# Patrologia Latina, volume 118 — English translation

# Patrologia Latina, vol. 118

## Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal Library

A complete, uniform, convenient, economical library of all the holy Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reprinting of all the surviving monuments of Catholic tradition from the first twelve centuries of the Church, based on the most accurate editions, carefully collated with one another and with several manuscript codices, and corrected with the greatest diligence; continually elucidated by dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged by the discovery of all works completed after the extensive editions produced during the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each volume and each author of importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with titles distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating its subject matter; expanded by works both doubtful and apocryphal, and by works possessing some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which whatever each Father has written on any topic may be seen at a glance; the other of Sacred Scripture, from which the reader may readily discover which Fathers, and in what passages of their works, have commented on the individual texts of the individual books of Scripture.

This is the most accurate edition, and one easily preferable to all others if one considers the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the corrections, the variety and number of the works reprinted, the exceptionally convenient format of the volumes, consistently similar throughout the entire work, the low price, and above all this collection itself: a single, methodical, chronological work containing six hundred fragments and minor treatises previously scattered here and there, but gathered for the first time in our library from works concerned with every age, place, language, and form.

## Second Series

In which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and writers of the Latin Church from Gregory the Great to Innocent III, edited by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the universal library of the clergy, or of the complete courses in each branch of ecclesiastical scholarship.

The Patrology has been printed in two editions, one Latin and the other Greek-Latin. The two hundred volumes of the Latin edition are sold for one thousand francs; for the Greek-Latin edition the supplied text gives “eight hundred and one thousand three hundred,” with the units elliptically or uncertainly printed. The purely Latin edition embraces all authors, both Western and Eastern; the Eastern authors, however, are presented in it only in Latin translation.

# The Second Part of the Complete Works of Haymo, Bishop of Halberstadt

[Col. 0009]

## Of the Homilies [Note: Title of the edition that we follow. Editor.]

Or sermons to the people on the Gospels of the temporal cycle and of the saints, as they are now read in the churches throughout the year, printed together for the first time. The two parts—namely, the winter and summer volumes—have been prepared with the greatest diligence possible. (G)*

[Col. 0009]

Several other homilies of the same Haymo on the Epistles of the holy apostle Paul, which are used in churches and had previously been printed nowhere, have been added. Finally, a single special homily by the same Haymo has been added on that reading from the Apocalypse: “I saw the holy city, Jerusalem,” etc.; this too had never before been printed anywhere. (Cologne, from the workshop of John Prael, in the year 1536.)

## To the Most Illustrious and Most Learned Man, Highly Skilled in Both Laws, Lord Jerome Unicorn

Canon of the metropolitan church at renowned Cologne, and counselor and vicar in spiritual matters to the most illustrious prince, the archbishop of Cologne, John Prael, printer, sends his respectful greetings.

[Col. 0009]

[Col. 0009A] Your prudent, pious, and truly generous spirit toward sound learning, your singular diligence in seeking out the very best writers, and finally your favor toward me have brought it about that, partly in the common interest of scholarship and partly on my own account, I think I owe something—or rather a great deal—to your name. If only, most learned Jerome, I had not so long lacked the opportunity and ability to oblige you, rather than possessing an ever-burning desire which has compelled me by this obligation—not, I say, to free myself from it (for I prefer to remain indebted to you in this respect), but at least to give you a suitable testimony of it. You thereby cause very many men to become your clients through such an honorable service, while you so advance the cause of learning, of students, and also of those whose work distributes literary monuments daily into the hands of men, that, by Hercules, you deserve the gratitude of all learned and good men.

My gratitude too is all the greater because, given the smallness of my abilities and resources, I can scarcely offer anything [Col. 0009B] worthy of your refined judgment and your broad command of affairs. Nevertheless, trusting in your kindness and generosity, I gladly make use of the opportunity into which I have now conveniently fallen, so that in this way some token of my regard may be dedicated to your name.

[Col. 0010A] For through the efforts of several friends, who took some care for my affairs, it has come about that Bishop Haymo—a lucid and familiar writer, and one versed in that pure and genuinely Christian theology, beyond what might have been expected from a man of such an age—was entrusted to us for printing, with commentaries on several Epistles of Saint Paul and then on a passage from the Apocalypse. This work will greatly please you—for you are not slightly learned, nor inexperienced in this field of study. Thus I have heard from friends at whose urging and advice this work was given by me to the press: that it would greatly please all learned and sincerely Christian men.

I therefore judged it worthwhile to follow that opinion, especially at a time when our craft is ill spoken of by some because, without much regard for religion or subject matter, all sorts of things are printed everywhere and indiscriminately, while works first find a printer when their profit is expected to be more certain, more rapid, and greater.

I cannot honestly deny that I hope for money from a work, or that I desire profit in order to maintain my household; yet, on the other hand, I cannot imagine success arising from bad, useless, or disreputable material, even if some people emerge quite successfully from handling such merchandise. For my part, neither have such works been offered to me [Col. 0011A] nor have I ever sought them. As the proverb says, good merchandise finds a buyer.

Saint Haymo is often reprinted and sold; he is purchased by learned men and pleases good men. Therefore I too seemed likely to accomplish something worthwhile if I committed these homilies to the press—homilies which I received as a gift from friends, written with sufficient correctness—and joined them to the other work of homilies printed recently. These homilies correspond to that work, although I could not complete them all because the time of the fair pressed me; I shall add the others to the earlier ones at once.

I judged that all of them should be dedicated to you, most distinguished man: first, because the republic of letters owes you much for seeking out books of this kind; [Col. 0012A] then because, with the greatest zeal permitted by your courtly affairs, you read such writings and writers; finally, so that by this small service I might in some measure win your favor—a small service, but one which, I hope, will be especially pleasing to you.

I thought it ridiculous to commend the writer to one who could judge him far more rightly than I. We have been content with the writer’s reputation and the judgment of our friends.

Accept, therefore, most gracious Jerome, whatever service this may be, benevolently and with your customary generosity. Consider not how much I was able to give in this gift, but how much the one who is given may be able to benefit. Farewell, and may Christ preserve you for us for a long time.

Cologne, the Kalends of December, 1536.

# Homilies on the Temporal Cycle

[Col. 0011]

## Homily One: The First Sunday of Advent

[Col. 0011B]

> “At that time, when Jesus had drawn near to Jerusalem and had come to Bethphage, at the Mount of Olives,” and so forth. (Matthew 21.)

Not only are the works and miracles performed by the Lord full of mysteries, but even the places where he taught or traveled should sometimes be understood as not lacking in mysteries. This is confirmed at the beginning of the present reading, where the Lord, as he approaches Jerusalem, is said first to have come to Bethphage, at the Mount of Olives.

The Mount of Olives is not far from Jerusalem. It is a very fertile and beautiful mountain, planted with trees, especially olive trees, from which it also received its name. On its slope was formerly the village of Bethphage, belonging to the priests, where they prepared the victims that they were to offer in the Lord’s temple.

Spiritually, however, the Mount of Olives signifies the Lord Jesus Christ, who is the mountain of richness, the mountain of mercy, because he came mercifully to redeem the human race—for the Greek word ἔλεος (*eleos*) is interpreted in Latin as *misericordia*, “mercy.”

This is that mountain of which the prophet Isaiah says:

> “And it shall come to pass in the last days that the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be prepared on the top of the mountains, and shall be exalted above the hills, and shall be high indeed.” (Isaiah 2.)

And Daniel says:

> “I saw a stone cut out of the mountain without hands; it grew into a great mountain and filled the whole earth.” (Daniel 2.)

Bethphage, however, which is interpreted as “house of the mouth” or “of the jaws,” signifies the Church, which without interruption keeps open the mouth—what is commonly called the *bucca*—in confession of the Lord, saying with the Psalmist:

> “Let us come before his face with confession, and let us sing joyfully to him in psalms.” (Psalm 94.)

Spiritually, too, that same Church is refreshed and nourished by God. It can say with the Prophet:

> “The Lord shepherds me, and I shall lack nothing,”

and so forth. (Psalm 22.)

Bethphage is therefore rightly said to be on the slope of the Mount of Olives, because the Church was formed from the side of Christ hanging on the cross, when one of the soldiers opened his side with a lance, and immediately there came forth the blood of redemption and the water of baptism.

Jerusalem, which is interpreted as “vision of peace,” signifies the heavenly homeland, where there is complete and true peace arising from the vision of the Creator.

The Lord is therefore beautifully described as coming to Bethphage at the Mount of Olives while he is making his way to Jerusalem, because anyone who desires to come to the vision of heavenly peace must first believe in the Lord Jesus Christ in the heart and confess him with the mouth.

Just as the priests at Bethphage prepared and cleansed the victims that they were to offer in the Lord’s temple, so each believer in the present Church must purify himself from every vice and sin by good works, so that he may become an acceptable sacrifice to God, according to the exhortation of the apostle Paul:

> “I beseech you, by the mercy of God, that you present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God, your reasonable service.” (Romans 12.)

The same Apostle prepared such a sacrifice when he said:

> “I chastise my body and bring it into servitude, lest perhaps, after preaching to others, I myself should become rejected.” (1 Corinthians 9.)

> “Then he sent two of his disciples, saying to them: Go into the village that is opposite you.”

Spiritually, the two disciples who are sent into the village signify two orders of preachers, one of whom was sent to the Jewish people and the other to the nations. It is clear that Peter and Paul particularly assumed these roles, as the Apostle testifies:

> “He who worked through Peter for the apostleship of the circumcision also worked through me among the nations.” (Galatians 2.)

According to the literal interpretation of some, they are said to have been Peter and Philip, because Philip preached in Samaria, interpreting the name “Samaria” as “Asia.”

Alternatively, the two disciples whom the Lord sent before him signify understanding and action. For anyone who has undertaken ecclesiastical leadership and the power of binding and loosing must ensure that understanding and action precede him, because one without the other cannot be supreme and pre-eminent before the Creator. He said to his disciples:

> “You know these things; blessed shall you be if you do them.” (John 13.)

The disciples therefore go ahead first, and Jesus follows afterward, because the Lord comes into the hearts of those who possess a right understanding of faith and the practice of good living. Scripture says:

> “A good understanding belongs to all who practice it; its praise endures for ever and ever.” (Psalm 110.)

The village to which they are sent is, in the literal sense, understood as the city of Jerusalem. No one should think it absurd if a royal city is called a village or fortress, because Scripture customarily sometimes calls a city a village and a village a city.

Spiritually, however, the village to which they are sent signifies the world. It is said to be opposite them because, at the beginning of their preaching, the world tried to resist their teaching, just as the Jews said to the apostles:

> “As for this sect, we know that it is opposed everywhere.” (Acts 28.)

The apostles also reproached them, saying:

> “It was necessary that the word of God should first be spoken to you; but since you reject it and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the nations.” (Acts 13.)

What he adds—

> “And immediately you will find a donkey tied, and a colt with her; untie them and bring them to me”—

he says according to the custom of the province.

For it was customary in those regions, in each city and village, to keep ready a donkey or any animal suitable for riding. If one of the citizens needed to make a journey of one day, he used the support of this conveyance; the inhabitants of the city jointly provided for the maintenance of the conveyance.

This custom was therefore observed at Jerusalem when the Lord sent his disciples there, saying:

> “You will find a donkey tied, and a colt with her,”

and so forth.

Spiritually, the domesticated donkey signifies the Synagogue, which had been tamed and worn down under the yoke of the Law and trained in the observance of legal ceremonies.

The wanton and untamed colt, however, which ran here and there without a bridle, signifies the gentile people. Bound by no teaching of the Law and instructed in no knowledge of God, uncertain and wandering, they pursued the idols fashioned by their own hands.

Of it, according to another Evangelist, it is rightly said:

> “Upon which no man has ever sat.”

For no prophet or patriarch had yet exercised preaching and instruction over the gentile people.

It is not only the tied donkey but also the colt that is said to be found, because not only the gentile people but also the Jews were bound by the chains of sin. The Apostle testifies to this when he says in his Epistle to the Romans:

> “There is no distinction between Jew and Greek; for all have sinned and lack the glory of God.” (Romans 10.)

And again:

> “Tribulation and distress upon every soul of man who does evil, of the Jew first and also of the Greek.” (Romans 2.)

He rightly ordered them to be untied first and brought to him afterward, because the order of things required that people first be freed from the bonds of unbelief and afterward be presented to him through faith.

The bonds are sins, as Solomon says:

> “Each person is bound by the cords of his own sins.” (Proverbs 5.)

The other Evangelists mention only the colt, wishing to express solely the calling of the nations. Matthew, however, mentions both animals—the donkey and the colt—to signify that some from both peoples would believe in Christ.

It was as though he sent the apostles to untie the donkey when he expressly sent them to preach to the Synagogue, saying:

> “Do not go into the way of the nations, and do not enter the cities of the Samaritans, but go rather to the sheep that have perished from the house of Israel.” (Matthew 10.)

He sent them, as it were, to the colt when, after his resurrection, he commanded them:

> “Go into the whole world, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.” (Matthew 28.)

What does he add?

> “And if anyone says anything to you, say: The Lord has need of them; and immediately he will let them go.”

This is what, according to the Evangelist Luke, is indicated by the colt that the disciples untied: it is said to have had many masters, because the people of the Jews and of the nations were devoted not to one error but to many.

The masters who opposed its release are to be understood as unclean spirits, who had once claimed tyrannical power over the human race after sin.

When they saw that through the apostles’ preaching the people were being converted to the faith, they said: “Why are you untying the colt?” For they had tried with every effort to resist the apostles’ preaching, stirring up kings and tyrants against it, so that the human race would not be freed from their chains.

But after the disciples said, “The Lord has need of them,” they immediately released them, because after such signs and miracles—namely, raising the dead, expelling unclean spirits from human bodies, and many other works—had made it known that the disciples were sent by God, the demons were compelled, unwillingly and against their will, to abandon the human race.

The power of the demons was weakened as soon as faith in Christ became manifest through the apostles’ preaching, to such an extent that idols were destroyed by the hands of those people at whose expense and through whose labor they had been built.

Therefore, through the possessed man, they also said to the Lord:

> “What have we to do with you, Son of God? Have you come here before the time to torment us?” (Matthew 8.)

> “Now all this was done so that what had been spoken through the prophet might be fulfilled: Say to the daughter of Zion: Behold, your king comes to you, meek, and sitting upon a donkey and a colt, the foal of a beast of burden.”

In this passage the Evangelist Matthew preserves his customary practice. Since he wrote the Gospel for Hebrews in the Hebrew language, whenever the occasion permitted he confirmed his narrative with testimonies from the Law and the Prophets.

Thus, after saying that the Lord had sent the disciples to untie the donkey and the colt, he immediately brought forward the prophet’s testimony:

> “Say to the daughter of Zion: Behold, your king comes,”

and so forth. (Zechariah 9.)

This testimony is found in the prophet Zechariah. It was fulfilled not only because it had been foretold, but it had also been foretold because it was to be fulfilled.

In order to remove every excuse of ignorance from the Jews, when the prophet foretold the Lord’s coming he also showed the character of the Lord who was coming, saying:

> “Say to the daughter of Zion,”

and so forth.

Historically, he calls Jerusalem the daughter of Zion, because Zion was situated in its higher part—a place not only safer for defense but also higher for contemplation.

It is as though the prophet said:

“O you Jews, whom the Lord’s coming in the flesh will find, recognize your king by these signs. When you see him coming meek—not proud, but humble; not terrifying in the splendor of arms, as Nebuchadnezzar and Antiochus once came for your destruction, but coming for your restoration; not sitting upon a foaming horse, lover of discord, which digs the earth with its hoof and scents war from afar, but upon a donkey, a lover of peace, or upon a colt, the foal of a donkey; not to take away from you a temporal and earthly kingdom, but to confer upon you, if you believe, a heavenly and eternal one; not to lead you captive into a foreign land, but to restore you free to your own.”

What he says, “your,” has this meaning, as though he were saying: “Your, I say—not another’s, not a stranger’s, but your own, born from you, nourished among you, and coming for your salvation.”

What follows, “meek,” shows his meekness not only in words but also in his riding upon the beast of burden.

Spiritually, Zion, which is interpreted as “watchtower” or “contemplation,” signifies the Church, which daily contemplates with a pure heart him who said:

> “I am the beginning, I who also speak to you,”

and again:

> “I am the light of the world.” (John 8.)

“Say therefore to the daughter of Zion”—that is, to the Church:

> “Behold, your king comes, sitting upon a donkey and a colt”—

that is, dwelling not in the minds of the proud but in those of the humble, so that you may learn from him who is meek and humble in heart.

For whoever desires to share in the kingdom of this king must be humble and meek, not returning evil for evil or abuse for abuse, so that he may be numbered among those of whom it is said:

> “The meek shall inherit the earth and shall dwell upon it for ever and ever.” (Psalm 36.)

And again:

> “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth.” (Matthew 5.)

The meek king wishes to have meek subjects, as he himself says:

> “Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart, and you shall find rest for your souls.” (Matthew 11.)

In Scripture the donkey is not always used in a bad sense nor always in a good one. Sometimes, under the name of donkeys, the foolishness of fools is signified; sometimes the wantonness of the profligate; sometimes the simplicity of a righteous man.

The foolishness of fools is signified, as it is written:

> “You shall not plow with an ox and a donkey together.” (Deuteronomy 22.)

That is: Do not join a fool with a wise man in preaching.

The wantonness of the profligate is signified where the prophet says:

> “Whose flesh is like the flesh of donkeys, and whose discharge is like the discharge of horses.” (Ezekiel 23.)

The simplicity of an innocent man is signified where the prophet Isaiah says:

> “Blessed are you who sow beside all waters, sending forth the foot of the ox and the donkey.” (Isaiah 32.)

Thus, in this passage, the donkey or colt brought for the Lord to ride signifies a simple or innocent soul.

The Lord sits upon the donkey when he inhabits a simple mind, as he says through the prophet:

> “Upon whom shall my Spirit rest, if not upon the humble and quiet one who trembles at my words?” (Isaiah 66.)

It is as though the Lord, sitting upon the colt, were making his way toward Jerusalem when, inhabiting a simple mind, he teaches it to hasten eagerly toward the vision of inner peace.

This is well signified in the true sacred history, where it is written that Achsah, the daughter of Caleb, sat upon a donkey and sighed. (Judges 1.) For Achsah, daughter of Caleb, seems to sigh while sitting upon a donkey when the mind of a simple man groans out of desire for heavenly life.

The apostles’ obedience followed the Lord’s command. Hence it is added:

> “The disciples went and did as Jesus had commanded them, and they brought the donkey and the colt.”

Above we have already said that the donkey and colt signify both peoples, namely the Jews and the nations.

Thus the disciples, sent as it were to bring the donkey, brought it when they caused some from the Synagogue to come to the faith of Christ. We read in the Acts of the Apostles that, when Peter preached, three thousand men believed on one day, and five thousand on the next, while a large crowd of priests obeyed the faith.

They also brought the colt, as it were, when, although most of those people did not believe, they went forth and preached everywhere, the Lord working with them and confirming the word through the signs that followed.

But because the order of the argument requires that a person first be instructed in faith and then be able to have God as a rider, it is rightly added:

> “They placed their garments upon them, and made him sit upon them.”

The apostles’ garments signify their teaching. Thus they placed their garments upon the donkey and the colt so that Jesus might sit more comfortably when they instructed human hearts through their teaching, so that they might be able to have God dwelling within them.

It is asked how he is said to have sat upon both animals within so short a space of the journey. If he sat upon the donkey, the colt was left without a rider; but if he sat upon the colt—which is more fitting—the donkey remained free of a rider.

This could have happened because he first sat upon the donkey and afterward, as he approached Jerusalem and the crowds came to meet him, wished to sit upon the little donkey, as the Evangelist John says:

> “As Jesus drew near Jerusalem, he found a young donkey and sat upon it.”

But according to the spiritual understanding, as we said above, the meaning is clear: he is said to have sat upon both animals because from both peoples he called some to his faith.

> “The very large crowd spread their garments on the road. Others cut branches from the trees and spread them on the road. The crowds that went before and those that followed cried out, saying: Hosanna to the Son of David; blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.”

In this passage we must consider, according to the order of the persons, the quality of their merits.

Some placed their garments upon the donkey so that Jesus might sit more comfortably. Others spread their garments on the road so that the donkey’s foot would not stumble. Others spread branches from the trees on the road, making the donkey’s path level and beautiful. Those who could not approach more closely followed and cried out:

> “Hosanna to the Son of David,”

and so forth.

Those who placed their garments upon the donkey were the apostles, because by their teaching they prepared human minds to be God’s dwelling place.

Those who spread their garments on the road were the holy martyrs. When they handed over their bodies to punishment for God’s sake, they spread their garments, as it were, showing simpler people the road by which they could reach heaven.

Those who cut branches from the trees and spread them on the road were the holy confessors. When they bring forth the many and necessary judgments of the Fathers who preceded them for our instruction, they are like people cutting branches from spiritual trees and adorning the road to the heavenly homeland.

The crowds going before and following signified the faithful of both Testaments, namely the Old and the New.

They cry out with one voice because there is one faith among those who preceded the Lord’s coming and those who follow it. The apostle Peter testifies to this when he says:

> “Through the grace of the Lord Jesus we believe that we shall be saved, just as they also were. What they foretold as future, we now believe to have happened.” (Acts 15.)

Let us hear what they cry out:

> “Hosanna to the Son of David.”

“Hosanna” is the cry of those who rejoice and praise at the same time.

They also profess him to be the Son of David, because the Savior descended to us, born from David’s line, as the Apostle says:

> “Who was made for him from the seed of David according to the flesh.” (Romans 1.)

This verse, which the children also sang to the Lord at the entrance of the temple, is taken from Psalm 117, almost all of which is sung in the person of the Lord, and its words concern his coming.

For when the Prophet had said:

> “The stone which the builders rejected has become the cornerstone,”

(Psalm 117), he inserted the following:

> “O Lord, save me; O Lord, grant success. Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.”

In Hebrew this reads:

> “Hosanna Adonai Hosanna.”

Symmachus, translating more explicitly in his customary manner, rendered it:

> “I beseech you, Lord, save me.”

Thus “Hosanna” is properly a Hebrew word, and in our language it means “save” or “bring salvation.”

Therefore, when the crowds cried “save” or “bring salvation,” they clearly believed him to be the Savior.

They also professed that the one who comes in the name of the Lord is blessed, because the Son came not in his own name but in the name of the Father; nor did he seek his own glory but that of the Father, as he said to the unbelieving Jews:

> “I have come in my Father’s name, and you do not receive me; if another comes in his own name, him you will receive.” (John 5.)

And again:

> “I have not come of myself, but my Father sent me.” (John 8.)

# Homily Two: The Second Sunday of Advent

[Col. 0018]

> “At that time, Jesus said to his disciples: There will be signs in the sun, moon, and stars, and on earth distress among the nations, because of the confusion caused by the roaring of the sea and the waves,”

and so forth. (Luke 21.)

Foreseeing—or condescending to and taking thought for—human weakness, the Lord wished to announce long beforehand the tribulations and distresses that would come near the end of the world, so that they might be endured all the more easily when they came, the more clearly they were remembered as having been foretold by him long before.

Arrows that can be foreseen usually strike with less force.

The elect who will be in the flesh near the end of the world will therefore endure the tribulations and distresses of the world more lightly insofar as they remember that these things were first foretold by the Redeemer himself.

For when the disciples asked the Lord about his coming and about the consummation of the world, as the Evangelist related above, he replied:

“For you will hear of wars and uprisings of wars; do not be terrified. These things must happen first, but the end will not come immediately.” Then he said to them: “Nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom. There will be great earthquakes in various places, and pestilences and famines, and terrors from heaven, and there will be great signs.” After inserting certain remarks about the persecution of the wicked [Col. 0018B] and the endurance of the elect, he added what we heard at the beginning of this reading, saying: “There will be signs in the sun and moon and stars.” Here it must be noted that, for the punishment of wicked human beings, even the elements of the world are said to be thrown into turmoil. The Lord enumerates them individually, saying: “Nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom.” Behold the disturbance among human beings. “There will be great earthquakes in various places.” Behold the manifestation of wrath from above. “There will be pestilences.” Behold the disorder of bodies. “There will be famine.” Behold the barrenness of the earth. “There will be terrors from heaven, and great signs.” Behold the disorder of the air. “There will be signs in the sun and moon and stars.” Behold the disturbance of the heavenly bodies. “Because of the confusion caused by the sound of the sea and the waves.” Behold the confusion of the rivers.

For it is just that senseless people [Col. 0018C] who have sinned in everything should be struck in everything—that is, if they sinned through the serenity of the air, they should be struck through the storm. Thus, in the remaining matters, let them be struck by the very senseless things themselves, and let what is written in Solomon be fulfilled: “The world will fight on his behalf against the senseless” (Wis. 5). What signs, however, will occur in the sun, moon, and stars is explained more clearly by another evangelist, namely Matthew, who says: “In those days the sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light, and the stars will fall from heaven.” Spiritually, the name “sun” signifies the Lord Jesus Christ. Of him it is written: “But for you who fear God, the sun of righteousness will rise.” And again: “The sun rose, and they gathered together” (Ps. 103). By the name “moon,” however, the Church is signified in this passage, as it is written in Habakkuk: “The sun was raised at its rising, and the moon stood in its order” (Hab. 3).

“In those days”—that is, in that final tribulation—“the sun will be darkened,” because the Lord Jesus Christ will not manifest the power of his strength. “The moon will not give its light,” because the Church will not shine with the splendor of miracles. Hence John says in the Apocalypse: “The sun became black like a sackcloth of hair, and the whole moon became like blood” (Rev. 1). And the Apostle says: “There must be heresies, so that those who are approved may become manifest” (1 Cor. 11). For when the Lord does not display the power of his strength, the Church will be bloodstained with the blood of martyrdom as a testimony to the truth, just as the prophet Joel says: “The sun will be turned into darkness and the moon into blood, before the great and manifest day of the Lord comes” (Joel 2).

By the name “stars” hypocrites are signified in this passage: although they possess a profession of faith, they shine in the Church like stars and heavenly bodies. But when the final tribulation approaches, the stars will fall from heaven, because at that time many will withdraw from the Church in body, from which they had already withdrawn in mind. For the Lord will permit Antichrist to rage against the saints and to pursue his violence against them stubbornly, so that their endurance may be tested. As the Apostle says (2 Thess. 2): “He who opposes and exalts himself above everything that is called God or is worshiped.” Hence it is said in the Apocalypse: “The dragon sent out his tail and dragged down a third of the stars of heaven” (Rev. 12).

For this reason Daniel, when he foretold the times of Antichrist, said among other things: “Strength was given him against the continual sacrifice for sin, and truth will be cast down to the ground; he will act and prosper” (Dan. 8). And again: “He was raised up to the height of heaven, and he cast down some of the stars in his strength, and trampled them.”

“And on earth there will be distress among the nations.” The signs from heaven will not suffice for the vengeance of wicked human beings; on earth also there will be distress among the nations. The inhabitants of the same earth will press upon one another and rise against one another in envious contention, just as the Lord says: “Father will rise against son, and son against father, and daughter against her mother, and daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law; and a man’s enemies will be those of his own household” (Luke 12). Hence Isaiah says: “A man will rush upon a man, each upon his neighbor. The child will be tumultuous against the old man, the lowly against the noble” (Isa. 3). And Paul says: “In the last days perilous times will come, and people will be lovers of themselves; they will turn away their hearing from the truth and turn instead to fables” (2 Tim. 3).

Therefore Matthew, describing the greatness of that tribulation more explicitly, says: “Then there will be such tribulation as has not been from the beginning until now, nor will be.” Not only heaven and earth, but also the sea and the rivers will rise up for the punishment of wicked human beings. Hence it is added: “Because of the confusion caused by the sound of the sea and the waves.”

The confusion, sound, and waves of the sea have not yet newly arisen; but since we see that most of what was foretold has been fulfilled, we cannot doubt the few things that remain. [Col. 0019D] Already nations have risen against nations and kingdoms against kingdoms, as we have seen and heard; we have experienced earthquakes in various places; we know that pestilences, famines, terrors from heaven, and great signs have occurred. Signs in the sun, moon, and stars are reported by some to have been seen frequently. But the confusion caused by the sound of the sea and the waves, because it has not yet come, is without doubt believed to be coming.

Some report that, near the end of the age, the sea, rivers, and streams will emit voices and roarings according to their nature and size, lamenting their own destruction with mournful sounds, and thereby striking no small terror into those who hear them. For since everything must come to an end, everything is shaken near the end of the age. [Col. 0020A] Hence John says in the Apocalypse: “And the sea is no more.”

“As people faint with fear.” Spiritually, for people to wither in the final tribulation means for the wicked to fail in the richness of faith and charity. Many will wither away from the faith in that tribulation who were thought faithful in a time of prosperity, just as the Lord says concerning the seeds cast upon the rock: “When the sun rose, they withered.” The foolish virgins will suffer this dryness when they say to the prudent: “Give us some of your oil, because our lamps are going out” (Matt. 25).

It is rightly said: “Because of fear and expectation of what will come upon the whole world.” That tribulation is in some way bearable after which joy is hoped for; but that tribulation is harsh, severe, and intolerable which, while it torments in the present, threatens greater things in the future. Both things will happen to the wicked in that tribulation: they will suffer evils in the present and await greater ones in the future. They will have punishments outwardly and fear inwardly, and they will be unable to possess security of soul either concerning the present or concerning the future. Therefore it is rightly said: “Because of fear and expectation of what will come upon the whole world.”

“For the powers of heaven will be shaken; and then they will see the Son of Man coming in a cloud, with great power and majesty.” Some wish to understand the powers of heaven in this passage as the teachers and rulers of the Church. If, they say, the Church is spiritually heaven, as in the words, “Heaven is my throne” (Isa. 66), and “The soul of the righteous is the seat of wisdom” (Wis. 7), then the powers of heaven may appropriately be understood as the rulers of the Church, namely bishops and priests.

They wish to understand of these the statement that is written: “The terrified angels will be cleansed” (Isa. 41), interpreting the word “angels” as referring to priests, in accordance with what Malachi says: “The lips of the priest guard knowledge, and they seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts” (Mal. 2). The powers of heaven are said to be shaken because, in that strict judgment, the prelates of the churches will also render an account, not only for their own actions but also for the souls entrusted to them, just as the Lord says: “From the one to whom much has been entrusted, much will be demanded.” And another Scripture says: “The mighty will suffer mighty torments” (Wis. 6).

We, however, understand the powers of heaven in this passage specifically as angels, archangels, thrones, dominations, virtues, principalities, and powers, cherubim and seraphim, concerning whom it is written: “Praise the Lord, all his angels; praise him, all his powers” (Ps. 148). These powers are said to be shaken because the angels will not only accompany the Lord’s coming but will also go before him, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “The Son of Man will send his angels, and they will gather out of his kingdom all scandals” (Matt. 13). And again: “The angels will go out and separate the wicked from the midst of the righteous.” And elsewhere: “The Lord will come to judgment with the elders” (Isa. 3). And Solomon says: “Her husband is noble at the gates when he sits with the elders [Col. 0021A] of the land” (Prov. 31).

Or certainly, they are said to be shaken in another sense, so that the terror and strictness of the judgment may be shown. For, for example, when a king exercises a severe and strict judgment over his subjects, not only those who are judged for their own merits are afraid, but also those who are accustomed to remain at his side. So when almighty God punishes the wicked in judgment, so that the terror and strictness of the judgment may be displayed, even those who are established in eternal stability are said to fear.

Hence blessed Job aptly says: “The pillars of heaven tremble and are terrified at his nod” (Job 26). What, then, will become of such people when the pillars are shaken? What will the little reed of the desert suffer when the cedar of Lebanon is shaken? What will wretched mortal human beings do when the angels are afraid? “And if the righteous,” as the Apostle Peter says, “will scarcely be saved, where will the ungodly and the sinner appear?” (1 Pet. 4).

The prophet Zephaniah had seen the strictness of this day when he said: “The day of the Lord is near, near and exceedingly swift. The sound of the day of the Lord is bitter; the mighty man will be afflicted there. That day is a day of wrath, a day of tribulation and distress, a day of calamity and misery, a day of cloud and storm, a day of trumpet and shouting” (Zeph. 1). And again: “Woe to those who desire the day of the Lord! Why do you desire it? Just as a man flees from the face of a lion and a serpent bites him, so the day of the Lord will be darkness and not light” (Amos 5).

And as Matthew says: “Woe to pregnant women and nursing mothers in those days” (Matt. 24). And again: “Then two will be in one bed,” and so forth. And Luke says: “Behold, days will come in which they will say: Blessed are the barren, and the wombs that have not borne, and the breasts that have not nursed. Then they will begin to say to the mountains: Fall upon us, and to the hills: Cover us” (Luke 23).

Whoever therefore desires to be secure on that day must, while he lives in this body, place the strictness of that day before the eyes of his mind. For each person will be more secure there in proportion as he is now more fearful in observing the Lord’s commandments. “Blessed is the man who fears the Lord,” the Prophet says; “he will greatly delight in his commandments” (Ps. 111). And Solomon says: “Blessed is the man who is always fearful, but whoever is hard of heart will fall into evil” (Prov. 28).

In the terror of that day, the generosity of almsgiving will provide great security, when the Judge himself, placed at the right hand, will say: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world. For I was hungry, and you gave me food; I was thirsty, and you gave me drink; I was a stranger, and you welcomed me; naked, and you clothed me; sick and in prison, and you came to me” (Matt. 25).

“For blessed is he,” the Prophet says, “who understands concerning the needy and the poor; on the evil day the Lord will deliver him” (Ps. 40). Hence the voice of righteous men says: “Almsgiving will be a great confidence before the Most High God for all who practice it,” and so forth (Tob. 4). And again: “My son, almsgiving delivers from death and does not permit a person to go into darkness” (ibid.).

It must be noted that the stronger the signs become manifest, the nearer the Lord’s coming is understood to be. For just as, when a king is going to come to some palace or city, messengers are sent one after another, but when those who are accustomed to sit at his side begin to appear, there is no doubt about his arrival, so signs in the sun, moon, and stars, and many other things, will precede that coming of the Lord. But when the angels who always attend him begin to appear, the Lord’s coming is immediately recognized as near.

Therefore, after saying, “The powers of heaven will be shaken,” he added: “And then they will see the Son of Man coming in a cloud, with great power and majesty.” They will see the Son of Man in judgment because he will come to judgment in the form of a servant—that is, in the human form which he assumed for us—as it is written: “Behold, he will come in the clouds, and every eye will see him, even those who pierced him, and all the tribes of the earth will mourn over him” (Rev. 1). And again: “They will see him whom they pierced” (John 19).

They will see him in great power and majesty, though they had refused to listen to him speaking in humility. For it is fitting that the very Son of God, who was unjustly judged in human form, should in that same form justly judge all people in judgment, as he himself says in the Gospel: “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John 8). And again: “He gave him authority to execute judgment, because he is the Son of Man.”

But after these things had been said to terrify the wicked, the Lord immediately turned his speech to console the elect, saying:

“When these things begin to happen, look up and raise your heads, because your redemption is drawing near.” It is as though the Lord were saying: When you see, through the repeated disasters and continual blows of the world, the sign of its end approaching, do not weep over the destruction of the world; do not fear for yourselves. For when the end of the world—which you did not love—comes, you will find the joy that you have always sought.

In the holy Scriptures, the head is often used for the mind, as Solomon says: “The eyes of the wise are in his head” (Eccl. 2). If we consider bodily vision, the eyes of the wise are not only in the head, but those of the foolish are there as well. Yet the eyes of the wise are said to be in his head because he possesses spiritual discernment in his mind. For just as the limbs of the body are governed by the head, so thoughts are discerned by the mind. And just as the head is the principal member of the body, so the mind is the governing power of the heart.

Thus, when he commands heads to be raised in this passage, he commands the mind to prepare itself for eternal reward. These words show that the elect ought not so much to fear the day of judgment as to desire it. Every day they ask for one thing in prayer, saying: “Your kingdom come.” This is what those do who remember that, with God’s grace preceding them, they have performed good works, as John says: “Beloved, if our heart does not condemn us, we have confidence on the day of judgment” (1 John 3).

And so that the human mind would not remain sluggish in understanding these things, the Lord added a comparison drawn from visible realities. Hence it follows:

“And he told them a parable: Look at the fig tree and all the trees. When they are already producing fruit from themselves, you know that summer is near.” He himself explained it by adding:

“So also you, when you see these things happening, know that the kingdom of God is near.” It is as though the Lord were saying: Just as the approach of summer is recognized from the fruit of a tree, so you should recognize from the ruin of the world that the kingdom of God is near and approaching.

Hence another evangelist, namely Matthew, beautifully says, in order to show the swiftness of the Lord’s coming to judgment: “So also you, when you see all these things happening, know that he is near, at the doors” (Matt. 24).

The kingdom of God is aptly compared with summer because, just as in summer the sun appears brighter and more radiant and illuminates the world, so after the judgment every human frailty and every temptation will pass away. And when the sun of righteousness, the Lord Jesus Christ, appears in the glory of his vision, he will glorify the saints with greater splendor, when what the Lord says elsewhere is fulfilled: “Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Matt. 13). Then what the Apostle says will also be fulfilled: “What we now see through a mirror and in an enigma, then we shall see face to face” (1 Cor. 13).

Just as in winter we see trees stripped of leaves, deprived of fruits, and almost dead, so in the present life the saints, putting their members to death upon the earth, appear humble and despised, saying with the Prophet: “For your sake we are put to death all day long; we are reckoned as sheep for slaughter” (Ps. 43).

And just as, when summer approaches, trees that have come back to life are again clothed with leaves, adorned with flowers, and decorated with fruits, so on the day of judgment the saints, rising from earth and dust, clothed in the robe of immortality, will appear joyful and flourishing, as the Psalmist says: “The righteous will flourish like a palm tree, and like a cedar of Lebanon he will multiply” (Ps. 91).

The Apostle Paul had looked upon spiritual trees as dead in the present life, as though it were winter, when he said: “For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God” (Col. 3). He considered that, as summer approached, they would again be clothed with leaves and adorned with spiritual flowers when he said: “When Christ, your life, appears, then you also will appear with him in glory.”

The prophet David likewise had looked upon spiritual trees as dead when he said: “Going, they went and wept, casting their seeds” (Ps. 125). And he had looked upon them as destined to be brought to life again as summer and the kingdom approached when he said: “But coming, they will come with rejoicing, carrying their sheaves.”

Hence the holy Church, rejoicing that after the Lord’s resurrection she was filled with the fruit of righteousness, heard the Lord say to her in the Song of Songs: “Come, my chosen one, my beautiful one, my dove, my undefiled one. You are altogether beautiful, my beloved, and there is no blemish in you. For winter has now passed, the rain has gone away and departed; flowers have appeared in the land, the season of pruning has come; let us rise early and go to the vineyards” (Song 2).

Or, in another interpretation, we may understand the fig tree as the Synagogue. This is the fig tree to which, according to another parable of the Gospel, the Lord is read to have come, seeking fruit on it and finding none, and said: “May fruit never come from you again forever” (Matt. 21).

When, therefore, we see this fig tree—that is, the Synagogue—bringing forth from itself the fruit of belief, we should know that the kingdom of God is near, because near the end of the age, through the preaching of Elijah and Enoch, the Synagogue will believe in part, as the Apostle testifies when he says: “When the fullness of the nations has entered, then all Israel will be saved” (Rom. 11). And again: “It is not the spiritual that comes first, but the natural, and afterward the spiritual” (1 Cor. 15).

Hence the Lord also promised through the prophet Malachi, saying: “Behold, I will send you Elijah the Tishbite, who will turn the hearts of fathers toward their children and the hearts of children toward their fathers” (Mal. 4).

“Amen I say to you, this generation will not pass away until all things have happened.” *Amen* is properly a word of the Hebrews, and it is an adverb of affirmation. Although it can be interpreted as “truly” or “faithfully,” it has not been translated by anyone; out of honor and reverence for the Lord, who frequently used this word in his speech, it has therefore been left without translation.

“This generation,” if understood of the Jewish people, will not pass away—that is, they will not cease to exist in sufficient number—until all the things foretold by the Lord have been fulfilled. If, however, it is referred to the whole mass of the human race, it is plainly evident that the human race will not pass away until everything foretold by the Lord has been completed.

The Lord’s incarnation was foretold, and it was fulfilled. His passion and resurrection were foretold, and they were fulfilled. His glorious ascension was foretold, and it was completed. The Church that would exist throughout the whole world was foretold, and we see its fulfillment with our own eyes. The signs in the sun, moon, and stars were foretold, and they have been fulfilled. The sound of the sea and the waves was foretold; no one doubts that it will come. The day of judgment was foretold; because it has not yet been fulfilled, it is without doubt believed that it will be fulfilled. Universal judgment and eternal life were foretold, and we await their completion.

With what firmness, however, the things foretold by the Lord must be believed, he himself makes clear when he adds:

“Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away.” Nothing among visible things is more enduring than heaven and earth; nothing among human things passes more quickly than words, which cannot even be completed except by passing away. When the Lord therefore says, “Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away,” he shows that what seems fixed to us is transitory in his sight, while what seems transitory to us is firm and stable in his words. His speech forms fixed and enduring judgments even as it passes away.

But one may ask: When the Lord says, “Heaven and earth will pass away,” how can what Ecclesiastes says stand: “One generation passes away, and another generation comes, but the earth stands forever” (Eccl. 1)? If, according to the Lord’s words, heaven and earth will pass away, how is the earth said to stand forever?

To this it must be answered that one heaven is the atmospheric heaven, another the starry heaven, and another the ethereal heaven. The atmospheric heaven is near the earth; hence we speak of the birds of heaven, which we see flying above the air. Rain is said to fall from heaven when, in fact, it rains from the clouds that we see.

This atmospheric heaven and the earth are therefore said to pass away, as the Psalmist says: “In the beginning you founded the earth, Lord, and the heavens are the work of your hands; they will perish” (Ps. 101)—not so that they will cease entirely to exist, but so that they will be changed into something better. This change itself is called passing away.

Something is said to pass away not only when it perishes in such a way that it will never exist again, but also when it is changed so as to become better. Thus gold and silver objects pass through fire, not so that they cease to exist, but so that they may become more beautiful.

Because heaven and earth have been polluted by our iniquities, they must be purified through fire on the day of judgment, as the Psalmist says: “Fire will go before him and will burn his enemies round about.” Some report that the fire of judgment will burn in the air to the same extent that the waters of the flood covered the earth. This change of heaven and earth is called passing away.

For just as a person throws off a cloak or any garment in order to put on another that is more fitting, so almighty God will purify heaven and earth through fire, so that, once purified, they may remain in a better state. Hence the Psalmist also says: “And like a cloak you will change them, and they will be changed” (ibid.).

For this reason the Apostle Peter says (2 Pet. 3): “The heavens that now exist and the earth, preserved by the same word, are kept for fire on the day of judgment.” And again: “The day of the Lord will come like a thief, in the night; on it the heavens will pass away with great force, and the elements will be dissolved by heat.”

Hence the Lord says through Isaiah: “Behold, I create a new heaven and a new earth”—not so that they must be created from nothing, but so that they may be changed into something better (Isa. 65). Likewise, John says in the Apocalypse: “Behold, I make all things new” (Rev. 21).

## HOMILY III. THE THIRD SUNDAY OF ADVENT

(Matt. 11.) “At that time, when John heard in prison about the works of Christ, he sent two of his disciples and said to him: ‘Are you the one who is to come?’” and so forth.

At the beginning of this reading we must ask why John the Baptist, a prophet and more than a prophet, who had pointed out the Savior to others with his finger, saying, “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1), and who had been astonished when he came to be baptized, saying, “I ought to be baptized by you, and you come to me?” (Matt. 3), now, while he was in prison, sent disciples to ask him, as though he did not know who he was: “Are you the one who is to come, or should we expect another?”

Did he, then, not know the one whom he had pointed out to others, and over whom he had seen the Holy Spirit descending and remaining in the form of a dove, and had heard the Father’s voice thunder: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (ibid.)? Had he not borne much testimony about him, saying: “He who is from the earth speaks from the earth; he who comes from heaven is above all” (John 3)?

No. John’s question was necessary for his disciples rather than for himself. What he asked—“Are you the one who is to come, or should we expect another?” (Matt. 11; Luke 7)—must therefore be answered as follows: in this question, as we have said, he was not looking after his own interests but those of his disciples. He asked not because of his own ignorance, but because of the unbelief of the disciples who were asking.

That John’s disciples still possessed some sharpness or envy toward the Lord, whom they did not yet recognize as the true God, is shown by the preceding text of the Gospel. On that day John’s disciples came to Jesus, saying: “Why do we and the Pharisees fast frequently, but your disciples do not fast?” (Matt. 9). And again: “John’s disciples came to him”—that is, to John—“saying: ‘Rabbi, the one to whom you bore witness, behold, he is baptizing, and everyone is going after him’” (John 3). It was as though they had said: “We are being left behind, and everyone is following him.”

John, therefore, placed in prison and knowing that he would die for the testimony of the truth, did not wish to leave in error the disciples whom he had prepared to believe in Christ. Consequently, under the pretext of asking a question, he sent them to inquire, so that, while they went to question him and saw the signs and miracles that he performed, they might recognize and believe that he was the true God, and thus be freed from their error.

There is also another reasonable explanation for why John sent his disciples to question Christ. He knew that Christ had been born of a virgin and had come into the world for the redemption of humanity. But he did not yet know whether, upon dying, Christ would himself free those who were unjustly held in hell. Therefore he did not say, “Are you the one who came?” but, “Are you the one who is to come?”

It was as though he said: “I am shut up in prison and will be beheaded by Herod; I am going down to the underworld. Tell me whether I should announce your coming to the dead below, as I announced it to those above, or whether it is not fitting for the Son of God to taste death and, for the accomplishment of this mystery—that is, the liberation of souls—to send someone other than you.”

“And Jesus answered and said to them: ‘Go and report to John what you hear and see. The blind see, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead rise, the poor are evangelized.’”

This response of the Lord belongs to the preceding interpretation: he did not answer John’s question but the thoughts of those who were asking. When questioned about his death, he enumerated the powers of his miracles in order to draw the minds of those who saw them toward belief in him.

It was as though he said: “Compare the works you see in me with the prophetic oracles you have read, so that you may recognize that I am the one of whom the prophet once rejoiced to say: ‘The Lord himself will come, and he will save us’” (Isa. 35).

“The blind see,” so that the prophetic word might be fulfilled: “Then the eyes of the blind will be opened” (Isa. 35).

“The lame walk,” so that this might be fulfilled: “Then the lame man will leap like a deer” (ibid.).

“Lepers are cleansed,” because, as the prophet says: “He himself took away our iniquities and bore our illnesses; by his bruise we have been healed” (Isa. 53).

“The deaf hear,” so that this might be fulfilled: “And the ears of the deaf will be opened” (Isa. 35).

“The dead rise,” so that the word might be fulfilled: “The dead will live; my slain will rise” (Isa. 26).

“The poor are evangelized,” so that the ministry of those of whom it is said might be fulfilled: “The Lord will give the word to those who evangelize with great power” (Ps. 67).

Spiritually, John bound in prison signifies the law bound in the hearts of the Jews. Since it was understood not spiritually but carnally, it lay as though shackled and bound.

“John therefore sent two disciples to Christ to ask him: ‘Are you the one who is to come, or should we expect another?’” The law likewise sent scribes and Pharisees to question the Savior: “If you are the Christ, tell us openly” (John 10). And again: “Tell us by what authority you do these things” (Luke 20).

The Lord appropriately answers them: “Go and report to John what you hear and see: ‘The blind see,’” and so forth. Through these bodily illnesses the weakness of souls was signified. He enumerated the healings of the sick because he did not come to call the righteous but sinners to repentance.

He says, “The blind see,” as though he were saying in other words: “The time of my grace has now appeared, so that the true light, shining in the world, may illumine the eyes of those who were sitting in darkness and the shadow of death. With the eye of the mind cleansed, they begin to look upon the one who says in the Gospel: ‘I am the light of the world’” (John 8), so that in them may be fulfilled: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God” (Matt. 5).

“The lame walk.” That is, those who previously limped along the way of God now, instructed by the reading of both Testaments, strengthened by love of God and neighbor, and possessing a firm step of mind, run along the way of God’s commandments and hasten to reach their heavenly homeland from earthly things, so that in them may be fulfilled: “Blessed are the meek, for they will possess the earth” (Matt. 5).

“Lepers are cleansed.” That is, those who had been made unclean and defiled by various crimes of sin now desire to be purified through baptism and repentance. They mourn not only their past sins but also sigh from desire for eternal life, and they maintain humility in prosperity and patience in adversity, so that in them may be fulfilled: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called sons of God” (ibid.).

And so that they may receive the cleansing of the soul, they grow toward such perfection that they not only inflict no evils but also bear with equanimity the evils inflicted by others, so that in them may be fulfilled: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake.”

“The deaf hear,” because those who previously had closed ears for hearing the word of God but open ears for hearing insults now, conversely, close their ears so that they may not hear bloodshed, and desire to hear the word of God with ardent spirit. So that they may fulfill it in their works, they hunger and thirst, so that in them may be fulfilled: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they will be satisfied” (ibid.).

“The dead rise.” That is, those who lay dead in sins as though insensible now, by putting their members to death, begin to live spiritually. They extend to others, as far as they are able, the mercy they have experienced in themselves, desiring to fulfill what Scripture says: “Have mercy on your soul, pleasing God” (Eccl. 30), so that in them may be fulfilled: “Blessed are the merciful, for they will obtain mercy” (Matt. 5).

“The poor are evangelized.” That is, those who were poor and lacking in virtues and filled with vices now, conversely, so that treasures may be stored up in heaven, despise temporal riches. Through the communion of charity and the grace of the Holy Spirit, they do not cease announcing to others the good they have learned, so that in them may be fulfilled: “How beautiful are the feet of those who evangelize peace, who evangelize good things” (Rom. 10). And those who were previously poor and empty in virtues now begin to be poor in spirit, so that in them may be fulfilled what the Lord says in the Gospel: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5).

“And blessed is the one who is not scandalized because of me.” This conclusion of the Lord pertains to John’s question. When questioned about his death, he first enumerated the powers of the signs and then answered what had been asked, saying: “Blessed is the one who is not scandalized because of me”—that is, because of my death.

It was as though he said: “The things I do are indeed wondrous and great, because I restore sight to the blind, hearing to the deaf, the ability to walk to the lame, and life to the dead. Yet, although I do all these things, I do not ultimately disdain to endure death for the redemption of the human race. It is necessary for people who venerate the signs in me not to despise my death to their own scandal.”

For many, after previously marveling at the Lord’s powers, despised in him the most shameful death of the cross. Having seen so many signs and such great powers of miracles, a person could avoid scandal and instead marvel. But the minds of unbelievers took grave offense against him when, after the signs of miracles had been enumerated, they saw him seized, bound, scourged, and placed in a tomb. They were also scandalized when they saw dead the one whom they had seen raising the dead.

Of such people the Apostle says: “But we preach Christ crucified: a scandal indeed to the Jews, but foolishness to the Gentiles” (1 Cor. 1).

“While they were departing, Jesus began to say to the crowds concerning John: ‘What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A reed shaken by the wind?’” It was as though he said: Lest the crowds standing around should think that John’s question arose either from envy or from ignorance, after his disciples had departed the Lord extols John with marvelous and great praises, saying concerning him to the crowds: “‘What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A reed shaken by the wind?’” It was as though he said: Did you come out into the wilderness for this—to see a man like a reed, who through fickleness of mind would doubt me, whom he had shortly before proclaimed to you? He presented this not by affirming it, but by denying it.

A reed—*arundo*—is a cane, so called from its dryness. It is recognized as naturally possessing three characteristics. First, it grows in moist and watery places; second, it is beautiful on the outside but hollow within; third, whenever it is touched by any breeze, it bends and turns toward another side. It signifies the minds of carnal people, who, because they love the wantonness of lust, are born, as it were, in watery and moist places. Hence the Prophet says: “The beasts have rotted in their dung” (Joel I). And again: “They have been compared to foolish beasts and have become like them” (Psalm XLVIII).

When, through hypocrisy, they pretend to be holy though they are not, they appear outwardly polished like a reed, but inwardly they are empty. [Col. 0029B] Such were the scribes and Pharisees, whom the Lord sternly rebuked, saying: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, for you are like whitewashed tombs, which appear beautiful to people on the outside, but within are full of the bones of the dead and of every impurity” (Matthew XXIII). Thus you appear righteous to people on the outside, but within you are full of hypocrisy and iniquity.

And because they do not have God dwelling in their hearts, they provide access to unclean spirits. Thus the Lord says concerning the devil to blessed Job: “Under the shadow he sleeps in the secret place of the reed, in moist places” (Job XL). But when they are lifted up by human praises and cast down by criticisms, they are bent toward another side, like reeds touched by the wind.

For if a carnal mind hears the breeze of passing praise, it is delighted, becomes cheerful, and rejoices. But if the wind of criticism proceeds from the same mouth—from which the favor of human praise was accustomed to come—it is immediately provoked to anger.

John, however, was not such a man. Born of chaste and long-lived parents, he was both a lover and guardian of virginity. Nor was he beautiful outwardly and empty inwardly, because the holiness that he displayed outwardly he preserved much more fully within. Neither could the wind of criticism or praise lift him up or cast him down in the manner of a reed; rather, he remained unmoved amid adversity and prosperity, preserving humility in prosperity and patience in adversity. Concerning his praise it is rightly added:

“‘But what did you go out to see? A man clothed in soft garments?’” The Lord introduced this also by denying, not affirming it. John was not clothed in soft garments, because he wore clothing made of camel hair, from which a rough haircloth is woven.

Therefore, let those who think that there is no sin in elegant dress or in the excess of costly garments learn from John’s example to restrain their desires. If it were not a virtue to be clothed in inexpensive garments, the Lord would never have praised John for the roughness of his clothing. And if it were not a sin to wear costly and excessive garments, he would never, when speaking of the punishment of the purple-clad rich man, have first said that he was clothed in purple and fine linen.

Nor would blessed Paul the Apostle restrain women from desiring costly clothing, saying: “Not in costly clothing, nor with braided hair, gold, pearls” (1 Timothy II). Here we should consider how shameful it is for men to desire what the teacher of the Church strove to restrain in women.

Each of us has his own conscience as witness that costly clothing is sought for no reason except empty glory. If a person were in a hidden place where no one could see him, he would not care what kind of clothes he wore. But when he goes out in public, he seeks costly garments—not to appear holier, but to appear more honorable and more beautiful to many.

Instructed, therefore, by these examples, let us seek clothing sufficient both to cover nakedness and to ward off cold, because, as the Apostle says: “We brought nothing into this world, and neither can we take anything away. But having food and clothing, let us be content with these” (1 Timothy VI).

According to the spiritual interpretation, John was not clothed in soft garments because he knew how to correct the vices of sinners not by flattering them and fostering their faults, but by rebuking them. Thus he reproved King Herod himself for his unlawful marriage, saying: “It is not lawful for you to have your brother’s wife while he is alive” (Mark VI).

Every teacher likewise clothes himself in rough garments after the example of John when he rebukes sinners with harsh denunciations, as it is said through Solomon: “The words of the wise are like goads, and like nails driven deeply” (Ecclesiastes XII). The words of the wise are rightly compared to nails and goads, because they do not know how to soothe the faults of wrongdoers by concealing them, but prick them by striking them, as John did when he said to the Jews: “Brood of vipers, who showed you how to flee from the coming wrath?” (Luke III).

Conversely, a teacher is clothed in soft garments when he does not rebuke the vices of sinners, but nourishes them by flattering them or remaining silent. Since this is sometimes done through fear and sometimes through love, it is rightly added:

“‘Behold, those who wear soft garments are in the houses of kings.’” This is openly to say: Those who, through fear of persecution or love of praise, do not rebuke the vices of sinners serve not a heavenly king but an earthly one. They conform themselves to such people so that they may acquire temporal possessions.

“‘But what did you go out to see? A prophet? Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet.’” The Lord did not deny that John was a prophet; rather, he affirmed that John was more than a prophet. The office of a prophet is to foretell what is to come, but not to point it out. John, however, was both a prophet and more than a prophet, because he not only foretold the coming of the one who would come after him but also pointed him out with his finger, saying: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John I).

Concerning this John the Lord says elsewhere to the disciples: “Among those born of women none has risen greater than John the Baptist” (Matthew II). But because the Lord had denied that John was a reed shaken by the wind, because he had said that John was not clothed in soft garments, and because he had shown that John was not merely a prophet but also more than a prophet, he made clear what kind of man he was by adding:

“‘For this is he of whom it is written: Behold, I send my angel before your face, who will prepare your way before you.’” This testimony is written in Malachi, specifically concerning John. When the prophet foretold the coming Lord, he also revealed the person of his forerunner when he said: “Behold, I send my angel” (Malachi III).

The name is lofty, but his merit is not inferior. In his work he fulfilled what he received in his name. Since *angelus* is Greek for what is called *nuntius*—“messenger”—in Latin, he is rightly called an angel, because he came to announce the Lord’s advent, saying: “The one who is stronger than I will come after me, whose sandal strap I am not worthy to loosen” (Matthew III). And: “His winnowing fan is in his hand, and he will thoroughly cleanse his threshing floor” (ibid.).

Nor does John alone deserve a share in this name [Col. 0031B]; all priests and ministers of the Church who preach the word of God in the Church and announce the coming judgment will deserve a share in the angelic name, according to what Malachi says: “The lips of the priest guard knowledge, and they seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts” (Malachi II).

Not only priests, but also faithful laypeople, if they announce to their brothers the good that they know according to the measure of their knowledge, will belong to the company of angels. For in the ornament of the tabernacle, not only bowls but also cups were commanded to be made. Not only more abundant teaching is acceptable to God, but also the least, according to what John says in the Apocalypse: “Let the one who hears say, ‘Come’” (Revelation XXII). And the Apostle says: “We have become a spectacle to the world, to angels, and to human beings” (1 Corinthians IV).

John prepared the way of the Lord not by removing stones or leveling rough places, but by preparing human minds when he announced, saying: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is drawing near” (Matthew III). Or he prepared the way of the Lord when he washed human bodies by baptizing them, although he did not forgive sins—prefiguring the one who was to baptize not only in water but also in the Holy Spirit, and to forgive sins to human beings.

## HOMILY IV. WEDNESDAY OF THE FOUR EMBER DAYS

“(Luke I.) At that time, the angel Gabriel was sent by God to a city of Galilee whose name was Nazareth,” and so forth.

Angels are designated by personal names so that their names may also indicate what they are capable of accomplishing in their work. Indeed, in that holy city which the vision of almighty God makes complete in knowledge, they do not receive proper names because their persons could not otherwise be known; rather, when they come to us to perform some ministry, among us they also derive their names from their ministries.

Gabriel, therefore, is sent to the virgin Mary. He is called “the strength of God.” He came to announce the one who, in order to conquer the powers of the air, deigned to appear in humility. Concerning him the Psalmist says: “The Lord, strong and mighty, the Lord, mighty in battle” (Psalm XXIII). And again: “The Lord of hosts—he is the king of glory.”

Through the strength of God, therefore, the one who is Lord of hosts and mighty in battle was to be announced—the one who came to wage war against the powers of the air.

Understand the sixth month as March, on whose twenty-fifth day our Lord is handed down as both conceived and suffering, just as he was born on the twenty-fifth day of December. If it is believed that on the former day the spring equinox occurs, as some think, or that on the latter day the winter solstice occurs, it is certainly fitting that he who enlightens every person coming into this world (John I) should be conceived or born with the increase of light.

But if anyone argues that before the time of the Lord’s birth and conception the light either grew or overcame the darkness, we reply that John was then evangelizing the kingdom of heaven before his coming, and that even now it is commanded to preachers: “Make a way for him who ascends above the setting sun” (Psalm LXVII).

Why, however, John was conceived around the autumnal equinox and born around the summer solstice, he himself teaches when he speaks either in his own person or, as many think, in the person of the Old Testament: “He must increase, but I must decrease” (John III).

“To a virgin betrothed to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David; and the name of the virgin was Mary.”

For many reasons the Savior wished to be born not of an unmarried virgin but of a betrothed woman. First, so that through the lineage of Joseph, whose relation Mary was, Mary’s origin might also be known. For it is not the custom of Scripture to construct genealogies of women. The statement that they were “of the house of David” may also be understood of both.

Second, it was so that she would not be stoned by the Jews as an adulteress, since he preferred that some people should doubt his parentage rather than her chastity. At the same time he removed an occasion for shameless virgins, lest they should say, through false suspicions, that the Savior’s mother had also been disgraced.

Third, so that when she fled into Egypt and returned, she would have the comfort of a husband who would be at once the guardian and witness of her perfect virginity.

Fourth, so that her childbirth would not be exposed to the devil. If he had known that he was born of a virgin, he might perhaps have feared to hand him over to death as someone superior to other human beings.

Mary in Hebrew means “star of the sea,” while in Syriac she is called “lady.” And rightly so, because she was worthy to give birth both to the Lord of the whole world and to the perpetual light of the age.

“And the angel entered to her and said: ‘Hail, full of grace; the Lord is with you; blessed are you among women.’”

She is rightly called “full of grace,” since she attained the grace that no other woman had deserved: namely, to conceive and give birth to the very author of grace.

“When she heard this, she was troubled by his words and considered what kind of greeting this might be.”
