Learn the virgin from her conduct; learn the virgin from her modesty; learn the virgin from the oracle; learn the virgin from the mystery. It belongs to virgins to tremble and to fear at every entrance of a man, and to revere every word spoken by a man.

Let women learn the purpose of modesty and imitate the one who was alone in her inner chamber, seen by no man. The angel found her alone, without a companion, alone without a witness; lest she should be corrupted by any ignoble affection, she was greeted by the angel.

Learn, virgin, to avoid wanton speech. Mary herself feared the angel’s greeting. Yet, he says, she was considering what kind of greeting this might be (Luke I). She did so with modesty, because she was afraid; with prudence, because she marveled at a new formula of blessing, which had nowhere been read or previously encountered.

“And the angel said to her: ‘Do not be afraid, Mary, for you have found grace with God.’”

Because he saw her troubled by an unusual greeting, one reserved for her alone, he commands her not to fear, calling her by name as though addressing a familiar acquaintance. And because he had called her full of grace, he further confirms and more abundantly explains that same grace, saying:

“‘Behold, you will conceive in your womb and bear a son, and you will call his name Jesus.’”

Jesus is interpreted as “savior” or “salutary.” Speaking to Joseph, the angel explained the mystery of this name: “For he,” he said, “will save his people from their sins.” He did not say “the people of Israel,” but “his people,” that is, those called from uncircumcision and circumcision into the unity of faith. Gathered together from different sides, they would become “one flock and one shepherd” (John X).

“‘He will be great and will be called the Son of the Most High, and the Lord God will give him the throne of David his father.’”

It was also said of John that he would be great, but great as a human being; this one, as great as God. John was great before the Lord, but of this one it says: “He will be great, and he will be called the Son of the Most High.”

The same one, therefore, is the Son of the Most High who was conceived and born in the virgin’s womb; the same is the human being created in time from his mother, who is God, born before time from the Father.

If the same human being is God, let Nestorius cease saying that only a human being was born from the virgin and that this person was received by the Word of God into an inseparable association, not into the unity of person. Otherwise he is shown to assert not one Christ, true God and human being, but two—which it is impious to say—and thus to proclaim not a Trinity but a quaternity.

The Catholic faith, however, just as it most rightly confesses every human being to consist of flesh and soul, so also confesses the human being and the Word to be one Christ. This is also signified by the angel’s words, which affirm that he will be given the throne of David his father.

For by saying that the one whom he declares to be called the Son of the Most High would have David himself as father, the angel demonstrates one person of Christ in two natures. He received David’s throne so that he himself might summon to an eternal kingdom the people to whom David and his sons once provided the governance of a temporal kingdom—the kingdom prepared for them from the foundation of the world.

“‘And he will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there will be no end.’”

Isaiah also says: “His dominion will be multiplied, and there will be no end of peace. Upon the throne of David and over his kingdom he will sit, to establish it and strengthen it in judgment and justice” (Isaiah IX).

He did not say “in the acquisition of glory and earthly treasures,” nor “in the victory over many nations and the destruction of proud cities,” but “in judgment and justice.” Through these things the kingdom of Christ is multiplied and strengthened both in each individual believer and throughout the Church across the world.

By the house of Jacob he means the whole Church, which was either born from a good root or, though it was a wild olive tree, was nevertheless grafted by the merit of faith into the good olive tree. After the triumph of his passion, the Savior addresses it, saying: “You who fear the Lord, praise him; glorify him, all the seed of Jacob” (Psalm XVI).

He is not therefore declared, by a verb referring to the future, to be destined to become great, to be called the Son of the Most High, to receive David’s scepter, and to reign in the house of Jacob because—as heretics think, and in their madness depart from the truth—Christ did not exist before Mary. Rather, it is because the human being assumed into God was glorified with the glory that the Word of God had with the Father before the world existed.

That is, the human being, full of grace and truth together with God, received both the same name of Son and the same person of Christ.

“Mary said to the angel: ‘How will this happen, since I do not know a man?’”

She reverently explained the purpose of her mind: namely, that she had decided to lead a virginal life. Because she was the first among women to take care to devote herself to such a service, she rightly deserved to surpass other women in a unique blessedness.

“‘How,’ she said, ‘will this happen?’” She did not say, “From where shall I know this?” but, “How will this happen, since I do not know a man?” She was asking about the manner of the obedience to which she was to submit, not demanding a sign in which she might believe.

It was not fitting that the virgin chosen to give birth to God should be doubtful through distrust; rather, she was cautious through prudence, since a human being could not easily know the mystery that had remained hidden in God for ages.

Because she had read: “Behold, a virgin will have a child in her womb and will bear a son” (Isaiah VII), but had not read how this could happen, she asked the angel about what she had not found in the prophet.

“The angel answered and said to her: ‘The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you.’”

You will conceive, he says, not by the seed of a man whom you do not know, but through the work of the Holy Spirit, with whom you are filled. Conception will occur in you; there will be no lust of desire. There will be no heat where the Holy Spirit casts his shadow.

In the words “the power of the Most High will overshadow you,” the twofold nature of the incarnate Savior may also be signified. A shadow is usually formed by light and a body. The person overshadowed is refreshed by as much light or solar heat as is sufficient; but if the sun’s own heat cannot be endured, it is moderated by the interposition of a light cloud or some other body.

Blessed, therefore, is the Virgin, because, being a pure human being, she could not bodily contain the whole fullness of divinity. The power of the Most High overshadowed her—that is, incorporeal light took a human body in her.

Concerning this the prophet beautifully says: “Behold,” he says, “the Lord will ascend upon a light cloud and will enter Egypt” (Isaiah XIX). This means: Behold, the Word of God, coeternal with the Father and light born from light before the ages, will assume, at the end of the ages, flesh and a soul unburdened by any weight of sin, and will proceed into the world from the virgin’s womb like a bridegroom from his chamber.

“‘And therefore the holy one who will be born from you will be called the Son of God.’”

To distinguish our holiness from his, Jesus is uniquely declared to be holy at birth. We, even if we are made holy, are not born holy, because we are bound by the very condition of corruptible nature, so that each of us rightly says with the Prophet in lamentation: “Behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and my mother bore me in sins” (Psalm I).

He alone is truly holy who, in order to overcome the condition of corruptible nature itself, was not conceived through the union of bodily intercourse.

“‘He will be called the Son of God.’” What do you say to this, Nestorian, who deny that blessed Mary is the mother of God and strive to attack the fitting truth? Behold, he said that God would come upon her and that the Son of God would be born. How, then, is the Son of God not God? Or how can she who gave birth to God not be *Theotokos*—that is, “Mother of God”?

“And behold, Elizabeth your kinswoman has also conceived a son in her old age. And this is the sixth month for her who is called barren, because no word will be impossible with God.”

So that the virgin would not doubt that she could give birth, she received the example of an old, barren woman who was to bear a child, so that she might learn that all things are possible for God, even those that appear contrary to the order of nature.

If anyone is troubled by how Elizabeth is called the kinswoman of blessed Mary, since Mary descended from the house of David but Elizabeth from the daughters of Aaron, let him observe that their ancestors, by giving their children to one another in marriage, could have united the two tribes.

If this explanation should not satisfy someone who stubbornly insists that such a union could not have occurred contrary to the prohibition of the law, let him read Exodus, where it is written: “Aaron took as his wife Elizabeth, daughter of Amminadab, sister of Nahshon, and she bore him Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar” (Exodus VI).

Let him see that, before the promulgation of the law, by heavenly providence the priestly lineage had already been joined to the royal lineage, so that the Lord Jesus Christ, who was to be the true king and priest according to the flesh, might also receive that flesh from both lines—from David and from Aaron.

Hence in both tribes the mystical anointing is celebrated according to the law, foreshadowing alike the name and the generation of Christ. David himself, entering the house of God, received the holy bread and the sword as king and priest, prefiguring the one who would come from his seed, who would fight by royal right for your freedom and offer the bread of his flesh for the release of your freedom.

“Mary said: ‘Behold, I am the handmaid of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word.’”

What devoted humility: she desires the angel’s promise to be fulfilled and calls herself, though chosen to be a mother, a handmaid, openly showing that she claims no merit for herself in obeying the Lord’s commands.

“Let it be done,” she says: let flesh be conceived in a virgin without the seed of a man; let complete flesh be born from the Holy Spirit. Let the holy one who is born from a human mother without a human father be called the Son of God.

## HOMILY V. FRIDAY OF THE FOUR EMBER DAYS

“(Luke I.) At that time, Mary arose and went into the hill country with haste, to a city of Judah, and so forth.”

After receiving the Virgin’s consent, the angel immediately returns to heavenly things. She goes to the hill country and hastens to visit Elizabeth, not as though she were unbelieving concerning the oracle or doubtful concerning the example, but as one joyful because of her desire and devout because of her duty. At the same time she offers a figurative example: every soul that has conceived the word of God in its mind should immediately ascend, by the step of love, the lofty summits of virtue, so that it may enter the citadel of the city of Judah—that is, of confession and praise—and be able to remain there, as it were, for three months, until the perfection of faith, hope, and charity.

“And she entered the house of Zechariah and greeted Elizabeth.”

Learn from Mary, virgin, humility, so that you may be chaste in body and devout in heart. A younger woman visits an older woman; a virgin greets a wife. For the more chaste a virgin is, the more humble she ought to be. By honoring her elders, she commends the discipline of chastity through the testimony of humility.

Alternatively: Mary comes to Elizabeth, the Lord to John. The former comes so that Elizabeth may be filled with the Holy Spirit; the latter, so that John may be consecrated by baptism. The humiliation of the greater is certainly the exaltation of the lesser. Finally, it follows:

“And it happened that, when Elizabeth heard Mary’s greeting, the infant leaped in her womb, and Elizabeth was filled with the Holy Spirit.”

Observe the distinction and the particular force of each word. Elizabeth first heard the voice, but John first perceived grace. She heard according to the order of nature; he leaped because of the mystery. She perceived Mary’s arrival; he perceived the Lord’s.

These women speak of grace; those infants inwardly perform the mystery of divine mercy before they begin to advance through their mothers. Through a twofold miracle, the mothers prophesy by the spirit of their little ones. The infant leaped, and the mother was filled. The mother was not filled before the son. But when the son was filled with the Holy Spirit, he also filled his mother.

“And she cried out with a loud voice and said: ‘Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb.’”

It should be noted that she embraces the prophecy about Christ already stated, not only through the miracles of events but also through the precision of the words. For this is the fruit that was promised to the patriarch David under oath: “From the fruit of your womb I will set upon your throne” (Psalm CXXXI).

At the same time, it should be observed that Mary is blessed by Elizabeth with the same word with which she was blessed by Gabriel, so that she might be shown worthy of reverence by angels and human beings alike and rightly preferred to all women.

“And from where is this granted to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?”

She does not inquire as one ignorant of the matter, for she recognizes that it is the work of the Holy Spirit: namely, that she is being greeted by the mother of her Lord for the perfecting of her own pledge. Rather, struck by the novelty of the miracle, she confesses that this is not the accomplishment of her own office but a divine gift.

“For behold, when the voice of your greeting came to my ears, the infant in my womb leaped for joy.”

Elizabeth was ashamed of the burden of giving birth as long as she did not know the mystery of faith. But once she who had hidden herself because she had conceived a son began to boast because she was giving birth to a prophet, she who had previously been ashamed began to bless, and she who had previously doubted was strengthened.

“For behold,” she said, “when the voice of your greeting came to my ears, the infant in my womb leaped for joy.” Thus she cried out with a loud voice when she perceived the Lord’s coming, because she believed the birth to be sacred when she recognized the birth of a prophet, rather than affectedly taking on faith in the conception.

“And blessed is she who believed, because those things will be fulfilled that were spoken to her by the Lord.”

You see that Mary did not doubt but believed, and therefore obtained the fruit of faith. “Blessed,” she says, “is she who believed”—and truly blessed, for, surpassing the priest, when he had denied, the virgin corrected the denial also through her pledge.

It should likewise be noted how greatly grace enriched Elizabeth’s mind when Mary entered, and how the spirit of prophecy enlightened her at once concerning the past, present, and future. By saying, “Blessed is she who believed,” she clearly indicates that through the Holy Spirit she recognized the angel’s words that had been spoken to Mary.

By adding, “Those things will be fulfilled that were spoken to you by the Lord,” she foresaw what would also follow Mary in the future. By calling her “the mother of her Lord,” she understood that she carried the Redeemer of the human race in her womb.

“And Mary said: ‘My soul magnifies the Lord, and my spirit has rejoiced in God my Savior.’”

The Lord has exalted me with so great and unheard-of a gift, she says, that it cannot be explained by any service of the tongue, but can scarcely be grasped even by the feeling of the innermost heart. Therefore I offer all the powers of my soul in praises of thanksgiving; whatever I live, perceive, and discern, I joyfully devote to contemplating the greatness of the one whose greatness has no end.

For my spirit also rejoices in the eternal divinity of the same Jesus—that is, of the Savior—whose flesh is made fruitful by temporal conception in me. Similar is the Psalmist’s saying: “My soul will rejoice in the Lord and delight in his salvation” (Psalm XXXIV). For he himself revered the Father and the Son with equal love.

“‘Because he has looked upon the humility of his handmaid; for behold, from now on all generations will call me blessed.’”

She rejoices that the one whose humility has been regarded is rightly to be called blessed by human beings. Conversely, the one whose pride is despised and condemned wastes away under the name of Eve—that is, of woe or calamity. For it was fitting that, just as death entered the world through the pride of our first mother, so the entrance to life should again be opened through Mary’s humility.

“‘Because he who is mighty has done great things for me, and holy is his name.’”

She looks back to the beginning of the song, where it was said: “My soul magnifies the Lord.” Only that soul to which the Lord deigns to do great things can magnify him with worthy praises and exhort those who share the same desire and purpose, saying: “Magnify the Lord with me, and let us exalt his name together” (Psalm XXXIII).

For whoever refuses, insofar as he is able, to magnify the Lord whom he has come to know and to sanctify his name will be called least in the kingdom of heaven.

His name is called holy because, in the summit of his unique power, it transcends every creature and is set far apart from all that he has made. This is better understood in Greek, where the word *ἅγιον* (*hagion*, “holy”) signifies, as it were, being outside the earth. In imitation of him, we too are commanded, according to our measure, to be set apart from all who are not holy and not devoted to God, as the Lord says: “Be holy, because I am holy” (Leviticus XX).

Whoever consecrates himself will rightly appear to be outside the world. He too can say: “While walking upon the earth, we have our way of life in heaven.”

“‘And his mercy is from generation to generation for those who fear him.’”

Turning from particular gifts to God’s general judgments, she describes the condition of the whole human race. In the following verses she explains what the proud and the humble deserve, what the children of Adam receive through free choice, and what the children of God receive through grace.

He has not done great things only for me, she says, he who is mighty; rather, in every nation and generation, whoever fears him and practices righteousness is acceptable to him.

“‘He has shown strength with his arm; he has scattered the proud in the thoughts of their hearts.’”

By “his arm” she signifies the Son of God himself. This does not mean that the Father is defined by the form of human flesh and that the Son clings to him like a bodily limb. Rather, because all things were made through him, he is called the arm of the Lord.

Just as your arm is the means by which you work, so the word of God is called God’s arm, because through that Word he worked the world. Why does a human being extend an arm in order to accomplish something, unless it is because what he has said does not immediately come to be? If he possessed such power that what he said came to be without any movement of his body, his word would be his arm.

Therefore, when we hear that the Son of God is the arm of God the Father, let bodily custom not obstruct us. Rather, insofar as he grants us the ability, let us contemplate the power and wisdom of God through whom all things were made.

“‘He has brought down the mighty from their thrones and exalted the humble. He has filled the hungry with good things and sent the rich away empty.’”

What she said about his arm, and what she previously said about generation after generation, must also be joined to these following verses individually, since throughout all the generations of the age the proud continually perish and the humble are exalted through the loving and just dispensation of divine power.

“‘He has helped Israel his servant, remembering his mercy.’”

Israel is beautifully called the Lord’s servant, because he has been taken up by him for salvation—obedient and humble—according to what Hosea says: “Because Israel was a child, and I loved him” (Hosea XI).

For whoever refuses to be humbled cannot be saved, nor can he say with the prophet: “Behold, God is my helper, and the Lord is the protector of my soul” (Psalm LIII). “Whoever humbles himself like a little child is greater in the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew XVIII).

“‘As he spoke to our fathers, Abraham and his seed forever.’”

By Abraham’s seed he signifies not a carnal but a spiritual seed: not only those descended from him by flesh, but those who, whether in circumcision or in uncircumcision, follow the footsteps of his faith.

For Abraham himself believed while still uncircumcised, and it was credited to him as righteousness; he then received circumcision as the seal of that same faith, so that through faith he might become the father of both peoples, as the Apostle fully explains in his letter to the Romans.

The coming of the Savior, therefore, was promised forever to Abraham and his seed—that is, to the children of promise, to whom it is said: “If you belong to Christ, then you are Abraham’s seed, heirs according to the promise” (Galatians III).

It is fitting that the mothers prophetically anticipate the birth both of the Lord and of John, so that, just as sin began through women, good things might also begin through women. And she who perished through the deception of one woman might, through two women proclaiming together, have life restored to the world.

## HOMILY VI. SATURDAY OF THE FOUR EMBER DAYS

“(Luke III.) At that time, in the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, while Pontius Pilate was governing Judea, and Herod was tetrarch of Galilee, while Philip his brother was tetrarch of the region of Ituraea and Trachonitis, and Lysanias was tetrarch of Abilene,” and so forth.

Herod, Philip, and Lysanias, who governed Judea together with the Roman governor Pilate, were sons of that Herod under whom the Lord was born. Their brother Archelaus likewise reigned among them for ten years. The Jews accused him before Augustus because of his intolerable savagery of spirit, and he perished in perpetual exile at Vienne.

In order to make the kingdom of Judea less powerful, that same Augustus arranged for it to be divided into tetrarchies. Pilate, sent into Judea in the twelfth year of Tiberius Caesar, assumed the administration of the people and remained there for ten continuous years, almost until the very end of Tiberius.

«Under the high priests Annas and Caiaphas, the word of the Lord came to John, son of Zechariah, in the wilderness.» Both of them—Annas and Caiaphas—were high priests when John began his preaching; but Annas administered during one year, and Caiaphas during the year in which the Lord ascended the cross. Three others had exercised the high-priesthood in between, but the Evangelist mentions especially those whose tenure was connected with the Lord’s Passion. For at that time, while legal prescriptions had been set aside by force and bribery, the honor of the high priesthood was bestowed on no one by merit of life or lineage; rather, by Roman authority, the dignity of the supreme priesthood was granted now to one man, then to another. Finally, Josephus reports the matter in these words:

“Valerius Gratus, having removed Annas from the priesthood, appointed Ishmael, son of Bassi, as high priest. But not long afterward, having also deposed him, he substituted Eleazar, son of Annas the high priest, in the high priesthood. After a year, he likewise removed him from office. Octavianus the emperor reigned for fifty-six years and entrusted the office of the high priesthood to a certain Simon, son of Cantharus. After he too had held it for no more than a single year, he accepted Joseph as his successor—Joseph whose name was also Caiaphas.”

Thus the entire period during which our Lord is described as having taught on earth is confined within the span of four years, during which these four successions of high priests, mentioned by Josephus, are recorded, scarcely one of them serving for a full year. Since John came to preach the one who would redeem some from Judea and many from the nations, the times of his preaching are marked by the king of the nations and the rulers of the Jews. And since the Gentiles were to be gathered while Judea was to be scattered because of the guilt of its unfaithfulness, the very description of earthly rule also makes this evident. For in the Roman state one ruler is described as presiding, whereas in the kingdom of Judea many were ruling in its several divisions. In the words of our Redeemer it is said: «Every kingdom divided against itself will be laid waste» (Luke XI). It is therefore clear that Judea had come to the end of its kingdom, since it lay subject to so many divided rulers.

It is also fittingly demonstrated not only under which kings but under which priests these events took place, so that John the Baptist might preach the one who would exist as both king and priest. Luke the Evangelist designated the times of John’s preaching by the kingship and the priesthood.

«And he came into the whole region of the Jordan, preaching a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins.»

It is clear to all who read that John not only preached the baptism of repentance but also gave it to some; nevertheless, he could not give his own baptism for the forgiveness of sins. For the forgiveness of sins is granted only in the baptism of Christ. It must therefore be observed that when it says, “preaching a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins,” John was preaching a baptism that would release sins, although he was unable to give it. Just as he went before the incarnate Word of the Father with the word of preaching, so too the baptism of repentance, by which sins cannot be forgiven [the sentence breaks off in the supplied text].

«As it is written in the book of the words of Isaiah the prophet» (Isaiah XL): «The voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord; make straight the paths of our God.»

When John the Baptist himself was asked who he was, he replied: «I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness.» He was therefore called a voice by the prophet because he went before the Word. He also cries in the wilderness because he announces the comfort of redemption to abandoned and forsaken Judea.

What he was crying out is made clear when it adds: «Prepare the way of the Lord; make his paths straight.» Everyone who preaches right faith and good works—what else does he do but prepare a way for the coming Lord to the hearts of his hearers, so that the power of grace may penetrate them and the light of truth illumine them? He makes straight paths for God when, through the word of good preaching, he forms pure thoughts in the mind.

«Every valley shall be filled, and every mountain and hill shall be brought low.»

What is signified here by the name “valleys” except the humble? And by “mountains and hills” except proud people? At the coming of the Redeemer, therefore, the valleys were filled, while the mountains and hills were brought low, because, in his words, «everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted» (Luke XVIII). A filled valley rises, whereas a humbled mountain or hill decreases.

For in faith in the Mediator between God and human beings, Jesus Christ the man, the Gentiles received the fullness of grace, while Judea, through the error of its unfaithfulness, lost the very thing by which it had been swollen with pride.

«And crooked things shall become straight, and rough ways into smooth roads.»

Crooked things become straight when hearts distorted by the injustice of evil are directed toward the rule of justice. Rough ways are changed into smooth roads when harsh and wrathful minds, through the infusion of heavenly grace, return to the gentleness of meekness. For when the word of truth is not received by a wrathful mind, the roughness of the road, as it were, drives back the step of one who is advancing. But when a wrathful person, having received the grace of meekness, accepts a word of correction or exhortation, the preacher finds a smooth road there where previously, because of the roughness of the way, he could not proceed—that is, could not set down the step of his preaching.

«And all flesh shall see the salvation of God.»

Since “all flesh” means every human being, no human being in this life could see “the salvation of God,” namely Christ. Where, then, does the prophet direct the eye of prophecy in this statement, if not toward the final day of judgment? There, when Christ appears with the heavens opened, the angels ministering, and the apostles seated on the throne of his majesty, all—both the elect and the reprobate—will see him together, so that the righteous may rejoice without end in the gift of their reward, while the wicked may groan forever under the punishment of their retribution.

## HOMILY VII. THE FOURTH SUNDAY OF ADVENT

(John I.) «At that time, the Jews sent priests and Levites from Jerusalem to John to ask him: Who are you?» and so forth.

It may prompt us to inquire why the Jews, sending priests and Levites from Jerusalem to John, asked him so earnestly and insistently, saying: «Who are you?» But the answer is readily and truly apparent. Among the Jews, through their frequent use of the Law, it was a familiar matter that Moses had said: «God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers, like me; you shall listen to him according to everything that he speaks to you» (Deuteronomy XVIII). It had also been made known through the prophecies that Christ would come into the world and preach a new teaching.

Therefore, because they had heard that John had been born, through an angelic promise, from an aged father and a barren mother; because they had heard that at his birth his father’s tongue had been loosed; because they saw him, as a young man, pursuing the wilderness and preaching an unprecedented repentance for the forgiveness of sins, or an unprecedented doctrine; because they saw him preserving extraordinary abstinence and not only teaching baptism but also administering it—they judged among themselves that he was the Christ who had been promised to them. For this reason they sent priests and Levites from Jerusalem to John to ask him: «Who are you?»

That they sent him to be questioned because they were moved by this suspicion is plainly declared by another Evangelist, namely Luke, who says: «Now while the people were expecting, and all were reasoning in their hearts about John, whether perhaps he might be the Christ» (Luke III).

«They sent priests and Levites from Jerusalem to ask him: Who are you?» But let us hear what the herald of truth says about himself.

«And he confessed, and did not deny; and he confessed: I am not the Christ.»

If you ask what he confessed and what he did not deny: he confessed what he was not; he did not deny what he was. He confessed that he was not Christ, but he did not deny that he was Christ’s forerunner. He confessed that he was not the judge, but he did not deny that he was the judge’s herald. He confessed that he was not the bridegroom, but he did not deny that he was the bridegroom’s friend. He confessed that he was not the Word, but he did not deny that he was the voice.

For he chose to stand firmly within himself, lest human opinion should vainly carry him above himself. He preferred to be numbered humbly among Christ’s members rather than undeservedly usurp Christ’s name and be cut off from Christ’s body. While others considered him great, he regarded himself as small. While others thought great things about him, he felt the least about himself, preserving what Scripture says: «The greater you are, humble yourself in all things, and you will find grace before God» (Ecclesiasticus III).

«And they questioned him: What then? Are you Elijah? He said: I am not.»

They questioned John about his identity because they had the promised coming of Elijah in the prophecy of Malachi, where the Lord says: «Behold, I will send you Elijah the Tishbite, who will turn the hearts of fathers to their children and the hearts of children to their fathers» (Malachi IV). But, supposing that what had been foretold about the Lord’s second coming had been spoken of his first, they asked John, after he had confessed that he was not the Christ: «What then? Are you Elijah? He said: I am not.»

From this answer a considerable question arises for us if we recall another Gospel passage. For elsewhere we read that, when the disciples questioned the Lord about the coming of Elijah, he replied: «Elijah has already come, and they did not recognize him, but they did to him whatever they wished. And if you wish to know, he himself is Elijah, John» (Matthew XI, XVII). Since, then, the Lord says that John himself is Elijah, why does John, when questioned, say, “I am not Elijah”? Nothing could appear more discordant than “he is” and “I am not.” Does truth think one thing while the forerunner and prophet of truth thinks another? Does the judge announce one thing while the herald cries another? No.

Or could Elijah and John be one at the same time? We quickly understand how both statements can be true if we recall the words of the angel spoken to Zechariah when he foretold that John would be born. Among other things, he says: «He himself will go before him in the spirit and power of Elijah» (Luke I). These words show that John was not Elijah in person, but that he was Elijah in spirit. Just as Elijah will precede the Lord’s second coming, when he comes to judge the world, so John preceded the Lord’s first coming, when he came to redeem the world. And just as the former will be the herald of the Judge, so the latter became the forerunner of the Redeemer.

Therefore, what the Lord says concerning the spirit, John denies concerning the person; and what John denies concerning the person, the Lord affirms concerning the spirit. Although they were separated in time, they were united in spirit. Since the Lord was speaking to spiritual disciples, to whom it had been granted to know the mystery of the kingdom of God, it was fitting that he should give a spiritual judgment concerning John, saying: «John himself is Elijah.» But when John was questioned by Jews who knew how to consider only the letter, not the spirit, it was fitting that he should speak not of the spirit but of his own person and say: «I am not Elijah.»

Finally, if anyone carefully examines the activity of the two heralds, he understands that one and the same spirit worked in both. Elijah was in the wilderness, and so was John. Elijah fasted for forty days and nights (1 Kings XIX), and John maintained an unprecedented abstinence, for he ate locusts and wild honey (Mark I). Elijah had a leather belt around his loins (2 Kings I), and so did John (Matthew III). Elijah divided the Jordan River with his cloak (2 Kings XIX), and John baptized in the Jordan River (John I). Elijah suffered persecution from King Ahab and the most wicked queen Jezebel (1 Kings XIX), and John was beheaded by Herod on account of Herodias (Mark VI).

«Are you the prophet? And he answered: No.»

John denied that he was a prophet because he understood that he was more than a prophet. The office of a prophet is to foretell what is to come, not to point it out. John was therefore more than a prophet, because he not only foretold the one who was to come but also pointed him out with his finger as having come, saying: «Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world» (John I).

But the priests and Levites who had been sent to John continue to inquire more diligently who he is, saying:

«Who then are you, so that we may give an answer to those who sent us? What do you say about yourself?»

But he who had denied that he was Christ, and had said that he was neither Elijah nor a prophet, reveals what he thinks of himself when he adds:

«I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness.»

John fittingly called himself a voice because he preceded the Word. In human speech, the voice comes first and afterward the word, since a word cannot be formed unless a voice has first sounded. John therefore rightly confesses himself to be a voice, because he preceded the Word—the one of whom John the Evangelist says: «In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and God was the Word» (John I). And again: «The Word became flesh and dwelt among us» (ibid.).

So that human blindness would not suddenly stumble against the Lord’s brightness when he appeared, John was sent before the Lord like a lamp before the sun, a voice before the Word, and a herald before the judge, so that through his preaching the hearts of human beings might be prepared to see God. As it is said through John the Evangelist: «There was a man sent by God, whose name was John. He came as a witness, to bear witness to the light, so that all might believe through him. He was not the light, but came to bear witness to the light.»

John therefore cried in the wilderness, that is, among the Jewish people. Since “wilderness” means an abandoned place, the Jewish people are rightly designated by the name “wilderness”: they abandoned the Lord and were abandoned by him, as the Lord elsewhere reproaches them, saying: «Behold, your house will be left desolate» (Luke XV).

In this wilderness John cried when he preached repentance to sinners, saying: «Broods of vipers, who showed you how to flee from the coming wrath? Therefore produce fruits worthy of repentance» (Luke III).

But let us hear what else he cried: «Make straight the way of the Lord, as Isaiah the prophet said.»

The way of the Lord is directed toward the heart when the heart humbly inclines itself to hear God’s commandments. Alternatively: the way of the Lord is directed toward the heart when the hand performs the good that the heart understands.

Any teacher, following John’s example, directs the way of the Lord when he persuades people to turn away from evil and do good, so that, once the entrance of the heart has been cleansed, it may have as its inhabitant the one who says: «Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone opens to me, I will enter him and dine with him, and he with me» (Revelation III).

When we thus prepare the way of the Lord for ourselves, Jesus will deign to come to our hearts through faith, as he himself says in the Gospel: «If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him» (John XIV).

Hence the Psalmist says to preachers: «Make a way for him who ascends above the setting sun; the Lord is his name» (Psalm LXVII).

But because the priests and Levites questioned John more out of a desire to criticize than from a wish to learn, the Evangelist discreetly took care to make this known when he added:

[Col. 0044D] «And those who had been sent were from the Pharisees.»

It was as if he were saying: They were asking John about his actions who were more accustomed to envy teaching than to imitate it.

«And they questioned him and said to him.»

But those who had been sent, having received an answer concerning his person, also questioned him about his ministry, saying:

«Why then do you baptize, if you are not the Christ, nor Elijah, nor the prophet?»

It was as if they were saying: What authority do you have to dare to teach a new doctrine and give people a baptism previously unheard of, since you are neither Christ, nor Elijah, nor the prophet?

And because, according to the judgment of the apostle Peter (1 Peter III), we must always be ready to give an account to everyone who asks for the reason of the faith that is in us, John was questioned about why he baptized and answered:

«I baptize in water.»

Here it should be noted that he said he baptized in water, not in the Spirit, because he washed bodies but did not forgive sins. Of this it is written: «John was in the wilderness, preaching the baptism of repentance» (Mark I). And again: «John baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit» (Acts I).

Why, then, did he baptize if he did not forgive sins? Did his baptism therefore appear useless? No. Certainly, in order to preserve the order of his forerunning—he who by his birth had preceded Christ who was to be born—he also preceded, by baptizing in water, the one who would baptize in the Spirit.

For priests today also baptize in water, since through an outward ministry they immerse the bodies of those being baptized in water. But only he baptizes in the Spirit who forgives sins through the Holy Spirit. Of him it was said by the Father’s voice to this same John: «He upon whom you see the Holy Spirit descending like a dove and remaining upon him is the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit.»

And just as he preceded the Word by preaching, so his baptism, in which sins were not forgiven, preceded the true baptism of that one, in which sins would be released.

Hence, according to another Evangelist, namely Matthew, John is said to have answered well: «I indeed baptize you with water for repentance,» and shortly afterward he added: «He himself will baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire» (Matthew III). The name “fire” designates the Holy Spirit. Of this the Savior says: «I came to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire except that it burn?» (Luke XII).

Nor should it be thought that John’s baptism benefited people very little. Although it did not forgive sins, he nevertheless understood that all who were baptized by him remained bound by the chain of sin. Therefore, as soon as our Redeemer and purifier appeared—the one able to forgive sins—they necessarily had to seek him.

Concerning him the words of his forerunner continue:

«But one stands among you whom you do not know.»

By “the one who stands among you” he means the Lord Jesus Christ. Although he is exalted above all, he deigned to take flesh from the Jews and dwell among human beings, as he himself says to the disciples: «I am among you as one who serves» (Luke XXII).

He says that he stood among them but was not known because, through his humanity, he appeared visibly to human beings and to the Jews, while to many he remained unknown through his divinity. Hence John the Evangelist says: «He came to his own, and his own did not receive him» (John XI).

Of him it continues:

«He is the one who will come after me, who was made before me.»

This means: He will come after me—that is, he was born after me and will begin to preach after me—but he was made before me, that is, he was preferred to me in dignity and placed above me. When he says, «he was made before me,» this concerns the excellence of his dignity. John himself explains the reason for this precedence elsewhere, saying: «Because he was before me» (John III).

It was as if he were saying: He surpasses me, although he was born afterward, because the circumstances of his birth do not confine his times. He who was born after me from a mother without a human father was begotten before every creature, without any beginning, from a Father without a mother.

Elsewhere this same John says of him: «I must decrease, but he must increase» (John III). And by the greatness of this comparison he reveals how small he considers himself, adding: «I am not worthy to unfasten the strap of his sandal» (John I).

Here we should observe that, although John’s holiness was great, his humility is shown to be no less. Though he was so holy that the crowds thought he was the Christ, he was so humble that he judged himself unworthy to unfasten the strap of Christ’s sandal.

If we follow the spiritual meaning, the strap of the sandal is the bond of the mystery. A sandal is made from the skin of a dead animal. Since a sandal customarily protects the feet, the Lord’s sandal rightly signifies the incarnation of his humanity. When the invisible God appeared visibly to us in the human being whom he assumed, divinity came to us as though shod, as he says through the Psalmist: «I will extend my sandal over Edom» (Psalm LIX).

Edom, which is interpreted as “bloody,” signifies the Gentile people, who were bloodstained by various crimes of sin. The Lord extended his sandal over Edom, as it were, when through the mystery of his incarnation he manifested himself to the Gentiles.

But John did not presume to unfasten the strap of his sandal, because he did not presume to scrutinize the secret of his incarnation—how, with the Holy Spirit overshadowing her, the Virgin conceived—even though he himself pointed him out with his finger as he came in the flesh.

The mysteries of divinity are lofty and inscrutable, and no mortal can investigate them, as it is said through the prophet: «Who will recount his generation?» (Isaiah LIII). The apostle Paul considered this inscrutable depth when he said: «O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments and how unsearchable his ways! For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counselor?» (Romans XVI). And the Psalmist says: «How magnificent are your works, O Lord!» (Psalm XC).

There is also another point concerning the strap of the sandal that can be examined more subtly. It was customary among the ancients that, if someone did not wish to take the wife of his deceased brother, the man who approached her as bridegroom by right of kinship would loosen his sandal strap; for this reason that man’s house was called “the house of the barefooted” in Israel, as we learn from the example of Ruth the Moabite.

Christ appeared among human beings as the bridegroom of holy Church, as it is said in the Psalm: «Like a bridegroom coming forth from his chamber» (Psalm XVIII). And the same John says: «He who has the bride is the bridegroom. But the friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices greatly because of the bridegroom’s voice» (John III).

Hence the Lord himself says in the Gospel: «Can the children of the bridegroom fast as long as the bridegroom is with them?» (Matthew III).

When people saw John’s extraordinary holiness and thought that he was the Christ, they wanted to believe him to be the bridegroom of holy Church, as the Lord says concerning them: «You came to John, and you wished to rejoice for a while in his name.» But John declares himself unworthy to unfasten the strap of his sandal. Since he denied that he was the Christ, which people thought he was, he did not undeservedly usurp the name of bridegroom; and consequently he denied that he was the bridegroom of holy Church.

It was as if he were saying: “I am not the bridegroom, but the friend of the bridegroom.”

«These things took place in Bethany beyond the Jordan, where John was baptizing.»

We read that there were two Bethanys. One is on the slope of the Mount of Olives, where the Lord raised Lazarus; it is also called Bethphage. There is another Bethany beyond the Jordan, where John was baptizing and where these events are reported to have taken place. John the Evangelist also mentions it, saying: «John was baptizing in Aenon near Salim, because there was much water there.»

Spiritually, Bethany is interpreted in our language as “house of obedience.” It is therefore fitting that the Lord’s forerunner is said to have baptized in Bethany, which means “house of obedience,” so that people may understand that, if they desire to be freed from original sin—which came about through the disobedience of the first human being—they must receive the sacrament of baptism with a humbled body and believing heart.

For, as the Savior says elsewhere: «Unless someone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God» (John III).

Jordan is interpreted as “their descent”—whose, if not that of those being baptized? People are baptized in the Jordan, as it were, because before they come to baptism they are children of wrath and children of the devil. But when they descend into baptism, their sins descend, and they rise as children of peace and adopted children of God.

## HOMILY VIII. ON THE VIGILS OF THE NATIVITY OF THE LORD

(Matthew I.) «At that time, when Mary, the mother of Jesus, had been betrothed to Joseph, before they came together, she was found to be with child by the Holy Spirit,» and so forth.

When Matthew the Evangelist narrated the birth of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ—who, though the eternal Son of God before the ages, appeared in time as the son of a human being—he proceeded in a brief discourse from Abraham to Joseph, the husband of Mary, showing all those born and begetting according to the common order of human generation. Then, as he was about to speak of Christ himself and to show how his generation differed from that of the others, he made it clear that the others were born through the customary union of male and female, whereas he was born into the world through a virgin, as the Son of God.

Indeed, it was fitting in every way that, when God wished to become human for the sake of human beings, he should be born not from anyone other than a virgin; and that, when a virgin was to give birth, she should produce no son other than one who was God.

«When,» he says, «Mary, the mother of Jesus, had been betrothed to Joseph, before they came together, she was found to be with child by the Holy Spirit.»

Luke the Evangelist sufficiently explains in what order and in what city the conception took place. Since this is known very well to your holiness, we must say only a few things about what Matthew writes.

First of all, it should be noted that in the phrase «before they came together,» the verb “to come together” does not signify sexual intercourse itself, but the time of the wedding rites that ordinarily preceded it, when the woman who had previously been betrothed begins to be a wife. Thus “before they came together” means before they properly celebrated the solemnities of the wedding: «she was found to be with child by the Holy Spirit.»

Afterward they did come together in the order mentioned, when Joseph, at the angel’s command, took his wife; but they did not have intercourse, because it follows: «and he did not know her.»

She was found to be with child by no one other than Joseph, who, by marital privilege, knew almost everything about his future wife and therefore quickly detected her swelling womb with a curious gaze.

It continues:

«Joseph her husband, being righteous and unwilling to expose her, resolved to dismiss her secretly.»

When Joseph saw that his betrothed had conceived, though he knew very well that she had not been touched by any man, he was righteous and wished to act justly in all things. He therefore judged it best neither to disclose this to others nor to take her as his wife, but secretly to change his intention concerning the wedding and allow her to remain in the condition of a betrothed woman, as she was.

For he had read in Isaiah that a virgin from the house of David would conceive and bear God. He knew that Mary derived her lineage from that same house and therefore did not doubt that this prophecy might be fulfilled in her.

But if he had wished secretly to dismiss her and not take her as his wife, and she had given birth while remaining betrothed, surely there would have been few who would have considered her a virgin rather than supposing her to be a prostitute. Therefore Joseph’s decision was suddenly changed by a better plan: in order to preserve Mary’s reputation, he would accept her as his wife after celebrating the wedding feast, but would guard her chastely forever.

For the Lord preferred that some people should remain ignorant of the manner of his generation rather than that the chastity of his mother should be disgraced.

For it continues:

«While he was considering these things, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared to him in a dream, saying: Joseph, son of David, do not be afraid to take Mary your wife. For that which has been born in her is from the Holy Spirit. She will bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus. For he himself will save his people from their sins.»

These words make known both the manner of his conception and the dignity of his birth: he would be conceived from the Holy Spirit and would bear Christ. Although the angel does not call him Christ openly, nevertheless, by explaining the etymology of the name Jesus, showing him to be the author of salvation, and naming him the Savior of the peoples, he plainly indicates that he is the Christ.

Through these words Joseph was to learn what he had not known, so that he might completely withdraw his mind from touching the Mother of God. Yet he is commanded to take her, through a dispensation of just necessity, as his wife in name only: so that she would not be stoned by the Jews as though she were an adulteress, and so that, when fleeing into Egypt, she would have the comfort of a male companion who could provide familial care, protect feminine weakness, and serve as a witness to her perpetual virginity.

Catholic interpreters also offer other reasons why Joseph ought to take the Mother of God as his wife; whoever wishes may find them in their own works.

The Evangelist also adds to the virgin birth an example from prophetic speech, so that the miracle of such great majesty might appear all the more certain, since he would believe that it had not only happened but also recall that it had been foretold by a prophet. Indeed, it is customary for this Evangelist, Matthew, to confirm everything he narrates by prophetic testimonies.

He wrote his Gospel especially for those who believed from among the Jews but were nevertheless unable to detach themselves from the ceremonies of the Law, although they had been reborn in Christ. Therefore he took pains to raise them from the carnal understanding of the Law and the prophets to the spiritual understanding that concerns Christ, so that they might receive the mysteries of the Christian faith with all the greater confidence when they recognized that these were nothing other than what the prophets had foretold.

«Behold,» he says, «a virgin will have a child in her womb and will bear a son, and they will call his name Emmanuel,» which is interpreted, «God with us.»

The name of the Savior, whom the prophet calls “God with us,” signifies both natures in his one person. He who was born before the ages from the Father as God himself became, in the fullness of time, Emmanuel—“God with us”—in his mother’s womb, because he deigned to assume the weakness of our nature into the unity of his person, when the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.

In a wondrous manner he began to be what we are without ceasing to be what he was, assuming our nature in such a way that he did not lose what he was.

“Then Joseph, rising from sleep, did as the angel of the Lord had commanded him. And he took his wife, and he did not know her.” He took her as his wife in name, for the reasons “we have mentioned,” but did not know her in the marital act, because of the mysteries he had learned. If anyone wishes to oppose this interpretation of ours and insists that the blessed [Col. 0049D] Mother of God was never taken by Joseph as his wife after the celebration of their marriage, let him explain this passage of the holy Gospel better and likewise show that among the Jews it was permissible for a man to have carnal relations with his betrothed; and we shall gladly yield to his sound interpretation—provided only that we do not believe anything was done toward the Lord’s mother that could be disgraced by public opinion.

But when it is added, “until she bore her firstborn son,” no one should understand it as though he knew her after the son was born, as some perversely suppose. Your Fraternity should know that there were heretics who, because it says, “he did not know her until she bore her firstborn son,” believed [Col. 0050A] that Joseph knew Mary after the Lord’s birth, and that from this union arose those whom Scripture calls the Lord’s brothers. They also used the designation “firstborn” to support their error. May the Lord God avert this blasphemy from the faith of you all, and grant us, in Catholic devotion, to understand that the parents of our Savior were illustrious in an ever-undefiled virginity, and that those who are called the Lord’s brothers were not their children but their relatives, according to the usage of Scripture. For this reason the evangelist did not concern himself with whether Joseph knew her after the Son of God was born: he had thought that no one would doubt that spouses to whom, while remaining chaste in virginity, the birth of the Son of God was granted by singular grace could in no way thereafter violate the rights of chastity.

It should also be noted that first [Col. 0050B]borns are not, as the heretics suppose, only those who are followed by other brothers. Rather, according to the authority of Scripture, all who first open the womb are called firstborns, whether any brothers follow them or none. Nevertheless, the Lord may be understood to be called “firstborn” for a special reason, in accordance with what John says of him in the Apocalypse: “He is the faithful witness, the firstborn from the dead, and the prince of the kings of the earth” (Apoc. I). The apostle Paul likewise says: “For those whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, so that he might be the firstborn among many brothers” (Rom. II).

He is “the firstborn among many brothers”: “For as many as received him, he gave them power to become children of God.” He is rightly called their “Firstborn,” because he surpasses all adopted children in dignity, even those who, by being born, preceded the time of his In[Col. 0050C]carnation. Indeed, they can most truthfully testify with John: “He who came after us was made before us” (John I). That is, although he was born in the world after us, by the merit of his virtue and kingdom he is rightly called the Firstborn of us all.

He can also appropriately be called firstborn in his very divine birth, because before he brought forth any creature, the Father begot the Word, coeternal with himself. Hence the Word himself—the Son, that is, the power and wisdom of God—says: “I came forth from the mouth of the Most High, firstborn before every creature” (Eccli. XXIV). He was born God from God, and, having been created in his humanity, he surpassed every creature by right.

“And he called his name,” it says, “Jesus.” Jesus is called in Hebrew; in Latin [Col. 0050D] it means “saving” or “Savior.” The certainty of this name’s designation is clear from the prophets. Hence those words, sung with great desire for the vision of him: “My soul shall rejoice in the Lord and shall delight in his salvation” (Ps. XXXIV). And again: “My soul has fainted for your salvation” (Ps. CXVIII). Elsewhere: “But I will glory in the Lord; I will rejoice in the Lord my Jesus” (Hab. III). And above all: “O God, save me by your name” (Ps. LIII). It is as though he said: “Glorify in saving me the glory of your name, by which you are called Savior.”

Jesus, therefore, is the name of the Son who was born from the Virgin, as the angel explained, signifying that he himself would save his people from their sins. He who saves from sins—that is, certainly from the corruptions [Col. 0051A] of mind and body that arose because of sins—will save them.

Christ, however, is a title of priestly or royal dignity. For priests and kings under the Law were called *christs* from *chrisma*, that is, from the anointing with holy oil. They signified him who, appearing in the world as the true king and high priest, was anointed with the oil of gladness above his companions. From this anointing, that is, from the chrism, he himself was called Christ; and those who share in that same anointing, that is, in spiritual grace, are called Christians.

Through the fact that he is Savior, he would save us from sins; through the fact that he is high priest, he would reconcile us to God the Father; through the fact that he is king, he would graciously bestow upon us the eternal kingdom of the Father.

## “Now the generation of Christ was as follows”

It is asked why he did not say “of Jesus Christ,” but only “of Christ,” [Col. 0051B] reserving the name for what the angel would soon say. “Generation”: Christ himself generated in the flesh. It is as though he said: “The generation which is Christ was as follows.” This may be explained in two ways: either with reference to the place in the genealogy where it says, “Jacob begot Joseph, the husband of Mary, from whom Jesus was born, who is called Christ”; or with reference to what follows:

“All the generations from Abraham to David are fourteen generations; from David to the deportation to Babylon, fourteen generations; and from the deportation to Babylon to Christ, fourteen generations.”

## “Now the generation of Christ was as follows. When the mother of Jesus, Mary, had been betrothed to Joseph, etc.”

Thus the generation of Christ was as follows—that is, this genealogy pertains in this way to Christ.

“When she had been betrothed.” [Col. 0051C] Christ was born not from an unmarried virgin but from a betrothed woman for these reasons: so that the genealogy might be traced through a man rather than through a woman, according to the custom of Scripture; so that she would not be stoned by the Jews as an adulteress; so that, when she fled into Egypt, she would have the support of a husband; so that her childbirth might be concealed from the devil, who would think that he had been born not from a virgin but from a wife; so that the disgrace of a violated virgin might not be burned into public memory.

The Lord preferred that some should doubt his own origin rather than his mother’s chastity. This was also so that his mother’s dishonor would not become a veil of excuse for virgins; so that, when the Lord said, “I have not come to abolish the Law but to fulfill it,” no one could object that he had been born in violation of the Law; so that a husband might be supplied as a witness to her chastity, able to remove and avenge the reproach if he did not acknowledge the mystery; so that Mary would not seem to conceal her guilt [Col. 0051D] by a lie—for, since childbirth is the reward of marriage for women, a betrothed woman had no reason to lie; so that Herod and the Jews would not be given an excuse for persecuting him as one born of adultery; so that continence might be commended to married believers by mutual consent; and so that it might be shown how the human race could multiply without injury to virginity, provided it were not subject to transgression.

“Betrothed,” that is, not yet married.

“His mother.” It says “his mother,” not “Joseph’s wife.” At the very entrance of the passage the names of both are placed, corresponding to their deeds.

“Before they came together.” This indicates that the time of the wedding was near, not that it necessarily followed that they would come together afterward, as Helvidius says.

“She was found.” [Col. 0052A] She was found by no one other than Joseph, who, with the marital authority he possessed over his future wife, knew everything.

Here Matthew omitted many things that Luke narrated, saying: “In the sixth month, the angel Gabriel was sent by God to a city of Galilee named Nazareth, to a virgin betrothed to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David; and the virgin’s name was Mary. And the angel entered to her and said, ‘Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with you,’ etc.”

Matthew clearly carried the genealogy down to the point at which he said, “Joseph, the husband of Mary, from whom Christ was born.” Therefore he left the conception, which he had passed over, to be narrated by Luke.

“In the womb.” This should not be understood as though he received something into the womb from elsewhere, but as something possessed within, through the coming of the Holy Spirit, as in the saying: “A woman shall encompass a man.”

[Col. 0052B]

## “By the Holy Spirit”

It is asked: if Joseph found her carrying a child by the Holy Spirit, why did he wish to dismiss her? The reason is that he neither knew everything nor was wholly ignorant. He knew that she was carrying a child, not from carnal intercourse but through spiritual power. But he did not know by what Spirit she had conceived; this was revealed to him as though he were ignorant, when the words “by the Spirit” are followed by “holy,” and the rest.

It is also asked why Matthew anticipated what the angel was soon to say. This was because of spiritual fervor, so that the reader’s mind would not hesitate, even for the briefest lines, and so that “every word might stand by the mouth of two or three witnesses” (Deut. XV; II Cor. XIII).

## “Joseph, her husband”

In Scripture, betrothed women are called wives, and betrothed men husbands or males.

“When he was just.” Since those who are conscious of crimes are liable [Col. 0052C] to sin, why is Joseph called just while concealing the crime? The purpose is to commend the reliability of his testimony. In many copies the phrase “when he was a just man” is added, showing that Joseph was just according to human justice, since in comparison with God’s justice human justice is reckoned as nothing.

Thus what follows is rightly added: “And he did not wish to.” He not only conceals the matter but does not dare to touch the temple of the Lord’s body; rightly, the just man does not corrupt the temple of justice.

“To expose her.” It is as though he said: “He did not wish to take as his wife the woman whom he suspected to be an adulteress.” Or otherwise: he did not wish to expose her to punishment, since he knew that she had not conceived from a man. The word “exposure” is more often found in an evil than in a good sense. The Greek expression likewise signifies this without impropriety: παραδειγματίσαι, that is, “to make [Col. 0052D] public,” “to disclose,” and make the conception known to everyone.

“Privately.” This was so that, whether he dismissed his wife and thereby brought upon her the guilt of another’s intercourse, or released her and thereby freed himself as though innocent of adultery, he would not incur blame.

Behold, the heavenly Adam sets new things against the old. On the first occasion, woman was made from man alone, without a mother; on the second, man was born from woman alone, without a carnal father. It was fitting that the new redemption should come from women, from whom the ancient transgression had proceeded. The earthly Adam was formed from incorrupt earth; the second Adam was formed from the incorrupt flesh of the Virgin Mary (I Cor. XV).

## “While he was considering these things, behold, an angel of the Lord”

[Col. 0053A]

To a good and just man, considering good and just things, a good and just messenger appears. Therefore “of the Lord” is added, to distinguish him from the apostate angels. Many think this angel was Gabriel, in accordance with Luke’s account. Not because he alone is the messenger of all births, but because his name is interpreted as “strength of God,” and victory in warfare has been entrusted to him; therefore he is rightly sent as the messenger of those who are to come, at the births of John and Christ.

Appropriate consolation is likewise brought to one who is thinking about God, just as Christ was shown to the two men walking on the road.

“He appeared in a dream.” The language of appearing signifies an unusual event. Divine speech is distinguished in two ways: either through angels or through God himself. When it occurs through God himself, he teaches the heart inwardly by inspiration alone, without words or syllables. He opens the hearing but is not known to produce a sound, as the Spirit said to Philip: “Join yourself to this chariot [Col. 0053B]” (Acts VIII).

When it occurs through an angel, it takes several forms. Sometimes it is through words without any image, as when Christ said, “Father, glorify your Son” (John XVII), and the answer immediately came: “I have glorified him, and I will glorify him again,” and so forth.

Sometimes it is through events without words, as when Ezekiel saw the appearance of amber in the midst of fire (Ezek. I), signifying through this the Incarnation of Christ.

Sometimes it is through words and events, as when Adam saw the Lord walking in Paradise after midday (Gen. III), signifying that the light of truth would withdraw from him.

Sometimes it is through images shown to the eyes of the heart, as when Jacob saw a ladder resting on the heavens (Gen. XXVIII), and Peter, in ecstasy, saw a vessel full of living creatures (Acts X).

Sometimes it is through images assumed from the air before the bodily eyes, as when Abraham not [Col. 0053C] only saw three men but received them into his house and also fed them (Gen. XVIII).

Sometimes it is through heavenly substances, as when, after the Lord’s baptism, a voice sounded, saying: “This is my Son” (Matt. III).

Sometimes it is through earthly and heavenly things together, as when, before Moses, he joined fire and a bush on the mountain (Exod. III). This signified that he would be a teacher of the people, who would receive the flame of the Law yet would not abandon the thorn of sin; or that from that people would come one who would place the fire of divinity upon the thorns of our humanity.

Sometimes he inspires secrets through a hidden presence into human hearts; hence Zechariah says: “And the angel who spoke in me said to me” (Zech. II).

When it is said that he appeared to blessed Joseph, he appeared through an image shown to the eyes of the heart.

“Joseph, son of David.” He speaks with the affection of one who reassures, signifying that Joseph was known [Col. 0053D] and familiar, while his name and lineage are identified. From this it appears that Joseph and Mary belonged to the same tribe, in accordance with the saying: “No one shall marry outside his tribe” (Num. XXXVI).

Here it should be noted that he called him “son of David” not so much according to the flesh as according to the spirit, declaring that, as a just man propagated from the lineage of a just man, he had deserved this designation.

“Do not fear.” It is evident that fear was the reason he had wished to dismiss her: he was afraid to profess a spiritual marriage. Observe that the fear by which he had been prevented from taking her as his wife is not suppressed but addressed by the command not to fear taking her into his presence. Fear is expelled first, so that he might more willingly hear what would afterward be said.

“Your wife.” Scripture commonly calls betrothed women wives or spouses. Or [Col. 0054A] Mary is called his wife because she was to raise the Savior under the same yoke.

“That which has been born,” he says, not “that which has been sown from outside,” “is of the Holy Spirit.” Here what Joseph knew and what he did not know is made clear. Yet the Holy Spirit should not for this reason be regarded as Christ’s father, as though God the Father begot the Word while the Spirit begot the man. Rather, Christ’s birth was accomplished through the Spirit’s ministry.

## “She will bear a son”

She will bear him without the pain of childbirth, just as he was conceived without the will of sin. Here four uncertainties concerning every person being born are indicated, for she will bear a son who will be called Jesus, and he will save his people.

“And you shall call.” O Joseph, do not contradict the voices of the prophets. It should be noted that according to Matthew the child’s name [Col. 0054B] was foretold to Joseph, while according to Luke it was foretold to Mary, because Jesus came for the salvation of both sexes.

The etymology of the name Jesus follows when it says: “For he himself will save his people.” Truly they are his own, those who can be saved.

“From their sins.” This is directed against the Jews, who think that the people were to be liberated through Christ from captivities, not from sins.

“Their.” Note that salvation belongs to him, whereas sins belong to us.

## HOMILY IX: ON THE HOLY DAY OF THE NATIVITY OF THE LORD

*(John I.)* “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and God was the Word. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made,” and so forth.

As we celebrate each year the day of the Lord’s birth, on which he was born in time [Col. 0054C], let us turn the eyes of our mind toward contemplating the nature of divinity. Since the sayings of three evangelists—Matthew, Mark, and Luke—describe the manner of his human birth, we ought to consider the sayings of the blessed evangelist John concerning the consubstantial essence of God the Father.

As we are about to speak of his Gospel, it seems appropriate to recall briefly but reasonably why this disciple, so beloved by the Lord, is placed last in the order of the prophets. Because he wrote his Gospel last, he is rightly placed last. By then three Gospels had already been written and disseminated throughout the whole world: through Matthew in Judea, and through Mark and Luke among the nations.

After the Lord’s Ascension, John himself preached his Gospel in the regions of Asia for nearly sixty [Col. 0054D] years, without any written aid. But after Domitian, the most impious emperor and most cruel tyrant, had exiled him to the island of Patmos because of his unconquerable steadfastness in preaching the Gospel, heretics broke out against the Church: Marcion, Cerinthus, Ebion, and other sons of the devil, whom he calls Antichrists in his epistle. They attempted to divide the Church by various doctrines, saying that Christ had not existed before Mary.

Later, when, by the permission of the most devout emperor Nerva, John had returned from exile and was staying at Ephesus, he is said to have been asked by all the bishops and presbyters to speak to them about the divinity of the Lord and to leave it written as a memorial for future generations. As we have said, they already had a full account of the Lord’s temporal [Col. 0055A] birth in the books of the three evangelists; thus, after John’s departure from the world, the faithful would have something with which to strengthen themselves and destroy the false doctrines of the heretics.

At first he refused to do this. But when they persisted in prayer, he consented to do it only on the condition that they all pray together to the Lord after a three-day fast. When everyone had carried this out most willingly, on the third day, after the fast had been completed, John is said to have been filled with such great grace—corresponding to the meaning of his name—that he was caught up beyond all other men to contemplate the nature of divinity. Seeing the King in his beauty, he drew from the purest fountain of divinity what he might offer to us who thirst[Col. 0055B]ed. Thus, throughout the text of his Gospel, inserting only a few matters concerning the Savior’s human actions, he left a sufficient written account of his divinity.

Therefore he is rightly said to have reclined at supper upon the Lord’s breast. Since all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden in the breast of Jesus, John tasted from it how sweet the Lord is and imparted to us, who were hungry, the food of eternal life.

Thus he is rightly described among the four living creatures as possessing the form of an eagle. Just as the eagle flies higher than the other birds and, more than all living creatures, gazes upon the sun’s radiance with unblinking eyes, so John perceived more profoundly than all other human beings what pertains to divinity, and contemplated the nature of the eternal Sun more exaltedly than all mortals, saying:

“In the beginning was the [Col. 0055C] Word, and the Word was with God, and God was the Word.”

The other evangelists describe Christ as born in time; John recalls that he existed before all times, saying: “In the beginning was the Word.”

The others recall that he suddenly appeared as a man among human beings; John shows that he always remained with God the Father, saying: “And the Word was with God.”

The others describe him as a true man; John confirms that he is true God, saying: “And God was the Word.”

The others assert that he was born bodily from the Virgin Mary and lived among human beings in time; John demonstrates that he was always with God the Father, saying: “He was in the beginning with God.”

The others recount the signs and mighty works he performed among human beings; John reveals that, because he was God, he created every creature through the Son, when he says:

“All things were made through [Col. 0055D] him, and without him nothing was made.”

In a wondrous order, the blessed evangelist John, at the beginning of his Gospel, both strengthens the faith of believers and condemns the false doctrine of heretics.

There were heretics who said: “If Christ was born, then there was a time when he did not exist.” The evangelist destroys their error at the very beginning of his Gospel when he says: “In the beginning was the Word.” He did not say, “In the beginning the Word began to exist,” but “In the beginning was the Word,” showing that no time preceded his nature, but that he himself always existed before all times, as he says in the Gospel: “I am the beginning, who also speak to you” (John VIII). [Col. 0056A]

And in Proverbs: “The Lord possessed me at the beginning of his ways, before he made anything from the beginning. From eternity I was established, and from ancient times, before the earth was made” (Prov. VIII). And again: “When he prepared the heavens, I was there, arranging all things with him” (ibid.).

Hence the Psalmist says: “Before the mountains were made, or the earth and the world were formed, from age to age you are God” (Ps. LXXXIX).

Again, there were other enemies of the truth who, wishing to deny the three persons of the Holy Trinity, said: “The Father is the Son when he wishes; when he wishes, he is the Holy Spirit. The Son is the Father when he wishes; when he wishes, he is the Holy Spirit. The Holy Spirit is the Father or the Son when he wishes; nevertheless he is one and the same.”

The truthful evangelist [Col. 0056B] disperses their utterly false error when he adds: “And the Word was with God.” If one was with another, it is evident that the person of the Father is one, that of the Son another, and that of the Holy Spirit another. The Father is not, as they falsely claim, at one time changed into the Son, nor the Son into the Father, nor the Holy Spirit into the Father or the Son. Rather, the Father is always Father, the Son always Son, and the Holy Spirit always Holy Spirit.

For the divine nature or substance cannot be changed, as the apostle James testifies: “With whom there is no change or shadow of alteration” (James I).

Again, there were other sons of the devil who believed Christ to be merely human and denied that he was true God. The evangelist cuts away their deception with a spiritual sword when he adds: “And [Col. 0056C] God was the Word.”
