The Son is appropriately called the Word, coeternal with the Father, because just as we reveal the inner intention of our heart through a word, so God the Father brought into being through the Son all things that are seen. The Psalmist testifies to this when he says: “By the word of God the heavens were established, and by the breath of his mouth all their power” (Ps. XXXI).

Or the Son is called the Father’s Word because, as the Apostle says, he is “the power and wisdom of the Father” (I Cor. I). Of him the Psalmist says elsewhere: “My heart has uttered a good word” (Ps. XLIV).

There were yet others who did believe Christ to be God, but thought that he had his beginning from Mary. One of them, it is said, spoke in madness: “I do not envy Christ because he was made God; for if I wish, I can become like him.”

The holy evangelist crushes their most wicked error when he further adds: [Col. 0056D] “He was in the beginning with God.” He shows that Christ did not receive an increase from time but always existed with the Father in a coeternal substance.

There were also other enemies of the truth who asserted that some creatures were made by God and others by a certain prince of darkness. The evangelical passage destroys them when it adds: “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made.”

Those things that subsist were made through him, as it is written: “He who remains forever created all things together.” They were not partly good and partly evil, as those heretics thought, but all were “very good,” as it is written: “He saw all that he had made, and they were [Col. 0057A] very good” (Gen. I).

That some creature appears to be evil happened because of human sin, as a certain wise man says: “The teeth of beasts, scorpions, and serpents were all created for punishment.” For sin, since it does not possess a nature of subsistence, was not created by God but invented by the devil, and therefore it is nothing. Whatever does not subsist is nothing, as the Apostle says concerning the worship of idols: “We know that an idol is nothing” (I Cor. VIII).

There were also other heretics who, investigating the substance of the divine nature more subtly than they ought, said that the only-begotten Son of God, in the form of divinity, was made by God rather than begotten by the Father. Arius was one of these. By this they asserted that he was less than the Father, proclaiming that he was not begotten from God but made by God.

The evangelist, armed with faith, tramples upon their [Col. 0057B] error or madness when he says: “All things were made through him.” If all things were made through him, he himself was not made, for he made all things. Therefore he is not a creature but the Creator, not a product but the Maker, and he is to be believed equal to the Father, as he himself says in the Gospel: “I and the Father are one” (John X).

Since the rational wisdom of God created another rational creature, so that you would not suppose that his will was changeable—as though he suddenly wished to make another creature that he had not made in his eternal disposition—the evangelist adds something necessary, saying:

## “What was made. In him was life”

This verse should be punctuated so that we first say, “What was made,” and then continue, “in [Col. 0057C] him was life.” The meaning is this: What was made by him appeared in time, whether living or lacking life; but in him was life. That is, in his eternal wisdom even those things that do not live were alive before they were created, namely before the beginning of the world, because it had been determined that they would later come into being. In this sense they were as though already made, since every creature was imagined in the Son of God.

To make this clearer, let us give an example from visible things. A carpenter goes into the forest, looks at a tree, and considers making from it a chest or some other vessel. Although the tree remains not yet cut, its future length and breadth are already considered in his wisdom. Its construction is shown to live in his art, even though the tree itself does not yet live [Col. 0057D] in that form; and if the vessel were later destroyed by age or fire, he would still know how to make another vessel of the same size and quality.

In the same way, before almighty God created the world, before he formed the creatures of the world into their proper kinds, not only those things that live but also those that lack life were alive in his wisdom.

But lest you should think that every creature in this world possesses life and is illuminated, it is rightly added:

“And life was the light of human beings.”

This means plainly that the very life and wisdom through which all things were created, and in which they are said to live according to a certain reason, as we have said, is the light of human beings—that is, of rational creatures, not of irrational ones.

For it is not beasts and cattle but human [Col. 0058A] beings who are illuminated, because they are rational. Although beasts live, they are not illuminated so as to possess wisdom, understanding, and the spirit of discernment.

To some creatures God grants being, life, and sensation, but not discernment, as to animals; to others being and life, but not sensation, as to trees; to others being, but neither life nor sensation, as to stones. To human beings he grants being, life, sensation, and discernment. Hence those who were created in the image of God are rightly illuminated.

Yet any human being who is merely animal does not perceive the things that belong to the Spirit of God (I Cor. II). But because eternal divine wisdom has left those who live carnally no excuse based on ignorance, it rightly continues:

## “And the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it”

[Col. 0058B]

The darkness consists of wicked people: murderers, adulterers, robbers, the unclean, and perpetrators of similar deeds. Concerning them John says: “Everyone who hates his brother is in darkness, and walks in darkness, and does not know where he is going, because the darkness has blinded his eyes” (I John II).

Hence the Apostle says to believers: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Eph. V).

The light shines in the darkness because those who live carnally cannot claim ignorance as an excuse when they are wise enough to do evil but do not know how to do good. Because they darken the rational sense by which, while living carnally, they could know both the Lord and his will, the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness does not comprehend it.

It sometimes happens [Col. 0058C] that those who live carnally shine with greater sharpness of understanding than those who live simply, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “The children of this age are more prudent in their generation than the children of light” (Luke XVI).

Therefore the light shines in the darkness because, although wicked people do not see the light—that is, Christ—their evil deeds are seen by the light, namely by Christ, before whose eyes everything is naked and open. The Psalmist testifies to this when he says: “The face of the Lord is against those who do evil” (Ps. LIII).

For example, if a blind man is placed in the sun, he does not see the sunlight, but is confused by it all around him. In the same way, the people just mentioned do not see God, but are seen by God. Thus, because God sees them, the light shines in the darkness—that is, in those very [Col. 0058D] people.

Or certainly, the light shines in the darkness because the wisdom through which we recognize that we are human beings and understand that we do something—when compared with irrational beasts, to which we have become similar—does not comprehend the true light, that is, God, although we ourselves are darkness.

Hence the evangelist rightly says: “And the darkness did not comprehend it.” “For,” as the Apostle says, “there is no sharing of light with darkness, no agreement of Christ with Belial, and no portion of the believer with the unbeliever” (I Cor. VI).

But because the human mind, placed in darkness, could not endure the ineffable light of God when it came suddenly, the light itself that was to come sent a man of great merit before it, like a lamp before the day [Col. 0059A] and the morning star before the sun. Through his testimony and preaching, the blindness of the human mind might be prepared to see the true light, and God and man might be recognized.

If the Lord’s light had appeared to us suddenly, we would have been blinded by it rather than illuminated. The Lord therefore wished gradually to announce his coming to us through patriarchs and prophets. For example, when we stand in a valley, we cannot see the rising sun; yet when we climb to the summit, we see its rising shine forth and know that it will soon radiate fully. In the same way, the Lord wished through his saints to draw our minds toward contemplation of his light.

John was one of these mountains, and concerning him it continues:

## “There was a man sent from God”

In the first word [Col. 0059B] his virtue of obedience is commended, when it says: “There was a man sent from God.” He did not come from himself, that is, through his own presumption, but was sent by God.

To come from oneself is one thing; to be sent by God is another. The one comes from himself who presumptuously seeks his own glory in what he teaches. Hence it is said of false prophets: “They themselves were coming, and I did not send them; they were speaking, although I had not commanded them” (Jer. XXV).

John was not one of these, but belonged rather to those to whom the Savior says in the Gospel: “I chose you from the world, that you should go and bear fruit, and that your fruit should remain” (John XV).

The one who seeks the praise of God and the gain of souls in what he teaches is sent by God. Such was Moses, to whom it was said: “Come, and I will send you to Egypt.” Such was the prophet [Col. 0059C] Isaiah, who, when the Lord said, “Whom shall I send, and who will go for us to this people?” replied: “Behold, here am I; send me” (Isa. VI).

Such was John the Baptist, of whom it is said: “There was a man sent from God.”

After calling him “that man,” the text continues: “Whose name was John.”

For what purpose he was sent by God is revealed when it adds:

## “He came as a witness, to bear witness to the light”

Why did he bear witness to the light? This is explained when it continues: “So that all might believe through him.”

It did not say, “so that all might believe in him,” because “cursed is the man who trusts in man” (Jer. XVII), but “so that all might believe through him”—that is, through his testimony, all might believe in Christ.

To believe someone, to believe through someone, and [Col. 0059D] to believe in someone are different things. “To believe someone” and “to believe through someone” can be applied to a faithful human being. But “to believe in someone” belongs only to God.

For example: “I believe Paul, and through Paul I believe,” that is, through his preaching; yet I do not believe in Paul, but in the God whom he preaches.

## “He was not the light, but he came to bear witness to the light”

It is asked why the evangelist says of John, beloved of the Lord and greater than those born of women, “He was not the light,” when the Lord says to his disciples: “You are the light of the world” (Matt. V).

The answer is readily apparent: one light illuminates, while another is illuminated. The light that illuminates neither receives a beginning nor is confined by an end; it neither increases nor suffers diminution, but remains always [Col. 0060A] equal. Compared with this light—that is, Christ—all human beings, both lesser and more perfect, are reckoned darkness. Even our righteousness, if compared with his righteousness, will be considered unrighteousness.

Human beings are illuminated so that they may be light by him who says in the Gospel: “I am the light of the world. Whoever follows me will not walk in darkness but will have the light of life” (John V).

Such was John, of whom the Lord says elsewhere: “He was a burning and shining lamp.” Burning with devotion and love, shining in speech.

Nevertheless, John is said not to be the light in comparison with the true light, which illuminates everyone and is illuminated by no one. The difference between the light that illuminates and the light that is illuminated is as great as the difference between a lamp, the morning star, and the sun.

That, then, is the principal light concerning which it [Col. 0060B] continues:

## “He was the true light that enlightens every person coming into this world”

By saying “every person coming into this world,” it shows that, whether human beings are illuminated by spiritual grace or by natural intelligence, they can be illuminated only by the one from whom all wisdom proceeds, with whom it always was and is before all ages.

“In the world he was, and the world was made through him, and the world did not know him.”

Here the evangelist clearly indicates three distinctions in the word “world.” For sometimes “world” signifies the saints, sometimes the structure of the earthly globe, and sometimes those who love the world. Thus, what he says, “In the world he was,” refers to the saints, concerning whom the Lord says elsewhere: “The Son of Man did not come to destroy the world, but that the world might be saved through him” (John XII). And the apostle Paul says: “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself” (I Cor. V).

But what he adds, “And the world was made through him,” refers to the structure of the earthly globe, in accordance with what the Lord says to his disciples in the Gospel: “Go into all the world.” But what he adds, “and the world did not know him,” refers to those who love the world. Concerning them the Lord says elsewhere: “Righteous Father, the world has not known you.”

In saying, “In the world he was,” he shows that, by his divinity, he is present everywhere, because he is confined or excluded by no place; rather, he himself is above and he himself below, he himself within and he himself outside. It is read, “In the world he was,” that is, in the earthly globe. Some, however, interpret “in the world” as referring to holy human beings.

“The world was made through him,” because every creature was made through him and by him from nothing. “And the world did not know him,” that is, those who love the world. For those who love the world are rightly called “the world,” because in mind and desire they inhabit the world.

The Jews visibly saw him performing signs, but they did not recognize him. For heaven recognized him when, at his birth, it sent a new star; the sea recognized him when it offered itself to be trodden beneath his feet; the earth recognized him when it trembled at his death; the sun recognized him because it hid its rays at his death. But, as we have said, those who loved the world—that is, the Jews—did not recognize him. Concerning them it is further added:

“He came to his own, and his own did not receive him.”

He came to his own because he not only assumed flesh from the stock of the Jews, but also taught and preached among them and displayed ineffable signs and wonders. “But his own did not receive him,” that is, the Jews, whom in former times he had specially adopted as his own, whom he had made dwell in the promised land after expelling their enemies, to whom he had given knowledge of the Law, to whose instruction he had sent prophets, and from whom he had chosen to be born.

Or certainly, “he came to his own” because he appeared in the world through his humanity, though he had made the world through his divinity. To come and depart belong to humanity; to remain and to exist belong to divinity.

“But his own did not receive him,” that is, human beings whom he had made in his own image and likeness, for the most part refused to believe in him. But did everyone remain alienated from knowledge of him? No. For it follows:

“But to all who received him.”

They received him who believed him to be the Son of God sent by the Father. But what benefited them from receiving him? “He gave them,” he says, “the power to become children of God, to those who believe in his name.”

Here God’s abundant mercy is shown: those who were not worthy to be servants are even called children—not by nature, but by the grace of adoption—so that here, through faith, we might become heirs of God and, through grace, co-heirs with Christ, in accordance with what the same John wrote at the end of his Gospel, saying: “These things have been written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Son of God, and that, believing, you may have life in his name” (John XX).

What, then, is kinder or more merciful than that the only Son of God, unwilling to remain alone, should take our flesh, make us children of God, and adopt us as brothers, so that what he possessed by nature we might possess by grace? Concerning them he himself says in the Gospel: “Whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven is my brother, sister, and mother” (Matt. VII). And after the resurrection he deigned to call the disciples brothers, saying: “Go, announce to my brothers.”

No one comes to this adoption unless he believes by faith in his name, because, as it is written: “The righteous person lives by faith, without which it is impossible to please God” (Rom. I; Hebr. XI). And lest you should think that this birth is carnal and not spiritual, it is rightly added:

“Who were born not from bloods, nor from the will of the flesh, nor from the will of man.”

In this passage, when he wrote “from bloods,” he acted contrary to the rule of grammatical art, because among grammarians *sanguis* (“blood”) is always expressed in the singular and never in the plural according to the rule. But the evangelist was not concerned to observe the rule of grammatical art, so that he might express the meaning more perfectly. For if he had said “from blood,” he would seem to signify only the seed of the man and would not fully express what he intended. But when he says “from bloods,” he indicates the union of man and woman alike.

Therefore, lest anyone ask why he had said “from bloods,” he explains by adding: “Nor from the will of the flesh, nor from the will of man.” He used “flesh” for “wife,” in accordance with what is written: “This now is bone from my bones, and flesh from my flesh.” And: “The two shall be one flesh” (Gen. II). And the Apostle says: “No one has ever hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it” (Eph. V).

Or “from bloods,” that is, from vices and sins, as it is said through the Psalmist: “Deliver me from bloods, O God, God of my salvation” (Ps. L).

“But they were born from God.”

How and in what manner human beings are born from God, so that they may be children of God by adoption, the Lord makes clear elsewhere, saying: “Unless someone is born again from water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (John III). And again: “What is born from flesh is flesh, and what is born from spirit is spirit” (ibid.). For one nature is carnal and the other spiritual; one is visible and the other invisible.

“And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.”

This verse depends upon what precedes, as though the evangelist were saying: In order that human beings might become children of God by adoption, that Word which was in the beginning, God with God—that Word, I say—became flesh, that is, God became human. Yet he was not changed into flesh: assuming what he was not, he did not cease to be what he was. Remaining God, he became human.

He who made all things in the form of God—that is, while he was God—was made in the form of a servant. He who had made all things became human, so that the one who had perished might be found.

When he says, “The Word became flesh,” however, by the name “flesh” he signifies a complete human being, consisting of a rational soul and flesh. For Scripture’s usage is sometimes to signify the whole human being by the soul alone, and sometimes by the flesh alone.

The whole human being is signified by the name “soul,” as it is written: “Jacob went down into Egypt with seventy souls” (Gen. XLVI). Again, the whole human being is signified by the name “flesh,” as it is written in the Prophet: “All flesh shall see the salvation of God” (Luke III). For souls did not descend into Egypt without bodies, nor could flesh without a soul see the salvation of God. Rather, as we have said, in one place the whole human being is signified by the soul alone, and elsewhere by the flesh alone.

Thus, in this passage also, when he says, “The Word became flesh,” he says nothing other than that God became a human being consisting, as we have said, of a rational soul and flesh. For there were certain heretics who said that the Lord assumed flesh without a soul. If he did what is lesser, then surely he also assumed what is greater. He who assumed flesh for the liberation of souls undoubtedly assumed a human soul.

Concerning this he himself says: “I have power to lay down my soul and to take it up again” (John XVI). And again: “My soul is sorrowful even unto death” (Matt. XXVI).

What is added—“And he dwelt among us”—refers especially to those to whom he appeared visibly and with whom he lived bodily.

Or otherwise, “he dwelt among us” so that we might dwell in him. He dwells in us by protecting us, and we dwell in him so that we may be protected by him.

But in order that he might dwell among us, “though he was in the form of God, he did not consider equality with God something to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of human beings and found in appearance as a human being” (Phil. II).

“And we saw his glory, glory as of the Only-Begotten from the Father.”

They saw his glory in his humanity, though they could not see it in his divinity; what they could not see before the incarnation, they saw after the Word became flesh. Thus they especially saw the glory of God concealed in a human being when they were privileged to behold him shining through miracles.

Those also saw his glory more clearly who contemplated him transfigured on the mountain before his Passion, hearing above the voice of the Father thunder: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. III). One of these was this John, to whom such things were revealed and through whom such signs were displayed—signs that no one could perform unless he were the Father’s Only-Begotten.

After the resurrection also, the Holy Spirit deigned to overshadow and fill these same disciples, so that through these things they might recognize both the only-begotten Son of God and the firstborn from his mother.

There is, however, a distinction between “only-begotten” and “firstborn”: not all firstborn are only-begotten, but all only-begotten children are called firstborn. We call someone “firstborn” not only because others follow him, but also because no one precedes him.

Because the evangelist Matthew says, “Until she had given birth to her firstborn son” (Matt. II), the heretics who desired to defame the virginity of blessed Mary sought an opportunity. For they said that she had other sons from Joseph after the Lord, and they wanted these to be the ones who are called the Lord’s brothers in the Gospel. They did not consider that in Scripture brothers are called so in various ways.

Sometimes they are called brothers by nature, as Cain and Abel, Esau and Jacob, Peter and Andrew. Sometimes by kinship, as Abraham and Lot, in accordance with what Abraham himself says: “Please let there be no quarrel between me and you, nor between my shepherds and your shepherds, for we are brothers” (Gen. XIII). Likewise Jacob and Laban, when Laban himself says: “Because you are my brother, will you serve me for nothing?”

Sometimes they are called brothers by nation, as all the Jews were called brothers. Moses, the bearer of the Law, says: “If you appoint a king over yourself, you may not set over you a man of another nation, but one who is your brother,” that is, from your own nation.

Sometimes they are called brothers by affection, as all Christians are called brothers, when the Lord says to the disciples: “For you are all brothers” (Matt. XXII).

In the same way, the Lord’s brothers were called so by kinship, because they were from his lineage.

Therefore the Lord is called not only the Only-Begotten but also the Firstborn—not only because no others were born from Mary after him, but because no one preceded him.

What is added—“full of grace and truth”—means that the singular grace of God was given by the Father to the Son in the humanity he assumed, so that from the moment he began to be human he was perfect God and perfect human being.

He did not receive the same grace in measure, as ordinary human beings do; rather, having become human, he was full of grace, as the Apostle says: “In him the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily” (Col. II). And John the Baptist says: “From his fullness we have all received, grace upon grace.”

Concerning this fullness of grace the Psalmist says: “God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Ps. XLIV). He was also full of truth, as he himself says in the Gospel: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John XIV).

## HOMILY X: ON SAINT STEPHEN, THE PROTOMARTYR

*(Matt. XXIII.)* “At that time Jesus said to the crowds of the Jews: ‘Behold, I send to you prophets and wise men and scribes; and some of them you will kill and crucify, and some of them you will scourge in your synagogues,’” and so forth.

The preceding text of the Gospel recounts how the Lord, in conflict with the Jews, convicted them of being murderers and sons of murderers. While they built the tombs of the prophets and adorned the monuments of the righteous, they said: “If we had been in the days of our fathers, we would not have been their partners in the blood of the prophets.”

In this they showed themselves to be the sons of those who had killed the prophets, because, filled with envy, they persecuted Christ and his disciples. Therefore the Lord adds, saying: “Thus you testify against yourselves that you are sons of those who killed the prophets. And you—fill up the measure of your fathers.” It is as though he were saying: “What was lacking to them, you desire to complete. They killed the members; you persecute the head. They killed the prophets; you desire to kill the Lord of the prophets himself, who was foretold by them. They did not kill me and my disciples because they did not see us; you, seeing us, desire to fulfill their longing.”

What follows is appropriate to them: “Serpents, offspring of vipers, how will you escape the judgment of Gehenna?” They are rightly called “vipers,” because just as vipers are born from vipers and serpents from serpents, so they, drawing a poisonous disposition from poisonous parents, attempted to persecute Christ and his disciples.

It also corresponds to them that the nature of vipers is said to be such that the father dies at conception and the mother at childbirth. Although the kinds of vipers and serpents are diverse, it is nevertheless reported that there are only two vipers in the regions of Arabia, where no human habitation exists. For not only is a person killed by their breath if he approaches, but even a bird is killed if it flies overhead.

Their conception occurs slowly, but whenever it takes place, it happens in such a way that, as we have said, the father dies at conception and the mother at childbirth. At the time of conception the male puts his head into the female’s mouth; but she, tightening her jaws out of excessive love, cuts off his head. When the time of childbirth arrives, the mother’s belly is torn open, and the offspring emerge. Thus the father dies at conception and the mother at childbirth.

Hence the viper is so called because it gives birth by force or causes death by force.

The Jews were like this by analogy, because they delivered Christ—who had come to beget them spiritually—to the gibbet of the cross with blood-stained hands, saying: “Crucify him, crucify him. If you release this man, you are not Caesar’s friend” (Matt. XXVII).

They also persecuted the Church, which was destined to be their spiritual mother: first in the apostles, through whom the holy Church was governed, and then in their successors, concerning whom it is now said: “Behold, I send to you prophets and wise men and scribes.”

At the beginning of this reading, however, the doctrine of the heretics is overthrown—those who said that the God of the Old Testament was one God and the God of the New Testament another—when he says: “Behold, I send to you prophets and wise men and scribes.” It is as though he were saying: “I who once sent prophets, wise men, and scribes to your fathers am the very same one, and not another, who now send prophets, wise men, and scribes.”

There were prophets in the Old Testament: Isaiah, Jeremiah, and many others. There were wise men, such as Solomon and Samuel, and many more. There were also scribes, such as Moses, who wrote the Law, and Ezra, who recovered the Law after the Babylonian captivity, when the libraries had been burned. Concerning him it is written: “Ezra went up from Babylon, and he was a ready scribe in the Law of Moses” (I Esdr. VII).

In the New Testament we read that Agabus and the four daughters of Philip prophesied (Acts II and XXI). Everyone who warns people to avoid future evils and love good things is a prophet.

There were also wise men, such as the apostles and the evangelists, who left us written accounts of the Lord’s words and deeds. Concerning them the Lord says in the Gospel: “Every scribe instructed in the kingdom of heaven is like a householder who brings forth from his treasure new things and old” (Matt. XIII).

But their fathers killed Isaiah, Jeremiah, and many others. These people, however, threw James the Just from the pinnacle of the Temple; they stoned Stephen, whose solemnity we celebrate today; they crucified Peter and Andrew; and they beheaded Paul.

That they scourged and persecuted them in their synagogues and drove them from city to city, the book of the Acts of the Apostles recounts fully when it says: “The disciples went away from the presence of the council rejoicing, because they had been considered worthy to suffer dishonor for the name of Jesus” (Acts V).

“So that all the righteous blood may come upon you.”

It is asked how all righteous blood can be said to come upon those to whom the Lord was speaking, since they themselves did not shed all righteous blood. The answer is that they joined themselves by imitation to the generation of the wicked; therefore, in the repayment of vengeance, they are said to be participants with them.

“From the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah, son of Barachiah, whom you killed between the Temple and the altar.”

There is no uncertainty about who Abel was or that he was killed by his brother out of envy. That he was righteous is read not only in Genesis, where his offerings are said to have been acceptable to God and where his blood is said to have cried out to the Lord (Gen. IV), but also here, where testimony is now given to him: “From the blood of righteous Abel.”

But it is asked who this Zechariah was, since we read of many Zechariahs. And so, lest anyone be given an opportunity to err, the phrase “whom you killed between the Temple and the altar” is added. Different people have held different opinions about him.

Some said that this was Zechariah, who is listed as the eleventh among the twelve Minor Prophets, the name of his father agreeing with the passage, since he was the son of Barachiah. But the place of his death does not agree, because it is not found that he was killed between the Temple and the altar—especially since in his time the Temple was being rebuilt by those who had returned from captivity, and since that same Zechariah, because he prophesied prosperity for the people, was held in great honor by them.

Others said that this was Zechariah, the father of John the Baptist, and that he was killed by the people because he preached the coming of the Lord. But this opinion derives more from the fantasies and ravings of apocryphal writings than from the truth.

When these possibilities are excluded, the mind returns to the Books of Kings, where we read that, after King Uzziah had died and the most wicked queen Athaliah had taken his place and was killing all the royal offspring, Jehoiada the high priest took one of the king’s sons, the younger one, named Joash, and hid him in the Temple of the Lord for six years.

In the seventh year he anointed him king and entered into a covenant with him and with all the people, that he should walk in the Law of God. And he did so throughout all the days of Jehoiada’s life.

After Jehoiada died, his son Zechariah succeeded him in the priestly dignity and office. He was a good and righteous man. When Joash began to turn away from the Law of the Lord, Zechariah frequently rebuked him. Because of this he incurred the king’s hatred, to such an extent that one day, when Zechariah publicly rebuked him, the angry king ordered him to be stoned in the portico of the house of the Lord.

As he was dying among the stones, he said: “May God see and judge.” And, as Scripture itself adds: “Joash did not remember the kindness that Jehoiada his father had shown him, but killed his foster-brother, the son of the man who had nourished him” (IV Kings II).

This, therefore, is the Zechariah who was killed by King Joash, whose righteousness the Lord bears witness to, saying: “From the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah, son of Barachiah, whom you killed between the Temple and the altar”—that is, between the Temple building and the altar of incense.

Solomon made a bronze altar, as the history of the Kings relates, before the doors of the house of the Lord, in the portico of the Temple, so that sacrifices might be offered upon it every morning and evening. For the golden altar that was in the house of the Lord could not bear all the burnt offerings that were offered.

Near the bronze altar there was the fountain of Siloam, where red stones also appear. Hence simple people suppose that they were stained by the blood of this righteous man.

But although we have a Zechariah and the place of his death agrees, the name of his father seems to differ: there he is read as the son of Jehoiada, while here he is called the son of Barachiah.

A prudent reader might answer that, according to an ancient custom, he was perhaps known by two names, being called Jehoiada in one place and Barachiah in another. We, however, say that wherever Scripture appears deficient in the Latin language, we must have recourse to the Greek or Hebrew character of the language from which that same Scripture took its origin, so that through an appropriate interpretation what sounds inconsistent literally may appear harmonious.

Thus *Joiada* is interpreted as “the righteousness of the Lord,” *Barachias* as “the memory of the Lord,” and *Zacharias* as “blessed by the Lord.” Since, therefore, the blessing of the Lord arises from the righteousness of the Lord and from the memory of the Lord, according to a fitting interpretation there seems to be no discrepancy whether he is read as the son of Barachiah or the son of Jehoiada.

For in the Gospel used by the Nazaraeans, instead of “son of Barachiah,” “son of Jehoiada” is written.

Nor should it be thought without reason that, when the Lord mentioned the blessed martyrs, he wished to name these two in particular, namely Abel and Zechariah, since from the beginning of the world many others had been killed for his name. He wished to set forth such examples that through their martyrdom the sufferings of all who had suffered or were to suffer for his name might be signified.

By Abel, who was killed in the field not because of preaching but because of envy, and who is said or read not to have resisted, those are signified who are simple in teaching but firm in faith. Knowing only Christ and him crucified, they choose to die for his name rather than deny his faith.

By Zechariah, who was a priest of pontifical rank and was killed not in the field but between the Temple and the altar because of his preaching, those are signified who are masters and teachers of the Church and who have suffered martyrdom because of their steadfastness in preaching the Gospel or because of their rebuke of the reprobate.

The first of these after the Lord’s Passion was blessed Stephen the Levite, whose festival we celebrate today. Appointed by the apostles to preach, he taught that Christ was the Son of God on the authority of the divine Law, and was stoned by the hands of the reprobate.

Yet he did not lose his patience among the stones. Rather, in prayer he displayed a pure conscience, pleading for those who stoned him and saying: “Lord Jesus, do not hold this sin against them, because they do not know what they are doing” (Acts VII).

“Amen I say to you, all these things will come upon this generation.”

If anyone is troubled by how all these things are said to come upon one generation, since that generation did not itself kill either Abel or Zechariah, let him understand that sacred Scripture is speaking of two generations: the generation of the good and the generation of the wicked.

Of the good we read: “The generation of the upright will be blessed” (Ps. CXI). And again: “This is the generation of those who seek the Lord, who seek the face of the God of Jacob” (Ps. XXIII).

Of the wicked, however: “A crooked and perverse generation.” And again: “A generation that did not direct its heart,” and “a people without counsel and without understanding.”

Hence the Lord also says in the Gospel: “An evil and adulterous generation seeks a sign” (Matt. II).

All persecutors of the faithful, from the first Cain to the last who will come, are counted as one generation, because although they are separated in time, they are united in evil will. Likewise, those who by good works join themselves to the generation of the upright will receive a reward with them in the future.

“Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets and stone those who are sent to you, how often I wanted to gather your children as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you were unwilling.”

When the Lord speaks to Jerusalem, we should not think that he is speaking to stones or buildings, but metaphorically to the people themselves, so that by “the inhabited” you may understand “the inhabitants.” He mourned them with paternal affection because he quickly foresaw that their destruction was coming, in accordance with what we read elsewhere: “When Jesus saw the city, he wept over it, saying: ‘If only you had known, even you.’”

When he added, “You who kill the prophets and stone those who are sent to you,” he showed that in former times prophets had been sent for the salvation of that same people.

But it is asked how the Lord can say, “How often I wanted to gather your children as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you were unwilling,” when elsewhere it is written: “Whatever the Lord willed, he did in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in all the deeps” (Ps. CXXXIV).

Since he does everything he wills, how did he will to gather the children of Jerusalem and yet did not gather them?

The answer is that almighty God does not wish to have human service that is compelled, but service that is spontaneous and voluntary, so that in our good will he may find something to reward from his own gratuitous generosity. Therefore the merciful and almighty God, who does not desire the death of a sinner but that he should turn and live, did not abandon the children of Jerusalem because he was unable to gather them. Rather, because they were unwilling to exercise free will, he did not wish to gather them.

What he says, “How often I wanted to gather your children,” and so forth, means this: “I wanted to, but you were unwilling. I did what was mine to do, but you did not do what was yours. For your salvation I sent prophets to you, but you killed them. I myself came to you, and you did not wish to receive me.”

For almighty God wills all human beings to be saved, yet not all are saved because they persist unrepentant in hardness of heart.

Nor should it be passed over without consideration that he compared himself to a hen when he said that he wished to gather the children of Jerusalem. A hen is a simple and very gentle bird. When she warms and feeds her chicks, she raises her feathers and makes herself entirely bristling; she lowers her wings, softens her voice, and makes herself appear completely weak, so that she may make her chicks stronger. She even places herself in the way of beasts and birds lying in wait, offering herself to death for the safety of her chicks.

In accordance with this likeness, therefore, the Lord compared himself to a hen. In order to make us strong from weakness and raise us from earthly things to heavenly ones, he presented himself as weak to the weak when he descended from heaven to earth, knowing that “it is not the healthy who need a physician, but those who are ill” (Matt. IX). And in his Passion he made himself, as it were, wholly bristling, though he had appeared gentle and meek.

Concerning him Isaiah says: “And we saw him without appearance or beauty” (Isa. LIII). He softened his voice when, hanging on the cross, he said: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matt. XXVII). And, so that our liberation might be complete, he also offered himself to death for us.

Nor should it seem unworthy that our Redeemer, in the humanity he assumed, compared himself here to a hen, since he also likened himself to worms, as he says through the prophet: “But I am a worm and not a human being” (Ps. XXI).

He fittingly compared himself to a hen, for he is also said to have called his persecutor Herod a fox, saying: “Go and tell that fox that today and tomorrow I shall perform miracles, and on the third day I shall depart” (Luke XIII).

The fox is a cunning little animal, known to lie in wait for and be hostile to the hen. In the same way Herod, cunning and crafty, persecuted the hen because he despised the Lord with his host. He lay in wait for his chicks because he did not cease persecuting the apostles.

Thus the persecutors of the Lord are compared to foxes, as it is said through the prophet: “They themselves sought my life in vain. They will enter into the lower regions of the earth; they will be handed over to the power of the sword; they will become portions for foxes” (Ps. LXII).

The two wings of the hen with which she shelters her chicks are the Lord’s two Testaments. Or the two wings of the hen are Moses and Aaron, through whom the Lord liberated the Israelite people from Egyptian slavery; or Jesus and Zerubbabel, through whom he brought that same people back from the Babylonian captivity.

But ungrateful for these and other benefits, the people not only refused to believe, but also delivered their nurturer to death. Therefore what follows rightly happened to them:

“Behold, your house will be left to you desolate.”

If anyone looks with bodily eyes, he will see that this word of the Lord was fulfilled even literally. The house of the Lord, which had shone nobly, built in Jerusalem, was destroyed to the ground by Titus and Vespasian because of their unbelief, so that not one stone was left upon another.

Therefore, when the disciples had earlier shown the Lord the buildings of the city, he said to them: “Do you see all these things? Amen I say to you, not one stone here will be left upon another that will not be destroyed” (Matt. XXIV).

It is said: “Behold, your house will be left to you desolate.” It is called “their house” because it was left desolate, though once it had been called the house of the Lord, when offerings and sacrifices were made there. Now it is called “your house” because it was left desolate.

Spiritually, however, the house of the Jews was left desolate because, while they persisted in unbelief, they did not receive Christ as a guest in their hearts. He says: “Behold, I stand at the door and knock; if anyone opens to me, I will enter in to him, and I will dine with him, and he with me” (Rev. III).

The prophecy of Jeremiah was fulfilled, when he says: “I have abandoned my house, I have left my inheritance; my inheritance has become for me like a hyena’s den”—a small but rustic animal that digs up graves at night and feeds on the corpses of the dead (Jer. XII).

The Jews are rightly compared to it, because, denying Christ, they gave themselves over to every impurity and iniquity. They were scattered from nation to nation and from kingdom to another people, left without God, without the Law, and without priesthood. The prophecy was fulfilled in them which says: “They will suffer hunger like dogs and go around the city” (Ps. LVIII).

“For I say to you, you will not see me from now on until you say: ‘Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.’”

This sentence was fulfilled literally at the time when the Lord, seated upon a donkey’s colt and approaching Jerusalem, was honorably received by the crowds. They went out to meet him with palm branches, saying: “Hosanna to the Son of David; blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.”

This verse should be understood spiritually rather than literally. Its meaning is: “I say to you, you will not see me from now on until you say: ‘Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord’”—that is, you will not have me dwelling with you in your hearts until you believe that I have been sent by the Father as the Son of God for the salvation of humanity.

## HOMILY XI: ON SAINT JOHN THE EVANGELIST AND APOSTLE
(JOHN XXI.) “At that time, Jesus said to Peter: ‘Follow me.’ Peter turned and saw the disciple whom Jesus loved following,” and so forth.

In the sequence of this reading, blessed John the Evangelist commends three things to us: namely, the privilege of the Lord’s love toward him, the manner of his bodily end, and the composition of the Gospel. He commends the privilege of his being loved when he says: “Peter turned and saw the disciple whom Jesus loved following.” He shows the manner of his bodily end when he says: “Jesus did not say to him, ‘He shall not die,’ but, ‘So I want him to remain.’” He describes the Gospel when he adds: “This is the disciple who bears witness concerning these things and wrote them.”

But so that we may understand the beginning of this reading more fully, let us briefly consider what comes before. For above the same evangelist John reported that, while the disciples were sitting together in a room after the Lord’s resurrection, Simon Peter said to them: “I am going fishing.” The other disciples said to him: “We are coming with you.” Simon Peter therefore went aboard, together with Thomas, who is called Didymus, and Nathanael, who was from Cana in Galilee, and the sons of Zebedee, and two other of his disciples. After they had labored all night in fishing without success, Jesus stood on the shore in the morning and filled their net with a great multitude of fish. When they had come ashore, he said: “Come, eat.”

During that meal the Lord asked Peter three times whether he loved him. After his threefold denial, when Peter confessed his love for the third time, the Lord entrusted his sheep to him for the third time, saying: “If you love me, feed my sheep,” or “my lambs.” After entrusting the sheep to him, he also wished to disclose what he would suffer for those same sheep, saying: “Amen, amen, I say to you: when you were younger, you girded yourself and walked where you wished; but when you grow old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will gird you and lead you where you do not wish to go.” “Now this he said,” the evangelist adds, “signifying by what death he would glorify God.”

And lest the suffering of the cross should seem harsh and intolerable to Peter, the merciful Teacher sought to ease it by his own example, saying: “Follow me”—that is, imitate me. It was as though the Lord were saying: “You will endure the suffering of the cross all the more readily when, in bearing it, you remember to follow my footsteps. Just as I did not hesitate to bear the cross for your salvation, so you too must remember that you ought to suffer for confession of my name. For you will obtain the more glorious palm of martyrdom the more closely you follow the path of the Teacher in order to attain it.”

To follow the Lord means to imitate him, as he himself says: “If anyone wishes to come after me,” and so forth (Matt. XVI). And again: “Whoever serves me, let him follow me” (John XII). The apostle Peter followed the Lord, because he did not hesitate to bear the cross for the sheep entrusted to him, just as the Lord himself graciously embraced it for the redemption of the human race, fulfilling what the apostle John says: “Whoever says that he remains in Christ ought himself also to walk just as he walked” (John II).

What the Lord and Peter did after this, the evangelist does not expressly state. Nevertheless, by saying: “Peter turned and saw the disciple whom Jesus loved following,” he quietly indicates that as soon as the Lord said to Peter, “Follow me,” Peter rose from the place of the meal and began to leave. Desiring to fulfill the Lord’s command even literally, Peter followed him with bodily steps.

That disciple whom Jesus loved—namely, John, whose Gospel this is—also followed the Lord and Peter. For he did not consider himself unworthy to follow him, since he knew that the Lord had embraced him with a glory of greater love than the others. Nor is it incredible that Peter and John followed the Lord bodily, because they did not yet understand what the Lord’s words to Peter, “Follow me,” signified spiritually.

But because blessed John did not wish to make his own person known by name, he identified himself by merit when he said: “He saw the disciple whom Jesus loved.” Jesus loved him—not in such a way as to exclude the others and love him alone, but by loving one of them in a particular way. He proved that he loved them all when, before his Passion, he said to them: “As the Father loved me, so I loved you; remain in my love” (John XV).

Yet he loved this one more than the others, because virginal integrity had made him worthy of a greater love. For histories relate that, when he wished to marry, the Lord called him away from the wedding; and because he had withdrawn him from carnal embrace, he made him more worthy of spiritual love.

In saying, “He saw the one whom Jesus loved following,” blessed John the Evangelist preserved the custom of the saints: while concealing his proper name, he indicated his own person by another designation. Holy men have this practice: whenever they speak of great and wondrous things concerning themselves, they pass to another person and speak of themselves as though of someone else. Moses did this when he spoke of himself as of another, saying: “Now Moses was a very meek man, more than all the men who dwelt upon the earth” (Num. XII). Likewise blessed Job, about to say, “There was a man who was simple and upright, fearing God,” first spoke of himself as of another, saying: “There was a man in the land of Uz, whose name was Job” (Job I).

Preserving this humility, blessed John did not wish to place his own name anywhere in the whole course of his Gospel. Blessed John the Evangelist gives another indication by which he may be recognized when he adds: “Who also reclined at supper upon the Lord’s breast and said: ‘Lord, who is it that will betray you?’”

At the final supper that the Lord held with his disciples, as the preceding text of the Gospel relates, that disciple reclined upon the breast of the Teacher. When the Lord said, “One of you is about to betray me,” and everyone was troubled, Peter signaled to John, who asked the Teacher: “Lord, who is it that will betray you?” And lest a dreadful suspicion should torment the consciences of them all, he gave them certainty, saying: “The one who dips his hand with me in the dish—he will betray me.”

The fact that this disciple reclined upon the breast of the Teacher was not only a sign of present love, but also a sign of a future mystery. Since all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden in the breast of Jesus, it is rightly said that he reclined upon the breast of the Teacher who was to describe his divinity more deeply and profoundly than the others.

[Col. 0072C] “When Peter had seen him, therefore, he said to Jesus: ‘Lord, but what about this man?’” Because the apostle Peter understood the stretching out of hands, the girding by another, and being led where he did not wish to go as a sign of his own Passion, he wished to know by what death his brother and fellow disciple would also pass to life. And seeing him following, he said:

“‘Lord, but what about this man?’ Jesus said to him: ‘So I want him to remain until I come; what is that to you? You follow me.’”

It was as though he were saying: “I do not wish him to complete the course of his present life through the suffering of martyrdom. Rather, I want him to remain in this way until, once the peace of the Church has been established, I lead him to eternal life through the passage of natural death.”

We must not suppose that the Lord denied that John would suffer many tribulations for his faith. Rather, he foretold that John would not complete his present life through martyrdom. For in the Acts of the Apostles we read that he was publicly beaten with rods, when the disciples went away from the presence of the council rejoicing because they had been deemed worthy to suffer insults for the name of Jesus (Acts V).

It is also written that the most impious Caesar Domitian cast him into a cauldron of boiling oil, from which he emerged as free from bodily pain as he had been untouched by the corruption of the flesh. For in Ecclesiastical History we read that he was given poison to drink and suffered no harm, the Lord’s saying being fulfilled in him: “And if they drink any deadly thing, it shall not hurt them.”

Afterward, because of his unconquerable perseverance in preaching the Gospel, the same ruler banished him into exile on the island of Patmos. There, deprived of human companionship, he obtained the consolation of angels. With his own hand he wrote the Apocalypse, which the Lord graciously revealed to him concerning the condition of the Church, both present and future.

Therefore, when the Lord said, “So I want him to remain until I come,” he did not deny that John would die bodily, but foretold that he would not complete his life through the suffering of martyrdom.

The disciples, however, began at that time to understand the statement about remaining in such a way that they thought John would no longer die. Hence the evangelist adds:

“This saying therefore went out among the brothers that that disciple would not die.”

But John himself corrected their error when he added: “Jesus did not say, ‘He will not die,’ but, ‘So I want him to remain until I come.’”

John truly died the death of the body, because from the day when it was first said to the first human being, “On whatever day you eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, you shall surely die” (Gen. II), no one tastes life without tasting death. Finally, even if Elijah and Enoch are believed still to be alive, we must understand that they postponed bodily death for a time; they did not escape it altogether, since they are to be killed in the time of Antichrist.

Although the Lord, in the form of his humanity, accepted death, no one can escape bodily death, as the Psalmist testifies when he says: “Who is the man who shall live and shall not see death?” (Ps. LXXXVIII)—“no one” is understood.

Finally, as we find in the writings of the Fathers, when John was living at Ephesus, worn down by advanced age to such an extent that he could scarcely go to church, supported by the hands of his disciples, and knowing that the day of his death was near, he ordered a tomb to be prepared for him. On the Lord’s Day, after the celebration of the Masses and an admonition addressed to the disciples, he strengthened himself by receiving the body and blood of the Lord.

Then, bidding farewell to the brothers, he descended into the excavated place of burial that he had prepared for himself. As though upon a bed, he gathered himself into the tomb; and after completing his prayer, he was laid beside his fathers in the sight of the disciples, as free from bodily pain as he had been untouched by the corruption of the flesh.

In that place the earth is said gradually to have bubbled up from below, so that some believed he was still alive. But because, after the other apostles had been brought to completion through the suffering of martyrdom, he alone ended his life by a natural death in the peace of the Church, the Lord said: “So I want him to remain until I come.”

This means: “I do not want him to end his present life by the violence of a persecutor. Rather, I want him to remain in this way until, coming to life, I lead him to everlasting life and glorify him with eternal reward.”

Spiritually, through these two disciples we may understand the two lives of the faithful, in which the Church consists: namely, the active and the contemplative. One of these is characterized by labor, the other by rest.

Through Peter, to whom it was said, “Follow me,” the labor of the active life is expressed. To this belong giving food to the hungry, drink to the thirsty, clothing to the naked, receiving the stranger, visiting the sick, burying the dead, correcting the one who has gone astray, teaching the ignorant, and, for truth and justice, fighting even unto death if necessity requires.

Those who have been placed in positions of authority must also foresee, with attentive concern, how their subjects may have food and clothing.

Through John, concerning whom it was said, “So I want him to remain until I come,” the sweetness of the contemplative life is signified. To this belongs, after all cares and anxieties have been set aside, devoting oneself continually to reading and prayer; and, through frequent contrition expressed in tears, sighing most sweetly for the remission of sins and the attainment of eternal life.

Nevertheless, no one is unaware that both disciples, and both lives, are perfect. The active life generally belongs to all the faithful who, keeping themselves undefiled by this world, exercise mind, hand, and tongue in good works.

The contemplative life, however, is given especially to those who, after long exercises in monastic life, choose secluded places in the desert, where, without the hindrance of human beings, they may devote themselves to reading and prayer, cleave to God alone, and, insofar as human frailty permits, sometimes join themselves in mind to the assemblies of angels, saying with the Psalmist: “Behold, I fled away and remained in solitude” (Ps. LIV).

The difference between the active and contemplative lives is that the active life begins here and ends here, whereas the contemplative life begins here but will be perfected more fully in the future.

For who will give food to the hungry in that life, where no one hungers, since there is living bread? Who will give drink to the thirsty, where there is a living fountain, and whoever tastes from it will never thirst forever? Who will clothe the naked, where there is the robe of immortality? Who will visit the sick, where there is no one who becomes sick? Who will bury the dead, where the dwelling is the land of the living?

Therefore, as we have said, the active life has its beginning and end here, while its reward remains. The contemplative life has its beginning here, but will have its perfection in the future, because “what it now sees through a mirror and in an enigma, then it will see face to face” (1 Cor. XIII).

Hence it is rightly said of John: “So I want him to remain until I come”—that is: “Those whom I have intoxicated with a taste of my contemplation, I want always to advance until, when I appear on the day of judgment, they pass from faith to sight together with eternal reward.”

Blessed John now commends to us the composition of his Gospel when he says:

[Col. 0074D] “This is the disciple who bears witness concerning these things and wrote them.”

John bore witness to the Lord by teaching; he bore witness by living rightly; he bore witness by writing the Gospel; and he bears witness also every day, whenever the Gospel he wrote is read or heard by the faithful in the Church.

It may perhaps be pleasing if we briefly recall what occasion led him to write the Gospel. After the Lord’s Ascension, for nearly sixty years he preached the Gospel without any written aid. But when, as we have said, he had been banished into exile on the island of Patmos by the most impious Caesar Domitian because of his unconquerable perseverance in evangelizing, the heretics Marcion, Cerinthus, Ebion, and the other sons of the devil—whom he himself calls Antichrists in his Epistle—burst into the Church of God and attempted to divide it by various doctrines, saying that Christ had not existed before Mary.

Afterward, when, with the permission of the most devout ruler Nerva, he had returned from exile and was living at Ephesus, all the bishops and presbyters of Asia are said to have asked him to speak to them about the divinity of the Savior and to leave a written record for the memory of future generations. They already had sufficient writing about the Savior’s humanity in the books of the three evangelists, and they especially wished to refute the heresy that claimed Christ had not existed before Mary.

At first he refused to do this. But when they persisted in prayer, he consented only on the condition that they all pray together to the Lord for three days with fasting. When they had done so, he is said to have been filled with such abundant grace of the Holy Spirit that his mind was carried away to contemplate the divinity of the Father, the Son, and the same Holy Spirit. He drank from the purest fountain of eternal life, so that he might offer its drink to us who thirst.

Hence the beginning of his Gospel is: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.” And throughout the entire text of his Gospel, inserting only a few matters concerning human actions, he left a sufficient written testimony concerning the divinity of the Savior.

How firmly and without any doubt the things written by John ought to be believed, he himself makes clear when he adds: “And we know that his testimony is true.”

Let us therefore, together with the other faithful, believing as true the things he wrote, preserve the things he taught, so that we may reach what he promised. May he deign to grant this, he who, with the Father, and so forth.

## HOMILY XII. ON THE HOLY INNOCENTS

(MATTHEW II.) “At that time, an angel of the Lord appeared in a dream to Joseph,” and so forth.

The divine readings are connected with one another, and one frequently depends upon another, so that sometimes the beginning of what follows is more easily understood by considering what precedes. We readily perceive this in the present reading if we briefly attend to what comes before.

The Gospel reading above reported that, when Herod had sent the Magi who came from the East to Jerusalem on to Bethlehem, he said to them: “Go and inquire carefully about the child, and when you have found him, report back to me, so that I too may come and worship him” (Matt. II).

But because he intended to kill the one whom he professed that he would worship, after receiving an answer in a dream that they should not return to Herod, they went back to their own country by another way. Immediately the evangelist added: “When they had departed, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared in a dream to Joseph.”

Here we must consider that the heavenly angel, the minister of God, forestalled Herod’s plots by warning Joseph to flee into Egypt with the child, lest Herod should be able to vent the fury of his anger upon the child Jesus as he did upon the others.

Perhaps someone will ask why the angel appeared to Joseph in a dream, when he is recorded to have appeared to the shepherds while they were awake and to have announced the Lord’s birth. The answer is that this difference in the angels’ appearances commends both Joseph’s holiness and his prudence.

The shepherds were uneducated, being shepherds, and could not discern divine mysteries. It was therefore necessary for the angel to appear to them visibly and to disclose the hidden mystery openly. Joseph, however, was not only holy but also prudent. It was not necessary for the angel to appear to him while he was awake, but only in a dream, because, as the Apostle says, “tongues are for a sign, not to believers but to unbelievers” (1 Cor. XIV).

And because Joseph was able prudently to discern that angelic vision, he shared not only the bodily origin but also the name of that Joseph who had seen in a dream that he would be preferred above his brothers, and who, by prudently interpreting dreams, had been placed in authority as prefect—or lord—of Egypt (Gen. XLI).

As far as the moral sense is concerned, the angel appeared to Joseph in a dream to show that those will attain the fellowship of angels who, as though asleep, are separated from the world’s hindrances and from carnal cares.

Thus the person who sets aside the world’s unnecessary anxieties and opens the eye of the mind to the love of God is awake even while sleeping, as the voice of the Church says: “I sleep, but my heart is awake” (Song V).

Let us hear what the angel appearing in the dream says: “Rise, take the child and his mother, flee into Egypt, and remain there until I tell you.”

Here we must note that he did not say, “Take your son,” as the Jews falsely wished to claim, but “Take the child”—that is, take him as a bearer and foster-father, not as his true father.

He did not say, “Take your wife,” as the Photinians wished to claim, although fiancées may also be called wives, but “Take his mother”—that is, take her as the guardian of chastity and supporter of weakness, not as a violator of virginity.

The child Jesus fled before Herod’s persecution, not because he feared death—for he had come to die for human beings—but so that, at the proper time, he might endure not the death the persecutor wished to inflict, but the death he himself had ordained. He showed that he had the power to lay down his life and to take it up again (John X).

The order of events was necessary: first, by performing miracles, he had to make himself known as God, and afterward to endure death—namely, the most shameful death of the cross—for our redemption.

For it was fitting that, since the first human being had fallen by sin through forbidden wood, he should be restored through the wood of the holy cross. If he had then been killed, who would have recognized him as Lord, except Mary, Joseph, Elizabeth, and the few others to whom the Holy Spirit had revealed it?

By all the others who knew him he was thought to be Joseph’s son. Therefore he postponed death; he did not fear it. He showed his faithful that the fury of persecutors is not to be feared where they see that his death benefits the life of others, but that death is to be fled where they see that it brings benefit to no one, in accordance with what the Lord says elsewhere: “When they persecute you in one city, flee into another” (Matt. X).

Why the angel so carefully warned Joseph to flee into Egypt with the child and his mother, he makes clear when he says: “For it will happen that Herod will seek the child in order to destroy him.”

“He will seek him,” he says, “to destroy him, but he will not find him to kill him.”

How ready Joseph was, with what zeal and concern, to obey the angelic commands is shown when it is added:

“He arose, took the child and his mother by night, and withdrew into Egypt.”

He did not fear the darkness of night and wait for daylight; he did not fear the cruelty of the faithless nation and turn aside elsewhere. Rather, “he arose, took the child and his mother by night, and withdrew into Egypt.”

The Lord’s great power is evident, but his humility shines no less brightly. He wished to flee before the face of a persecutor, he whose ministers are angels. The Lord fled into Egypt, full of idols, leaving behind the cradle of the Jewish nation, and showing even by the position of his body what he would later say: “I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance” (Mark IX).

“And he was there until the death of Herod.”

Some report that this occurred after four years; others, after two. Spiritually, however, Mary and Joseph signify the Law and the Synagogue. Egypt, which is interpreted as “darkness” or “sorrow,” signifies the world, which after the Lord’s Incarnation sat in the darkness of ignorance and in the shadow of death, sorrow, and distress, as the Apostle says: “Tribulation and distress upon every human soul that works evil, of the Jew first and also of the Greek” (Rom. II).

As though carried by Mary and Joseph, the Lord came into Egypt when, with the Law and the Synagogue going before him, he illumined the world, which lay in the darkness of error, by his visitation. Thus the prophecy of Isaiah was fulfilled: “Behold, the Lord ascends upon a light cloud and will enter Egypt, and the heart of Egypt will melt within it, and the images of Egypt will be shaken,” and the rest that follows.

The light cloud is the virgin Mary, who was not burdened with male seed. The Lord, ascending as upon a light cloud, entered Egypt when, taking flesh from the virgin, he appeared visibly to the world.

“So that what was spoken through the prophet might be fulfilled: ‘Out of Egypt I called my son.’”

It is customary for this evangelist, namely Matthew, frequently to confirm his narrative by the utterances of the prophets. Because he was the first to write his Gospel for Hebrews in the Hebrew language, whenever an appropriate opportunity arose he took care to confirm his narrative from their books.

Therefore, after saying that the Lord had been carried into Egypt by his parents at the angel’s command, he immediately added the prophetic utterance: “Out of Egypt I called my son.”

This testimony is found in the prophet Hosea according to the Hebrew truth, but it is not found among the Septuagint interpreters. Because, at the command of King Ptolemy, they were translating the Scriptures into Greek, the Jews say, with prudent reasoning, that they acted so that wherever the Son was explicitly mentioned, they either interpreted the passage differently or omitted it altogether. They feared that Ptolemy, who appeared to be a worshiper of the one God, might, by failing to understand the Trinity, fall into belief in several gods.

Hence many passages are read in our codices that are not found among the Septuagint interpreters, such as this one (Judg. XIII): “Out of Egypt I called my son”; and this: “He shall be called a Nazarene”; and this: “They shall look upon him whom they pierced.”

Some, however, have wished this testimony to be taken from the Book of Numbers—namely, from Balaam’s prophecy, where it is written: “God called him out of Egypt, and his glory is like that of a unicorn” (Hos. XI).

Although this may be understood of the Jewish people, who were called from Egypt to the promised land, it may also be understood of the Son of God, who, after Herod’s death, returned to the land of Israel at the angel’s command.

[Col. 0078B] “Then Herod, seeing that he had been mocked by the Magi, sent and killed all the boys who were in Bethlehem and in all its territories, from two years old and under, according to the time that he had carefully learned from the Magi.”

When he says, “Then Herod, seeing that he had been mocked by the Magi,” he refers back to what was said earlier in the Gospel, when Herod, sending the Magi to Bethlehem, said: “Go and inquire carefully about the child” (Matt. II), and so forth.

But after receiving an answer in a dream that they should not return to Herod, they went back to their own country by another way. When Herod saw that his plots had been frustrated, he became very angry because he had been mocked by the Magi. Since he could not destroy the child secretly, he immediately burst into open persecution.

“And he sent and killed all the boys who were in Bethlehem and in all its territories.”

He thought that if all the boys were killed, the one he sought could not escape. The wretched man did not consider that “there is no counsel, no wisdom, no prudence against the Lord.”

Therefore he ordered the boys “from two years old and under” to be killed—that is, from a child of two years down to a child of one night old.

The words, “according to the time that he had carefully learned from the Magi,” are explained by the histories of Josephus and Hegesippus. At the time when Herod had heard from the Magi that the king of the Jews had been born, his adversaries accused him, and he was summoned by the emperor and went to Rome.

When he had appeared before Caesar and the entire senate, being clever in mind and eloquent in speech, he cleared himself with the greatest force and dignity of all that had been brought against him. Although his enemies had expected otherwise, he was raised to still greater glory by the emperor, who gave him a royal diadem and confirmed his authority to reign in Judea.

When, after two years, he had returned to Judea in great glory, he remembered what he had heard from the Magi about the birth of the king of the Jews. Thus: “He sent and killed all the boys who were in Bethlehem and in all its territories, from two years old and under, according to the time that he had carefully learned from the Magi,” judging, as we have said, that once all had been killed, not one could escape.

The fact that persecution began when the Lord was born signifies that throughout the whole period of the present life there would be people who persecute God’s elect, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you” (John XV). And the Apostle says: “All who wish to live devoutly in Christ will suffer persecution” (2 Tim. III). And as Scripture says: “The furnace tests the potter’s vessels, and temptation through tribulation tests righteous people” (Eccl. XXVII).

The fact that the boys were killed for the Lord signifies that the crown of martyrdom is reached through the merit of humility, for, as the Lord says, everyone who humbles himself will be exalted.

The innocence of the boys signifies the humility of the simple. Concerning such people the Lord says: “Allow the little children to come to me, for of such is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. XIX). And again: “Unless you turn and become like little children, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven.”

When the boys, as we have said, were killed for Christ, but Christ, who was being sought, was not found, it is shown that persecutors can mistreat and kill the bodies of martyrs, but cannot take Christ away either from the living or from the dying. They can say: “Whether we live, we live to the Lord; whether we die, we die to the Lord. Therefore, whether we live or die, we are the Lord’s” (Rom. XIV).

Those who were two years old when they were killed signify those who are perfect in work and doctrine. By living well and teaching rightly, they rebuke the wickedness of others and struggle even to the shedding of blood.

Those who were younger signify the simple, who know Christ and him crucified alone and prefer to die rather than deny his faith.

The fact that the boys were killed not only in Bethlehem but also in all its territories signifies that persecution would arise not only in Judea, from which the Church had taken its origin, but also extend to the ends of the earth.

The fact that the Lord fled into Egypt because of Herod’s persecution signifies that the elect, because of the persecution of the wicked, are sometimes driven from their own homes and sent into exile.

The fact that, after Herod’s death, he returned again to the land of Israel at the angel’s command signifies that those same elect, after the falsehood of heretics has been suppressed, will return to their own places. We read of this concerning Hilary of Poitiers, Athanasius of Alexandria, and many others.

[Col. 0079D] “Then was fulfilled what was spoken through Jeremiah the prophet, saying: ‘A voice was heard in Rama, lamentation and great wailing: Rachel weeping for her children; and she refused to be comforted, because they are not.’”

The evangelist Matthew confirms our preceding account when he introduces the utterances of the prophets into his own words.

When he says, “A voice was heard in Rama,” the name Rama does not simply refer here to a city or place, as some think, but rather signifies “on high.” For to say, “A voice was heard in Rama,” is the same as saying that the storm of persecution had spread far and wide.

The literal question is how Rachel is said to have wept for her children, since Bethlehem, where the boys were killed, was not in the tribe of Benjamin, which descended from Rachel, but in the tribe of Judah, who was born of her sister Leah.

The answer is that the tribes of Judah and Benjamin, as ancient history relates, received their inheritances next to one another, and the boundary line of Benjamin reached near Bethlehem. Since Herod had ordered the boys to be killed not only in Bethlehem but also in all its territories, we understand that on this occasion many from the tribe of Benjamin were slain. Rachel their mother is said to have wept for them with a voice raised on high, so that the enormity of the persecution might be intensified: the mother herself is said to have done what is known to have been carried out by her tribe.

A prudent reader may add another point here. As the history in Genesis relates (Gen. XXXV), Rachel was buried near Bethlehem, beside the road that leads to Hebron, as the inscription of her monument testifies. Therefore, what is established as having been done by others is said, in prophetic fashion, to have been done by her herself, since that place bore its distinguished name from her burial there (John LXXX).

Spiritually, however, Rachel—which is interpreted as “sheep” or “beginning of sight”—signifies the Church. She is rightly called “the beginning of sight,” because, once the eye of the heart has been cleansed, she desires to contemplate the beauty of him who says: “I am the beginning, who also speak to you” (John VIII).

She is also the hundredth sheep whom the merciful shepherd, having found her, placed upon his own shoulders and thus carried back to the flock (Luke XV).

Rachel therefore weeps for her children because the Church groans on account of the persecution of the faithful. She does not wish to be consoled concerning those who are no more, because she does not wish to receive the consolation that they might return once more to the struggles of this world, they who reign with Christ, crowned through martyrdom.

“After Herod had died.” Therefore Herod, who had made himself the perpetrator of so many crimes that he would not withdraw his hand even from persecuting the Lord himself, could not remain unpunished.
