The answer is that in this passage “to see” is used in the sense of “to feel” or “to experience.” This usage is extremely common in Scripture, so that “to see” is sometimes used for “to feel” or “to experience,” as the Lord says in the Gospel: “If anyone loves my words, he will never see death.” Therefore, when the evangelist says that he would not see death, it is as though he said that he would not taste or experience death in himself.

“And he came in the Spirit into the Temple.”

He is not thought to have come into the Temple in an ecstasy, as John testifies in the Apocalypse that he was in heaven (Revelation 12), but, warned by the same Spirit from whom he had received the answer, and understanding that the hour had arrived in which he would see the Lord, he came bodily into the Temple to satisfy his desire by seeing the Lord and to prophesy many things about him before witnesses.

Hence it follows:

“And when his parents brought in the child Jesus, to do for him according to the custom of the law, he also took him into his arms.”

Behold, the promise of the Holy Spirit was fulfilled, because Simeon was deemed worthy not only to see the Lord but also to carry him in his arms—that is, in his embrace. And it is a wondrous thing: the old man carried the one by whom he himself was carried. Great here is the Lord’s power, but no less evident is his humility, since the one whom heaven and earth cannot contain was carried in the arms of one man.

He carried Christ in his humanity, while Christ carried him through his divinity. The old man bore Christ as an infant, while Christ governed him in his old age. Blessed indeed was Simeon, who was deemed worthy not only to see Christ but also to carry him in the flesh; yet no less blessed are the souls that did not see and believed. Hence the Lord said to one who touched him: “Because you have seen me, you have believed; blessed are those who have not seen and have believed” (John 20).

Typically, the aged Simeon signifies the world. When, after five thousand years and more, it recognized Christ as having been born, it carried the child, as it were, in its old age. He took him into his arms, with which we customarily carry burdens, so that we may learn to take upon ourselves Christ’s yoke, which is easy, and his burden, which is light.

Spiritually, the Church carries in good works the one whom Simeon carried bodily in his hands, because hands and arms signify works. The Apostle Paul admonishes us, saying: “Glorify and carry the Lord in your heart” (1 Corinthians 6).

Therefore, on this day, the faithful who celebrate the solemn rites of Mass carry lights in their hands, recalling that ineffable light whom Simeon carried in his hands on this day. Figuratively, when the old man carries him, he teaches us that, having stripped off the old man with his deeds, we should carry and put on the new—that is, Christ—so that in some way we may return from condemnable old age to spiritual infancy, according to the Apostle’s saying: “The night,” that is, unbelief, “has passed; but the day has drawn near” (Romans 13).

What greatness Simeon recognized in the one whom he saw as small is shown when it follows:

“And he blessed God.”

He blessed God—not because human blessing can confer anything upon God, from whom every blessing proceeds, as the Apostle says: “Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ” (Ephesians 1)—but he is said to have “blessed God” as though it meant: he praised the Lord well, or spoke well of him, or prophesied worthily and well concerning him. For it is the custom of the saints always to bless God, whether in prosperity or adversity, saying with the Psalmist: “I will bless the Lord at all times; his praise shall always be in my mouth.”

Let us hear what he says as he blesses:

[Col. 0106A] “Now dismiss your servant, Lord, according to your word, in peace.”

In these words he shows that he had wished to remain in the world for no other reason than to see the Lord born. As soon as he had seen him, carried him, and praised him with his mouth, he blessed God, leaping for joy and, as it were, asking permission to depart from the world: “Now dismiss your servant, Lord, according to your word, in peace.”

It was as though he said: Because I see peace, dismiss me in peace—namely, into that peace which he was to commend to his disciples, saying: “I give you peace; I leave you peace” (John 14). For he knew that he would pass from a laborious life to a place of peace and rest, from which, after the Lord’s resurrection, he would proceed to the heavenly realm.

Nor did Simeon alone desire to pass from this life to another. Many of the saints attained this perfection, wishing to lay down the burden of the flesh and pass, as it were, into Abraham’s bosom, that is, into rest, and requesting the coming of the one who would open for them the gate of heavenly life.

Thus Jeduthun, “the leaper” or “one who leaps over desires,” when he saw the evils of the world increasing and grew hot in spirit, said: “Make known to me, O Lord, my end, and what is the number of my days, that I may know.” And again: “Behold, you have made my days old.” And David: “Do not take me away in the midst of my days, throughout generation and generation,” and so forth.

But the fathers of the New Testament depart from this life with so much greater security as they believe more certainly that another life has been prepared for them. This is the conduct of the perfect. Such was the Apostle Paul, who, secure because of his good works, said: “I desire to depart and to be with Christ.” To depart and to be with Christ is much better; but to remain in the flesh is necessary for your sake—that is, for the sake of the disciples. And again: “While we are in the body, we are absent from the Lord” (2 Corinthians 5).

Why Simeon wished to be dismissed he makes clear by adding:

“For my eyes have seen your salvation.”

God’s salvation is Jesus; for wherever “savior” or “salvation” is read among us, the Hebrew has *Jesus*.

What follows is:

“Which you have prepared before the face of all peoples.”

It is evident that all peoples could not see God’s salvation—that is, Christ—in the flesh, because he preached personally only in Judea. Yet it is said to have been prepared before the face of all peoples because, through the preaching of the apostles, it came to the knowledge of all peoples, as it is written in the Gospel: “But they went forth and preached everywhere” (Mark 16). Thus the prophecy was fulfilled which says: “Their sound has gone out through all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Psalm 19). And again: “There are neither speech nor language in which their voices are not heard.”

Alternatively, God’s salvation is said to have been prepared before the face of all peoples because it will appear to everyone at the judgment—not only to the righteous but also to the unrighteous—as it is written: “All flesh shall see the salvation of our God” (Luke 3). And John says in the Apocalypse: “Every eye will see him, even those who pierced him, and all the tribes of the earth will mourn over him.”

For what purpose the Lord came at his first advent is declared when it follows:

“A light for the revelation of the Gentiles, and the glory of your people Israel.”

God’s salvation was indeed a light to the Gentiles, because the Gentiles who sat in darkness and the shadow of death were illumined by his coming. The prophecy of Isaiah was fulfilled: “The people of the Gentiles who walked in darkness saw a great light” (Isaiah 9). “Upon those dwelling in the region and shadow of death, light has dawned.” Hence he himself says in the Gospel: “I am the light of the world. Whoever follows me does not walk in darkness but will have the light of life.”

God’s salvation was also glory to Israel, because it became great glory for those among them who wished to believe in him when the Son of God deigned to assume flesh from their lineage. For he taught among them and sanctified them by his miracles. But because only a few Jews, whereas many Gentiles, were going to believe in him, he placed the revelation of the Gentiles before the glory of Israel.

The Psalmist is also read to have done this. After prophesying the Lord’s advent in the flesh, saying, “The Lord has made known his salvation; in the sight of the Gentiles he has revealed his righteousness,” he added: “He has remembered his mercy and his truth toward the house of Israel” (Psalm 98).

HOMILY XV. ON THE EPIPHANY OF THE LORD.

(Matthew 2). “At that time, when [Col. 0107C] Jesus was born in Bethlehem of Judea, in the days of King Herod,” and the rest. In the opening of this reading the blessed evangelist Matthew commends three things to us: the person of the one being born, the place of his birth, and the time. For it was fitting that nothing of authority should be lacking in that birth of the Lord. He indicates the person, therefore, when he says, “when Jesus was born”; the place, when he adds, “in Bethlehem of Judea”; and the time, when he says, “in the days of King Herod.”

Having said Bethlehem, he rightly adds “of Judea,” to distinguish it from the other Bethlehem, which the book of Joshua proves to be in Galilee. The Lord beautifully chose to be born in Bethlehem. For Bethlehem is interpreted “house of bread,” because there the patriarch Jacob fed his flocks, giving it the name Bethlehem [Col. 0107D] on account of the mystery of its future significance; it had previously been called Ephrath. For the place in which the Lord was to be born was called Bethlehem beforehand, since the true bread was indeed to appear there through the material of flesh—the bread which refreshes the minds of the elect with eternal satisfaction, namely he who says in the Gospel: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven”; and of whom the Psalmist says: “He gave them bread from heaven,” and, “Man ate the bread of angels” (Psalm 77). Sedulius too sang beautifully of him:

“Christ was bread, Christ the rock, Christ upon the waters.”

He also rightly chose to be born in the days of Herod, so that the prophecy of Jacob might be fulfilled [Col. 0108A], who said: “The sceptre shall not be taken away from Judah, nor a ruler from his loins, until he comes who is to be sent, and he shall be the expectation of the nations” (Genesis 49). For from the time when they came up from Egypt they had leaders, kings, and princes from their own people. But when the rulers from Judah had failed, Herod, the first man of foreign birth, had seized the kingdom of the Jews.

Since Herod has been mentioned, it seems fitting briefly to recall how he came to the height of the Jewish kingdom. When those descended from the line of Mattathias had held the leadership of the Jewish kingdom for a number of years, power at last came to a certain man of their lineage, named Alexander. After some time he died, leaving a wife with two little sons, [Col. 0108B] one called Aristobulus and the other Hyrcanus. When they had grown up, they began to quarrel with one another from a desire to rule.

At that time there was a man named Antipater, strong in body and exceedingly rich in resources, born of a certain Herod, who was a temple-attendant of Apollo. Hyrcanus therefore called him into friendship and alliance against his brother. Since Antipater aided him not only with arms but also with resources, he instructed him also to seek the assistance of Roman commanders, because at that time the Romans excelled other men in faith, wisdom, and strength in arranging affairs of kingdoms. To pass over the details: when Aristobulus was captured by the Romans and led under guard to Rome, the leadership of the Jewish kingdom came to Hyrcanus. Then, remembering the benefit [Col. 0108C] conferred on him by Antipater, Hyrcanus cultivated him as a friend and associate, so far as to entrust to him under his own authority the administration of some part of the Jewish kingdom.

This Antipater had a wife named Cypris, an Arabian by birth, by whom he had sons; one he named Phasael and the other Herod. When, worn out by advanced old age, he ended his present life, he left to his son Herod the authority which he had received from Hyrcanus among the Jews. Herod, a shrewd and cautious man, began vigorously to conduct the affairs that concerned him, and married Hyrcanus’s granddaughter, the daughter of Aristobulus. But after some time Hyrcanus was captured in a battle he had undertaken against the Arabs, and was also kept in exile. Then Herod first obtained Hyrcanus’s authority, as it were in his stead. But when, after some time, Hyrcanus returned to Judea with his ears cut off, Herod pretended to receive him in peace; afterward, however, having killed him by treachery, he fraudulently obtained his authority. Having first received authority from Cassius, a Roman commander, and afterward from the emperor himself, he brought the Jewish kingdom under his power [Col. 0108D].

Thus Herod, the first foreigner, acquired the kingdom of the Jews under his power by this fraud. While he reigned, the Lord Jesus Christ, foretold according to the prophets, was born in the town of Bethlehem in Judea. Since the rulers from Judah had failed and an alien, stranger, and usurper had seized the Jewish kingdom, the time was at hand when the true King should be born. On the thirteenth day after his birth, the magi came from the east to Jerusalem [Col. 0109A],

“saying, ‘Where is he who has been born King of the Jews? For we saw his star in the east and have come to worship him.’”

They fittingly came from the east who sought the East, namely him of whom it is written: “Behold the man; East is his name”; and again: “The East from on high has visited us” (Luke 1). It was not by chance but by divine dispensation that the magi first sought the newborn king at Jerusalem, the metropolitan city of the Jews: so that they might learn the place of his birth from the Jews, and the Jews might hear from them that their king had been born. If they went with them to worship, they would be saved; but if they refused to go, they would be without excuse. Yet they showed others the place of his birth from their own books, while themselves remaining like foolish and blind men in darkness. They became like milestones that show the road to travellers, but remain stupid and motionless as the travellers pass by: thus the Jews showed others the place of Christ’s birth but themselves remained obtuse.

The city called Jerusalem here by the Evangelist was built by Shem, Noah’s son. It was first called Salem, and later Jebus after its Jebusite inhabitants. Hence its name Jerusalem is compounded from both names. In the time of King Solomon, raised to greater honour by his wisdom and splendour, it was called Hierosolyma, as though *Hierosolomonia*. Thus one of the poets says: “Hiero, whom Salomonia bore to the king.”

By their own words the magi confessed that the one they sought was at once man, king, and God. They show that they seek a man when they say, “Where is he who has been born?”; a king, when they add, “King of the Jews”; and they confess that he is God when they add, “For we saw his star in the east and have come to worship him.”

But perhaps someone asks why a star, an indication of the Lord’s birth, appeared to the magi in the east, whereas an angel announced that same birth to the shepherds in Judea. The answer is that it was fitting for the shepherds, who were Israelites and knew the God of heaven, that a rational creature—that is, an angel—should appear and instruct them concerning the Lord’s birth; whereas for the magi, as Gentiles and lacking reason, an irrational creature, a star, should appear. Shining in the sky with an unwonted radiance, it showed that the king of heaven had been born on earth. Thus, instructed, the former by an angel and the latter by a star, they might run to the cornerstone and be made from the two peoples into one wall, joined by him of whom the Apostle says: “He himself is our peace, who made both one and joined the middle wall, destroying enmities in his flesh; and coming, he preached peace to those who were far off and those who were near” (Ephesians 2).

But perhaps someone asks whether this star remained in the starry heaven like the others, or moved through the air or over the earth. The answer is that it was neither fixed in the starry heaven nor on the earth, but moved through the air, so as to be the guide and forerunner of the magi as far as the newborn child. It is believed neither to have existed before nor to have remained afterward; rather, when a new man was born into the world, a new star appeared in the sky. For all the elements recognized that their Creator had come into the world. Heaven recognized him, because immediately at his birth it sent forth a new star; the sea recognized him, because it offered itself to be trodden beneath his feet; the sun recognized him, because at his death it hid the rays of its light; rocks and stones recognized him, because they were split when he died; the earth recognized him, because it trembled when he rose again (Matthew 27). Yet the hard and foolish hearts of the Jews still do not recognize him whom irrational creatures recognized.

Nor should this be passed over: there were Priscillianist heretics who said that every person is born under the fate of the stars. To support their error, they wished to invoke the fact that, as soon as the Lord was born, his star appeared in the east. We reply to them, on the contrary, that it was not the child who came to the star, but the star to the child. If it were permissible to speak in this manner, the child might more readily be believed to be the star’s fate than the star the child’s fate. They said that those born under the sign of Libra would become bankers; yet many peoples have no bankers, although many persons among them, as in other lands, are born under that sign. They also said that those born under Aquarius would become fishermen, although without doubt many people are born under the same star, as in other regions, who are not fishermen.

For in France and in the kingdoms of many peoples, kings customarily succeed by descent. No one is ignorant that, under the same sign and at the same hour in which a king’s son is born, many of servile condition are born in the same kingdom under the same star. Yet when the king’s son grows up, he is exalted to the dignity of kingship, while those born with him remain in servitude until death. But lest these arguments seem slight for destroying the heresy of the Priscillianists, let us also bring forward the authority of Holy Scripture. We read that at one and the same hour Rebecca their mother bore two sons from the same womb, Esau and Jacob; yet one was chosen and the other rejected, the Lord saying: “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated” (Romans 9). If fate existed, either both would have been chosen or both rejected. From all this we recognize that not fateful accidents but divine providence orders and disposes human life.

But astrologers customarily object that the fateful constellation arises at the instant of the midwife’s touch. We answer them, conversely, that a human being is not born in an instant but undergoes delays in being born. And if fate were to be believed in, as many fates would have to be believed as there are limbs of a human body. Therefore the star that appeared in the east did not help the newborn child in any respect; rather, it was a sign of his birth, and by its radiance it illumined the minds of the magi to seek him who had been born.

Perhaps someone also asks who these magi were, or from what people they came, who so eagerly sought the newborn child in order to worship him. We set forth different opinions concerning them, so that he may choose what he judges sounder. Some said that they came from Tarsus or Arabia and wished the prophecy to have been fulfilled in them literally: “The kings of Tarshish and the islands shall offer gifts; the kings of the Arabs and of Sheba shall bring presents”; and again: “All shall come from Sheba, bringing gold and incense and proclaiming praise to the Lord.” Others said that they came from the region of the Persians, as a certain learned man says:

“Then he commands the swift Persians to hasten their steps.”

Most thought that they were Chaldeans, because the Chaldeans considered the stars of heaven gods and were most skilled in the art of astronomy. Others also said that they were descended from the line of the prophet Balaam. As soon as they saw the new star, they understood that the king had been born, and, recalling Balaam’s prophecy (Numbers 24), “A star shall rise from Jacob, and a man shall arise from Israel, and he shall rule the nations,” they were the first to hasten with gifts to worship him.

But whichever of these they were, it must be known that they were the first fruits of the Gentiles and signified the Gentiles who would believe in Christ. They are rightly said to have been three magi, because the Gentile people, coming to faith, learned to confess the undivided Trinity as God. Or they were three because those who worship God ought to possess three chief virtues: faith, hope, and charity. Or indeed they were three because those who desire to see God ought to guard their thought, speech, and action from evils, and occupy memory, understanding, and will with good things. Or again, the three magi came with three gifts because the Gentile people, coming to faith, brought with it three natural disciplines: physics, ethics, and logic—that is, natural, moral, and rational knowledge.

“But when King Herod heard it, he was troubled, and all Jerusalem with him.” Herod, as we have said, held the Jewish kingdom deceitfully and craftily. As soon as he heard that the king of the Jews had been born, he was troubled in mind, fearing a successor and fearing to lose justly what he held unjustly. He did not understand that the latter had not come to take away an earthly kingdom but to confer an eternal one upon believers.

Since it is said that not Herod only, but all Jerusalem with him, was troubled, it must be understood that not all were troubled in the same way by the one question of the magi. Some were troubled through envy, like Herod; others through fear, like the Jews, who, hearing that a king of the Jews was being sought, feared that some occasion of trouble would arise for them, both from Herod and from the Romans. Others, however, were troubled neither through envy nor fear, but from joy alone: such as the aged Simeon, the widow Anna, and others like them, who had learned through the revelation of the Holy Spirit that Christ’s birth was near. When they heard that what they had desired with all their wishes had occurred, they were troubled by excessive joy. For we learn from Peter’s example that the human mind is customarily troubled by great joy: when he saw the Lord transfigured on the mountain, he was troubled and did not know what to say.

“Then, summoning all the chief priests and scribes of the people, he inquired of them where Christ was to be born.” In the fact that Herod, having heard of the birth of a new king, questioned the priests and teachers of Scripture, he left us an example worthy of imitation: whenever something new arises in the Church, we should always return to the authority of Scripture, because it is written, “Do everything with counsel,” and we should give the answers that we know our fathers gave or upheld. In accordance with Solomon’s saying [Col. 0112B], “Let us not transgress the ancient boundaries,” which our fathers established, let us fulfill what is said through the prophet Jeremiah: “Stand upon the roads, and ask about the ancient paths, which is the good way, and walk in it” (Jeremiah VI). But when Herod asked the priests and scribes where Christ was to be born, they answered what they had read and learned, saying:

“In Bethlehem of Judah,” confirming this by prophetic authority, saying:

“And you, Bethlehem, land of Judah, are by no means least among the rulers of Judah.” For they knew not only that Christ would be born, but also where Christ would be born. Since the Holy Spirit wished to remove every opportunity for unbelief, he foretold through the prophets not only [Col. 0112C] that Christ would be born, but also designated the place where he would be born, saying through Micah: “And you, Bethlehem, land of Judah, are by no means least,” and so forth—as if he were saying: O Bethlehem, which lies in the land of Judah, you appear smaller in the multitude of your people, narrower in the breadth of your walls, lower in the height of your towers; but you will by no means be least. Why? Because “from you will come forth a ruler who will govern my people Israel.”

One has already gone forth from you, but another will go forth. David, the son of Jesse, went forth, born in time and dying in time; the Son of God will go forth from the womb of the Virgin Mary, born in time but remaining eternally. David went forth, handsome and beautiful, but [Col. 0112D] he will go forth who is “beautiful beyond the sons of men.” David went forth, governing the kingdom of Israel rationally for a time; and the Son of God will go forth, defending Israel—that is, those who see God—from the attacks of demons with spiritual weapons, and in the future leading them to the pastures of the heavenly kingdom.

“Then Herod secretly summoned the magi and carefully learned from them the time when the star had appeared to them.” After Herod had learned the place of Christ’s birth from the authority of Scripture, he turned his mind to crafty ambushes, considering how he might secretly destroy the one whom he had openly heard they were seeking. Having secretly summoned the magi—that is, privately—he carefully learned from them the time when the star had appeared to them. He did this so that, if the magi did not return to him, as later [Col. 0113A] happened, he might kill the one he feared by slaughtering all the boys in Bethlehem from the time when he had heard that the king of the Jews had been born. The fool did not understand that “there is no wisdom, no prudence, no counsel against the Lord.”

“And sending them to Bethlehem, he said: ‘Go and inquire carefully about the child, and when you have found him, report to me, so that I too may come and worship him.’” With the same cunning by which Herod had fraudulently seized the kingdom of the Jews, he persisted also in plotting the Lord’s death, promising to worship the one whom he intended to kill. His example is now followed by pretenders, that is, hypocrites, who display outwardly an appearance of holiness that they do not possess inwardly. Although with Herod they seek God with a deceitful heart, they are not deemed worthy [Col. 0113B] to find him, because just as the Lord is near to all who call upon him in truth, so salvation is far from sinners. Hence Herod is rightly interpreted as “leathery” or “the glory of skin,” because when hypocrites outwardly desire to glory as though in a good work, inwardly they are alike foul and savage in their cunning, according to what the Lord says: “Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly are ravenous wolves” (Matthew VII).

“When they had heard the king, they departed.” This did not happen by chance, but by God’s will: the star that had gone before the magi left them as they approached Herod, so that they might announce to the Jews that Christ had been born and learn from them, on the authority of [Col. 0113C] Scripture, the place of his birth. But after they had departed from Herod, “behold, the star which they had seen in the east went before them, as before, until it came and stood over the place where the child was.”

We therefore learn that the Lord’s grace may appropriately be represented by this star, and the devil by Herod. When the magi entered Herod’s presence, the star abandoned them, because divine grace deserts those who submit themselves to the devil’s service. But if they leave Herod—if, by repentance, they shake the devil’s yoke from their necks and begin to seek God—divine grace will appear to them again; it will enlighten them again and once more show them the way by which the Lord may be found.

It often happens that the soul rejoices with greater gladness when it receives God’s grace after sin than it rejoiced in possessing it before [Col. 0113D] sin. Thus, when the Lord explained in the Gospel the parable of the lost and recovered sheep, he said: “I tell you, there will be more joy in heaven over one sinner who repents than over ninety-nine righteous persons who have no need of repentance” (Luke XV). And concerning the return of the prodigal son, when the elder son had become sorrowful, he heard from his father: “Son, you ought to rejoice, because your brother was dead and has come to life; he was lost and has been found” (Luke XV). Hence it is rightly said now of the magi:

“But when they saw the star, they rejoiced with exceedingly great joy; and entering the house, they found the child with Mary his mother.” No one doubts that the star had shown the magi in the east that the king of the Jews had been born. By standing over the house where [Col. 0114A] the child was, it gave a certain sign and indication, so that they might recognize without doubt that he was the one whose birth in Judea they had learned of while they were in the east.

How great he was whom they saw to be small is made clear when it is added: “And falling down, they worshiped him.” For the one whom they worshiped with their faces bowed to the ground, they undoubtedly believed to be God. And because they understood that he had become mortal man for our sake, they proclaimed him by their mystical gifts as God, king, and likewise man. Hence it follows: “And opening their treasures, they offered him gifts: gold, frankincense, and myrrh.”

Gold is fitting for a king; frankincense is offered in God’s sacrifice; with myrrh the bodies of the dead are embalmed. Holy faith never [Col. 0114B] ceases to offer all these things truly to Christ, while it believes him to be one and the same true God, true king, and true man, and truly recognizes that he died for us.

When, therefore, the magi believed the one and the same child to be God, king, and likewise man, they offered him gold, frankincense, and myrrh together. There were, however, certain heretics who offered him gold and frankincense but refused to offer myrrh, because they believed him to be God reigning everywhere but disdained to believe that he had become man. Again, there were others who offered him only myrrh and refused to offer gold and frankincense, because they believed him to be merely a man, and did not understand divinity in him.

But let us shun the examples of these people and offer gold to our king [Col. 0114C], so that we may believe him to reign everywhere. Let us also offer frankincense, so that we may confess him to be the true God and Creator of all things, existing without beginning. Let us offer him myrrh as well, and have no doubt that for our salvation he assumed a mortal body.

Alternatively, the opening of the treasures signifies the inner hearts of the saints. Gold signifies the splendor of speech, as Solomon says: “A desirable treasure rests in the mouth of the wise” (Proverbs XXI). Frankincense, which is offered in God’s sacrifice, signifies pure prayer accompanied by contrition of heart. Myrrh, with which the bodies of the dead are embalmed, signifies the mortification of vices.

We therefore offer gifts to our king as often as we devote the secret places of our hearts to his praises, as it is said through the Psalmist: “Your vows are upon me, O God [Col. 0114D]; I will render praises to you” (Psalm LVI). When our treasures are opened, we offer him gold whenever we attribute to his grace everything that we rightly understand and say. We offer something like frankincense when in our prayer we present a contrite heart and a humbled spirit, saying with the Psalmist: “Let my prayer be directed like incense in your sight” (Psalm CXL). We offer something like myrrh when, for his love, we mortify the desires of our flesh, fulfilling what the Apostle says: “Put to death your members that are upon the earth,” namely, “fornication, uncleanness, covetousness,” and things like these (Colossians III).

“And having received an answer in a dream not to return to Herod, they went back to their own region [Col. 0115A] by another way.” So that Herod might not be able to carry out his cruelty against the child by cunning, the angel forestalled his plots, warning the magi in a dream not to return to Herod.

But the magi left us an example worthy of imitation in their conduct when they returned to their own region by another way. Our own proper region is paradise, because we were created for this purpose: if the first man had not sinned, we would have enjoyed the delights of paradise without bodily death. Since we fell from it through sin, it is necessary that we return to it through repentance, as if by another way. We who fell by pride, disobedience, and tasting what was forbidden must return to it by another way—that is, by humbling ourselves, obeying, and abstaining not only from what is unlawful but also from what is lawful. May he himself deign to grant [Col. 0115B] this, who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY XVI. ON THE OCTAVE OF THE EPIPHANY

(John I.) “At that time, John saw Jesus coming toward him, and said: ‘Behold the Lamb of God,’” and so forth.

In the brevity of this reading we must consider how fully the inseparable essence of the Trinity is commended to us. For when the Son is baptized, the Father’s voice is heard, and the Holy Spirit is seen in the form of a dove; one deity in substance and three in persons are thereby declared.

In this passage also the holiness of the Lord’s forerunner is commended. Though he was a man born of human beings, by divine grace he was brought to such greatness that he not only [Col. 0115C] baptized the Son of God in human form, but also heard the Father’s voice thunder from above and saw the Holy Spirit in the form of a dove.

But let us examine everything in order.

“John,” he says, “saw Jesus coming toward him.” This vision must not be understood as pertaining only to bodily eyes, but also to spiritual ones. He saw him walking in the body, but understood that divinity dwelt in him; and therefore he cried out, saying: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world.”

It was as if he were saying: Behold the innocent one among sinners, the just one among the rejected, the pious one among the impious. For although he assumed true human flesh from Adam, he nevertheless took no sin from Adam’s origin. Therefore he is able to take away the sins of the world. Although he was a man among human beings, no [Col. 0115D] trace of sin could be found in him, for, as the apostle Peter says: “He committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth.”

The Lord is called a lamb not according to nature but figuratively, because just as a lamb was offered in sacrifice for the sins of the people, so he offered himself as a sacrifice to the Father for us, as a pleasing fragrance, and washed away the stains of our sins with his blood, as it is said through John in the Apocalypse: “He loved us and washed us from our sins in his blood” (Revelation I).

The paschal lamb in the Old Testament also held this type and figure. In remembrance of Israel’s deliverance, it was commanded to be sacrificed every year at Passover, signifying that lamb whose sacred passion [Col. 0116A] Isaiah foretold, saying: “He will be led like a sheep to the slaughter, and like a lamb before its shearer he will be silent, and he will not open his mouth” (Isaiah LIII).

This is that lamb of whom John says in the Apocalypse: “I saw a lamb standing as though slain, having seven horns and seven eyes” (Revelation V). And again: “I saw a lamb standing upon Mount Zion, and with him one hundred and forty-four thousand who were purchased from the earth.”

By what order this lamb takes away the sins of the world, the apostle Peter indicates when he says: “You were not redeemed with perishable things, gold or silver, from your vain manner of life inherited from your fathers, but with the precious blood, as of an unblemished and spotless lamb, Christ” (1 Peter I).

The Lord did not take away the sins of the world only when he offered himself as a unique sacrifice for the world; he also [Col. 0116B] takes away the sins of the world daily, when through communion in his body and blood he washes the souls of the faithful from the stains of sins. In accordance with this, when he handed on to his disciples the mystery of his body and blood, he said: “This is the cup of my blood of the New Testament, which will be poured out for you and for many for the forgiveness of sins. Do this whenever you drink it in remembrance of me” (Mark XIV).

Let us hear what testimony his forerunner bears to the Lord:

“This is he of whom I said: ‘After me comes a man who has been made before me.’” [Col. 0116C] In these words he reveals both the human and divine nature when he says: “After me comes a man who has been made before me.”

It was as if he were saying: “After me he comes,” because he was born after me and will begin preaching after me. “He has been made before me,” because he has been preferred to me in dignity. For in Scripture “before” does not always refer to time; sometimes it refers to dignity, as it is written concerning Joseph’s sons: “He placed Ephraim before Manasseh” (Genesis XLVIII)—that is, he showed that Ephraim would be greater in grace and dignity.

Or certainly, when he says, “After me comes a man,” he indicates the order of human nature. But when he adds, “He has been made before me,” he shows the excellence of divine power. It was as if he were saying: Although he was born after me, he surpasses me because the sequence of times of birth does not restrict him in his divinity.

Hence he appropriately adds: “Because he was before me.” In these words he indicates the one of whom John said at the beginning of his Gospel: “In [Col. 0116D] the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John I).

The Lord is beautifully called a man by his forerunner, for “man” is derived from strength. This name is especially fitting for him who, like a meek and humble lamb, alone was able to overcome the savagery of the lion. Concerning him it is written: “Behold, a man; his name is the Rising One” (Zechariah VI).

“And I did not know him.” Although it is manifest to all the faithful that John knew the Lord—he had sensed him while still in his mother’s womb and had borne witness to him, saying, “I ought to be baptized by you, and you come to me?” (Matthew III), along with many similar statements—what does he mean now by saying, “I did not know him”?

This must be understood in the following way: when he baptized him, he grew [Col. 0117A] so greatly in his knowledge of him that, in comparison with that knowledge, he considered himself to have known nothing of what he had previously understood about him. Therefore he says, “And I did not know him,” as if he were saying: I did not know him so perfectly, since I had not yet discovered such greatness of divinity in him.

When the Lord’s baptizer heard the Father’s voice thunder from above and saw the Holy Spirit descending in the form of a dove, there is no doubt that through this sight and hearing he made great progress in divine knowledge.

But because God the Father revealed his Son to John so that through John’s preaching he might be shown to others, it rightly follows: “But the reason I came baptizing in water was that he might be manifested to Israel.” This is plainly to say: I was not sent to baptize in water so that by baptizing [Col. 0117B] I might be able to take away sins, but so that in that baptism I might foreshadow the baptism of the one who was to come after me and baptize in the Holy Spirit.

He alone baptizes in the Holy Spirit who, through the Holy Spirit, forgives sins in baptism. He says in the Gospel: “Unless one is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (John III). Concerning this baptism, as he was about to ascend into heaven, he said to his disciples: “You will be baptized with the Holy Spirit not many days from now” (Acts XI).

The Lord makes clear elsewhere that this occurs invisibly, not visibly (John III). After saying of the same Spirit, “The Spirit breathes where he wills, and you hear his voice, but you do not know where he comes from or where he goes,” he immediately added: “So is everyone who is born of the Spirit.”

And because everyone who receives divine knowledge ought to announce it to others [Col. 0117C], it rightly follows concerning this same John:

“And John bore witness, saying: ‘I saw the Spirit descending like a dove from heaven, and it remained upon him.’”

In these words we must ask not only why the Holy Spirit is sometimes said to have been seen in the form of a dove and sometimes in tongues of fire, but also why he appeared over the Lord in the form of a dove and over the apostles in fire, so that he was seen neither over the Lord in fire nor over the apostles in the form of a dove. Each of these matters must therefore be explained.

Because the dove is a simple bird, the Holy Spirit rightly appeared in the form of a dove, [Col. 0117D] to show that he dwells in the hearts of those who are meek and humble of heart, preserve harmonious unity with their brothers, and pursue peace and holiness with everyone, according to what is written: “Upon whom will the Holy Spirit rest, if not upon the humble and quiet one, who trembles at my words?” This is signified by the kisses of doves.

But because fire kindles and illuminates whatever it touches, the same Spirit rightly appeared in the vision of fire, because he inflames the heart he touches with love and enlightens it to perceive his will.

This is the fire of which the Savior says in the Gospel: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire except that it burn?” (Luke XII). Of this fire it is said through Moses [Col. 0118A]: “In his right hand was a fiery law” (Deuteronomy XXXIII); and through the Apostle: “For our God is a consuming fire” (Hebrews XII).

By this fire the hearts of those people had been warmed who said: “Was not our heart burning within us while he spoke to us on the road and opened the Scriptures to us?” (Luke XXIV).

We quickly understand why he appeared over the Lord in the form of a dove and over the apostles in fire if we consider more carefully the quality of each person. Since the dove, as we have said, is a simple bird, the Holy Spirit rightly appeared over the Lord in the form of a dove, because at his first coming he came not to punish our sins in zeal but to forgive them in meekness.

But because the apostles, as ordinary human beings, had not only to be refined [Col. 0118B] of the rust of their sins but also to be kindled with zeal for righteousness in order to preach the Gospel, the same Spirit rightly appeared over them in tongues of fire.

But since we have heard from today’s reading that the Holy Spirit appeared in the form of a dove, let us return more attentively to consider the nature of the dove, so that if we wish to receive the Holy Spirit, we may preserve in our minds what the dove possesses in its body.

The dove is said to possess seven natural characteristics: first, it lacks the bitterness of gall; second, it is accustomed to utter groans instead of singing; third, it flies or mourns in a flock; fourth, it delights in sitting near flowing waters, so that it may more easily guard against the hawk’s arrival; fifth, it eats nothing living; sixth, it does not defend itself with claws or beak like other birds, but strikes with its wings [Col. 0118C] in defending itself; seventh, it builds its nest in rocks.

The dove therefore lacks the bitterness of gall; and we, in accordance with the apostle Peter’s admonition, should put away all anger, deceit, and envy (1 Peter II).

The dove has groans instead of song; and we, placed in the valley of tears, should mourn not only for the remission of sins but also in our misery for the reception of eternal life. Let us grieve after the example of the one who said: “Every night I wash my bed; I drench my couch with my tears” (Psalm VI), so that what the Lord says may be fulfilled in us: “Blessed are you who weep now, for you will laugh” (Luke VI).

The dove flies in a flock; and let us love unanimity [Col. 0118D], offering for the Lord’s sake whatever good we can not only to our friends but also to our enemies, so that we may be counted among those of whom it is said: “The multitude of believers had one heart and one soul” (Acts IV); and again: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is when brothers dwell together” (Psalm CXXXII).

The dove is accustomed to sit near flowing waters so that it may more easily beware of the hawk’s arrival; and so that we may foresee and avoid the devil’s snares, let us devote ourselves gladly to meditation on the Scriptures, so that what is said in praise of the Church may be fulfilled in us: “Your eyes are like the eyes of doves” (Song V), which have been washed with milk and sit beside abundant streams; and again: “Your eyes are like the eyes of doves” (Song IV), apart from what lies hidden within.

The dove eats nothing living; and we, [Col. 0119A] according to the Apostle’s teaching (Colossians III), should put to death our members that are upon the earth, namely, fornication, uncleanness, and covetousness, which is the service of idols.

The dove does not defend itself with claws or beak; and whenever we suffer persecution from the unjust, let us not be stirred to revenge, but rather, following the examples of the saints, let us love patience, lest our tongue become a weapon, an arrow, and a sharp sword. Let us fear what the apostle Paul says: “If you bite and devour one another, take care that you are not consumed by one another” (Galatians V), so that this may be fulfilled: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called sons of God” (Matthew V).

The dove builds its nest in rocks; and let us place all our hope and strength in the rock that is Christ, saying with the Psalmist: “You have exalted me upon a rock; you have led me, because you have become my hope, a tower of strength against the enemy” (Psalm LX).

Moses had placed his nest [Col. 0119B] in the openings of this rock when he was deemed worthy to hear from the Lord: “There is a place with me, and you shall stand there in the opening of the rock” (Exodus XXXIII).

If, therefore, we wish to have the Holy Spirit dwelling in our hearts, let us diligently hold fast to these spiritual virtues, so that what is said in praise of the whole Church in the Song of Songs by the voice of the bridegroom may apply especially to us: “Come, my bride, my chosen one, my dove, in the openings of the rock, in the caverns of the wall. Show me your face; let your voice sound in my ears” (Song II).

The Lord wanted his disciples to be such people [Col. 0119C], to whom he said: “Be wise as serpents and simple as doves” (Matthew X).

The seven characteristics of the dove are beautifully enumerated because the Holy Spirit, who appeared on this day over the Redeemer of the world, has seven principal gifts, of which Isaiah says: “The Spirit of the Lord will rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and piety, and he will be filled with the spirit of the fear of the Lord” (Isaiah XI).

The Scriptures of the Old and New Testaments agree with one another in wondrous harmony. We read that when Noah wished to know whether the waters of the flood had subsided, he sent out a dove, which returned to him in the evening carrying in its mouth a branch of an olive tree with green leaves (Genesis VIII).

Now, when the Lord had been baptized, the heavens were opened [Col. 0119D] and the dove appeared to his forerunner. Just as baptism is prefigured by the flood, so the anointing of the Holy Spirit, which is bestowed upon the faithful in baptism, is expressed by the dove that carried in its mouth a branch of an olive tree with green leaves. Concerning this anointing John says: “His anointing teaches you about everything” (1 John II).

But what the baptizer adds in his own voice:

“And I did not know him,”

must be understood as we explained above: in comparison with what he later came to know, he had previously known little about him. Therefore a certain sign of his knowledge is given when it follows:

“But the one who sent me to baptize in water said to me: ‘The one upon whom you see the Spirit descending and remaining, this is he who baptizes in the Holy Spirit.’”

Here it is asked why the Father [Col. 0120A] wished to give such a sign for recognizing his only-begotten Son, when the same Son promises his disciples, saying: “I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete, so that he may remain with you forever—the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father. The world cannot receive him, because it neither sees him nor knows him; but you will know him, because he will remain with you and will be in you” (John XIV).

If the Spirit therefore remains in the disciples, what is so remarkable if he descended upon and remained with the only-begotten Son of God?

The answer is readily apparent: they received him in one way, and he in another. For the Spirit was given to them according to measure, whereas in him “all the fullness of divinity dwells bodily” (Colossians II).

They received the Spirit in time; but he possessed the fullness of that same Spirit [Col. 0120B] from the moment when, through the overshadowing of the Holy Spirit, he was conceived within the Virgin’s womb, as it is said through the Psalmist: “God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Psalm XLIV).

We may also say that the same Spirit always remains in the minds of the faithful for one purpose, and comes to them in order to depart for another. He remains with them so that they may live soberly, justly, and piously in this world; but he departs from them so that they may not always perform bodily works.

The Spirit came to them in such a way that, if they changed their will from a good purpose, he would depart from them. But in the Lord it was not the case that the Spirit’s grace became greater from the time of his baptism. Rather, the Spirit appeared visibly [Col. 0120C] at his baptism so that the faithful might understand that through his baptism they receive the gifts of the same Holy Spirit.

How truthfully and without any doubt the things recalled in this reading must be believed, the Lord’s forerunner took care to make clear when he added:

“And I saw and bore witness that this is the Son of God.”

Here it must be considered that in this brief reading the teachings of two heretics are destroyed: those of Manichaeus and Photinus. One denied that Christ was truly human; the other denied that he was truly God.

Let Manichaeus therefore be ashamed when he hears: “After me comes a man.” Let Photinus also be ashamed when the Lord’s forerunner cries out: “I saw and bore witness that this is the Son of God.”

Let the meek hear and rejoice, believing without doubt that this is the Son [Col. 0120D] of Man, who was baptized as a man, and that this same one is the Son of God. Let them confess with Peter: “You are the Son of the living God” (Matthew XVI).

## HOMILY XVII. THE FIRST SUNDAY AFTER THE EPIPHANY

(Luke II.) “At that time, when Jesus was twelve years old, as they were going up to Jerusalem,” and so forth.

The teachers of ecclesiastical instruction and transmitters of divine Scripture reasonably describe the evangelist Luke as possessing the likeness of a calf among the four living creatures, as is found in Ezekiel and in John’s Apocalypse. For just as a calf was offered in sacrifice to the Lord [Col. 0121A] in the temple by the priests, so Luke, more particularly than the other evangelists, took care to recall the things that the Lord did in or around the temple.

He began the opening of his Gospel with the priest Zechariah, saying—for the priests themselves offered a calf on the day of their ordination:

“There was in the days of Herod, king of Judea, a certain priest named Zechariah, of the division of Abijah, and his wife was from the daughters of Aaron. And it happened that, while he was serving as priest in the order of his division before God, according to the custom of the priesthood, he was chosen by lot to offer incense, and he entered the temple of the Lord.”

After this he reports that the Virgin Mary came to the house of that same priest and remained there with her kinswoman Elizabeth for three months.

He also narrates that the Lord was not only [Col. 0121B] circumcised on the eighth day, but was presented in the temple on the thirty-third day; that gifts were offered for him; and that he was received and blessed by the prophet Simeon.

He traces the Savior’s genealogy not through King Solomon but through Nathan, the prophet and priest, the son of David.

In the present reading, therefore, he describes the Savior, when he was twelve years old, coming with his parents to the temple and remaining there without their knowledge. At the end of his Gospel also he shows the Lord Jesus Christ ascending into heaven as a true priest while blessing his disciples, saying: “He lifted up his hands and blessed them. And it happened that, while he blessed them, he withdrew from them and was carried up into heaven; and they worshiped him and returned [Col. 0121C] to Jerusalem with great joy, and they were continually in the temple, praising and blessing God.”

How diligently the Savior’s parents observed the law we can quickly understand if we briefly attend to the earlier part of this Gospel. The Evangelist says:

“And the parents of Jesus went every year to Jerusalem on the solemn day of Passover.”

The Lord not only wished to observe the law, which he had not come to abolish but to fulfill; he also chose parents who were observers of the law. For he himself had commanded in the law that every male among them should appear three times a year before the Lord, in the place that God had chosen.

Here we see with what care they observed the greater commandments of the law, since they did not neglect even the lesser ones. It was the custom of the Jews [Col. 0121D], as we have said, to go up to Jerusalem every year to worship the Lord and offer gifts to him, in remembrance of their departure from the land of Egypt and the sacrifice of the lamb.

As the Lord’s parents therefore went up according to this custom for prayer, Jesus, having reached the age of twelve, went up with them.

But when you hear that he was made, do not doubt that he was the Maker. He was made in the form of a servant, though he had made all things in the form of God, as it is written: “All things were made through him” (John I). Concerning him the Apostle says: “He was made from the seed of David according to the flesh” (Romans I).

And, so to speak, he who had made everything was made so that the one who had been rightly made but had perished through wrongdoing might be found again. In his humanity he ascended in his twelfth year [Col. 0122A], while in his divinity he has no passage of time.

The Lord, at the age of twelve, beautifully wished to reveal the beginnings of his childhood by questioning the priests, thereby prefiguring through this number the mystery of apostolic preaching and making the knowledge of his divinity known to the world.

The number twelve is perfect and, divided into its parts, signifies perfection. It is divided into three fours and four threes. Whether you multiply three by four or four by three, you complete the number twelve.

The same number also consists of the parts of the number seven, namely, the first even number and the first odd number—that is, three and four. Three pertains to the indivisible Trinity; four to the four books of the holy Gospel. Seven signifies the fullness of time, because the course of the present life revolves through seven days. Twelve likewise [Col. 0122B] refers either to the twelve apostles or to the twelve patriarchs.

Since, therefore, the faith of the Holy Trinity and the teaching of the four Gospels were to be announced to the world through the preaching of the twelve apostles, the Lord rightly went up to the temple at the age of twelve.

“When the days had been completed and they were returning, the boy Jesus remained in Jerusalem, and his parents did not know it.” Someone may perhaps wonder how Jesus, who had been raised with such care by his parents—especially since they did not doubt that he was the Son of God—could remain in Jerusalem without their knowledge.

It must be understood that, apart from the divine mystery, this happened not through the parents’ negligence [Col. 0122C] but rather through the custom of the Jews. Their custom was that, when they went up to the Lord’s temple to celebrate the solemn feast, the men formed separate groups and the women separate groups, for the sake of the purity of chastity. Children of lesser age, however, were free to go with whichever parent they wished, whether with their father or with their mother.

Because of this custom, it happened that the boy Jesus remained in Jerusalem without their knowledge: Mary thought that he was with Joseph, and Joseph assumed that he was with Mary. And this is what follows:

“But supposing him to be in their company, they traveled a day’s journey and sought him among their relatives and acquaintances.”

How great was the affection of love they had toward him is shown when it follows:

[Col. 0122D] “And when they did not find him, they returned to Jerusalem, seeking him. And it came to pass that after three days they found him in the temple.” It is not without mystery that the Lord was found by his parents in the temple after three days. For there are three periods: before the Law, under the Law, and under grace. Since, therefore, he who appeared visibly to the world not before the Law or under the Law, but under grace, is rightly said to have been found in the temple after three days. Or, alternatively, he wished to be found in the temple after three days to show that those will attain to his vision who perfectly possess faith, hope, and charity, and who believe the faith of the holy Trinity with a pure heart and preserve it in their works. Or again, he wished to be found in the temple after three days so that we might understand that we shall deserve to arrive happily at his vision if we guard our thoughts, speech, and actions from evil deeds, and occupy our memory, understanding, and will in his service.

Where he was found is shown when it says: “In the temple, in the midst of the teachers.” What he was doing is made clear when it adds:

“Listening to them and questioning them.” For he was not found somewhere idle or engaged in frivolous talk, but in the temple, listening to the teachers and questioning them. At the same time the Lord offered us an example of the humility that must be learned, since he is found in the temple not teaching but learning and asking questions, fulfilling the Mosaic injunction: “Ask your fathers, and they will tell you; your elders, and they will declare it to you (Deut. XXXII).” So that we may not be ashamed to learn from teachers, he questions the teachers in the temple who teaches the angels in heaven. In this action not only is human pride confounded, but presumption and rashness are also restrained. For there are some who wish to teach before they have reached the years of puberty; and therefore they become teachers of error, because they were not disciples of truth. Thus the apprenticeship of one who is to be placed at the summit of governance must be tested over a long period and through many exercises, and one who desires to teach must learn for a long time. Hence Solomon says: “A time for keeping silence and a time for speaking (Eccli. III).” He does not say first a time for speaking and afterward a time for keeping silence, but first a time for keeping silence and afterward a time for speaking, so that we may understand that by first keeping silent we must learn what we are afterward to teach by speaking. Again the same man admonishes us, saying: “At every time of your leisure, write down wisdom; but those who are diminished in activity will acquire it (Eccli. XXXVIII).”

On the contrary, if the Son of God, who was going to preach at the age of thirty, is found at the age of twelve not teaching but listening and questioning in the temple, he thereby shows that the proper time must be observed, whether for the priesthood or for ecclesiastical teaching. At this age Joseph, that is, at thirty years, was appointed lord of Egypt. At this age David, who in childhood had crushed the mouths of lions and bears, assumed the government of the kingdom. At this age the prophet Ezekiel saw the heavens opened over the river Chebar. And although childish simplicity is better than senile foolishness, it must nevertheless be observed in both cases that gravity of character and mature age agree in the conduct of those chosen for ecclesiastical teaching. Hence also, in the Law, the Lord rightly commanded concerning the Levites that they should minister with their brothers in the temple up to the age of fifty, but after the age of fifty should become guardians of the vessels. For what are the holy vessels except the souls of the saints? And because after the age of fifty the vigor of life begins to fail, this command shows that those are to be chosen to guard souls who, through long exercises, have learned to extinguish the stimulus of lust or the heat of desire. Finally, even if Daniel and Jeremiah are read to have been sent to prophesy in childhood, it must be understood that the Lord’s miracles are not to be drawn into examples for imitation. The Lord’s marvelous works are rather to be revered [Col. 0124A] than imitated, since they cannot be performed by everyone.

“And all were astonished at his understanding and his answers, and so forth.” They saw him small in body and age, but great in his questions and answers, considering him a human being and not God. We, however, should not be astonished with the Jewish elders at his understanding and answers, but should believe him to be true God and true man, from whom all wisdom comes, and with whom it always was and is before the ages. He also speaks in Proverbs, saying: “I, Wisdom, dwell in counsel; through me kings reign. Counsel and justice are mine; I came forth from the mouth of the Most High (Prov. VIII).”

How deeply, meanwhile, the spirit of the blessed virgin, the Mother of God, was wounded by the loss of her son is declared in this passage:

“And his mother said to him: Son, why have you done this to us? and so forth.” The Virgin Mother had sought him for three days in anxious sorrow. After finding him, placed between grief and joy, she reproached him with loving correction, as though he had presumed to do such things, saying: “Son, why have you done this to us? Behold, your father and I, grieving, were seeking you.” She calls Joseph his father, not because he was truly his father, as the Photinians maintained, but because, in order to preserve Mary’s reputation, he was regarded by everyone as his father. But who his true Father is, he himself reveals when he answers them:

“Why were you seeking me? Did you not know that I must be in the things that belong to my Father?” In these words he should not be thought to have angered his mother. Nor should we omit the fact that in this reading the Lord commends both his natures to us when, found in the temple, he says: “I must be in the things that belong to my Father.” As a human being, he went up to Jerusalem with his parents; but as God, without their knowing it, he remained in the temple. As a human being, he questioned the elders; but as God, he answered matters at which the elders marveled. As a human being, he is found in the temple; but as God, once found in the temple, he said: “I must be in the things that belong to my Father.” Since that house had been built in God’s honor, he demonstrated that he was the Son of God when, found in the temple, he said: “I must be in the things that belong to my Father.” The temple, the prophets, and the frequent meditation on the divine Scriptures belonged to that Father. And he beautifully demonstrated in these works of his that he was the Son of God.

“And when they saw him, they were astonished.” For the Lord not only questioned humbly but also answered subtly.

“And all who heard him were astonished at his understanding and his answers.” It is proper for sons to possess their father’s inheritance and to remain and exist in it. Therefore the Lord Jesus Christ remained and dwelt in the temple to show that he was not of lesser power than the Father. For those who have one majesty do not have unequal power, as he himself says: “I and the Father are one (John X),” and: “Everything that belongs to the Father is mine.”

[Col. 0125A] “And they did not understand the word that he spoke to them.” Because they were not yet able to grasp the mystery of the divine nature, they did not understand the word that he spoke to them—namely, what he had said about the Father. And because he saw that they could not understand his divinity, he accommodated himself to them through his humanity, in order to lift their hearts toward his divinity. Hence it is also added:

“And he went down with them and came to Nazareth, and was subject to them.” Let children, then, learn to obey their parents, by whom they were not only begotten but also nourished through labor and care, since the child Jesus did not disdain to be subject to his parents. It is most honorable to show great reverence and honor to parents, because they nourished us when we were small and, as we advanced in age, instructed us in wisdom. After raising the eyes of their minds—who knew only human things—to contemplate his divinity, he said to them: “Did you not know that I must be in the things that belong to my Father?” Then he went down to Nazareth, came with them, and was subject to them. By this example we are to understand that we must not only be subject to our parents, but also refresh and support their old age or weakness with devoted care, according to what is commanded in the divine Law: “Honor your father and your mother, that it may be well with you upon the earth and that you may live long (Exod. XXVIII).” Hence the Apostle commands children to obey their parents in all things, for this is good and acceptable before God (I Tim. V). And again: “If anyone does not care for his own, and especially for those of the household of faith, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever (ibid.).”

“And his mother kept all these words in her heart.” That is, she kept in her heart everything she had heard about him, whether from the angels, the shepherds, the magi, Simeon, or the prophetess Anna, and also everything she saw him do, ruminating on it like a clean animal. She did not wish to cast her pearls before swine or give what was holy to dogs, but awaited the time of his perfect maturity, when he would be shown to be God by performing miracles and when these things were to be written down so that they might all be narrated in order. Hence the same evangelist said a little earlier: “pondering them in her heart.” For she compared what she saw taking place in him with what she had read about him in the prophetic oracles, and believed him to be God all the more truly because she saw being fulfilled in him the things she had read about him.

“And Jesus advanced in wisdom and age.” In this brief verse two heresies are destroyed: those of the Manichaeans and the Apollinarians. The Manichaeans, who said that God had not assumed true flesh, are refuted when it says: “Jesus advanced in age.” The Apollinarians, who said that he did not possess a true soul, are refuted when it says: “He advanced in wisdom.” For just as age belongs here to the body, so wisdom belongs to the soul. If he had not possessed true flesh, he could in no way have advanced and grown in age. And if he had not possessed a rational and true soul, he could in no way have advanced and grown in wisdom. Just as the body grows through the stages of life, so the soul advances by growing in wisdom. Therefore he who came to free body and soul in us assumed, for our salvation, a true body and a true soul from the Virgin.

What follows is:

“And in grace with God and men.” By a singular grace from God the Father, it was granted to the child Jesus that from the moment he began to be human—that is, from his conception by the Holy Spirit—he should be perfect God and perfect man. Concerning him the evangelist John says: “We saw his glory, glory as of the Only-Begotten from the Father (John I).” And he rightly said first that he advanced with God and afterward with men, because one must first please God and afterward men—not for any other reason than that they themselves may please God, as the Apostle says: “Providing what is good not only before God but also before all men (Rom. XIII).” And again: “Let us provide what is good in the midst of a crooked generation (Phil. II).” And Peter says: “Having your conduct honorable among the nations (I Pet. II).”

HOMILY XVIII. SECOND SUNDAY AFTER EPIPHANY.

(John II.) “At that time, a wedding took place at Cana of Galilee,” and the rest. Whenever the miracles of our Lord and Savior are read, they are not to be drawn into examples, but rather admired and revered. Whenever we read that the Lord came after being invited either to a wedding or to a banquet, we must not attribute this to the allurements of gluttony, as the scribes and Pharisees did, who called him a wine-drinker and a friend of tax collectors (Matt. XI), but must believe that he came for the sake of a particular mystery—that is, to win souls. For just as a skilled fisherman and an experienced hunter spread nets in a place where they know that a multitude of fish, birds, or beasts will gather, so that when many assemble some may be caught, so the Lord wished to come to a banquet or a wedding so that, where many gathered, some might be caught in the net of his preaching.

For this reason he is read to have been invited by a Pharisee and to have reclined in his house; and now, called to a wedding, he is remembered not only to have come but also to have consecrated it by his miracle [Col. 0126D]. Here it should be noted that when the Lord came to celebrate a wedding according to earthly custom, he not only showed that the marital union is good, but also destroyed the heresy of Marcion and Tatian, who wished to condemn marriage. For if marriage were not good, the Son of the Virgin would in no way have come to it, nor would he have deemed it worthy to consecrate it by his miracle. And if marriage were not good—marriage which takes place for the love of children—the Lord would never have created male and female at the beginning, nor would he have said: “For this reason a man will leave his father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two will be one flesh (Gen. II).”

Hence, when the disciples asked the Lord whether it was permissible to dismiss one’s wife for any cause, he said, to show that a marriage lawfully celebrated is good: “What God has joined, let no human being separate. For whoever dismisses his wife, except on account of fornication, commits adultery (Matt. XIX).” Therefore the Apostle, following the Teacher’s judgment, says: “Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the Church. And whoever loves his wife loves himself (Eph. V).” And again: “Because of fornication, let each man have his own wife, and let each woman have her own husband. Let the husband render the debt to his wife, and likewise the wife to her husband. The wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband does. Likewise, the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife does (I Cor. III).” And again: “To those joined in marriage I command—not I, but Christ—that a woman should not depart from her husband; but if she departs, let her remain unmarried, or else be reconciled to her husband (ibid.).” “For marriage is honorable,” says Solomon, “and the marriage bed undefiled (Hebr. XIII).” Fornicators and adulterers the Lord will judge.

The marital union is therefore good, widowhood in continence is better, and virgin integrity is more perfect. To confirm these things, the Lord was born from the undefiled womb of a virgin; immediately after his birth he was blessed by Anna the widow; and when he had become a young man, he is read to have come after being invited by those celebrating a wedding. These things have been said according to the literal sense.

Spiritually, however, it is customary throughout Scripture for the union of Christ and the Church to be called a wedding, as in the Gospel: “The kingdom of heaven is like a king who made a wedding for his son (Matt. XXII).” And again: “When you are invited to a wedding, do not recline in the first place (Luke XIV).” At a wedding two are joined, the bridegroom and the bride. The bridegroom is Christ, of whom the Psalmist says: “Like a bridegroom coming forth from his bridal chamber (Ps. XVIII).” And the evangelist John says: “He who has the bride is the bridegroom (John III).” His bride is the holy Church, to whom the Prophet says: “I will espouse you to myself in justice and the holiness of truth (Hos. II).” And in the Song of Songs: “Come, my bride, my chosen one (Song II).”

The bridal chamber of this bridegroom was the undefiled womb of his mother. From it, as we have said, Christ came forth like a bridegroom from his bridal chamber. He therefore came to a wedding celebrated according to earthly custom because, in order to join the Church to himself, he appeared as a human being among human beings.

The place of the wedding was first in Judea, where the Lord was born, where he not only taught but also performed mighty works, and from which the apostles were chosen. The first celebrants of the wedding were the apostles, concerning whom the Lord says in the Gospel: “The sons of the bridegroom cannot mourn as long as the bridegroom is with them. The time will come when the bridegroom will be taken away from them, and then they will fast (Matt. IX).”

But since no one can come to this spiritual wedding unless, first touched by zeal for God, he has rejected evil works and learned to love good works, it is rightly reported to have taken place at Cana of Galilee. Cana, a village of Galilee, is interpreted as “zeal.” For Galilee is said in our language to mean “transmigration.” By this interpretation it is shown that he reclines happily at this wedding who, touched by the zeal of the love of God, has passed over from earthly love to heavenly desire, and who can say with the Psalmist: “The zeal of your house has consumed me (Ps. LXVIII).” And with the Apostle: “We, contemplating the glory of the Lord with unveiled face, are transformed from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord (II Cor. I).”

The Psalmist did this also. When he saw the impious exalted and raised up like the cedars of Lebanon, counting all transitory things as nothing and growing hot in spirit, he said: “I passed by, and behold, he was not; I sought him, and his place was not found (Ps. XXXVI).”

And it is rightly reported to have taken place on the third day, after the things that the evangelist mentioned above. For there are three periods: before the Law, under the Law, and under grace. Since God appeared visibly to join the Church to himself not before the Law or under the Law, but under grace, he is rightly remembered to have come to the wedding on the third day. Concerning this union the Apostle Paul says: “For I am jealous over you with God’s jealousy, since I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ (II Cor. XI).”

Hence, in praise of the Church, it is said: “Behold, you are beautiful, my beloved; behold, you are beautiful; your eyes are like those of doves (Song I, II).” And again: “Your eyes are more beautiful than wine, and your teeth whiter than milk.” And John says in the Apocalypse: “I saw the holy city, Jerusalem, descending from heaven, like a bride adorned for her husband (Apoc. XXI).”

Or certainly, because no one can take part in this wedding unless he has confessed the indivisible Trinity of the Lord, it is rightly also narrated that he came to the wedding on the third day. Or again, he wished to come to the wedding on the third day to show that whoever reclines in the Church through faith must guard memory, will, and understanding from evil and exercise them in good; or because he must preserve in his works the three principal virtues, namely hope, faith, and charity, concerning which the Apostle says: “Let faith, hope, and charity remain in you; these three, but the greatest of these is charity (Rom. XIII; I Cor. XIII).”

The number three is perfect because of faith in the holy Trinity. Or the number three is perfect because we read that, when the Lord said to the prophet Jonah: “Go to Nineveh, the great city, and say to this people: ‘Forty more days, and Nineveh will be overthrown (Jonah III),’” after he preached, the king immediately descended from his throne and commanded the people to undertake a three-day fast. When this had been done, the people ceased from their wickedness, turned to the Lord, and the Lord heard them and the plague ceased.

“And the mother of Jesus was there.” Spiritually, the mother of Jesus signifies the Synagogue, which, by proclaiming through the prophetic oracles that God would come into the world, as though from a certain spiritual womb of the Law, gave birth for us to the Son of God.

“And Jesus and his disciples were invited to the wedding.” Everything, therefore, that is related in the sequence of this reading must be understood according to the literal sense, while nevertheless demonstrating something to us through its signification.

We have already said above that the wedding signifies the union of Christ and the Church. The statement that Jesus was invited to the wedding declares that he did not appear in the world without the testimony of the Law and the prophets. For the holy fathers and prophets invited the Lord to the wedding when they not only foretold that he would come into the world but also desired with all their prayers that he might deign to come for our redemption.

Do you wish to hear how he was invited? Hear Isaiah saying: “Would that you would tear open the heavens and come down (Isa. LXIV).” And the Psalmist, desiring his coming, says: “Lord, incline your heavens and come down (Ps. CXLIII).” And that venerable old man, already near death, said: “I will await your salvation, Lord (Gen. XLIX).”

His disciples were also invited with him, because, so that the authority might be stronger, not only the Lord’s incarnation but also their preaching was foretold. Thus Isaiah says in the person of the Lord: “Behold, I and the children whom the Lord has given me, for a sign and portent to Israel (Isa. VIII).”
