“And when the wine failed, the mother of Jesus said to him: ‘They have no wine.’” It must not be thought that it happened by chance or accident that the wine failed when the Lord came to the wedding. Rather, it happened so that an occasion for a miracle might arise, so that, when he changed the water into wine, the God concealed in the human being might appear—namely, the one who brings forth bread from the earth and gladdens the human heart with wine.

Therefore his holy mother, understanding that the time of perfect maturity had arrived, when he would make himself known to the world as Lord through miracles and would be believed to be not the son of Joseph but the Son of God and of the Virgin Mary, said: “They have no wine.”

Spiritually, when the Lord came to the wedding, the wine failed because that unmixed wine of the Law had lost its former savor and sweetness. The Law tasted like wine in the times of Moses, Joshua, Samuel, David, and the others who understood and observed it. But by the time the Lord appeared in the world, as Pharisaic superstition increased [F., *superstitionibus*, “superstitions”] and the Jewish people grew cold in their love of God, it had departed from its ancient flavor, just as the Lord reproached the Jews, saying: “You are the ones who have abandoned God’s commandment on account of your traditions (Matt. XIX).” When the mother of Jesus said to him, “They have no wine,” it was the voice of the Synagogue urging Christ to perform miracles.

“Jesus said to her: ‘What is there between me and you, woman?’” The Lord should not be thought to have dishonored his mother, since he commands that parents be honored. Rather, when she sought something higher than mere humanity possesses, he lifted the eyes of her mind to contemplate the power of divinity. It was as though he said: “What does your humanity have in common with the miracle you seek, since it belongs to divine power to perform mighty works?”

“‘My hour has not yet come.’” By this expression he does not signify a fated hour, as the heretics wished, but the hour of his passion. It was as though he said: “The hour of my passion has not yet come, when I will truly reveal what the humanity that I assumed from you is capable of.” That hour was fulfilled when, hanging on the cross, he said: “Woman, behold your son (John XIX).” It was as though he said: “Behold what I assumed from you: it can suffer and die; but the miracle you seek cannot be performed without divinity.”

When you hear the Mother of God called “woman,” do not doubt her virginity. It is the usage of Scripture to call all females women, not only married women but also unmarried women. Thus, concerning Eve, the first mother of all, when she was formed, it is said: “The Lord built the rib that he had taken from Adam into a woman (Gen. II).” Following this usage, the Apostle called the Mother of God, who remained a virgin before and after childbirth, a woman, saying: “God sent his Son, made from a woman, made under the Law (Gal. IV),” although without doubt he is believed to have been born from a virgin. For this name does not designate corruption but sex.

To make it understood that the Lord did not deny devotion to his mother, but rather foretold the order of his passion, it is rightly added:

“His mother said to the servants: ‘Whatever he tells you, do.’” For she understood from the Lord’s words that she had not angered him; and therefore she confidently commanded the servants to fulfill the commands of the son who was giving orders.

“Now there were six stone water-jars placed there for the purification of the Jews, each holding two or three measures.” Water-jars are vessels prepared for receiving water. The term is derived from the characteristic usage of the Greek language, since water is called ὕδωρ (*hydōr*) in Greek. Since they are said to have been placed there for the purification of the Jews, the custom of the Jews, especially the Pharisees, was to have vessels containing water at banquets and weddings, for Jewish purification, the washing of hands, or whatever else might be necessary.

That Pharisee in the Gospel indicates this, when he dared to reproach the Lord himself, the fountain of living water, because he had not washed before the meal (Mark VII). But because the time was already approaching when he who appeared to be a pure human being would be shown to be true God, it is rightly added:

“Jesus says to them: ‘Fill the jars with water.’ And they filled them to the brim.” These were changed into wine. Indeed, the Lord could have filled the empty jars with wine, since before they existed he created them from nothing; but he first ordered them to be filled with water, and thus changed the water into wine. For, when he came, he gave no other law than the one he had given through his servant Moses, but by interpreting that law spiritually he changed it for the better, because he disclosed the spiritual understanding hidden within it, just as he himself says in the Gospel: “I have not come to abolish the law, but to fulfill it” (Matt. V). [Col. 0130D]

Thus, in a spiritual sense, he changed water into wine when, after his resurrection, as he walked with the disciples, he opened their understanding so that they might understand the Scriptures. Beginning with Moses and the prophets, he interpreted for them in all the Scriptures the things concerning him. They were so inebriated by the sweetness of this taste that afterward they said: “Was not our heart burning within us” because of Jesus, “while he spoke to us on the way and opened the Scriptures to us” (Luke XXIV)?

Spiritually, the jars signify the hearts of the saints, which contain water within themselves—that is, knowledge of the Scriptures. [Col. 0131A] That water signifies knowledge of the Scriptures is attested by Solomon, who says: “Deep water is the word from a man’s mouth, and an overflowing torrent is a fountain of wisdom” (Prov. XVIII). They are rightly said to be made of stone, because the hearts of the saints, adhering to that stone of which the apostle Peter says, “Approaching him, the living stone, you yourselves also, as living stones, are being built into a spiritual house” (1 Pet. II), are firm and steadfast against the temptations of the devil. For, as the Apostle says, the rock signifies Christ (1 Cor. X).

They are rightly said to have been six, because there are six ages of this world, in which almighty God has deigned to send spiritual jars—that is, holy men—for our instruction and cleansing. [Col. 0131B] The first age of the world was from Adam to Noah; the second, from Noah to Abraham; the third, from Abraham to David; the fourth, from David to the Babylonian captivity; the fifth, from the Babylonian captivity to Christ’s coming in the flesh; and the sixth, from the Lord’s first coming, when he came to redeem the world, to his second coming, when he will come to judge the world.

Throughout these ages, therefore, almighty God did not cease to send holy men who, inspired by the Holy Spirit, poured out the water of the divine utterances for the instruction of others. In the first age of the world we read that God made man from the mud of the earth, in his own image and likeness. When he wished to make a woman for his consolation and assistance, [Col. 0131C] he cast a sleep upon him, took one of his ribs, built it into a woman, and placed them in the paradise of delight. He then commanded them, saying: “Eat from every tree of paradise, but do not touch the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. For on whatever day you eat from it, you shall die the death” (Gen. II).

Afterward, however, seduced by the serpent, which was more cunning than all the animals, they not only touched the forbidden fruit of the tree but also ate it. Their eyes were opened, and when they realized that they were naked, they made themselves loincloths from fig leaves. As the Lord was walking in the paradise toward the evening breeze, Adam and his wife hid themselves among the trees of paradise. When God sought him, saying, “Adam, where are you?” he answered: “I heard your voice, Lord, and I was afraid because I was naked, and I hid myself.” [Col. 0131D] God then said to him: “Who told you that you were naked, unless it is because you ate from the tree from which I had commanded you not to eat?” Therefore the earth is cursed in your work. When you work it, it shall not give you its fruits, but it shall produce thorns and thistles for you; and in the sweat of your face you shall eat bread until you return to the earth from which you were taken, because you are earth and into earth you shall go; dust you are, and into dust you shall return (Gen. III).

Whoever, therefore, hearing these things, fears to transgress God’s commandment, reflecting within himself and saying, “If God did not spare those inexperienced and newly formed people, perhaps he will not spare us either, if, after the many falls of others, we neglect our own salvation,” finds in the first age a jar full of water. [Col. 0132A]

But if he understands something deeper—so that he understands by Adam, who was made from immaculate earth, the Lord Jesus Christ; and by Eve, who was formed from the side of the sleeping Adam, the holy Church, which was formed from the side of Christ hanging on the cross, when “one of the soldiers opened his side with a lance, and immediately blood and water came out” (John XIX)—the jar that he had found full of water has been changed into wine.

Let us see, still in that same age, another jar full of water. For we read (Gen. IV) that the same first man, after his sin, fathered two sons, namely Cain and Abel. Abel was a shepherd of sheep, and Cain a farmer. [Col. 0132B] Abel took from his sheep and from their fat and offered a burnt offering to the Lord, while Cain offered from the fruits of the earth. The Lord looked upon Abel and his offerings, but upon Cain and his offerings he did not look.

Therefore Cain became angry and, driven by envy, said to his brother: “Let us go outside.” And when they were in the field, he rose up against his brother and killed him. God said to him: “Where is Abel your brother?” He denied it not only falsely but also insolently, saying: “I do not know. Am I my brother’s keeper?” God then said to him: “What have you done? Behold, your brother’s blood cries out to me from the earth. Therefore now you shall be cursed upon the earth, which has opened its mouth and received your brother’s blood from your hand. You shall be a wanderer and a fugitive all the days of your life.”

Whoever, therefore, hearing these things, chooses to live innocently and simply with Abel and fears to harbor envy or hatred toward his brother, lest perhaps he be reckoned under the curse with Cain, finds in the first age another jar full of water. [Col. 0132C]

But if he turns his mind to spiritual understanding, so that he understands by Abel the Lord Jesus Christ; by his killing, the Lord’s Passion; by the earth that opened its mouth and received his blood, the holy Church, which daily opens its mouth in confession of the Lord; and by Cain the murderer, the Jewish people, who did not fear to shed the Lord’s blood because of envy and were therefore reckoned wanderers and fugitives—the jar that he had found full of water has been changed for him into wine.

In the second age we read that, when those who descended from Adam’s stock transgressed the Lord’s commandment, [Col. 0132D] Noah, a righteous man, was found. The Lord said to him: “The end of all flesh has come before me, and my spirit shall not remain in man forever, since he is flesh. I will destroy,” he said, “all flesh by a flood. Make yourself an ark, therefore, from planed wood, and enter it—you, your sons, your wife, and your sons’ wives—so that you may live. For I have found you righteous in this generation” (Gen. VI).

Fulfilling the Lord’s command, he labored for a hundred years on the construction of the ark. On the appointed day he entered the ark, he and his sons, his wife, and his sons’ wives. The Lord rained upon the earth for forty days and forty nights, and the flood came; all flesh in which there was the breath of life died. [Col. 0133A]

Afterward, wishing to learn whether the waters had subsided, Noah sent out a raven, which did not return to him. Then he sent out a dove a second time, and in the evening it returned to him, carrying in its mouth a branch of olive with green leaves.

Whoever, therefore, hearing these things, chooses to be saved with the few elect, after the example of Noah, rather than perish with the many reprobate, finds in the second age a jar full of water.

But if he has learned to interpret this history spiritually, so that he understands by Noah, the builder of the ark, the Lord Jesus Christ, builder and ruler of the Church; by the flood that destroyed sinful people, baptism, in which sins are destroyed; by the raven that went out and did not return, the heretics who went out from us but were not of us; [Col. 0133B] and by the dove that brought a branch with green leaves, the anointing of the Holy Spirit given to the faithful in baptism—the jar full of water that he possessed has been changed for him into wine.

In the third age we read that Abraham was a righteous man. God said to him: “Go out from your land, from your kindred, and from your father’s house, and come into the land that I shall show you” (Gen. XII). Obeying God, he immediately departed, not knowing where he was going. As he progressed more and more in faith and love toward God, God gave him in his old age, by promise, an only-begotten son named Isaac.

Later God said to him (ibid.): “Take your only-begotten son Isaac, whom you love, and go into the land of vision; there you shall offer him as a burnt offering upon one of the mountains that I shall show you” (Gen. XXII). He “rose, immediately saddled his donkey, and took with him two servants and his son Isaac.” [Col. 0133C] On the third day, lifting his eyes, he saw from afar the place that God had shown him and said to his servants: “Wait here with the donkey; I and the boy will hurry on there, and after we have worshiped, we shall return to you.”

When he had placed the wood upon his son Isaac, he laid him upon the altar, “stretched out his hand, and took the sword to sacrifice his son. And behold, the angel of the Lord called from heaven, saying: Abraham, Abraham. He answered: Here I am. And he said to him: Do not stretch out your hand against the boy, nor do anything to him. Now I know that you fear God, since you have not spared your only-begotten son for my sake. Blessing, I shall bless you, and I shall multiply your offspring like the stars of heaven and like the sand that is on the seashore.” [Col. 0133D]

Turning back, he “saw a ram caught by its horns among the thorns.” He took it and offered it as a burnt offering in place of his son.

Whoever, therefore, hearing these things, considers in his heart with what devotion he ought to obey God, when Abraham preferred to obey God rather than spare his only-begotten son, possesses in the third age a jar full of water.

But if, in this deed of Abraham, he seeks a spiritual understanding, so that he understands by Abraham God the Father, and by Isaac his only-begotten son, the Lord Jesus Christ, who is the Father’s only-begotten Son; by Isaac’s sacrifice, the Lord’s Passion, since, about to suffer for us, he himself carried the wood on which he was to suffer; and if, in the fact that Isaac was released by the Lord’s voice and a ram was sacrificed in his place, he understands that the Lord’s humanity endured suffering but that his divinity remained incapable of suffering—the jar that he had possessed full of water has been changed for him into wine. [Col. 0134A]

In the fourth age we read (1 Kings XIX) that David was not only a courageous man but also humble and merciful. When, after Saul had been rejected, he was chosen by God to reign, he suffered persecution from Saul, to such an extent that Saul often wished to kill him. When the Lord delivered Saul into David’s hands, and David could have killed him, he spared him not only once but also a second and a third time, for the Lord’s sake, saying: “Far be it from me to lay my hand upon the Lord’s anointed” (1 Kings XXVI).

For this reason Saul’s kingdom was destroyed, and David’s kingdom was exalted over Israel. If you, hearing these things, wish to imitate David’s humility and gentleness, so that, when you are able to harm your enemies, you forgive them for God’s sake, you have found in the fourth age a jar full of water. [Col. 0134B]

But if you understand Saul, the rejected and envious man, as the Jewish people who persecuted the Lord; and David as the Lord Jesus Christ, who is strong and mighty in battle and the Lord of hosts, and who prayed for his Jewish persecutors, saying, “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke XXIII); and if you understand that their kingdom was therefore scattered, while the Lord’s kingdom remains forever, then the fourth jar, which you had found full of water, has been changed for you into wine.

In the fifth age we read (2 Kings XXV) that the Jewish people transgressed the Lord’s commandment, abandoning the God of their fathers and worshiping idols. [Col. 0134C] Therefore the Lord handed them over to Nebuchadnezzar, king of the Chaldeans, who led them captive into Babylon and destroyed the city of Jerusalem. There, because of the vengeance due to sin, they remained in great affliction for seventy years.

Afterward, God took pity on that people and raised up Jesus son of Josedec, the high priest, and Zerubbabel, prince of the Jews, who brought them back to Jerusalem and restored the Lord’s temple.

If you, hearing these things, fear to sin, lest captivity or some temporal tribulation come upon you because of sin, you have found in the fifth age a jar full of water.

But if you turn your mind to a higher understanding, so that you understand by the Israelite people the human race; by Nebuchadnezzar, who took the people captive, the devil; by Babylon, which is interpreted as “confusion,” hell, where after the transgression the devil dragged the human race into captivity; [Col. 0134D] by Jerusalem, which is interpreted as “vision of peace,” the heavenly homeland; and by Jesus the high priest, our Lord Jesus Christ, who became a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek (Ps. CIX), who recalled his elect from Babylonian captivity to the heavenly homeland—your jar, which previously contained water, has been changed for you into wine.

In the sixth age we read (1 Tim. II) that the Lord Jesus Christ himself, author and redeemer of all, having become man for human beings, was circumcised on the eighth day, and thirty-three days afterward was presented in the temple, and a legal offering was presented for him—not because any necessity compelled him, but by his own free will, solely in order to fulfill the law. [Col. 0135A]

If, hearing these things, you consider with how much care and devotion you ought to observe the commandments of the Gospel that were spoken through him, since he himself deigned to observe with such diligence the law that he had given through his servant, you have found in the sixth age a jar full of water, more abundant and purer than all the others, from which you can be not only cleansed but also satisfied.

But if you understand something deeper in this deed of the Lord, so that you understand that, in refusing to be presented first in the temple of the material building before he had been circumcised, and in waiting for the day of purification although he had no need of it, he signifies that we cannot be spiritually joined to the Church of God or become participants in Christ’s body and blood unless we have first been cleansed from original sin through baptism, then the jar that you had possessed full of water has been changed for you into good wine. [Col. 0135B]

And if you wish to investigate something still more sacred, so that you understand that, in wishing first to be circumcised before entering the temple, the Lord Jesus Christ signifies that we shall in no way enter the temple of eternal blessedness, which is in heaven, where God’s praise is sung without end, unless in the present life we have been purified through confession, almsgiving, and other good works, and have guarded our heart with every care, so that we may deserve to offer a worthy sacrifice to God in heaven, then the jar that had been changed into good wine has been changed into the purest wine. [Col. 0135C] You have been spiritually inebriated by its sweetest delight, so that you can say with the prophet: “And your cup, making drunk, how glorious it is!” (Ps. XXII). And again: “The rushing of the river gladdens the city of God” (Ps. XLV). And once more: “The children of men will hope under the protection of your wings, and they will be inebriated by the abundance of your house, and you will give them drink from the torrent of your delight” (Ps. XXXV).

This is the wine desired by the one who said in the Song of Songs: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth, for your breasts are better than wine, fragrant with the finest perfumes” (Song I).

Whoever, therefore, considering the examples of the saints through each of the ages, learns to live well and spiritually to understand their teaching, will find in each age jars from whose draught he may be both cleansed and satisfied.

Most beautifully, too, what is said about these same jars applies to the minds of the saints: “Each holding two or three measures.” For μέτρον (*metron*) in Greek, *mensura* in Latin, means a measure of three *modii*. He does not say that some held two and others three, but that each held two or three measures. [Col. 0135D]

When holy men mention only the Father and the Son, they hold, as it were, two or three measures. But when they mention the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit together, those same men hold three measures.

Thus the spiritual jar of David held, as it were, two measures when he spoke of the Father and the Son, saying: “You have made all things in wisdom” (Ps. CIII). The same jar held, as it were, three measures when he said: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the breath of his mouth all their host” (Ps. XXV). [Col. 0136A]

The Lord showed two measures in the Gospel when he said: “I and the Father are one” (John X). He showed three when elsewhere he said: “Go and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. XXVIII).

The holy teachers, that is, the spiritual jars, receive three measures when they preach to others that the Trinity is undivided and to be believed; two when they commend to their hearers love of God and of neighbor.

The servants, who are said to have filled the jars, signified the apostles or the teachers of the Church, through whose teaching the world received a draught of wisdom. Of them it is rightly said: “And they filled them to the brim.” [Col. 0136B] For they showed that from the beginning of the world no time had been empty of the instruction of the faithful, in which they did not disclose spiritual teaching through words and examples.

Or certainly they filled them to the brim because they showed that greater perfection exists through the grace of the New Testament than through the Old, since the teaching of the Gospel that they preached filled the whole world; or because the teachers of the Church left us nothing lacking in the works of the saints that might demonstrate imperfection.

“Jesus says to them: ‘Draw some out now and take it to the master of the feast.’ And they took it.” The *architriclinus* is called the ruler of the dining room, because ἀρχός (*archos*) in Greek means “ruler” in Latin; a *triclinium*, meanwhile, is a house having three rows. [Col. 0136C]

We may also understand this master of the feast literally as one of the leading Jews, such as Nicodemus or Gamaliel, or his disciple Saul, who afterward became Paul.

Spiritually, however, just as the masters of the Church are signified by the master of the feast, so the Church itself is signified by the dining room, which has three orders: the married, the continent, and the virgins.

The Lord ordered wine made from water to be given to the master of the feast, for spiritual teaching is entrusted to those who know how to distinguish between the Old and New Testaments—that is, between the law and the Gospel.

“When the master of the feast tasted the water made wine, and did not know where it came from, while the servants who had drawn the water knew, the master of the feast calls the bridegroom.” [Col. 0136D]

This bridegroom, according to the literal sense, is understood by some to be the apostle John. When he had married, after seeing the Lord’s miracle he abandoned the wedding and followed him as a virgin; hence he is also called the Lord’s beloved.

Spiritually, however, the bridegroom is understood to be Christ himself.

“And he says to him: ‘Every man first sets out the good wine, and when they have become drunk, then what is worse. But you have kept the good wine until now.’”

It belongs to teachers to discern how far the law differs from the Gospel, the killing letter from the life-giving Spirit, and good from evil. Thus the master of the feast had discernment between wine and water. For as much as water differs from wine, so much does the letter of the law differ from the spiritual grace of the Gospel.

In the Lord’s presence, therefore, the elements themselves were changed, when the carnal law, through his own interpretation, was understood spiritually, so that whoever tasted this sweetness would marvel and say: “Every man first sets out the good wine.” [Col. 0137A]

“This Jesus did as the beginning of his signs in Cana of Galilee.”

Therefore the Lord fittingly wished to consecrate the beginning of his signs with this miracle, changing water into wine, so that the faithful might say that he came to teach no other law than the one he had given through his servant Moses, but to change that same law for the better by interpreting it spiritually.

It is rightly said: “And he manifested his glory.” He manifested, through this sign, that he himself was the King of glory and the Lord of hosts, and that he himself was the bridegroom of the Church. [Col. 0137B] He manifested that he was the one who could create all things from nothing and who, whenever he wished, could also change the elements.

As for what follows: “And his disciples believed in him,” it must not be thought that they believed in him for the first time then, especially since they are said to have been invited by him to the wedding. Rather, those who had believed previously believed more firmly when they saw the miracle; and, whereas they had previously believed him to be a man, when they saw this sign they believed him to be true God and man.

## HOMILY XIX. THIRD SUNDAY AFTER EPIPHANY

(MATT. VIII.) “At that time, when Jesus had come down from the mountain, great crowds followed him,” and the rest.

Above, the evangelist related how the Lord, sitting on the mountain, delivered the order of the eight beatitudes, [Col. 0137C] saying: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. V), and the other things that follow. And, so that they might believe that what they had heard in his words was true, he took care to add a miracle afterward, saying: “And when he had come down from the mountain, great crowds followed him.”

Spiritually, we can understand the mountain on which the Lord sat as heaven, in which he remained with the Father and always remains equal to him. He came down from the mountain when, for us and for our salvation, he came into the valley of tears and assumed our humanity, so that he who was invisible in his own nature might become visible in ours, and that we, who could not see him in his exalted state, might at least recognize him in our weakness.

Therefore, in accordance with a fitting interpretation, the disciples alone approached him on the mountain; [Col. 0137D] but when he came down from the mountain, many crowds followed him. Before his incarnation, God was known only in Judea, and “Israel was his great name.” But after he descended even to the assumption of our human nature, many crowds of the nations immediately followed him through faith.

Isaiah had foretold them long before, saying: “And it shall come to pass in the last days that the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be prepared on the top of the mountains, and it shall be exalted above the hills, and it shall be very lofty. And all nations shall come to it, and many peoples shall go and say: House of Jacob, come, and let us walk in the light of our God” (Isa. II).

And the Psalmist says: “All the nations that you have made shall come and worship before you, O Lord, and they shall glorify your name forever” (Ps. LXXXV). [Col. 0138A]

John also saw this crowd in the Apocalypse. After describing twelve thousand sealed from each of the tribes of Israel, he added: “After this I saw a great crowd that no one could number, from every people, tribe, and language” (Rev. VII).

The crowds follow the Lord when the faithful imitate the footprints of his humanity. To follow the Lord means to imitate him, as he himself says: “Whoever serves me, let him follow me” (John XII). And again: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Luke IX).

“Behold, a leper came and worshiped him, saying: ‘Lord, if you are willing, you can cleanse me.’” [Col. 0138B]

If anyone attends only to the literal sense in this passage, it is clear that this leper possessed no small faith. He did not doubt that he was God, since he worshiped him as a suppliant. Nor did he doubt his power, since he asked only for his will, saying: “Lord, if you are willing, you can cleanse me.”

Therefore faith immediately obtained its effect, for it follows:

“And Jesus, stretching out his hand, touched him, saying: ‘I am willing; be cleansed.’”

Here the Lord’s great power is evident, but his humility is no less clearly revealed. The law cast the leper outside the camp, and the scribes and Pharisees scarcely deigned to look at him; yet he did not refuse to touch the man whom he could have cleansed without touching him, showing that his touch is salvation for believers.

It is asked why the Lord touched the leper when the law commanded that he not be touched. First, so that he might show us an example of humility and compassion and make clear that our neighbors should not be despised on account of any weakness. [Col. 0138C] Second, so that he might show that he was not a servant of the law but the Lord of the law: although he walked according to the law, he could cleanse anyone he wished even above the law.

When he says, “I am willing; be cleansed,” the two expressions should not be joined and read as though he said, “I am willing to cleanse,” as certain Latins have thought. Rather, one must first say “I am willing,” and then add “be cleansed.” Thus, to each of the leper’s words the Lord responded with a corresponding word.

The leper had said: “Lord, if you are willing.” The Lord replied: “I am willing.” The leper had said: “You can cleanse me.” The Lord replied: “Be cleansed,” in the imperative mood, of course.

“And immediately his leprosy was cleansed.” Between the Lord’s speaking and doing there is no difference: “For he spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created” (Ps. XXXII). [Col. 0138D]

Allegorically, this leper signifies the human race, which incurred the leprosy of sin when it despised the Lord’s commandment in paradise. Therefore, according to the evangelist, he is rightly described not merely as a leper but as being full of leprosy, since, when the Lord came in the flesh, he found the human race polluted by various errors and iniquities.

But when the Lord descended from the mountain—that is, appeared in the flesh—the leper met him. For the human race understood that, being polluted by the leprosy of iniquity, both from the Jews and from the nations, it could receive cleansing in its soul in no other way than through faith in him who committed no sin and in whose mouth no deceit was found. [Col. 0139A] The Apostle bears witness to this when he says: “There is no distinction between Jew and Greek. For all have sinned and lack the glory of God, being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus” (Rom. X).

But the Lord, who had come to confer salvation, did not disdain to touch the leper in order to raise him to salvation. He cured the leper, as it were, by touching him when, through assuming the likeness of our flesh, he freed us from the sins of the soul.

Although he could have cured the leper by a word, he preferred to cure him by touching him, because, by assuming the mortality of our flesh, he purified us from the contagion of sins. He thus showed himself to be the one of whom it had been prophesied through Isaiah:

“We saw him without appearance or beauty, and we desired him, despised and the last of men, a man of sorrows and acquainted with weakness. His face was as though hidden and despised, and therefore we did not esteem him. Truly he himself bore our sicknesses, and he himself carried our pains. We considered him as a leper, struck by God and humbled. But he was wounded because of our sins; he was crushed because of our iniquities” (Isa. LI). [Col. 0139B]

Hence the apostle Peter also says: “He himself bore our sins in his body upon the tree, so that, having died to sins, we might live to righteousness; by whose bruising we were healed” (1 Pet. II).

“And he said to him: ‘See that you tell no one, but go, show yourself to the priest, and offer the gift that Moses prescribed as a testimony to them.’”

[Col. 0139C] What does it mean that the Lord, who elsewhere commanded a man healed from a legion of demons, saying, “Go into the city to your own people, and announce to them how great things God has done for you” (Mark 5), now says to the leper who has been cured, “See that you tell no one”? In this action he surely instructs us, whom empty glory frequently tempts, showing that vainglory must also be avoided in a good work. For if he who, as the Son of God, had no fear of vainglory commanded his miracle to be concealed, much more ought we, whom vain glory secretly ensnares, to beware of boasting, so that, according to his own saying, “Your left hand must not know what your right hand is doing” (Matthew 6). Here again he admonishes us, saying: “But when you pray, enter your room, and, having shut the door, pray to your Father; and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you” (ibid.).

[Col. 0139D] In what he says, “Go, show yourself to the priest,” we must consider that the Lord is recorded to have sent no others whom he had restored to bodily health to the priests, except lepers alone. He did this not only here, but also elsewhere, when ten leprous men met him and cried, “Jesus, Master, have mercy on us!” He commanded them, saying: “Go, show yourselves to the priests” (Luke 17). We believe that he did this for several reasons. First, to show honor to the priests; second, so that he would not appear to contradict the Law, since the Law prescribed that if anyone had been cleansed from leprosy, he should go to the priest; third, to provoke the minds of the priests toward their own cruelty, and to remove every excuse from those who would not believe. [Col. 0140A] When they saw the leper cleansed, if they believed in the one who had cleansed him, they would find salvation; but if they refused to believe, they would be without excuse. Hence it is rightly said, “as a testimony to them,” that is, to the priests.

Alternatively, by the mountain on which the Lord taught his disciples, a higher teaching is understood, to which only the disciples came, because those who can grasp spiritual matters through prolonged meditation must be instructed in them. But those who are immature in understanding and earthly in faith must be instructed, as it were, in the valleys—that is, admonished through more accessible teachings. Thus, when he taught the disciples on the mountains and cured the leper in the valleys, he showed that in preaching, the discourse of teachers must be shaped according to the capacity of their hearers. The imperfect must not be abandoned on account of the perfect; rather, they must be corrected and [Col. 0140B] endured alongside them.

Those who are such that they can hear with the apostles, “To you it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God” (Luke 5), must be instructed more deeply and profoundly through the types and figures of allegories. But those who are immature in understanding must be instructed by the letter alone. The Lord also teaches us this elsewhere by his example, when a certain man said to him, “Good Teacher, what must I do to possess eternal life?” (Matthew 19). As though he were placed in a valley, he answered him: “You know the commandments: You shall not kill. You shall not commit adultery. You shall not bear false witness. You shall not covet your neighbor’s property,” and so forth.

[Col. 0140C] When the man replied, “I have kept all these things from my youth,” the Lord immediately showed him the mountain of perfection, adding: “One thing is still lacking for you: if you wish to be perfect, go, sell everything you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; then come, follow me.” And because those burdened by love of riches climb this mountain with difficulty, he went away sorrowful, because he had many possessions.

The Apostle Paul likewise followed this example. As though he were dwelling with certain people in the valleys, he said to them: “I could not speak to you, brothers, as spiritual people, but as carnal—as infants in Christ. I gave you milk to drink, not food” (1 Corinthians 3). With others, as though he had climbed the mountain, he said: “We speak wisdom among the perfect” (1 Corinthians 2).

[Col. 0140D] In the moral sense, this leper who met the Lord as he descended from the mountain signifies every sinner. For just as leprosy displays a variegated color on the skin, so sin has various forms in the mind. Whoever commits adultery, murder, theft, robbery, sacrilege, and similar acts displays, as it were, leprous skin upon his soul.

If such a person wishes to receive cleansing, he must meet the Lord—that is, he must acknowledge himself a sinner with tears and groans, and beseech the Lord’s mercy with a contrite heart, saying with the Prophet: “Have mercy on me, O God, according to your great mercy. For I acknowledge my iniquity, and my sin is always before me. Against you alone I have sinned, and I have done evil in your sight” (Psalm 50). And again: “I made my offense known to you, and I did not conceal my injustices. I said, ‘I will confess my injustice against myself to the Lord,’ and you forgave the wickedness of my sin” (Psalm 32).

[Col. 0141A] Nor should he despair of forgiveness, provided he does not neglect to perform worthy penance. For how merciful the Lord is toward converted sinners is shown when it follows: “And Jesus, stretching out his hand, touched him, saying: ‘I will; be cleansed.’” And because he is the true physician, who came not to call the righteous but sinners to repentance (Matthew 9), he is rightly said to have touched the leper.

The hand of the Lord in Scripture sometimes signifies the power of his majesty, and sometimes the mystery of the Incarnation. It signifies the power of majesty, as the Psalmist says: “Into your hands, O Lord, I commend my spirit” (Psalm 30). It signifies the mystery of the Incarnation, as the same writer says elsewhere: “Send forth your hand from on high” (Psalm 144).

God wills to cleanse the leper, [Col. 0141B] because, as the Apostle says, “He wants no one to perish, but all to turn to the knowledge of the truth” (1 Timothy 2). Hence he himself says through the Prophet: “As I live, says the Lord God, I do not desire the death of the sinner, but rather that he should turn and live” (Ezekiel 18). And again: “On whatever day the sinner is converted,” and so forth. And in the Gospel: “I tell you, there will be joy in heaven over one sinner who repents” (Luke 15).

The Lord does not require a span of years or a long duration of time in penance, but God does not despise a contrite and humbled heart, because past evils do not harm us if they no longer please us. He first touched the leper and afterward cleansed him, because he first inflames our mind by his grace to perform penance, and afterward, when we rightly ask, he mercifully releases us from what we have done wrong.

[Col. 0141C] But because we must confess our sins themselves to priests in the Lord’s place and perform penance according to their counsel, it is rightly added: “See that you tell no one, but go, show yourself to the priest,” and so forth.

Perhaps there are also some who believe that it is sufficient for them to confess their sins to God alone with a contrite heart, and that it is unnecessary to confess them to priests, provided only that they cease from their evil works. If their opinion were true, the Lord would never have sent to priests the lepers whom he himself had cleansed.

[Col. 0141D] Finally, if sins did not have to be confessed to priests and examined according to their judgment, he would certainly not have directed Paul—whom he had addressed on the road—to the priest Ananias, saying: “Go into the city, and there you will be told what you must do” (Acts 9). That confession of sins to priests is greatly beneficial is proved by the Apostle James, who says: “Confess your sins to one another, and pray for one another, so that you may be saved” (James 5). And John says: “If we confess our sins, God is faithful and just, so that he may forgive us our sins and cleanse us from all sin” (1 John 1).

This is also figuratively demonstrated in the Old Testament, when the Lord gives Moses the following command concerning lepers. For it is written:

“And the Lord spoke to Moses” (Leviticus 13): “A man on whose skin a variegated color appears shall come to the priest and show himself to him. He shall shut him up in a separate house by himself for seven days; and after seven days, having examined him, if he sees that the leprosy has increased, he shall add another seven days. [Col. 0142A] After fourteen days, having examined him again, if he sees that the leprosy is still increasing, he shall know that it is persistent leprosy. Then he shall judge him to be a leper and expel him outside the camp. He shall remain with his beard untrimmed, his head covered, his garment torn, and his mouth uncovered, declaring himself unclean throughout the whole period of his separation.

“But if the one suffering from this condition has been cleansed, he shall come to the priest and offer for his cleansing a round loaf of bread and a sextarius of oil for preparing the lamps, and he shall offer two living sparrows, one for sin and the other as a burnt offering.”

How all these things ought now to be carried out spiritually in the Church must briefly be explained. Leprosy, as we said, signifies sin. Therefore, whoever has leprosy appear on his skin—that is, whoever has sin in his soul—must come to the priest and show him the place of the leprosy, that is, humbly confess his sins to him.

[Col. 0142B] The priest is to shut him up in a separate house by himself for seven days—that is, he is to indicate that he must do penance throughout the whole period of his life, which turns through seven days. After seven days, having examined him, if he sees that the leprosy has increased, he is to add another seven—that is, wherever the sin is repeated, the measure of penance must be increased. For those who sin habitually are to be judged more strictly than those who fall suddenly.

After fourteen days, having examined him again, if he sees that the leprosy is still increasing—that is, if he sees that the sin has become habitual—he shall know that it is persistent leprosy. Let him remain outside the camp, either separated bodily from the Church, or judging himself in his mind unworthy of the company of the saints.

[Col. 0142C] Let him have an untrimmed beard, so that he may display even in his face the squalor of penance. His head should be covered, because one who does public penance ought to cease from the office of preaching. Let him remain with his mouth uncovered and his garment torn—that is, let him disclose his conscience through confession.

But if the one suffering from this condition has been healed, let him come to the priest and offer for his cleansing a round loaf of bread—that is, let him extend the sweetness of charity to whomever he can, not only to friends but also to enemies. The sweetness of charity is beautifully signified by the round loaf, because, just as bread is the chief food in human life, so charity is the chief among all virtues.

[Col. 0142D] Let him also offer a sextarius of oil—that is, clothed in the compassion of mercy, let him forgive those who sin against him with clemency—and let this be offered for preparing the lamps, so that, just as he destroyed many by his example when he sinned, so by living more carefully he may rebuild many through his satisfaction.

Let him also offer two living sparrows—that is, let him subject his body and soul to divine service, so that, just as he presented his members to serve uncleanness and iniquity leading to iniquity, so he may serve righteousness leading to sanctification.

[Col. 0143A] Or certainly, let him offer two living sparrows, that is, two kinds of compunction: fear and love. Of these it is rightly said: “One for sin and the other as a burnt offering”—that is, one in the sacrifice that was offered for sin, and the other in thanksgiving, where it was offered not out of fear of sin but out of love for God and desire for him. For every sinner is first pierced by fear, and afterward by love.

“When he had entered Capernaum, a centurion approached him, asking him and saying: ‘Lord, my servant lies at home paralyzed and is suffering terribly.’”

After the healing of the leper, we come to another miracle, in which not only the Lord’s power appears worthy of wonder, but also the centurion’s humility appears worthy of imitation.

[Col. 0143B] First, however, we must ask why Matthew says that the centurion approached the Lord, when Luke reports that he did not come himself but sent Jewish elders on his behalf. For it is written in Luke (Luke 7):

“A certain centurion’s servant was about to die and was precious to him. And since he did not dare to approach Jesus, he sent Jewish elders to him, who came saying: ‘Lord, he is worthy that you should grant this to him. For he loves our nation; indeed, he himself built us a synagogue.’”

The evangelists should not therefore be thought to have intended contradictory accounts. One describes the will; the other, the actions. When Matthew says that he himself approached, he described the man’s intention, because he approached in will. When Luke says that he did not come himself but sent the Jewish elders on his behalf, he shows the centurion’s humility and how the event took place in bodily terms. Since he was a Gentile, he did not dare approach the Lord bodily by himself.

But let us hear what the Lord answered him:

[Col. 0143C] “And Jesus said to him: ‘I will come and cure him.’”

In these words our pride is put to shame if we compare this reading with another passage in the Gospel. For elsewhere, in the Gospel according to John (John 4), we read that there was a certain royal official whose son was ill at Capernaum:

“When he heard that Jesus had come from Judea into Galilee, he went and asked him to come down and heal his son, for he was beginning to die. And Jesus said to him: ‘Unless you see signs and wonders, you do not believe.’ And he said: ‘Lord, come down before my son dies.’ Jesus said to him: ‘Go; your son lives.’”

Why, then, did the Lord refuse to go when asked on behalf of the royal official’s son, but was ready to go, even without being asked, on behalf of the centurion’s servant? Who does not know that a royal official possesses greater authority than a centurion? In this action, as we said, our pride is put to shame, because among human beings we consider not nature but power. Those whom we see as powerful, we fear, revere, and honor; but the poor we despise, neglect, and look down upon.

[Col. 0143D] Yet the Son of God, who came from heaven to earth to show that pride must be avoided, humility loved, and human nature cherished, refused to go when asked on behalf of the royal official’s son, but was ready to go, even when not asked, on behalf of the centurion’s servant. “The exalted Lord looks upon the humble from nearby, but the proud he regards from afar” (Psalm 138), because, as the Apostle Peter testifies concerning him, “God is not a respecter of persons, but in every nation whoever works righteousness is acceptable to him” (Acts 10).

[Col. 0144A] “And the centurion answered and said: ‘Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof, but only say the word, and my servant will be healed.’”

The centurion’s great faith is revealed in this, but his humility is shown to be no less remarkable. In the action of this centurion, three virtues worthy of imitation are displayed for us: humility, faith, and prudence.

He possessed great humility because, when the Lord said, “I will come and cure him,” he judged himself unworthy and replied: “Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof.” He possessed perfect faith because, although he was a Gentile, he believed that by a mere word the Lord could restore health to the servant, saying: “Only say the word, and my servant will be healed.”

[Col. 0144B] For unless he confidently believed that the Lord was omnipotent, he would never have approached him to ask for the well-being of his little servant. He also possessed no small measure of prudence, since, having seen him walking bodily, he understood that the Lord was present everywhere through his divinity.

Nor should we think that charity was lacking in him, since while many came to the Lord to ask for the health of themselves, their children, or their loved ones, he came only for the health of a servant. Thus, still persevering in the constancy of his faith, he added:

“For I too am a man under authority, having soldiers under me; and I say to this one, ‘Go,’ and he goes; and to another, ‘Come,’ and he comes; and to my servant, ‘Do this,’ and he does it.”

[Col. 0144C] It is as though he were saying: “If I, although I am a man under the authority of a ruler, have soldiers under me, and say to this one, ‘Go,’ and he goes; and to another, ‘Come,’ and he comes; and to my servant, ‘Do this,’ and he does it—how much more can you, since you are God, wholly everywhere, present everywhere, powerful everywhere? If you say to illness, ‘Depart,’ will it not depart? If you say to health, ‘Come,’ will it not come? Therefore, you do not need to weary yourself by coming bodily, since you can cure by your word alone.”

Spiritually, however, by the centurion’s subordinates we can understand the natural virtues in which certain Gentiles excelled: not committing adultery, not stealing, not robbing, not killing, having mercy on the needy, helping the afflicted, and similar things. Thus we read concerning the Gentile Cornelius (Acts 10) that he was a just and good man, giving alms with all his household to the people and fearing God.

[Col. 0144D] Or certainly, by the centurion’s subordinates we may understand the good and evil thoughts that are never absent from our heart, which we ought to keep subject to us. Thus, if we say to the evil thoughts, “Depart,” let them depart; and to the good, “Come,” let them come, and let us rejoice together with them.

To our servant, that is, to our body, let us say, “Do this,” and it will do it. That is, let us command it to accomplish the things that belong to the Spirit of the Lord, according to the Apostle’s saying: “I chastise my body and bring it into servitude, lest, after preaching to others, I myself should be rejected” (1 Corinthians 9).

“When Jesus heard this, he marveled.”

The Lord marveled at the centurion’s faith, which he wonderfully administered in his heart—not because anything could be astonishing to him who works all things wondrously, but so that he might teach us that we too ought to marvel at him.

Marveling at and likewise praising his faith, the Lord said to those who followed him:

“Amen, I say to you, I have not found such faith in Israel.”

[Col. 0145A] He does not say this concerning the patriarchs and prophets, who once saw him—for if “Israel” is interpreted as “seeing God,” they did see him—but concerning carnal Israel, that is, the Jewish people, or concerning those who were present, among whom he performed signs and miracles and proclaimed the word of life, which they were unwilling even to receive. They did not believe as quickly as the centurion.

Therefore, in the centurion not only was the faith of the Gentiles praised, but it was also prefigured, when he says:

“But I say to you that many will come from the east and the west, and will recline with Abraham and Isaac and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven.”

[Col. 0145B] By the east and the west the four regions of the world are designated, from all of which people from the nations would come to the faith, not only through the preaching of the apostles but also through that of their successors. Concerning them the Psalmist says: “Let those redeemed by the Lord say so, whom he redeemed from the hand of the enemy; from the regions he gathered them, from the rising and the setting of the sun, from the north and from the sea” (Psalm 106).

That many were called to the faith through the preaching of the apostles, as we have said, the same Psalmist shows elsewhere when he says: “Their sound has gone out through all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Romans 10). And again: “There are no languages or speeches whose voices are not heard” (Psalm 19).

[Col. 0145C] Or, as some wish, the Hebrews came from the east, because they were the first to know the Lord, and the Gentiles from the west, because they received knowledge of the Lord last.

Alternatively, those came from the east who, under God’s protection, committed no criminal sins; those came from the west who, after perpetrating many disgraces, are converted to almighty God.

Or, from the east came those who served God from infancy or childhood; from the west, those who were converted to God’s service in old age or extreme decrepitude.

To recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven means that the nations rest in the faith of the patriarchs and believe that the one whom the holy patriarchs prophesied would come has indeed come.

A terrible sentence is pronounced concerning the Jews when he says:

“But the children of this kingdom will be cast into the outer darkness.”

[Col. 0145D] He calls the Jews “children of the kingdom,” who are rightly called children of the kingdom because, for love of an earthly kingdom, they refused to believe in the heavenly King, saying to Pilate: “We have no king but Caesar” (John 19).

Again, choosing an earthly kingdom and rejecting the heavenly one, they said: “What shall we do? For this man performs many signs. If we leave him so, everyone will believe in him, and the Romans will come and take away our place and our nation” (John 11).

The Jews had been placed under Roman power, and therefore, deceived by this pretext, they feared that if a new king were heard to be reigning in Judea, they would be defeated and expelled from the kingdom. Thus, because the Jews loved an earthly king more than the heavenly one, they lost not only the heavenly king but also the earthly one.

[Col. 0146A] For, scattered from nation to nation and from one kingdom to another people, they were left without God, without law, without a leader, and without a priest. Just as those who love God more than the world are called children of God, so those who have planted the roots of their hearts steadfastly in love of an earthly kingdom are called children of the kingdom.

Where such people are to be sent is made clear when it follows: “They will be cast into the outer darkness.”

Here we must consider that, although darkness is always within and not outside—for when the door of a house is closed, there is darkness inside, while outside there is light—they are sent after death into outer darkness who, while they lived, shut themselves within inner darkness, that is, blindness of mind.

[Col. 0146B] It is asked why it is called “outer darkness,” when darkness is always within. We must answer that inner darkness is called blindness of mind, while outer darkness means the infernal punishments that are outside us. For in hell they are inward, but those who suffer there are said to be sent into outer darkness, that is, into infernal punishments.

What they suffer there is shown when it follows: “There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.”

The eyes commonly weep because of excessive smoke, and the teeth gnash because of excessive cold. Therefore, when he says, “There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth,” he shows metaphorically through bodily members that the reprobate will endure in punishment both immeasurable cold and intolerable heat, as blessed Job says: “Let him pass from the waters of snow to excessive heat, and let his sin descend even to hell. Let mercy forget him. His sweetness shall be worms” (Job 24).

[Col. 0146C] If anyone doubts the resurrection of his body, he can understand from this passage that it will indeed take place. For the eyes are of flesh, and the teeth are made of bones. Therefore, when he says, “There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth,” he shows that we will rise in the same form in which we remain in the present age.

Hence blessed Job says elsewhere: “I believe that my Redeemer lives, and on the last day I shall rise from the earth. And again I shall be clothed with my skin, and in my flesh I shall see God, whom I myself shall see, and not another, and my eyes shall behold him” (Job 19)—that is, it will not be another form on my behalf; I myself shall see him.

The Lord also showed this when, after his resurrection, he spoke to the disciples, saying: “See my hands and my feet, for I myself am” (Luke 24). And again: “Touch and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see me have.”

[Col. 0146D] “And Jesus said to the centurion: ‘Go; as you have believed, so let it be done for you.’ And the servant was healed from that hour.”

Here we must consider how greatly each person’s own faith helps him, when another person’s faith was of such benefit. Because of the centurion’s faith, the servant’s health was restored.

Faith is indeed a great virtue, and, as the Apostle says, “without it it is impossible to please God” (Hebrews 11). Concerning it the Prophet Habakkuk also says: “But my righteous one lives by faith” (Habakkuk 2). Commending this faith to his disciples, the Lord says: “If you have faith like a grain of mustard seed, you will say to this mountain, ‘Move from here,’ and it will move; and to the mulberry tree, ‘Be uprooted and planted in the sea,’ and it will obey you” (Luke 17).

And because the faith of the Gentiles was prefigured in the Gentile centurion, this man, who believed so perfectly, is rightly called a centurion by the Evangelist.

[Col. 0147A] A centurion is so called because he has one hundred soldiers under him. The number one hundred is perfect: it passes from the left hand to the right, and, forming a circle, takes the shape of a crown. It signifies the crown that Christ’s soldiers will receive for spiritual combat. One of them said: “I have fought the good fight; I have finished the course; I have kept the faith. From now on, the crown of righteousness is laid up for me” (2 Timothy 4).

## HOMILY XX. FOURTH SUNDAY AFTER EPIPHANY

[Col. 0147B]

(Matthew 8.) “At that time, as Jesus was boarding a boat, his disciples followed him. And behold, a great disturbance arose on the sea,” and so forth.

In the sequence of this reading, the Lord Jesus Christ was pleased to commend the truth of both his natures, namely, the divine and the human. As man, he boarded the boat; but as God, he stirred up the sea. As man, he slept in the boat; but as God, he commanded the winds and the sea.

He did not assume the function of a boat because he was unable to dry up the sea, as he once did before the children of Israel, or to walk upon the waves of the sea—for he also granted Peter the ability to walk upon the waves—but he performed the things proper to a human being, so that he might indicate that he had truly become human for our sake.

Allegorically, [Col. 0147C] the boat that the Lord boarded signifies the standard of the cross. He boarded the boat, as it were, when, for our liberation, he allowed himself to be raised upon the wood of the cross, as he himself said to the Jews: “When you have lifted up the Son of Man, then you will know that I am” (John 8).

Therefore Mark rightly records that he boarded the boat near sunset, in order to suggest the mystery of his Passion, concerning which the Prophet says: “The sun knew its setting” (Psalm 104).

His disciples followed him because they imitated the footsteps of his Passion. To follow the Lord means to imitate him, as he himself says: “Whoever serves me must follow me” (John 12). And again: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Luke 9).

But when the Lord boarded the boat,

[Col. 0147D] “a great disturbance arose on the sea,” because, while he hung upon the cross, an uproar arose among the Jewish people. The sea was swelling, as it were, when the Jewish people roared and cried out: “Crucify, crucify” (John 19), such a one.

The disturbance of the sea became so great “that the boat was covered by the waves.” For the persecution of the Jews increased so greatly that the very chief of the apostles denied Christ, and he himself and the others sat in a locked room because of fear of the Jews.

“But he was sleeping,” because he postponed the power of his resurrection until the third day. And Christ’s death is beautifully compared with sleep, because no one is awakened from sleep more easily than he rose from the tomb. Concerning this sleep he says through the Prophet: “I slept and was drowsy, and I rose” (Psalm 3).

[Col. 0148A] “And his disciples approached him and awakened him, saying: ‘Lord, save us; we are perishing.’”

It was not that they could assist him in his resurrection, since he raised himself by his own power. But because they themselves, in a certain measure, awakened him when they doubted his resurrection, it is rightly said:

“And he said to them: ‘You of little faith, why did you doubt?’”

A person of little faith is one who believes partly and partly does not believe. For one who doubts entirely is an unbeliever. The apostles were therefore called people of little faith because they doubted his resurrection in part, as Matthew testifies when he says: “The eleven disciples went into Galilee, to the mountain where Jesus had appointed them; and when they saw him, they worshiped him, but some doubted” (Matthew 28).

[Col. 0148B] Therefore, according to the Evangelist Mark, their unbelief and hardness of heart are rightly rebuked at the end, because they did not believe those who had seen him risen. Those who had heard the Lord say, “O foolish ones and slow of heart to believe in all that the prophets have spoken” (Luke 24), were reproved for this smallness of faith.

“Then he rose and commanded the winds and the sea, and there was a great calm.”

[Col. 0148C] The Lord rose and commanded the winds and the sea when, revealing his resurrection to the disciples, he caused doubt to cease in their minds and restrained the fury of the roaring Jewish people, fulfilling the prophecy that says: “The earth trembled and became still when God arose for judgment, to save all the meek of the earth” (Psalm 76).

“Moreover, the men were amazed, saying: ‘What sort of man is this, that the winds and the sea obey him?’” It should not be thought that the apostles said this, but rather the sailors and the others who were in the boat. But if anyone stubbornly insists that the apostles said it, let him recognize that they are called “men” because they were still thinking in human terms. For if anyone considers the nature of divinity, it is not surprising that he could command the winds and the sea, since he could create all things from nothing. For he himself was in the boat who, in the beginning, set a limit for the sea, saying: “Thus far you shall come, and you shall proceed no farther, and here your swelling waves shall be broken” (Job 38).

We can also refer this voyage of the Lord to the general persecution of the Church, since the boat sometimes signifies the Church, as it is said through the prophet: “Those who go down to the sea in ships, doing their work upon many waters; they have seen the works of the Lord and his wonders in the deep” (Psalm 106). Whoever, then, desires to cross the sea of this world must necessarily enter the bosom of this boat—that is, join himself to the members of the Church in faith and works. For the Lord may be said to have boarded the boat when he came to the Church through the preaching of the disciples.

“But a great disturbance arose on the sea.” For the persecution of the pagans, instigated by the devil, rose up against the Church, so that “the little boat was covered by the waves”—namely, so that, as the persecution increased, the Church could scarcely remain hidden among the few faithful [Col. 0149A] and no one would dare publicly confess the name of Christ unless he was prepared to die immediately for Christ. History reports that this happened in the time of Diocletian and Maximian, and of the others who persecuted the Church with no ordinary severity.

“But he was sleeping,” because he was not displaying the power of his strength. For he was as though sleeping in the boat when he permitted the wicked to prevail against the devout, so that the elect might be crowned more gloriously through patience, while the wicked might be condemned more severely for their cruelty.

“And they came and woke him, saying: ‘Lord, save us; we are perishing.’” This occurred when the faithful and ecclesiastical men, realizing that by their own strength they could neither endure nor overcome that storm of persecution, fled with all their desires to him who says in the Gospel: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15), saying to him with the Prophet (Psalm 43): “Awake; why do you sleep, O Lord? Awake, and do not reject us forever.” And also: “Arise, O Lord, help us and deliver us for the sake of your name.”

“Then, rising, he commanded the winds and the sea.” The Lord rose and commanded the winds and the sea when he caused the persecutions stirred up by the devil to become quiet, converting some of them to his faith and physically punishing others who persisted in unbelief.

“And there was calm” for the Church, to such an extent that the emperors, kings, and princes themselves submitted their necks to the yoke of the Christian faith and afterward honored those against whom they had previously burned with persecution. This happened so fully that people were amazed, saying: “What sort of man is this, that the winds and the sea obey him?” [Col. 0149C]

But what we have said generally about the universal Church can also be applied morally to each individual soul of a righteous man. Whoever renounces impiety and worldly desires, crucifying his members with their vices and desires (Galatians 5), desires, as though boarding the boat with the Lord, to cross the sea of this world.

But immediately a great disturbance arises on the sea, because the storm of temptation, rising from the devil’s envy, seeks to shake the mind of the righteous man from its good purpose—sometimes outwardly through the persecutions of wicked people, sometimes inwardly through the impulse of evil thoughts, and sometimes through the weakness of the flesh itself, when the goads of temptation arise.

When the disciples therefore board the boat with the Lord, a great disturbance occurs on the sea, because the more a person advances in God, the more he finds in the world that he must bear with greater difficulty. So it was with the Israelites, who were harassed by Pharaoh with a double affliction precisely when, instructed by Moses, they happened to flee for divine help, at the time when they were called through Moses and Aaron to the promised land. The Lord also demonstrated this by his own example when, after fasting, he endured the devil’s temptations. For the devil often tempts us more fiercely after our conversion, grieving that we have withdrawn from his service.

But he who neither sleeps nor slumbers, guarding Israel, is as though sleeping in the boat when he permits the mind of the righteous man to be wearied more severely amid the storms of temptation. When that man realizes that he cannot overcome by his own strength either the devil’s temptations or even the goads of his own flesh [Col. 0150A], he approaches and wakes the Lord: he draws near to him through devotion of mind, humbly acknowledges his weakness, and most devoutly begs for divine power.

If he senses that the Lord is delaying the fulfillment of his desires, he joins prayers to prayers until, through continual groaning, he arouses divine help for his assistance. Hence it is rightly added: “Then, rising, he commanded the winds and the sea.” The Lord rises and commands the winds and the sea when he causes the tumult of evil thoughts to become quiet in the faithful soul.

Then there is a great calm, because, once the roots of evil thoughts have been driven out, the soul begins, as though naturally through good habit, to guard the virtues which it had previously guarded with fear. The soul rejoices with the prophet and sings: “Depart from me, you evildoers, and I will search out the commandments of my God” (Psalm 118).

“Jesus boarded the little boat.” In the sacred Scriptures one and the same thing commonly has a twofold or threefold significance. Thus the boat sometimes signifies the banner of the cross, sometimes the womb of the undefiled Virgin, and sometimes the holy Church.

It signifies the holy Church, as in the passage: “Jesus boarded the little boat” (Matthew 8), and: “Sitting, he taught the crowds from the boat” (Luke 5).

It signifies the womb of the undefiled Virgin, as it is read elsewhere: “Jesus boarded the boat, crossed over, and came to his own city” (Matthew 9).

It signifies the banner of the holy cross, as in this passage: “Jesus boarded the little boat” (Matthew 8).

In each and the same miracle both natures of the Lord, namely the divine and the human, are commended to us. For as man he boarded the boat, but as God he stirred up the sea; as man he slept in the boat, but as God he commanded the winds and the sea and made them quiet.

But why did he wish to board a boat when he was going to cross the sea? Could he not cross over the sea who enabled Peter to walk upon the waves? Or could he not dry the sea before his own feet, who long ago had dried up the Red Sea before the children of Israel leaving Egypt and had made them cross on dry ground? Certainly he could. But he assumed the service of the boat for this reason: so that, doing everything that belongs to man, he might show himself to be truly human.

After he had wondrously performed miracles in our lands [Col. 0150D], he crossed over to the sea in order to perform there a great miracle and demonstrate that he was the Son of God, who does great wonders, brings forth the sea and rivers, and brings the winds out of his treasuries. For he is the one who made the sea and the dry land, who set a limit for the sea, saying: “Thus far you shall come, and you shall proceed no farther, and here your swelling waves shall be broken” (Job 38).

Typically, as we have said, the banner of the cross is understood through this little boat. A boat is a hollow piece of wood, extremely useful for carrying loads over the waters and especially necessary in places where no shallows are found. The Lord, however, intending to cross the sea’s waves, boarded a boat because, having trodden upon the waves of this world, he was going to ascend the cross in order to suffer [Col. 0151A].

It was fitting that, since the first man had found death through the forbidden wood by disobedience, he should regain life through the wood of the holy cross by obeying God.

“But his disciples followed him.” Just as he deigned to suffer, be crucified, and die for the redemption of the human race, so his disciples did not hesitate to endure many torments for his name and for the sheep entrusted to them. For both Peter and Andrew were crucified; Paul was beheaded; and the others also endured various torments.

Or they followed him because, by devoting themselves to good works, they imitated his footsteps. To follow the Lord means to imitate him, as he himself says: “Whoever serves me must follow me” (John 12). And again: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself” (Luke 9), and so forth. Hence it is also commanded in the Law: “You shall walk after the Lord your God” (Deuteronomy 10). Likewise, in the Song of Songs, the Church says to the Bridegroom: “Draw me after you; we shall run in the fragrance of your ointments” (Song of Songs 1).

“And behold, a great disturbance arose on the sea, so that the little boat was covered by the waves.” If the boat which the Lord boarded signifies the banner of the cross, then in this passage the sea likewise signifies the Jewish people, which was shaken by a great revolt. The Jews were disturbed, and his disciples fled.

Was the sea not surging when, while Pilate said, “I find no cause of death in him” (John 19), the people cried out: “Take him away, take him away; crucify him,” and: “If you release this man, you are not Caesar’s friend”? The sea surged when some said: “If this man were not a criminal, we would not have handed him over to you” (John 18), while others, grieving, said: “Truly this was the Son of God” (Mark 15).

“He himself, however, was sleeping.” Christ’s sleep signifies death. He slept then when, hanging upon the cross, he said: “It is finished,” and, bowing his head, gave up his spirit (John 19). Christ’s death is rightly compared with sleep, because no one rises from sleep so easily or so quickly as Christ rose from death.

For he was awakened like a sleeping Lord, as the Psalmist says (Psalm 77), and like a powerful man overcome with wine. Through the same Psalmist he also says: “I slept and took my sleep, and I rose” (Psalm 3). And again: “In peace, in the same place, I shall sleep and rest” (Psalm 4).

The Lord’s sleep, therefore, pertains not to his divinity but to his humanity. He sleeps according to his humanity, while he never slept according to his divinity, as the Psalmist bears witness, saying: “He will neither sleep nor slumber who guards Israel” (Psalm 120).

“And his disciples came to him and woke him, saying: ‘Lord, save us; we are perishing.’” The disciples approached and woke the Lord because they understood that they could not overcome the savagery of the Jews unless they were strengthened and gladdened by his resurrection, which they desired to take place as quickly as possible.

Or they approached him to awaken him because, trusting in his omnipotence, they clung to him in mind and desire, according to the Psalmist’s words: “Draw near to him and be enlightened, and your faces shall not be put to shame” (Psalm 53).

Or they approached him because they desired with all the strength of their minds that his resurrection should occur, as the Evangelist Luke makes clear when he says: “The disciples rejoiced when they saw the Lord” (Luke 24).

“And he said to them: ‘Why are you timid, you of little faith?’” One who does not believe is called unbelieving; one who believes perfectly is called great in faith; but one who believes in part, yet does not believe perfectly, is called of little faith.

The disciples therefore had little faith when they doubted while the Omnipotent One was present; and while the Creator was present, they feared a creature.

Nor are they reproved for their smallness of faith only here, but also in other passages. For during the Lord’s Passion they had little faith, although shortly before they had said: “Let us also go and die with him” [Col. 0152B] (John 11). But when they saw him seized, bound, and scourged, they abandoned him and fled (Matthew 26).

Peter also had little faith, because, although he had previously said to the Lord, “Even if I must die with you, I will not deny you” (ibid.), he denied him at the voice of a single servant girl.

They are shown to have had little faith not only during the Passion but also in the resurrection, because they doubted that he would rise. Thus, when he appeared after his resurrection to those sitting in the upper room—that is, in a closed house—they were troubled and frightened, thinking that they saw a spirit.

To confirm their faith, he showed them his hands and feet, saying (Luke 24): “See my hands and my feet, for I am he myself.” And again: “Touch and see, because a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see that I have.”

Thomas was not removed from this smallness of faith. When the disciples told him, “We have seen the Lord,” he did not believe them, saying: “Unless I see in his hands the mark of the nails and put my hand into his side, I will not believe.”

To strengthen his faith, the Lord made himself tangible, saying: “Put your finger here and see the place of the nails, and bring your hand to my side; and do not be unbelieving but believing” (John 20).

“Then, rising, he commanded the winds and the sea”—namely, when, rising on the third day, he not only strengthened and gladdened the hearts of the disciples but also caused the savagery and revolt of the Jews to become quiet, turning their joy into sorrow. They even promised money to the soldiers guarding the Lord’s tomb and reporting his resurrection, saying: “Say that his disciples came by night and stole his body” (Matthew 28).

“And there was a great calm.” For some of those who had consented to the Lord’s death were converted to the faith of Christ through the preaching of the apostles: when Peter preached, three thousand believed in one day, and another five thousand on another occasion.

“Moreover, the men were amazed, saying: ‘What sort of man is this, that the winds and the sea obey him?’” The apostles did not say this, but the sailors who were with the Lord in the boat. For the apostles already knew how to say that this was Christ, the Son of the living God. The others, however, who saw only the Lord’s humanity and did not understand his divinity, said “What sort of man?” and the rest—not by asking but by expressing amazement [Col. 0153A].

Hence they are rightly called “men,” because they were thinking in human terms, as though they had said: “This man is greater than our fathers. Moses divided the waters of the sea with a staff, and Elijah the waters of the Jordan with his cloak; this man, by a mere word, makes seas and storms become quiet.”
