Although this reading appears to pertain particularly to the apostles, we can nevertheless refer it to the universal Church. After Christ, having conquered death through the trophy of the holy cross, ascended to heaven, the sea was, as it were, stirred up: for the more the Church grew through the faith of the elect and the number of believers multiplied, the more it experienced a greater persecution from the wicked and a harsher unbelief from heretics rising up against it.

But because he permitted such a powerful persecution to rage against the elect, after he had been awakened by the prayers of the saints, he rose and commanded the winds and the sea. For he caused that persecution and unbelief to become quiet and granted peace and tranquility to his elect.

There was a great calm because, after rulers and powerful men came to the faith of Christ through the apostles’ preaching, such rest was given to the Church that even those who had destroyed it rebuilt it with their own hands.

And although the sea surged and the storm grew, the boat in which the Lord was sleeping was not submerged. For although the Church could be disturbed by hostile persecutions, it did not, with the Lord guiding it, depart from the faith of uprightness. It had been founded upon the firm rock, of which the Apostle says: “The rock, however, was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10) [Col. 0153C].

What was fulfilled in the apostles and in the universal Church commonly also takes place morally in every holy man. Whoever crucifies his members with their vices and desires, and for whom the world has been crucified and he himself to the world, has Christ dwelling within him.

Jesus boarded the boat when he inhabits the mind of the holy man, because, as the wisest Solomon says, “The soul of the righteous is the seat of wisdom.”

When this man wishes to withdraw from vices and sins so that he may be free for God alone—that is, attentive to him—he feels the devil’s temptations rising up against him and its persuasions opposing his mind. The more he wishes to draw near to God, the more he finds that he must bear with greater difficulty.

“For all who wish to live devoutly in Christ suffer persecutions” (2 Timothy 3), as in the example of the Israelites, who were afflicted more harshly by Pharaoh when they were called through Moses and Aaron to the promised land.

Hence a certain wise man, Solomon, admonishes us, saying: “My son, when you approach the service of God, stand in justice and fear, and prepare your soul for temptation” (Sirach 2).

Jesus sleeps when he permits the pleasures of the flesh and the devil’s persuasions to rise up against the mind of the holy man. But when that man understands that he cannot overcome those temptations by his own strength, he has recourse to God’s omnipotence.

Hence it is added: “And they came and woke him, saying: ‘Lord, save us; we are perishing.’” For he does not cease to implore God’s mercy with all the strength of his mind, saying with the Psalmist (Psalm 43): “Arise; why do you sleep, O Lord?” And again: “Arise, O Lord, help us,” and so forth.

“And rising, he commanded the winds and the sea,” when he causes the temptations of the devil rising against the mind of the holy man to become quiet and allows him to serve him freely.

Then there is a great calm, because he will afterward guard the things he previously possessed without fear, just as he has begun to preserve them naturally through good habit, saying with the Psalmist: “Depart from me, you evildoers, and I will search out the commandments of my God” (Psalm 118).

Thus, after crossing the sea and trampling upon the waves of this world, he happily reaches the harbor. Of such people it is said through the prophet: “Those who go down to the sea in ships, doing their work upon many waters, they have seen the works of the Lord and his wonders in the deep” (Psalm 106).

They go down to the sea—that is, into this world; in ships—that is, in souls; doing their work—that is, doing good, breaking their flesh with its vices and desires, and sighing for heavenly things; upon many waters—that is, among a numerous people, living among whom they take care in all things not to defile themselves in anything.

But just as a man sailing in a boat through the sea is not touched by the sea, so the righteous, dwelling in this world among the people, do not cling to their wickedness.

## HOMILY XXI: THE SUNDAY OF SEPTUAGESIMA

(Matthew 20) “At that time, Jesus told his disciples this parable: ‘The kingdom of heaven is like a householder who went out early in the morning to hire laborers for his vineyard,’” and so forth.

When “the kingdom of heaven” or “the kingdom of God” is read in the Gospel, it does not always have one and the same meaning. Sometimes it signifies the Lord Jesus Christ, sometimes sacred Scripture, sometimes the heavenly homeland, and sometimes the present Church.

It signifies the Lord Jesus Christ, as he himself says: “The kingdom of God is within you” (Luke 17).

It signifies sacred Scripture, as is said to the unbelieving Jews: “The kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a nation producing its fruits” (Matthew 21).

It signifies the heavenly homeland, as in the passage: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for the sake of justice, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 5).

It signifies the present Church, as he says elsewhere: “Whoever loosens one of these least commandments and teaches people to do so will be called least in the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 19).

Therefore, in this passage “the kingdom of heaven” signifies the present Church. It is compared to a householder so that, through something known, we may learn to believe what is unknown, and so that our mind may be carried from visible things to invisible realities.

Since this is a parable, let us attend to what the householder, his vineyard, the laborers, and their reward signify allegorically.

This householder represents the figure of almighty God, who is compared to a householder because, just as a householder orders the members of his household, so almighty God orders, rules, and disposes human beings in the world.

The vineyard of this householder is the holy Church. From the beginning of the world to the end of the age, as many saints as it brings forth, it generates, as it were, that many branches.

This vineyard was first planted among the Jewish people, but after the Lord’s incarnation it was extended to the ends of the earth, as the Psalmist says: “You brought a vine out of Egypt; you drove out the nations and planted it. You were its guide in its sight; you planted its roots, and it filled the land. Its shade covered the mountains, and its branches the cedars of God. It stretched out its branches to the sea and its shoots to the river” (Psalm 79).

This is that vineyard of which, in the Song of Songs, the voice of the Bridegroom says: “Let us rise early and go to the vineyards; let us see whether the vine has blossomed and whether the flowers are bringing forth fruit” (Song of Songs 7).

And again: “A vineyard was planted for the peaceful one, in her that possesses peoples. He entrusted it to keepers; a man gives a thousand silver pieces for its fruits” (Song of Songs 8).

The same vineyard is also described through Isaiah: “I will sing for my beloved the song of my kinsman concerning his vineyard: My beloved had a vineyard on a fertile hill. He fenced it and cleared it of stones; he planted it as a choice vine. He built a winepress in its midst and surrounded it with a wall. He expected it to produce grapes, but it produced wild grapes” (Isaiah 5).

The same prophet reveals what this vineyard is when he adds: “For the vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel, and the men of Judah are his delightful plant” (ibid.).

In this vineyard a person labors with greater faithfulness the more firmly he believes in God and the more carefully he keeps his commandments, abandoning earthly things and longing for heavenly things. And the more abundantly he labors in it, the richer the fruits he produces, the more he seeks not his own but another’s gain. Whoever seeks what is his own and not what belongs to Jesus Christ does not labor in Christ’s vineyard.

The householder therefore went out early in the morning to cultivate this vineyard, because from the beginning of the world almighty God has never ceased to send holy men. By living well they cultivated this vineyard, and by teaching well they called many to its cultivation.

That those who labor faithfully in this vineyard—that is, in the Church—will receive a reward is made clear when it is added:

“After agreeing with the laborers for a denarius a day, he sent them into his vineyard.” The denarius promised to those laboring in the vineyard signifies the reward of eternal life.

This is entirely appropriate, for the image of a king is expressed on a denarius, while man was made in the image and likeness of God, as the Lord himself says: “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Genesis 2).

But man violated this image when he sinned. The householder therefore makes an agreement with the laborers for a denarius a day because he promises those who work well the glory that the first man would have possessed without labor if he had not sinned.

But because, after sin, the human condition cannot remain long in the present age, as the elect succeed one another he called laborers in different periods to cultivate the vineyard. Hence it is added:

“And going out about the third hour, he found others standing idle in the marketplace, and he said to them: ‘Go, you also, into my vineyard, and whatever is just I will give you.’ They went away. Again he went out about the sixth and the ninth hour and did likewise. About the eleventh hour he went out and found others standing there, and he said to them: ‘Why are you standing here idle all day?’ They said to him: ‘Because no one has hired us.’ He said to them: ‘Go, you also, into my vineyard.’”

The variety of hours at which laborers are sent to cultivate the vineyard signifies the various times at which holy laborers—namely, the faithful—were sent to cultivate the spiritual vineyard.

The morning of the world was from Adam to Noah; the third hour, from Noah to Abraham; the sixth, from Abraham to Moses; the ninth, from Moses to the coming of the Lord; and the eleventh, from the coming of the Lord to the end of the age.

To mention a few among the many, let us give some examples. The laborers of the early morning, that is, of the first hour of the day, were Abel and Enoch and all the others who pleased God in that age.

At the third hour, the laborers were Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, together with the twelve patriarchs.

At the ninth hour the number of laborers began to increase, when Moses and Aaron, Joshua, Samuel, David, Isaiah, Jeremiah, and many others were sent.

At the eleventh hour, the laborers sent to cultivate the vineyard—that is, the Church—were the holy apostles. They cultivated this vineyard with greater zeal and care because they had been instructed more perfectly by Truth itself.

Hence one of them said: “We are those upon whom the ends of the ages have come” (1 Corinthians 10).

If we refer this comparison to both peoples, namely the Jews and the Gentiles, the laborer of the first, third, sixth, and ninth hours was the Jewish people in its ancient fathers, and it flourished like a single spiritual vine in its elect.

At the eleventh hour the Gentiles were called, because after the Lord’s ascension they believed through the preaching of the apostles. Of them it is said: “Why are you standing here idle all day?”

They stood idle all day because, from the very beginning of the world until the Lord’s incarnation, they remained alienated from the worship of God. No patriarch had been sent to instruct them; no prophet had been sent. Hence, making excuse, they say: “Because no one has hired us.”

What does “No one has hired us” mean except that no one called us to cultivate the spiritual vineyard?

By these words we must stir our consciences and consider carefully what we shall say in our defense on the day of judgment if we are found sluggish in good works—although we were born of Christian parents, received the word of life almost from our cradles, and were nourished with the milk of the Scriptures together with the milk of the flesh.

We must therefore be as much more diligent in good works as we shall be less able to plead ignorance in our defense—namely, when we shall be without excuse because we have received the call and knowledge of God. For those who sin knowingly and those who sin unknowingly are not constrained in the same way, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “The servant who did not know his master’s will and did not act rightly will be beaten with few blows; but the one who knew and did not act rightly will be beaten with many blows” (Luke 12).

Morally, we can also refer these varieties of hours to the stages of our own life.

The morning is the childhood of a human being; the third hour is adolescence. For just as at the third hour the sun begins to ascend higher and to unfold the rays of its brightness, so in adolescence the natural heat of the blood increases.

The sixth hour is youth. For just as at the sixth hour the sun, positioned in the middle of the sky, emits rays that are not only brighter but also hotter, so youth is found to be capable, eager, suitable, and strong for doing good work.

The ninth hour is old age. For just as at the ninth hour the sun begins to decline toward sunset, so in old age not only the heat of the blood but also a person’s natural and innate strength declines.

The eleventh hour is the age that in our language is called decrepitude, so that it is understood to have gone beyond old age. Hence the Greeks call those who are very old not γέροντας (*gerontas*, “old men”), but πρεσβύτας (*presbytes*, “elders”), indicating by this term that they are more than merely old.

The laborers are therefore sent into the vineyard at different hours because, at different ages, human beings are called by divine grace to do good works.

Those who serve God with devoted minds from childhood are hired into the vineyard, as it were, at the first hour.

Others, when they are converted to God’s service in adolescence, are called to cultivate the vineyard at about the third hour.

Others live carnally during adolescence; if they are converted to the Lord in youth, shake off their sluggishness and laziness, abandon their former ways, and practice good works, they are sent into the vineyard at about the sixth hour.

If someone has been sluggish in good works during childhood, adolescence, and youth, it is necessary that in old age, as at the ninth hour, he convert to God’s service and be ashamed of having been idle in God’s service, since he will not have much time left to labor. Let him consider what the Apostle says: “Do you not know that God’s patience is leading you to repentance?” (Romans 2), and let him beware of what follows: “By your hardness and impenitent heart you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath” (ibid.).

But if someone is so negligent and lazy that even in old age he remains sluggish in good works, let him at least come to his senses in the age of decrepitude and, by turning to God, withdraw himself from the devil’s snares in which he was held captive. Let him wash away his past evils with tears and, as far as he can, devote himself to good works.

For if he is converted at the eleventh hour, let him not fear to undertake the labor even then, when he will be able to labor little for God. Just as he fears the sentence of the strict Judge, so let him trust in the mercy of the one who did not come to call the righteous but sinners to repentance.

The most compassionate and merciful God does not reject or despise those who are converted even in old age; rather, in his most kindly mercy he receives and embraces them.

He did not lie who said: “As I live, says the Lord, I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he turn and live” (Ezekiel 33). And again (ibid.): “On whatever day the sinner turns and groans, all his sins will be consigned to oblivion.”

But because the cunning of the ancient enemy commonly deceives lukewarm Christians in this matter—persuading them to sin while promising them a long life, as though they could wash away in old age or decrepitude what they committed in adolescence or youth—it is nevertheless necessary that, because we do not know the hour of our calling, we be prepared for good works at all times.

This deception must be countered by the variety of the human condition. Since we do not know which of us will be called from this life in childhood, which in adolescence, which in youth, which in old age, and which in decrepitude, just as the time of departure is uncertain for all, so each person’s determination to do good must be certain, because the Lord says: “You also must be ready, for the Son of Man will come at an hour when you do not expect him” (Luke 12; Matthew 24).

For just as laborers, as we have said, are sent into the vineyard at different hours, so human beings are called from this life at different ages. Some at the first hour, that is, in childhood; others at the third hour, that is, in adolescence; others at the sixth, that is, in youth; others at the ninth, that is, in old age; and others at the eleventh, that is, in decrepitude, which is called advanced age.

Because the hour of each person’s calling is uncertain throughout these ages, everyone must be prepared for good works, lest, when he is able, he refuses to do good and begins to wish to do it when he will no longer be able.

Hence the merciful Lord admonishes us, saying: “Run while you have the light of life, lest the darkness of death overtake you” (John 12). And Solomon says: “Whatever your hand is able to do, do it diligently” (Ecclesiasticus 18). For neither work, nor reason, nor wisdom, nor knowledge will exist in the underworld.

And again: “Do not delay turning to God, nor postpone from day to day, because the wrath of God will come suddenly and in the end will destroy you” (Ecclesiasticus 5).

And Isaiah says: “Seek the Lord while he may be found; call upon him while he is near” (Isaiah 55).

The remembrance of death greatly helps to overcome the pleasure of sin, as it is said through a certain wise man, namely Solomon: “In all your works remember your last things, and you will never sin” (Ecclesiasticus 7).

“But when evening had come, the lord of the vineyard said to his steward: ‘Call the laborers and give them their reward’” [Col. 0158D].

Evening is the end of the day, according to the interpretation given above. In this passage evening signifies the time of the Lord’s incarnation, as Paul says: “We are those upon whom the ends of the ages have come” (1 Corinthians 10). And as John says: “Little children, it is the last hour” (1 John 2).

Just as the householder is understood to be almighty God and his vineyard the holy Church, so the steward is the Lord Jesus Christ, who says in the Gospel: “I am the true vine, and my Father is the cultivator, and you are the branches” (John 15).

The householder therefore calls the steward to give the laborers their reward because almighty God created us through the Son, redeemed us through the Son, and will reward us through him, as the Son himself says: “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5).

How greatly he has caused the riches of his goodness to abound in us who believed after his incarnation is shown when it is said: “Beginning with the last and proceeding to the first.” This means: beginning with the laborers of the eleventh hour and continuing to the laborers of the first hour.

“Therefore, when those who had come at the eleventh hour arrived, they received a denarius each.” In these words it is shown how greatly the Lord’s incarnation benefits us who believed after his resurrection. For not only did those who came last receive the same denarius that had been promised to the first, but they received it before them. For the holy Fathers who preceded the Lord’s coming, although they lived justly and devoutly, did not immediately enter the gate of the heavenly kingdom when they were released from the flesh; rather, they were held in the places of the underworld, though not in places of punishment, as blessed Jacob testifies when he says: “You will bring down my gray hairs with sorrow to the underworld” (Gen. XLII). And again: “I shall go down mourning for my son into the underworld” (Gen. XXXVII). Hence it is also said through blessed Job (ch. XXX): “I know, Lord, that you will deliver me over to death, where the whole house of the living has been established. And if I descend into the underworld, you will free me from there.” But to us, who believed after the Lord’s incarnation, it has been granted as a great gift that, if we live perfectly, we may receive eternal life without any delay when released from the flesh. And this is what it means that the first, who came last, received the denarius.

[Col. 0159C] “But when the first came, they supposed that they would receive more. Yet they too received a denarius each, and upon receiving it they murmured against the master of the household, saying: ‘These last have worked one hour, and you have made them equal to us, who have borne the burden of the day and the heat.’” Since we have said above that the denarius signifies the reward of eternal life, the question arises why these are said to have received the denarius and to have murmured, when no one who murmurs receives the kingdom of God, and no one who has received it can afterwards murmur. But the answer must be that the murmuring in this passage does not express a malicious intention against God; rather, it signifies the devout complaint of the saints to God. Since the ancient Fathers happened to live for a long time in the present life, they necessarily had to remain for a long time subject to the burden of the day and the heat in the sufferings of the flesh. Their actions may therefore be said to have murmured when they appeared to see those who believed after the Lord’s incarnation receive, after a brief tribulation, the reward that they themselves had awaited amid long tribulation.

To make this easier to understand, it seemed appropriate to bring forward one example from among many, namely the patriarch Abraham. His action may be said to have murmured when he saw the thief, rescued by divine grace from the very jaws of death, enter paradise before him (Matt. XXVII). Did not the thief come at the eleventh hour, he who confessed Christ on the cross, and yet received the reward of the denarius before Abraham, who was called at the third hour and endured the burden of the day and the heat for a long time? For the thief confessed Christ on the cross, but from the cross he ascended to paradise, the Lord saying: “Amen I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke XXIII).

We may also understand it in this way: Christians now ascend to heaven before those who lived before the Lord’s coming did. For after leaving the body, those earlier people remained in the underworld for a long time; but these, after leaving the body, ascend to heaven without delay, if they are just. This is what it means that Christians ascend after their departure from the body before those earlier people ascended after their departure from theirs. And because eternal life is owed to no one as a debt, but is given through gratuitous mercy, [Col. 0160B] the master of the household rightly calls one of them and says:

“Friend, I am not doing you an injustice. Did you not agree with me for a daily denarius? Take what is yours and go.” It is clear, as we have said, that this pertains to the people of the Jews and of the Gentiles. For many Jews who believed after the Lord’s ascension did not wish to admit the Gentiles into their fellowship or equality; instead, they judged that the Gentiles ought to be treated as proselytes. They said that it was unworthy for the Gentiles, after the worship of idols, to be made equal to those whose fathers God had addressed (Exod. XVI), to whom he had shown many wonders, to whom he had given the law, and from whom he had assumed flesh.

This is what those who had come first into the vineyard said when they murmured against the last: “These last have worked one hour,” [Col. 0160C] and so forth. But because the Lord Jesus Christ extended the bosom of his mercy even to gather in the Gentiles, one of them is rightly told: “Friend, I am not doing you an injustice,” and so forth. Indeed, he who is not a respecter of persons, but in every nation is acceptable to him who practices righteousness (Rom. II), rightly says: “I also wish to give this last one as I have given you.” For through his grace—he who (Matt. IX) came not to call the righteous but sinners to repentance—not only were the Gentiles made equal to the Jews, but they were also found more ready to believe.

“Or is it not lawful for me to do what I wish? Or is your eye evil because I am good?” Thus the Apostle, restraining human complaints against God, says: “O man, who are you to answer back to God? Does the thing formed say to him who formed it, ‘Why have you made me thus?’ Or does the potter not have authority over the clay, to make from the same lump one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?” (Rom. IX). Certainly he does. For God, constrained by no necessity, but solely through goodness, gives life to whomever he wishes. Hence it is also added:

“Thus the last will be first, and the first last.” The Jews were once first, when long ago they believed in the God of heaven and lived according to the law. The Gentiles, however, were last (Deut. XXVIII), strangers to the knowledge of God and to the covenant of the law because of their unbelief. But when the Lord came, those who seemed to be first became last through refusing to believe, while those who had been last became first through believing; those who had been the head became the tail, and those who had been the tail became the head, according to what the Lord says: “For judgment I have come into this world, so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind” (John IX).

Hence the rare faith of the Jews is condemned when it is further added: “For many are called, but few are chosen.” This pertains especially to the Jewish people, among whom many were called, but few were found who would believe in the Lord. Concerning the calling of the Gentiles it is said elsewhere: “Many will come from the east and the west, and will recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. VIII).

Since, then, we have said that the variety of the hours at which the workers are called into the vineyard pertains to the differences of ages, it is worthwhile to observe how what we have said occurred among two peoples is fulfilled in the Church. For the evangelist says: “When evening had come,” and so forth. But because in this parable we follow a twofold interpretation, morally evening comes for each of us as the end of the present life. Although some are called from this life before they reach mature age, if they do not have evening by reason of age, they nevertheless have it by reason of their departure.

Thus the workers are called at evening to receive their reward because they receive the reward for their good works when they are called from this life, as the Psalmist testifies when he says: “When he gives sleep to his beloved, this is the Lord’s inheritance” (Ps. CXXVI).

God calls us in two ways: in the present to labor, and in the future to rest. Therefore whoever desires the future reward must not refuse labor in the present. Those who faithfully undertake labor for God will faithfully arrive at the reward, when they are to hear: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart, and you will find rest for your souls” (Matt. XI).

And because it often happens that some who are converted later and are called from this life receive their reward before those who began to labor earlier, the voice of the master of the household rightly says to the steward: “Beginning with the last and proceeding to the first,” and so forth. Their actions may be said to have murmured against those converted later, when they see those people rewarded before themselves.

What follows—“But when the first came, they received a denarius each, and upon receiving it they murmured against the master of the household, saying: ‘These last have worked one hour, and you have made them equal to us, who have borne the burden of the day and the heat’”—often occurs in the Church, and especially in the monastic order. Those bear the burden of the day and the heat who, nourished in the regular disciplines from childhood, are compelled to toil in vigils, fasts, and manual labor.

There are others who live carnally in the world until old age or even extreme old age, but who are converted near the end of life and quickly arrive at their reward after a brief tribulation. When, after a brief labor, they are called to rest, those who bear the burden of the day and the heat seem to murmur at their reception, seeing that those who entered the spiritual warfare last are rewarded while they themselves have remained in the contest.

But there must be no murmuring against God’s goodness, because such delay does not diminish the reward but increases it. For God, the just judge, will repay the elect according to their works; and they will receive a greater reward in proportion to the greater labor they endure while awaiting it, as the Apostle testifies: “Each will receive his reward according to his labor” (I Cor. III). All will receive one denarius because one kingdom has been prepared for all the elect; nevertheless, according to the diversity of merits, different rewards have been prepared in the kingdom of heaven, as the Lord says: “In my Father’s house there are many dwelling places” (John XIV).

Thus the heretic Jovinian is proved to have lied when he said that there would be no difference between a simple righteous person and a wise righteous person, between a virgin and a woman who had been corrupted, or between one of lesser merit and one of greater merit. The Apostle contradicts him, showing that different rewards have been prepared for different merits in the resurrection, saying: “There is one glory of the sun, another glory of the moon, and another glory of the stars. For star differs from star in glory; so also is the resurrection of the dead” (I Cor. XV).

Hence Daniel, when he foretold that many would rise from the dust of the earth, wishing to show that those who live well and devote themselves to gaining souls would receive a greater reward, said: “Those who are learned will shine like the splendor of the firmament, and those who instruct many in righteousness like stars for endless eternities” (Dan. XII).

That no one should murmur against God’s justice, but that all should rejoice in his goodness, is made clear when it is added: “Friend, I am not doing you an injustice. Did you not agree with me for a daily denarius? Take what is yours and go,” and so forth. God would seem to do an injustice if he failed to return as a reward what was owed as a debt. But since he gives to no one by debt, and gives only through gratuitous mercy to those whom he wishes, no one can murmur against God’s justice: for he has mercy on whom he wishes, and he hardens whom he wishes. He has mercy through goodness alone, and hardens through no iniquity; for even if his judgments are sometimes hidden, they are nevertheless not unjust.

What is added—“Thus the last will be first, and the first last”—we see happening daily in the Church, because some who are converted to the Lord later surpass, through the fervor of their minds and devout dedication, those who live lukewarmly and negligently.

But when the parable ends with the words, “Many are called, but few are chosen,” this should be feared more than explained. We all know that we have been called; whether we are chosen, however, we do not yet know. God calls us in many ways: through faith, through baptism, through repentance, through prosperity, through adversity, through dreams, and through revelations.

There are some who possess faith and shine with the words of doctrine, yet because they are sluggish in good works they are rejected from God’s election, since, as the Apostle James says: “Faith without works is dead” (James II). Of such people the Apostle Paul says: “They profess that they know God, but by their deeds they deny him” (Titus I). And the Lord says in the Gospel: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but he who does the will of my Father who is in heaven will enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. VII).

Such people will say on the day of judgment: “Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, perform many miracles, and cast out demons?” They will be answered: “Amen I say to you, I do not know you. Depart from me, workers of iniquity.” Therefore we must be as diligent in good works as we know ourselves to be without excuse regarding our calling, lest at the time of judgment, when we remain outside the door with the foolish virgins, we hear: “I do not know you,” instead of being received with the wise into the bridegroom’s chamber.

## HOMILY XXII: SUNDAY OF SEXAGESIMA

(Luke VIII.) “At that time, when a very great crowd had gathered and people were hurrying to Jesus from the cities, he spoke by way of a parable: ‘A sower went out to sow his seed,’ and so forth.”

While the Lord Jesus Christ was preaching the Gospel of the heavenly kingdom, many crowds followed him, differing in mind just as they differed in body. Some followed out of love, some out of envy, some for healing, and some out of admiration. The Lord so adapted his discourse to them that, in one and the same parable, each person heard what applied to him; and, accommodating himself to the weakness of all, he used comparisons drawn from visible things in his holy discourses, so that through visible things they might learn to recognize invisible realities.

Thus, as Matthew says: “Jesus spoke with his disciples in parables, and without parables he did not speak to them.” This does not mean, as some maintain, that he never at any time spoke without parables; rather, in the preaching that Matthew describes there, he spoke only in parables. For just as, as we have said, they followed him in four different ways, so, according to some, he also adapted his discourse in four different ways, speaking to them in parables and without parables, through likenesses and unlikenesses.

Sometimes the Lord opened certain matters in his words and closed others, so that through what we understand we might not grow proud, but instead regard what we do not understand as God’s gift. Thus, when many crowds gathered and hurried to him from the cities, he proposed the comparison of a man who went out to sow his seed. For by the variety of the soils he indicated that different kinds of human hearts were present in that crowd: some in which the seed of God’s word would perish after being harmed in various ways, and others in which it would bear good fruit through perseverance.

Here we must consider that the Lord graciously explained this comparison himself in order to suggest to us that allegorical meanings should be sought in the other comparisons that he did not explain. He showed what the field is, what the seed is, what the good soil signifies, and what the rocky and thorny soil signify. [Col. 0164A] But he left us one matter to investigate, namely the sower. We should understand no one better as the sower than the Lord Jesus Christ himself, who, having become human, sowed the seed of God’s word in human hearts, according to what he says in another parable: “He who sows the good seed is the Son of Man.”

Thus, according to the other evangelists, he is appropriately said to have left the house, gone to the sea, and boarded a boat before speaking this comparison, demonstrating by the position of his body what he was bringing forth from his mouth. For just as a prudent farmer, after uprooting brambles and thorns and cultivating the field with the plowshare, leaves his house, carries seed with him, and scatters it upon the earth so that he may receive it multiplied, so the Lord Jesus Christ, after cultivating the field—that is, the heart of the Jews—through the preaching of patriarchs and prophets, went out from the house, that is, appeared visibly in the world. He boarded a boat because he dwelt in the Church through faith, and he sowed spiritual seed, that is, the word of God, in the hearts of his hearers—not because he himself had nowhere to gather a harvest, but so that he might gather us into the Father’s granary.

Even today, when preachers and teachers preach the word of Christ, it is as though Christ himself were sowing the seed. For “unless the Lord builds the city, those who build it labor in vain” (Ps. CXXVI); and unless the Lord illumines the hearts of the hearers, the discourse of teachers labors in vain. Hence Paul, considering his own preaching and the obedience of the disciples as nothing belonging to himself, said: “I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth” (I Cor. III).

But because not everyone received his preaching in the same way, it is made clear when it is added: “And as he sowed, some fell beside the road, and it was trampled, and the birds of the sky ate it.” It often happens that when a person sows a field, a road lies beside it, and some part of the seed falls upon it. But the seed that falls on the road perishes through a double injury: either it is trampled by passersby, or it is snatched away by the birds of the sky.

It is called a road because those who pass along it carry something across it. The road signifies a heart worn down by the path of evil thoughts. The seed of God’s word that falls into such a heart is either crushed by passersby—that is, by unclean thoughts—or carried away by the birds of the sky—that is, by unclean spirits. They are called birds of the sky in two ways: either because they fell from heaven through pride, or because they move through the aerial heaven.

“And another fell upon the rock, and when it had grown it withered, because it had no moisture.” The rock in this passage signifies a hard and unteachable heart, which is not easily split open by the plowshare of God’s word. If the seed of God’s word falls into such a heart, even if it sprouts, it does not reach maturity, because it does not establish a root in the moisture of perseverance. The drying up of moisture at the root of the seed signifies, in another parable, the lack of oil for adorning the virgins’ lamps.

“And another fell among thorns, and the thorns that sprang up with it choked it.” The thorns signify vices and sins, concerning which it was said to the first man: “When you work the earth, it will not give its fruits, but it will produce thorns and thistles for you.” A mind devoted to vices therefore cannot make the seed of God’s word fruitful.

“And another fell on good soil, and when it had grown it produced a hundredfold fruit.” The good soil is the good heart of a person, prepared not only to hear the word of God but also devoted to doing what it hears. Therefore it produces a hundredfold fruit, that is, perfect fruit, because the number one hundred is used in Scripture for perfection.

Thus, concerning the person who abandoned all his possessions for God, it is said: “He will receive a hundredfold and possess eternal life.” This does not mean that one who abandoned one wife will receive a hundred wives, but that in the present he will receive such perfection that he will not again seek what he abandoned, and in the future he will possess eternal life. Isaac signified such soil producing a hundredfold when it is written: “Isaac sowed, and in that same year he found a hundredfold” (Gen. XXVI).

“When he had said this, he cried out.” But let us hear what he cried: “He who has ears to hear, let him hear.” Whenever this little admonition is inserted in the Gospel or in the Apocalypse, it indicates that something mystical is being proposed for investigation. For everyone in that crowd had bodily ears; and when he says to all who had bodily ears, “He who has ears to hear, let him hear,” he is seeking other ears, that is, hearts.

There is a spiritual hearing when the soul desires to hear the word of God with fervent love. Job showed that he possessed such hearing when he said: “I heard you by the hearing of the ear, O Lord” (Job XLII). Isaiah also says: “The Lord God has given me an ear.”

When the comparison was finished, he cried out among the crowds in order to show teachers that they should cry out in preaching—not merely through loudness of voice, but through the urgency of their preaching—according to what is said through Isaiah: “Cry out, do not cease; raise your voice like a trumpet, and announce their sins to my people and their transgressions to the house of Jacob” (Isa. LVIII). And again: “Cry out with strength, you who announce peace.”

“His disciples were asking him what this parable meant.” We should not think that immediately after the comparison ended the disciples questioned him in the presence of the crowds. Rather, as Mark says, when he was alone in the house, they asked him what this parable meant.

[Col. 0165D] “He said to them: ‘To you it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God, but to those who are outside everything is presented in parables.’” The house in which the disciples questioned the Lord spiritually signified the Church, which became the house of God through faith. Concerning it, it is written: “I will enter your house; I will worship toward your holy temple in your fear” (Ps. V).

Those hear the mystery of God who enter his tabernacle. Whoever therefore wishes to know the mystery of God should enter the house with Jesus—that is, having become faithful, should hold fast to the unity of the Church—for he is the one who makes people dwell with one heart in the house, as it is said through the Psalmist (Ps. LXVII).

But those who are outside—that is, pagans, Jews, and heretics—hear all Scripture in parables because they cannot grasp its mystery. When the Lord’s disciples questioned him privately, it is understood that a master should not be questioned by his disciples in the presence of everyone, but privately, lest he be embarrassed if he does not have an answer ready, or so that he may have the opportunity to consider what he says.

It is beautifully said: “To you it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God, but to the others in parables,” so that he might show that no one should glory in his own merits, as the Pelagians did when they said that a person could be justified without God’s grace. Nor should anyone presume on his own wisdom or virtue, since the apostles did not possess the mystery of the kingdom of God from themselves, but received it as something given by God, according to what one of them, namely James, says: “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, descending from the Father of lights, with whom there is no change or shadow of alteration” (James I).

And as the Lord himself says: “Without me you can do nothing” (John XV). Hence he glorifies the Father, saying: “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones. Yes, Father, because this was pleasing before you” (Matt. XI).

But in what follows:

“So that seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not understand,”

he especially strikes at the Jews. They had once been seeing and hearing, when they knew God’s will and fulfilled it in action. Hence their prophets were called “Seeing Ones,” because they saw what others could not see. The Gentiles, however, were not seeing and not hearing because they did not know the Lord.

But when the Lord came into the world, those who had been seeing and hearing became blind and deaf through pride, when they refused to believe in him. The prophecy of Isaiah was fulfilled, which says: “Make the heart of this people blind, and make their ears heavy, and close their eyes” (Isa. VI), “lest they see with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their heart, and be converted, and I heal them.”

Those who had not been seeing or hearing were illumined through believing, according to what the Lord says in the Gospel: “For judgment I have come into this world, so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind.”

When the Lord explained the parable, he added: “This, then, is the parable: The seed is the word of God. Those beside the road are the ones who hear; then the devil comes,” and so forth.

The seed is beautifully compared to the word of God, because just as seed sown in the earth appears small and is afterwards multiplied as it grows, so the word of God, when it is sown in the hearts of hearers, appears small; but when the hearers have grown in good works, then the word of God likewise produces abundant fruit in virtues along with them.

And just as the body is nourished by multiplied seed, so the soul is nourished by the word of God, the Lord saying: “Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God” (Matt. IV).

And just as a farmer rejoices when he gathers multiplied seed into his granary, so when a person reaches the maturity of perseverance, he becomes worthy to be gathered into God’s granary, where he will neither hunger nor thirst, nor will heat or sun strike him; rather, he will always rejoice and always be glad.

The Psalmist seemed to behold the small seed at the time of sowing when he said: “Going, they went and wept, casting their seeds” (Ps. CXXV). But he seemed to behold the same seed multiplied when he said: “Coming, they will come with rejoicing, carrying their sheaves.”

Therefore, just as seed is sown in hope of fruit, so the word of the Lord must be taught for the sole reward of eternal life. In seed there is one time of sowing and another of harvesting: what is sown in this life is received in the future, when, as the Apostle says: “Whatever a person sows, that he will also reap; for he who sows in the flesh will reap corruption from the flesh, but he who sows in the spirit will reap eternal life from the spirit” (Gal. VI).

The Apostle rejoiced that this seed was in the hearts of the disciples, saying: “I give thanks to my God always for you all, for the grace of God that was given to you in Christ Jesus, because in everything you have been enriched in him, in every word and in every knowledge, so that you lack nothing in any grace” (I Cor. I).

“Those beside the road are the ones who hear; then the devil comes and takes the word from their heart, lest they believe and be saved.” Mark writes about this seed as follows: “These are the ones beside the road, where the word is sown; and when they have heard, immediately Satan comes and takes away the word that was sown in their hearts.”

Matthew, however, writes: “Everyone who hears the word of the kingdom and does not understand it: the evil one comes and snatches away what was sown in his heart.”

From these words of the Lord’s explanation we learn that the passersby signify evil and unclean thoughts. There are some who hear the word of God, but while they allow unclean desires to dwell in their hearts, the seed of God’s word cannot produce spiritual fruit. When an unclean action follows an unclean thought in their hearts, the word of God is, as it were, trampled by passersby so that it cannot become fruitful.

To such people it is said through the prophet, in the person of Judah: “You have laid your body like the earth, and like a road for those who pass by” (Isa. LI). And again: “They said to your soul, ‘Bend down, so that we may pass over you’; and he who gathers wages put them into a pierced purse.”

For just as a pierced purse gathers wages uselessly from above while spilling them below, so the person who does not retain the word of God in the storehouse of memory hears it in vain. Hence every animal that does not chew the cud is rightly regarded as unclean in the law (Lev. II), because those people are excluded from God’s sacrifice from whose memory the devil takes away the word of life, lest they believe and be saved.

And because the devil deceives people in various ways so that they do not retain the word of God, the evangelists also designate him by various names. By the evangelist who wrote this Gospel, the devil is called *diabolus*, that is, “slanderer,” “accuser,” or “one flowing downward”; in Hebrew, *Belial*, which is interpreted as “without a yoke.” By Mark he is called Satan, that is, “the adversary”; and by Matthew he is called “the evil one,” for he has a thousand arts of doing harm.

The same being who is called the devil by Luke, Satan by Mark, and the evil one by Matthew causes those whom he deceives to flow downward; he is an adversary to the souls of the faithful; and he drags those whom he has deceived into perpetual evil. He has as many names as he has devices for doing harm. Concerning him the blessed Apostle Peter says: “Be sober and watchful, because your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, goes about seeking whom he may devour. Resist him, strong in faith, knowing that the same suffering is being accomplished in your brotherhood throughout the world” (I Pet. V).

“For those upon the rock are the ones who, when they hear, receive the word with joy, but they have no roots; they believe for a while, and in the time of temptation they fall away.” As we learn from the Lord’s explanation, there are some who, when they hear the word of God preached, promise with all their desires that they will keep what they hear. But when the opportunity for sin arrives, they suddenly forget what they had previously promised.

For example, when some hear the Lord saying: “Woe to you who are rich, for you have your consolation” (Luke VI), and: “It is difficult for those who have money to enter the kingdom of heaven,” they detest greed. But when the hour of remorse has passed, they not only retain their own wealth immoderately, but also desire or seize the possessions of others.

Similarly, when others hear the Apostle saying: “Adulterers will not possess the kingdom of God” (I Cor. VI), they detest sexual impurity, sometimes to the point of being pierced with tears. But when the beauty of the flesh appears before their eyes, they forget what they had previously promised, and so readily return to sin as though they had previously made no decision at all against sin.

Concerning such people Solomon says: “As a dog returns to its vomit, so a fool returns to his folly” (Prov. XXVI). By contrast, he himself admonishes us: “At all times let your garments be white, and let oil not fail from your head” (Eccles. IX).

Hence it was said of the holy woman: “Her face was not again changed in different directions” (I Sam. I), that is, she showed herself throughout her life to be as she had been at the time of prayer.

When such people hear the word of God, it seems to germinate in them, but it does not reach maturity because they do not fight against the heat of temptation. Thus, according to the evangelist Matthew (Matt. XIII), when the sun rose they withered—that is, when temptation arose, they fell away.

In Scripture the sun, when used in a good sense, signifies the Lord Jesus, as it is written: “For you who fear God, the sun of righteousness will rise” (Mal. IV). But when used in an evil sense, it signifies the heat of temptation, as is said concerning the reprobate: “They were scorched by the sun.”

Prosperity inflates some people, while adversity breaks others, so that they do not bring the seed they have received to maturity. Against both kinds of harm the Apostle strove to preserve the seed he had heard when he said: “By the weapons of righteousness on the right and on the left, through glory and dishonor, through ill repute and good repute, as deceivers and yet truthful, as unknown and yet known” (II Cor. VI), and so forth.

For he loved all people equally. The divine seer Balaam signified all these people in his own action. When he saw the camp of the Israelites, he said: “May my soul die the death of the righteous, and may my end be like theirs” (Num. XXIII). But afterwards, touched by the heat of greed, he gave counsel for the destruction of those whose death he had wished to resemble.

“What fell among thorns” are those who have heard, but, as they go their way, are choked by anxieties and pleasures of life, and do not produce fruit.”

It would seem very strange if anyone wished to interpret the thorns as riches, unless the Lord Himself had explained this in His own words—especially since thorns prick, whereas riches flatter. Yet if we consider the matter carefully, riches are thorns: for just as thorns tear and bloody the body with their prickings and make it shameful and disfigured in the eyes of men, so the love of riches makes the wretched and unhappy soul so before the eyes of God. And just as thorns are difficult to handle and can scarcely be handled without injury, so the avaricious and greedy, because they are held by the love of riches, are harsh, bitter, and unmanageable not only toward strangers but even toward their own relatives, in accordance with what is said through Solomon: “A merciful man does good to his own soul, but the miser rejects even his relatives” (Prov. XI).

Hence, appropriately, according to the other evangelist, namely Matthew, the Lord calls riches not merely riches but deceptive riches, saying: “They are choked by the deception of riches, and they do not produce fruit” (Matt. XIII). For they are deceptive because they cannot remain with us for long. Either we spend them and leave them behind, or, while they remain, they reject us. Hence the apostle Paul commands Timothy: “Command the rich of this age not to be proud, nor to hope in the uncertainty of riches, but in the living God, who gives us all things abundantly for enjoyment, to do good, to become rich in good works” (I Tim. VI), and so forth.

Or certainly they are deceptive because they do not extinguish the poverty of the mind; rather, the more they are acquired, the more they inflame the possessor’s spirit toward acquisition, as Solomon testifies when he says: “The miser will not be satisfied with money, nor will his soul be satisfied with good things” (Eccl. V).

The only true riches, however, are those which make us rich here in faith and afterward establish us as heirs of the kingdom of heaven. The Lord urged us to seek and love these when He said: “Lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither rust nor moth destroys, and where thieves do not break in and steal. For where your treasure is, there your heart also is” (Matt. VI). If you truly desire to be rich, love the true riches; if you seek the summit of true honor, hasten as quickly as possible to that heavenly homeland.

But these riches are deceptive, since they can scarcely, or not at all, be acquired without sin, in accordance with what the Apostle says: “Those who desire to become rich fall into temptation and the devil’s snare, and into many foolish and harmful desires that plunge a person into destruction and perdition” (I Tim. VI). Hence the rich must greatly fear what the Lord solemnly cries out, saying: “Woe to you who are rich, for you have your consolation” (Luke VI). And again: “How difficult it is for those who have money to enter the kingdom of heaven” (Luke XVIII). And again: “It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven” (Mark X).

Hence also the apostle James says: “Come now, you rich; weep and howl over the miseries that will come upon you. Your riches have rotted, your garments have been eaten by moths, your gold and silver have rusted, and their rust will be a testimony against you, and it will consume your flesh like fire” (James V). And Isaiah says: “Woe to you who join house to house and connect field to field, all the way to the boundary of the place” (Isa. V).

It should be noted, however, that there are two things that join riches: anxieties and pleasures. Since anxiety does not coexist with pleasure, we must understand that at one time the love of riches pricks the mind through anxiety, and at another relaxes it through pleasure. In acquiring riches, a person is anxious lest he lose them—as merchants run at different times from kingdom to kingdom so that they may acquire them—to such an extent that, if anyone should wish to take them away, they raise arms against him. In possessing them, however, there is pleasure, because their spirit, satisfied with those riches, rises both in luxury and in other wicked and sensual pursuits.

Whoever, therefore, has such a heart cannot make the word of God fruitful in it. For just as the density of thorns does not allow the dew of heaven and the warmth of the sun to reach the root of the seed, so the love of riches does not permit spiritual richness to enter the mind. Therefore, if we wish to bear fruit from the seed mentioned above, we must mortify the desire for riches. For, as the Apostle says: “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in worldly affairs” (II Tim. II).

But having spoken of the three kinds of soil, let us hear what the Lord says about the good soil.

“What fell into good soil are those who, hearing the word in a good and excellent heart, retain it and bear fruit with patience.”

The good soil, therefore, is the good human heart. Good soil is opposed to the three kinds of soil, and good soil produces good fruit, just as a good person brings forth good from the good treasure of his heart. But because not all believers bear fruit equally, and grace is not given equally to all, it is rightly said: “These are those who, hearing the word in a good and excellent heart, retain it.” For being excellent is greater than being good. Almost everyone in the Church hears the word, but not everyone advances equally: one advances more, another less.

Whoever rightly orders his temporal possessions produces good fruit; whoever abandons all temporal things for love of perfection produces excellent fruit. Or certainly, the one who uses marriage chastely for the love of legitimate children produces good fruit, while the one who vows continence or virginity to the Lord produces excellent fruit.

Hence the evangelist Matthew, wishing to show a distinction among the righteous themselves, says concerning the seed sown in good soil: “It produced fruit, one thirtyfold, another sixtyfold, and another hundredfold” (Matt. XIII). And Mark says: “It bore one thirtyfold, one sixtyfold, and one hundredfold” (Mark IV).

Thus, in the three kinds of produce, he shows three orders in the Church: the married, the continent, and virgins. The thirtyfold fruit belongs to the married, who preserve chaste love among themselves and live soberly, justly, and devoutly. This is indicated figuratively by the joining of the fingers: just as, in the number thirty, finger joined to finger signifies the chaste union between husband and wife, of which it is written: “The two shall be one flesh” (Gen. II).

The sixtyfold fruit is produced by widows and the continent, who, having experienced the pleasure of the flesh, endure a longer tribulation. This too is shown in the counting of the fingers: just as, in the number sixty, one finger is pressed by another, representing the tribulation they have experienced, as the Apostle says: “Such people will have tribulation in the flesh” (I Cor. VII).

Virgins produce the hundredfold fruit, promising the Lord the incorruption of the flesh. They will receive so much greater a reward as they offer God a richer and more difficult fruit. Its perfection is shown in the counting of the fingers: just as the number one hundred passes from the left hand to the right and, forming a circle, takes the shape of a crown, so it displays the unfading crown of the virgin. The Lord promises this through the prophet, saying: “Thus says the Lord to the eunuchs who keep my commandments and choose what I desire: I will give them a place in my house and within my walls” (Isa. LVI). “I will give them a named place and an everlasting name that shall not perish.” If they have fled pollution not only in mind but also in body, let them hear what John says in the Apocalypse: “These are those who have not been defiled with women, for they are virgins” (Rev. XIV).

Or certainly, those who confess faith in the Holy Trinity produce the thirtyfold fruit. But because faith without works is dead, they add the sixtyfold to the thirtyfold when they add good works to their confession of faith. Since there are six days in which work is permitted, good works are signified by the sixtyfold fruit. But because the one who believes rightly and lives well awaits a future reward, they produce the hundred-and-thirtyfold fruit, so that they may receive eternal glory.

Since patience is necessary in every good work, it is rightly added: “And they bear fruit with patience.” Good soil therefore produces through patience, because none of the good things we do are truly good if we do not patiently endure the evils of the wicked. True patience is that which is conquered by no fury, separated by no tribulation, and disturbed by no persecution. It is necessary not only under divine chastisements but also in enduring the persecution of our neighbors, so that in all things the soul that perseveres may bear fruit with patience. For the person who refuses to tolerate the wicked was not good.

The Lord also shows elsewhere what kind of virtue this is when He says: “By your patience you will possess your souls” (Luke XXI). And again: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God” (Matt. V). And elsewhere: “Have salt in yourselves, and have peace among yourselves” (Mark IX). Therefore Paul, following the example of his teacher, commanded his disciples, saying: “Pursue peace” (Heb. XII).

## HOMILY XXIII. SUNDAY OF QUINQUAGESIMA

### (LUKE XVIII)

“At that time Jesus took his twelve disciples and said to them: ‘Behold, we are going up to Jerusalem, and everything that has been written by the prophet concerning the Son of Man will be fulfilled,’ etc.”

The preceding text of the Gospel reading related how the Lord taught that temporal riches must be shunned and voluntary poverty loved, saying: “How difficult it is for those who have money to enter the kingdom of heaven” (Luke XVIII); “for it is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God” (Mark X). Those who heard Him said: “Who, then, can be saved?” He said to them: “The things that are impossible with human beings are possible with God.” He also showed that the apostles, who had left everything for the sake of the kingdom of God, would receive much more in this present time and, in the age to come, eternal life. After this He added:

“Jesus took his twelve disciples.”

Thus, after restoring health to the sick, rebuking the hardness of the rich, and rewarding the apostles’ voluntary poverty with an eternal promise, He proceeds to the trophy of His passion, to show that neither perfect salvation can be attained nor earthly things abandoned and heavenly things grasped unless He died for the salvation of all—He who is the salvation of us all.

Although He had promised them eternal life, He places the sufferings of tribulation before it, so that, if the lofty position pleased them, the pain of tribulation might first exercise them. In view of the tribulations just mentioned, we should consider that the Lord, foreseeing that the minds of the disciples would be disturbed by His passion, wished to announce that same passion to them long beforehand, so that they would be less disturbed at the time of the passion insofar as they remembered that it had been foretold by their loving teacher. Arrows that are foreseen strike less severely.

He foretold not only the punishment of His passion but also the glory of His resurrection, so that, when they saw Him dying—as had been foretold—they would not in the least doubt that He would also rise again. The announced passion would cause them sorrow, but the foretold resurrection would make them rejoice.

Foreseeing also the future foolishness of the pagans, who would say that He endured passion for us not willingly but under compulsion, He foretold the passion beforehand, so that we might understand that the one who could foretell both the place and the time of His passion could have avoided it, unless He had willingly endured it for our redemption. Death did not compel Him; rather, He Himself chose the death He desired, in accordance with what He said to the judge at the time of His passion: “I have authority to lay down my life, and I have authority to take it up again” (John X). And again: “No one takes my life from me, but I lay it down of my own accord, and I take it up again” (John X).

By these words He destroys not only the foolishness of the pagans but also the madness of the heretics, who said that there was one God of the Old Testament and another of the New. Before His passion He foretold the fulfillment of what had been predicted about Him in the Scriptures, showing that He Himself is the God of the Old and New Testaments, the one who would do and teach what the prophets had foretold that He would do and teach in the Old Testament.

Clearly, therefore, He Himself is the God of the Old and New Testaments, as He says through the Prophet: “I am God, and I do not change” (Mal. III). And again: “Before me no god was formed, and after me there shall not be” (Isa. XLIII).

Appropriately, the Savior took twelve disciples and revealed to them the secret of His passion and resurrection because of the perfection of the number twelve. For the number twelve is perfect, and, divided into its parts, signifies a certain perfection. It consists of the first odd number and the first even number, that is, of three and four. For whether you multiply three by four or four by three, they complete the number twelve.

Three pertains to perfection because of the indivisible Trinity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; also because of the three periods—before the law, under the law, and under grace; and because of the three principal virtues, namely faith, hope, and charity.

Four likewise pertains to perfection because of the four Gospels and the four principal virtues; also because of the four seasons of the year, or because of the four living creatures said to be full of eyes before and behind, surrounding the throne of God.

The number twelve itself is also perfect because of the twelve patriarchs, the twelve apostles, the twelve months of the year, and the twelve hours of the day; or because of the twenty-four elders who, in a doubled number, adore the Lamb in the Apocalypse, “casting their crowns before the throne of God” (Rev. IV).

Because He was going to announce to the world, through the preaching of the twelve apostles, both faith in the Holy Trinity and the teaching of the four Gospels, He rightly took twelve apostles and revealed to them the secret of His passion, saying: “Behold, we are going up to Jerusalem,” and so forth. When they saw that everything in Him had been fulfilled which they had heard foretold by Him, they were to remember the command in which He says: “What I tell you in darkness, speak in the light; and what you hear in the ear in private rooms, proclaim upon the housetops” (Luke XII).

It should be noted that He says: “Behold, we are going up to Jerusalem, and everything that has been written concerning the Son of Man will be fulfilled.” The question arises why He says, “Everything that has been written concerning the Son of Man will be fulfilled,” since at the time of the passion not everything that had been foretold about Him had been completed. His glorious ascension still remained, as did the sending of the Holy Spirit from heaven, His coming for judgment, the preaching of the disciples, the calling of the Gentiles, and many other things that had been foretold about Him, as no one doubts.

The answer is that Scripture often uses the rhetorical figure of synecdoche, sometimes putting the whole for the part and sometimes the part for the whole. The part is put for the whole, as it is written: “Jacob went down into Egypt with seventy souls” (Gen. XLVI). Did souls descend without bodies? Certainly not. Rather, by the better part of the human being, which is the soul, the whole person is understood.

The whole is put for the part, as it is read elsewhere: “All flesh shall see the salvation of God” (Luke III). This does not mean that the flesh of birds, serpents, and beasts will see the Savior coming for judgment, but “all flesh,” that is, every human being.

In the Lord’s passion, too, it is said of the thieves that both blasphemed the Lord, whereas another evangelist shows more clearly that one blasphemed Him while the other believed. Thus, in this passage also, He put the whole for the part by reference to the greater part when He said: “Everything will be fulfilled.” This manner of speech is customary not only in Scripture but also in our everyday conversations, when we say: “Everyone went up into the city,” or “The whole city cried out”—not meaning that no one remained outside the city or that no one in the city was silent, but signifying the whole by reference to the greater part.

So here too “everything will be fulfilled” signifies the whole by reference to the greater part—not that everything was completed in the passion, but that, because the greater part had been completed, everything that was to be completed is said to have been completed. What had been foretold by different Fathers at different times was fulfilled in one and the same Son of Man, the Lord Jesus Christ.

To make this clearer, let us give an example. Suppose someone spent twenty denarii, then five, and later fifteen; he also gave thirty, and three times ten at different times. If he gathered all of these into one sum, he would find the total of one hundred. Thus the Lord’s incarnation, passion, and resurrection were foretold at different times by different Fathers, but were fulfilled in one Mediator between God and human beings. Therefore the firmness of faith remains immovable, because everything that was to happen in Christ had previously been foretold.

In foretelling His passion, He preferred to be called the Son of Man rather than the Son of God, to show that, insofar as He was the Son of Man, He could be seized, scourged, suffer, and be crucified, while His divinity remained incapable of suffering. What things, then, were to be fulfilled in Him at the time of His passion, He makes clear when He adds:

“For He will be handed over to the Gentiles, mocked, scourged, and spat upon; and after they have scourged Him, they will kill Him, and on the third day He will rise.”

No believer doubts that all these things were foretold about Him and fulfilled in Him, and the diligent reader can easily find them.

That He was to be handed over had been foretold by Jeremiah, who says: “He handed me over, the one whom I loved.” And the Psalmist says: “I was handed over, and I did not escape” (Ps. LXXVIII). This was fulfilled at the time of the passion, when Judas Iscariot, one of the Twelve, went to the chief priests, saying: “What will you give me, and I will hand Him over to you?” (Matt. XXVI). They appointed thirty pieces of silver for him, and, after receiving the money, he handed Him over to the servants of the high priest, saying: “The one whom I kiss is He; seize Him.”

That He was to be mocked, the Psalmist says in His person: “I have become a reproach to my neighbors, a scorn and derision to my enemies” (Ps. XXX). And again: “My loins are filled with mockery” (Ps. XXXVII). Jeremiah says: “Mocking men rose up against me.” This was fulfilled at the time of the passion, when they placed a crown of thorns upon His head, gave Him a reed in His right hand, and, kneeling before Him, mocked Him, saying: “Hail, King of the Jews.”

That He was to be scourged, the prophet Zechariah foretold in His person: “With a rod they will strike the prince of Israel’s sons” (Zech. XIII). And again: “I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered” (ibid.). This was fulfilled in the passion, when He was ordered to be beaten with scourges, Pilate saying: “Therefore, after scourging Him, I will release Him.”

That He was to be spat upon, the prophet Isaiah had foretold in His person: “I did not turn my face away from those who rebuked me and spat upon me” (Isa. L). And Job says: “Wicked men rose up against me without mercy, and they did not spare to spit in my face” (Job XXX). This was fulfilled at the time of the passion, when they spat in His face.

That He was to be killed, Daniel had foretold, saying: “Christ will be killed, and He will have no one,” and so forth (Dan. IX). Hence Moses says to the children of Israel: “Your life shall hang before your eyes, and you shall not believe in your life” (Deut. XXVIII), but you shall fear. This was fulfilled when, hanging on the cross, He bowed His head and gave up His spirit.

That after His death He would rise on the third day is written in the prophet Hosea: “He will revive us after two days; on the third day He will raise us up, and we shall live in His presence” (Hos. VI). And Zephaniah says: “Wait for me, says the Lord, on the day of my resurrection to come” (Zeph. III). And He Himself says through the Psalmist: “I slept and took my sleep, and I rose” (Ps. III). And elsewhere: “Raise me up, and I will repay them.” This was fulfilled on the third day after the passion, when the women who had come to the tomb before dawn heard from the angel: “You seek Jesus; He is not here; He has risen” (Mark XVI).

“And they understood none of these things. This saying was hidden from them, and they did not understand what was being said.”

In the Gospel according to John we read that, when the Lord spoke veiledly to the Jews about His passion, saying: “When you have lifted up the Son of Man, then you will know that I am” (John VIII), and: “If I am lifted up from the earth, I will draw all things to myself” (John XII), they immediately understood and replied: “You have a demon; who is seeking to kill you?” (John VII). We had heard that Christ remains forever; yet, when He openly foretold His passion, the apostles understood none of these things.

What does it mean that the Jews heard such veiled words that the evangelist considered them worthy of explanation, saying: “He said this to signify by what death He was going to die” (John XII), and they immediately understood, whereas the apostles heard openly and did not understand? Clearly, piety concealed this from the apostles, while impiety revealed it to the Jews.

The human mind has this characteristic: what it absolutely does not want, it believes either with difficulty or slowly; what it wants to happen in every way, it understands easily and believes even more easily. Since the Jews desired to discover how they might kill Him, they immediately understood when they heard something about His passion, even if they heard it secretly. The apostles, however, neither desired nor believed that Christ, the Son of God, could die; therefore, although they heard His passion foretold openly, they did not understand.

How harsh and grievous His passion seemed to the minds of the disciples, Peter indicates. When the Lord elsewhere foretold His passion, Peter took Him aside privately and said: “Far be it from you, Lord; this shall not happen. For it is not fitting that the Son of God should taste death” (Matt. XVI).

In the sacred Scriptures, the word is understood in three ways: sometimes it is used for the Lord Himself, sometimes for an event, and sometimes for a saying. It is used for the Lord in: “In the beginning was the Word” (John I), and: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established” (Ps. XXXII).

It is used for an event when, in Exodus, we read concerning Moses after he had killed the Egyptian: “How has this matter become known?” (Exod. II). Likewise it is read elsewhere: “Whoever speaks a word against the Son of Man, it will be forgiven him” (Matt. XII), and so forth.

Thus, in the present passage, it is used for a saying when it is said: “This saying was hidden from them,” that is, this statement.

But because the disciples did not understand what they had heard openly about the Lord’s passion, the narrative proceeds to a miracle. A blind man was enlightened in their presence, so that they might learn to doubt nothing concerning the one whom they saw shining forth through such miracles. Hence it continues:

“It happened that, when He drew near Jericho, a certain blind man was sitting beside the road, begging.”

Jericho is a city beyond the Jordan in the Promised Land. The children of Israel are said to have first come to it after crossing the river Jordan. In the time of Joshua it was miraculously overthrown by the Lord after the Lord’s ark had been carried around it for seven days. In the time of King Ahab it was rebuilt by Ahiel the prince, as the history of Kings relates (III Kings XVI). In accordance with Joshua’s pronouncement, he founded it in his firstborn and established its gates in his youngest.

Interpreted in our language, Jericho means “moon.” The moon, which waxes and wanes at monthly intervals, sometimes signifies in Scripture the decline of our mortality: we grow by being born and diminish by dying; we increase in prosperity and decrease in adversity.

The Lord, as it were, approached Jericho when He assumed the weakness of our flesh or its mutability, so that He who was immutable in Himself might become mutable in what was ours.

As He approached Jericho, however, a certain blind man was sitting beside the road and begging. Hence a certain versifier says:

> The son of Timaeus, blinded in the world,  
> Encounters the Lord.

Spiritually, this signifies the human race, which incurred blindness of mind when it lost the light of truth, opened its eyes to desire the forbidden tree, and fell into the darkness of error. Not only the Gentile people but also the Jewish people were held in this darkness. They arose from the root of sin and were bound by the chain of original sin, as the Apostle testifies when he says: “There is no distinction between Jew and Greek; for all have sinned and lack the glory of God” (Rom. III).

Hence Matthew appropriately placed two blind men, indicating that some from both peoples would be enlightened through the Lord’s incarnation.

When the Lord therefore approached Jericho, the blind man was enlightened—namely, the human race. For when He clothed Himself with the mortality of our flesh, He restored us to His immortality.

He was sitting beside the road because he had departed from the way of truth. It is rightly said that this blind man both sat beside the road and begged, because there are some who neither sit beside the road nor beg. There are others who sit beside the road but do not beg. There are still others who both sit beside the road and beg.
