The way is Christ, who says: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (Job XIV). Those who neither sit beside the way nor beg are those who neither believe in God nor seek spiritual riches from Him. Those who sit beside the way but do not beg are perverse and false Christians: they believe in God, but, sluggish in good works, do not strive to seek spiritual riches from Him. Of them the Apostle says that they “profess to know God, but deny Him by their actions” (Titus I).

Those who sit beside the way and beg are those who believe in God and do not cease to seek heavenly glory through constant prayers. Concerning such people the Lord says: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied” (Matt. V).

“And when he heard the crowd passing by, he asked what it was.”

The passing crowd signifies the order of the patriarchs and prophets. They are called “passing” because, being born in succession and begetting in succession, they passed from this age, yet left behind many things written about the Lord’s incarnation, passion, and resurrection, and about the redemption of the human race.

When the blind man—that is, the human race—heard this, he asked what it was.

“They told him that Jesus of Nazareth was passing by.”

When he heard from them that Jesus of Nazareth was passing by—that is, when he had learned from their books about the Lord’s incarnation, passion, and resurrection—he began to cry out with a believing voice, saying:

“Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me.”

In these words the Catholic faith is beautifully commended. It confesses and believes in the Mediator between God and human beings, true God and true man. If he had not believed Him to be true God, he would not have asked Him to have mercy on him; and if he had not believed Him to be the same true man, he would not have said: “Jesus, Son of David.”

For in Latin speech Jesus means “savior” or “salutary.” He cried out “Jesus” without abandoning “Son of David,” and he invoked “Son of David” without passing over the Savior. He thereby showed that the Mediator between God and human beings, the Lord Jesus Christ, must be believed to be perfect God and perfect man in one and the same person, from divine and human substance.

He is called the Son of David because He assumed flesh from David’s lineage for our redemption, as the angel’s voice says to Mary: “The Lord God will give Him the throne of David His father” (Luke I). And the Apostle says: “Who was made for Him from the seed of David according to the flesh” (Rom. I).

Jesus of Nazareth is rightly said to be passing by because He did not remain in the world like other mortals. After He had preached and suffered, having overcome the devil, He returned victoriously to the Father.

His passage was from heaven into the womb, from the womb into the tomb, and from the tomb again into heaven. The apostle Peter speaks of this passage: “He went about doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil” (Acts X). Admiring His passage, the Church says in the Song of Songs: “Behold, he comes, leaping upon the mountains, passing over the hills” (Song II).

“Those who went before rebuked him so that he would be silent.”

Those who went before and wished to impose silence on the blind man signify the crowds of unclean spirits. At the beginning of faith, they attempted to turn the human race away from belief in the Lord, not only by persuasion but also by rebuke—that is, by stirring up persecutions and tribulations.

But let us hear what the blind man did.

“But he cried out much more: ‘Son of David, have mercy on me.’”

The blind man cried out more and more because, the more intensely the human race feels itself oppressed by unclean spirits, the more ardently it strives to cry out to the Lord, saying with the Prophet: “Lord, you have become our refuge from generation to generation” (Ps. LXXXIX).

Hence it is rightly said:

“Jesus stood still and ordered the blind man to be brought to Him.”

The Lord ordered the blind man to be brought to Him spiritually when He sent the apostles to preach to the human race, saying: “Go into all the world and preach the Gospel to every creature” (Mark XVI). And again: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. XXVIII).

They brought him to Him when they went forth and preached everywhere, and so forth.

“When he had drawn near, He asked him, saying: ‘What do you want me to do for you?’”

After the blind man had been brought to Him, He asked what he wanted—not because He was ignorant of it, since almost everyone present knew it, but so that He might grant the light He was about to bestow from His goodness in response to his request and approve his confession.

The merciful Lord wishes His freely given gifts to become our merits. That is, He does not want our good to be unwilling and forced, but spontaneous and voluntary; and what He freely bestows on us, He wishes to attribute to our petitions.

Therefore, although He knows what we need before we ask—saying: “Do not be anxious about your life, what you shall eat” (Matt. VI), and so forth—He nevertheless urges us insistently to ask when He says: “Ask, and you will receive; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you. For everyone who asks receives, and whoever seeks finds, and to the one who knocks it will be opened” (Matt. VII).

“But he said: ‘Lord, that I may see.’”

Concerning this blind man a certain versifier says:

> The blind man asked the Lord for neither gold nor many rewards,  
> But for light; and, shining, he gleamed among the stars.

In his example, all radiant things make their request. From his petition we learn that in prayer we should seek neither gold, nor silver, nor earthly riches, nor long life, nor vengeance against enemies, but the ineffable light—that is, that we may be able to see Him “who enlightens every human being coming into this world” (John I), in accordance with His own admonition: “Seek first the kingdom of God and His righteousness, and all these things will be added to you” (Matt. VI).

How great the power of faith is becomes clear when it is added:

“And Jesus said to him: ‘Look up; your faith has saved you.’”

If this man was enlightened through faith, then whoever does not believe is an unbeliever, because he remains in darkness and is in darkness. When He says, “Your faith has saved you,” it is understood that faith is a great virtue, without which it is impossible to please God (Heb. XI).

For just as unbelief is the mother and root of all vices, so faith is the source of all virtues, as the Prophet says: “But the righteous person lives by faith” (Hab. II). Commending it to His disciples, the Lord said: “Have faith in God” (Mark XI). And again: “If you have faith like a grain of mustard seed, you will say to this mountain, ‘Move from here,’ and it will move” (Luke XVII).

Since no one ought to remain ungrateful for God’s benefits, it is rightly said of him:

“Immediately he saw, and followed him, glorifying God.” [Col. 0179C] For the more a person is enlightened by God, the more fully and diligently he ought to devote himself to good works. Thus this blind man, having immediately received his sight, did not remain idle, but followed God, glorifying him. For it was fitting that the one who had been enlightened by the Lord should not turn back, but should follow God. To follow the Lord is to imitate him, as he himself says: “Whoever serves me, let him follow me (John XII),” and so forth. And again: “Whoever wishes to come after me (Matthew IX),” and the rest.

Here it should be noted that some neither see nor follow; others see but do not follow; and still others both see and follow. Those who neither see nor follow are the pagans and Jews, who neither understand what is good nor practice it. Those who see but do not follow are those who understand what is good but disdain to practice it, such as false and lukewarm Christians, [Col. 0179D] of whom the Lord says in the Gospel: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven (Matthew VII).” And: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me (Isaiah XXIX; Mark VII).” Those who see and follow are the most perfect Christians, who believe in God and complete in deed the good that they understand. Hence the Apostle Paul says: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation (Romans X).” The Apostle Peter exhorts them, saying: “Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example, so that you might follow his footsteps (1 Peter II).”

“And all the people, when they saw it, gave praise to God.” Those who were present glorified the Lord not only because of the miracle that had occurred, [Col. 0180A] but also because of the faith of the blind man himself. So we too, when performing good works, ought in our holy conduct to show ourselves such that God may be glorified in us, as he himself admonishes, saying: “Let your light shine before men, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven (Matthew V).”

But what we have said generally to concern the human race can also be referred specifically to each sinner. Whoever commits a criminal sin in deed—such as adultery, homicide, theft, robbery, sacrilege, and similar acts—and harbors hatred in his heart is blind in mind, as the Apostle John testifies when he says: “Everyone who hates his brother is in darkness, and walks in darkness, and does not know where he is going, because the darkness has blinded his eyes (1 John II).”

But whoever desires to be enlightened and to lay aside the blindness of his mind [Col. 0180B] must not cease asking in prayer; rather, he must always beg spiritually. That is, he should come to the Church and humbly confess the sins he has committed; wash away past sins with tears; and willingly open the ears of his heart to hear the divine word. For there, in the examples and words of the saints, he will find that he may obtain satisfaction for past offenses and prudence for the future. But if he begins to think about eternal life and, after sinning, returns to it with tears, then he sits blind beside the road and begs. To him what is said rightly applies: “And when he heard the crowd passing by, he asked what this was.”

The passing crowd is the unanimous chorus of the saints, [Col. 0180C] or it signifies their actions and teaching. They are called “passing by” because they have no abiding city here, but seek the one that is to come with all their desire. For the saints’ passing by means not fixing the root of the heart in love of the world, but hastening toward eternal life with the whole force of one’s desire.

Thus one of them, when he had seen the impious person exalted and raised up, said: “I passed by, and behold, he was no more (Psalm XXXVI),” and so forth. When, from the examples and sayings of the saints, the sinner hears the punishment of sinners terribly threatened, and hears the Apostle crying out: “Do not be deceived: neither adulterers, nor robbers, nor those who have intercourse with males will possess the kingdom of God (1 Corinthians VI),” while pardon is promised to the penitent, he is pierced in heart and asks what this means.

And when he has learned from their words [Col. 0180D] that everything earthly and transitory is nothing, he hears, as it were, Jesus of Nazareth passing by. If he desires to receive the light of the heart, the blind man shows by his own example what he ought to do, when he cried out, saying: “Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me.”

The blind man cries out to the Lord when the sinner, asking pardon for his sins, humbly groans, saying with the Prophet: “For I acknowledge my iniquity, and my sin is always before me. Against you alone I have sinned, and I have done what is evil before you (Psalm L).”

But because unclean spirits rise up against the one whom they see returning to forgiveness, it is rightly added: “And those who went before rebuked him, telling him to be silent.” Those passing by therefore wanted to impose silence on the blind man, [Col. 0181A] because unclean spirits oppose the sinner so that he may not return to repentance.

In many ways, too, unclean spirits try after confession to drag the mind back, so that it may not persevere in conversion—sometimes by persuasion, sometimes by rebukes. Against all these things the Scripture admonishes us to strengthen the mind, when Solomon says: “My son, when you approach the service of God, stand in righteousness and fear, and prepare your soul for temptation (Ecclesiasticus II).”

Nor do only unclean spirits begin to rebel more harshly; the very habit of sinning does so when it senses that, after its customary evils, a person wishes to turn toward the virtues. For example, when a drunkard rises to return to sobriety, the urge to drink immediately rises against him. When an adulterer vows chastity, the pleasure of the flesh immediately rises against him [Col. 0181B] and seeks to draw him back to his former offenses, so that he may not be converted to the Lord, because “the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh (Galatians V).” These two oppose one another, so that we do not do what we wish and cannot behold God with a pure mind.

But what a person of this kind ought to do, whether against the temptation of unclean spirits or against the pleasure of the flesh, is taught by the example of this blind man, when it is added: “But he cried out much more: Son of David, have mercy on me.” The more fiercely someone feels himself attacked by the temptation of evil spirits or by the very habit of sinning, the more forcefully he ought to fight in prayer, because of what the Lord says: “This kind is driven out only by prayer and fasting (Matthew IX).”

Hence the Apostle [Col. 0181C] Peter admonishes the faithful in his epistle, saying: “Be prudent and watchful in your prayers, because your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, prowls around seeking someone to devour. Resist him, strong in faith (1 Peter V).”

For divine mercy will not deny assistance to the penitent if he does not cease asking in prayer, does not presume anything on the basis of his own merits, but trusts in the mercy of the one to whom it is said through the Prophet: “In the Lord we shall perform valor, and he himself will bring our enemies to nothing (Psalm LIX).”

How great a mercy the Lord shows to the penitent, and what assistance he provides to those fighting against sin, is made clear when it follows: “But Jesus, standing, commanded him to be brought to him.” The one who had previously been passing by now stands because of the temptations [Col. 0181D] inflicted by demons upon human minds. When we suffer the phantoms of temptations in prayer, we seem to hear the Lord passing by; but if we persevere in praying, seeking, asking, and knocking, he commands that we be brought to him as though he were standing.

For when tranquility of mind has been restored, he manifests, however faintly, the sweetness of his contemplation, because, as he himself says: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God (Matthew V).”

And because in prayer we ought above all to seek eternal glory, the blind man, rightly asked by the Lord, “What do you want me to do for you?” replied: “Lord, that I may see.”

Faith is especially necessary in prayer, so that we may firmly believe, with God’s gift, that we can receive the good we seek, [Col. 0182A] in accordance with what the Lord says: “Amen, I say to you: Whatever you ask for in prayer, believe that you will receive it, and it will be done for you (Matthew XXI).”

And since whoever does not neglect to repent worthily should not despair of pardon, it is rightly said: “Receive your sight; your faith has saved you.” Concerning this it is rightly added: “And immediately he saw, and followed him, glorifying God.”

It often happens that the more someone has been freed from serious sins through repentance, the more gratefully he recognizes the mercy of his liberator. Hence it is rightly said: “And all the people, when they saw it, gave praise to God.” The higher someone stands in rank, the graver his crime; but the more he has been freed by God from serious sins and delivered from deeper darkness, [Col. 0182B] the more gloriously he will implore the Lord’s mercy.

## HOMILY XXIV. ON ASH WEDNESDAY

(Matthew VI.) “At that time Jesus said to his disciples: ‘When you fast, do not become like the hypocrites, gloomy,’” and the rest.

Fasting is indeed pleasing to almighty God, provided only that it is performed worthily and irreproachably. There were Scribes and Pharisees who, during their fast, disfigured their faces [Col. 0182C] so that they might appear to people to be fasting. If, then, those who disfigured their faces in order to appear to people to be fasting were hypocrites, it is clear that whoever holds one thing in his heart and does another in deed is a hypocrite—like the Scribes and Pharisees, who, although they had joy in their minds because of empty glory, nevertheless displayed sadness in their faces.

“For they disfigure their faces.” In place of the word we customarily read, *exterminant* (“they disfigure”), blessed Jerome teaches that one should read *demoliuntur* (“they demolish”). For *exterminare* means to lead outside one’s proper boundaries. It is more accurately read: “They demolish their faces,” that is, they distort them; they do not wash themselves, and they deliberately display a continuous pallor upon their faces.

“So that they may be seen by men.” That is, so that they may obtain human praise from it.

“But when you fast, anoint your head.” That is, while you fast, present yourself as festive. The Palestinians, according to whose custom the Lord speaks, anointed their heads with oil on feast days and treated them with precious ointments. The meaning therefore is: When you fast, present yourself as festive [Col. 0182D] and cheerful, as though you were not fasting but rather celebrating a solemn feast.

In the allegorical sense, oil is understood both negatively and positively. It is understood negatively when it signifies flattery. Hence the Psalmist says: “May the oil of the sinner not fatten my head (Psalm CXL).” It is understood positively, as the same Psalmist says: “God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions (Psalm XLIV).”

Oil signifies charity, because just as oil surpasses all liquids, so charity excels all virtues. Hence Paul, speaking of it, says: “I show you a still more excellent way (1 Corinthians XII).” And elsewhere: “Now these three remain: faith, hope, and charity. But the greatest of these is charity (1 Corinthians XIII).”

By the head the principal [Col. 0183A] part of our mind is signified. Our fasting will then be pleasing if it has been seasoned with love of God and neighbor.

“Do not store up treasures for yourselves on earth, where rust and moth destroy, and where thieves break in and steal.” Through these three kinds—rust, moth, and thieves—the Lord shows that nothing among earthly possessions of wealth is secure.

Some things are devoured by rust, such as gold, silver, and other metals. Other things are not devoured by rust but are eaten by moths, such as silk garments and other valuables. Still other things are devoured neither by rust nor by moths, but thieves dig them out and steal them, such as gems and similar objects.

Therefore, [Col. 0183B] because the substance of our whole life and the possession of all things are uncertain, the Lord urges us to store up treasure in heaven. But how can someone store up treasure in heaven unless he sends his wealth ahead of him by giving alms?

We can understand rust, moth, and thieves as spiritual wickednesses. Rust signifies pride, for pride causes the minds it has invaded to perish from their state of uprightness. Moth signifies envy, for envy tears apart the heart it corrupts, depriving it of all integrity. Thieves signify evil spirits, because they keep watch in order to steal the treasures of our souls.

There is no rust in heaven, because pride has no place there: [Col. 0183C] the devil and his followers have already fallen from it. There is no moth there, that is, envy, because no one will envy the blessedness of the saints. There are no thieves there, that is, demons, because they fell from there together with their head.

“Where your treasure is, there also is your heart.” This should be understood not only of money but also of every vice. If a rich man’s treasure has been buried beneath the earth, his heart will also be there, meditating lest thieves carry it away or it be lost through some corruption.

The treasure of a gluttonous person is his belly, because he is always thinking how he might fill it. The treasures of a lustful person are amusements and pleasures. Whoever clings to any vice serves and obeys that vice.

## HOMILY XXV. THURSDAY AFTER ASH WEDNESDAY

[Col. 0183D]

(Luke VII.) “At that time: A certain centurion’s servant, who was ill and near death, was precious to him,” and the rest.

Someone might ask, either piously in order to find an answer or impiously in order to criticize, why the Evangelist says that the servant—who is subsequently shown not to have died but to have been healed—was near death. The brief answer is that he truly was near death, unless he had been restored to life by the faith of his master, who pleaded, and by Christ’s compassion, which showed mercy.

Thus King Hezekiah, according to a certain human understanding of nature, was near death [Col. 0184A] when he heard from the words of the truthful prophet: “Set your house in order, for you shall die and not live (Isaiah XXXVIII).” But by the hidden judgment of divine Providence, which has arranged all things in measure, number, and weight, he was to obtain fifteen additional years of life through tears and prayers.

“When he had heard about Jesus, he sent the elders of the Jews to him, asking him to come and save his servant.” It happened by a heavenly dispensation that the elders of the Jews were sent to the Lord, and that, while they were present, the servant who was ill was healed, so that they would be without excuse if they did not believe while a Gentile believed.

Yet it is asked how Luke’s account—that the centurion sent messengers—accords with Matthew’s, which says that he himself approached the Lord. To those who ask piously, the answer is readily apparent: Matthew, for the sake of brevity, said that he himself approached, because his desire and will had truly been conveyed to the Lord, even though others carried his request. He was also mystically [Col. 0184B] commending to us what is written: “Draw near to him and be enlightened (Psalm XXXIII).”

Since the Lord praised the centurion’s faith—by which one truly draws near to Jesus—to such an extent that he said, “I have not found such faith in Israel,” the wise Evangelist preferred to say that the man himself had approached Christ rather than those through whom he had sent his words.

Luke, however, disclosed the whole matter as it happened, so that from this we might understand how the other Evangelist could say that he approached without having lied. Just as that woman (Matthew IX) who suffered from a flow of blood, although she touched the fringe of his garment, nevertheless touched the Lord more by believing than did the crowds that pressed around him, so the centurion approached the Lord all the more because he believed all the more. [Col. 0184C]

“For he loves our nation, and he himself built the synagogue for us.” The one who reports that the synagogue was built by the centurion clearly shows that, just as we customarily call the Church not merely an assembly of the faithful but also the place where they assemble, so they too customarily called the synagogue both the assembly and the place of assembly, as we taught above.

“Now Jesus was going with them.” Great was the Lord’s sublimity: he was able to heal by a word alone. Yet no less was his humility, by which he deigned to visit the sick servant. As one powerful, compassionate, and asked to save him, he proceeded there; and in the middle of the journey, when asked, he saved him by a word, so that no one would think that he went bodily because of a lack of power rather than as an example of humility.

Elsewhere he did not wish to come to save the official’s son, lest he seem to have honored the rich. [Col. 0184D] Here, lest he seem to have despised a servile condition, he immediately allowed himself to go to the centurion’s servant.

“When he was already not far from the house, the centurion sent friends to him, saying: ‘Lord, do not trouble yourself. For I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof.’” Because of the conscience of his Gentile life, he thought himself more burdened by the Lord’s condescension than helped by it. He also thought himself unable to have Christ as a guest, since, although endowed with faith, he had not yet been instructed in the sacraments.

But whatever our weakness does not presume, divine grace knows how to give. Another centurion, who, like this one, prefigures the believing people from the Gentiles, received the gift of the Holy Spirit, [Col. 0185A] by the great merit of his faith and righteousness, before he was baptized. This man too, although not yet catechized, deserved to have his faith praised by the Lord and his servant saved.

Of him it is beautifully said allegorically that, although he had Jesus not far from his house, he nevertheless did not dare invite him under his roof. Those who love him are near to his salvation; and whoever uses the natural law rightly, doing the good he knows, thereby draws near to the one who is truly good.

But those who have joined crimes to the error of paganism can be compared to those concerning whom the Lord says elsewhere, when crowds were flocking to him: “For some of them have come from far away (Mark IX).”

“Therefore I did not consider myself worthy to come to you.” We who believe from the Gentiles cannot ourselves come to the Lord, whom we are now entirely unable to see in the flesh. [Col. 0185B] But all of us who have recognized the sufferings of our servitude ought already to approach by faith the one who sits at the right hand of the Father.

We ought already to send the elders of the Jews—that is, the highest men of the Church who have gone before us to God—by humbly entreating them to become our patrons. They should bear witness for us that we love the Church and, insofar as we are able, strive to build it, and should intercede for us with the Lord for our sins and those of our people.

“But say the word, and my servant will be healed.” Great was the centurion’s faith: he confessed that words were sufficient in Christ and applied this to the mysteries of our healing. For although we knew Christ according to the flesh, we know him now no longer in that way.

“For I too am a man placed under authority, [Col. 0185C] having soldiers under me.” He says that he is a man subject to the authority of a tribune or governor, yet able to command those beneath him. The implication is that he who is God and powerful above all has much more an innumerable army of angelic power that obeys his commands.

“And I say to this one, ‘Go,’ and he goes; and to another, ‘Come,’ and he comes; and to my servant, ‘Do this,’ and he does it.” He wishes to show that the Lord can accomplish what he wills not only through the presence of his body but also through the ministries of angels. Bodily illnesses, or hostile powers through which human beings are often reduced to weakness, must be driven away both by the Lord’s word and by the ministries of angels.

Alternatively, the soldiers and servants who obey the centurion are natural powers, [Col. 0185D] of which many who come to the Lord bring no small supply with them. Concerning these it is said in praise of Cornelius the centurion: “For he was a righteous man who feared God with all his household, gave alms to the people, and always entreated God (Acts X).”

“When Jesus heard this, he marveled.” He marveled because he saw that the centurion understood his majesty. But who had produced in him that faith or understanding except the one who marveled at it? Even if someone else had produced it, why would the one who knew beforehand marvel?

It should therefore be noted that, when the Lord marvels at something, he signifies that it ought to be marvelous to us, who still need to be instructed in this way. For whenever such emotions are attributed to God, they are not signs of a disturbed mind [Col. 0186A] but of a teacher instructing his disciples.

“And turning, he said to the crowds that followed him: ‘Amen, I say to you, I have not found such faith even in Israel.’” He is speaking not of all the patriarchs and prophets of former times but of the people of the present age. The centurion’s faith is placed before theirs because they had been taught by the admonitions of the Law and the Prophets, whereas he believed spontaneously, without anyone teaching him.

“And those who had been sent, returning to the house, found the servant who had been ill in good health.” The master’s faith is proved, and the servant’s health is confirmed. Thus a master’s merit can assist servants—not only through the merit of faith but also through the care of discipline.

Matthew explains this more fully: when the Lord said to the centurion, “Go, and as you have believed, let it be done for you,” the servant was healed from that hour. But blessed Luke’s custom is to abbreviate what he has seen fully explained by the other Evangelists, [Col. 0186B] or even deliberately to pass over it; whatever he has found them to have treated briefly, however, he carefully clarifies by touching upon it.

Mystically, as I said, the centurion, whose faith is preferred to that of Israel, signifies the elect from the Gentiles. They are surrounded, as though by a centurion’s military force, by spiritual virtues; yet, sublime in perfection, they seek from the Lord nothing earthly, but only the joys of eternal salvation for themselves and their own.

The number one hundred, which is transferred from the left to the right, is customarily used as a sign of heavenly life. Hence Noah’s ark was built over one hundred years. Abraham, at the age of one hundred, received the son of promise. Isaac sowed and found a hundredfold in that same year (Genesis XXVI). The court of the tabernacle is one hundred cubits long (Exodus XXVII). [Col. 0186C] “I will sing of mercy and judgment (Psalm C),” and other passages of this kind.

Therefore men of such merit must necessarily implore the Lord for these people, because they are still oppressed by the spirit of servitude in fear, so that, as they are gradually advanced to higher things, perfect love may cast out fear.

## HOMILY XXVI. FRIDAY AFTER ASH WEDNESDAY

(Matthew V.) “At that time Jesus said to his disciples: ‘You have heard that it was said to the ancients: You shall love your neighbor and hate your enemy,’” and the rest.

Some think that the commandments of the New Testament are impossible [Col. 0186D] and say that the commandments of the New Testament are more burdensome than those of the Old. They must be answered that the commandments of almighty God are not impossible but rather perfect. For if they were nearly impossible, they could never have been observed by any saint. But since we read that the saints have observed them in some measure, it is clear that they are not impossible but perfect.

For we read that this commandment of the Lord—“Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you (Luke VI)”—was fulfilled both by blessed Stephen and by David. Stephen prayed for his persecutors (Acts VII), while David mourned the death of his most savage enemy, Saul (1 Samuel I).

But it must be asked how this agrees with what the Lord commands in the Old Testament: [Col. 0187A] “Love your friends and hate your enemies (Leviticus XIX).” The answer is that almighty God commanded us not to hate in our enemies what they are as human beings, but what they are as evil people. Wisdom speaks of God: “You hate nothing that you have made (Wisdom XI).”

If he hates nothing that he has made, how is it said through Malachi: “I loved Jacob, but I hated Esau (Malachi I)”? The Lord hated sin in Esau, but he did not hate human nature. God does not hate a person because he is human; he hates him insofar as he is a sinner.

“And pray for those who persecute and slander you.” To persecute is to inflict violence; to slander is to seek an opportunity to cause harm.

But it must be asked: Since the Lord commands us to pray for those who persecute and slander us, [Col. 0187B] what are we to make of certain imprecations against persecutors found in the books of the Prophets and in the Gospel, which are thought to be curses? For example: “Let their table become a snare before them (Psalm LXVIII).” And when the Apostle Paul had been struck by an officer of the high priest, he replied: “God will strike you, whitewashed wall (Acts XXIII).” And the Lord says in the Gospel: “Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida (Matthew XI)!”

The answer is that these words were spoken not with the desire of one pronouncing a curse but with the concern of one foretelling what would happen. The Lord and the Prophets foresaw the future ruin of the impious, and they proclaimed that ruin not by wishing for it but by prophesying it.

Again it is asked: Since the Lord commands us to pray for our enemies, why does John forbid prayer for certain brothers who are sinning unto death? For he says in his Epistle: “There is a sin [Col. 0187C] unto death; I do not say that anyone should pray for it (1 John V).”

The answer is that among brothers there are often certain sins more serious than the persecutions of the impious. A sin unto death means persevering in sin unto death. Or the person commits a sin unto death who, after acknowledging God, attacks the fellowship of the brethren and harasses it with the jaws of injury.

“So that you may be sons of your Father.” That is, you ought to do these things so that you may be sons of your Father, who makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil. Literally, this alone is to be understood. For the Lord distributes these two creatures, through which all crops are born and nourished, [Col. 0187D] equally over Christians and pagans, the good and the evil.

“For if you love those who love you,” and so forth. The meaning is: If publicans and sinners, guided by nature, extend themselves to such goodness that they love those who love them, how much more ought you to be broader in charity, so that you love not only your friends but also your enemies?

“Do not even the publicans do this?” Among the Romans, publicans were called tax collectors who exacted taxes from the people.

“And if you greet only your brothers,” and the rest. If you greet those who are your brothers by nature or are joined to you by a bond of friendship, what more are you doing than the Gentiles?

*Ethnos* (ἔθνος) is Greek; in Latin it is *gens*, “a nation” or “people.” Hence they are called *ethnici*, “Gentiles.” A Gentile is one who remains as he is born, namely, in the same rite, profession, and paganism.

“Therefore be perfect, just as your heavenly Father is perfect.” [Col. 0188A] “Just as” does not indicate equality of quality but rather likeness. Just as God is perfect in the nature of his power, so you too should be perfect according to the measure of your weakness. Just as God makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil and sends rain upon the just and the unjust, so you should extend your love and the sun of your charity not only to friends but also to enemies.

“Take care not to perform your righteousness before men in order to be seen by them.” Take care—that is, beware of displaying righteous deeds for the purpose of being seen by people and seeking human praise from them.

It is not a sin to perform righteous deeds before people; it is a sin to perform righteous deeds before people for the purpose of seeking praise from them. Hence the Lord also said above: “Let your light shine before men, [Col. 0188B] so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven (Matthew V).”

“Therefore, when you give alms, do not sound a trumpet before you.” The Lord drew this saying from the custom of the Scribes and Pharisees. On feast days and fast days, when they were about to give alms, they ordered trumpets to be sounded before them, so that at the sound of the trumpet a multitude of poor people would gather. When the people who had come together for the feast saw this, they would magnify and exalt them with their praises, as though they were worshipers of God, and would also load them with their own gifts. [Col. 0188C]

Or we can understand this in a deeper sense. In sacred Scripture, a trumpet usually signifies manifestation. Hence the Apostle Paul says: “We shall all indeed rise, but we shall not all be changed. In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet. For the trumpet will sound, and the dead will rise incorruptible, and we shall be changed (1 Corinthians XV).” That is, the resurrection will be openly manifested.

“Amen, I say to you, they have received their reward.” That is, praise from human beings.

“But when you give alms, let your left hand not know what your right hand is doing.” The meaning of the statement “Let your left hand not know what your right hand is doing” is this: [Col. 0188D] When you give alms, do not display that almsgiving publicly, lest you seem to glory in another’s misery.

Whoever has done something good out of a desire for human approval has had his left hand aware of his deed. The left hand signifies the desire for human praise; the right hand signifies the intention of good will.

“When you give alms, let your left hand not know what your right hand is doing.” That is, let the desire for human praise and approval not be mixed with your good will.

“So that your almsgiving may be in secret,” that is, in a good conscience. There are many who give alms with good will, although they lack the means to give. Hence the Psalmist says: “The man who shows mercy and lends is gracious [Col. 0189A] (Psalm CXI),” showing that even in mercy there is a certain grace belonging to almsgiving.

“But when you pray, enter your room, and after shutting the door, pray to your Father in secret.” Above, the Lord said that those who gave alms at the sound of a trumpet were hypocrites; that those who fasted improperly were hypocrites; and that those who prayed in the corners of the streets in order to be seen by people were altogether hypocrites. From this it is understood that whoever performs good works for the sake of human approval is a hypocrite.

The corners of the streets are crossroads and junctions. They are the places where one road crosses another and forms a crossroads. They stood at the crossroads so that people coming from every direction might see them [Col. 0189B] intent upon prayer and magnify them as friends of God and observers of the Law.

“Amen, I say to you, they have received their reward,” that is, human praise. They obtained as their reward the human praise that they desired from people.

“But when you pray.” The Lord trained a good athlete, as though he were saying: You who pray for the sake of eternal life, “enter your room,” that is, the secret place of your heart.

“And after shutting the door” of your mouth, “pray to your Father.” Pray not in a loud voice but in contrition of spirit, as Hannah, the mother of Samuel, did (1 Samuel I). When she prayed, she merely moved her lips, but no sound of hers could be heard.

Or “after shutting the door” of the heart against evil thoughts, [Col. 0189C] so that when you pray evil thoughts may have no access or entrance into your heart. Or “after shutting the door,” that is, the door of our senses.

## HOMILY XXVII. SATURDAY AFTER ASH WEDNESDAY

(Luke XIV.) “At that time Jesus was saying to a certain leader of the Pharisees: ‘When you make a lunch or a dinner, do not invite your friends, or your brothers, or your relatives, or your neighbors, or the rich,’” and the rest.

He does not forbid brothers, friends, and rich people to hold banquets for one another as though this were a crime. Rather, like the other transactions of human necessity in which sinners lend to sinners so that they may receive equal returns, he shows that such banquets have no value for obtaining the rewards of heavenly life.

Finally he adds: [Col. 0189D] “Lest they also invite you in return, and, he says, a repayment be made to you.” He does not say, “and sin be committed,” but “and, he says, a repayment be made to you.”

Something similar is what he says elsewhere: “And if you do good to those who do good to you, what credit is that to you? For sinners do the same (Luke VI).”

Nevertheless, there are certain reciprocal banquets of brothers, friends, relatives, and rich neighbors that receive not only repayment in the present but also condemnation in the future. Indeed, they are counted by the Apostle among the works of darkness: “Let us walk honorably as in the day, not in revelries and drunkenness (Romans XIII).”

Revelries are luxurious banquets, which are either celebrated through everyone’s contributions or customarily provided in turn by members of a convivial group, so that no one is ashamed to say or do something dishonorable. They gather for this purpose: that shameful things may be done there [Col. 0190A] and that an abundance of wine may stimulate various pleasures of lust.

“But when you give a banquet, invite the poor, the weak, the lame, and the blind, and you will be blessed, because they have nothing with which to repay you. For you will be repaid in the resurrection of the righteous.”

He says “the resurrection of the righteous” because, although everyone will rise, [Col. 0190B] it is not improperly named almost as their own, since they do not doubt that they will be blessed in it. Therefore, whoever invites the poor to a banquet will receive a reward in the future. Whoever invites friends, brothers, and the rich receives his reward.

But even if he does this for God’s sake, following the example of Job’s sons, as with the other duties of brotherly love, the one who commanded it himself rewards him.

Whoever invites gluttons and lustful people because of wantonness will be punished with eternal punishment in the future.

“Upon hearing these things, one of those reclining at table said to him: ‘Blessed is he who shall eat bread in the kingdom of God.’” The bread that is eaten in the kingdom of God is not, as Cerinthus held, to be understood as bodily food, but rather as that bread which says: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven. If anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever” (John 6). That is, if anyone, having been perfectly incorporated into the sacrament of my incarnation, is deemed worthy to enjoy the vision of my divine majesty, he will rejoice in the perpetual blessedness of immortal life. But because some receive this bread merely by faith, as though by worshiping it, they disdain to attain its sweetness by truly tasting it.

## HOMILY XXVIII. THE FIRST SUNDAY IN LENT

### (Matthew 4)

“At that time, Jesus was led by the Spirit into the wilderness, to be tempted by the devil. And when he had fasted forty days,” and the rest. In the sequence of this reading the Lord was pleased to manifest to us both his natures, namely, the divine and the human. The fact that he fasted for forty days and forty nights is a declaration of divine power; but when, after those days had been completed, he became hungry as a human being, he was tempted by the devil as a human being, yet as God he overcame the devil’s temptations.

But perhaps those of limited understanding do not know by what spirit Jesus was led into the wilderness, especially because what follows says: “The devil took him to the holy city,” or to a high mountain. Yet it is easily recognized that he was truly and without any ambiguity led into the wilderness by the Holy Spirit, if we briefly consider what precedes in this Gospel. For the Evangelist says (Matthew 3): “Jesus came from Galilee to the Jordan, to John, to be baptized by him.” After he had been baptized, he immediately came up from the water. And behold, the heavens were opened to him, and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove and coming upon him. And behold, a voice from heaven said: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.” Immediately he added: “Then Jesus was led by the Spirit into the wilderness, to be tempted by the devil.” Thus he shows that Jesus was led into the wilderness not by another spirit, but by that very Holy Spirit who had descended upon him in the form of a dove.

The other Evangelists, namely Mark and Luke, also make this clearer. Mark says: “And immediately the Spirit drove him into the wilderness, and he was in the wilderness forty days and forty nights, and was tempted by Satan; and he was with the wild beasts, and angels ministered to him” (Mark 1). Luke, however, says: “Jesus, filled with the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan and was driven by the Spirit into the wilderness for forty days, and he ate nothing during those days. And when they were completed, he was hungry” (Luke 4). From these words we understand most clearly that the Holy Spirit led him to the place where the evil spirit would find an opportunity to tempt him. The devil had to be given an opportunity to tempt, so that Christ might have an opportunity to conquer. For he permitted himself to be tempted by the evil spirit in order to show us an example of combat.

The apostle Paul says this in his Epistle to the Hebrews, when speaking of the Lord: “For we do not have a high priest who cannot sympathize with our weaknesses, but one who was tempted in every respect as we are, without sin” (Hebrews 4). Let us therefore approach the throne of glory with confidence, so that we may receive mercy and find grace for timely help.

But when the human mind hears that its Creator and Redeemer, who had no sin whatsoever, was tempted by the devil, it trembles in fear at its own frailty. Yet whoever is frightened by human weakness ought to recover confidence from the compassion of his Creator. For he who was pleased to become human for our sake permitted himself to be tempted for us in human nature, so that by his temptation he might exclude ours; and not only grant us courage to fight against the devil, but also restore our confidence in conquering him.

To some, perhaps, it may also seem incredible that the Lord was tempted by the devil. But we understand that there is nothing to fear in his temptation, and that it is not incredible if we weigh his other deeds. For we know with certainty that the devil is the head of all the reprobate, and that all the wicked are members of this head. Was Pilate not one of his members? Were not the Jews who persecuted him and the soldiers who crucified him his members? Certainly they were. Since, then, being killed is something greater than being tempted, what is surprising if he wished to be tempted by the devil, when he permitted himself to be crucified by the devil’s members? Nor is it incredible that he who endured the greater thing from the members endured the lesser thing from the head.

But we must carefully consider that immediately after his baptism the Lord endured the devil’s temptations, so that we may understand that we are pressed more fiercely by the devil’s temptations when we have begun to withdraw from his servitude or dominion and desire to live justly and devoutly with Christ. This is shown elsewhere in the Gospel, when, as the demon was departing from the boy, it threw him down, tore him violently, and cried out before leaving him (Luke 9). For just as a king wages war not against subject nations but against rebellious ones, so the devil attacks more vigorously those whom he sees withdrawing from his service and hastening toward the easy yoke of Christ.

The elect then experience more severe demonic temptations when they wish to begin some good undertaking. We learned this from the example of the Israelites, who are said to have been afflicted more harshly by Pharaoh precisely when, through Moses and Aaron, they were called to the promised land. Against the darts of these temptations a certain wise man urges us to take up spiritual weapons, saying: “My son, when you approach the service of God, stand in justice and fear, and prepare your soul for temptation” (Ecclesiasticus 2). And the Apostle says: “Put on the armor of God, so that you may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil. For our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against rulers and authorities, against the rulers of the darkness of this age, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places” (Ephesians 6).

And as though you might ask what these weapons are, the same Apostle explains, adding: “Stand therefore, having girded your loins with truth, and having put on the breastplate of righteousness, and having shod your feet in readiness for the Gospel of peace; in all things taking up the shield of faith, with which you may be able to extinguish all the flaming arrows of the evil one. And take the helmet of salvation and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (ibid.).

When the Lord was about to fight the devil, he withdrew into the wilderness, to show us that, if we wish to overcome his temptations perfectly, we must avoid not only the crowds of demons but also the fellowship of wicked people. For just as the fellowship of good people greatly helps, so the company of the wicked does great harm to weak minds; and the Psalmist bears witness, saying: “With the holy you will be holy, and with the innocent you will be innocent. And with the chosen you will be chosen, and with the perverse you will become perverse” (Psalm 17).

Therefore Solomon warns us, saying: “Do not be a friend to an angry man, nor walk with a furious man, lest you learn his ways and take a stumbling-block for your soul” (Proverbs 22). And so whoever desires to escape the snares of temptation ought sometimes to flee the company of the wicked bodily, but always in mind, following the example of the one who, placed in a royal court or among popular crowds, said: “Behold, I have fled far away, and I remained in solitude” (Psalm 54).

“And when he had fasted forty days and forty nights, afterward he was hungry.” By fasting for forty days and forty nights, the Lord, who was about to overcome the devil, showed that fasting and prayer are necessary weapons against the devil’s temptations, in accordance with what he himself says in the Gospel: “This kind is not driven out except by prayer and fasting” (Matthew 17). And Paul says: “Everyone who competes in the contest exercises self-control in all things” (1 Corinthians 9).

When, therefore, he fasted for forty days and nights, he taught that throughout the whole course of the present life the elect have a struggle against the temptations of the ancient enemy. Or certainly the Lord fasted for forty days and forty nights because he was about to preach the Gospel, to show that the Old Testament does not differ from the New. For we read that two outstanding Fathers fasted for forty days and nights, namely Moses and Elijah. One of them was the lawgiver, the other an eminent prophet. Moses therefore signifies the Law, and Elijah prophecy.

To show, then, that he would teach nothing different in the Gospel from what the Law and the Prophets had foretold about him, the Lord wished to fast for forty days and forty nights. For, as he himself says in the Gospel, he had not come to abolish the Law and the Prophets but to fulfill them (Matthew 5). Accordingly, when he was transfigured on the mountain, Moses and Elijah are rightly said to have been seen with him, proclaiming the departure of his passion in Jerusalem.

Or certainly, by fasting he showed that the elect would be in affliction throughout all the days of the present life. There is also another matter concerning this number forty that ought to be considered. This number begins from one but is multiplied by addition: if you add two to one, the result is three; add three, and the result is six; add four, and the result is ten. Thus, just as one, two, three, and four make ten, so one, two, three, and four multiplied fourfold make forty.

The number ten belongs to the Old Testament, because of the Decalogue of the Law; but the number forty belongs to the grace of the New Testament, because there are four books of the holy Gospel. The same number also signifies the course of the present life, because the world is divided into four regions: east, west, north, and south. From these regions of the world the faithful are gathered, as it is written: “Those whom he redeemed from the hand of the enemy, he gathered from the regions, from the rising and the setting of the sun, from the north and from the sea” (Psalm 106).

We arrive at the number forty as though multiplying ten by four, when, by understanding the Law spiritually, we explain it more broadly through the grace of the New Testament. For the Law increases when it is interpreted spiritually, because its commandments grow all the more as they are examined more subtly.

There is also another matter concerning this number forty that a careful reader may add. The ten commandments given to Moses were written on two tablets: on one there were three, and on the other seven. The three pertain to love of God, because God is the inseparable Trinity, whom we are commanded to love with all our heart, all our mind, and all our soul. The seven pertain to love of neighbor, whom we are also commanded to love as ourselves. And appropriately so, because our whole human being, inner and outer, consists of seven qualities.

The inner person consists of understanding, memory, and will; the outer of earth, water, fire, and air—that is, of what is hot and cold, dry and moist. Thus seven and three make ten. Let us therefore join the seven to the three so that we may reach the perfect number, namely, that with the whole affection of love we may cling to our Creator.

And because by living unworthily we have transgressed the commandments of the Decalogue, let us afflict our flesh through repentance, so that we may be able to reach the perfect number forty. Nor should it seem burdensome if, for the common benefit, we insert here something further concerning this number forty.

From the present day until holy Easter there are forty-two days to come, comprising six weeks. If we subtract the six days that fall on Sundays, no more than thirty-six days remain for abstinence. Since the annual cycle turns through 365 days, if we consider the matter correctly, this season of Lent is a tithe of our life.

For it is fitting that those who have lived for themselves throughout the whole year should at least during these holy days live for God, so that we may give God a tithe not only of our possessions but also of our bodies. And if we wish to enter the kingdom of heaven, our righteousness must exceed that of the scribes and Pharisees, so that while they gave tithes of their possessions, we may give tithes of our days.

Let us be eager in abstinence, constant in prayers, and generous in almsgiving. Let us mortify our flesh through abstinence and our mind through compunction, so that, according to the Apostle, we may “present our bodies as a living sacrifice” (Romans 12). A sacrifice is offered and yet lives, because a person does not depart from the present life and nevertheless afflicts his flesh through abstinence.

He offers God a sacrifice that is all the more acceptable because he does not seek outside himself, as a lamb does, something to sacrifice to God, but seeks it within himself, as Scripture says: “A sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit; a contrite and humbled heart God will not despise” (Psalm 50).

Just as gluttony is the fuel of all vices, so abstinence is the nurse of all virtues. Let us recall the goodness of abstinence from the beginning. As long as our first parents remained in paradise, they abstained from the forbidden food. But after they satisfied the desires of their appetite, they immediately lost the beauty of paradise.

After this, Moses, who fasted, received the Law of God; the people, who ate, fashioned idols. Hence it is written: “The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play” (Exodus 32). Jonathan also deserved the sentence of death because, unknowingly, he violated the fast imposed by his father (1 Samuel 14).

Daniel and the three young men, who practiced remarkable abstinence in the king’s court, not only escaped the lions’ teeth and felt nothing of the furnace of fire, but also received knowledge for interpreting sacred mysteries (Daniel 3). John, too, because he practiced remarkable abstinence, deserved not only to see the Redeemer but also to baptize him.

Why say more? The mediator between God and human beings, himself made human, fasted for forty days and forty nights in order to overcome the devil, showing that fasting and abstinence are invincible weapons against the devil’s snares.

Invited by these examples, let us embrace the virtue of abstinence with our whole heart, so that we may be able both to extinguish future evils and to wash away past sins, following the example of the Ninevites, who escaped the threatened anger of God through three days of abstinence (Jonah 3).

But because almsgiving is the companion of fasting, it is fitting that what we subtract from our body through abstinence we distribute to the poor through mercy. God therefore does not approve a fast that almsgiving does not adorn. For fasting without almsgiving is like a lamp without oil.

Thus the Lord himself, through the prophet, rebuked certain people who fasted but refrained from almsgiving, saying: “When you fasted and mourned, did you fast and mourn for yourselves?” (Zechariah 7). He takes the benefit of abstinence for himself and does not distribute it to the poor, but reserves it for himself in the future.

But whoever fasts and gives alms must guard his heart against all anger, hatred, and impatience. For he afflicts himself in vain in body if he preserves hatred in his heart, just as the Lord rebukes certain people who fast, saying: “Behold, on the day of your fast your own will is found, and you demand all your debts. Behold, you fast for quarrels and strife, and you strike with an impious fist” (Isaiah 58).

Conversely, the Lord says through Joel: “Sanctify a fast” (Joel 1). To sanctify a fast means, together with abstinence of the flesh, to give alms and perform the other works of piety.

Therefore, in accordance with the Apostle, who says: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (2 Corinthians 6), it is fitting that during these days we present ourselves as ministers of God, in much patience, in fastings, in vigils, in chastity, and in sincere love.

How much the Lord loves peaceful harmony among us, he himself makes clear in the Gospel when he cries out: “If you offer your gift at the altar, and there remember that your brother has something against you” (Matthew 5), and so forth. We shall celebrate the day of resurrection all the more securely the more strictly we observe the days of the present time.

Accordingly, the Lord himself shows what reward—or rather, how great a glory—awaits those who fast with a simple heart and give alms. After saying through the Prophet (Isaiah 58): “This is the fast that I have chosen: break your bread for the hungry, and bring the poor and homeless into your house; when you see the naked, cover him, and do not despise your own flesh,” he added: “Then your light will break forth like the dawn, and your healing will quickly arise. Your righteousness will go before you, and the glory of the Lord will gather you. Then you will call, and the Lord will answer; you will cry, and he will say, ‘Here I am’” (ibid.).

For an appropriate reason, therefore, the teachers of the Church established that the season of Lent should be observed before the Lord’s passion, so that we may understand that the affliction of the present life produces future immortality. To confirm this, the Lord himself, who fasted for forty days before his passion, also spent forty days with his disciples after his resurrection, completing each period with the number forty, to show that the present life is a time of affliction and the future a time of joy.

When he fasted for forty days before his passion, he seemed to cry out: “Unless you repent, you will all perish in your sins” (Luke 13); and Peter said: “Abstain from fleshly desires, which wage war against the soul” (1 Peter 2).

But when after his resurrection he lived with his disciples, making their hearts joyful, he seemed to promise that ineffable joy of which he says elsewhere: “I will see you again, and your heart will rejoice, and no one will take your joy from you” (John 14). And again: “Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age” (Matthew 28).

He fasted not only for forty days but also for forty nights, so that whether prosperous circumstances flatter us—which are signified by days—or adversities terrify us—which are signified by nights—the Christian mind may remain unmoved, as did the one who said: “By the weapons of righteousness on the right and on the left, through glory and dishonor, through ill repute and good repute, as deceivers and truthful, as unknown and known” (2 Corinthians 6).

After it had been said, “When he had fasted forty days and forty nights,” it was rightly added, “afterward he was hungry,” so that his true humanity might be shown. We do not read this about Moses and Elijah, because there is no doubt that, after fasting, they hungered as ordinary human beings. But it was fitting that this should be written about him who was God in such a way that he was also human.

Or certainly he became hungry after fasting so that an opportunity to tempt him might be given to the devil. When the devil saw him fasting for forty days and nights, he perhaps would not have dared to tempt him unless he saw him hungry. When he saw him hungry after the fast, he presumed to tempt him as a human being. Hence it follows:

“And the tempter approached and said to him: ‘If you are the Son of God, command that these stones become loaves of bread.’” Because bread is suitable for one who is hungry, the devil persuaded the one whom he saw hungry to make bread from stones.

But someone may perhaps ask how the devil found an opportunity to tempt the Lord, and why he believed him to be the Son of God. The answer is that he may have heard the voice of God the Father thundering: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 17). Therefore, although he heard from the Father’s testimony that he was God, he postponed believing that he was human.

For if he did not consider him God, he would never have said through a possessed man: “What have you to do with us, Son of God? Have you come here to torment us before the time?” (Matthew 8). But because he saw in him what belonged to a human being, he remained ignorant until his death whether he was God.

Thus our Lord Jesus Christ so ordered his works that the devil could not recognize his coming, while through the power of his miracles he manifested to the world that he was God. He was conceived as God but born as a human being. As God he was worshiped by the Magi; as a human being he was carried by his parents into Egypt. As God he fasted; as a human being he became hungry. As a human being he slept; as God he commanded the winds and the sea. As God he fed many thousands of people with a few loaves; as a human being he needed earthly food. Finally, as a human being he was crucified, but as God he rose again.

Three things concerning the Lord remained hidden from the prince of this world: his conception, his birth, and his passion. For, as the Apostle says: “If they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Corinthians 2).

But because the devil wished to test his divinity, he approached him to tempt him and said: “If you are the Son of God,” and so forth. In this temptation the devil is held bound in two ways. If he considered him merely human and not God, why did he tempt him to make bread from stones, since this is not impossible for God? As we have said, he spoke as one doubtful and uncertain.

“He answered and said: ‘It is written: Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God.’” Great is the Lord’s power, but his patience is shown to be no less great. For although by a single word he could have either turned his tempter into a stone or plunged him into the abyss, he endured his temptations, showing us that when we are tempted we must not be afraid, but must beware lest we consent to temptations.

“For blessed is the man who endures temptation, because, when he has been tested, he will receive the crown of life that God has promised to those who love him” (James 1).

The Lord wished to overcome the devil not by power but by authority, showing us that whenever we are tempted by the devil, we must always have recourse to the authority of Scripture. We must do what Scripture teaches, not what the devil suggests.

When the Lord says, “Man shall not live by bread alone,” this is literally true, because human life is not sustained by bread alone; rather, God created various foods for human use, namely, the flesh of cattle, birds, and fish, as well as different kinds of fruits. But when he adds, “but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God,” he shows that there is one life of the body and another of the soul.

The life of the body is the soul; the life of the soul is God. And just as the body dies if it is not nourished with bodily food, so the soul dies unless it is refreshed by the word of God—not so that it ceases to exist, but so that it becomes evil. For “man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God.”

“Then the devil took him to the holy city.” In this passage the Evangelist calls Jerusalem the holy city—not because it was holy at that time, but because he preserved its former name. Or certainly he calls it holy in comparison with the other cities in which idols were worshiped.

“And he set him on the pinnacle of the temple.” The pinnacle of the temple was the priestly platform, which rose above the entire height of the temple. There the priests, when they were about to speak the word to the people, were accustomed to ascend so that they could be heard and seen more easily.

For in Palestine—that is, the promised land, which is called Palestine because the Philistines lived there—they do not build houses in our manner, but make them flat on top for sitting or walking. Around the roof they also build a wall, so that people may walk upon it more safely. Hence Moses commanded the people, saying: “When you build a new house, you shall make a wall around the roof, lest you incur guilt if your neighbor falls and plunges headlong” (Deuteronomy 22).

In accordance with this model, the house of King Uzziah is believed to have been built; of him it is written: “For he fell through the lattice of his house and died” (2 Kings 1). The pinnacle was therefore higher than the whole temple. From it James, the brother of the Lord, is said to have been thrown down because he proclaimed in Jerusalem the resurrection from the dead.

The devil is therefore said to have taken the Lord to this pinnacle, not by his own power, but by the Lord’s permission and will. The Lord himself ascended the pinnacle by his own will, in order to give the devil an opportunity to tempt him.

It should be noted that, while persuading him to leap, the devil said:

“If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down.” He does not urge those whom he deceives to climb upward, but persuades them to fall downward. Thus Symmachus aptly interpreted the name of the devil as “flowing downward,” so that what he expressed in his will would also be heard in his name.

The devil not only urged the plunge, but, so that he might more easily be believed, also appealed to the authority of Scripture, saying:

“For it is written: ‘He has commanded his angels concerning you, and they will lift you up in their hands, lest you strike your foot against a stone.’”

From this passage we learn that the devil misinterprets Scripture. For this was not written about the person of the Lord, but is sung concerning the person of a righteous man who needs the help of angels, lest he strike against a stone—that is, against the Law written on stone tablets. Or it may refer to Christ, who is spiritually the rock, as the Apostle says: “The rock was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10). And the Prophet says: “Behold, I will place in Zion a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense” (Isaiah 8).

For if the devil had wished to speak the truth, he should have said what follows in the same psalm: “You will tread upon the asp and the basilisk; you will trample the lion and the dragon” (Psalm 90). For he is the asp who kills human souls with the poison of temptations. He is the basilisk who tries to destroy souls by the breath of wicked persuasion. He is the lion who, prowling about, seeks someone to devour. He is also the dragon who drags the people he deceives into the depths of punishment and swallows them up.

But the Lord walked upon the asp and the basilisk and trampled the lion and the dragon. By his own power he broke the snares of the ancient enemy, so that he cannot harm any Christian unless we willingly subject ourselves to him.

But the devil, cunningly evading the issue, kept silent about this verse, which he knew had been written about himself. Instead, he directed against the Lord, as though against a weak human being, what is sung concerning the righteous man, saying: “It is written that he has commanded his angels concerning you, and they will lift you up in their hands,” and so forth.

From this passage we also learn that angels are assigned to guard the lives of the saints, as the Apostle bears witness, saying: “Are they not ministering spirits, sent out for service on behalf of those who are to inherit salvation?” (Hebrews 1). And the Lord says in the Gospel concerning the little ones: “Their angels always see the face of my Father” (Matthew 18).

Hence in the Acts of the Apostles, when Peter knocked at the door, it was said: “It is not Peter, but his angel” (Acts 12). For this reason the angel said to Tobit: “When you were praying, I presented your prayers before God” (Tobit 12).

“Jesus said to him again: ‘It is written: You shall not tempt the Lord your God.’” It should be noted that the Lord took his useful testimonies against the devil from the book of Deuteronomy, mentioning the second Law in order to demonstrate that it was holy and just, and to shatter the enemy’s false darts with true shields.

David once prefigured this victory when he fought the Philistine in single combat. He set aside the royal armor and took five smooth stones from the stream, placing them in his shepherd’s bag. He cast one of them with a sling, struck the Philistine on the forehead, and brought him down to the ground; then he cut off his head with the Philistine’s own sword, granting great grace and glory to his people (1 Samuel 17).

Who better than the Lord Jesus Christ is signified by David, whose name is interpreted as “strong of hand,” since Christ took flesh from David’s lineage? He is rightly called strong of hand because he alone struck down the devil, of whom it is written: “The Lord is strong and mighty; the Lord mighty in battle” (Psalm 23).

About to fight the Philistine, David chose five smooth stones, but by striking the Philistine on the forehead with one he brought him down to the ground. In the same way, the Lord took up the five books of Moses to refute the devil’s cunning. With one of them he struck the Philistine on the forehead, because from the book of Deuteronomy he opposed three testimonies to the devil’s threefold temptation. Thus he obtained victory over the ancient enemy and brought great joy to those who believe in him.

“Again the devil took him to a very high mountain and showed him all the kingdoms of the world and their glory.” What is said about the pinnacle should also be understood about the mountain. We must not suppose that the devil could take the unwilling Lord to a high mountain; rather, the Evangelist presents the devil’s evil intention as though it were an accomplished deed.

The Lord himself ascended the mountain by his own will, so that there might be an opportunity for the devil to tempt and for Christ to triumph. For if there had been no opportunity to tempt, there would have been no triumph in conquering.

Some, following the literal sense, assert that this mountain was Olympus, which is said to be so much higher than the others that it appears to contain clouds within itself. Others say that it was Tabor, which is reported to have been very high. But whatever mountain it was, the Lord nevertheless ascended it voluntarily, as we have said.

Spiritually, however, the mountain on which the devil tempted the Lord signifies pride. When, therefore, the devil tempted the Lord on a mountain, this is understood to mean that he persuades those whom he deceives to raise themselves up in the pride of their minds. Of him it is said through blessed Job: “He sees every lofty thing; he is king over all the sons of pride” (Job 41). And the Apostle says: “Pride is the beginning of every sin” (Ecclesiasticus 10). For just as the devil fell from heaven through pride, so he makes all whom he deceives sin through pride.

By the glory of the world he means gold, silver, precious stones, and the other desirable things of the world, in which lovers of the world chiefly glory.

But we must not suppose that he could have shown all the kingdoms of the world and their glory to the Lord simultaneously from any source other than himself. Rather, he who created all things through his divinity saw all things simultaneously, as he wished, through his humanity—whether the whole world as it is, or gathered together into a sphere, so that, as we have already said above, an opportunity might be given to the devil to tempt him.

Nor is it surprising that the Lord was able to survey the whole world in this way, since he also granted this as a gift to certain holy people, so that they could see it gathered together into a sphere. But in what he says:

[Col. 0200A] “I will give you all these things, if you will fall down and worship me”: by this he is proved a liar. Nor does he have the power to give all the kingdoms of the world, or their glory, to whomever he wishes, since he did not dare to harm even the substance of blessed Job before he had been permitted by God, when the devil himself said to the Lord: “Stretch out your hand and touch all that he possesses, and he will curse you to your face” (Job 1). We can also readily recognize this from the fact that we read of holy men who were exceedingly rich in possessions of silver and gold—something that certainly would not have been the case if all the kingdoms of the world had been in the devil’s power.

Because everyone who worships the devil first falls from God’s sight through consent to an evil deed, the devil’s words are: “If, falling down, you will worship me.” Here we must consider that he first said “fall,” and afterward “worship.” A person falls when he consents to sin. It is as though he worships the devil after his fall when he commits the sins themselves in deed, just as the Apostle says of the greedy: “And greed, which is the service of idols” (Eph. 5). And of such people the Psalmist says: “There they fell who work iniquity; they were cast out, and they could not stand” (Ps. 35).

But it is asked why the holy evangelists—Matthew, that is, and Luke—seem to disagree in their account of the temptations, especially since they agree about the first but differ about the second and third. For what Matthew placed second, Luke placed third; and what Luke placed third, Matthew placed second.

To this we must reply that both wrote the truth, since Luke preserved the order in which the events literally took place: the first occurred in the desert, the second on the mountain, and the third in the city. Matthew, however, considered more subtly the order of the temptations by which the devil first deceived the human being in paradise. For the devil tempted the first human being in paradise in three ways: through gluttony, vainglory, and greed (Gen. 3). He tempted him through gluttony when he persuaded him to eat the forbidden food; through vainglory when he said, “You will be like gods”; and through greed when he added, “Knowing good and evil.” Greed is present not only in the desire for money, but also in the ambition for honor, when an honor not owed is sought beyond one’s nature or proper measure. Thus, concerning the only-begotten Son of God, who did not wish to seek this, the Apostle Paul said: “He did not regard it as robbery to be equal with God” [Col. 0200D] (Phil. 2).

But because the devil had overthrown the human being in paradise through these three means, when he was about to tempt the Lord he returned to his customary weapons, thinking that he could wound him with the same arrows by which he had destroyed the first human being. He tempted him through gluttony when he said, “If you are the Son of God, command that these stones become bread.” Through vainglory when he said, “If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down.” Through greed when he added, “I will give you all these things, if, falling down, you will worship me.”

But the Lord, who had come to free the human race from the devil’s power, shut out his temptations by the very entrance through which the devil thought he held the first human being. Here we should consider that we, who were created from the stock of the first human being and redeemed through the second human being, are continually tempted in these three ways—especially during these days of Lent, when the devil sees our religious devotion burning more earnestly with love for God.

Gluttony therefore tempts us when it persuades us either to anticipate the appointed hour or, at the appointed hour, to eat beyond measure, and it suggests that we provide luxurious or excessive banquets. But if it finds us watchful in this matter, it tempts us through greed, so that what we remove from the body by abstinence we may not distribute generously to the poor, but instead reserve for ourselves in the future through covetousness. If we give it no consent even in this, it tempts us through vainglory, so that in fasting or giving more abundant alms we may seek human praise rather than God’s.

But instructed by the Lord’s example, let us conquer the appetite of gluttony through abstinence, greed through generosity, and vainglory through humility, according to the admonition of blessed John, who says: “Little children, do not love the world, nor the things that are in the world, because everything that is in the world is the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the pride of life” (1 John 2) [Col. 0201B]. The desire of the flesh pertains to gluttony; worldly ambition to greed; and the desire of the eyes to vainglory.
