That the human race is especially drawn away from the Lord’s will by these three temptations, in which the devil was overcome by the Lord, is indicated by that Gospel parable (Luke 14) in which those invited to the dinner refused to come and offered three excuses. The first said: “I have bought a farm, and I must go out and see it.” The second said: “I have bought five yoke of oxen, and I am going to test them.” The third also said: “I have taken a wife, and therefore I cannot come.”

Therefore, foreseeing the devil’s cunning and protected on the right and on the left by the weapons of righteousness, let us strive with all our efforts to resist him.

“Then Jesus said to him: Go, Satan.” Some think that the devil heard the same sentence as Peter did, but the two are very different. To Peter, who ignorantly opposed the mystery of the Passion, it was said: “Get behind me, Satan,” which means: “Follow me”—that is, “Imitate me, you who are opposed to my will.” To the devil, however, he does not say, “Get behind me,” but simply, “Go, Satan,” with “into hell” understood.

“For it is written: You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve.” This testimony, like the preceding ones, is written in Deuteronomy. Here we should consider that when the devil said, “I will give you all these things if, falling down, you will worship me,” the Lord replied, “You shall worship the Lord your God.” He thereby showed that the devil ought to have worshiped him as his God and Creator, rather than tempting him to be worshiped who was a creature.

But it is asked: Since the Lord says, “You shall serve him alone,” why does the Apostle Paul say that we should serve one another through charity? How, then, are we commanded to serve the Lord alone when service is spoken of as common?

We can easily recognize that the two are not contradictory if we attend to the character of the Greek language from which Scripture was translated. Among the Greeks, “service” is expressed in two ways: λατρεία (*latreia*) and δουλεία (*douleia*). Λατρεία is the service owed to God alone through worship and veneration, by which we honor the author and creator of all things. Hence the compound word εἰδωλολατρεία (*eidololatreia*) is formed from εἴδωλος (*eidōlos*, “idol”) and λατρεία: foolish people wished to offer idols the honor and service owed to God alone.

Δουλεία, however, is the service that is common and is to be rendered by believers to one another. Hence a servant is called δοῦλος (*doulos*) among them. We are therefore commanded to serve one another through charity, which pertains to δουλεία; and we are again commanded to serve God alone, which pertains to λατρεία, so that we may offer his honor to no creature.

When the Apostle says, “Servants, obey your earthly masters” (Eph. 6), this pertains to δουλεία. But when he says elsewhere, “We are the circumcision, serving God in spirit” (Phil. 3), this pertains to λατρεία; accordingly, in that same passage the Greek has λατρεύοντες (*latreuontes*, “serving in worship”) [Col. 0202B].

“Then the devil left him.” He left one whom he had never held, because, having been overcome by the one he had tempted, he ceased from the temptation. Although he withdrew from him then after being overcome, he came to him at the time of the Passion, as the Lord himself says: “The prince of this world is coming, and he has nothing in me” (John 14). From this we learn that the ancient enemy can be overcome, but does not know how to rest.

And when he had withdrawn from the temptation: “Behold, angels approached and ministered to him.” Most beautifully, at the conclusion of this reading, both natures of the Lord—divine, that is, and human—are disclosed to us, provided that we compare this passage with the reading from Luke’s Gospel. For we read in Luke (Luke 22) that when, as the time of the Passion drew near, the Lord prayed at greater length, an angel of the Lord descended from heaven and strengthened him.

As testimony to both natures, therefore, an angel strengthened him, and angels ministered to him. Because he is God, angels ministered to him; because he is truly human, an angel strengthened him. For to him who in his humanity was made a little lower than the angels, all things are subjected beneath his feet through his divinity.

As far as the literal sense is concerned, those who live in the regions across the sea report that no mountain is as high as Olympus, whose summit, they assert, is above the clouds, and that neither rain nor showers touch it there. Blessed Augustine relates that men who were exceptionally strong and robust climbed it in summer, carrying a sponge to their noses, along with flour or ashes. They made some mark in the flour or ashes, and when they returned the following year and climbed there again, they found it just as they had left it. This shows that it is above the clouds, and that neither shower nor rain reaches it, nor does the wind blow there.

Spiritually, however, the high mountain signifies the devil himself, concerning whom it is written elsewhere: “He was wounded by the mountain of Tyre”; and the prophet says: “How you have fallen from heaven, Lucifer, who rose in the morning, who said in your heart: I will ascend into heaven; I will set my throne above the stars of heaven” (Isa. 13). [Col. 0203A]

The devil is rightly represented by a mountain, because he urges all his followers toward higher things—that is, toward pride. Of him blessed Job says: “He sees every high thing, and he is king over all the sons of pride” (Job 41). Conversely, the Lord always urges his own toward humility, saying: “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. 11).

“And their glory.” By the glory of the world he means gold, silver, clothing, precious stones, and the other desirable or transitory things of the world. Another evangelist says that he showed him everything in a moment and the blink of an eye. This is fitting, because everything that is seen is momentary and transitory, as it is written: “The world passes away, and its desire, and everything is vanity” (1 John 2).

Another says that the devil told the Lord: “All the things you see are mine, and I give them to whomever I wish. But if you, falling down, worship me, they will all be yours” (Matt. 4). The devil deceived him and said this through arrogance, not through power. Far be it from us to understand that the whole world belongs to him. It cannot be so; rather, it belongs to him who created all things from nothing. The Prophet declares whose it is, saying: “The earth is the Lord’s and its fullness, the world and all who dwell in it” (Ps. 23).

## HOMILY XXIX. MONDAY AFTER INVOCAVIT

(Matt. 25.) “At that time Jesus said to his disciples: When the Son of Man comes in the seat of his majesty, and all his angels with him” [Col. 0203C].

After two days he would celebrate the Passover, and he fittingly foretells that he will come in majesty to judge the human race, so that those whom the ignominy of punishment had terrified might also be lifted up by the glory of the kingdom.

The Son of Man is fittingly said to come in majesty, because “the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5). At the judgment, only the form of the Son of Man will appear.

“Then he will sit upon the seat of his majesty.” We should understand this seat of God’s majesty either as the cloud in which he ascended into heaven and with which he will also descend for judgment, or as the angels and holy human beings over whom he presides as he conducts judgment throughout the world.

[Col. 0203D] “And all the nations will be gathered before him, and he will separate them from one another, as a shepherd separates sheep from goats.” Sheep are placed first as a sign of the elect, because of their innocence. The elect are called sheep because they are imitators of the one of whom it is said: “He was led like a sheep to the slaughter” (Isa. 53). The reprobate, however, are represented by goats, because the goat is a wanton and unruly animal and because in the Old Testament it was offered for the sins of the people.

“And he will place the sheep at his right hand, but the goats at his left.” With God there is neither right nor left; rather, by the right hand the greatness of glory is signified, and by the left the greatness of punishment. He will therefore place the sheep at his right hand, that is, the elect in the greatness of glory; but the goats at his left, that is, sinners in eternal punishments.

“And the King will say to those who are at his right hand: Come, blessed of my Father; possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.” We must understand this according to God’s foreknowledge and predestination. “The kingdom,” he says, “which I prepared for you from the foundation of the world—come and possess it.” Almighty God prepared the kingdom for his elect, and he prepared the elect themselves for the kingdom.

“Then the righteous will answer him, saying: Lord, when did we see you hungry and feed you?” and so forth. The righteous speak in this way either because of the Lord’s terror and greatness or because of the greatness of the reward. For all the good deeds performed in this age are judged unequal to the greatness of that glory [Col. 0204B].

“Amen I say to you: As long as you did it to one of these, my least brothers, you did it to me.” Although Christ is received in all the poor and alms are given to him in all of them, in this passage he specially designates those who are poor not in body but in spirit: those who have abandoned their possessions for God, as the apostles and their imitators did. Over these the Lord extended his hands, saying: “Behold my mother and my brothers” (Matt. 12).

“And these will go into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life.” Just as, in God’s knowledge and predestination, the kingdom was prepared for the saints from the foundation of the world, so the punishments of hell are said to have been prepared for the devil and his angels. Origen therefore dogmatizes in vain that the devil and all the reprobate will leave hell after a period of a thousand years and be transferred to the glory of eternal life, since the Lord says: “These will go into eternal punishment.” For just as the glory that the saints will receive on the day of judgment will be eternal and without end, so without doubt punishment will be given eternally to the reprobate.

## HOMILY XXX. TUESDAY AFTER INVOCAVIT

(Matt. 21.) “At that time, when Jesus had entered Jerusalem, the whole city was stirred, saying: Who is this?” and so forth.

The Lord had entered Jerusalem with a great crowd singing hymns and praises to him. When the people who had gathered for the feast saw the Lord arriving in Jerusalem with such a crowd, the whole city was stirred, saying: “Who is this?” When it says, “the whole city was stirred,” this must be understood as a metonymy, by which the container indicates what is contained—that is, by “the city,” the people dwelling in it are indicated. They ask, saying: “Who is this?”

“But the people”—that is, the common crowds who were walking with the Lord—“said: This is Jesus the prophet from Nazareth of Galilee.” Beginning with the lesser, they extend their answer toward the greater. “This is,” they say, “Jesus the prophet.” They do not say “the Christ,” but “the prophet,” as though they were still less knowledgeable and did not yet believe in him perfectly. Nevertheless, they were not entirely mistaken. He had also been called a prophet by Moses, who said: “The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers, like me; you shall listen to him” (Deut. 13). He also called himself a prophet, saying: “A prophet is not without honor except in his own country” (Matt. 13), and: “It is not fitting for a prophet to perish outside Jerusalem” (Luke 13).

He is said to be from Nazareth of Galilee because he was brought up there after returning from Egypt.

Allegorically, Jerusalem signifies the highest vision of peace, namely, the heavenly homeland. When Jesus entered Jerusalem—that is, when through the mystery of the Ascension he penetrated the heavens—the army of the heavenly powers was stirred at his coming, saying: “Who is this?” The Psalmist explains this more openly when, speaking in the person of the angelic powers, he says: “Who is this King of glory?” And those who were walking with the Lord answered them: “The Lord of hosts, he is the King of glory” (Ps. 23). Isaiah pronounces the same meaning, though in different words, saying (Isa. 63): “Who is this who comes from Edom, with garments dyed from Bozrah?” And he immediately added, in the response of the angels who accompanied the Lord: “This one is beautiful in his robe, walking in the multitude of his strength.”

“And Jesus entered the temple of God,” and so forth. The Lord gave us an example, so that whenever we go out into a city or village, we may first seek the house of God for the sake of prayer, and afterward carry out what we must do with God’s help.

Having entered the temple, he “was casting out all who were selling and buying in the temple.” We must begin with the custom of the Jews, who were sellers and buyers. For the law commanded (Deut. 16) that all the people of the kingdom of Judah should appear three times a year before the Lord, and when they gathered at the temple they were given the command: “You shall not appear before God empty-handed” (Exod. 15).

In that most august temple, to which the whole kingdom of Judah gathered, many victims were offered—oxen, rams, sheep, goats, and sparrows. But because many came from distant regions and could not bring victims and sacrifices with them, the priests kept victims of various kinds prepared, suitable for sacrificial use, so that those who came to the Lord’s temple could buy a sacrifice.

Thus a double profit accrued to the scribes and Pharisees. They received the price of their goods, and what was bought they again converted to their own uses. But because the poverty of the poor prevented their fraud—the poor not only lacked victims, but also lacked the money with which to buy what was necessary—they devised another fraud by which they could plunder the people. They placed money-changers in the temple, so that they might lend money at interest to each person in need.

But because the law prohibited usury, and money brought in could produce no profit without interest, they devised another fraud by which they could strip the people. In place of money-changers they installed *collybistae*, who demanded *collybia*—that is, sweetmeats or cheap little gifts—from the people to whom they lent money, so that what they were not permitted to accept in coins they might at least receive in things purchased with coins.

For example, fried chickpeas, a raisin, various kinds of fruit, and other things bought with coins: finding such practices in the temple, the Lord cast them all out. What would he have done if he had found people there indulging in luxury and drunkenness, when he cast out those who were offering things in the Lord’s temple? When it says that he cast them out of the temple, we should not think that such things were being done inside the temple itself, but in the porticoes attached to the temple.

“And he overturned the seats of those selling doves.” Doves do not sit on seats, but rather in cages, so that the Lord would overturn the seats of the doves. Some, however, maintain that the sellers of those doves were sitting on seats. Yet this scarcely holds, because a seat is not for merchants, but rather for teachers and instructors.

When the Lord overturned the seats of those selling doves, destroyed the tables of the money-changers, and expelled buyers and sellers alike from the Jewish temple, he indicated by one action another action that was to be performed. The sellers and buyers in the Church are those who either confer sacred orders for a price or receive them for a price.

The tables of the money-changers are called God’s altars because of the greed of priests who attend the altar for the purpose of acquiring earthly profit from it. Just as the Lord at that time expelled sellers and buyers alike from the bodily temple that was in Jerusalem, so now he expels sellers and buyers every day from the spiritual temple—that is, from the holy Church. That means both those who obtain ranks of dignity through money and those who confer those same ranks for a price. Even if they are not expelled from the present Church, they are at least excluded from the future one.

“And he overturned the seats of those selling doves.” We should understand the doves as the gift of the Holy Spirit, because for this reason the Holy Spirit appeared in the form of this animal over the baptized Lord. What the Lord physically did at that time therefore signifies that he would destroy the dignity and ministry of those who do not bestow the grace of the Holy Spirit—which is granted especially through the laying on of the hands of bishops—unless they have first received payment [Col. 0206D].

“It is written: My house shall be called a house of prayer.” A person should approach the temple for this reason: to practice pure and frequent prayer there. But it is converted into a den of thieves when anyone desires to acquire temporal profit for himself from the sacred ministry.

Spiritually, however, the temple of God is the mind of each believer. Hence the Apostle Paul says: “The temple of God is holy, and you are that temple” (1 Cor. 3). But this temple of God is converted into a den of thieves when in our minds we devise injuries against our neighbors. For while we carefully plan in our hearts how we may be able to harm them, thieves sit in our minds as though in a cave, carrying off plunder from passersby [Col. 0207A].

“And the blind and the lame came to him in the temple, and he healed them.” After expelling those who practiced unlawful things in the temple of God, he healed the blind and the lame, clearly indicating that just as those people were healed of their bodily blindness and weakness, so those others, if they wished to turn back, would be healed of their spiritual blindness.

“But when the chief priests and scribes saw his wonders which he performed,” and so forth. Many ask which of the Lord’s miracles should be regarded as greatest among all his signs. Some prefer the raising of Lazarus; some the giving of sight to the man born blind; some his changing water into wine; and many his transfiguration on the mountain before the disciples. To blessed Jerome, however, this appears to be the foremost and greatest of all the miracles.

For this was a great and extraordinary miracle: that one man—and one so despised at that time that he could be crucified—should drive from the temple, by flogging them with a whip made of cords, the whole crowd gathered from every kingdom of Judah, something that an immense army could not have done. In this deed, a certain star-like splendor of divinity radiated from his face, and those who were terrified by it lacked the courage to resist the Lord.

But the Pharisees, not daring to lay hands on the Lord, terrified by his divinity, nevertheless slandered his works, saying:

[Col. 0207C] “Do you hear what these people are saying?” As though they were saying: “This praise is not fitting for a human being, but for God alone.” In saying this, they did not think that he was the Son of God.

But we should consider with what danger bishops receive human praise, since it was charged as a crime that the Son of God was being praised by human beings. The Lord tempered his reply to them in such a way that he neither said what they wished to hear—“They are giving true testimony about me”—nor said, “They are mistaken; forgive their youth.” Instead, he confirmed the children’s words by the sayings of the prophets, saying: “Have you never read: From the mouth of infants and nursing children you have perfected praise?”—when he kindled the hearts and mouths of the simple crowds to faith in the Lord.

[Col. 0207D] “And leaving them”—that is, leaving behind his obstinate and slanderous opponents—“he went out beyond the city to Bethany.” By this he signified that he would leave the Jews because of their faithlessness and migrate to the peoples of the Gentiles, since Bethany is interpreted as “house of obedience.”

Here we should also note the Savior’s poverty. He was so poor that in so great a city he found no one whose hospitality he could enjoy. He flattered no one so much as to enjoy anyone’s hospitality. Rather, by day he came into the city and carried out his preaching there; at night he returned to Bethany and enjoyed the hospitality of Lazarus and his sisters.

## HOMILY XXXI. WEDNESDAY AFTER INVOCAVIT

[Col. 0208A]

(Matt. 12.) “At that time the scribes and Pharisees came to Jesus, saying: Teacher, we wish to see a sign from you,” and so forth.

They asked the Lord to show them signs from heaven as though the signs he had already performed earlier had not been signs. But we must ask what sort of signs they requested the Lord to perform.

Perhaps they asked him to make fire fall from heaven in the manner of Elijah, as happened at that time when fire descended from heaven and struck the captains of fifty together with their fifty men. Or perhaps they asked that, as in the time of Samuel, thunder should roar in summer, contrary to the custom of that land, lightning should flash, and rain should pour down (1 Sam. 12). But since they slandered the things they saw the Lord doing every day before their own eyes, they would have slandered these even more if they had happened. They would have said that this did not occur through the Lord’s power, but through various conditions of the air.

Or, as the Evangelist John says (Matt. 12), they asked him to make manna rain down for them from heaven, as he had once done for their ancestors in the desert, so that they might live without labor or fatigue.

“An evil and adulterous generation.” He calls the Jewish people an evil generation because of their contempt and transgression. It was transgressive of the divine commandments and adulterous because, having abandoned its own husband—that is, God—it had joined itself to the idols of the nations.

“It seeks a sign”—that is, a sign from heaven—“and no sign shall be given it except the sign of the prophet Jonah.” You ask, he says, to see a sign from me, but you will not be given a sign of my divinity from heaven; rather, a sign of my humanity from the underworld.

“For just as Jonah was in the belly of the sea creature three days and three nights, so the Son of Man will be in the heart of the earth three days and three nights.” The story of Jonah is well known (Jonah 1): when he fled from the face of the Lord toward Tarshish, he was swallowed up by a sea creature and remained there three days and three nights. By this act he signified the Lord’s death, when the Lord lay hidden in the heart of the earth—that is, in the tomb—for three days and three nights.

But it is asked why the Lord is said to have lain in the tomb three days and three nights when it is clear that he did not remain there for that many complete days and nights. He was crucified on Friday at the sixth hour; at the ninth hour he gave up his spirit; in the evening, after sunset, he was taken down from the cross and placed in the tomb. He lay there for only thirty-six hours.

Here, however, we must observe the rule of Scripture, by which the whole is frequently indicated through a part. Just as we reckon Friday together with the preceding night, so we reckon Sunday night together with the following day. According to this reckoning, the Lord is found to have remained three days and nights in the tomb.

We often find such an expression in Scripture and also in ordinary speech—for example, when we say that a woman carries a child for ten months, although it is clear that she bears it for only nine months, with the child emerging at the beginning of the tenth [Col. 0209A].

“But the men of Nineveh will rise in judgment with this generation and condemn it,” and so forth. When the men of Nineveh are said to rise in judgment with that generation, it is plainly established that both the good and the reprobate will rise equally in the judgment.

“And they will condemn it”—not by authority, but by comparison—because they repented at the preaching of Jonah.

“And behold, one greater than Jonah is here.” “Here” is neither a noun nor a pronoun, but rather an adverb of place. “Behold,” he says, “I am here among you, and I am greater than Jonah; therefore the Ninevites will exercise judgment against you.” Jonah preached to them for only three days, whereas I have been preaching among you for a much longer time. Jonah preached to a foreign people, namely the Assyrians, whereas I preach to the Jews, once the people of God. Jonah performed no miracle, whereas I have performed many signs among you.

“The Queen of the South will rise in judgment with this generation and condemn it.” The Queen of the South—that is, Sheba—who came from the ends of the earth to hear Solomon’s wisdom, condemned this generation, not by authority but by comparison.

She will rightly condemn the Jews’ savagery, since she herself came through many difficulties of land and sea to hear Solomon’s wisdom. But the Jews, although they had Christ present among them, refused to hear his teaching. In the faith of the Ninevites and of the Queen of Sheba, the faith of the Gentiles is preferred to that of the Israelite people.

“But when the unclean spirit has gone out from a person, it wanders through dry places, seeking rest, and does not find it.” This can be understood in two ways, but the saying properly concerns the Jews. Hence the Lord speaks in its conclusion: “So will it also be with this most evil generation.”

The unclean spirit went out from the Jews when, receiving the law of God at Mount Sinai, they said: “Whatever the Lord has said to us, we will do, and we will obey him” (Exod. 24). Once the evil spirit had gone out from the Jews, it wandered through dry places—that is, through the hearts of the Gentiles, untouched by any dew of heaven. But there it found no rest, because through the preaching of the apostles and the grace of baptism it was expelled from there.

[Col. 0209D] “Then he says: I will return to my house from which I came.” That is: “I will return to the Jews whom I previously left.”

“And coming, he finds it swept clean”—that is, through circumcision—“and empty”—that is, having ceased from good works—“and adorned” with the traditions of the scribes and Pharisees.

“Then he goes and takes with him seven other spirits more wicked than himself, and entering in, they dwell there”—that is, the fullness of demons and vices.

“And the last state of that person becomes worse than the first.” For the Jews who now blaspheme Christ in their synagogues are worse than the Gentiles once were when they worshiped idols in Egypt.

Yet we can also refer this saying to every sinner. The unclean spirit goes out from a person when that person is regenerated from water and the Holy Spirit. It “wanders through dry places,” namely through the hearts of believers, which are dry—that is, separated from every flow of desire. It seeks rest and does not find it because it encounters the warfare of the elect.

“Then he says: I will return to my house from which I came”—that is: “I will return to the one whom I left at the time of baptism.”

“And coming, he finds it swept clean”—that is, purified by baptism—“and empty”—that is, empty of good works—“and adorned” through hypocrisy, that is, through pretense.

“Then he goes and takes with him seven other spirits more wicked than himself, and entering in, they dwell there.” Just as the number seven is sacred in relation to Christ because of the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, which Isaiah recounts as resting upon the Lord, so this number is also consecrated to the devil because of the fullness of all vices.

There are seven principal vices; the eighth is pride, through which the devil himself fell. The first is γαστριμαργία (*gastrimargia*), which is interpreted as the desire of the belly, or gluttony; the second is fornication; the third is φιλαργυρία (*philargyria*), that is, greed or the love of riches; the fourth is anger; the fifth is sadness; the sixth is *acedia*, which is anxiety of mind or weariness; the seventh is κενοδοξία (*kenodoxia*), that is, vainglory and emptiness; the eighth is pride, which is the devil himself, who fell from heaven through pride.

“And the last state of that person becomes worse than the first.” For it would be better not to know the way of truth than to turn backward after having recognized it. It would have been better for Judas the betrayer not to follow Christ than to betray him after recognizing him. It would have been better for Simon not to be baptized than to perish after baptism in the snare of condemnation.

For although every person who serves vices is utterly wicked, the worst of the wicked is the one who, while serving all the vices, nevertheless pretends through hypocrisy to possess virtues.

“While he was still speaking to the crowds, behold, his mother and brothers were standing outside, seeking to speak with him.” The Lord was occupied with performing miracles and engaging the people in work and teaching. While he was preaching and rebuking the Jews, his mother and brothers stood outside.

“But someone said to him: Behold, your mother and your brothers.” It appears that the person who reported this to the Lord did not do so with a simple intention, but rather with the cunning of a tempter, to discover whether the Lord would place the preaching of the Gospel before familial affection or not.

But he understood that person’s thought and wickedness. He did not place affection before religious duty—he who praised the bodily relationship—but said:

“Who is my mother, and who are my brothers?” In saying this, he did not deny that blessed Mary was his mother. Rather, as we have said, he placed the divine word before bodily relationship. He could not deny his mother, since he commands us to love our parents, saying: “Honor your father and your mother” (Deut. 5; Matt. 15).

“And stretching out his hand toward his disciples, he said: ‘Behold, my mother and my brothers.’” [Col. 0211A]

We must not understand the Lord’s brothers, who are called so in the Gospel, as Joseph’s sons by another wife, as certain heretics suppose; for just as blessed Mary remained in virginity, so blessed Joseph was the guardian of perpetual virginity. Rather, the Lord’s brothers are understood to be the sons of Mary, his maternal aunt: James, John, and Jude.

Brothers are spoken of in four ways. First, by physical kinship, as Jacob and Esau; second, by kinship of the flesh, as Laban called Jacob his brother because he was his uncle. Thus Abraham says to Lot: “Let there be no quarrel, I beg you, between me and you, and between my shepherds and your shepherds, for we are brothers” (Gen. XIII). Lot was not Abraham’s brother, but rather his nephew.

Third, they are called brothers because of unity of nation, namely because they were born from the same people, as it says in Genesis: “If you choose a king over you, choose from among your brothers whomever you wish”—that is, from your own people. Fourth, they are called brothers through affection and devotion, as all who believe in Christ are called brothers.

The Lord’s brothers are called so in one of these ways: namely, by kinship of his flesh. While the Lord was spiritually preaching to the crowds, his mother and brothers stood outside; and now, while the Lord teaches the nations in the Church, his mother and brothers—that is, the Synagogue—stand outside, meaning that they remain alienated from the fellowship of the Church. Yet when they themselves enter the Lord’s house, they will not be rejected by him; rather, what the Lord said will be fulfilled in them: “Whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven, he is my brother, sister, and mother.” [Col. 0211C]

It must be asked, however, how anyone can become the Lord’s mother. Whoever does the Father’s will is his brother and sister. There is nothing surprising about both sexes being included, but he becomes the Lord’s mother who gives birth to the word of God in the hearts of his hearers. Every believer, so long as he is being instructed, is a son; but when he instructs others, he is a mother. The Apostle Paul showed maternal affection toward his hearers, saying: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you” (Gal. IV).

## HOMILY XXXII. THURSDAY AFTER INVOCAVIT

(JOHN VIII.) “At that time, Jesus was saying to those Jews who had believed in him: ‘If you remain in my word,’” and so forth.

He says “remain” because you have been initiated into spiritual teaching, because you have begun to exist in it. If you remain—that is, in the faith which has begun to exist in you who believe—observe where you will arrive; see what the beginning is and where it leads. You have loved the foundation; look toward the summit, and from this humility seek another height.

Faith has humility. Knowledge, immortality, and eternity do not have humility, but rather an uprightness arising from height: no falling away, but eternal stability; no assault by the enemy, no fear of failing. It is a great thing to begin from faith, but it is greater to arrive through faith. Listen, then, where it leads, and see how great faith is.

Thus he also said to the Jews: “If you remain in my word,” in which you have believed, “you will truly be my disciples.” He added: “And you will know the truth.” Whoever knows the truth knows God, because God is truth, as the Lord himself says: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John XIV).

Let us therefore believe so that we may know the truth, because no one can arrive at knowledge of the truth without faith. What is it that we shall know? That which “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man.” For what is faith except believing what you do not see? Faith, therefore, is believing what you do not see; truth is seeing what you have believed.

What is it that we are promised we shall see? The Lord says elsewhere what it is that we shall see, when he says: “Whoever loves me will be loved by my Father; and I will love him, and I will manifest myself to him” (ibid.). This is the promise; this is the reward of faith, which works through love; this is the satisfaction for which the Psalmist longed, saying: “I shall be satisfied when your glory is manifested” (Ps. XVI).

O Lord, make us worthy to love you and not to love the world, so that we may be able to reach that freedom which is attained through knowledge of the truth, concerning which you added: “And the truth will set you free.”

What does “it will set you free” mean? It makes you free. In the same way, “it saves” means nothing other than “it will make you safe.” We have therefore heard what the free truth said; let us hear what proud falsehood replies.

“The Jews therefore said: ‘We are Abraham’s seed, and we have never been slaves to anyone; how can you say: You will be free?’”

The Lord had not said, “You will be free,” but “The truth will set you free.” Yet they understood nothing else in that word than carnal freedom. They exalted themselves because they were Abraham’s seed and said: “We are Abraham’s seed, and we have never been slaves to anyone. How can you say: You will be free?”

O empty pride, O false boasting! How could you say truthfully, “We have never been slaves to anyone”? Was Joseph not sold? Were the holy prophets not led into captivity? Finally, was not that very people of his, which made bricks in Egypt under harsh labor, serving—not at least in silver and gold, but in mud?

If you have never served anyone, O ungrateful people, what is it that God continually reproaches you for? How did he free you from the house of slavery? Or perhaps your fathers served? But you who say, “We have never served anyone”—if you have never served anyone, how then did you pay tribute to the Romans?

You even set a snare of entrapment for Truth himself, asking, as it says (Luke XX): “Is it lawful to pay tribute to Caesar?” If he had said, “It is lawful,” you would have seized him as though he had wished to deprive Abraham’s seed of its freedom; but if he had said, “It is not lawful,” you would have accused him before the rulers of the earth of forbidding tribute to be paid to kings.

Then, when the coin was produced, you were defeated and forced to answer your own trap. For there you were told: “Give back to Caesar what belongs to Caesar, and to God what belongs to God” (Matt. XXII), after you yourselves had answered that the coin bears Caesar’s image.

For just as Caesar seeks his own image on the denarius, so God seeks his own image in a human being. God does not seek something alien from a human being, but what he himself established in the human being. Therefore God became human, so that in the human being he might restore what he had formed in the human being.

Let us therefore hear what the Lord answered the Jews, who were lying and swelling with vain claims of freedom.

[Col. 0213B] “Amen, amen, I say to you: everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin.”

Who would not tremble at these words, if every human being is a sinner and every human being is a slave of sin? But let us listen more attentively in these words to how we are freed from this slavery. He inspires terror, but applies a remedy. For the Lord says: “Amen, amen, I say to you.” What is “amen, amen” except “I tell you the truth”? Neither the Greek translator nor the Latin one dared to transfer this word into another language, so that it might retain the honor of a hidden veil: the testimony of truth in Christ.

Truth says, “Truly, truly, I say to you.” He repeats and reiterates the word of truth, so as to awaken the sleeping, make the hearers attentive, and prevent contempt for him who says: “Amen, amen, I say to you: everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin.” [Col. 0213C]

O miserable slavery—to serve sin, to serve the devil, who is the author of sin! Often people flee wicked masters so as not to serve evil, yet they do not flee sin. How much easier it would be to flee sin and serve a human being with a free conscience!

Moreover, a human being who is a slave to another is sometimes wearied by his master’s commands and finds rest by fleeing. But where will the slave of sin flee? The avenging conscience drags him along with it. Wherever he flees, he does not escape; rather, his evil conscience follows him—or rather, it does not depart from him, for the sin he committed is within him.

He committed sin in order to obtain some bodily pleasure. The pleasure passes, but the sin remains. What delighted him disappears, while what torments him remains: evil slavery. Sometimes people flee wicked masters and, by fleeing, find rest from slavery. But how will those be free from slavery who do not wish to be free from sins?

How much easier it is for a person to abandon sin and flee to Christ, the defender and author of true freedom! Only the Lord frees from this slavery to sin, because he did not have sin. He alone came into the world without sin; he alone can free from sin. He came without sin and became a sacrifice for sin.

Since, then, everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin, hear what hope we have of freedom.

“But the slave,” he says, “does not remain in the house forever.”

The Church is the house; the sinner is the slave. Let a person not remain in sin, lest he be a slave of sin, so that he may be able to remain in the house—that is, in the Church. Let him remain in the body of his head, so that he may be a son, not a slave. [Col. 0214A]

It is one thing to sin and another to remain in sin. Whoever remains in sin is a slave of sin; whoever flees from sin will be a slave of righteousness. Thus he inspired terror and gave hope: he inspired terror so that we would not love sin; he gave hope so that we would not despair of release from sin.

“Everyone,” he says, “who commits sin is a slave of sin. But the slave does not remain in the house forever.” What hope, then, do we have, since we are not of sin? Hear your hope:

“The Son remains in the house forever. Therefore, if the Son sets you free, you will truly be free.”

This is our hope, brothers: that we may be freed by the Free One, and that by freeing us he may make us his servants. We were slaves of desire; we become free servants of love. [Col. 0214B]

The first freedom is not to remain in sin, but to serve righteousness, as the Apostle says: “When you were slaves of sin, you were free with respect to righteousness” (Rom. VI). But now you have your fruit leading to sanctification, and its end is eternal life.

Perfect freedom, however, is to serve Christ God: to love him who truly freed us, who truly is the Son of God, and who is Lord in the form of a servant—not a servant, but Lord in the form of a servant. For that form of flesh was servile; although it was in the likeness of sinful flesh, it was not sinful flesh. He promised freedom to those who believed in him.

But the Jews, as though they were boasting of their own freedom, disdained becoming free, even though they were slaves of sin. They said they were free because they were Abraham’s seed. What did the Lord answer them? Let us hear.

[Col. 0214C] “I know,” he says, “that you are Abraham’s children, but you seek to kill me.”

I recognize the origin of your flesh, not the faith of your heart. You are Abraham’s children, but according to the flesh; therefore you seek to kill me.

“For my word,” he says, “does not find room in you”—that is, it has no place in you. If my word found room in you, it would surely make room for you. What does “it does not find room in you” mean? It means that it does not find room in your heart, because your heart does not receive it.

You have certainly heard the Lord saying: “I know that you are Abraham’s children.” Hear what he says afterward:

“I speak what I have seen with my Father; and you do what you have seen with your father.”

What do they do, and what did he say to them? You seek to kill me; they never saw this in Abraham.

He said: “What I have seen with my Father, I speak.” I saw truth; I speak truth, because I am truth. If the Lord speaks truth because he himself is the Father’s truth, which he saw with the Father, and says that he saw it, then he himself is the Word who was the Word with God.

Where, then, did they see with their father the evil they do, which the Lord rebukes and condemns? When we hear more clearly in what follows who their father is, then we shall understand what they saw with such a father.

For he has not yet named their father. A little earlier he mentioned Abraham, but he meant the origin of the flesh, not likeness of life. Now he is about to name another father of theirs, one who neither begot them nor created them as human beings, yet they were his children insofar as they were evil, not insofar as they were human; insofar as they imitated him, not insofar as they were created.

[Col. 0215A] “They answered and said to him: ‘Our father is Abraham.’”

As though he were about to say something against Abraham, or as though he would dare to criticize Abraham in any respect. It was not that the Lord did not dare to criticize Abraham, but that Abraham was such a man that the Lord would not criticize him, but rather praise him.

Yet they seemed to be provoking him to say something evil about Abraham, so that they might have an opportunity to do what they were planning. “Our father is Abraham.”

Let us hear how the Lord answers them: while condemning them, he praised Abraham.

[Col. 0215B] “Jesus says to them: ‘If you are Abraham’s children, do the works of Abraham. But now you seek to kill me, a man who has spoken to you the truth that I heard from God; Abraham did not do this.’”

There he is praised; they are condemned. They sought to kill the Lord, but Abraham was not a murderer.

“I do not say,” he says, “that I am the Lord of Abraham”—and if I said this, I would speak the truth, for elsewhere he said: “Before Abraham was, I am,” when they wished to stone him. But for the moment I say only what you see, what you behold, what you think I alone am: namely, that I am a human being.

Why, then, do you wish to kill a human being who tells you what he heard from God, unless you are not Abraham’s children? And yet earlier he said: “I know that you are Abraham’s children.” He does not now deny their origin, but condemns their deeds. Their flesh was from him, but their life was not.

Thus Christians have become Abraham’s seed by the grace of God, not from Abraham’s flesh. They were made coheirs; God disinherited those others and adopted these. They are the ones of whom John the Baptist said elsewhere: “God is able to raise up children for Abraham from these stones” (Luke III).

Those, therefore, will be Abraham’s children who imitate Abraham’s works. For this reason the Lord added: “If you are Abraham’s children, do the works of Abraham.” Prove your nobility by deeds, not by words.

“But you seek to kill me, a man who has spoken to you the truth that I heard from God; Abraham did not do this. You do the works of your father.”

Since he still does not say who their father is, let us see what they answered him. They began, in some fashion, to understand that the Lord was not speaking about descent from the flesh, but about the formation of one’s life.

Because it is the custom of Scripture—which they read—to call idolatry “fornication” spiritually, when the soul, like a prostitute, is subjected to mute and false gods, they answered accordingly:

[Col. 0215D] “We were not born of fornication; we have one Father, God.”

Since they had so often boasted of Abraham and been rejected, let us now see how they refused to be rejected by the truthful mouth. Abraham’s conduct was such that they did not imitate it, yet they boasted of being descended from him. So they changed their answer, I suppose saying to themselves:

“Whenever we mention Abraham, he will say to us: ‘Why do you not imitate him, whose lineage you boast of?’ We cannot imitate that holy, just, and wholly innocent man. Let us call God our Father and see what he will say to us.”

Did falsehood find something it could say? Let us hear what they say, and hear what they hear.

“We have one Father,” they say, “God.”

[Col. 0216A] “Jesus therefore said: ‘If God were your Father, you would certainly love me, for I proceeded from God and came. For I did not come of myself, but he sent me.’”

You call God Father; at least recognize your brother. Here he touched upon what he often says: “I did not come of myself, but he sent me; for I proceeded from God and came.”

Christ’s mission, therefore, is his incarnation. But the Word’s proceeding from God the Father is an eternal procession, without time, through whom time was made. Thus he proceeded from him as God and equal, as the only Son, as the Father’s Word.

He came to us “because the Word became flesh, so that he might dwell among us” (John I). His coming is his humanity; his dwelling is his divinity.

“Why,” he says, “do you not understand my speech? Because you cannot understand my word.”

They could not understand because they could not hear. But why could they not hear, unless because they were unwilling to be corrected by believing? And this is why:

[Col. 0216B] “You are of your father the devil.”

As long as you mention fathers, as long as you change fathers—now Abraham, now God—hear from the Son of God whose children you are: “You are of your father the devil.”

God, the creator of all creatures, certainly created the human being. How, then, does he say here: “You are of your father the devil”? Whatever has been created by God is good; and every human being, insofar as he is God’s creature, is good. But insofar as he subjects himself through free choice to the devil, he is of the devil as father.

Human nature is good, but it was corrupted through evil will; and in that respect he was of the devil as father. What God made cannot be evil, unless the human being makes himself evil.

The Jews, therefore, were called children of the devil not by being born, but by imitation. It is also the custom of sacred Scripture often to call people children on the basis of imitation or habitual conduct. Thus the Prophet says to the Jews: “Your father was an Amorite and your mother a Hittite” (Ezek. XXIX).

The Amorites were a nation from which the Jews did not derive their origin. The Hittites likewise had their own nation, entirely unrelated to the Jewish people. But because the Amorites and Hittites were impious, and the Jews imitated their impieties, they found parents who were not those from whom they were born, but whose ways they followed and with whom they were likewise condemned.

It may perhaps be asked where the devil himself came from. From the same place as the other angels, certainly. But the others remained in their obedience; he fell through disobedience and pride as an angel, and became the devil.

But now hear what the Lord says: “You,” he says, “are of your father the devil, and you wish to carry out the desires of your father. You seek to kill me, a man who tells you the truth.” He envied the human being and killed the human being.

When the devil envied the human being, he clothed himself in a serpent, spoke to the woman, and through the woman poisoned the man. Thus they died by listening to the devil, whom they would not have listened to if they had wished to listen to God. They ought to have obeyed the Creator, not the deceiver.

[Col. 0217A] “He was a murderer from the beginning.”

Observe the kind of being he is: the devil is called a murderer. The devil did not come to the human being armed with a sword or girded with iron; he sowed an evil word and killed.

Do not therefore think that you are not a murderer when you persuade your brother to do evil. If you persuade your brother to do evil, you kill. Hear the Psalm: “The sons of men: their teeth are weapons and arrows, and their tongue a sharp sword” (Ps. LVI).

You wish, then, to carry out the desires of your father; therefore you rage against the flesh, because you cannot rage against the mind.

“He was a murderer from the beginning”—certainly in the first human being; from that moment he was a murderer. From when could murder occur? From when the human being was made. A human being could not be killed unless the human being had first been made.

“And he did not stand in the truth, because truth is not in him.”

Not in the way truth is in Christ, so that he himself is truth, God. If he had stood in the truth, he would have remained in the holiness of his origin. But he did not stand in the truth, because truth is not in him.

“When he speaks falsehood, he speaks from his own resources, because he is a liar and its father.”

The devil was a liar from himself, and he himself generated his falsehood; he had heard falsehood from no one before him. Just as the Father begot the Son, who is truth, so the devil generated falsehood as though it were a son. He generated falsehood because he did not stand in truth.

For everyone who remains in God remains in truth, because God is truth. But whoever departs from God will be a liar, as the Psalmist says: “Every human being is a liar” (Ps. CXV).

Insofar as a human being departs from God, he is a liar; insofar as he turns away from the truth, he is a sinner. For every sin is not truth but falsehood, because by departing from God it does not possess truth.

The devil was created good, but became evil through himself, turning away from the highest good. Therefore he spoke falsehood from his own resources, because he found within himself the source of his being a liar.

The human being, deceived by the devil, became a liar and therefore a child of the devil—not by nature, but by imitation.

Let us therefore depart from the father of falsehood and run to the Father of truth. Let us embrace truth, so that we may receive true freedom.

The Jews had seen in their father what they were saying—but what was it except falsehood? The Lord, however, had seen with his Father what he should speak—but what was it except the eternal Word of the Father, coeternal with the Father?

Therefore he added:

[Col. 0217D] “I speak the truth to you, and you do not believe me.”

A liar speaks falsehood, but truth brings forth truth. The devil is a liar, but Christ is truth and the defender of truth; for from the mouth of truth nothing other than truth can proceed.

## HOMILY XXXIII. FRIDAY AFTER INVOCAVIT

(JOHN V.) “At that time, it was a feast day of the Jews, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem. Now there is at Jerusalem a pool called the Sheep Pool, and so forth.”

We were speaking to you also now about the Gospel reading, in which two miracles of human healing are read: one invisibly accomplished through angelic administration, the other visibly exhibited through the Lord’s presence. But the mysteries of both have been explained briefly, lest an extensive explanation of the lengthy reading prove burdensome to anyone.

The Sheep Pool, which was surrounded by five porticoes, is the Jewish people, fortified on every side by the guardianship of the Law so that they ought not to sin. For rightly the Law, which was written in the five books of Moses, is represented by the number five.

Rightly the people who used sometimes to serve certain purifications of life and at other times to be troubled by the covenants of unclean spirits are signified by the water of the pool, which was accustomed sometimes to remain calm in the wind and at other times to be disturbed when the winds rushed upon it.

And rightly that pool is called “probatica,” for τὰ πρόβατα in Greek means “sheep.” There were indeed among that people those who knew how to say to the Lord: “But we are your people and the sheep of your flock; we shall give thanks to you forever” (Ps. LXXVIII).

In common usage, however, the pool is said to have been called probatica—that is, “the animal pool”—because the priests used to wash victims in it.

The multitude of sick people lying in the aforementioned porticoes, awaiting the movement of the water, signifies the crowds of those who, hearing the words of the Law, grieved that they could not fulfill it by their own strength; and therefore, with longing, they sought the help of the Lord’s grace.

They were blind because they did not yet possess the perfect light of faith; they were lame because they could not fulfill through the steps of their actions the good things they knew; they were withered because, although they possessed whatever eye of knowledge they had, they lacked the richness of hope and love.

Such people lay in the five porticoes, but they were healed only when the angel came into the pool. For through the Law came knowledge of sin, but the grace of forgiveness came only through Jesus Christ.

The angel signifies him: descending invisibly into the pool, he moved the water to announce its healing power. The angel of great counsel descended clothed in flesh—that is, the messenger of the Father’s will—into the pool of the Jewish people, and stirred sinners who had been made so by his teaching, so that he might be killed. Through his bodily death he was sufficient not only to heal those spiritually sick, but also to raise the dead.

The movement of the water therefore indicates the Passion, which occurred when the Jewish people were stirred up and thrown into turmoil. And because believers were redeemed through it from the curse of the Law, those who had until then lain sick in the porticoes were healed as though they were descending into the disturbed water of the pool.

For the letter of the Law taught them what ought to be done and what ought to be avoided. Yet it neither retained those brought out from their former seats of ignorance within its porticoes nor healed the sick.

The grace of the Gospel, however, which through God and the mystery of the Lord’s Passion heals all the diseases of our sins—sins from which we could not be justified by the Law of Moses—sends the chosen sick from the porticoes of the Law into the turbid water of the pool so that we may be healed.

For through the water of baptism it washes away the sins which the Law had revealed. The Apostle bears witness, saying: “For all of us who were baptized in Christ Jesus were baptized into his death. We were buried with him through baptism into death, so that, just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too might walk in newness of life” (Rom. VI). [Col. 0219A]

It is rightly said that whoever first descended after the movement of the water was healed of whatever disease held him, because there is one Lord, one faith, one baptism. Whoever is instructed in the mysteries of Christ within Catholic unity is healed, whatever sickness of sins holds him.

But whoever separates himself from unity cannot attain the salvation that comes from the One.

We have spoken about the first miracle of the Gospel reading, which the Lord performed. Now let us speak to your fraternity about the second, which he himself performed; in it also one person is presented as healed.

This is not because the almighty mercy of the Savior could not have healed all whom it found lying sick there, but so that he might teach that, apart from the unity of Catholic faith, no place of salvation is open to anyone.

“Now there was a certain man,” he says, “who had been in his illness for thirty-eight years.”

This man, held by illness for so many years, signifies any sinner weighed down by the immense magnitude or multitude of his crimes; even the length of time during which he suffered corresponds to the guilt he signifies.

For he had been ill for two years short of forty. The number forty, which is produced by multiplying ten four times, is customarily understood in Scripture as representing the perfection of right conduct, because whoever performs the duty of perfect conduct fulfills the Decalogue of the Law through the four books of the holy Gospel.

The one who is two short of that perfection is plainly deficient in the love of God and neighbor, which the Scriptures of both Law and Gospel commend.

The Lord also taught this mystically when he healed the sick man, saying:

“Rise, take up your pallet, and walk.”

To rise means to shake off the sluggishness of the vices in which you have long languished and to raise yourself for the practice of the virtues by which you may be saved forever.

“Take up your pallet”—that is, carry it. Love your neighbor by patiently bearing his weaknesses, since he patiently and for a long time supported you while you were still weighed down by the burden of temptations.

“For bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ” (Gal. VI). And as he says elsewhere: “Bearing with one another in love, eager to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Eph. VI).

“Walk,” then: love God with your whole heart, whole soul, and whole strength. And so that you may deserve to reach the vision of him, advance each day by the steps of good works from virtue to virtue.

Do not abandon the brother whom you carry by bearing with him, because of love for the one toward whom you are journeying; nor, because of love for your brother, turn away from the course of right walking while seeking to remain with the one with whom you desire to dwell.

Rather, so that you may be perfectly saved: “Rise, take up your pallet, and walk”—that is, leave your former sins and come to the aid of your brothers’ needs.

In everything you do, take care not to fix your mind in this world, but hasten to behold the face of your Redeemer.

Rise by doing good; carry your pallet by loving your neighbor; and walk by awaiting the blessed hope and the coming of the glory of the great God.

But what astonishing madness possessed the faithless! They ought to have believed and been spiritually healed at the unexpected healing of a man who had long been ill. Instead, they were scandalized and directed accusations both against the one who had been healed and against the Savior.

Against the healed man, because he had carried his pallet on the Sabbath; against the Savior, because on the Sabbath he had commanded both that the man be saved and that he carry his pallet—as though they themselves knew more about the Sabbath than such great divine power.

[Col. 0220A] “The Jews,” he says, “were saying to the man who had been healed: ‘It is the Sabbath; it is not lawful for you to carry your pallet.’”

They foolishly defended the letter of the Law, failing to understand the dispensation of the one who had once distinguished the Law’s decrees through a servant and who, now coming himself, had determined to transform that same Law through grace, so that what carnal people had long observed carnally according to the letter, they might thereafter recognize as spiritually observed.

On the carnal Sabbath, which was kept according to the letter, the people were commanded to rest from every servile work on the seventh day.

The spiritual Sabbath is that, in the light of spiritual grace—which is understood as sevenfold—we remain free from the unrest of vices not on one day only, but every day.

For if, according to the Lord’s word, “everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin” (John VIII), it is plainly evident that sins are rightly understood as servile works. From these we are commanded to walk free, as though on the seventh day, through the reception of spiritual grace—not merely refraining from evil, but also devoting ourselves to good deeds.

The Lord showed this figuratively in this reading as well, when he commanded the man who had been ill for two years short of forty not only to rise on the Sabbath, but also to take up his pallet and walk.

He thereby indicated that those who waste away through the long sickness of vices and are empty of love of God and neighbor—being two short, as it were, of the perfect sum of virtues—can now rise from vices through the gift of the Holy Spirit. Once their sluggishness has been shaken off, they ought to hasten with the fervor of fraternal love toward the vision of their Creator.

The fact that the man who was healed recognizes Jesus not while he is still in the crowd, but afterward in the temple, teaches us mystically that, if we truly desire to recognize the grace of our Creator, to be strengthened by his love, and to reach his vision, we must carefully flee the crowd—not only of thoughts that disturb us and of evil affections, but also of wicked people who can obstruct the purpose of our sincerity, whether by showing evil through their example, mocking our good works, or forbidding them.

Let us diligently take refuge in the house of prayer, where, calling upon the Lord with private freedom, we may give thanks for the benefits received from him and pray with humble devotion for those yet to be received.

Indeed, let us take care to become the holy temple of God himself, in which he may deign to come and make his dwelling, hearing the Apostle say: “Your bodies are temples of the Holy Spirit, who is in you” (II Cor. VI).

Among these matters, my brothers, we must look more carefully at the fact that, finding in the temple the man whom the Lord had healed, he said to him: [Col. 0221A]

“Behold, you have been made well; now do not sin any more, lest something worse happen to you.” By these words it is clearly shown that he was languishing on account of sins, and that he could not be healed except after those sins had been forgiven. But the one who healed him outwardly from infirmity also saved him inwardly from crime. Therefore he prudently warned him beforehand, lest by sinning again he bring upon himself a sentence of condemnation more severe.

This should not, however, be understood as though everyone who falls ill becomes ill on account of sins. A person is often afflicted so that he may not grow proud in God’s gifts, as is read concerning the Apostle Paul (II Cor. XII); often he is troubled so that he may be tested, just as blessed Job’s patience was troubled and tested (Job I, II); often illness is given as chastisement. For God scourges every son whom he receives (Heb. XII). [Col. 0221B] To some, however, illness is given for the glory of God, as is read concerning the man born blind and concerning Lazarus (John IX, XI): the Lord knows for whose sake he commands anyone to be ill, or permits it.

He often acts in human beings by a hidden judgment, but never by an unjust one. Let us learn humbly to submit to the scourge of our most merciful Redeemer, judging that we suffer less than we deserve, always mindful of that saying: “Blessed is the person who is corrected by the Lord” (Prov. III). And he himself says in the Apocalypse: “I rebuke, reprimand, and chastise those whom I love” (Apoc. III).

But when the long-ailing sick man had been healed inwardly and outwardly—that is, raised up both from the scourge of chastisement and from the sins by which he had deserved it—the Jews, sick inwardly in the opposite way, now began to suffer a worse illness, namely by persecuting Jesus because he was doing these things on the Sabbath. [Col. 0221C] They persecuted him, not as though they were following the authority of the Law together with the examples of divine action. For the Lord completed the creation of the world in six days and rested from all his works on the seventh; and he commanded the people to work for six days and rest on the seventh. They did not understand that the carnal decrees of the Law were gradually to be changed by spiritual interpretation, when he appeared who is not only the Lawgiver but also the end of the Law, Christ, for righteousness to everyone who believes (Rom. X).

Nor did they observe that on the seventh day the Creator ceased not from the work of governing the world and the soul, nor from the daily renewal of created things, but from the institution of new creatures. When it is said (Gen. II) that God rested on the seventh day from all his works, this is therefore to be understood as meaning that God ceased from creating new creatures. [Col. 0221D]

## HOMILY XXXIV. ON THE SATURDAY AFTER INVOCAVIT

(Matt. XVII.) “At that time: Jesus took Peter, and James, and John his brother,” and the rest.

The Lord Jesus Christ, through the preaching and teaching of the Gospel, imposed upon the faithful not only the labors of the present life but also promised future blessedness. Therefore, after he had said above (John XII), “Whoever loves his life will lose it,” and so forth, “Whoever hates his life in this world preserves it for eternal life,” lest the harsh and difficult persecution of martyrdom [Col. 0222A] seem unbearable, he offered the example of his own passion and resurrection, saying that he would suffer many things in Jerusalem and rise again on the third day.

But lest the unheard-of glory of the resurrection seem incredible, he took three chosen disciples aside and showed them the form of that same resurrection in his transfiguration. And beautifully, because he was about to show his disciples the form of that same resurrection, he led them apart, since, if we desire to share in that resurrection, we must be separated from the crowds of evil spirits and the disturbances of the world—always in mind, and sometimes also in body. For just as the company of the good greatly helps, so the fellowship of the wicked frequently harms weakened minds, as the Psalmist testifies when he says: “With the holy man you will be holy, and with the innocent man you will be innocent; with the chosen man you will be chosen, and with the perverse man you will become perverse” (Ps. XVII).

Therefore Solomon admonishes us, saying: “Do not be a friend to an angry man, nor walk with a furious man, lest perhaps you learn his ways and take offense against your soul” (Prov. XXII).

He also fittingly led those whose heart he showed to have been glorified up onto a high mountain, to teach us that we shall then deserve happily to attain the glory of the future resurrection if, abandoning earthly things, we desire what is lofty and heavenly, saying with the Apostle: “But our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. III). Hence also we await the Savior, our Lord Jesus Christ.

We ascend the mountain with the Lord when, despising the fleeting joys of the world, we desire the heavenly homeland, as the Psalmist did when he said: “As the deer longs for the springs of waters, so my soul longs for you, O God” (Ps. XLI).

Nor should we pass over without consideration the fact that he is said to have shown his resurrection to the disciples after six days and after the events narrated above. Since there are six days in which it is permitted to work, the number six often signifies the labor of the present life. And as though after six days he showed his splendor to the disciples, so the elect, after the labors of the present life, are to attain the glory of the future resurrection. For, as the Apostle says: “If we suffer with him, we shall also reign with him” (Rom. VIII); and: “If we share in his sufferings, we shall also share in his resurrection” (II Cor. I).

What is said, then:

“And his face shone like the sun; but his garments became white like snow.” [Col. 0222D]

The form of that same resurrection is demonstrated. Since, according to his promise, “the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Matt. XIII), he showed in himself what is destined to occur in his members. Can the brightness of the sun be compared with the Lord, or with the saints concerning whom the Apostle says: “Star differs from star in brightness; so also is the resurrection of the dead” (I Cor. XV)?

But because nothing more brilliant than the sun appears among visible things, the splendor of the future life was signified by the sun’s brightness. In that life, as Daniel says: “Those who are learned will shine like the splendor of the firmament, and those who instruct many in righteousness like stars for everlasting eternities” (Dan. XII).

And since, as we have said, we know of nothing brighter than the sun, the glory at the resurrection not only of the Lord but also of the saints is compared with the sight of the sun, because he could find nothing clearer than the sun by which to provide human beings with an example.

No one should suppose that the glorified majesty of the Lord’s body, or the glory of the saints’ bodies, will be seen in the judgment by the reprobate. They will see only him whom they pierced, and all the tribes of the earth will mourn over him. But when the wicked have been removed after the judgment, so that they may not see the glory of God, the righteous will enter perpetually to contemplate the glory of his kingdom, themselves also transformed according to their measure into the glory of incorruption.

Therefore the Apostle says: “He will reform the body of our lowliness, conforming it to the body of his glory” (Phil. [Col. 0223B] III).

By the Lord’s garments, which became white like snow, the Church is signified. According to the Apostle, he chose her (Eph. V) without stain or wrinkle, so that she might be clean and immaculate in his sight, as it is said through John in the Apocalypse: “I saw the holy city, the new Jerusalem, descending from heaven, prepared like a bride adorned for her husband” (Apoc. XXI).

For just as a garment is woven from many threads, so the Church is adorned with many virtues, according to Isaiah’s saying: “As I live, says the Lord, you will be clothed with all these things as with an ornament” (Isa. XLIX). And the Apostle says: “For as many of you as were baptized in Christ have put on Christ” (Gal. III).

That is, at the time of the resurrection they are cleansed from every stain of iniquity and likewise from every darkness of mortality. [Col. 0223C] The Lord’s garments became white like snow because in the future life the Church will attain the glory “which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart.” David longed to reach this glory when he said: “You will wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow” (Ps. L).

Therefore it is fittingly said of these same garments by another evangelist, namely Mark: “They became exceedingly white, like snow, such as no fuller on earth can make them” (Mark IX). For no teacher or preacher, however spiritual, is able in the present life to disclose in words how great the future glory of the saints will be.

But lest any doubt remain in the hearts of the apostles, suitable witnesses are brought forward after the transfiguration of the Lord’s body. Hence it follows:

[Col. 0223D] “Behold, Moses and Elijah appeared with him, speaking.”

The other evangelist, namely Luke, more clearly explains in what form they appeared and what they spoke with him, saying: “And behold, Moses and Elijah were seen speaking with him, splendid in majesty, proclaiming his departure at Jerusalem” (Luke IX).

By Moses and Elijah we understand the declarations of both the Law and the Prophets, who proclaimed his departure at Jerusalem, because the Law and the Prophets foretold that the Lord would suffer and rise again. Alternatively, through Moses and Elijah we can understand both Testaments, namely the Old and the New.

With one voice, then, Moses and Elijah foretold the Lord’s departure, because the faithful of both Testaments perceive the Lord’s coming with a concordant faith: what the former foretold as future, the latter announces as already accomplished.

In yet another way, through Moses, who had not yet paid the debt of death, we can understand two orders of saints: those who preceded the Lord’s final coming by dying, and those who will be found alive in the flesh at the time of judgment. They are therefore fittingly said to have appeared with him in glory, because both those who have been raised and those who have been changed will be caught up in the clouds to meet Christ in the air (I Thess. IV), and so will always be with the Lord.

Then the Lord’s promise will be fulfilled: “Father, grant that just as you and I are one, so they also may be one in us” (John XVII)—not by equality, but by participation in glory.

But how greatly the Apostle Peter delighted in the splendor of this vision, he showed when he answered Jesus:

[Col. 0224B] “Lord, it is good for us to be here.”

Here he showed that the highest and principal good in the future life is to be with the Lord, not in the present world, which is wholly placed in evil and where, in the words of the Apostle Paul, the days are evil. He had perceived this good, and it is good to cling to God.

That he did not wish to depart from this vision, he showed when he added: “If you wish, let us make three tents here: one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah.”

He said this, as another evangelist reports, not knowing what he was saying, because when human nature is led beyond the measure of its weakness, it sometimes does not even recognize its own ignorance. He did not know what he was saying when he judged that temporal tents were necessary in that eternal glory. For there the construction of a material tent is not necessary, where the highest good is the perfect vision of the Lord, as it is said through John concerning the heavenly city of Jerusalem: “I saw no temple in it, for the Lord God Almighty is its temple, and the Lamb” (Apoc. XXI).

The nature of its future construction the Psalmist declares when he says: “Jerusalem, which is built as a city, whose fellowship is in unity” (Ps. CXXI). And the Lord says in the Gospel: “In my Father’s house there are many dwelling places” (John XIV).

One and the same matter must also be carefully considered: according to the Psalmist’s saying, “The wicked man does not dwell with him, nor will the unjust remain before his eyes” (Ps. V). Therefore, asking the Lord in this way, let us say with the Prophet: “Lord, who will dwell in your tent? Or who will rest upon your holy mountain?” (Ps. XIV.) Let us show ourselves to be those of whom it follows: “The one who walks without blemish and practices righteousness” (Ps. XIV), and the rest that follows.

But while Peter was thinking about visible construction of tents:

[Col. 0224D] “While he was still speaking, behold, a bright cloud overshadowed them.”

They were to understand that, once the elect had been received into eternal tents, bodily tents would not be necessary; there, sheltered by the overshadowing cloud, they would be protected from the assembly of the wicked and from the multitude of those who work iniquity. Then what is said elsewhere through the Psalmist would be fulfilled: “You will hide them in the hiding place of your face from the disturbance of men; you will protect them in your tent from the contradiction of tongues” (Ps. XXX).

For if he protected and illuminated the people walking through the wilderness for forty years by the shade of a column, much more will he make the elect, received into his life, secure and likewise defended without the construction of tents.

But to instruct the minds of the apostles concerning the divinity of the only-begotten Son of God, after the testimony of Moses and Elijah, the Father’s voice bore witness from the cloud, saying: “This is my beloved Son.” That is: the one whom you see as a human being in human form is my beloved Son.

It is as though he were saying: “This is my Son, not adopted but proper; not created from elsewhere but begotten from me; with me he has one power, one [Col. 0225B] substance, and one eternity.”

Concerning him it follows: “In whom I am well pleased.” For human nature displeased God when, by sinning, it became a transgressor of his commandment, as he himself said to Noah: “My spirit will not remain in man forever, because he is flesh. I repent that I have made them” (Gen. VI).

But in the sole Mediator between God and human beings he says that he was well pleased, because he did not have in his humanity the sin that would stain his divinity: “For he committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth.”

For what the Father’s voice says concerning the Son, “In whom I am well pleased,” is the same as what the Son testifies elsewhere, saying: “And the one who sent me is with me, and he has not left me alone, because I always do what pleases him” (John VIII).

It is also fittingly said of him by the Father’s voice: [Col. 0225C] “Listen to him,” so that we might understand him to be the one of whom it had been prophesied through Moses (Deut. XVIII): “The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers like me; you shall listen to him, according to everything he speaks to you. And whoever does not listen to that prophet shall be destroyed from among the people.”

Blessed, then, were the apostles, who deserved not only to see the Lord’s glory but also to hear the Father’s voice thunder. Nor shall we be wholly strangers to this blessedness if we believe in the one whom they believed; if, imitating how they lived, we live likewise; and if we love with all our innermost being the one whom they loved.

But because human weakness cannot bear the weight of divinity, it is rightly added:

[Col. 0225D] “And when the disciples heard this, they fell upon their faces and were very much afraid.”

But the compassionate teacher kindly consoles and raises those whom human weakness weighed down, both by word and by touch. Hence it follows:

“And Jesus approached and touched them, saying: Rise, and do not be afraid.”
