By touching them, therefore, he drives away fear and grants confidence, because his touch is the healing of the whole world. And since, according to his saying, “Everyone who humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke XVIII), they are commanded to rise after their fall, because after the labors of the present life the elect are to be raised up to glory, according to the Psalmist’s saying: “Rise after you have sat” (Ps. CXXVI).

“But when they lifted up their eyes, they saw no one except Jesus alone.”

They were to understand that Moses [Col. 0226A] and Elijah had appeared for this purpose: to bear witness to the Lord’s glorification.

But when they were coming down from the mountain, Jesus commanded them, saying:

“Tell no one of the vision until the Son of Man has risen from the dead.”

He indicates the time of the future preaching. For he knew that the apostles’ minds were too weak to bear witness to so great a vision until they had been more fully instructed by the grace of the Holy Spirit and more perfectly strengthened. He also knew that carnal minds would not believe these things unless they were first moved to faith by his visible resurrection.

Therefore he did not forbid the vision to be spoken of altogether, but forbade them to speak of it before the resurrection, showing the appointed time of preaching—when it would no longer seem incredible, since it was also displayed visibly through the state of the resurrection.

## HOMILY XXXV. THE SECOND SUNDAY IN LENT

(Matt. XV.) “At that time: Jesus went out from there—[from] Gennesaret—and withdrew into the region of Tyre and Sidon. And behold, a Canaanite woman came out from that region, crying out and saying: Have mercy on me, Lord, Son of David,” and the rest.

The Gospel reading above relates how the Lord had a dispute with the Pharisees and Scribes. Since they did not believe but even blasphemed, he departed from there and withdrew into the region of Tyre and Sidon.

Tyre and Sidon were cities of the Gentiles, which had been assigned by lot to the Jewish people, [Col. 0226C] but were not possessed by them, because their inhabitants had not believed. Situated in the heart of the sea, they were not easily captured by enemies.

Hiram, a most powerful king, lived there; he supplied Solomon with timber and stones for building the house of the Lord (III Kings V). Against Tyre the prophet Ezekiel spoke at length (Ezek. XXVII), saying that it was situated in the heart of the sea, rich in wealth but full of vices, and prophesying that King Nebuchadnezzar would come for its destruction.

Tyre is said to derive its name from the location or character of the place, because *Tyria*—that is, the most precious purple—is found there. Fish are also found there, called shellfish, which, when cut with iron, release drops like blood; silk is dyed with these, and from it a more precious purple is woven.

In our language Tyre is interpreted as “the lot of God.” It signifies the human race, which before the transgression of the first man was in God’s lot, but departed from that lot when the first man sinned.

The Lord approached the boundaries of Tyre when he came into the world for the redemption of the human race, in order to call the human race itself back from the devil’s lot to his own lot, fulfilling the prophecy that says (Hos. I, II; Rom. IX; I Pet. II): “I will call ‘Not my people,’ ‘My people’; and ‘Not having obtained mercy,’ ‘Having obtained mercy.’ And it shall be: In the place where it was said to them, ‘You are not my people,’ there they shall be called sons of God.”

And again: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance” (Ps. II). And: “The nations that have not sought you will run to you.” [Col. 0227A]

Sidon is likewise said to derive its name from the location or character of the place, because a great number of fish are caught there. For the Phoenicians call fish *sidon*. An abundance of the most precious glass is also said to be found there.

In our language Sidon is interpreted as “useless hunting.” It too signifies the human race, which before the Lord’s incarnation was uselessly hunted by the devil. For just as a hunter pursues a beast with the most savage dogs, desiring to tear its flesh apart, so the devil pursued the human race before the incarnation, in order to drag its soul into the destruction of death.

But the Lord approached the boundaries of Sidon so that he might draw the human race from the devil’s useless hunting into useful hunting—through those hunters of whom it is said through the Prophet: “I will send my fishermen, and they will fish for them; and hunters, and they will hunt them from every mountain and every hill” (Jer. XVIII).

When the Lord, therefore, leaving the Scribes and Pharisees, withdrew to the region of Tyre and Sidon, by the very position of his body he showed that the Jews were to be abandoned because of their faithlessness and that the Gentiles were to be called to the faith, according to what he said elsewhere to the unbelieving Jews: “The kingdom of God will be taken from you and given to a nation producing its fruits” (Matt. XXI).

This is immediately made manifest when it follows: “And behold, a Canaanite woman came out from that region.”

The Canaanite woman was a Gentile woman, born from the stock of Ham, who had deserved a curse. Another evangelist (Mark VII) calls her a Syrophoenician. She cries out after the Lord, [Col. 0227C] because he had not come to call the righteous but sinners to repentance (Mark II).

Allegorically, however, this Canaanite woman represents the Church gathered from the Gentiles. The Church is also compared with a woman, not because of softness, but because of the union with a husband and the fruitfulness of offspring. Before the Lord’s coming she remained barren and sterile; but when the Lord came, the Church was joined to him and began to bear spiritual children, fulfilling the prophecy that says: “Rejoice, barren woman who do not give birth” (Isa. LIV).

This is the woman of whom Solomon says: “Who will find a strong woman? Her price is from far away and from the remotest boundaries” (Prov. XXXI). Concerning her also the Lord speaks figuratively in the Gospel: “The kingdom of heaven is like leaven, which a woman took and hid in three measures of flour, until the whole was leavened” (Matt. XIII). And again: “When a woman gives birth, she has sorrow, because her hour has come” (John XVI).

This woman spiritually gives birth to as many children every day as she regenerates believers through the water of baptism and the grace of the Holy Spirit.

It should be noted that the woman is first said to have come out from her own region and then to have cried out after the Lord, because unless the Church had first anathematized her former errors, she could not have attained knowledge of God.

For necessary order demands that the one who desires to receive virtues first renounce vices and crimes, as the Psalmist says: “Who is the man who desires life and wishes to see good days? Let him restrain his tongue from evil, and his lips from speaking deceit. Let him turn away from evil and do good; let him seek peace and pursue it” (Ps. XXXIII).

But let us hear what she cries: “Have mercy on me, Lord, Son of David.”

In these words she embraces the Catholic faith, briefly indeed but completely. For she believed him to be God in such a way that she did not deny him to be human; she confessed him to be human in such a way that she believed him to be the same true God.

She believed him to be true God when she said, “Have mercy on me.” She confessed him to be true man when she added, “Son of David.” She calls him Son of David because our Savior assumed flesh from David’s stock, as the Apostle says: “Who was made for him from the seed of David according to the flesh” (Rom. I). And the Prophet says: “Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and I will raise up for David a righteous shoot; and he will reign as king and will be wise” (Jer. XXIII).

When the mother pleaded with the Lord for her daughter, saying, “My daughter is grievously tormented by a demon,” she showed that those who first believed from among the Gentiles poured out prayers to the Lord for the liberation of those who were still held in error.

As we said above, the mother signifies the Church, while her daughter prefigures each sinful soul. The daughter is grievously tormented by a demon when, in the entirety of her body, she is subject to vices and crimes such as adultery, theft, murder, robbery, sacrilege, and the like.

The mother therefore prayed for her daughter because the Church watches anxiously over the correction of those who are subject to sins and vices: sometimes by persuading, sometimes by exhorting, sometimes by rebuking her more sharply, and sometimes by offering the assistance of prayer. [Col. 0228C]

Not only should teachers impose correction upon those subject to them, but also prayer, so that those whom they cannot correct by words they may at least help by prayers. Thus the Apostle acted when, regarding the fall of certain disciples as his own, he said: “Who is weak, and I am not weak?” (II Cor. XI.) And again: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you” (Gal. IV).

“He did not answer her a word.”

This was not because of the arrogance of the Scribes and Pharisees—that the Lord did not answer the crying woman—but for various reasons he initially delayed answering her, though afterward he not only gave her an answer but also kindly granted what she requested.

First, so that the woman’s constancy might be tested, whether she would persevere in prayer or not; second, so that he might remove from the Jews an occasion for unbelief, lest they perhaps say: “The Christ promised to us is this man, yet he teaches the Gentiles and heals the Gentiles, and therefore we do not wish to believe in him”; third, so that he might stir the hearts of the disciples to mercy.

But far be it from us to believe that they were without mercy, since they walked with the author of mercy. The evangelist shows that their hearts were moved to mercy when he adds: “And his disciples approached and pleaded with him.”

At that time the disciples pleaded for the Canaanite woman; afterward they pleaded for the Church called from the Gentiles. They not only handed themselves over even to death, but also commended her to the Lord in their prayers—as the Apostle Paul did when leaving certain disciples, saying: “I commend you to God and to the word of his grace” (Acts XX)—saying: “Send her away,” which means: “Forgive her sins and grant her virtues.”

“Because she cries out after us.”

The woman cried out after the apostles because the Church loves not only their teaching but also imitates their actions. To cry out after the apostles means to follow in their footsteps.

“But he answered and said: I was not sent except to the sheep that have perished from the house of Israel.”

It is asked why he says, “I was not sent except to the sheep that have perished from the house of Israel,” when elsewhere he is read to have said: “I have other sheep that are not of this fold; these also I must bring, and they will hear my voice, and there will be one flock and one shepherd” (John X). [Col. 0229B]

The answer is that he was speaking of his bodily presence, since he is not read to have taught any Gentiles in person, except for the two days in Samaria, so as to remove from the Jews an occasion for unbelief, as was said above.

Nevertheless, while he walked among the Jews, taught, and performed signs, he proclaimed the future salvation of the Gentiles, saying: “I have other sheep that are not of this fold”; and elsewhere: “He will put the wicked to a miserable death and lease his vineyard to other farmers” (Matt. XXI).

Therefore, the one who had first said, “Do not go into the way of the Gentiles, and do not enter the cities of the Samaritans” (Matt. X), later said: “Go into all the world and preach the Gospel to every creature” (Mark XVI).

This was fulfilled after his ascension through the preaching of the apostles. What he did not accomplish bodily, he fulfilled after the resurrection through his disciples in a spiritual manner.

But it must not be passed over why he said, “I was not sent except to the sheep that have perished,” since those who have perished ought rather to be counted among goats than among sheep.

The answer is that those whom the Lord found lost through their own merit he made sheep of his grace. Of these the Apostle Peter says: “You were like sheep going astray, but now you have returned to the shepherd and bishop of your souls” (I Pet. II). He knew himself to have been in this error when he said: “I have gone astray like a sheep that has perished” (Ps. CXVIII).

But when that woman, who had earlier been rejected and not heard, heard that the disciples were pleading for her, she finally regained confidence, came to God, and worshiped him, saying:

[Col. 0229D] “Lord, help me.”

For she who sought salvation did not doubt his power.

“He answered and said: It is not good to take the children’s bread and throw it to the dogs.”

The children were once the Jews, concerning whom the Lord said to Pharaoh through Moses: “Let my son Israel, my firstborn, go” (Exod. IV). The dogs are the Gentiles, because of the filthiness of idolatry.

The word “dog” also has various meanings in Scripture. Sometimes it is used for evil, sometimes for good. It signifies good teachers, as it is said through the Psalmist: “The tongue of your dogs from the enemies, from him” (Ps. LXVII); evil people, of whom Isaiah says: “Mute dogs, unable to bark” (Isa. LVI); sometimes heretics, as the Apostle says: “Beware of dogs, beware of evil workers, beware of the mutilation” (Phil. III); sometimes a sinner and false Catholic who repeats his evil deeds, as Solomon says: “As a dog returns to its vomit, so a fool returns to his folly” (Prov. XXVI); sometimes the Jews, as it is said through the Psalmist: “Many dogs have circumcised me” (Ps. XXI); and sometimes the Gentiles, as in this passage, as was said above: “It is not good to take the children’s bread and throw it to the dogs.”

It is as though he were saying: “It is not good that the bread of teaching should be taken away from the children—that is, from the Jews, because from the beginning they worshiped and adored God—and given to you Gentiles, who have served many impurities and idols.”

Understanding this wisely and humbling herself accordingly, the woman said:

[Col. 0230B] “Yes, Lord.”

It is as though she were saying: “I know, Lord, and I believe that it is so. After the worship of idols, we are not worthy to receive the children’s bread. But because you have deigned to come into the world, extend the lap of your mercy even to gather the Gentiles, so that where sin abounded, your grace may abound all the more (Rom. V), and so that by your mercy what is impossible through our merit may become possible.”

“For even the little dogs eat from the crumbs that fall from the table of their masters.”

Since we cannot receive great things, let us at least be nourished by the small and superfluous—that is, since we are not worthy to share in the children’s table, let us at least be nourished by the crumbs that fall from the table of their masters.

The table in this passage signifies Sacred Scripture, which, according to the capacity of its hearers, contains various foods and arrangements of words, serving us the bread of life. Concerning it the Prophet says: “You have prepared a table before me in the presence of those who trouble me” (Ps. XXII).

The crumb, which is the inner part of the bread, signifies spiritual understanding in the Scriptures. “The little dogs therefore eat from the crumbs that fall from the table of their masters” when converted Gentiles seek within themselves the spiritual understanding that the Jews were unwilling to receive.

When the Lord saw that the prudent woman understood this, he answered her:

“O woman, great is your faith. Let it be done for you as you wish. And her daughter was healed from that hour.”

Here it should be considered that, at the mother’s request, her daughter was freed from the demon, so that we may understand that infants in baptism, who cannot speak, are released from original sin through baptism by the faith of their parents.

The Lord also admired her faith, as he had admired that of the centurion, to whom he said:

“Truly I say to you, I have not found such great faith in Israel.” And therefore, because this woman had faith, her daughter immediately obtained the effect of healing. For we recognize three principal virtues in this woman’s words and actions: faith, perseverance, and humility. She had faith because, although she was a Gentile, she did not doubt that she could obtain from the Lord the salvation of her daughter; perseverance because, although she had been rejected, she persisted in prayer until she received what she asked for; humility because, when she had been compared by the Lord to dogs, she, thinking humbly of herself, likened herself to little dogs.

Let us therefore imitate this woman, who by believing first became our mother in faith, we who have come from the Gentiles. Let us have faith, so that, believing in one God, we may believe that whatever we rightly ask of him we can obtain, according to the promise of the one who says: “Truly I say to you, whatever you ask for in prayer, believe that you will receive it, and it will be done for you (Mark XI)”; and again: “If you have faith like a mustard seed, you would say to this mountain: ‘Move from here,’ and it would move (Matthew XVII).” “For the righteous,” as Scripture says, “lives by faith, and without faith it is impossible to please God (Habakkuk II, Hebrews XI).”

Let us have perseverance, so that if divine providence hears our prayers only after a delay, we may join prayers to prayers until we obtain what we ask, saying to him with the Psalmist: “Guide me in your truth and teach me, for you are God my Savior, and I have waited for you all day long (Psalm XXIV).” For just as a householder sleeps, and yet, if roused by our prayers, he answers, “Do not trouble me; the door is already shut, and my children are with me in bed. I cannot get up and give you anything (Luke XI),” nevertheless, if he sees us asking with the greatest persistence, even if he does not rise and give because he is our friend, he will rise because of our importunity and give us as much as we need.

The one who wishes to receive is commanded to persist in prayer up to the horn of the altar, that is, up to faith, as the Psalmist says: “Appoint the solemn day, amid the leafy branches, up to the horn of the altar (Psalm CXVII).” And if we do not feel ourselves worthy to obtain what we ask, let us seek the prayers of spiritual brothers as our aid, so that, just as this woman obtained what she asked when the apostles intervened on her behalf, so we may believe that we are helped more by common prayers than by our own individual ones.

Let us have humility, so that, while others think greater things of us, we may judge ourselves the least, following the example of this Canaanite woman, who, having been compared by the Lord to dogs, compared herself to little dogs. He had this humility in his heart who, despised by others, said: “I will play, and I will become even more worthless than I have been, and I will be humble in my own eyes (2 Samuel VI).” Hence the wise man said: “The greater you are, humble yourself in everything, and you will find grace before God (Ecclesiasticus III).”

We have already said above that through this woman’s daughter every sinful soul is signified. Although neither soul can sin without flesh nor flesh without soul, nevertheless there are certain vices that seem to pertain especially to the flesh, and others to the soul. Theft, adultery, murder, fornication, drunkenness, sacrilege, and similar offenses pertain to the flesh; envy, however, anger, pride, hatred, resentment, deceit, vainglory, hypocrisy, and similar offenses pertain to the soul.

Therefore, whether it is the soul or the flesh that has been defiled by these vices, let it go out from its borders—that is, let it leave behind its former sins, which must be condemned; let it mortify the desires of the flesh, break its own wills, devote itself to fasts, vigils, almsgiving, and prayers, and persist in prayer until it deserves to hear from the Lord, together with the Canaanite woman: “Great is your faith; let it be done for you as you wish.”

But this must not be passed over: this woman, asking on behalf of her daughter, is introduced at the fifteenth miracle. For this number is agreeable to the mysteries of the Church, because of the mystery of the hebdomad and the ogdoad; it consists of seven and eight. For on the fourteenth day after the departure from Egypt, the Israelite people were commanded to celebrate the Passover. We read fifteen Songs of Ascents in the Psalter, from “To the Lord, when I was in distress (Psalm CXIX)” to “Behold, now bless the Lord (Psalm CXXXIII).” Fifteen years were added to Hezekiah’s life. Paul testifies that he remained with Peter for fifteen days, conferring about the Gospel that he was going to preach to the Gentiles, lest he should run or have run in vain.

The seven, therefore, refer to the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, and the eight to the resurrection. And because the Church, enlightened by the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit, has learned to believe, hope for, and love the resurrection, she is rightly introduced in the fifteenth place as one who will plead for her daughter. And because the Church, inflamed by zeal for divine love, has learned to despise the present life and love the eternal one, she is rightly called Canaanite. For *Chana* is interpreted as “zeal.”

## HOMILY XXXVI. Monday after *Reminiscere*

[Col. 0232C] (John VIII). “At that time Jesus said to the crowds of the Jews: ‘I am going away, and you will seek me,’” and so forth. “I am going away,” he says, “and you will seek me,” not out of desire but out of hatred. For after he had withdrawn from the sight of human beings, both those who hated him and those who loved him sought him: the former by pursuing him, the latter by desiring to possess him.

It is good to seek Christ’s soul, but in the manner in which the disciples sought it; and it is evil to seek Christ’s soul, but in the manner in which the Jews sought it: the former sought him in order to possess him, the latter in order to destroy him. Finally, because these people sought him with an evil and perverse heart, he added what follows: “You will seek me?”—that is, do not suppose that you will seek me rightly.

“You will die in your sin.” This means: to seek Christ wrongly is to die in one’s sin. A person dies in his sin who remains in sin until death. He does not seek Christ who does not seek the salvation of his soul through repentance. To him the Prophet cries: “Seek the Lord while he may be found (Isaiah LIX).” Whoever does not seek him now, while he has time and he is merciful, will find him angry.

He said to the Jews, “You will die in your sin,” because he knew beforehand that they would remain in their sin. He used the singular, “in sin,” and the plural, “your,” because he knew that all those to whom he was speaking had one will: an equal wickedness in destroying the one who had come to save them.

In another place he said to the disciples: “Where I am going, you cannot come (John XIII).” He did not take away their hope, but foretold a delay. When the Lord said this to the disciples, they could not then come where he was going, but they were going to come later. These, however, would never come there, to whom he said in his foreknowledge: “You will die in your sin.”

When they heard these words, they spoke as those who think in carnal terms, judge according to the flesh, and hear and understand everything carnally:

“Will he perhaps kill himself, since he says, ‘Where I am going, you cannot come’?”

Foolish words, completely full of ignorance! For if he killed himself, why could they not come where he had gone? Were they themselves not going to die? What, then, does “Will he perhaps kill himself?” mean, because he said, “Where I am going, you cannot come,” if he was speaking of human death, when no human being fails to die?

Therefore, when he said, “Where I am going,” he meant not the place to which one goes at death, but the place to which he himself was going after death. Since they did not understand this, the Lord answered them, for they were earthly-minded:

“You are from below.” You are earthly-minded because, like the serpent, you eat the earth; you feed on earthly things, delight in earthly things, gape after earthly things, and do not have your heart above.

“You are from below; I am from above. You are of this world; I am not of this world.”

How, then, was he not of this world, through whom the world was made and who is always everywhere? All are of the world, but the world came first, and humanity afterward. But Christ existed before the world; before Christ there was nothing. He “was the Word in the beginning, and all things were made through him (John I).” Thus he was from above.

From what above? From the Father himself, than whom nothing is higher, because he begot the Word equal to himself, coeternal with himself, his only-begotten Son, without time, through whom he established time. Therefore Christ existed before all creatures and before all times, because he was begotten from the Father as coeternal with the Father.

“You are of this world; I am not of this world. Therefore I told you that you will die in your sins.”

He explained to us what he meant by “You are of this world.” He said that they were of this world because they were sinners, because they were unrighteous, because they were unbelievers, because they were earthly-minded.

Were the apostles and the saints of God not of this world? They were, indeed, because they were born from Adam; but Truth itself says of them: “I chose you from the world (John XV),” that is, from the carnal way of life which, in this passage, seems to be signified by the name “world.” Therefore, because they were of the world, they became not of the world, but began to belong to the one through whom the world was made.

These, however, remained in the world, to whom it was said: “You will die in your sins.” Let no one say, “I am not of this world.” Whoever you are, human being, you are of this world. But the one who made the world has come to you, and he will free you from this world.

If the world delights you, you always wish to remain unclean. But if this world does not delight you, you will already be clean, and you will not hear what the Jews heard: “You will die in your sin.” And the more a person sins, the more he is in the world, and the more unclean he is. The more one cleanses oneself from sin, the more one rises above being of the world.

The Jews rightly heard, “You will die in your sins,” because you could in no way be without sin, since you were born with sin. Nevertheless, he added: “If you believe in me, although you were indeed born with sin, you will not die in your sin.” For he continued: “If you do not believe that I am he, you will die in your sins.” Therefore, if you believe that I am he, you will not die in your sins.

Hope was restored to the despairing; those who were asleep were roused. Their hearts awoke, and consequently many believed, as the continuation of the Gospel itself testifies, where it says:

[Col. 0234B] “As he was saying these things, many believed in him.”

Among this people to whom the Lord was speaking, therefore, there were some who were going to die in their sin, and there were also some who were going to believe in the one who was speaking and be freed from every sin.

Nevertheless, attend to what the Lord Christ said: “If you do not believe that I am he, you will die in your sin.” What does “if you do not believe that I am he” mean? Since he added nothing, he commended much. He said, “I am,” and did not add what he was—whether Christ, or the Son of God, or the one whom the prophets foretold, or the Savior of the world, or anything else that is read about him in Scripture.

What he said, “I am,” is profound, because God had said to Moses: “I am who I am.” In the same way he used the Word of eternal being before the Jewish people, as he had earlier spoken to Moses through the angel in the flame of fire in the bush, when he was going to send him to free his people (Exodus III).

What does he mean here by saying, “I am,” except: I am that very one who then, in the angel, commissioned Moses my servant to free my people; I am the one who has now come incarnate through myself, made human, to free the human beings whom I created and who had been lost?

For whatever can at some time be changed, either for the better or for the worse, in a certain manner begins, from what it previously was, to be something else or to be otherwise than it was. God alone, however, is always the same: unchangeable truth, unchangeable, eternal, unchangeable nature, unchangeable substance; and whatever can be said of him is always the same as it was and will be.

There seems to be nothing more fitting in this passage, in the words spoken by the Lord, “I am,” than: I am God; you will die in your sin. But since they were always earthly-minded, always hearing and responding according to the flesh, let us hear what they said to him:

“Who are you?”

For when you said, “Unless you believe that I am he,” you did not add who you were. Who are you, that we should believe? And he said:

“The Beginning.”

Behold what the Beginning is: it cannot be changed; the Beginning remains in itself and renews all things. It is the Beginning to which it was said: “But you are the same, and your years will not fail (Psalm CI).”

“The Beginning,” he said, “who also speaks to you.”

He answered: Believe that I am the Beginning, and he added, “who also speaks to you”—that is, because I have become humble for your sake, I have descended to these words. For if the Beginning had remained with the Father as it is, and had not taken the form of a servant and spoken as a human being to human beings, how would they have believed in him, when weak hearts could not understand the intelligible Word without a voice, nor see invisible things?

Therefore, he says, believe that I am the Beginning, because, in order that you may believe, I not only exist, but also speak to you.

The words of our Lord Jesus Christ in his conversation with the Jews were so measured that the blind did not see, while the eyes of the faithful were opened.

“The Jews therefore said: ‘Who are you?’ And he said: ‘The Beginning, who also speaks to you.’”

Why does the Lord Jesus call himself the Beginning? Because all things were made through him. For he is the Wisdom of God, as the Psalmist says: “You made all things in wisdom (Psalm CVII).” If, then, God made all things in Wisdom—that is, in his Son, coeternal and consubstantial with him—the Son is certainly the Beginning of all things.

Can the Father also be called the Beginning? Certainly the Father too is rightly called the Beginning; nevertheless there are not two beginnings. Just as the Father is God and the Son is God, yet there are not two gods but one God, so the Father and the Son are one Beginning.

The Holy Spirit, therefore, is also the Beginning; nevertheless there are not three beginnings—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—but one Beginning. Just as the Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God, yet there are not three gods but one God; and just as the Father is almighty, the Son almighty, and the Holy Spirit almighty, yet there are not three almighty beings but one Almighty.

That which the Father is in relation to himself is God; that which he is in relation to the Son is Father. That which the Son is in relation to himself is God; that which he is in relation to the Father is Son. And that which the Holy Spirit is in relation to himself is God; that which he is in relation to the Father and the Son is the Holy Spirit, because he is the Spirit of the Father and the Son, proceeding from the Father and the Son, of one substance, power, and majesty with the Father and the Son.

“I have many things,” he said, “to speak and judge concerning you.”

In another place, however, he said: “I judge no one (John VIII),” showing that his present coming was for the purpose of saving, not judging, because he had come to save the world, not to judge the world. But when he now says, “I have many things to speak and judge concerning you,” he speaks of the future judgment. For he ascended in order to come to judge the living and the dead.

No one will judge more justly than the one who was judged unjustly. “I have many things,” he says, “to speak and judge concerning you, but the one who sent me is truthful.”

See how he gives glory to the Father—the Son equal to the Father. He offers us an example of giving glory to God and seeking God’s glory, not our own. It is as though he were saying: O faithful human being, if I, the Son of the Father, equal to the Father, consubstantial with the Father, coeternal with the Father, give glory to the one from whom I am, how are you proud before the one whose servant you are?

“I have many things,” he says, “to speak and judge concerning you, but the one who sent me is truthful.” It is as though he were saying: I speak the truth because I am the Truth born from the Truthful One. The Father is truthful; the Son is Truth. For the Lord himself says most openly: “I am the way, and the truth, and the life (John XIV).”

Therefore, if the Son is Truth, what is the Father, except what Truth says: “The one who sent me is truthful”? The Son is Truth; the Father is truthful. As the Son is from the Father, so Truth is from the Truthful One.

The Father is truthful, but not from Truth; the Son is Truth, but from the Father, because the Son is from the Father, not from himself. Therefore, in another place he says: “I have not come of myself (John VII),” that is, I am not from myself.

The Father is truthful, not by participating in Truth but by begetting Truth. For the Father begot the Son, who says of himself: “I am the way, and the truth, and the life.”

When the Lord Jesus had said, “The one who sent me is truthful,” they did not understand that he was speaking to them about the Father. They did not yet have the eyes of their hearts opened, so that they could understand the equality of the Truthful One and Truth.

“He therefore said to them: ‘When you have lifted up the Son of Man, then you will know that I am he, and that I do nothing of myself, but as the Father taught me, so I speak.’”

What does this mean? He seems to have said nothing other than that they would know after his Passion who he was. Without a doubt, therefore, he saw there some whom he himself, together with all his saints, had chosen in foreknowledge before the foundation of the world, and who would believe after his Passion.

These are the ones whom we continually commend and set before others for imitation with great exhortation. After the Lord’s Passion, resurrection, and ascension, when the Holy Spirit had been sent and miracles were being performed in the name of the one whom the Jews, pursuing him as though he were dead, had despised, they were pierced in their hearts.

Those whom they had killed in their fury, and whose blood they had poured out in their rage, they drank through faith: those three thousand and those five thousand Jews whom he saw there when he said: “When you have lifted up the Son of Man, then you will know that I am he.”

It was as though he were saying: I am delaying your knowledge in order to complete my Passion; in your appointed time you will know who I am.

Not all of those who heard him were going to believe then, that is, after the Lord’s Passion. For a little earlier he says: “As he was saying these things, many believed in him,” and yet the Son of Man had not been lifted up.

He calls the lifting up the lifting up of the Passion, not of glorification; of the cross, not of heaven. For he was lifted up there when he hung upon the wood, but that lifting up was humiliation. Then he became obedient to the Father unto death, even death on a cross. Therefore God exalted him (Philippians II), and so forth.

There was one exaltation when he was raised upon the cross, and another when he ascended into heaven: the former was an exaltation of humiliation, the latter of glorification.

The exaltation of the cross had to be accomplished through the hands of those who would afterward believe, to whom he says: “When you have lifted up the Son of Man,” and he added: “then you will know that I am he.”

What does “I am” mean except that he is of one substance with the Father? As we said above, it was said to Moses: “I am who I am (Exodus III).” The Lord uses of himself a word of substance, so that it may be understood that his substance is eternal and that the substance of the Father and the Son is one.

Nevertheless, so that he would not himself be understood to be the Father, he immediately added: “And I do nothing of myself”—that is, I am not from myself.

But what he added, “As the Father taught me, so I speak,” has a very profound meaning. The heart must be cleansed in order to understand what he says: “As the Father taught me, so I speak.”

It must not be understood as though a human father were speaking to a human son, but in a more exalted and sacred sense. One thing is meant by what the Evangelist says, “In the beginning was the Word (John I),” and another by what he says, “The Word became flesh.”

We must think one way about Christ’s divinity, in which he is equal to God the Father, and another way about his humanity, in which he is like us. What the Lord says, “I and the Father are one (John X),” must not be understood in the same way as what he says, “The Father is greater than I (John XIV).”

Therefore, do not think corporeally that the Father spoke to the Son, since the incorporeal Father begot the Son. Nor did he teach him as though he had begotten an ignorant son; rather, his teaching him means that he begot him knowing.

And this is what “The Father taught me” means: the Father begot me knowing. For if, as few understand, the nature of Truth is simple, then for the Son to be is the same as for him to know.

Therefore he has from the one by whom he has being that he knows. It is not that he first existed from him and afterward came to know from him; rather, just as the Father gave him by begetting the gift of knowing, so he gave him being.

Because, as has been said, the nature of Truth is simple, being and knowing are not two different things but the very same thing.

He said these things to the Jews, and added:

“And the one who sent me is with me.”

He had already said this earlier, but he repeatedly recalls the great truth: “He sent me, and he is with me.”

If he is with you, Lord, then one was not sent by another, but both came. And yet, although they are alike, one was sent and the other sent, because “sending” is incarnation. The incarnation belongs to the Son alone, not to the Father.

The Father therefore sent the Son, but he did not depart from the Son. “The one who sent me,” he says, “has not left me alone.” By whose authority I was incarnate as by a father’s authority, he is with me; he has not abandoned me.

Why has he not abandoned me? “Because I always do what pleases him.”

This is eternal equality—not beginning at some point and continuing thereafter, but without beginning and without end. For God’s generation has no beginning in time, because time itself was made through the one who was begotten.

## HOMILY XXXVII. Tuesday after *Reminiscere*

(Matthew XXI). “At that time Jesus spoke this parable to the crowds of the Jews: ‘A certain man had two sons,’” and so forth.

This man, the householder who is read to have had two sons, is Almighty God, the householder and creator of two peoples. The first son is the Gentile people, which took its beginning from Noah and his sons. It is called first insofar as antiquity is concerned. To it the Lord gave, through the natural law, the command that it should work in his vineyard, saying (Tobit IV): “What you do not want done to you, do not do to another.” And: “Whatever you want people to do to you, do to them also (Matthew VII).”

At first that people refused to labor in the Lord’s vineyard, but afterward, at the Lord’s coming, moved by repentance, it turned to works of righteousness. The other son was the Jewish people, to whom the Lord gave the law through Moses and commanded them to work in his vineyard.

[Col. 0238A] “And he answered: ‘I go, Lord.’” For he said: “Whatever the Lord commands us, we will do, and we will obey him (Exodus XXIV).” “And he did not go.” Because he lied about all the things that he had promised would be established.

“Which of the two did the Father’s will?” They said: “The first.”

The Jews condemn themselves by their own judgment. For the first son, that is, the Gentile people, did the Father’s will: at first it went astray, but afterward corrected itself through repentance.

Some interpret this parable not as concerning two peoples but as concerning the righteous and sinners. The tax collectors and sinners, who at first rejected God’s commands, afterward, when John preached, accepted him and were cleansed by his baptism.

On the other hand, the scribes and Pharisees, who applauded themselves because of a false righteousness, despised receiving John’s baptism and thus proved disobedient to the divine commands. Therefore, at the conclusion of this parable, the Lord added:

“Because tax collectors and prostitutes will go before you into the kingdom of God.”

We may understand the kingdom of God as Holy Scripture, according to what he says elsewhere: “The kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a nation producing its fruits (Matthew XXI).” Into this kingdom of God the tax collectors and prostitutes—that is, the Gentiles—went before the Jews.

## HOMILY XXXVIII. Wednesday after *Reminiscere*

(Matthew XX). “At that time, as Jesus was going up to Jerusalem, he took his twelve disciples aside privately and said to them: ‘Behold, we are going up to Jerusalem,’” and so forth.

The Lord had already frequently foretold his Passion, including the time, place, and manner of his Passion. Why, then, does he repeat it again? Because he had spoken about many other matters, and the memory of his Passion could slip from the minds of his disciples. Therefore he repeated the prediction of the dishonor of his Passion, both to prepare their souls for temptation and so that, when they came to Jerusalem, they would be less frightened because they remembered that the Lord had foretold it so often.

“And the mother of the sons of Zebedee approached him with her sons, worshiping and asking something from him.”

The mother of the sons of Zebedee was the aunt of the Savior, namely the mother of James and John. But what did this woman mean by asking him for glory and rank for her sons after she had heard from the Lord about the dishonor and suffering of his Passion? He had said nothing about the glory of the kingdom, but only about the punishment of his Passion.

Perhaps, however, she was prompted to ask for rank for her sons because she had understood the Lord’s statement that he would rise on the third day. For, following the Jewish fable, she thought that after his resurrection the Lord would reign bodily on earth for a thousand years and distribute earthly rank to his chosen ones.

Thus, moved by feminine fervor, she approached the Lord so that after his resurrection he might give her sons the power to sit, one at his right hand and the other at his left.

[Col. 0239A] “But Jesus answered and said: ‘You do not know what you are asking.’”

The mother had made the request, but the Lord rebuked the disciples because, through the power of his divinity, he understood that the request the mother had brought to him had arisen from the sons’ urging. Nor is it surprising that the Lord says to these two disciples, “You do not know what you are asking,” when the Evangelist says of the apostle Peter that he did not know what he was saying.

“Can you drink the cup that I am going to drink?”

By the name of the cup—and, as another Evangelist puts it, by baptism—he signifies the Passion. Hence the Psalmist says: “What shall I repay the Lord for all that he has repaid me? I will take up the cup of salvation (Psalm CXV).” And immediately he explained what the cup of salvation was, saying: “Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints.”

Passion is also often signified by baptism, as the Lord says: “I have a baptism with which I must be baptized (Luke XII),” that is, I must endure a Passion.

The Lord therefore asks whether they can drink the cup that he was going to drink—that is, whether they could endure the same Passion that he was going to suffer for them. In these words he openly shows that punishment is endured first, and afterward one reaches the kingdom.

“You will indeed drink my cup,” that is, you will endure my Passion.

We must ask how this is to be understood. There is no doubt concerning James, that he drank the Lord’s cup, because he was beheaded by Herod. But there is doubt concerning John, since he did not end this life through the punishment of martyrdom.

Nevertheless, although he did not pass from this world through the shedding of blood, he too drank the Savior’s cup. For he was thrown by the most wicked emperor Domitian into a cauldron of boiling oil, and he drank poison before the emperor and remained unharmed. It is also read that he was scourged together with the other apostles.

Although he did not pass from this life through punishment and the shedding of blood, he nevertheless drank the cup of the Passion, because his spirit and will were always prepared to endure the Passion.

“But to sit at my right hand or at my left is not mine to give you.”

We must consider what he means when he says, “It is not mine to give you”—namely, to you who are proud and desirous of empty glory. The meaning is: the kingdom of God is not for the giver but for the recipient. Such as you are, you cannot receive the kingdom of God; you must become what you ought to be.

“It is not mine to give you,” that is, to the proud and haughty. Therefore first become humble, and thus you will reach the dignity of the kingdom. Prepare yourselves to be such as are fit for the kingdom of heaven.

Some teachers, however, think that what these disciples asked was granted, so that one would sit at the Lord’s right hand and the other also at his left. When James entered the heavenly kingdoms through the martyrdom of beheading, he sat, as it were, at the Lord’s right hand. Because John the Evangelist endured for a very long time, for many years beyond the other apostles, he sat, as it were, at his left hand.

For the left hand signifies the present life, while the right hand signifies heavenly blessedness, as it is said in the Song of Songs: “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand embraces me (Song of Songs II).”

“But for those for whom it has been prepared by my Father.” Namely, for the humble and gentle, who hear me saying: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart (Matthew XI).”

“When the ten heard this, they became indignant at the two brothers.”

The former asked carnally, and the latter became carnally indignant. Yet the apostles were not indignant against the mother, who had brought her sons’ request, but against the sons, because they understood that this request had arisen from the sons’ own will.

The Lord, however, being gentle and humble, neither accused the mother of greed nor accused the apostles of envy and resentment, but set before both groups an example of humility, saying that the greater in the kingdom of heaven is rather whoever makes himself lower in service.

“You know that the rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, and those who are greater exercise authority among them.”

The Lord sets before them the example of the Gentiles, whose rulers exercise authority among them. Having presented this example, he added:

“It will not be so among you,” that is, you will not contend in the same way over leadership and glory as the Gentiles do.

“Just as the Son of Man did not come to be served but to serve.”

This means that the Son of Man did not come to seek honors and dignities in this world, but rather to serve others himself. The Lord sets himself before us as an example of humility.

What did the Lord provide for his apostles? Food and clothing and the other necessities of the body, the preaching of the divine word, and, finally, he humbled himself so greatly that he endured the cross and Passion for them. This too he provided for us.

Hence the Lord says: “And to give his life as a redemption for many.” He did not say “for all,” but “for many,” because although the Lord endured the cross for the whole human race, his Passion benefited only those who were reborn to life by the same Spirit by whom he was conceived in his mother’s womb.

## HOMILY XXXIX. Thursday after *Reminiscere*

(John V). “At that time Jesus said to the crowds of the Jews: ‘I can do nothing of myself, but as I hear, I judge.’”

Perhaps he said, “I can do nothing of myself,” as though he had said: I am not from myself but from the Father. For the Father is from no other, whereas the Son is from the Father, and so forth.

He said, “As I hear, I judge,” because the work of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is one. “As he hears, he judges.” He will hear, namely, through the unity of substance and the distinctiveness of knowledge.

He does not judge from himself because he is not from himself. The Father alone is from no other; the Son is begotten from the Father, as we have said. The Son will hear from the one from whom he was begotten, because he is not from himself but from another, from whom he was begotten. From the one from whom he has understanding, he also has knowledge. From that one, therefore, comes his hearing, which is nothing other than knowledge.

The very words he said, “As I hear, I judge,” can also be understood according to the nature of his humanity, which the Son of God assumed from the Virgin. When he was speaking about the resurrection of souls, he did not say “I hear” but “I see.”

“As I hear, I judge, and my judgment is just.” From where does the human judgment come? Because he continues: “I do not seek my own will, but the will of the one who sent me.”

This sending is the incarnation of Christ, which took place for this purpose: that the Father’s will might be accomplished through him for the salvation of the human race.

It appears that in this passage, from these words of our Savior, he wishes to make known to us that there are two natures in him, and that he truly possesses a soul, in which alone there is will. For it was joined to divinity with so great a union that its entire will was spiritual, yet not animal—that is, carnal. For he continued:

“If I bear witness about myself, my witness is not true.” For, as he said in what follows: “If I glorify myself, my glory is nothing; but it is my Father who glorifies me, he who sent me” (John 8). But here it is said: “If I bear witness about myself, my witness is not true” (ibid.). And shortly afterward: “The Father who sent me, he himself bears witness about me” (ibid.). At one time he demonstrates in himself the nature of man; at another he signifies that, in the majesty of God, he is equal to the Father; at another he claims for himself the unity of divinity with God the Father; at another he displays the frailty of human flesh; at another he says that his teaching is not his own; at another that he does not seek his own will; at another he signifies that his own witness is [Col. 0241C] not true; and at another that it is true. For here he says: “If I bear witness about myself, my witness is not true.” And shortly afterward: Even if I bear witness about myself, my witness is true. How, then, is his witness not true, except according to the frailty of the flesh? Likewise, what he said—“I have not come to do my own will” (John 6)—and, “The Son can do nothing of himself,” together with many other statements of this kind, do not weaken the Son, deceive him, or separate him from the Father. Indeed, these things have been set forth so that his true humanity may shine forth, just as it does in the following statements: “I am in the Father and the Father is in me” (John 14); and again: “I and the Father are one” (John 10); and: “Whoever sees me sees the Father also” (John 14). And by the statement, “Just as the Father raises [Col. 0241D] the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whomever he wishes,” his true divinity is confirmed. For the will of the Father and the Son is one, their operation is one, and finally their grace and governance are the same. But the teacher of the nations teaches these things when he writes: “Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians 1).

“Another is he who bears witness about me.” In what follows he shows who that other one is who bears witness about him, when he says: “The Father who sent me, he himself bears witness about me” (John 8). The Father’s testimony concerning the Son was given at the baptism, when a voice came from heaven: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 17). The Father also gave similar testimony on the holy mountain, in the hearing of [Col. 0242A] three disciples, concerning his Son. “And I know that his testimony is true.” Everything true is true from the truth. For God is truth. And whatever is true is true from God. Here, moreover, he explained what the testimony is: “The works,” he says, “that I do bear witness about me.” Then he added: “And the Father who sent me bears witness about me.” He says that the very works he performed he received from the Father. The works, therefore, bear witness; the Father who sent him bears witness.

John bore witness about Christ like a lamp—not to heal friends, but to confound enemies. For it had already been foretold in the person of the Father: “I have prepared a lamp for my Christ. I will clothe his enemies with confusion, but upon him my sanctification will flourish” [Col. 0242B] (Psalm 131). Suppose that, as though placed in the night, you fixed your attention on a lamp, admired the lamp, and rejoiced in the light of the lamp. But he says that the lamp is the sun, in which you ought to rejoice. And although it burns during the night, he commands you to await the day.

It is not, therefore, because that man’s testimony was unnecessary. For why would he have been sent if he were unnecessary? Rather, it was so that a person might not remain with the lamp and imagine that the lamp’s light was sufficient for him. Therefore the Lord neither says that the lamp was superfluous, nor does he say that one ought to remain with the lamp. “Search the Scriptures,” he says, “in which you think you have eternal life. They themselves bear witness about me, and you refuse to come to me so that you may have life.” Why do you think that you have eternal life in the Scriptures? Ask the one to whom they bear [Col. 0242C] witness, and understand what eternal life is.

And because they appeared to reject Christ on account of Moses, as though he were another lamp: all human beings are lamps, since they can both be kindled and extinguished. Lamps shine when they possess wisdom and burn with the Spirit. Even if they burned, they have been extinguished and have already become foul. The servants of God remained good lamps through the oil of his mercy, not through their own strength; for God’s grace—grace freely given—is the oil of the lamps. “I have labored more than all of them,” says one such lamp. And lest he seem to burn by his own strength, he added: “Yet not I, but the grace of God that is with me.”

Every prophet before the Lord’s coming is a lamp, concerning whom the apostle Peter says (2 Peter 1): “We possess the prophetic word made more certain, to which you do well to pay attention as to [Col. 0242D] a lamp shining in a dark place, until the day dawns and the morning star rises in your hearts.” The prophet, therefore, is a lamp, and all prophecy is one great lamp.

What of the apostles? Are they not lamps? They too are plainly lamps. For he alone is not a lamp. He is not kindled and extinguished, but is “the true light, which enlightens every person coming into this world” (John 1). Concerning John it is said: “He was not that light, but came to bear witness about the light” (ibid.). Concerning Christ, however: “He was the true light, which enlightens every person coming into this world.” What, then, is the meaning of the fact that Truth itself says of the apostles, “You are the light of the world,” while of John the Evangelist it says, “He was not that light”? Neither was John a lamp from himself, nor were [Col. 0243A] the apostles light from themselves. He was a lamp from the light, Christ; they were illumined by the light, who is the true sun rising in the hearts of believers.

“I have a testimony greater than John. For the works that the Father gave me to complete—the very works that I do—bear witness about me, because the Father sent me. And the Father who sent me, he himself has borne witness about me.” Above he said, “I do not receive testimony from a human being.” Here he gave the reason why he did not receive testimony from a human being: because he has the Father’s testimony and the testimony of his works, and possesses testimony greater than that of human beings.

Therefore this sending is Christ’s incarnation; Christ’s incarnation is our redemption; and our redemption is in the Truth itself, which says: “I came so that they may have life, and have it abundantly” (John 10). [Col. 0243B]

He then added to this testimony concerning the Father that the Jews—or rather, all unbelievers, whose minds have been blinded—cannot receive the truth of his divinity, saying:

“You have never heard his voice, nor seen his form, and you do not have his word remaining in you.” The Apostle says: “It is not the hearers of the law who are justified, but the doers of God’s word” (Romans 2); that is, the Son of God does not remain in their hearts because they do not keep what they hear.

When he says, “You have neither heard his voice nor seen his form,” he shows by this that the substance of divinity is incomprehensible and invisible, and that his voice cannot be heard by bodily ears. Rather, it must be understood or loved through spiritual understanding by the grace of the Holy Spirit, according to what is granted to each person. [Col. 0243C]

“Search the Scriptures, because you think that in them you have eternal life.” And “they are the ones that bear witness about me, yet you refuse to come to me so that you may have life.” “You refuse to come” means, “You refuse to believe,” because without faith it is impossible to please God. Our coming to Christ means believing that he is truly the Son of God and that through him we truly have salvation.

For all Holy Scripture bore witness to Christ—whether through figures, through prophets, or through the ministries of angels. Thus Moses bore witness to Christ, John bore witness to Christ, and the other prophets and apostles bore witness to Christ. To all these testimonies he adds the testimony of his works, because through them all it was God alone who bore witness to his Son. [Col. 0243D]

“I do not receive glory from human beings,” that is, I do not seek human praise, because “I have not come to be served but to serve” (Matthew 20); that is, I did not come to receive fleshly honor from human beings, but to give human beings spiritual honor.

“But I know you, that you do not have the love of God in yourselves.” They did not have the love of God because they did not believe in him, because he did not come to do his own will but the will of the one who sent him. Therefore he added:

“I have come in my Father’s name, and you did not receive me,” that is, you did not believe in me, who came into the world so that the Father’s name might be glorified. “If another comes in his own name, him you will receive.” Who is the one who comes in his own name except the one who seeks his own glory and not that of the one who sent him? Whom were the Jews going to receive except the Antichrist, who is to come seeking his own glory? And this will be their punishment for sin: because they refused to believe the truth, they will believe the lie. [Col. 0244A]

“How can you believe, you who receive glory from one another and do not seek the glory that comes from God alone?” We must consider with greater attention how great an evil is the ambition for boasting and human praise, on account of which Truth itself says that certain people cannot believe, because they were desirous of worldly glory. What is the desire for human praise except an exaltation of the mind above? A person wishes to be esteemed for possessing something that he does not strive to have within himself. One desires to appear one way inwardly, another outwardly. [Col. 0244B]

Humility seeks glory from God alone; pride seeks it from human beings. Therefore John the Baptist was praised so excellently by Truth itself that he was not a reed shaken by the wind: he was not pliable under the breath of human praise or hateful reproach, and for that reason he did not seek human glory.

“Do not think that I will accuse you before the Father. There is one who accuses you: Moses, in whom you especially hope.” I do not accuse you because I did not come to condemn but to save. Moses, however, accuses you because you are unbelieving toward his voice. “He wrote about me,” when he said (Deuteronomy 18): “The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers, like me; you shall listen to him.” But pay attention to what follows: “Every person who does not obey that prophet shall be destroyed from the people of God.” [Col. 0244C]

If you do not believe his writings, how will you believe my words? For whatever the Law and the Prophets wrote, in every respect they indicated that Christ would come. If the Jews had believed the Law or the Prophets, they would certainly have believed Christ as well.

## HOMILY XL. FRIDAY AFTER REMINISCERE

(Matthew 21.) “At that time Jesus said to his disciples and to the crowds of the Jews this parable: ‘There was a certain householder who planted a vineyard,’” and so forth.

The scribes and Pharisees, who had earlier said to the Lord, “By what authority are you doing these things?”, hear through hidden parables what they were not worthy to hear through open speech. For almighty God the Father is the founder and ruler of his households. His vineyard is the house of Israel. This people is commonly called by that name in sacred speech, as Isaiah says (chapter 5): “I will sing for my beloved the song of my kinsman concerning his vineyard.” “My beloved had a vineyard in a fertile place,” and so forth, until he says: “The vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel.”

The Psalmist also says: “You brought a vine out of Egypt” (Psalm 79). Almighty God therefore planted a vineyard, because, after expelling its inhabitants, the Canaanites, from the land of promise, he settled the Israelite people in it. [Col. 0244D]

“And he surrounded it with a hedge,” that is, with the walls of cities and the protection of angels. “And he dug a winepress in it.” The winepress signifies the altar. For just as grapes are pressed in a winepress, so the blood of offerings and sacrifices was poured out upon the altar. Alternatively, by the winepress we should understand the suffering of the holy prophets, since this name is commonly used to designate the suffering of the saints. Hence we find certain psalms entitled “For the winepresses,” in which the suffering of the saints is commemorated. [Col. 0245A]

“And he built a tower.” The tower means that most august temple which the Lord built in the middle of Jerusalem, first through Solomon, then restored through Ezra and Nehemiah, and finally through Judas and his brothers.

“And he leased it to tenant farmers,” that is, he entrusted it to the scribes and Pharisees, so that they might bring forth from the Law the fruit of good works. [Col. 0245B]

“And he went away to a foreign land.” This does not mean a change of place, because God is everywhere and absent nowhere, as he says through Jeremiah (chapter 23): “I am a God who is near, and not far away.” Rather, he is said to have gone away because he left the cultivators of the vineyard the freedom to work according to their own will.

“When the time of the fruits drew near, he sent his servants to the tenant farmers, so that they might receive its fruits.” The time of the fruits is the time when the fruits of good works are to be rendered. He sent his servants to the tenant farmers—namely, Aaron and Moses.

“And the tenant farmers seized his servants and beat one.” They beat Moses and Aaron, not indeed with blows, but by their conduct and words. For they even wanted to stone them. We read in the Psalm: [Col. 0245C] “Moses was troubled on their account, because they provoked his spirit” (Psalm 105).

They beat David when they said: “We have no share in David, nor inheritance in the son of Jesse” (2 Samuel 20). They also killed some of the prophets and stoned others.

“Again he sent other servants, more than the first.” The servants sent for the second time signify the company of the prophets. “And they treated them in the same way,” that is, they stoned some, like Naboth; they beat others, like Isaiah, whom they cut with a wooden saw; and they scourged others, like Jeremiah.

“Finally he sent his son to them, saying: ‘Perhaps they will respect my son.’” The Lord speaks doubtfully—not because he himself is uncertain, since he possesses perfect knowledge, but because the Lord speaks doubtfully when our unbelief is rebuked. [Col. 0245D]

“But when the tenant farmers saw the son, they said among themselves: ‘This is the heir. Come, let us kill him.’” From this passage it is understood that the Jews killed Christ not through ignorance but through envy. For when they said, “The whole world has gone after him” (John 12), they understood him to be the one of whom the prophet says: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance” (Psalm 2).

They therefore thought that, once he had been killed, they could transfer his inheritance to themselves—that is, remove his teaching from the hearts of the nations and implant in their hearts their own righteousness, which came from the Law.

“And they seized him, threw him outside the vineyard, and killed him,” because the Lord suffered outside the gate. Or they threw him outside the vineyard and killed him in this sense: first they cast him out of their hearts through unbelief, and afterward they killed him. [Col. 0246A]

“When, therefore, the lord of the vineyard comes, what will he do to those tenant farmers?” The Lord asks the scribes and Pharisees what the householder will do when he comes to those tenant farmers—not because he does not know what he will do, but so that he may convict them by their own answer. They were convicted by their own judgment: namely, that because of their negligence the knowledge of the Scriptures was to be transferred to the nations.

“They say to him: ‘He will destroy those evil men evilly, and will lease his vineyard to other tenant farmers,’” that is, he will give the knowledge of the Scriptures to the nations, who will render its fruit to him in its seasons—that is, who will render the fruit of good works in their own times. [Col. 0246B]

Jesus says to them: “Have you never read in the Scriptures: ‘The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone’?” Those whom he previously called tenant farmers and vinedressers he now calls builders—namely, the scribes and Pharisees. Not because they were builders, but because they ought to have built up the people by their examples and teaching.

“They rejected the stone” when they said: “We do not want this man to reign over us” (Luke 19), and, “We do not know where he is from.” But “the stone has become the cornerstone.” A corner joins two walls, and Christ became the cornerstone, joining in himself two peoples who came from different directions, making peace for those who were near and for those who were far away. [Col. 0246C]

“This was done by the Lord.” Everything in this matter was done by the Lord. For the joining of the two walls by that stone through its unity—that is, the joining of the two peoples in one Church—was not the work of human strength but of divine power. The meaning is: How will the Psalmist’s prophecy be fulfilled unless you reject me and crucify me?

“And it is marvelous in our eyes.” This is marvelous: that from two peoples one Church should be formed. Therefore I tell you that this parable concerns you.

“I tell you, the kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a nation producing its fruits.” He calls the kingdom of God the knowledge of the divine Scriptures. [Col. 0246D] “The kingdom of God will be taken away from you”—that is, the knowledge of the Scriptures—and only the barrenness of the letter will remain with you. “And it will be given to a nation”—that is, to a Gentile people—producing its fruits, namely, its works.

“And whoever falls upon this stone will be broken.” It is one thing to fall upon the stone and another to fall beneath the stone. A person falls upon the stone—that is, upon Christ—when, by sinning, he offends him while still retaining hope of pardon through repentance. Whoever denies Christ falls upon him; that is, divine judgment rushes upon him and crushes him completely, so that no fragment remains from which water might be drawn.

This may also be understood in another way. In the present life sinners fall upon the stone and are broken through repentance. But the stone will fall upon them on the day of judgment, because the Lord Jesus will come to judgment with all the powers above. [Col. 0247A]

“When the chief priests and Pharisees heard his parables, they understood that he was speaking about them.” Although the scribes and Pharisees were hard-hearted, and although they refused to believe in Christ, they nevertheless understood plainly that his parables concerned them. Therefore they sought to seize him, but they feared the crowds, because the crowds regarded him as a prophet.

The fickleness of the crowd must be observed. The one whom they now regard as a prophet they will later, during his Passion, cry out against, saying: “He is guilty of death” (Matthew 26), and, “Crucify him, crucify him!”—persuaded, of course, by the scribes and Pharisees.

## HOMILY XLI. SATURDAY AFTER REMINISCERE

[Col. 0247B]

(Luke 15.) “At that time Jesus said to his disciples: ‘A certain man had two sons, and the younger of them said to his father: “Father, give me the portion of the substance that falls to me,”’” and so forth.

When the scribes and Pharisees were murmuring about the reception of sinners, the Savior set forth three parables in succession. In the first two, which are to be discussed, he indicated how greatly he rejoices with the angels over the salvation of penitents; in the third, which follows, he demonstrated not merely his own joy and that of his people, but also rebuked the murmuring of those who were envious.

The man who is said to have had two sons is understood to be God the Father, the father of two peoples and, as it were, the author and creator of two stocks of the human race. The elder son signifies those who remained in the worship of the one God; the younger signifies those who deserted God even to the point of worshiping idols. [Col. 0247C]

The portion of the substance that fell to the younger son is the rational sense in the human being. To live, understand, remember, and excel through a vigorous intelligence is a substance of the divine gift. The younger son asks this from his father when, delighted with his own power, a human being seeks to govern himself by free will and asks to depart from the Lord his creator.

“He divided the substance between them”: to the faithful, he gave the protection of his grace, which they desired; to the unfaithful, he granted only the gift of natural intelligence, with which they were content.

“And not many days later, after gathering everything together, the younger son departed to a distant region. And there he squandered his substance by living extravagantly.” He went far away not by changing his place but by changing his mind. Behold: the more anyone now sins through evil conduct, the farther he withdraws from God’s grace.

It says that this happened “not many days” later, so that, after everything had been gathered together, he might depart to a distant region. For not long after the creation of the human race, the soul chose by free will to carry with it a certain power, as it were, belonging to its nature, and to desert the one by whom it had been created. It presumed upon its own powers, which it consumes all the more quickly the more it deserts the one from whom they were given. [Col. 0247D]

Thus he calls this a prodigal life: one that loves to squander its substance and parade itself in outward display, becoming inwardly empty when a person pursues the things that proceed from it and abandons the one who is interior to him.

“After he had spent everything, a severe famine arose in that region.” Everything he squandered signifies the adornments of nature that he consumed. The famine in the distant region is the poverty of the word of truth amid forgetfulness of the Creator, concerning which it is said in the Prophets: “The Lord will send a famine upon the land, not a famine of bread nor a thirst for water, but of hearing the word of God” (Amos 8).

“He began to be in need, and he went and attached himself to one of the citizens of that region.” He rightly began to be in need, since he had abandoned the treasures of God’s wisdom and the height of heavenly riches. [Col. 0248A]

The one citizen of that region to whom the needy man attached himself is surely the one who, by the merit of his perversity, has been placed over earthly desires and is called by the Lord the prince of this world. Concerning him the Apostle says: “The god of this age has blinded the minds of unbelievers” (2 Corinthians 4).

“And he sent him into his estate to feed pigs.” To be sent into an estate means to be subjected to the substance of the world and to worldly desire. In another parable, someone who despised the spiritual banquets to which he had been invited said: “I have bought an estate, and I must go out and see it” (Luke 14). To feed pigs means to perform those things in which unclean spirits delight. [Col. 0248B]

“And he desired to fill his belly with the pods that the pigs were eating.” The pods with which he fed the pigs are worldly teachings, sounding with sterile sweetness. In varied speech and verse they resound with praises of idols and stories about the gods of the nations, in which demons delight.

When this man desired to be filled, he wanted to find something solid and upright in such things, something pertaining to the blessed life, but he could not. This is what the words mean: “And no one gave him anything.” [Col. 0248C]

“But when he came to himself”—that is, when he brought his attention back from those things that outwardly entice and deceive in vain to the interior of his conscience—he said: “How many hired servants in my father’s house have an abundance of bread, while I am perishing here from hunger.”

How could he have known this, since he was in such great forgetfulness of God, as all idolaters were, unless this recollection already belonged to one recovering his senses, when the Gospel was being preached? [Col. 0248D]

The hired servants of the father therefore have an abundance of bread because those who strive to perform worthy deeds with an eye to future reward are daily refreshed by the nourishment of heavenly grace. But those perish from hunger who, placed outside the father’s dwelling, desire to fill their belly with pods—that is, those who live without faith and seek the blessed life through the studies of empty philosophy.

Just as bread, which strengthens the human heart, is compared with the word of God, by which the mind is refreshed, so the pod—which is itself empty within, soft outside, and does not nourish the body but fills it, so that it is more a burden than a benefit—is rightly compared with worldly wisdom. Its speech is sonorous through the applause of eloquence, but empty of the power that brings benefit. [Col. 0249A]

“I will arise and go to my father, and I will say to him: ‘Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you.’” How merciful and loving he knew his father to be, since, though offended by his son, he did not disdain to hear the name “father.”

“‘I will arise,’” he says, because I have recognized that I am lying down; “and I will go,” because I have withdrawn far away; “to my father,” because under the prince of pigs I am wasting away in miserable poverty.

“‘I have sinned’ against heaven and before” the angelic spirits and holy souls, in which he signifies that God’s dwelling is located. “Before you” means in the very inner chamber of the conscience, into which the eyes of God alone could penetrate. [Col. 0249B]

“‘I am no longer worthy to be called your son; make me like one of your hired servants.’” He does not dare aspire to the affection of a son, who does not doubt that everything belonging to the father is his own; rather, he desires the status of a hired servant, already intending to serve for a wage. Yet he testifies that he cannot even merit this except by his father’s gracious favor.

Where, then, are the Pelagians, who trust that they can be saved by their own service, contrary to the clearest statement: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15)?

“And rising, he came to his father.” To come to the father is to be established in the Church through faith, where there can already be a legitimate and fruitful confession of sins.

“While he was still far away”—and before he understood God, yet already seeking him devoutly—“his father saw him.” The impious and proud are appropriately said not to be seen, as though they were not before his eyes. For only those who are loved are usually said to be held before someone’s eyes. [Col. 0249C]

“And he was moved with compassion, and he ran and fell upon his neck.” The Father did not abandon his only-begotten Son, in whom he ran and descended even to our distant pilgrimage, because “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself” (2 Corinthians 5). The Lord himself says: “The Father, remaining in me, does his works” (John 14).

What does it mean to fall upon his neck except to bend and humble his arm in an embrace? And to whom was the Lord’s arm revealed? Surely to our Lord Jesus Christ.

“And he kissed him.” To be consoled by the word of God’s grace toward the hope of pardon for sins is, after a long journey, to receive from the father the kiss of love upon one’s return. [Col. 0249D]

“And the son said to him: ‘Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you; I am no longer worthy to be called your son.’” Now, having been established in the Church, he begins to confess his sins.
