He does not say everything he had promised to say, but stops at: “I am no longer worthy to be called your son.”

For he desires that, by grace, what he confesses himself unworthy of by his merits should be granted to him. He did not add what he had conceived before and had said: “Make me like one of your hired servants.” When he had no bread, he had desired even to be a hired servant; after the kiss of his most noble father, he now disdains this.

For he understood that there is no small distance between a son, a hired servant, and a slave. A slave is one who still restrains himself from vices through fear of Gehenna or of present laws. A hired servant is one who acts through hope and desire for the heavenly kingdom. A son is one who acts through affection for the good itself and love of the virtues. [Col. 0250A]

The blessed Apostle, summing up the whole substance of salvation in the perfection of these three virtues, says: “Now faith, hope, and love remain, these three; but the greatest of these is love” (1 Corinthians 13).

Faith is what, through fear of future judgment and punishment, causes us to avoid the contagion of vices. Hope calls our mind away from present things and causes it to despise all bodily pleasures in expectation of heavenly rewards. Love succeeds by directing us toward love of Christ and toward the fruit of spiritual virtues, kindling the mind; it causes us to detest with complete hatred whatever is contrary to them. [Col. 0250B]

Thus this prodigal, after returning to himself, feared the punishment of dreadful hunger. Having become like a slave, as it were, he also desired the status of a hired servant, already thinking about a wage. But his father ran to him and, unwilling merely to grant lesser things, passed him without delay through both stages and restored him to his former dignity as a son. He made him think not about the wage of a hireling but about the inheritance of a parent.

“But the father said to his servants: ‘Quickly bring out the first robe and put it on him.’” The first robe is the garment of innocence that the created human being received but lost after being misled. After the transgression, he recognized that he was naked and, having lost the glory of immortality, took on a garment of skin—that is, mortality. [Col. 0250C]

The servants who bring it out are the preachers of reconciliation. They bring out the first robe when they assert that mortal and earthly human beings will be so exalted that they will become not only fellow citizens of the angels but also heirs of God and coheirs of Christ.

“And put a ring on his hand and shoes on his feet.” The ring is either the seal of sincere faith, by which all the promises are stamped with a firm impression upon the hearts of believers, or the pledge of those nuptials by which the Church is betrothed.

The ring is rightly placed on the hand, so that faith may shine through works and works may be strengthened through faith. The shoes on the feet signify the duty of evangelizing, so that the course of the mind, directed toward heavenly things, may be preserved unharmed and clean from the pollution of earthly matters; fortified by the examples of those who came before, it may walk securely over serpents and scorpions. [Col. 0250D]

The hands and feet, therefore—that is, works—are adorned: the hands, so that we may live rightly; the feet, so that we may hasten toward eternal joys. “For here we have no lasting city, but we seek the one that is to come” (Hebrews 13).

“And bring the fattened calf and kill it.” The fattened calf is the same Lord, but according to the flesh. He is rightly called fattened, because his flesh has been suffused by God with the highest spiritual power, so that it is sufficient for the salvation of the whole world and can send up to God, as a pleasing fragrance, the scent of sacrifice and intercede for all.

To bring the calf and kill it means to preach Christ and make known his death. For then he is, as it were, freshly killed for each one of us when that person believes that he was killed. His flesh is eaten when the mystery of his Passion is received by the mouth for cleansing and contemplated in the heart for imitation. [Col. 0251A]

“And let us eat and celebrate, because this son of mine was dead and has come to life again; he was lost and has been found.” It is not only the son who came to life again and was found who eats and celebrates. The father and his servants also feast upon the flesh of the holy calf that was killed for the son. The father’s food is our salvation, and the father’s joy is the remission of our sins—not only the Father’s, but also the Son’s and the Holy Spirit’s. For just as there is one will and one operation in the divinity, so there is one delight of the holy and undivided Trinity.

Therefore blessed Abraham, receiving three angelic guests (Genesis 18), is read to have killed and offered a tender and choice calf, together with milk, bread, and butter, for a feast. Whoever desires to refresh—that is, gladden—the blessed Trinity through the duties of right devotion must also celebrate, with the sincerity of a devout confession, the death in the flesh of the only-begotten Son of God, who is one, in the same person of the Trinity. [Col. 0251B]

It should be noted that first the robe, then the ring, then the shoes are provided, and only afterward is the calf sacrificed. For unless a person has put on the hope of immortality, unless he has fortified his works with the ring of faith, and unless he has proclaimed that faith by devout confession, he cannot take part in the heavenly sacraments.

“And they began to celebrate.” These banquets and festivities are now celebrated throughout the world, as the Church has spread and been extended. For that calf is both offered to the Father in the Lord’s body and blood and feeds the entire household. [Col. 0251C]

“Now his elder son was in the field.” The elder son is the people of Israel. Although he did not go away to a distant region, he is nevertheless said to have remained not at home but in the field. For that people neither deserted the Creator to worship idols nor penetrated into the interior meaning of the Law it had received. Content only with guarding the letter, it was accustomed both to perform and to hope for external and earthly things, hearing through the Prophet: “If you are willing and obey me, you shall eat the good things of the land” (Isaiah 1).

“And when he came and drew near to the house, he heard symphony and chorus.” The son approaches the house when that people—among whichever Israelites possess understanding, for many such people have been found and are often found among them—rejects the servile labor of works and considers, from those same Scriptures, the freedom of the Church. [Col. 0251D]

He hears symphony and chorus: those filled with the Spirit preaching the Gospel in harmonious voices. To them it was said (1 Corinthians 1): “I beseech you, brothers, that you all say the same thing, and that the soul and heart of those living in harmony be one in the praises of God.”

“And he called one of the servants and asked what these things meant.” He calls one of the servants when he takes up one of the prophets to read, and, searching in him, asks in a certain manner why these celebrations are taking place in the Church, celebrations in which he does not see himself included. The father’s servant, the prophet, answers him:

“‘Your brother has come, and your father has killed the [Col. 0252A] fattened calf, because he has received him back safe.’” Your brother was at the ends of the earth; therefore there is greater rejoicing, singing, and a new song to the Lord, because his praise comes from the ends of the earth. And for the sake of the one who was absent, the one concerning whom it was said, “May your burnt offering be made fat” (Psalm 20), was killed.

“Now he became angry and did not want to go in. Therefore his father went out and began to plead with him.”

He becomes angry even now, and still does not wish to enter. When, therefore, the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, his father will go out at the appointed time, so that all Israel also may be saved. On the part of Israel from which blindness has come, there has been something like an absence in the field, until the fullness of the younger son—those who had long been established in the idolatry of the Gentiles and have now been brought back to the father—should enter to eat the fattened calf. For one day the Jews’ open calling to the salvation of the Gospel will come. This manifest calling he calls the father’s going out, to plead with the elder son.

“But he answered and said to his father: Behold, for so many years I have served you, and I have never transgressed your command.”

The question arises how that people can be said never to have transgressed God’s command. The answer readily presents itself: the statement is not about every command, but chiefly about one of the most necessary, since they were commanded to worship no other God. Nor is this son understood to represent all Israelites, but those among them who never turned from the one God to idols. Although, like a son placed in the field, he desired earthly things, he nevertheless desired those goods from the one God. This is also confirmed by the testimony of his own father, when he says: “You are always with me.” He does not rebuke him as though he were lying; rather, approving his perseverance, he invites him to the perfection of a better and more joyful rejoicing.

“And you have never given me a young goat, so that I might feast with my friends.”

A sinner is surely customarily signified by the name “young goat,” but far be it from me to understand the Antichrist here. For it is absurd that the one to whom it is said, “You are always with me,” should have wished from his father to believe in the Antichrist; nor is it at all permissible to understand this son as one of those Jews who will believe in the Antichrist. How would he feast upon that young goat if it were the Antichrist, when he would not believe in him? Or, if feasting upon the slaughter of the young goat means rejoicing in the destruction of the Antichrist, how does the son whom the father receives say that this was not granted to him, when all the sons of God will rejoice in the condemnation of that adversary?

Clearly, then, he complains that the Lord himself was denied to him for feasting, while he regarded Him as a sinner. For when the Lord appeared to that people as a young goat—that is, when they considered Him a violator of the Sabbath and a profaner of the Law—he did not deserve to rejoice in His feasts. Thus, what he says, “You have never given me a young goat, so that I might feast with my friends,” amounts to this: “You have never given me for feasting the one who appeared to me to be a young goat”; by not granting Him to me, You denied Him to me precisely because He appeared to me as a young goat.

As for his saying, “with my friends,” this may be understood either as referring to the leaders together with the people, or to the people of Jerusalem together with the other peoples of the Jews.

“But after this son of yours, who has devoured his substance with prostitutes, came, you slaughtered for him the fattened calf.”

The prostitutes are the superstitions of the Gentiles. To squander one’s substance with them is, after abandoning the one marriage-bond of the true God, to fornicate with a multitude of demons through the most shameful desire.

“But he said to him: Son, you are always with me, and everything that is mine is yours. But it was necessary to feast and rejoice, because this brother of yours was dead and has come to life; he had perished and has been found.”

When he says, “Everything that is mine is yours,” this should not be understood as though the brothers also were not included, so that he would suffer distress as though in an earthly inheritance. How could everything belong to the elder if the younger also has his share? Everything is possessed by perfected, purified, and already immortal sons in such a way that each thing belongs to everyone and everything belongs to each one. For just as desire holds nothing without distress, so love holds nothing with distress.

When, therefore, we have obtained that blessedness, what is above will be ours for contemplation; what is equal will be ours for fellowship; and what is below will be ours for dominion. If anyone is troubled by how Truth, praying to the Father, can say, “Everything that is mine is yours, and what is yours is mine” (John XVII), which seems to sound much like what is said here to the Son, “Everything that is mine is yours,” let him know that everything belonging to the Father belongs to the only-begotten Son. Through this He is also God himself, born from the Father and equal to the Father.

For when speaking of the Holy Spirit He likewise says, “Everything that the Father has is mine” (John XVI). The Holy Spirit was not going to receive these things from the creature, which is subject to the Father, and the Son was not going to receive them from the creature when He says, “He will take from what is mine”; rather, He was to receive them from the Father, from whom the Spirit proceeds and from whom the Son is born.

Whether, then, you wish to refer these two sons to the two peoples, or, as some prefer, to any two persons—the penitent and the righteous, or the one who appeared righteous to himself—the elder should rejoice with the younger, because his brother was dead and has come to life; he had perished and has been found.

## HOMILY XLII. THE THIRD SUNDAY IN LENT.

[Col. 0253D] (Luke XI.) “At that time, Jesus was casting out a demon, and it was mute. And when He had cast out the demon, the mute man spoke, and the crowds marveled,” and so forth.

Since the Evangelist was going to say that the Lord had cast a demon out of a man, he rightly placed at the beginning of this reading a word by which he might express the essence of the Divinity, saying: “Jesus was casting out a demon.” For he did not say “was,” in the sense of having come to be, because being belongs to God alone: to remain eternal and unchangeable, for whom past things do not pass away and future things do not follow, but who always remains eternally, as He himself said to Moses: “I am who I am” (Exodus III). And: “You shall say to the children of Israel, ‘He who is has sent me to you’” (ibid.). And again: “I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob” (ibid.). And in the Apocalypse: “I am Alpha and Omega” (Apocalypse I). And in the Gospel: “Amen, amen, I say to you, before Abraham came to be, I am” (John VIII).

Therefore, to show that the Son of God is always with the Father, he said “was,” and not “came to be.”

According to Matthew, this demoniac was not only mute but also blind, and is said to have been wondrously healed by God, so that he both spoke and saw. Here we should note that in one and the same man the Lord performed three miracles together: the blind man sees, the mute man speaks, and the man possessed by a demon is delivered.

Allegorically, however, he signifies the human race, which then subjected itself to its possessor, the devil, when, persuaded by the devil, it despised God its Creator. It lost the dignity of seeing God when it opened its eyes to desire the forbidden tree, as it is written: “The woman saw that the tree was beautiful to look upon and pleasing in appearance; she took and ate, and gave some to her husband, who ate, and the eyes of both were opened” (Genesis II).

It likewise lost speech, because after subjecting itself to sin it ceased from the praise of God. “For,” as Scripture says, “praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner” (Ecclesiasticus XV).

But when the Lord came into the world, this demoniac was healed. For after God united human nature to Himself, He drove the powers of unclean spirits from human hearts, as He himself said: “Now is the hour for the ruler of this world to be cast out” (John XII).

Then he received again the faculty of seeing God, when he began to behold Him through faith, from whose vision he had withdrawn himself by sinning. The prophecy was fulfilled which says: “The people who sat in darkness saw a great light; for those dwelling in the land and shadow of death, light has arisen” (Isaiah IX). Hence the apostle Paul says to believers: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Ephesians V).

He likewise received speech again when the human race opened mouths that had previously been silent to confess God, saying with the Psalmist: “Lord, open my lips” (Psalm L). And with Isaiah: “The Lord God has given me a learned tongue” (Isaiah L).

He began not only to praise God but also to detest the worshipers of idols, saying with the Psalmist: “Let all who worship carved images be confounded, those who glory in their idols” (Psalm XCVI)—“for all the gods of the nations are demons, but the Lord made the heavens” (Psalm XCV). And with Jeremiah: “Let the gods who did not make heaven and earth perish from heaven and from among those who are under heaven” (Jeremiah X).

Hence it is rightly added: “And when He had cast out the demon, the mute man spoke, and the crowds marveled.”

From this we can understand that the demons who possessed him had come from outside and dwelt within him. He had lost externally the faculty of seeing and speaking, because as soon as the demon departed he recovered sight and speech, so that the crowds marveled.

According to the anagogical, that is, higher, sense, the crowds who marveled are to be understood as unclean spirits. Seeing the human race freed from their power and enlightened, they were terrified by fear and amazement together. Hence, through the possessed man, they said: “What have you to do with us, Son of God? Have you come to torment us before the time?” (Matthew VIII).

But because where the good person advances the evil person becomes worse, it is rightly added:

“But some of them said.”

These words should not be thought to have been spoken by some of the crowd, but by the scribes and Pharisees, who followed God for the purpose of criticizing Him and made these accusations, as the other Evangelists testify. While the crowds everywhere marveled at the Lord’s signs, they, filled with envy, tried by sinister interpretation to distort what they could not deny, so that they might withdraw the simpler people from belief in Him.

Therefore, seeing the mute and blind demoniac healed, they said, while the crowds marveled: “He casts out demons by Beelzebub, the prince of demons.”

As some say, the name was formed from Beel, which is Baal, and from this Beelzebub was compounded. For Beelzebub was the idol Baal, who was called the god of Accaron. King Ochozias sent messengers to him to inquire whether he would recover from his illness or not. The prophet Elijah met them and said (IV Kings I): “Is there no God in Israel, that you are going to consult Beelzebub, the god of Accaron? Therefore say to the man who sent you: ‘From the bed to which you have gone, you shall not come down, but you shall surely die.’”

The transgression associated with this idol was discovered in ancient times. For, as some report, there was a man named Beel, the father of King Ninus, who built the city of Nineveh. After Beel died, his son erected a statue of him and commanded his subjects to worship it, claiming that his father had been transferred among the gods. From that time the most wicked custom grew up, so that foolish people offered idols the honor due to God.

Later he was called Beelphegor because he was worshiped by many after being set up on Mount Phegor, which was on the borders of Midian. There the Israelites who had departed from Egypt transgressed at Balaam’s instigation, when, as the Psalmist says: “They were initiated into Beelphegor and ate the sacrifices of the dead” (Psalm CV).

In the time of the Judges he was called Baalberith, that is, “god of the covenant,” because the children of Israel entered into a covenant with him, abandoning the God of their fathers. It was his custom, especially in the mountains rather than in the valleys, to give an answer. Hence he was also called the god of the mountains. Thus the Syrians, defeated by Israel and supposing that he was worshiped by them, said (III Kings XX): “Their gods are gods of the mountains, and therefore we cannot overcome them.”

Worshiping the image of this idol, they set it up near Jerusalem in the valley of Topheth, in a most pleasant place, where they offered it not only incense and sacrifices but also their sons and daughters, transferring them to it as sacrifices through fire. Manasseh, that most cruel murderer of his own children, is said to have done this.

Because of this place the Lord very often issued terrible threats through the prophets, especially through Jeremiah, saying: “They have placed their abominations in the house in which my name was invoked, and they have defiled it. And they built the high place of Topheth, which is in the valley of the son of Ennon, to burn their sons and daughters in fire—things which I did not command and which never entered my heart. Therefore, behold, days are coming, says the Lord, and it shall no longer be called Topheth or the valley of the son of Ennon, but the valley of slaughter. And they shall bury in Topheth, because there will be no place for burial on account of the multitude of corpses. And the corpses of this people shall be food for the birds of the air and the beasts of the earth, and there shall be no one to drive them away” (Jeremiah VII)—that is, to defend them.

Because of the shedding of blood that frequently occurred there, many flies gathered in the same place. Hence an appropriate name was given to it: Beelzebub, that is, “prince of flies,” or “the one who has flies.” For *zebub* means “fly.”

Some have thought that the end of this name should be written with *d* or *l*, reading *Beelzebul*, and asserting that the original author of this idol was Zebul, the servant of Achimelech, who killed his seventy brothers upon one stone. But the interpretation of the name itself shows that it should be written with no other letter than *b*, because, as we said above, Beelzebub means “prince of flies.”

Therefore, because the scribes and Pharisees could not deny the miracle performed by the Lord, they attempted to obscure it by saying that it had been accomplished by the power of this demon. Thus, blaspheming, they said: “He casts out demons by Beelzebub, the prince of demons.”

“And others, tempting Him, were seeking from Him a sign from heaven.”

It is useless for those who refuse to believe what they see with their eyes to seek signs concerning invisible things. They did not want to believe that the blind man had been made to see and the mute man to speak by God, so they turned to crafty arguments, seeking a sign from heaven—for example, that He should cause thunder to flash from heaven after the manner of Samuel, or bring down fire from heaven in the likeness of Elijah.

If He had done this, they would certainly have slandered that as well, saying that it had not been done by God but had resulted from hidden disturbances of the air. They would even have claimed that Pharaoh’s magicians in Egypt had performed many signs from heaven.

It was not impossible for God to show a sign from heaven; rather, they were unworthy to see a sign from heaven who, loving the earth, dared to tempt the King of heaven. To them that saying is more appropriately directed in which the Lord says: “This evil and adulterous generation seeks a sign, and no sign will be given to it except the sign of the prophet Jonah.”

Those called hypocrites also appear to resemble these people, because those who seek God falsely do not find Him. For “salvation is far from sinners” (Psalm CXVIII), and “He is near to all who call upon Him” (Psalm CXLIV)—not in pretense, but in truth.

“But He, when He saw their thoughts, said.”

Because He knew that they did not wish to believe external signs, He immediately answered their thoughts, so that at least in this way they might be compelled to believe that He possessed Divinity, since He saw the secrets of the heart. It was as though He said: “By the same majesty by which I look upon the thoughts of the heart, I can also display signs from heaven.”

For it belongs to the Lord alone to see the thoughts of the heart, as Scripture says: “You alone, O God, know the hearts of the children of men” (II Chronicles VI). And again: “A human being sees what is on the face, but God sees what is in the heart.”

“Every kingdom divided against itself will be desolated, and house will fall upon house.”

According to the literal sense, this is so. For if a kingdom is divided against itself, so that the king thinks one thing, the leaders another, the commanders another, and the soldiers another, it suffers desolation. Likewise, if a household is divided, so that the husband thinks one thing, the wife another, the children another, the parents another, the servants another, and the masters another, it too will certainly suffer ruin.

A house is said to fall upon a house when the father’s soul is stirred against the son and the son’s against the father, and similarly in the remaining relationships. By this comparison the Lord warns His tempters to withdraw from the kingdom of the devil, which they recognize cannot stand for long when divided against itself.

It was as though He said: “If every kingdom divided against itself cannot stand—a fact you cannot deny in any way—withdraw as quickly as possible from the kingdom of the devil, which you cannot doubt will soon fall.”

The devil’s kingdom is in those over whom he reigns through sin. Although it is united in an evil will, it is nevertheless divided in its activity. One commits adultery, another murder, another theft, another sacrilege; yet all proceed from the one root of an evil will.

“But if Satan also is divided against himself, how will his kingdom stand, because you say that I cast out demons by Beelzebub?”

In these words the Lord, by a most prudent syllogism, closes off His tempters on every side, so that they could not find a suitable answer. We read that He did this not only here but frequently in many other places, as when they came to Him saying: “Tell us, by what authority do you do these things?” And He said to them: “You also tell me one word, and I will tell you by what authority I do these things” (Matthew XXI). If you do not do this, neither will I tell you by what authority I do these things.

“The baptism of John—where was it from, from heaven or from human beings?” But they considered among themselves, saying: “If we say, ‘From heaven,’ He will say to us, ‘Why then did you not receive it?’ If we say, ‘From human beings,’ the crowd, which was baptized by John, will stone us.” And, finding nothing to say, they were silent.

So also here: because they did not wish to confess that Christ cast out demons by the power of God, and could not affirm that Satan cast out Satan, and found no free response, the mouths of those speaking wickedness were stopped. Therefore, “they will be delivered into the hands of the sword, and they will become the portions of foxes” (Psalm LXII).

To expose their malice He added further, saying:

“If I cast out demons by Beelzebub, by whom do your sons cast them out?”

He calls their disciples their sons, since they were undoubtedly born from their lineage. He had already given them power to drive out demons and to tread upon every power of the enemy, saying: “In my name cure the sick, cleanse lepers, enlighten the blind, cast out demons. You have received without payment; give without payment” (Matthew XX).

It was as though He said: “If my disciples—your sons, certainly—cast out demons in my name, why do you attribute the same work in me to Beelzebub, the prince of demons, and not to God?”

“Therefore they themselves will be your judges.”

That is, my disciples, the weak and contemptible things of the world that I chose in order to confound the strong, who attribute the healing of demons to God and not to Beelzebub, “will be your judges”—namely, “when the Son of Man comes and sits upon the throne of His majesty, they too will sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matthew XIX).

Or certainly He calls their sons exorcists, who according to ancient custom existed among that same people. Through their invocations or adjurations demons were driven from human beings. Josephus, the historian of the Hebrews, bears witness to this. In his ancient books, among the other things he recalled about Solomon’s wisdom, he added the following:

“The Lord granted Solomon that he should also cast out demons, and he established incantations by which illnesses are customarily alleviated. This treatment is recognized to remain very powerful among us to the present day. For I myself saw a certain Eleazar, one of our people, in the presence of Vespasian and Titus and another army assembled with them, treating those who were tormented by demons.

“The method of treatment was as follows. He placed beneath the nostrils of the man tormented by the demon a ring whose base contained a seal displayed by Solomon, and the man immediately fell down. Then Eleazar adjured the demon by the oath of Solomon, reciting the incantations that Solomon had composed over it, saying: ‘Thereupon, through the nostrils of the man, he drew out the demon.’ And, adjuring and charging it not to return to him again, he bore witness to this.

“To demonstrate that Eleazar possessed this power, he placed in the middle a basin full of water, or some other vessel, and commanded the demon, when it had departed from the man, to overturn it, giving everyone proof that it had left the man. When this happened, they marveled at Solomon’s wisdom.”

In comparison with these exorcists, therefore, the Lord constrains the scribes and Pharisees, saying: “If I cast out demons by Beelzebub, by whom do your sons cast them out?” It was as though He said: “If the expulsion performed by exorcists is attributed to God and not to demons, why does the same work in me not receive the same reverence?”

“Therefore they themselves will be your judges”—not by authority, but by comparison. Just as the queen of the South, coming from the ends of the earth to hear Solomon’s wisdom, will judge those who refused to hear Christ, who is greater than Solomon; and just as the Ninevites, repenting at the preaching of Jonah, will judge those who refused to hear the Savior, who is greater than Jonah, so these exorcists, who attributed the healing of demons to God, are said to judge those who attributed the healing of demons to Beelzebub and not to God.

“But if I cast out demons by the finger of God, surely the kingdom of God has come upon you.”

The finger of God is understood to be the Holy Spirit, as the Evangelist Matthew makes clearer when he says: “But if I cast out demons by the Spirit” (Matthew XII).

The Holy Spirit is beautifully represented by the finger of God, because just as we perform or grasp something with our fingers, so the Father and the Son perform all things through the Holy Spirit. The Psalmist says: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the spirit of His mouth all their power” (Psalm XXXII).

By this finger the tablets of the Testament were written. Concerning this finger the magicians in Egypt, when defeated, also said: “This is the finger of God.” The prophet admired its most beautiful operation when he said: “For I shall see Your heavens, the works of Your fingers” (Psalm VIII).

Or certainly the Holy Spirit is rightly understood by the finger of God because, just as we have no other limbs in which we possess such division as in the fingers, so the gifts of the Holy Spirit are diverse according to the qualities of those who receive them. The Apostle bears witness, saying: “To one is given through the Spirit a word of wisdom; to another a word of knowledge according to the same Spirit; to another faith in the same Spirit; to another the grace of healings in one Spirit; to another the working of miracles; to another prophecy; to another the discernment of spirits; to another kinds of tongues; to another the interpretation of words. But one and the same Spirit works all these things, distributing to each one as He wills” (I Corinthians XII).

When He says that the kingdom of God has come upon them, He may be speaking of Himself, as He says elsewhere: “The kingdom of God is within you” (Luke XVII). Or He wishes that judgment of discernment to be understood by which the devout are distinguished from the impious and the righteous from the wicked.

After silencing the plots of the accusers, who said that He cast out demons by Beelzebub, He speaks freely of His victory and likewise of the expulsion of demons, adding:

“When a strong man, armed, guards his courtyard, the things he possesses are at peace.”

By the strong man armed He means the devil, whose courtyard was the world, which he had subjected to himself through the transgression of the first man. While the strong man guarded it, everything he possessed was at peace, because before the Lord’s coming no one was so righteous that he could resist him perfectly and remove the human race from his power.

For this work the coming of the One who was to enter the world without sin was awaited. Concerning Him it is added:

“But when one stronger than he comes upon him and conquers him.”

The stronger one is the Lord Jesus Christ, of whom the Psalmist sang: “The Lord is strong and powerful, the Lord powerful in battle” (Psalm XXIII).

He alone conquered the devil, since the ancient enemy could find no trace of sin in Him. He himself says in the Gospel: “The ruler of this world is coming, and he has nothing in me” (John XIV).

Because, therefore, the devil sharpened the weapons of persecution against Him who was without sin, he rightly lost his power over sinners, the Lord saying: “Now is the hour for the ruler of this world to be cast out” (John XII). And again in the Gospel: “I saw Satan falling from heaven like lightning” (Luke XII).

The Lord did not come merely to free one person from a demon, but also to drive his power out of the entire human race. Hence it is added:

“He will take away all his armor in which he trusted.”

The devil’s armor is vices and sins, such as the Apostle lists: “The works of the flesh are manifest: fornication, impurity, licentiousness, the service of idols, sorcery, enmities, disputes, rivalries, anger, quarrels, dissensions, factions, envy, murders, drunkenness, revelries, and things like these. Those who do such things will not obtain the kingdom of God” (Galatians V).

But the Lord took away the devil’s armor when He changed vices into virtues in converted people, so that in place of pride they loved humility, in place of licentiousness chastity, and in place of greed generosity.

Or otherwise: the devil’s armor was kings and rulers, in whom he trusted as though in weapons, because as long as he held the leaders in his power, he did not fear that he could easily lose their subjects. The Lord took this armor from him when He converted not only subjects but also emperors, kings, and rulers to His faith.

How completely the Lord had triumphed over the ancient enemy is also shown when it is added:

“And he will distribute his spoils.”

It belongs to the victor to distribute spoils. The spoils were those same human beings whom the devil, like a most violent robber, had carried off from paradise. The Lord distributes them when He sends His disciples into every part of the world for the purpose of winning human beings.

Just as a king, joyful after the triumph of victory, divides spoils among his soldiers, so the Lord distributed the regions of the world to His disciples for preaching: to Peter and Paul, Rome; to Andrew, Achaia; to James, Judea; to John, Asia; to Philip, Ethiopia; to Bartholomew, India; and the same should be understood of the others.

“Whoever is not with me is against me, and whoever does not gather with me scatters.”

Although this saying can be understood of the Jews and heretics, it applies especially to the devil, who from the beginning was a thief and a liar and did not stand in the truth. Because he departed from God, he was against Him—that is, contrary to His will. The Apostle bears witness: “What agreement is there between Christ and Belial? Or what share does a believer have with an unbeliever? Or what fellowship does light have with darkness?” (II Corinthians VI.) None.

For the things the Lord commands and the devil suggests are contrary to and different from one another. The Lord commands humility; the devil suggests pride. The Lord commands chastity; the devil suggests licentiousness. The Lord commands concord; the devil suggests discord.

And because he does not gather with Him, he scatters, as it is said elsewhere of him under the figure of a wolf: “The wolf snatches and scatters the sheep” (John X).

“When the unclean spirit has gone out from a person, he wanders through dry and waterless places.”

That this comparison pertains especially to the Jewish people the Evangelist Matthew clearly declares, when, after the parable has ended, he records that the Lord said: “So will it also be with this most wicked generation” (Matthew XII).

There is no doubt that when the Jews worshiped the Lord and observed the precepts of the Law, the unclean spirit went out from them. He wanders through dry and waterless places—that is, through deserts and the hearts of unbelievers, who were dry because they lacked the richness of the Holy Spirit and waterless because they were strangers to the flood of baptism.

But when, at the Lord’s coming into the world, the Gentiles had driven the unclean spirit from themselves through the water of baptism and the grace of the Holy Spirit, “seeking rest and not finding it, he says: ‘I will return to my house from which I came.’” This means: “I will return to the Jews, whom I left.”

“And when he has come, he finds it swept with brooms and adorned.”

For Matthew says: “He finds it empty, swept with brooms, and adorned” (Matthew XII).

The house of the Jews was empty because it did not have Christ as its guest, as the Lord says: “Behold, your house will be left to you desolate” (Matthew XXIII).

“Swept with brooms”: by circumcision and carnal ceremonies.

“Adorned”: by the superstitions of the scribes and Pharisees.

“Then he goes and takes with him seven other spirits more wicked than himself, and entering, they dwell there.”

The house that he finds empty is invaded not only by him who had left it, but he also takes with him seven other spirits more wicked than himself—that is, the seven principal vices: pride, gluttony, fornication, greed, anger, sadness, and vainglory.

For just as the number seven, when used in a good sense, signifies all the virtues given to the faithful through the grace of the Holy Spirit, so, when used in an evil sense, it signifies all the vices opposed to the virtues.

“And the final state of that person becomes worse than the first.”

For the Jews are now much worse than they were before they received the Law: they have been abandoned by God, left without Law and priesthood, scattered from nation to nation and from kingdom to kingdom, to another people.

But we must take great care lest perhaps the vices of the Jews pass over to us. He says: “When the unclean spirit has gone out from a person.” For the whole Catholic Church believes that through the water of baptism and the grace of the Holy Spirit, after all sins have been forgiven, the power of the demon is excluded.

Then he wanders through dry and waterless places—that is, testing the hearts of other Christians who are dry through abstinence and waterless because they are strangers to the flow of lust. Seeking rest in such people, he does not find it, because he flees chaste and pure minds and seeks dark and lustful ones.

Concerning this the Lord says to blessed Job: “He sleeps under the shade, in the secrecy of the reed, in moist places” (Job XL).

But when he has been driven out by zeal for divine love, he says: “I will return to my house from which I came.” Then he begins to test in various ways the mind of the person whom he had abandoned through baptism.

But because there are many lukewarm Christians, it is rightly added concerning that same house: “And when he has come, he finds it empty, swept with brooms, and adorned.”

“Empty”: that is, sluggish and inactive in good works.

“Swept with brooms”: that is, washed from past sins through baptism.

“Adorned”: outwardly clothed in Christianity but with simulated virtues.

“Then he goes and takes with him seven other spirits more wicked than himself, and entering, they dwell there.”

It often happens that one whom before baptism he held only through original sin, afterward he possesses through many vices.

“And the final state of that person becomes worse than the first.”

For, as the apostle Peter says concerning such people: “It would have been better for them not to have known the way of truth than, after knowing it, to turn back” (II Peter II).

The Lord says of such people in the Gospel: “No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God” (Luke IX).

For the punishment owed to one who sins greatly is not equal to that owed to one who sins little, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “The servant who knew his master’s will and did not do it will deservedly be beaten with many blows” (Luke XII).

“Now it happened that, as He was saying these things, a certain woman from the crowd raised her voice and said.”

This woman is shown to possess great devotion. Among crowds of malicious, critical, and slanderous people, she confessed with believing lips the faith in the Lord’s incarnation that she had conceived in her heart, saying: “Blessed is the womb that bore you, and the breasts that nursed you.”

In these words she not only confounds the present accusers who said that He cast out demons by Beelzebub, but also destroys the future error of those who would say that the Lord had not assumed true flesh from the Virgin Mary.

For if He was carried in a womb and nursed at breasts, it is plainly evident that He received flesh consubstantial with that of His mother—especially since, according to the physicians, in the womb of a pregnant woman the fluid of blood and milk flows from one source: blood, from which the human being is formed; milk, by which he is nourished.

Therefore, if the Lord Jesus Christ, like other human beings, sucked milk and was nourished, He certainly assumed true flesh, not an appearance of flesh, as the apostle Paul says: “Who was made for Him from the seed of David according to the flesh” (Romans I).

Matthew says of Him at the beginning of his Gospel: “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham.”

Spiritually, however, this woman signifies the holy Church, which among crowds of Jews, pagans, and heretics confesses the Lord Christ with a believing voice. By her voice the womb of the Virgin Mary is truly proclaimed blessed (Luke I), for she deserved to bear the Redeemer of the whole world, as she herself says concerning herself: “From now on all generations will call me blessed.”

And Elizabeth says: “Blessed are you because you believed.”

He confirms the woman’s words when He adds:

“Rather, blessed are those who hear the word of God and keep it.” As though he had said: According to your judgment, that womb is blessed above all which bore me; but all those also are blessed who hear the word of God and keep it. Whoever delights in Mary’s blessedness should gladly hear the word of God and keep it; [Col. 0262D] he will be blessed. Therefore, whoever willingly hears the word of God conceives Christ; but if he carries it out in his deeds, he gives birth to Christ. Hence, when someone said to the Lord (Matt. XII), “Behold, your mother and your brothers are standing outside, seeking you,” he replied: “Whoever does the will of my Father is my brother, sister, and mother.” For everyone who, hearing the word of God, fulfills it, conceives and gives birth to Christ daily. And he spiritually carries the one whom Mary’s womb carried bodily.

He rightly added “and keep it” after saying “Blessed are those who hear the word of God,” because hearing the word of God is not enough to attain eternal blessedness unless each person strives to keep it, as the Lord says to his disciples: [Col. 0263A] “You know these things; blessed are you if you do them” (John XIII). Hence, when John had said in the Apocalypse, “Blessed is the one who hears the words of the prophecy of this book,” he added, “and keeps what is written in it” (Rev. I). For, as the Apostle says, it is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but the doers of the law will be justified (Rom. I). To hear and not to do belongs more to defiance than to blessedness. Hence James says: “For the one who knows the good and does not do it, for him it is sin” (James IV). And James also says: “Be doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving yourselves. For if anyone is a hearer of the word and not a doer, he will be compared to a man observing the face of his birth in a mirror. For he observed himself and went away, and immediately forgot what he was like. But whoever has looked closely into the law of perfect freedom and has remained in it—not becoming a forgetful hearer, but a doer of the work—this person will be blessed in his deed” (James I).

## HOMILY XLIII. MONDAY AFTER OCULI

(Luke IV.) “At that time the Pharisees said to Jesus: ‘How many things we have heard have been done,’” and so forth.

Their insane unbelief nevertheless confesses, though unknowingly, a sound faith when it calls Christ the Lord a craftsman and names him a physician. For he is truly a craftsman, because “all things were made through him” (John I); and a physician, because all things in heaven and on earth have been restored through him. As he testifies concerning himself: “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick” (Mark II).

And since we have said with what instrument he fashions, let us also say by what method he heals. “Passing by, he saw a man blind from birth, spat on the ground, made mud from the spittle, smeared it over his eyes, and said to him: ‘Go and wash in the pool of Siloam,’ which is interpreted as ‘Sent.’ He went, therefore, and washed, and came back seeing” (John IX).

Recognize, then, the manner of this great medicine, and rejoice, because through it you have deserved to be illumined. The mud from the earth is Christ’s flesh. The spittle from the head is his divinity, because God is Christ’s head. The spittle mixed with mud illumines us when we are baptized in the pool of Siloam, because “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we saw his glory” (John I), which previously, because darkness barred the way, we could not grasp.

[Col. 0263D] Therefore, through Christ the craftsman you were created so that you might exist. Through Christ the physician you were recreated so that, after your wounds, you might be healthy—although his fellow citizens, mocking him, urge him to cure himself, that is, to perform mighty deeds in his own homeland. Yet another Evangelist rightly excuses him, because he could not perform a mighty deed there, except that he healed a few sick people by laying hands on them; and he marveled because of their unbelief, lest perhaps anyone should think that affection for one’s homeland ought to be weaker in us. He loved his fellow citizens, but they themselves freely deprived themselves of love and of their homeland.

“He said: ‘Amen, I say to you, no prophet is accepted in his own homeland.’” That the Lord Christ is called a prophet in Scripture is also testified by Moses, who says: “The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers, like me; you shall listen to him” (Deut. XVIII).

Not only he, who is the head and Lord of the prophets, but also Elijah, Jeremiah, and the other lesser prophets were held in lower esteem in their homeland than in foreign regions, because it is almost natural for citizens always to envy their fellow citizens. They do not consider the present works of the man, but remember his fragile infancy, as though they themselves had not also passed through the same stages of life to reach maturity.

“‘Truly I say to you, there were many widows in Israel in the days of Elijah, when heaven was shut for three years and six months, when a great famine occurred in the land; and Elijah was sent to none of them except to a widow in Sarepta of Sidon.’”

He says: This—that I withdraw divine benefits from disdainful fellow citizens—does not conflict with the deeds of the prophets. For just as, when famine once oppressed the whole land, no one was found in Judea worthy of Elijah’s hospitality, but a widow from a foreign people was sought, who on account of her faith deserved to be visited by so great a prophet; and just as, although many lepers were present there, only Naaman the Syrian, because he had sought healing devoutly, deserved to be cured by the prophet Elisha—so you too will be deprived of the heavenly gift for no other reason than envy and unbelief.

If you examine the deeds of the prophets allegorically as well, you will certainly find that, in his homeland, from which he was not received because of unbelief, the Lord denounced the pride of the Jews. By the name Capernaum, which is interpreted as “field of consolation,” he proclaimed the salvation of the nations; there, every day, greater signs are brought about through the apostles and their successors, not so much in the healing of bodies as in the healing of souls.

Thus, the widow to whom Elijah was sent signifies the Church of the nations. Long deserted by her creator, she did not know the people of true faith; like a needy woman, she nourished a poor son with a scant allowance—that is, she taught without experiencing the fruits of the word—until the prophetic utterance came. Israel’s fleece had been dried up, as it were, and, with heaven’s door closed, it was perishing from famine in Judea. The prophetic word was nourished there and nourished others at the same time: received, clearly, by believers and itself refreshing believers.

Hence this widow is rightly said to have lived in Sarepta of Sidon. Sidon is interpreted as “useless hunting”; Sarepta as “fire” or “the distress of bread,” because “where sin abounded, grace abounded all the more” (Rom. V). Where attention was devoted to acquiring superfluous things, as though to bird-catching; where the fire of famine burned cruelly and spiritual bread had previously become scarce—in that place flour and oil are blessed by the prophetic mouth, that is, the fruit and gladness of charity, or the grace of the Lord’s body and the anointing of chrism; and they are made fruitful by the unfailing gift of the heavenly word. To this day, the oil of spiritual joy and the flour of blessing have not failed in her vessels, while the other nations do not believe, wretched in their lack of divine bread and devoted to useless hunting.

Indeed, she herself most beautifully testifies that, before she died, she intended to make a mystical bread for herself and wanted to gather two pieces of wood: not only by the name of the wood but also by the number of pieces of wood, expressing the sign of the cross, by which the bread of eternal life has been prepared for us.

[Col. 0265A] “And there were many lepers in Israel under the prophet Elisha, and none of them was cleansed except Naaman the Syrian.”

Because the history is well known, we must briefly explain its mystery. This Naaman the Syrian, whose name is interpreted as “beauty,” represents the people of the nations, once stained by the leprosy of unbelief and crimes, but cleansed through the sacrament of baptism from every defilement of mind and body.

Advised by the captured young girl—that is, by the grace of heavenly inspiration, which the nations seized because the Jews could not preserve salvation—he is instructed to wash seven times, because assuredly only that kind of baptism which regenerates from the Holy Spirit saves.

Hence his flesh is rightly said to have appeared after the washing like the flesh of a little child, either because grace, the mother, brings all who are baptized in Christ into one infancy, or because that child is to be understood of whom it was said: “A child is born to us, a son is given to us” (Isa. IX), to whose body the entire offspring of believers is united through baptism.

And so that you might know that all the sacraments of baptism were prefigured here—in baptism we are commanded to renounce Satan and confess the faith—Naaman denies that he will henceforth sacrifice to foreign gods and declares that he will serve the Lord alone in all things. He is also glad to take with him a portion of the holy land, because those who have been baptized ought also to be strengthened by participation in the Lord’s body.

Therefore Naaman rightly takes precedence: while water washes his body, faith cleanses his heart. That is, the people of the nations are placed above the Jews, who are filthy with the leprosy of obstinacy.

Rightly, too, the widow of Sarepta—that is, the Church desiring to be refreshed by the wood of the cross—is restored, while the Jews perish from hunger for the word, by the sacred bread of the body and the anointing of the life-giving Spirit. It is thus demonstrated that the Lord denied the doctrine of his mighty works to his fellow citizens not because of his own inability, but because of their envy.

Finally, by this example he abandoned the whole nation—not because it was not loved, but because it wanted itself to be loved—to teachers scattered throughout the world, clearly for the salvation of the nations. But what the Lord testifies by word concerning the Jews, the Jews themselves testify by deed concerning themselves. For it follows:

“And everyone in the synagogue was filled with anger when they heard these things. And they rose up and drove him out of the city.”

The sacrileges of the Jews, which the Lord had previously foretold through the prophet, saying, “They repaid me evil for good” (Ps. XXXIV), the Gospel teaches to have been fulfilled. For while he himself spread benefits among the peoples, they inflicted injuries upon him. It is no wonder that they lost salvation, since they drove the Savior from their borders.

Morally, the Lord—and the apostles whom he taught by his own example to become all things to all people—neither rejects the willing nor binds the unwilling, nor resists those who drive him out, nor is absent from those who ask. Thus, elsewhere, when the Gerasenes could not endure his mighty works, he left them behind as though they were weak and ungrateful.

Understand at the same time that his bodily passion was not imposed by necessity but was voluntary: he was not captured by the Jews, but offered himself. For when he wills, he is captured; when he wills, he slips away; when he wills, he is hung; when he wills, he is not held.

“And they led him,” he says, “to the brow of the hill on which their city had been built, so that they might throw him down. But he, passing through the midst of them, went away.”

O inheritance of the disciples, worse than their teacher! The devil tempts God by word; the Jews, by deed. He says, “Throw yourself down”; these attack him in order to throw him down.

The Lord had indeed climbed the brow of the hill to be thrown down, but through their midst, when the minds of the raging crowd suddenly changed or were stunned, he descended—because he preferred still to heal rather than to destroy—so that, seeing their efforts at wickedness frustrated, they might thereafter cease demanding his death.

For the hour of his passion had not yet come; it was to take place not on just any Sabbath, but on the eve of Passover. The place of his passion had not yet arrived: it was not to be Nazareth but Jerusalem, symbolized by the blood of sacrifices. Nor had he chosen this kind of death, since he had been proclaimed from the beginning as one who would be crucified.

He therefore did not will to be thrown down by the people of Nazareth, stoned by the people of Jerusalem, killed by Herod among the children of Bethlehem, or brought to completion by any other form of death. For what token of royal power would stand out in such a death, by which the brows of the faithful might be armed?

Only the standard of the cross was awaited. Its figure could be drawn even by the swiftest motion of the right hand against the assaults of the evil enemy, and that same figure could nevertheless be regarded as a type of singular sovereignty, so that, as the Apostle says when expounding the triumph of the cross, “in the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven and on earth and under the earth” (Phil. II).

For this is what the peaks of that same cross signify: they reach toward heaven; its lower ends seek the depths; its lower horns are covered by the earth.

## HOMILY XLIV. TUESDAY AFTER OCULI

(Matt. XVIII.) “At that time, Jesus looked upon his disciples and said to Simon Peter: ‘If your brother sins against you, go and rebuke him between you and him alone,’” and so forth.

This saying pertains to what he said above: “Woe to the world because of scandals” (Matt. XVIII), and: “Whoever causes one of these little ones to stumble, it would be better for him that a millstone be hung around his neck and he be drowned in the depths of the sea.”

Since, therefore, the Lord had previously warned that scandals must be avoided, he now teaches how those same scandals can be avoided: namely, through peace, concord, and the forgiveness of sins.

If our brother sins against us, we can forgive him; indeed, we must forgive him. But if he sins against God, that does not lie within our power; it rests in God’s judgment. For it is written: “If a man sins against a man, he may be appeased; but if a man sins against the Lord, who will pray for him?” (1 Sam. II).

He is your brother, who has the Father with us in heaven and can say with us: “Our Father, who are in heaven” (Matt. VI).

“Go and rebuke him between you and ‘him alone.’” Why alone? Clearly, lest, if you reprove him publicly, he put shame aside and withdraw from correction.

“If he listens to you, you have gained your brother.” You acquire not only a reward for yourself, but also, as the Apostle James says: “Whoever causes a man to turn from his iniquity will save his soul from death and will cover a multitude of sins” (James V)—both his own sins and those of the person whom he causes to turn from his iniquity. For everyone who rebukes his brother by personal admonition has gained him.

“But if he does not listen to you, take with you one or two more, so that every word may stand by the testimony of two or three witnesses.” He commands that one or two be brought either for the sake of testimony, so that every word may stand by the testimony of two or three witnesses, or also because, having felt no shame when rebuked by one, he may at least feel shame when rebuked by two.

“But if he does not listen to them, tell it to the Church,” that is, to the assembly of the faithful, so that the person who did not correct himself when rebuked by one or two may at least be put to shame by the general gathering of the faithful.

“But if he does not listen to the Church, let him be to you as a pagan and a tax collector.” *Ethnos* in Greek is called *gens* in Latin, hence *ethnicus*, that is, “gentile.” A gentile is one who remains until death in the same rite in which he was born. Tax collectors, in general, are those who accumulate wealth for themselves by lawful and unlawful means.

When he says, “Let him be to you as a pagan and a tax collector,” he clearly shows that those who secretly practice the works of unbelievers under the name of the faithful are worse than those who are openly unbelieving.

“Amen I say to you, whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven.” The Lord had said above: “If he does not listen to the Church, let him be to you as a pagan and a tax collector.” Someone who is rebuked in this way and does not amend himself might say: If you despise me, I will despise you; if you condemn me, you will also be condemned by my own mouth. The Lord confirms the judgment of the Church by his own sentence, saying: “Whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven.”

“Again I say to you, if two of you agree on earth about anything they ask, it will be done for them by my Father who is in heaven.” Every saying of the Lord urges us toward concord: “If two of you,” he says, “agree on earth about anything.”

“For where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them.” We can establish this with many examples. When the apostles were speaking about his resurrection, he was present. When two disciples were walking to Emmaus, a third joined them and revealed his identity to them in the breaking of bread (Luke XXIV). He is also present with us daily when we are gathered in the name of Jesus.

For his name is Jesus. Jesus is interpreted as “Savior.” We are gathered in the name of Jesus whenever we come together to discuss either our own salvation or the salvation of our brothers.

Allegorically, “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them” means this: if body, soul, and spirit agree as one, so that neither flesh resists the spirit nor the spirit resists the flesh, whatever we ask of the Father we shall obtain. For the request is good in which the spirit does not dissent from the flesh, nor the flesh resist the spirit.

“Then Peter came to him and said: ‘Lord, how often will my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? Up to seven times?’”

Moved by the Lord’s words, in which he had said above, “If your brother sins against you, rebuke him between you and him alone,” Peter asks how often he ought to forgive a brother who sins against him. He asks in the form of a question, “Up to seven times?”—that is, must I forgive the person who has sinned against me up to seven times?

Jesus says to him: “I do not say to you up to seven times, but up to seventy times seven.” According to blessed Jerome, this means 490 times: we should forgive a brother who sins against us as many times in a day as he is unable to sin against us.

But it is better to understand simply what he says, “seventy times seven,” as seventy-seven times rather than 490. For every number, when it passes through a number adverbially, increases its total. For example, *septies septuagies septuaginta*—“seven times seventy times seventy”—passes from the noun into the adverb, and the result is 490. But when numbers are expressed adverbially, the total does not increase; the number remains within its own limits, as in this passage, where he says “seventy times seven.”

The Lord therefore commands that we forgive a brother who sins against us seventy-seven times, so that we forgive him as many times as he is unable to sin against us.

## HOMILY XLV. WEDNESDAY AFTER OCULI

(Matt. XV.) “At that time, scribes and Pharisees came to Jesus from Jerusalem, saying,” and so forth.

What extraordinary madness on the part of the scribes and Pharisees, who accuse the Lord because he does not follow human traditions, when he is himself the Son of God! They say:

“Why do your disciples transgress the traditions of the elders? For they do not wash their hands when they eat bread.”

This had arisen from the tradition of the scribes and Pharisees. It was their custom that, if they happened to speak with a gentile, or touch something dead, or see something unclean, they would wash either the whole body or even a part of the body.

“But he answered and said to them: ‘Why do you also transgress the commandment of God for the sake of your tradition?’”

The Lord refutes a false accusation with a truthful response, saying: “Why do you also transgress the commandment of God for the sake of your tradition?” As though he were saying: Why do you accuse my apostles because they transgress human precepts in order to fulfill the precepts of God, when you transgress the precepts of almighty God for the sake of human traditions?

“For God said: ‘Honor your father and your mother, and whoever curses father or mother shall die the death’” (Exod. XX).

In Scripture, honor is understood in two ways: both as reverence and respect, and as the giving of a gift. Hence the Apostle Paul also said: “Let presbyters be held worthy of double honor” (1 Tim. V), and: “Honor widows who are truly widows.” In that passage honor means not merely greeting and reverence, but also giving.

“Honor your father and your mother,” both in the reverence of service and in the giving of gifts. Conversely, when he says, “Whoever curses father or mother,” cursing means not only harsh speech but also the withholding of benefit.

Almighty God, foreseeing the weakness and advanced age of parents, commanded their children, once their parents had reached old age, to honor them not only through service but also through the giving of gifts.

The scribes and Pharisees saw that what was given to parents diminished their own profits, and they devised this trick: they falsely claimed that the commandment “Honor your father and your mother” was to be understood by the Jews as referring instead to the father or mother—that is, to the Temple and the Synagogue. Thus, they said, almighty God had not commanded them to honor their physical parents, but rather to distribute whatever they had to the Temple and the Synagogue.

When the simple heard this, they were led astray by error and offered in the Temple whatever they were able to possess. When it happened that their father or mother asked them for some assistance, they said:

“Whatever gift there may be from me will benefit you”—that is, will the gift which I once offered to God benefit you if I spend it for your needs?

Hearing this, the parents preferred to lose their lives through poverty rather than touch anything consecrated.

This statement, “Whatever gift there may be from me will benefit you,” can also be understood otherwise, as though he were saying: The gift that I offer to God from my substance will benefit you just as it benefits me. By saying this, however, he did not honor his father or mother.

“Hypocrites, Isaiah prophesied well about you, saying: ‘This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me’” (Isa. XXIX).

He did not say that something good came from your wickedness, but what he said fits you well: “This people honors me with their lips.” The Jewish people honored God the Father with their lips, because they boasted that they believed in him; but their heart was far from him, because in their speech they sought to trap him and hand him over to Roman authority.

“But in vain they worship me, teaching doctrines and commandments of men.” In vain, he says, they worship me, placing their doctrines before the commandments of God.

“And having summoned the crowds to himself, he said to them: ‘Hear and understand.’” God does not want his hearers merely to hear, but after hearing also to understand.

[Col. 0270A] “It is not what enters the mouth that defiles a person.”

If what enters the mouth does not defile a person, it is rightly asked why the Apostle Paul forbids us to eat food sacrificed to idols, or why he says: “You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons” (1 Cor. VII).

The answer is that the creature itself is clean and good; but when it has been consecrated to idols, it becomes filthy and unclean because of the invocation of demons and idols. Therefore, we are commanded not to eat such things.

The whole religion and holiness of the Jews consisted especially in the distinction between clean and unclean foods. But what almighty God set forth distinctly in the Old Testament, he commanded to be used without distinction in the New Testament.

Almighty God commanded that hands be washed not with bodily water, but with the purity of good works, so that we might be worthy for the word of God to come into our hands. Thus we often read in the Old Testament: “The word of the Lord came to the hand of Jeremiah,” and to Isaiah and the others. The word of the Lord came into their hands because their works were such that they were worthy for the word of God to come to them.

“Then his disciples came and said to him: ‘Do you know that the Pharisees, when they heard this word, were scandalized?’”

From this passage it is understood that in some circumstances people must avoid scandal, while in others it should be disregarded as worthless. The Lord also teaches this by his own example.

We read elsewhere (Matt. XVII) that those who collected the tribute from the people came to Peter and said: “Does your teacher not pay the didrachma?” When he entered the house, Jesus anticipated him, saying: “What do you think? From whom do the kings of the earth collect tribute: from their own sons or from foreigners?” He said: “From foreigners.” And he said to him: “Then the sons are free. But so that we do not scandalize them, go to the sea, cast a hook, and take the first fish that comes up; and when you have opened its mouth, you will find a stater. Take it and give it for me and for you.”

There he avoided scandal; here, where the scribes and Pharisees were scandalized against the Lord without cause, he regarded their scandal as worthless.

From this it is understood that scandal must be avoided where an offense to the faith may occur. But where the truth itself is endangered, it is better to incur scandal than to abandon the truth. For *skándalon* (σκάνδαλον) is Greek; in Latin it is called an offense, or a stumbling and falling of the foot, or a striking of the feet; more precisely, it is called in Latin a disturbance of the mind.

“Every planting that my heavenly Father has not planted will be uprooted.”

If every planting that the heavenly Father has not planted will be uprooted, then will the planting planted by the Apostle Paul be uprooted, since he said (1 Cor. III): “I planted, Apollos watered”?

The question is resolved by what follows: “But God gave the growth.” If every planting that the Father did not plant will be uprooted, then will the planting that he himself planted not be uprooted?

The answer is that every planting planted by the heavenly Father cannot be uprooted by anyone unless he himself gives consent to its being uprooted. Hence Jeremiah says: “I planted you as a choice vine; how have you turned into the bitterness of a foreign vine?” (Jer. II).

“Leave them,” that is, permit them to remain in their condemnation. “They are blind and leaders of the blind”—understand, of the peoples.

“But if the blind lead the blind, both will fall into a pit.”

Knowing that their minds were incorrigible, the Lord therefore said: “If the blind lead the blind, both will fall into a pit.” The scribes and Pharisees were blind, and they were not only blind but also leaders of the blind. For they not only sent themselves into perdition, but also dragged others after them.

It is clear that if the teacher is blind, he himself and those who listen to him will fall into the pit of eternal condemnation.

“But Peter answered and said to him: ‘Explain this parable to us.’ But he said: ‘Are you also still without understanding?’”

What had been said plainly and openly by the Lord, Peter thought had been spoken as a parable. Hence the Lord reproves him, saying: “Are you also still without understanding?”

From this it is understood that a listener is defective if he wishes obscure statements to be understood plainly, or wishes plainly stated things to be turned into obscurity.

“Do you not understand that everything that enters the mouth goes into the stomach and is expelled into the latrine?”

Some people find fault with the Lord at this point, saying that he was ignorant of natural science, since what enters the mouth is not immediately expelled into the latrine, but the liquid of that food is first dispersed through the veins and then expelled through certain passages, which in Greek are called *poroi*.

But in criticizing him they reveal their own ignorance. For although the most refined liquid is first dispersed through the veins, as soon as it has traversed the whole body it goes into the latrine.

“But what proceeds from the mouth comes from the heart, and these things defile a person.” He explains what those things are that defile a person, saying:

“For from the heart proceed evil thoughts.”

From this passage it is understood that the ruling faculty of the soul is not, according to Plato, in the brain, but rather in the heart: “For from the heart proceed evil thoughts.”

It is also understood here that the devil is not the author of evils, but rather their instigator. He can be an instigator, but not an author. For he cannot search out the inner recesses of our hearts, but can infer what we are thinking from the movements of the body.

For example, if he sees us frequently looking at a beautiful woman, he understands from the movement of our eyes that our heart has been wounded by the dart of love. From this reasoning it is proved that he is not the author, but the instigator and augmenter of evil thoughts.

## HOMILY XLVI. THURSDAY AFTER OCULI

[Col. 0272A]

(John VI.) “At that time Jesus said to the crowds: ‘Work not for the food that perishes, but for the food that remains unto eternal life,’” and so forth.

Carnal food perishes, but spiritual food remains; the Son of Man will give it to you. The Father therefore signified this righteous Son of Man.

Do not understand this as though there were other sons, “sons of man,” of whom it is said: “But the sons of men will hope in the protection of your wings.” This Son of Man, set apart from the sons of men by a certain grace, removed from the number of human beings, is the Son of Man.

This Son of Man is also the Son of God; this human being is also God. Hence the Truth itself, which was then speaking to the Jews and now speaks to everyone through the words of evangelical preaching, showed what he is—not what many then judged him to be, or even now judge him to be. He added:

“For God the Father has sealed him.”

What does it mean to seal, unless it means to place something distinctive? It means to indicate something, to place something by which it is not confused with other things. To seal is to place a mark upon something. Whenever you place a mark on anything, you do so so that it may not be confused with other things and become unrecognizable to you.

The Father, therefore, sealed him. What does “sealed” mean? He gave him something distinctive, so that he would not be compared with other human beings. Hence it is said: “God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Ps. XLIV).

Therefore, he says: Do not despise me because I am the Son of Man, but seek from me not food that perishes, but food that remains unto eternal life. I am the Son of Man in such a way that I am not one of you. I am the Son of Man in such a way that God the Father sealed me.

What does “sealed” mean? He gave me something distinctive, by which I would not be confused with the human race, but through me the human race would be liberated.

“Therefore they said to him: ‘What shall we do, so that we may work the works of God?’”

He had said to them: “Work for food not that which perishes, but that which remains unto eternal life.” They ask: What shall we do? By observing what will we be able to fulfill this command?

“Jesus answered and said to them: ‘This is the work of God, that you believe in the one whom he sent.’”

This, then, is eating food not that which perishes, but that which remains unto eternal life.

Faith is distinguished from works, as the Apostle says: a person is justified by faith without the works of the law. There are works that appear good without faith in Christ, but are not good. “For Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Rom. X).

He therefore did not separate faith from works, but said that faith itself is a work; for it is faith itself that works through love. He did not say, “This is your work,” but said: “This is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he sent,” so that “whoever boasts may boast in the Lord” (1 Cor. I).

Since he was inviting them to faith, they still sought signs by which they might believe.

“Therefore they said to him: ‘What sign do you do, so that we may see and believe you? What do you work?’”

Was it not enough that they had been fed from the five loaves? They knew this indeed, but preferred manna from heaven to that food.

The Lord Jesus was presenting himself as one superior to Moses. For Moses did not dare to say of himself that he would give food not that which perishes, but that which has eternal life.

They were paying attention to one who promised more, and as though they had not yet seen him do greater things. They considered what Moses had done and still wanted something greater to be done by the one who made such great promises.

“What do you do,” they say, “so that we may believe you and know what you work?” They were comparing the ancient miracles with this miracle and therefore judged the things Jesus was doing as though they were lesser.

“Our fathers,” they say, “ate manna in the desert, as it is written: ‘He gave them manna to eat,’” and you do not perform things such as Moses did. He did not give barley loaves, but manna from heaven.

“Therefore Jesus said to them: ‘Amen, amen, I say to you, Moses did not give you bread from heaven, but my Father gives you the true bread from heaven. For the true bread is the one who descends from heaven and gives life to the world.’”

Therefore that is the true bread which gives life to the world, and it is the very food of which I spoke shortly before: “Work for the food that does not perish but remains unto eternal life” (John VI).

That manna, then, signified this, and all those signs were mine. You loved my signs, but despise what was signified.

“Therefore they said to him: ‘Lord, give us this bread always.’”

Just as the Samaritan woman, to whom it was said (John IV), “Whoever drinks of this water will never thirst,” immediately understood it bodily and, desiring nevertheless to be free from want, said, “Lord, give me this water,” so these people also say: “Lord, give us this bread that will refresh us and not fail.”

“Therefore Jesus said to them: ‘I am the bread of life. Whoever comes to me will not hunger, and whoever believes in me will never thirst.’”

“Whoever comes to me” means the same as “whoever believes in me.” And what he said, “will not hunger,” is to be understood together with “will never thirst.” Both signify eternal satisfaction, where there is no want.

You desire bread from heaven; you have it before you, and you do not eat it. But I told you that you have both seen me and have not believed.

## HOMILY XLVII. FRIDAY AFTER OCULI
## (John 4)

“At that time, Jesus came to a city of Samaria called Sychar, near the plot of land which Jacob gave to his son Joseph,” and so forth. When the Evangelist had mentioned the plot of land in which Jacob’s well was located, he added:

“But Jesus, wearied from the journey, was sitting thus upon” the well which holy Jacob had left to his son Joseph.
