I believe that this plot of land was left not so much to Joseph as to Christ, whose figure the holy patriarch Joseph bore—he whom truly the sun adores, and the moon, and all the stars bless. The Lord therefore came to this plot of land so that the Samaritans, who were attempting to claim for themselves the inheritance of the patriarch of Israel, might recognize their possessor and be converted to Christ, who has become the patriarch’s legitimate heir.

For the Evangelist says: “But Jesus, wearied from the journey, was sitting thus upon” the well. The mysteries of the Gospel, signified in the words and deeds of our Lord Jesus Christ, are not evident to everyone; and some, by interpreting them less carefully and less soberly, often bring ruin instead of salvation and error instead of knowledge of the truth. Among these is the mystery written here: that the Lord came to Jacob’s well at the sixth hour of the day, sat down exhausted from the journey, asked a Samaritan woman for a drink, and the other things which are said to require examination and discussion in this passage.

Regarding this matter, the first point to be held is what must be guarded with the greatest vigilance throughout all the Scriptures: that the exposition of the divine mystery be made according to the faith. At the sixth hour of the day, therefore, our Lord came to the well. I see in the well a dark depth. I therefore urge you to understand it as signifying the weak parts of this world, that is, the earthly parts, to which the Lord Jesus came at the sixth hour—that is, in the sixth age of the human race—as though in the old man’s old age, from which we are commanded to strip ourselves so that we may put on the new man, who has been created according to God.

The life of the old man, therefore, which is lived according to the flesh under temporal conditions, is concluded in the old age of the sixth age. In this old age, as I have said, our Lord, the creator and restorer of the human race, arrived, so that, when the old man was dying, he might establish the new man in himself and, stripped of earthly clay, transfer him to the heavenly realms.

Thus, as has been said, the well now signifies the earthly labor and terror of this world through its dark depth. And because the outer man is old, while the inner man is new, the Apostle said: “Even if our outer man is being corrupted, yet our inner man is renewed day by day” (2 Cor. 4). This is altogether most fitting, since all visible things belong to the outer man, to which Christian discipline bids us renounce.

The Lord came to the well at the sixth hour, that is, in the middle of the day, from which this visible sun now begins to decline toward its setting. For, when we are called by Christ, our delight in visible things diminishes, so that the inner man, refreshed by love of invisible things, may return to the inner light which never fails, according to the apostolic teaching—not seeking the things that are seen, but those that are not seen. “For the things that are seen are temporal, but the things that are not seen are eternal” (1 Cor. 13).

That he came to the well wearied signifies the weakness of the flesh; that he sat signifies humility. For he took upon himself the weakness of the flesh for our sake, and he deigned to appear as a man among human beings with such humility. Concerning this weakness of the flesh the prophet says: “A man placed in suffering and knowing how to bear weakness” (Isa. 53). Concerning humility, the Apostle speaks, saying: “He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death” (Phil. 2).

Nevertheless, the fact that he sat—because teachers ordinarily sit—may be understood in another way, not as indicating the modesty of humility but the person of a teacher.

But one may ask why he requested a drink from the Samaritan woman, who had come to fill her water jar, when he himself later proclaimed that he could give those who asked him the abundance of the spiritual fountain. Clearly, God thirsted for the faith of that woman, who, because she was a Samaritan—and Samaria was accustomed to represent idolatry—was in need of this. For they, separated from the Jewish people, had devoted the honor of their souls to images of mute animals, that is, to golden calves.

Our Lord Jesus Christ had come to bring the multitude of the nations, which had served images, to the stronghold of Christian faith and uncorrupted religion. “It is not,” he says, “the healthy who need a physician, but those who are ill” (Matt. 9). Therefore he thirsts for the faith of those for whom he shed his blood.

Jesus therefore said to her:

“Woman, give me a drink.”

And so that you may know what our Lord was thirsting for, shortly afterward his disciples came, having gone into the city to buy food.

“They said to him: Rabbi, eat. But he said to them: I have food to eat which you do not know. His disciples therefore said to one another: Surely no one has brought him something to eat? Jesus said to them: My food is to do the will of him who sent me and to complete his work.”

Can some other will of the Father who sent him be understood here, according to which he wished him to complete his work, except that he should convert us from the destructive error of the world to faith in him? Therefore, his food is of the same nature as his drink. For this reason he thirsted for this in the woman: to do the Father’s will in her and to complete his work.

But she, understanding him carnally, replied:

“Since you are a Jew, how can you drink from me, although I am a Samaritan woman? For Jews do not associate with Samaritans.”

Our Lord said to her:

“If you knew the gift of God, and who it is who says to you, ‘Give me a drink,’ you would rather have asked him, and he would have given you living water.”

By this he showed her that he had not asked for such water as she had understood. But because he himself thirsted for her faith, he desired to give the Holy Spirit to her who was thirsting. For we rightly understand this living water as the gift of God, just as he himself says: “If you knew the gift of God.”

And, as the same John testifies elsewhere (John 7), saying that Jesus stood and cried out: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. Whoever believes in me,” as Scripture says, “rivers of living water will flow from his belly.”

Quite consistently he says: “Whoever believes in me, rivers of living water will flow from his belly,” because we first believe so that we may deserve these gifts. These rivers of living water, therefore, which he wished to give that woman, are the reward of the faith for which he first thirsted in her.

He then explains the meaning of this living water: “Now he said this,” he says, “about the Spirit, whom those who were going to believe in him were to receive. For the Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified.”

This gift, then, is the Holy Spirit, whom after his glorification he gave to the Church, as another Scripture says: “Ascending on high, he led captivity captive and gave gifts to human beings” (Eph. 4).

But the woman still thinks carnally, for she replied:

“Lord, you have neither” a drawing vessel “and the well is deep; whence have you [the means] to give me” living water? “Surely you are greater than our father Jacob, who gave us this well and drank from it himself, and his sons, and his livestock?”

Now the Lord explains what he had said:

“Everyone,” he says, “who drinks from this water will thirst again. But whoever drinks from the water which I” shall give “will not thirst forever; but the water which I” shall give “will become in him a fountain of water springing up” into eternal life.

But the woman still embraces the wisdom of the flesh, replying:

“Lord, give me this water, so that I may not thirst, nor come here to draw.”

Jesus says to her:

“Go, call your husband, and come here.”

Since he knew that she had no husband, the question is why he said this. For when the woman said:

“I have no husband,” Jesus said to her: “You have spoken well, ‘I have no husband’; for you have had five husbands, and the one whom you now have is not your husband. You have spoken this truth.”

But these things must not be understood carnally, lest we appear to be like this Samaritan woman even now. Rather, if we have already tasted something of that gift of God, let us treat these matters spiritually.

Some understand the five husbands as the five books which were given through Moses. What was said—“and the one whom you now have is not your husband”—they understand as having been said by the Lord about himself, so that the meaning is this: First you served the five books of Moses, as though five husbands; but the one whom you now have, that is, the one whom you hear, is not your husband, because you have not yet believed in him.

But since, not yet believing in Christ, she was still held by the union of those five husbands—that is, of the five books—it may be asked how it could have been said, “You have had five husbands,” as though she no longer had them, when she was still certainly living subject to them.

Moreover, since the five books of Moses preach nothing other than Christ, as he himself says: “If you believed Moses, you would perhaps believe me also; for he wrote about me” (John 5), how can it be understood that a person withdraws from those five books in order to pass over to Christ, when one who believes in Christ does not abandon those five books but, by understanding them spiritually, embraces them much more blessedly?

There is therefore another interpretation: the five husbands may be understood as the five bodily senses.

One is the sense belonging to the eyes, by which we see this visible light and the various colors and forms of bodies. The second belongs to the ears, by which we perceive the movements of voices and all sounds. The third belongs to the nostrils, by which we take delight in the varied sweetness of odors. The fourth is taste in the mouth, which perceives sweet and bitter things and judges all flavors. The fifth, throughout the whole body, distinguishes by touch hot and cold, soft and hard, smooth and rough, and whatever else we perceive by touching.

The first age of a human being is therefore steeped in these five bodily senses by the necessity of mortal nature. For after the sin of the first human being we were born in such a condition that, before the light of the mind had been restored, we devoted ourselves to bodily senses and passed through bodily life without any understanding of truth.

Infants and little children must necessarily be like this, since they are not yet able to receive reason. And because these senses are natural, govern the first age, and have been granted to us by God the craftsman, they are rightly called husbands, as though legitimate ones. For nature has contributed them not through the fault of its own errors but through God’s craftsmanship.

But when someone reaches an age in which life can be capable of reason, if that person is able immediately to grasp the truth, he will no longer use those senses as rulers. Instead, he will have as a husband the rational spirit, to whom he will reduce those senses to the service of slavery, subjecting his body together with his soul—not now to five husbands, that is, to the five bodily senses to which it had been subject—but having the divine Word as its legitimate husband, to whom it is joined and clings, when the human spirit itself has also clung to Christ.

“For Christ is the head of the man.” Embracing spiritual things and eternal life, the soul enjoys them without fear of any separation, as the Apostle says: “Who will separate us from the love of Christ?” (Rom. 8)—the implied answer being, “No thing.”

But because that woman was held by error, signifying the multitude of the world subjected to various superstitions, after that time of the five bodily senses by which the first age is governed, she had not received the Word of God as her husband; rather, the devil possessed her in an adulterous embrace.

Therefore the Lord, seeing that she was carnal—that is, thinking carnally—says to her:

“Go, call your husband, and come here.”

That is: Remove yourself from the carnal affection in which you are now established, because from there you cannot understand what I am saying. And call your husband—that is, be present in spirit with understanding.

For the spirit of a human being is, in a certain way, like the husband of the soul; it governs the animal affection as its spouse. This is not the Holy Spirit, who is given inseparably with the Father and the Son, but the spirit of the human being, concerning whom the Apostle says: “No one knows what is in a human being except the spirit of the human being which is in him” (1 Cor. 2).

For that Holy Spirit is the Spirit of God, concerning whom he says again: “So also no one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God.”

When this human spirit is present—that is, attentive—and submits itself to God in devotion, a person understands what is spoken spiritually. But when the devil’s error dominates in the soul as though understanding were absent, the spirit is adulterous.

“Call, therefore,” he says, “your husband”—that is, the spirit which is in you, by which a human being can understand spiritual things. If the light of truth illumines it and it is itself present, I will speak with you, so that you may receive spiritual water.

And when she says, “I have no husband,” he says: “You have spoken well, for you have had five husbands”—that is, the five senses of the flesh ruled you in your first age—“and the one whom you now have is not your husband,” because there is not in you a spirit that understands God, with whom you could have a legitimate marriage. Rather, the devil’s error dominates, corrupting you through adulterous defilement.

And perhaps, for those who understand, he indicated by the name “five husbands” that the five aforementioned bodily senses are signified.

After five carnal replies, in her sixth reply this woman names Christ. Her first reply was: “Since you are a Jew, how do you ask me for a drink?” The second: “Lord, you have nothing with which to draw, and the well is deep.” The third: “Lord, give me this water, so that I may not thirst, nor come here to draw.” The fourth: “I have no husband.” The fifth: “I see that you are a prophet; our fathers worshiped on this mountain.”

For this reply is carnal. A place on earth had been given to carnal people where they might pray; but the Lord said that spiritual people would pray in spirit and truth.

After he had spoken this, the woman’s sixth reply confesses Christ to be the teacher of all the righteous. She says:

“I know that the Messiah is coming, who is called Christ. Therefore, when he comes, he will announce everything to us.”

But she is still in error, because she does not see that the one whose coming she hopes for has already come. Nevertheless, through the Lord’s mercy this error is now expelled like an adulterer.

Jesus says to her:

“I am he who speaks with you.”

When she heard this, she did not reply, but immediately left her water jar and hurried into the city, so that she might not only believe the Gospel and the Lord’s coming but also proclaim it.

Nor should the fact that she left her water jar and departed be passed over carelessly. For perhaps the water jar signifies love of this world, that is, desire, because human beings draw pleasure for themselves from the dark depth whose image the well bears—that is, from earthly conduct—and, having tasted it, burn again with desire for it, just as the one who drinks that water will thirst again.

But once she had believed in Christ, it was necessary for her to renounce the world. By leaving the water jar, she showed that she had abandoned worldly desire, believing with the heart unto righteousness and confessing with the mouth for salvation what she had believed.

For the woman says:

“Lord, I see that you are a prophet.”

The husband is beginning to come, but he has not yet fully arrived, because she thought the Lord a prophet. Indeed, he was also a prophet, for he says concerning himself: “A prophet is not without honor except in his own country” (Mark 6). Likewise, it was said to Moses concerning him: “I will raise up for them a prophet from among their brothers, like you” (Deut. 18)—like you in the form of the flesh, that is, not in the eminence of majesty.

Thus we find the Lord Jesus called a prophet. Accordingly, this woman is no longer greatly in error. “I see,” she says, “that you are a prophet.” She begins to exclude the adulterous husband when she says: “I see that you are a prophet,” and she begins to ask about what had usually troubled her.

For there had been a dispute between the Samaritans and the Jews, because the Jews worshiped the Lord in the temple built by Solomon. The Samaritans, situated far from it, did not worship there. For this reason the Jews rejoiced that they were better, because they worshiped in the temple.

They said: “Why do you rejoice and claim that you are therefore better than we are, because you have a temple which we do not have? Did our fathers, who pleased God, worship in the temple? Did they not worship on this mountain where we are? We therefore,” they said, “pray to God better on this mountain, where our fathers prayed.”

Both groups were contending in ignorance, because, having no husband, the one group was puffed up on behalf of the temple and the other on behalf of the mountain, against each other.

But the Lord now teaches the woman, as though her husband had begun to be present.

The woman says to him:

“Lord, I see that you are a prophet. Our fathers worshiped on this mountain, and you say that one must worship in Jerusalem.”

Jesus says to her:

“Woman, believe me.”

For the Church will come, as it is said in the Song of Songs (Song 2): “My beloved speaks to me.” And again: “Rise, hurry, my beloved, my beautiful one, my dove, my undefiled one, and come. For winter has now passed, the rain has gone away, the flowers have appeared in our land, the time of pruning has come. The voice of the turtledove has been heard in our land.”

Now that the husband is already present, the woman rightly hears: “Believe me.” For there is already in you one who believes, because your husband is present. You began to be present in understanding when you called me a prophet.

“Woman, believe me, because unless you believe, you will not understand.” Therefore, believe me.

“For the hour is coming when you will worship the Father neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem. You worship what you do not know; we worship what we know, because salvation is from the Jews. But the hour is coming—and now is.”

What hour is this?

“When true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth.”

Not on this mountain, not in the temple, but in spirit and truth.

God is spirit. If God were a body, he ought to be worshiped on a mountain, because a mountain is bodily; he ought to be worshiped in a temple, because a temple is bodily. God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth.

“We worship what we know; you worship what you do not know, because salvation is from the Jews.”

He gave much to the Jews. But do not understand these as the rejected Jews: that wall, namely Israel, was joined so that, reconciled in the cornerstone—which is Christ—they might be united. One wall is from the Jews and one from the nations; the walls are far apart, but they are joined when they meet at the corner.

The foreigners and outsiders were strangers and aliens to the covenants of God. Accordingly, this was said: “We worship what we know.” It was spoken in the person of the Jews, but not of all Jews—not of the rejected Jews, but of those such as the apostles were, such as the prophets were, such as all those holy people were who sold all they possessed and placed the proceeds of their goods at the apostles’ feet (Acts 2).

“For God did not reject his people whom he foreknew” (Ps. 93).

The woman says to him:

“I know that the Messiah is coming, who is called Christ. Therefore, when he comes, he will show us everything.”

When he comes, he will reject the mountain and overturn the temple. He will teach us everything, so that we may know how to worship in spirit and truth.

She knew who could teach her, but although he was already teaching, she did not yet recognize him. She was therefore already worthy to whom he might be revealed.

Messiah means “anointed.” “Anointed” is *unctus* in Latin, χριστός (*christos*) in Greek, and Messiah in Hebrew.

“So the woman says to him: I know that the Messiah is coming, who is called Christ. Therefore, when he comes, he will announce everything to us.”

Jesus says to her:

“I am he who speaks with you.”

The woman is now being ordered in faith and guided toward a good life. After she heard, “I am he who speaks with you,” what more could she say? Christ the Lord had wished to reveal himself to the woman to whom he had said: “Believe me.”

And immediately his disciples came and were amazed that he was speaking with a woman. They were amazed because he had come to seek the lost woman, having come to seek what had perished. They were amazed at something good; they did not suspect anything evil. Yet no one said: “What are you seeking?” or “Why are you speaking with her?”

The woman therefore left her water jar. Having heard, “I am he who speaks with you,” and having received Christ the Lord into her heart, what could she do except now abandon the water jar and run to proclaim the Gospel?

She cast away desire and hurried to announce the truth. The water jar was a vessel from which water was drawn. In Greek it is called ὑδρία (*hydria*), because water is called ὕδωρ (*hydōr*) in Greek—as though one were to say “a vessel of water.”

She cast away the water jar, which was no longer useful but had become a burden. For she eagerly desired to be satisfied with that water so that she might announce Christ, having cast off the burden.

She ran to the city and said to those people:

“Come and see a man who told me everything I have ever done.”

Gradually, lest they become angry and indignant with her and investigate the matter, she added:

“Could this be the Christ?”

They went out of the city and came to him. Meanwhile his disciples asked him, saying:

“Rabbi, eat.”

They had gone to buy food and returned.

But he said to them:

“I have food to eat which you do not know.”

Therefore the disciples said to one another:

“Surely someone has brought him something to eat?”

What wonder is it if that woman did not understand the water? The disciples had not yet understood the food.

But he heard their thoughts and instructed them as a teacher—not indirectly, as he had instructed the woman whose husband he was still seeking, but openly:

“My food,” he says, “is to do the will of him who sent me.”

Therefore his drink itself was present in that woman: to do the will of him who sent him. For this reason he said: “I thirst; give me a drink”—namely, so that he might work faith in her, drink her faith, and transfer her into his body. For his body is the Church.

“Therefore,” he says, “my food itself is to do the will of him who sent me, so that I may complete his work.”

“Do you not say that there are still four months and the harvest comes?”

He was burning with zeal for the work and preparing to send laborers. You count four months until the harvest; I show you another harvest, white and ready.

“Behold, I say to you: Lift up your eyes and see the regions, because they are already white for the harvest.”

Therefore he is about to send reapers.

“For in this the saying is true: one is he who sows and another he who reaps.”

So that both the one who sows and the one who reaps may rejoice together.

“I sent you to reap what you did not labor for. Others labored, and you have entered into their labors.”

For where labor had already been done, seed had certainly been sown; and what had been sown had already become mature and desired the sickle and the threshing floor.

Where, then, were the reapers to be sent? Where the prophets had already preached. For they were the sowers.

If they were not sowers, how had the woman reached the point of saying: “I know that the Messiah is coming”? This woman was already ripe fruit, and the harvests were white and were seeking the sickle.

“I sent you to reap what you did not sow. Others sowed, and you entered into their labors.”

What did Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob themselves labor for? Read their labors. For in all their labors there is a prophecy of Christ. Therefore Moses and the other patriarchs, and all the prophets, were sowers; they endured much in that cold season when they were sowing.

Thus the harvest was already ready in Judea. It was rightly like a ripe crop there when so many thousands of people brought the proceeds of their possessions, placed them at the apostles’ feet (Acts 2), and, with their shoulders freed from worldly burdens, followed Christ the Lord.

Truly it was a ripe harvest. What happened from it? A few grains were taken from that harvest and sowed throughout the world; and another harvest arises, which is to be reaped at the end of the age.

For this harvest the apostles are not sent, but angels. “The reapers,” he says, “are angels.”

This harvest therefore grows among the weeds and awaits cleansing at the end. But that other harvest was already ripe, where the disciples were first sent, where the prophets had labored.

Nevertheless, see what was said: “So that both the one who sows and the one who reaps may rejoice together.” They had labors belonging to different times, but they will enjoy the same joy and receive the reward together: eternal life.

Many Samaritans from that city believed in him because of the word of the woman who testified: “He told me everything I have ever done.”

When the Samaritans had come to him, they asked him to remain with them. He stayed there two days. Many more believed because of his word. And they said to the woman:

“We no longer believe because of what you said; for we ourselves have heard him, and we know that this is truly the Savior of the world.”

This too should be observed gradually, because the reading has ended. The woman first announced him, and the Samaritans believed because of the woman’s testimony and asked him to remain with them. He stayed there two days, and more believed.

And when they had believed, they said to the woman:

“We no longer believe because of your word, but we ourselves have come to know, and we know that this is truly the Savior of the world.”

First through report, afterward through presence: this is what happens today with those who are outside and are not yet Christians. Christ is announced through Christian friends. As though through that woman—that is, through the Church announcing him—they come to Christ and believe through this report.

He remains with them for two days, that is, he gives them the two commandments of love. And many more believe in him more firmly, because he truly is the Savior of the world.

## Homily XLVIII. Saturday after *Oculi*

### (John 8)

“At that time, Jesus went to the Mount of Olives, and at dawn he came again into the temple,” and so forth.

The Mount of Olives signifies the exaltation of the Lord’s Passion and mercy. For in Greek, mercy is ἔλεος (*eleos*), while an olive grove is called ἐλαιών (*elaiōn*); and the anointing, ἄλειμμα (*aleimma*), ordinarily brings relief to tired and suffering limbs.

Moreover, the fact that oil surpasses other liquids in power and purity, and that whatever liquid one wishes to pour over it immediately sinks beneath it while the oil rises above it, not inappropriately suggests the grace of heavenly mercy, concerning which it is written: “The Lord is sweet to all, and his mercies are over all his works” (Ps. 144).

The time of dawn also demonstrates the rising of this same grace, since, once the shadow of the Law had been removed, the light of evangelical truth was to be revealed.

The Lord therefore goes to the Mount of Olives to declare that the stronghold of mercy remains established in him. He comes again at dawn into the temple to signify that, with the light of the New Testament beginning, this same mercy is to be disclosed and offered to his temple—that is, to the faithful.

“And all the people,” he says, “came to him. And sitting down, he taught them.”

The Lord’s sitting signifies the humility of his incarnation, through which he deigned to have mercy on us. It is rightly said that, when Jesus taught while sitting, all the people came to him, because, after he had become near to human beings through the humility of his incarnation, his word was received more willingly by many.

By many, I say, his word was received; for by more people it was rejected through proud impiety. “The meek heard and rejoiced.”

Finally, the Jews, testing him, brought a woman caught in adultery and asked what he ordered to be done with her, since Moses had commanded that such a woman be stoned. If he too decided that she should be stoned, they would mock him as though he had forgotten the mercy he was always teaching. If he forbade her to be stoned, they would gnash their teeth against him and condemn him as a supporter of crimes and an opponent of the Law.

“But Jesus, bending down, was writing on the ground with his finger.”

Through Jesus’ bending down, humility is expressed; through the finger, which is flexible through the articulation of its joints, the subtlety of discernment is expressed. Through the ground, moreover, the human heart is shown, which usually produces the fruits of either good or evil actions.

When the Lord was therefore asked to judge the sinful woman, he did not immediately give judgment. Instead, first bending down, he wrote on the ground with his finger, and only then judged after being earnestly entreated.

He was typologically instructing us: whenever we see the errors of our neighbors, we should not judge them by reproving them before we have humbly returned to our own conscience, carefully carved it with the finger of discernment, and distinguished through diligent examination what pleases and what displeases the Creator in it, according to the Apostle’s saying:

“Brothers, if a person is overtaken in any transgression, you who are spiritual should instruct such a one in a spirit of gentleness, considering yourself, lest you also be tempted” (Gal. 6).

“But when they persisted in questioning him, he raised himself and said to them: Let the one among you who is without sin first cast a stone at her.”

Because the scribes and Pharisees were stretching snares of ambushes for the Lord from both sides, thinking that he would either prove merciless in judging or unjust, he foresaw their deceits. Like a thread passing through a spider’s web, he passed through them, displaying everywhere both the judgment of justice and the gentleness of compassion.

Behold the restraint of mercy: “The one among you who is without sin.” Behold again the justice of judgment: “Let him be the first to cast a stone at her.”

It is as though he had said: If Moses commanded you to stone a woman of this kind, see that he commanded not sinners but righteous people to do this. First fulfill the justice of the Law yourselves, and, innocent in your hands and pure in heart, come together to stone the guilty woman.

First fulfill the Law’s spiritual decrees—faith, mercy, and love—and then turn to judging bodily matters.

After judgment had been given:

“The Lord, bending down again, was writing on the ground.”

According to the custom of human behavior, it may be understood that he wished to bend down before those wicked tempters and write on the ground so that, directing his attention elsewhere, he might give them a free opportunity to leave. He foresaw that, struck by his reply, they would depart more quickly than they would ask further questions.

Finally, “when they heard this, they went out one by one, beginning with the elders.”

But figuratively he warns us by the fact that, both before and after giving judgment, he bent down and wrote on the ground. This teaches us that, both before reproving a sinful neighbor and after rendering to that person the ministry of deserved correction, we should examine ourselves through a fitting investigation of humility, lest perhaps we be entangled either in the same crimes which we reprove in them or in other offenses of whatever kind.

It may happen, for example, that the person who judges a murderer deserving death is himself found before the eyes of the Creator to be guilty in himself through hatred of his brother. Similarly, one who accuses a brother of the crime of fornication may fail to see in himself the offense of pride.

For this reason the judge of another’s crime is commanded to write it in his own heart with the finger of discernment, lest he perhaps be found guilty in himself.

What remedy, then, what hope of salvation remains for us in such dangers except that, when we see someone sinning, we immediately bend down toward the ground—that is, humbly consider how cast down we are by the condition of our weakness if divine mercy does not sustain us?

Let us write on the ground—that is, let us weigh the matter with careful discernment. For our heart does not condemn us in all our ways.

It is fitting that the one who bent down and wrote on the ground speaks the words of mercy after rising, because what he promised through fellowship with human weakness he bestows on human beings as a gift of compassion through the power of divine strength.

“Jesus, raising himself,” he says, “said to her: Woman, where are those who accused you? Has no one condemned you?”

She said:

“No one, Lord.”

No one dared to condemn you, a sinful woman, because each had begun to see in himself what he recognized as more deserving of condemnation.

But the one who drove away the crowds of accusers by presenting the weight of justice—let us see with what gift of mercy he raises up the accused woman.

It follows:

“Jesus said: Neither will I condemn you. Go, and now do not sin anymore.”

Because he is merciful and compassionate, he releases past sins. Because he is just and loved justice, he forbids her to sin any longer.

## Homily XLIX. Fourth Sunday in Lent, or *Laetare*
(JOHN VI.) “At that time: Jesus went away across the Sea of Galilee, which is the Sea of Tiberias,” and so forth.

The Sea of Galilee, which is also called Tiberias, is designated by various names according to the character of the surrounding regions. It is called the Sea of Galilee because of the neighboring land or province of Galilee. It is called the Sea of Tiberias because of the city of Tiberias, which was formerly called Paneas but, after it had been rebuilt by Herod in honor of Tiberius Caesar, was named Tiberias. It is also called the Lake of Gennesaret, because it seems by its rippling waves to generate a breeze from itself. It is called the Lake of Chinnereth because of the adjacent city of Chinnereth and because of the convenience of its harbor. Some also call it the Asphalt Sea. For it extends 140 stadia in length and forty in width.

It was not called a sea because its waters are bitter; they are sweet for drinking and suitable for fishing. Rather, it is an idiom of the Hebrew language to call gatherings of waters “seas,” just as it is written in Genesis: “He called the gatherings of waters seas” (Gen. I).

Spiritually, this navigable sea signifies the present age, which, when shaken, cannot remain at rest. Hence it is properly called *mare* (“sea”), from *meando* (“moving”), because it is always advancing and receding. Just as the sea cannot remain still and tranquil, so the world is stirred by disturbances and upheavals: now it is lifted up by prosperity, now cast down by adversity; it grows by being born and diminishes by dying. The Lord therefore crossed this sea when, trampling upon the waves of the world, he showed us the path of heavenly life. The Apostle Peter speaks of his crossing: “He went about doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil” (Acts X).

“And a great multitude followed him, because they saw the signs that he performed upon those who were sick.”

The crowds that followed him signify the Church of the elect, gathered from all nations. For it follows the Lord daily, not by the movement of its feet but by imitation in its deeds. To follow the Lord is to imitate him, as he himself says: “Whoever ministers to me, let him follow me” (John XII). Hence it is also commanded in the Law: “You shall walk after the Lord your God” (Lev. XVIII). For this reason John admonishes us, saying: “Whoever says that he remains in Christ ought himself to walk as he walked” (1 John II).

But the reprobate are rolled about in this sea like fish. Entangled in carnal desires, they cannot in any way touch the shore of eternal life. Hence it is fittingly called the Sea of Galilee, which is interpreted as “wheel” or “rolling.” Just as a moving wheel turns in a circle but completes no journey, so those who have planted the roots of their hearts in the loves of the world are mobile and restless, yet in no way undertake the journey of heavenly life. Of them the Prophet says: “The ungodly walk in a circle” (Ps. XI).

But we, who do not have here a lasting city but seek the future one with all our desire, should despise the examples of such people, cross the sea with the Lord, forget what lies behind, and stretch forward toward what lies ahead. According to our calling, let us follow him to the prize of eternal reward, so that with this crowd we may be specially instructed, healed, and refreshed by him.

“Then Jesus went up onto a mountain, and there he sat with his disciples.”

The mountain onto which the Lord went after crossing the sea signifies heaven, into which he ascended victoriously after the triumph of the holy cross, having trampled upon the raging waves of the world. That he sat there with his disciples shows that where the Head went before, the members would also follow, as he himself says in the Gospel: “Father, I will that where I am, there my minister also may be” (John XII). And again: “Wherever the body is, there the eagles will also be gathered” (Luke XVII).

Alternatively, this mountain signifies more sublime doctrine. The Lord on the mountain is the word on high. Whoever therefore wishes to receive more sublime doctrine should raise his heart from earth to heaven—that is, pass from love of the world to love of God.

The Lord teaches, heals, and refreshes the crowds in the valleys, and he ascends the mountain with his disciples to show that, in the preaching of teachers, the discourse must be shaped according to the capacity of the hearers. The weak are not to be abandoned on account of the perfect; rather, they are to be endured and corrected together with them.

The Lord, as it were, remained with someone in the valleys when he answered the man who asked, “What must I do to possess eternal life?” (Luke XIX): “If you wish to find life, keep the commandments: You shall not kill, you shall not commit adultery, you shall not steal, you shall not bear false witness, you shall not covet your neighbor’s property; honor your father and mother.” But when that man sought something more sublime and said, “I have kept all these things from my youth,” he immediately showed him the mountain of perfection, saying: “One thing is still lacking to you. If you wish to be perfect, go, sell everything that you possess and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; then come and follow me.” But because those who have riches [the printed reading *velamant* is corrupt or uncertain] ascend this mountain with difficulty, “he went away sorrowful, because he was very rich.”

Paul, as it were, remained with his disciples in the valleys when he said: “I could not speak to you, brothers, as spiritual people, but as carnal—as infants in Christ. I gave you milk to drink, not food” (1 Cor. III). He had, as it were, ascended the mountain when he said to them: “We speak wisdom among the perfect” (1 Cor. II). He remained, as it were, in the valleys when he said: “Because of fornication, let each man have his own wife, and let each woman have her own husband” (1 Cor. VII). He had, as it were, ascended the mountain when he said: “Concerning virgins, I have no commandment of the Lord, but I give counsel. It is good for them if they remain thus, according to my counsel. I wish, however, that all people were as I am” (ibid.).

For one and the same teaching is not equally suitable for everyone, since recent converts must be admonished in one way and the perfect in another; married people in one way and virgins in another; the chaste in one way and the lustful in another; drunkards in one way and the sober in another; the proud in one way and the humble in another; those who seize what belongs to others in one way and those who distribute their own possessions in another.

Often, one medicinal antidote cures one illness while aggravating another. Bread strengthens the life of the strong but kills the little ones. Poison is the life of a serpent but the death of a human being.

This, then, is the discernment to be observed in preaching: when a teacher sees that some people cannot grasp spiritual understanding, he should teach them according to the literal sense, yet should not on their account abandon those who are more perfect.

The patriarch Jacob showed us this by his example. When he was tending the sheep of his uncle Laban and receiving various things as his wages, he took poplar and almond rods, stripped some of them in part, left others partly with their bark, and placed them in the watering troughs, so that the sheep might conceive varied offspring while looking at them (Gen. XXX).

What does Jacob, the shepherd of sheep, signify except a shepherd of the Church? What do the sheep signify except faithful hearers? Hence it was said to the first shepherd: “If you love me, feed my sheep” (John XXI).

Water signifies sacred Scripture, of which Solomon says: “The word from a man’s mouth is deep water, and a flowing stream is a fountain of wisdom” (Prov. XVIII). The rods are the meanings of that same Scripture. Some of them are to be stripped of their bark and others left with their bark, so that the more perfect may be instructed allegorically, while those of lesser capacity may be taught according to the literal sense.

“Now the Passover, the feast of the Jews, was near.”

Passover was not named from the Passion, as some think, but from “passing over.” From the time when the Lord, passing through Egypt, struck down the firstborn of the Egyptians and freed the children of Israel, Passover was commanded to be celebrated. In Hebrew it is called *phase*, and in Latin *transitus*, “passing over.” Since the Evangelist was about to say that the Lord satisfied five thousand people with five loaves, he first stated: “The Passover, the feast of the Jews, was near,” so that we might understand that we are spiritually fed by him when we celebrate the passing over—that is, when we pass from vices to virtues and from love of the world to love of God.

“When Jesus therefore had lifted up his eyes and had seen that a very great multitude was coming to him.”

The Lord’s eyes have a twofold meaning in Scripture. Sometimes they signify the gifts of the Holy Spirit; sometimes they signify the gaze of compassion.

They signify the gifts of the Holy Spirit, as it is read in Zechariah: “Upon one stone are seven eyes” (Zech. III). John also says in the Apocalypse: “And I saw, and behold, in the midst of the throne and of the four living creatures, and in the midst of the elders, a Lamb standing as though slain, having seven horns and seven eyes, which are the seven spirits of God sent into all the earth” (Rev. V).

They signify the gaze of compassion, as it is read in the Psalm: “The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous” (Ps. XXXV). And again: “The Lord looked down from heaven; he saw all the sons of men” (Ps. XXXII).

Since all things are naked and open to his eyes, he is said to see us when he grants us the gifts of his compassion or frees us from the pressure of tribulation. Thus he says to Moses: “I have surely seen the affliction of my people who are in Egypt, and I have heard their groaning, and I have come down to deliver them” (Exod. III).

In this passage, therefore, the lifting of the Lord’s eyes signifies the gaze of compassion, because he first looked mercifully upon the crowds whom he later fed. With these eyes the Lord looked upon Peter when he went outside and wept bitterly (Matt. XXVI).

“He says to Philip: ‘Where shall we buy bread, so that these people may eat?’”

The Lord questioned Philip, not in order to learn something from him but in order to teach him. We understand this more easily if we consider the different ways in which a question is asked. There are three: either from the desire to reprimand, from the wish to learn, or from the intention to teach.

It is asked from the desire to reprimand when the scribes and Pharisees questioned the Lord in order to accuse him—for example, concerning a woman caught in adultery (John VIII), concerning the denarius (Matt. XXII), and in similar cases.

It is asked from the wish to learn when the apostles questioned the Lord, saying: “Lord, when will these things happen? Or what will be the sign of your coming?” (Mark XIII), and in other such instances.

It is asked from the intention to teach when the angel questioned John in the Apocalypse, saying: “Who are these clothed in white robes, and from where have they come?” (Rev. VII). When John answered, “My lord, you know,” the angel immediately taught him, saying: “These are those who came out of the great tribulation, washed their robes, and made them white in the blood of the Lamb.”

The Lord questioned his disciple not to reprimand him, nor to learn anything from him, but to teach him. The Evangelist carefully made this clear when he immediately added:

“But he said this to test him.”

What does it mean that the Lord is said to have tested his disciple, when the Apostle James says: “Let no one, when he is tempted, say that he is tempted by God, for God is not a tempter of evil; indeed, he tempts no one” (James I)? If God tempts no one, why does the Evangelist say, “He said this, testing him”?

The brief answer is that there is one temptation of the devil, by which he tests a person in order to destroy him, and another temptation of God, by which he tests a person in order to prove him. We understand this better if we examine the different kinds of temptation more carefully.

There is the devil’s temptation, by which he tests a person in order to destroy him. Wishing to be delivered from it, we say daily in prayer: “Do not lead us into temptation” (Matt. VI).

There is another temptation that arises from the weakness or pleasure of the flesh. James speaks of it: “Each person is tempted when he is drawn away and enticed by his own desire” (James I). The Apostle likewise says: “Let no temptation overtake you except what is human” (1 Cor. X).

There is also a temptation by which God tests a person in order to prove him. Through Moses this is said to the Israelites: “The Lord your God tests you, to know whether you love him or not” (Deut. XIII). And through a certain wise man: “The furnace tests the potter’s vessels, and the trial of tribulation tests righteous people” (Ecclus. XXVII).

By this kind of temptation God tested Abraham, so that he who was known to God might appear proved to human beings. In this way the Prophet desired to be tested when he said: “Prove me, Lord, and test me” (Ps. XXV).

In this way, then, the Lord tested Philip, so that he who was ignorant of such a great ministry might be made knowledgeable and instructed. He was to learn that, in the presence of him who brings bread forth from the earth and wine that gladdens the human heart, he should not doubt that a few loaves could satisfy a great multitude.

This temptation, therefore, is not to be feared but rather endured and even desired for the sake of testing, as the Apostle James admonishes when he says: “Consider it all joy, my brothers, whenever you fall into various temptations, knowing that temptation produces endurance, endurance produces testing, and testing produces hope. Blessed is the man who endures temptation, for when he has been proved, he will receive the crown of life that God promised to those who love him” (James I).

“Philip answered him: ‘Two hundred denarii worth of bread would not be sufficient for them, so that each might receive even a little.’”

Philip is interpreted as “mouth of the lamp.” In this passage he signifies the Jewish people, which was once the mouth of the lamp, when it sprang forth with open mouth to praise God.

By his statement that “two hundred denarii worth of bread would not be sufficient for them, so that each might receive even a little,” he signifies the rare or limited faith of that same people. It did not believe that, through the bodily presence of the Lord and the small number of the apostles, a person could attain knowledge and understanding of both Testaments. For the two hundred denarii signify the two Testaments.

“One of his disciples, Andrew, the brother of Simon Peter, says to him: ‘There is one boy here who has five barley loaves and two fish. But what are these among so many?’”

If we examine the literal sense, Andrew seems in this passage to have a somewhat greater faith than Philip when he says: “There is one boy here who has five barley loaves and two fish.” But he doubted in faith when he added: “But what are these among so many?”

He signifies the prophetic word, which had faith when it foretold that God would come in the flesh. But when that same people largely refused to believe in him when he came, it doubted in faith. Isaac prefigured this people: when he blessed his son with dimming eyes, he foretold many things that would happen to him, yet he did not recognize who was actually present (Gen. XXV).

In Scripture, “boy” sometimes signifies purity and sometimes lightness or instability of mind. It signifies purity when it is said of the Lord: “Behold my chosen servant, whom I have chosen” (Isa. XLII). And when he himself said to his disciples: “Children, do you have anything to eat?” (John XXI).

It signifies lightness or instability of mind when the Lord says concerning the Jews: “To what shall I compare this wicked generation, or to what shall I liken it? It is like children sitting in the marketplace, calling to one another and saying: ‘We played music for you, and you did not dance; we mourned, and you did not lament’” (Matt. XI). The age of childhood is talkative and fickle unless restrained by the rod of discipline.

This boy therefore signifies the Jewish people, which, because of the lightness or instability of its mind, did not remain firm in faith and knowledge of God. He had five loaves because the Jewish people received the five books of Moses: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy. In the Hebrew language these are called *Beresith*, *Veellehsemoth*, *Vaicra*, *Vaidabber*, and *Ellehaddebarim*.

They are rightly said to have been barley loaves because of the hardness of the Law. Barley has a dense husk, and its inner substance is not easily reached. This signifies the obscurity of the Law, because before the Lord’s coming it was so veiled that no one could understand it spiritually, until the one who had given the Law came and bestowed its blessing.

If the five loaves signify the five books of Moses, we may also understand by the two fish two other books—namely, the oracles of the Prophets and the songs of the Psalms. After the authority of the Law, these were held in greater sanctity among that people. They recited one by singing it from memory and the other by frequently reading it in their synagogues.

These two books are rightly understood by the two fish, because they foretold that a people would arise in the Church that would preserve in its conduct what the fish possesses by nature.

A fish has four characteristics. First, it cannot live without water. Second, it is accustomed to leap above the water. Third, the more it is struck by the waves, the stronger it becomes. Fourth, fish neither beget nor are begotten through intercourse.

Just as a fish cannot live without water, so that people cannot enter everlasting life without the font of baptism, the Lord saying: “Unless someone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (John III).

And just as a fish leaps above the waters, so the same spirit, despising earthly things, raises itself to heavenly things on the wing of contemplation, saying with the Apostle: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. III).

And just as a fish becomes stronger the more it is struck by the waves, so the perfect Christian advances in God to the degree that he finds in this age something harder to endure, saying with the Prophet: “You brought us into a snare; you placed tribulations upon our back; you set people over our heads. We passed through fire and water, and you brought us into refreshment” (Ps. LXV).

And just as the fish of the world neither beget nor are begotten through intercourse, so in the Church there are those who reject marital union and pursue virginal integrity, fulfilling what the Lord says in the Gospel: “Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning” (Luke XII).

Alternatively, by the two fish we may understand the two orders that were more prominent among that people, namely, the royal and the priestly orders, by which they were governed and instructed. The Lord Jesus graciously took both into himself, so that he might become for us both king and priest: king by governing us well, and priest by offering himself to God as an immaculate sacrifice for us.

“Then Jesus said: ‘Make the people sit down.’”

To make people sit down is, spiritually, to make them rest in faith. The Lord commanded the disciples to make the people sit down when he sent them into the world to preach, saying: “Go into all the world, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved” (Mark XVI).

They made them sit down when, “going forth, they preached everywhere, while God worked with them and confirmed the word by the signs that followed.”

It should not be omitted, however, that, as we learn from the account of another Evangelist, “they made them sit down for the meal, by fifties and hundreds.” This arrangement of those sitting signifies the variety of those living in the Church.

Those seated by fifties are penitents. The number fifty suits penitents because the fiftieth Psalm is sung in penitence, and the fiftieth year is called a jubilee in the Law—that is, the year of remission. Those seated by hundreds are people who, under God’s protection, have no need of public penance.

Alternatively, those seated by fifties are married people, and those seated by hundreds are virgins. Or again, those seated by fifties are those who arrange earthly matters well, while those seated by hundreds are those who, out of love for perfection, abandon everything for God.

“Now there was much grass in the place.”

Grass is the vegetation of the meadows, which, while green, is pleasing to the sight and pleasant for sitting and walking upon. But when it has been cut by the sickle, it suddenly loses its former greenness.

Grass therefore signifies either carnal pleasure or the fragility of the flesh. Although it appears delightful and beautiful to those who love it, once cut down by the sickle of death it is reduced to the dryness of dust, as Isaiah says: “All flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of grass. The grass withered, and the flower fell, because the spirit of God blew upon it” (Isa. XL).

The people truly are grass. The Prophet had seen the dryness of this grass when he said: “A human being is like grass; his days are like a flower of the field, so he will bloom” (Ps. CII). And Job: “A human being, born of woman, living for a short time, is filled with many miseries” (Job XIV). He comes forth like a flower and is crushed; he flees like a shadow and never remains in the same condition.

The crowd whom the Lord fed therefore sat upon the grass, so that we might understand that, if we desire to be spiritually refreshed by him, we must restrain the pleasures of the flesh under the rule of the mind, according to the Apostle’s words: “Let not sin reign in your mortal body, so that you obey its desires; but put to death your members that are upon the earth—that is, fornication, uncleanness, and greed” (Rom. VI; Col. III), and other things of this kind.

“Then the men sat down, about five thousand in number.”

It should not be passed over without consideration that no woman is mentioned as having been present at this meal of the Lord, but only men. For “man” (*vir*) is so called from strength (*vires*).

Hence the Lord says to blessed Job: “Gird your loins like a man” (Job XXXVIII)—that is, “Restrain lust like a strong man.” And in Wisdom: “O men, I call to you” (Prov. VIII). It is as though he were saying: Those who possess a weak and womanish mind cannot hear my words.

For this reason, in praise of Joseph, who bravely endured the tribulations of Egypt, it is said: “He sent a man before them” (Gen. XLV).

Since only men are said to have been present at this meal of the Lord, we are mystically admonished that, if we desire to taste how sweet the Lord is, we should be men—that is, strong against the temptations of the devil. The Apostle admonishes us: “Act like men and be strengthened; let all that you do be done in charity” (1 Cor. XVI). And the angel says in the Apocalypse: “Be strong in battle and fight against the ancient serpent.”

Nor will a woman remain unfed at this meal of the Lord if, in her female body, she courageously suppresses the devil’s temptations. Conversely, a man becomes womanish in mind if he is found soft and lax in his conduct against the assault of temptation. To the condemnation of such people it is said: “And the effeminate will rule over them” (Isa. III).

It is rightly reported that there were five thousand men, because of the perfection of the number five. The number five pertains to the five bodily senses: sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch. We must carefully guard these senses if we wish to take part in the Lord’s banquet.

Let us guard our eyes from unlawful sight, so that they do not see what they may desire, in accordance with the Lord’s statement: “Whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. V). And again: “You shall not covet your neighbor’s property” (Exod. XX). Thus we may be able to say with Job: “I have made a covenant with my eyes that I would not even think about a virgin” (Job XXXI). In order that we may do this, let us pray continually with the Prophet: “Turn my eyes away, so that they do not see vanity” (Ps. CXVIII).

Let us guard our ears, so that they do not willingly listen to words of cursing, detraction, falsehood, and vulgarity, but may always be open to hearing the divine word, so that with Job we may say: “By the hearing of the ear I have heard you, O Lord” (Job XLII). Hence the Prophet admonishes us: “Hedge your ears with thorns, so that they do not hear the words of detractors” (Ecclus. XXVIII).

Let us guard our nostrils from unlawful odors, so that we are not drawn into sin through the enticements of fragrance, but, as the Apostle says, “may be the good fragrance of Christ to God in every place” (2 Cor. II).

Let us guard our tongue from cursing, detraction, falsehood, murmuring, and idle speech. And, to preserve silence, let us sometimes refrain even from good words, according to the Prophet’s statement: “I said, ‘I will guard my ways, so that I do not sin with my tongue.’ I placed a guard over my mouth; I was silent, humbled myself, and kept silence even from good things” (Ps. XXXVIII).

For, as Solomon says, “death and life are in the power of the tongue” (Prov. XVIII). And: “Whoever guards his mouth preserves his soul from distress” (Prov. XXI). Our entire religion is in a certain sense defiled unless we impose moderation upon the tongue. For, as the Apostle says: “Bad conversations corrupt good morals” (1 Cor. XV). And James: “If anyone thinks that he is religious but does not restrain his tongue and deceives his own heart, that person’s religion is worthless” (James I).

Let us guard our hands from the shedding of blood, from persecution, and from injuring our neighbor. Let us always keep them ready for almsgiving and most eager to perform what is good, so that with the Prophet we may say: “I will wash my hands among the innocent, and I will go around your altar, O Lord” (Ps. XXV).

If we do this, we attain the perfection signified by the number one thousand. For the number one thousand, beyond which counting does not increase, signifies the perfection of those who possess complete and consummate virtue. As the Apostle says, they lack nothing in any grace while awaiting the revelation of our Lord Jesus Christ (1 Cor. I).

“Then Jesus took the loaves, and, when he had given thanks, distributed them to those who were seated. Likewise, also from the fish, as much as they wanted.”

Another Evangelist says that Jesus took the loaves, gave thanks, blessed them, broke them, and gave them to his disciples to distribute; and they distributed them to the crowd (Matt. XIV).

We have already said above that the loaves signify the Law of Moses and the fish the oracles of the Prophets and the songs of the Psalms.

Jesus took the loaves, broke them, and gave them to the disciples when, after his resurrection, he opened their understanding of the Law—namely, when, beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, he interpreted for them the Scriptures concerning himself in all things. He also took the fish, broke them, and gave them to the disciples when he showed them the spiritual meaning in the Psalms and the Prophets, saying (Luke XXIV): “Thus it is written in the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms concerning me. And thus it was necessary for Christ to suffer, to rise from the dead, to enter into his glory, and for the forgiveness of all sins to be preached in his name.”

The disciples distributed these things to the crowd when they preached the same understanding throughout the whole world. Of them it is said: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Ps. XVIII).

When the Lord was about to refresh the crowd, he gave thanks to the Father—not because he needed to ask anything from him, since he gives all that is requested together with the Father, but to show that all holy and righteous things must be sought from him of whom the Apostle James says: “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights” (James I).

“When they had been filled, he said to his disciples: ‘Gather up the fragments that remain, so that they do not perish.’”

Here the Lord’s great power is shown, but his no less remarkable humility is also revealed. It is a great power to satisfy five thousand people with five loaves; but it is a wonderful humility not to allow the fragments that remained to perish.

If Scripture is signified by the loaves, as has been said, we may also understand by the remaining fragments its more obscure meanings. What the common people cannot grasp, the Lord commanded the apostles to gather. For the more obscure meanings, which the simple multitude cannot comprehend, the teachers of the Church—namely, bishops and priests—ought to store within their own breasts, so that in a time of need they may be found capable not only of teaching but also of defending them.

Hence the Apostle Paul, when describing the virtues of a bishop, shows that knowledge of the Scriptures should be sought in him, saying: “He must hold firmly to the trustworthy word according to the teaching, so that he may be able to exhort with sound doctrine and refute those who contradict it” (Titus I).

Although holy simplicity is better than learned wickedness, both qualities nevertheless suit the teachers of the Church: their life should be holy for the sake of example, and their tongue learned for the instruction of others.

Hence the Lord says: “Every learned scribe in the kingdom of heaven is like a householder who brings forth from his treasure things new and old” (Matt. XIII). And again: “Who, do you think, is the faithful and wise servant whom the Lord has appointed over his household, to give them their measure of wheat at the proper time? Truly I say to you, he will set him over all his goods” (Matt. XXIV).

“So they gathered them and filled twelve baskets with fragments from the five barley loaves and the two fish, which remained over for those who had eaten.”

The sign grew and increased the wonder, because not only were five thousand people satisfied from five loaves, but so many fragments also remained that twelve baskets could be filled.

The twelve apostles are appropriately represented by the twelve baskets. A basket is woven from cheap and very small rods. Likewise, the apostles were chosen not from kings and princes, nor from the philosophers and wise men of this world, but from simple people and fishermen. Thus they were woven together like baskets from cheap and very small rods. Of them the Apostle says: “God chose the weak things of the world to confound the strong” (1 Cor. II).

There is also another reason why the apostles are suitably compared with baskets. In baskets manure is placed, and they carried it onto dry ground—that is, into the hearts of the Gentiles—so that they might produce more abundant fruits and the prophecy might be fulfilled: “The beautiful places of the wilderness will grow fat, and the hills will gird themselves with exultation. The rams have been clothed with sheep; the valleys will abound in grain” (Ps. LXIV).

“Those people, therefore, when they had seen the sign that Jesus had performed, said: ‘This is truly the prophet who is to come into the world.’”

The Evangelist rightly calls them “people,” because they understood only human things. Having seen such a great miracle, they ought to have said: “This is truly the Son of God who has come into the world.” But because they were human and understood human things, they kept silent about the Son of God and confessed him to be a prophet.

Yet they are not entirely wrong when they confess the Lord to be a prophet, because, as he himself says concerning himself: “A prophet is not without honor except in his own country and in his own house” (Mark VI). And again: “It is not fitting for a prophet to perish outside Jerusalem” (Luke XIII).

But we, taught by him and instructed by the Holy Spirit, should avoid their example and confess with Peter that he is the Son of the living God, who for us and for our salvation came into the world and will come again to judge the living and the dead.

## HOMILY L. MONDAY AFTER LAETARE

(JOHN II.) “Jesus went down to Capernaum, he and his mother, his brothers, and his disciples, and there they remained for not many days. And the Passover of the Jews was near, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem,” and so forth.

The Evangelist rightly says that Jesus went down to Capernaum. Capernaum is interpreted as “most beautiful village,” signifying this world, to which our Lord Jesus Christ is said to have descended for the salvation of the human race, without ever departing from his Father’s dwelling.

Some people are accustomed to be troubled by what is said at the beginning of this Gospel reading: that when the Lord descended to Capernaum, not only his mother and disciples but also his brothers followed him. Nor were there lacking heretics who thought that Joseph, the husband of Mary ever-virgin, had begotten from another wife those whom Scripture calls the Lord’s brothers; others, with even greater impiety, thought that he had begotten them from Mary herself after the Lord’s birth.

But we, dearest brothers, must know and confess without any scruple of doubt that not only the blessed Mother of God but also the most blessed Joseph, the witness and guardian of her chastity, always remained entirely free from every conjugal act. Those who were not her children but her relatives are called, according to the customary usage of Scripture, the Savior’s brothers and sisters.

Finally, Abraham speaks in this way to Lot: “Please, let there be no quarrel between me and you, or between my shepherds and your shepherds, for we are brothers” (Gen. XIII). And Laban says to Jacob: “Because you are my brother, will you serve me for nothing?” (Gen. XXIX).

It is clear, however, that Lot was the son of Haran, Abraham’s brother, and Jacob was the son of Rebecca, Laban’s sister; yet they are called brothers because of their relationship.

According to this rule in the sacred Scriptures, as I have said, we must understand that Mary’s or Joseph’s relatives are also very frequently called the Lord’s brothers.

But the fact that Jesus went up to Jerusalem as the Passover approached certainly gives us an example of how vigilantly we ought to submit to the Lord’s commands, since he, appearing in the weakness of a human being, observed the same decrees that he established by the authority of his divinity.

So that servants would not think that they could escape punishments or receive rewards without frequent prayers and sacrifices of good works, the Son of God himself went up, even among servants, to pray and offer sacrifice to God.

Let us see what he found them doing when he came to Jerusalem and what he did there.

“And,” he says, “he found in the temple those selling oxen and sheep and doves, and the money-changers sitting there. And when he had made something like a whip from cords, he drove them all out of the temple, the sheep and oxen as well; he poured out the money-changers’ coins and overturned their tables.”

The oxen, sheep, and doves were bought for the purpose of being offered in the temple. The money-changers sat at the tables so that the price of the victims might readily be assessed between their buyers and sellers. Thus, things that were bought for the purpose of being offered to the Lord in that same temple appeared to be sold there lawfully. But the Lord himself, unwilling that any earthly commerce—even commerce considered respectable—should take place in his house, drove out all the dishonest traders together with those who were conducting the trade.

What then, my brothers? What do we suppose the Lord would do if he found people divided by quarrels, occupied with frivolous talk, unrestrained in laughter, or entangled in any other crime—he who, when he saw people in the temple buying victims to be sacrificed to him, hastened to drive them out? We have said these things on account of those who, having entered the church, not only neglect the purpose of prayer but also pursue others with slander, adding sins to sins and, as it were, weaving for themselves an extremely long cord by the continual increase of those sins, without fearing that they will be condemned when bound by it at the examination of the strict Judge.

For twice, indeed, in the holy Gospel we read that the Lord, coming into the temple, drove out such traders: here, namely, in the Gospel of John, that is, in the third year before his passion, as we recognize from the following writings of this evangelist; and in the very year in which he suffered, when he came to Jerusalem seated on an ass five days before Passover (Matthew 21). But everyone who thinks rightly understands that the same thing takes place in the temple of the Lord’s holy Church through his scrutiny and daily visitation. Therefore these matters are greatly to be feared, beloved, and to be shuddered at with worthy dread. We must carefully guard against his coming unexpectedly and finding something perverse among the good for which we ought deservedly to be scourged and driven from the Church. Above all, we must be watchful in that place which is specially called a house of prayer, lest we do anything foolish, lest we hear the Apostle say to us, as he said to the Corinthians (1 Corinthians 11): “Do you not have houses for carrying on or speaking about ordinary affairs, or do you despise the church of God?” And lest we hear the prophet, when he spoke to the Jews, saying: “My beloved has committed many crimes in my house” (Jeremiah 11).

Indeed, we ought to rejoice because in baptism we ourselves are the temple of God, as the Apostle testifies when he says: “For the temple of God is holy, which you are” (1 Corinthians 3). We ourselves are the city of the great King, of which it is sung: “Its foundations are in the holy mountains” (Psalm 86), that is, the foundations of the Church rest upon the firmness of the faith of the apostles and prophets. But we must fear no less what the Apostle stated beforehand: “But if anyone violates the temple of God, God will destroy him” (1 Corinthians 3). And the righteous Judge himself says: “I will destroy from the city of the Lord all who work iniquity” (Psalm 101).

We ought to rejoice because the solemnity of Passover is being celebrated in us when we strive to pass from vices to virtues; for Passover means “passage.” We ought to rejoice because he deigns to visit our breasts—that is, his own city—and because that same Passover deigns, by the presence of his mercy, to illumine our good action. But we must be very much afraid that he may find us doing in his city something other than what he loves, and that he may show himself to us as a strict creditor, in a form we do not love: that is, lest, finding in the temple money-changers or sellers of sheep and doves, he condemn us.

The oxen signify the teaching of heavenly life, the sheep works of purity and piety, and the doves the gifts of the Holy Spirit. For, since a field is customarily cultivated with the help of oxen, the Lord’s field is the heart cultivated by heavenly teaching and properly prepared to receive the seeds of God’s word. Sheep innocently provide their fleeces for clothing people. And the Spirit descended upon the Lord in the form of a dove.

Those sell oxen who offer the word of the Gospel to their hearers not out of divine love but with an eye to earthly profit. The Apostle rebukes such people because they proclaimed Christ insincerely. Those sell sheep who perform works of piety for the sake of human praise. Of them the Lord says that they have received their reward (Matthew 6). Those sell doves who give the grace of the Spirit they have received not freely, as commanded, but in exchange for a reward. They confer the laying on of hands, through which the Spirit is received, not for monetary gain, perhaps, but for the favor of the crowd; they bestow sacred orders not for the merit of life but for the sake of favor.

Those lend money who serve, in the Church, not heavenly things hypocritically but earthly things openly, seeking their own interests and not those of Jesus Christ. But the Lord shows what reward awaits such deceitful workers when, having made a whip from cords, he drives them all out of the temple. Those are driven out from the portion and lot of the saints who, placed among the saints, either hypocritically perform good works or openly perform evil ones. He also drives out the sheep and oxen, because he shows that both the life and the teaching of such people are alike rejected.

The cords with which he scourged and drove the wicked from the temple are the accumulations of evil actions, from which the strict Judge receives the material for condemning the reprobate. Thus Isaiah says: “Woe to those who drag iniquity with cords of vanity” (Isaiah 5). And Solomon says in Proverbs: “His own iniquities capture the wicked, and he is bound by the cords of his sins” (Proverbs 5). For one who piles sin upon sin, so that he may be condemned more severely, gradually lengthens by his actions the cords with which he will be bound and scourged.

He also poured out the money of the money-changers whom he had driven out and overturned their tables, because, when the reprobate are condemned at the end, he will also remove the form of the very things they loved, in accordance with what is written: “And the world will pass away, and its desire” (1 John 2).

“And to those who sold doves he said: ‘Take these things away from here, and do not make my Father’s house a house of commerce.’”

He commanded that the selling of doves be removed from the temple because the grace of the Spirit ought to be received freely and given freely. Hence that magician Simon, who wanted to buy it with money in order to sell it at a higher price, heard: “May your money be with you for destruction. You have neither part nor lot in this word” (Acts 8).

It should be noted, however, that not only are those sellers of doves who, by bestowing sacred orders, seek payment in money, praise, or even honor, and make the house of God a house of commerce; so also are those who exercise a spiritual rank or grace in the Church, which they received through God’s generosity, not with a simple intention but for the sake of some human recompense, contrary to the words of the Apostle Peter: “Whoever speaks, let him speak as the words of God; whoever ministers, let him do so as from the strength which God supplies, so that in all things God may be glorified through Jesus Christ” (1 Peter 4).

Therefore, all such persons, when the Lord comes, [lacuna: to be removed from the Church; Note: Col. 0297D, something is missing here], should remove these things from their own actions, lest they make the house of God a house of commerce.

Nor should we pass over the fact that Scripture carefully commends both natures of our Savior, namely, the human and the divine. In order that he may truly be understood as the Son of God, let us hear what the Lord himself says: “Do not make my Father’s house a house of commerce.” For he plainly shows himself to be the Son of God the Father when he calls the temple of God the house of his Father.

Again, in order that he may be recognized as the true Son of man, let us recall that at the beginning of this reading, when he descended to Capernaum, he is said to have had his mother as his companion. It continues:

“His disciples remembered that it was written: ‘Zeal for your house has consumed me.’”

Out of zeal for the house of the Father, the Savior drove the wicked from the temple. Let us also be zealous, dearest brothers, for the house of God, and, as far as we can, let us strive to ensure that nothing wrong is done in it. If we see a brother who belongs to the house of God swollen with pride, accustomed to slander, enslaved to drunkenness, weakened by lust, troubled by anger, or subjected to any other vice, let us strive, insofar as opportunity permits, to chastise him and correct what has been polluted and perverted. And if we cannot correct anything of this kind, we should not endure it without the sharpest inward grief.

Above all, in that very house of prayer, where the body of the Lord is consecrated and where the presence of angels is always believed to be present, let us act with all our strength to ensure that nothing foolish is done and that nothing occurs which might impede our own prayer or that of our brother.

It continues:
