“Then the Jews answered: ‘What sign do you show us, since you do these things?’ Jesus answered and said to them: ‘Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.’”

Only afterward did the evangelist explain which temple he meant: namely, the temple of his body, which, after they had destroyed it through the passion, he himself raised from the dead after three days. Since they were asking the Lord for a sign as to why he should have cast the customary commerce out of the temple, he answered most appropriately that he should drive the wicked from the temple because that temple signified the temple of his body, in which there was absolutely no stain of any sin. Nor was it without reason that he cleansed the figurative temple of crimes, since he who could raise from the dead, by the power of divine majesty, the temple of God’s Word, destroyed by human beings through death, had cleansed it.

“Then the Jews said to him: ‘This temple was built in forty-six years, and will you raise it up in three days?’”

This is how they understood it, and so they answered. But lest we too should understand the Lord’s spiritual saying carnally, the evangelist subsequently explained which temple he was speaking about. When they say of the temple, “It was built in forty-six years,” they refer not to its first but to its second construction. For Solomon completed the first one in the greatest peace of his reign after a work of one hundred and seven years. After it had been destroyed by the Chaldeans, it began to be rebuilt seventy years later, at the command of Cyrus, when the Persian released the captives.

But the children of the exile, who were carrying out the work under the leaders Zerubbabel and Jeshua, were unable to complete it before forty-six years had elapsed because of the opposition of the neighboring peoples. This number of years also corresponds most fittingly to the perfection of the Lord’s body. For writers on natural history report that the form of the human body is completed in that many days: during the first six days from conception it has the likeness of milk; during the following nine it is changed into blood; then during twelve it becomes solid; during the remaining eighteen it is strengthened until the complete outlines of all the limbs are formed; and from that point onward, during the remaining time until birth, it increases in size.

Six, nine, twelve, and eighteen make forty-five. If we add one to these—that is, the very day on which the body, now distinguished into its members, begins to grow—there are as many days in the building of the Lord’s body as we find years in the construction of the temple.

And because that man-made temple symbolized the Lord’s most holy flesh, which he took from the Virgin, as we learn from this passage, it also symbolized his body, which is the Church, and the body and soul of each of the faithful, as we find in many places in Scripture.

The first Adam, after his sin, heard: “You are earth, and you will return to earth” (Genesis 3). But the second Adam said of himself: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2).

The first was scattered throughout the entire world; in the second he was gathered together. This is signified by the name Adam, which is written with four letters: ἄλφα (alpha), δέλτα (delta), again ἄλφα (alpha), and μῦ (mu). These four letters designate the four parts of the world in which Adam was scattered through his children. Therefore these four letters are read at the beginnings of the names of the regions of the world.

For ἄρκτος (arktos), “north,” begins with alpha; δύσις (dysis), “west,” begins with delta; ἀνατολή (anatolē), “east,” also begins with alpha; and μεσημβρία (mesēmbria), “south,” begins with mu. These are the regions of the world, beginning with these four letters.

If these letters are considered according to Greek reckoning, they make forty-six: alpha is one, delta four, alpha again one, and mu forty. Added together, they are forty-six. Mystically, they designate the years during which the temple of Christ’s body was built in the Virgin’s womb, as we said above.

The flesh of Christ, which was taken from Adam, was destroyed by the Jews and was rebuilt by him from himself, according to the Scriptures of the prophets. And therefore the evangelist says:

“For he was speaking about the temple of his body. When he had risen from the dead, his disciples remembered that he had said this about his body, and they believed the Scripture”—that is, the statements of the prophets who foretold that Christ would rise on the third day—“and the word which Jesus had spoken”—that is, what he said: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.” This means: “On the third day I will raise up what you destroy on the cross.”

It continues:

“When Jesus was in Jerusalem at Passover, on the feast day, many believed in his name when they saw the signs which he performed. But Jesus himself did not entrust himself to them, because he knew them all. And because he had no need for anyone to testify about a human being, for he himself knew what was in a human being.”

They did not believe in him in such a way that they were worthy for Christ to dwell in them. Their faith may be compared with that of catechumens, who believe in Christ, but Christ does not entrust himself to them. For “unless someone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (John 3). Christ entrusts himself to no one except one who is worthy to enter the kingdom of God.

For this reason ecclesiastical custom does not give catechumens communion in the body and blood of Christ, since they have not been born again of water and the Spirit. Only those who have been so born are entrusted with participation in the body and blood of Christ.

## HOMILY 51. TUESDAY AFTER LAETARE

### (John 7)

“At that time: When the feast was already half over, Jesus went up into the temple and taught; and the Jews were amazed, saying: ‘How does this man know letters, since he has not studied?’” And so forth.

The one who had remained hidden now taught and spoke openly, and he was not afraid. His remaining hidden was an example; his speaking openly was an exercise of power. But when he taught, the Jews were amazed. All of them, I think, were amazed, but not all were converted.

Why were they amazed? Because many knew where he had been born and how he had been raised. They had never seen him learning letters, yet they heard him disputing about the law and producing testimonies from the law—things which no one can produce unless he has read them, and no one can read unless he has learned letters. Therefore they were amazed.

Their amazement provided the Teacher with an opportunity to insinuate the truth more deeply. From their amazement and words, the Lord said something profound and worthy of careful examination. What, then, did the Lord answer them when they were amazed at how he knew letters which he had not learned?

“My teaching,” he said, “is not mine, but his who sent me.”

Here is the depth of the matter. He appears to have spoken contradictory words in a few syllables. For he did not say, “This teaching is not mine,” but “My teaching is not mine.” How is it mine and not mine? The question is how both can be true: mine and not mine.

If we carefully consider what the holy evangelist himself says in the same Gospel—“In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1)—the solution to this question depends upon it. What, then, is the Father’s teaching except the Father’s Word? Christ himself is therefore the Father’s teaching, or the Father’s Word.

But because the Word cannot belong to no one, but must belong to someone, he called himself his own teaching and not his own, because he is the Father’s Word. The Lord Christ seems to have said, “My teaching is not mine,” as though he were saying: “I am not from myself.”

Although we call and believe the Son equal to the Father, and although there is no difference of nature or substance between them, nor any interval between the one who begets and the one who is begotten, nevertheless, while preserving and guarding this truth, we say that one is the Father and the other the Son. The Father would not be the Father if he did not have a Son; the Son would not be the Son if he did not have a Father.

Yet the Son is God from the Father, while the Father is God but not from the Son: God from God, light from light. The Father is light, the Son is light—not two lights, but one light. The Father is God, the Son is God—not two gods, but one God, Father and Son.

The Holy Spirit, proceeding from the Father and the Son, is also God. As the Father is God, as the Son is God, so also the Holy Spirit is God: not three gods, but one God; one light, one substance, one nature, one majesty, one eternity, one greatness, one power, one goodness.

The Lord Christ therefore saw that not everyone would understand this profound mystery. In what follows he gave the counsel that to understand is to believe. For God said through the prophet: “Unless you believe, you will not understand” (Isaiah 7, according to the Septuagint).

This is what the Lord also added afterward:

“If anyone wills to do his will, he will know concerning the teaching whether it is from God or whether I speak from myself.”

What does this mean: “If anyone wills to do his will”? But I had said: If anyone believes—and I had given this counsel: If you have not understood, believe. Understanding is the reward of faith. Therefore do not seek to understand in order to believe; believe in order to understand, for unless you believe, you will not understand.

Since, then, I had given obedience to faith as the means of reaching the possibility of understanding, and since I had said that the Lord Jesus Christ himself joined these things together, in the sentence that follows we find him saying: “If anyone wills to do his will,” that is, to believe. But because “he will know,” that is, understand, everyone understands.

Yet because the words “If anyone wills to do his will” refer to believing, and because this must be understood more carefully, we need our Lord himself as interpreter, so that he may show us whether true belief belongs to doing the will of his Father.

Who does not know that doing the will of God means performing his work—that is, doing what pleases him? The Lord himself says openly elsewhere: “This is the work of God: that you believe in him whom he sent” (John 6). He says, “that you believe in him,” not merely “that you believe him.”

But the one who believes him does not immediately believe in him. For the demons believed him, but did not believe in him. Again, we can say of his apostles: We believe through Paul, but we do not believe in Paul; we believe through Peter, but we do not believe in Peter.

“He believed in him who justifies the ungodly, and his faith is counted as righteousness.” What, then, does it mean to believe in him? It means to love through believing, to cherish through believing, to be inscribed among his members through believing, and to be incorporated into his members.

The very faith which God requires from us is therefore the faith that works through love. If you understand the words of God, understand that Christ is the Son of God and that the Father’s teaching is not from himself: not from nothing, not from other subsisting beings, but from the Father alone, remaining in the Father and equal to the Father.

“He who speaks from himself seeks his own glory.”

This will be the one who is called Antichrist, exalting himself, as the Apostle said, above everything that is called God and that is worshiped. The Lord, announcing that he would seek his own glory rather than the glory of the Father, says to the Jews: “I have come in my Father’s name, and you did not receive me. Another will come in his own name; him you will receive” (John 5).

He indicated that they would receive Antichrist, who will seek the glory of his own name, puffed up rather than solid, and therefore unstable and destined to ruin.

But our Lord Jesus Christ gave us a great example of humility. He is indeed equal to the Father. Indeed, “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1). Indeed, he himself said—and said most truly: “I have been with you for so long, and you have not known me? Philip, whoever has seen me has seen the Father” (John 14). Indeed, he himself said—and said most truly: “I and the Father are one” (John 10).

If, then, he is one with the Father, God equal to the Father, God from God, God with God, coeternal, immortal, equally unchangeable, equally beyond time, equally the creator and administrator of times—nevertheless, because he came in time, took the form of a servant, and was found in appearance as a human being, he seeks the glory of the Father, not his own.

What ought you, a human being, to do when you seek your own glory whenever you do something good, yet meditate accusations against God whenever you do something evil? Pay attention to yourself: you are a creature; acknowledge the Creator. You are a servant; do not despise the Lord. You have been adopted, but not through your own merits. Seek the glory of him from whom you, an adopted human being, have received this grace—the glory which he sought who was uniquely born from him.

“But he who seeks the glory of the one who sent him is truthful, and there is no injustice in him.”

In Antichrist there is injustice, and he is not truthful; there is no one by whom he was sent. For he was not sent; he was permitted to come.

Therefore, all who belong to the body of Christ, lest we be led into the snares of Antichrist, let us not seek our own glory. But if he sought the glory of the one who sent him, how much more should we seek the glory of the one who made us?

It continues:

“Did not Moses give you the law,” he said, “and none of you keeps the law?” For if you had kept the law, you would recognize Christ in the very letters and would not kill him while he was present.

“Why do you seek to kill me?”

For this reason you seek to kill me: because none of you keeps the law. “The crowd answered him”: See what they answered: “You have a demon. Who seeks to kill you?”

It was almost worse to say, “You have a demon,” than to kill him. For the one who was driving out demons was told that he had a demon. What else could a turbulent crowd say? What else could stirred-up filth smell like except something rotten?

The crowd is troubled. By what? By the truth. The brilliance of the light troubled the crowd’s diseased eyes. But the eyes that lack health cannot bear the brilliance of the light.

The Lord, however, is not altogether troubled. Tranquil in his truth, he did not return evil for evil or abuse for abuse. If he had said to them, “Rather, you have a demon,” he would certainly have spoken the truth. For why would they say of the truth, “You have a demon,” unless the falsehood of the devil had provoked them?

Let us hear more calmly what he answered, and let us live calmly.

“I performed one work, and you are all amazed.”

It is as though he were saying: What would you do if you saw all my works? For the works they saw in the world were his works. He performed one deed and they were troubled, because he had made a man well on the Sabbath. They did not understand that the Lord was the Son of man and Lord of the Sabbath, who established the Sabbath for the sake of humanity, not humanity for the sake of the Sabbath.

He did not destroy the Sabbath by making a man well on the Sabbath, because the observance of the Sabbath was given to human beings for the salvation of human beings.

“For this reason Moses gave you circumcision.” It was rightly done that you received circumcision from Moses, “not because it is from Moses, but from the fathers.” Abraham was the first to receive circumcision from the Lord.

“And on the Sabbath you circumcise a man.”

Moses convicts you. In the law you received the command to circumcise on the eighth day; in the law you received the command to rest on the seventh day. If the eighth day of the one who has been born falls on the seventh day, the Sabbath, what do you do? Will you rest in order to observe the Sabbath, or will you circumcise in order to fulfill on the Sabbath the mystery of the eighth day?

“But I know,” he says, “what you do: you circumcise a man.” Why? Because circumcision pertains to a sign of salvation, and human beings ought not to rest from salvation on the Sabbath.

Therefore, you should not be angry with me either, because I saved the whole man on the Sabbath.

“If a man receives circumcision on the Sabbath,” he says, “so that the law of Moses may not be broken”—for something salutary was instituted through Moses in that regulation of circumcision—“why are you angry with me,” who works salvation “on the Sabbath?”

Perhaps that circumcision signified the Lord himself, with whom they were angry when he healed and saved. For circumcision was commanded to be performed on the eighth day. And what is circumcision except the stripping away of flesh?

That circumcision therefore signifies the stripping away from the heart of fleshly desires. It was not given without reason, nor was it commanded to be performed on that particular member. For through that member the human race is brought forth, and through one human being came the resurrection of the dead.

And because “through one man sin entered the world, and through sin, death” (Romans 5), everyone is born with a foreskin, because every human being is born with the fault inherited from the race.

God cleanses no one, whether from the fault with which we are born or from the faults we add by living wickedly, except through the stone knife—that is, through our Lord Jesus Christ. “For the rock was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10).

They circumcised with stone knives, and by the name of the rock they represented Christ; yet they did not recognize him when he was present, and even desired to kill him.

But when you circumcise a man on the Sabbath, understand that this signifies the good work which I performed when I saved the whole man on the Sabbath. For he was healed so that he might be sound in body, and he believed so that he might be sound in soul.

“Do not judge according to appearance, but judge a just judgment.”

What does this mean in this context? You circumcise according to the law of Moses on the Sabbath; do not be angry with me personally, who am the truth. Pay attention to the truth and judge a just judgment. If you judge according to the truth, you will condemn neither Moses nor me. And once you know the truth, you will know me, because “I am the truth” (John 14).

Brothers, it is a matter of great labor in this world to escape the vice which the Lord noted here: not to judge according to appearance, but to preserve a right judgment.

The Lord admonished the Jews, but he admonished us no less. He convicted them and instructed us; he rebuked them and sharpened us. Let us not think that this was not said to us merely because we were not there at that time. Let us therefore hear the Gospel as though the Lord were present.

Let us not say: “Oh, how fortunate were those who were able to see him!” Many of those who saw him bodily killed him; many among us who did not see him have believed.

Who is the one who does not judge according to appearance, except the one who loves equally? Whoever loves everyone equally judges equally concerning everyone.

Let us not think that this saying concerns those whom we honor in different ways according to the honor of their ranks, but those whose cases we are commanded to judge.

The Lord Jesus therefore went up to the feast not openly but secretly—not because he was afraid of being seized, but to signify that even on the very feast celebrated by the Jews, the mystery was hidden and profound. But soon the power that had been thought to be timidity appeared.

He spoke openly at the feast, so that the crowds were amazed and said what we heard when the reading was read:

“Is this not the man whom they seek to kill? And behold, he speaks openly, and they say nothing to him. Have the rulers truly recognized that this is the Christ?”

Those who knew with what savagery he was being sought were amazed at the power by which he was not seized. Since they did not fully understand his power, they supposed that the rulers had recognized that he was the Christ; for this reason, they had spared the one whom they had sought so intensely to kill.

Then what did those same people say among themselves?

“Have the rulers truly recognized that this is the Christ?”

They raised for themselves the question by which it might seem to them that he was not the Christ. For they added:

“But we know where this man is from. When the Christ comes, no one knows where he is from.”

What did the Jews mean when they said, “When the Christ comes, no one knows where he is from,” when, upon Herod’s inquiry, they pointed out the place of his birth in accordance with the prophecy of the prophet Micah?

They certainly knew the definite place of his birth, according to the words of the prophets. But we must consider what they thought they knew and what they said they did not know. They knew the place of his birth through the statements of the prophets, but through the impiety of their hearts they did not know his divine birth, by which he was eternally born from God the Father, as Isaiah says: “Who will declare his generation?” (Isaiah 53).

Finally, the Lord himself answered both matters: the frailty of his humanity and the majesty of his divinity, saying:

“Jesus therefore cried out as he taught in the temple: ‘You know me, and you know where I am from.’”

He rightly said: “You know me, and you know where I am from”—that is, you know my birth according to the flesh, the nobility of my parents, and the appearance of my face. But according to divinity you do not know me, because “I have not come from myself, but the one who sent me is true, whom you do not know.”

But in order that you may know him, believe in the one whom he sent. And know that “no one has ever seen God except the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father; he has made him known” (John 1). No one knows the Father except the Son, and the one to whom the Son wills to reveal him.

Finally, after he had said, “But the one who sent me is true, whom you do not know,” to show them how they might know what they did not know, he added:

“I know him.”

Therefore, ask me so that you may know him. Why do I know him? “Because I am from him, and he sent me.”

He magnificently showed both truths: “I am from him,” because the Son is from the Father; and whatever the Son is, he is from the one whose Son he is.

For this reason we call the Lord Jesus God from God. We do not call the Father God from God, but simply God. We call the Lord Jesus light from light, but the Father simply light.

This is what belongs to the words, “I am from him.” But when you see me in the flesh, “he sent me.” When you hear, “He sent me,” do not understand a difference of nature, but the authority of the one who begets.

“Then they sought to seize him, and no one laid hands on him, because his hour had not yet come.”

This means that he did not wish it. For he who was born by his will suffered by his will. Just as he foresaw the hour of his birth, so he predestined the hour of his passion.

If the hour of our death is according to his will, how much more did the hour of his passion come according to the decision of his own will?

Great, therefore, is the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ: that he was made in time, through whom times were made; that he was made among all things, “through whom all things were made” (John 1); that he was made what he had made.

He was made what he had made: he became human, though he had made humanity, so that what he had made would not perish.

According to this dispensation, the hour of his birth had already come and he had been born, but the hour of his passion had not yet come. Therefore he had not yet suffered, because the hour in which he wished to suffer had not yet arrived.

For this reason we read that, on the cross, when everything had been completed according to the Scriptures of the prophets, he said: “It is finished.” And, bowing his head, he gave up his spirit (John 19).

When he willed it, the things written about him had been completed, and when everything had been completed, he released his spirit by his own power.

“Many from the crowd believed in him.”

The Lord was saving the humble and the poor, while the rulers were raging. And therefore they not only failed to recognize the physician but also desired to kill him.

## HOMILY 52. WEDNESDAY AFTER LAETARE

### (John 9)

“At that time, as Jesus was passing by, he saw a man blind from birth.” And so forth.

The things which our Lord Jesus Christ did are astonishing and wonderful, both his works and his words. They are works because they were performed; they are words because they are signs.

If, then, we consider what this event signifies, the human race is that blind man. This blindness occurred in the first human being through sin, from whom we all derive not only the origin of death but also the origin of iniquity.

For if blindness is unbelief and illumination is faith, whom did Christ find faithful when he came? Therefore the evangelist says of Christ: “And as Jesus was passing by.”

Christ passed by in this way: he did not stand in the way of our sins, as the Lord himself says in a certain parable (Luke 10): “A Samaritan came along the road,” the one who came to heal the wounded man who was half-dead.

He passed by to illuminate the blind man, who is said to have been wounded in the parable; here, in the event itself, the blind man is illuminated.

He therefore saw a blind man—not blind in just any way, but blind from birth. For all human beings, except that one alone who was born from the Virgin, were born blind through original sin, that is, born with the sin which they drew from the root of the sin of their first parent.

The disciples therefore asked him: “Rabbi”—they called him their teacher, because they desired to learn. They put their question to the Lord as to a teacher: “Who sinned, this man or his parents, that he should be born blind?” Jesus answered: “Neither this man sinned, nor his parents.” What does he mean? If no human being is without sin, were the parents of this blind man without sin? Was he himself born without original sin, or had he added nothing to it by living? If, then, both his parents had sin and he himself had sin, why did the Lord say, “Neither this man sinned, nor his parents,” unless he answered the question actually put to him: why was he born blind? His parents did have sin, but it was not through sin committed in him that he was born blind. If, then, he was not born blind because of his parents’ sin, why was he born blind? Hear the teacher instructing, seeking one who believes, so that he may produce understanding: he himself states the reason why that man was born blind. “Neither this man sinned, nor his parents, but that the works of God might be manifested in him.” Not merely what I am going to do in this one blind man, but so that what must be done by me in the blindness of the whole human race might be manifested. Then he continued:

“I must work the works of him who sent me while it is day.” Remember how he attributes the whole glory to the one from whom he is, because that one has a Son who is from him, while he himself has no one from whom he is. What are the works of the Lord, for the sake of which the Son of God came into the world, except to illuminate the blindness of the human race, heal its wounds, seek what was lost, and restore what was deformed? But what does he mean by saying, “I must work the works of him who sent me while it is day? The night is coming, when no one can work”? It is clear that in this passage the Lord expressly and definitively called himself “day,” that is, the light of the world: “As long as I am in this world,” he says, “I am the light of the world.” Therefore he himself works as long as he is in this world. Do we suppose, brothers, that he was here then but is not here now? If we suppose this, then after the Lord’s ascension that fearful night has already come, in which no one can work. But if that night came after the Ascension, what is the meaning of his saying to his disciples as he ascended into heaven: “Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age” (Matt. XXVIII)—he who was then present in the world in bodily presence, but is now present everywhere in the world by divine power?

We have heard about the day; let us hear what this night is. What, then, shall we say about this night? When will it be, when no one will be able to work? This night will belong to the impious; this night will belong to those to whom at the end it will be said: “Go into the eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. XXV). But fire’s flame has also been called night. Hear, for there is also a night spoken of concerning a certain servant (Matt. XXII): “Bind him hand and foot, and cast him into the outer darkness.” Let a person therefore work, lest that night overtake him, in which no one can work. Now is the time for him to work through love; and if we work now, this is the day, this is Christ. Hear him promising, and do not suppose that he is absent: “Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age” (Matt. XXVIII). There will be night where no one can work, but only receive what he has worked for. The time of working is one thing; the time of receiving is another. For he will repay each according to his works. Let us hear the Apostle exhorting us with anxious concern to work. He says: “While we have opportunity, let us do good” (Gal. VI). We have heard what Christ said, admonishing the good and terrifying the wicked; but let us see what he did.

[Col. 0307A] “When he had said these things, he spat on the ground, and made clay from the spittle, and smeared it upon his eyes, and said to him: Go and wash in the pool of Siloam, which is interpreted as ‘Sent.’” What the Lord did is obvious. The blind man was illuminated, but a great mystery is commended in the human race. He spat on the ground and made clay from his saliva, because “the Word became flesh” (John I), and he anointed the blind man’s eyes. He had been anointed, yet did not see; he sends him to the pool called Siloam. The evangelist considered it important to commend to us the meaning of this pool, and said: “which is interpreted as ‘Sent.’” You now recognize who was sent. Unless he had been sent, none of us would have been released from iniquity. He therefore washed his eyes in the pool that is interpreted as “Sent.” He was baptized in Christ. If, then, when he baptized him in himself, so to speak, he illuminated him, perhaps when he anointed him he made him a catechumen. The depth of so great a sacrament can indeed be explained and treated in different ways, but this will suffice for your charity. The catechumen is anointed—that is, he is taught to believe in Christ. He is sent to the pool of baptism, so that he may be illuminated, recognize the true light, receive the remission of sins, be made from a son of wrath a son of God, and, once illuminated, come to proclaim Christ.

“Therefore the neighbors and those who had previously seen him, because he was a beggar, were saying: Is this not the man who used to sit and beg? Some were saying: It is he; but others: No, he is like him.” His opened eyes changed his appearance. “But he was saying: It is I.” A welcome voice, lest he be condemned for being ungrateful.

“So they said to him: How were your eyes opened? He answered: The man called Jesus made clay and anointed my eyes, and said to me: Go to the pool of Siloam and wash. And I went, and washed, and I saw.” Behold, he has become an announcer of grace; he evangelizes and confesses. That blind man, now seeing, confessed, and the hearts of the wicked were constricted, because they did not have in their hearts what he already had in his face.

“They said to him: Where is he? He said: I do not know.” In these words his mind was still like that of one who had been anointed but did not yet see. But let us suppose, brothers, that he had that anointing in his mind: he proclaims, yet does not know whom he proclaims.

[Col. 0307D] “So they bring to the Pharisees the man who had been blind. Now it was the sabbath when Jesus made the clay and opened his eyes. Again the Pharisees asked him how he had come to see. But he said: He put clay on my eyes, and I washed, and I see. Therefore some of the Pharisees said”—not all, but some; for some were already being anointed. What, then, did those say who neither saw nor were anointed? “This man is not from God, because he does not keep the sabbath.” Rather, it was he who kept the spiritual sabbath—that is, not having sin—who was without sin. “Everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin” (John VIII). But these men, as I said, neither seeing nor anointed, observed the sabbath carnally and violated it spiritually. “Others were saying: How can a sinful man perform such signs?” Behold, these are the anointed. “And there was a division among them.” That day was divided between light and darkness.

“So they say to the blind man again: What do you say about him who opened your eyes? What do you think about him? What is your judgment of him?” They were seeking a way to slander the man, so that he might be expelled from the synagogue but found by Christ. But he steadfastly expressed what he thought. For he said: “He is a prophet”—still anointed in heart, certainly, and not yet confessing the Son of God, but not lying. Yet the Lord himself says of himself: “A prophet is not without honor except in his own country” (Matt. XI).

“So the Jews did not believe about him that he had been blind and had received his sight, until they called his parents, the man who had received his sight, and asked them, saying: Is this your son, whom you say was born blind? How then does he now see? His parents answered them and said: We know that this is our son and that he was born blind. But how he now sees, we do not know; or who opened his eyes, we do not know. Ask him; he is of age; let him speak for himself.” It was as though they were saying: We know that this is our son and that he was born blind; but we would rightly be compelled to speak for a child if he could not speak for himself. This man, once blind, speaks; now he sees. We know him as blind from birth; we know that he spoke before; now we see him seeing. Ask him, so that you may be instructed.

[Col. 0308C] “His parents said these things because they feared the Jews. For the Jews had already conspired that if anyone confessed him to be the Christ, he should be expelled from the synagogue. Therefore his parents said: He is of age; ask him. So they called again the man who had been blind and said to him: Give glory to God.” What does “Give glory to God” mean? Deny what you have received. This plainly is not giving glory to God, but rather blaspheming God. “Give,” they say, “glory to God” (John V).

“We know that this man is a sinner.” Then he said to them: “If he is a sinner, I do not know. One thing I know: though I was blind, now I see.” So they said to him: “What did he do to you? How did he open your eyes?” And he, now becoming angry at the Jews’ obstinacy, seeing though he had been blind, and unable to endure the blind,

“answered them: I have already told you, and you heard. Why do you want to hear it again? Surely you do not also want to become his disciples?” What does “surely” mean here, except: I am already one? Surely you too now see? But I do not see you seeing.

“They reviled him and said: You are his disciple.” May such a curse fall upon us and upon our children! It is a curse if you examine the heart, not if you weigh the words. “But we are disciples of Moses. We know that God spoke to Moses.” For you have the Lord saying: “If you believed Moses, you would believe me also” (ibid.). For he wrote about me in this way: You follow the servant and turn your back upon the Lord.

[Col. 0309A] “The man answered and said to them: Here is the astonishing thing: you do not know where he is from, and yet he opened my eyes. We know that God does not hear sinners; but if anyone is a worshiper of God and does his will, he hears him.” He is still speaking as one who has been anointed, for God has heard sinners. If God did not hear sinners, that publican would have said in vain, lowering his eyes to the ground and striking his breast: “Lord, be merciful to me, a sinner” (Luke XVIII). Through this confession he deserved justification, just as this blind man deserved illumination. But sinners must wash their hearts with the tears of repentance, so that they may be heard; so that what happened in this blind man’s face may happen in their hearts; and so that they may perceive that God hears them—he who came into the world to save sinners.

“From the beginning of the world it has not been heard that anyone opened the eyes of a man born blind. If this man were not from God, he could do nothing”—freely, steadfastly, and truthfully. For these things that were done by the Lord—by whom could they be done except by God? Or when could such things be done by the disciples, unless God dwelt in them?

“They answered and said to him: You were born entirely in sins.” What does “entirely” mean? With your eyes closed; but he who opened your eyes also saves the whole of you. He who gave illumination to your face will give resurrection to your heart. “You were born entirely in sins, and you are teaching us?” And they threw him out. They had made him their teacher: they questioned him so many times in order to learn, and then threw out the one they had questioned when he taught them.

“When Jesus heard that they had thrown him out, and when he had found him, he said to him: Do you believe in the Son of God?” Now he washes the face of his heart.

“He answered and said”—as though still one who had been anointed: “Who is he, Lord, that I may believe in him?” And Jesus said to him: “You have both seen him, and he who speaks with you is he.” Then he fell down and worshiped him. Finally, with the face of his heart washed and his conscience cleansed, recognizing that he was not the son of Joseph, as he had previously believed, but the Son of God whom he saw, he said: “I believe, Lord.” But it is not enough to say, “I believe.” Do you wish to see what kind of belief he had? “Falling down, he worshiped him.” If he had not believed that the Son of God was the one he saw, he would certainly not have worshiped him. Therefore, sinners, devote yourselves to prayers. Confess your sins; pray that they may be blotted out; pray that they may be diminished; pray that, as you advance, they themselves may cease.

# HOMILY LIII. THURSDAY AFTER *LAETARE*

*(John V.)* “At that time Jesus said to the crowds of the Jews: My Father is working until now, and I am working,” and so forth.

The Father and the Son are working, so that the diversity of the natures created in the world’s first formation may remain. Therefore it is said in the Psalms: “He fashioned their hearts one by one” (Ps. XXXII). He reforms not unknown kinds of souls, but souls of the same substance that was created in the first man. Consequently, when the Psalmist referred not only the primordial creation of the world but also the daily governance of creation to the praise of the Creator, he said, among other things: “You made all things in wisdom” (Ps. CIII). If we rightly confess Christ as the power of God and the wisdom of God, and God governs all things in this wisdom, it is plainly established that the Father is working until now, and the Son is also working.

“Therefore,” he says, “my Father has not worked only during the first six days, as you suppose; rather, he is working until now—not by instituting a new kind of creation, but by propagating what he created in the beginning, so that it may not perish. ‘And I am working’”—that is, until now, arranging, governing, and increasing all things with him. It is as though he openly said: Why are you envious of me? Why do you censure me, blind teachers of the Law, because in the form of a man I have worked the salvation of one man on the sabbath, when in the nature of divinity, together with God the Father, I am always peacefully working the whole human race—or rather, the entire structure of the world, and all things visible and invisible? But they were less capable of understanding so great and such a mystery.

“Therefore they sought all the more to kill him, because he not only broke the sabbath, but also called God his own Father, making himself equal to God.” They were especially distressed because the one whom they knew as truly a man through the weakness of the flesh wished to be believed to be truly the Son of God—that is, not adopted by grace like the other saints, to whom the Prophet says: “I said: You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High” (Ps. LXXXI), but equal to the Father in every respect by nature.

It should certainly be noted that the words “making himself equal to God” are spoken with reference to the person of the Jews, who thought that the Lord Jesus, by preaching, was making himself something he was not, rather than truly declaring what he was. The Jews were therefore stirred up and indignant—rightly so, because a man dared to make himself equal to God; but wrongly, because they did not understand God in the man. They saw the flesh but did not know the God; they saw the dwelling but ignored its inhabitant. For that flesh was a temple; God dwelt within it.

Jesus was not therefore comparing the flesh with the Father, nor was he comparing the form of a servant with the Lord—not what was made for our sake, but what he was when he made us. You know who Christ is—I am speaking to Catholics—because you have rightly believed not merely in the Word, but that “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” [Col. 0310D] (John I). Recall what you know about the Word: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (ibid.). Here there is equality with the Father; but “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.” In respect of this flesh, the Father is greater; thus the Father is both equal and greater: equal to the Word, greater than the flesh; equal to him through whom he made us, greater than him who was made for our sake.

“So the Jews were stirred up and troubled,” because Christ made himself equal to the Father. They understood him only as a man, not as God: they saw the flesh and did not believe in the divinity.

“For he said: The Son cannot do anything of himself except what he sees the Father doing.” The Father does not perform one set of works that the Son sees him doing, while the Son performs another set of works that he has seen the Father doing; rather, the Father and the Son perform the very same works alike. Whatever he does, the Son also does in the same way. It is not that when the Father does one thing the Son likewise does another; whatever the Father does, the Son also does in the same way.

But the Son does those things which the Father does, and the Father does them through the Son. If the Father does through the Son the things he does, the Father does not perform one set of works and the Son another; rather, the works of the Father and the Son are the same. And how does the Son do them—both the same things and in the same way? Perhaps you will say: “The same things, but you say ‘in the same way.’” The same things, he says, and in the same way. How could they be the same without being done in the same way, when everything the Father does he does through the Son, as it is said: “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (ibid.)?

He therefore said “in the same way” because the Son does the same things as the Father, since the substance and operation of the Father and the Son are one in divinity, and their will, power, life, and essence are one. All things are equal in the Father and the Son, except that the Father is Father and the Son is Son. There is distinction in the persons, but unity in the nature.

“For the Son cannot do anything of himself except what he sees the Father doing.” We must not understand this statement carnally, as though the Father and the Son were two men, one showing and the other seeing; one speaking and the other listening. For neither does the Father have lesser power, nor does the Son of God have greater power; there is no difference of divinity between Father and Son, but one majesty. Therefore he added: “For whatever things the Father does, these the Son also does in the same way.”

He displays the sign of one nature and one operation, because the operation of the Father and the Son is shared, since they have one nature and likewise one operation. Therefore he continued:

“The Father loves the Son, and shows him everything that he himself does.” He said this to show that all this showing by the Father is instruction for our faith, and so that no ignorance could at all be understood in the Son, to whom the Father would show all the works he himself was doing. He immediately said:

“And he will show him greater works than these, so that you may marvel. For just as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so the Son also gives life to whom he wills.” He says that the Father shows the Son those things that cause them to marvel; and he immediately taught what those things were and that they were the same: “For just as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so the Son also gives life to whom he wills.”

Power is made equal through the unity of an undissimilar nature and through the showing of works. This is not instruction arising from ignorance, but instruction for our faith. It does not bring knowledge of unknown things to the Son, but brings us the confession of his birth. For the Father’s showing consists in doing through the Son what he is going to do.

The greater works are the resurrection of the dead, which will occur on the last day, greater than the healing of this sick man, who was healed by Christ’s word and from which the whole occasion of this discourse arose. He says: “so that you may marvel.” It is difficult to see how the eternal Father, who is coeternal with the Son and who knows all things that are with the Father, should show something to the Son as though in time. What, then, are those greater works? The works are therefore greater: to raise the dead than to heal the sick. But just as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so the Son also gives life to whom he wills.

The Father does not give life to some and the Son to others; one power brings about one giving of life, and this power must also be honored with one honor. Therefore he continued:

“For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son, so that all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father. Whoever does not honor the Son does not honor the Father who sent him.”

The Father judges no one because the person of the Father is assumed in man and will not be seen in the judgment; only the form of the Son will be seen—the form that was unjustly judged and justly judges the living and the dead. Nor will the Son be seen in the judgment in the nature in which he is consubstantial with God the Father, but in the nature in which he is consubstantial with his mother and became man.

This is how we should understand, “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son,” as though it were said: No one will see the Father in the judgment of the living and the dead, but all will see the Son, because the Son is also the Son of Man, so that even the impious may see him, when they too will see him whom they pierced.

So that we may not seem to infer this rather than demonstrate it openly, we bring forward the Lord’s own clear and certain statement, which we have shown to be the reason he said: “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son.” The judge will appear in the form of the Son of Man, a form that belongs not to the Father but to the Son; not the form of the Son in which he is equal to the Father, but that in which he is less than the Father, so that he may be visible in the judgment to the good and the wicked, “so that all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father.”

Whoever does not honor the Son does not honor the Father. For what is it to “honor the Father” except to have the Son? It is one thing when God is commended to you because he is God, and another when God is commended to you because he is Father. When he is commended to you because he is God, the Creator is commended to you; the Almighty is commended to you; a certain supreme, eternal, invisible, unchangeable Spirit is commended to you. But when he is commended to you because he is Father, nothing other than the Son is commended to you. For he cannot be called Father if he does not have a Son, just as the Son cannot be called Son if he does not have a Father.

But perhaps you may honor the Father as greater and the Son as lesser, saying: I honor the Father; I know that he has a Son, and there is no error in the Father’s name. I do not understand the Father apart from the Son, yet I honor the Son as lesser. Let the Son himself correct you and call you back, saying: “Let all honor the Son,” not less, but “just as they honor the Father.” “Therefore whoever does not honor the Son does not honor the Father who sent him.”

“I,” you say, “want to give greater honor to the Father and lesser honor to the Son.” There you remove honor from the Father, where you give greater honor to the Son. For what else does this view seem to imply except that the Father either did not wish or was unable to beget a Son equal to himself? If he did not wish to, he was envious; if he was unable to, he failed. Do you not see, therefore, that wherever you wish to give greater honor to the Father, there you are insulting the Father? Accordingly, honor the Son as you honor the Father, if you wish to honor both Son and Father.

“Amen, amen, I say to you, whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life. He will not come into judgment, but has passed from death into life.” Pay attention also to this: “whoever hears my word.” He did not say, “Believe me,” but “believes him who sent me.” Let him hear the Son’s word, so that he may believe the Father.

Why does he hear your word and believe another? When we hear someone’s word, do we not believe the very person speaking, and give our trust to the one speaking to us? What, then, did he mean by saying, “whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me,” except that his word is in me? And who is the one who hears my word except the one who hears me and the one who believes in me? He believes the one who sent me because, when he believes him, he believes his word; and when he believes his word, he believes me, because I am the Word of the Father.

For he would not pass from death to life unless he had first been in death. He was therefore dead and came to life; he had perished and was found. A certain resurrection is therefore already taking place, and all are passing from one kind of death to one kind of life: from the death of unbelief to the life of faith, from the death of falsehood to the life of righteousness. This, then, is also a resurrection of the dead. Let him unfold it more fully, and let it shine upon us as it has begun to do.

“Amen, amen, I say to you, the hour is coming—and now is—when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live.” This is proper to the godly: they hear concerning his incarnation in such a way that they believe he is the Son of God; that is, they receive him as having become lesser than the Father in the form of a servant for their sake, while believing that he is equal to the Father in the form of God. Therefore it follows:

“For just as the Father has life in himself, so he has given the Son also to have life in himself.” What he says—“He has given the Son to have life in himself”—may briefly be stated as: He begot the Son as life possessing life in himself. For he did not exist without life and then receive life; rather, he is life by being born. The Father is life without being born; the Son is life by being born. The Father is from no father; the Son is from God the Father. The Father is Father for the sake of the Son; the Son, both in being Son and in what he is, is for the sake of the Father; and what he is, he is from the Father.

He said “he gave life to the Son” so that he might have it in himself, as though he were saying: The Father, who is life in himself, begot the Son, who would be life in himself. For “gave” he intended “begot,” just as if we were to say to someone: God gave you existence. He continues and says:

“And he gave him authority to execute judgment, because he is the Son of Man.” I think nothing could be clearer. The Son of God, equal to the Father, does not receive this authority to execute judgment; he possesses it with the Father in secret. But he received it so that the good and the wicked might see him judging, because he is the Son of Man. The vision of the Son of Man will indeed be displayed to the wicked as well. The vision of the form of God, however, is granted only to the pure in heart, because they will see God—that is, only to the godly, to whose love he promises this very thing: that he will show himself to them. Therefore see what follows:

“Do not marvel at this,” he says. What prevents us from marveling except that which truly amazes everyone who does not understand? He would therefore say that the Father gave him authority to execute judgment because he is the Son of Man, whereas one might rather expect him to say, “because he is the Son of God.” But because the wicked cannot see the Son of God insofar as he is equal to the Father in the form of God, it is necessary that, when the living and the dead are judged before him, both the righteous and the wicked should see the judge.

“Do not marvel,” he says, “because the hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear the voice of the Son of God. And they will come forth: those who have done good, to the resurrection of life; those who have done evil, to the resurrection of judgment.” It was therefore necessary that he receive this authority precisely because he is the Son of Man, so that all who rise might see him in the form in which he can be seen by human beings—some for condemnation, others for eternal life.

What, then, is eternal life except that vision which is not granted to the impious? “That they may know you,” he says, “the one true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (John XVII). And how will they know Jesus Christ himself except in the same way as the one true God, who shows himself to them? Not in the way in which he will show himself even to those who are to be punished, in the form of the Son of Man.

In accordance with that vision he is good—the vision in which God appears to the pure in heart, as the Psalmist says: “How good is the God of Israel to the upright in heart” (Ps. LXXII). But when the wicked see the judge, he will not appear good to them, because they will not rejoice in him in their hearts. Rather, then all the tribes of the earth will mourn—meaning, of course, all the wicked and unbelievers.

For this reason also, when the man who had called him “Good Teacher” asked him for advice about attaining eternal life, he answered: “Why do you ask me about the good? No one is good except one, God” (Matt. XIX), although elsewhere the Lord himself calls a human being good: “The good man brings forth good things from the good treasure of his heart, and the evil man brings forth evil things from the evil treasure of his heart” (Matt. XII).

But because that man was seeking eternal life, and eternal life consists in that contemplation in which God is seen not for punishment but for everlasting joy, the Lord Jesus Christ shows us two resurrections in these words. The first is in faith, rising from sins, concerning which he says: “Amen, amen, I say to you, the hour is coming when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God.” The other is the one of which he says: “Amen, amen, I say to you, the hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear the voice of the Son of God.” The former is the resurrection of souls; the latter will be the resurrection of bodies.

Whoever does not rise in this first resurrection will not rise to him there. “The hour is now,” when the dead should rise. The hour will come at the end of the age when the dead will also rise. But if they rise now in mind, then they will rise in the flesh. Now they rise in mind through the Word of God, that is, through the Son of God; then they will rise in the flesh through the Word of God made flesh, the Son of Man.

The Father himself will not come to judge the living and the dead, yet the Father does not withdraw from the Son. How, then, will he not himself come? Because he himself will not be seen in the judgment. “They will see him whom they pierced.” That form will be the judge which stood beneath a judge; that form will judge which was judged. It was judged unjustly; it will judge justly. The judge will appear in such a form as can be seen by those by whom he has been crowned.

There is a distinction between the word he spoke above, “the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God,” and what he says here: “The hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear the voice of the Son of God.” There he said “will hear,” meaning “will obey”; therefore that resurrection is to life. But the future resurrection of which he says, “they will hear the voice of the Son of God,” means that they will hear so as to rise for judgment.

Here he did not add “to life,” because not all will rise to glory; many will rise to punishment. Therefore he added concerning the future resurrection: “Those who have done good, to the resurrection of life; those who have done evil, to the resurrection of judgment”—that is, condemnation, because here he used “judgment” for punishment. Then will come the final separation, separating the good from the evil, the wheat from the chaff. Then the impious will go into eternal fire, but the righteous into eternal life.

# HOMILY LIV. FRIDAY AFTER *LAETARE*

*(John XI.)* “At that time Lazarus of Bethany was sick, from the village of Mary and Martha, his sisters,” and so forth.

Because many things in this miracle of Lazarus’s resurrection are clear, we do not need to explain each one individually. In the preceding reading the evangelist makes clear that the Lord withdrew from the hands of those who had wanted to stone him and went across the Jordan, where John was baptizing. While the Lord was there, Lazarus became sick in Bethany, a village near Jerusalem.

“Now Mary was the one who anointed the Lord with ointment and wiped his feet with her hair; her brother Lazarus was sick. So the sisters sent to him, saying:” We now understand that they sent word where the Lord was. Since he was absent—across the Jordan, of course—they sent to the Lord, announcing that their brother was sick, so that, if he was willing, he might come and free him from his illness. He delayed healing him so that he could raise him.

What, then, did his sisters announce? “Lord, behold, the one whom you love is sick.” They did not say, “Come,” for only the fact was reported to the one who loved him. They did not dare to say, “Come and heal him”; they did not dare to say, “Give the command there, and it will happen here.” Why are these women not praised, if the faith of that centurion is praised for saying: “I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof, but say the word only, and my servant will be healed” (Luke VII)? These women said none of this, but only: “Lord, behold, the one whom you love is sick.” It is enough that you know; surely you do not love and then abandon him.

Someone may ask how Lazarus could signify a sinner and still be loved by the Lord in this way. Let him hear the Lord saying: “I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners” (Matt. IX); he would certainly not say this if he did not love sinners who have been converted.

“When Jesus heard this, he said to them: This illness is not unto death, but for the glory of God, so that the Son of God may be glorified through it.” This glorification did not increase him, but benefited us. Therefore he says, “it is not unto death,” because that death itself is not unto death, but rather unto the miracle by which people would believe in Christ and avoid true death.

For there are heretics who deny that the Son of God is God. Let them hear: “This illness,” he says, “is not unto death, but for the glory of God.” The glory of which God? Hear what follows: “So that the Son of God may be glorified through it” (John XI). Through what? Through that illness.

[Col. 0316B] “Now Jesus loved Martha and her sister Mary and Lazarus.” He was sick, they were sad, and all were chosen; but he was also the Savior of the sick, indeed the raiser of the dead and the consoler of the sorrowful.

“When he heard that he was sick, he then remained in the same place for two days.” They sent the message, and he remained there. The time was prolonged until the four days were completed—not without reason, because perhaps—indeed, certainly—the number of days itself conveys some mystery.

“Then after this he says to his disciples: Let us go again into Judea.” He had nearly been stoned there, and for that reason seemed to have left, lest he be stoned. He departed as a man, but by returning, as though he had forgotten the danger, he displayed his power. “Let us go,” he says, “into Judea.” Then, after he had said this, see how frightened the disciples were.

“The disciples say to him: Rabbi, just now the Jews were seeking to stone you, and you are going there again?” Jesus answered: “Are there not twelve hours of the day?” What does this answer mean? They said: “Just now the Jews wanted to stone you, and you are going there again so that they may stone you?” And the Lord: “Are there not twelve hours of the day?”

“If anyone walks in the day, he does not stumble, because he sees the light of this world. But if anyone walks in the night, he stumbles, because the light is not in him.”

He spoke of the day, certainly, but for our understanding—as though it were still night—let us invoke the day, so that it may drive away the night and enlighten the heart with light. What, then, did the Lord intend to say? As far as I can see, insofar as the height and depth of the meaning lie open to me, he wished to rebuke their hesitation and unbelief. They wanted to give the Lord advice, so that he would not die, although he had come to die, lest they themselves should die. Thus, in another place, holy Peter loved the Lord but still did not fully understand why he had come; he feared that he might die. And he displeased Life—that is, the Lord himself.

Therefore, when human beings wished to give advice to God, disciples to their teacher, servants to their Lord, and the sick to their physician, he rebuked them and said: “Are there not twelve hours in the day? If anyone walks in the day, he does not stumble.” Follow me, if you do not wish to stumble. Do not give me advice, since you ought to receive advice from me.

What, then, is meant by “Are there not twelve hours in the day?” It is because, to show that he himself was the day, he chose twelve disciples. “If I am the day,” he says, “and you are the hours, do the hours give advice to the day? The hours follow the day; the day does not follow the hours.”

If they are the hours, then what is Judas doing there, himself among the twelve hours? If he was an hour, he was shining; and if he was shining, how was he drawing the day toward death? But in this saying the Lord was foreseeing not Judas himself, but his successor. When Judas fell, Matthias succeeded him, and the number twelve remained. For he did not choose twelve disciples without reason, except because he himself is the spiritual day.

Let the hours, then, follow the day; let the hours proclaim the day. Let the hours be illumined by the day. Let the hours be enlightened by the day. Through the preaching of the hours, let the world believe in the day. Therefore he said, in brief: Follow me, if you do not wish to go astray.

“After this he said to them: Lazarus, our friend, is asleep, but I am going to awaken him from sleep.”

He spoke truly: to the sisters he was dead, but to the Lord he was asleep; he was dead to human beings, who could not raise him. For the Lord raised him from the tomb with as much ease as you awaken a sleeping person from bed.

According to his power, therefore, he called him asleep, since other dead people are also often called asleep in Scripture, as the Apostle says: “Concerning those who sleep, brothers, I do not want you to be ignorant, so that you may not grieve like the rest, who have no hope” (I Thess. IV). He therefore called them asleep because he declared that they would rise again. And in another place: “We shall all indeed sleep, but we shall not all rise” (I Cor. XV), signifying our death by the name of sleep.

For when the body is abandoned by the soul, it sleeps in the tomb until the resurrection on the last day. But souls, when they leave their bodies, receive different destinies: joy for the good, torments for the wicked. When the resurrection has taken place, however, the joy of the good will be greater and the torments of the wicked more severe, when they will be tormented together with their bodies.

When the Lord had spoken of his friend’s sleep, the disciples replied, showing how they understood it:

“Lord, if he is asleep, he will be safe.”

For dreams are ordinarily signs either of death or of recovery for a sick person.

“But Jesus had spoken of his death, whereas they thought that he was speaking about ordinary sleep. Then Jesus said to them plainly.”

He had spoken somewhat obscurely when he said, “He is asleep.” Therefore he said plainly:

“Lazarus has died, and I am glad for your sake, so that you may believe, because I was not there.”

He had been reported sick, not dead, so that the one who had created him might remain hidden, as would the one into whose hands the soul of the dying man had gone. This is what he meant when he said, “I am glad for your sake, so that you may believe, because I was not there”: they were now beginning to marvel that the Lord could say that he was dead, although he had neither seen nor heard it.

Here we must remember that even then the faith of the disciples themselves, who had not yet believed in him, was being built up by miracles—not so that it might begin to exist, but so that what had already begun to exist might grow, although he used a form of speech as if they were then beginning to believe. For he did not say, “I am glad for your sake, so that your faith may increase or be strengthened,” but “so that you may believe”—which must be understood as meaning, so that you may believe more fully and more firmly.

“But let us go to him.” Then Thomas, who is called Didymus, said to his fellow disciples: “Let us go too, so that we may die with him.” Jesus therefore came and found that he had already been four days in the tomb.

Many things can indeed be said about the four days, in keeping with the obscure passages of Scripture, which produce many meanings according to the diversity of those who understand them. Let us also say what it seems to us that the dead man of four days signifies.

Just as in the case of the blind man we understand, in a certain way, the human race, so perhaps in this dead man also we shall understand many things; for one reality can be signified in different ways.

When a human being is born, he is born already with death, because he draws sin from Adam. Hence the Apostle says: “Through one man sin entered the world, and through sin, death; and so it passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned” (Rom. V). There you have one day of death: the human being draws from death a descent into death.

Then he grows and begins to approach the years of reason, so that he may recognize the natural law, which all have fixed in their hearts: What you do not want done to you, do not do to another. Is this said only of pagans, and is it not read, in a certain way, in nature itself? You want to commit theft? Surely you do not want to suffer it. There is the law in your heart: What you do not want to suffer, do not do.

And people transgress this law: there is the second day of death.

A law was also given divinely through Moses, the servant of God. It was said there: “You shall not kill, you shall not commit adultery, you shall not bear false witness. Honor your father and your mother; you shall not covet your neighbor’s property” (Exod. XX). There is the written law, and it too is despised, and the third day of death is reached.

The Gospel is preached, the kingdom of heaven is proclaimed everywhere, Christ threatens Gehenna and promises eternal life. This too is despised; people transgress the Gospel. There is the fourth day of death.

Rightly, then, he already stinks. But is mercy to be denied to such people? Far from it. He does not disdain to approach even such people in order to raise them up.

“Many of the Jews had come to Martha and Mary to console them concerning their brother. When Martha heard that Jesus had come, she went to meet him; but Mary remained at home. Martha therefore said to Jesus: Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died. But even now I know that whatever you ask of God, God will give you.”

She did not say, “But now I ask you to raise my brother.” She said only this: I know that you can, if you wish; whether you will do so, however, is a matter of your judgment, not of my presumption.

Jesus said to her: “Your brother will rise.”

Martha said to him: “I know that he will rise on the last day.”

I am certain about that resurrection; about this one I am uncertain.

Jesus said to her: “I am the resurrection and the life.”

You say that your brother will rise on the last day; that is true. But through whom will he rise then? He can also rise now, because “I am the resurrection and the life.” He is life because he is resurrection. “For if he believes in me, he will not die forever.”

What does this mean by: “Whoever believes in me, even if he has died, will live”? Will he live as Lazarus died and will live? For he is not the God of the dead, but of the living.

Concerning the fathers who had long since died—that is, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob—he gave the Jews this answer: “I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob” (Exod. III; Luke XX). He is not the God of the dead, but of the living. For all of them live.

Believe, then, and even if you have died, you will live; but if you do not believe, even while you are alive you are dead.

Where, then, does death exist in the soul? Because faith is not in it. Where does death exist in the body? Because the soul is not there.

Therefore the life of your soul is faith. Just as the soul is the life of the body, so faith is the life of the soul.

“Whoever believes in me, even if he has died in the flesh, will live in the soul,” until the flesh rises, never afterward to die. This is what he means: whoever believes in me, even if he dies, will live.

“And everyone who lives”—in the flesh—“and believes in me,” even if he dies for a time because of the death of the flesh, “will never die forever,” because of the life of the spirit and the immortality of the resurrection. This is what he says: “Everyone who lives and believes in me will never die forever.”

“Do you believe this?” She said to him: “Certainly, Lord. I have believed that you are the Christ, the Son of God, who has come into this world.”

When I believed that you are the resurrection, I believed that you are life; I believed that whoever believes in you, even if he dies, will live; and that whoever lives and believes in you will never die forever.

“When she had said this, she went away and secretly called her sister Mary, saying: The Teacher is here and is calling you.”

It should be observed how she called it silence although she spoke softly. For how could she have been silent when she said, “The Teacher is here and is calling you”? It should also be observed that the evangelist did not say where, when, or how the Lord called Mary, so that this might rather be understood from Martha’s words, while the truth of the narrative was preserved.

“As soon as she heard this, she rose quickly and went to him. For Jesus had not yet come into the village, but was still in the place where Martha had met him. The Jews, therefore, who were with her in the house and were consoling her, when they saw Mary, that she had quickly risen and gone out, followed her, saying: She has gone to the tomb to weep there.”

Why did it matter to the evangelist to narrate this? So that we might see what caused more people to be present when Lazarus was raised. The Jews thought that she was hurrying for this reason: to seek consolation for her grief through tears. They followed her, so that the very great miracle of a man dead four days and rising again might find many witnesses.

“Mary, therefore, when she came to where Jesus was, seeing him, fell at his feet and said to him: Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died. When Jesus saw her weeping, and the Jews who had come with her also weeping, he groaned in spirit and troubled himself, and said: Where have you laid him?”

By groaning in spirit and troubling himself, he conveyed something to us. For who could trouble him, unless he himself troubled himself? First, then, attend to his power, and only afterward inquire into the meaning.

You are troubled unwillingly; Christ is troubled because he wished to be. Jesus was saddened, it is true, but because he wished to be. Jesus was hungry, it is true, but because he wished to be. Jesus slept, it is true, but because he wished to. Jesus died, it is true, but because he wished to.

It was in his power either to be affected in this way or not to be affected. For he assumed a true soul and flesh, joining to himself the nature of the whole human being in the unity of one person.

The Apostle’s soul too was enlightened by the Word; Peter’s soul and Paul’s soul were enlightened by the Word; the souls of the other apostles and of the holy prophets were enlightened by the Word. But of none of them was it said: “The Word became flesh” (John I); of none was it said: “I and the Father are one” (John X).

The soul of Christ and the flesh of Christ, together with the Word of God, are one person, one Christ.

And so, where supreme power is present, infirmity is troubled according to the inclination of the will. This is what he says: “He troubled himself.”

What, then, does Christ’s troubling himself mean, except that he shows you how you ought to be troubled when you are weighed down and oppressed by such a mass of sins?

You have examined yourself, you have seen yourself, you have reckoned with yourself: I did that, and God spared me; I committed that, and he endured me; I heard the Gospel, and despised it; I was baptized, and returned again to the same things. What shall I do? Where shall I go? Where shall I escape?

When you say these things, the spirit already groans, because faith groans. In the voice of one who groans, the hope of one who will rise again appears.

Therefore your faith is from Christ, and Christ is in your heart. Let Christ, then, groan in your heart.

Thus Christ wept for his dead friend, whom he had come to raise. Why did he weep, unless because he taught human beings to weep, oppressed by the weight of sins? Why did he groan and trouble himself, unless because the faith of a person rightly displeased with himself ought to groan in this manner in the accusation of evil works, so that the habit of sinning may yield to the force of repentance?

And he said: “Where have you laid him?”

You know that he is dead, and do you not know where he has been buried? What meaning does this also have? I would not dare to say that he does not know. What does he not know? Rather, he behaves as though he does not know.

How do we prove this? Hear the Lord saying in the judgment: “I do not know you; depart from me” (Matt. VII). What does “I do not know you” mean? I do not see you in my light; I do not see you in that justice which I know.

So here also, as though he did not know such a sinner, he said: “Where have you laid him?” Such is the Lord’s voice in paradise after Adam had sinned: “Adam, where are you?” (Gen. III).

They said to him: “Lord, come and see.”

This means: See and have mercy. For the Lord sees when he has mercy. Hence it is said to him: “See my humiliation and my labor, and forgive all my sins” (Ps. XXIV).

“Christ wept.” Then the Jews said: “See how he loved him.”

What does “he loved him” mean? He did not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance (Mark II).

But some of them said: “Could not this man, who opened the eyes of the man born blind, have caused this man not to die?”

He who did not wish to make him not die is about to do something greater: raise him after death.

“Jesus therefore, again groaning within himself, came to the tomb.”

He also groans within you, if you intend to live again. To every person who is oppressed by a most evil habit it is said: “He came to the tomb.”

“Now it was a cave, and a stone had been placed over it.”

The dead man is beneath the stone; the guilty person is beneath the law. For you know that the law given to the Jews was written on stone; but all the guilty are under the law. Those who live rightly are not under the law, for the law was not laid down for the righteous.

What, then, does it mean to remove the stone? It means to preach grace. For the Apostle Paul says that he is a minister of the New Testament, not of the letter but of the spirit. For “the letter,” he says, “kills, but the spirit gives life” (II Cor. III).

The letter that kills is like a stone pressing down.

“Remove the stone,” he says; remove the burden of the law and preach grace.

Martha, the sister of the one who had died, said to him: “Lord, he already stinks, for he has been dead four days.”

Jesus said to her: “Did I not tell you that if you believe, you will see the glory of God?”

What does “You will see the glory of God” mean? It means that he raises even one who stinks and has been dead four days. “For all have sinned and lack the glory of God” (Rom. III). And: “Where sin abounded, grace abounded all the more” (Rom. V).

“So they removed the stone. But Jesus, lifting his eyes upward, said: Father, I give you thanks because you have heard me. I knew, however, that you always hear me; but because of the people standing around I said this, so that they may believe that you sent me.”

When he had said this, he cried out in a loud voice.

He groaned, he wept, and he cried out in a loud voice, so that you may consider in your mind how difficult it is for one oppressed by the mass of an evil habit to rise. Yet he rises, secretly brought to life within by grace.

He rises after the loud voice with which he cried out: “Lazarus, come out!”
