“And immediately the man who had been dead came out, his feet and hands bound with strips of cloth, and his face was bound with a cloth.”

You marvel that he came out with his feet bound, and do not marvel that he rose after four days? In both cases the power was the Lord’s, not the dead man’s strength.

He came out and was still bound, still wrapped up; nevertheless, he had already come out. What does this signify?

When you despise, you lie dead; and if you despise all that I have said, you lie buried. You rise when you confess.

For what does it mean to come out except to be made manifest, as though stripping away what is hidden? But God brings you to confess by crying out—that is, by calling with great grace.

Therefore the dead man came out still bound, still guilty, so that his sins might be loosed. To the attendants, therefore, he said:

“Unbind him and let him go.”

He who raised the dead man could have loosed his bonds. But for the sake of the unity of holy Church and indivisible charity, this is said to the attendants, that is, to Christ’s disciples: “Unbind him.”

For without the unity of catholic faith and the charity of ecclesial holiness, sins are not loosed.

“Many of the Jews who had come to Mary and had seen what Jesus did believed in him. But some of them went to the Pharisees and told them what Jesus had done.”

Not all the Jews who had gathered around Mary, but some of them—perhaps those who had not believed—went to the Pharisees and told them what Jesus had done, either announcing it so that they too might believe, or rather betraying him so that they might rage against him. In any case, and by whomever it was done, this report reached the Pharisees.

# HOMILY LV, ON THE SATURDAY AFTER *LAETARE*

## (JOHN VIII)

“At that time Jesus said to the crowds: I am the light of the world. Whoever follows me does not walk in darkness,” and so forth.

Here he plainly teaches not only by what authority he forgave the woman’s sins, as is related shortly above, but also that he himself is “the true light that enlightens every person coming into this world” (John I).

Human frailty could not have seen his perpetual radiance unless it had been veiled by the cloud of flesh, through which, as through a kind of exceedingly clear mirror, the brightness of the divine light might become known to human minds. These minds must be purified by faith so that they may be made worthy of beholding so great a light.

Therefore he continues: “Whoever follows me does not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life.”

Whoever now obeys my commands and examples will not fear the darkness of condemnation in the future, but will have rather the light of life, where he will never die at all.

Therefore, my brothers, let us follow Christ, the light of the world, lest we walk in darkness. The darkness to be feared concerns conduct, not the eyes; and if it concerns the eyes, it concerns not the outward but the inward eyes. By it one distinguishes not white from black, but the just from the unjust.

Before our Lord Jesus Christ came, he kindled and sent before him many prophetic lamps. Among these was also John the Baptist, to whom the great Light himself, the Lord Christ, bore witness such as he bore to no other human being. For he said: “Among those born of women there has not arisen anyone greater than John the Baptist” (Matt. XI).

Yet he who was greater than anyone born of women says concerning our Lord Jesus Christ: “I indeed baptize you with water. But he who comes after me is mightier than I, whose sandals I am not worthy to carry” (Matt. III).

See how the lamp submits itself to the day.

The Lord himself testifies that John was a lamp: “He was,” he says, “a burning and shining lamp, and you were willing to rejoice for a time in his light.”

“The Pharisees therefore answered: You bear witness concerning yourself; your testimony is not true.”

Let us see what they heard; let us also hear, but not as they did: they heard while despising, we while believing; they wanted to kill Christ, while we desire to live through Christ. For the present, let this difference distinguish our ears and minds, and let us hear what the Lord answered the Jews.

“Jesus answered and said to them: Even if I bear witness concerning myself, my testimony is true, because I know where I come from and where I am going.”

He wanted the Father to be understood. If the Son glorified the Father, being equal to him, by whom he was sent, how much more ought a human being to glorify him by whom he was created?

“I know where I come from and where I am going.”

This person who is now speaking to you possesses what he did not abandon, and yet he came. For by coming he did not depart from there, nor by returning did he abandon us—he who said: “Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age” (Matt. XXVIII).

The testimony of the light is therefore true, whether it displays itself or otherwise, because without light the light cannot be seen, and without light nothing else that is not light can be seen either.

Just as light displays both itself and the things around it, so Christ displays both himself and illuminates others—those who are around him in charity and follow him, not by the steps of their feet but by the works of charity.

We read in the holy Scriptures that two comings of our Lord Jesus Christ were foretold by the prophets: one of mercy, which has been accomplished; the other of judgment, which is to come.

The first dispensation of our Lord Jesus Christ was therefore medicinal, not judicial. For if he had first come to judge, he would have found no one to whom he could repay the rewards of justice.

Because he saw that all were sinners and that absolutely no one was free from the death of sin, his mercy had first to be brought forward, and afterward judgment had to be exercised.

For the Psalm had sung concerning him: “I will sing of mercy and judgment to you, O Lord” (Ps. C). It does not say, “of judgment and mercy.” For if judgment came first, there would be no mercy; but first mercy, afterward judgment.

What is the first mercy? The Creator of humanity deigned to become human; he became what he had made, so that what he had made might not perish.

What can be added to this mercy? Yet something was added. Rejected by the human beings for whose salvation he had come into the world, he endured mockery, scourging, spitting, the insults of enemies, and the most shameful death of the cross.

He endured all these things because he wished to save the human being whom he had created.

No kind of death was more intolerable than the cross, because of its prolonged tortures; yet nothing is more glorious than to carry the sign of the cross upon one’s forehead.

Hence the Apostle, proclaiming the glory of the cross, says: “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Gal. VI).

Because he came to judge no one, he consequently answered the Jews:

“You judge according to the flesh; I judge no one.”

He endured an unjust judgment in order to carry out a just one; but in enduring what was unjust, he acted in mercy.

Finally, he humbled himself so greatly that he reached the cross. He delayed the exercise of his power, but he made his mercy public.

How did he delay his power? Because he did not wish to come down from the cross, although he was able to rise from the tomb.

How did he make his mercy public? Because, hanging on the cross, he said: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke XXIII).

Whether, then, because he had not come to judge the world but to save the world, he said, “I judge no one”; or, as I have recalled, because he had said, “You judge according to the flesh,” he added, “I judge no one”—we are to understand that Christ does not judge according to the flesh, according to which he himself was judged by human beings.

But so that you may not now recognize Christ as judge, hear what follows:

“And if I judge, my judgment is true.”

There you have judgment also. But recognize the Savior, lest you experience judgment.

Why, then, did he say that his judgment was true? “Because I am not alone,” he says, “but I and the Father who sent me.”

What is Christ’s being sent except his incarnation? “Christ was sent” means the same as saying, “Christ was incarnate.” He was sent by the Father, and yet he never departed from the Father. He was here through the incarnation, and he is here now through divinity.

Faith therefore cleanses our hearts so that understanding may fill our hearts. And so that we may understand: the mystery of our salvation is lofty, deep, and secret. There is one substance, one divinity, one majesty of the Father and the Son.

The Father did not suffer; the Son alone suffered. Let us therefore understand the sending of the Son as the incarnation of the Son; but do not believe that the Father was incarnate.

How, then, is his judgment true, unless he is truly the Son of the Father? Therefore he said: “My judgment is true, because I am not alone, but I and the Father who sent me.”

In another place he said the same thing: “I and the Father are one” (John X).

One in substance, two in person. He said “one” because of the unity of substance; he said “are” because of the distinction of persons.

Hear what he said: “I and the Father who sent me.” Distinguish the persons: recognize that the Father is Father; recognize that the Son is Son, lest you reach the abyss of Sabellius. And do not say “one thing and another thing,” but say “one person and another person.” Not one thing and another in substance, but one person and another in person.

The Father is not greater, nor is the Son lesser, in the glory of divinity; rather, believe: “We are one.”

In the word “one,” spoken by Truth itself, free yourself from Arius; in the word “are,” free yourself from Sabellius. If “one,” then they are not different; if “are,” then they are not one person.

He had spoken of judgment: “I judge no one.” Now he wishes to speak of testimony.

“In your law,” he says, “it is written.”

He says “your,” as though he were saying, “In the law given to you by God,” just as we say, “Our daily bread,” although we have asked God to give it to us.

What is written in their law? “The testimony of two human beings is true.”

Do two human beings always give true testimony? Did not two false witnesses bring false testimony against Susanna (Dan. XIII)? And when the Jews were seeking false testimony against Christ, the evangelist says: “At last two false witnesses came” (Matt. XXVI).

Were they not false witnesses because there were two of them? What shall we say about two or three? The entire people lied against Christ.

If, then, the entire people, consisting of a great multitude of human beings, was found to give false testimony, how should this be understood: “At the mouth of two or three witnesses every word shall stand” (Deut. XIX), unless the Trinity is commended in this way through a mystery—the Trinity in which there is perpetual stability of truth?

If you wish to have a good case, have two or three witnesses: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

Finally, when Susanna, a chaste woman and faithful wife, was being pressed by two false witnesses, the Trinity supported her in her conscience and in secret. That Trinity brought forth Daniel as one witness from secrecy, and he convicted the two.

Therefore, because it is written in your law that the testimony of two human beings is true, accept the true testimony, lest you experience judgment: “For I,” he says, “do not judge anyone, but I bear witness concerning myself.”

I defer judgment; I do not defer testimony.

Let us choose, brothers, the testimony of God, because the testimony of God is true. And just as he is the witness of everything we do, he will be the judge of everything we have done.

He seeks no other witness than himself, who examines all the secrets of our hearts, and what proceeds from them and from what source. He is therefore a witness because he does not seek another from whom to learn who you are or what your life is like—he who repays each person according to his works.

The Jews therefore answered the Lord, who was speaking about his Father, and said:

“Where is your Father?”

They understood Christ’s Father carnally, because they judged Christ’s words according to the flesh. The one who was speaking was flesh in the open, but the Word in secret: a manifest human being, a hidden God.

Let us see, then, what the Lord answered them.

“Where,” they say, “is your Father?” For we heard you say, “I am not alone, but I and the Father who sent me.” We see only you; we do not see your Father with you. How do you say that you are not alone but are with your Father? Come, show us that your Father is with you.

And the Lord: Do you see me and not see my Father? This is what follows; this is what he himself answered in his words, whose exposition we have already set forth above.

See what he said:

“Jesus answered: You know neither me nor my Father. If you knew me, perhaps you would know my Father also.”

You say, then, “Where is your Father?” as though you already knew him, as though I were entirely what you see. Since you do not know me, therefore I do not show you my Father.

You seek a human being because you judge according to the flesh. But because, according to what you see, I am one thing, and according to what you do not see I am another, I speak of my Father as hidden.

He is hidden first, so that you may know me; then you will also know my Father: “For if you knew me, perhaps you would know my Father also.”

He who knows everything does not doubt when he says “perhaps,” but rebukes. Consider how that very “perhaps,” which seems to be a word of doubt, is spoken as a rebuke.

It is a word of doubt when it is spoken by a doubting human being—doubting because ignorant. But when a word of doubt is spoken by God, from whom nothing is hidden, that doubt rebukes unbelief; it does not express uncertainty in the divine nature.

Human beings sometimes doubt, by way of rebuke, concerning things they hold as certain—that is, they use a word of doubt while not doubting in their hearts. For example, if you are angry with your servant and say: “Do you despise me? Consider that perhaps I am your master.”

The Apostle likewise, speaking to certain people who despised him, says: “I think that I too have the Spirit of God” (I Cor. VII). By saying “I think,” he seems to doubt, but he was rebuking, not doubting.

And the Lord Christ, elsewhere rebuking the future unbelief of the human race, says: “When the Son of Man comes, do you think he will find faith on earth?” (Luke XVIII).

He therefore knows all things, through whom all things were made, and yet he rebukes by seeming to doubt: “If you knew me, perhaps you would know my Father also.”

He rebukes unbelievers and admonishes believers, so that they may know that the Father and the Son have one knowledge, and thus know that knowledge of the Son of God is also knowledge of the Father.

Therefore, when the chosen disciple asked him to show them the Father, he answered: “For so long I have been with you, and you have not known me? Philip, whoever sees me sees the Father also” (John XIV).

If the Son were unlike the Father, would he say to his disciples, “Whoever sees me sees the Father also”? Would he say to the Jews, “If you knew me, you would know my Father also”?

“Jesus spoke these words in the treasury, teaching in the temple.”

Great confidence, without fear. For he would not have suffered if he had not wished to; nor would he have been born if he had not wished to.

What does it mean that Jesus spoke these words in the treasury while teaching in the temple?

The treasury is where treasures are stored. Jesus spoke to the Jews in the treasury while he spoke to the crowds in parables. For Christ’s treasury was that in which all the mysteries lay hidden, destined to be opened when he himself, who had lain hidden in the letter, spoke—not in proverbs, but openly explaining everything to his faithful.

The treasuries also adjoined the temple, because Christ himself is the temple, concerning which he said: “Destroy this temple” (John II). All the mysteries of the ancient law adhered to him and all looked toward him, until he came to open each treasury of the mysteries, opening the understanding of his faithful so that they might understand what had lain hidden, as the evangelist says: “Then he opened their understanding, so that they might understand the Scriptures” (Luke XXIV).

Finally, let us hear what follows:

“No one seized him, because his hour had not yet come.”

Clearly, everything is according to his own dispensation; everything is according to his will. For he who was born by his will also suffered by his will.

If he had not wished to suffer, he would not have suffered; but if he had not suffered, his blood would not have been poured out; and if that blood had not been poured out, the world would not have been redeemed.

Let us therefore give thanks both for the power of his divinity and for the mercy of his weakness: for the hidden power that the Jews did not know, concerning which it was said to them just now:

“You know neither me nor my Father.”

And let us give thanks for the flesh he assumed, which the Jews did know, and whose homeland they knew. Hence elsewhere he said to them: “You know me, and you know where I am from.”

Let us recognize both in Christ: the source from which he is equal to the Father, and the source from which the Father is greater than he. The one is the Word; the other is flesh. The one is God; the other is human. Yet there is one Christ, God and human.

# HOMILY LVI. THE FIFTH SUNDAY IN LENT, WHICH IS CALLED THE SUNDAY OF THE LORD’S PASSION
(JOHN 8.) “At that time Jesus said to the crowds of the Jews and to the chief priests: ‘Which of you will convict me of sin? If I speak the truth, why do you not believe me?’” and so forth.

After the Lord had convicted the Jews and shown that they were sons of the devil, saying (John 8), “You are of your father the devil, and you want to carry out your father’s desires,” and after he had shown that their claim to noble descent—which is read earlier in the same account, when they boasted, “We are Abraham’s offspring, and we have never been enslaved to anyone”—was of no benefit without nobility of mind, he added, saying: “Amen, amen, I say to you, everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin. But a slave does not remain in the house forever.”

Thus, to show that if they wished to imitate him they could become sons of God, he added what stands at the beginning of this reading: “Which of you will convict me of sin?” The pronoun *quis* (“who”), though indefinite, sometimes has the force of a question and sometimes of a denial. It has the force of a question, as it is said through the Psalmist (Psalm 14): “Lord, who will dwell in your tent? Or who will rest on your holy mountain?” The answer to this question immediately follows when it is added: “The one who walks without blemish and practices righteousness.” It has the force of a denial, as Solomon says: “Who can say, ‘My heart is clean; I am pure from sin’?” (Proverbs 20). And again: “But in the underworld, who will confess to you?” (Psalm 6), where “no one” is to be understood in each case.

Thus, in this passage also it is used negatively when the Lord says: “Which of you will convict me of sin?”—that is, “no one.” No one could convict him of sin, for he had come into the world without sin in order to release sinners from sin. Other human beings can rebuke those like themselves for sins, whether past sins or future sins that may be committed. But no one can convict the Lord Jesus Christ either of past or of future sins, because although he took flesh from Adam’s flesh, he nevertheless did not derive any guilt of sin from Adam’s origin.

The apostle Peter says of him with complete truth: “He committed no sin, and no deceit was found in his mouth” (1 Peter 2). And the Lord himself says of himself: “The ruler of this world is coming, and he has nothing in me” (John 14). Not only were his conception and holy birth without sin, but all his conduct, preaching, display of power, and life among human beings also appeared irreproachable, as he himself says in the Gospel: “If I have spoken wrongly, testify about the wrong” (John 18). And again: “The works that I do in my Father’s name testify on my behalf” (John 10).

To show that they could be freed from sins if they wished to believe in him, he continued, saying: “If I speak the truth, why do you not believe me?” He himself is the Truth, who says: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14). It is as though he said: “When you do not believe me, who am the Truth and who have come from the Father of truth, speaking the truth to you, you clearly show yourselves to be children of him who was a liar from the beginning and did not stand in the truth, because truth is not in him.”

[Col. 0328A]

“Whoever is of God hears the words of God.” In these words each person can test his own conscience, whether he is of God or not. For whoever willingly hears the word of God and still more willingly fulfills it in action should have no doubt that he is of God, since, as the Lord says in the Gospel, “A bad tree does not produce good fruit” (Matthew 7).

But whoever, foolish and hardened, scorns hearing the word of God—or, even if he hears it with the bodily ear, makes no effort or exertion to put it into practice—clearly shows that he is not of God. Such were those to whom the Lord says: “For this reason you do not hear, because you are not of God.”

A question arises from these words: Why does the Lord say to the Jews, “You are not of God,” when elsewhere it is written: “God saw everything that he had made, and it was very good” (Genesis 1)? And again: “He who remains forever created all things together” (Sirach 18). The answer is that he does not deny that they are of God by nature, but by vice. For one thing is nature in a human being, and another is sin. Nature in a human being, created by God, is very good; sin was invented by the devil.

Good can exist without evil, but evil cannot exist without good, because the deprivation of good is nothing other than the invention of evil. Thus, by their created condition they were of God, but by their vice they were not of God.

We understand this more clearly if we attend briefly to what comes earlier in this reading. We read that he acknowledged these same Jews as sons of Abraham, saying (John 8): “I know that you are Abraham’s sons.” A little later, however, he denied that they were Abraham’s sons, adding: “If you are Abraham’s sons, do the works of Abraham.” Thus, by the descent of the flesh they were Abraham’s sons, but by imitation of his humility and faith they were not Abraham’s sons.

So, as was said, by nature they were of God, but by vice they were not of God. This manner of speaking is so common in Scripture that it is also found in ordinary speech. For example, I see a sinful human being: when we name the human being, we understand the nature; when we add “sinful,” we understand the vice. Similarly, we call people good and people bad: good because they were created by God, bad because they are vicious. We also speak of a good angel and a bad angel—not because he can be bad by nature, but because he made himself bad by vice.

But what the Lord testifies in words about the Jews—that they were not of God—they themselves demonstrate by their deeds. For, instead of being corrected by the rebuke through which they ought to have been amended, they became worse. For, as the account continues:

[Col. 0329A]

“They answered and said to him: ‘Are we not right in saying that you are a Samaritan and have a demon?’”

That their statement that the Lord had a demon was intended as an insult is clear. But what insult they intended by calling him a Samaritan must be recalled for the sake of those who do not know the history.

We read in the Books of Kings (3 Kings 12) that the ten tribes of the children of Israel, at the prompting of Jeroboam—who sinned and made Israel sin—abandoned the God of their fathers and worshiped the golden and silver calves that he had set up at Bethel and Dan. Therefore the Lord raised up against them Shalmaneser, king of the Assyrians, who led them captive into foreign nations, though in such a way that he settled other peoples in their territory.

When these peoples worshiped their own gods there, the Lord sent savage beasts against them, namely bears and lions. As many were dying from their bites and attacks, they sent messengers to the king, saying: “The land in which we dwell is excellent, but it devours its inhabitants, because we do not know how to worship the ordinances of the God of the land.”

Then the king, after taking counsel, sent one of the Hebrew priests to teach them to worship the ordinances of the God of the land. At that time those peoples worshiped the God of heaven, but they did not abandon their idols.

The tribes of Judah and Benjamin, in which kings of David’s line ruled—as the Lord had promised him that he would give him a lamp from his offspring forever—had not yet been led into captivity, but remained in Jerusalem. From that time they were called Jews, not, as some think, after Judas Maccabaeus.

So great a discord grew between the Jews and the Samaritans just mentioned that no Jew considered it worthy to converse familiarly with them, share a meal, or maintain any association with them. This is shown by the Samaritan woman, who is reported to have said to the Lord, as we read in the Gospel: “How can you, though you are a Jew, ask me for a drink, since I am a Samaritan woman? For Jews do not associate with Samaritans” (John 4).

Whenever the Jews wished to attack someone with an insult, they called him a Samaritan. Therefore, angered against the Lord, and unable to find any true evils with which to reproach him, they brought false accusations against him, saying that he had a demon and was a Samaritan. Although he could have answered them truthfully, “You have a demon,” he did not wish to do so; instead, he patiently kept silent about the true evil that he recognized in them, showing us an example of patience, so that whenever we suffer insults from those near us, we may patiently keep silent about their real faults, lest such a correction appear to arise not from love but from revenge.

[Col. 0330A]

“Jesus answered and said to them: ‘I do not have a demon.’”

It should be noted that two accusations were brought against him, but he denied one and, by remaining silent, accepted the other. He denied having a demon, but he did not deny being a Samaritan.

*Samaritanus* (“Samaritan”) is interpreted as “guardian.” The Lord therefore did not wish to deny that he was a Samaritan, for he knew that he was our guardian—he of whom the Prophet entrusted his own frailty to be guarded when he said: “Guard me, Lord, like the apple of the eye” (Psalm 16). And again: “Guard me from the snare that they have set for me” (Psalm 140). And: “He who guards Israel will neither slumber nor sleep” (Psalm 120). And: “The Lord guards the little ones” (Psalm 114).

For he is that Samaritan who, finding his neighbor wounded, bound up his wounds, placed him on his own animal, brought him to an inn, and cared for him (Luke 17). Of him the prophet Isaiah says: “The burden of Dumah calls to me from Seir: ‘Guardian, what of the night? Guardian, what of the night?’ The guardian said: ‘Morning comes, and also night. If you seek, seek; turn back and see’” (Isaiah 21).

“But I honor my Father, and you have dishonored me.” In many places in the Gospel we find that the Son honored the Father. For he not only referred the mystery of his incarnation to the Father’s glory, but also his preaching, the display of miracles, and the healing of the sick, as he himself says: “I have not come of myself, but my Father sent me” (John 8). And again: “My teaching is not mine, but his who sent me, the Father’s” (John 7). And elsewhere: “The Father is greater than I” (John 14). And again: “Holy Father, I have made your name known to the people whom you gave me” (John 17). And again: “I do nothing of myself” (John 8). And in his passion: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matthew 26).

But the Jews dishonored the Son who honored the Father when they said: “He casts out demons by Beelzebul, the prince of demons” (Matthew 12). And again: “Are we not right in saying that you are a Samaritan and have a demon?” (John 8). And: “This man is not from God, because he does not keep the sabbath” (John 9). And: “If this man were not a criminal, we would not have handed him over to you” (John 18).

[Col. 0330D]

“I do not seek my own glory; there is one who seeks and judges.”

Although the Son of God performed many signs and displayed many powers, he did not seek his own glory. Instructed by his example, we should say that we do not glory in the good we do, lest that sentence be directed against us which says: “Why are you proud, earth and ashes?” (Sirach 10).

Therefore the Apostle restrains the presumption of one who boasts in himself, saying: “What do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (1 Corinthians 4).

But it is asked why he says, “I do not seek my own glory; there is one who seeks and judges,” when elsewhere he is said to have declared: “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5). If the Father has given all judgment to the Son, why does the same Son, after receiving an insult, say: “There is one who seeks and judges”?

The answer is that in Scripture “judgment” has a twofold meaning. Sometimes it refers to discernment, and sometimes to condemnation. If it did not refer to discernment, the Psalmist would never say: “Judge me, O God, and discern my cause from an ungodly nation” (Psalm 42). And: “O God, save me by your name” (Psalm 53).

And if it did not refer to condemnation, the Savior would not have said in the Gospel: “The hour is coming when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who have done good will come forth to the resurrection of life, but those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgment” (John 5).

Thus, in this passage “judgment” refers to discernment, when he says: “I do not seek my own glory; there is one who seeks and judges.” It is as though he said: “My Father is the one who distinguishes between my cause and yours.”

For when God the Father sent his Son into the world, he showed his cause to be entirely distinct not only from that of the reprobate but also from that of the righteous. Others are born with sin; he was born without sin. Others receive the Holy Spirit in measure, but in him the entire fullness of divinity dwells bodily, as Isaiah says: “The spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and piety; and the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him” (Isaiah 11).

The Psalmist speaks of this distinction: “God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Psalm 44).

With respect to that judgment by which the reprobate will be sent into condemnation, the Father is not said to judge anyone, but to have given all judgment to the Son. For it is just and fitting that the Son of God, who was unjustly judged by human beings, should appear as judge of the living and the dead at the universal judgment and separate the good from the evil, as he himself says: “When the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty, all the nations will be gathered before him, and he will separate them from one another, as a shepherd separates sheep from goats” (Matthew 25).

Elsewhere in the Gospel we read of this judgment: “The Father gave him power to execute judgment, because he is the Son of Man” (John 5). And the Apostle says: “We must all appear before the tribunal of Christ, so that each may receive according to what he has done, whether good or evil” (2 Corinthians 5).

Nor should it seem impossible to anyone that one word, “judgment,” should have two meanings, since many such cases are found in Scripture. There is a temptation that brings glory, and there is a temptation that brings sin. There is servile fear, which perfect love casts out, and there is chaste fear, which endures forever. So there is also judgment that pertains to discernment and judgment that pertains to condemnation.

But the Lord does not withhold the benefit of his preaching, even from the ungrateful. For those whom he saw would not be corrected by rebuke, he invited to correction by a gentle promise, saying:

[Col. 0331D]

“Amen, amen, I say to you: If anyone keeps my word, he will never see death.”

“Amen” is always doubled in the Gospel so that what he says may be believed all the more certainly.

It is asked why he says, “If anyone keeps my word, he will never see death,” when we read that the holy fathers kept the Lord’s word and nevertheless did not escape bodily death at all, except Elijah and Enoch—although, even if they are still alive, they will not escape bodily death.

For when our first parent despised the commandment of life, he subjected himself and his offspring to the condition of death, according to the sentence with which the Lord threatened: “On whatever day you eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, you shall die” (Genesis 2). Hence Scripture says: “Who is the person who will live and not see death?” (Psalm 88)—with “no one” understood.

This law was established for the human condition, so that whoever tastes life may also taste death, especially since it is written of the Lord: “And the exits of death belong to the Lord God” (Psalm 67).

Why, then, does he say, “If anyone keeps my word, he will never see death”?

The answer is that there is one death of the soul and another of the body. The soul dies through sin, as it is written: “The soul that sins shall itself die” (Ezekiel 18). The body dies as punishment for sin, because, as Scripture says: “When sin is fully grown, it gives birth to death” (James 1).

The Lord therefore includes both kinds of death when he says: “Let the dead bury their own dead” (Luke 9)—that is, let the dead in soul bury the dead in body. For the life of the body is the soul, and the life of the soul is God. Just as the body dies without the soul, so the soul dies without God.

It is therefore of this death—the death of the soul, everlasting death, the death of Gehenna—that he says: “If anyone keeps my word, he will never see death.” For whoever keeps the Lord’s command, although he falls into bodily death, will nevertheless be freed from the death of the soul, singing with the Prophet: “Though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for you are with me” (Psalm 22).

Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “I am the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in me, even if he has died, will live; and everyone who lives and believes in me will never die” (John 11). And John says in the Apocalypse: “Blessed and holy is the one who has a share in the first resurrection” (Apocalypse 20).

In such persons the second death—that is, the death of the soul—has no power: that is, when the soul passes in this world from vices to virtues.

To make this more easily understood, let us give an example. Some people were told: “Worship the idols, or you will be killed.” Fearing bodily death more than death of the soul, they worshiped and fell into the death of the soul, nor did they escape bodily death forever. Of such people it is written: “The death of sinners is most grievous” (Psalm 33).

Others were told: “Worship the idols, or you will be thrown into a furnace of blazing fire.” But, fearing the death of the soul more than bodily death, they confidently replied: “Our Lord is able to deliver us from the furnace of blazing fire and from your hands, O king. But if he does not wish to, let it be known to you that we do not worship your gods, and we do not adore the golden statue that you have erected” (Daniel 3).

And because they loved the life of the soul more than they feared bodily death, they escaped the latter for a time. Even if they had died in the furnace, “precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his holy ones” (Psalm 115).

But it is asked why he said, “He will never see death,” since death rather takes away sight than gives it. The answer is that in this passage “to see” means “to feel” or “to experience.”

Thus a pit is called “blind,” not because it lacks eyes—which it never had—but because it makes those who are within it unable to see. Likewise, we call lupines “sad,” not because they themselves can be sad or joyful, but because they make those who taste them sad on account of their bitterness. So death is said to be seen because it makes its bitterness felt.

But because the Jews had fallen into the death of the soul without seeing it at all, they said:

[Col. 0333A]

“Now we know that you have a demon. Abraham died, and the prophets did too; and you say, ‘If anyone keeps my word, he will never taste death.’”

As they understood, so they answered. It is as though they said: “Even if until now we have been uncertain whether you have a demon, we now truly believe it, when you say, ‘If anyone keeps my word, he will not taste death,’ although Abraham died.”

The Lord was speaking of the death of the soul, but they understood him to be speaking of bodily death and answered with a kind of quarrel:

“Are you greater than our father Abraham, who died? The prophets also died. Whom do you make yourself?”

It is as though they said: “You are exalting yourself excessively, raising yourself needlessly, lifting yourself beyond measure, when you presume to place those who keep your words above Abraham and the prophets, who plainly kept the Lord’s word and nevertheless died bodily.”

And because he saw that they were seeking temporal glory, not enduring glory, he urged them toward humility, saying: “If I glorify myself, my glory is nothing” (John 8).

It is as though he said: “My glory could be nothing if I wished to glorify myself. Therefore your glory is nothing, because you seek glory from one another and do not desire the glory that comes from God alone.” For it is written: “Let another praise you, and not your own mouth; a stranger, and not your own lips” (Proverbs 27).

Hence it is added:

[Col. 0333C]

“My Father is the one who glorifies me, whom you say is our God.”

If anyone reviews the history of the holy Gospel, he can easily discover how the Father glorified the Son. The Father glorified the Son when, after he had been baptized, a voice sounded from heaven, saying: “You are my beloved Son; in you I am well pleased” (Mark 1).

He also glorified him when he was transfigured before the disciples on the mountain and the same voice sounded, saying: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; listen to him” (Matthew 17).

He glorified him when he performed through him such powers and signs that he showed him, the man, to be God. Thus, when the Son said: “Glorify me, Father, with yourself, with the glory that I had with you before the world existed” (John 17), the Father answered: “I have glorified [it], and I will glorify [it] again” (John 12).

The Son glorified the Father elsewhere when he said: “I have not come of myself, but my Father sent me” (John 8). He also glorifies him when he referred the works and powers that he performed to the Father’s glory, saying: “My teaching is not mine, but that of the Father who sent me” (John 7).

Hence it is written elsewhere: “Holy Father, I have glorified you on earth; I have finished the work that you gave me to do” (John 17).

There was no other reason that made the Jews angry with the Lord more than the fact that he said that their God was his Father, as the same John shows elsewhere when he says: “For this reason the Jews sought all the more to kill Jesus, because he not only broke the sabbath, but also called God his own Father, making himself equal with God” (John 5).

But although they were angry, although they were indignant, although they raged, the Truth nevertheless always spoke the truth, showing us that whenever scandal arises on account of the truth, it is better to endure the scandal than to abandon the truth.

[Col. 0334B]

“And you have not known him.”

The Jews showed by this that they had not known the Father, because they did not believe in his Son, who had been sent by him. For if they had known the Father, they would certainly also have believed in his Son, as the Son himself says to them: “If God were your Father, you would certainly love me, because I came forth from God and have come” (John 8).

It is rightly added: “But I know him.” The Son knows the Father in one way, and we know him in another. We, illuminated by him in time, perceive little of his subtle nature. But for him to know the Father means always to be co-eternal and consubstantial with him, as he himself says: “As the Father knows me, so I know the Father” (John 10).

“And if I said that I do not know him, I would be like you, a liar.” Since, as Scripture says, “Every human being is a liar” (Psalm 115), while God alone is truthful—as he himself says, “I am the truth” (John 14)—the Jews were much worse liars, for they said that the Son of God had a demon.

“But I know him, and I keep his word.” It is as though he said: “You cannot see the invisible God, but from the works that I perform in his name you can recognize that I have been sent by him,” as he himself says: “If you do not believe me, believe the works at least” (John 10). And again: “The works that I do in my Father’s name themselves testify about me” (ibid.).

And because I show by this that I know him—that I keep his word—you plainly falsely boast that you know him, whose commandments you despise. Therefore the apostle John says: “If anyone says, ‘I love God,’ but does not keep his commandments, he is a liar” (1 John 2).

[Col. 0334D]

“Abraham your father rejoiced that he might see my day; he saw it and was glad.”

Perhaps someone will ask where or when the blessed patriarch Abraham is found to have seen Christ’s day and rejoiced. But if we examine his works carefully and consider them spiritually, we quickly understand where and when he saw Christ’s day and rejoiced.

For we read in Genesis that, when he was old and advanced in years, he called to himself the oldest servant of his household and said to him: “Place your hand under my thigh, and swear to me by the God of heaven that you will not take a wife for my son from the daughters of Canaan, among whom I dwell, but that you will go to my land and to my kindred, and from there take a wife for my son Isaac” (Genesis 24).

What is the meaning of such an oath? What does the God of heaven have to do with Abraham’s thigh, or Abraham’s thigh with the God of heaven? If he swore by the thigh, why by God? And if by God, why by the thigh?

Surely offspring of the flesh is signified by the thigh. When, therefore, he made the servant swear by the God of heaven and by the thigh, he showed that he understood that one would be born from his lineage who belonged to his thigh and yet was rightly believed to be the God of heaven.

Thus Abraham saw Christ’s day and rejoiced. He could rejoice with unspeakable joy when he foresaw that Christ would be born from his lineage, through whom not only he himself would be saved, but the whole world would also be redeemed, and the Lord’s promise to him would be fulfilled: “In your offspring all the nations will be blessed” (Genesis 22).

Or, alternatively: Abraham saw Christ’s day and rejoiced when, as a figure of the holy Trinity, he received three angels as guests at midday (Genesis 18). He saw three and adored one, because he believed in unity within the Trinity. There, therefore, he understood the person of Christ; and then he saw his day and rejoiced.

Hence Scripture itself immediately adds: “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness” (Romans 4).

And because those frequently mentioned impious Jews could not penetrate the profound mystery of divinity, they wandered with blind minds in the age of Christ’s humanity, saying:

[Col. 0335B]

“You are not yet fifty years old, and have you seen Abraham?”

Because they saw the Lord Jesus Christ as a human being, they did not consider that God was joined to him. Looking only at his humanity, they said that he was not yet fifty years old.

But because the Lord Jesus Christ, true God, without beginning and without end, is present everywhere, he had seen Abraham before fifty years had passed, and continued to see him. But he who, in his humanity, was less than fifty years old, in order to show that in his divinity he existed before all ages, added:

“Amen, amen, I say to you: Before Abraham came to be, I am.”

Here it should be noted that, to show that he was true God, he did not say, “I was,” but “Before Abraham came to be, I am.” “I am” is a verb of the present tense; it expresses neither past nor future, but what is always present. Therefore it belongs only to the one for whom past things do not pass away and future things do not arrive, but for whom being always means remaining eternal and unchangeable.

Hence, when Moses asked: “If the children of Israel say to me, ‘What is his name?’ what shall I say to them?” he answered: “This is what you shall say to the children of Israel: ‘I am who I am’; ‘He who is has sent me to you’” (Exodus 3).

He is not only before Abraham, but also before every beginning, as he himself says: “I am the beginning, who also speak to you” (John 8), to whom, in praise of Wisdom, it is said: “The Lord possessed me at the beginning of his ways” (Proverbs 8). And again: “I came forth from the mouth of the Most High” (Sirach 24).

After they saw that they had been defeated by the Lord, so that they could not oppose word to word, they were moved by the gall of envy and attempted to kill him with stones. Hence it is added:

[Col. 0336A]

“So they took up stones to throw at him.”

They rightly ran to stones, for they had stony hearts. To them aptly applied what had been said through the Prophet to their fathers: “Your neck is an iron sinew, and your forehead bronze” (Isaiah 48).

They did not belong to those of whom the Lord says through the Prophet: “I will take away from you your heart of stone and give you a heart of flesh” (Ezekiel 11). Rather, they were hard in the solidity of rocks, because although they saw with their own eyes the Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, whom their prophets had promised to them, performing miracles, preaching, and acting as they had in their Scriptures, they did not recognize him but wanted to stone him.

And because he had not come to conquer his enemies by power but by humility, it is rightly added: “But Jesus hid himself and went out of the temple.”

Woe to the Jews from whom he hid himself. For he hid himself bodily from their sight because they did not deserve to see him with their minds. The Lord did not hide himself from the hands of his persecutors because he feared dying—he had come to die for us—but for the sake of humility, so that at the fitting time he might undergo the fitting death, namely, crucifixion.

For it was fitting that, because the first human being had fallen through a forbidden tree, he should be restored through the wood of the holy cross, as is made clearer in what follows.

But at the end of this reading both natures of the Lord—namely, the divine and the human—are beautifully demonstrated to us if we compare this passage with the other. We read that when they led him to the brow of the mountain on which their city had been built, intending to hurl him down from there, “he passed through the midst of them and went on his way” (Luke 4).

And in the same John, when the rulers and priests sent soldiers to seize him, Jesus went out to meet them and asked them: “Whom are you seeking?” They answered: “Jesus of Nazareth.” He said to them: “I am he.” As soon as he said, “I am he,” they went backward and fell to the ground (John 18).

Thus, as a human being, he hid from the eyes of those who were stoning him; but as God, he passed through the midst of his persecutors and struck his enemies down. He who struck down his enemies by a single word is God. But he who hid bodily, as a human being among other human beings, was truly human.

HOMILY LVII. MONDAY AFTER *JUDICA*.

[Col. 0336D]

(JOHN 7.) “At that time the rulers and Pharisees sent attendants to seize Jesus.”

They sent officers to seize him whom they could not seize, since he still did not wish to be seized. But those who had come to seize the innocent heard him teaching.

“Then Jesus said to them: ‘I am with you for a little while longer.’”

What you now wish to do, you will do—but not now, because now I do not wish it. Why do I not wish it now? “Because I am with you for a little while longer, and then I am going to him who sent me.” I must fulfill my dispensation and thus reach my passion.

[Col. 0337A]

“You will seek me and will not find me, and where I am, you cannot come.”

Here he already foretold his resurrection. They did not wish to recognize him while he was present, and afterward they sought him when they saw that a multitude already believed.

For great signs were also performed when the Lord had risen, and when he ascended into heaven great works were then performed through the disciples—but he performed them through them, just as he had performed them himself. For he had said to them: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15).

Why could they not come? Because they did not wish to believe, since no one can be saved without faith.

“Therefore the Jews said”—not to him, but to one another: “Where is this man going, that we will not find him? Surely he is going to the dispersion of the nations and is going to teach the Gentiles?”

They did not know what they were saying, but because he wished it, they prophesied. For the Lord was going to the Gentiles—not by the presence of his body, but by divine power in his disciples, of whom he said through the Prophet: “How beautiful are the feet of those who proclaim peace, who proclaim good things!” (Isaiah 52; Romans 10).

Christ was going to the Gentiles in these feet, and through them he was going to teach the Gentiles, so that the Gentiles might receive the faith that the Jews rejected. Those who did not know the truth prophesied, though they did not understand Christ when he said: “Where I am, you cannot come.”

Why can you not come? Because you do not wish to believe. What does he mean by saying, “Where I am,” except “in the bosom of the Father, co-eternal with the Father”? He was speaking on earth, but he showed that he was in the Father’s bosom.

Before the other dispensations of our Lord, the teachings of our salvation, and the Jews’ doubts concerning the Lord Jesus Christ—things he said by which some would be confounded and others instructed—on the last day of that festival, which was called the Feast of Booths, or the construction of tabernacles, a festival about which your charity has already heard us speak, the Lord Christ called out. He did not merely speak, but cried out, so that whoever thirsted might come to him.

We thirst; let us come. Not with our feet, but with our affections; not by changing our place, but by loving. Yet even according to the inner person, the one who loves migrates. To migrate bodily is one thing, and to migrate in the heart is another. One migrates bodily who changes his place by bodily movement. One migrates in the heart who changes his affection by movement of the heart. If you love something else, though you once loved this, you were not there.

Therefore the Lord cries out to us, for he stood and cried:

[Col. 0337D]

“If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. Whoever believes in me, as Scripture says, rivers of living water will flow from his belly.”

What this means, the Evangelist explained; we must not linger over it. For he immediately explained what the Lord meant when he said, “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. And whoever believes in me, rivers of living water will flow from his belly,” saying:

“Now he said this about the Spirit, whom those who believed in him were to receive.”

Let us know only this: the Lord Jesus was crying out about charity. He cried out, then, and says that we should come and drink, if there is an inner disposition [Col. 0338A]. And he says that, when we have drunk, rivers of living water will flow from our belly. The belly of the inner person is the consciousness of his heart. Having drunk this liquid, the purified conscience comes to life again; and, drawing from the spring, it will itself also become a spring.

What is the spring, or what is the river, that flows from the belly of the inner person? Goodwill, by which he wishes to benefit his neighbor. Those who believe in the Lord therefore drink. For if someone thinks that what he has drunk ought to be sufficient for him alone, living water does not flow from his belly. But if he hastens to benefit his neighbor, he does not dry up for that very reason: because he flows forth.

We shall now see what it is that those who believe in God drink—for, naturally, we are Christians, and if we have believed, we drink. Each person ought to recognize in himself what he drinks, if he drinks from what he drinks. The spring will not abandon us if we do not abandon the spring. The evangelist explained and said from what source the Lord had cried out, to what kind of drink he had invited them, and what he had offered to those who drank, saying:

“Now he was speaking about the Spirit whom those who believed in him were to receive. For the Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified.”

Which spirit does he mean, if not the Holy Spirit? For each human being has his own spirit within him, that is, his mind. The mind of every person is his spirit, concerning which the apostle Paul says: “For who knows what belongs to a human being except the spirit that is in him?” (I Cor. II.)

But what does he mean by saying: “For the Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified”? Was the Holy Spirit not in the holy people [Col. 0338C] of God—in the prophets and patriarchs, who foretold many future things through the Holy Spirit? Accordingly, we also read of Elizabeth (Luke I) that she was filled with the Holy Spirit, and the evangelist similarly says of Zechariah: “And Zechariah was filled with the Holy Spirit, and he prophesied.”

What, then, does he mean by saying that the Holy Spirit had not yet been given? We have many indications of the Holy Spirit’s earlier presence before the Lord was glorified by the resurrection of his flesh. The prophets who foretold Christ’s coming did not have another Spirit; but there was to be a certain future manner of giving this gift, which would cause people gathered together after receiving the Holy Spirit to speak in the languages of all nations.

After his resurrection, when he first appeared to his disciples, he said to them: “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John XX). This, then, is what was meant by the statement, “The Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified”; and he breathed upon their faces. By that breath he first gave life to the human being whom he had made and raised from the clay. By that breath he gave a soul to his limbs, signifying that it was the same Spirit whom he breathed upon their faces, so that they might rise from the clay and renounce works of clay.

Then, for the first time after his resurrection—which the evangelist calls his glorification—he gave the Holy Spirit to his disciples. Afterwards, as the book of the Acts of the Apostles demonstrates (Acts I, II), he remained with them for forty days and ascended into heaven while they watched and followed him with their sight. After ten days had passed there, [Col. 0339A] at Pentecost, he sent the Holy Spirit to them from above; they had been gathered together, as I have said, in one place. Having received the Holy Spirit, they spoke in the languages of all nations.

Perhaps someone asks why those who have been baptized in Christ and live according to his commandments of charity do not speak in the languages of all nations, although it is certain that they have received the Holy Spirit. The reason is that the Church itself, which is Christ’s body, speaks in the languages of all nations. This was prefigured then in the primitive Church, which was founded among the Jewish people alone but is now gathered from all nations. Just as one person then spoke in the languages, so now the unity of the holy Church speaks in all languages.

We too have received the Holy Spirit if we love the Church, if we are joined together by charity, and if we rejoice in the Catholic name and faith. Therefore, the more each person loves the Church of Christ, the more he has the Holy Spirit. We have the Holy Spirit, then, if we love the Church. We love it if we remain in its unity and charity, which the Apostle confidently placed above all virtues.

Whoever possesses this will possess every good thing, because without it nothing will benefit a person, whatever he may be able to possess. Concerning it the blessed apostle James says: “Whoever offends in one point has become guilty of all” (James II). Concerning it Truth itself also says: “By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (John XIII).

## HOMILY LVIII. TUESDAY AFTER *JUDICA*

[Col. 0339C]

(John VII.) “At that time: Jesus was walking in Galilee, for he did not wish to walk in Judea, because the Jews were seeking to kill him,” and so forth.

He was thereby offering an example to our weakness; he had not lost his power, but was comforting our frailty. It was going to happen, as I said, that one of his faithful would hide himself so as not to be found by persecutors. And so that hiding might not be held against him as a crime, he went before us in the Head with what would be confirmed in the members. Christ could walk among the Jews and not be killed, since he said: “I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it up again.” He displayed this power when he wished, when at his voice those who had come with weapons to seize him fell backward.

“Now the feast of the Jews, the Feast of Tabernacles, was near.” The Feast of Tabernacles was a festival during which the Jews were commanded to live for seven days in booths beneath the branches of trees, in memory of their dwelling in the wilderness. This was the festival that the Jews celebrated with great solemnity so that they might remember the Lord’s benefits, since he had led them out of the land of Egypt.

According to Jewish usage, a feast is called not one day but all the days belonging to that festival, as though they were one feast-day, because of the customary unity of the celebration.

[Col. 0340A] “So his brothers said to him: ‘Leave here and go to Judea.’” The Lord’s brothers were called, according to the very common usage of Holy Scripture, the relatives of holy Mary, ever-virgin. Abraham and Lot, for example, are called brothers, although Abraham was Lot’s uncle. Laban and Jacob are likewise called brothers, although Laban was Jacob’s maternal uncle.

Therefore, when you hear of the Lord’s brothers, understand a blood relationship to Mary, not any offspring from her giving birth again. We have said who the brothers were; let us hear what they said:

“Leave here and go to Judea, so that your disciples may see the works that you are doing.”

The Lord’s works were not hidden from the disciples, but they were hidden from these men. These brothers—that is, Christ’s relatives—were able to have Christ as their relative. Yet they were disdainful of believing in him precisely because of that closeness. Therefore the evangelist immediately continued:

“For not even his brothers believed in him.”

Why did they not believe in him? Because they were seeking human glory, saying to him:

“Leave here and go to Judea, so that your disciples may see the works that you are doing. For no one does anything in secret while he himself seeks to be known openly. If you do these things, reveal yourself to the world.”

These words show that they were seeking his glory in a carnal manner, as though they had said: “You perform wonders, but secretly. Go to Judea, so that the leaders of the nation and the capital city of the kingdom may see your wonders. Make yourself known; appear to everyone, so that everyone may praise you.”

What, then, does the Lord Jesus say to this? Let us hear:

“My time has not yet come, but your time is always ready.” The Apostle says: “When the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son” (Gal. IV).

The time of Christ’s glory had not yet come when he said these things. That is what those appeared to be seeking who urged him to go to Judea, perform miracles, and make himself known to the world, lest he be considered insignificant because he remained hidden. But he wished to proceed to exaltation by humility and to reach the very height by the way of humility.

“Your time,” that is, the world’s glory, “is always ready.” There is indeed a time of glory, so that he who came in humility may come in exaltation; he who came to be judged may come to judge; he who came to be killed by the dead may come [Col. 0340D] to judge the living and the dead.

“You go up to this feast.” What does “this” mean? The place where you seek human glory. What does “this” mean? The place where you wish to extend carnal joys; do not think about eternal ones.

“For I am not going up to this feast, because my time has not yet been fulfilled.” At the feast you seek human glory, but “my time,” that is, my glory, “has not yet come.” My feast-day will not be these days, running their course and passing away, but the feast that remains forever: joy without end, eternity without corruption, serenity without cloud.

“When he had said these things, he remained in Galilee. But when his brothers had gone up, then he also went up to the feast, not openly, but as though in secret.”

For this reason he did not go up to “this” feast: he did not wish to glory temporarily, but to teach something beneficially, correct people, admonish them about the eternal feast, turn them away from love of the world, and convert them to God.

What does it mean that he went up to the feast as though secretly? This work of the Lord is not without significance. All the Jewish feast-days were figures. Christ therefore went up secretly among them because Christ was hidden in them: hidden from the earlier people, but now revealed to the better people. What that people did in shadow, we do in manifest light.

Some, however, wish to understand this response of the Lord—“I am not going up to this feast” (John VII)—as referring to his Passion, because Christ ascended the cross not at the Feast of Tabernacles but at the paschal festival, during which the lamb was accustomed to be killed.

“But the Jews were seeking him at the feast,” before he went up. His brothers went up first, and he did not go up at the time they expected and wanted, so that what he said might now be fulfilled: “Not to this”—that is, not to the day you want, whether the first or the second. He went up later, as the Gospel says, in the middle of the feast, when so many days of the feast had already passed that only the remaining days were left. For, as we must understand, they celebrated the festival over many days.

“So they were saying: ‘Where is he?’ And there was much murmuring about him among the crowd.” Why the murmuring? Because of disagreement. What was the disagreement?

“For some were saying: ‘He is good.’ Others were saying: ‘No, but he is leading the crowds astray.’”

This is now said about all his servants who excel in some grace. Some say, “He is good”; others, “No, but he is leading the crowds astray.”

Why is this so? Because our life is hidden with Christ in God. The body of Christ suffers this from lovers of the world until the end of time, just as he then suffered it from the Jews who murmured. The grain has not yet been separated from the chaff (Matt. III), so that the grains of wheat may be gathered into the granary and the chaff burned with eternal fire. What was said, then, about the Lord serves for the consolation of any Christian about whom the same thing may be said.

[Col. 0341D] “Yet no one spoke openly about him because of fear of the Jews.”

“Some were saying, ‘He is good’; others were saying, ‘No, but he is leading the crowds astray.’” Their sound will appear like that of dried-up streams: “He is leading the crowds astray” sounded more loudly; “He is good” they whispered more softly.

But now, brothers, although that glory of Christ which will make us eternal has not yet come, his Church nevertheless grows in such a way—for he has deigned to spread it throughout the world—that it may even be whispered, “He is leading the crowds astray,” while “He is good” resounds more loudly.

For a new heresy secretly whispers in corners: “Christ is adoptive.” But the voice of the universal holy Church resounds more clearly: “Christ is the Son of God.” They hiss still more insolently with serpent-like mouths, “Christ has been called God,” but the unanimity of all the faithful cries out more distinctly and firmly: “Christ is God; he is good; he is true God,” as the outstanding preacher testifies, saying: “Whose are the fathers, from whom is Christ, who is God over all, blessed.”

## HOMILY LIX. WEDNESDAY AFTER *JUDICA*

(John X.) “At that time, the Dedication took place in Jerusalem, and it was winter. Jesus was walking in the temple in Solomon’s Portico,” and so forth.

The Dedication was the solemnity of the temple’s dedication, which the people of God had been accustomed to celebrate every year, according to the ancient tradition of the fathers. But it should be noted that this Dedication mentioned here does not concern the temple’s first dedication but its last. This is easily gathered from the fact that it is reported to have taken place in winter.

The first dedication of the temple was carried out by Solomon in autumn; the second, by Zerubbabel and the priest Jesus, in spring; the third, by Judas Maccabaeus, in winter, when it is specifically recorded that it was established that the same dedication should be recalled every year in solemn ceremonies. We heard just now, when the Gospel was being read, that it was observed even until the time of the Lord’s incarnation. In our own time this dedication is also known to be preserved in the churches of Christ as a salutary custom.

We must consider why the evangelist said that this Dedication took place in winter. It was entirely because of the hardness and unbelief of the Jews, which are often represented under the name of cold.

“And Jesus was walking in the temple in Solomon’s Portico.” If, then, the Son of God wished to walk in the temple where the flesh and blood of brute animals were offered, how much more gladly will he visit the house of our prayer, where the sacraments of his own flesh and blood are celebrated.

If he did not disdain to walk through the portico where a once-mortal and earthly king, however powerful, used to stand in prayer, how much more does he desire to visit and illuminate the innermost places of our hearts—provided that he sees them to be Solomon’s Portico, that is, provided that he sees them possessing his fear, which is “the beginning of wisdom” (Ps. CX).

For we must not think that the only house is the one in which we gather for prayer or the celebration of the mysteries. Much more are we called and are the temple of God when the Apostle plainly says: “You are the temple of the living God, as God said: ‘I will dwell in them and walk among them’” (II Cor. VI).

The evangelist shows why he said that this occurred in winter when he adds:

“The Jews surrounded him.” They surrounded him, then, to test him, not out of a desire to recognize the truth.

“And they were saying: ‘How long will you keep our soul in suspense? If you are the Christ, tell us plainly.’” They were not asking in a disposition of faith, but were plotting against the one whom they questioned and preparing an accusation [Col. 0343A], so that they might find a way to accuse him. They did not wish to believe him to be God, but only a mere human being who would come as a king more exalted than all others.

In this same madness their descendants continue to wander even to the present day, and will continue until they accept the Antichrist in place of Christ. Even if he had answered that he was the Christ, they were thinking of handing him over to the governor’s authority for punishment, as though, by resisting Augustus, he were unlawfully claiming imperial power.

But he, concerned for our salvation—for whose sake these things were to be written—tempered his answer in such a way as to close the mouths of his accusers and plainly disclose to the faithful that he is the Christ. They were asking about Christ as a human being, but he openly relates the mysteries of his divinity, by which he is equal to the Father.

What, then, did the Jews who surrounded the Lord say? Let us see.

“How long,” they said, “will you keep our soul in suspense? If you are the Christ, tell us plainly.”

Christ did not come to take away the soul of those who believe in him, but to give the soul life. The Jews themselves took away their own soul through unbelief, since they gathered to test Christ, not to believe in Christ.

“Jesus answered them: ‘I speak to you, and you do not believe.’”

He showed specifically who he was when he said, “I speak to you”—that is, “I am the Word of God, coeternal with the Father”—“because the works that I do in my Father’s name, these testify about me.”

He is the Son of God, who did not seek his own glory but the glory of the one who sent him, because the Father’s and the Son’s glory is one. But the hearts of unbelievers could not receive this faith [Col. 0343C]. Concerning them he says:

“But you do not believe.” He gives the reason why they did not believe:

“Because you are not of my sheep.”

They are sheep by believing; they are sheep by following the shepherd; they are sheep by not despising the Redeemer; they are sheep by entering through the door; they are sheep by going out and finding pasture.

How, then, did he say to these people, “You are not of my sheep”? Because he saw that they were destined for eternal destruction, not purchased for eternal life by the price of his blood.

“My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me, and I give them eternal life.”

He says, “I know them.” It is the custom of Holy Scripture to say that God knows whatever he chooses. The Apostle says (II Tim. II): “The Lord knows those who are his”; and that he does not know what he does not approve as worthy of eternal life. Hence he will say to the wicked: “I do not know you” (Matt. VII).

He continues concerning the sheep: “And I give them eternal life.” These are the pastures that he promised his sheep above, where no grass withers, everything is green, everything flourishes, everything remains whole, and whatever is received once is possessed forever.

“And they shall never perish.” Here one must understand implicitly: “This is how you will perish, because you are not of my sheep.”

“And no one will snatch them from my hand,” that is, from my power.

“What my Father gave me is greater than all.”

What the Father gave the Son is greater than all: that he should himself be his only-begotten Son, equal and consubstantial. What did he give? Certainly, he gave it by begetting him, because he did not beget one inferior to himself, nor one later in time, but one coeternal, always God without a beginning in time.

It must not be said, “He did not exist before he was born.” He who was coeternal with the Father was never unborn. Let whoever understands grasp it; let whoever does not grasp it believe. Let him be nourished by faith so that he may be able to grasp the Word of God, because the Word is the Son.

The Son is therefore always Son and always equal. He is equal not by growing but by being born: always born from the Father, Son from God, God from God, coeternal from the eternal. The Father, however, is not God from the Son; the Son is God from the Father. Therefore the Father, by begetting, gave him to be God; by begetting, he gave him to be equal. This is what is greater than all.

For this reason John transcended all the heights [Col. 0344B] of creatures, the thousands of angelic armies, and all great things, and reached what is greater than all, saying:

“In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John I).

This is what is greater than all: that I should be his Word, that I should be his only-begotten Son, that I should be the radiance of his light.

Therefore no one snatches the sheep from my hand, and no one can snatch them from the hand of my Father. The Father’s hand and the Son’s hand are one hand—that is, one power, one divinity, one majesty, one eternity, one equality. The Lord himself possessed this equality in divinity before the world existed, with the Father; in humility, he received it at the time of the incarnation.

“And no one can snatch them from my Father’s hand.” He plainly indicates that his hand and the Father’s hand are one and indistinguishable—that is, that their power is one—and therefore that he must be believed to be the Christ, who was not made like the other saints by grace in time, but has always truly existed as the Son of God (John X). He makes this even clearer in the following statement, saying:

“I and the Father are one.”

“One,” he says, “we are; our substance is one, our divinity is one, our eternity is one, perfect equality, no dissimilarity.”

With these words he not only explained the Jews’ present question—whether he himself was the Christ—but also showed how detestable would be the faithlessness of the heretics whose future coming he foresaw.

Let Sabellius be silent when he hears, “I and the Father,” for by a perverse teaching he asserted that the Father and the Son were one person. For “I and the Father” indicates two persons. Let Arius likewise blush when he hears, “We are one,” for he asserted two natures in the Father and the Son, whereas “one” signifies one nature, just as “we are” signifies two persons.

Let us follow the apostolic faith that the blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, confessed: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matt. XVI).

The Jews, hearing the Lord’s words, had hastened this far. But when he said, “I and the Father are one,” they could not endure it. As was their custom, hard-hearted, they ran to stones, as the evangelist says:

“They took up stones to stone him.”

The Lord did not suffer what he did not wish to suffer, and he suffered nothing except what he wished to suffer. Still addressing them as they desired to stone him, he says:

“The Jews took up stones to stone him. Jesus answered them: ‘I have shown you many good works from my Father. For which of these works are you stoning me?’”

But they answered: “We are not stoning you for a good work, but for blasphemy, and because, although you are a human being, you make yourself God.”

They were responding to what he had said: “I and the Father are one.” Behold, the Jews understood what the Arians do not understand. They were angry because they perceived that “I and the Father are one” could not be said except where the Father and the Son are equal.

But see what God answered the perverse. He saw that they could not bear the splendor of the truth, and he tested them in his words.

[Col. 0345B] “Is it not written in your law”—that is, the law given to you—“‘I said, You are gods’?”

Through the prophet, in the psalm, God says to everyone: “I said, You are gods.” The Lord generally called all those Scriptures “the law,” although elsewhere he specifically calls the law distinct from the prophets, as in: “The law and the prophets were until John” (Luke XVI). Again: “On these two commandments depend the whole law and the prophets” (Matt. XXII).

At times he divides the same Scriptures into three parts, saying: “It was necessary that everything written about me in the law of Moses, the prophets, and the psalms should be fulfilled” (Luke, last chapter). Here, however, he also called the psalms “the law,” where it is written: “I said, You are gods.”

“If he called them gods to whom the word of God came—and Scripture cannot be broken—do you say of the one whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world, ‘You are blaspheming,’ because I said, ‘I am the Son of God’?”

If the word of God came to human beings so that they might be called gods, how is the very Word of God, who is with God, not God? If human beings become gods through the word of God, how is the one from whom they receive participation not God? If illuminated lights are gods, how is the light that illuminates not God? If those who are somehow warmed by a saving fire become gods, how is the one from whom they are warmed not God?

You approach the light, you are illuminated, and you are numbered among the children of God. If you withdraw from the light, you are darkened and counted among the darkness. Yet that light does not approach itself, because it does not withdraw from itself.

If, then, the word of God made you gods, how is the Word of God the Father not God? Therefore he sanctified his Son and sent him into the world.

Perhaps someone may say: “If the Father sanctified him, then at some time he was not holy.” To this we must answer: He sanctified him in the very manner in which he begot him, so that he should be holy. By begetting him, he gave him holiness, because he begot him holy. For if whatever is sanctified was previously not holy, how do we say to God the Father, “Hallowed be your name”?

“If I do not perform my Father’s works, do not believe me. But if I do them, and if you do not wish to believe me, believe the works, so that you may know and believe that the Father is in me and I am in the Father.”

The Son does not say, “The Father is in me and I am in him,” in the same way that human beings can say it. For, if we think rightly, we are in God, and if we live rightly, God is in us [Col. 0346A]. The faithful, participating in his grace and illuminated by him, are in him and he is in them—but not as that only-begotten Son is in the Father and the Father in him, as an equal in the one to whom he is equal.

Finally, we can sometimes say, “We are in God, and God is in us,” but we cannot say, “I and God are one.”

Can we not say, “You are in God,” because God contains you? And, “God is in you,” because you have become God’s temple? Yes. But does it follow that, because you are in God, you are God? Or because God is in you, can you say, “Whoever sees me sees God,” as the Only-Begotten said: “Whoever sees me sees the Father also” (John XIV)? And again: “I and the Father are one”?

No. Recognize what belongs properly to the Lord and what is the servant’s gift. The Lord’s proper possession is equality with the Father; the servant’s gift is participation in the Savior.

## HOMILY LX. THURSDAY AFTER *JUDICA*

(John VII.) “At that time, when some of the crowd had heard Jesus’ words, they were saying: ‘This is truly the prophet,’” and so forth.
