When Christ was speaking on the last day of the festival the things set out above in this Gospel passage, disagreement about him arose among the crowd. Some thought that he was the Christ; others said that the Christ would not arise from Galilee.

Those who had been sent to seize him returned free from guilt and filled with admiration. They bore witness to his divine teaching when they said to those who had sent them:

[Col. 0346C] “Why did you not bring him?” They answered: “No one has ever spoken as this man speaks.”

For no human being speaks in this way. He spoke in this way because he was God and human being.

Yet the Pharisees, rejecting their testimony, said to them:

“Have you too been led astray?” For we see that you have been delighted by his words.

“Has any one of the rulers believed in him, or any of the Pharisees? But this crowd, which does not know the law, is accursed.”

Those who did not know the law were the ones believing in him who had given the law. Those who taught the law were despising the one who had given it, so that what the Lord himself had said might be fulfilled: “I came so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind.”

The Pharisees, who were teachers, became blind; the people who did not know the law and believed in the author of the law were enlightened.

Nicodemus, however, one of the Pharisees, who had come to the Lord at night—himself not yet believing, but fearful—for he had come to the light at night because he wanted to be illuminated but was afraid of being known, answered the Jews:

“Does your law judge a person unless it first hears him and learns what he does?”

For those wicked men wanted to condemn before they had investigated. Nicodemus knew, or rather believed, that if they would only listen to him patiently, perhaps they would become like those who had been sent to seize him and had preferred to believe him rather than seize him.

They answered out of the prejudice of their hearts:

[Col. 0347A] “Are you also a Galilean?” That is, as though to say, “Have you been led astray by a Galilean?”

The Lord was called a Galilean because his parents were from the city of Nazareth. I said “parents” with reference to Mary, not to male seed. For on earth he sought only a mother, since he already had a Father above. Both of his births were wondrous: the divine birth, without a mother; the human birth, without a human father.

So they said to Nicodemus, as though they were teachers of the law: “Search the Scriptures and see that no prophet arises from Galilee.” But the Lord of the prophets arose from there according to the order of the prophets.

“And they returned,” the evangelist says, “each to his own house.”

## HOMILY LXI. FRIDAY AFTER *JUDICA*

[Col. 0347B]

(John XI.) “At that time, the chief priests and Pharisees gathered a council against Jesus, and they were saying: ‘What are we to do, because this man is performing many signs?’” and so forth.

Yet they were not saying, “Let us believe in him.” These utterly ruined men were thinking more about how to harm and destroy him than about how to secure their own safety so that they would not perish; nevertheless, they were afraid and thought they were taking precautions. For they said:

“What are we to do, because this man is performing many signs? If we let him go on in this way, everyone will believe in him. And the Romans will come and take away our place and our nation.”

They did not wish to lose temporal things, and they did not recognize eternal life; thus they lost both. For because of the Lord’s Passion and glorification, the Romans took away from them both their place and their nation, by warfare and deportation. What was said elsewhere also followed them: “The children of the kingdom will go into the darkness” (Matt. VIII).

They feared that, if everyone believed in Christ, no one would remain to defend the city of God and the temple against the Romans, because they perceived Christ’s teaching as opposed to that very temple and to their ancestral laws.

“But one of them, named Caiaphas, since he was high priest that year, said to them: ‘You know nothing at all, nor do you consider that it is better for you that one man should die for the people, and not that the whole nation should perish.’”

He did not say this from himself; but, since he was high priest that year, he prophesied.

[Col. 0347D] Here he also taught that the spirit of prophecy can proclaim future things through wicked people. Yet the evangelist attributed this to a divine sacrament because he was the high priest, that is, the chief priest.

You may wonder how he is called the high priest of that year when the Lord had established one chief priest, with one successor appointed upon his death. It should be understood that, through ambitions and disputes among the Jews, it was later established that there should be several who would minister in annual rotations.

For this is said concerning Zechariah: “It happened that, while he was serving as priest in the order of his division before God, according to the established arrangement of the priesthood, he was chosen by lot to enter and burn incense. And he entered the temple of the Lord,” and so forth [Col. 0348A] (Luke I).

This shows that there were several of them and that they had their rotations. For only the chief priest was permitted to offer incense, and they also served for one year by lot, with others succeeding them in another year; from among them the one who was to offer incense was chosen by lot.

What, then, does it mean that Caiaphas prophesied that Jesus was going to die for the nation, and not only for the nation, but also to gather into one the children of God who were scattered? The evangelist added this. Caiaphas prophesied only about the Jewish nation, in which there were sheep concerning whom the Lord himself says: “I was sent only to the sheep that had perished from the house of Israel.”

But the evangelist knew of other sheep that were not of this fold, which had to be brought in so that there might be one flock and one shepherd. These things were said according to predestination, because they were not yet his sheep, nor yet children of God, since they had not yet believed.

“From that day, therefore, they planned to kill him. But Jesus no longer walked openly among the Jews; he departed into the region near the wilderness, to a city called Ephraim, and there he stayed with his disciples.”

This was not because his power had failed, since, if he had wished, he could have lived openly among the Jews and they could have done nothing to him. Rather, in the weakness of human nature he was showing his disciples an example of how to live. It thereby becomes clear that it is not a sin if his faithful, who are his members, withdraw themselves from the eyes of their persecutors and avoid the fury of the wicked by hiding rather than inflaming it further by displaying themselves.

## HOMILY LXII. SATURDAY AFTER *JUDICA*, AT THE VIGIL OF PALMS

[Col. 0348C]

(John VI.) “At that time, Jesus said to the crowds of the Jews: ‘Amen, amen, I say to you: Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves,’” and so forth.

You do not know, in fact, how it is given or what the manner of eating this bread is. Nevertheless: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves.” He was certainly not speaking these words to corpses but to living people.

Therefore, lest they understand this life as referring to the present life and object to it, he continued by adding:

“Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life.”

He does not possess this life, then, who does not eat this bread and drink this blood. For without him, human beings who are not by faith in his body can somehow possess temporal life in this world; but they can never possess eternal life, which is promised to the saints.

But lest they think that eternal life was being promised in this food and drink—which they take carnally and do not understand spiritually through faith—in such a way that those who received it would no longer die bodily, he deigned to meet this thought. For after saying, “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life,” he immediately added and said:

“I will raise him up on the last day.”

Thus, in the meantime, he may have eternal life according to the spirit, in the rest that receives the spirits of the saints; but, as regards the body, it too will not be deprived of eternal life in the resurrection of the dead on the last day.

“For my flesh,” he says, “is truly food, and my blood is truly drink.” Since people seek food and drink so that they may not hunger or thirst, this is truly provided only by that food and drink which makes those who partake of it immortal and incorruptible—that is, the fellowship of the saints themselves, where there will be complete and perfect peace and unity.

For this reason, as men of God before us have also understood, our Lord Jesus Christ commended his body and blood to us in those things which are brought together into one from many [Col. 0349B]. One of these, namely bread, is made into one from many grains. The other, namely wine, is made into one from many grapes. Finally, he now explains how what he is saying comes about, and what it means to eat his body and drink his blood.

“And whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him.” Therefore, to eat that food and drink that drink is to remain in Christ and to drink him as he remains in oneself. But whoever does not remain in Christ, and in whom Christ does not remain, certainly does not spiritually eat his flesh, even though carnally and visibly he presses the sacrament of Christ’s body and blood [Col. 0349C] with his teeth. Rather, being unclean, he eats and drinks the sacrament of so great a reality to his own judgment when he presumes to approach Christ’s sacraments—sacraments which no one else receives worthily except one who is clean. Of such people it is said: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5).

“As the living Father sent me,” he says, “and I live because of the Father, so whoever eats me will himself live because of me.” The Son does not become better through participation in the Father, for he was born equal to him; whereas through participation in the Son, by the unity of his body and blood—which that eating and drinking signifies—we become better. We therefore live because of him when we eat him, that is, when through him we receive eternal life, which we did not possess from ourselves.

But he himself lives because of the Father, having been sent by him [Col. 0349D], because “he emptied himself, becoming obedient even unto the wood of the cross.” “As the living Father sent me, and I live because of the Father, so whoever eats me will himself live because of me.” It is as though he said: My self-emptying, in which he sent me, caused me to live because of the Father—that is, to refer my life to him as to one greater. But participation causes someone to live because of me, because he eats me. Thus I, humbled, live because of the Father; that person, made upright, lives because of me.

He did not speak of that nature in which he is always equal to the Father, but of that in which he was made lesser than the Father. Of this he also said above: “As the Father has life in himself, so he has granted the Son to have life in himself [Col. 0350A]” (John 5)—that is, he begot the Son possessing life in himself.

“This is the bread that came down from heaven,” so that by eating it we may live, since we can possess eternal life from ourselves. “Not as your fathers ate manna and died,” he says. “Whoever eats this bread will live forever.” That they died, therefore, he wishes to be understood in this sense: they do not live forever. Certainly, those who eat Christ will also die temporally; but they live forever because Christ is the sign of eternal life.

Whoever eats and drinks does so if he remains and is remained in, if he dwells and is dwelt in, if he clings so as not to be abandoned. Thus he taught and admonished us through mystical words that we should be in his body, under him as the head, among his members [Col. 0350B], eating his flesh and not abandoning his unity.

But many of those who were present, because they did not understand, were scandalized. In hearing these things, they thought only of flesh—the flesh that they themselves were. Yet the Apostle speaks truly: “To set the mind on the flesh is death” (Romans 8). The Lord says that we are to eat his flesh, and yet to set the mind on the flesh is death. Since he says of his flesh that it is food of eternal life, we must therefore not understand flesh according to the flesh, as in these words:

“Therefore many, when they heard,” not of the disciples generally, but “of his disciples, said: ‘This is a hard saying; who can hear it?’” If the disciples found this saying hard, what of his enemies? And yet it had to be said in such a way that it would not be understood by everyone [Col. 0350C]. God’s secret should make people attentive, not hostile. But these men quickly fell away when the Lord Jesus Christ spoke such things. They did not believe that he was saying something great, or that some grace was working through those words; instead, they understood them as they wished, and in the human manner, as though Jesus, who was present among them, intended to distribute among his believers the flesh with which the Word was clothed, as if it had been cut into pieces. “‘This is a hard saying,’ they said; ‘who can hear it?’”

“But Jesus, knowing in himself that his disciples were murmuring about this”—for they said these things among themselves, thinking that he would not hear them—he who knew what was within them heard them inwardly and answered: “Does this scandalize you?” Because I said [Col. 0350D], “I give you my flesh to eat and my blood to drink,” does this scandalize you?

“What if you see the Son of Man ascending to where he was before?” What does this mean? Here he resolves what had disturbed them; by this he will draw them out of that by which they had been scandalized; here it will plainly be seen what they did not understand. They thought that he would distribute his body, but he said that he would ascend into heaven, whole and entire. “When you see the Son of Man ascending to where he was before,” then surely you will see that he does not distribute his body in the manner you suppose; then surely you will understand that his grace is not consumed by being bitten.

In these words it is clearly understood that Christ is one person, since he said that the Son of Man [Col. 0351A] was previously in heaven. He was speaking on earth, yet said that he was in heaven. What does this imply except that we are to understand Christ as one person, God and man, not two persons—lest our faith become a quaternity rather than a Trinity?

Christ, therefore, is one: Word, soul, and flesh; one Christ, Son of God and son of man. One Christ, Son of God eternally, son of man in time. Yet the one Christ, according to the unity of his person, was in heaven when he was speaking on earth. The son of man was in heaven in the same way that the Son of God was on earth: the Son of God on earth in the flesh he had assumed; the son of man in heaven in the unity of his person.

He soon explains more fully what difference there is between spirit and flesh, and what it means to wish to eat Christ carnally rather than receive him spiritually. For he says:

[Col. 0351B] “It is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh profits nothing.” Shortly before he said: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves”; and now he says: “The flesh profits nothing”—that is, if you wish to understand what I say carnally. “The flesh profits nothing” if you understand this flesh as something to be eaten like other food, like the meat bought in butcher shops.

“It is therefore the Spirit who gives life.” Through the Spirit, the flesh profits, although by itself it profits nothing, because “the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.” For through the flesh the Spirit accomplished something for our salvation. The flesh was the vessel that contained him, and through it the Spirit saved us, using the organ of flesh for the salvation of the human race, just as the devil used the serpent as an instrument for the overthrow of our first parent [Col. 0351C].

“It is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh profits nothing”—as they understood flesh, not as I give my flesh to be eaten. Therefore he says: “The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life.”

For we have said that, in speaking of the eating of his flesh and the drinking of his blood, the Lord commended this to us: that we should remain in him and he in us. We remain in him when we are his members; he remains in us when we are his temple. To make us his members, unity joins us together; and what produces unity if not the love of God? Hence the Apostle says: “God’s love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Romans 5).

Therefore it is the Spirit who gives life, for the Spirit makes the members alive [Col. 0351D]. Nor does the Spirit make alive any members except those that he finds within the body that he himself animates. For the spirit that is in you, O human being, by which you exist as a human being, does it give life to a member that it finds separated from your flesh? I mean your spirit, your soul. Your soul gives life only to the members that are in your flesh. If you remove one of them, it is no longer given life by your soul, because it is not joined to the unity of your body.

These things are said so that we may love unity and fear separation. A Christian should fear nothing so much as being separated from the body of Christ. For if he is separated from the body of Christ, he is not his member; and if he is his member, he is not animated by his Spirit. “Whoever,” the Apostle says, “does not have the Spirit of Christ [Col. 0352A] does not belong to him.”

“Therefore it is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh profits nothing. The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life.” What does “they are spirit and life” mean? They are to be understood spiritually. If, therefore, you have understood them spiritually, they are spirit and life for you. If you have understood them carnally, even then they are spirit and life in themselves, but they are not so for you, O human being, because you do not understand them spiritually, nor do you know how to revere them through faith.

“But there are some among you who do not believe.” And for this reason they do not understand, because they do not believe. For the prophet said: “Unless you believe, you will not understand” (Isaiah 7, according to the Septuagint). Through faith we are joined together; through understanding we are given life. Let us first cling through faith, so that afterward we may be given life through understanding.

“For Jesus knew [Col. 0352B] from the beginning who those were who believed, and who would betray him.” Judas was there among those who were scandalized. Christ did not remain silent about him, nor did he openly identify him, so that all might be afraid, even though one would perish. But after he had spoken of and distinguished believers from unbelievers, he stated the reason why they did not believe.

“For this reason I said to you,” he says, “that no one can come to me unless it has been granted him by my Father.” Faith will be given by the Father to believers, so that no one may boast in his faith as though it came from himself and belonged to him by right, but may recognize it as given by God, as a gift of grace.

“From that time many of his disciples went back and no longer walked with him.” They went back—not after Christ, but after Satan. They returned backward in this way [Col. 0352C]: cut off from the body of Christ and no longer returning to him, because they had never been faithfully fixed in his body. And these were not few, but many. Let us therefore hear what he said to the few who remained.

“Then Jesus said to the Twelve: ‘Do you also want to leave?’” Judas did not depart then; but because he remained with the Lord, he was not yet revealed. Later he was made known.

Peter answered on behalf of all: one for many, unity for the whole. For the evangelist says:

“Simon Peter answered him: ‘Lord, to whom shall we go?’” As though he were saying: Are you driving us away from yourself? Give us another like you, to whom we may go if we leave you. If we depart from you, “to whom shall we go?”

“You have the words of eternal life.” See how Peter [Col. 0352D], with the Lord granting and the Holy Spirit renewing him, understood. Why else than because he believed the words of eternal life? You have eternal life in the ministry of your body and blood.

“And we believe, and we have come to know.” He did not say, “We have come to know and believe,” but “We believe and have come to know.” For we believe in order to come to know. If we wished first to know and then to believe, we would be able neither to know nor to believe.

What do we believe, or what have we come to know? “That you are the Christ, the Son of God.” That is: You yourself are eternal life, and in your flesh and blood you give nothing except what you are.

Jesus answered: “Did I not choose you Twelve [Col. 0353A], and one of you is a devil?” He was speaking of Judas, the son of Simon Iscariot. For he was going to betray him, although he was one of the Twelve.

He was one of the Twelve not in faith but in number; not in truth but in pretense. But how are we to understand “Did I not choose you Twelve?” when that one is said to be the son of the devil? It must be understood that the eleven were chosen in one way, and that one in another.

The eleven were chosen to remain in Christ and for their sound to go out through the whole world. That one was chosen so that through him the dispensation of divine mercy might be fulfilled for the salvation of the human race. Thus the goodness of God makes good use of his wickedness.

In the sale of Joseph [Col. 0353B], God likewise made good use of the wickedness of his brothers, so that from their evil deed the goodness of God might be shown for the salvation of many. In the same way, Judas’s evil was turned into our good. What the wicked person does by misusing God’s good things harms himself; he cannot destroy God’s goodness.

Why did Christ choose twelve? The number twelve is sacred. Since one of that number perished, the honor of the number was not thereby taken away, for another was substituted in the place of the one who perished. The consecrated number remained—the number twelve—because they were to proclaim the Trinity throughout the whole world, that is, through the four quarters of the earth. They were therefore chosen four at a time, so that the holy Trinity might be preached through the four parts of the world.

The year also runs according to the number twelve, and the order of the signs in the heavens, through which the sun and moon are known to move, is divided according to the number twelve. For this reason the Lord Christ sent the first preachers into the world in this number.

The number was not violated when Judas perished [Col. 0353C]; another was substituted in his place. Concerning the most sacred significance of this number, Christ himself says in the Gospel, speaking of the supreme glory of the saints: “When the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty, you also will sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matthew 19).

## HOMILY LXIII. PALM SUNDAY

*(Matthew 21.)* “At that time, when they had drawn near to Jerusalem and had come to Bethphage,” and the rest.

When they had drawn near—namely, the Lord and his apostles—to Jerusalem, Jesus was making his way toward the Passion, because the time of his Passion was already at hand. Five [Col. 0353D] days before the Paschal festival, he came into Jerusalem with a large crowd. After this occasion he did not leave there until he had suffered and risen there.

“To the Mount of Olives.” The Mount of Olives was not far from Jerusalem, but, as we find in the *Book of Antiquities*, it was a distance of one thousand paces away.

Bethphage is a village—“village,” I say, because in the land of promise all the larger settlements were fortified with walls, and therefore villages and country estates are designated by one term. Bethphage is interpreted as “house of the mouth” or “of the jaws.” The reason is that the priests in the Lord’s temple, after completing their turn of service over eight days and finishing the divine mystery, moved at night to that same village, where they consumed and ate the victims and sacrifices that they received from the people during the day [Col. 0354A].

Or certainly it is interpreted as “house of the mouth” or “of the jaws” because the priests continually meditated on the Lord’s law there in their hearts and “chewed it over” with their mouths.

When the Lord had therefore come to this Mount of Olives and to this village, Bethphage:

“He sent two disciples, saying to them: ‘Go into the settlement that is opposite you.’” He called Jerusalem a “settlement” contemptuously. The city that had previously been called the city of the great king and the holy city, when the time of the Lord’s Passion was approaching—because it was going to kill the Lord—was no longer called a city, but contemptuously a settlement.

Of this place it is rightly said, “which is opposite you,” because it was opposed both to Christ’s teaching and to the apostles’ teaching.

Spiritually [Col. 0354B], Bethphage signifies the primitive Church. It is rightly said that Bethphage was a village situated on a mountain, because the whole Church of Christ stands upon a mountain—that is, upon Christ. Hence the prophet says: “Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord,” and so forth (Micah 4).

It is also rightly said to be situated on the side of the mountain, because the consecration and redemption of the primitive Church proceeded from the Lord’s side. For we read that, when the Lord was hanging on the cross and had already given up his spirit, one of the soldiers opened his side with a lance, and immediately blood and water came out. The holy Church is redeemed by that blood, while it is daily cleansed from sins by the water.

When the Lord therefore came through the mystery of the Incarnation to save the Jewish people, he sent two disciples to Jerusalem—that is, into this world—so that through their preaching they might bring the rebellious hearts of the Gentiles under the faith of Christ [Col. 0354C] and subject all nations to his faith.

And rightly it is said, “which is opposite you,” because the whole world was unwilling to receive the yoke of faith. He sent two disciples—that is, two orders of preachers, namely, of the Jews and of the Gentiles.

Or he sent two because of the twofold commandment of love, by which we are commanded to love God with all our heart and our neighbor as ourselves.

Or he sent them in pairs because of teaching and action, since a teacher ought to be perfect both in doctrine and in works.

“Go, and you will find a donkey tied, and a colt with her.” According to the literal sense, the great humility of the Savior is commended here. As he made his way to Jerusalem, he did not wish to ride upon a proud or decorated horse; rather, he sought a donkey and its colt—lowly animals—to sit upon.

According to the spiritual understanding [Col. 0354D], these two animals clearly signify the burden of the two peoples. The donkey, accustomed to carrying loads, signifies the Jewish people, who had borne the burden of the law for a long time. The colt, which is wanton and free, signifies the people of the Gentiles, who before the Lord’s coming walked as though free and wandering, without the teaching of the law and the prophets.

Both are rightly said to have been tied, because when the Redeemer came into the world, he found both peoples bound by the chains of their sins. Hence the Apostle Paul says: “There is no distinction, for all have sinned and lack the glory of God” (Romans 10).

[Col. 0355A] “Untie them.” Untie the Gentiles from the bonds of their sins.

“And bring them to me”—through your preaching and miracles. Although Almighty God abandoned the Gentiles for a time in order to save them, he did not despise them forever in order to destroy them. For what the Psalmist said must be fulfilled: “You will save humans and animals, O Lord” (Psalm 35).

“And if anyone says anything to you, say: ‘The Lord has need of them.’” The Lord commanded his apostles that, during the time of their preaching, they should not yield to the rulers and kings of the Gentiles who tried to prevent them from teaching and saving the peoples.

For we read in the other evangelists (Mark 11; Luke 19) that when the disciples came to the house and were untying the colt, the owners of the house [Col. 0355B] said: “What are you doing, untying the colt?” But they replied that the Lord desired its service.

As soon as the holy apostles, having received the divine command, preached to the world, the kings and rulers of the Gentiles immediately began to oppose them, so that they would not untie the colt—that is, so that they would not turn the Gentile people away from the worship of idols. But the disciples steadfastly explained to them that the Lord desired their service.

Here one may ask why the disciples say of animals, “The Lord has need of them,” when the Church sings to him: “You have no need of my goods” (Psalm 15). The Lord has need of the Gentiles—so that from their multitude he may build for himself “a Church without spot or wrinkle”—in order that the losses suffered by the heavenly homeland through the fall of wicked angels might be repaired by the multitude of the Gentiles.

“And immediately he will send them back.” When the ministry of those animals [Col. 0355C] had been completed, the animals were indeed returned to their former master, but the figure represented by those animals remained with the Lord.

We must not therefore suppose that, after the animals—that is, the people of believers—have been brought to the Lord, they are again released to their former masters, that is, to the service of demons. Rather, this saying, “And immediately he will send them back,” is to be understood in this way: when people are brought to the faith of Christ, they are immediately sent back—not into demonic servitude, but into freedom of will.

“Now all this happened.” What does “all” mean? That the Lord sent the disciples into the city to bring the animals, so that he might be carried into the royal city upon lowly animals.

It is the custom of blessed [Col. 0355D] Matthew the evangelist, whenever he narrates something fulfilled concerning our Lord Jesus Christ, also to say that it had previously been foretold by prophetic testimonies.

“Say to the daughter of Zion.” This example is taken from the prophet Zechariah (Zechariah 9). The holy prophet knew through the Holy Spirit the unbelief of the Jews; and, with the Holy Spirit revealing in advance that, when the Lord came to Jerusalem, they would oppose him and treat him with blasphemies and insults. He therefore took care beforehand to restrain the presumption of their hearts and strove to foretell the coming of the Redeemer, indicating by what signs they might recognize him.

The prophet’s voice is addressed to the apostles and the others who accompanied the Lord, saying [Col. 0356A]: “Say to the daughter of Zion.” You apostles and all the others who accompany the Lord as he goes toward Jerusalem, “say to the daughter of Zion”—that is, to the people of Jerusalem gathered for the festival.

Historically, he calls Jerusalem the daughter of Zion. Zion was a lofty citadel in the middle of the city, holding dominion over the city’s buildings.

“Behold, your king”—not a foreigner, not an outsider like Herod, but one who takes his bodily origin from you.

“He comes to you.” It is not without significance that he said “to you.” This means: If you understand his coming and receive him devoutly, “he comes to you”—that is, to save you. But if you do not understand his coming, he will be rejected; he will come against you, that is, to destroy you.

“Gentle.” These are the signs of your king: gentle, not fierce or cruel like the other kings who formerly ruled over you, but mild, as he himself said: “Learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart” (Matthew 2).

[Col. 0356B] “Seated on a donkey and a colt”—that is, he did not come to you seated on a horse, a lover of strife and discord, but seated on a donkey, a lover of peace and tranquility.

Allegorically, we should understand Zion as that part of the holy Church which exists in those saints who already reign with Christ and contemplate his glory. The daughter of Zion, however, should be understood as the present Church, which still lives as a pilgrim on earth, separated from Christ.

She is rightly called the daughter of the heavenly city because those who went before us to the heavenly homeland taught us faith and good works, and also regenerated us through sacred baptism.

The prophet’s voice therefore addresses the preachers, saying: You holy preachers who still live as pilgrims on earth, separated from Christ, say to the holy Church: “Behold, your king.”

At his first coming [Col. 0356C], the king of the holy Church came gently to redeem her. At his second coming, he will also come gently, to withdraw her from this world and transfer her into the number of the heavenly citizens.

According to the literal sense, it is not easy to believe that the Lord sat upon both animals during so short a journey. For teachers report that from the Mount of Olives to Jerusalem there is a distance of only one thousand feet. Either he sat upon the donkey while the colt walked free; or—and this is more likely—he sat upon the colt while the donkey went without a rider.

But wherever the historical account fails, or contains something unbecoming, we must turn to the spiritual understanding. For even if the Lord could not sit upon both animals, according to the mystery he nevertheless rules over both peoples, namely the Jews and the Gentiles; and by ruling them he leads them to Jerusalem—that is, to the vision of the heavenly homeland.

[Col. 0356D] “And the disciples went.” Having received the command to preach, the apostles traveled throughout the whole world and scattered everywhere the seed of divine faith.

“And they placed their garments upon them.” The apostles’ garments, which they placed upon the bare backs of the animals, signify their teaching and commandments. Through these they warmed the hearts of the Gentiles, so that they could have the Lord as their rider. Unless those who believed in Christ had been adorned with the apostles’ garments, they would never have deserved to have the Lord as their rider.

[Col. 0357A] “But a very great crowd.” The very great crowd that spread its garments beneath the feet of the animals carrying the Lord signifies the multitude of martyrs who spread their garments—that is, their bodies—upon the road of this life, so that they might make a path for the animals carrying the Lord, that is, for the simple, by which to walk toward the heavenly homeland, and so that we too might reach Jerusalem—that is, the heavenly homeland—with an unhindered step.

It may also be understood in another way: the animals carrying the Lord bore the apostles’ garments upon themselves, as befitted their greater dignity, while the confused and common crowd trampled its garments beneath their feet.

The garments of the crowds [Col. 0357B] signify the ceremonies of the old law; the apostles’ garments demonstrate the teaching and commandments of the New Testament. Thus the Lord-bearing animals have the apostles’ garments upon them and trample the crowds’ garments beneath their feet, because all who believe in Christ attend to the apostles’ commandments above themselves, while they consider the commandments, new moons, and institutions of the Old Testament as worthless.

Whenever we despise circumcision, violate the Sabbath, and reject the new moons, what else are we doing but trampling the garments of the crowds beneath our feet?

“Others were cutting branches from the trees.” By the trees we should understand the divine Scriptures. Those cut branches from the trees who extract various useful things from the Scriptures for the benefit of those who are journeying toward the heavenly homeland.

It may also be understood in another way [Col. 0357C]. By the trees we can understand pagans; by the branches of the trees, the children of pagans. Whoever detaches the children of pagans from the rite and superstition of their fathers cuts branches from the trees.

“But the crowd that went before and the crowd that followed.” Remembering the marvelous deeds that the Lord had performed among them—raising the dead, healing lepers, walking upon the sea without his footsteps being submerged, and performing other such wonders—when he drew near to his Passion, they strove with devoted minds to offer him praise and thanks for the miracles and good works that he had performed among them, saying:

“Hosanna to the Son of David,” and so forth.

Spiritually, however [Col. 0357D], the fact that the crowd which went before the Lord and the crowd which followed him praised the Lord together with one harmonious voice signifies that the Jewish people, who preceded in faith, and the Gentiles who followed them praise Almighty God with equal and harmonious faith.

The same faith that existed in the patriarchs and prophets before the Savior’s coming exists in all the nations after his resurrection.

“Hosanna to the Son of David.” *Hosanna* is composed of two Hebrew words. *Osia* among them means “save” or “make safe,” while *na* is the interjection of one who pleads. When compounded, the name becomes *hosanna* through the elision of the vowel *i* and the doubling of the consonant *n*, although it would more correctly be said *osiana*. It is interpreted as “save” or “make safe,” with “your people Israel,” or “the whole world,” understood; or, as others wish, it is interpreted as “salvation,” so that the sense is: “Hosanna to the Son of David,” that is, “Salvation to the Son of David.”

[Col. 0358A] “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.” When it says, “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord,” this is understood to mean that the Son came from the Father into the world. Whatever he did according to the flesh in this world, he referred entirely to the glory and name of his Father, saying: “The Father who remains in me does his works” (John 4).

The addition, “Hosanna in the highest,” means that the Incarnation and Passion of the Lord the Savior were not salvation only for human beings, but also salvation and joy for the angels in heaven. For the multitude of believers is transferred to heaven, and the number of angels, which had been diminished when wicked angels fell, is restored by the multitude of the Gentiles.

[Col. 0358B]

## HOMILY LXIV. ON HOLY PALM SUNDAY

The Passion of Our Lord Jesus Christ according to Matthew.

*(Matthew 26–27.)* “At that time Jesus said to his disciples: ‘You know that after two days the Passover will take place,’” and the rest.

We read that the Lord came to Jerusalem six days before Passover, amid crowds and palm branches. From the day on which he entered Jerusalem riding on a donkey [Col. 0358C] up to this day on which he spoke these things to his apostles, we understand that four days had passed and that two days remained until Passover.

Allegorically, the two days signify the two Testaments, the Old and the New, which lead their followers and observers to the glory of eternal life. “After two days,” that is, after the manifestation of the two Testaments, the true Passover was celebrated in the world.

*Pascha* is not Greek, as some claim, but Hebrew. In Hebrew, *pesach* is interpreted as “passing over.”

First, it is called a passing over because on that day the Lord passed over Egypt, destroying the Egyptians and freeing the Israelite people.

Second, because on that day the destroyer passed through the kingdom of Egypt and killed its firstborn.

Third, because during this festival our Redeemer passed from this world to the Father, as John more fully declares: “Before the feast of Passover, Jesus, knowing that his hour had come to pass from this world to the Father” (John 19).

Fourth, so that we might be mystically instructed that through Christ’s Passion we were to pass from this mortality to true immortality.

[Col. 0358D] “And the Son of Man will be handed over to be crucified.” Those are mistaken who think that the Lord shrank from or feared the Passion, since he not only foretold his Passion two days beforehand but had foretold the same Passion long before. When that Passion was at hand, he did not wish to avoid the plot; while others were unwilling to go, he freely offered himself to the Passion.

The Lord was handed over in many ways. First, God the Father [Col. 0359A] handed him over, as the Apostle Paul says: “God did not spare his own Son, but handed him over for us all” (Romans 8).

Then the Son himself handed himself over, as the same Paul says: “He handed himself over for us” (Ephesians 5).

Third, Judas handed him over to the Jews; the Jews handed him over to Pilate for judgment; and Pilate handed him over to the soldiers for crucifixion.

“Then the chief priests and the elders of the people gathered in the courtyard of the high priest, who was called Caiaphas.” The wickedness and malevolence of the Jews are condemned in this passage. Instead of preparing themselves as Passover approached—smoothing the walls of the temple, sweeping the pavement, preparing the victims and sacrifices that were to be offered at the solemnity of Passover, and preparing themselves to celebrate the feast of Passover—they gathered to deliberate how they might hand the Lord over to death.

[Col. 0359B] “But they said: ‘Not on the feast day, lest perhaps there be a tumult among the people.’” The simple wording seems to suggest that the Jews were guarding against seizing the Lord on the feast day because they feared a riot among the crowds. But that interpretation does not hold. Rather, it should be understood that they feared he might be taken from their hands with the help of the people, because everyone regarded him as a prophet.

“Lest perhaps there be a tumult”—that is, lest there be an uprising—“among the people.”

“Now when Jesus was in Bethany, in the house of Simon the leper.” The evangelist rightly thought it necessary to relate what the Lord did in Bethany six days before Passover, the day before he went to Jerusalem riding on a donkey.

When he says “in the house of Simon the leper [Col. 0359C],” we must not suppose that Simon was still a leper at that time. Rather, he had once been a leper and had been miraculously healed by the Lord; his former name remained in memory of that healing. Matthew is likewise called “the tax collector,” not because he was still a tax collector, but because he had formerly been one.

And it is fitting that the Lord is said to have been in Bethany before the Passion. For Bethany is interpreted as “house of obedience,” clearly showing that he came to the Passion through complete obedience.

“Then a woman approached him, carrying an alabaster jar of costly ointment.” This woman was Mary Magdalene, from whom the Lord had cast out seven demons. At first, when she approached the Lord in the house of the Pharisee, she washed his feet with her tears and wiped them with her hair. [Col. 0359D] Later, having become familiar with the Lord, she approached to anoint his very head. And because she loved greatly, she merited the forgiveness of many sins.

Alabaster is a type of precious marble, streaked with various colors, which physicians say is excellent for preserving ointments unspoiled.

“Costly.” Another Evangelist explains how costly this ointment was, relating that it was made from genuine nard. Nard is an aromatic shrub with a rich and delicate root, holding first place among all the species from which ointments are prepared. Genuine—that is, faithful and uncorrupted—not adulterated, as physicians commonly adulterate the purity of ointments with certain herbs. Another Evangelist, to show that this ointment was extremely costly, [Col. 0360A] relates that it was made from spikes of nard. The finest ointment is made from the root, but that made from the spikes is more expensive.

Mystically, Mary’s devotion signifies the faith of the Church. She anoints the Lord’s head when she proclaims the power of his divinity, saying with the apostle John: “In the beginning was the Word” (John 1). She anoints his feet when she proclaims the weakness of his humanity, saying with that same John: “And the Word became flesh” (ibid.).

“But when the disciples saw this, they were indignant, saying: Why this waste?” Here Matthew and John seem to differ, since John alone attributes this indignation to Judas, giving the reason why he was indignant at the pouring out of the ointment—namely, because he was a thief and, having the money box, carried what was put into it. But this is a figure of speech called synecdoche, which often puts the singular for the plural and very frequently the plural for the singular. By this form of expression, then, we can say that Matthew has used the plural for the singular, saying that the disciples were indignant. It should be said, however, that if the other disciples were indignant, Judas was so not for the sake of the poor but out of envy, grieving that what was poured on the Lord’s head was being taken away from his money bags.

“For this could have been sold for much”—that is, for a great price—“and given to the poor.”

“But Jesus, knowing this, said to them: Why do you trouble this woman? She has performed a good work for me.” The gentle and kindly Teacher does not rebuke the disciples for their indignation against the woman; nor does he add at the end that his own betrayer and traitor was suffering from envy toward him. Instead, he said: “She has performed a good work for me.” [Col. 0360C]

“For you will always have the poor with you, but you will not always have me.” This too seems contrary to the saying in which the Lord says: “Behold, I am with you all days, until the consummation of the age” (Matthew 28). But that statement is to be understood of his divinity, whereas this one concerns his humanity; for according to his humanity he was not going to remain with them forever. “For,” he says, “you will always have the poor,” and you will be able to show them mercy, “but you will not always have me.”

“For by pouring this ointment on my body, she has done it for my burial.” The sense of these words is: The ointment that you think is the cause of waste is an act of service for my burial. “For by pouring this ointment on my body, she has done it for my burial.” That is, she has anticipated anointing my body while I am still alive, which she will do for the dead, if she is permitted. For we read that, after the Lord had been placed in the tomb, Mary, together with the other holy women, bought spices and other costly ointments, so that when they came they might anoint the Lord’s body. Yet she could not fulfill this, because the Lord’s resurrection came first. This is what the Lord’s words “she has done it for my burial” refer to: what she would have done for me when I was dead, if permitted, she diligently offered to me while I was alive.

[Col. 0361A] “Amen I say to you, wherever this Gospel is preached throughout the whole world, what she has done will also be told in memory of her.” It should be noted that the Lord, who was to suffer and be crucified by the Jews two days later, foretells that his Gospel will be preached throughout the entire world. Thus, among the other miracles of the Savior, Mary’s kindness is also proclaimed, and her devotion is praised by everyone: that she anointed the Lord’s head, poured her tears over his feet, and wiped them with her hair. Yet it is not so much Mary’s devotion that is proclaimed as the faith and devotion of the holy Church. “What she has done”—understand, this work—“will also be told in memory of her.”

“Then one of the Twelve, called Judas Iscariot, went to the chief priests.” By saying “then he went,” he shows that this man did not betray the Lord and Savior unwillingly, but voluntarily went to his destruction and, driven by greed, promised his downfall. [Col. 0361B]

“What will you give me, and I will hand him over to you?” He did not set a price for them but left it to their discretion what they wished to give him, so that he might be thought to be selling not the Lord but something like a worthless slave.

“But they fixed for him thirty pieces of silver.” This fulfilled what almighty God had complained through Zechariah, saying: “If it is good in your eyes, bring me my payment; but if not, refrain. And they weighed out my payment, thirty pieces of silver, a handsome price at which I was valued by them” (Zechariah 11). For all the benefits that the Lord [Col. 0361C] had performed among them, they valued him at the price of thirty pieces of silver. It should be understood, however, that Joseph was not sold for twenty gold pieces, as some think, according to what the Septuagint version indicates, but rather for twenty pieces of silver, so that a slave would not be sold at a higher price than the Lord.

“And from then on he sought an opportunity to hand him over.” That is, he sought a suitable place where he could betray him. Another Evangelist reveals what opportunity he was seeking: namely, to hand him over without the crowds, that is, without the support of the people, because he feared that with the people’s help he might be freed from their hands.

“On the first day of Unleavened Bread the disciples approached Jesus.” He calls the fourteenth day of the first month the first day of Unleavened Bread, when the lamb was sacrificed toward evening. The remaining seven days were called Unleavened Bread because they were without leaven. For during those days it was not permitted to eat anything leavened. Yet Unleavened Bread is also used for Passover, and Passover for Unleavened Bread, as here, where he calls the Passover festival itself Unleavened Bread.

“Where do you want us to prepare for you to eat the Passover?” We understand here that Judas approached him together with the other disciples. “You are poor,” they say, “and we poor have followed you, poor as you are; for love of you we have abandoned whatever we were able to possess. Where, then, do you want us to prepare the Passover for you to eat?”

[Col. 0362A] “But Jesus said: Go into the city to a certain man, and say to him: The Teacher says, My time is near; I am celebrating the Passover with my disciples at your house.” It is characteristic of the Hebrew language to speak without naming particular persons, and this practice has been observed here. The Lord fittingly does not state the name of the one at whose house he is going to celebrate the Passover, showing that no one is excluded from the Passover celebration who wishes to celebrate it with the Lord. “And say to him: The Teacher says, ‘My time’”—that is, the time of my passion—“is near; I am celebrating the Passover with my disciples at your house.”

“And the disciples did as Jesus had appointed them, and prepared the Passover.” Another Evangelist says that, when the disciples went, they found a large upper room [Col. 0362B] furnished, and there they prepared it. It is not without great mystery that the Lord celebrated the Passover in an upper room. For the upper room signifies the height of spiritual understanding. Having therefore passed beyond the instruments of the carnal letter, he celebrated the Passover in an upper room—that is, in the height of the New Testament—giving us an example, so that if we wish to celebrate the Passover with the Lord, we may transcend what is low and earthly and celebrate the Passover with the Lord in the upper room, that is, at the height of divine contemplation.

“When evening came, he was reclining with his twelve disciples.” Evening signifies the final age, in which the true Sun set by suffering the cross that he endured for the salvation of the human race. At this evening, therefore, he reclined with his twelve disciples—that is, through the shedding of his blood he prepared eternal rest for them.

“Amen I say to you, one of you is going to betray me.” The Lord could indeed have named the betrayer, but he did not wish to do so, lest, bound by shamelessness, he fall into the abyss of denial. He therefore warns him generally for his salvation, so that, corrected by the warning, he might do penance.

“And they were very sorrowful, and began individually to say: Surely it is I, Lord?” And indeed they were very sorrowful, because they could not only contemplate the Lord’s death but could scarcely even hear of it. Thus the apostle Peter, hearing the Lord speak of his passion, said: “Far be it from you; you will not die” (Matthew 16). All the apostles knew that they had conceived no such thing against the Lord, but, conscious of their weakness, trusting the Teacher more than their own weakness, they said: “Surely it is I, Lord?”

“But he answered and said: The one who dips his hand with me in the serving dish is the one who will betray me.” He had already said above: “One of you is going to betray me,” but because the man who had been warned had not done penance, he now identifies him more openly, saying: “The one who dips his hand with me in the serving dish is the one who will betray me.” A *paropsis* is a square vessel, so called because it has equal sides. It is a vessel for food, which the Evangelist Mark calls a dish, a clay vessel. It is therefore understood that there was on the Lord’s table a vessel containing food and sauce, in [Col. 0363A] which Judas dipped his hand with the Teacher in order to feign a good conscience.

“The Son of Man indeed goes”—understand, to his passion—“as it is written of him.” But woe to “that man through whom the Son of Man will be betrayed.” Even to this day, woe to the man who hands over the body of his Redeemer not to the Jews but to his sinful members, corrupting the integrity of faith. There are many who detest Judas’s crime, because he acted impiously and betrayed his Teacher; yet while reproving him, they take no care to avoid the same reproach in themselves. For when they overthrow the truth for money, what else do they do but betray Christ? For he said: “I am the truth” (John 14). When they violate brotherly love by some breach, what else do they do but betray Christ? Hence it is written: “God is love” (1 John 4).

“It would have been better for that man if he had not been born.” This is not to be understood as though Judas had existed, or could have existed, before he was born, unable then to do either good or evil. It should simply be understood to mean that it is better not to exist than to exist evilly.

“But Judas, who betrayed him, answered and said: Surely it is I, Rabbi?” His saying “Rabbi” is a sign of unbelief, or even an attempt at self-excuse: he calls him not Lord but Teacher, as though he had some excuse because he had betrayed not the Lord but at least a teacher.

“While they were dining, Jesus took bread, and [Col. 0363C] blessed it and broke it,” and so forth. When the rites of the Passover had been completed, the Lord proceeded to reveal the sacraments of the new Passover. After he had dined, he gave them bread and wine, clearly in the mystery of his body and blood. Since bread strengthens the human heart and wine increases the blood in a person, rightly is that same bread changed into the Lord’s flesh and that same wine transferred into the Lord’s blood—not by figure or shadow, but in truth. For we believe that it is truly Christ’s flesh, and likewise his blood. But because human weakness is not accustomed to eat raw flesh or drink blood, that same flesh has been transferred into bread and that same blood into wine.

Yet it is rightly asked why we receive so great a sacrament daily while fasting, when the Lord, after the meal had ended, [Col. 0363D] offered his disciples the bread of his body and the cup of his blood in mystery. The answer is that it was fitting first for the symbolic Passover to be completed, and thereafter for the true Passover to be introduced. Later, the fathers of the New Testament—the apostles and their successors—established that, in veneration of so great a sacrament, it should be received daily by those who are fasting.

It should also be considered that no one offers bread alone, or wine without an admixture of water. Since, according to John, the waters are the peoples, water is mixed with wine so that we may understand that Christ’s passion was accomplished for us. Christ’s passion was not celebrated without benefit to the human race, nor could we be saved without Christ’s passion. For if wine alone, without an admixture of water, were offered, it could be understood that we might be saved without Christ’s help and passion. But water is joined to wine, and bread is made with water, so that it may plainly be understood that neither can Christ’s passion occur without our salvation, nor can our salvation exist without his help.

“He took bread,” which was his body; “he blessed it and broke it,” to show that his body was filled with every blessing and was to be broken through the passion, yet was still filled with the fullness of divinity. “And he gave it to his disciples and said: Take and eat.” This stands against those who distribute the Eucharist to the dead. For when the Lord says “take,” he immediately adds, [Col. 0364B] “and eat,” because it is not enough to receive it unless each person eats it for his salvation; what they could not receive during life, they cannot receive after death.

“Likewise, taking the cup, he gave thanks and gave it to them, saying: Drink from it, all of you.” Thus we know that whoever receives it ought to drink.

“For this is my blood of the New Testament.” By saying “this is the blood of the New Testament,” he speaks in distinction from the Old Testament. In the Old Testament the blood of goats and calves was poured out, and those who were to be cleansed were sprinkled with it.

“Which will be poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins.” Christ’s blood was poured out for all, but it does not benefit all; it benefits only those who believe [Col. 0364C] in his passion, and those who are regenerated by the same Holy Spirit by whom Christ was conceived in Mary’s womb.

“But I say to you, I will not drink from this fruit of the vine from now on, until that day when I drink it new with you in my Father’s kingdom.” According to the literal sense, he promises that he will never drink from the fruit of the vine until he rises from the dead. After he rose, however, he not only ate but also drank with his disciples, as the apostle Peter declares, saying: “We who ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead” (Acts 10).

But those who understand more deeply seek a spiritual mystery here. By the name of the vine the Israelite people are signified, as in the Psalm: “You brought a vine out of Egypt” [Col. 0364D] (Psalm 79). And again in Isaiah: “The vineyard of the Lord of Sabaoth is the house of Israel” (Isaiah 5). He therefore says: “I will not drink from this fruit,” that is, from the offspring of this vine, “until I drink it new in my Father’s kingdom.” Here he calls the faith of believers his Father’s kingdom. He says, then: From this hour of my passion I will no longer receive carnal sacrifices and ceremonies, until I drink the sweetest wine—that is, their faith—with you in my Father’s kingdom.

For after the resurrection he drank that wine. He drank the sweetest wine from the fruit of this vine, namely, in those who believed after the resurrection through the preaching of the apostles. As we read in the Acts of the Apostles, when Peter preached, five thousand believed on one day, three thousand on another, and afterward many thousands. In these he drank the sweetest wine after his resurrection.

“And after singing a hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives.” This is what the Psalmist says: “The poor will eat and be satisfied, and they will praise the Lord who seek him” (Psalm 21). From this arose the custom that, when we are nourished by heavenly bread or refreshed by earthly food, we sing a hymn to God.

Alternatively, we may understand the hymn as the prayer through which he commended the disciples to the Father, which John gives in full and which begins as follows: “Father, the hour has come; glorify your Son, so that your Son may glorify you” (John 17). In it he prayed not only for the apostles but also for all who would believe in him through their word. The fact that the Lord went out to the Mount of Olives after the meal plainly gave us an example, so that, after we have been nourished by divine food, we may hasten as quickly as possible to the summit of virtue.

“Then Jesus said to them: You will all be scandalized because of me on this night.” *Skándalon* (σκάνδαλον) in Greek is called in Latin *offensio*, or a striking of the feet. The Lord foretells that they would be scandalized because of him, so that when the hour of scandal came they would not despair because of the scandal but would instead turn to penance. And he fittingly says “on this night,” because just as those who become drunk become drunk at night, so those who suffer scandal suffer it at night—that is, in the darkness of unbelief and ignorance.

“For it is written: I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered.” This is written in the prophet Zechariah in different words and from the perspective of another person. There the prophet’s person speaks to the Lord (Zechariah 12): “Strike the shepherd”—that is, Christ, who says: “I am the good shepherd” (John 10)—“and the sheep of the flock will be scattered,” that is, the apostles, who, abandoning him, all fled.

“But after I have risen, I will go before you into Galilee.” This was fulfilled when the twelve apostles went after the resurrection to Galilee, to the mountain where Jesus had appointed them. And when they saw him, they worshiped him.

“But Peter answered and said to him: Even if all are scandalized because of you, I will never be scandalized.” [Col. 0365D] These words are not words of rashness but rather of the great ardor that Peter had for the Lord. With the same ardor with which he spoke and acted in other matters, he spoke these words as well. But Peter, who was weak, presumed upon his weakness, whereas the Lord, conscious of all things, foretold what was going to happen.

“Then Jesus came with them to a village called Gethsemane.” Gethsemane is a valley near Jerusalem, where the place in which the Lord prayed is still shown, with a church built over it. Gethsemane is interpreted as “the valley of the fat ones,” or “of fatness.” It was not without reason that he sometimes prayed on a mountain and sometimes in a valley. On the mountain he prays to teach us to possess humility and contrition of heart at the time of our prayer. And he does so in the valley of the fat ones, or of fatness, so that our prayer may be seasoned with the fatness of charity.

Or it may be understood otherwise: each person prays on the mountain who seeks the rewards of the heavenly homeland. Yet he also prays in the valley who asks God for earthly things—namely, the death of enemies, vengeance upon adversaries, and an abundance of temporal resources.

“And taking Peter and the two sons of Zebedee, he began to be sorrowful and distressed.” He was sorrowful not because he feared the approaching passion for which he had come to suffer, but because of Judas’s destruction, the scattering of the Jewish people, the scandal of the disciples, and the overthrow of wretched Jerusalem. For these reasons the Lord was sorrowful.

[Col. 0366B] “Then he said to them: My soul is sorrowful unto death.” Those who think that the Lord did not possess a true soul are mistaken. For if he did not have a true soul, why does he say: “My soul is sorrowful unto death?” It should also be noted that he does not say “because of death” but “unto death”—that is, until I redeem my apostles and all believers through the shedding of my blood.

“Remain here and keep watch with me.” The Lord is not commanding bodily wakefulness, which at that time was not present, but rather spiritual watchfulness of the mind, lest the minds of the apostles or the faithful grow numb in the sleep of unbelief.

“And going forward a little, he fell on his face.” The Lord fell on his face to show the humility of his mind through the humility of his body. [Col. 0366C]

“My Father.” He speaks with the affection of one who entreats.

“If it is possible, let this cup pass from me.” He prays that, if it can be done, so long as the human race is saved without his passion, the cup of passion may pass from him—not because he feared suffering that same passion, but because he grieved that the Jews were committing so great a crime in his passion.

Or it may be understood otherwise: “If it is possible, let this cup pass from me”—that is, if it is possible for Nineveh to be saved unless the gourd withers; that is, if it can happen that the Gentiles throughout the world are delivered without the destruction and ruin of the Jews, let the cup of passion pass from me. But because he had said these things to the Father from the weakness of the flesh, he returns to himself; and what he had denied through weakness, he confirms from the person of his divinity, saying: “Nevertheless, not as I will, but as [Col. 0366D] you will”—that is, let not what I speak from the standpoint of humanity happen, but let happen that for which, by your will, I descended to earth.

“And he came to the disciples and found them sleeping.” For they were weighed down by sorrow as well as by the Lord’s passion.

“And he said to Peter: Could you not watch with me for one hour?” As though he were saying: How will you be able to die for me, when you could not watch for me for one hour?

“Watch and pray, so that you do not enter into temptation.” It is impossible for a person, as long as he is in this life, not to be tempted. Hence both the righteous and sinners say daily in prayer: “Lead us not into temptation” (Matthew 6). The Lord therefore does not command us to pray that we may not be tempted, but that we may not be led into temptation. For being tempted is one thing, and being led into temptation another. A person is tempted when either in mind or in body he is titillated by the pleasure of some vice; but he is led into temptation if he begins to consent to his pleasure.

For example, a certain martyr was tempted when he was forced to deny the Lord, but he was not led into temptation. For if he had denied the Lord, he would indeed have been led into temptation.” This, then, is what the Lord commanded them to pray for: that they might not enter into temptation—that is, that they might not withdraw from the faith of Christ out of fear of their persecutors and thereby be forced to deny him.

“The spirit is indeed willing”—to endure the passion—“but the flesh is weak.” He explains why he earlier said, “My soul is sorrowful unto death”: namely, that his spirit was willing to endure the passion, “but the flesh was weak” for enduring punishments.

“Again, a second time he went away and prayed, saying: My Father, if this cup cannot pass unless I drink it, your will be done.” That is, if the human race cannot be saved without my passion, or if the whole world cannot attain salvation unless the Jewish people fall into destruction, your will be done. Let not what I speak from the standpoint of humanity happen, but let happen that for which, by your will, I descended to earth.

“And leaving them, he went away again and prayed a third time, saying the same words.” He prayed three times, so that “every word may stand on the testimony of two or three” (Deuteronomy 19). [Col. 0367C] He prayed not for himself but for us, namely, so that this prayer might be the confirmation of the disciples.

“Then he came to his disciples.” After he had prayed to the Father and obtained the salvation of his disciples, he came to them and said:

“Sleep now and rest. Behold, the hour has drawn near, and the Son of Man will be handed over into the hands of sinners. Rise, let us go. Behold, the one who will betray me has drawn near.” We understand that, after he had said that the disciples should sleep and rest, he was silent for a little while so that what he had said might be fulfilled, and then said: “Rise, let us go.”

“While he was still speaking, behold, Judas, one of the Twelve.” One not by merit but by number, just as the Lord said above: “Did I not choose you twelve, and one of you is a devil?” (John 6).

“But the one who betrayed him gave them a sign, saying: The one whom I kiss is he; seize him.” Wretched Judas thought that the Lord had performed signs by magical arts. Recalling that he had been transfigured on the mountain before three disciples, and also thinking that at the hour of his passion he might change his appearance into another form, he therefore gave his persecutors a sign: whoever he kissed, they were to seize. He imagined that the Lord would elude his persecutors and transform himself into another form.

“And immediately approaching Jesus, he said: Hail, Rabbi. And he kissed him.” What utter madness in wretched Judas! He offers the kiss of peace to the one whom he wishes to hand over to his persecutors. Here was fulfilled what is said through the Psalmist: “The one who ate my bread has magnified his treachery against me” (Psalm 40).

“Friend, why have you come?” This can be understood and punctuated in two ways. It should be punctuated in such a way that we say, “Friend, why have you come?” and read it as the voice of the Lord questioning, rebuking the wretched man, and grieving that he had fallen from the highest rank of the apostleship into apostasy. The sense is: “Friend, why have you come?”—that is, into how great an evil have you been cast down, that from being an apostle you should become an apostate, and from being a teacher of truth, a teacher of error?

But if we make a complete division there and say, “Friend, why have you come,” with the implied command “complete it,” it would be as though he said: Abandon the kiss of peace and fulfill the office of a betrayer.

“And behold, one of those who were with Jesus stretched out his hand, drew his sword, and striking the servant of the chief priest, cut off his ear.” The apostle Peter is recorded as having done this according to John, with the same ardor of mind with which he did everything else. The servant of the chief priest whose ear was cut off was called Malchus, which is interpreted as “king.” In this servant nothing other than the Jewish people are signified. His right ear was cut off because, with spiritual understanding taken away from them, only the aridity of the letter remained in them, like a left ear.

But the Lord restored that man’s right ear by the touch of his hand, because in those who will believe around the day of judgment he will restore spiritual understanding. Hence the same man is called both king and servant of the chief priest. How can he be both king and servant? If king, how servant? He is king in those who will receive the faith of Christ; servant in those who will remain in the slavery of sin.

“Then Jesus said to him: Put your sword back in its place. For all who take the sword will perish by the sword.” According to the literal sense, not all who take up the sword perish by the sword. For many persist in murder and yet are not killed by the sword. But he shows that the passage must be understood more deeply, as though he were saying: By the same rashness with which you punish or judge another, you must be punished by the Lord.

“Or do you think that I cannot ask my Father, and he will provide me with more than twelve legions of angels?” As though he were saying: I do not need the help of twelve apostles, for if I wish to ask my Father, I can obtain from him twelve legions of angels. Among the ancients a legion consisted of six thousand. Twelve legions therefore make seventy-two thousand. So many nations, moreover, are said to have been divided at the tower of Babel into different languages. The sense is: I do not need the help and defense of twelve apostles, for if the whole world conspired for my death, I could ask my Father, and he would provide me with a thousand angels against each nation.

“As though against a robber you have come out with swords and [Col. 0369A] clubs”—and tumult—“to seize me,” and at night, “though I appeared openly to you by day and taught daily in the temple.” It is foolish, then, to seek me with swords when I willingly hand myself over to your power.

“But all this happened so that the Scriptures of the prophets might be fulfilled.” That is, so that the prophets’ predictions concerning Christ’s passion might be fulfilled, which would take too long to enumerate. One of them is: “They pierced my hands and my feet” (Psalm 21), and so forth. And: “Like a sheep he will be led to slaughter” (Isaiah 53). And again: “Because of the iniquities of my people I was led to death.”

“Then they seized Jesus and led him to Caiaphas the chief priest, where the scribes and Pharisees [Col. 0369B] had assembled.” Almighty God had commanded through Moses that the lawful succession of priests should continue forever. But when the time of the Lord’s passion approached, priestly dignity had been destroyed. It was so corrupted that whoever could buy the priesthood with money was made a priest. The succession of lineage was no longer preserved there, but rather the consideration of greed.

This Caiaphas, as Josephus relates, had bought the high priesthood from the Romans for one year. It is not surprising if an unjust priest pronounces an unjust sentence against the Lord.

“But Peter followed him from a distance, as far as the courtyard of the chief priest.” The divine words say one thing while signifying that another is to be understood. According to the literal sense, Peter followed him from a distance because [Col. 0369C] he feared that he too might be seized with him. Allegorically, he followed him from a distance because he was about to deny him shortly afterward.

“And entering inside, he sat with the attendants, to see the outcome.” He entered the courtyard of the chief priest after him either out of love for the Lord or also out of human curiosity, to see his end: whether they would spare him and release him after punishing him, or whether they would condemn him to death.

“Finally, two false witnesses came and said: This man said: I can destroy the temple of God and rebuild it after three days.” It is very surprising that they are called false witnesses when they say things that we read the Lord said elsewhere. But a false witness is one who interprets words in a different sense from the one who spoke them, as these men did, changing not only the meaning but also the words.

For what he had said about the temple of his body, they interpreted as referring to the material temple that was in Jerusalem. Yet in these words they construct a certain accusation against the Lord. They said: “I can destroy the temple of God.” But he had said (John 2): “Destroy this temple”—that is, you destroy it, not I, since it is unlawful for us to lay hands upon ourselves. They said: “And after three days I will rebuild it,” so that he might appear to be speaking of the material temple. But he had spoken of his living and animate body: “And in three days I will raise it up,” as though awakening it from sleep.

“And the chief priest rose and said to him: Do you answer nothing to what these men testify against you?” [Col. 0370A] The chief priest provokes him to answer the false witnesses, so that the one whom the false witnesses could not condemn might be convicted by his own response. But the Lord foresaw that whatever he said would be turned into an accusation. Therefore he answered the chief priest nothing, but said a few things to Pilate.

“Jesus said to him: You have said it”—understand, that I am. The Lord answered Pilate and the chief priest with the same words, so that he might condemn each by his own sentence.

“Nevertheless I say to you, from now on you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of the power of God and coming on the clouds of heaven.” He says to those Jews whom he knew would believe after his resurrection: “Nevertheless I say to you, from now on”—that is, from this hour or the time of my passion—“you will see”—that is, you will understand and believe—“the Son of Man seated at the right hand of the power of God and coming on the clouds of heaven,” namely, to judge.

“Then the chief priest tore his garments, saying: He has blasphemed. Why do we still need witnesses?” The same fury that earlier had shaken him from his seat now also provokes him to tear his garments. It was the custom among the Jewish people that whenever they heard anything harsh or blasphemous against the Lord, they tore their garments, so that by the tearing of the garments they might show the sorrow of their hearts. We read that Paul and Barnabas did this in a certain city when the people wanted to offer victims and sacrifices to them, worshiping them as gods.

Spiritually, the tearing of the chief priest’s garments signified that the dignity of the priesthood among the Jewish people was to be torn apart. In the priest’s being shaken from his seat, it was signified that the high priest’s seat would remain empty among the Jewish people.

“But they answered and said: He is guilty of death.” This fulfilled what the Psalmist had formerly said in the person of the Lord: “Many dogs have surrounded me” (Psalm 21).

“Then they spat in his face and struck him with blows.” This fulfilled what had been foretold through the prophet: “I did not turn my face away from those who rebuked me and spat upon me” (Isaiah 50).

“But others struck him in the face with the palms of their hands, saying: Prophesy to us, Christ; who is the one who struck you?” This fulfilled the prophetic saying: “I gave my cheeks to those who plucked them, and my jaws to those who struck them” (ibid.).

“And one maidservant came up to him, saying, ‘You also were with Jesus the Galilean.’” What does it mean that, in the Lord’s Passion, it was not a man but a woman who compelled Peter to deny him? This was divinely arranged, so that this sex might not appear exempt from the Lord’s Passion; rather, both sexes might be seen to have sinned in the Lord’s Passion, and with a fitting parallel: just as a woman first enticed the first parent to sin, so also the woman doorkeeper was compelling Peter to deny him.

“And again he denied him with an oath, [Col. 0371A] ‘I do not know the man.’” Some excuse the apostle Peter, saying that he did not deny Christ the Lord, but rather the man, as though he were saying: “I know the God; I do not know the man”—as though it were a lesser fault to deny the man than to deny God, when it is established that he is truly God and man.
