But those who wish to defend Peter are compelled to accuse Christ of falsehood, since he said: “Before the cock crows, you will deny me three times.”

“But your speech makes you plainly known.” The speech of those who accused and of those who were accused was indeed one and the same, so that their manner of speaking was not dissimilar, since all were Hebrews. But because every province or city has its own native sound of speech, which one cannot avoid, they therefore say: “For your speech makes you plainly known.” As we read in the Book of Judges, when the Ephraimites were crossing the fords of the Jordan and were compelled by their enemies to say *shibboleth*, which means “ear of grain,” because they could not pronounce it they said *sibboleth*.

“And Peter remembered Jesus’ word, which he had said: ‘Before the cock crows, you will deny me three times.’ And he went out and wept bitterly.” As another Evangelist says, “The Lord looked at Peter” (Luke XXII). The Lord’s look signifies his mercy, by which he looked upon Peter in his doubt and confirmed him in faith; for he also looks upon sinners and turns their hearts toward repentance. This too should be noted: when the cock crowed, Peter returned to repentance, because, whenever we sin through bodily negligence, we ought to return to repentance through the admonition of preachers. For preachers are often signified by the name of cocks.

“When morning came, all the chief priests and elders of the people took counsel against Jesus, so that they might hand him over to death.” The Jews’ diligence is noteworthy: throughout the whole night they labored toward evil, so that they might shed innocent blood; and when morning came, they took counsel and handed Jesus over to Pilate. He was not handed over to Pilate alone but, as John makes clearer, was first led to Annas, then to Caiaphas, who at that time held primacy among the high priests; third, he was led to Pilate; finally, to Herod. And, as the Evangelist Luke says, Herod despised him with all his soldiers and, after clothing him in a white garment, sent him back to Pilate. He was sent to them all, so that they might all mock him and no one might be exempt from Christ’s Passion.

“And they led him away bound and handed him over to Pontius Pilate the governor.” It was customary that anyone whom they handed over to death should be brought bound before the governor.

“Then Judas, who betrayed him, seeing that he had been condemned, moved by remorse, returned the thirty pieces of silver to the chief priests and elders, saying: ‘I sinned by betraying innocent blood.’” Judas saw that the Lord had been sentenced to death and that he himself was soon to be condemned to eternal death as well, because he had betrayed the Lord and Teacher. Moved by remorse, he returned the thirty pieces of silver that he had received from the chief priests—as though it lay within his power to alter the sentence of the persecutors. But although he changed his will, it did him no good then, because he did not alter the outcome he had previously set in motion. But if Judas sinned, as he himself said, “I sinned by betraying innocent blood,” what did those deserve who provoked the disciple to betray his Teacher’s blood? “‘What is that to us?’—that is, ‘What does it concern us?’ ‘You see to it.’” “You,” they say, “proved that when you accepted it; you see what you are going to do.”

“And throwing the pieces of silver into the temple, he departed and went away and hanged himself.” The weight of impiety excludes the enormity of avarice. It did Judas no good that he repented of the Lord’s betrayal, since he was unable to undo the guilt he had incurred. Thus, whoever sins against his brother in such a way that he can amend what he did against him may be forgiven; but whoever sins in such a way that he cannot amend what he has done will not be forgiven. For repentance is invoked in vain by the voice as long as the guilt remains. Of Judas and those like him the Psalmist says: “And his prayer shall be counted as sin” (Psalm CVIII). Judas’s prayer, therefore, was counted as sin, because he not only could not undo his former sin but also joined murder to the Lord’s betrayal.

“It is not lawful to put them into the *corban*, because it is the price of blood.” *Corban* in Hebrew is interpreted in Latin as “gift.” By this name the treasury is called, that is, the place where the treasure offered by the people was kept. Here was fulfilled what the Lord reproached the scribes and Pharisees with before his Passion, saying: “Straining out a gnat and swallowing a camel” (Matthew XXIII). For if it was not lawful to put the price of blood into the *corban*, much less was it lawful to shed innocent blood itself.

“And after taking counsel, they bought with it the potter’s field as a burial place for strangers.” They did this with one intention, yet even by doing it they provided for our salvation. For, according to the Lord’s interpretation, the field signifies this world; the potter is the Lord himself, who fashioned the sea and the world and all that is in them. Thus, with the price of Christ’s blood the field was bought, because we, who were strangers to God’s covenant, began through Christ’s blood to have rest for soul and body.

“Then what was spoken through the prophet Jeremiah was fulfilled, saying: ‘And they took the thirty pieces of silver,’” and so forth. This example is not found written in Jeremiah, although we find something similar in Zechariah. Accordingly, the Evangelist Matthew did not take care either to name Zechariah first or afterward to correct it, because everything that the Holy Spirit spoke through the mouths of the prophets is both common to all and proper to each individually. Whatever Jeremiah said must be attributed to Zechariah, and what Jeremiah said and the other prophets also uttered belonged, of course, to Zechariah. For, as I said, everything that the Holy Spirit spoke through the mouths of the prophets was both common to all and proper to each individually.

“And the governor questioned him, saying: ‘Are you the king of the Jews?’ Jesus said to him: ‘You say so.’” The meaning is: “Because I am.” It should be noted that what had been brought against him by the scribes and Pharisees Pilate also asks him: whether he claimed to be the king of the Jews, just as the scribes and Pharisees had accused him. But the Lord so tempered his answer that he spoke the truth and yet his words did not expose him to their accusation.

“And when he was accused by the chief priests and elders, he answered nothing.” We should observe that the Lord gave only a brief answer when Pilate questioned him, because Pilate was sentencing him to death not by his own judgment but on the basis of the people’s accusation. To the chief priests, however, he answered nothing, judging them unworthy of a response. Or certainly he did not answer for this reason: if he had cleared himself by giving an appropriate answer, the benefit of the Passion would have been postponed, and the human race could not have been saved without his Passion.

“Now on the solemn day the governor was accustomed to release for them one prisoner whom they wished.” The Jews had this custom in memory of their liberation from Egypt: on the feast day they rescued one prisoner from death, in memory of their deliverance when they were freed from Egypt.

“At that time they had a notorious prisoner called Barabbas.” Barabbas was being held in prison because of sedition and murder, as Luke testifies.

“While he was seated on the tribunal.” A tribunal is the seat of a judge, just as a throne is the seat of a king and a chair is the seat of a teacher.

“His wife sent to him, saying: ‘Have nothing to do with that just man.’” The devil then first understood that through the Lord’s Passion he would be deprived of the power he held in the world and stripped of the spoils he possessed in the underworld and over them. Therefore he tried to ensure that, at least through Pilate’s wife, he might turn the Lord away from death.

“For I have suffered many things today in a dream because of him.” It should be noted that dreams are often revealed by God to Gentiles, not on account of their merits but either for the sake of things to come or as a warning for others. Thus we read that Nebuchadnezzar saw in a dream the distribution of all the kingdoms of the earth (Daniel II); and likewise we read that Pharaoh saw a dream which, after Joseph had wisely interpreted it, resulted in his being appointed ruler in the land of Egypt (Genesis XLI).

“But the chief priests and elders of the people persuaded the crowds to ask for Barabbas and to destroy Jesus.” It is no wonder that the Jews lack quiet and peace, since they chose the leader of sedition and handed over the author of peace—that is, the Lord—to death.

“But they said: ‘Barabbas.’” Barabbas, whose name is interpreted as “son of the teacher” or “son of their father,” bears the type of Antichrist, whom the Jews will receive in place of the Lord at the end of the age, just as the Lord says to them: “I have come in my Father’s name, and you did not receive me. Another will come in his own name; him you will receive” (John V). He is rightly called the son of their father, that is, the son of the devil, who is their father, as the Lord reproaches them, saying: “You are from your father the devil” (John VIII), because whoever performs someone’s works is his son.

If *Barabbas* is read with two *r*s, it is interpreted as “son of the teacher,” because *rabbi* means “teacher.” But if it is read with one *r* and two *b*s, its interpretation will be “son of their father,” because *abba* in Hebrew is called “father” in Latin.

“Now Pilate, seeing that he was accomplishing nothing but that rather a riot was arising, took water and washed his hands before the people, saying: ‘I am innocent of the blood of this just man; you see to it.’” Perhaps Pilate had read in the Psalm: “I will wash my hands among the innocent” (Psalm XXV). Therefore he washed his hands so that he might appear free from the crime of the Lord’s Passion, as though he were saying: “I wanted to release him and show him to be innocent, but because the charge of rebellion against Caesar is being brought against me, you see to it. I am the minister of the laws; your own voice has shed the blood.”

“And the whole people answered, saying: ‘His blood be upon us and upon our children.’” This curse persists among the Jews to this day and will persist until the day of judgment. For it was not enough for them to condemn themselves, who were present at that time; they also bound every generation not yet born under the guilt of this curse. The Lord’s blood—that is, the Lord’s vengeance—remains upon the Jews and upon their entire offspring until the end of the age.

“But after scourging Jesus, he handed him over to them to be crucified.” It seems inconsistent that the one who earlier had wanted to release the Lord should now have scourged him and, after scourging him, handed him over to their power. This may be resolved in two ways: he scourged him in order to satisfy the laws of the Romans, whose custom was that anyone sentenced to death should first be scourged and then killed. Or he scourged him so that, satisfied with his punishments, they might stop demanding his death by crucifixion.

[Col. 0374D] “They gathered the whole cohort.” Among the Romans, a cohort consisted of thirty soldiers.

“And stripping him of his own garments, they put a scarlet cloak around him.” To disgrace the Lord, they put a scarlet cloak around him in place of royal purple; in place of a golden crown, they placed a crown of thorns on his head; and in place of the imperial scepter, they gave him a reed in his right hand. In all these things the sacrament of our salvation is celebrated. The Lord’s being clothed in a scarlet garment—that is, a red garment—signifies the taking on of our sins, since, although he was without sin, he took our sins upon himself. His receiving a crown of thorns on his head signified that he himself would take away from us our sins, which are understood by the thorns, and by his Passion would undo the curse spoken to the first man: “Your earth shall produce thorns and thistles for you” (Genesis III). His carrying the reed in his right hand signified that he would write down the sacrilege of the Jews. Or it also signified that the prophecies of the prophets were being fulfilled in his Passion. For we commonly write with a reed; and with the reed he killed poisonous creatures.

“Hail, King of the Jews,” as though they were saying: “You who claimed to be the king of the Jews.”

“And spitting on him, they took the reed and struck his head.” This happened to the Lord bodily once; heretics do it spiritually every day, striking his head and spitting in his face. “For the head of Christ is God,” as the apostle Paul testifies (1 Corinthians XI). Whoever denies that his divinity was in Christ strikes Christ’s head, as Arius does, saying that the Son is less than the Father. Whoever denies that he came in the flesh spits in his face, as Manichaeus does, saying that Christ did not have true flesh.

“And after they had mocked him, they stripped him of the cloak and put his own garments on him.” As long as the Lord endured mockery and spittle and had the crown of thorns on his head, he was not clothed in his own garments but in another’s. But as soon as the hour of contempt had passed, he resumed his own garments. For what he suffered and what he endured in being scourged did not belong to his divinity. But when he rose on the third day, he resumed, as it were, his own garment, signifying that he was to taste death for a time and, after the Passion had been completed, rise again from the tomb.

The prophecy spoken of him was fulfilled: “In order to do his work, his work is foreign; in order to perform his task, his task is strange to him” (Isaiah XXVIII). For in order to perform his own work, that is, the salvation of the human race, his work was foreign to him, because the Passion he endured was foreign to his divinity.

“And as they went out, they found a man of Cyrene, named Simon; they compelled him to carry his cross.” Matthew is not opposed to the Evangelist John, who wrote that the Lord carried his own cross. It should be understood that, when he first went out from the praetorium, he carried his cross himself; then, when Simon came upon them, they compelled him to carry the Lord’s cross as far as the place where it was to be fastened. This is not without a great mystery. Simon, whose name is interpreted as “obedient,” signifies the Gentile people. Hence he is rightly said to have been from Cyrene, which is interpreted as “heir.” For the Gentile people are promised by God the Father to the Son: “I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and your possession to the ends of the earth” (Psalm II).

“To a place called Golgotha, which is the place of the Skull.” Some think that the place was called the place of the Skull because of the burial of the first parent, since his head—that is, his skull—was buried in that same place. This is plainly false, because, as the Book of Joshua reports, he was buried not near Jerusalem but between Hebron and Kiriath-arba. The more accurate meaning, therefore, is that we call that place “the Skull” according to an ancient custom. A place was assigned outside every city where the heads of condemned persons were severed. Their heads were therefore severed there, at the skull-place, and the place was rightly called “the place of the Skull,” that is, after the heads of the condemned. The Lord was deservedly crucified there, so that where the altars of the condemned had previously been raised, there the standards of martyrdom might be raised. Or, “where sin abounded, grace abounded all the more” (Romans V).

“And they gave him wine mixed with gall to drink.” Here was fulfilled what is said through the Prophet: “They gave me gall for food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink” (Psalm LXVIII). They gave him what they themselves were. For they themselves were vinegar, having degenerated from the wine of the patriarchs and prophets, and they could give him nothing other than what they were.

But when it says: “And when he had tasted it, he would not drink,” he did not accept it. He tasted the wine mixed with gall but did not drink it, clearly signifying that he accepted Passion and death for a time but did not wish to be held by that same death forever.

“After they had crucified him, they divided his garments, casting lots.” They divided the Lord’s garments, but over the tunic, which was seamless and could not be divided, they cast lots. The Lord’s garments signify his elect. His four-part garment signifies the Church divided throughout the four quarters of the world. His seamless tunic, woven from above, signifies the unity of that Church, because the unity of the whole kingdom consists in the body of the holy Church. This unity is governed not by human judgment but by divine dispensation, through the love of Almighty God, concerning which the apostle Paul says: “I show you a still more excellent way” (1 Corinthians XII). Therefore that tunic is rightly said to have been woven from above.

“And they placed above his head the charge against him, written.” They wrote above his head the charge of death: “This is the king of the Jews.” They wrote this in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin letters, as the Evangelist John says (John XIX), because at that time these three languages held primacy among the other languages. Hebrew, because of the Jews who gloried in the Law; Greek, because of the philosophers among the Gentiles; and Latin, because of the Romans, who at that time ruled all nations. Whether the Jews wish it or not, every language and every nation confesses that Jesus is the king of the Jews—that is, of all who believe in him and confess him.

“Then two thieves were crucified with him, one on his right and one on his left.” Literally, what was spoken through the prophet was fulfilled: “And he was reckoned among the wicked” (Isaiah LIII). Allegorically, however, the two thieves who were crucified with the Lord signify two classes of people who, under confession of Christ’s name, undertake either the contest of martyrdom or the disciplines of a stricter life. Those who take such things upon themselves solely with an eye to reward are made equal in praise and merit to the thief on the right. Those who undertake either the contest of martyrdom or the disciplines of a stricter life for some other reason are represented by the faithlessness of the thief on the left: under confession of Christ’s name, they undertake the disciplines of that stricter life, but not out of love for it.

“But those passing by blasphemed him.” They are called “passing by” because they passed beyond life—that is, Christ—shaking their heads against the Lord, although previously they had moved their feet away from the straight path of righteousness.

“He saved others; he cannot save himself.” Whether they wish it or not, the Jews confess that the Lord Jesus saved others. But because he saved others, it follows that he could also save himself if he wished. Yet if the Lord had then descended from the cross in response to their taunts, yielding even to their insults, he would not have shown us the power of patience. Instead, the Lord endured insults and bore mockery. For he did something greater: he did not wish to descend alive from the cross, but rose dead from the tomb—and they did not believe him. It was greater to rise from death than to descend alive from the cross.

“And the thieves who were crucified with him also reproached him in the same way.” This should be understood by synecdoche. It was not both thieves who insulted the Lord; rather, as Luke makes clear in his more detailed account, while one persisted in blasphemy, the other rebuked him from the cross, saying: “Do you not even fear God, since you are under the same condemnation? We are receiving what our deeds deserve, but this man has done nothing wrong.” And turning to Jesus, he said: “Remember me, Lord, when you come into your kingdom” (Luke XXIII).

We may also say that at first both thieves had blasphemed the Lord, but when one saw the greatness of the signs—the darkening of the sun, the shaking of the earth, and the opening of the tombs—he immediately repented, while the other persisted in blasphemy.

“Now from the sixth hour darkness came over the whole land until the ninth hour.” According to the three Evangelists, the Lord was crucified at the sixth hour. As for what Mark confirms—that he was crucified at the third hour—we must refer it to the voices of the Jews, by whose cries he was crucified at the third hour. The Lord is rightly read as having been crucified at the sixth hour, since at that same hour we read that the first man sinned in paradise; and it was fitting that he should be redeemed at that same hour through the Passion of the Son of God.

Some, understanding the matter contrary to the truth of the holy Gospel, say that a natural eclipse of the sun occurred, which the apostles, not understanding, interpreted as relating to the Lord’s Passion. They must be answered that an eclipse of the sun can occur only at the new moon. It is established, however, that at the Paschal festival, when the Lord was crucified, there was a full moon. And lest this darkness of the sun be said to have been sudden and momentary, it lasted not merely one hour but three: from the sixth hour to the ninth hour. It should be believed that, just as the sun suffered darkness over the earth, so the moon beneath the earth withdrew its rays of light. Here the prophecy of Joel was fulfilled: “The sun shall be turned into darkness and the moon into blood” (Joel II). It withdrew its rays either so that it might not see its Lord dying on the cross, or so that the Jews, the ministers of iniquity, might not enjoy its light.

“And about the ninth hour Jesus cried out with a loud voice, saying: ‘Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani?’” Just as thirsting, becoming weary, and sleeping do not belong to divinity but to humanity, so this voice also proceeded from his humanity, not from his divinity. According to his divinity he is never abandoned by the Father; according to his humanity he appeared for a time to be abandoned by the Father, when he was permitted to be fastened to the cross. *El* means “God”; *i*, “my”; *lama*, “why?”; *sabachthani*, “you have abandoned me.”

“This man is calling Elijah.” We understand that these words were spoken not by the Jews but by the Roman soldiers, because they did not understand the Hebrew expression. But if someone were contentious and said that they were spoken not by Romans but rather by Jews, he would not depart from the faith, since, according to their customary practice, whatever the Lord said they twisted into disgrace.

“And immediately one of them ran, took a sponge, filled it with vinegar, put it on a reed, and gave him to drink.” They offered him what they themselves were, because they had already degenerated from wine—that is, from the good works of the patriarchs and prophets. The porous sponge signifies the heart of the Jews, full of malicious deceits. Hyssop, a lowly herb that cleanses the chest, signifies Christ’s humility. They surrounded the sponge with hyssop because they surrounded Christ’s humility, and they thought they had outwitted the one whom they had surrounded with various deceits. The reed on which the sponge was placed signifies Scripture, which was being fulfilled by this deed.

“Jesus, crying out again with a loud voice, gave up his spirit.” This was a sign of divine power: he gave up his spirit. No one can give up his spirit except the Creator of all spirits. He used “spirit” for “soul,” because the soul is indeed a spiritual nature, as we read in the Psalm: “You take away their spirit, and they fail” (Psalm CIII).

“And behold, the veil of the temple was torn in two, from top to bottom.” There were two veils in the temple: one inside, before the ark, and another outside, before the altar. Blessed Jerome therefore appears to think that the outer veil was torn, so that the heavenly mysteries, which had been kept hidden in the Old Testament, might be opened to us. And not only was the veil of the temple torn; the powers of the angelic authorities were also heard there saying: “Let us depart from these places, or seats.”

“And the earth was shaken, and the rocks were split.” Literally, the shaking of the earth and the splitting of the rocks signify the terror of created things, which could not endure the death of their Lord. But if we seek a higher understanding there, the shaking of the earth and the splitting of the rocks signify that the hearts of earthly people must be shaken toward repentance.

“And many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep arose.” Just as Lazarus was raised, so these too were raised, so that they might bear witness to the Lord when he rose. Although the tombs were opened while the Lord hung on the cross, none of those saints rose until the Lord had risen, so that he himself might be the firstborn from the dead.

“They came into the holy city.” He calls Jerusalem the holy city, not because it was holy at that time, but because it had once been holy on account of the worship of the one God, its former name remaining.

“And they appeared to many.” Not to everyone, but only to those who were worthy of seeing them.

“But the centurion and those who were with him, guarding Jesus, when they saw the earthquake and the things that were happening, were greatly afraid, saying: ‘Truly this was the Son of God.’” In the faith of the centurion, who was a Gentile, the faith of all the nations is signified. When the centurion believed, the Jews not only did not believe but were also afraid, because, while the nations were receiving Christ, the Jews remained in their unbelief.

“There were also many women there, looking on from a distance, who had followed Jesus from Galilee, ministering to him.” It was customary among the Jews, and was not counted as blameworthy, for devout women to minister to their teachers from their own resources. The apostle Paul avoided this so as not to cause scandal among the Gentiles, saying: “Do we not have the authority to lead about sisters?” (1 Corinthians IX). These women, therefore, who had ministered to the living Lord, followed him even as he proceeded to his Passion, so that they might serve him in death whom they had served in life.

“Among them was Mary Magdalene.” This is Mary Magdalene, from whom the Lord had cast out seven demons. She was called Magdalene after the town of Magdala.

“And Mary of James,” namely, the mother of James and Joseph, who are called the Lord’s brothers in the Gospel. This Mary was the Lord’s maternal aunt.

[Col. 0379D] “When evening had come, a rich man from Arimathea, named Joseph, arrived, who himself was also a disciple of Jesus. He went to Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus.” Arimathea is Ramathaim, the city of Elkanah and Hannah. Joseph is called rich not to boast, as though the Lord appeared to have a rich disciple, but to show that he could not otherwise obtain the Lord’s body from the governor unless he were rich. At that time no one was permitted to enter the governor’s presence unless he was powerful and wealthy. He is said to be rich and no less just. For if he had not been rich, he could not have obtained the Lord’s body; but if he had not been just, he would in no way have been worthy of the Lord’s burial. Justice is joined with power so that he may obtain Christ’s body.

“And having received the body of Christ, Joseph wrapped it in a clean linen cloth.” The Lord’s simple burial condemns the ambition of the rich, who cannot be without riches even in their tombs. From this we may also understand simply that, just as the Lord’s body was wrapped in a clean cloth and placed in the tomb, so the mystery of the holy altar may not be celebrated in cloth woven with gold, but in a clean linen cloth. By its symbolism, the one who wrapped Jesus in a clean linen cloth is the one who receives his sacrament with a pure mind.

“And he placed it in his own new tomb, which he had cut in the rock.” The Lord is rightly placed in a new tomb, not an old one, lest, while others remained there, they should pretend that others had risen when the Lord rose. Those who saw the tomb report that it was a round chamber cut from the underlying rock, and so high that a person inside could touch its top with an outstretched hand. It had an entrance on the eastern side, to which that great stone was fitted. On its northern side the Lord’s body lay, having a length of seven or eight feet and projecting three palms above the rest of the pavement. The stone was of a red-and-white color, a kind that most fittingly suits the person of the Savior, to whom the Church says in the Song of Love: “My beloved is white and red” (Song V). White, because he committed no sin; red, because he was stained with the blood of his own Passion.

“And he rolled a great stone against the door of the tomb and departed.” This was accomplished by divine providence: they rolled a great stone against the tomb’s entrance so that, if a small one had been rolled there, the scribes and Pharisees might have fabricated the accusation that Jesus’ body had been stolen by women or disciples.

“Mary Magdalene was there,” and so forth. The holy women who had loved the Lord more closely followed him even in death, as far as the burial.

“On the next day, which is after the day of Preparation, the chief priests and Pharisees gathered before Pilate.” The next day—that is, the Sabbath. The Lord was crucified on Friday, rested in the tomb on the Sabbath, and rose on the eighth day, which is the first. This is a beautiful order: since man was made on the sixth day and God rested from all his works on the seventh, so the Lord on Friday redeemed the human race through his Passion, rested in the tomb on the Sabbath, and rose on the eighth day. This too is clearly accomplished for our salvation. For throughout the six ages of the world we suffer with the Lord; in the seventh, which is the present age, after the Lord’s coming, we rest with him in soul, awaiting the eighth day and the general resurrection, so that, having received our bodies, we may be immortal in body and incorruptible in mind.

“Lord, we remember that while that deceiver was still alive he said: ‘After three days I will rise.’” By the terms “deceiver” and “thief,” the Jews, though unwillingly, speak the truth. The Lord is a deceiver not from truth to falsehood or from good to evil, but, on the contrary, from iniquity to righteousness. The apostles were thieves, because they strove to take from the Jews and transfer to the nations of the Gentiles the faith of Christ that the Jews had rejected.

“So they went and secured the tomb, sealing the stone with the guard.” It was not enough for the scribes and Pharisees to kill the Lord on the cross; they also placed guards at his tomb. As far as lay within their power, they opposed the one who was rising. But the greater their diligence in placing guards over the tomb, the more certain they made us concerning faith in his resurrection.

**HOMILY LXV. MONDAY OF PALM SUNDAY**
[Col. 0381B] (JOHN XII.) “At that time, six days before Passover, Jesus came to Bethany, where Lazarus was dead, whom he had raised,” and so forth. Knowing that the Jews had conspired to kill him, the Lord did not flee the hands of those plotting against him. Rather, confident in the glory of his resurrection, he first came to Bethany, near the city of Jerusalem, where he had raised Lazarus from the dead; then also to Jerusalem, where he would suffer and rise from the dead. He came to Jerusalem so that he himself might die there, but to Bethany so that the raising of Lazarus might be impressed more firmly upon everyone’s memory, and so that the wicked rulers, who did not fear killing the one who could raise the dead, might be confounded more and more and proved without excuse. Neither provoked by the benefit of the raising nor terrified by the divine power of the one who raised him, they might withdraw their minds from their unjust slaughter.

Nor should we read casually the reason why Jesus came to Bethany six days before Passover. The number six has great significance in the sacred Scriptures, and many works of the Lord our God are shown to have been completed according to the number six. For the number six, divided into its own constituent parts or joined together, is evidently perfect in itself. It has three parts contained within its denomination: one, two, and three. Its sixth part is one; its third is two; its half, therefore, is three. One, two, and three are recognized as making six. Nothing else can be produced from these three parts when joined together except six alone, nor can the number six be divided into any other parts except these three: one, two, and three.

[Col. 0381D] For it is well known that the Lord himself, creator of all things, completed the creatures of this world in six days; and it is established that on the sixth day he made the human being, whom, after he had been destroyed by the serpent’s deceit, the Son of God himself—through whom he had been created—came to Bethany six days before Passover to free. Thus the one who was created on the sixth day might be freed on the sixth day of the week. For I think that no one is unaware that Christ suffered on the sixth day of the week.

Therefore, in the sixth month, when the archangel announced it, the holy Virgin is also read to have conceived our same Redeemer through the inspiration of the Holy Spirit. He likewise, at the sixth hour, having reached perfect maturity and sitting beside a well, deigned to open to the Samaritan woman the streams of the divine fountain. In the sixth age of the world, too, the Creator himself, the Redeemer of the world, is already read—according to the testimony of sacred history—to have come.

The three parts—one, two, and three—from which, as we have said, six consists, also contain a certain mystery in the dispensation of human salvation. In the first period, under the law of nature, the holy fathers served God as though in a certain unity. In the second period, the law was added to nature, so that what evil custom had corrupted in nature, the law might restore in writing. There were then two: nature and law. In the third period, heavenly grace came through Jesus Christ, and there are three: nature, law, and grace. The law of nature does not destroy what is good, nor does grace dissolve the law; rather, it fulfills it and restores nature to its former nobility. Yet nature and the law could not be fulfilled without grace. Nor was free choice, or the commandment of the law, given to human beings in such a way that they would not need grace, as the Pelagian heresy asserts.

And lest the contrivers of accusations should say that Lazarus had been raised in some apparition, a supper was held there for the Lord, and Lazarus himself was one of those reclining with him. Thus, when they saw or heard him alive, speaking, eating, and familiarly conversing with his companions, they might at least in this way recognize the power of the one who had raised him and receive grace.

Mystically, however, this supper of the Lord, where Martha served and Lazarus reclined among the others, is the faith of the Church, which works through love. At this supper Martha serves: every faithful soul offers the Lord the work of its love.

“Lazarus, however, was one of those reclining with him.” Those who, after the death of sins, have been raised to righteousness rejoice in the presence of the truth together with those who have remained in their own righteousness; penitents are nourished together with the innocent by the gifts of heavenly grace.

And rightly is that same supper celebrated in Bethany, which is a city on the side of the Mount of Olives and is interpreted as “house of obedience.” For the house of obedience is the Church, which faithfully obeys the Lord’s commands. It is also the city established upon the mountain of mercy, which can never be hidden. It is the one constructed from the side of its Redeemer and imbued with what came forth from his side as he died for it—namely, the water of cleansing and the blood of sanctification. There, too, Mary, Lazarus’s other sister, displayed a sign of great love, as the Gospel reading shows in what follows.

[Col. 0382D] “She took a pound of costly ointment of genuine nard, anointed Jesus’ feet, and wiped his feet with her hair.” By this she gives not only an indication of her own devotion but also signifies the pious service of other faithful souls toward God.

“Mary took a pound of costly ointment of genuine nard.” What else is expressed by the pound of ointment except the perfection of righteousness? The ointment is said to have been made from genuine nard. What else is suggested by ointment except the good odor of reputation? This ointment is made from genuine nard, that is, faithful nard. For *pistis* (πίστις) is called *fides*—“faith”—in Latin. Without faith it is impossible to please God (Heb. 11), and without catholic faith a good reputation cannot come into being.

O human being, anoint Jesus’ feet by living well; follow the Lord’s footsteps; wipe them with your hair. If you possess anything superfluous, distribute it to the poor. This is to wipe Jesus’ feet with your hair: what is superfluous for you is necessary for the Lord’s feet, that is, for the least members in the Church, concerning whom the Lord will say at the end: “As long as you did it to one of the least of these, you did it to me.”

The fragrance of piety—that is, the Church—is the good reputation of a religious life. For a good life is a good odor. Hear the Apostle: “We are the good odor of Christ,” he says, “in every place” (2 Cor. 2). And in the Song of Songs: “Your name is poured-out ointment” (Song 1). Again: “While the king was at his table, my nard gave forth its odor” (ibid.). Here it is clearly shown what Mary did once, and typologically what the whole Church and every perfect soul always do.

[Col. 0383B] “Then one of his disciples, Judas Iscariot, who was about to betray him, said: ‘Why was this ointment not sold for three hundred denarii and given to the poor?’”

Woe to the wicked betrayer; woe to his accomplices in wickedness, who even now persecute Christ’s members and do not cease to envy in their neighbors the reputation for virtue which they themselves do not deserve to possess. Indeed, we might suppose that Judas spoke this out of concern for the poor; but the true witness, who knew his mind, exposes him when he says: “He said this not because he cared about the poor, but because he was a thief, and, having the money box, he used to carry what was put into it.”

Judas did not perish only when, corrupted by money, he betrayed the Lord; rather, he was already lost when he followed the Lord. He had the Lord’s money box and carried what was put into it for the service of the poor, though with an unfaithful mind he was accustomed to steal it.

Seeing that his heart was already darkened by the filth of greed, and foreseeing that it would be polluted by the worse filth of betrayal, the Lord entrusted to his faith whatever they had in their purses and allowed him to do with it whatever he wished, as though the honor conferred on him, or the memory of the money entrusted to him, might turn his mind away from selling the Lord. But because the greedy person is always in want, and the wicked never remembers benefits in good faith, he proceeded from stealing the money he carried to betraying the Lord, who had entrusted money to him for safekeeping.

“Then Jesus said: ‘Leave her alone, so that she may keep it for the day of my burial.’”

As though Judas had asked innocently, the Lord explained simply and gently what Mary’s service signified: namely, that he was going to die and would be anointed with spices for burial. Therefore Mary, although she greatly desired to anoint his dead body and would not be permitted to do so, was granted the opportunity to offer him while he was still alive the service which, after his death, she would be unable to perform, since the resurrection would swiftly forestall her.

Thus Mark rightly testifies that the Lord said of her: “She has done what she could; she has anticipated anointing my body for burial” (Mark 14). This plainly means: “Because she could not touch my body after I was dead, she did the one thing she could: she anticipated giving the living one the service of burial.”

[Col. 0383D] “For you always have the poor with you, but you will not always have me.”

Here, with great restraint and patience, the Lord does not accuse Judas of greed or say that he spoke about money for the sake of the poor. Rather, he demonstrates by reason that those who ministered to him from their resources while he lived among human beings were not to be blamed, since he himself would remain bodily with the Church for only a short time, whereas the poor to whom alms could be given would always be present in it.

“Then the great crowd of the Jews learned that he was there, and they came not only because of Jesus, but also to see Lazarus, whom he had raised from the dead.”

Curiosity, not charity, brought these people to Jesus. But let us, dearest brothers, reverse the matter: if we know where Jesus is, where he makes his dwelling, where he finds Bethany—that is, the house of the obedient soul—in which to dwell, let us come there through contemplation, not merely because of the human being whom he raised from the death of the soul and granted spiritual life, but so that, by imitating that person’s good life, we may thereby deserve to reach the vision of Jesus.

For we know with certainty where Jesus is: he rose after death and ascended into heaven; there he has an everlasting dwelling. That is the true city, heavenly Bethany, which no one can enter unless he is obedient.

“The chief priests planned to kill Lazarus also, because many of the Jews were going away on his account and believing in Jesus.”

O blind craftiness of the blind! They wished to kill the one who had been raised, as though the one who had been able to raise the dead could not raise the slain. Indeed, he taught that he could do both: he raised Lazarus, who had died, and himself, who had been killed.

After the Lord had raised the four-day dead man, while some Jews were astonished and others came to believe when they saw, and still others perished through what they saw; and after Jesus had reclined in the house, with Lazarus also reclining, the one who had been raised from the dead; after the ointment had been poured over his feet, so that the house was filled with its odor—we have treated these matters above as far as we could. Now we must consider what is established to have occurred before the Lord’s passion. For the evangelist says:

[Col. 0384C] “On the next day, the great crowd that had come for the feast, when they heard that Jesus was coming to Jerusalem, took branches of palm trees, went out to meet him, and cried out: ‘Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, the King of Israel.’”

The branches of palm trees signify praises and the victory by which the Lord was to overcome death by dying, and triumph over the devil, the prince of death, by the trophy of the cross.

“‘Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.’” It should certainly be noted that *osia*, a Hebrew word, is composed of two corrupted elements and one intact element. Among the Jews, it means “save” or “save alive.” *Na*, however, is the interjection of one making a plea, just as among the Latins *heu* is the interjection of one grieving, and *papae* the interjection of one expressing amazement.

Finally, in the Psalm where the Seventy translators rendered, “O Lord, save me” (Ps. 68), the Hebrew is written: *Anna adonai osiana*. Our translator Jerome, elucidating it more carefully, rendered it as follows: “I beseech you, Lord, save; I beseech you.” The *o* as an interjection of one pleading signifies the same thing as *obsecro*, “I beseech,” Lord, through the very word of supplication.

Thus *osanna* means “save, I beseech you,” with a letter or vowel consumed—the one that ends the first word—when *osi* is pronounced in full, through the force of the vowel-letter *aleph*, from which the following word *anna* begins. This is what metricians call synaloepha when scanning words, although in scanning they pass over the written letter. In the word *osanna*, however, the letter *yod* is not even written; rather, while the meaning intended by the speakers remains intact, it is entirely omitted.

“Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, the King of Israel” should be understood as referring to the name of the Father, although it may also be understood as “in his own name.” For he himself is Lord, as it is written elsewhere: “The Lord rained from the Lord.” His own words direct our understanding more clearly: “I have come in my Father’s name, and you did not receive me; another will come in his own name, and him you will receive” (John 5).

Christ is the teacher of humility, who “humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even the death of the cross” (Phil. 2). He does not therefore lose his divinity when he teaches us humility. In the former he is equal to the Father; in the latter he is like us. By being equal to the Father, he created us to exist; by being like us, he redeemed us so that we would not perish.

The crowd was saying these praises: “Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, the King of Israel.” The rulers of the Jews could not endure this voice because of their mental envy, when such a great multitude proclaimed Christ their king. But what was it to the Lord to be king of Israel? What great thing was it for the King of the ages to become king of human beings?

Christ was not King of Israel in order to exact tribute, arm an army with the sword, and defeat enemies. He was King of Israel in order to rule the mind, provide for it forever, and lead believers, those who hope and love, into the kingdom of heaven. Therefore, for the Son of God, equal to the Father, the Word through whom all things were made, to will to be King of Israel is condescension, not promotion; a sign of mercy, not an increase of power. For the one who was called King of the Jews is Lord of the angels in heaven.

[Col. 0385D]

“And Jesus found a young donkey and sat upon it.”

This is stated briefly here. How it happened is read in full in the other evangelists. Prophetic testimony is added to this event, so that it might become clear that the wicked rulers of the Jews did not understand the one in whom what they read was being fulfilled. Jesus therefore found a young donkey and sat upon it.

“As it is written: ‘Do not fear, daughter of Zion; behold, your king is coming to you, seated upon a donkey’s colt.’”

This daughter of Zion, to whom these things are divinely spoken, was among those sheep that heard the shepherd’s voice. She was among that multitude which praised the Lord who was coming with such devotion and escorted him in such a great procession.

It was said, “Do not fear”: recognize the one whom you praise, and do not tremble when he speaks, because that blood will be poured out through which your offense will be erased and your life redeemed.

He sits upon the colt of a donkey, upon which no one had sat—this is found in the other evangelists. It is understood as the people of the Gentiles, who had not received the law of the Lord. He sits upon the donkey because both animals were brought to the Lord, signifying the people who came from the people of Israel: not an untamed people, but one that recognized the Lord’s manger.

“These things his disciples did not understand at first, but when Jesus was glorified.”

That is, when he displayed them through the power of his resurrection, they then remembered that these things had been written about him. Recalling, according to Scripture, what had been fulfilled before the Lord’s passion or during it, they found there also this event: that, in accordance with the words of the prophets, he would sit upon the colt of a donkey.

[Col. 0386B] “The crowd that was with him when he called Lazarus out of the tomb and raised him from the dead therefore bore witness.”

For this reason the crowd also came to meet him, because they had heard that he had performed this sign.

The Pharisees therefore said to one another: “You see that we are accomplishing nothing? Behold, the whole world has gone after him” (John 12).

The crowd troubled the crowd. Why do you envy this, blind crowd—that the world is going after the one through whom the world was made?

“There were also some Gentiles among those who had gone up to worship at the feast. These therefore came to Philip, who was from Bethsaida of Galilee, and asked him, saying: ‘Sir, we wish to see Jesus.’ Philip came and told Andrew; Andrew and Philip in turn told Jesus.”

Let us see what the Lord answered them. Behold, the Jews wished to kill him, while the Gentiles wished to see him. Yet those who cried, “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, the King of Israel,” were also among the Jews. Behold: some from circumcision, others from uncircumcision, like walls coming from opposite directions and converging in the one faith of Christ through the kiss of peace. Let us therefore hear the voice of the cornerstone.

“Jesus,” he says, “answered them, saying: ‘The hour has come for the Son of man to be glorified.’”

Someone might perhaps think that he said he was glorified because the Gentiles wished to see him. It is not so. Rather, he saw that those same Gentiles would believe in him throughout all the nations after his passion and resurrection. For, as the Apostle says: “A partial blindness has happened in Israel until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter” (Rom. 11).

Taking occasion, therefore, from these Gentiles who desired to see him, he announces the future fullness of the Gentiles. He promises that the hour of his glorification is already immediately at hand: when this had occurred in heaven, the Gentiles would believe in him. Hence it was foretold: “Be exalted above the heavens, O God, and your glory over all the earth” (Ps. 56).

This is the fullness of the Gentiles of which the Apostle says: “A partial blindness has happened in Israel until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter.” But the humility of the passion had to precede the height of glorification. Therefore he immediately added:

[Col. 0387A] “Amen, amen, I say to you: unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit.”

He was saying that he himself was the grain that had to be put to death and multiplied: put to death through the unbelief of the Jews, multiplied through the faith of all peoples.

Now, exhorting his disciples to follow the footsteps of his passion, he says:

“‘Whoever loves,’ he says, ‘his soul will lose it.’”

This can be understood in two ways. “Whoever loves will lose”—that is, if you love, you will lose. If you desire to preserve your life in Christ, do not fear dying for Christ.

Or in another way: “Whoever loves his soul will lose it.” Do not love it in this life, lest you lose it in eternal life. This latter meaning seems more fully to accord with the Gospel sense.

It continues: “And whoever hates his soul in this world preserves it for eternal life.” Therefore, in what was said above—“whoever loves”—we are to understand “in this world”; that person will certainly lose it. But whoever hates it, certainly “in this world,” preserves it for eternal life.

Great and astonishing is the saying: how love of one’s soul can cause a person to perish, while hatred prevents perishing. If you have loved badly, then you have hated; if you have hated well, then you have loved. Blessed are those who hate in order to preserve, lest they lose through loving.

Here, by “soul,” the present life is signified, or even the enjoyment of this life, which must be lost so that you may happily find in the kingdom of God the will that you bravely conquered in this world. For the holy martyrs hated this present life for Christ’s name, preferring to lose this present life rather than deny Christ, fulfilling what follows:

“If anyone serves me, let him follow me.”

What does “let him follow me” mean except “let him imitate me”? “Christ suffered for us,” the Apostle Peter says, “leaving us an example, so that we might follow his footsteps” (1 Pet. 2). Behold the meaning of the saying: “If anyone serves me, let him follow me.”

With what fruit? With what reward? With what recompense?

“And where I am, there also will my servant be.”

The reward of love, and the payment for the work by which one serves, is to be with the one whom one serves. For where can it be well without him? Or how could it be bad with him?

Hear it more clearly: “If anyone serves me, my Father will honor him.” With what honor, except that he should be with his Son? For what he said above—“Where I am, there also will my servant be”—he explains when he says, “My Father will honor him.”

An adopted son can never receive greater honor than to be where the only Son is—not made equal to the divinity, but admitted to eternity.

What it means to serve, and what work is promised so great a reward, must be considered. “If anyone serves me, let him follow me”: he wished this to be understood as though he had said, “If anyone does not follow me, he does not serve me.”

Therefore, the person serves Jesus Christ who seeks not his own interests but those of Jesus Christ. This is what “let him follow me” means: let him walk in my ways, not his own, as it is written elsewhere: “Whoever says that he remains in Christ ought himself to walk as he walked.”

Even if he offers bread to one who is hungry, he ought to do it out of mercy, not boastfulness; he should seek nothing else there except the good work, with the left hand unaware of what the right hand does—that is, so that the intention of greed may be removed from the work of charity.

To such a person it is said: “When you did it to one of my least, you did it to me.” And not only those things that pertain to temporal mercy, but all works performed for Christ will then be good, because Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes.

The believer is Christ’s servant, even unto that great work of love which is to lay down one’s soul for one’s brothers. For this too is to lay it down for Christ, because he will say this concerning his members: “When you did it for these, you did it for me.”

Concerning such an hour the Lord also deigned to make and call himself a servant, when he said: “The Son of man did not come to be served but to serve, and to lay down his soul for many” (Matt. 20).

From this, then, each person is a servant of Christ from the same source from which Christ is also a servant. When someone serves Christ in this way, his Father honors him with that great honor: that he should be with his Son, and that his faith should never fail.

But he speaks generally of everyone: “If anyone serves me.” For everyone who serves Christ well here will receive his reward with Christ. Therefore each person ought to serve Christ according to his measure: by living well, giving alms, and preaching his name and teaching to those whom he can.

The person who exhorts those living well to persevere in living well serves Christ. The person who humbly obeys one admonishing him serves Christ. And the person who serves Christ happily in this world will reign happily with Christ in the world to come.

When the Lord Jesus had foretold his passion in the grain of mustard seed and had exhorted his servants to follow him, he again adapted his own feeling to our weakness and said:

[Col. 0388C] “Now my soul is troubled.”

Why is your soul troubled, Lord Jesus? Did you not assume a soul and become a complete human being precisely so that you might suffer in it? I see you transferring our weakness to yourself and taking our cause upon yourself.

You are troubled because you wished to be troubled, just as you wished to be born. For shortly before, where he raised Lazarus, it was said that he “troubled himself.”

By these words he drew us from our weakness into his own weakness. For the voice of the Lord’s strength is heard when he says: “The hour has come for the Son of man to be glorified.” The voice of our weakness is heard when he says: “Now my soul is troubled.”

O Lord, mediator, God above us and human being for our sake, I recognize your mercy. For by being troubled through the will of your love, though you are so great, you console many in your body who are troubled by the necessity of their weakness, so that they may not perish through despair.

Hear, then, O soldier of Christ, what he next adds after saying, “Now my soul is troubled”:

“And what shall I say?” he says. “‘Father, save me from this hour.’ But for this reason I have come to this hour. Father, glorify your name.”

He taught you what you should think, what you should say, whom you should invoke, in whom you should hope, and whose certain and divine will you should set before your own human and weak will.

Do not therefore think that he distrusts from above simply because he wishes you to progress from the beginning. He also deigned to be tempted by the devil; certainly, if he had not wished it, he would not have been tempted by him. And he gave the devil the answers that you ought to give in temptations.

He was tempted, but he was not endangered, so that he might teach you, when endangered in temptation, to answer the tempter, and, instead of following the tempter, to emerge from the danger of temptation.

As here he says, “Now my soul is troubled,” so there also he said: “My soul is sorrowful even unto death” (Matt. 26). And again: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (ibid.). He assumed the weakness of a human being in order to teach the one who is thus troubled and sorrowful to say what follows: “Nevertheless, not what I will, but what you will, Father” (ibid.).

For in this way the human being is raised from human things to divine things, when the divine will is placed before the human will.

What else is “Glorify your name” except “in his passion and resurrection”? What else, therefore, does it mean except that the Father should glorify his Son, who also glorifies his name in the comparable sufferings of his servants?

[Col. 0389B] “Then a voice came from heaven, saying: ‘I have glorified it, and I will glorify it again.’”

“I glorified it” before I made the world; “and I will glorify it again” when he rises from the dead and ascends into heaven.

It can also be understood in another way. He glorified it when he was born from a virgin; when, with a star as his herald from heaven, he was worshiped by the Magi; when he was recognized by holy people filled with the Holy Spirit; when he was manifested as the Spirit descended in the form of a dove; when he was pointed out by a voice from heaven; when he was transfigured on the mountain; when he performed many miracles; when he healed and cleansed many; when he fed such a great multitude with a few loaves; when he commanded the winds and waves; and when he raised the dead.

And he was glorified again when he rose from the dead; when death would no longer rule over him; when God would be exalted above the heavens and his glory would be over all the earth.

“The crowd standing by and hearing said that it had thundered. Others said: ‘An angel has spoken to him.’ Jesus answered and said: ‘This voice has come not for my sake but for yours.’”

Here he shows that the voice did not announce to him something he did not know—since he already knew it—but to those to whom it was necessary that it be announced. And just as that voice came in the realm of divinity not for his sake but for theirs, so his soul was troubled by an act of will not for his sake but for the sake of others.

“Now is the judgment of the world.”

We do not think that this was said about the future judgment that will take place at the end of the world, when the good and the evil will be separated by an eternal division, but about the judgment that ordinarily takes place daily in the holy Church of God.

The devil possessed the human race and held the guilty under the bond of sins. He ruled in the hearts of unbelievers, leading them to worship the creature after abandoning the Creator; he dragged the deceived and captive along. But through faith in Christ, which was strengthened by his death and resurrection, and through his blood, which was poured out for the remission of sins, thousands of believers are freed from the devil’s domination, joined to Christ’s body, and, under so great a head, his faithful members are given life by his one Spirit.

This is what he called judgment: this separation and the expulsion of the devil from those redeemed by him. Finally, notice what he says. As though we were asking what he meant by “Now is the judgment of the world,” he immediately explained it, saying:

“Now the prince of this world will be cast out.”

We have heard what kind of judgment he said it was. It is therefore not that judgment which will come at the end, when the living and the dead will be judged, some separated to the left and others to the right, but the judgment by which the prince of this world will be cast out.

How, then, was he within, if he said that he would be cast out?

“Now,” he says, “the prince of the world will be cast out.” This should be understood of what is happening now, not merely of what would happen afterward on the last day.

The Lord therefore foresaw—and knew—that after his passion and glorification many peoples throughout the whole world would believe. The devil was within their hearts; when they renounced him through faith, he would be cast out.

But someone may say: “Was he not cast out from the hearts of the ancient patriarchs, prophets, and other righteous people?” Certainly. How, then, was it said, “Now he will be cast out”? How should we understand it except that what had then been accomplished in very few human beings was now foretold as about to happen immediately among many great peoples?

The statement “the Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified” can pose a similar question and have a similar solution. The prophets did not announce future things without the Holy Spirit; nor did the elderly Simeon and the widow Anna fail to recognize the infant Lord in the Holy Spirit; nor did Zechariah and Elizabeth fail to prophesy through the Holy Spirit such great things about him who had not yet been born but had already been conceived.

Rather, the Spirit had not yet been given—that is, that abundance of spiritual grace through which the assembled believers would speak in the languages of all, and thus the future Church would be announced in the languages of all nations; through which peoples would be gathered by spiritual grace, sins would be forgiven far and wide, and thousands upon thousands would be reconciled to God.

What, then, someone may ask, does it mean that the devil is cast out from the hearts of believers? Does he no longer tempt any of the faithful?

Indeed, he does not cease tempting them. But it is one thing to reign within, another to attack from without; one thing to wound, another to kill. If he wounds, there is one who can heal.

For just as it was said to those engaged in combat, “I write these things to you so that you may not sin” (1 John 2), so those who are wounded hear what follows: “And if you sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous; he is the propitiation for our sins.”

What do we pray when we say, “Forgive us our debts” (Matt. 6), except that our wounds may be healed? And what else do we ask when we say, “Do not lead us into temptation” (ibid.), except that the one who lies in wait may not break out against us from any external quarter; that he may deceive us by no fraud and overthrow us by no devices, since he does not occupy the place of the heart from which he has been cast out by faith?

But “unless the Lord guards the city, the one who guards it watches in vain” (Ps. 126). Therefore do not presume upon yourselves, if you do not wish to call back inside the devil who has been cast out.

Let us not, however, suppose that the devil is called “the prince of the world” in such a way that we believe he can rule heaven and earth. Rather, the wicked human beings dispersed throughout the whole world are called “the world,” just as a house is named after those who inhabit it.

Accordingly, we say that a house is good or a house is bad—not when we praise or condemn the structure of its walls and roofs, but when we speak of the conduct of good or evil people. So, then, “the prince of this world” means the prince of wicked human beings who inhabit the world.

The good are also called “the world,” since they likewise are dispersed throughout the whole earth. Hence the Apostle says: “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself” (2 Cor. 5). These are the people from whose hearts the prince of the world is cast out.

When he had therefore said, “Now the prince of this world will be cast out,” he immediately added:

[Col. 0391B] “And I, if I am lifted up from the earth, will draw everything after me.”

What does he draw except those from whom the devil is cast out? He did not say “everyone,” but “everything.” For not everyone has faith. He therefore did not refer this to the universality of human beings, but to the wholeness of the creature: namely, spirit and soul and body; that which we understand, that by which we live, and that by which we are visible and corruptible.

When he said, “Not a hair of your head will perish,” he meant that he draws everything after him.

Or, if “everything” is to be understood as human beings themselves, we can say that everything predestined for salvation is included: concerning all of these he said that nothing would perish, when above he was speaking about his sheep.

Or certainly, “everything” may mean every kind of human being: in all languages, in all ages, in all ranks of honor, in every variety of intelligence, and in every profession of lawful and useful arts; and whatever else may be said according to the innumerable differences by which human beings differ from one another through sins alone—from the highest to the lowest, from king to beggar.

“Everything,” he says, “I will draw after me,” so that I may be their head and they may be my members.

“But if I am lifted up,” he says, “from the earth”—that is, “when I have been lifted up.” For he does not doubt that what he has come to fulfill will happen.

This refers to what he said above: “But if it dies, it bears much fruit.” For what else did he call his exaltation except the passion of the cross? The evangelist himself did not leave this unsaid; he added and said:

“This he said, signifying by what death he was going to die.” The crowd answered him: “We have heard from the Law that the Christ remains forever. How then do you say, ‘The Son of Man must be lifted up’? Who is [Col. 0392A] this Son of Man?” They had retained in memory that the Lord constantly said that he was the Son of Man. For here he does not say, “If the Son of Man is lifted up from the earth,” but, as he had said above, when the Gentiles who wished to see him were announced: “The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified.” Thus, retaining these words in mind, and understanding his present statement, “When I have been lifted up from the earth,” as referring to the death of the cross, they asked him and said: “We have heard from the Law that the Christ remains forever. How then do you say, ‘The Son of Man must be lifted up’?” “If he is the Christ,” they say, “he remains forever; if he remains forever, how will he be lifted up from the earth—that is, how will he die through the suffering of the cross?” For they understood that this was what he had said, which they were [Col. 0392B] planning to do. Thus the wisdom poured into them did not disclose the obscurity of these words to them, but rather their aroused conscience did.

“Jesus therefore said to them: ‘The light is still with you for a little while.’” This is the basis of your understanding that the Christ remains forever. “Walk while you have the light, so that darkness may not seize you.” Walk, draw near, understand everything: both the Christ who was to die and the one who would live forever; both the blood he would pour out to redeem, and the one who would ascend on high in order to lead you there. Darkness, however, will not seize you if you believe in Christ’s eternity in such a way that you do not deny in him the lowliness of death. “And whoever walks in darkness does not know where he is going,” but he may stumble against the stone of stumbling and the rock of [Col. 0392C] offense, which the Lord was to the blind Jews; just as to those who believed he became the stone that the builders rejected, made the cornerstone. For this reason they disdained believing in Christ: their impiety despised him when dead and mocked him when slain, although he himself was the death of the grain that was to multiply, and the exaltation of the one who drew all things after himself.

“While you have the light, believe in the light, so that you may be sons of light.” When you have heard something true, believe in the truth, so that you may be reborn in the truth. “Jesus said these things, and he went away and hid himself from them.”

## HOMILY LXVI. TUESDAY OF PALMS

The Passion of Our Lord Jesus Christ according to Mark.

[Col. 0392D] (MARK XIV, XV). “At that time, it was Passover and Unleavened Bread after two days,” and so forth. Passover, which in Hebrew is called *pasḥah* (*phase*), is named not from *passion*, as most people suppose, but from *passing over*, because the destroyer, seeing the blood on the doors of the Israelites, passed over them and did not strike them. Or the Lord himself, giving aid to his people, passed over them from above; explaining the sacramental meaning of the term more profoundly, the evangelist John says: “Before the feast of Passover, Jesus, knowing that his hour had come to pass from this world to the Father.” Here he plainly declares that the day of this solemnity was mystically called “Passover” by the Law for this reason: the Lamb of God, who would take away the sins of the world, was on that day to pass from this world—or [Col. 0393A] he himself would pass over, or he would lead us through a saving passage, as though out of Egyptian slavery.

This, then, is the precise distinction—according to the Scripture of the Old Testament—between Passover and Unleavened Bread: Passover is the name of the single day on which the lamb was killed in the evening, that is, on the fourteenth day of the moon of the first month. On the fifteenth day of the moon, when the people went out from Egypt, the festival of Unleavened Bread followed; this solemnity was established for seven days, that is, until the evening of the twenty-first day of the same month. Yet the evangelists commonly use “the day of Unleavened Bread” for Passover, and “Passover” for the days of Unleavened Bread. Mark says: “It was Passover and Unleavened Bread after two days” (Mark XIV). Luke says: “The feast day of Unleavened Bread, which is called Passover” (Luke XXII). [Col. 0393B] Likewise John, when the events were taking place on the following day, that is, on the fifteenth day of the moon, says: “They themselves did not enter the praetorium, so that they would not be defiled, but so that they might eat the Passover” (John XVIII).

They did this because they had been commanded both to celebrate the day of Passover with unleavened bread and, as though making Passover perpetual, were commanded always to pass from this world. For after the lamb was sacrificed in the evening on one day, seven consecutive days of Unleavened Bread followed, because Christ Jesus, having once suffered in the flesh for us in the fullness of time, commanded us to live throughout the entire period of this world—which is measured by seven days—in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth. He also continually urges us, with every effort, to flee earthly desires, as though they were the bonds of Egypt, and, like those who withdraw from worldly conduct into secret solitude, [Col. 0393C] to undertake the path of the virtues.

“And the chief priests and scribes were seeking how they might seize Jesus by deceit and kill him. But they were saying: ‘Not during the feast, lest perhaps there be a disturbance among the people.’” Those who ought to have been preparing victims for the approaching Passover, smoothing the walls of the temple, sweeping the floors, cleansing the vessels, and purifying themselves according to the rite of the Law so that they might become worthy to eat the lamb, gathered together and took counsel about how to kill the Lord. As the simple wording shows, they were not afraid of an uprising, but were taking care lest he be snatched from their hands with the help of the people.

“And when he was in Bethany, in the house of Simon the leper, and was reclining at table.” He who was about to suffer for the whole people and redeem all nations with his blood [Col. 0393D] remained in Bethany, the house of obedience, which had once belonged to Simon the leper—not because he remained a leper at that time, but because, having formerly been a leper, he was later cleansed by the Savior, while his former name remained, so that the power of the healer might be displayed. For in the catalogue of the apostles Matthew is called “the tax collector” by his former vice and occupation, although he had certainly ceased to be a tax collector.

Some wish to understand Simon the leper as a part of the people that had believed in the Lord and had been healed by him. Simon himself is also said to mean “obedient.”

“A woman came with an alabaster jar of costly perfume of pure nard, and, breaking the alabaster jar, poured it over his head.” This woman was Mary Magdalene, the sister of Lazarus, whom Jesus [Col. 0394A] raised from the dead, as John explicitly records. He also testifies that this event took place six days before Passover, on the day before Jesus came to Jerusalem seated on a donkey, with palms and the praise of the crowds.

She is the same woman, not another, who formerly—as Luke writes—was a sinner and, coming for this purpose, wet the Lord’s feet with tears of repentance and anointed them with the perfume of confession. Because she loved much, she obtained from the merciful Judge the forgiveness of many sins. Now justified and made familiar to the Lord, she poured holy oil not only over his feet, as that same John relates, but also over his head, as Matthew and Mark testify.

Alabaster is a kind of white marble streaked with various colors, which they hollow out for perfume vessels, because such vessels are said to preserve perfumes exceptionally well without spoiling. It is found around Egyptian Thebes and Damascus in Syria, whiter than elsewhere, but the finest is found in India.

[Col. 0394B] Nard is an aromatic shrub with, as they say, a strong and thick root, though short, black, brittle, and nevertheless full of oil. It emits a fragrance like cypress; it has a harsh taste and a small, dense leaf whose tips spread into spikes. For this reason perfumers celebrate both the spikes and the leaves of nard with a double excellence. This is what Mark means when he says, “the costly perfume of pure nard”: the perfume that Mary brought to the Lord was made not only from the root of nard but, to make it more precious, had also been enriched by the addition of its spikes and leaves, increasing its fragrance and potency.

[Col. 0394C] Natural philosophers report of nard that it is primary among perfumes; therefore it was rightly offered for anointing the Lord’s head and feet. There are indeed many varieties of it, but in all of them the plants provide evidence of its preciousness.

Mystically, this devotion of Mary ministering to the Lord signifies the faith and piety of the holy Church, which speaks in the Song of Love, saying: “While the king was at his table, my nard gave forth its fragrance” (Song I). Mary’s hands fulfilled these words once in their literal sense, and she does not cease to fulfill them spiritually every day in all the members of the Church, which, spread throughout the whole world, glorify themselves and say: “But thanks be to God, who always leads us in triumph in Christ Jesus and manifests through us the fragrance of the knowledge of himself in every place; for we are the good fragrance of Christ to God in every place” (II Cor. II).

[Col. 0394D] Whoever acknowledges, praises, and proclaims with worthy reverence the power of his divine nature, which he possesses together with the Father, certainly pours precious perfume over his head. But when he receives with equally worthy reverence the mysteries of the humanity he assumed, he pours upon the Lord’s feet the perfume of *nardus pisticus* (faithful nard)—that is, the faithful word—because he commends by devout preaching and venerates with devoted service that nature of his by which he deigned to touch the earth, that is, to live among human beings.

“But some were indignant among themselves and said: ‘Why has this waste of perfume been made? For this perfume could have been sold for more than three hundred denarii and given to the poor.’” Here Mark, like Matthew, speaks by synecdoche, using the plural number [Col. 0395A] in place of the singular. For John, speaking more distinctly, testifies that Judas said this, and that he said it out of greed, because he was a thief and, having the money box, carried away what was put into it.

It can also be understood that the other disciples either felt this or said it, or that Judas persuaded them by saying it; and that Matthew and Mark expressed the will of them all, Matthew in general terms and Mark even in their words. But Judas said it because he was a thief, while the others said it out of concern for the poor. John, however, wished to mention only Judas because he believed that on this occasion his habit of stealing should be disclosed.

As for what follows—“And they were hostile toward her”—I do not at all think this was said of the good apostles who were devoted to Christ, but rather of that one man, referred to in the plural number, who was proved neither to have [Col. 0395B] clung faithfully to the Lord and his disciples nor to have cared for the poor.

“But Jesus said: ‘Leave her alone. Why do you trouble her? She has performed a good work for me. For you will always have the poor with you, and whenever you wish you can do good to them; but you will not always have me.’” Here another question arises: why did Jesus say to the disciples after the resurrection, “Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age” (Matt. XXVIII), while here he says, “You will not always have me”?

It seems to me that in this passage he is speaking of bodily presence, because after the resurrection he would not be with them in the same way as he was then, in every fellowship and intimacy. Remembering this, the Apostle [Col. 0395C] says: “Even if we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him in that way” (II Cor. V).
