“What she had, she did: she anticipated anointing my body for burial.” What you consider a waste of perfume is an act of burial. It is not surprising if she has given me the good fragrance of her faith, since I am about to pour out my blood for her.

“Amen I say to you: wherever this Gospel is proclaimed throughout the whole world, what she has done will also be told in memory of her.” Observe his knowledge of future events: though he was to suffer within a few days, he knew that his Gospel would be celebrated throughout the whole world.

It should also be noted that, just as Mary obtained glory [Col. 0395D] throughout the world, wherever the holy Church has been spread, because of the service of pious devotion that she offered to the Lord, so, by contrast, the man who did not fear to disparage her service with a rash tongue was branded far and wide with the mark of treachery and rightly became hateful both to God and to human beings. But the Lord, rewarding the good with praise that they deserved, passed over in silence the future insults of the impious man.

“And Judas Iscariot, one of the Twelve, went away to the chief priests to betray him to them.” Unhappy Judas! What he thought he had done by the pouring out of the perfume, he now wished to compensate by putting a price on his teacher. He does not even demand a fixed sum, so that his betrayal might at least seem profitable; rather, as though handing over a worthless slave, he placed him in the power of [Col. 0396A] the eminent men, leaving them to give whatever they wished.

By saying, “He went away to the chief priests to betray him to them,” the evangelist shows that he had not been invited by the leaders, nor compelled by any necessity, but had undertaken the plan of his criminal mind of his own accord.

“When they heard this, they rejoiced and promised to give him money. And he was seeking how he might betray him at a convenient opportunity.” Many people today recoil from the crime by which Judas sold his Lord, teacher, and God for money as monstrous and abominable, yet they do not guard against committing the same crime. For when they give false testimony against anyone for gifts, they certainly deny the truth for money and sell God for money. He himself said: “I am the truth” (John XIV).

When they stain the fellowship of brotherhood with some [Col. 0396B] plague of discord, they betray the Lord, because God is love. Therefore those who despise the rights of truth and love betray God, who is love and truth, especially when they sin not through weakness or ignorance, but, in imitation of Judas, seek an opportunity to exchange truth for falsehood and virtue for crime when no witnesses are present.

“On the first day of Unleavened Bread, when they sacrificed the Passover, the disciples say to him: ‘Where do you want us to go and prepare for you to eat the Passover?’” He calls the fourteenth day of the first month the first day of Unleavened Bread, when they were accustomed, after removing the leaven, to sacrifice—that is, to kill—the lamb in the evening.

Explaining this, the Apostle says: “For Christ our Passover has been sacrificed” (I Cor. V). Although he was crucified on the following day, [Col. 0396C] that is, on the fifteenth day of the moon, on this night, when the lamb was sacrificed, he both handed over to his disciples the mysteries of his flesh and blood to be celebrated and, having been seized and bound by the Jews, consecrated the beginning of his own sacrifice, that is, of his Passion.

“And he sends two of his disciples and says to them: ‘Go into the city, and a man carrying a jar of water will meet you.’” This is an indication of his foreknowing divinity: while speaking with his disciples, he knows what will happen elsewhere.

Appropriately, as the disciples prepare the Passover, a man carrying a jar—or, according to another evangelist, an amphora—of water meets them, to show that this paschal mystery was to be celebrated for the perfect offering of the whole world. Water signifies the bath of grace; the jar [Col. 0396D] signifies the fragility of those through whom that same grace was to be ministered to the world. Hence they say: “But we have this treasure in earthen vessels” (II Cor. IV).

Thus the disciples prepare the Passover where water is brought in a jar, to indicate that the time was at hand when, for true worshipers of the Passover, the typical blood, offered on the threshold and doorposts, would be presented, and the baptism of the life-giving fountain would be completed for the removal of the world’s crimes.

“Follow him, and wherever he enters, say to the master of the house: ‘The Teacher says: Where is my lodging, where is the room in which I may eat the Passover with my disciples?’” The names of both the water-carrier and the master of the house have deliberately been omitted, so that it might be indicated that an opportunity is granted to all who wish to celebrate the true Passover—that is, to be imbued with Christ’s sacraments and to receive him as a guest into the [Col. 0397A] lodging of their minds.

“And he will show you a large upper room furnished and prepared; there prepare for us.” The large upper room is the spiritual Law, which, coming out from the narrowness of the letter, receives the Savior in a lofty place. For one who still observes the letter that kills—what else will he understand as great except a beast? Such a person celebrates a lesser Passover, because he has not yet learned to comprehend the majesty of the Spirit in the words of God.

But whoever has found in the house—that is, in the Church—the bearer of water, the herald of grace, prepares through Christ, who illuminates the face of the letter, a banquet for Christ in the high chamber of the mind, transcending the letter. For he recognizes that all the mysteries of the Passover, as well as the other decrees of the Law, are his mysteries.

[Col. 0397B] “When evening came, he arrived with the Twelve. And while they were reclining and eating, Jesus said: ‘Amen I say to you: one of you will betray me, the one who is eating with me.’” He had foretold his Passion, and he foretells the betrayer, giving him an opportunity for repentance, so that when he understood that his thoughts and hidden plans were known, he might repent of his deed. Yet he does not identify him specifically, lest, openly convicted, he become more shameless. He casts the crime into the number, so that the guilty man may repent.

“But they began to be sorrowful and to say to him one by one: ‘Surely it is not I?’” The eleven disciples certainly knew that they were not contemplating anything of this kind against the Lord, but they trusted the teacher more than themselves. [Col. 0397C] Fearing their own weakness, they sorrowfully asked about a sin of which they had no consciousness.

“He said to them: ‘One of the Twelve, the one who dips his hand with me into the dish.’” O marvelous patience of the Lord! He had first said, “One of you will betray me.” The betrayer persists in evil; he is accused more plainly, yet Judas’s name is not specifically identified. While the others are sorrowful, withdrawing their hands and forbidding food to their mouths, he, with the recklessness and shamelessness with which he was about to betray, even puts his hand into the dish with the teacher, so that audacity might falsely imitate a good conscience.

“The Son of Man indeed goes, as it is written of him. But woe to that man through whom the Son of Man will be betrayed.” Corrected neither the first nor the second time, he does not withdraw his foot from betrayal. [Col. 0397D] Rather, the Lord’s patience nourishes his shamelessness, and he stores up wrath for himself on the day of wrath. He foretells the punishment, so that the threatened torments may correct the man whom shame had not overcome.

But even today and forever, woe to that man who approaches the Lord’s table in wickedness, who, with his inner being polluted by some crime, does not fear to participate in the most holy offerings of Christ’s mysteries. He too, in imitation of Judas, betrays the Son of Man—not indeed to sinful Jews, but nevertheless to sinful members, namely his own, with whom he presumes to profane that incomparable and inviolable sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood.

He sells the Lord who is shown to love and care for earthly, transitory, and even criminal things [Col. 0398A] rather than for him, neglecting the fear and love of the Lord. “It would have been better for that man if he had not been born.” This should not be taken to mean that he existed before he was born, since nothing can be well with anyone except one who exists. It is simply said that it is much better not to exist than to exist badly.

“And while they were eating, Jesus took bread, blessed it, broke it, gave it to them, and said: ‘Take; this is my body.’” When the solemnities of the old Passover had been completed—solemnities celebrated in remembrance of the ancient liberation of God’s people from Egypt—he passed to the new Passover, which he wished the Church to celebrate in remembrance of its redemption. Thus, in place of the flesh of the lamb, he substituted the sacrament of his body and blood, showing himself to be the one concerning whom “the Lord swore and will not change his mind: ‘You are a priest forever [Col. 0398B] according to the order of Melchizedek’” (Ps. CIX).

He himself breaks the bread that he offers to the disciples, to show that the breaking of his body would not occur without his own will and direction, but—as he says elsewhere—that he has authority to lay down his life and authority to take it up again (John X).

For the sake of the sacrament, he first blessed this bread before breaking it, because he himself, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, filled with the grace of divine power the human nature that he assumed and in which he was to suffer. He blessed and broke the bread because he deigned to subject the assumed human being to death in such a way as to demonstrate that the power of divine immortality truly resided in him, and thus to teach that he would [Col. 0398C] be raised from death all the more swiftly.

“And taking the cup, giving thanks, he gave it to them. And they all drank from it.” As his Passion drew near, he is also said to have given thanks after taking the bread. Therefore the one who receives the scourges of another’s iniquity gives thanks. He who had done nothing worthy of being struck humbly blesses in his Passion, to show what each person ought to do under the scourge of sin, if he himself bears with equanimity the scourges of another’s guilt. He also shows what a subject should do when corrected, if, placed under the scourge, he who is equal to the Father gives thanks to the Father.

“And he said to them: ‘This is my blood of the New Testament, which will be poured out for many.’” Because bread strengthens the body, while wine produces blood in the flesh, [Col. 0398D] the one is mystically referred to Christ’s body and the other to his blood. Yet because we must remain in Christ and Christ in us, water is mixed with the wine of the Lord’s blood; for, as John testifies, the waters signify the peoples.

Nor is anyone permitted to offer either water alone or wine alone, just as a grain of wheat cannot become bread by itself without the addition and preparation of water. Otherwise such an offering would signify that the head should be separated from the members, and it might appear either that Christ could have suffered without the love of our redemption, or that we could be saved and offered to the Father without his Passion.

When he says, “This is my blood of the New Testament,” he refers by contrast to the Old Testament, which was consecrated by [Col. 0399A] the blood of goats and calves, as the lawgiver said while sprinkling: “This is the blood of the Testament that God commanded for you.” For it is necessary that the copies of heavenly things be cleansed by these sacrifices, but that the heavenly things themselves be cleansed by better sacrifices than these, as the Apostle demonstrates throughout his Epistle to the Hebrews, distinguishing the Law from the Gospel with most beautiful exposition and complete reasoning.

“Amen, amen I say to you: I will no longer drink from the fruit of the vine until that day when I drink it new in the kingdom of God.” The Synagogue is called the Lord’s vine or vineyard throughout Scripture; Isaiah, however, bears clearer witness in the song he composed about it: “The vineyard of the Lord of hosts,” he says, “is the house of Israel” (Isa. V).

[Col. 0399B] For a long time the Lord had fruit from this vineyard, although many of its branches had been turned into the bitterness of a foreign vine. Nevertheless, even though many from that people departed from the straight path of faith, there were some who remained faithful; throughout the entire period of the Law there were very many whose pious thoughts and supreme virtues delighted God.

But when the Lord had suffered in the flesh and risen from the dead, the time came for that legal and figurative observance to cease, and for the things performed according to the letter, transferred into a spiritual meaning, to be held more perfectly in the New Testament with the help of the grace of the Holy Spirit.

As he was therefore going to his Passion, the Lord said: “I will no longer drink from the fruit of the vine until that day when I drink it new in the kingdom of God.” It is as though he plainly said: “I will no longer take delight in the carnal ceremonies of [Col. 0399C] the Synagogue, in which even these rites of the paschal Lamb held the first place. For the time of my resurrection will come; that day will come when, placed in the kingdom of God—that is, exalted in the glory of immortal life—I will be filled with new joy together with you over the salvation of that same people, begotten from the fountain of spiritual grace.”

“And after singing a hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives.” This is what we read in the Psalm: “The poor will eat and be satisfied, and they will praise the Lord, those who seek him” (Ps. XXI).

That hymn may also be understood as the one that, according to John, the Lord sang while giving thanks to the Father. In it he prayed, with his eyes lifted upward, both for himself and for the disciples and for those who would believe through their word.

[Col. 0399D] Appropriately, after filling the disciples with the sacraments of his body and blood and enriching them with a hymn of devout intercession to the Father, he leads them up to the Mount of Olives, so that it might figuratively signify that through the reception of his sacraments and through the aid of his intercession we ought to ascend to higher gifts of virtue, the charisms of the Holy Spirit, with which we are to be anointed in the heart.

“And Jesus said to them: ‘You will all be scandalized because of me on this night.’” He foretells what they are going to suffer so that, when they have suffered it, they will not despair of salvation but will be freed through repentance. He significantly added, “You will be scandalized on this night,” because just as those who become drunk do so at night, so those who suffer scandal endure it in darkness and at night.

But let us [Col. 0400A] say: “The night has passed, and the day has drawn near” (Rom. XIII). For it is written: “I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered.” This is written in other words in the prophet Zechariah; and, unless I am mistaken, it is said by the prophet’s voice to God: “Strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered.” The sixty-eighth Psalm, which is sung entirely of the Lord, also agrees with this meaning: “For the one whom you struck, they themselves pursued.”

The good shepherd is struck so that he may lay down his life for his sheep, and from many flocks of error there may become one flock and one shepherd.

“But Peter said to him: ‘Even if all are scandalized, yet not I.’” This is neither recklessness nor a lie, but the faith of the apostle Peter and his ardent affection for the Lord Savior.

[Col. 0400B] “And Jesus said to him: ‘Amen I say to you: today, on this very night, before the rooster crows twice, you will deny me three times.’” Peter was making his promise out of the ardor of faith, while the Savior, as God, knew what was to come.

Note that Peter denies during the night, and denies three times. After the rooster crowed, and the diminishing darkness announced that light was near, he turned and wept bitterly, washing away the filth of his denial with tears.

There is no contradiction in the fact that, while Mark says, “Before the rooster crows twice, you will deny me three times,” the other evangelists simply say, “Before the rooster crows, you will deny me three times.” For Peter’s entire denial is a threefold denial. He remained in the same denial of mind and intention to lie until, reminded of what had been foretold to him, [Col. 0400C] he was healed by bitter weeping and anguish of heart.

If this whole denial—that is, the threefold denial—began after the first crowing of the rooster, the three who said that Peter would deny him three times before the rooster crowed would appear to have spoken falsely. Again, if he had completed the entire threefold denial before the rooster began to crow, Mark would be found to have reported superfluously, in the person of the Lord: “Amen I say to you: on this night, before the rooster crows twice, you will deny me three times.”

But because the whole denial can be understood as occurring before the first crowing, they paid attention to this point. Although in words the denial began before the first crowing and was completed before the rooster’s second crowing, that whole threefold denial had already been conceived in Peter’s disposition and fear. [Col. 0400D] It makes no difference over how many intervals of time it was prolonged before being uttered in three statements, since his heart already possessed the whole denial before the first crowing of the rooster. Great fear had taken up residence in him, so that, when questioned once, then again, and a third time, he could deny not only the Lord but also deny him repeatedly.

Thus, for those who attend more correctly and carefully, just as the man who looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart (Matt. V), so whenever Peter expressed in words the fear that he had conceived intensely in his mind, so that it could persist until the third denial of the Lord, the whole threefold denial must be assigned to the moment when sufficient fear of the threefold denial seized him.

“And they come to an estate called Gethsemane.” The place of Gethsemane where [Col. 0401A] the Lord prayed is shown to this day at the foot of the Mount of Olives; now a church is built above it. Gethsemane is interpreted as “the valley of the rich” or “of richness.”

Since not only the Savior’s words and deeds but also the places and times in which he acts and speaks are, as has often been said, filled with mystical figures, when the Lord prays on the mountain he silently admonishes us that we should seek only heavenly things in prayer and petition for celestial blessings. When he prays in a valley—and in the valley of the rich or of richness—he equally intimates that humility must be preserved in prayers and the richness of eternal love.

A person praying to the Lord should not dare to boast of his merits, after the example of the proud Pharisee; rather, with humble voice and mind he should cry out: “God, [Col. 0401B] be merciful to me, a sinner” (Luke XVIII). Nor should one whose heart is dry of love for his neighbor kneel down to win the Creator’s favor, like the man who, unwilling to forgive his brother the hundred denarii that he owed him, vainly begged the Lord to forgive him ten thousand talents (Matt. XVIII).

Nor should one whose breast is empty of love for the Creator seek any temporal thing in prayer rather than the Creator’s vision, lest he be counted among those of whom the Lord himself says: “They have received their reward” (Matt. VI). Indeed, what is it other than a certain dryness of mind to set one’s thoughts on earthly things? Those who, through holy desires, are already inwardly nourished by heavenly understanding and delights grow rich as though by abundant food.

The Psalmist longed to be fattened by this richness when he said: [Col. 0401C] “Let my soul be filled as with marrow and fatness” (Ps. LXII). As regards the dispensation of the Lord’s Passion itself, it was fitting that the Lord, as death approached, prayed in the valley of richness, because through the valley of humility and the richness of charity he underwent death for us. “For he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the Father unto death, even death on a cross” (Phil. II). “No one has greater love than this: that someone lay down his life for his friends” (John XV).

“And he takes Peter, James, and John with him, and he began to be afraid and distressed. And he said to them: ‘My soul is sorrowful even unto death.’” Christ fears, while Peter does not fear. Christ fears; Peter says, “I lay down my life for you.” Christ says: [Col. 0401D] “My soul is troubled.” Both are true, and both are fully rational: the one who is lower does not fear, while the one who is higher assumes the disposition of one who fears.

The former, as a human being, is ignorant of the force of death; the latter, as God established in a body, displays the weakness of the flesh, so that the impiety of those who deny the mystery of the Incarnation might be excluded. Finally, he said these things, yet Manichaeus did not believe, Valentinus denied, and Marcion judged him to be a phantom.

He so fully conformed the human being whom he demonstrated to possess a true body to the human condition that he said: “Nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will.” He therefore assumed my will; he assumed my sorrow. I confidently call it sorrow, because I [Col. 0402A] proclaim the cross. The will is mine, which he called his own, because as a human being he assumed my sorrow, spoke as a human being, and therefore said: “Not as I will, but as you will.”

The sorrow is mine, which he assumed with my disposition. Therefore he grieved for me, who had nothing for which he needed to grieve for himself; and, while the delight of eternal Divinity was set aside, he was affected by the distress of my weakness. “My soul,” he says, “is sorrowful unto death.” The Lord is not sorrowful because of death, because it was the condition of bodily feeling, not fear of death, that troubled him. For since he assumed a body, he had to assume everything proper to a body, so that he might hunger, thirst, be angry, and be sorrowful; but Divinity does not know change through such emotions.

“Remain here and keep watch. And when he had gone a little farther, he fell upon the ground.” [Col. 0402B] Because he commanded, “Remain here and keep watch,” he does not prohibit sleep, whose time had not yet come amid the impending danger, but rather the sleep of unbelief, both bodily and mental.

After giving them the command to remain and keep watch with him, he went a little farther and fell on his face upon the ground, displaying the humility of his mind through the posture of his flesh.

“And he prayed that, if it were possible, the hour might pass from him, and he said: ‘Abba, Father, all things are possible for you; take this cup from me.’” What was that voice but the sound of our infirmity? Many who are still weak are distressed by the death that awaits them. Let them have a right heart; let them avoid death as far as they can; but if they cannot, let them say what the Lord himself said—not for his own sake, but for ours. For what did he say: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me”? Behold, Christ has a human will; now see the right heart: “Yet not what I will, but what you will.” “I have not come,” he says, “to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me” (John 6). He called “his own will” that which he temporally assumed from the Virgin; but “the will of him who sent him” he indicated as that which the eternal Son had timelessly and eternally in common with the Father. He prays that the cup may pass from him in order to show truly that he was also human; but, remembering why he was sent, he fulfills the dispensation for which he was sent, and cries out: “Yet not what I will, but what you will.” “If death dies without my dying”—that is, according to the flesh—“let the cup pass,” he says. But because this will not happen in any other way, he says: “Not what I will, but what you will.”

But in invoking the Father by the twofold name, “Abba, Father,” he shows that he is the God and Savior of both peoples, namely, of the Jews and of the Gentiles. For *Abba* signifies the same as *Father*, but *Abba* is Hebrew, while *Father* is Greek and Latin. Thus, to teach that both peoples would believe in him and that he should be invoked by both, he himself first invokes him in both languages. For he is the good shepherd who gives his life for his sheep and makes one sheepfold out of two flocks (John 10). Therefore, with the voice of both flocks, he implores the Father’s help, so that we, instructed by his example in both respects, whenever we sense adversity threatening, may invoke God the Father—*Abba* among the Hebrews—and seek heavenly protection with one devotion of faith and love.

Accordingly, the distinguished teacher, taking from the Lord the model of instruction, addresses his hearers in this way: “You have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, in whom we cry, ‘Abba, Father’” (Romans 8). *Abba* belongs, of course, to him who comes from the people of Israel; *Father* to us who have come from the nations to faith in Christ.

“And he came and found them sleeping. And he said to Peter: ‘Simon, are you sleeping? Were you unable to keep watch for one hour?’” The one who had earlier said, “Even if all are scandalized, I will never be scandalized,” now cannot overcome sleep because of the magnitude of his sorrow.

“Keep watch and pray, so that you do not enter into temptation.” It is impossible for the human soul not to be tempted. Hence, in the Lord’s Prayer, we say, “Do not lead us into temptation” (Matthew 6)—not wholly rejecting the temptation that we cannot bear, but asking for the strength to endure amid temptations. Therefore, even here he does not say, “Keep watch and pray so that you may not be tempted,” but “so that you do not enter into temptation”; that is, so that temptation may not finally overcome you and hold you within its downfall. For example, the martyr who shed his blood in confessing the Lord was indeed tempted, but was not bound in the nets of temptation. The one who denies, however, falls into the snares of temptation.

“The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak.” This was said against the presumptuous, because whatever they believe, they think they can attain. Therefore, as much as we trust in the ardor of the mind, so much should we fear the frailty of the flesh. Nevertheless, according to the Apostle, it is by the spirit that the works of the flesh are put to death.

This passage stands against the Eutychians, who say that there was one operation and one will in the Mediator of God and human beings, our Lord and Savior. For when he says, “The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak,” he reveals two wills: the human, namely, that of the flesh, and the divine, namely, that of the Godhead. The human will, because of the weakness of the flesh, refuses suffering; but his divine will is most ready, since to fear in suffering belongs to human frailty, whereas to accept the dispensation of suffering belongs to divine will and power.

“And again he went away and prayed, saying the same words.” He alone prays for all, just as he alone suffers for all. But the apostles’ eyes were languishing and weighed down, with denial close at hand.

[Col. 0403D] “And he came a third time and said to them: ‘Sleep now and rest. It is enough. The hour has come; behold, the Son of Man will be handed over into the hands of sinners.’” When he had said, “Sleep now and rest,” and added, “It is enough,” and then continued, “The hour has come; behold, the Son of Man will be handed over,” it is evidently understood that, after saying to them, “Sleep and rest,” the Lord remained silent for some time, so that what he had announced beforehand might take place, and then added: “Behold, the hour is approaching,” or, “The hour has come.” For this reason “It is enough” has been placed after those words—that is, “Because you have rested, it is now enough.” But because that intervening silence of the Lord is not itself mentioned, the passage constrains the interpretation, so that another punctuation or delivery must be sought in those words.

[Col. 0404A] “Rise; let us go. Behold, the one who will betray me is near.” After he had prayed a third time and had obtained that the apostles’ ensuing fear should be corrected by repentance, he proceeds confidently toward his persecutors, secure concerning his Passion, and willingly offers himself to be killed. He said to the disciples: “Rise; let us go. Behold, the one who will betray me is near.” Let them not find you as though you were afraid and drawing back; let us go willingly toward death, so that they may see the confidence and joy of the one who is about to suffer.

“Now the betrayer had given them a sign, saying: ‘Whomever I kiss, he is the one; seize him and lead him away carefully.’ And when he had come, immediately approaching him, he said: ‘Rabbi.’ And he kissed him.” It was shameless and criminal confidence to invoke his teacher and offer a kiss to the one he was betraying. Yet he still retains something of a disciple’s modesty, since he did not openly betray him to the persecutors, but did so through the sign of a kiss. The Lord accepts the betrayer’s kiss, not to teach us to feign, but so that he would not appear to flee betrayal, while at the same time fulfilling what David said: “I was peaceful with those who hated peace” (Psalm 119).

“One of those standing nearby drew a sword, struck the servant of the high priest, and cut off his ear.” Peter did this, as the evangelist John explains, with the same love of mind by which he had earlier done many things. For he knew how Phinehas, by punishing sacrilegious people, had received the reward of justice and an everlasting priesthood. Luke adds that the Lord, touching the servant’s ear, healed him. Does the Lord therefore forget his own mercy, who does not even allow his enemies to be wounded? The righteous man is subjected to death, while he himself heals the wounds of his persecutors, mystically teaching that even those who, by consenting to his death, had contracted a wound in their souls may deserve salvation if they produce a worthy fruit of repentance.

“And Jesus answered and said to them: ‘Have you come out with swords and clubs to seize me as though I were a robber? Every day I was among you in the temple teaching, and you did not seize me.’” It is foolish, he says, to seek with swords and clubs the one who willingly handed himself over to your hands; and to investigate by means of a betrayer as though he were hiding by night and avoiding your eyes, the one who taught in the temple every day. But you gather against me in darkness for this reason: your power is in darkness.

“Then all his disciples, leaving him, fled.” The Lord’s saying was fulfilled, in which he had said that all the disciples would be scandalized because of him on that very night. Even if they fled when the crowd allowed it, at the Lord’s request, as John writes, they nevertheless displayed the fear and timidity of their minds; they were readier to seek the protection of flight than to show confidence in suffering.

“But a certain young man was following him, clothed in a linen garment over his naked body, and they seized him. But he, abandoning the linen garment, fled from them naked.” Since he says “clothed in a linen garment over his naked body,” the word *body* is understood: that is, he had no other clothing than the linen garment itself. Who this young man was, the evangelist does not say. Whoever he was, he proves that the Lord’s love remained greater in him than in the others, because, while they had already fled, he did not cease to follow him, drawn by the bond of love, until he was seized by the enemies. Yet he did not possess perfect love, since, once captured, he could flee from the company of the Savior. For just as perfect love casts out fear, so fear occupying the mind reveals imperfect love.

But we should observe more carefully that, when the evangelist writes about this young man, he does not say that he fled from the Lord’s company or from following the Lord; rather, he says: “After abandoning the linen garment, he fled from them naked.” He fled from the enemies, whose presence and deeds he detested. For he did not flee from the Lord and Savior, his teacher, whose love he preserved fixed in his heart even while absent in body.

Nor does anything prevent us from understanding that this young man was John, the disciple loved by the teacher more than the others. The fact that he was still a young man at that time is also indicated by the long life he afterward lived in the flesh. It could have happened that, slipping from the hands of those who had seized him for the moment, he soon put his garment back on and returned; and, in the uncertain light of night, mingled with the crowds leading Jesus as though he were one of them, until he reached the high priest’s courtyard, where he was known, as he himself records in his Gospel.

Just as Peter, who washed away the guilt of his denial with repentant tears and completely uprooted it by confessing his love for the Lord, shows the restoration of those who fall in martyrdom, so the other disciples, who reached the moment of the arrest by fleeing, teach caution in flight to those who feel themselves less capable of enduring punishments. For them it is much safer to seek the protection of hiding places than to expose themselves to the danger of combat.

Thus this young man also, who abandoned his linen garment and fled naked from the impious, signifies both the deed and the intention of those who, in order to be safer from the assaults of enemies, cast aside whatever they seem to possess in this world. They have learned to serve the Lord naked rather than, by clinging to worldly possessions, give the adversaries material with which to tempt them and draw them back from God, following the example of blessed Joseph (Genesis 39), who, leaving his cloak in the adulterous woman’s hands, leapt outside, preferring to serve God naked rather than, clothed in worldly desires, serve a prostitute.

“And they led Jesus to the high priest.” The high priest signifies Caiaphas, as the evangelist John writes: he was the high priest of that year. Josephus likewise gives corresponding testimony, saying that he had bought the high priesthood for himself from the Roman prince without deserving the dignity. It is no wonder if an unjust priest judges unjustly.

“But Peter followed him from a distance, as far as inside the courtyard of the high priest.” He rightly followed from a distance the one whom he was soon to deny when near. For he could never have denied him if he had clung closely to Christ. Nevertheless, in this he is especially worthy of our admiration: he did not abandon Jesus even while he was afraid. That he fears belongs to nature; that he follows, to devotion; that he denies, to sudden weakness; that he repents, to faith.

Alternatively, in that Peter followed the Lord, who was going to his Passion, from a distance, the Church is signified: it will indeed follow—that is, imitate—the footsteps of the Lord’s Passion, but in a very different manner. The Church suffers for itself; he suffers for the Church.

“And he was sitting with the servants and warming himself by the fire.” There is the fire of love, and there is the fire of desire. Of the former it is said: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire except that it burn?” (Luke 12). Of the latter: “All are adulterers; their hearts are like an oven” (Hosea 7). The former, descending upon the believers in the upper room of Zion, taught them to praise God in various languages; the latter, kindled in Caiaphas’s courtyard by the impulse of the evil spirit, armed the harmful tongues of the faithless to deny and blaspheme the Lord. What the wicked council was doing inside the house of the high priest, the fire kindled outside in the courtyard amid the cold of night materially foreshadowed in a symbolic way.

Therefore, whoever is burdened by sin can say with the prophet to the Lord: “For I have become like a wineskin in the frost; I have not forgotten your righteous judgments” (Psalm 119). But those in whom troubled rivers of vice overwhelm the flame of love hear from the Lord: “Because iniquity has increased, the love of many will grow cold” (Matthew 24).

At that cold, the Apostle Peter, temporarily benumbed, wanted to warm himself as though by the servants’ coals, because he was seeking the comfort of temporal advantage through the companionship of the faithless. But soon, when the Lord looked upon him, he abandoned the fire of the wicked in his body and infidelity in his heart. After the Lord’s resurrection, refreshed by the holy fire, he completely cleansed the excess of his threefold denial by a threefold confession of love.

For then, after that memorable catch of fish had been completed, when he came to the Lord, he saw with his disciples coals laid out, and a fish placed upon them, together with bread. Immediately, when he saw them, he set the secrets of his heart aflame with the coals of love.

“And some who had risen brought false testimony against him, saying: ‘We heard him say: “I will destroy this temple made with hands, and after three days I will build another not made with hands.”’” How are they false witnesses if they say what we read that the Lord said? A false witness, however, is one who does not understand words in the same sense in which they are spoken. The Lord had spoken about the temple of his body, but they slandered him through the very words, adding or changing a few things as though they were making a legitimate accusation.

The Savior had said: “Destroy this temple.” They change this and say: “I will destroy this temple made with hands.” “You,” he says, “destroy it, not I,” because it is unlawful for us to inflict death upon ourselves. Then they alter it to: “And after three days I will build another not made with hands,” so that he appears to have spoken specifically about the Jewish temple. But the Lord, to show that the temple was a living and breathing one, had said: “And I will raise it up in three days.” To build is one thing; to raise up is another.

“And the high priest, rising, stood in the midst and questioned Jesus, saying: ‘Do you answer nothing to what these men are accusing you of?’ But he was silent and answered nothing.” A headlong and impatient anger, finding no place for accusation, drives the high priest from his seat, so that he displays the madness of his mind through the movement of his body. The more Jesus remained silent before those unworthy of his answer—false witnesses and impious priests—the more the high priest, overcome by fury, provoked him to answer, seeking an opportunity for accusation from any statement he might make. Nevertheless, Jesus remains silent. For, as God, he knew that whatever he answered would be twisted into slander. Again the high priest questioned him and said:

“‘Are you the Christ, the Son of the Blessed?’ Jesus said to him: ‘I am.’” In Matthew it is written that, when the high priest questioned him under oath as to whether he was the Christ, he answered: “You have said so.” For this Mark substituted “I am,” evidently to show that what Jesus said—“You have said so”—had the same force as if he had said, “I am.”

“And you will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of the Power and coming with the clouds of heaven.” Therefore, if contempt, weakness, and the cross are an offense to you in Christ, O Jew, pagan, and heretic, see that through these things the Son of Man will sit at the right hand of God the Father; and that, born as a human being from the Virgin’s womb, he will come in his majesty with the clouds of heaven.

Hence the Apostle, after describing the humiliation of the cross, saying, “He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross” (Philippians 2), added: “Therefore God also exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, in the glory of God the Father.”

“Then the high priest, tearing his garments, said: ‘What further need have we of witnesses? You have heard the blasphemy.’” The one whom fury had driven from the priestly seat is now provoked by rage to tear his garments. He tears his garments to show that the Jews had lost their priestly garment, or glory, and possessed an empty high-priestly seat.

It is also Jewish custom, when they hear something blasphemous and seemingly directed against God, to tear their garments. We likewise read that Paul and Barnabas did this when, in Lycaonia, they were being honored with the worship of gods (Acts 14). But Herod, because he did not give glory to God and yielded to the people’s excessive favor, was immediately struck by an angel.

At a deeper level of mystery, it happened that, during the Lord’s Passion, the Jewish high priest himself tore his garments, while the Lord’s tunic could not be torn even by the soldiers who crucified him. This signified that the priesthood of the Jews, because of the crimes of their high priests, would be torn apart and completely separated from its state of integrity.

But the solidity of the holy universal Church, which is customarily called the garment of its Redeemer, can never be torn apart. Rather, even if Jews, Gentiles, heretics, or bad Catholics despise the humility of the Lord and Savior, nevertheless, until the consummation of the age, its purity will remain inviolate in those whom the lot of election finds among them.

“And some began to spit on him, to cover his face, to strike him with blows, and to say to him: ‘Prophesy.’ And the servants struck him with slaps.” Here the prophecy was fulfilled that says: “I gave my cheeks to those who struck me, and I did not turn my face away from the shame of spitting” (Isaiah 50).

But the one who was then struck with the fists or slaps of the Jews is also struck now by the blasphemies of false Christians. The one who was then spat upon by the saliva of unbelievers is still dishonored by the madness of those who are unbelievers in name only, and is provoked by insults.

They covered his face, not so that he himself would not see their crimes, but so that, as they had once done to Moses, they might hide from themselves the grace of knowing him. For if they believed Moses, they would perhaps also believe the Lord. This veil remains upon their heart unrevealed to this day, but it has been removed from us who believe in Christ.

For it was not without reason that, when he died, the veil of the temple was torn in two. The holy mysteries that had been hidden throughout the whole period of the Law and concealed from carnal Israel were revealed to the worshipers of the New Testament.

When they say to him, “Prophesy,” and, according to the other evangelists, “Who is it who struck you?”, they speak as an insult to the one whom they wanted the people to regard as a prophet. But through the dispensation of the one who suffers, everything happens for our sake, just as Peter urges (1 Peter 4): since Christ suffered in the flesh, let us arm ourselves with the same thought and prepare ourselves to endure insults and mockery for his name.

“And while Peter was below in the courtyard, one of the high priest’s maidservants came. When she saw Peter warming himself, she looked at him and said: ‘You also were with Jesus the Nazarene.’ But he denied it, saying: ‘I neither know nor understand what you are saying.’” What does it mean that a maidservant is the first to expose him, when men could certainly have recognized him more easily, unless it was so that this sex also might appear to have sinned in the Lord’s death, and this sex might be redeemed through the Lord’s Passion? Therefore, a woman is the first to receive the mysteries of the Resurrection and to preserve the commands, so that she might erase the ancient error of transgression.

“And he went outside, before the courtyard, and the rooster crowed.” The other evangelists are silent about this crowing of the rooster, but they do not deny that it happened, just as some have passed over in silence many other things that others recount.

“Again, when another maidservant saw him, she began to say to those standing nearby: ‘This man is one of them.’ But he denied it again.” We should not think that this was the same maidservant who had accused him earlier. For Matthew says quite clearly: “As he was going out through the gate, another maidservant saw him and said to those who were there” (Matthew 27).

From this denial of Peter we learn that one denies Christ not only by saying that he is not the Christ, but also by denying, while being one, that one is a Christian. The Lord did not say to Peter, “You will deny my disciple,” but “You will deny me.” He therefore denied Christ when he denied that he was his disciple.

“And after a little while those standing nearby said to Peter: ‘Truly, you are one of them, for you are also a Galilean.’” This does not mean that Galileans spoke a different language from the people of Jerusalem, since both were Hebrews, but that each province and region has its own characteristics and cannot avoid its native manner of speech.

Thus, in the Acts of the Apostles, when those upon whom the Holy Spirit had come were speaking in the languages of all nations, among the others who had come from different parts of the world, those who lived in Judea are also reported to have said: “Look, are not all these who are speaking Galileans? And how do we each hear our own language in which we were born?” (Acts 11).

And Peter, speaking to the brothers in Jerusalem, says: “It became known to all the inhabitants of Jerusalem, so that that field was called in their language Haceldama” (Acts 1). Why was their language so called, unless the same name sounded one way among them—that is, the people of Jerusalem—and another way among the Galileans?

“But he began to curse and to swear: ‘I do not know this man whom you are talking about.’ And immediately the rooster crowed a second time.” Sacred Scripture often indicates the merit or character of events by the course of times. Thus Peter, who denied at midnight, repented at the crowing of the rooster. After the Lord’s Resurrection, in the daylight, he likewise professed three times that he loved the one whom he had denied three times.

For the one who had gone astray in the darkness of forgetfulness corrected himself at the recollection of the light that was already hoped for, and, having attained the presence of that true light, fully raised up everything within him that he had distorted. I think that this rooster should be understood as some teacher who, awakening us when we lie down and rebuking the sleepy, says: “Awake, you righteous, and do not sin” (1 Corinthians 15).

“And Peter remembered the word that Jesus had said to him: ‘Before the rooster crows twice, you will deny me three times.’ And he began to weep.” How harmful are the conversations of the wicked! Peter himself, among unbelievers, denied knowing even the man whom he had already confessed among his fellow disciples to be the Son of God. But while he was held in Caiaphas’s courtyard, he could not perform his repentance. He goes outside, as the other evangelists recount, so that, separated from the council of the impious, he might cleanse the filth of his fearful denial with free-flowing tears.

“And immediately, in the morning, the chief priests, with the elders and scribes and the whole council, taking counsel, bound Jesus, led him away, and handed him over to Pilate.” He was led not only to Pilate but also to Herod, so that both might mock the Lord. And observe the priests’ diligence in evil: they stayed awake all night in order to commit murder.

“And they handed him over to Pilate bound.” For they had this custom: whoever they had condemned to death, they handed over to the judge bound. Nevertheless, it should be noted that they did not bind him for the first time then. Rather, immediately after seizing him in the garden at night, they bound him, as John explains, and thus led him first to Annas.

[Col. 0410A] “And Pilate questioned him: ‘Are you the king of the Jews?’” Since Pilate asked about no other charge except whether he was the king of the Jews, the Jews are convicted of impiety, because they could not find even a false accusation to bring against the Savior.

“But he answered and said to him: ‘You say so.’” He answered in such a way that he spoke the truth, while his statement did not expose itself to slander. Observe that he answered Pilate, who was passing judgment amid vices, in some measure, but did not wish to answer the priests and rulers, judging them unworthy of his speech.

“Pilate again questioned him, saying: ‘Do you answer nothing? See how many things they accuse you of.’ But Jesus still answered nothing.” The one who condemns Jesus is indeed a pagan, but he refers the charge back to the Jewish people: “See how many things they accuse you of.” Jesus did not wish to answer anything further, lest, by dissolving the charge, he be released by the governor and the benefit of the cross be postponed.

“But the chief priests stirred up the crowd so that he would release Barabbas to them instead.” To this day the Jews bear the consequence of the request they obtained with such effort. For when they were given the choice, they chose a robber instead of Jesus, a murderer instead of the Savior, and a destroyer instead of the giver of life. They deservedly lost salvation and life and subjected themselves so greatly to robberies and sedition that they also lost the homeland and kingdom they loved more than Christ. To this point they have not deserved to regain the freedom—whether of soul or of body—that they sold.

“But Pilate, answering again, said to them: ‘What then do you want me to do with the king of the Jews?’ But they cried out again: ‘Crucify him!’ Pilate said to them: ‘Why, what evil has he done?’” Pilate gave many opportunities to release the Savior. First, he contrasted him with a robber; then he said: “What then do you want me to do with the king of the Jews?” When they answered, “Let him be crucified,” he did not immediately agree but, following the prompting of his wife, who had sent him word, as Matthew writes, “Have nothing to do with that righteous man” (Matthew 27), he himself also answered: “Why, what evil has he done?” By saying this, Pilate acquitted Jesus.

“But they shouted even more loudly: ‘Crucify him!’” Thus was fulfilled what he had said in the twenty-first Psalm: “Many dogs have surrounded me; the assembly of the wicked has besieged me.” Isaiah also speaks suitably in this passage: “I expected him to execute judgment” (Isaiah 5). And the words of Jeremiah: “My inheritance has become for me like a lion in the forest; they raised their voices against me” (Jeremiah 12). They committed iniquity and not justice, but an outcry.

“But Pilate, wishing to satisfy the crowd, released Barabbas to them and handed Jesus over, having scourged him, to be crucified.” Jesus is to be understood as having been scourged by Pilate himself, and by no one else. For John writes plainly: “Again they all cried out, saying: ‘Not this man, but Barabbas.’ Now Barabbas was a robber” (John 18). Then he adds: “So Pilate took Jesus and scourged him.”

“And the soldiers, weaving a crown of thorns, placed it upon his head.” They did this, and it should be believed that they handed him over to the soldiers to be mocked for this reason: so that, once the Jews had been satisfied with his punishments and insults, they would cease thirsting for his death. This happened because, since it was written, “Many are the scourges of the sinner” (Psalm 32), when he was scourged we might be freed from blows, as Scripture says: “The scourge will not approach your dwelling” (Psalm 91).

“And the soldiers led him into the courtyard of the praetorium and summoned the whole cohort. They clothed him in purple and, weaving a crown of thorns, placed it upon him, and began to salute him: ‘Hail, king of the Jews!’” Since the soldiers had been told that he was the king of the Jews, and since the scribes and priests had brought this charge against him—that he was usurping authority over the people of Israel—they did this in mockery. They stripped him of his former garments and clothed him in purple, which ancient kings used to wear.

Instead of a diadem, they placed upon him a crown of thorns; instead of a royal scepter, they gave him a reed, as Matthew writes, and they worshiped him as though he were a king. We should understand all these things mystically. For just as Caiaphas said, “It is better that one man should die for the people” (John 11), not knowing what he was saying, so these men, whatever they did, although they acted with another intention, nevertheless bestowed mysteries upon us who believe.

It should be noted that where Mark says, “They clothed him in purple,” Matthew writes: “They stripped him and wrapped him in a scarlet cloak” (Matthew 27). The mockers used that scarlet cloak in place of royal purple; it was a kind of red purple, very similar to scarlet. It may be that Mark also mentioned purple because of the color of the cloak, even though it was scarlet.

Mystically, the purple with which the Lord was clothed signifies his flesh, which he exposed to sufferings. Concerning it, the preceding prophecy had said: “Why then is your garment red, and your clothing like that of those who tread in the winepress?” (Isaiah 63).

In the crown of thorns that he wore is signified the taking upon himself of our sins, for which he is shown to have become mortal, in accordance with the testimony of his forerunner, who said of him: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1). The Lord himself confirms that thorns are placed as a sign of sins, when he said to the first human being, after his fall into sin: “Your land shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you” (Genesis 3). This is plainly to say: “Your conscience will not cease to produce for you the pricks and stings of vices.”

But where, according to Luke’s Gospel, the Lord is clothed by Herod in a white garment, while in the other evangelists he is said to have been mocked by Pilate’s soldiers in purple or scarlet clothing, the two accounts, considered together, express on the one hand the innocence and purity of the humanity he assumed, and on the other the reality of the Passion, through which he would attain the glory of the immortal kingdom.

For just as purple imitates the color of the blood poured out for us, so it also signifies the form of the kingdom into which the Lord entered after his Passion and whose entrance he opened for us. Since the Apostle says, “All of you who were baptized into Christ have clothed yourselves with Christ” (Galatians 3), and Isaiah says to the Lord concerning the elect, “You will clothe yourself with all these as with an ornament” (Isaiah 49), in these two garments of the Lord—not according to the shameful judgment of his enemies, but according to the most glorious election of the Lord himself—the whole multitude of his elect may most fittingly be signified, distinguished into venerable martyrs and the rest of the faithful people.

He is clothed in a white garment when he is surrounded by the pure confession of the righteous. He is clothed in purple or scarlet when he exults in the triumph of victorious martyrs.

“And they struck his head with a reed, spat upon him, and, bending their knees, worshiped him.” The soldiers of Pilate did these things then; heretics and pagans, who are truly the soldiers of the devil, do them even now.

Because God is the head of Christ, those strike his head who deny that he is true God. And because Scripture is customarily written with a reed, they strike Christ’s head as though with a reed when, contradicting his divinity, they attempt to confirm their error by the authority of Sacred Scripture.

They spit in Christ’s face who, from the inner madness of a blind mind, reject the presence of his grace with accursed words and deny that Jesus Christ came in the flesh.

The soldiers worshiped him in mockery, as though he had falsely claimed to be God. But today there are people guilty of more serious madness: they worship him with certain faith as the true God, but then, by their perverse actions, immediately despise his words as though they were fables and place his promises of the kingdom far behind the attractions of temporal things.

“And they led him out to crucify him. And they compelled a passerby, Simon of Cyrene, who was coming from the countryside, the father of Alexander and Rufus, to carry his cross.” This Simon appears to have been a man of great renown at that time, since even his sons are designated by name, as though already known to everyone.

But we must take care lest anyone think it contradictory that John writes that the Lord himself carried his cross, while the other evangelists report that this Simon of Cyrene carried it. First it was carried by the Lord, and afterward it was placed upon Simon to carry, since they happened to encounter him as they were going out.

This also accords sufficiently with the order of the mystery: the Lord himself suffered for us, leaving us an example so that we might follow his footsteps (1 Peter 2).

And because this Simon is said to have been not a Jerusalemite but a Cyrenian—and Cyrene is a city of Libya, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 2)—the peoples of the nations are rightly signified through him. Once strangers and foreigners to the covenants, they are now, through obedience, fellow citizens and members of God’s household, and, as it is said elsewhere, “heirs indeed of God, and joint heirs with Christ” (Romans 8).

Accordingly, Simon is aptly interpreted as “obedient,” and Cyrene as “heir.” Nor should it be passed over that this same Simon is reported to have come from the countryside. A countryside is called a *pagus*, from which we call those people pagans who are alien to the city of God and, as it were, without the urban way of life.

But Simon, coming out from the *pagus*, carries the cross behind Jesus when the people of the nations, abandoning pagan rites, obediently embrace the footsteps of the Lord’s Passion.

“And they brought him to the place called Golgotha, which is interpreted as ‘the place of the Skull.’” Outside the city and beyond the gate are places where the heads of warriors are cut off, and they took the name “Calvary,” that is, the place of those who have been beheaded.

For this reason the Lord was crucified there: so that, where formerly there had been a field of the condemned, the standards of martyrdom might be raised. And just as for the salvation of all he became the curse of the cross, was scourged, and was crucified, so for the salvation of all he is crucified as though he were guilty, among the guilty.

[Col. 0413B] “And they gave him wine mixed with myrrh, but he did not accept it.” God speaks to Jerusalem: “I planted you as my true vineyard; how have you been changed into the bitterness of a foreign vine?” (Jer. II). A bitter vine produces bitter wine and offers it to the Lord Jesus, so that what is written might be fulfilled: “They gave me gall for food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink” (Ps. LXVIII). What is said—“but he did not accept it”—or, according to Matthew (Matt. XXVII), “when he had tasted it, he would not drink,” indicates that he indeed tasted the bitterness of death for us, but rose again on the third day. For when Mark says, “he did not accept it,” this means that he did not accept it in order to drink it; he did taste it, as Matthew testifies. And what Matthew says, “he would not drink,” Mark had expressed as “he did not accept it.” Moreover, what Mark calls “wine mixed with myrrh” is to be understood as what Matthew called “mixed with gall.” For Matthew used “gall” to signify bitterness, and wine mixed with myrrh is extremely bitter; although it may also be that both gall and myrrh made the wine exceedingly bitter.

“And crucifying him, they divided his garments, casting lots over them to determine what each should take.” John the Evangelist explains this more fully (John XIX): the soldiers divided the other garments into four parts, according to their number, but cast lots for the tunic, which was seamless and woven from the top throughout. The Lord’s four-part garment represented his four-part Church, spread throughout the whole world, which consists of four regions, and distributed equally—that is, harmoniously—among all those regions. The tunic for which they cast lots signifies the unity of all the parts, held together by the bond of charity. For since charity, according to the Apostle, has the more excellent way, surpasses knowledge, and is above all commandments, it is rightly said that the garment symbolizing it was woven from the top throughout. What else is commended by the casting of lots except the grace of God? Thus it comes to all through one, when the lot pleases everyone; for the grace of God also comes to all through one, and when the lot is cast, the decision is entrusted not to anyone’s person or merits but to God’s hidden judgment. And because, as the Apostle says, our old self was crucified together with him, so that the body of sin might be destroyed and we might no longer serve sin (Rom. VI), as long as our works are accomplishing the destruction of the body of sin, as long as the outward person is being corrupted so that the inward person may be renewed day by day, it is the time of the cross. These are indeed good works, but they are still laborious; their reward is rest. Yet it is said, “rejoicing in hope,” so that with cheerfulness we may undertake the future rest amid our labors. This cheerfulness is signified by the height of the cross in the transverse beam, where the hands are fastened. By the hands we understand works; by the breadth, the cheerfulness of the one who works, since sorrow causes narrowness; and by the height, to which the head is attached, the expectation of reward from the lofty justice of God, who will repay each according to his works: eternal life to those who seek glory, honor, and incorruption through endurance in good work. Thus the length, by which the whole body is extended, signifies endurance itself. Hence those who endure are called long-suffering. The depth, fixed into the earth, prefigures the mystery’s hiddenness. I shall explain these words of the Apostle as an account of the cross’s meaning, where he says: “Rooted and founded in charity, so that you may be able to comprehend with all the saints what is the length, breadth, height, and depth” (Eph. III).

“And it was the third hour, and they crucified him.” Some think that the Lord was crucified at the third hour, while darkness began from the sixth hour and lasted until the ninth, so that the three hours from his crucifixion until the darkness began are understood to have elapsed. This could indeed be understood most appropriately, unless John said that at about the sixth hour Pilate sat on the tribunal, in the place called Lithostrotos, and in Hebrew Gabbatha. For what follows is: “It was the preparation of Passover, about the sixth hour, and he says to the Jews: Behold your king” (John XIX). If, then, at about the sixth hour, while Pilate was sitting on the tribunal, he was handed over by the Jews to be crucified, how was he crucified at the third hour, as some have thought because they did not understand Mark’s words? Mark had already said: “And crucifying him, they divided his garments.” If, therefore, he intended to mention the time when that event occurred, it would have been enough to say: “It was the third hour.” Why did he add, “and they crucified him,” unless he wished, by way of recapitulation, to signify something that would be found useful when Scripture itself was being read in those times when it was known throughout the churches at what hour the Lord was suspended on the wood—so that either this error might be corrected or this falsehood refuted? But because he knew that the Lord was crucified by the soldiers, not by the Jews, he wished secretly to show that those who cried out for him to be crucified had crucified him more than those who performed their service for their ruler according to their duty. It is therefore understood that it was the third hour when the Jews cried out for the Lord to be crucified. It is most truthfully shown that they crucified him at the time when they cried out, especially since they wished it not to appear that they had done this. For this reason they handed him over to Pilate, as their words sufficiently indicate according to John. Thus Mark shows that they did at the third hour precisely what they most wished not to appear to have done, indicating most truthfully that the Lord was killed more by the tongue of the Jews than by the hand of the soldiers.

“And there was an inscription of the charge against him written above: The King of the Jews.” The inscription placed above his cross, on which was written “The King of the Jews,” showed that even by killing him they could not bring it about that they would not have him as king, because by his most manifest power he will repay them according to their deeds. Hence he sings in the Psalm: “But I have been appointed king by him over Zion, his holy mountain” (Ps. II). And appropriately, since he is both king and priest, when he offered to the Father the outstanding sacrifice of his flesh upon the altar of the cross, he displayed in the inscription also the dignity of the king who had been proclaimed king, so that he might make known to all who wished to read—that is, to hear and believe—that through the cross’s gallows he had not lost his power but rather confirmed and strengthened it.

“And with him they crucify two robbers, one on his right and the other on his left.” The robbers who were crucified with the Lord signify those who, under faith in and confession of Christ, undertake either the struggle of martyrdom or any stricter discipline of self-restraint. But whoever undertook these things solely for eternal and heavenly glory is clearly represented by the merit and faith of the robber on the right. Those, however, who renounce the world either with an eye to human praise or with any other less worthy intention rightly imitate the mind and actions of the blasphemer and the robber on the left. Of such the Apostle says: “If I deliver my body so that it may burn, if I give all my possessions as food for the poor, if I perform many other works of piety so that I may appear to have received spiritual gifts, but do not have charity, it profits me nothing” (1 Cor. XIII). Blessed are those who leave their possessions for the Lord and for the Gospel. “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. V).

“Likewise the chief priests, mocking him, said to one another with the scribes: He saved others; he cannot save himself.” Even unwillingly, the scribes and chief priests confess that he saved others. Thus your own sentence condemns you. For the one who saved others certainly could have saved himself, if he had wished.

[Col. 0415D] “Christ, the King of Israel, let him now descend from the cross, so that we may see and believe.” A deceitful promise. What is greater: to descend alive from the cross, or to rise dead from the tomb? He rose, and you do not believe; therefore, even if he descended from the cross, you likewise would not believe. “And those who were crucified with him reviled him.” How is this true, since one of them reviled him, according to Luke’s testimony, while the other restrained him and believed in God? We must understand that Matthew and Mark, touching the matter briefly, used the plural number for the singular here, just as in the Epistle to the Hebrews we read the plural expression “they closed the mouths of lions” (Heb. XI), although only Daniel is understood; and “they were sawn asunder,” although only Isaiah is understood. For what is more ordinary, for example, than for someone to say, “The peasants insult me,” even if only one insults him? It would then be contrary if Luke had revealed that one did so, while they had said that both robbers reviled the Lord. Yet even then one could be understood under the plural number. But when it is said “the robbers,” or “those who were crucified with him,” and “both” is not added, this could be said not only if both had done it, but also because one did it and, according to customary speech, could be signified by the plural number. Since, however, according to Luke’s testimony, one robber blasphemes the Lord, saying, “Save yourself and us,” while the other rebukes him with a fitting reprimand and entreats the Lord with faithful supplication, saying, “Lord, remember me when you come into your kingdom” (Luke XXIII), we see the same thing happening in the Church to this day, when true and false Christians alike are touched by the afflictions of the world. Those who carry the mysteries of the Lord’s passion with a feigned mind wish to be freed by the Lord for the joys of the present life; they do not, with a sincere intention and together with the Apostle, glory in the cross alone of our Lord Jesus Christ. The true Christians, rather, desire to be rescued from present troubles so as to commend their spirit into the hands of its author and, together with him, desire to share in the heavenly kingdom. Hence the one who prayed to the Lord with doubtful faith was rightly rejected completely by the Lord and considered unworthy of any response. But the prayers of the one who sought eternal salvation from him the Lord soon deigned to receive with merciful hearing. For whoever, placed in tribulations, seeks only temporal consolations from the Lord is recompensed with temporal things and deprived of eternal joys. Those who truly long for the good things of the heavenly homeland reach them without any doubt, through Christ’s mercy.

“And when the sixth hour had come, darkness came over the whole earth until the ninth hour.” The most brilliant light of the world withdrew its rays, lest it see the Lord hanging there or the impious blasphemers enjoy its light. It should be noted that the Lord, at the sixth hour—that is, after the sun had already risen—celebrated the mysteries of his resurrection. He marked the appointed time and displayed the event corresponding to that time: he who died for our sins and rose for our justification. For it is also written that when Adam sinned, he heard the voice of the Lord God walking in the garden at the evening breeze (Gen. III). “After noon” signifies the light of faith having declined; “at the breeze,” the fervor of charity having cooled; and “walking,” because God was heard to withdraw from the sinful human being. Reason—indeed, the wealth of divine mercy—therefore required that at the same hour when he had then closed paradise to Adam in his transgression, the Lord should now open its gate to the repentant robber; and that at the hour when the first Adam, by sinning, brought death into this world, the second Adam should at that same hour destroy death by dying.

“And at the ninth hour Jesus cried out with a loud voice, [Col. 0417A] saying: Eloi, Eloi, lamma sabachtani? Which is translated: My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” “Why,” and so forth. He used the beginning of the twenty-first Psalm. The words in the middle of the verse, “Look upon me,” are superfluous. For in Hebrew it reads: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” Do not be surprised at the humility of the words or at the complaints of one who has been forsaken, when you recognize the form of a servant and see the scandal of the cross. Just as hunger, thirst, and weariness were not proper to the Godhead but to bodily suffering, so also the words “Why have you forsaken me?” were proper to the bodily voice, by which the body according to its nature ordinarily has no desire to be deprived of the life joined to it. Although he himself said this, he was specifically displaying the body’s frailty while remaining the power and wisdom of God. Thus he speaks as a human being, carrying my movements—the feelings by which, when we are placed in dangers, we think we are abandoned by God—or he is troubled as a human being, weeps as a human being, and is crucified as a human being.

“And some of those standing nearby, when they heard this, were saying: Behold, he is calling Elijah.” Not all of them, but some, whom I think were Roman soldiers, did not understand the particular character of the Hebrew expression but, from his saying “Eli, Eli,” thought that he was calling Elijah. If, however, you wish to understand these as Jews who said this, they are also acting according to their customary manner, slandering the Lord in his weakness because he is supposedly imploring Elijah’s aid.

“But one ran and, filling a sponge with vinegar and placing it around a reed, gave him a drink, saying: Let us see whether Elijah comes to take him down.” John explains more fully why vinegar was given the Lord to drink, saying: “Afterward, knowing that all things had now been accomplished, so that the Scripture might be fulfilled, Jesus said: I thirst. A vessel full of vinegar had been placed there. They, putting a sponge full of vinegar around hyssop, offered it to his mouth” (John XIX). Before he accepted the vinegar and gave up his spirit, he saw that all things that had to happen had been accomplished; and, so that this too might be fulfilled, he said: “And in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink” (Ps. LXVIII). “I thirst,” he said, as though he were saying: “You have done this one thing short; give what you are.” For the Jews themselves were vinegar, degenerating from the wine of the patriarchs and prophets. They had a heart filled with the iniquity of this world, as though from a full vessel, like a sponge made fraudulent by hidden places that were in some way cavernous and twisted. The hyssop around which they placed the sponge full of vinegar, because it is a humble herb and cleanses the breast, we appropriately understand as Christ’s humility, which they surrounded and which they thought they had outwitted. Hence the Psalm says: “You shall sprinkle me with hyssop, Lord, and I shall be cleansed” (Ps. L). We are cleansed by Christ’s humility, because unless he had humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death—even death on a cross—his blood would not have been poured out for the remission of sins, that is, for our cleansing. By the reed on which the sponge was placed, Scripture is signified, for Scripture was fulfilled in the deed. Just as a language is called Greek, Latin, or any other language because it signifies the sound expressed by the tongue, so a letter may be called a reed because it is written with a reed. But we very commonly call the sounds of the human voice “tongues”; to call Scripture a “reed” is less customary and therefore more mystically figurative.

“But Jesus, uttering a loud cry, breathed his last.” What the Lord said with this loud cry Luke clearly indicates: “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit. And having said this, he breathed his last” (Luke XXIII). John writes that, after he had received the vinegar, he said: “It is finished. And bowing his head, he gave up his spirit” (John XIX). Between the words “It is finished” and “bowing his head, he gave up his spirit,” that loud cry was uttered, which John omitted but the other three Evangelists recorded.

“And the veil of the temple was torn in two, from top to bottom.” The veil of the temple is torn so that the ark of the Testament and all the mysteries of the law that had been covered might appear and pass over to the people of the nations. Formerly it had been said: “God is known in Judah; his name is great in Israel” (Ps. LXXV). Now, however: “Be exalted above the heavens, O God, and your glory over all the earth” (Ps. LVI). And in the Gospel he had previously said: “Do not go into the way of the Gentiles” (Matt. X); but after his passion: “Go into all the world and teach all nations” (Matt. XXVIII).

“When the centurion who stood opposite him saw that he had breathed his last while crying out in this way, he said: Truly this man was the Son of God.” The evident cause of the centurion’s wonder is explained: seeing the Lord breathe his last in this way—that is, give up his spirit—he said, “Truly this man was the Son of God.” For no one has power to give up his spirit except the one who is the creator of souls. It should also be considered that the centurion, standing before the cross amid the very scandal of the passion, confesses him to be the true Son of God, while Arius preaches a creature in the Church. Therefore, rightly, the faith of the Church is represented by the centurion: once the heavenly mysteries have been disclosed through the Lord’s death, she immediately confirms Jesus, both truly a righteous man and truly the Son of God, while the Synagogue remains silent.

“There were also women looking on from a distance, among whom were Mary Magdalene, and Mary the mother of James the younger and of Joses, and Salome. And when he was in Galilee, they followed him and ministered to him.” He calls James “the younger” the James who was Alphaeus’s son, who was also called the brother of the Lord because he was the son of the Lord’s maternal aunt, whom John mentions in his Gospel, saying: “There stood by the cross of Jesus his mother, and his mother’s sister, Mary of Clopas.” He seems to call her Mary of Clopas from her father or from her kinship. He called James “the younger” to distinguish him from James the elder, namely the son of Zebedee, whom the Lord called and chose among the first Apostles. It is a Jewish custom—and, according to the practice of that ancient people, it was not considered blameworthy—for women to provide their teachers with food and clothing from their own resources. Because this could cause scandal among the nations, Paul recalls that he rejected it: “Do we not have the authority to lead around believing women as sisters, as the other Apostles do?” (1 Cor. IX). They ministered to the Lord from their resources, so that he might reap their material goods, while they reaped spiritual goods. This was not because the Lord of creatures needed food, but so that he might show the model for teachers: they ought to be content with food and clothing from their disciples. But let us see what kind of companions he had: Mary Magdalene, from whom he had cast out seven demons; Mary the mother of James and Joses, his maternal aunt; and the others whom we read about in the other Gospels.
