“When evening had already come, since it was the preparation, which is before the Sabbath, Joseph of Arimathea, a noble councillor, came.” A councillor is one who belongs to the order of the curia and administers the office of the curia; he is also commonly called a *curialis* because he oversees civic duties. Arimathea itself is Ramathaim, the city of Elkanah and Samuel, in the Canaanite region near Diospolis. *Paraskeuē* (παρασκευή), in Greek, means “preparation.” By this name the Jews who lived among the Greeks called the sixth day of the week, because on that day they customarily prepared what was necessary for the Sabbath rest, in accordance with what was once commanded concerning the manna: “On the sixth day you shall gather twice as much” (Exod. XVI), and so forth. Since the human being was made on the sixth day and the whole creation of the world was completed, while on the seventh the Creator rested from his work—and hence he also wished this day to be understood as the Sabbath, that is, as rest—the Savior was rightly crucified on that same sixth day and fulfilled the mystery of the restoration of humanity. Therefore, when Jesus had received the vinegar, he said, “It is finished”: that is, on the sixth day everything he had undertaken for the restoration of the world was now completed. On the Sabbath, resting in the tomb, he awaited the outcome of the resurrection that was to come on the eighth day. Here an example shines before us both of our devotion and of our blessed reward: in this age of the world we must suffer for the Lord and, as it were, be crucified to the world. In the seventh age—that is, when a person pays the debt of death—our bodies must remain in the tombs, while our souls remain with the Lord in hidden peace, and after good works must rest until, at last, with the coming of the eighth age, the bodies themselves, glorified by the resurrection, receive together with their souls the incorruption of the eternal inheritance.

“Joseph, it says, came from Arimathea, a noble councillor, who himself was also awaiting the kingdom of God. And he entered boldly before Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus.” This Joseph is praised as having possessed great dignity in the world, but greater merit before God. For it was fitting that one who would bury the Lord’s body should be such a man: he would be worthy of that ministry through the merits of his righteousness and would be able to obtain the means of carrying it out through the nobility of his worldly power. For no unknown or ordinary person could approach the governor and obtain the body of one who had been crucified.

“Joseph bought a linen cloth, and taking him down, wrapped him in the linen cloth.” Even in the Lord’s simple burial, the extravagance of the rich is condemned, for they cannot be without riches even in their tombs. According to the spiritual understanding, we can also perceive that the Lord’s body was wrapped not in gold, gems, or silk but in clean linen; although this too signifies that the one who received Jesus with a pure mind wrapped him in a clean linen cloth. Hence the custom of the Church has arisen that the altar sacrifice should be celebrated not in silk or dyed cloth but in earthly linen, just as the Lord’s body was buried in a clean linen cloth, according to what we read in the pontifical records was established by blessed Pope Sylvester.

Concerning the Lord’s tomb, those who in our time came to Jerusalem from Britain report that it was a round chamber cut out of the underlying rock, of such height that a person standing inside could scarcely touch the ceiling with an outstretched hand. It had an entrance from the east, to which that great stone was rolled and set in place. In the northern part of this tomb was the sepulcher itself, that is, the place of the Lord’s body, made from the same rock. It was seven feet long and three palms in measure, rising higher than the rest of the pavement. This place was open not from above but entirely from the southern side, through which the body was carried in. The color of the tomb and of the little chamber is said to be a mixture of reddish and white.

# HOMILY LXVII. THURSDAY OF PALM WEEK, AT THE LORD’S SUPPER

(John XIII.) “At that time: Before the feast of Passover, Jesus, knowing that his hour had come to pass from this world to the Father,” and so forth. Passover is not, as some think, a Greek name but a Hebrew one. In its own language, Passover means “passing over,” because the Lord’s people first celebrated Passover when, fleeing from Egypt, they crossed the Red Sea. This figure was fulfilled in Christ according to the truth, when through his passion he passed from this world to the Father. We too must pass from this world to the Father—from temporal things to eternal things, from iniquity to righteousness, from the deceiving devil to Christ the Savior.

“When he had loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end.” He loved them so that they themselves might pass from the place where they were to their head, who had passed from here, through his love. “To the end” means that he loved them eternally. Or “to the end” means in Christ, because Christ is the end of the law.

“And when supper had taken place.” We should not understand this to mean that supper had already been completed and finished. They were still eating when the Lord rose and washed his disciples’ feet; afterward he reclined again and gave the morsel to his betrayer. “Supper had taken place” means that the meal had already been prepared for the disciples dining with their teacher.

“When the devil had already put it into the heart of Judas, son of Simon Iscariot, to betray him.” If you ask what had been put into Judas’s heart, it was certainly this: that he should betray him. This putting is a spiritual suggestion, not entering bodily ears but entering a heart that consents to iniquity. For just as the good Spirit sends good thoughts, so the evil spirit suggests evil thoughts. The difference lies in what the human mind consents to, whether it is abandoned through its deserts or assisted by divine grace. Without faith in God, the betrayer came to the banquet, not believing that the one whom he did not intend to betray was God. He seemed to be tolerated by the one whom he thought could be deceived, yet he himself was deceived; and God’s goodness used his wickedness for the salvation of others.

“Knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands”—therefore, also the betrayer himself. For if he did not have him in his hands, he certainly would not use him as he wished. The Lord knew what he was doing for his friends, since he patiently made use of his enemies. He also knew “that he had come forth from God and was going to God.” He neither abandoned God when he came forth from him nor abandoned us when he returned.

“He rises from supper and lays aside his garments.” As the Evangelist was about to speak of such great humility in the Lord, he first wished to commend his exalted status. This is the point of his saying: “Knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands.” He fulfilled not the office of the God who is Lord but of the human servant. So great is the usefulness of human humility that even divine majesty commended it by its example. “He rises from supper”: he descended from the heavenly heights. “He laid aside his garments”: that is, he emptied himself. “Having taken a linen cloth, he girded himself”: putting on the form of a servant.

“He pours water into a basin”: that is, he poured out his blood upon the earth, so that he might cleanse in himself the footsteps of those who believed in him, which had been soiled by earthly sins, and wipe them with the linen cloth he wore—that is, with the cloth of his body with which he had girded himself—because his entire passion is a cleansing. When he took the form of a servant, he did not abandon what he had; he assumed what he did not have.

“Then he came to Simon Peter.” This should not be understood as though, after washing the feet of the others, he came to the first Apostle. Rather, because he began there, Peter was astonished that the Son of God should wash his feet: the Lord washing the servant’s feet, God washing a human being’s feet. When he began to wash the disciples’ feet, he came to the one with whom he had begun, namely Peter. Then Peter—as any of them would also have been astonished—was astonished and said: “Lord, are you washing my feet?” You are God; I am human. You are Lord; I am a servant. You are Redeemer; I am a sinner.

“Jesus answered and said to him: What I am doing, you do not know now, but afterward you will understand.” You do not yet understand the mystery of this deed, but afterward you will understand.

“For if I do not wash you, you will have no part with me. Peter said: You shall never wash my feet.” He used “forever” to mean “never.” But frightened by the Lord’s reply, he said:

“Lord, not only my feet but also my hands and head.” Since you threaten that my limbs must be washed by you, I do not withhold the lower parts alone; I also offer you the higher ones. Do not deny me a share with you; I deny you no part of my body to be washed.

“Jesus answered him: Whoever has been washed has no need except to wash his feet, but is entirely clean.” How is he entirely clean and yet still needs to have his feet washed, unless he is clean in the washing of holy baptism? In baptism all our sins are forgiven. But just as a foot that treads the earth cannot be without dirt, so no one can live without sins, for which we pray every day: “Forgive us our debts” (Matt. VI). Again soiled by the dust of earthly dwelling, a person needs to be washed again through the grace of divine mercy, although by that same grace he had previously been cleansed entirely, as the Apostle John testifies: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John I). Therefore, the one who intercedes for us washes our feet every day; and that we need to wash our feet every day we confess in the Lord’s Prayer when we say: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.” “And you are clean, but not all of you.” The Evangelist explains this in the words that follow; let us therefore pass on to the rest.

[Col. 0422C] “After he had washed their feet.” That is, when the cleansing of our redemption had been completed through the shedding of his blood, he took his garments, rising from the tomb on the third day, made immortal and clothed in the same body in which he had died on the cross. “And when he had reclined again”: that is, he ascended again into heaven, sitting at the right hand of God and reclining in the majesty of the Father’s divinity, from which he will come again to judge the living and the dead. For what follows is: “He said to them: Do you know what I have done for you?” He said this in fulfillment of what he had previously promised when he answered the Apostle Peter: “What I am doing, you do not know now, but afterward you will understand.” Now is the fulfillment of that earlier promise.

“You call me Teacher and Lord, and you speak well.” Indeed, because you speak the truth. “For so I am.” He said this not out of arrogant display but in service to the truth.

“If I, then, the Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet.” If I, God and Lord, have forgiven you your sins, you also ought to forgive one another’s sins. This is what the Apostle says: “Forgiving one another, if anyone has a complaint against another; as the Lord has forgiven you, so you also must forgive one another” (Col. III). Therefore, let us forgive one another’s offenses and pray for one another’s offenses, and thus in a certain way wash one another’s feet. Although some may rightly wish to perform this bodily as an act of charity and an example of humility, spiritually it must be done by everyone in the heart, so that we forgive one another our debts, just as we ask God to forgive us our debts.

“Amen, amen, I say to you: A servant is not greater than his lord, nor an apostle greater than the one who sent him. If you know these things, you will be blessed if you do them.” He said this because the teacher of humility had washed the disciples’ feet, so that by word and example he might instruct them in the duty of charity.

“Not concerning all of you”—that is, I do not call all of you blessed. “I know whom I have chosen”: for this blessedness, so that they might be followers of my commandments. “But that the Scripture may be fulfilled: He who eats bread with me will lift up his heel against me.” That is, he will trample me. He eats bread not for his salvation but for his punishment: he ate in order to conceal himself as a betrayer, not to advance as a lover. What does he mean when elsewhere he said, “Did I not choose you twelve, and one of you is a devil?” (John VI), while here he says, “I know whom I have chosen”? That Judas was chosen not for blessedness but for the treachery of perdition, for the salvation of the world, not for his own, because it was said of him: “It would have been better for that man if he had not been born.” But those concerning whom he has just said, “I know whom I have chosen,” were chosen for the blessedness of eternal glory.

“From now on I tell you, before it happens, so that when it has happened you may believe that I am.” That is, I am the one of whom that Scripture spoke beforehand, where it says: “He who eats bread with me will lift up his heel against me” (Ps. XL).

“Whoever receives anyone whom I send receives me; and whoever receives me receives the one who sent me.” When he said this, he did not divide the unity of nature but showed the authority of the one who sends. Each person should receive the one who is sent in such a way that in him he receives or recognizes the one who sent him. If, then, you attend to Christ in the Father, you will find the teacher of the disciple; but if you attend to the Father in the Son, you will find the begetter of the Only-Begotten. Thus, in the one who was sent, he receives the one who sent him without any error.

“When Jesus had said these things, he was troubled in spirit, and testified, and said: Amen, amen, I say to you, one of you will betray me.” The approaching passion, the imminent danger, and the betrayer’s hand, whose intention he had foreknown, troubled him. He was therefore troubled in spirit by so great a crime on the betrayer’s part. Our weakness was troubled in him, not his power. Just as he suffered for us, so he was troubled for us. He who died by his own power was troubled by his own power, so that our disturbance might not fall into despair but, through compassion for our neighbors, might be turned away by repentance for our sins. His disturbance is therefore our consolation.

“Amen, amen, I say to you, one of you will betray me.” “One” in number, not in merit; in outward appearance, not in virtue; by bodily association, not by a spiritual bond; joined by flesh, not united by the fellowship of the heart. What does “of you” mean except that the one who will betray me will go forth from you?

[Col. 0424A] “The disciples therefore looked at one another, uncertain of whom he was speaking.” Such pious charity toward their teacher existed among them that, nevertheless, human weakness stirred each of them against the other. Each person’s conscience was known to himself, but the other’s was unknown.

“Now there was reclining one of his disciples in Jesus’ bosom, whom Jesus loved.” What he had said, “in his bosom,” he shortly afterward says, “upon Jesus’ breast”; it was John, as is later made clear. For this was the custom of those who ministered the sacred writings to us: whenever one of them was recounting a divine history, when he came to himself, he would speak as though of another, and thus insert himself into the arrangement of his narrative as a writer of events, not as the preacher of his own deeds. Blessed Moses did this also, narrating everything about himself as though about another.

He did not love one above all others, but loved something in him that he did not love in the others: namely, that he should pass from this life in peace and not end this life through suffering. “In the bosom of Jesus”—that is, in the secret place from which he poured forth that wondrous mystery unheard of throughout all ages: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1).

“And Simon Peter signaled to him and said to him.” He says it by signaling, not by speaking; by indicating, not by uttering. What does he say by signaling? What follows: “Who is he of whom he speaks?” Peter said these words by a bodily movement, not with the sound of his voice.

“Therefore, when he had reclined upon the breast of Jesus.” This is certainly the bosom of the breast—the secret place of wisdom.

“He says to him: ‘Lord, who is it?’ Jesus answered him: ‘It is the one to whom I shall give the dipped morsel.’ And when he had dipped the bread, he gave it to Judas, the son of Simon Iscariot. And after the morsel, Satan then entered into him.” The betrayer was exposed; the hiding places of darkness were laid bare. What he received was good, but he received it to his own harm, because the evil man received the good in an evil manner. Here we are taught how carefully we must beware of receiving a good thing wrongly. For it makes a great difference not what is received, but who receives it; nor what is given, but what sort of person is the one to whom it is given.

Therefore, after this morsel, Satan entered into the Lord’s betrayer, so that he might more fully possess one already delivered over to him—one into whom he had previously entered in order to deceive him. The presumption involved in the sacrament increased the sin of the betrayal: bread entered the ungrateful man’s belly, and the enemy entered his mind. Perhaps, therefore, that dipped morsel signified the hypocrisy of the one who came to the supper as a feigned friend and went to the Master as a false disciple.

“‘What you are doing, do quickly.’” He did not command the crime, but foretold Judas’s evil and our good. For what was worse for Judas, and what better for us, than that Christ should be betrayed by him for our benefit? He said this because he was more ready for suffering than anger for vengeance—not so much raging toward the destruction of the treacherous man as hastening toward the salvation of the faithful. [Col. 0425A] “‘What you are doing, do quickly.’” Not because it lies in your power whom you will betray, but because this is what the one who can do all things wills.

“Now none of those reclining knew why he had said this to him. For some thought, because Judas had the money box, that Jesus had said to him: ‘Buy what we need for the feast,’ or that he should give something to the poor.” The Lord therefore had a money box, preserving what the faithful offered and distributing it both for the needs of his own and to others in need. Here the pattern of ecclesiastical funds was first established, so that we might understand that the command not to think about tomorrow was not given to prevent the saints from keeping any money, but to prevent them from serving money instead of God.

“When he had received the morsel, he went out immediately. [Col. 0425B] And it was night.” It was night because the son of darkness had gone out. He went out, therefore, for the service of his own destruction and for the administration of our salvation—not with concern for our salvation, but with the intention of his own bargain. Here what the Psalmist says is fulfilled (Psalm 12): “Day pours forth the word to day,” that is, Christ was bringing forth the word of salvation to his disciples; “and night declares knowledge to night,” that is, Judas revealed to the Jews the malice of a betrayer.

Now the Lord’s words must be considered with greater attention; the words he spoke privately to his disciples that very night, before the hour of the betrayal, are most profound in their mysteries. Therefore, where the interpreter will have to labor greatly, the hearer must not be negligent. The sayings of the Most High must be considered more deeply: he conceals them so that we may seek, and reveals them so that we may find. [Col. 0425C] He is the one who closes and opens: he closes so that we may seek; he opens so that we may find; so that the seeker may receive the fruit of his toil, and the giver may have praise and gratitude for his goodness.

“And Jesus said: ‘Now the Son of Man has been glorified, and God has been glorified in him.’” Something great is signified by this glorification. Judas went out, and Jesus was glorified; the son of perdition went out, and the Son of Man was glorified. When he went out, therefore, all who belonged to the world remained in the world, and they remained with their purifier. Something similar will happen when this world, conquered by Christ, passes away, and, with the weeds separated from the wheat, the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father.

About this future glorification of the saints he spoke using the past tense. For what is future in the saints is said to have already happened in God’s predestination: “Now the Son of Man has been glorified,” as though he were saying: Behold what will occur in that glorification of mine, where there will be no evil person and no good person will perish. Yet he did not say, “Now the Son of Man has been signified” by a sign, just as it was not said, “The rock signified Christ,” but rather, “The rock was Christ.”

When he had said, “Now the Son of Man has been glorified,” he added, “And God has been glorified in him.” For the glorification of the Son of Man consists in God being glorified in him. He is not glorified in himself, but God is glorified in him; then God also glorifies him in himself. Finally, as though explaining this, he adds and says:

[Col. 0426A] “If God has been glorified in him, God also has glorified him in himself.” This means: If God has been glorified in him who did not come to do his own will, but the will of the one who sent him, then God has also glorified him in himself, so that the human nature in which the Son of Man exists—the nature assumed by the eternal Word—might also be granted immortal eternity. “And immediately,” he says, “he will glorify him,” namely, by his resurrection, not like ours at the end of the age, but immediately thereafter.

## HOMILY LXVIII. GOOD FRIDAY OF THE PARASCEVE

The Passion of Our Lord Jesus Christ according to John.

(John 18–19.) “At that time, Jesus went out with his disciples across the brook Cedron,” and so forth. Κεδρῶν is a plural genitive in Greek, which can be rendered in Latin as Cedrorum, “of cedars.” Then the time approached of which it is written in the Psalmist: “He will drink from the brook on the way,” that is, on the way of this life he drank from the brook of suffering; “therefore he will lift up his head” (Psalm 109), which the Apostle explained in this way: “Christ, obedient to the Father unto death, and death on a cross; therefore God also exalted him” (Philippians 2).

“Where there was a garden, into which he entered, he and his disciples.” He was rightly seized in the garden of our misery, so that he might lead us into the garden of his blessedness. In the garden of delights—that is, in paradise—the first father of the human race sinned, and from there he was expelled into this valley of tears. Therefore Christ, the second Adam, desired to be seized in a garden, so that the sin which the first man committed in the garden of paradise—whose name means “garden of delights”—might be erased.

“Now Judas, who betrayed him, also knew the place, because Jesus had often gone there with his disciples.” What he narrates here, namely the Lord’s entry into the garden with his disciples, did not happen immediately after the prayer had ended, whose words are introduced by “When Jesus had said these things.” Certain other events intervened, which are omitted by this evangelist but are read in the other evangelists, just as they contain many things which those others likewise omitted from their narratives.

The statement, “When Jesus had said these things,” serves to prevent us from thinking that he came into the garden before he had finished those words and that prayer which are recorded. “And Judas, who betrayed him, knew the place.” The order of the words is: “He who betrayed him knew the place, because,” he says, “Jesus had often gone there with his disciples.” There, then, the wolf covered with sheep’s clothing, and tolerated among the sheep by the household master’s profound plan, learned how to scatter the flock for a brief time by plotting against the shepherd.

“Judas, therefore,” he says, “having received a cohort and attendants from the chief priests and Pharisees, came there with lanterns, torches, and weapons.” The cohort was not a cohort of Jews but of soldiers. It should therefore be understood as having been received from the governor, as though for the purpose of seizing an accused man, with the proper order of lawful authority preserved, so that no one would dare resist those who were making the arrest. [Col. 0427A] So great a force of enemies was assembled that no one would dare either oppose or defend Jesus against those who were apprehending him. In this way his power was concealed and weakness was displayed, so that these measures might seem necessary to his enemies against him. Thus the good one makes good use of the wicked and brings good out of evil.

“But Jesus,” as the evangelist continued, “knowing all that was to come upon him,” knew and desired to be seized, because he came into the world for this purpose: that what he willed might take place. “He went forth and said: ‘Whom do you seek?’” He came forward prepared for suffering and asked whom they were seeking, not as though ignorant of their intention, but so that they might know that he himself was the one they sought.

“They answered: ‘Jesus of Nazareth.’” Jesus was called Nazarene because he was brought up in Nazareth, so that the prophecy might be fulfilled: “He shall be called a Nazarene.” “He says to them: ‘I am he.’” He did not hide himself but revealed himself, because by his own will he laid down his life for the world.

“Now Judas, who betrayed him, was also standing with them. When therefore he said to them, ‘I am he,’ they went backward and fell to the ground.” Where then was the cohort of soldiers, and the attendants of the chief priests and Pharisees? Where were the terror and the protection of their weapons? Surely a single voice saying, “I am he,” struck, repelled, and threw down such a savage crowd of hatred, terrible with weapons, without any weapon at all. For God was hiding in the flesh, and eternal day was so concealed in human limbs that they sought him, to kill him, with lanterns and torches—their darkness seeking the light.

[Col. 0427C] “‘I am he,’ he says, and he cast down the impious. What will he do when he comes to judge, who did this when he was to be judged? What will he be able to do when he reigns, who was able to do this when he was about to die?” And now everywhere throughout the Gospel Christ says, “I am he,” while the Jews await the Antichrist, so that they may go backward and fall to the ground.

Why, then, did those who came to seize him not hold him, when they heard him say, “I am he”? They sought to seize and kill him; he sought to redeem and give them life, for which reason he came to us. He displayed his power to those who sought him, because he had the power to lay down his life; when he laid it down, he showed this power at the hour of his Passion, so that the mystery of our redemption might be fulfilled.

“Therefore he asked them again: ‘Whom do you seek?’” If you are seeking him, why do you not seize him? Is it not because the hour for seizing him is not in your power, but in the power of the one who came to be seized?

“They said: ‘Jesus of Nazareth.’ Jesus answered: ‘I told you that I am he. If therefore you seek me, let these go.’” See the enemies: they do what he commands. “Let these go”—those whom he does not wish to perish. But were they not later going to die? Why, then, would he lose them if they died at that time, unless because they did not yet believe in him in the way that all who do not perish believe?

“Simon Peter, therefore, having a sword, drew it and struck the servant of the high priest and cut off his right ear. The servant’s name was Malchus.” This evangelist alone also gives the servant’s name, just as Luke alone records that the Lord touched and healed his ear.

Malchus, however, means “one who will reign.” What, then, does the ear cut off for the Lord and healed by the Lord signify, except hearing renewed by the amputation of the old condition, so that it may exist in newness of spirit and not in the oldness of the letter? Whoever receives this from Christ—who could doubt that he will then reign with Christ? He was called a servant because of legal servitude, but he is said to have been healed because of evangelical freedom.

Nevertheless, the Lord disapproved Peter’s action and forbade him to go further, saying:

“Put your sword into its sheath. Shall I not drink the cup which the Father has given me?” “Shall I not drink it?” should be read either interrogatively or reproachfully, as though he had said: “Shall I not drink the cup which the Father commanded me to drink?” Why do you wish to resist the will of the almighty Father, indeed the cup of your salvation?

In his action, that disciple wished to defend the Master, still ignorant of the dispensation of the Father’s will—namely, what he had willed would come to pass through this event. As for the cup of suffering, which he says was given to him by the Father, it is surely what the Apostle says: “If God is for us, who is against us? He who did not spare his own Son, but handed him over for us all” (Romans 8). Yet the author of this cup is also the one who drinks it; hence the same Apostle says: “Christ loved us and handed himself over for us as an offering and sacrifice to God, for a pleasing fragrance” (Ephesians 5).

[Col. 0428C] “Therefore the cohort, the tribune, and the attendants of the Jews seized Jesus and bound him.” They seized the one to whom they had drawn near, for that day was present, while they themselves remained darkness and did not hear: “Draw near to him, and be enlightened” (Psalm 33). When they seized him in that manner, they moved farther away from him. “And they bound him”—the one whom they ought rather to have wished to set free.

After the persecutors, with Judas’s betrayal, had seized and bound the Lord—who loved us and handed himself over for us, and whom the Father did not spare but handed over for us all—

“They led him first to Annas.” John does not omit the reason why they did this, for he says:

[Col. 0428D] “For he was the father-in-law of Caiaphas, who was high priest that year. Now Caiaphas was the one who had given the counsel to the Jews that it was expedient for one man to die for the people.” He was led first to Annas and afterward to Caiaphas, so that their blood relationship might make them partners in the crime.

At Moses’ command, it had been prescribed that high priests should succeed their fathers, so that the succession of generations might be preserved among the priests. Josephus reports that this Caiaphas had purchased the priesthood from Herod for only one year’s payment. It is therefore not surprising if an unjust high priest judged unjustly. Often one who enters the priesthood through avarice conducts himself in it through injustice, so that a criminal beginning may be completed by a disastrous end.

[Col. 0429A] “Simon Peter,” he says, “was following Jesus, and another disciple.” Who this disciple was should not be asserted rashly, since it is not stated. John, however, customarily identifies himself in this way and adds, “whom Jesus loved” (John 13). Perhaps, therefore, this too was the one who stood beside Jesus’ cross, to whom he entrusted the care of his mother.

Matthew also says of Peter: “Peter was following him from a distance” (Matthew 26). He followed the Lord from a distance because he was going to deny him, in order to see the outcome. He may have been eager to know, either out of love for the Master or out of human curiosity, what the high priest would decide concerning Jesus—whether he would hand him over to death or release him after having him scourged.

“But that other disciple,” he says, “was known to the high priest, and entered with Jesus into the courtyard of the high priest. Peter [Col. 0429B] was standing outside at the door.” He was standing outside because he was going to deny the Lord; he was not in Christ, since he did not dare confess Christ.

“Therefore the other disciple, who was known to the high priest, went out, spoke to the doorkeeper, and brought Peter in. The maidservant who was the doorkeeper said to Peter: ‘Are you also one of this man’s disciples?’ He said: ‘I am not.’” Here we recognize the truth of what the Truth had said shortly before: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15). Behold, the strongest pillar trembled entirely at the breath of a single breeze. Where was the boldness of the one who made promises and presumed greatly upon himself? Where are those words he spoke when he said: “Why can I not follow you now? I will lay down my life for you” (John 13)?

This is not following the Master: it is denying that one is a disciple. Is a life not laid down for the Lord in such a way that the voice of a maidservant is feared lest this should happen? Certainly, in this passage we must consider how dangerous it is for a Christian to deny that he is a Christian. For Peter did not here say that he denied Christ, but that he denied being Christ’s disciple; nevertheless, Christ himself had foretold: “You will deny me three times.” Whoever denied that he was Christ’s disciple denied Christ; likewise, whoever denies that he is a Christian out of some fear also denies Christ.

“Now the servants and attendants were standing at a charcoal fire, because it was cold, and they were warming themselves.” The cold of unbelief was in their hearts, so much so that even the chief of the apostles grew numb in that cold, because he had not yet been inflamed by the warmth of the Holy Spirit. After receiving the gift of the Holy Spirit, he not only himself feared no longer to confess Christ before the emperor and the Roman people, but even beardless boys and girls, inflamed by the warmth of the Holy Spirit, confessed Christ publicly unto death and did not fear to die for him—the one whom the key-bearer of heaven had feared to confess at the voice of a single maidservant.

“Then the high priest questioned Jesus about his disciples and about his teaching.” He did not question him out of a love of knowing the truth, but to find a charge on the basis of which Jesus might also be accused and handed over to the Roman governor for condemnation.

“Jesus answered him: ‘I have spoken openly to the world; I have always taught in the synagogue and in the temple, where all the Jews gathered, and I have said nothing in secret.’” What does it mean that he says he spoke openly and said nothing in secret, when elsewhere, while speaking to the crowds in parables, he said to the apostles: “To you it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God, but to the others in parables” (Mark 4)?

He should be understood to have said, “I have spoken openly to the world,” as though he had said: Many heard me speaking openly, and yet it was not openly for all. The very fact that he spoke openly was, in a certain sense, both open and not open. It was open because many heard, and again it was not open because they did not understand. And when he spoke separately to the disciples, he certainly was not speaking in secret. For who speaks in secret when he speaks before so many people, since it is written: “Every word shall stand on the testimony of two or three witnesses” (Deuteronomy 19), especially if he tells a few what he wishes to become known through them to many? Thus even what seemed to have been said by him secretly was, in a certain sense, not said in secret. For it was not spoken in such a way that those to whom it had been said would keep silent about it, but rather so that it might be proclaimed everywhere.

“Why do you question me? Question those who heard what I spoke to them. Behold, they know what I said.” As though he had said: Why do you question me, when you do not desire to hear the truth from me but wish to condemn me? Question those instead whose words will not arouse your hostility. Thus the Lord tempered his response so that he would neither appear to conceal the truth nor to defend himself.

“When he had said these things, one of the attendants standing nearby struck Jesus on the face, saying: ‘Is this how you answer the high priest?’” Here what had been prophesied about him is fulfilled: “I gave my cheeks to those who struck them” (Isaiah 50). He struck him as though he were guilty because of his answer, but the one unjustly struck replied gently:

“If I have spoken wrongly, testify about the wrong. But if I have spoken rightly”—that is, truthfully—“why do you strike me?” Everyone who speaks against the truth speaks wrongly. If I have not spoken the truth, testify against me concerning the lie I told. But if I have spoken rightly, that is, truthfully, why do you strike me?

What could be truer, gentler, or more just in this response? If we consider who it was that received the slap, would we not want the one who struck him either to be consumed by heavenly fire, swallowed up by the opening earth, or seized by a demon and thrown about? For what of these could not the one through whom the world was made have done by his power, had he not preferred to teach us patience—the one by whom the world is conquered?

Perhaps someone here asks why he did not offer the other cheek to be struck. In accordance with his command, he not only offered the other cheek to the one striking him, but also handed over his whole body to be crucified. The Lord prefers to keep his commands in the tranquility of the heart rather than display them through ostentation of the body.

“And Annas sent him bound to Caiaphas the high priest.” These two, Annas and Caiaphas, were leaders among the priests and administered the priesthood in alternating annual terms; it was Caiaphas’s year when Christ suffered. We should believe that it happened according to Caiaphas’s wishes that he was led first to Annas, so that it might seem a lesser fault if he were condemned by the judgment of another fellow priest as well.

But after the evangelist had said that Annas sent him bound to Caiaphas, he returned to the point in the narrative where he had left Peter, in order to explain what had happened in Annas’s house concerning his threefold denial.

“Now,” he says, “Simon Peter was standing and warming himself.” This repeats what he had already said earlier; then he joins what followed: “Therefore they said to him: ‘Are you also one of his disciples?’ He denied it and said: ‘I am not.’” He had already denied him once at the maidservant’s voice; behold, terrified again by the same fear, he spoke—or rather denied—again. Then, so that the third denial might also be completed and the word of God proclaiming it fulfilled:

“One of the servants of the high priest, a relative of the man whose ear Peter had cut off, said to him: ‘Did I not see you in the garden with him?’ Peter therefore denied again, as before, and immediately the cock crowed.” Behold, the physician’s prediction was fulfilled and the sick man’s presumption was convicted. For what Peter had said did not happen: “I will lay down my life for you”; rather, what Christ had foretold happened: “You will deny me three times.”

Yet this threefold denial born of fear is washed away by a threefold confession born of love. Love had not yet come which would cast out fear; servile fear still prevailed in his heart. The one who had foretold these things to him had not yet looked upon him. But we must believe that this occurred through God’s great dispensation, so that the one to whom Christ, returning to the Father, was going to entrust his sheep might learn through his own weakness to show mercy to another and forgive the faults of his brothers, while remembering his own sin; and that he might be able to share the weakness of others, since he was not ignorant of his own fall.

When Peter’s threefold denial had been completed, the evangelist returned to the order of his narrative at the point where he had left it:

“So they lead Jesus to Caiaphas, into the praetorium.” He had said that he was sent to Caiaphas by Annas, his colleague and father-in-law. But if he was taken to Caiaphas, why into the praetorium? This must mean either the place where the governor Pilate lived, or that Caiaphas went into the praetorium to Pilate on account of Christ’s condemnation, or that Pilate had a praetorium in Caiaphas’s house. The place was so spacious that it could have accommodated them both, with the master dwelling in one part and the judge in another.

Behold how great was the priests’ diligence in evil: they stayed awake all night in order to commit murder. “Now it was morning.” And they—that is, those who were leading Jesus—“did not enter the praetorium,” that is, the part of the house occupied by Pilate. If it was Caiaphas’s house, why did they not enter the praetorium? The evangelist explains the reason: “So that they would not be defiled, but might eat the Passover.”

The days of Unleavened Bread had begun, during which they considered it a defilement to enter another person’s dwelling. O impious and foolish blindness! They thought they would be polluted by entering another’s dwelling, yet did not see themselves defiled by their own crime. They feared contamination from the house of a foreign judge, but did not fear the blood of an innocent brother.

We should understand the distinction between Passover and the days of Unleavened Bread. Properly speaking, Passover was the day on which the lamb was killed toward evening, at the fourteenth moon; the seven days that followed were called the days of Unleavened Bread. They were the days during which nothing leavened was to be found in their houses. Nevertheless, the Passover day is also found included among the days of Unleavened Bread, as it is read in another Gospel: “On the first day of Unleavened Bread the disciples came to Jesus, saying: ‘Where do you want us to prepare for you to eat the Passover?’” (Matthew 26). The evangelist continues:

“So Pilate went outside to them and said: ‘What accusation do you bring against this man?’ They answered and said to him: ‘If he were not a criminal, we would not have handed him over to you.’” The Jews had this custom: the one whom they judged worthy of death they would bind and hand over to the governor.

Let those who were freed from unclean spirits, the sick who were healed, the lepers who were cleansed, the deaf who heard, the mute who spoke, the blind who saw, and the dead who rose be questioned and answer whether Jesus is a criminal. But they were saying this of the sort of people concerning whom he had himself foretold through the Prophet: “They repaid me evil for good” (Psalm 34).

“Pilate therefore said to them: ‘Take him yourselves and judge him according to your law.’” The Gentile judge was more just than they. It was as though he were saying: You have a law; judge him according to your law. You know better what your law judges concerning such matters; judge according to what you know to be just.

The Jews therefore said: “It is not lawful for us to kill anyone.” What is this that their frenzied cruelty is saying? Did they not kill the one whom they offered to be killed? Did they not perhaps kill him while crying out, “Crucify, crucify”?

What did they mean by saying, “It is not lawful for us to kill anyone,” when the law commands murderers, adulterers, and those guilty of such crimes to be killed or stoned? Unless perhaps they said this because of the holiness of the feast-day: that it was not lawful for them according to the law to kill a man on the feast-day, out of reverence for which day they had also refused to enter the judge’s praetorium.

How is it, O Jews, O false Israelites, that you did not kill the one whom you seized, whom you led away, whom you handed over to the governor, and whom you demanded to be crucified? Hear what was spoken against you, for the Prophet was already crying out: “The sons of men: their teeth are weapons and arrows, and their tongue a sharp sword” (Psalm 56). Behold with what weapons, with what arrows, with what sword you killed the just man.

Then the evangelist continues:

“So that the word of Jesus might be fulfilled, which he spoke, signifying by what death he was going to die.” It is therefore to be understood that the Lord was not signifying another death than the death of the cross, but the fact that the Jews were handing him over to the Gentiles to be killed. Yet their crime was less than that of the Jews, who in this way wished to make themselves seem strangers to his killing—not so that their innocence might be demonstrated, but so that their madness might be exposed.

The evangelist continues:

“Pilate therefore entered the praetorium again, called Jesus, and said to him: ‘Are you the king of the Jews?’” In these words Pilate showed that the Jews had brought this charge against him, namely that he claimed to be the king of the Jews.

“Jesus answered: ‘Do you say this of yourself, or have others told you about me?’” The Lord certainly knew both what he himself was asking and what Pilate was going to answer. Nevertheless, he wished it to be said—not for his own sake, since he knew everything, but for our sake, so that what he wished us to know might be written down.

“Pilate answered: ‘Am I a Jew? Your nation and the chief priests have handed you over to me. What have you done?’” He removed from himself the suspicion that he might have said of his own accord that Jesus was the king of the Jews, showing that he had received this from the Jews by saying, “What have you done?”

He sufficiently indicated that this had been brought against him as a crime, as though he were saying: If you deny that you are a king, what have you done that you should be handed over to me? It would not be surprising if a man who called himself a king were handed over to a judge for punishment. But if he did not say this, it would be necessary to ask him what else he might have done that made him worthy of being handed over to the judge.

“Jesus answered: ‘My kingdom is not of this world. If my kingdom were of this world, my servants would certainly fight so that I would not be handed over to the Jews. But now my kingdom is not from here.’” This is what the good teacher wished us to know. First, however, the vain human opinion concerning his kingdom had to be exposed—whether the opinion of the Gentiles or of the Jews, from whom Pilate had heard it—as though he deserved to be punished by death because he had sought an unlawful kingdom, or because rulers commonly envy those who are destined to rule.

The Lord could have answered Pilate’s first question, when he said, “Are you the king of the Jews?” by saying, “My kingdom is not of this world.” But by questioning Pilate in return about whether he said this of himself or had heard it from others, and by Pilate’s answer, he wished to show that the Jews had presented this to him as a crime. He thus disclosed to us the thoughts of men, which he knew to be vain.

But when he said, “My kingdom is not of this world,” that is, it is not a kingdom in this world, hear this, all kings of the earth: Christ did not come to take away a kingdom, but to give one; not to diminish, but to increase. He did not deny that he was a king; he denied that he ruled carnally in this world.

For what is the kingdom except those who believe in him? At the end of the age he will hand over the kingdom to God the Father—that is, he will lead it to God the Father, so that he may reign with it without end.

But to prove that his kingdom was not of this world, he added: “If my kingdom were of this world, my servants would certainly fight so that I would not be handed over to the Jews.” He did not say, “But now my kingdom is not here,” but “It is not from here.” His kingdom is here until the end of the age, but in his saints, of whom he said in another Gospel: “The kingdom of God is within you” (Luke 17).

For the holy Church is the kingdom of God. Hence the angel also said to holy Mary: “And he will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there will be no end” (Luke 1). He wished to demonstrate a spiritual kingdom, in which he reigns in heaven, not the carnal kingdom that the impious often possess in this world. Concerning his kingdom he says shortly before: “You are not of the world, but I chose you out of the world” (John 15).

“Pilate therefore said to him: ‘So you are a king?’ Jesus answered: ‘You say that I am a king.’” He did not fear to confess that he was a king, but said, “You say,” so that he might speak the truth while leaving his words inaccessible to calumny. “You say” is as though he were saying: You speak carnally, as a carnal man.

Then he adds: “For this I was born, and for this I came into the world, to bear witness to the truth.” The syllable of this pronoun should not be lengthened, as though he had said, “I was born for this matter,” but shortened, as though he had said, “For this purpose I was born,” or “For this reason I was born,” just as he says, “For this I came into the world.” In the Greek Gospel there is no ambiguity in this expression.

It is therefore clear that here he recalled his temporal birth, by which he came into the world incarnate—not that birth without beginning by which he was God and through which the Father made the world. He was born from the Virgin in order to bear witness to the truth.

But because faith does not belong to everyone, he added: “Everyone who is of the truth hears my voice.” He hears with the inner ears—that is, he obeys my voice—which amounts to saying: He believes in me.

When Christ bears witness to the truth, he certainly bears witness to himself, for his voice is: “I am the truth” (John 14). Here he commends the grace by which we have been called. He therefore says: “Everyone who is of the truth hears my voice.” He is not of the truth because he hears his voice; rather, he hears because he is of the truth—that is, because this gift has been bestowed upon him from the truth. What else is this than, by Christ’s gift, to believe in Christ?

The evangelist continues:

“Pilate said to him: ‘What is truth?’” He did not wait to hear what Jesus would answer, perhaps because he was not worthy to hear. Instead:

“When he had said this, he went out again to the Jews and said to them: ‘I find no cause in him. It is your custom that I release one man to you at the Passover. Do you want me to release to you the king of the Jews?’”

I believe that when Pilate said, “What is truth?” the custom of the Jews immediately came to his mind—the custom by which he used to release one man to them at the Passover. For this reason he did not wait to hear from Jesus what truth was, lest there be delay, since he had recalled the custom by which someone could be released to them at Passover.

This custom of release may perhaps have remained among the Jews because of the Passover and the memory of their liberation from Egypt, since they had been freed from slavery at Passover. But all who heard shouted again, all saying:

“Not this man, but Barabbas.” Barabbas was a robber.

This Barabbas is interpreted as “the son of their master,” that is, of the devil, who was master either to this robber in his crime or to the Jews in the impiety of their faithlessness.

We do not condemn you, O Jews, because at Passover you released a guilty man, but because you killed an innocent man. Yet unless this had happened, the true Passover would not have taken place. The Jews who had gone astray held the shadow of the truth, and, through deceitful human beings, the truth of that same shadow was fulfilled by a marvelous dispensation of divine wisdom. In order that the true Passover might take place, Christ was sacrificed like a sheep.

“Then Pilate took Jesus and scourged him.” We must believe that Pilate did this for no other reason than that the Jews, satisfied with his humiliations, might think that this was enough for them and cease raging against him until his death. To this belongs what the same governor allowed his cohort to do, as follows:

[Col. 0435B] “And the soldiers, plaiting a crown of thorns, placed it on his head; and they clothed him in a purple garment, and they came toward him and said: ‘Hail, King of the Jews’; and they struck him with slaps.” Thus were fulfilled the things Christ had foretold about himself; thus martyrs were instructed to endure everything their persecutors might choose to do; thus the dreadful power was concealed for a little while, while patience was commended beforehand for imitation; thus the kingdom that was not of this world overcame the proud world, not by the violence of fighting but by the humility of suffering. Thus that grain, destined to be multiplied, was sown amid horrible punishment, so that afterward it might spring forth in glory.

“Pilate went out again and said to them: ‘Behold, I am bringing him out to you, so that you may know that I find no case against him.’ Jesus therefore went out, wearing the crown of thorns and the purple garment, and he said to them: ‘Behold the man.’” From this it is clear that Pilate was not unaware that these things had been done by the soldiers, whether he had permitted them for the reason stated above—namely, so that his enemies might see these mockeries of him with the greatest satisfaction and no longer thirst for blood. Jesus went out to them, wearing the crown of thorns and the purple garment: not glorious in authority, but full of disgrace. “And he said to them: ‘Behold the man.’” If you envy a king, now spare him, because you see him cast down. He has been scourged, crowned with thorns, clothed in a garment of mockery, taunted with bitter insults, and struck with slaps: disgrace is boiling over; let envy grow cold. But it does not grow cold; rather, it burns more fiercely and increases.

[Col. 0435D] “When the chief priests and the attendants had seen him, they cried out, saying: ‘Crucify, crucify him!’ Pilate said to them: ‘Take him yourselves and crucify him, for I find no case against him.’ The Jews answered: ‘We have a law, and according to the law he ought to die, because he made himself the Son of God.’” Behold another, greater envy. The former had seemed small, as though he were seeking kingship by an unlawful assumption of royal power; yet Jesus falsely claimed neither of these things. Both are true: he is both the only-begotten Son of God and the king appointed by God over his holy mountain, Zion. And he would now demonstrate both, if he did not prefer to be all the more patient in proportion to his greater power.

“When Pilate had heard this saying, he was more afraid. And he entered the praetorium again and said to Jesus: ‘Where are you from?’ But Jesus gave him no answer.” This silence of our Lord Jesus Christ is found, when the accounts of all the evangelists are compared, to have occurred more than once: before the chief priests, before Herod, and before Pilate. Nevertheless, because of those to whom he refused to answer, the likeness of a lamb was applied to him, so that in his silence he might be regarded not as guilty but as innocent.

[Col. 0436A] “Jesus answered: ‘You would have no power against me unless it had been given you from above. Therefore the one who handed me over to you has the greater sin.’” Behold, he answered, and yet he did not answer everywhere—not as a guilty or deceitful man, but as a lamb, that is, as one simple and innocent, he did not open his mouth. Accordingly, where he did not answer, he was silent like a sheep; where he answered, he taught like a shepherd. Let us therefore state what he said, which he also taught through the Apostles: “There is no authority except from God” (Rom. XIII). And the one who, through envy, hands over an innocent man to a power for execution sins more greatly than the power itself, if that power kills him through fear of another, greater power. The Lord had given Pilate such power that it was itself also under Caesar’s power. Therefore he said: “You would have no power against me”—that is, whatever power you have, you would not have it at all unless this very thing, whatever it is, had been given you from above. But because I know how great it is—for it is not so great that you are altogether free to act as you please—“therefore the one who handed me over to you has the greater sin.” He handed me over to your power out of envy, whereas you are going to exercise that same power against me out of fear. Even through fear, a human being ought not to kill another human being, especially an innocent one; but to do so out of jealous hatred is much worse than to do so out of fear. And therefore the truthful teacher did not say: “The one who handed me over to you has the sin,” as though the other had none; rather, he said: “has the greater sin,” so that Pilate might understand that he too had sin. For the former sin is not nonexistent merely because this one is greater.

[Col. 0436B] “From that point Pilate was seeking to release him.” What does the phrase “from that point” mean, as though he had not sought this before? Read what precedes, and you will find that he had long been seeking to release Jesus. “From that point,” therefore, must be understood as meaning “because of this,” that is, for the reason that he should not incur the sin of killing an innocent man handed over to him, although he sinned more mildly than the Jews who had handed him over for execution. “From that point,” then, means “for this reason, so that he might not commit this sin”: he was not seeking to release him only now, but had sought to do so from the beginning.

“But the Jews cried out, saying: ‘If you release this man, you are not Caesar’s friend. Everyone who makes himself a king opposes Caesar.’” They thought they could impose a greater fear upon Pilate by frightening him with Caesar, so that he would kill Christ, than they had earlier when they said: “We have a law, and according to the law he ought to die, because he made himself the Son of God.” Pilate did not fear their law so as to kill him; rather, he feared killing the Son of God. Now, however, he could not disregard Caesar, the source of his authority, as he could the law of a foreign people. He continued:

[Col. 0437A] “When Pilate had heard these words, he brought Jesus out and sat down on the tribunal, at the place called Lithostratos, but in Hebrew Gabbatha. It was the preparation-day of the Passover, about the sixth hour.” At what hour the Lord was crucified, because of the testimony of the other evangelist who said: “It was the third hour, and they crucified him” (Mark XV), and because a major dispute usually arises when we reach the passage where his crucifixion is narrated, we shall discuss it, if the Lord wills.

When Pilate had sat down on the tribunal:

“He said to the Jews: ‘Behold your king.’ But they cried out: ‘Take him away, take him away, crucify him!’ Pilate said to them: ‘Shall I crucify your king?’” He still tries to overcome the terror they had inspired concerning Caesar, wishing to break them through their disgrace by saying: “Shall I crucify your king?” He could not calm them by means of Christ’s disgrace; but Pilate was soon overcome by fear. Hence it follows:

[Col. 0437B] “The chief priests answered: ‘We have no king but Caesar.’ Then he handed him over to them to be crucified.” He would have seemed most openly to act against Caesar if, when they professed that they had no king but Caesar, he had wished to impose another king upon them by releasing with impunity the man whom they had handed over to him to be killed for this very claim. Yet it is not said: “He handed him over to them so that they might crucify him,” but: “so that he might be crucified”—that is, by the judgment and authority of the governor, as the evangelist says: “So he handed him over to them to be crucified.”

But did Pilate not earlier desire the same thing, when he said: “Take him yourselves and crucify him,” or even above: “Take him yourselves and judge him according to your law”? Why, then, did they so insist, saying: “It is not lawful for us to kill anyone,” and press in every way for him to be killed not by them but by the governor, refusing for that reason to accept him for execution—if now they accept him for execution? Or, if this is not the meaning, why is it said: “Then he handed him over to them to be crucified”? The evangelist said that he handed him over to them for this reason: to show that they were implicated in the crime from which they had tried to distance themselves. For Pilate would not have done this unless he intended to fulfill what he saw them desiring. Hence it also follows:

[Col. 0437D] “They took Jesus and led him out.” This may already refer to the soldiers or to the governor’s attendants. For later it is stated more clearly: “When the soldiers had crucified him.” Nevertheless, even if the evangelist handed the whole matter over to the Jews, he does so rightly. They themselves took what they had demanded with the utmost boldness, and they themselves did whatever they had forced to be done. With Pilate sitting in judgment on the tribunal and condemning the Lord Jesus Christ, about the sixth hour they took him and led him out.

“And carrying his own cross, he went out toward the place called the Place of the Skull, which in Hebrew is called Golgotha, where they crucified him.” What does the evangelist Mark mean when he says: “It was the third hour, and they crucified him” (Mark XV), whereas John says: “It was the preparation-day of the Passover, about the sixth hour, when he sat on the tribunal”? The Lord was crucified at the third hour according to the speech of the Jews, and at the sixth hour by the hands of the soldiers. We are to understand that the fifth hour had already passed and that some part of the sixth had begun when Pilate sat on the tribunal, which is why it is called “about the sixth.” When he was led away to be crucified, in due course, with two thieves, and when the events narrated took place beside his cross, the sixth hour was completed. From that hour until the ninth, the sun was darkened and darkness occurred, as the authority of the three evangelists—Matthew, Mark, and Luke—testifies.

[Col. 0438A] But because the Jews tried to transfer the crime of Christ’s death from themselves to the Romans, that is, to Pilate and his soldiers, Mark suppressed the hour at which Christ was crucified by the soldiers—an hour that had already begun to be the sixth—and instead remembered and specified the third hour. At that hour they can be understood to have been crying out before Pilate: “Crucify, crucify,” so that not only those who hung Jesus on the wood at the sixth hour, namely the soldiers, might be found to have crucified him, but also the Jews, who cried out at the third hour that he should be crucified.

“Carrying his own cross, he went out toward the place called the Place of the Skull, which in Hebrew is called Golgotha, where they crucified him, and with him two others, one on each side, with Jesus in the middle.” These two were thieves, as we learn from the accounts of the other evangelists, with whom Christ was crucified and between whom he was crucified. Concerning him prophecy had already said: “And he was numbered among the transgressors” (Isa. LIII).

[Col. 0438C] “Pilate also wrote a title and placed it above the cross. It was written: ‘Jesus the Nazarene, King of the Jews.’” Many of the Jews read this title, because the place where Jesus was crucified was near the city. It was written in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin. These three languages predominated there above the others: Hebrew because of the Jews who gloried in the Law, Greek because of the wise among the nations, and Latin because of the Romans, who already at that time ruled many—indeed almost all—nations.

“So the chief priests of the Jews said to Pilate: ‘Do not write, “The King of the Jews,” but that he himself said, “I am the King of the Jews.”’ Pilate answered: ‘What I have written, I have written.’” O ineffable power of divine action, even in the hearts of those who were ignorant! Was there not some hidden voice sounding inwardly to Pilate, in a kind of—if one may say so—loud silence, what had been prophesied so long before in the words of the Psalms: “Do not corrupt the inscription of the title”? For will it not be true merely because Jesus said: “I am the King of the Jews”? But what are you saying, insane chief priests? If what Pilate wrote cannot be corrupted, can what Truth said be corrupted?

[Col. 0439A] But is Christ King only of the Jews, or also of the nations? Indeed, also of the nations. For after the prophecy had said: “Yet I have been appointed king by him over Zion, his holy mountain” (Ps. II), proclaiming his command so that he would not be said to have been appointed king only for the sake of Mount Zion among the Jews, it immediately added: “The Lord said to me: ‘You are my Son; today I have begotten you. Ask of me, and I will give you the nations’” (Ps. II), and so forth.

Why, then, do we wish to understand a great mystery in this title, on which was written: “King of the Jews,” if Christ is also King of the nations? Because the wild olive has been made a sharer in the richness of the olive; the olive has not been made a sharer in the bitterness of the wild olive. In the fact that the title was truthfully written concerning Christ—“King of the Jews”—who are to be understood as Jews except the seed of Abraham, the children of the promise, who are also children of God? For the Apostle says that not the children of the flesh are children of God, but the children of the promise are counted as Abraham’s seed (Rom. IV). And he was speaking to the nations when he said: “But if you belong to Christ, then you are Abraham’s seed, heirs according to the promise” (Gal. III).

[Col. 0439B] Christ, therefore, is King of the Jews—but of Jews by circumcision of the heart and by the spirit, not by the letter. Their praise is not from human beings but from God; they belong to Jerusalem, which is free, our mother, eternal in heaven, the spiritual Sarah who casts out the slave woman and her children from the household of freedom. Therefore Pilate wrote what he wrote, because the Lord said what he said.

“So the soldiers, when they had crucified him, took his garments and made four parts, a part for each soldier, and the tunic.” From this it appears that there were four soldiers who obeyed the governor in crucifying him. For he plainly says: “So the soldiers, when they had crucified him, and so forth,” with “took” to be supplied. The meaning is therefore: “They took his garments and made four parts, a part for each soldier; and they took the tunic.” He spoke in such a way that we understand no lot was cast for the other garments, but for the tunic, which they took together with the others but did not divide in the same way. Concerning it he continues, explaining:

[Col. 0439C] “The tunic was seamless, woven from above throughout.” Why they cast lots for it he relates by saying:

“So they said to one another: ‘Let us not tear it, but let us cast lots for it, whose it shall be.’” It is therefore evident that in the other garments they had equal shares, so that it was unnecessary to cast lots. Perhaps the division of the garments into four parts and the casting of lots for the tunic signified something.

The fourfold garment of our Lord Jesus Christ prefigured his fourfold Church, spread throughout the whole world, which consists of four regions, and distributed equally—that is, harmoniously—among all those regions. For this reason he says elsewhere that he will send his angels to gather his elect from the four winds. What does this mean except from the four parts of the world: east, west, north, and south?

[Col. 0439D] The tunic on which the lot was cast signifies the unity of all the parts, which is held together by the bond of charity. Concerning charity the Apostle says: “I show you a still more excellent way” (I Cor. XII). And elsewhere he says: “To know the charity that surpasses knowledge, which is the bond of perfection” (Eph. III). If, then, charity has a more excellent way, surpasses knowledge, and is above all commandments, rightly the garment by which it is signified is said to have been woven from above. It is seamless, so that it may never be torn apart. It reaches to one point, because it gathers all into one, just as it did the Apostles. For although their number was twelve—that is, divided into four parts—and all had been questioned, Peter alone answered: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” And it was said to him: “I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. XVI), as though he alone were to receive the power of binding and loosing, although he had said the former on behalf of all, that is, together with all, representing the person of that unity. He spoke on behalf of all because unity exists in all.

Therefore, after saying “woven from above,” he added “throughout.” If we refer this to what it signifies, no one is excluded from it who is found to belong to the whole. This whole, as the Greek language indicates, is called the catholic Church.

[Col. 0440B] But what is commended by the lot except the grace of God? Thus, in one thing, it reaches all, when the lot pleased everyone, because God’s grace likewise reaches all through one thing. When a lot is cast, the matter is entrusted not to anyone’s person or merits but to the hidden judgment of God. Therefore, one should not say that this signified nothing good merely because it was done by evil men—not by those who followed Christ, but by those who persecuted him.

For what are we to say about the cross itself, which was likewise made and driven into Christ by enemies and impious men, and yet is rightly understood to signify what the Apostle says: “What is the breadth, length, height, and depth” (Eph. III)? It is broad in the transverse beam, where the hands of the one hanging are extended, and signifies good works in the breadth of charity. It is long from the transverse beam to the ground, and signifies perseverance through the length of time to the end. It is high at the top, where it extends upward again from the transverse beam, and signifies the heavenly end toward which all works are directed, because everything done well and perseveringly is to be done for the sake of the height of divine rewards. It is deep also in the part fixed in the earth; there it is hidden and cannot be seen, but all its visible prominence rises from it, just as all our good proceeds from the depth of God’s grace, which cannot be comprehended or judged.

[Col. 0440D] And even if the cross of Christ signifies only what the Apostle says—“Those who belong to Christ have crucified their flesh with its passions and desires” (Gal. V)—how great a good is that? Yet this does not happen unless a good spirit, desiring what is contrary to the flesh, has made that cross of Christ which the enemy, that is, the evil spirit, made.

Finally, what is the sign of the cross—which all refused—except the cross of Christ? What is a sign unless it is applied either to the foreheads of believers, or to the water from which they are reborn, or to the oil with which they are anointed in chrism, or to the sacrifice by which they are nourished? Without it, none of these is accomplished in life. How, then, can nothing good be signified through what evil men do, when through the cross of Christ, which evil men made, every good thing is signified for us in the celebration of his sacraments?

After the Lord had been crucified, and the division of his garments, including the casting of lots, had been completed, let us see what the evangelist John next relates.

[Col. 0441A] “The soldiers indeed did these things. But standing beside the cross of Jesus were his mother, and his mother’s sister, Mary of Clopas, and Mary Magdalene. When Jesus therefore saw his mother and the disciple standing whom he loved, he said to his mother: ‘Woman, behold your son.’ Then he said to the disciple: ‘Behold your mother.’”

This is surely that hour in which Jesus, about to change water into wine, said to his mother: “What is there between me and you, woman? My hour has not yet come” (John II). He had foretold this hour, which had not yet come then: the hour when his mother would have to recognize him dying, though she had given birth to him mortally.

[Col. 0441B] At that time, as he was about to perform divine works, he reproved the mother of his humanity, as though she were unknown to him—not the mother of his divinity. But now, suffering human things, he commended her with human affection, since from her he had become human. For then he who had created Mary was being revealed through power; now he whom Mary had borne hung upon the cross.

A moral lesson is therefore presented here. He does what he teaches ought to be done, and by his example the good teacher instructs his followers that dutiful children should provide care for their parents. Thus the wood on which the limbs of the dying man were fixed also became the teacher’s chair from which he taught.

“And from that hour the disciple took her into his own home.” Speaking about himself, he is accustomed to mention in this way the disciple whom Jesus loved. Jesus certainly loved everyone, but he loved this disciple more familiarly than the others, so much so that at the supper he made him recline upon his breast. I believe that by this means he commended more profoundly the divine excellence of the Gospel that he was to proclaim.

[Col. 0441C] “After this, the Lord, knowing that everything had now been accomplished, so that the Scripture might be fulfilled, said: ‘I thirst.’ A vessel full of vinegar was standing there. So they placed a sponge full of vinegar around hyssop and brought it to his mouth. When Jesus had received the vinegar, he said: ‘It is finished.’ And bowing his head, he gave up his spirit.”

Who can arrange the things he does in such a way as this suffering man arranged them? Yet he was the man who is the mediator between God and human beings, the man of whom it is written beforehand: “He is both man, and who recognizes him?” All those through whom these things were being done saw the man, but did not recognize God. He appeared as a man because the Lord was hidden. He who appeared suffered all these things; and the very one who was hidden arranged all these things.

He saw, therefore, that everything that had to occur before he received the vinegar and gave up his spirit had been completed, and also that this saying might be fulfilled: “And in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink” (Ps. LXVIII). “I thirst,” he said, as though saying: “You have left this undone; give what you are.” The Jews themselves were the vinegar, having degenerated from the wine of the patriarchs and prophets. As though from a full vessel, they were filled with the iniquity of this world, possessing hearts like a sponge, fraudulent through its cavernous and twisted hiding places.

[Col. 0442A] As for the hyssop around which they placed the sponge full of vinegar, since hyssop is a lowly herb and cleanses the chest, we appropriately understand it as the humility of Christ, which they surrounded and which they thought they had ensnared. Hence the saying in the Psalm: “You shall sprinkle me, Lord, with hyssop, and I shall be cleansed” (Ps. L). We are cleansed by Christ’s humility, because unless he had humbled himself, becoming obedient to the Father unto death, even death on a cross (Phil. II), his blood would not have been poured out for the remission of sins, that is, for our cleansing.

Nor should it trouble us that they were able to bring the sponge to his mouth when he had been lifted up from the earth on the cross. For, as we read in the other evangelists, in a detail omitted here, this was done on a reed, so that such a drink might be raised on the reed to the height of the cross. By the reed Scripture is signified, which was being fulfilled through this act. Just as one speaks of a tongue—Latin or any other language—to signify the sound produced by the tongue, so a reed can be called the letter that is written with a reed. Yet we very commonly call the sounds of the human voice “languages.” It is less customary to call Scripture a reed, and therefore the figure is all the more mystical.

“When Jesus had received the vinegar, he said: ‘It is finished.’” What does this mean except what prophecy had shortly before foretold? Moreover, nothing remained that still had to be done before he died. Like one who had power to lay down his life and to take it up again (John X), after completing everything that he had awaited in order to complete it, he bowed his head and gave up his spirit. Who sleeps in this way whenever he wishes, as Jesus died when he wished? Who lays aside his garment whenever he wishes in such a way as Jesus laid aside his soul when he wished? Who dies when he wishes in such a way as Jesus died when he wished? How great a power of the judge is to be hoped for or feared, if so great a power appeared in the one who died?

[Col. 0442C] After the Lord Jesus had completed everything that he knew beforehand ought to be completed before his death, he gave up his spirit when he wished. Let us now see, as the evangelist narrates, what followed.

“The Jews,” he says, “because it was the preparation-day, so that the bodies might not remain on the cross on the Sabbath—for that Sabbath was a great day—asked Pilate that their legs might be broken and that they might be taken away.” It was not that the legs should be taken away, but that those whose legs were broken for the purpose of causing their death should be removed from the wood, so that, hanging on crosses, they would not defile the great festival day with the horror of their prolonged punishment.

[Col. 0442D] “The soldiers therefore came and broke the legs of the first man and of the other who had been crucified with him. But when they came to Jesus and saw that he was already dead, they did not break his legs. Instead, one of the soldiers opened his side with a lance, and immediately blood and water came out.”

The evangelist used his words attentively. He did not say that the soldier struck his side, or wounded it, or anything similar, but that he “opened” it, so that there might in some way be opened there the door of life, from which the sacraments of the Church flowed, without which one does not enter the life that is true life. That blood was poured out for the remission of sins; that water provides the saving drink, and supplies both washing and drinking.

This was prefigured when Noah was commanded to make a door in the side of the ark through which the animals that were not destined to perish in the flood might enter; by them the Church was prefigured. For this reason the first woman was made from the side of the sleeping man and was called “woman,” the mother also of men.
