A great good is signified here, as well as the great evil of transgression that preceded it, in the condition of one lying down and sleeping. Here too the second Adam slept on the cross with his head bowed, so that from his side there might be formed for him a spouse who flowed forth from the side of the sleeping man. O death, from which the dead come back to life!

[Col. 0443B] “For these things happened so that the Scripture might be fulfilled: ‘You shall not break a bone of him’” (Exod. XII). And again another Scripture says: “They shall look upon him whom they pierced” (Zech. XII).

He supplied two testimonies from the Scriptures for the individual events that he narrated as having occurred. Because he had said: “When they came to Jesus, they did not break his legs,” the testimony “You shall not break a bone of him” pertains to this. This command was given to those who were ordered to celebrate the Passover by sacrificing a lamb under the old law, which had gone before as the shadow of the Lord’s Passion. Hence “our Passover” was sacrificed, concerning whom the prophet Isaiah also foretold: “He was led like a sheep to be slaughtered” (Isa. LIII).

[Col. 0443C] Likewise, he had added: “But one of the soldiers opened his side with a lance.” The other testimony pertains to this: “They shall look upon him whom they pierced.” In it Christ was promised as the one who would come in the flesh in which he was crucified.

“After this, Joseph of Arimathea, because he was a disciple of Jesus, though secretly because of fear of the Jews, asked Pilate to take away the body of Jesus. Pilate permitted it. So he came and took the body of Jesus. Nicodemus also came—the one who had first come to him by night—bringing a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about a hundred pounds.”

The sentence should not be divided in such a way that we say “first bringing a mixture of myrrh.” Rather, the word “first” belongs to the preceding sense. Nicodemus had first come to Jesus by night, as John himself narrated earlier in his Gospel. Here, then, we should understand that Nicodemus came to Jesus not only at that time, but came then for the first time; afterward he came repeatedly, so that by listening he might become a disciple. This is certainly now being made known to almost all nations through the revelation of the body of blessed Stephen.

[Col. 0443D] “There was a garden in the place where he was crucified, and in the garden a new tomb in which no one had yet been placed.” Just as no one before or after him was conceived in the womb of the Virgin Mary, so no one before or after him was buried in this tomb.

“There, because it was the preparation-day of the Jews and because the tomb was nearby, they placed Jesus.” He wishes the burial to be understood as hurried, lest evening come on, since, because of the preparation-day—which among us the Jews more commonly call the “pure supper”—it was no longer permitted to do anything.

HOMILY LXIX: ON THE VIGIL OF EASTER

(COL. III.) “Brothers, if you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God.” And so forth.

Beloved brothers, with the favor of his merciful kindness, let us faithfully venerate the honorable solemnity of our Lord Jesus Christ and marvel at his ineffable mercy, since for the sake of our redemption he not only assumed human flesh, but also deigned to undergo various kinds of punishment for our salvation. Thus, even after the long sleep of our sluggishness and laziness, we may awaken—not unwillingly but voluntarily—roused by the sweetness of the holy Christian religion in the assembly of this most holy solemnity, and rise willingly and devoutly with every care, according to what the Apostle says in the present reading: “If you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God.”

[Col. 0444B] “Set your minds on the things that are above, not on the things that are on earth.” It is as though he were saying: We who are being restored according to the image of the holy Trinity should be renewed according to that same image. We who fell most grievously through the threefold sin into consent to evil works should, having been raised three times from the font and having received remission of all sins through Christ’s grace, rise to life just as he rose on the third day.

If we wish to rise with Christ, however, let us first die to the world and to carnal desires. Let us put off the old man—that is, evil will, or corrupt practice and the worst pleasures—and put on kindness, so that with complete devotion we may do good to our neighbors and, after the love of God, place nothing before love of neighbor, but love them as ourselves.

He continues: “Set your minds on the things that are above, not on the things that are on earth”—seeking only the things that are heavenly, not those that are earthly; dying to the earth but living to God; pursuing heavenly wisdom, not earthly wisdom. For he adds:

[Col. 0444D] “For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God.” When we have died to the world and to its resources and desires, our life is hidden in God, because we are children of God. Hence it follows:

“When Christ, your life, appears, then you also will appear with him in glory.” For it is not yet apparent what we are or what kind of people we have become for judgment. But when Christ appears to judge the living and the dead, then we too shall appear with him in glory, rising again. For Christ is born, suffers, and rises for us and on our behalf, so that through him we may be reborn to life amid tribulations and rise with him through virtues.

[Col. 0445A] Everything has been restored through him on this night. On this night he himself rose as the firstfruits, so that afterward we might all rise. On this night our captivity is loosed, and the life lost in Adam is restored. On this night the first-formed Adam rises; the exile returns to his homeland, paradise. From this night of the Lord’s resurrection onward, paradise is open to all and closed to no one except by that person’s own act; it is opened to no one except by Christ.

Therefore, let us guard ourselves with every care, lest, because of the works of the devil that drag us into destruction, we ourselves close to ourselves the open way of the heavenly kingdom. Rather, through works of righteousness and mercy, let us make the way to the kingdom of heaven level for ourselves.

Let us therefore recall in our humility the humility of our Lord, undertaken for us. Let us keep vigil humbly on this night; let us pray humbly to God, who has illuminated this night with the glory of his light. To him we say: “My God, enlighten my darkness” (Ps. XVII). Let us ask him to grant light to our hearts, so that just as with rejoicing eyes we behold this splendor of lights, so with an enlightened mind we may see the splendid glory of this night. Let us pray to him to hear us keeping vigil at his solemnity—he who slept for our salvation.

[Col. 0445B] Let us therefore keep vigil and pray outwardly; let us celebrate this vigil. God speaks to us in his readings; let us speak to God in our prayers. If we obediently hear his words, he whom we ask dwells within us. To him be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

HOMILY LXX: ON THE HOLY DAY OF EASTER
[Col. 0445C] (MARK XVI.) “At that time: Mary Magdalene, and Mary the mother of James, and Salome bought spices so that, coming, they might anoint Jesus.” And the rest. This most sacred reading commends to us the devotion of the holy women; it also commends the appearance of the angels and, greater than these, the Lord’s resurrection. But let us examine everything in order.

For the evangelist says: “Mary Magdalene,” and so forth. These women, as the evangelist Luke records, had followed the Lord from Galilee, ministering to him from their own means; for among the Jews it was permitted, and was not considered blameworthy, for women to provide preachers with food and clothing from their possessions. The apostles maintained this custom after the Lord’s resurrection, or ascension, [Col. 0445D] as the apostle Paul proves; but he himself, in order to avoid scandal among the Gentiles, refused to use this custom, saying: “Do we not have the authority to lead about a believing sister as wife, as do the other apostles, and the brothers of the Lord, and Cephas?” (I Cor. IX). *Cephas* is called Peter in Latin. It is as though he were saying: “We do have this authority.”

And in the Acts of the Apostles we read concerning those same apostles: “All these continued with one accord in prayer with the women and Mary the mother of Jesus” (Acts I). But the women who had followed the Lord, seeing him seized, bound, scourged, and crucified, while the disciples who had earlier said, “Let us also go, that we may die with him” (John XI), were fleeing, remained with him themselves. Thus was fulfilled at the time of the Lord’s passion what had formerly been said through blessed Job in his person: “When my flesh had been consumed, my bone clung to my skin, and only lips were left around my teeth” (Job XIX). For, as though the flesh had been consumed and the skin had cleaved to the bone, so, when the disciples fled, the women persevered with the Lord.

But those who had loved him more closely while he was alive could not be separated from him when he was dead. For when they saw him buried, they sat opposite the tomb, as the evangelist reports, and noted the place so that, after leaving, they might buy spices; and during that night they prepared as many ointments as they could. On the Sabbath, however, they kept silent according to the commandment of the law. After sunset, they labored over whatever remained to be done in preparing the ointments. But early on the first day of the week, before it grew light, they came to the tomb with the spices they had prepared, longing at least to anoint his most sacred body when dead, since they had loved him exceedingly while alive.

This is what Mark says: “Mary Magdalene, and Mary of James, and Salome bought spices,” and so forth. The women are fittingly designated by one name, so that those who shared one will and equal desire might also share one designation. The reading of the Gospel distinguishes their names by adding further names, when it says: “Magdalene, of James, and Salome.”

Mary Magdalene was named from the town of Magdala. She was also the sister of Lazarus, the woman who, as Luke relates, had once been a sinner in the city; but because she loved greatly, many sins were forgiven her. Mary of James was named from her son James. She was the Lord’s maternal aunt—that is, his mother’s sister—and the mother of James and Joseph. Mary Salome was named either from a village or from a man. For they relate that she had two husbands, Cleophas and Salome, and they wish her to be the woman elsewhere called Mary of Cleophas.

Now *Mary* in Syriac is interpreted among us as “star of the sea,” or “mistress.” It signifies the Church, which shines like the lights in the world amid a crooked and perverse generation, holding the word of life. Although this symbolism spiritually suits the Mother of God, through whose virginal birth the Sun of justice shone upon the world, it can also suit these women, who came to the tomb with spices and first announced the splendor of the Lord’s resurrection to the world.

In the mystical sense, the holy Church is represented by these most devout women, whose names are rightly appropriate to her. *Magdalus*, from which Mary Magdalene was named, as we have said, is interpreted as “tower,” and signifies the Church. A tower is not only higher but also a dwelling, not easily accessible to enemies. Thus it signifies the Church, which both abandons earthly things and desires heavenly ones, fighting against spiritual wickedness and daily seeking help from God on high so that it may overcome the snares of the ancient enemy. It entrusts its strength not to itself but to the Lord, praying with the Prophet: “Be to me, Lord, a tower of strength against the face of the enemy” (Ps. LX).

For this is that strong and impregnable tower to which the voice of the bridegroom says in the Song of Songs: “Your neck is like the tower of David, built with battlements. A thousand shields hang upon it, every kind of armor of the mighty” (Song IV). And Solomon says of it: “The name of the Lord is a most strong tower; the righteous runs to it and is exalted.”

Mary of James is interpreted as “she who supplants.” She too signifies the Church, which knows how to trample down vices so that it may receive virtues. Mary Salome is interpreted as “peaceful.” She too suits the Church, which preserves invisible peace not only in prosperity but also in adversity, saying with the prophets: “With those who hated peace, I was peaceful” (Ps. CXIX). And again: “His place was made in peace, and his dwelling is in Zion” (Ps. LXXV).

The most devout women therefore come with spices to visit the Lord’s tomb, because the Church, through the diligence of devotion, approaches God daily, saying with the Psalmist: “Let my prayer be directed like incense in your sight” (Ps. CXL). Spices signify the prayers of the saints. What are called *aromata* in Greek are called *odoramenta*, “fragrant substances,” in Latin; thus they signify the fragrance of devout prayer, as John says in the Apocalypse: “They had bowls full of fragrant substances, which are the prayers of the saints” (Rev. V). And again: “An angel stood beside the altar of the temple, holding a golden censer in his hand, and many incenses were given to him, so that he might burn them before the golden altar that is before the eyes of the Lord” (Rev. VIII).

Although spices are always fragrant, they give off a greater fragrance when placed upon fire. So the prayers of the saints smell all the sweeter before God the more they have been refined by the fire of compunction. To such an extent that the king, delighted by their sweetness, says: “Who is this who comes up through the wilderness like a column of smoke from spices of myrrh and frankincense and every perfumer’s powder?” (Song III). To him the holy soul, presuming nothing of itself, says: “Draw me after you; we shall run in the fragrance of your ointments” (Song I).

For we buy spices to carry to the tomb when, about to enter a church for prayer, we cleanse our consciences of the filth of our thoughts, saying with the Prophet: “My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready; I will sing and make melody to the Lord.”

Those women, then, see angels who come to the tomb with spices, because those souls belong to the fellowship of angels that combine a reputation for good works with constancy in prayer. Such was the man who said: “We are the good fragrance of Christ to God in every place” (II Cor. II).

Let us therefore imitate those same holy and most devout women, so that, just as they sought the Lord with their whole desire in the tomb, the proper place of the dead, so we too may seek him with every affection of mind—not in a tomb, but with spices, that is, with prayers—in heaven, where we know that he has ascended.

“Very early on the first day of the week they come to the tomb, when the sun had risen.”

Here we must inquire why this evangelist says, “Very early on the first day of the week they come to the tomb,” when Matthew describes it thus: “In the evening of the Sabbath, as it begins to dawn toward the first day of the week, Mary Magdalene and the other Mary came to see the tomb.” A prudent reader can easily answer that, in the intention and desire of their minds, they began to come in the evening, as Matthew says; but because the darkness of night hindered them, they reached the Lord’s tomb bodily very early, according to Mark.

Or certainly, when Matthew says, “In the evening of the Sabbath, as it begins to dawn toward the first day of the week, they came to see the tomb” (Matt. XXVII), he wished the entire night to be understood from the part of the night in which they came, because Scripture sometimes signifies the whole by a part. But, so that this may be understood more clearly and plainly, it should be known that just as a day has an evening, so does a night. There is, however, this difference between them: the evening of day customarily grows dark into night, whereas the evening of night grows light into day.

Therefore, to show that Matthew had described not the evening of the day but that of the night, after saying “in the evening of the Sabbath,” he added, “which begins to dawn toward the first day of the week.” Thus what Mark says, “very early,” and what Matthew says, “in the evening of the Sabbath,” are one and the same.

At the Lord’s resurrection, even the order of time was changed. From the beginning of the world until the Lord’s resurrection, day preceded and night followed. From the Lord’s resurrection onward, the preceding night belongs to the day that follows, because he who rose from the dead during the last part of that night made the night itself bright and shining and, in a certain sense, changed it into day. Of this it is written: “The night shall be illuminated like the day” (Ps. CXXXVIII). And again: “The night is my illumination in my delights” (ibid.).

It was fitting formerly that day should precede night, because the first man, departing from the true light, fell into the darkness of error. It is also fitting now that day should follow night, because through the Lord’s resurrection we have been freed from the darkness of error and turned toward the true light, as the Apostle says: “The night has advanced, but the day has drawn near” (Rom. XIII).

Again, however, what Mark says—“They come to the tomb when the sun had risen”—seems contrary to John, who says: “While it was still dark, Mary Magdalene came to the tomb.” Here it must be said that, because of the greatness of her love, Mary Magdalene first came alone to the tomb while it was still dark, as John relates; afterward she came again with the two other women of the same name, when the sun had risen, as Mark records.

There is also another explanation by which the evangelists are understood to have said nothing contradictory. Every day we see that, when the approach of daybreak begins and the sun, leaving the earth’s hollows, begins to open its rays of light, there is light in the east while darkness remains in the west. Therefore, if we consider the eastern regions, Mark appears to have said nothing contradictory when he says, “when the sun had risen”; if we consider the western regions, John’s words, “while it was still dark,” do not seem discordant.

Someone may ask why John, naming only one woman, asserts that she saw angels, while Mark mentions three. The answer is that, as we have said, Mary Magdalene either came first and afterward came again with the others, or the three came together, and John, naming one, did not deny that the others had come.

According to the spiritual understanding, darkness was in the women’s hearts when they sought God as though he were dead among the dead. The sun rose for them when they believed the resurrection they had heard announced. In Scripture, the name “sun” sometimes signifies the Lord Jesus Christ, as it is written: “The sun knew its setting” (Ps. CIII), that is, Christ knew his passion. And again: “For you who fear the Lord, the sun of justice shall rise, and healing in its wings” (Mal. IV).

When it says “one of the Sabbaths,” we should understand the first day of the week—that is, the first day after the Sabbath—which, out of honor and reverence for the Lord’s resurrection, we call the Lord’s Day. Just as we speak of the first feria, the second feria, the third feria, and the remaining days in order, so the Jews called them the first of the Sabbath, the second of the Sabbath, and the third of the Sabbath.

And just as Scripture says “Song of Songs” and “Holy of Holies” because of their greatness, so this day may be called the Sabbath of Sabbaths because of the glory of the Lord’s resurrection. This day is both one of the seven and outside the seven. Within this week it takes its beginning and receives its completion. It is the first in such a way that it is the third, and the third in such a way that it is also the eighth: first in creation, third in resurrection, eighth in recurrence.

Therefore, he who deigned to rise on this day showed that the number eight pertains to the resurrection. He rose on that day itself to show that the human race would rise in the eighth age of the world. Hence Solomon says: “Give a portion to seven, and also to eight” (Eccles. XI).

Just as God rested from his works on the seventh day, so the seventh age is called the rest of the saints, when souls without bodies are at rest. In the eighth age they will receive their bodies and will be at rest. As a type or figure of this, eight souls were saved in Noah’s ark.

For this is the day of which it is said: “This is the day that the Lord has made; let us rejoice and be glad in it” (Ps. CXVII).

“And they said to one another: ‘Who will roll away the stone for us from the entrance of the tomb?’”

The evangelist Matthew says that, when Joseph had buried the Lord in his new tomb, he rolled a large stone to the entrance of the tomb and departed, while the Jews sealed it with guards. These women, therefore, coming to visit the Lord’s tomb, considered the weakness of their sex and recalled the size of the stone, which is said to have been so large that it could scarcely be moved by twenty men. They said: “Who will roll away the stone for us from the entrance of the tomb?”

Although they said such things, they did not abandon the journey they had begun, believing that what seemed impossible to human weakness could be made possible by divine power. The steadfastness of these women was beautifully prefigured in the Books of Kings, when the Philistines, returning the captured ark of the Lord to the land of Israel, yoked two nursing cows to a cart and shut up their calves at home.

And just as it is written: “The cows went straight along the road that leads to Beth-shemesh, proceeding and lowing, yet not turning aside to the right or to the left” (I Kings VI), so these women, proceeding to visit the Lord’s tomb, said as though lowing and groaning: “Who will roll away the stone for us?” and so forth. Yet neither because of the weakness of their sex, nor because of the size of the stone, nor because of fear of the guards did they turn aside from the journey they had begun.

Let us therefore imitate the steadfastness of these women, so that, walking along God’s way, we may not turn aside from the straight path because of the temptation of demons, the fear of human beings, or concern for our relatives. For a reward is promised to those who begin, but it is given to those who persevere, the Lord saying: “The one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. LXIV).

“And looking up, they saw that the stone had been rolled away.”

How and in what manner the stone was rolled away is explained by another evangelist, Matthew, who says: “For an angel of the Lord descended from heaven, and coming near, rolled away the stone and sat upon it” (Matt. XXVIII).

The angel therefore rolled away the stone, not to open a path for the Lord as he emerged, but to give everyone evidence of his departure—that is, so that all might believe that he had risen from the dead. For in his resurrection he did not need the assistance of angels, since by his own power he shattered the bars of hell.

“For it was very large.”

Spiritually, this stone placed at the entrance of the tomb signifies the bondage of hell [the manuscript reading *oblationem* is evidently an OCR corruption of *obligationem*, “bondage”], by which even the righteous were held subject through the transgression of the first guilt. It is said to have been very large because the bondage of original sin was so hard and insoluble that no one is read to have been so just that he could free himself or others from it, until he came who was made free among the dead.

But the Lord Jesus Christ, who is the angel of great counsel, rolled away the stone from the entrance of the tomb because, rising from the dead on this day, he removed from the way to paradise the cherubim and the flaming, turning sword. Hence it is written: “Lift up your gates, O princes, and be lifted up, eternal gates, and the King of glory shall enter” (Ps. XXIII).

He alone did not rise from the dead; he also freed all the souls of the righteous from the prison of hell, fulfilling the prophecy of Hosea, who says: “I shall be your death, O death; I shall be your bite, O hell” (Hos. XIII). And the Lord says: “When I am lifted up from the earth, I shall draw all things to myself” (John XII).

The unique power of his resurrection was prefigured by that most powerful Samson. We read of him in the Book of Judges (Judg. XVI) that, when he had entered the city of Gaza to visit a prostitute, the Philistines, hearing of his entrance, fortified the city and carried away the guards. They rejoiced as though they had already captured him. But let us hear what Samson did. He not only went out at midnight; he also carried both gates of the city, with their posts, upon his own shoulders to the mountain, leaving the guards empty-handed and deceived.

Whom did that most powerful Samson signify except the Lord Jesus Christ, of whom it is written: “The Lord is strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle”?

When he entered the city, he loved the prostitute—that is, Christ loved the Church, which after the worship of idols was called to the feast of Christ. What does the city of Gaza signify except hell? What do the Philistines signify except the Jews? When Samson entered Gaza, the Philistines rejoiced; so the Jews rejoiced when the Lord had been buried and had descended to the prisons of hell, thinking that they had extinguished his name.

But what did our Samson, the Lord Jesus Christ, do? He not only came forth free; he also carried away the gates. For he not only came forth free from hell but also freed all the souls of the righteous from hell and recalled them to the mountains—that is, to the heavenly places.

To him the prophet Zechariah says: “You also, by the blood of your covenant, have led out your prisoners from the pit in which there was no water” (Zech. IX).

And so that no one might doubt the resurrection, he also raised some from the body, because, as it is written, “many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep arose” (Matt. XXVII).

“And entering the tomb.”

After the devout women saw that the stone had been rolled away from the entrance of the tomb, they entered it without any delay. But some who consider only the tombs customary among us may wonder how the Lord’s tomb had been constructed so that it could contain so many women together with the angels.

The answer is that, as those who saw it testified and left a written account for our memory, it was built in the following manner. There was a large stone in a garden, stained with purple drops and shining white in color. A tomb had been hewn into its side, large enough to hold eight or nine people and so high that anyone standing on its floor could reach the ceiling with an outstretched hand.

On its northern side the Lord’s tomb was cut out. It had, they say, a length of seven and a half feet and a width of three and a half palms. The entrance of the cave opened toward the east. For those entering, the place of the Lord’s body was on the right, since the Lord’s body lay in the tomb with his head toward the west and his feet toward the east; his right hand was toward the south and his left toward the north. From that time the custom arose of burying Christian bodies in this arrangement.

The Lord rightly chose such a place for his burial, where there was no possibility of digging beneath it, so as to remove every opportunity for the Jews to make accusations. Otherwise, if it had been enclosed by a wall or some other construction, they might have said that his disciples had stolen him.

After the Lord’s ascension and resurrection, Christians, fired by the zeal of divine love, built a church of astonishing size and circular form in the same place. They paved its floor with white marble, adorned the roof above with golden plates, and decorated the inner surfaces of the walls with golden veneers. Over the tomb they placed a golden cross of extraordinary beauty, hanging before it a silver lamp with lights.

The Lord’s tomb was made so marvelous that even the prophecy of Isaiah was literally fulfilled, where he says: “On that day the root of Jesse, which stands as a sign for the peoples, him the nations will implore, and his tomb will be glorious” (Isa. XI).

“They saw a young man sitting on the right, clothed in a white robe.”

The evangelist John says that, when Mary Magdalene looked into the tomb, she saw two angels in white sitting, one at the head and one at the feet, where the body of Jesus had been placed.

Here we should consider how beautifully both natures of the Lord, divine and human alike, are commended to us. The head signifies divinity, as the Apostle says: “The head of Christ is God” (I Cor. XI). The feet signify humanity, concerning which Moses says: “Those who draw near to his feet will receive instruction from him” (Deut. XXXIII).

The angel sits, as it were, at the head when John cries: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John I). He sits, as it were, at the feet when the same evangelist says: “And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (ibid.).

Mark describes the same angel as sitting on the right, to indicate that the Lord had passed from mortality to immortality. For just as the left signifies the present life, so the right signifies the immortality of the future life, as Solomon testifies when he says: “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand embraces me” (Song I).

The angel, the witness of his resurrection, rightly appeared on the right, to show that he had passed from corruption to incorruption and from mortality to immortality, because, as the Apostle says, “Christ, rising from the dead, dies no more; death shall no longer have dominion over him” (Rom. VI). And again: “And if we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know him so no longer” (II Cor. V).

And to declare that the enemy of the human race had been completely overcome by the Lord, the angel wished to appear not standing but sitting. Standing belongs to one who fights; sitting belongs to one who reigns or judges. A king sits upon the throne of his glory, while a soldier rests after victory. Because the Lord had crushed the head of the ancient serpent and freed all God’s elect from its power, the witness of his resurrection rightly appeared not standing but sitting, as has been said.

He also appeared well clothed in a white robe, displaying through his very clothing the unspeakable joy of the Lord’s resurrection. Although in the Old Testament angels are very often recorded as having been seen by human beings, you will not easily find anyone appearing clothed in a white robe, because this privilege was reserved for the Lord’s resurrection.

And because it is customary among the Palestinians, when celebrating feast days, to put on white garments, by appearing clothed in a white robe the angel showed that he was celebrating the feast of the Lord’s resurrection. If someone asks whether it was his feast or ours, it may be understood as both his and ours.

The Lord’s resurrection was the angels’ feast, because the number of angels that had been diminished when an angel apostatized is completed from the souls of the faithful. It is our feast because, freeing us from destruction, he restored us to the fellowship of the angels.

Thus, at both his feast and ours, the angel appeared in white garments to display the unspeakable joy of this celebration. If there is joy in heaven before the angels over one sinner doing penance, what joy do we suppose there was when they saw so many thousands of holy souls pass over into their fellowship?

“For this is the day that the Lord has made; let us rejoice and be glad in it” (Ps. CXVII).

“And they were astonished.”

It is customary for mortals that, when they see something above them, they are afraid within themselves. From the time when the first man departed through sin from the fellowship of the angels, we have fallen into such misery that we cannot see the citizens above without fear.

Therefore, the holy women were astonished not only because they saw the angel clothed in a white robe, but also because they saw that the place of the tomb was empty. The same angel, the witness of the Lord’s resurrection, appeared in such a form that, through his appearance itself, he might offer both terror to the reprobate and consolation to devout minds.

The evangelist Matthew makes this clear, saying: “His appearance was like lightning, and his clothing like snow.” In the lightning, terror is shown; in the snow, the consolation of gentleness.

Because the angel appeared with a face like lightning and a whiteness like snow, he showed that the Lord Jesus, who is called the angel of great counsel, will appear at the final and general resurrection both terrifying to the reprobate and gentle to the righteous.

He will appear, as it were, with a face like lightning to those to whom he will say: “Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. XXV). He will appear, as it were, in snowy whiteness to those to whom he will say: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (ibid.).

The angel, the witness of the Lord’s resurrection, displayed this description when the guards were terrified before him and became like dead men, while the women, so that they would not be afraid, immediately received gentle consolation. Hence it follows:

“He said to them: ‘Do not be frightened.’”

It was as though he said: “Let those who do not love the arrival of the citizens above be afraid; let those who guard the Lord’s tomb with evil intent be terrified. But you should not fear, since you see your fellow citizens.”

And he immediately demonstrates why the women should not fear when he adds: “You are seeking Jesus.” *Jesus* in the Hebrew language is called *savior*, or *salutary*, in Latin. It was as though he said: “You who are seeking the Savior should not fear the Savior’s messenger, but should love him all the more.”

And lest anyone think that he was speaking of some other Jesus, he added: “The Nazarene.” The Lord was called Nazarene because he was conceived and brought up in the city of Nazareth. But because *Nazarene* is interpreted as “holy,” this name rightly suits him especially, since he is the Holy of Holies, the King of kings, and the Lord of lords. Of him the Prophet says: “You will not permit your holy one to see corruption” (Ps. XV).

And lest anyone in Nazareth be called by that name, he added:

“Crucified.”

He was crucified for us so that, through the wood of the holy cross, he might exclude the wood of transgression.

“He has risen.”

He rose according to his humanity, while his divinity suffers no fall. Therefore he who never fell wished to rise, so that the one who refused to stand might be raised up.

When he says, “He is not here,” he speaks of bodily presence. For through the power of his divinity he is wholly everywhere and present everywhere, as he himself says through the Prophet: “I fill heaven and earth” (Jer. XXIII).

And to drive every doubt from their hearts, he added: “Behold the place where they laid him.” It was as though he said: “If you do not believe my words, at least believe the empty tomb, and drive every doubt from your hearts.”

“But go, tell his disciples and Peter.”

In this passage the Lord’s special mercy toward the female sex must be considered. So that woman might not always be held in disgrace because a woman had first offered death to a man, he wished through women to announce the resurrection first to men. It was as though he said to humanity: “From whose hand you received the cup of death, from her mouth hear the joy of resurrection.”

But it may be asked why, after naming the disciples, Peter is designated by name. The angel says: “Tell his disciples and Peter.” The answer is that, as the Gospel history relates, when the Lord was going to his passion, Peter, overcome by fear, had denied him three times. Perhaps, among the other disciples, he would not have dared to approach to see the Lord after the Lord’s resurrection unless the angel had expressly named him.

He is therefore called by name so that he would not despair because of his denial. Someone may also wonder why the Lord permitted a disciple so beloved by him to fall into so grave a crime that he denied his Lord and teacher at the voice of a single servant girl.

It should be understood that this happened through the Lord’s most provident dispensation. Since he had decided to set Peter above the whole Church, he permitted him to deny himself, so that from his own weakness he might learn how he ought to show mercy to others who sinned.

First, therefore, he showed Peter to himself, and then placed him over the others, so that he might understand that he owed severity toward vices but compassion toward nature. Elsewhere the Lord says to him: “I have prayed for you, Peter, that your faith may not fail; and you, once converted, strengthen your brothers” (Luke XXII).

When it says, “He will go before you into Galilee; there you will see him, as he told you,” this is the same thing he had said when going to his passion: “After I have risen, I will go before you into Galilee” (Matt. XXVI).

It is fittingly foretold that the disciples would see the Lord after his resurrection in Galilee, because he had already passed from corruption to incorruption and from mortality to immortality. For *Galilee* is interpreted as “made transmigration,” or “migration.”

Because he passed from corruption to incorruption and from mortality to immortality, he is rightly said to be seen in Galilee. As the apostle Peter says: “Christ died once for our sins, the just for the unjust, so that he might offer us to God” (I Pet. IX). And again: “Although he died through weakness, yet he lives through the power of God” (II Cor. XV).

Or, according to another interpretation, Galilee, which is interpreted as “rolling” or “wheel,” signifies the Gentile people. When he is foretold to be seen in Galilee, it shows that the Jews are to be abandoned because of their unbelief, while the Gentiles are to be gathered through faith—those who, before the Lord’s coming, lived without knowing God in the revolving course of the world.

Or otherwise, he is announced as to be seen in Galilee after the resurrection because those will deserve to reach the sight of him who now pass from vices to virtues and from love of the world to love of God, turning away from evil and doing good.

Hence Galilee is aptly called “revelation” according to another interpretation, because what we now see in appearance we shall then see in reality, with unveiled face. Thus the Apostle says: “Now we see through a mirror, in an enigma; then face to face” (I Cor. XV). And again: “But we, brothers, contemplating the glory of the Lord with unveiled face, are transformed from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord” (II Cor. XVIII).

May he deign to bring us to that vision, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

HOMILY LXXI. MONDAY OF EASTER.

(Acts X.) “In those days Peter, standing in the midst of the people, said: ‘Men and brothers, you know what word came to pass throughout all Judea, beginning from Galilee after the baptism that John preached, Jesus of Nazareth.’” And the rest.

In the present reading that you have heard, dearest brothers, the apostle Peter briefly embraced everything contained in the Creed: that Jesus is the Christ and that he is Lord of all.

Standing in the midst of the people, he said: “Men and brothers, you know what word came to pass throughout all Judea, beginning from Galilee after the baptism that John preached, Jesus of Nazareth.”

Here everything is demonstrated together: that Christ was sent to reconcile the world to God; that John proclaimed him beforehand; that he was anointed with the Holy Spirit; that, with God dwelling in him, he was declared through miracles; that he was crucified and raised from the dead; that he will come at the end as judge of all; and that he will illuminate his Church throughout the whole world through faith.

Finally, it follows:

“How God anointed him with the Holy Spirit and with power.” Jesus was therefore anointed not with visible oil, but with the gift of spiritual grace, which fully contained everything signified by visible ointment. When he was baptized, he anointed the Church, since the sevenfold Spirit is invoked through the laying on of the bishop’s hands; in this likeness, the Holy Spirit descended upon him after his baptism in the form of a dove (John I). Then he also deigned to prefigure his Church, in which those baptized chiefly receive the Holy Spirit. For he is to be understood as anointed when “the Word became flesh,” that is, when human nature, without any preceding merits of good works, was united to God the Word in the Virgin’s womb, so that the divine and human natures might together be one person. For this reason we confess him to have been born of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary.

“Who went about doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil, because God was with him.” That is, the Father always remained with the Son. This is better understood than to suppose that it signifies the Son’s divinity dwelling with the man whom he assumed, thereby dividing Christ into two persons and falling into the gravest error [Note: [Col. 0455D] Something is missing here, or something is superfluous.]. It continues:

[Col. 0456B] “And we are witnesses of all that he did in the region of the Jews and in Jerusalem.” Those who have been sent throughout the whole world to preach the Gospel rightly testify that they are witnesses, as we read in the Psalm: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Psalm XVIII).

God the Father works through the two natures in Christ: through the one which Christ shares with God the Father, insofar as he is God; and through the other, by which he became human from the Virgin Mary. Through these two natures in the one Son of God, he likewise brings about two resurrections of the human race, namely, of souls and of bodies.

Souls too have their own death, in ungodliness and sins; according to this death they were dead, of whom the same Lord says: “Let the dead bury their dead” (Luke IX), so that those dead in soul might bury the dead in body. The death of the soul occurs, plainly, when God abandons it because of the enormity of its sins. The death of the body occurs when it is abandoned by the soul.

We say that those raised from these two kinds of death have undergone two resurrections. Now, in the Church, the resurrection of souls takes place through the Son of God—that is, through the Word of God—when those brought to life by God’s grace rise from the death of iniquity. This is the first resurrection. Those who possess it will faithfully rise in the second resurrection, which is that of the body, to eternal life.

The wicked too will rise, each in his own flesh, so that they may be punished with the devil and his angels (Matthew XXV). This must be known with complete certainty: no one will be delivered except through God’s undeserved mercy, and no one will be condemned except through his deserved judgment. Then the saints will understand more fully what good God’s grace has bestowed upon them, and what they would have attained if divine mercy had not freely chosen them as a gift.

Then God himself will be the fellowship of the saints, the delight of the blessed, and everything that they may rightly desire: life, salvation, abundance, glory, honor, peace, eternal blessedness, and blessed eternity. To him be honor and glory now and always and forever and ever. Amen.

# HOMILY LXXII. MONDAY OF EASTER

(LUKE XXIV.) “At that time: Two of Jesus’ disciples were going that same day to a village which was sixty stadia from Jerusalem, named Emmaus.” And so forth.

At the beginning of this reading, some are accustomed to ask who these two disciples were who, on the very day of the resurrection, departed from Jerusalem and hastened to the village of Emmaus. That they were not among the twelve apostles the evangelist demonstrates at the end of this reading, when he says that they returned to Jerusalem and found the eleven gathered together. Hence it appears that they belonged to the seventy disciples, not to the twelve apostles.

The name of one is indeed disclosed below: he is said to have been called Cleophas. Some, however, think that the other was called Emmaus, like the village to which they were going; for this reason, they suppose, the evangelist may have considered it unnecessary to repeat one name in a brief verse. Others also believe that this was Luke the evangelist, who wrote this Gospel and, out of humility, concealed his own name.

It is the custom of the saints that, when they speak of great and wondrous things concerning themselves, they speak of their own person as though of another, in order to preserve humility. Thus Moses is found to have done, speaking of himself as though of another when he said: “Now Moses was a very meek man, more than all the people who dwelt on the earth” (Numbers II). Similarly, blessed Job says of himself as though of another: “There was a man in the land of Uz whose name was Job” (Job I).

Those who think that Luke was one of these two disciples say that, following this example, he concealed his own name. But whoever either of them may have been, it must be understood that they departed from Jerusalem in doubt concerning the Lord’s resurrection, as they themselves demonstrate not only by their words but also by their actions.

They had waited in Jerusalem until the third day, expecting him to rise on the third day, as he himself had promised. Since they had not seen the fulfillment of his promise, they departed from Jerusalem in doubt. Their weakness, however, must be forgiven, because, as the evangelist says, the Spirit had not yet been given: “for Jesus had not yet been glorified” (John VII).

Accordingly, the length of the journey they were undertaking seems appropriately to correspond to their minds. Sixty stadia are counted from Jerusalem to Emmaus. A stadium is called so from *stare*, “to stand,” or from *statuere*, “to establish,” because some prize was set at a fixed place for the exercise of runners. Although among the ancients the measure of the stadium varied, they nevertheless report Hercules as the originator of the standard stadium; he is said to have run one hundred and twenty-five paces in a single breath. Thus, if correctly calculated, sixty stadia make seven and a half miles.

Six pertains to good works, because there are six days in which work is permitted; seven pertains to the rest of souls, because on the seventh day God rested from all his works; eight pertains to the resurrection, because the Lord rose on the eighth day. Solomon says: “Give a portion to seven, and also to eight” (Ecclesiastes XI).

It is as though these disciples had run the sixth mile with the Lord when they had seen him living in good works in this present life. It is as though they had reached the seventh mile when they had learned that he had been placed in the tomb. They had indeed completed the eighth half-mile, because they had previously believed that he would rise, yet they departed from Jerusalem in doubt concerning his resurrection.

Although they departed from Jerusalem in doubt concerning the Lord’s resurrection, they had not altogether withdrawn from love for him. Hence it is rightly added:

“And they were speaking with one another about all these things that had happened.”

It should be noted that they were not speaking about trivial matters, empty things, matters belonging to detraction, or things that provoke laughter. Rather, they were speaking with one another about all that had happened: how he had lived innocently and without reproach in the world; how he had performed signs and miracles; how he had been handed over to crucifixion through the hatred and accusations of the Jews; and how he had foretold that he would rise, though they had not yet seen this.

Since they were speaking about these and similar things concerning him, it happened that they also saw bodily the one whom they supposed to be absent. Thus, even in a literal sense, the Lord fulfilled his promise, in which he says: “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them” (Matthew XVIII). Hence it is added:

“And it came to pass, while they talked and questioned one another, that Jesus himself, drawing near, went with them.”

Here it should be noted that the Lord shaped his appearance according to the condition of their minds. They loved the Lord in their hearts, but they doubted his resurrection. The Lord appeared to them in bodily form, but did not reveal who he was. Because they loved him, they saw him; because they doubted his resurrection, they did not recognize the one whom they saw.

Since this doubt had arisen in their minds through the snares of the ancient enemy, it is rightly added:

“But their eyes were held, so that they would not recognize him.”

Their eyes were held either by the doubt itself or by the temptation of the ancient enemy, so that they could not recognize the one whom they saw. He who had risen from the dead by his own power appeared to his disciples in whatever form he wished. Hence another evangelist rightly says: “After this he appeared in another form to two of them” (Mark XVI).

“And he said to them: ‘What are these words that you are exchanging with one another as you walk, and why are you sad?’”

The Lord did not ask because he was ignorant of what the disciples were saying. Rather, through their conversation he sought a confession of the heart, so that what he says elsewhere might be fulfilled in them: “Either you will be justified by your mouth, or you will be condemned by your mouth” (Matthew XII).

They were rightly walking sadly, since faith in the resurrection had not yet gladdened them. What the Lord had promised had not yet been fulfilled in them: “Your sorrow will be turned into joy” (John XVI). Rather, they were still held by the sentence that says: “But the world will rejoice, while you will be sorrowful” (ibid.). One of them, whose name was Cleophas, showed the reason for their sadness when he said:

“Are you the only stranger in Jerusalem, and have you not known the things that have happened there in these days?”

It was as though he were saying: “How could you alone remain unaware of the things that have happened in Jerusalem in these days, especially when, because of their importance, they could be unknown to no one?”

But we must not pass over the fact that the Lord wished to appear to his disciples after his resurrection in the guise of a stranger. He was a stranger to them because he was far removed from their mortality. Or certainly he appeared in the guise of a stranger in order to summon their minds to mercy, so that they might love him at least as a stranger, since they did not yet recognize him as God.

He also appeared in the guise of a stranger so that we, who are his members, might understand that in this life we are strangers and sojourners. A stranger is so called as one who goes farther away or traverses what belongs to another. By this name are designated those who, driven from their native soil, sigh with lamentation for their return.

We too, who have lost the joys of paradise, remain in a foreign homeland as long as we are in this life. Therefore, it is necessary that every day, with lamentation, we hasten to return to our own homeland, saying with the Apostle: “While we are in the body, we are absent from the Lord; for here we have no lasting city, but we seek the one that is to come” (1 Corinthians V).

David sensed that he was in this pilgrimage when he said: “For we are strangers and sojourners before you, as all our fathers were” (Psalm XXXVIII). And again: “Woe is me, that my sojourning has been prolonged! I have dwelt with the inhabitants of Kedar; my soul has been a long-time sojourner” (Psalm CXIX).

But the Lord inquires more carefully into the causes of their sorrow, saying:

“What things?”

They revealed why they were sad, saying:

“Concerning Jesus of Nazareth, who was a man, a prophet mighty in deed and word before God and all the people.”

They testify that he was a man and a prophet, but remain silent about his being the Son of God—either because they were departing from Jerusalem in doubt concerning his resurrection, or because they feared the plots of the Jews. For the Jews had already conspired that anyone who openly confessed him would be expelled from the synagogue.

Since *Jesus* is called *Salvator*, “Savior,” in Latin, he is rightly designated by this name, since his resurrection brought salvation to believers, as the apostle Peter says: “There is salvation in no one else, nor is there any other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved” (Acts IV).

Since *Nazaraeus* is interpreted as “holy,” this name suits him who committed no sin, and in whose mouth no deceit was found. Of him it is written: “Know that the Lord has made his holy one wondrous” (Psalm IV). And again: “You will not permit your holy one to see corruption” (Psalm CXV).

Although they did not know whom they were seeing, the disciples rightly called the Savior a man. For *vir*, “man,” is derived from *vires*, “strengths,” and this name is especially suited to him who alone, by rising from the dead, was able to break the devil’s strength. Of him it is written: “Behold the man; his name is Rising” (Zechariah VI).

Let us therefore also learn, strengthened by him, to be men, so that we may resist the devil’s temptations courageously and endure all adversity manfully, as did the one to whom it was said: “Gird your loins like a man, and, like a strong man, restrain lust” (Job XXXVIII).

For this reason Joseph is also praised in these words: “He sent a man before them” (Genesis XLV). The Psalmist likewise admonishes us, saying: “Act manfully, and let your heart be strengthened, all you who hope in the Lord” (Psalm XXX).

Although the disciples were not altogether without doubt concerning his resurrection when they called the Lord the prophet of prophets, for he himself says of himself: “A prophet is not without honor except in his own country” (Matthew XIII). And again: “It is not fitting for a prophet to perish outside Jerusalem” (Luke XIII). In his person it is also said through Moses: “God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers, like me; you shall hear him” (Deuteronomy XVIII).

He is called mighty first in deed and then in word, because what he taught by words he demonstrated by examples, as it is written: “Jesus began to do and to teach” (Acts I). Preaching is properly ordered when you first fulfill by your deeds what you later teach in words, following the example of the Lord, who says: “Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart, and you will find rest for your souls” (Matthew XI).

He is rightly said to have been mighty first before God and then before all the people, so that in every work we may strive above all to please God. We must not first please human beings; rather, we ought first to please God and then human beings—not for our own glory, but so that those people themselves may please God, seeing that we please him. The Lord admonishes us accordingly, saying: “Let your light shine before human beings, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew V).

The Apostle likewise says: “Providing what is good not only before God but also before all human beings” (Romans XII). And again: “Please everyone, just as I also please everyone in all things, not seeking my own advantage but that of many, so that they may be saved” (1 Corinthians X).

“And how the chief priests and our rulers handed him over to the sentence of death and crucified him.”

Here the disciples recall what the preceding Gospel text explains: namely, how he was handed over to crucifixion by the chief priests because of their envy.

But it must be asked why they say that he was handed over by the chief priests, when we read that Judas handed him over, saying: “What will you give me, and I will hand him over to you?” (Matthew XXVI).

From this question another arises: how can Judas or the Jews be said to have handed him over, when we read that the Father handed him over, as the Apostle says: “God did not spare his own Son, but handed him over for us all” (Romans VIII)?

The Son himself also handed himself over, as the same Apostle says elsewhere: “Who loved me and handed himself over for me” (Galatians II). And again: “Walk in love, just as Christ also loved us and handed himself over for us” (Ephesians V).

If, then, the Father handed over the Son and the Son handed himself over, are Judas and the Jews without guilt if they did what the Father and the Son did? Certainly not. Rather, different intentions are expressed by the one word “handed over.”

Judas handed him over because of greed; the Jews handed him over because of envy; Pilate is said to have handed him over when he permitted him to be crucified; the Father handed him over for our liberation; the Son handed himself over because of his love for us.

Therefore the Father and the Son are not only to be loved but also glorified. Judas and the Jews, however, are not only to be detested but also condemned, because what the Father and the Son did out of love, they did out of greed.

That these disciples were departing from Jerusalem in doubt is shown by their own words, when they said:

“But we had hoped that he was the one who would redeem Israel.”

“We had hoped” is a verb in the imperfect tense. By saying not “we hope” but “we had hoped,” they showed that they doubted his resurrection.

Instructed only to a limited degree by the grace of the Holy Spirit, they had hoped that, by rising from the dead, the Savior would redeem Israel—that is, that he would restore the kingdom of Israel in bodily form, much nobler than the kingdom once ruled by David.

This suspicion had moved the two who persuaded their mother to ask him, saying: “Lord, say that these two sons of mine may sit, one at your right hand and the other at your left, in your kingdom” (Matthew XX). The same doubt held those who questioned him after the resurrection, saying: “Lord, will you at this time restore the kingdom to Israel?” (Acts I).

“And now, besides all these things, today is the third day since these things happened. But certain women from among us also terrified us. They were at the tomb before dawn, and, not finding his body, they came saying that they had even seen a vision of angels who say that he is alive. Some of our companions went to the tomb and found it just as the women had said, but they did not see him.”

The preceding Gospel text adequately relates what the disciples recall briefly: namely, how the women who had followed the Lord from Galilee came to the tomb with the spices they had prepared; and, after receiving from the angel the announcement of his resurrection, reported it to the disciples.

At that time two of them—Peter and John—ran to the tomb and found it as the women had said, but they did not see him himself.

“And he said to them: ‘O foolish ones and slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken.’”

It is rightly not only the disciples’ foolishness that is rebuked, but also their slowness. Since they saw everything fulfilled in the Lord’s teaching, miracles, and passion just as the prophets had foretold concerning him, they should not have doubted his resurrection—especially since they remembered that the Lord himself had foretold everything that was to happen to him before he suffered.

The indolence and lukewarmness not only of those disciples but also of us is rebuked, for we are unwilling to learn even excellent things and do not strive to fulfill by our deeds what we learn. Thus we are found slow to learn and sluggish in action. To such people it is rightly said:

“Was it not necessary that the Christ should suffer these things and so enter into his glory?”

This should be read interrogatively, with *it was necessary* understood. It was necessary for Christ to suffer, not for his own sake but for ours.

He is said to enter into his glory, from which he never departed, because he causes us to enter, although we had been driven far from it through sin. Just as he is said to see and confess because he causes us to see and confess something, so too he is said to enter into his glory through the passion.

Therefore the Lord entered into his glory, showing that we must enter the kingdom of God through many tribulations. Christ, our head, loves his members so greatly that he is frequently said himself to do what he makes us capable of doing.

Because they were foolish and slow in understanding Scripture, the Lord, after his loving rebuke, adds an explanation. Hence it is added:

“Beginning with Moses and all the prophets, he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself.”

He interpreted throughout all the Scriptures, especially those passages relating to his passion and resurrection, in order to remove every doubt from their minds and strengthen their spirits to believe in the resurrection. Such passages include: “They pierced my hands and my feet” (Psalm XXI); “They divided my garments among themselves, and for my clothing they cast lots” (ibid.); and “Unjust witnesses rose up against me” (Psalm XXVI), along with other passages of this kind.

But someone may ask why the Lord is said to have begun with Moses when he interpreted the Scriptures to the disciples, since we read that there were many fathers before Moses who prophesied his passion and resurrection both by their words and by their deeds.

What did the death of Abel signify (Genesis IV) if not Christ’s passion? Just as Abel was unjustly killed by his brother, so the Lord was innocently killed by the Jews.

What is signified by the translation of Enoch (Genesis V) if not the Lord’s ascension? What is signified by Noah, who guided the ark through the flood (Genesis VII), if not the Lord, who is the head of the Church?

And what is represented by Abraham, who sacrificed his son (Genesis XXII), if not God the Father, who did not spare his own Son? The sacrifice of Isaac likewise prefigured Christ’s passion.

Jacob, the shepherd of sheep (Genesis XXX), signifies our Lord Jesus Christ, who says in the Gospel: “I am the good shepherd” (John X). Similarly, Joseph’s sale prefigured the sale of Christ.

But, as we have said, someone may ask why the Lord is said to have begun with Moses when he interpreted the Scriptures to the disciples, since we read that there were many fathers before Moses who prophesied his passion and resurrection both by their words and by their deeds.

The answer is that, although there were many fathers before Moses, we know their deeds because Moses wrote them down. We do not doubt that he was the first writer of truthful history. From which book, then, did the Lord begin to interpret their Scriptures? He began with Moses because Moses was the first to write down their deeds, as we have said. For from that point onward a human being wrote, when there was no human being.

“And they drew near to the village to which they were going, and he pretended to go farther.”

Since pretending is usually characteristic of hypocrites, what does it mean that the Lord is said to have pretended? A reasonable answer is evident: we do not always use “pretend” to mean “simulate,” but sometimes also “arrange” or “compose.” Hence those who shape clay are called *figuli*, potters, and those who compose poems are called *fictors*, that is, composers of poems.

From these examples we learn that the simple Truth did nothing through duplicity. Rather, he arranged or presented himself before the eyes of the disciples in such a way that it might become clear whether they would love him, whom they recognized as God, at least as a stranger.

But far be it from us to believe that they were alien to the compassion of love, since they were walking with the author of mercy. For it is added:

“And they urged him, saying: ‘Stay with us, because evening is coming on and the day is now declining.’”

From their example we learn that strangers and guests should not only be received when they are present but also invited and urged when they are absent. He himself demonstrates how great the virtue of hospitality is, promising that at the judgment he will say to the faithful: “I was a stranger, and you welcomed me. And as long as you did it for one of the least of mine, you did it for me” (Matthew XXV).

We learn the same from the deeds of Abraham and Lot, who, by frequently receiving strangers, sometimes received angels. Hence the Apostle admonishes us, saying: “Let brotherly love remain among you, and do not forget hospitality. Through it some, by receiving angels as guests, have pleased God” (Hebrews XIX; Genesis XIX).

The apostle Peter likewise exhorts us: “Be hospitable to one another without grumbling” (1 Peter IV). Blessed Job also bears witness concerning himself, saying: “The stranger did not remain outside; my door was open to the traveler” (Job XXXI).

“And he entered with them. And it came to pass, while he reclined with them, that he took bread, blessed it, broke it, and gave it to them. And their eyes were opened, and they recognized him.”

Because faith without works is dead, we may understand from this that they recognized the God whom they had not recognized either from seeing him or from his interpretation of the Scriptures as soon as they carried out in action what the Scriptures command.

“They recognized him in the breaking of the bread.” For, as the Apostle says: “It is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but the doers of the law will be justified” (Romans II). And as the Lord says: “Blessed are those who hear the word of God and keep it” (Luke II).

We too, according to our measure, recognize the Lord in the breaking of the bread if, with a pure heart and chaste body, we receive the mystery of his body and blood with fitting reverence.

“And he vanished from their sight. And they said to one another: ‘Was not our heart burning within us while he spoke to us on the way and opened the Scriptures to us?’”

For, as the Apostle says: “Our God is a consuming fire” (Hebrews XII). After the Lord vanished from the disciples’ sight, they declared with what ardor they had been kindled by his speech on the way, saying: “Was not our heart burning within us concerning Jesus while he spoke to us on the way?” and so forth.

They had been kindled by the fire of which the Lord says: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire except that it burn?” (Luke XII). The one who said, “My heart grew hot within me, and in my meditation the fire will burn” (Psalm XXXVIII), knew that he had been kindled by this fire.

Since everyone who learns something good through God’s teaching ought, through the mystery of love, to announce it to others, these disciples prove this, for it is added:

“And rising up at that same hour, they returned to Jerusalem.”

They were not prevented by the fatigue of the journey, nor did they fear the obstacle of the evening hour. Rising at that very hour, they returned to Jerusalem to announce to the apostles what they had discovered on the way concerning the Lord’s resurrection. Hence it is rightly added:

“And they found the eleven gathered together and those who were with them, saying: ‘The Lord has truly risen and has appeared to Simon.’ And they themselves recounted what had happened on the way, and how they had recognized him in the breaking of the bread.”

The evangelist does not explain where or when this happened, but he does not conceal that it happened, saying: “The Lord has truly risen and has appeared to Simon,” that is, to Peter, as the Apostle bears witness: “He was seen by Cephas, and afterward by the eleven” (1 Corinthians XV).

It is believed that after the resurrection the Lord appeared first of all the men to Peter, not only to strengthen the order of his apostleship but also to restore his mind, which had faltered during the passion.

# HOMILY LXXIII. TUESDAY OF EASTER

(ACTS XIII.) “In those days: Paul rose, and, indicating silence with his hand, said: ‘Men, brothers, sons of the race of Abraham, and those among you who fear God, to you the word of this salvation has been sent,’” and so forth.

All those to whom this apostle was speaking were sons of Abraham according to the flesh, just as they themselves said elsewhere: “We are Abraham’s offspring, and we have never been slaves to anyone” (John VIII). And again: “Abraham is our father.” The Lord said to them: “I know that you are Abraham’s children.”

They were not children of Abraham by imitation, however, for the Lord said to them: “You are from your father the devil” (John VIII). Thus the Jews were sons of the devil, not by birth but by imitation. “You are,” the Lord says, “from your father the devil, and you wish to do the desires of your father.” Behold from where they are sons of the devil. What are his desires? “He was a murderer from the beginning, and you are seeking to kill me.” Behold how they are sons of the devil by imitation.

They were also sons of Abraham by the origin of their flesh, these people to whom the Apostle was speaking; and they were sons by imitation because of the chastity of their fear, to whom he specifically said: “And those among you who fear God, to you the word of this salvation has been sent.”

This is the word of which Isaiah says: “The Lord sent a word into Jacob, and it fell upon Israel” (Isaiah IX). That is, God sent his Son, concerning whom John says: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John I).

He sent it to Jacob—that is, to the Jews—and it came to Israel—that is, to the gentile people. God the Word is himself the Son of God.

Therefore, when the Father sent him as the Word from the Father, it was by his Word that he was sent. The same Son was sent by the Father and by the Son, because the Son himself is the Father’s Word: the Word of God that was in the beginning with God, and God was the Word.

He was in the very Wisdom of God at the time when the Word was to become flesh and dwell among us. When the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, born of a woman (Galatians IV), so that the incarnate Word might appear to human beings.

[Col. 0465B] “For those who dwell in Jerusalem and its rulers, because they did not recognize Jesus or the voices of the prophets, which are read every Sabbath.”

It is also written in the Acts of the Apostles: “For Moses, from ancient times, has in every city those who proclaim him in the synagogues.” These testimonies clearly show that the reading of the Law and of the prophets was always carried out by the Jews in the synagogues on the Sabbath.

“And when they had completed everything that was written about him.”

John relates these words in this way: “Afterward, knowing that all things had been completed, so that the Scripture might be fulfilled, Jesus said: ‘I thirst’” (John XIX). After Jesus had accomplished everything that had to be accomplished before his death, he handed over his spirit when he wished and as he wished.

“Taking him down from the tree.” In the wilderness, a bronze serpent was hung upon a tree by Moses, so that the Lord might be signified as dead in the serpent and eternal in the bronze: that is, he was judged dead according to his humanity, yet was like bronze according to his divinity.

What should be said to the Jews who object with the testimony: “Cursed is everyone who hangs upon a tree” (Deuteronomy XXI)? A person who hangs upon a tree is cursed, but one who is guilty, not one who is innocent. The punishment of sin cannot be a curse upon innocence.

For if Mordecai had been hanged upon the prepared tree and had fulfilled the sentence of the king’s cruelty, would they now judge him worthy of a curse? Certainly not.

For this reason our Lord hung upon the tree: so that, by being hung upon the tree, he might absolve us from the offense committed through the tree of perdition.

“They placed him in a tomb.” Jesus was placed in a new tomb in which no one had yet been placed. Just as no one before him or after him was conceived in the Virgin’s womb, so no one before him or after him was buried in this tomb.

“But God raised him from the dead.” The bitter root of the cross vanished; the flower of life rose with its fruits in glory. This is Aaron’s staff, which blossomed after its dryness. The staff becoming green after being dry is Christ rising after death. He is the flower of virgins, the crown of martyrs, the glory of those who practice continence, “who was seen for many days.”

That is, for forty days. Yet he did not appear to them continuously throughout all those forty days. He appeared whenever he wished, to whom he wished, and in whatever manner he wished, “to those who had come up with him from Galilee to Jerusalem.”

Without departing from the historical sense, let us consider the spiritual meaning. Galilee is interpreted as “a transmigration that has taken place”; Jerusalem as “vision of peace.” Those go up with the Lord from Galilee to Jerusalem who, first rejecting here the fuel of vices, pass over to the heights of virtue.

They are the ones who pass over with our Redeemer from passion to resurrection and will one day joyfully see the Lord in the heavenly Jerusalem—those who, in this manner, having abandoned their vices, have passed over to the heights of the virtues.

“And we announce to you the promise that was made to our fathers.”

For it was said to Abraham: “In you all the families of the earth will be blessed” (Genesis XXII). To Jacob: “And in you and in your seed all the tribes of the earth will be blessed” (Genesis XXVIII).

The Apostle explains this, saying: “He did not say ‘in seeds,’ as of many, but ‘in your seed,’ which is Christ” (Galatians III). Christ is indeed the seed of Abraham, in faith in whose name blessing was promised—that is, signified—to all the families of the earth, namely, to Jews and gentiles.

“I will give you the holy and faithful things of David.”

That is: whatever I promised faithfully to David, I, the faithful guarantor, will fulfill for you—namely, that Christ would be born from his lineage.

# HOMILY LXXIV. TUESDAY OF EASTER

[Col. 0466C]

(Luke 24.) “At that time: Jesus stood in the midst of his disciples.” And the rest. The divine readings are linked to one another, and frequently one depends upon another, so that sometimes the beginnings of what follows are more easily understood by considering what came before. We readily recognize this in the present reading if we attend briefly to the preceding passages of this Gospel. For after the evangelist had related that the Lord appeared to two disciples on the road, and after he had narrated that they recognized him in the breaking of the bread, he immediately added: “And rising at that same hour, they returned to Jerusalem and found the Eleven gathered together, and those who were with them, saying that the Lord had truly risen and had appeared to Simon. And they themselves related what had happened on the road, and how they had recognized him in the breaking of the bread” [Col. 0466D]. “While they were speaking about these things to one another, Jesus stood in their midst.”

Hence it is evident that this appearance took place on the very day of the Lord’s resurrection. The evangelist John more clearly explains the manner of this appearance, saying: “When it was evening on that day, the first day of the week, and the doors were shut where the disciples were gathered for fear of the Jews, Jesus came and stood in the midst” (John 20). Here we should consider that the Lord is said to have stood in the midst of them while they were speaking about him, so that we may understand that we shall then have him dwelling with us when, whenever we gather together, we speak and do those things that pertain to his praise and our salvation [Col. 0467A], according to what he himself says: “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them” (Matthew 18).

But let us hear what the Lord said when he appeared to the disciples: “Peace be with you.” And beautifully, when rising from the dead, he first commended peace to the disciples, so that he might show that through his passion the angelic and human natures had been reconciled. For from the time when the first man withdrew from God by sinning, there had been discord between human beings and angels. But because, by redeeming human nature, the Lord restored it to fellowship with the angels, when rising from the dead he bestowed peace upon the disciples as a special gift.

“For he is our peace,” the Apostle says, “who made both one and joined together the middle wall, dissolving the enmity in his flesh, so that he might create the two in himself as one new man, making peace, and reconcile both to God in one body” [Col. 0467B]. And coming, he preached peace to those who were far away and peace to those who were near” (Ephesians 2). Or certainly, when rising from the dead, the Lord commended peace to the disciples in order to show that those would attain to his vision who preserve harmony of peace in heart and body, according to what he says elsewhere: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God” (Matthew 5).

“For great peace,” says the Psalmist, “belongs to those who love your law, O Lord, and there is no scandal for them” (Psalm 118). But lest they think that he was someone else, whose body they saw glorified after the resurrection, he immediately added: “I am he.” Here we should consider that he did not say, “I was,” but “I am.” For *sum*, the substantive verb, expresses neither the past nor the future, but always the present [Col. 0467C]; and it specially suits him for whom the future does not succeed and the past does not pass away, but who always possesses being throughout eternity, as he himself said to Moses: “I am who I am. Thus you shall say to the children of Israel: ‘He who is has sent me to you’” (Exodus 3).

But because human eyes could not see an immortal body without fear, they needed to be strengthened by the Lord. For he said: “Do not be afraid.” Human nature’s weakness has this characteristic: whenever it sees something above itself, it fears what is beneath it. Hence it follows:

“But being troubled and terrified, they thought that they were seeing a spirit.” This sudden disturbance of the disciples became a great error for the Manichaeans [Col. 0467D]. For they, who denied that God had assumed true flesh, wanted to take as support for their error the fact that after the resurrection the Lord had been thought by the apostles to be a spirit. But the Lord himself proved this error of the disciples false when he recalled their minds from it, saying:
