“Why are you troubled, and why do thoughts arise in your hearts?” Here it should be noted that he did not say, “thoughts descend into your hearts,” but “arise.” Good thoughts descend, because they are given from above by the Lord, as the Apostle James bears witness, saying: “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights” (James 1). But evil thoughts arise, because they are sent from below by unclean spirits [Col. 0468A]. Dew descending from above moistens the earth in one way, while ash is carried into the air by the force of the winds in another. And in order to remove every doubt concerning his resurrection from the minds of the disciples, he offered his hands and feet to be touched, saying:

“See my hands and feet, for I am he myself. Touch and see, because a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see me have.” And when he had said this, he showed them his hands and feet.

Not only his hands and feet but also, according to John’s Gospel, he offered his side, which had been pierced by the lance, so that, seeing the marks of the nails in his hands and feet and the opening made by the lance in his side, they might recognize that the one whom they had seen crucified three days earlier had risen [Col. 0468B].

Here someone may ask how, after the resurrection, the Lord’s body could have been incorruptible and tangible, since everything incorruptible is intangible and everything tangible is corruptible. But in a wondrous and ineffable manner the Lord after the resurrection presented his body as tangible and demonstrated it to be incorruptible: by displaying it as tangible, he restored them to faith; by showing it to be incorruptible, he invited them to their reward. Or certainly, after the resurrection he exhibited his body as both tangible and incorruptible in order to show that he was of the same nature but possessed a different glory.

But because our universal resurrection was prefigured in the Lord’s resurrection, when the Lord after the resurrection presented his body as tangible and demonstrated it to be incorruptible [Col. 0468C], he showed that our bodies after the resurrection would be incorruptible in such a way that they could also be tangible. Hence the heretic Eutyches both lies and is refuted. He says that after the resurrection our bodies will be like wind and air; and just as a sunbeam can be seen, so he wants to maintain, in support of his error, that our bodies will indeed be visible but intangible, on the basis of what the Apostle says: “Flesh and blood shall not possess the kingdom of God” (1 Corinthians 15).

He does not understand that “flesh” has various meanings in Scripture. Sometimes the term “flesh” designates the very nature of flesh; sometimes the weakness of that same flesh; sometimes sins, which arise from the flesh; and sometimes the genealogy of kinship. The term “flesh” designates the substance of flesh itself, as it is written: “This now is bone from my bones and flesh from my flesh” (Genesis 2) [Col. 0468D]. At other times the term “flesh” designates the weakness of flesh, as it is written: “And he remembered that they are flesh” (Psalm 77), that is, weak. At times the genealogy of kinship is expressed by the term “flesh,” as it was said to Peter: “Flesh and blood has not revealed this to you” (Matthew 16). And as the Apostle Paul says: “Immediately I did not consult flesh and blood” (Galatians 1).

The term “flesh” also signifies vices and sins that arise from the flesh, as it was said: “My spirit shall not remain in man forever, because he is flesh” (Genesis 6). Therefore, when the Apostle says, “Flesh and blood shall not possess the kingdom of God,” he did not deny that the nature of flesh would rise again; rather, he showed that the vices arising from the flesh cannot reign with Christ. Hence he added immediately: “Nor will corruption possess incorruption” (1 Corinthians 15) [Col. 0469A].

For the rest, we must believe that our flesh will rise in the resurrection, in the truth of its substance, without corruption or the weakness of death, in accordance with what blessed Job testifies, saying: “I know that my Redeemer lives, and on the last day I shall rise from the earth, and again I shall be clothed with my skin, and in my flesh I shall see God, whom I myself shall see, and not another; my eyes shall behold” (Job 19).

But in this passage [Col. 0469B] the deceitful folly of the pagans is accustomed to mock Christian simplicity, saying: “With what presumption do you Christians suppose that your God can raise your bodies from the dust, when, as you say, he himself, rising from the dead, could not heal the marks of his passion in his own flesh?”

To this true faith replies that this was not a matter of inability but rather of mercy. For it is greater to raise flesh than to heal the marks of passion in that same flesh. But since he who could do the greater could certainly have done the lesser, he would have done so unless for various reasons he had left the marks of his passion in his own flesh.

First, so that he might more easily restore the disciples’ doubtful faith in his resurrection to belief. For although the apostles believed slowly, when they saw the marks of the nails in his body they would have believed much more slowly had they not recognized the signs of his passion in his body. Hence one of them, when the others were saying, “We have seen the Lord,” affirmed with an oath: “Unless I see in his hands the mark of the nails, and put my finger into the place of the nails, and put my hand into his side, I will not believe” (John 20) [Col. 0469C].

Or certainly, when rising from the dead, the Lord wished to preserve the marks of his passion in his flesh because, coming for judgment, he will appear to everyone in the same form, to the just and to the unjust alike. Thus the just, seeing how great and how many things the Author of the human race endured for their deliverance, may advance in his praise and thanksgiving; while the unjust may be punished all the more severely because they contemptuously despised God’s more abundant benefits, as it is written: “They shall look upon him whom they pierced” (Zechariah 12).

Again, another Scripture says: “Behold, he is coming with the clouds, and every eye shall see him, and those who pierced him. And all the tribes of the earth shall mourn over him” (Revelation 1) [Col. 0469D]. And elsewhere: “Then all the tribes of the earth shall mourn, and they shall see the Son of Man coming in the clouds of heaven with great power and majesty” (Matthew 24).

The Lord also preserved the marks of his passion in his flesh for another reason: because, as our advocate, he intercedes with the Father for us in his humanity, while in his divinity he gives all things with the Father. He displays to the Father the very wounds that he endured for our redemption, so that he may move him to pity for those human beings for whom the only-begotten Lord did not refuse to endure such great things; and thus he may summon to mercy the one who never ceases to show mercy.

Or certainly, after the resurrection the Lord wished to preserve the marks of his passion in his flesh so that those very signs of the passion might eternally proclaim the victory he had obtained over the ancient enemy. For, by way of example, when a most courageous soldier, at the command of his emperor, has gone into battle and happens to return to his homeland victorious but wounded, he does not wish to be healed by physicians in such a way that the traces of his wounds do not appear. Rather, appearing without disfigurement, they show his courage to all who see him. Likewise, when rising from the dead, the Lord wished the marks of his passion to appear in his flesh, so that those very signs might demonstrate throughout infinite ages that he was the victor over the devil [Col. 0470A].

And because the minds of the disciples, placed between sorrow and joy, did not yet fully believe that he had risen, he continued to reveal a clear proof of the resurrection. Hence it follows [Col. 0470B]:

“While they still did not believe, but were marveling for joy, he said: ‘Do you have anything here to eat?’ But they offered him a piece of broiled fish and a honeycomb. And when he had eaten before them, he took the remains and gave them to them.”

Therefore, after the resurrection he ate and drank before the disciples, not because he needed to be sustained by bodily food, but to show that he had risen in the reality of the flesh, because eating properly belongs to the body, not to the spirit. He ate and drank before the disciples so that they might proclaim his resurrection with all the greater assurance, since they had not only touched his flesh with their hands but had also seen him eating with their bodily eyes. Thus afterward they could confidently say: “He was seen after the resurrection [Col. 0470C], not by all the people, but by witnesses foreordained by God—by us, who ate and drank with him after he had risen from the dead—and he commanded us to preach to the people and testify that he is the one appointed by God as judge of the living and the dead.”

Nor should we believe that the kind of food he ate after the resurrection was without a mystery.

“They offered him,” he says, “a piece of broiled fish and a honeycomb.” What is signified by the broiled fish except that the Mediator between God and human beings suffered? For, like a fish, he deigned to lie hidden in the waters of the human race; like a fish, he was caught by the hook of passion; but in the resurrection he proved sweeter than honey. His sweetness had been tasted by the one who said: “How sweet are your words to my throat, O Lord, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth” (Psalm 118) [Col. 0470D].

A honeycomb is honey in wax. Honey, therefore, in wax is the sweetness of divinity joined to the form of humanity.

“And when he had eaten before them, taking the remains he gave them.” The fact that the Lord gave the remains of the food to the disciples signifies that he showed them that they must imitate his passion, according to what he says elsewhere: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Luke 9). Hence one of them said: “Christ suffered for us” (1 Peter 2), and so forth.

Therefore he gave them the remains of the broiled fish and the honeycomb: he showed that his passion was bitter in the sorrow of the heart, but exceedingly sweet in the glory of the resurrection. Hence one of them, who bore in his own body, as it were, the marks of Christ’s passion, said: “Brothers, I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that will be revealed in us” (Romans 8) [Col. 0471A].

“And he said to them: ‘These are the words that I spoke to you when I was still with you.’” Was he not, then, with those to whom he was speaking visibly? He was indeed with them through the presence of his body, but he was far from them through participation in their weakness, because they were corruptible and mortal, whereas he was incorruptible and immortal. And therefore, while speaking with them bodily, he said: “These are the words that I spoke to you when I was still with you.”

“For it is necessary that everything written about me in the law of Moses and the prophets and the psalms be fulfilled” [Col. 0471B]. Here he invoked not only the Law but also the oracles of the prophets and the psalms in order to confirm his passion and resurrection. For, since he himself says, “Let every word be established on the testimony of two or three witnesses” (Deuteronomy 15), if anyone refused to believe the testimonies of the Law concerning him, he should at least not presume to disbelieve the many testimonies contained in the oracles of the prophets and the psalms, but should judge them worthy of belief.

“Then he opened their understanding, so that they might understand the Scriptures.” And because they could not understand the Scriptures by themselves, he opened their understanding so that they might understand the Scriptures, so that what they heard bodily they might understand spiritually. What had been written about him in the Law, the prophets, and the psalms he makes clear when he adds:

“And he said to them: ‘For thus it is written, and thus it was necessary for Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead on the third day’” [Col. 0471C].

It was necessary for Christ to suffer and to rise, not for himself but for us, so that through his undeserved passion he might free us from the punishment we deserved, and through his holy resurrection show that we would reign with him. For, as the Apostle says, “he died for our sins and rose for our justification” (Romans 4).

Hence he rightly did not wish to delay his resurrection beyond the third day, so that he might rest in the tomb through two nights and one day. Night pertains to sin, and human nature was held bound by two deaths: the death of the soul because of sin, and the death of the flesh because of the punishment of sin. Because the Mediator between God and human beings died only in the flesh, in order to free us from the death of the soul, he rightly wished to rest in the tomb for two nights and one day, since by his single death he condemned our double death [Col. 0471D].

Why he wished to die and rise for us is made clear when it is added: “And that repentance and the forgiveness of sins should be preached in his name.” Therefore, let it not seem harsh or severe that it is said, “that repentance should be preached in his name,” because what follows is exceedingly sweet: “for the forgiveness of sins.”

Where these things were to be preached is made clear when it is added: “To all nations.” By this statement [Col. 0472A] the heresy of the Donatists is confounded. They wanted to introduce a local God and therefore said that his faith existed only in Africa, failing to heed what the Lord himself says: “To all nations.”

Through the ministry of the apostles, repentance and the forgiveness of sins were preached among all nations, fulfilling the prophecy that said: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world.” And lest anyone despair of pardon because of the greatness of his sins, it is added: “Beginning from Jerusalem.”

Therefore, no one should despair that he can obtain forgiveness because of the greatness of his sins, provided that he repents lawfully, since he knows that forgiveness was granted even to the people of Jerusalem, who with bloody hands and lying voices shed the very blood by which the human race was redeemed. For, as the Lord says through the prophet: “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live” (Ezekiel 18) [Col. 0472B].

## HOMILY LXXV. WEDNESDAY OF EASTER.

(Acts 3.) “In those days, Peter opened his mouth and said: ‘Men of Israel, and you who fear God, hear.’” And the rest. We should note that he calls men from the race of Israel, and those who fear the Lord, to hear the word of God.

They are called *men* from *strengths*, because they do not know how to fail through endurance or to vaunt themselves with any arrogance in prosperity [Col. 0472C]; rather, fixed with steadfast spirit and strengthened by contemplation of heavenly things, they always remain undaunted.

“Those who fear the Lord,” he says, “hear,” that is, those who have reverence for his name. For no one deserves to hear his words unless he is known to fear him. The fear of the Lord, because it is just and upright, renews hearing, grants love, and kindles the ardor of charity.

“The God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, the God of our fathers.” He could have said, “the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob,” but he names God three times—God of Abraham, God of Isaac, God of Jacob—so that you may understand God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. And lest the threefold naming of God cause you offense, he added, “of our fathers.” Wisely he distinguished the persons and united the nature.

“He glorified his Son,” when, after the exceedingly wondrous resurrection, God granted that the whole world should believe in him in the very fact that he had become human [Col. 0472D]. He glorified him with the glory of the resurrection, glorified him with the glory of the ascension, and glorified him with the glory of his sitting at the right hand.

“Whom you indeed handed over.” For Pilate answered the Lord by saying: “Am I a Jew? Your nation and your chief priests handed you over to me; what have you done?” (John 18)—with the implied addition, “so that you should be handed over to me.”

The priests handed over the Lord out of envy; Judas handed him over out of greed; the Father handed him over for our liberation; the Son handed himself over out of love for us. Of the Father the Apostle says: “He did not spare his own Son, but handed him over for us all” (Romans 8). Of the Son he says: “He loved us and handed himself over for us” (Galatians 2).

“And you denied him before the face of Pilate” [Col. 0473A], saying: “Crucify, crucify such a man. We have no king except Caesar. We have a law, and according to the law he must die, because he has made himself the Son of God,” while Pilate was judging that he should be released.

For, as the Gospel says, Pilate was seeking an opportunity to release Jesus, saying: “I find no cause in him,” and neither did Herod. Pilate sends him to Herod; Herod sends him back to Pilate. Piety runs between two forms of impiety, yet impiety cannot condemn piety.

The accused is present, but no guilt is found. “You handed this man over to me,” he says, “as though he were turning the people away; and behold, having questioned him before you, I find no cause in him concerning the charges you bring against him. You say that he orders tribute not to be paid to Caesar; I have proved that what you allege is false. You say that he teaches against the Law; I have proved that he does not destroy the Law but fulfills it. Everything you have alleged has been found to be the opposite” [Col. 0473B].

“And you asked that a murderous man be given to you.” The Gospel says that there was a man called Barabbas, bound because he had committed murder during a rebellion. For Barabbas, who is interpreted as “son of their father,” signifies the devil, who stirs up many rebellions throughout the whole world—murders, adulteries, and every crime. For as soon as Jesus was crucified, this Barabbas was released and suffocates the Jewish people.

“But you killed the Author of life” [Col. 0473C], the one who fashioned the human being from the mud of the earth and breathed into his face the breath of life, and the human being became a living soul; the one who said: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14); and of whom John says: “This is the true God and eternal life” (1 John 5).

“And now, brothers, I know that you acted through ignorance.” For, as the Apostle says, “if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Corinthians 2).

“But God, who foretold through the mouth of all the prophets that his Christ would suffer, has fulfilled it in this way.” Hence the Lord himself said to Cleopas and another disciple: “O foolish ones and slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken! Was it not necessary that the Christ should suffer these things and so enter into his glory? And beginning with Moses and all the prophets, he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself” (Luke 24) [Col. 0473D].

For if Moses and all the prophets spoke of Christ, and of his entering into his glory through the anguish of his passion, how do those who boast that they are Christians show themselves to be so, when, according to the measure of their strength, they neither desire to investigate how the Scriptures pertain to Christ nor wish to attain through the passions of tribulations the glory that they desire to possess with Christ?

## HOMILY LXXVI. WEDNESDAY OF EASTER.

(John 21.) “At that time: Jesus revealed himself again at the Sea of Tiberias. He revealed himself in this way: Simon Peter and Thomas, who is called Didymus, were together” [Col. 0474A]. And the rest.

Although we ought always to retain the memory of the Lord’s resurrection in our minds and recite it with our mouths, nevertheless we should speak of it especially on these days, on which it is believed to have taken place and is venerated. It should not seem burdensome to hear what the holy evangelists considered useful to write.

For it is not only glorious that he appeared to the disciples after the resurrection; the number of those to whom he appeared and the places in which he was seen are also full of mysteries. The Evangelist took care to make this clear in the sequence of the present reading, when he so carefully expressed the manner of his appearance, saying: “Jesus revealed himself again at the Sea of Tiberias. He revealed himself in this way,” and so forth.

And appropriately, at his seventh appearance he appeared to seven disciples [Col. 0474B], because those will attain to his vision who, illumined by the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit, tread upon the waves of the present age through divine love and keep watch over the winning of souls. For the number seven, which consists of three and four—that is, of the first odd number and the first even number—signifies the gifts of the Holy Spirit, through whose grace both faith in the Trinity is known and the teaching of the four Gospels is preserved.

But someone may ask why Peter returned to fishing after his conversion, since the Truth says: “No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God” (Luke 9). The answer is brief but readily apparent: the work that is repeated after conversion without fault is the work that was practiced without fault before conversion.

We recognize this more easily if we compare the occupations of Peter and Matthew the evangelist and fellow apostle [Col. 0474C]. We know that Peter was a fisherman and Matthew a tax collector. We read that Peter returned to fishing after his conversion, whereas we do not read that Matthew returned to the profits of the tax office. For it is one thing to seek one’s livelihood justly by fishing, and another to persist in the profits of a tax office through quarrelling.

“And they went out and got into the boat, and that night they caught nothing.” Just as the boat signifies the world, so that night signifies ignorance, as in the saying: “The night has advanced, and the day has drawn near” (Romans 13). For all those who labored before the Lord’s coming labored, as it were, in night, because they could not possess as fully as people do now the hope of rising again or of possessing eternal life [Col. 0474D].

Thus throughout the whole night they caught nothing, because unless the Lord illumines the heart of the hearer by his grace, the teacher’s discourse labors as though in night, as the Psalmist testifies: “Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labor in vain” (Psalm 126).

But in order that teachers may teach rightly and hearers may hear worthily, the mercy of him of whom it follows must be sought:

“But when morning had come, Jesus stood on the shore; yet the disciples did not know that it was Jesus.” Here someone may perhaps ask why the Lord stood on the shore after the resurrection, when before the passion he had not only walked upon the waves of the sea before the disciples [Col. 0475A] but had also given Peter his hand so that he could walk upon the sea.

The answer is that the Lord did this not because of inability but because of a mystery. The sea, as we have said, signifies the world. The disciples were therefore in the sea because they were still laboring amid the waves of this age. But the Lord stood on the shore because he was free from their corruption and mortality. It was as though he said in words: “I no longer appear to you in the sea, because I no longer live among the waves of the world in common with you.” This is what he says elsewhere: “These are the words that I spoke to you when I was still with you” (Luke 24).

“Jesus therefore said to them: ‘Children, have you any relish (*pulmentarium*)?’ They answered him: ‘No’” [Col. 0475B]. The Lord did not question the disciples because he was ignorant, but so that through their common conversation he might demonstrate his knowledge.

And beautifully he called his disciples children. For *puer*—“child”—is derived from purity. This name rightly suits the disciples, because without deceit or pretense they clung to the Lord with the purest love of heart. In their person it had formerly been said through Isaiah: “Behold, I and my children, whom the Lord has given me” (Isaiah 8).

He wanted all believers to be such little ones when elsewhere he said: “Unless you turn and become like little children, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 18). And again: “Let the little children come to me, for of such is the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 19).

“Jesus said to them: ‘Cast the net on the right side of the boat, and you will find some’” [Col. 0475C]. Twice in the holy Gospel we read that, at the Lord’s command, nets were cast for a catch: first before the passion, and now a second time after the resurrection.

There is, however, this difference between the two catches. In the first catch, they are commanded to cast the nets, but the side on which they should cast them is not indicated; in this one, they are specifically commanded to cast them on the right side. In the first, the net is torn because of the multitude of fish; in this one, many fish are caught, but the nets are not torn.

Hence it is evident that the first catch signifies the Church as she exists in the present life, while this catch, which took place after the resurrection, signifies what she will be in the future. The good are never found alone except in heaven, and the wicked are never found alone except in hell. In the present Church, however, citizens of both groups are found, because many enter the Church through faith who will not reach the kingdom of heaven through good works. Of them the Psalmist says: “I announced and spoke; they were multiplied beyond number” (Psalm 39) [Col. 0475D].

In this catch, therefore, which took place after the resurrection, it was fitting that only good fish should be caught, signifying the number of the elect.

“So they cast the net, and now they were unable to draw it in because of the multitude of fish.” The present passage demonstrates that outward miracles frequently instruct inward faith: the one whom they had not recognized by sight and conversation, they recognized through the catch of fish. Thus, after laboring throughout the whole night and catching nothing, at his command they immediately caught such a multitude of fish that they were unable to draw in the net.

“That disciple whom Jesus loved said to Peter: ‘It is the Lord’” [Col. 0476A]. And because among all virtues virginal integrity excels by a certain privilege, rightly the incorrupt virgin was the first to recognize the incorruptible body of the Lord—namely, John, whose Gospel this is.

But when all had heard that it was the Lord, the one who loved him more than the others hastened to come first. Hence it follows: “Simon Peter, when he heard that it was the Lord, girded himself with his tunic” (for he was naked), “and threw himself into the sea, and came to Jesus.”

In many passages of the Gospel it is shown that Peter loved the Lord more than the other disciples [Col. 0476B]. For when the Lord foretold that he would suffer in Jerusalem, saying: “Behold, we are going up to Jerusalem, and the Son of Man will be handed over to the hands of sinners, and they will condemn him to death” (Matthew 20), Peter took him aside privately and said to him: “Far be it from you, Lord; this shall not happen to you” (Matthew 16). It was not fitting, he meant, that the Son of God should taste death.

And when the moment of that same passion was approaching, and the Lord said: “All of you will suffer scandal because of me on this night,” Peter, trusting in the greatness of his love, said: “Even if all are scandalized because of you, I will never be scandalized.” And when the Lord continued to foretell what would happen, saying: “Amen I say to you, before the cock crows, you will deny me three times,” he contradicted him: “Even if I must die with you, I will not deny you” (Matthew 26) [Col. 0476C].

And, as this reading relates, when he saw the Lord standing on the shore, he girded himself with his tunic and threw himself into the sea.

Spiritually, we may understand this to mean that after he recognized that the Lord had risen, he put on again the tunic of faith or love with which he had stripped himself when denying him. And he threw himself into the sea—that is, he began to preach his name among the swelling powers of the world, the one whom previously, at the voice of a single woman, he had denied three times. For he says: “We must obey God rather than human beings” (Acts 5).

“But the other disciples came in the boat,” that is, burning with the same faith or love with which the apostle Peter had been inflamed, they followed him. Hence it is also fittingly said: “For they were not far from land, but about two hundred cubits, dragging the net of fish.”

Because in two hundred cubits the number one hundred is doubled, this number signifies perfect charity, which consists in love of God and of one’s neighbor. For the one who perfectly loves God and neighbor is not far from the land of the living [Col. 0476D].

“But when they had come onto the land, they saw burning coals laid out, and a fish placed upon them, and bread.” Literally, this seems almost to say that the fish and the bread had both been placed upon the coals. But we should understand that the item that needed cooking—that is, the fish—had been placed upon the coals, while the bread had been set aside separately.

It should also be noted that the very kind of food is not without a mystery. For, as we read in another Gospel reading, the disciples offered the Lord a honeycomb with a broiled fish [Col. 0477A]. Here, however, bread and fish are mentioned.

He himself was, as it were, broiled like a fish at the time of his passion, but at the time of the resurrection he displayed the sweetness of bread. Of himself he says (John 6): “I am the living bread that came down from heaven.” And again: “The bread that I will give is my flesh for the life of the world.”

“Jesus said to them, ‘Bring some of the fish that you have just caught.’ Simon Peter went up and dragged the net ashore, full of large fish, one hundred and fifty-three. And although there were so many, the net was not torn.”

It is clear, and requires no explanation, why Peter was the first of them all to drag the net with the fish ashore. For the Church was specially entrusted to him, and the power of binding and loosing was given to him when the Lord said to him: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it. And I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven. Whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven” (Matthew 16). For after the resurrection the Lord also said to him: “Simon, son of John, do you love me more than these? Feed my sheep” (John 21).

But this must be carefully considered: the Evangelist would never have expressed the number of the fish so precisely if he believed that no mystery was present in that number. For he says: “Simon Peter went up and dragged the net ashore, full of large fish, one hundred and fifty-three.” This number begins with one, but is multiplied by increasing it up to seventeen. For if you multiply seventeen by three, you will find fifty-one. Again, if you multiply fifty-one by three, you will find one hundred and fifty-three.

The ten pertain to the number of the Decalogue of the Law, because ten commandments were given to Moses. The seven pertain to the spiritual grace of the New Testament, on account of the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, or on account of faith in the Holy Trinity and the teaching of the four Gospels. The number fifty pertains to rest, because the fiftieth year was called the jubilee, that is, the year of remission. Since, therefore, those will attain true rest who spiritually fulfill the Decalogue of the Law through the grace of the Holy Spirit, we multiply, as it were, the sum of ten and seven by three, so that we may arrive at the number fifty.

And because true rest is found in unity, one is rightly added to fifty, since this was said of the primitive Church: “The multitude of believers had one heart and one soul” (Acts 4). And because the observance of the Law and spiritual grace consist in faith in the Holy Trinity, we arrive, as it were, at fifty-three. For since, as was said above, this fishing signifies the Church as it will be in the future, it was fitting that so many fish should be caught, through which the total number of the elect who will reign with the Lord might be signified.

But in order to remove every doubt concerning his resurrection from the minds of the disciples, the Lord was graciously willing not only to appear to them but also to eat in their presence. Hence it follows:

“Jesus said to them, ‘Come and have breakfast.’”

Beautifully, he wished to celebrate the final meal with seven disciples, because those will celebrate an eternal banquet with the Lord after the universal judgment who in the present age have been filled with the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit.

What follows—“And none of those reclining at table dared to ask him, ‘Who are you?’ knowing that it was the Lord”—means this: no one presumed to ask who he was, because no one could doubt that he himself was the Christ. His identity was so evident and manifest that it was clear to all who saw him who he was; and therefore it was superfluous to ask who he was, since none of those reclining at table could doubt his identity.

“And Jesus came and took bread and gave it to them, and likewise the fish.”

The Lord therefore gave the disciples fish because he showed that his passion was to be imitated. He also gave them bread with the fish because, after enduring the passion, he promised the joys of eternal satisfaction.

But when it is said:

“This was now the third time that Jesus was manifested to his disciples, after he had risen from the dead,”

this refers not to the number of appearances but rather to the days. For on the first day, when he rose from the dead, he was seen five times by human beings. Again, on another day, when after eight days he appeared to the disciples in the room where Thomas was. And the third time was when he appeared to the disciples while they were fishing by the Sea of Tiberias—his seventh appearance to the disciples.

## HOMILY LXXVII. THURSDAY OF EASTER

(JOHN 20.) “At that time: Mary was standing outside at the tomb, weeping.” And so forth.

In many passages of Scripture the praiseworthy virtue of perseverance is shown, but we learn how great this virtue is at the very beginning of this reading if we briefly attend to what precedes in this Gospel.

Above, the Evangelist reported that, while it was still dark, Mary Magdalene came to the tomb and saw that the stone had been removed from the tomb. She therefore ran and came to Simon Peter and to the other disciple whom Jesus loved, and said to them: “They have taken the Lord from the tomb, and we do not know where they have placed him.” They ran, entered the tomb, and found it just as the women had said. Immediately afterward it is written of them: “Then the disciples went away again to their own homes.” But of her it follows: “Mary was standing outside at the tomb, weeping.”

Here we must consider how great a love for the Lord had inflamed this woman’s mind: even when the disciples were leaving the tomb, she did not leave. And because she did not cease seeking him, she deserved to see him first. Thus we learn that perseverance is necessary in every good work, as the Lord says: “The one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matthew 10).

For this reason the Law commands that the tail of the victim be offered in sacrifice. The end of the body is in the tail, and the one who completes a good work to the end offers an acceptable sacrifice to God.

For this reason also Joseph is said to have been clothed among his brothers in a long robe reaching to the ankles. The end of the body is at the ankle. Spiritually, that person is clothed in such a robe who brings a good work to completion.

For this reason the Psalmist also admonishes us, saying: “Establish the solemn day amid the dense branches, even to the horns of the altar” (Psalm 117). The end is at the horn of the altar, and the one who celebrates the solemn day in his mind perseveres in good work to the end.

How greatly this woman was afflicted with grief for the Lord is shown when it is said: “Mary was standing outside at the tomb, weeping.” For she was weeping because she did not see the one whom she greatly desired; she was weeping because she thought that the body had been stolen from the tomb.

“While she was weeping, she bent down and looked into the tomb.”

She had already seen that the tomb was empty, since she had reported to the disciples that the Lord had been stolen from the tomb. Why did she bend down again, unless because she desired to see again? For one glance is not enough for someone who loves greatly.

Just as when we lose something, although we run here and there searching for it, we nevertheless look repeatedly toward the place where we remember having had it, so this woman, although she was seeking the Lord’s body here and there, nevertheless, anxious over his absence, looked repeatedly at the tomb where she knew he had been placed.

Thus, although she did not immediately deserve to see the Lord, she was not deprived of the vision of angels. Hence it follows:

“And she saw two angels in white, sitting, one at the head and one at the feet, where the body of Jesus had been placed.”

Someone may perhaps wonder why John describes them as sitting at the Lord’s resurrection, whereas Luke, describing the same resurrection, mentions that they stood beside the woman.

To this we must answer that, just as sitting is a sign of royal dignity, so standing is characteristic of one who helps or fights. And because the same Mediator between God and human beings became both king and priest for us, he describes some as sitting and others as standing.

And because the one whose resurrection they had come to testify to must be believed to be both God and man, one is remembered as having sat at the head and one at the feet. The head signifies the height of divinity, as the Apostle says: “The head of Christ is God” (1 Corinthians 11). The feet express his humanity, as it is said through Moses: “Those who draw near to his feet will receive instruction from him” (Deuteronomy 33).

Thus the angel sits, as it were, at the head when the Evangelist proclaims: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1). The angel sits, as it were, at the feet when the same Evangelist adds: “And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (ibid.).

And because it is customary among the Palestinians to celebrate feast days dressed in white garments, when the angels appeared in white garments they showed that they were celebrating a festival.

If someone asks whether it was their festival or ours, the answer is: both theirs and ours. It was the Lord’s resurrection that constituted the angels’ festival, because through human beings he recovered the number of angels diminished by the apostate angel. It was also our festival, because, having freed us from darkness and the shadow of death, it restored us to the dignity of the angels.

“They said to her: ‘Woman, why are you weeping?’”

The angels asked not only the causes of her grief but also what she was seeking—not to lessen her desire to seek, but to increase it. Just as when we weep because of the loss of loved ones, if someone asks us the causes of our tears, our weeping grows greater, so they asked about the causes of her sorrow in order to increase her desire for weeping, knowing that those who mourn are blessed, for they will be comforted.

But she reveals why she was weeping when she adds: “Because they have taken away my Lord, and I do not know where they have placed him.”

Here we should note that she did not say, “They have taken away the body of my Lord,” but “They have taken away my Lord,” although she knew that only the Lord’s body had been placed in the tomb. Holy Scripture sometimes customarily uses the whole for the part; therefore, while she was seeking only the Lord’s body, she said that the Lord had been taken from the tomb.

“When she had said this, she turned around and saw Jesus standing, but she did not know that it was Jesus.”

Appropriately, in order that Mary might deserve to see God, she is said to have turned around. For the one who turns around directs his eyes toward the place where previously his back had been.

She turned around, as it were, when, setting aside the clouds of doubt, she began partly to believe in Christ’s resurrection. Yet the Lord moderated his appearance to her in such a way that, because she loved him but did not believe that he had risen, she both saw him and failed to recognize him. Hence it follows:

“Supposing that he was the gardener, she said to him: ‘Lord, if you have taken him away, tell me where you have placed him, and I will take him.’”

In these words we should also consider how great a fire of love had filled the woman’s mind. Before she had identified the person she was addressing, she spoke as though he already knew whom she was seeking, saying: “If you have taken him away, tell me where you have placed him, and I will take him.”

Love has this particular characteristic: whoever loves someone greatly thinks that everyone loves that person.

Yet the woman was not entirely mistaken when she thought the Lord was the gardener. For just as it belongs to a gardener’s work to uproot harmful plants so that the good may also flourish, so the Lord Jesus Christ daily uproots vices from his garden—that is, from his Church—so that virtues may be able to flourish.

And although the female sex is physically weak for carrying burdens and fearful of bearing the corpses of the dead, whatever would be impossible for others she considered light and possible because of the greatness of her love, saying: “If you have taken him away, tell me where you have placed him, and I will take him.”

“Jesus said to her: ‘Mary.’ She turned and said to him: ‘Rabboni,’ which means ‘Teacher.’ Jesus said to her: ‘Do not touch me.’”

Because earlier the Lord had addressed the woman by the common designation of her sex, and he was not recognized, he also called her by her proper name, so that at least she might recognize the one who recognized her. For he said: “Mary.”

Since the number of the elect is certain before God, great grace is given to some when they are remembered as known to God by their proper names. Such was Moses, to whom it was said: “I know you by name” (Exodus 33), and: “You have found favor before me.”

Therefore, after the woman was called by her proper name by the Lord, she immediately recognized the one who recognized her, saying: “Rabboni,” which means “Teacher.”

What the woman did after this the Evangelist does not state. Nevertheless, from the Lord’s words—“Do not touch me”—he makes clear that, as soon as the woman recognized the Lord, she wished to hold his feet in worship.

The Lord says to her: “Do not touch me.” We should not suppose that after the resurrection he absolutely refused the touch of women, since it is said of the two women leaving the tomb that they approached and held his feet. Rather, he forbade the touch of this woman because he did not perceive her mind to be sound in faith.

But why he did not wish to be touched by the woman is made clear when it follows: “For I have not yet ascended to my Father.”

Did she wish to touch him bodily after the ascension? No. In her mind he had not yet ascended to the Father. Since she was seeking him, dead, among the dead, she did not believe him equal to the Father.

“But go to my brothers and say to them: ‘I am ascending to my Father and your Father, my God and your God.’”

The Redeemer’s great condescension toward the apostles is revealed here. Those who had not been worthy to be servants are called brothers, in accordance with what is said in his person through the Psalmist: “I will proclaim your name to my brothers; in the midst of the assembly I will praise you” (Psalm 21).

Nor will we be strangers to this dignity if we become participants through holiness of conduct, the Lord himself saying: “Whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven is my brother and sister and mother” (Matthew 12).

What greater reward can an adopted servant receive than to be called the brother of the one who is the only Son? Therefore, although we were not worthy to be called servants, we are called brothers.

But when he said, “I am ascending to my Father and your Father, my God and your God,” why did he not say “our Father” and “our God” in common?

Clearly, he is Father to him in one way and to us in another, because what he possesses by nature we have received by the grace of adoption. He is his God because he descended to us and was made a little lower than the angels by assuming our humanity. He is their God because through him they have deserved to ascend to the Father.

“Mary Magdalene came announcing to the disciples: ‘I have seen the Lord, and he said these things to me.’”

The most merciful compassion of God toward the female sex is shown here. Because death had been brought into the world through a woman, and so the female sex would not always be held in disgrace, he wished through the female sex to announce to men the joys of the resurrection, through the same sex by which the sorrow of death had been announced.

It was as though he were saying to human beings: “From the hand of the one from whom you received the cup of death, hear the joys of the resurrection.”

After the woman heard, “Go, tell my brothers,” and so forth, it is rightly added: “Mary came announcing to the disciples,” because everyone who understands rightly ought to announce it to others, in accordance with what is written in the Apocalypse: “Let the one who hears say, ‘Come’” (Revelation 22).

## HOMILY LXXVIII. FRIDAY OF EASTER

(MATTHEW 28.) “At that time: The eleven disciples went to Galilee, to the mountain where Jesus had appointed them.” And so forth.

Obedience accompanies the Lord’s command to the disciples. When the Lord foretold that he would suffer and rise again, he also designated the place where he would be seen by the disciples, saying: “After I have risen, I will go before you into Galilee” (Mark 14).

And when the angel announced to the women that his resurrection had already taken place, he said: “Go, tell his disciples and Peter that he has risen. Behold, he will go before you into Galilee; there you will see him, as he told you” (Mark 16).

Lifted up by this promise, the disciples, as the present Gospel reading relates, “went to Galilee, to the mountain where Jesus had appointed them.”

This should not be passed over without consideration: after his resurrection the Lord promised that he would be seen in Galilee and, as the present reading records, he showed himself there. For Galilee in our language is interpreted as “transmigration accomplished.”

He is seen in Galilee after the resurrection so that, by the name of the place itself, he might indicate that he had already passed over from corruption to incorruption, from lowliness to glory, and from mortality to immortality, as the Apostle says: “Even if we once knew Christ according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him in that way” (2 Corinthians 5). And again: “Christ, rising from the dead, dies no more; death will no longer rule over him” (Romans 6).

Or certainly, when he is seen in Galilee—that is, in “transmigration”—he mystically admonishes us that, if we wish to see him now “through a mirror and in a riddle,” and afterward “face to face” (1 Corinthians 13), we should strive to pass over from vices to virtues and from love of the world to love of God, saying with the Apostle: “But we, with unveiled face, contemplating the glory of the Lord” (ibid.), and so forth.

Let no desire for the world hold us here; let no passing pleasure of ours persuade the mind to remain here, so that with the Apostle we may be able to say: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Philippians 3).

Therefore he is rightly seen not only in Galilee but also on a mountain, for the mountain in this place signifies the height of perfection. The disciples saw the Lord on the mountain because those who now trample upon earthly desires will one day deserve to see him in the heights of heaven.

The disciples rightly worshiped the Lord after the resurrection, since even before the passion they had recognized through his miracles that he was God.

But when it is said, “Some doubted,” this is what the Evangelist Luke means when he says that, seeing the Lord while they were sitting together in the room, they thought they were seeing a spirit (Luke 24).

One of them, having heard the others say, “We have seen the Lord” (John 20), doubted that this could have happened and said: “Unless I see the marks of the nails in his hands, and put my finger into the place of the nails, and put my hand into his side, I will not believe.”

Hence the Evangelist Mark also says: “He appeared to the eleven as they reclined at table, and reproached their unbelief and hardness of heart” (Mark 16), and so forth.

Their doubt was the confirmation of our faith: the more they doubted, the more carefully they investigated; and the more perfectly they discovered the truth, the more firmly they showed what we ought to believe. They not only strengthened our faith but also destroyed the perversity of heretics.

“And Jesus came and spoke to them.”

Because he knew that some of the disciples doubted his resurrection, he graciously drew near to them and also conversed with them, so that they might recognize through conversation the one whom they had not recognized as God through sight.

He said: “All authority has been given to me in heaven and on earth.”

He speaks this with respect to the humanity he assumed, in which he was made a little lower than the angels. In his humanity, therefore, he received authority over all things, while in his divinity he is omnipotent over all things, as he himself says: “Everything that the Father has is mine” (John 16). And again: “I and the Father are one.”

For he says that he has received authority not only on earth but also in heaven, because, by rising again, he raised above the angels the humanity that he had handed over to suffering for our sake. The Apostle bears witness to this when he says: “Therefore God also exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow—of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth” (Philippians 2).

This authority does not reject sinners but gathers them. Therefore, after saying, “All authority has been given to me in heaven and on earth,” he added:

“Go, therefore, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.”

Here the proper order for baptism is shown, since teaching is said to precede baptism. He says: “Teach all nations”; then he adds: “Baptizing them.”

The person who is to be baptized must first be taught, so that he may first learn to believe what he can afterward receive through baptism. For just as faith without works is dead (James 2), so works, if they do not arise from faith, are of no benefit.

This is not observed in the case of infants, because they are believed to be saved in holy baptism through the faith of their parents or of those who receive them. Nevertheless, when they reach the age of understanding, they must be taught not only what they ought to believe in their hearts but also what they ought to observe in their conduct.

Hence it is rightly added: “Teaching them to observe everything that I have commanded you.”

Therefore, they are not to be taught other things, but what Christ commanded—and not some of these things, but all of them.

It should also be noted that he did not say, “Baptizing them in the names of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit,” but “in the name,” to signify that God is an undivided Trinity. For although he is three in names, he is one in nature, since God is the Father, God is the Son, and God is the Holy Spirit.

And lest the apostles’ weakness doubt that it was unequal to teaching all nations, the gracious Teacher offered great consolation when he added: “And behold, I am with you all days, until the consummation of the age.”

Hence it is asked why he says, “Behold, I am with you all days, until the consummation of the age,” when elsewhere he is reported to have said: “Little children, I am with you only a little while, and you will seek me and will not find me” (John 13).

To this we must answer that the Mediator between God and human beings, the Lord Jesus Christ, must be believed to be true man and true God. At times he speaks of the humanity he assumed; at other times, of the power of his divinity.

Thus, what he says—“I am with you only a little while”—refers to the humanity he assumed, in which he could go from place to place. But what he says here—“Behold, I am with you all days, until the consummation of the age”—refers to the majesty of his divinity, through which he is present everywhere, wholly present everywhere. He neither comes in time nor departs in time, but always remains equally and ineffably, as it is said to him through the Psalmist: “You are the same, and your years will not fail” (Psalm 101).

When he promised that he would remain with the apostles until the consummation of the age, he showed that until the consummation of the age there would be future elect with whom he would deign to remain.

Since much longer periods were to follow the apostles up to the consummation of the age, this promise must not be thought to pertain only to the apostles, but to all the elect who will exist until the consummation of the age, in accordance with what he himself says elsewhere: “This Gospel will be preached to all nations, and then the end will come” (Matthew 24).

## HOMILY LXXIX. SATURDAY AFTER EASTER

(JOHN 20.) “At that time: On the first day of the week Mary Magdalene came early, while it was still dark, to the tomb.” And so forth.

If someone compares this woman’s former deeds with the present reading, he will recognize how merciful God is toward converted sinners.

For this is that woman who, as Luke says (Luke 7), when she was a sinner in the city and learned that Jesus was reclining in the house of Simon the leper, brought an alabaster jar of ointment. Standing behind him at his feet, she began to bathe his feet with tears, wiped them with her hair, kissed his feet, and anointed them with ointment.

This is the woman of whom Mark writes: “When Jesus had risen early on the first day of the week, he appeared first to Mary Magdalene, from whom he had cast out seven demons” (Mark 16).

But because, according to the Savior’s word, many sins had been forgiven her because she loved greatly, she persevered in that fervor of love even to the Lord’s passion. She could not be separated from the dead one whom she had loved with supreme love while he was alive.

Finally, as the Evangelists relate, as soon as she saw the Lord placed in the tomb, she bought spices and, early on the first day of the week before daylight—as the present Gospel reading relates—came to the Lord’s sepulcher.

And although the female sex is ordinarily timid about walking in darkness, this woman, who loved the Lord with all her heart, feared nothing. For perfect love was in her, the love that casts out fear.

But it is asked why John says, “Mary Magdalene came early, while it was still dark, to the tomb,” whereas Mark says that she came very early, after the sun had risen.

We can answer simply that it could have happened that, because of the greatness of her love, she first came alone to the tomb before daylight, and afterward, when the sun had risen, returned to the tomb with two women of the same name.

For we should not think that the holy women came to the Lord’s tomb only once in the day, but frequently.

Or certainly, by saying that she came to the tomb while it was still dark, John describes the western part of the world, while Mark, by saying that the sun had risen, describes the eastern part.

Every day we see that, when the sun leaves the earth’s concave regions and begins at first light to restore daylight to the earth, there is light in the east while darkness remains in the west. When John says that it was still dark, he has the western regions in view; when Mark says that the sun had risen, he considers the eastern regions.

Spiritually, darkness was in the woman’s heart when she came to the Lord’s tomb, because, ignorant of his resurrection, she was seeking the living among the dead. The sun then rose in her mind when she not only saw that he had risen but also believed it.

“And she saw that the stone had been removed from the tomb.”

Matthew describes more clearly how and when the stone was rolled away, saying: “For an angel of the Lord descended from heaven, came, rolled away the stone, and sat upon it” (Matthew 28).

We should not think that the angel assisted the Lord in his resurrection. Rather, he rolled away the stone in order to show human beings that the resurrection had taken place.

But after the woman saw that the stone had been removed from the tomb, since she did not yet believe that the Lord had risen, she believed that he had been stolen and hurried to announce what she had seen to the disciples.

She is truly the woman who, in the words of the Song of Songs, speaks as the voice of the Church: “Upon my bed at night I sought him whom my soul loves; I sought him, but I did not find him. I will rise and go around the city, seeking him whom my soul loves. The watchmen who guard the city found me. ‘Have you seen him whom my soul loves?’ And it happened that, when I had passed them, I found him whom my soul loves. I held him and would not let him go until I brought him into the house of my father and into the chamber of my mother” (Song of Songs 3).

Hence it follows:

“So she ran and came to Simon Peter and to the other disciple whom Jesus loved, and said to them: ‘They have taken my Lord from the tomb, and we do not know where they have placed him.’”

When they heard this, Peter and John, who loved him more than the others—and John is the author of this Gospel—went out. Hence it is rightly said:

“Then Peter and the other disciple went out and came to the tomb. The two were running together, but the other disciple ran ahead faster than Peter and came first to the tomb. And when he bent down, he saw the linen cloths lying there, but he did not enter. Then Simon Peter came, following him, and entered the tomb. He saw the linen cloths lying there, and the cloth that had been on his head, not lying with the linen cloths but rolled up separately in one place.”

This running of the disciples must not be thought devoid of mystery. John would not have said that he arrived first and did not enter if he had not perceived a mystery in his very hesitation.

Through the two disciples, therefore, two orders of peoples are spiritually prefigured: the Jews and the Gentiles.

Peter, the older, signifies the Gentile people; the younger John signifies the synagogue of the Jews.

John ran first but did not enter the tomb, because the synagogue was first in knowledge of God and understanding of the Law, but refused to enter into faith.

Simon Peter came following him and entered, because the Gentile people, converted after the Lord’s incarnation, came later, but entered faith first, in accordance with the Lord’s word in the Gospel: “The first will be last, and the last first” (Matthew 20).

“And he saw the linen cloths lying there, and the cloth that had been on his head, not lying with the linen cloths but rolled up separately in one place.”

What is signified by the linen cloths except good works? Linen, which is woven with labor but worn with beauty, signifies the works of the good: they are completed through the diligence of devoted labor, but they clothe the soul with beauty. Of these it is said through the prophet in the voice of the Church: “As I live, says the Lord, you will clothe yourself with all these as with an ornament” (Isaiah 49).

By the cloth with which the sweat of laborers is usually wiped—and from this it received its name—the labor of the Lord’s passion is expressed. Hence he himself says through the Prophet: “I have labored in crying out; my throat has become hoarse” (Psalm 68).

Alternatively, by the cloth that had been placed over his head, his divinity can be understood. For the Apostle says: “The head of Christ is God” (1 Corinthians 11).

It is found separately because the Creator surpasses every creature. The cloth of the Lord’s head is therefore found not with the linen cloths but separately in one place, because the Lord’s passion was far different from our passion: what we scarcely endure with sin, he endured without sin; and we suffer tribulations for ourselves, whereas he suffered for us and not for himself.

It is rightly said to have been found rolled up. Linen that is rolled up reveals neither its beginning nor its end. And because the one who suffered in his humanity had neither beginning nor end in his divinity, the cloth of his head is rightly found rolled up.

It is also rightly said to have been found in one place, because the Lord is not in division of minds but dwells in the hearts of those who maintain unity with a pure heart.

The one Lord loves unity. Therefore, what is one cannot be divided, because where there is division Christ cannot dwell, since he is the one who makes those of one mind dwell in a house (Psalm 67).

Hence it is also said of the primitive Church: “The multitude of believers had one heart” (Acts 4), and so forth.

“Then the disciple who had come first to the tomb also entered.”

After Peter entered, John, who had come first, also entered, because, as the Apostle says: “When the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then all Israel will be saved” (Romans 11).

And not first the spiritual, but the natural, and afterward the spiritual.

“And he saw and believed.”

What should we think that he saw or believed? That the Lord had risen from the dead? No. He saw the linen cloths lying there and believed, as the woman had said, that the Lord had been stolen from the tomb.

For if he had believed in his resurrection, the Evangelist would certainly not have added:

“For they did not yet understand the Scriptures, that he had to rise from the dead.”

Here the great usefulness of understanding the Scriptures is demonstrated, since the apostles are said to have been ignorant of the Lord’s resurrection precisely because they did not yet understand the Scriptures. That is, because, through the revelation of the one from whom all wisdom proceeds, they had not yet learned to understand them spiritually. They had not yet heard: “Thus it is written in the Law and the Psalms and the Prophets concerning me,” and so forth, “unto the forgiveness of sins” (Luke 24).

But if the apostles did not believe that the Lord had risen because they did not know the Scriptures, let the madness of those who refuse to discern what is excellent cease—those who criticize others who wish to discern, and envy in others the very things they either cannot or will not do.

## HOMILY LXXX. ON THE OCTAVE OF EASTER

(1 JOHN 5.) “Beloved: Everything born of God conquers the world; and this is the victory that conquers the world, our faith. Who is the one who conquers the world except the one who believes that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God?” And so forth.

When the Epistle was read, dearly beloved brothers, you heard the Apostle John instructing us and saying: “Everything born of God”—that is, the spiritual race that serves God—“conquers the world”—that is, it conquers lovers of the world, or it conquers the works of unbelief and the desire for the world, or every form of idolatrous worship, through observance of Christ’s commandments.

“And this is the victory that conquers the world, our faith.”

Therefore, with firm faith in Christ we conquer the world, all earthly desires, every earthly love and sin, and also the devil, who is the prince and inventor of sin.

“Who is the one who conquers the world except the one who believes that Jesus is the Son of God?”

What the world—that is, the lover of the world—does not believe, let us believe, and let us faithfully obey his commandments.

“This is the one who came through water and blood, Jesus Christ.”

It is as though he were saying: This is the one who came to erase the curse of the earth by his baptism in the Jordan and to redeem the world by his holy blood.

“Not in water only, but in water and blood.”

For he did not come to redeem the world by baptism alone, but also by his own death and the outpouring of his blood.

“**It is the Spirit who bears witness, because Christ is the truth.**” For the Holy Spirit, through whom the remission of all sins is granted to us in baptism, makes us sons of God by adoption: those whom the Lord himself redeemed through the death of the cross and his blood; and through the grace of that same Holy Spirit, whom we received in baptism, we have received the light of true faith and the knowledge of God, from which we must attain eternal salvation.

“**For there are three who bear witness on earth: the water, the blood, and the Spirit.**” Some understand the Holy Trinity to be mystically signified here—the Trinity that bore witness to Christ. In the water they understand the Father to be signified, because he says of himself: “They have forsaken me, the fountain of living water” (Jer. II). In the blood, Christ himself, who poured out his blood for the salvation of the world. In the Spirit, that same Holy Spirit. This Holy Trinity bears witness to Christ, as he himself speaks through the Gospel: “I am the one who bears witness concerning myself, and the Father who sent me bears witness concerning me. And when the Paraclete comes, whom I shall send to you from my Father, the Spirit of truth, he will bear witness concerning me” (John VIII, XV).

“**And these three are one**”—that is, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. One in nature, one in divine substance, equal in all things, and coeternal in every respect, differing in nothing. In this substance of the Trinity nothing is created, because nothing there has a beginning; nor is anything there understood to be superior, because nothing is found to be earlier or later. In what the Trinity is, it is one, eternal, and true. This is the one faith, because this is the true faith; and therefore this is the catholic faith: to believe the holy Trinity to be of one substance, and to recognize in the Son of God the true natural reality of our flesh and soul.

By this faith we are justified; by this faith we are cleansed. By this faith we are saved; in this faith we have believed, because it grants us remission of all sins. Therefore let there be a most certain hope for us all: the true resurrection of the flesh, which has already taken place in Christ, will follow in us. This flesh of all dead human beings, whether faithful or unfaithful, will rise at the end; but the flesh of the faithful will rise to glory, and the flesh of the unfaithful will rise to punishment. The faithful souls will rejoice forever with their bodies. The souls of the unfaithful likewise will be tormented forever with their bodies; and thus whatever the souls receive there in their flesh, they will not lose, since joy will never be taken away from the good, nor punishment ever removed from the wicked.

We therefore receive eternal life through the holy Church. [Col. 0489A] In this Church alone there is eternal life, because its King is eternal life. One part of this Church already rejoices and reigns in heaven, while another still journeys and labors on earth. It is the one holy Church, in which we are now justified and in which we shall then be glorified. Let us love this good mother unanimously, like good children. Let no one despise the sighs of this mother; let no one reject her admonitions; let no one depart from her bosom. For he will attain the inheritance of God the Father who preserves in faith and love the unity of the mother Church.

Remain, therefore, in the catholic Church; humbly obey the divine words; diligently keep God’s commandments. For those who despise the Lord’s commandments will burn forever, while those who keep them will rejoice without end. And just as eternal death and eternal misery will belong to those who despise them, so eternal life and eternal joy will be given to those who obey, through Jesus Christ, the Son, our Lord, who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

# HOMILY LXXXI. ON THE OCTAVE OF EASTER

**(JOHN XX.)** “At that time: When it was evening on that day, the first day of the week, and the doors were closed where the disciples were gathered because of fear of the Jews.” And so forth.

Whenever we read that the disciples were afraid during the Lord’s Passion, and that after his resurrection they remained in a room because of fear of the Jews, this should not be received with indignation, but should be excused on account of their weakness. For they were fragile and infirm, and had not yet been strengthened by the fullness of the grace of the Holy Spirit, because, as the Evangelist says: “The Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified” (John VII).

But those who had previously remained in a room because of fear of the Jews, after visibly receiving the Holy Spirit, were strengthened with such courage that they confessed the Lord without any trembling before rulers and priests. In the apostles we see, by a certain likeness, what usually happens with water: although naturally liquid, when touched by excessive frost it reaches such hardness that it is changed into the hardest crystal stone, so that it can scarcely be cut with iron. Thus, before the gift of the Holy Spirit, the disciples, weighed down by the weakness of the flesh, were afraid; but after they had been fortified by the grace of the Holy Spirit, they were made so strong that those who had previously remained in a room because of fear of the Jews afterward went away rejoicing from the presence of the council, saying that they were “worthy to suffer dishonor for the name of Jesus” (Acts V).

Let us see with what great courage the apostle Peter was made firm after receiving the Holy Spirit. He had previously denied his Lord and master at the voice of a servant girl; afterward, before terrifying rulers and fearsome authorities, he confessed him with a free voice, saying: “We must obey God rather than human beings”; and again: “Whether it is right in your sight to listen to you rather than to the Lord, judge for yourselves; for we cannot refrain from speaking of what we have seen and heard” (Acts IV).

When it says “the first day of the week,” we must understand the very day of the Lord’s resurrection, which, on account of the honor and reverence due to that resurrection, we call the Lord’s Day. Five times on that same day the Lord, rising from the dead, wished to appear to human beings.

First, he appeared to Mary Magdalene, from whom he had cast out seven demons, as she wept at the tomb. Second, he appeared to that same Mary together with another woman called by the same name, as they went to announce his resurrection to his disciples; then they approached and held his feet. Third, he appeared to Simon Peter. Although the Evangelist does not make clear how or in what manner he appeared to him, he does not conceal that he did appear. Fourth, he appeared to the two disciples going to the village of Emmaus, when they recognized him in the breaking of the bread. When they had returned to Jerusalem and found the eleven gathered together, saying that the Lord had truly risen and had appeared to Simon, Jesus then came for the fifth time and stood in the midst of them.

This is what the Evangelist now says: “When it was evening,” and so forth.

It may reasonably be asked how the Lord, possessing a true body after the resurrection, could enter to the disciples through closed doors. But since this marvelous deed cannot easily be understood in itself, let us recall to mind one of his other, still more marvelous deeds or miracles. For the universal Church confesses that he was born of a Virgin. What wonder, then, if he brought incorruptible and immortal limbs to his disciples through closed doors, when he brought a mortal and corruptible body forth from the closed womb of the Virgin? If, therefore, he did what is greater, it is not surprising that he could do what is lesser.

For divine mysteries cannot be fully comprehended by human reason, as the Psalmist testifies, saying: “Your thoughts have become exceedingly deep” (Ps. XCI). Hence the prophet says elsewhere: “Who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor?” (Isa. XL.) The apostle Paul likewise, to show that the greatness of God’s mysteries cannot be fully comprehended, says: “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and how inscrutable his ways!” (Rom. XI.) But let us hear what he said while standing in their midst.

“**Peace be with you.**” Beautifully, after the resurrection, the Lord first commended peace to his disciples, clearly showing that the discord between angels and human beings had been pacified through his resurrection. From the time when the first human being, by sinning, was separated from the fellowship of the angels, great discord existed between them. Hence, in the Old Testament, angels are frequently read to have been worshiped by human beings. But after the Lord’s resurrection they do not allow themselves to be worshiped by human beings on earth, because they worship the God who became human in heaven.

For this reason, as John says in the Apocalypse, when he wished to worship an angel, the angel prevented him, saying: “See that you do not do this; I am your fellow servant and the fellow servant of your brothers who bear witness to Jesus. Worship God” (Apoc. XIX). Showing, therefore, that this peace had been restored through his resurrection, he said to the disciples: “Peace be with you.”

For, as the Apostle says: “He himself is our peace, who made both one and broke down the middle wall of the dividing barrier, abolishing the law of commandments expressed in decrees, that he might create in himself the two into one new human being, and reconcile both in his body, by killing the enmities in his flesh through the cross. And coming, he proclaimed peace to those who were near and to those who were far away; for through him we all have access to God in one Spirit” (Eph. II).

“**And when he had said this, he showed them his hands and his side.**” The Evangelist Luke, who wrote about this appearance, says that when “Jesus stood in the midst of them, they were terrified and troubled, and supposed that they saw a spirit” (Luke XXIV). To remove their doubt and strengthen their faith, he showed them his hands and his side, so that through the marks of the nails and the opening in his side they might understand that he was the one whom they had previously seen fastened with nails and pierced with a spear.

The apostles’ disturbance, therefore, is a confirmation of our faith. “Then the disciples rejoiced when they saw the Lord.” Rightly did the disciples, who had been saddened by the Lord’s Passion, rejoice at his resurrection, so that what the Lord had foretold to them might be fulfilled: “I will see you again, and your heart will rejoice” (John XVI). Nor could they have been without great joy when they saw the Lord living, whom they had at least wished to behold dead.

“**Then he said to them again: Peace be with you.**” Once and again, after his death or after his resurrection, he commended peace to the disciples, so that he might find in peace those whom he had left in peace before his Passion. For when he was going to his Passion, he commended peace to them, saying: “My peace I give you; my peace I leave you” (John XIV). Rising from the dead, he confirmed it again, saying: “Peace be with you.” As if he were saying: “I left you in peace; in peace I shall find you.”

Or certainly he commended a twofold peace to the disciples, to show that those are worthy of his vision who preserve peace and harmony with a pure heart and possess a twofold love, namely, of God and of neighbor. But the wicked do not retain this peace. Although adulterers may appear to have peace with adulterers, fornicators with fornicators, plunderers with plunderers, and murderers with murderers, nevertheless they do not possess true peace, as the Psalmist or prophet testifies, saying: “There is no peace for the wicked, says the Lord” (Isa. LVII); and the Apostle says: “Without peace and holiness no one will see God” (Heb. XII).

The faithful hold this same peace more firmly when they preserve patience amid adversity. Of such people the Psalmist says: “Great peace have those who love your law, and nothing causes them to stumble” (Ps. CXVIII). Commending this peace to his disciples, the Lord says: “Have salt in yourselves, and have peace among yourselves. As the Father sent me, so I send you” (Mark IX).

In Scripture, sending sometimes refers to the Incarnation and sometimes to the giving of love. It refers to the Incarnation when the Apostle says: “When the fullness of time had come, God sent forth his Son, born of a woman, born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law” (Gal. IV); and again: “God sent his Son in the likeness of sinful flesh” (Rom. VIII). It refers to direction [sending] when the same Apostle says: “God sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, ‘Abba, Father.’”

But the Lord comprehended both kinds of sending in one verse when he said: “As the Father sent me, so I send you.” God the Father sent his Son, appointing him to become incarnate; the Son sent the apostles when he directed them throughout the whole world to preach that same Incarnation. Or, just as God the Father sent his Son to endure various insults and sufferings, so the Son sent the apostles not to receive the honor and glory of this age, but to endure afflictions, injuries, insults, and various persecutions.

“**When he had said this, he breathed on them and said: Receive the Holy Spirit.**” We read twice that the apostles received the Holy Spirit through a manifest giving: first, now, while the Lord remained on earth, and afterward, when he presided in heaven.

It may be asked why the Lord said to the disciples: “Receive the Holy Spirit.” Had they not previously received the Holy Spirit, when he had given them power to trample upon every power of the enemy, saying to them: “In my name cast out demons; heal lepers.
