You have received without payment; give without payment” (Matt. X)? And how did they do this if they did not have the Holy Spirit? They certainly had him. The Lord also confirms our assertion when he says to the Jews: “If I cast out demons by Beelzebul, by whom do your sons cast them out?” (Luke XI.)

Therefore they must be believed to have had the Holy Spirit previously. For unless they had been enlightened by the grace of the Holy Spirit, they would neither have cast out demons, nor performed miracles, nor believed him to be the true God. But at first they had the Holy Spirit in order to live well; afterward they received that same Spirit more perfectly, so that they might be fit to preach, so that they might believe with the heart unto justification and confess with the mouth unto salvation.

Thus what had been said through Moses was fulfilled: “They sucked honey from the rock, and oil from the hard rock” (Deut. XXXI). We never read that the people who received manna as food for forty years sucked honey or oil from the rock, but only water. What was not fulfilled historically in them, we believe was completed spiritually in the apostles. For “the rock,” as the Apostle says, “was Christ” (1 Cor. X).

The sweetness of honey and the pleasantness of oil signify the grace of the Holy Spirit, which is found to be sweeter than every delight, as the Psalmist says: “How sweet are your words to my throat, Lord; sweeter than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth” (Ps. CXVIII).

Thus, as it were, the apostles sucked honey from the rock when, while Christ remained on earth, they received the Holy Spirit from him. And as it were oil from the hard rock when, after he had taken his seat in heaven, they deserved to receive that same Holy Spirit visibly from heaven in tongues of fire. Of this oil it is written: “The yoke will decay before the oil” (Isa. X)—that is, the yoke of sin before the presence of the Holy Spirit.

Or otherwise: as the Apostle says, “God’s love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. V). They rightly received the Holy Spirit in these two ways, because the same love is fulfilled in two commandments, namely, love of God and of neighbor. On earth the Spirit is given so that neighbor may be loved; from heaven the Spirit is given so that God may be loved.

And because through love of neighbor we arrive at love of God, rightly the Spirit is first given on earth and afterward from heaven, as the apostle John says: “Whoever does not love his brother whom he sees, how can he love God whom he does not see?” (1 John IV.)

Beautifully, he gave the Holy Spirit by breathing, to show that he himself was the one who had breathed the breath of life into the face of the first human being (Gen. II). Or certainly, because breath is drawn from within and brought outward, he gave the Holy Spirit by breathing to show that all divinity is in him, and that the Holy Spirit proceeds from him just as from the Father. For, as the Apostle says, “in him the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily” (Col. II).

Hence ecclesiastical custom has also established that priests breathe upon the faces of those who are to be regenerated through the grace of the Holy Spirit.

For this must not be passed over: through the giving of the Holy Spirit the remission of all sins is granted, and this remission itself is effected in seven ways.

First, through the sacrament of baptism.

Second, through receiving the Eucharist. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man” (John VI), and so forth.

Third, through martyrdom.

Fourth, through almsgiving, because, as it is written: “Just as water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin” (Ecclus. III).

Fifth, through repentance: “Repent,” says the Apostle, “and turn back, so that your sins may be blotted out” (Acts III).

Sixth, through love, because, as the Apostle says: “Love covers a multitude of sins” (1 Pet. IV).

Seventh, when we forgive those who sin against us, because, as the Lord says: “If you do not forgive others their sins, neither will your heavenly Father forgive you your sins” (Matt. VI).

Because, therefore, the remission of sins is granted through the Holy Spirit, it is rightly said that the same Spirit was given to the disciples:

[Col. 0493D] “**Whose sins you forgive are forgiven them; and whose sins you retain are retained.**”

And truly great grace was given to the apostles: not only were they absolved from their own sins through the Holy Spirit, but they also received power to forgive the sins of others. Bishops and priests now retain their place and office in the Church; they possess the power of binding and loosing, just as it was specially said in the person of all to the first shepherd: “I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven. Whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven” (Matt. XVI).

Hence the law figuratively commands concerning lepers that if anyone had been struck with leprosy, he should show himself to the priest, and at the priest’s judgment should either be expelled outside the camp or received. This does not mean that the priest himself could cleanse a leper or make an unclean leper clean, but that it belongs to the priest’s ministry to distinguish between leprosy and leprosy—that is, between a greater and a lesser sin.

With careful examination it must be determined who are worthy to be received within the Church and who, because of their sins, are to be rejected outside it. For not only the quality and quantity of the sin must be considered in judgment, but also the person of the sinner and the penitent’s satisfaction. By his sentence the pastor can absolve those whom he sees, through contrition of heart and worthy amendment, to have been released by God.

Great is the honor, but heavy the burden of this honor. For it is very difficult that one who does not know how to guard his own soul should undertake the judgment of other souls. There are some who turn the ministry of religion into the exercise of honor’s power, and think that they can absolve the guilty and bind the innocent. Of such people it is written: “They put to death souls that should not die, and they kept alive souls that should not live” (Jer. XIII).

For he kills, as it were, one who should not die when he condemns by his sentence someone who is not guilty of wrongdoing. And he makes alive, as it were, one who does not live when he thinks he can absolve someone who remains in sins. Of such people it is written elsewhere: “They treated the wound of my people with disgrace, saying, ‘Peace, peace,’ when there was no peace” (Jer. VI).

But whether the pastor’s sentence is pronounced justly or unjustly, it must be feared lest a fault that does not arise from the deed itself arise from pride.

“**Thomas, one of the twelve, who is called Didymus, was not with them when Jesus came. So the other disciples said to him: We have seen the Lord. But he said to them: Unless I see in his hands the mark of the nails, and put my finger into the place of the nails, and put my hand into his side, I will not believe.**”

Since Luke says that two of the disciples returned to Jerusalem and found the eleven gathered together, and so forth, what does John mean by saying that Thomas was absent, when he was one of them?

The answer is that Thomas was with them at first, but he went out for a time, and while he was gone Jesus came. This should not be thought to have happened by chance; rather, it occurred by divine providence, so that when the Lord appeared to the disciples, one chosen disciple would be absent—one who, on hearing of the resurrection, would doubt; doubting, would seek; seeking, would find; and would drive all doubt from our hearts.

Thomas’s disbelief benefited us much more than Mary’s very swift belief: for while he doubted, he sought carefully; seeking, he found; finding, he touched; and by touching he not only strengthened our faith but also excluded the error of heretics who said that Christ had not possessed a true body.

Because Thomas doubted not through malice but through ignorance, the merciful teacher did not wish to leave so beloved a disciple in unbelief; rather, to restore his faith, he deigned to appear again. Hence it follows:

“**And after eight days his disciples were again inside, and Thomas was with them. Jesus came through closed doors, stood in the midst, and said: Peace be with you.**”

Beautifully, the Lord commended peace to the disciples not only once and twice but also a third time, to show that through his resurrection the utterance of the first curse had been undone and, as some report, to remove the threefold curse that had been spoken to Adam: “Cursed is the ground because of your work; in labor you shall eat from it all the days of your life. Thorns and thistles it shall produce for you, and you shall eat the plants of the earth. In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread, until you return to the earth” (Gen. III).

But after peace had been commended generally to all the disciples, he dealt specially with Thomas’s doubt, saying:

“**Put your finger here, and see my hands; bring your hand and put it into my side; and do not be unbelieving but believing.**”

It is asked why he says, “Put your finger here and see,” when seeing properly belongs to the sight of the eyes. The answer is that in this passage “to see” is used for “to perceive” or “to understand.” This kind of expression is so common among us that it seems to extend through all the senses. For example, we say: “Listen and see how melodiously he sings”; “Smell and see how sweetly it fragrances”; “Touch and see how smooth it is”; “Taste and see how sweet it is.”

Therefore, so that the disciple would not remain unbelieving, the Lord offered him his flesh to touch, so that afterward he might proclaim it with a free voice. In this act the Lord displayed two marvels that are comprehensible according to human reason: after the resurrection he offered his body to be touched and demonstrated it to be incorruptible, especially since what can be touched can also decay, while what cannot be touched cannot decay.

But in a wondrous and ineffable manner he demonstrated his body after the resurrection to be both touchable and incorruptible: by the one quality strengthening the faith of the apostles, and by the other inviting them to their reward.

Or certainly he demonstrated his body after the resurrection to be touchable and incorruptible in order to show that it was of the same nature as it had been before the Passion—that is, that he had flesh—and yet of another glory, namely, that the same flesh was incorruptible. And because in his own resurrection he wished to foreshadow ours, he showed that our bodies after the resurrection would be incorruptible and immortal, but not untouchable.

Therefore Eutyches lied when he said that our bodies after the resurrection would be subtler than wind and air, and that just as the sun’s ray can be seen but cannot be touched, so our bodies would be visible but untouchable. To support his error he took what the Apostle says: “Flesh and blood cannot possess the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. XV), not understanding that “flesh” has various meanings in Scripture.

Sometimes the condition of human nature itself is designated by the name flesh, as it is written: “This at last is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh” (Gen. II).

Sometimes the fragility of that same flesh is meant, as the Psalmist says: “And he remembered that they were flesh” (Ps. LXXVII).

Sometimes the offspring of kinship is meant, as the Apostle says: “Immediately I did not consult flesh and blood” (Gal. XI).

And the Lord says: “Flesh and blood has not revealed this to you” (Matt. XVI).

Sometimes sin is designated by the name flesh, as the Lord says to Noah: “My spirit shall not remain in human beings forever, because they are flesh” (Gen. VI)—that is, sinners. And the Apostle says to the Romans: “You, however, are not in the flesh but in the Spirit” (Rom. VIII). For if they were not in the flesh, he would not have sent them letters in bodily form. But they are said not to be in the flesh because they did not succumb to carnal sins.

Therefore, when the Apostle says, “Flesh and blood cannot possess the kingdom of God,” he did not deny that human nature would rise; rather, he affirmed that the sins of that same flesh cannot possess the kingdom of God. The Apostle explained this immediately afterward, saying: “Nor can corruption possess incorruption” (1 Cor. XV).

Our bodies, therefore, will rise immortal and incorruptible, but not invisible and untouchable, as blessed Job testifies, saying: “I believe that my Redeemer lives, and on the last day I shall rise from the earth, and again I shall be clothed with my skin, and in my flesh I shall see God” (Job XIX).

Having said these things against Eutyches, let us return to the passage itself:

“**Put your finger here, and see my hands; bring your hand and put it into my side; and do not be unbelieving but believing.**”

Here we must note that, in order to remove every doubt from their hearts, he showed not only his hands and side but also, according to another Evangelist, his feet, which had been fastened with nails, saying: “See my hands and my feet. Touch and see, because a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see that I have” (Luke XXIV).

But at this point pagans commonly mock Christian simplicity, saying: “With what presumption do you Christians think that your God will raise your bodies from the dust, when, as you say, he himself rose from the dead but could not heal the marks of his Passion in his body so that they would not appear?”

To this true faith responds that this was not impossible but rather an act of mercy. For it is greater to raise flesh from the dead than to heal the wounds of nails in flesh. Therefore, the one who did what is lesser and could do what is greater would have done so unless he had wished, for various reasons, to preserve those very wounds in his body.

First, he did so to invite or restore the apostles’ faith. Those who believed only slowly when they saw the marks of the nails would have believed still more slowly if they had not recognized the traces of the Passion in his mortal body.

Or, in another way, he wished to preserve the traces of his Passion in his flesh so that, interceding with the Father for us—for, as the apostle John says, “we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous, and he is the atoning sacrifice for our sins” (1 John II)—he might show him the scars of the nails and thereby invite him, who never forgets to show mercy, to have mercy.

Or certainly he wished to preserve the traces of his Passion so that at the universal judgment he might show them to all, both the just and the unjust. The just, seeing how great and what kind of things the Redeemer of the human race endured for their liberation, would burn more ardently with love for him and advance in praise; while the unjust would be confounded all the more grievously because they had proved ungrateful for such great benefits, as it is written: “Every eye will see him, even those who pierced him, and all the tribes of the earth will mourn over him” (Apoc. I).

Or certainly the Lord Jesus Christ wished to preserve the marks of the nails and the opening made by the spear in his flesh so that they might themselves display his victory over the ancient enemy. For example, when a very brave soldier, at the king’s command, enters single combat for the safety of his people and, having returned, brings victory back to his people after receiving a number of wounds, suppose that a physician says to him: “Do you wish me to heal you in such a way that the scars of your wounds do not appear, or so that they appear without disfigurement?” If he replies: “I want them to appear without disfigurement, so that they may reveal the sign of my victory to all who look upon me,” so also the Lord Jesus Christ wished to carry the wounds of his Passion into heaven, so that they themselves would demonstrate that he had won victory over the ancient enemy.

“**Thomas answered.**” Thomas is interpreted as “abyss.” This interpretation of his name rightly suits him, because just as the abyss possesses immense depth, so he, by touching the Lord’s body, understood the depth of divinity in him, concerning which it is written: “Your judgments are a great abyss” (Ps. XXXV).

He touched one thing with his body and believed another with his heart. He touched a human being; he believed in God. And therefore he exclaimed, saying: “**My Lord and my God.**”

“Lord” is derived from lordship; “God” from fear, as one of the wise says:

> “Fear first made gods throughout the world.”

And Solomon says: “Fear God and keep his commandments” (Eccles. XII). And again: “Fear God and turn away from evil. For this will be healing to your navel and refreshment to your bones” (Prov. III).

This name properly belongs to him essentially, who is King of kings and Lord of lords, and who must be feared, worshiped, and venerated above all things. Through the prophet it is said to him: “For you made all things, heaven and earth, and everything contained within the circuit of heaven; you are Lord of all” (Esther XIII).

How great a reward faith possesses is made clear when it follows:

“**Jesus said to him: Because you have seen me, Thomas, you have believed. Blessed are those who have not seen and have believed.**”

In this verse not only is Thomas’s faith praised, but our future salvation is also foretold, as if the Lord were saying: “You are indeed blessed because you have seen me and believed; but those also will be blessed who, not seeing me bodily, will believe in me with the mind.”

When he says, “Blessed are those who have not seen and have believed,” he uses the verb in the past tense because, in his presence, all future things are past.

“**Jesus did many other signs in the presence of his disciples that are not written in this book.**” If anyone compares the Gospel of Saint John with those of the other Evangelists, he will find many miracles of the Savior in their writings that are not found in John’s Gospel. John, who wrote his Gospel last, omitted many things in many places because he knew what had been written by the others.

Nor are all the Lord’s miracles written in the four books of the Gospels, as John himself testifies at the end, saying: “There are also many other things that Jesus did; if each one were written down, I suppose that the world itself could not contain the books that would be written” (John XXI).

The holy Evangelists wrote down as many of the miracles as they knew would suffice to strengthen the faith of believers. Hence it follows:

“**But these have been written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God.**” Since these things have been written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, let Photinus be ashamed, for he wished to believe him to be merely human and not God.

Instructed by the Gospel reading, let us believe that Jesus Christ, the Son of God, is in one and the same person perfect God and perfect human being: God before the ages, human in time; God from the Father, human from his mother.

What we gain from this belief is made clear when it continues: “**And so that, believing, you may have life in his name.**” Life, therefore, is given in the name of the one who gives himself to believers, who is “the way, the truth, and the life” (John XIV), as he says elsewhere: “This is eternal life: that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John XVII).

# HOMILY LXXXII. THE SECOND SUNDAY AFTER EASTER, “THE MERCY OF THE LORD”

[Col. 0498C]

**(1 PET. II.)** “Beloved, Christ suffered for us, leaving us an example, so that you might follow his footsteps.” And so forth.

Dearest brothers, in the apostolic reading that you have heard, blessed Peter urges us to imitate Christ’s example, saying:

“**Christ suffered for us, leaving us an example, so that you might follow his footsteps.**” This means what the Lord himself says in the Gospel (Matt. XVI; Luke IX): “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself”—that is, let him abandon his own desires and submit himself in every way to God’s will—“and let him take up his cross”—that is, let him put carnal pleasures to death—“and follow me,” resisting the desires of the world as far as he is able with the gift of divine grace.

By these means, and by other holy practices of this kind, we must follow Christ’s footsteps.

“**He committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth.**” As the prophet says of him: “He alone was without sin, who came to take away the sins of the world” (1 John III). And elsewhere: “He did not quarrel or cry out, nor did anyone hear his voice in the streets” (Matt. XII).

It continues:

“Though he was being reviled, he did not revile in return.” No deceit, falsehood, or slander was found in his mouth. Therefore, if we wish to imitate his example, we must avoid these same evils with every effort: we must lay aside all deceit and hatred, every kind of wickedness and pretense, envy and slander, and strive earnestly in good works to serve Christ the Lord.

“While suffering, he did not threaten.” He did not threaten vengeance for the insults he received; rather, he even prayed for those who crucified him, as he taught us elsewhere, saying: “Pray for those who persecute and slander you, so that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. V).

“But he entrusted himself to the one judging him unjustly.” Through his divinity he handed over the humanity that he had assumed to suffering, delivering it to the Jewish people who judged him so that he might be crucified. For if he who was without sin handed himself over on account of our sins, in order to redeem us from death, what worthy return can we make for his mercy, except that we should always faithfully prepare ourselves to do his will through sincere confession, tears of repentance, generosity in almsgiving, and works of mercy and piety, so that by worthy and holy conduct we may be able to possess eternal joys with him?

[Col. 0499A]

“He himself bore our sins in his body upon the wood.” For this reason he wished to suffer upon the wood of the cross: to erase the transgression of the wood that Adam had committed, and to open for us the way to the kingdom of heaven, which had been closed to the world through Adam’s sin.

“So that, having died to sins, we might live for righteousness; by whose bruising we have been healed.” Thus, just as previously we were dead to God through sin, so now through his passion and resurrection he might lead us to eternal immortality, reconcile us to God his Father, and grant us the power to die to the world and to all sins through confession, and to live for God through righteousness.

[Col. 0499B]

“For you were like wandering sheep.” The error of the sheep is understood to be the fault of the shepherds, who neglect to rebuke those who offend. “But now you have returned to the shepherd and bishop of your souls.” You have turned from the devil to Christ, from darkness to light, from death to life, from unbelief to faith, and from weakness to salvation. If you remain in this state to the end, striving in good works, you will be saved forever. For it is not the one who has begun the good work, but the one who has persevered in goodness, who will be saved. Our conversion pleases God when we complete with a persevering end the good work that we begin. Therefore, virtue consists not in having begun the good, but in having brought it to completion. A reward is promised to those who begin, but it is given to those who persevere, through the one who promised it, Jesus Christ our Lord, the true promiser and giver.

[Col. 0499C]

He lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit, God, forever and ever. Amen.

# HOMILY LXXXIII. THE SECOND SUNDAY AFTER EASTER, “The Mercy of the Lord”

(John X.) “At that time Jesus said to his disciples: ‘I am the good shepherd.’” And so forth.

The preceding text of the Gospel relates how the Lord distinguished between good and evil shepherds, saying of the evil ones: “He who does not enter the sheepfold through the gate, but climbs in by another way, is a thief and a robber.” But of the good ones: “He who enters through the gate is the shepherd of the sheep. To him the gatekeeper opens, and the sheep hear his voice. But they do not follow a stranger; rather, they flee from him, because they do not recognize the voice of strangers.”

[Col. 0500A]

When the Lord saw that they did not understand this proverb, he explained more clearly which shepherd he was speaking about, saying: “I am the good shepherd.” At the beginning of this reading, however, we must ask why the Lord wished to be called a shepherd. Is he called a shepherd because, in the manner of an earthly shepherd, he leads sheep to pasture and brings them back? No. Such names are applied to him by analogy, so that through visible things we may understand invisible things.

For just as he is called a sheep because of innocence, a lamb because of gentleness, a calf because of the offering of his flesh, a lion because of strength, and a rock because of firmness, so he is called a shepherd not only because he spiritually feeds and refreshes his faithful, but also because by his protection he defends them from the bites of wolves.

This is the true shepherd who grants us rational understanding and supplies spiritual insight. He is the true shepherd who, through the sacrament of his body and blood, refreshes us in the present and, in the future, brings us to the satisfaction of contemplating him. He says in the Gospel: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven” (John VI). And again: “If anyone enters through me, he will be saved, and he will enter and go out and find pasture” (John X). And again: “Whoever eats my flesh” (John VI), and so forth. And: “My flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink.”

[Col. 0500B]

Under the governance of this shepherd, the Prophet rejoiced that he had found abundant pasture when he said: “The Lord feeds me, and I shall lack nothing” (Ps. XXII). And again: “I shall be satisfied when your glory is revealed” (Ps. XVI).

This shepherd was promised to the faithful sheep when the Lord said through the prophet: “Behold, I will raise up for you one shepherd, my servant David, who will feed the sheep with judgment and righteousness” (Ezek. XXXIV). In the type or figure of this shepherd, the patriarch Jacob is said to have tended sheep.

For just as it belongs to a shepherd’s duty not only to lead the stronger sheep to pasture but also to provide medicine for the weak, so this shepherd not only bears with those in the Church who are more perfect, but also bends compassionately toward weak souls and provides the care of salvation through repentance.

[Col. 0500C]

Jacob’s words signify this when he says: “You know, my lord, that I have with me sheep that are nursing young and tender; if I make them labor more than they can bear while walking, all the flocks will die in one day” (Gen. XXXIII).

Hence it is said through the prophet Ezekiel: “Behold, I myself will seek out my sheep and visit them. As a shepherd visits his flock on the day when he is among his scattered sheep, so I will visit my sheep and gather them from all the places in which they were dispersed. I will seek what was lost, bring back what was cast away, bind up what was broken, strengthen what was sick, and guard what was fat and strong” (Ezek. XXXIV).

He is also the one who heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds. And again: “The Lord sets free those in chains; the Lord gives sight to the blind” (Ps. CXLV).

[Col. 0500D]

How greatly this shepherd’s kindness has compassion on weak sheep is shown by that Gospel parable (Luke XV) in which it is written that the good shepherd, leaving the ninety-nine sheep in the mountains, went to seek the one that had wandered in the valleys. When he found it, he placed it upon his own shoulders and so carried it back to the flock.

If we wish to approach the table of this aforementioned shepherd, we must prepare ourselves in good works, as Solomon testifies: “Have you approached the table of a powerful man? Pay close attention to what is set before you, knowing that you must prepare similar things” (Ecclus. XXXI).

Since, therefore, the Lord, as he went to his passion, handed over to us the mystery of his body and blood, we prepare similar things for him when, for love of him, we endure tribulations and distress, because, as the Apostle says, “through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God.” And the Psalmist says: “What shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me?” (Ps. CXV).

[Col. 0501A]

It is asked why the Lord called himself a shepherd when shortly before he had said that he was the gate, saying: “I am the gate.” The answer is that the gate is one thing, the gatekeeper another, and the shepherd another.

He is the gatekeeper who introduces us to faith, as he himself says in the Gospel: “No one comes to the Father except through me” (John XIV). “For no one knows the Father except the Son, and the one to whom the Son wishes to reveal him” (Luke X).

He is the gate because through him we enter into faith, as he himself says: “If anyone enters through me, he will be saved” (John X). And appropriately, after saying, “I am the shepherd,” he added, “good,” to distinguish him from those who unworthily usurp the name of shepherd because they are neither good nor worthy. Concerning them the Lord says above: “All who came before me were thieves and robbers” (John X).

There were, however, good shepherds, such as Peter, to whom the Lord said: “If you love me, feed my sheep” (John XX). And again: “You are the shepherd of the sheep.” Paul was such a shepherd, for he desired to become anathema for his brothers, saying: “I longed to be anathema for my brothers, my kinsmen according to the flesh, who are Israelites” (Rom. IX).

[Col. 0501B]

But one thing is good essentially, as in the case of the Lord, and another is good by designation, as in the case of the disciples; one is good by nature, and another by grace. They received from the Lord what enabled them to be good; he, however, received from no one but himself what enabled him to be good. Therefore, when they are compared with his goodness, they are found to be less good.

How much the good shepherd ought to love the sheep entrusted to him is made clear when it is added:

“The good shepherd gives his life for his sheep.”

He did what he commanded, and demonstrated by his example what he had taught in words. He first laid down his life for his sheep, showing good shepherds that, if necessity should arise, they must not fear death for the sheep entrusted to them.

[Col. 0501C]

Therefore, when he had entrusted his sheep to Peter’s care three times, he revealed what Peter would suffer for those same sheep, saying: “Amen, amen, I say to you: When you were younger, you girded yourself and walked where you wished; but when you grow old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will gird you and lead you where you do not wish to go.” The evangelist says that he said this to signify by what kind of death Peter would glorify him (John XXI).

Finally, the Apostle Paul was also prepared to die for the sheep entrusted to him, when he said: “I myself was spending and was being spent for your souls” (II Cor. XI). And again: “I am ready not only to be bound, but also to die in Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus. For I do not make my life more precious than myself” (Acts XX). And again: “It is better for me to die than that anyone should deprive me of my glory” (I Cor. IX).

But after the Lord had shown the work of the good shepherd, he also took care to disclose the vices of the evil shepherd, saying:

[Col. 0501D]

“But the hired man, who is not the shepherd.”

A hired man is one employed for wages. By this name evil shepherds are rightly represented: they undertake care of souls not for the love of God or because of love for the flock, but for earthly profits, seeking their own interests rather than those of Jesus Christ, as the Apostle says: “They consider godliness a means of gain” (I Tim. VI).

The Lord rebukes them through the prophet, saying: “They themselves reigned, but not through me; they became princes, and I did not acknowledge them” (Hos. VIII).

There are three things that hired men seek from sheep: milk, wool, and flesh. Evil shepherds, who desire to rule rather than to benefit, demand these three things from those subject to them: the milk of flattery, the wool of bodily service, and the flesh of carnal pleasure.

The Lord rebukes them through the prophet Ezekiel, saying: “Woe to the shepherds of Israel who fed themselves. Are not flocks fed by shepherds? You ate the milk, clothed yourselves with the wool, and slaughtered what was fat, but you did not feed my flock. You did not strengthen what was weak, heal what was sick, bind up what was broken, or bring back what was cast away; you did not seek what had perished, but ruled them harshly and with power” (Ezek. XXXIV).

[Col. 0502A]

Those whom they ought to have defended from outsiders they frequently oppress like robbers. Concerning them the Lord says in the Gospel: “Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly are ravenous wolves; you will know them by their fruits” (Matt. VII).

The Apostle foresaw such thieves in the Church when he said to the disciples: “I know that after my departure grievous, ravenous wolves will enter among you, not sparing the flock. And from among your own selves men will arise speaking perverse things, to draw the disciples after them” (Acts XX).

Rightly, then, it is added concerning such men: “They are not his own sheep.” For they do not recognize them as their own sheep, nor do they know them as strangers.

[Col. 0502B]

It is not easily recognized in a time of peace who is a shepherd and who is a hired man. But the arrival of a wolf reveals with what disposition each person watches over his flock. Hence it follows:

“He saw the wolf coming, abandoned the sheep, and fled; and the wolf snatched and scattered the sheep.”

By the name “wolf” in this passage are designated powerful and unjust men of every kind. When they plunder the possessions of the poor, they tear the flesh of the sheep apart like wolves.

But the hired man sees the wolf coming, abandons the sheep, and flees, because the carnal shepherd, fearing the loss of his earthly property, hides himself in silence. He flees not by changing his location, but by withdrawing his assistance. When he sees his subjects being oppressed by powerful men, he does not object in order to free the poor and needy from their hands; instead, he deceives them further by flattery.

[Col. 0502C]

Concerning such men it is said through the prophet: “All your princes have fled and have been bound with harsh bonds” (Isa. XXII). And again: “Your prophets, Israel, were like foxes in the desert” (Ezek. XIII).

Elsewhere, through the prophet, the Lord rebukes their blameworthy fear, saying: “You did not go up to oppose them, nor did you set up a wall for the house of Israel, so that you might stand in battle on the day of the Lord” (ibid.).

There is also another invisible wolf, which daily tears apart not bodies but the souls of sinners: namely, the one of whom the Apostle Peter says: “Your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour” (I Pet. V).

[Col. 0502D]

When he draws one person to pride, another to adultery, another to robbery, another to fornication, and another to murder, he tears the flesh of the sheep apart like a wolf.

But the hired man sees the wolf coming, abandons the sheep, and flees when the one who feeds God’s flock not for divine love is inflamed by no zeal against these vices, moved by no sorrow, and brings forward no weapons of preaching.

He flees when he hides himself in silence. He also flees when he sees his subjects being defiled by various vices and remains silent because he does not correct them, paying no attention to what the Apostle commanded Timothy: “I testify before God and Christ Jesus, who will judge the living and the dead: preach the word, be urgent in season and out of season; reprove, entreat, rebuke” (II Tim. IV).

Such men will have to give an account not only of their own sins but also of those of their subjects, as the Lord terribly threatens through Ezekiel, saying: “I have appointed you as a watchman for the house of Israel. If you do not announce his iniquity to the wicked person, I will require his blood from your hand” (Ezek. III).

[Col. 0503A]

It must also be considered how the hired man flees when a bear comes. By the bear, which is an ingenious and cunning animal, as some say, heretics are represented, for through perverse teaching they do not cease to deceive the gentle within the Church.

But the hired man and the one who is not the shepherd sees the bear coming and flees when he sees those under his care being deceived by heretics or perverse teachers within the holy Church, while the simple are misled, and he does not resist them by the authority of the divine Scriptures.

Concerning such men the Lord says through the prophet: “They are mute dogs unable to bark, seeing worthless things, sleeping and loving dreams; they are most shameless dogs who know no satisfaction. The shepherds themselves have no understanding” (Isa. LVI).

Concerning them it is further added:

[Col. 0503B]

“But the hired man flees because he is a hired man and has no concern for the sheep.”

If you ask why the hired man flees, you will find no more immediate reason than that he is a hired man. For the one who feeds the Lord’s flock not out of divine love but out of love for greed and power withdraws as soon as fear of losing these things arises—if not bodily, then at least in mind—because, in the words of the Psalmist, “there he trembles with fear where there was no fear” (Ps. LII).

Concerning such men it is said through the prophet Jeremiah: “Your hired men, who were in your midst, were like fattened calves; they fled together and could not stand” (Jer. XLVI).

They chiefly love what they can laudably lose—that is, earthly possessions—and do not fear losing what they cannot abandon without grave danger—that is, the souls of those under their care.

[Col. 0503C]

Concerning such men, under the figure of the ostrich, blessed Job says: “When she leaves her eggs on the ground, she forgets that a human foot may trample them and that the beasts of the field may crush them” (Job XXXIX).

There are also some rulers who, although they teach well, nevertheless, because they live badly, are counted more among hired men than among shepherds. Those whom they instruct by good teaching, they destroy by the example of their evil life.

Concerning them it is said through the prophet: “When you drank the purest water, you troubled the rest with your feet. And my sheep, which had been trampled by your feet, fed upon it; and what your feet had troubled, they drank” (Ezek. XXXIV).

But after exposing the vices of the hired men, the Lord turns his discourse to the duty of the good shepherd, saying:

[Col. 0503D]

“I am the good shepherd, and I know my sheep, and my sheep know me.”

This is plainly to say: “I know my own,” that is, I love them. “And my own know me,” that is, because they love me, they obey my voice.

Elsewhere the Lord says concerning them: “My sheep hear my voice, and I, the Lord, know them; they follow me, and I give them eternal life, and they shall never perish, nor shall anyone snatch them from my hand.”

Therefore other shepherds ought to imitate this good shepherd, so that those whom they come to know under their governance they may love with a pure and sincere heart.

[Col. 0504A]

Hence the first shepherd of the Church admonishes the other shepherds, saying: “The elders who are among you I beseech, as a fellow elder and a witness of Christ’s sufferings, and also a sharer in the glory that is to be revealed: feed the flock of God that is among you, watching over it not under compulsion but willingly, according to God; not for shameful gain but freely; not as domineering over the clergy, but becoming examples to the flock from the heart; so that when the chief shepherd appears, you may receive the unfading crown of glory” (I Pet. V).

[Col. 0504B]

For just as hired men are condemned more harshly not only for their own vices but also for the crimes of those under them, so good shepherds will receive a reward as great as the number of those whom they have gained through their example or preaching. Then, that is, they will deserve to hear that desirable voice: “Well done, good and faithful servant. Because you have been faithful over little, I will set you over much. Enter into the joy of your lord” (Matt. XXV).

Therefore, when the Lord was born, an angel rightly appeared to shepherds, and the glory of God shone around them, so that we may understand that God’s grace illuminates more perfectly in the present and rewards with a higher recompense in the future those who do not refuse, through divine love, to feed the Lord’s flock by teaching it well. For, as Daniel says: “Those who are learned will shine like the stars of the firmament, and those who instruct many in righteousness like the stars forever and ever” (Dan. XII).

[Col. 0504C]

“As the Father knows me, so I know the Father.”

The Father knows the Son not temporally but eternally, begetting the Son—namely, the Word and Wisdom—as coeternal and consubstantial with himself. Likewise, the Son knows the Father because he was begotten by the Father, as he himself says in the Gospel: “No one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son and the one to whom the Son wishes to reveal him” (Luke X).

“And I lay down my life for my sheep.”

It is as though he said: If I show that I know the Father and am known by the Father through this—that I lay down my life for my sheep—then every shepherd is shown to know God more truly in proportion as he watches more carefully over the flock entrusted to him, not only by admonishing and exhorting, but also, if necessity demands, by setting his own advantage aside for their needs.

[Col. 0504D]

“For no one has greater love than this: that someone should lay down his life for his friends” (John XV). Hence John also says: “If Christ laid down his life for us, we also ought to lay down our lives for our brothers” (I John III).

But did the supreme shepherd lay down his life only for the salvation of the Jews? No. For it was fitting that, when the Son of God died, he should die not only for one nation but for the entire people.

Therefore Caiaphas prophesied at the time of his passion, saying: “It is better for you that one man should die for the people and that the whole nation should not perish” (John XVIII). The evangelist says that he did not say this of himself, but, since he was high priest that year, he prophesied that Jesus was going to die for the nation—and not only for the Jewish nation, but also to gather into one the children of God who were scattered abroad.

Concerning these he says:

[Col. 0505A]

“And I have other sheep that are not of this fold.”

From the time when the Lord separated Abraham from the other nations and chose his descendants as his own special people, two peoples and two nations began to be named: the Jews and the nations.

But after he was born from Abraham’s own stock, he joined one Church from both peoples, so that what the Lord had promised him might be fulfilled: “In your seed all the families of the earth shall be blessed” (Gen. XXII).

Therefore, while he walked bodily among the Jews, he spoke of our calling: “And I have other sheep that are not of this fold,” that is, not of this nation and people. “I must bring them also,” that is, call them to my faith through the preaching of my apostles. “And they will hear my voice,” that is, they will obey my commands. “And there will be one flock,” that is, one Church gathered from both peoples, whether in the present or on the day of judgment, since the Jews will come to the faith.

[Col. 0505B]

“And one shepherd,” namely, the Lord Jesus Christ, of whom the Apostle Peter says to believers: “For you were once like wandering sheep, but now you have returned to the shepherd and bishop of your souls” (I Pet. II).

# HOMILY LXXXIV. THE THIRD SUNDAY AFTER EASTER, “Rejoice”

(I Pet. II.) “Beloved, I beseech you, as strangers and pilgrims, to abstain from carnal desires, which wage war against the soul.” And so forth.

The Apostle Peter fittingly admonishes and exhorts us, dearly beloved brothers, as your affection heard in the present reading: “I beseech you,” he says, “as strangers and pilgrims.”

We are strangers and pilgrims as long as we are in this land, as the Apostle Paul says: “For here we have no lasting city, but our citizenship is in heaven” (Heb. XIII).

[Col. 0505C]

A stranger, pilgrim, or guest does not think that he is in his own house. So we too, as far as we are able, with the Lord’s generosity, must altogether despise these things and meditate on heavenly matters, from which we are to live eternally.

“To abstain from carnal desires.” It is therefore good to abstain from carnal desires and always to desire heavenly things that can remain with us eternally. Carnal desires deceive and lead to destruction those who remain in them.

He adds concerning carnal desires: “Which wage war against the soul.” Carnal desires always try to drag us down to hell. We must resist them in every way and devote ourselves to good and righteous labors, to chastity and self-restraint, by which we may avoid punishments and merit eternal rewards.

[Col. 0505D]

“Maintaining your conduct honorable among the nations.” By showing good examples to others through the practice of good works, you should shine like lights in the world. “So that in the very matter for which they slander you as evildoers”—the wicked and malicious always disparage the deeds of good people and attempt to overturn them into a bad reputation, fearing that their evil pleasure, the depraved practice in which they remain and perish, may be destroyed and exposed by the deeds of others.

But when we hear this, we must persevere even more earnestly in good works, so that others too may be saved and these people may become without excuse if they refuse to turn from their wickedness.

[Col. 0506A]

It follows: “As they observe you through your good works, they may glorify God on the day of visitation.” As the Lord himself teaches in the Gospel: “Let the light of your good works shine before people,” so that “you” should by no means desire praise from them, but so that others, “seeing your good works, may glorify,” not you, but “your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. V), who seeks through his servants such good works for the salvation of his own people and of others.

“Be subject to every human creature for God’s sake.” Give honor to all people, each according to his dignity—not because of earthly desires, nor because of an appetite for human praise, nor for the gain of shameful profit, but solely for the sake of God, who teaches us, saying: “Learn from me, for I am gentle and humble of heart, and you will find rest for your souls” (Matt. XI). And again: “Everyone who humbles himself for the Lord’s sake will be exalted by the Lord” (Luke XVIII).

[Col. 0506B]

“Whether to the king as the one who is preeminent,” because he is the ruler of the people. When the Lord himself commands in the Gospel that due honor be rendered, saying: “Render to Caesar what is Caesar’s” (Matt. XXII)—that is, the tribute that is owed and the obedience of submission with fidelity—“and to God what is God’s”: right faith, firm hope, and perfect charity.

“Or to governors as sent by him for the punishment of evildoers.” Concerning them Paul also says: “Let every soul be subject to the higher authorities, for there is no authority except from God” (Rom. XIII). They are God’s ministers, sent to restrain human wickedness, so that those who do not wish to avoid evil voluntarily may avoid it, even unwillingly, through fear of them.

“And for the praise of those who do good.” Paul likewise says: “Do you wish not to fear the authority? Do what is good, and you will have praise from it” (Rom. XIII).

[Col. 0506C]

“For such is the will of God: that by doing good you may silence the ignorance of foolish people.” Be so cautious and so perfect in God’s work that they have nothing to criticize in you according to their evil will, “as free”—free from every sin through true repentance and pure confession—“and not as having freedom as a veil for wickedness.”

Let there be no fraud or wickedness in you. Rather, strive to serve God as your Lord with worthy and holy works, with complete faith and willingness, “as servants of God,” and in charity render to all, mutually, the service owed for God’s sake.

“Honor everyone” according to each person’s dignity. Yet devote the greatest effort to serving the poor and those least able, because Christ is especially honored in them, as he himself will say at the judgment: “What you did for one of the least of mine, you did for me” (Matt. XXV).

[Col. 0506D]

For it follows: “Love the brotherhood.” The Lord himself shows in the Gospel that all are brothers and neighbors, saying: “You are all brothers” (Matt. XXIII). Therefore he commands us to love one another when he says: “I give you this command: love one another” (John XV). And John says: “He who does not love his brother whom he sees, how can he love God whom he does not see?” (I John IV.)

For God is not truly loved without one’s neighbor, nor is one’s neighbor truly loved without God. And Paul says: “Love of neighbor does no evil” (Rom. XIII). Therefore love is the fullness of the law.

“Fear God; honor the king.” He therefore urges that proper honor be rendered to all and, according to the Lord’s command, that what belongs to Caesar be rendered to Caesar and what belongs to God to God.

He who fears God does good, because “the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ecclus. XVI). Every good thing is born from the fear of the Lord, and through the fear of the Lord all human wickedness is emptied out. For the one who fears God carefully guards himself from sins.

[Col. 0507A]

Therefore, let us fear God in such a way that we love him, because perfect love casts out servile fear.

“Servants, be subject in all fear to your masters, not only to the good and gentle but also to the difficult.” This is grace in Christ Jesus our Lord.

Because of fear of God and likewise love of him, it is worthy and just for every person to serve his own master faithfully, whether present or absent. Whatever good a person does for God’s sake is not lost, because he will repay each one according to his works.

For in human life the end is always sought: what a person is like at the final time of his life. For according to his end each person is either justified or condemned.

[Col. 0507B]

Therefore, each person must strive with the greatest urgency to complete the good things he has begun, so that he may receive an everlasting reward from the Lord, by his generosity, who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

# HOMILY LXXXV. THE THIRD SUNDAY AFTER EASTER, “Rejoice”

(John XVI.) “At that time Jesus said to his disciples: ‘A little while, and you will no longer see me; and again a little while, and you will see me, because I am going to the Father.’” And so forth.

“A little while, and you will no longer see me”—mortal, corruptible, and capable of being grasped, as you now see me—“and again a little while, and you will see me”—immortal, incomprehensible, and incorruptible.

Whenever we recite the Gospel reading, we must consider that it often happens that one part of it applies specifically to the disciples, to whom Christ spoke bodily, while another part applies generally to the universal Church. This is easily demonstrated in the present reading if its text is examined carefully.

[Col. 0507C]

What he says—“A little while, and you will no longer see me; and again a little while, and you will see me”—applies specifically to the disciples, to whom he was speaking through his bodily presence.

But what he later explained to them when they did not understand, saying: “Amen, amen, I say to you, you will weep and lament,” and so forth, up to “it will be changed into joy,” applies specifically to the apostles and also generally to the universal Church.

Since he was speaking these words to the disciples on the night when he was to be handed over, the time during which they would not see him was short: for he was seized that very night, crucified on the following day, and placed in the tomb; then they began not to see him.

[Col. 0507D]

After resting in the tomb through the night and the following day, he rose in the morning of the first day of the week and appeared to the disciples although the doors were not open.

Or certainly the short period during which they would see him was the time after his resurrection, when he appeared to them for only forty days with many proofs and, on the fortieth day, ascended into heaven while they watched.

Hence it is added:

“Because I am going to the Father.”

He speaks here not of his divinity but of his humanity. Again, he says that he is going to the Father according to his humanity, from whom he did not depart according to his divinity, as he himself says: “I and the Father are one” (John X).

[Col. 0508A]

For just as he did not abandon the Father when he appeared to the apostles, so he did not abandon the apostles when he returned to the Father, as he himself says: “Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age” (Matt. XXVIII).

Remaining therefore with the Father according to his divinity, he appeared to the disciples according to his humanity; and returning to the Father according to his humanity, he remained with the disciples according to his divinity, as he says elsewhere: “I came forth from the Father and came into the world” (John XVI).

To come and to return belong to humanity; to remain and to be belong to divinity. This is readily apparent to those who confess both natures—divine and human—in the one Mediator between God and humanity.

[Col. 0508B]

And he is rightly said to go to the Father, because as long as he lived among the disciples, clothed in flesh like theirs, he could be seized, bound, scourged, weighed down by sleep, wearied, crucified, and killed together with them, and could suffer these and similar things belonging to humanity.

But after the resurrection, having cast off the mortality of the flesh, he was so glorified by the Father and made impassible and immortal that he no longer suffers any of these things.

Concerning him Paul says: “Even if we once knew Christ according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him in that way” (II Cor. V). And again: “Christ, having risen from the dead, no longer dies” (Rom. VI), and so forth.

And because the devout minds of the disciples could not bear the bodily absence of their devout teacher without profound weariness and grief, this is made clear when it is added:

“Then some of his disciples said to one another: [Col. 0509C] “What does this mean that he says to us: ‘A little while, and you shall not see me; and again a little while, and you shall see me,’ and, ‘Because I am going to the Father’?” They were saying, therefore: “What does this mean that he says: ‘A little while’? We do not know what he is saying.”

The human mind has this characteristic: that what it absolutely does not want either it understands slowly or believes even more slowly. And so the disciples, because they neither wanted nor believed that their gracious Teacher would be separated from them bodily—although he plainly said, “A little while, and you shall no longer see me”—did not understand this. Hence, complaining among themselves, they said: “What does this mean that he says: ‘A little while’? We do not know what he is saying.”

In accordance with this sense, when elsewhere he foretold his passion to them, saying (Matt. XX): “Behold, we are going up to Jerusalem, and everything that has been written through the prophets about the Son of Man will be fulfilled” [Col. 0509D], and so forth, it is added: “And they understood none of these things; for this saying was hidden from them, and they did not understand what was being said.” Why? Because they did not understand that the one whom they did not wish to suffer could suffer.

But because they did not turn their complaints into cunning arguments, and instead decided humbly to question their gracious Teacher, he who searches the heart anticipated their thoughts and answered before he was questioned. Thus, although he had shown in many ways that he was God, he also declared himself to be God by discerning their hearts—namely, the one of whom it is written: “The Lord knows the thoughts of human beings, that they are futile” (Ps. XLIII); and the Psalmist says: “You understood [Col. 0510A] my thoughts from afar” (Ps. CXXXVIII); and again: “Human thought shall confess to you” (Ps. LXXV); and Solomon says: “You alone, O God, know the hearts of the children of human beings” (II Chron. VI); and again: “What is in the human heart your eyes see, O Lord”; and again: “A human being sees what is before his face, but God sees into the heart.”

Or perhaps he wished to anticipate their thoughts in order to show that they ought not to doubt the promises of one whom they saw so readily discerning the hidden things of their thoughts. Hence it is added:

“Now Jesus knew that they wanted to question him, and he said to them: ‘You are asking one another about this, because I said: “A little while, and you shall not see me; and again a little while, and you shall see me.”’”

It is as though he were saying: If this troubles you and disturbs your minds, because I said: [Col. 0510B] “A little while, and you shall not see me,” hear this further: “Amen, amen, I say to you, you shall weep and lament, but the world shall rejoice. You, however, shall be sorrowful, but your sorrow shall be turned into joy.”

The lovers of Christ wept when they saw that the one whom they had observed living in the world without guilt was seized as though guilty, bound, scourged, and crucified. For they could not see the death of the one whose life they had loved with such extraordinary affection without profound sorrow and tears. They had previously seen him raise the dead, yet now they saw him dead.

But, on the other hand, the world rejoiced—that is, the Jewish people, who are rightly called “the world” because of their love of the world—when they saw him crucified, since he was burdensome even for them to behold, and they supposed that his name had been erased.

But will the reprobate always rejoice [Col. 0510C] and the elect always be sorrowful? No. Let me say what he means: “Your sorrow shall be turned into joy.” The sorrow of the apostles was indeed turned into gladness when, as the evangelist Luke says, the disciples rejoiced at seeing the Lord. Conversely, the joy of the Jews was changed into mourning, to such an extent that, when they heard of his resurrection, they promised money to the soldiers, saying: “Say that his disciples came by night while we were sleeping and stole him; and if this reaches the governor’s ears, we will persuade him and make you secure” (Matt. XXVIII).

But because we said above that part of this reading applies generally to the universal Church, in his own words the Lord indicates mourning and weeping to the faithful when he says: “Amen, amen, I say to you, [Col. 0510D] you shall weep,” and so forth, up to “shall be turned into joy.”

Placed in the valley of tears and weighed down by the burden of sins, they weep not only for the remission of sins but also groan daily in expectation of the eternal life to come, saying with the Psalmist: “I shall wash every night” (Ps. VI), and so forth; and again: “You shall feed us with the bread of tears” (Ps. LXXIX); and again: “Woe is me, for my sojourn” (Ps. CXIX), and so forth; and elsewhere: “My tears have been my bread day and night” (Ps. XLI).

For they remember from where they have fallen and consider where they have arrived. And while they bring before the eyes of their minds the punishments of the reprobate and the glory of the righteous, they wash away the stains of their sins in the sight of the most merciful Judge with a fountain of tears, saying [Col. 0511A] with the Psalmist: “O Lord, all my desire is before you, and my groaning is not hidden from you” (Ps. XXXVII); and again: “O God, I have declared my life to you” (Ps. LV).

Nor do the saints weep only for their own sins; at times they also weep for the sins of others when they see them persisting in them irrevocably, as the apostle Paul did when he said: “I mourn many of those who sinned before and did not repent of the impurity they committed” (I Cor. XII).

But the world rejoices—that is, the lovers of the world—when they are raised to honors, enjoy bodily health, possess an abundance of goods, and beget children. They are rightly called “the world,” because they place all their desire in the love of the world and love no other life. Of them the Lord says in [Col. 0511B] the Gospel: “Righteous Father, the world has not known you” (John XVII); and the apostle John says: “The whole world lies in the power of evil” (I John V).

But their shadowy and smoky joy is turned into sorrow, because, as blessed Job says: “They spend their days in prosperity, and in a moment they descend to the underworld” (Job XII). To them the Lord says in the Gospel: “Woe to you who laugh, for you shall weep” (Luke XII). Through the prophet he also reproaches them, saying: “Behold, my servants shall rejoice, but you shall be confounded. Behold, my servants shall exult in gladness, but you shall cry out because of sorrow of heart, and you shall howl because of the contrition of your spirit” (Isa. LXV).

The brief sorrow of the righteous, however, shall be changed into eternal gladness when this mortal nature shall put on immortality and this corruptible nature shall put on incorruption. Those who now sow in tears shall then reap in joy. And when what the Lord says is fulfilled—“Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. V)—and what Job says—“The mouth of the truthful shall be filled with laughter” (Job VIII)—then the joy of the reprobate shall be turned into sorrow, when, after the universal judgment, they see the saints crowned in glory and themselves [Col. 0511C] hurled into Tartarus.

Then they shall begin to mourn, saying: “These are the ones whom we once held in derision and made the object of reproach. We fools considered their life madness and their end dishonorable. How are they now counted among the sons of God, and their lot is among the saints?” (Wis. V.)

But because the disciples were not yet capable of understanding the matters mentioned above, the Lord wished to give an illustration from [Col. 0511D] earthly things and introduced an example to console their sorrow, saying:

“When a woman gives birth, she has sorrow, because her hour has come.”

According to the literal sense, this is so: when a woman gives birth, she gives birth with grief and sorrow. For from the time when it was said to our first mother, “In sorrow you shall give birth to children” (Gen. III), it has been the nature of woman to give birth with grief and pain.

Spiritually, this woman signifies the holy Church. She is not called a woman because of softness, but because of her union with a man, of whom it is rightly sung: “Noble at the gates is her husband, when he sits with the elders of the land” (Prov. XXXI). She is compared to a woman because of the fruitfulness of her offspring, since this woman gives birth daily [Col. 0512A] to as many children as she regenerates through the faithful by the water of baptism and the grace of the Holy Spirit. Concerning this regeneration the Lord says elsewhere: “Unless one is born again of water and the Holy Spirit” (John III), and so forth.

This is that woman of whom the Lord speaks figuratively in the Gospel, saying: “The kingdom of heaven is like leaven which a woman took and hid in three measures of flour until the whole was leavened” (Matt. XIII). For the Church sowed the teaching of the holy Gospel in the three parts of the world—Asia, Africa, and Europe—until the whole was leavened, that is, until the entire human race heard the preaching of Christ.

Concerning her Solomon also says: “Who shall find a valiant woman? Her price is from afar and from the ends of the earth. The heart of her husband trusts in her, and he shall have no need of spoils [Col. 0512B]” (Prov. XXXI). In her type or figure, the queen of Sheba came from the ends of the earth to Jerusalem to hear the wisdom of Solomon.

But this woman has sorrow when she gives birth, because her hour has come. For the holy Church, when she keeps watch in preaching, is sometimes afflicted by external enemies, but is always pressed by internal ones. She wages war daily, not against flesh and blood, but against rulers and powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places, knowing that it is written: “Many are the tribulations of the righteous” (Ps. XXXIII); and again: “Through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God” (Acts XIV).

The Apostle knew that he belonged among the members of this woman when, with grieving voice, he lamented the fall of his spiritual children, [Col. 0512C] saying: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you” (Gal. IV); and the prophet, when he said: “Because of your fear, O Lord, we conceived and gave birth to the spirit of salvation” (Isa. XXVI).

“When she has given birth to the child.”

Just as a woman rejoices when a child has been born, so the Church rejoices when she sends the souls of the faithful into eternal life. Amid the pressures of tribulations she is always lifted up by the hope of rewards, recalling the Apostle’s words: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy of the glory to come that shall be revealed in us” (Rom. VIII).

What sort and what measure of joy there shall be there is made clear by these words: “She no longer remembers the anguish” that preceded, “because of [Col. 0512D] the joy” that follows, “because a human being has been born into the world.” Such glory is given to the saints that they will not only have no fear of what is to come, but will also forget their past afflictions, as is said through John in the Apocalypse: “God shall wipe away every tear from the eyes of the saints, and there shall no longer be mourning, nor crying, nor any pain, because the former things have passed away” (Apoc. XXI).

Of their spiritual joy the Psalmist also says: “The saints shall exult in glory; they shall rejoice in their dwelling places” (Ps. CXLIX). Such security shall exist there that they will even mock death, saying: “Where is your sting, O death? Where is your contention?” Where there is the fullness of life, there will be no image of death, because those who now struggle in combat [Col. 0513A] shall then be crowned in recompense.

It is rightly said that a human being has been born into the world when a faithful soul passes into the life to come. For just as in ordinary speech we are said to be born when we proceed from our mother’s womb into the world, so the faithful soul is believed to be born spiritually when it is granted to pass from the misery of the present life into blessed life.

Hence ecclesiastical custom has established that the days of blessed martyrs or confessors on which they departed from this life should be called not funeral days but birthdays, because they began to live more happily at the moment when, through the shadow of death, they were deemed worthy to reach eternal life. The Lord promises this life to the faithful, saying: “Whoever believes in me, even if he has died, shall live” (John XI).

That birth is much more blessed than this one, because in the first birth we are born on earth in order to die, whereas in the second [Col. 0513B] we are born into heaven in order to live without end, singing with the Psalmist: “One day in your courts is better than thousands” (Ps. XXXIX).

Explaining what he wished to be understood in the illustration he had offered concerning the woman, the Lord added:

“And so you also now have sorrow. But I shall see you again, and your heart shall rejoice, and no one shall take your joy from you.”

It is as though he were saying: Just as a woman has sorrow when she gives birth, so you shall be sorrowful because of my passion; and just as a woman rejoices when the child has been born, so my resurrection shall make you glad.

But what does he mean by saying: “I shall see you again”? Are we hidden for any interval of time from the sight of him before whose eyes all things are naked and open [Col. 0513C]? No. Rather, “I shall see you” means: “I shall rescue you from tribulation and free you from distress.” God is properly said to see us when, in his mercy, he releases us from the pressure of tribulation, as he himself said to Moses: “Seeing, I have seen the affliction of my people” (Exod. III), and so forth; and as the Psalmist prayed: “See my humiliation and rescue me” (Ps. CXIII).

The Lord therefore saw the apostles when he freed them from the distresses they had endured because of his passion.

Or certainly, “I shall see you” is equivalent, by a figurative expression, to: “I shall cause you to see.” God is said to see when he enlightens us so that we may see; likewise, he is said to know when he causes us to know, as he said to Abraham: “Now I know that [Col. 0513D] you fear God” (Gen. XXII), that is, “I have caused you to know.”

By saying, “And your heart shall rejoice,” we are given to understand that the hearts of the disciples, which had been saddened by his passion, rejoiced when they saw that he had risen from the dead. They were delighted with still greater joy when they saw the human nature united to God ascend into heaven amid the praises of the angels, as the evangelist Luke says: “And they worshiped him and returned to Jerusalem with great joy, and they were continually in the temple, praising and blessing God” (Luke XXIV).

It is asked, however, why he says: “No one shall take your joy from you,” since after his ascension they are read to have been frequently beaten, bound in chains, and thrown into prisons [Col. 0514A]. But it must be understood that the joy they received from his resurrection and ascension could be taken from them by no sorrow, persecution, or distress. Rather, as Scripture relates, they went rejoicing from the presence of the council, saying that “they were worthy to suffer disgrace for the name of Jesus” (Acts V).

Hence one of them, rejoicing, said: “Consider it all joy, my brothers, when you fall into various trials, knowing that tribulation produces endurance, endurance produces testing, and testing produces hope; but hope does not put us to shame, because the love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (James I; Rom. V).

The Lord promised this invisible and ineffable joy to the apostles when he said: “Ask, and you shall receive [Col. 0514B] so that my joy may be in you and your joy may be complete” (John XV).

The apostle Paul knew himself to share in this unspeakable joy, which no one could take from the apostles, when he said: “Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation, or distress, or famine, or persecution, or nakedness, or the sword? I am certain that neither death nor life, neither things present nor things to come, neither height nor depth, nor any other creature shall be able to separate us from the love of God which is in Christ Jesus” (Rom. VIII).

And so, if in proportion to our weakness we do not refuse to be sorrowful with the apostles in the present life, we shall be deemed worthy to attain that ineffable joy which he promised, when we enter into the presence of the Lord with exultation [Col. 0514C]. For, as the Apostle says: “If we are companions in suffering, we shall also be companions in consolation; and if we suffer with him, we shall also reign with him” (I Cor. I; Rom. VIII).

No one shall take that joy from you, because no change, no sorrow, and no fear of death will be able to exist in eternal gladness. Rather, as Scripture says, those who have been redeemed by the Lord shall possess joy and gladness; they shall come to Zion rejoicing, and everlasting joy shall be upon their heads.

## HOMILY LXXXVI. FOURTH SUNDAY AFTER EASTER, “Cantate”

(James I.) “Beloved, every good gift and every perfect gift is from above.” And so forth. This is understood generally of every virtue given by God, and specifically of [Col. 0514D] each individual one. It may also be understood specifically that the “good gift” refers to continence within marriage, and the “perfect gift” to virginity.

“Coming down from the Father of lights.”

God is called the Father of lights because from him all things were made: whether the invisible lights, such as the angels, concerning whom God said at the beginning, “Let there be light” (Gen. I); or those souls to whom Jesus said, “You are the light of the world” (Matt. V); or visible lights, the sun, moon, and stars.

“With whom there is no change.”

He who said, “I am who I am” (Exod. III), will not change. Movement and time, growth and decline, are wholly foreign to the divine nature.

“Nor shadow of alteration.”

God is not [Col. 0515A] overshadowed by darkness after light as day is; he is always the light of light, the creator and source of every light.

“For of his own will he brought us forth,”

namely, by grace, not by nature. For only the Word is substantially and properly called the Son of God; the others are called sons by the power received from him. “But to all who received him,” the evangelist says, “he gave power to become sons of God” (John I).

“By the word of truth.”

God the Father is Truth; the Son is his Word. Or, Christ is Truth; the Word of Truth is his Gospel. “Through the Gospel,” Paul says, “I begot you” (I Cor. IV).

“That we might be a beginning of his creation.”

The beginning of rational creation consists of the angels in heaven, Adam on earth, the patriarchs in the Church of the Old Testament, and the apostles in the Church redeemed by Christ’s blood [Col. 0515B]. For to one of them it is said: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I shall build my Church” (Matt. XVI). The apostle Paul calls this Church a new creation.

“But let every person be quick to hear, slow to speak.”

He knew that those to whom he was sending his letters wished to hold the primacy in speech and to teach rather than be taught; therefore he admonishes them to preserve humility. Quickness in hearing makes a person teachable; slowness in speaking makes one gentle.

“Slow to anger.”

He could not completely forbid what occurs naturally. He prescribed slowness, because anger diminishes when delayed.

Alternatively: “Slow to anger,” that is, according to the law of the Old Testament, slow to take vengeance. “For the law,” the Apostle says, “produces wrath” (Rom. IV), that is, “an eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth.”

“For the anger of man does not accomplish the justice of God [Col. 0515C].”

By “the anger of man” he means human anger, which, according to the practice of the Old Testament, always desires to exercise vengeance and, in the New Testament, where it is written, “Do not resist evil” (Matt. V), does not accomplish justice.

Alternatively: “The anger of man accomplishes justice,” with “the anger of God” understood. This anger is said in human terms to accomplish justice, as in Sodom, in Pharaoh, in Egypt, in the Red Sea, and among the Israelite people themselves in the desert. Hence the Psalmist sings: “The Lord was angry in fury against his people” (Ps. CV); and in many places we read that the anger of God, which always proceeds by the most just judgment, accomplishes perfectly righteous justice.

[Col. 0515D] “Therefore, putting away all uncleanness.”

Some have wished to understand “uncleanness” in this passage specifically as idolatry; others, as sexual impurity committed with women, with men, with animals, and things of that kind. Finally, so that you might understand it generally of every kind of wickedness, he added:

“And an abundance of wickedness.”

For just as a living root in the earth puts forth shoots, so wickedness hidden in the heart produces vices.

“With gentleness receive the implanted Word, which is able to save your souls.”

“With gentleness”—that is, without anger and dispute—receive it through right faith in a pure mind. “Implanted”: sent by God and received in our [Col. 0516A] minds, so that where sin abounded, grace might abound even more. “The Word,” he says—that is, the word of faith, the word of the Gospel; finally, that Word of which John says: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John I). He is also called the Savior, because he is able to save your souls.

## HOMILY LXXXVII. FOURTH SUNDAY AFTER EASTER, “Cantate”

(John XVI.) “At that time Jesus said to his disciples: ‘I am going to him who sent me, and none of you asks me, “Where are you going?”’” And so forth.

From the beginning of his preaching the Lord frequently showed that he loved his disciples, but he displayed his affection toward them especially when, as the moment of [Col. 0516B] his passion approached, he was about to depart from them bodily, as the same evangelist makes clear elsewhere when he says: “Knowing that his hour had come to pass from this world to the Father, having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end” (John XIII).

For just as a wise head of a household, when he has departed for a distant region, especially admonishes those subject to him how they ought to conduct themselves, so the Lord Jesus Christ, about to depart bodily from the apostles, graciously chose to show them especially how they ought to live in the world, saying: “By this everyone shall know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (ibid.); and again: “I give you a new commandment, that you love one another” (ibid.), and other things [Col. 0516C] of this kind.

On that same night on which he was to be betrayed by a disciple, he not only washed the disciples’ feet but also handed over to them the mystery of his body and blood. And while he spoke to them at length about his own divinity and that of the Father, he wished to foretell not only his resurrection but also his ascension, saying: “I am going to him who sent me.”

Here it must be asked why he says, “I am going to him who sent me,” when elsewhere he is read to have said to the disciples: “Behold, I am with you all days, until the consummation of the age” (Matt. XXVIII).

This question is easily understood by those who confess in the one Mediator between God and human beings both natures, namely, the divine and the human. He remains with the disciples [Col. 0516D] through his divinity, and he goes to the Father through his humanity, from whom he never departed through his divinity, as he himself says: “I and the Father are one” (John X).
