To come and to depart belong to humanity; to remain and to be belong to divinity. Therefore he remained with the disciples by virtue of the fact that “in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.” He goes to the Father by virtue of the fact that “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us,” as he himself says elsewhere: “I came forth from the Father and came into the world; again, I leave the world and go to the Father” (John XVI); and again: “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John III).

What he adds—“And none of you asks me, ‘Where are you going?’”—is as though he were saying: My ascension shall be so clear and glorious [Col. 0517A] that none of you will need to ask me where I am going, since everyone will see that I am ascending into heaven.

For when earlier he foretold that he would go to his passion, saying: “Little children, I am with you only a little while longer” (ibid.), and as he said to the Jews, “Where I am going, you cannot come” (John VIII), Peter questioned him, saying: “Lord, where are you going?” (John XIII). But when they had seen the glory of his ascension, they did not need to ask where he was going, because, as Luke relates in the Acts of the Apostles, while everyone watched, he was lifted up, and a cloud received him from their eyes.

And while they were gazing into heaven as he went, immediately two men stood beside them in white garments. They said: “Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven? This Jesus who [Col. 0517B] has been taken up from you into heaven shall come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven” (Acts I).

And because the Lord knew that these words would produce all the greater sorrow in the hearts of the apostles the more closely he foretold that he would depart from them, he added:

“But because I have spoken these things to you, sorrow has filled your heart.”

They could not hear of the bodily absence of the one by whose grace they had been chosen from the world, whose teaching instructed them, whose words formed them, and whose miracles delighted them, without profound grief. They felt him as their protector and defender [Col. 0517C] in all things, and they could not be separated from him without great sorrow.

Hence, when he foretold his passion elsewhere, Peter, wishing to prevent him, said: “May God be gracious to you, Lord; this shall not happen. For it is not fitting that the Son of God should taste death” (Matt. XVI). And when, reclining at the Last Supper, he said: “One of you is about to betray me,” they were greatly saddened and began, each one, to say: “Surely it is I, Lord?” (Matt. XXVI).

But the gracious Teacher took care to soothe this sorrow of theirs with kind consolation, saying:

“I tell you the truth: it is expedient for you that I go.”

It is as though he were saying: I who am the Truth tell you the truth. It is necessary that this form of a servant, which you see in me and love with sincere affection, be withdrawn for a time from your sight, so that you may be able to contemplate the form of divinity in me more perfectly, as he himself says elsewhere: “If you loved me, because the Father is greater than I” (John XIV).

Hence it is rightly added: “But if I do not go, the Paraclete will not come to you; but if I go, I shall send him to you.”

Could he have given the Holy Spirit while on earth, when it is plainly read that after the resurrection he breathed upon them and said: “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John XX)? He certainly could have. But as long as the apostles had God as a human being living, eating, and speaking with them, they delighted in his presence and raised the eyes of their minds less toward knowing his divinity.

After they knew that the Lord’s body had been placed at the right hand of the Father, they transferred all their desire to the place where they knew that the Head had gone [Col. 0518A] before them, in accordance with what the Lord says elsewhere: “Where your treasure is, there also is your heart” (Matt. VI); and again: “Where the body is, there the eagles will also be gathered” (Luke VII).

And therefore they were deemed worthy to receive the Holy Spirit visibly after the ascension with so much greater perfection as they burned more intensely with love for him. This is what he means by saying: “If I do not go, the Paraclete will not come to you.”

The Spirit is rightly called the Paraclete: for παράκλητος (*paraklētos*) in Greek means “comforter” or “advocate” in Latin. He is rightly called the Comforter because he not only then deigned to console the hearts of the apostles grieving over the Lord’s absence, but also daily grants the greatest consolation to those who mourn because of the sins they have committed, while he promises hope of forgiveness.

By the help of this consolation the one who said, “Your consolations [Col. 0518B], O Lord, have gladdened my soul” (Ps. XCIII), knew himself to have been strengthened. In Greek it reads: Αἱ παρακλήσεις σου εὔφραναν τὴν ψυχήν μου — “Your consolations have gladdened my soul.”

And again: “I remembered your judgments from of old, O Lord, and I was comforted” (Ps. CXVIII).

The same Spirit is also rightly called an Advocate, because he daily intercedes with the Father for our transgressions, as the Apostle says: “For we do not know what we ought to pray for as we should, but the Spirit himself pleads for us with inexpressible groanings” (Rom. VIII).

How greatly the apostles were to advance through the gift of this same Spirit is made clear when it is added:

“And when he comes, he shall convict the world concerning sin, and concerning justice, and concerning judgment.”

It is clear that the Lord Jesus Christ [Col. 0518C] himself convicted the world—that is, the lovers of the world—concerning sin, justice, and judgment.

He convicted them concerning sin because they did not wish to believe in him. Of them he says elsewhere: “If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin; but now they have no excuse for their sin, because they have seen me and hated me without cause” (John XV).

He convicted them concerning justice because they did not wish to imitate the justice and simplicity of the apostles. In comparison with them they shall rightly be judged, for he says to them: “If I cast out demons by Beelzebul, by whom do your sons cast them out? Therefore they shall be your judges” (Luke XI).

He convicted them concerning judgment because, although he had shown that the devil had already been judged, saying, “I saw Satan falling from heaven like lightning” (Luke X), they preferred to remain under his harshest [Col. 0518D] slavery rather than pass under the gentle yoke of their liberator.

But what the Lord did himself among the one nation of the Jews, he promises that the Holy Spirit will do among all nations through the preaching of the apostles. For the Holy Spirit convicts the world—that is, the lovers of the world—through the apostles concerning sin when he condemns the unbelief of the faithless, as the Holy Spirit says through the apostles to those who did not believe: “It was necessary that the word of God be spoken to you first; but because you reject it and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts XIII).

And beautifully, at the outset, the Lord set the sin of unbelief in a special place, because just as faith is the origin of all virtues, so unbelief is the foundation of all [Col. 0519A] vices; and just as the righteous person lives by faith, so the one who does not believe has already been judged.

“Concerning justice, because I am going to the Father, and you shall no longer see me.”

The justice of the apostles was especially confirmed in this: that although they had seen him as a humble human being, they believed him to be exalted God. Likewise, the justice of the rest of the faithful appears praiseworthy in this: that although they do not see him bodily, they love and believe in him with the mind.

Hence it is rightly said: “Concerning justice, because I am going to the Father, and you shall no longer see me.” This means: You shall not see me mortal, corruptible, hungry, and thirsty, such as the reprobate can still see me; but you shall see me immortal and incorruptible [Col. 0519B], such as only the eyes of the righteous were able to see me.

The Holy Spirit therefore convicts them concerning justice because they are reluctant to imitate the good works of the righteous, who, although they do not see God bodily, nevertheless show through good works that they love him.

“But concerning judgment, because the prince of this world has already been judged.”

He calls the devil the prince of the world, because he once claimed dominion over the hearts of those who love the world more than God the Creator. Concerning him the Lord says: “For the prince of this world is coming, and he has nothing in me” (John XIV).

The prince of the world has therefore already been judged, because through the presence of God his power has been driven from the hearts of the faithful, as the Lord says: “Now is the hour when the prince of this world shall be cast out” (John XII).

The Holy Spirit therefore convicts those concerning judgment whom the example of the condemned angel terrifies, so that they do not dare [Col. 0519C] to act proudly against God, as the apostle Jude says: “The angels who did not preserve their own principality but abandoned their dwelling he has reserved for the judgment of the great God.”

But because the Lord knew that the hearts of the apostles were still frail and needed to be strengthened by the coming of the Holy Spirit in order to convict concerning sin, justice, and judgment, he promises this, adding:

“I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now. But when that Spirit of truth comes—”

He is called the Spirit of truth because he proceeds from the Father of truth. What he adds—“He shall teach you all truth”—pertains not only to the present [Col. 0519D] life but also to the life to come.

No one can be so perfect in the present life as to be able to comprehend all truth, especially since the apostle Paul, who had been caught up to the third heaven, says: “For we know in part, and we prophesy in part” (I Cor. XIII); and the Psalmist says: “I considered [Col. 0520A] in order to know this; it is labor before me, until I enter the sanctuary of God and understand their final destiny” (Ps. LXXII).

“He shall teach you all truth,” therefore, because whatever each faithful person understands imperfectly about God, the Holy Spirit will cause him to understand more perfectly in the life to come, since, as the Apostle says: “Now we see through a mirror in a riddle, but then face to face” (I Cor. XIII).

Or certainly, when he says, “He shall teach you all truth,” this means that he shall spread truth—or love—in the hearts of the faithful, by which he teaches them to love all truth. And because the Father, the Son, and that same Holy Spirit have one substance and one divinity, it is rightly added:

“Indeed, he will not speak from himself.” The Holy Spirit will not speak from himself, because he proceeds from the Father and the Son; and those who have one essence and one nature cannot be divided, so that one should speak without the other. Rather, what the Father speaks, the Son speaks, and the Holy Spirit speaks. Hence it also follows: “But whatever he hears, he will speak.” He will hear, that is, from the Father, from whom he exists not temporally but eternally, not visibly but invisibly. For the Holy Spirit’s speaking is to teach our minds through hidden inspiration, in accordance with what the Lord says elsewhere: “The Spirit breathes where he wills, and you hear his voice, but you do not know where he comes from or where he goes” (John 3). What he adds—“And he will announce to you the things that are to come”—is clear according to the literal sense, because the Holy Spirit frequently announced future things to the faithful, to whom he granted the mystery of prophecy. But the Holy Spirit announces future things in a way that applies generally to all the faithful, because he inflames all whom he fills to love the eternal life that is to come. Concerning this he adds further:

“He will glorify me.” The Holy Spirit glorified the Son when he drove every fear from the hearts of the apostles and made them fit to preach the only-begotten Son of God, as it is written in the Acts of the Apostles: “They were all filled with the Holy Spirit, and they spoke the word of God with boldness” (Acts 4). The Holy Spirit also glorified the Son when, sent by him as he had been promised, he granted the apostles knowledge of all languages on the day of Pentecost. Hence it is read in the Acts of the Apostles: “They were all filled with the Holy Spirit, and they began to speak in various languages, as the Holy Spirit gave them utterance” (Acts 6). The Holy Spirit also glorified the Son when he adorned the Son’s preachers with such great and such remarkable powers that the whole world hastened to believe in him. When he says, “Because he will receive from what is mine and announce it to you,” one must understand: from what belongs to my Father. For the Father alone is from no one and proceeds from no one. The Son is said not to be from himself, because he was born from the Father. The Holy Spirit is said to receive from the Father because he proceeds indivisibly from the Father and the Son. Hence it also follows:

“Everything that the Father has is mine. And therefore I said: Because he will receive from what is mine and announce it to you.” That is, he will make those things known to you.

## HOMILY 88. FIFTH SUNDAY AFTER EASTER, “The Voice of Joy”

(James 1.) “My dearest brothers, be doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving yourselves.” And so forth. We must fulfill the divine words by our deeds if we wish to reach the heavenly kingdom. In the present reading, as you have heard, the apostle James exhorts us, saying: “Be doers of the word, and not hearers only” [Col. 0521A]. Doers of the word are those who keep the Lord’s commandment. “Deceiving yourselves.” Those who deceive themselves are involved in other affairs, desiring to hear the Gospel but not to fulfill it; or those who conceal from the priest, the divine physician, the wounds of their sins and do not wish to reveal them for their own salvation. He deceives neither Scripture nor the priest, but himself, since he follows not God’s will but the devil’s. Concerning such people he adds:

“For if anyone is a hearer of the word and not a doer, he will be compared to a man observing the face of his birth in a mirror. For he observed himself and went away, and immediately forgot what he was like.” It is customary for women to look at themselves in a mirror so that they may adorn themselves and be able to please their husbands. In the same way, we must carefully examine our souls in the mirror of the Gospel and weigh its teachings, considering what adornment we possess from fulfilling its sacraments, so that we may be able to please our husband, Christ the Lord [Col. 0521B]. But if, through imperfect observance of the Gospel, we have acquired too little adornment for our souls, we must hasten with all diligence to present that very adornment to ourselves through holy works. Otherwise, when our bridegroom Christ comes and calls us at an hour when we do not expect him, he may find us unprepared, and we may be shut out from the wedding feast of the heavenly kingdom. Finally, with the foolish virgins we may begin uselessly to cry out before the door and seek an entrance, when we are unable to find one. Let us therefore not forget the Lord’s commandments, which are the adornment of our souls [Col. 0521C]. Rather, serving his will, let us adorn ourselves with worthy conduct and holy behavior, so that when Christ our bridegroom comes to call us, we may deserve to reach eternal joys with him. It follows:

“But whoever looks attentively into the law of perfect freedom and perseveres in it, not becoming a forgetful hearer but a doer of the work, that person will be blessed in his deed.” He calls charity the law of freedom, concerning which Paul says: “You have been called in the freedom of the charity of Christ” (Galatians 5). And again: “Bearing one another’s burdens in charity” (ibid.). For if anyone strives to preserve himself in perfect charity—namely, loving God with all his heart, with all his soul, and with all his strength, and loving his neighbor as himself—he is shown to be not a forgetful hearer but a doer of the evangelical work [Col. 0521D]. And if he perseveres in that same contemplation of the divine law by putting it into practice, he will truly be blessed and will attain everlasting blessedness.

“If anyone thinks that he is religious, not restraining his tongue”—by praising himself and seeking to glorify himself before people for the good things he has done, like the Pharisee standing in the temple and reckoning up his good deeds, declaring that he was not like the tax collector (Luke 18)—“not restraining his tongue,” that is, not guarding his heart from pride or the desire for empty glory, or not guarding his tongue from detraction or blasphemy. For it is useless to abstain from certain vices if he has not restrained his tongue. Hence it is said in the Psalm: “Who is the person who desires life and wishes to see good days? Let him restrain his tongue from evil, and his lips from speaking deceit” (Psalm 33). For it follows: “But deceiving his own heart, this person’s religion is empty,” as long as his heart remains in its pride.

“Religion pure and undefiled before God and the Father is this: to visit orphans and widows in their tribulation.” The care of orphans and widows is entrusted to the Church, and great danger is threatened to priests if they are unwilling to resist those who oppose the truth. For whoever accepts the person of the powerful and is afraid to speak the truth is punished by the sentence of grave guilt. Many bishops of the Churches, fearing that they may lose friendships and incur the burden of hatred, do not rebuke sinners and are afraid to correct the oppressors of the poor [Col. 0522B]. Nor do they fear the severity of the account they will have to render because they remain silent about the peoples entrusted to them when the poor are oppressed by the powerful. Good priests bring the help of protection to rescue them. They do not fear anyone’s hostile displeasure, but openly rebuke, reprimand, and excommunicate the oppressors of the poor. They fear their plots to do harm less, even if those oppressors are able to cause harm. For the good shepherd gives his life for his sheep. Just as a shepherd customarily guards sheep through vigilance against beasts, so the priest of God must be watchful over Christ’s flock, lest the enemy lay it waste, lest the persecutor harass it, lest the greed of any powerful person disturb the life of the poor. Rather, through his vigilance and careful concern, they may deserve life and eternal salvation [Col. 0522C].

## HOMILY 89. FIFTH SUNDAY AFTER EASTER, “The Voice of Joy”

(John 16.) “At that time Jesus said to his disciples: Truly I say to you, if you ask the Father for anything in my name, he will give it to you.” And so forth. The Lord Jesus Christ, giver of virtues and rewarder of merits, knowing that human nature can possess nothing good except through his grace—he who says, “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15)—elsewhere exhorts and admonishes us to persist in praying and to be insistent in asking, saying: “Ask, and you will receive; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you” (Matthew 7). And so that no one would doubt that he could obtain what he asked, provided that he did not grow weary in prayer, at the beginning of this reading he offered great confidence to those who ask, saying: “Truly, truly I say to you, if you ask the Father for anything in my name, he will give it to you.” Here we should note that when he urges us to ask, he wishes his gratuitous gifts to become our merits. Therefore, although he knows what we need before we ask him, so that he may find in us something he can justly reward, he invites us to ask, saying: “Everyone who asks receives, and whoever seeks finds, and to the one who knocks it will be opened.” But those who understand less may be troubled by his saying, “If you ask anything in my name, he will give it to you,” since we read that not only lesser people but even the apostle Paul, who was of the highest perfection, asked for something and did not obtain it [Col. 0523A]. But so that the Lord’s truthful promise may shine more clearly for us, let us examine the various kinds of those who ask and distinguish the reasons for obtaining or not obtaining. For it sometimes happens that good things are requested in prayer, but because those who ask are evil, they do not deserve to be heard by the Lord. They vainly think that the Lord will hear their prayers when they disdain to hear him in his commandments, as Solomon testifies, saying: “Whoever closes his ear so as not to hear the law, his prayer will be accursed” (Proverbs 28). At other times carnal people ask for carnal things, and therefore they are not heard by the Lord. To them the blessed apostle James says: “You ask, and you do not receive, because you ask wrongly, so that you may remain in your desires” (James 4). At times good people ask for good things, but the evil merits of those for whom they ask prevent them from being heard. Such were those concerning whom the Lord says to Jeremiah: “But you, do not pray for this people, and do not take up praise and prayer for them, because I will not hear you” (Jeremiah 7). And again: “If Moses and Samuel were to stand before me, my soul is not toward this people” (Jeremiah 15). Yet we must not think that we are deprived of the fruit of our reward whenever, praying for wicked people, we do not deserve to be heard. For even if those for whom we ask are not worthy to receive, a reward will nevertheless be repaid to us for our good intention. Hence he did not simply say, “If you ask the Father for anything in my name, he will give it,” but added, “He will give it to you” [Col. 0523C]. This means: Even if those for whom you ask do not deserve to receive, a reward will nevertheless be given to you for your affection of charity, as the Psalmist says: “And my prayer will return into my own bosom” (Psalm 34).

At times the holy ask for holy things, but because their request is not fulfilled in the present, it remains to be fulfilled in the future. Thus the universal Church asks God daily in prayer, saying: “Your kingdom come” (Matthew 6). Although that kingdom does not come immediately when the prayer is finished, it is nevertheless undoubtedly believed that it will come after the universal judgment. At times holy people unknowingly ask in prayer for things contrary to their souls, yet by God’s hidden judgment they are heard not according to their will but for their salvation. For it is much more beneficial to be heard for salvation than according to one’s will. To make this clearer, let us set before us two people, one evil and the other good, arranged so that the good person is said to have asked and not obtained, while the evil person is said to have asked and obtained. But lest someone say in the silent judgment of his conscience that it is impossible for the one who was heard to be unjust before God and for the one who was not heard to be just, let the evil person be one whose wickedness no one can ignore, and let the good person be one whose holiness no one can doubt: namely, the apostle Paul and the devil. For who would deny that the devil is the author of wickedness, especially since blessed Job says of him: “He sees every lofty thing, and he is king over all the sons of pride” (Job 41)? Who, on the other hand, would doubt that the apostle Paul was holy after his conversion, especially since the judge himself bears witness concerning him, saying: “This man is a chosen vessel for me, to carry my name before the nations and kings and the children of Israel” (Acts 9)? No one. And yet the devil asked and obtained, while the Apostle asked and did not obtain. The devil asked that Job’s possessions be destroyed, and he heard: “Behold, everything he has is in your hand” (Job 1). The Apostle asked that the thorn of his flesh be taken away from him, and he did not obtain it. Which of them, then, was heard more fully—the devil or the Apostle? The devil was heard according to his will, but not for his salvation, because he became worse through the very thing by which he had attempted to inflict harm on the holy man. The Apostle was not heard according to his will, but for his salvation, because it was not beneficial for the thorn of his flesh to be taken away from him; it had been given to him for the guarding of humility, as he himself says: “And lest the greatness of the revelations should exalt me, a thorn in my flesh was given to me, an angel of Satan, to strike me. For this I besought the Lord three times, that it might depart from me, and he said to me: My grace is sufficient for you, for power is made perfect in weakness” (2 Corinthians 12) [Col. 0524B].

Therefore, whoever asks perseveringly, without doubting in faith, for those things that pertain to the salvation of his soul is undoubtedly heard, either in the present or in the future. Hence it is rightly said, “in my name.” His name is Jesus, that is, “savior” or “salutary.” Therefore, the one who asks in Jesus’ name is the one who seeks the salvation of his soul.

“Until now you have asked nothing in my name.” Had the apostles not asked before, saying (Mark 14): “Lord, tell us when these things will be,” or, “What will be the sign of your coming?” and similar questions? They certainly had. But the words “Until now you have asked nothing” can be understood in two ways. Either: You have asked nothing because you did not believe me to be equal to the Father, so as to ask in my name; or certainly: You have asked nothing because, in comparison with the things you ought to have asked, what you asked was nothing. Before the Passion, the apostles’ frail minds knew how to ask first for earthly and transitory things. Thus we read concerning the two sons of Zebedee, who persuaded their mother to ask him that one might sit at his right hand and the other at his left in his kingdom. But because, in comparison with what they ought to have asked, what she was asking was nothing, they immediately heard: “You do not know what you are asking.” Earthly and transitory things, when compared with eternal happiness, must be considered nothing [Col. 0524D]. But because they had until then been sluggish in asking for things that are eternal, they are stirred by the Lord’s words to ask, when he says: “Ask.” And so that they would not doubt that they would receive, it is rightly added: “And you will receive.” What they ought principally to ask is made clear when it follows: “So that your joy may be full.” The order of the words is therefore: Ask so that your joy may be full, and you will receive. Here it is shown that in prayer we ought to ask not for gold, not for silver, not for earthly riches, and not for the length of the present life, but for eternal life and the things that pertain to it, namely, the virtues of the soul [Col. 0525A]. Full and perfect joy cannot exist where the frailty of mutability varies everything so greatly that joy can scarcely remain with us for the space of a single hour. Suddenly happiness is swallowed up by sadness, joy is turned into grief, health is damaged by sickness, abundant possession is reduced by poverty, prosperity is overthrown by adversity, youth runs toward old age, and life hastens toward death. Therefore, when he says, “Ask and you will receive, so that your joy may be full,” he urges us to ask for that singular and blessed life where there is happiness without sadness, joy without grief, security without fear, and life without death. Those who attain it will obtain joy and gladness, and every pain and groaning will flee from them, when what the Lord promises elsewhere is fulfilled: “I will see you again, and your heart will rejoice, and no one will take your joy from you” (John 16). The devout petitioner had especially desired this when he said (Psalm 26): “One thing I have asked from the Lord; this I will seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life and see the delight of the Lord.” And again: “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living.”

“I have spoken these things to you in proverbs. The hour is coming.” We may understand this hour as the day of Pentecost. “When I will no longer speak to you in proverbs, but will announce the Father to you openly.” Certain comparisons are called proverbs; authors employ them as necessary for understanding more obscure meanings, so that through visible things people may at least be able to recognize invisible things [Col. 0525C]. Hence Solomon’s book received the name Proverbs, because through certain images or comparisons it urges the ignorance of little ones toward learning wisdom. The Lord therefore says that he spoke in proverbs because, adapting himself to the weakness of the disciples, he first used comparisons in his words so that they could more easily grasp them, just as the evangelist Matthew says: “Jesus spoke with his disciples in parables, and without parables he did not speak to them.” But when he promises that he will no longer speak in proverbs but will announce the Father openly, he shows that they will come, through the arrival of the Holy Spirit, to such perfection that it will no longer be necessary to speak to them as little ones in proverbs, since the Holy Spirit, when he comes, will announce the Father openly—that is, he will enable them to know perfectly how the Father is in the Son and the Son is in the Father. Whatever the Father can do, the Son can likewise do, according to what he himself says: “Everything that the Father has is mine” (John 16). Hence it also follows:

“On that day you will ask in my name.” This means: On that day, when the Holy Spirit comes and makes you know that I and the Father are one, you will ask in my name, because you will know that I am equal to the Father and will believe that I am able, together with the Father, to give everything. Or the words “You will ask in my name” have this meaning, as though he were saying: When the Holy Spirit comes and makes you despise earthly things perfectly, you will understand that only those things which pertain to the salvation of souls should be requested [Col. 0526A]. And because Christ appeared as man in such a way that he was perfect God, it is rightly added: “And I do not say to you that I will ask the Father concerning you.” Because he is human, he is read elsewhere as having asked the Father for the disciples, saying: “Holy Father, preserve them in your name, whom you have given me” (John 17). And again: “Father, while I was with them, I preserved those whom you gave me; but now I ask for them, not for the world. And I do not ask that you take them out of the world, but that you preserve them from evil” (ibid.). And elsewhere he says to Peter: “I have prayed for you, Peter, that your faith may not fail” (ibid.). But now he says that he will not ask the Father for the disciples, because in divinity he is almighty with the Father. He therefore asks the Father according to his humanity, because according to his divinity he grants everything that is requested together with the Father.

Or certainly, by saying, “And I do not say to you that I will ask the Father concerning you,” he shows that the saints will come to such blessedness in eternal life that they will need no one’s help or intercession, because they will be filled with eternal blessedness, as the Lord promises through the prophet Jeremiah, saying: “In those days and at that time a man will no longer teach his brother, nor his neighbor, saying: Know the Lord; for all will know me, says the Lord, from the least to the greatest” (Jeremiah 31). And therefore he did not say of the present, “I ask,” but of the future, “I will ask.” What he adds—“For the Father himself loves you, because you have loved me and believed that I came forth from God”—must not be understood as though the disciples’ love came first, so that they deserved to be loved by the Father through their own merit. Rather, by a gratuitous gift they were first chosen by the Father, so that they might be able to believe in and love the Son. Indeed, he himself says through the prophet: “I will love them freely” (Hosea 14). And in the Gospel: “You did not choose me, but I chose you” (John 15). Hence the apostle James says: “Of his own will he begot us by the word of truth” (James 1). For the same grace that follows a human being so that he may be able to do good precedes him so that he may desire to do good. If God’s grace did not precede the human will so that it might desire what is good, the Psalmist would by no means say: “I will guard my strength toward you, for God is my protector; my God’s mercy will precede me” (Psalm 58). And unless that same grace followed a person so that he might be able to do good, the same Psalmist would in no way say: “His mercy will follow me all the days of my life” (Psalm 22) [Col. 0526D].

“I came forth from the Father and came into the world; again I leave the world and go to the Father.” In this verse the Lord commended to us both his natures, namely, the divine and the human. Since God could not be seen by human beings in the form of divinity, he came forth from the Father and came into the world. In order to be seen, he showed himself visibly to the world in the form of a servant, as the Apostle says: “Although he was in the form of God, he did not consider equality with God something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of human beings and found in appearance as a human being” (Philippians 2). Again, he left the world and went to the Father when, having completed the mystery of his incarnation, he placed the human nature that he had assumed from us at the Father’s right hand, as the evangelist Mark says: “The Lord Jesus, after he had spoken to them, was taken up into heaven and sits at the right hand of God” (Mark 16) [Col. 0527A]. Therefore, just as he did not abandon the Father when he came into the world, so he did not abandon the elect when he returned to the Father, as he himself says elsewhere: “Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age” (Matthew 28). Remaining with the Father through divinity, he came into the world through humanity; returning to the Father through humanity, he remained with the elect through divinity, as he himself says: “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John 3).

“His disciples say to him: Behold, now you are speaking openly, and you are saying no proverb.” In these words the disciples show that in this final conversation, when the Lord spoke with them, he was discussing especially those things that delighted them to hear. Although they did not yet understand perfectly what he was saying, they answered as though they understood, saying: “Behold, now you are speaking openly, and you are saying no proverb.” Because he frequently anticipated their thoughts and brought forward, without being questioned, the things they wished to ask, they recognized in him an indication of the divine nature. Hence they add:

“Now we know that you know all things, and you do not need anyone to question you. By this we believe that you came forth from God.” It is proper to God to see the thoughts of human beings, as Scripture testifies, saying: “You alone, God, know the hearts of the children of human beings” (1 Chronicles 6). And again: “The things that are in the human heart your eyes see, O Lord.” And the Psalmist says: “You have understood my thoughts from afar” (Psalm 138).

## HOMILY 90. ON THE LITANIES, THAT IS, ON THE SUPPLICATIONS, AND THEIR ORIGIN

Because we commemorate the days of the litanies—that is, of the supplications—through the annual cycle, it is fitting, for the sake of the simpler among us, briefly to recall where they originated. They should not be thought to have entered into use without evangelical and apostolic authority [Col. 0527D]. Indeed, when the Lord was about to ascend into heaven, having frequently promised that he would send the Holy Spirit to the apostles, he said among other things: “But remain in the city until you are clothed with power from on high” (Luke 24). After they saw him ascend into heaven, they returned to Jerusalem, as the evangelist Luke says, with great joy, and they were always in the temple, praising and blessing God (ibid.). In order to deserve to receive the promised Holy Spirit, they devoted themselves to preparing through fasting and prayer, as the same Luke records in the Acts of the Apostles, saying: “They were all persevering with one accord in prayer, with the women and Mary the mother of Jesus, and his brothers” (Acts 1). After they had been filled with the Holy Spirit and sent to preach the Gospel to the nations scattered throughout the whole world, they are believed to have handed on these days for their successors to observe [Col. 0528A]. From that time Christian devotion began to celebrate them annually, so that believers might deserve to become participants in the gift of the same Holy Spirit.

The reason why we now observe them not after the Ascension but before the day of the Lord’s Ascension is this. When, because of their sins, the peoples of Gaul were being slaughtered with the ferocity of wolves, and no remedy for this scourge could be found, the bishops of Gaul are said to have assembled at Vienne, the principal city of Gaul, and to have jointly decreed that they should implore the Lord’s mercy through a three-day fast, following the footsteps of the ancient fathers. When the eye of divine mercy looked upon their prayers and mercifully removed the pestilence of this scourge, these days came into use as an annual celebration, to be observed throughout the provinces of Gaul before the day of the Lord’s Ascension [Col. 0528B].

Let us therefore also observe these days, according to the measure of our smallness, with the greatest reverence and devotion, with abstinence from flesh and humility of heart—not merely so that we may escape the rage of visible wolves, but also so that we may be able to overcome what is better, the temptations of invisible wolves, that is, of unclean spirits. For fasting is a very powerful weapon against the temptations of demons, as the Lord says: “This kind is not driven out except by prayer and fasting” (Matthew 17). Fasting helps not only against temptations but also raises the mind to the understanding of divine mysteries. Indeed, Moses fasted for forty days and forty nights in order to deserve to receive the law (Deuteronomy 9) [Col. 0528C]. Daniel, in order to be able to understand secret mysteries, not only practiced remarkable abstinence in the court of Babylon but also remained in prayer and fasting for three weeks, as he himself says: “I, Daniel, mourned for three weeks of days; I did not eat desirable bread, and flesh and wine did not enter my mouth. Nor was I anointed with ointment until the three weeks of days were completed” (Daniel 10).

Therefore, in order to deserve to become participants in the gift of the Holy Spirit, we ought to celebrate these days with complete purity, being more generous in abstinence and more abundant in almsgiving. Where our flesh feels affliction, there let the hunger of the poor feel consolation [Col. 0528D]. We ought to supplicate not only for our own needs but also for those of the whole Church: for the tranquility of peace, for the abundance of crops, for temperate weather, and for kings and governors, as the Apostle admonishes when he says: “I urge first of all that supplications, prayers, petitions, and thanksgivings be made for all people, for kings and all who are in high positions, so that we may lead a quiet and peaceful life in all piety and chastity. For this is good and acceptable before God our Savior, who desires all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth” (1 Timothy 2).

## HOMILY 91. MONDAY AFTER “The Voice of Joy,” DURING THE GREATER LITANIES

[Col. 0529A]

(James 5.) “My dearest brothers, confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, so that you may be saved.” And so forth. The apostle James urges us toward the best remedy for our salvation, as you heard when the present reading was read, beloved: “Confess,” he says, “your sins to one another.” This is not because God needs our confession—for everything we think, say, and do is present to him—but because we cannot otherwise be saved unless, as penitents, we confess what we have done wrongly as sinners. For whoever accuses himself in his sins leaves the devil nothing with which to accuse him again on the day of judgment. The penitent must wash away through repentance what he has done, and must not again call back what he has mourned. But whoever conceals his crimes will not prosper; whoever confesses and abandons them will deserve eternal forgiveness from the merciful God.

“And pray for one another so that you may be saved.” There are two kinds of human weakness, namely, of body and of soul. Therefore the Apostle urges us to pray to almighty God for both our weaknesses, asking one another to obtain the remedy of divine mercy, so that he may strengthen the body in his holy service and free the soul from eternal punishment. “For the continual prayer of a righteous person has great power.” The prayers of negligent people are not even able to obtain from another human being what they want; much less can someone obtain forgiveness from God for another by praying when he must himself ask humbly for forgiveness for his own sins and prays negligently for himself [Col. 0529C]. The prayer of the faithful must be continual if they desire to obtain what they ask. Since the Lord commands us to pray for our enemies, how much more should we pray for our friends and faithful companions? If we pray faithfully, we ought to pray earnestly not only for ourselves but also for our brothers, so that they may deserve to be saved, because persistence in prayer provides us with help in adversity. It follows:

“Elias was a human being like us, subject to suffering, and he prayed in prayer that it might not rain upon the earth, and it did not rain for three years and six months.” He saw the world covered, as it were, with the darkness of his people’s iniquity, heaven polluted, and the earth defiled by sacrifices to idols. Burning with zeal, he prayed that perhaps through hunger and the barrenness of the earth they might be converted to the Lord and repent of their sins. Compelled by such punishments, they turned from their way and from their many wickednesses, and, doing penance, they inclined God toward mercy. It follows:

“And he prayed again, and the sky gave rain, and the earth produced its fruit.” When righteous men are heard by the Lord in temporal matters as they pray for the guilt of others, this occurs for the sake of hope and salvation. When those for whom they pray are helped by a temporal remedy, the eyes of the wicked are opened to confess their sins, so that by repenting and confessing they may receive remedies for their souls [Col. 0530A]. And just as dry earth, watered by rains, produces necessary fruit, so their hardened hearts, watered by the compunction of tears and by the infusion of God’s grace—which they deserve through repentance—afterward produce the fruit of good works.

“But if anyone among you should wander from the truth, and someone should convert him, he should know that whoever causes a sinner to be converted from the error of his way will save his soul from death and cover a multitude of sins.” Namely, his own sins and those of others whom he converts from sin through his teaching. When any of our brothers disclose to us their sins, like wounds to physicians, by which they are afflicted, we must strive, with God as our guide, to bring them as quickly as possible to health, lest, because treatment is neglected, they progress toward something worse [Col. 0530B]. But the crimes of anyone which become known from whatever source, when the criminals themselves refuse to confess them, should be rebuked and treated like wounds by the fire of a pious correction, if they have not been healed by the gentle medicine of repentance. If even then they do not endure this with equanimity, and the remedy of a pious rebuke makes no progress in them—if, after being patiently borne with and salutarily reproved for a long time, they refuse to be corrected—then, like rotten parts of the body, they must be cut away by the sword of excommunication. Otherwise, just as flesh deadened by disease, if it is not cut away, corrupts the health of the remaining flesh through the contagion of its decay, so these people, who disdain to be corrected and persist in their illness, if they remain with their depraved conduct among the community of the saints, may infect them through the example of their destruction [Col. 0530C].

But those whose sins remain hidden from human knowledge, neither confessed by themselves nor made public by others, if they refuse to confess or amend them, will have as their avenger the God whom they have as their witness. What does it profit them to avoid human judgment if, while they remain in evil, they are going to eternal punishment, with God rendering recompense? But if they become judges of themselves and, as avengers of their own iniquity, inflict upon themselves here a voluntary penalty of the strictest correction, they will exchange eternal punishments for temporal ones. Through tears flowing from true compunction of heart, they will restrain the flames of eternal fire, by the gift of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY 92. MONDAY AFTER “The Voice of Joy,” DURING THE GREATER LITANIES

[Col. 0530D]

### (Luke 11)

“At that time Jesus said to his disciples: ‘Which of you will have a friend and will go to him at midnight?’” And so forth.

Knowing that, after the loss of free will, we can possess no good from ourselves, the Lord Jesus Christ urges and admonishes us not only to pray with the greatest devotion, but also with the greatest persistence, so that what nature has less capacity to accomplish in us may be obtained through prayer from him who says: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15). For while he was engaged in prayer, as the Gospel passage reported above relates, his disciples approached him and asked him, saying (Luke 11): “Lord, teach us to pray, just as John taught his disciples.” To them he said: “Thus, then, you shall pray: ‘Our Father who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name,’” and the rest that follows. In these words he briefly gathered what we ought chiefly to ask for in prayer; then, by adding a comparison, he explained with what persistence one ought to persevere in prayer, saying: “Which of you will have a friend and will go to him at midnight?”

Spiritually, this friend is understood to be almighty God. Although he is God and the creator of the whole creation, he has deigned to call his faithful servants friends, saying (John 15): “You are my friends.” And again: “I shall no longer call you servants,” but my friends. And once more: “But I have called you my friends” (ibid.).

“Night” in this passage signifies tribulation. For just as day pertains to joy, so night sometimes pertains to sadness. We must go to our friend at midnight, because under the pressure of tribulation we ought neither to prepare our minds for vengeance nor to despair or break down, but to implore the help of him who says: “In the world you will have tribulation, but have confidence, because I have overcome the world” (John 16). Although the Lord must always be entreated, he must be entreated especially when persecution rages and burns fiercely.

So that we may not fail in tribulation, we ought to ask his assistance, like the Psalmist, who said: “To the Lord I cried when I was in distress, and he heard me” (Psalm 119). And again: “From tribulation I called upon the Lord” (Psalm 117), and so forth.

What we ought to ask for in prayer he makes clear by adding: “Friend, lend me three loaves, because my friend has come to me from the road, and I have nothing to set before him.” This is what we must seek in prayer, this also is what we must ask: that he pour the knowledge and love of the Holy Trinity into our hearts. Or certainly, in prayer we ought to ask for three loaves, that is, faith, hope, and charity.

This friend who is said to come from the road is our mind, which departs from us as often as, through the broad desires of this world, it spreads itself abroad in thought. It returns to us from the road when the mind, setting itself before itself, begins to despise transitory things and to thirst for and desire those things that are eternal and enduring.

But lest it perish from hunger, the friend must be asked—that is, the Lord’s mercy must be implored—to lend us three loaves: namely, to grant, as has been said, the love of the Holy Trinity to our hearts. And because almighty God sometimes enlarges our desires, not in order to diminish the reward but to increase merit, it is rightly added:

“‘And he answering from within says: “Do not trouble me; the door is already shut, and my children are with me in the bedroom. I cannot rise and give you.”’”

The friend’s door is the understanding of the divine mystery, which Paul desired to have opened to him so that he might speak the word of God with confidence. This door, therefore, remains closed to us until it is opened to us by divine grace, so that we may come to know the divine mysteries.

The master of the household’s children are to be understood as the apostles or their successors. And it is rightly mentioned that they are with him in the bedroom, because they have already been received into eternal rest. Of them the Prophet says: “The saints shall exult in glory; they shall rejoice in their beds” (Psalm 149).

And beautifully those who are said to be in the bedroom are called “children,” because those will come to eternal rest who are pure and innocent, such as were those of whom the Lord said: “Children, do you have anything to eat?” (John 21.) And again: “Let the little children come to me, for of such is the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 19).

The apostle Peter desired his hearers to become such, saying to them: “Like newborn infants, long for rational milk without deceit, so that by it you may grow toward salvation” (1 Peter 2).

“‘And if he persists in knocking, I tell you, even if he will not rise and give him because he is his friend, yet because of his persistence he will rise and give him as many as he needs.’”

Here the comparison is made from the lesser, so that you may understand that if a human being, not because of friendship but overcome by annoyance, gives what he had previously refused, much more will the Lord give good things to those who ask, since he himself urges us to ask. For if he did not wish to grant them, he would certainly not invite us to ask.

Thus, when elsewhere he taught that we ought always to pray and not grow weary (Luke 18), he offered the comparison of an unjust judge whom a certain widow repeatedly approached, saying: “Vindicate me against my adversary.” For a long time he was unwilling. But afterward, overcome by annoyance, he said within himself: “Although I do not fear God or respect man, nevertheless, because this widow troubles me, I will vindicate her.”

God wishes us to be persistent in asking, so that his gratuitous gifts may become our merits. The ears of divine mercy are always open to our prayers, provided that we do not cease from our petitions and do not doubt in faith, as the apostle James testifies when he says: “If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask God, who gives generously to all and does not reproach, and it will be given to him. But let him ask in faith, without hesitating” (James 1). Therefore, explaining the proposed comparison, the Lord added:

“‘And I say to you: Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you. For everyone who asks receives; and whoever seeks finds; and to the one who knocks it will be opened.’”

Eternal life, therefore, must be requested through prayer, sought through living, and approached by knocking through perseverance in good works.

There are two things that we must carefully consider in prayer. First, that we ask for what God wills; second, that our life not disagree with our prayers. For the person who either asks for what displeases God or, if what he asks is good, makes himself unworthy of it by living perversely, persists in prayer in vain.

Hence the apostle James says: “You ask, and you do not receive, because you ask wrongly” (James 4). And likewise Solomon: “Whoever turns away his ear so as not to hear the law, his prayer will be accursed” (Proverbs 28).

What things are chiefly to be asked for in prayer God reveals elsewhere, saying: “Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you” (Matthew 6). And again: “Ask, and you will receive, so that your joy may be full” (John 16).

And lest we despair in prayer of receiving what we ask, the Lord adds another comparison, saying:

“‘Which of you, if his son asks him for bread, will give him a stone? Or if he asks for a fish, will give him a serpent instead of a fish? Or if he asks for an egg, will offer him a scorpion?’”

In this passage bread signifies charity. And fittingly so, because just as bread holds the chief place among human foods, so charity holds the chief place among the other virtues. The Lord demonstrated this when, being questioned by a learned scribe about which was the greatest commandment in the law, he replied: “You shall love the Lord your God,” and so forth, up to: “This is the first and greatest commandment” (Matthew 22).

Or certainly, charity is signified by bread because, although a table may be filled with various foods, it nevertheless appears poor without bread; likewise, the other virtues are proved to be nothing without charity, as the Savior says in the Gospel: “To everyone who has, it will be given, and he will abound” (Matthew 25).

Hence the Apostle says: “If I speak with the tongues of human beings and of angels, but do not have charity, I have become like sounding bronze or a clanging cymbal. And if I have prophecy and know all mysteries and all knowledge, and if I have all faith, so as to move mountains, but do not have charity, I am nothing. And if I distribute all my possessions as food for the poor, and if I hand over my body so that I may burn, but do not have charity, it profits me nothing” (1 Corinthians 13).

The opposite of this is the stone, that is, hardness of heart and lack of mercy.

The fish signifies faith, and quite appropriately. For just as a fish is nourished by water, so faith is strengthened by baptism, as the Lord says: “Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved” (Mark 16).

Or certainly, faith is represented by the fish because, just as a fish lies hidden beneath the waters, so faith concerns things that are not seen, as the Apostle says: “Faith is the substance of things hoped for, the proof of things not seen” (Hebrews 11).

Or again, faith is understood through the fish because, just as a fish grows more the more it is battered by the waves, so faith advances the more persecution it endures. Concerning this the Lord says: “If you have faith like a grain of mustard seed, you will say to this mountain, ‘Move from here,’ and it will move” (Matthew 17).

The opposite of this is the serpent, namely unbelief or poisonous thoughts, which try to kill the soul.

Hope is represented in the egg, because just as the offspring is not yet seen in the egg but is believed to be forthcoming, so hope is not seen by the eye but is hoped for in the mind, as the Apostle says: “For what a person sees, why does he hope for it? But if we hope for what we do not see, we await it with patience” (Romans 8).

The opposite of this is the scorpion, which carries its sting in its tail: that is, despair, which tries to draw us backward from the eternal eggs [ovis perennibus].

In these comparisons, therefore, the Lord shows that, although he himself is merciful and compassionate, he gives no evil thing to anyone who asks for good. He does not give a stone instead of bread, because he does not give a hard and merciless heart to one who loves charity. Nor does he give a serpent instead of a fish, because he does not drive one who seeks faith into unbelief. Nor does he offer a scorpion instead of an egg, because he does not compel one who possesses hope to fall into despair.

It belongs to his immense goodness sometimes to make bad people good, but never to compel good people to become bad. Hence he further concludes his statement, saying:

“‘If you, then, although you are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father from heaven give the good Spirit to those who ask him.’”

Here our condition is plainly revealed when he says: “Although you are evil.” We were created good by God but made evil through the fault of evil. If our goodness is compared with his goodness, it is not even called goodness.

Made evil, therefore, through evil intention, we have the Father in heaven through creation. It is as though the Lord had said: “If you, although you are evil, give good gifts to your children”—that is, bread, fish, eggs, and those things that human custom usually counts among the good things of the present life—“how much more will the Father from heaven give the good Spirit to those who ask him,” so that, illumined by his Spirit, they may learn not only to ask for faith, hope, and charity, but also deserve to receive them.

When he says, “He will give the good Spirit to those who ask him,” he comprehends all the virtues of the soul, since all the good things given to human beings by God are administered through the Holy Spirit, as the Apostle testifies: “The love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us” (Romans 5). And again: “To one are given kinds of tongues, to another the interpretation of speech, to another the discernment of spirits. But one and the same Spirit works all these things, distributing to each as he wills” (1 Corinthians 12).

### HOMILY XCIII. TUESDAY OF THE LITANIES, AFTER “THE VOICE OF JOY”

### (Matthew 7)

“At that time Jesus said to his disciples: ‘Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you.’” And so forth.

One of the hearers might have said to the Lord: How do you command us not to give what is holy to dogs, nor to cast pearls before swine, when we do not yet possess that holiness or those same pearls which we might cast before swine?

As though responding to this, the Lord continues: “Ask, and it will be given to you.” For he said three things: ask, seek, knock.

Ask God for health and strength of mind, so that you may be able to fulfill what is commanded you. Seek the way of truth, and you will find it. Knock at the door of the heavenly kingdom, of which it is written: “This is the gate of the Lord; the righteous shall enter through it” (Psalm 117).

In this order almighty God advances our petitions: first, if we ask for the ability to fulfill the divine commandments; then, if we diligently seek to discover the way of truth; finally, if we wish to enter the hall of the heavenly kingdom, if we knock through prayers and good works.

Let us set forth an example. You see a person who has become ill and is unable to walk with his feet. First, the medicine of health is applied to him, so that he may be able to walk. To this pertains the saying: “Ask, and you will receive.”

What good does walking do him if he does not know the right way by which he ought to proceed, unless the right way is shown to him? To this pertains the saying: “Seek, and you will find.”

What good is the journey to him if, after reaching a definite place, he finds the place he desires to enter closed? To this pertains the saying: “Knock, and it will be opened to you.”

Or it may also be understood in another way: ask by believing, seek by doing good, knock by persevering.

“‘Or which of you is there who, if his son asks him for bread, will give him a stone?’”

In these three comparisons the Lord wishes to signify three principal virtues.

Bread signifies charity, because just as a table filled with various foods is poor without bread, so the other virtues are made imperfect without charity. Conversely, the stone expresses hardness of heart, which is especially opposed to charity. If, then, we ask God the Father to give us charity, will he give us a stone—that is, hardness of heart?

“‘Or if he asks for a fish, will he give him a serpent instead of a fish?’”

In the fish, faith is understood, because just as a fish is battered amid the waves so that it may continually grow, so faith is tested and advances amid the adversities of this world.

Will he give us a serpent—that is, unbelief? Unbelief is represented by the serpent because it infused the poison of its malice into our first parents.

Luke adds the third comparison, for he says:

“‘Or if he asks for an egg, will he offer him a scorpion?’”

Hope is represented in the egg, because the offspring is not yet seen in the egg but is hoped for as something future. Likewise, hope that is seen is not hope; rather, hope is the expectation of future good works.

“‘Will he give him a scorpion?’” That is, despair. For the scorpion signifies despair because the scorpion strikes with its tail, and despair causes the greatest destruction at the end.

“‘If you, then, although you are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father, who is in heaven, give good things to those who ask him?’”

It is remarkable that the Lord called the apostles evil, unless perhaps we say that, in the person of the apostles, he censures the whole human race, because from its youth, as we read in Genesis, the human heart is inclined toward evil (Genesis 8).

Or certainly we can say that he specifically called those same apostles evil. Although by their special privilege they surpassed the goodness of the whole human race, nevertheless, in comparison with God they are evil, because in comparison with him no one is good. Hence he himself says: “No one is good except God alone” (Mark 10).

“‘You know how to give good things,’” and so forth. What does he call “good things” here? Those he mentioned above: bread, fish, and the other necessities of the body. They are good because they were created by God, since “the earth is the Lord’s and its fullness.”

“How much more will your Father who is in heaven give good things to those who ask him?” The meaning is: If you are generous toward your children in necessary things, how much more generous will almighty God be toward you in supplying you with food and clothing?

“‘Whatever you wish people to do to you, you also do to them.’”

This is the natural law, which consists in two commandments; and upon these two sayings the whole law and the prophets depend.

One of these is what is said to you: “Whatever you wish people to do to you.” The other is what is said elsewhere: “What you do not wish to be done to you, do not do to another” (Tobit 4).

For whatever the law and the prophets describe at greater length is briefly comprehended in these two commandments. Whoever observes these two will rejoice that he has fulfilled the whole law and the prophets.

“‘Enter through the narrow gate, which leads to eternal life, because the gate is wide and the way is broad that leads to destruction, and there are many who enter through it.’”

The Lord sets before us two ways: one is broad and spacious, leading to hell; the other is narrow, leading to heaven.

The broad way is the path of the pleasures of this world. The Lord rightly says that it is broad and spacious, and that many enter by it. For there is no need to seek it out: it presents itself willingly to those who wander.

The narrow way is the way that leads to life. It is found by few, and, though found by many, it is not held by many. Many have begun to travel this road, but, captured by the pleasures of this world, they turn back halfway along the journey.

The narrow way is the desire to complete the journey to heaven. Is it not indeed a narrow way that earns participation in the eternal kingdom through fasting and giving alms?

### HOMILY XCIV. WEDNESDAY OF THE LITANIES, AT THE VIGIL OF THE ASCENSION OF THE LORD

### (John 17)

“At that time: Jesus, lifting his eyes toward heaven, said: ‘Father, the hour has come; glorify your Son.’” And so forth.

The Son could have spoken these same words of prayer to the Father silently, but the Son’s prayer is instruction for the apostles, and also for those who do not wish to follow their examples or read their writings.

“He said: ‘Father, the hour has come.’” The hour of the Passion, therefore, is approaching.

“‘Glorify your Son.’” That is, with the glory of the resurrection. Let the humility of the Passion come first, so that the glorification of the resurrection may quickly follow.

It continues: “‘So that your Son may glorify you.’” The Father’s glorification is eternal and can neither be increased nor diminished. But this glorification pertains to the knowledge of God the Father, so that, when the glory of the resurrection had been accomplished in the Son, God the Father might become known throughout the whole world, whereas previously he had been known only among the Jews.

“‘Glorify your Son, so that your Son may glorify you.’” It is as though he had said: “Raise me from the dead, so that through me you may become known throughout the whole world.”

It continues:

“‘Just as you gave him authority over all flesh.’” That is, over every human being: the whole is signified by a part, “flesh” standing for “human being.”

He said this to show more and more clearly how he would glorify the Father. “Just as you gave authority,” he says, “over all flesh, so may the Son glorify you”—that is, make you known to all flesh that you have given him.

For you gave it in this way: “‘So that he may give eternal life to all whom you have given him. And this is eternal life: that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent.’”

The order of the words is: “that they may know you and Jesus Christ whom you have sent as the only true God.” The fullness of the knowledge of God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is complete, perfect, and eternal life. Perfect eternal life is supreme blessedness. Supreme blessedness exists only in eternal life.

“‘I glorified you upon the earth; I completed the work that you gave me to do.’”

Why did he use the past tense, “I glorified” and “I completed,” and immediately afterward add the future-tense verb, “I will do,” unless because all things are present to God and future things must be regarded in divine predestination as though they had already taken place? What was going to happen was, for him, as though it had already happened.

“‘I glorified you.’” It is as though he had said: “I will glorify you through the glory of preaching, which I will spread throughout the whole world through my disciples, when I complete the work of my Passion and resurrection that you gave me to do.”

“‘And now glorify me, Father.’” By saying, “I glorified you upon the earth,” and then asking the Father to glorify him now with that same Father, he clearly reveals the glory of both glorifications.

He glorified the Father upon earth by preaching him to the nations; the Father, by placing him at his own right hand, glorified him with himself. He then added:

“‘With the glory that I had with you before the world existed.’”

The order of the words is: “with the glory that I had with you before the world existed.”

This is the force of the statement, “And now glorify me”: just as then, so also now; then through predestination, now through completion. Do in the world what existed before you before the world existed. Do in its proper time what you established before all times.

In this passage we should understand the predestination of the glory of his human nature: that nature, which in him was to become immortal from mortal, was predestined with the Father before the world existed, so that what was predestined would also be accomplished in the world at its proper time. The Apostle said the same about us: “He chose us in him before the foundation of the world” (Ephesians 1).

Nor should we fear calling the Son of God predestined according to his humanity. He came into the world in his own time, but he was predestined before all times. That was predestined which did not yet exist but was to come into being, and which God willed to exist. Concerning this predestination the Apostle says in his Epistle to the Romans: “Who was made for him from the seed of David according to the flesh, who was predestined to be the Son of God in power” (Romans 1).

According to this predestination he was also glorified before the world existed, so that his glory from the resurrection of the dead might be with the Father, at whose right hand he sits.

“‘I manifested your name to the people whom you gave me from the world.’”

What he was going to accomplish through holy teachers throughout the whole world after the glory of his resurrection and ascension, and after the gifts of the Holy Spirit that were conveyed to the disciples, he spoke of as though it had already been accomplished.

This is like what he said shortly before: “I glorified you upon the earth.” In both places he used the past tense for a future event, as one who knew that it had been predestined to occur, and therefore said that he had done what he would certainly accomplish without any doubt.

It continues: “‘They were yours, and you gave them to me, and they have kept your word. Now they have known that everything you have given me is from you. For the words that you gave me, I gave to them; and they received them and truly understood that I came forth from you, and they believed that you sent me.’”

Although all these statements could also have been spoken concerning all future believers, as though already perfected while they were still to come, they may nevertheless be understood especially of the disciples, to whom he was then speaking in person.

For what follows:

“‘While I was with them, I was keeping them in your name; those whom you gave me I guarded, and none of them perished except the son of perdition’”—meaning Judas, who betrayed him and who was one of the Twelve—fits this interpretation better, namely, that he was speaking these things specifically to the apostles.

Then he adds:

“‘But now I am coming to you.’” It is clear that he was speaking of his bodily presence. “While I was with them, I was keeping them,” as though he would soon no longer be bodily present with them.

In this way he wished to signify the ascension that was soon to occur, concerning which he says: “But now I am coming to you.” He was going to the right hand of the Father, and from there he will come in bodily presence to judge the living and the dead, according to the rule of faith and sound doctrine.

For he was always with them spiritually, and with his whole Church in this world until the consummation of the age.

But let us return to what he said above: “I manifested your name to the people whom you gave me.” He did not mean the name by which you are God, but the name by which you are my Father, which cannot be manifested without the manifestation of that Son.

For he considered it impossible that the name by which he is God should be wholly unknown to any rational nature. This is the life of his divinity: that he cannot be entirely hidden from rational creation as an unknown reality, except among the few in whom rational nature has been excessively corrupted.

Almost all nations confess that God exists, although different errors prevent them from recognizing him correctly. When it is read in the Psalms, “God is known in Judah” (Psalm 75), this indicates that only the Jews knew and worshiped the true God according to legitimate worship.

But the fact that the Father of Christ—through whom Christ takes away the sins of the world—was unknown before Christ came into the world, except to those to whom God revealed this great and hidden mystery through the Spirit of prophecy, was preached to the nations after his coming into the world, believed in this world, and taken up into glory.

When he added, “whom you gave me,” this is what he had said shortly before: “No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him” (John 6).

“‘Whom you gave me from the world’” means those to whom he granted this through grace by regeneration, not those to whom nature granted it through birth.

What does the following mean: “They were yours, and you gave them to me”? He says that he received this authority from the Father according to his humanity, so that he might possess those whom the Father chose and predestined before the foundation of the world—not the Father alone, but the Son and the Holy Spirit also—so that the work of the Holy Trinity might be one, inseparable, and altogether equal.

It continues: “‘And they have kept your word. Now they have understood that everything you have given me is from you.’” That is, they have learned that there is nothing alien in me apart from you, and that whatever I teach is yours.

The Father gave him everything simultaneously when he begot him, because he also possesses everything. As the Lord himself says earlier in this Gospel: “Just as the Father has life in himself, so he has granted the Son also to have life in himself” (John 5)—that is, he begot the Son as one possessing life in himself.

“‘For the words that you gave me, I gave to them, and they received them’”—that is, they understood and retained them. The Father gave him words, as he said, and these he gave to them. But they truly received them when they received them not outwardly in their ears but spiritually; then they truly received them, because then they truly understood.

They truly understood because they truly believed. But these words, which the Son says the Father gave him, are understood to pertain to the unity of divinity. The Father gave words to the Son in the same way in which he begot the Word coeternal with himself.

It continues:

“‘I pray for them; I do not pray for the world, but for those whom you gave me.’”

He said these things, among others, while praying for those whom the Father had given him. By “the world” he wishes to be understood those who live according to the desire of the world and have not received the grace by which they are chosen from the world.

Therefore he says that he prays not for the world but for those whom the Father gave him. Through the fact that the Father has already given them to him, they have been made not to belong to that world for which he does not pray.

Then he adds: “‘Because they are yours.’” For the Father did not lose those whom he gave to the Son, since the Son continues and says:

“‘And all my things are yours, and your things are mine.’”

Here it sufficiently appears how everything belonging to the Father belongs to the only-begotten Son. It is plainly evident that he himself is also God and that he was born from the Father, equal to the Father.

This was also said concerning rational creation, which God chose and which is subject to the Father and the Son, so that it might belong equally to the Father and the Son.

“‘And I have been glorified in them,’” he says. He speaks of his glorification as though it had already occurred, although it was still future.

“‘I have been glorified in them’”—that is, through their preaching I have been glorified throughout the whole world. And because it was predestined to happen, he wished the future event to be regarded as certain; therefore he used verbs in the past tense.

“‘And now I am no longer in the world, but they are in the world.’”

He signifies the hour in which he was about to depart from this world and uses the present tense in place of the future, because what was soon to happen he spoke of as though it had already occurred.

When he says, “and they are in the world,” he signifies that those to whom he was speaking would depart from this world later. For it was necessary that they remain, through whom his holy name would be preached in the world.

And foreseeing what might trouble those who heard these things and whom he had chosen, he added:

“‘But now I am going to you,’” in the glory of the ascension, through which the human being was raised above the heights of the heavens and the dignities of all angelic powers, so that he might be placed at the right hand of God the Father.

### HOMILY XCV. ON THE HOLY DAY OF THE ASCENSION OF THE LORD

### (Acts 1)

“I composed the first account, O Theophilus, concerning all the things that Jesus began to do and teach.” And so forth.

The evangelist Luke, dearly beloved brothers, who wrote one of the four Gospels, also published the book of the Acts of the Apostles, from which the present reading is now heard. In it he first mentioned the final meal that the Lord shared with his disciples after his resurrection, as well as his ascension into heaven, which we celebrate today.

The beginning of that book is as follows: “I composed the first account”—that is, the Gospel—“O Theophilus,” bishop, who compels me to write this book of the Acts of the Apostles, “concerning all the things that Jesus began”—first by displaying signs, or doing those things that pertained to examples of life—“to do and afterward to teach,” because Jesus, establishing himself as a good teacher, did nothing except what he taught.

“Until the day on which, giving commands through the Holy Spirit to the apostles whom he had chosen, he was taken up.” Before his assumption he gave commands to observe and fulfill what is read either in this book or in the Gospels.

“To whom he also presented himself alive by many proofs, appearing to them for forty days after his Passion and speaking about the kingdom of God.”

Through this forty-day association with the disciples he signifies that he would fulfill everything, both what was open and what was hidden, that he had promised. To mention one of many examples, he said: “Behold, I am with you all the days until the consummation of the age” (Matthew 28).

“And while eating with them, he commanded them not to depart from Jerusalem, but to await the promise of the Father.”

He took food with the disciples in order to show, by allowing himself to be touched and handled, that the flesh which he had raised from death was the same true flesh (Luke 24).

It continues: “‘Which you have heard,’ he said, ‘from my mouth: for John baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit not many days from now.’”

The apostles had already been baptized with water, but not yet fully with the Holy Spirit, who was promised to them after that ascension.
