Neither the apostles themselves nor their successors in the Church to this day wished to baptize in any other way than John the Baptist—that is, in water. Nevertheless, when the name of Christ is invoked, the inward power of the Holy Spirit purifies souls and bodies simultaneously as the person is immersed in water; this did not happen in John’s baptism.

“Therefore, when they had gathered together, they asked him, saying: ‘Lord, will you at this time restore the kingdom of Israel?’”

They consequently inquire about the kingdom of God, asking whether it was to be restored immediately in the present age when the Holy Spirit came, or whether they ought to believe that it was reserved for the saints in the future.

“But he said to them: ‘It is not for you to know the times or moments that the Father has established by his own authority.’”

He showed that it is not beneficial for us mortals to know the day of our calling, so that, always uncertain about the Judge’s coming, we may live each day with such vigilance as though we ought to hasten to judgment on the following day.

“‘But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit comes upon you, and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem, and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth.’”

It is as though he had said: You ought not to think that, when the Holy Spirit comes upon you, the consummation of this world will immediately occur. Rather, he will provide you with power to bear witness about me.

“And when he had said these things, while they were watching, he was lifted up, and a cloud received him from their eyes.”

Everywhere creation offers obedience to its Creator. The stars announce him as he is born; they conceal him as he suffers; the clouds receive him as he ascends; and they will accompany him when he returns for judgment.

“While they were watching him go into heaven, behold, two men stood beside them in white garments, and they said: ‘Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven? This Jesus, who has been taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven.’” That is, he comes to be judged in the same form and substance of flesh in which he will come as judge. Let us therefore prepare ourselves for an ascent into heaven by worthy conduct, and let us recognize that we are pilgrims in this world. Even if certain comforts flatter us here, they must not be wickedly embraced but bravely rejected. Therefore, beloved brothers, if you wish to ascend into heaven, let us meanwhile strengthen this hope within us; let us burn with all our desires for it; let us meditate here on earth upon this: that we may be counted among the inhabitants of heaven. Then, when we are to cast off the mortality of the flesh, let us now cast off the oldness of the mind. The body will easily be lifted to the heights of heaven if the burden of sins does not weigh down the spirit. Therefore, beloved, let us rise toward him who made the dust of our lowliness into the body of his glory, and, so that we may deserve to be companions of his ascension, let us conform in all things to his humility and patience. We have undertaken the service of a great name and the discipline of a great profession. Those who follow Christ may not depart from the royal road, nor is it fitting that those striving toward eternal things should be occupied with temporal matters. And because we have been redeemed by the precious blood of Christ, let us glorify and bear God in our body, so that we may deserve to attain the rewards prepared for the faithful.

## HOMILY XCVI. ON THE HOLY DAY OF THE LORD’S ASCENSION

*(Mark 16.)* “At that time, while the eleven disciples were reclining, Jesus appeared to them and reproached their unbelief.” And so forth. As the Lord was about to ascend into heaven and withdraw from the disciples in bodily presence, he wished to reproach the hardness of their heart and their unbelief, so that the word of correction might cleanse the stains of doubt. He reproached them at the end—not because they were still persisting in unbelief, but because they had not believed at first, and had been slow to do so. For we read in the Gospel according to Luke that when devout women came very early to the Lord’s tomb and saw a vision of angels who said that he was alive, they ran and announced it to the disciples. But they did not believe them; rather, their words seemed to them like nonsense (Luke 24). Thomas, however, one of the twelve, who is called Didymus, when the other disciples said, “We have seen the Lord,” did not believe, saying: “Unless I see the marks of the nails in his hands and put my hand into his side, I will not believe” (John 20). And so they are reproached at the end for having at first been slow or hard in coming to belief.

They ought not to have doubted his resurrection, since, while he was mortal, they had seen him raise the dead—especially since they saw him undergo the kind of passion and death which they remembered he had foretold. Or certainly, as he was about to depart from them, he wished to reproach the disciples for their unbelief and hardness of heart, so that his final words might cling all the more firmly to their hearts the more harshly they had been spoken in reproach. For just as an evil mind sometimes becomes worse through reproof, so a good one always advances through correction, as Solomon says: “Reprove a wise man, and he will love you; teach a righteous man, and he will hasten to receive it” (Proverbs 9).

And because we customarily bind the final words of our dearest ones—when they are dying or departing for a distant region—to our memory by a certain bond of love, or whatever has been discovered by a more obscure investigation, the departing Lord reproached them for their hardness of heart and unbelief so that no trace of doubt might remain in the hearts of those who were to be sent to instruct the ignorance of others. The evangelist Mark records this as the final appearance (chapter 16), because after this he is not read as having been bodily seen speaking on earth, but as ascending into heaven through the air.

The evangelists describe him as having appeared to human beings ten times after his resurrection: first, to Mary Magdalene, weeping at the tomb; second, to that same Mary together with another woman of the same name, as they were going to announce his resurrection to the disciples, when he met them and said, “Hail”; and they approached and clasped his feet; third, to Simon Peter; fourth, to two disciples going to the village of Emmaus, when they recognized him in the breaking of bread; fifth, to the disciples sitting in a room because of fear of the Jews, when Thomas was not with them; sixth, after eight days, when Thomas was with them; seventh, to the disciples fishing at the Sea of Tiberias; eighth, in Galilee, when, as the evangelist Matthew says (chapter 28), “the eleven disciples went to Galilee, to the mountain where Jesus had appointed them, and when they saw him they worshiped him”; ninth, as the present reading relates, when he appeared to them while they were reclining and reproached their unbelief; tenth, no longer on earth but speaking through the air, when, as the evangelist Luke says (chapter 24), “he led them out as far as Bethany, and while he blessed them, with his hands raised, he was carried up into heaven.”

The Lord fittingly wished to appear to them while they were reclining, because peace and harmony are usually maintained among those reclining together. When, therefore, he appeared to them while they were reclining, he showed that those are worthy of his appearance who preserve unshaken peace even amid adversity, who can say with the Psalmist: “With those who hated peace, I was peaceable” (Psalm 119:7).

He appeared to eleven disciples because Judas had been separated from their company by betraying his Master, and Matthias had not yet been called by lot to the election. After reproaching their hardness of heart and unbelief, he immediately adds the duty of preaching:

“And Jesus said to them: ‘Go into the whole world and preach the Gospel to every creature.’” This may trouble those who understand less carefully, since it is said that the Gospel must be preached to every creature. Was it to be preached to senseless and irrational animals? No. By the name “every creature,” the human being is signified. For if the nature of the human creature is compared more subtly with the other creatures, it is found to have a certain communion and participation with them all.

There are stones, which neither live nor perceive. There are herbs and shrubs, which, although they live through their greenness, nevertheless do not perceive or discern. There are irrational animals, which live and perceive but do not discern. There are angels, who live, perceive, and discern. Thus the human being has a certain share with these creatures: existence with the stones, life with the trees, perception with irrational animals, and discernment with angels. The Gospel is therefore commanded to be preached to every creature when it is preached to the human being alone, because he is instructed for whose sake all things were made and with whom all things share a certain likeness.

Or certainly, by the name “every creature,” every nation of the Gentiles is designated. In these words the benefit of the Lord’s Passion is made manifest to us who have believed from among the Gentiles. For he who had previously said, “Do not go on the road of the Gentiles, and do not enter the cities of the Samaritans, but go rather to the sheep that have perished from the house of Israel” (Matthew 10), now, after his resurrection and as he was about to ascend into heaven, commanded: “Go into the whole world and preach the Gospel to every creature”—that is, to every nation of human beings.

The evangelist Matthew makes this clearer when he says (chapter 28): “Go into the whole world, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.” Therefore let the wretched Jew be ashamed, who says that Christ will come only for his salvation and not for that of others, when Christ himself says: “Go, baptize all nations.” Let the Donatists also be ashamed, who, wishing to confine him locally, said that he was only in Africa and not in the other parts of the world, when he himself likewise says: “Go into the whole world.”

But lest the nations suppose that they were being called to belief in God without reason, a reward is promised to those who believe, when it is added:

“Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved.” And because those whom a gentle promise does not persuade to believe must be frightened more harshly, it is rightly added: “But whoever does not believe will be condemned.”

In this passage the order of baptism is demonstrated to preachers, when it is said: “Whoever believes and is baptized.” Belief is placed first, and baptism follows afterward, because no uninstructed person ought to receive so great a mystery unless he has first been instructed and imbued by a teacher. After he has believed, let him be baptized.

Here a curious reader may object: What, then, will happen to little children who do not know how to speak? To this a true answer can be given: the faith of the parents alone benefits little children in baptism, provided that, when they reach the proper age, they are instructed and taught. “And fittingly the faith of those who are to be saved is placed upon the foundation” (Habakkuk 2), because, as Scripture says, “the righteous person lives by faith, and without faith it is impossible to please God” (Hebrews 11).

But just as faith is the origin of all virtues, so unbelief is the mother of destruction. Hence it is also added: “But whoever does not believe will be condemned.” For, as the Lord says elsewhere, “whoever does not believe has already been judged” (John 3), and again: “Unless someone is born of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (ibid.).

But perhaps someone says: “I have already believed, and I will be saved.” He speaks truly if he fulfills by deeds what he professes in words. For true faith is that which accomplishes by works what it confesses with the mouth, according to what the Lord says to the disciples: “You know these things; blessed are you if you do them” (John 13). Hence the Apostle also says: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Romans 10).

The Lord wishes his confessors to be doers. Otherwise, one who neglects to do good vainly flatters himself about faith alone, because, as the apostle James says (chapter 2), “Faith without works is dead.” “But there are very many of this kind, which is worse,” as the Apostle says (Titus 1), “who confess in words that they know God, but deny him in their deeds.” The Lord reproves such people in the Gospel, saying: “Why do you call me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ and do not do what I say?” (Luke 6.) And through the prophet: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isaiah 29).

But when the apostles were sent to preach the Gospel to every creature, lest they complain that they were unable to accomplish so great a work, signs of visible miracles are promised to them as assistance, when it is said:

“These signs will accompany those who believe: In my name they will cast out demons; they will speak in new tongues; they will pick up serpents; and if they drink anything deadly, it will not harm them. They will lay hands on the sick, and they will be well.”

No one who has read their deeds or lives is unaware that all these things were fulfilled, even literally, through the apostles and their successors. But a few examples from many should be recalled. In the name of Christ the apostles frequently cast demons out of possessed bodies, as we read that Paul did when a girl who had a pythonic spirit followed him for many days (Acts 16). “But he was distressed, and turning to the spirit he said: ‘In the name of Jesus Christ I command you to come out of her.’” And she was immediately healed.

They spoke in new tongues—not only the apostles on the holy day of Pentecost, when they received the Holy Spirit in tongues of fire, but also, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles (ibid. 2), when those who received the Holy Spirit through the laying on of their hands spoke in tongues and prophesied.

They picked up serpents, as we read that the apostle Paul did (ibid. 28). When he had sailed to a certain island and, after gathering a quantity of brushwood, had placed it on the fire, a viper, driven out by the heat of the fire, attacked his hand. When they thought that he would suddenly collapse and quickly die, he shook the creature from his hand, threw it into the fire, and suffered no harm.

“And if they drink anything deadly, it will not harm them.” We read in the Ecclesiastical History of Eusebius of Caesarea that John, the Lord’s disciple, because of his unconquerable steadfastness in preaching the Gospel, was given poison to drink and suffered no harm. In the same writings of the Fathers, Barnabas is also said to have drunk the same deadly potion without experiencing the danger of death.

“They will lay hands on the sick, and they will be well.” We read not only that health was restored to the sick through the laying on of the apostles’ hands, but also, as is recounted in the Acts of the Apostles (chapter 19), that handkerchiefs and aprons were taken from their bodies and placed upon the sick. The sick were even carried into the streets on beds and pallets so that, when Peter came, at least his shadow might overshadow someone among them; and they were healed of whatever illness afflicted them (ibid. 5).

This is what the Lord promises elsewhere when he says: “Whoever believes in me will also do the works that I do, and will do greater works than these” (John 14).

Perhaps someone also says that this same grace is no longer in the Church, because it does not shine forth with the same bodily miracles. Such a person should be answered that the same power is now in the Church as existed in former times. But the reason it shone forth in former times through bodily signs must be understood: so that faith might grow at the beginning of the nascent Church, it had to be nourished by bodily miracles. The signs of miracles were manifested for this purpose, so that the hearts of those who saw them might be drawn toward belief in visible things.

For example, when we plant shrubs, we pour water at their roots until we see that they have grown strong; once they have taken root, the watering ceases. Thus the young planting of the Church had to be watered with bodily miracles so that the growth of faith might advance. But after it had been firmly rooted in faith, outward miracles ceased, because, as the Apostle says, “Tongues are a sign, not for believers but for unbelievers” (1 Corinthians 14).

Every day, however, the Church performs spiritual works of power, the same works that it performed through the apostles in former times. Demons are cast out in the name of Christ (Mark 16) when, through the priestly ministry and the grace of exorcism, their power is driven from the minds of those who are baptized in the name of the holy Trinity.

“They will speak in new tongues” (ibid.) when those who were accustomed to lies, perjuries, slanders, and curses are converted to praising and blessing God. They speak in new tongues also when they exhort their neighbors, console the sorrowful, reprove the negligent, change their lips, and abstain from evil and wicked speech, saying with the Psalmist: “I said, ‘I will guard my ways, so that I may not sin with my tongue’” (Psalm 39). And again: “For all his judgments are before me, and I have not rejected his ordinances” (Psalm 18). “And I shall be blameless with him, and I shall guard myself from my iniquity.”

When they do not permit poisonous and unclean thoughts to rule in their own hearts or in the hearts of others, they likewise pick up serpents. When they hear words of slander and perverse counsels from their neighbors but do not consent to them so far as to put them into practice, they drink something deadly, but it does not harm them.

For anyone who either wavers in faith or trembles in good works is certainly sick in spirit. Therefore, whoever offers such a person the word of preaching or shows the example of a good work in order to make him firmer in good works lays hands on the sick, so that he may be well.

These signs are greater insofar as they are spiritual, and better insofar as through them it is not bodies destined soon to die that are healed, but souls destined to live forever. Outward signs await a smaller reward in the future insofar as they receive greater glory in the present; inward signs, however, await greater glory in the future insofar as they are less seen by human beings in the present.

Even the wicked can possess outward signs, such as those who will say: “Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, cast out demons in your name, and do many mighty works?” (Matthew 7.) They will be answered: “Truly, truly, I say to you, I do not know you. Depart from me, workers of iniquity” (ibid.).

For God does not concern himself through whom he performs mighty works, so as to save those whom he wishes to possess forever. But those who possess spiritual gifts cannot be wicked.

“And the Lord Jesus, after he had spoken to them, was taken up into heaven.” Therefore, after the Lord had sent the apostles into the world to preach the Gospel to every creature, and after he had promised that signs and mighty works would follow those who were to believe in his name, he ascended into heaven, showing that they would one day come there, where they recognized that their Head had gone before them, just as he asks the Father when he says: “Father, I desire that where I am, there my minister also may be” (John 12). And again: “Where the body is, there the eagles will also be gathered” (Luke 17).

The evangelist Luke agrees with these words. When he had related that the Lord said to the disciples, “You will be my witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth” (Acts 1), he immediately added: “And when he had said this, while they were watching, he was lifted up, and a cloud received him from their eyes” (ibid.).

Here it must be considered that the Lord wished to have witnesses and forerunners of his ascension in the Old Testament: one before the Law and the other under the Law, namely Enoch and Elijah. For just as Joseph, when he was sold, prefigured the Lord’s sale and Passion, so Enoch, who was translated, and Elijah, who was carried away in a fiery chariot, prefigured him who was to ascend above all the heavens.

Those men, as pure human beings weighed down by the burden of sins, required the assistance of angels; they were transferred to a certain more hidden region, not avoiding death altogether but postponing it for a time. Hence one is said to have been translated, the other carried away.

The Lord Jesus Christ, however, whom no mortality of corruption weighed down, did not need the assistance of angels in his ascension. By his own power he pierced the heights of heaven, as he himself says in the Gospel: “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John 3). And through the Prophet: “Now I will arise, says the Lord; now I will be exalted; now I will be lifted up” (Isaiah 33).

Here it must be noted that, with the passage of time, the purity of chastity increased, in accordance with what is said through Daniel (chapter 12): “Many will pass through, and knowledge will be multiplied.” Enoch’s was a passing-through: he was begotten through intercourse, and he begot through intercourse; he is read to have had a wife and children. Elijah was carried away: he was begotten through intercourse, but did not beget through intercourse, since he is not read to have had a wife or children. Yet he was not taken into the ethereal heaven, but rather into the air.

The Lord Jesus Christ was taken up: he overcame the author of death, was neither begotten through intercourse nor begetting through intercourse, and was taken not into the airy heaven but into the ethereal heaven. He was begotten before all ages from the Father without a mother, and at the end of the ages was born from a mother without a father.

The holy Fathers not only prefigured the Lord’s ascension by examples, but also foretold it in words. David says: “Be exalted above the heavens, O God, and your glory above all the earth” (Psalm 57). And again: “God has ascended amid rejoicing, and the Lord amid the sound of the trumpet” (Psalm 47). And elsewhere: “Ascending on high, he led captivity captive; he gave gifts to human beings” (Ephesians 4).

Today the gate of the heavenly kingdom has been opened to all, because the human being, assumed by God, has ascended above all the powers of the angels, as the Psalmist testifies, saying: “He ascended upon the Cherubim and flew; he flew upon the wings of the winds” (Psalm 18).

The Bride marveled at the singular flight of today’s ascension in the Song of Songs when she said: “Behold, he comes, leaping upon the mountains, bounding over the hills” (Song of Songs 2).

Today a new joy has arisen in the heaven of the angels, because the lost human being has been recalled by the Lord to the kingdoms of heaven.

When it says, “And he sits at the right hand of God,” God the Father must not be thought to possess a right hand as we do, since he is incorporeal and boundless; rather, he is wholly right, because he is wholly holy. Therefore, the power of equality is signified by the right hand of God. He is described as sitting at God’s right hand because, through his ascension, he joined the human being whom he assumed from among us to the Divinity. Of him the Psalmist says: “The Lord said to my Lord, ‘Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool’” (Psalm 110).

For just as the reprobate are to be placed on the left, so the elect are to be placed on the right, as the Judge himself testifies when he says: “He will place the sheep at his right hand, but the goats at his left” (Matthew 25).

He is therefore said to sit at the right hand of God so that his members may believe that they will come to be where they hear that their Head has gone before them, as the Apostle says: “If you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God” (Colossians 3).

It is asked why Mark says, “He sits at the right hand of God,” when Stephen reports: “Behold, I see the heavens opened and Jesus standing at the right hand of God” (Acts 7). What does it mean that the one speaks of him as sitting and the other as standing, unless sitting belongs to one who reigns, while standing belongs to one who fights or helps?

Mark describes him as sitting after the ascension because he now judges all things with the Father and will come at the end as judge of all. Stephen, however, placed in combat, saw him standing—the one whom he took as his helper—because he was fighting for Stephen, rewarding him so that he might conquer.

“But they went out and preached everywhere.” They preached everywhere so that the prophecy might be fulfilled which says: “Their sound has gone out through all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Psalm 19). And again: “There are no languages or speeches whose voices are not heard” (ibid.).

It must not be thought that immediately after the Lord’s ascension they were sent everywhere to preach. Rather, according to the Lord’s command, they remained in the city until they were clothed with power from on high. After they had received the gifts of the Holy Spirit, they first announced the word of God to the Jews, so that, when they did not believe, the transfer to the Gentiles might justly take place, as they themselves said: “It was necessary that the word of God be spoken to you first” (Acts 13).

Therefore, when long ago the prophet foretold that the Gentiles would become fellow members and co-heirs of the Church of God, he said: “It is too little for you to be my servant, to raise up the tribes of Jacob and restore the remnants of Israel.” And again: “I have given you as a light to the Gentiles.” And once more: “Lengthen your cords and strengthen your stakes. For you will penetrate to the right and to the left, and your offspring will inherit the nations” (Isaiah 49, 42, 54).

And lest you suppose that the apostles were fit to preach the Gospel everywhere by their own power, the evangelist added an essential point, saying: “The Lord working with them and confirming the word by the signs that followed.” The Lord confirmed the apostles’ preaching through the signs that followed, when he displayed such signs and mighty works through them that no one who witnessed the marvels could doubt that their teaching was from God.

He performed such signs through them that even certain persecutors and opponents, being pierced in heart, came to believe: while one person was raised bodily, many were raised spiritually; and while one was healed in body, many were healed in soul.

The apostles themselves, with God cooperating with them, also confirmed their preaching when they first fulfilled by their deeds what they preached to others in words. A teacher confirms his preaching when he first completes in practice what he teaches others, imitating that good Teacher of whom it is written: “Jesus began to do and to teach” (Acts 1).

## HOMILY XCVII. THE SUNDAY AFTER THE LORD’S ASCENSION

*(1 Peter 4.)* “Beloved: Be prudent and watchful in prayers.” And so forth. Beloved brothers, we ought to consider the apostolic words that we have heard in the present reading, in which blessed Peter admonishes and teaches us: “Therefore be prudent and watchful in prayers,” fulfilling in practice the things written in the Gospel.

“Above all, maintain constant mutual charity among yourselves.” This is believed to be greater than all the virtues, “because charity covers a multitude of sins”—namely, both one’s own sins and those of the person whom one converts to a better life through one’s teaching.

“Be hospitable to one another without grumbling.” Grumbling is harmful to good works. Therefore “the Apostle says that God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9).

“As each has received grace, administer it to one another, as good stewards of the manifold grace of God.” For God’s sake, diligently giving one’s own possessions to those in need.

“If anyone speaks, let him speak as the words of God.” That is, whoever preaches the command of God should attribute it not to himself but to God, and should speak as though speaking the words of God. He should not strive to understand these things according to human judgment, that is, according to carnal wisdom, but according to what the Holy Spirit has dictated; he should strive to understand them spiritually and fulfill them in his deeds.

“If anyone ministers, let him do so as from the strength that God supplies.” Let him attribute all God’s gifts to divine grace and dare to ascribe nothing to his own merits, because whatever good there is in a human being comes solely from God’s activity, not from human wisdom or power. Nevertheless, we ought humbly to offer our neighbors the good that we possess, because we know that the good things within us do not come from ourselves but proceed solely from God’s grace.

“So that in all things God may be glorified through Jesus Christ our Lord.” From all the good things that God grants through his generosity to human beings, praise and thanksgiving should always be offered to him, so that, remaining worthy through observance in that life of praise and thanksgiving, they may thereby deserve eternal life.

Therefore it is necessary that we frequently consider what we shall be like on the day of judgment, when we shall be presented before the purest gaze of the angels and give an account to the eternal Judge from the books of conscience. When all other proofs have been removed, it is certain that on that day the human being himself will be set before himself, his own soul will be shown to him as in a mirror of the heart, and witnesses against it will be brought not from outside or elsewhere but from within, from itself. Not foreign testimony will be added, but all the testimony will be familiar—namely, one’s own deeds.

Let us therefore conquer our pleasures and impulses while that most eagerly awaited and blessed time succeeds us in the happy transformation of eternal life, when what the Lord says will be fulfilled: “Human beings will be like the holy angels” (Mark 12).

Let us remain in continual tears and in our daily repentance. We have a priest in heaven who intercedes for us, of whom John also says: “If anyone sins, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous, and he is the propitiation for our sins” (1 John 2).

Behold, the spirit rejoices when we hear of the power of our advocate; yet fear again bites into our rejoicing, because the one who is our advocate is called righteous. We have causes of injustice, but the righteous advocate in no way undertakes unjust causes, nor does he consent to offer words in defense of injustice.

What, then, shall we do, beloved brothers? Behold, the answer comes to mind. Let us abandon and accuse the evils we have committed. It is written: “The righteous person is his own accuser at the beginning” (Proverbs 18). For any sinner who is converted in tears already begins to be righteous when he begins to accuse what he has done. Why should he no longer be righteous who already rages against his own injustice through tears?

Our righteous advocate, therefore, will not defend the righteous in judgment, because we recognize and accuse ourselves as unjust. Let us therefore place our confidence not in our tears or in our deeds, but in the relief provided by our advocate, who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY XCVIII. THE SUNDAY AFTER THE LORD’S ASCENSION

[Col. 0550D]

*(John 15–16.)* “At that time Jesus said to his disciples: ‘When the Paraclete comes, whom I will send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth.’” And so forth. In many places in the Gospel we read that the Lord promised to give, through the coming of the Holy Spirit, those things that the apostles possessed less fully with respect to perfection. At the beginning of this reading, however, he not only promises that same Spirit again, but also declares that by his gift they would be made fit to preach the Gospel, when he says: “When the Paraclete comes, whom I will send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father, he will bear witness about me.”

It is clear and requires no laborious explanation why he calls that Spirit the Paraclete. For *paracletus* (παράκλητος) is Greek; in Latin it means “consoler” or “advocate.” He is rightly called the Consoler because he not only consoled the apostles’ sorrowing hearts over the Lord’s absence, and comforted them in enduring tribulations and sufferings, but also daily gives great consolation to those who mourn their sins, by promising them hope of pardon.

The Prophet prayed to be consoled by him when he said: “Your consolations, O Lord, have gladdened my soul” (Psalm 94). In Greek this reads: “Αἱ παρακλήσεις σου, εὔφραναν τὴν ψυχήν μου”—“Your consolations have gladdened my soul.”

And again: “I remembered your judgments, O Lord, from of old, and I was consoled” (Psalm 119).

He is rightly called an Advocate because, being equal to the Father and the Son, he does not cease daily to intercede with the Father for our offenses, since, as the Apostle says: “We do not know what we ought to pray for” (Romans 8), and so forth.

He rightly declares that the same Spirit is sent by him and proceeds from the Father—not that he proceeds from the Father in one way and from the Son in another, or is sent by the Son in one way and by the Father in another, but because the sending itself is procession, and the procession itself is sending. There is no difference in the one who proceeds or in the one who sends, since they possess one essence and equal divinity.

The one who proceeds is not inferior to the one from whom he proceeds; nor is the one who is sent inferior to the one by whom he is sent, because what the Father is, the Son is, and the Holy Spirit is also. Since he is the co-eternal and consubstantial Spirit of both, just as he proceeds from the Father, so also from the Son; and just as he is sent by the Son, so he is sent by the Father.

That the same Spirit belongs to the Father, the Lord makes clear in the Gospel when he says to his disciples: “For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matthew 10). That he belongs to the Son, the apostle Paul shows when he says: “If anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to him” (Romans 8).

The same Spirit also comes from himself, because he is true God, as the Lord says: “The Spirit breathes where he wills” (John 3). And Paul, after enumerating the powers of that same Holy Spirit, added: “All these things one and the same Spirit accomplishes, distributing to each as he wills” (1 Corinthians 12).

He is called the Spirit of truth because he proceeds from the Father of truth. For the Father himself is truth, and likewise the Son, and likewise the Holy Spirit. What the Son says of himself—“I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14)—must also be understood of the Father and the Holy Spirit, because as the Father is, so is the Son, and so also is the Holy Spirit.

When he says, “He will bear witness about me,” it is clear that the Holy Spirit bore witness to the Son that he was God when, sent by him on the holy day of Pentecost as he had been promised, he granted the apostles knowledge of all languages (Acts 2). But he bore witness to him not only then. Before he suffered, he also bore witness to him when, after he had been baptized by John in the Jordan, the Spirit appeared above him in the form of a dove, and a voice was heard saying: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3). Hence John also says: “And I saw, and I bore witness that this is the Son of God” (John 1).

Or certainly, the Holy Spirit bore witness to the Son when he made the apostles strong enough to bear witness. Hence it is added:

“ And you also will bear witness, because you have been with me from the beginning.” He does not say “from the beginning of the world,” nor “from the beginning of his birth,” but “from the beginning of his preaching.” For at the beginning of his preaching the Lord chose his disciples, as the same John says elsewhere: “This was the beginning of Jesus’ signs, at Cana in Galilee, and his disciples believed in him” (John II). They were therefore able to bear his testimony all the more truly after his most glorious [Col. 0552B] ascension, the more clearly they had observed his works and powers from the beginning of his preaching. Hence they also said: “We are witnesses of all that he did in the region of the Jews and in Jerusalem, whom they killed by hanging him on a tree. God raised him on the third day and granted that he be made manifest, not to all the people, but to witnesses appointed beforehand by God—to us, who ate and drank with him after he had risen from the dead. And he commanded us to preach to the people and to testify that he is the one appointed by God as judge of the living and the dead. To him all the prophets bear witness, that through his name everyone who believes in him receives forgiveness of sins” (Acts X). But because persecution was to arise through that same preaching, it is rightly added:

“These things I have spoken to you so that you may not be scandalized.” For if, as the Apostle says, “all who wish to live devoutly in Christ suffer persecution” (II Timothy III), the apostles endured persecutions for the truth all the more harshly because they appeared earlier in the Lord’s preaching. The devout teacher consoles the minds of the disciples so that they would fear the rage of their persecutors less, since they recognized that these things had been foretold to them by their devout teacher. Hence, when elsewhere he foretold them that persecutions would come on account of their preaching, he set himself forward as an example of endurance, saying: “If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you; if they kept my word, they will also keep yours” (John XV). And again: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; rather, fear him who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna” (Matthew X). And elsewhere: “If you were of the world, the world would love what was its own. But because you are not of the world, and I chose you out of the world, therefore the world hates you” (John XV). To be scandalized is to fall away from the faith during persecution or to cease from preaching. But in order to make them stronger, he not only foretold persecutions to them but also showed them the kind of persecution, when he added:

“They will make you outcasts from the synagogues.” The Greek word συναγωγή (*synagōgē*) means in Latin “assembly” or “congregation.” For at that time it was no small disgrace to be expelled from the synagogue. Just as it is now shameful for someone to be driven outside the Church because of his crimes, so then it was disgraceful for anyone to be made an outsider from the synagogue. That they were frequently expelled from the synagogue is fully made clear by the book of the Acts of the Apostles, in which we read: “After setting them in the council, they warned them not to speak to anyone in the name of Jesus or teach, and when they went away from the presence of the council, they rejoiced because they had been considered worthy to suffer dishonor for the name of Jesus” (Acts V). But because many Jews, out of zeal to defend the carnal law, stirred up persecutions against the apostles, it is rightly added: “But the hour is coming when everyone who kills you will think that he is offering service to God.” In this passage “hour” may be understood as the time of persecution, during which the apostles were to suffer persecutions from the wicked. For they thought they were offering great service to God when they persecuted the preachers of the Gospel as destroyers of the law. Of them the Apostle says: “I testify that they have zeal for God, but not according to knowledge” (Romans XII). But they defend in vain the law given through a servant, while they lose the grace brought through the Son. For, as it is written: “The law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (John I). Hence it follows:

“And they will do these things to you because they have not known the Father nor me.” In this the Jews show that they do not know the Father: they persecute the preachers of the Son with such hatred, just as the same Son says elsewhere to his disciples: “Whoever receives you receives me, and whoever despises you despises me” (Matthew X).

“But I have spoken these things to you so that, when their hour comes, you may remember that I told you.” The devout teacher foretells the disciples that persecutions will come, so that they might endure them more easily when they arrived, remembering that he had foretold them. Arrows strike less severely when they can be foreseen, whereas sudden and unexpected events often disturb even the bravest soldiers in war. Therefore he wished not only here to foretell what was going to happen, but also in many passages, so that they might bear tribulations and distress more lightly because they had been fortified by the shield of foreknowledge. When he sent them to preach, saying, “Behold, I am sending you like sheep in the midst of wolves,” he immediately took care to make clear what they would suffer for that preaching, adding: “Beware of men, for they will hand you over to councils, and in their synagogues they will scourge you; and you will be led before governors and kings for my sake, as a testimony to them and to the nations” (Matthew X). And again: “Blessed will you be when people hate you, and when they separate you, reproach you, and cast out your name as evil, on account of the Son of Man. Rejoice on that day and exult, for behold, your reward is great in heaven” (Luke VI).

## HOMILY XCIX. AT THE VIGIL OF PENTECOST

[Col. 0554A]

(John XIV.) “At that time Jesus said to his disciples: ‘If you love me, keep my commandments.’” And so forth. What does it mean that he says that the Spirit, the Paraclete, would be given to those who love God and keep his commandments, when God is not loved and his commandments cannot be kept except through the Holy Spirit? What else does this mean except that the one who loves God through the Holy Spirit merits, by loving, to possess him more, and by possessing him more, to love him more? For *Paraclete* means “comforter.” The Holy Spirit is rightly called the Paraclete because he lifts up and refreshes the hearts of the faithful with desires for heavenly life, so that they do not fail amid the adversities of this age.

[Col. 0554B] “And I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete.” In this he shows that he himself is also the Paraclete. For previously they too had a Paraclete, namely the Lord himself, dwelling with them in the flesh; through the sweetness of miracles and the work of preaching, he used to raise and strengthen them so that they would not be scandalized because of the persecution of unbelievers. He said, “I will ask,” according to his humanity, although according to his divinity he gives all things with the Father. “So that he may remain with you forever.” For he remains forever with the saints, whom even in this life he always invisibly illumines within and, in the future, brings forever to contemplate the vision of his majesty. “The Spirit of truth, whom the world cannot receive, because it neither sees him nor knows him.” He calls “the world” those who are given over to love of this world. The world therefore cannot receive him—that is, worldly people cannot—because they do not have the invisible eyes of charity, by which alone the Holy Spirit can be seen, known, and, through knowing, understood.

[Col. 0554C] “But you will know him, because he will remain with you and will be in you.” He will be in order to remain forever. Unbelievers saw the Lord and Savior in the flesh before his Passion, but that he was the Son of God, that he was the Paraclete sent by God into the world, only the faithful were able to know. Unbelievers neither saw the Holy Spirit with their eyes nor wished to know him in their minds, because he did not appear to the disciples clothed in humanity. Rather, he chose to come to them and remain among them in such a way that he consecrated for himself a most pleasing dwelling in their very hearts. This is what he says: “But you will know him, because he will remain with you and will be in you.” He who invisibly remains with the elect in this life visibly displays to them the grace of his thought.

[Col. 0554D] “I will not leave you orphans; I will come to you.” It seemed to unbelievers that, when the Lord died on the cross, he would leave the disciples orphans. But he did not leave orphans those to whom he showed himself alive after his Passion through many proofs over forty days and, ten days after his ascension, gave them the gifts of the Holy Spirit from heaven. No one who recognizes the inseparable nature, truth, and operation of the Holy Trinity can doubt that Christ himself came to them.

[Col. 0555A] “A little while, and the world will no longer see me.” The “little while” lasted until the time when his Passion was completed, after which the wicked were no longer able to see him. Only the righteous, who had been saddened by his death, were worthy to see the joy of his resurrection. “But you will see me, because I live, and you will live.” What does “I live, and you will live” mean? Why did he say that he lives in the present, but that they would live in the future, unless he also promised them the life of the flesh—indeed, a resurrected life—such as was about to precede in him and follow in them? And because his resurrection was soon to occur, he used a verb in the present tense to signify its nearness; but because theirs was deferred until the end of the age, he did not say “you live,” but “you will live.” In two words, one in the present tense and one in the future, he elegantly and briefly promised two resurrections: his own, soon to come, and ours, to follow at the end of the age.

[Col. 0555B] “On that day you will know that I am in my Father, and you are in me, and I am in you.” On what day, if not the day of which he said, “And you will live”? At that time the apostles knew that Christ was in the Father through the unity of undivided divinity. They knew that they were in Christ through receiving his faith and sacraments; they knew that Christ was truly living and was in the Father, and that Christ was in them through love and observance of his commandments. The holy Church of God also knew this, but on that day of which he said, “And you will live”—the day of the resurrection, when they truly began to live—it would know these things much better and more fully, when they would know more perfectly all that must be known and would behold the very source of knowledge more closely and without end. And because he was promising this blessedness to everyone, not only to the apostles, he immediately adds:

[Col. 0555C] “Whoever has my commandments and keeps them is the one who loves me. Whoever loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and manifest myself to him.” Here we must consider with complete attention that truly to love Christ is not merely to confess that one loves him, but to keep Christ’s commandments—which we possess by learning—by putting them into practice. “Whoever has my commandments,” he says, “and keeps them is the one who loves me.” The one who has them in memory and keeps them in life; who has them in speech and keeps them in conduct; who has them by hearing and keeps them by doing; or who has them by doing and keeps them by persevering—he, he says, is the one who loves me. It should be noted that, when he said, using a verb in the present tense, “whoever loves me,” he adds in the future tense: “will be loved by my Father, and I will love him, and I will manifest myself to him.” The Son, together with the Father, even now loves those who love him, but now he loves them so that they may live rightly by faith, which works through love; then he will love them so that they may attain the vision of truth, which they had carried through faith. He did not add without reason, “and I will manifest myself to him.” For although according to his humanity he will manifest himself to all at the judgment, to the righteous and holy alone he will manifest the glory of his divinity, in which he is equal to the Father [Col. 0556A] and the Holy Spirit, for eternal blessedness.

## HOMILY C. ON THE HOLY DAY OF PENTECOST

(John XIV.) “At that time Jesus said to his disciples: ‘If anyone loves me, he will keep my word.’” And so forth. Since the Lord was about to promise the Holy Spirit to the disciples, he makes clear at the beginning of this reading what those who desire to become his dwelling place ought to be like, when he says: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word.” In these words he shows that the proof of true love is the presentation of a good work. For if the one who does not love the Lord does not keep his commandments, the person who confesses with words that he loves him, while not keeping his precepts in deeds, declares this without cause, as the Apostle John bears witness, saying: “If anyone says, ‘I love God,’ and hates his brother, he is a liar” (I John IV). And as the Apostle says concerning false professors of the faith: “They profess that they know God, but they deny him by their deeds” (Titus I). The Lord reproves such people in the Gospel when he says: “Why do you call me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ and not do what I say?” (Luke VI). And the Prophet says: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isaiah XXIX). For just as the righteous person lives by faith, so faith without works is dead, as the Lord says: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew VII), and so forth. Hence John, when he had said in the Apocalypse, “Blessed is the one who reads and the one who hears the words of the prophecy of this book” (Apocalypse I), immediately added: “and keeps what is written in it.” For love of God cannot be idle, since, as the Lord says, “the mouth speaks from the abundance of the heart” (Matthew XII). If it is true love, it either performs great works; or, if it refuses to act, it ought not to be called love. Just as an emperor recognizes that his soldiers love him when they observe the laws of his province, so we show the affection of our love toward God when we keep his commandments. Hence, shortly before this reading, he said: “Whoever has my commandments and keeps them is the one who loves me.” And again: “If you love me, keep my commandments.” In the love of God, one must observe not only the tongue [Col. 0556D] but also the hands, as the Lord says elsewhere to his disciples: “You know these things; blessed are you if you do them” (John XIII). God’s commandments must therefore be kept, because an exceedingly great reward has been prepared in keeping them. Concerning this reward it immediately follows: “And my Father will love him.” For what more can the Son promise his lover than that he will be loved by the Father? Therefore whoever loves the Son is also loved by the Father, because the same Son is one with the Father, as he himself says elsewhere to those who love him: “The Father himself loves you, because you have loved me and have believed that I came forth from God” (John XVI). It should also be noted that he says: “and we will come to him.” If God were not a Trinity, he would certainly not speak in the plural: “And we will come to him.” Wherever the Father comes, the Son comes, and the Holy Spirit comes. And wherever the Father remains, the Son remains, and the Holy Spirit also remains. For, as the Apostle says: “The love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Romans V). And again: “that Christ may dwell in our hearts through faith” (Ephesians III). But what follows should be received with a joyful heart: “And we will make our dwelling with him.” God comes to the hearts of some people, but does not make his dwelling there, because he visits them through the grace of compunction; but when the hour of compunction has passed and they return to iniquity, they drive God away from their hearts. Of them the Lord says elsewhere: “They believe for a time, but in the time of testing they fall away” (Luke VIII). But to the heart [Col. 0557B] of the elect he not only comes but also makes his dwelling, because their minds are so fixed in the love of the Divinity that they do not depart from his love in the time of testing. Rather, they cling to the Lord in such a way that, whether in prosperity or adversity, they always strive to bless him, saying with the Psalmist: “I will bless the Lord at all times” (Psalm XXXIII).

We must therefore consider with the utmost care how diligently the one who desires to receive so great and so worthy a guest ought to prepare the dwelling of his mind. If a king or a powerful friend were about to come to your house, you would prepare it with every effort, throwing out what was superfluous, bringing in what was necessary, and seeking out not only what belonged to usefulness but also what belonged to adornment. In the same way, as you are about to receive the Lord your God into the dwelling of your heart, cleanse your conscience from dead works and from superfluous and unclean thoughts. For the pure inhabitant seeks a pure house—one in which he who says, “Behold, I stand at the door and knock; if anyone opens to me, I will enter him, and I will dine with him, and he with me” (Apocalypse III), may not only come but also deign to remain. We must therefore cleanse the house of our mind from the filth of every vice and adorn it with the various flowers of the virtues, so that it may shine with humility, sparkle with chastity, and radiate with charity, in order that the Holy Spirit, coming into our hearts, may make his dwelling there.

But after these things have been explained concerning the elect, who love God not only in words but also in deeds, he immediately speaks of the reprobate:

[Col. 0557D] “Whoever does not love me does not keep my words.” For just as the one who observes God’s commandments proves, even when his tongue is silent, that he loves him, so the one who does not keep his word demonstrates that he does not love him. “And the word that you have heard is not mine, but the Father’s, who sent me.” When above he used “words” in the plural, he wished the teaching of the holy Gospel to be understood. But when he added in the singular, “And the word that you have heard,” he wished himself to be understood, for he is the Word and Wisdom of God, concerning whom John says elsewhere: “In the beginning was the Word” (John I), and so forth. Therefore he rightly says: “And the word that you have heard is not mine, but the Father’s, who sent me,” because the Son did not come from himself but from the Father, as he himself says: “I have not come from myself, but my Father sent me” (John VII). And just as the Son is not from himself, so he does not say that his teaching is his own, as he himself says: “My teaching is not mine, but that of the Father who sent me” (ibid.). And again: “The Father remains in me, and I in him” (John VI). And elsewhere: “I do nothing from myself” (John VIII). For he who is made from no one and proceeds from no one is the Father alone. The Son, however, is believed to have been born from the Father, and the Holy Spirit to proceed from the Father and the Son.

“These things I have spoken to you while remaining with you.” Was he not going to remain with the disciples, to whom elsewhere he promised, saying: “Behold, I am with you all the days until the consummation of the age” (Matthew XXVIII)? Certainly he was, but when he says, “These things I have spoken to you while remaining with you,” he is speaking of his bodily presence, through which he was soon to depart from them. The same applies to what he says elsewhere: “These are the words that I spoke to you while I was still with you” (Luke XXIV). Therefore, while speaking these things to them at the moment of his Passion, he would remain with them forever according to his divinity, but he speaks of departing according to his humanity. Yet he promises that he will teach them by the coming of the Holy Spirit what they could not fully understand concerning his divinity, when he adds:

[Col. 0558B] “But the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you all things.” The same is expressed elsewhere: “I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now. But when that Spirit of truth comes, he will teach you all truth” (John XVI). It is plainly evident, and requires no laborious exposition, that he will advance our minds toward understanding spiritual things. Why he calls that same Spirit the Paraclete is also clear: *paracletus* is a Greek expression, παράκλητος (*paráklētos*), meaning in Latin “comforter” or “advocate.” He is rightly called “comforter,” because he comforts the minds of the faithful with hope of heavenly rewards, so that they do not fail amid the adversities of this age. He is rightly called “advocate,” because he intercedes with the Father for the error of sinners, as the Apostle bears witness, saying: “For we do not know how to pray as we ought” (Romans VIII), and so forth. And beautifully he says that this same Spirit is sent by the Father in his name, because he is of one nature and the same power with the Father, as he himself says elsewhere: “When the Paraclete comes, whom I will send to you from the Father—the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father—he will bear witness concerning me” (John XV).

What he says, “He will teach you all things,” must be understood as meaning all things that are necessary, whether for understanding or for teaching. The Holy Spirit is rightly said to teach all things, because the teacher’s external speech labors in vain unless the Holy Spirit is present inwardly to illumine the heart of the hearer. Yet no one can be so perfect in the present life as to know everything about God, especially since the Apostle, who is said to have been caught up to the third heaven, says: “We know in part, and we prophesy in part” (I Corinthians XIII).

[Col. 0558D] When he adds, “And he will suggest to you all things whatsoever I have said to you,” the Holy Spirit is said to suggest because he makes us *suggerentes*, that is, suppliants. But one may ask how he suggests, since suggesting belongs to an inferior, whereas the Holy Spirit is believed to be equal to the Father. The answer is that this usage of speech is frequently found in the sacred Scriptures: God is said to do what he brings about in us so that we may do it, and to pray when he makes us pray. Just as the Holy Spirit is said to groan because he incites us to groan, so he is said to suggest because he instructs us to suggest—that is, he makes us ask in supplication for what we lack in virtues. And because “to suggest” sometimes means “to supply,” the Holy Spirit, coeternal and consubstantial with the Father and the Son, is said to suggest because he ministers divine knowledge to us through hidden inspiration—not from below, but from above.

[Col. 0559B] Hence the Apostle says: “The love of God has been poured into your hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to you” (Romans V). After the Lord promised the disciples that he would give them the Spirit, the Paraclete, he immediately commended peace, saying:

“I leave peace with you; I give you my peace.” He shows that those deserve to receive his Spirit and become temples of the Holy Spirit who preserve unbroken peace and concord with their brothers, according to the prophetic saying: “Upon whom will my Spirit rest, if not upon the humble, the quiet, and the one who trembles at my words?” (Isaiah LXVI). Hence John says in his Apocalypse: “I will dwell in them and walk among them” (II Corinthians VI). True peace is not kindled by any fury and is disturbed by no persecution; rather, amid the adversities of this age, the Christian mind stands unshaken, because, as the Prophet says: “Great peace belongs to those who love your law, and there is no scandal for them” (Psalm CXVIII). The Lord commended this peace to his disciples as a special gift when he said: “Have salt in yourselves, and have peace among yourselves” (Mark IX). And again: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called sons of God” (Matthew V). He knew that he possessed this peace who said: “With those who hated peace, I was peaceful” (Psalm XIX). A certain wise man briefly summed up the power and dignity of this virtue, saying:

Peace nourishes the soul; concord preserves peace.

Peace suppresses quarrels; concord binds together—and again:

[Col. 0559D] Quarrels fear peace; discord flees peace.

Peace drives away hatred; peace nourishes chaste love.

Even now the wicked cannot possess the sweetness of this virtue, although they appear to agree among themselves, as Scripture says: “There is no peace for the wicked” (Isaiah XLVI), says the Lord God. He therefore beautifully says: “I leave peace with you; I give you my peace.” It is as if he were saying: “I give it to those who are present; I leave it to those who will come. I leave it to those who are beginning; I give it to those who persevere.” And because peace will be more perfect in the future than in the present, he rightly said with the added qualification: “I give you my peace.” For there we will have not only no outward conflict with vices, but no inward conflict either, where there is supreme peace through the vision of the Creator.

[Col. 0560A] “Not as the world gives do I give to you.” There is a great difference between the peace of the world and the peace of God. The world gives peace to its lovers when adulterers agree with adulterers, drunkards with drunkards, the rapacious with the rapacious, and murderers with murderers. But this peace leads to perpetual discord; in the present it is frequently changed into quarrels, and sometimes ends when death intervenes. The peace that the Lord gives, however, both makes the Christian mind tranquil in the present through the love of the brotherhood and leads it in the future to fellowship in everlasting peace. Therefore, in the peace of God, people love one another not for the sake of earthly love but for the sake of the peace of charity, so that those who have one Father in heaven may be joined together in one bond of charity on earth, as it is said of the primitive Church: “The multitude of believers had one heart and one soul” (Acts IV).

[Col. 0560B] Their peace is not changed by quarrels, broken by discord, or ended when death intervenes; rather, it is strengthened, so that those who have one desire on earth may have one reward in heaven. And because the Lord had commended peace to his disciples, knowing that tribulations and distresses would come upon them, he added a word of exhortation so that they would not lose peace amid the pressures of the world, saying: “Let not your heart be troubled, nor let it be afraid. You heard that I said to you: ‘I am going away, and I am coming to you.’” Hence, when elsewhere he encouraged them to face his Passion, he said: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matthew X). And again: “Do not fear, little flock, because it has pleased your Father to give you the kingdom” (Luke XII). For he knew that the more tribulations and distresses they endured for his name, the more their glory would increase. As it is written: “As the furnace tests the potter’s vessels, so temptation tests righteous people through tribulation” (Ecclesiasticus XXVII).

In many places in the Gospel we read that, when the Lord said he would depart bodily from the disciples, they could not hear it without deep sorrow. Hence, when he had said elsewhere, “I am going to him who sent me” (John VII), he immediately added: “But because I have spoken these things to you, sorrow has filled your heart” (John VI). They could therefore be troubled and afraid because they heard that the one whom they loved with all their hearts would depart from them. But the devout teacher kindly consoles their sorrow when he says: “Let not your heart be troubled, nor let it be afraid,” on account of what I said: “I am going away and I am coming to you.” If someone is saddened because I am going away, he ought to rejoice because I am coming, according to what he says elsewhere: “Let not your heart be troubled: believe in God, and believe in me” (John XIV). For “if I go and prepare a place for you, I will come again and take you to myself, so that where I am, you also may be” (ibid.). And elsewhere: “I will not leave you orphans; I will come to you” (ibid.). Hence it follows:

[Col. 0560D] “If you loved me, you would certainly rejoice, because I am going to the Father, because the Father is greater than I.” Did the apostles not love the Lord, for whom they were even prepared to die, saying: “Let us go also, and let us die with him” (John XVI)? What then does he mean by saying, “If you loved me, you would certainly rejoice”? The answer is that he does not deny that the disciples loved him, but, accommodating himself to their weakness, prepares their human minds for divine love. There was one aspect of him that they loved principally, and another that they loved less perfectly. They principally loved in him the form of humanity, which they saw, but less perfectly the form of divinity, which they did not see. It is as if the Lord were saying: “If you principally loved in me the form of divinity, which ought to be loved, you would certainly rejoice because I am going to the Father, because the Father is greater than I.”

Arius wrongly interprets this statement, daring to say that the Son of God is less than the Father in divinity. Unhappy man, he did not understand that in the one mediator between God and human beings there is one nature of divinity and another of humanity. In the nature of divinity he is believed not to have been made by God but to have been born from God: God from God, light from light, coeternal and consubstantial with the Father, as he himself says: “I and the Father are one” (John X). In the nature of humanity, by which he was made a little lower than the angels, he is believed to be less than the Father, and according to that nature he says: “I am going to the Father, because the Father is greater than I.”

[Col. 0561B] “And now I have told you before it happens, so that when it happens you may believe.” The Lord wished to foretell what was going to happen to him not only to show himself to be God, who could know what was to come, but also to summon the minds of the disciples to faith by this sign—namely, so that they might believe those things more firmly when they saw them fulfilled exactly as he had foretold them. As he says elsewhere: “I have spoken these things to you so that, when their hour comes, you may remember that I told you” (John XVI). Hence, when he was about to raise Lazarus, after foretelling that he would die, he said: “I rejoice for your sake, so that you may believe that I was not there” (John XI).

But when he added:

[Col. 0561C] “I will no longer speak many things with you,” he is speaking of bodily speech. For, speaking these things to the disciples at the moment of his Passion, he was about to say only a few things to them bodily. Spiritually, however, he speaks every day whenever the holy Gospel is read or the authority of sacred Scripture is recalled to memory: “For the prince of this world is coming, and he has nothing in me.” If we understand “the prince of this world” in this passage to mean Pilate, it is clear that he found nothing in him, as he himself replied to the chief priests: “For what evil has this man done?” (Matthew XXVII). “I find no case against this man in the charges you bring against him; neither did Herod, for he sent him back to us, and behold, nothing deserving death has been done by him” (Luke XXIII).

But we understand the prince of this world more appropriately as the devil, who once claims power and tyranny over the minds of those who love the world rather than God. Against this prince the soldier of the camp of God had entered into combat, saying: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood” (Ephesians VI). And again: “I do not fight as one beating the air, but I discipline my body and bring it into servitude, lest after preaching to others I myself should become disqualified” (I Corinthians IX).

[Col. 0561D] This prince of the world therefore came to the Lord when, seeing him die as a human being, he thought that he could seize his soul as he had seized the souls of the others whom he held through original sin. But he found nothing in him because, as the Apostle Peter says: “He committed no sin, and no deceit was found in his mouth” (I Peter II). He therefore lost the power that he retained over others precisely because he sharpened the sword of his assault against one in whom he found nothing. For, as the Apostle says: “If they had understood, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (I Corinthians II). Concerning him the Lord says elsewhere: “Now is the hour for the prince of this world to be cast out” (John XII). And again: “I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven” (Luke X). Hence it follows:

“But so that the world may know that I love the Father, and just as the Father commanded me, so I do: arise, let us go from here.” In these words he shows that he suffered not by necessity but by his will. He was not bound by the chains of any sin, so that he had to suffer by necessity; rather, through love alone he freely endured the Passion for us, both to fulfill obedience to the Father and to free us from death’s destruction. What he says, “But so that the world may know that I love the Father,” means this: “I show that I love the Father in that I do not delay enduring tribulations and distresses for his name.” Or certainly: “I show that I love the Father in that, although I can avoid death, I do not delay undergoing death for his love, since I did not come to do my own will.”

Let us also imitate our Head, according to the measure of our ability, so that, although we cannot be without sin, we may not fear suffering persecutions for righteousness, because, as the Apostle Peter says: “Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example so that you might follow his footsteps. He committed no sin, and no deceit was found in his mouth” (I Peter II). And may what the Lord says in the Gospel be fulfilled in us: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness” (Matthew V). For this reason the Apostle Peter also admonishes us elsewhere, saying: “Let none of you suffer as a murderer, or a thief, or an adulterer. But if as a Christian, let him not be ashamed, but let him glorify God in this name” (I Peter IV).

## HOMILY CI. THE SECOND DAY OF PENTECOST

[Col. 0562D]

(John III.) “At that time Jesus said to his disciples: ‘God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son, so that everyone who believes in him should not perish but have life.’” And so forth. Here we should note that he repeats concerning the only-begotten Son of God the same promise that he had made concerning the Son of Man lifted up on the cross, saying: “So that everyone who believes in him should not perish but have eternal life.” For certainly the same one who is our Redeemer and Creator, existing as the Son of God before the ages, became the Son of Man at the end of the ages, so that he who had created us through the power of his divinity might restore us through the frailty of our humanity, in order to establish us in the blessedness of eternal life and restore the life that we had lost. It follows:

[Col. 0563A] “For God did not send his Son into the world to judge the world, but so that the world might be saved through him.” Therefore, insofar as it depends upon the physician, he came to heal the sick person; but the one who does not wish to observe the physician’s prescriptions is destroyed. He came to save the world. Why was he called the Savior of the world, unless it was to save the world, not to judge the world? Do you not wish to be saved by him? You will be judged by yourself. And what shall I say—“you will be judged”? See what he says:

“He who believes in him is not judged. But he who does not believe”—what did you expect him to say, except “he will be judged”? “He has already,” he says, “been judged.” The judgment has not yet appeared, but judgment has already taken place. The Lord knows who are his; he knows who will remain for the crown and who will remain for the flame; he knows his wheat in his threshing floor, and he knows the chaff; he knows the grain, [Col. 0563B] and he knows the weeds. He has already been judged who does not believe. Why has he been judged? “Because he has not believed in the name of the only-begotten Son of God. This is the judgment: that the light has come into the world, and people loved darkness more than light. For their works were evil.”

My brothers, whose works does the Lord find good? No one’s. For he finds everyone’s works evil. How, then, have some done the truth and come to the light? This follows:

“But he who does the truth comes to the light, so that his works may be revealed, because they have been done in God.” How, then, have some done a good work so as to come to the light, that is, to Christ? And how have some loved darkness? For if he found all to be sinners, and heals all from sin—and that serpent [Col. 0563C] in which the Lord’s death was prefigured heals those who had been bitten (Num. 21)—and if the serpent was raised because of the serpent’s bites, that is, the Lord’s death because of mortal human beings whom he found unrighteous, how is this understood: “This is the judgment, that the light has come into the world, and people loved darkness more than light, for their works were evil” (John 3)?

What does this mean? Whose works were good? Did you not come to justify the ungodly? But he says, “They loved darkness more than light.” There he placed the emphasis. For many loved their sins; many confessed their sins. For whoever confesses his sins and accuses his sins is already acting with God. God accuses your sins, and when you accuse them, you are joined to God. There are, as it were, two things: the human being and the sinner. What you hear called “human being,” God made; what you hear called “sinner,” that same human being made. Destroy what you have made, so that God may save what he made.

You ought to hate your own work within yourself and love God’s work within yourself. When what you have done begins to displease you, your good works begin there, because you accuse your evil works. The beginning of your good works is the confession of your evil works. You do the truth and come to the light. What does it mean to do the truth? Do not flatter yourself, do not indulge yourself, do not fawn upon yourself; do not say, “I am righteous,” when you are unrighteous—and you begin to do the truth.

You come to the light so that your works may be revealed, because they have been done in God. For even the fact that your sin displeased you would not displease you unless God were shining upon you and his truth were showing itself to you. But whoever, even after being admonished, loves his sins hates the light that admonishes him and flees from it, so that his evil works, which he loves, may not be reproved.

But whoever does the truth accuses his evils within himself. He spares himself nothing; he forgives himself nothing, so that God may forgive him, because what he wishes God to forgive, he himself acknowledges. And he comes to the light, giving thanks to it because it has shown him what he should hate within himself. He says to God: “Lord, turn your face from my sins” (Ps. 50). And because he says this in vain unless he also says, “For I acknowledge my iniquity, and my sin is always before me” (ibid.), let what you do not wish to be before God be before you. But if you place your sin behind you, God turns it back before your eyes—and he turns it back when there will already be no fruit of repentance. [Col. 0564B]

## HOMILY CII. TUESDAY OF PENTECOST

(John 10.) “At that time Jesus said to his disciples: ‘Amen, amen, I say to you: whoever does not enter the sheepfold through the door, but climbs in by another way, is a thief and a robber.’” And so forth.

Because of the Pharisees’ poisonous, proud, and incurable arrogance—for they boasted that they could see, although they were blind—the Lord Jesus composed these sayings, which are concealed in this parable. He graciously explained it to them, though they did not understand, and in it he profitably warned us, if we pay attention, not to glory in human wisdom or in moral distinction, but in the humility of the catholic faith, [Col. 0564C] which does not fail in Christ.

There are many pagans who, according to a certain manner of life in this world, are called good and innocent people, seeming to observe the things commanded in the Law: they honor their parents; they do not commit adultery; they do not perpetrate murder; they do not steal; they do not bear false witness against anyone; they do not covet their neighbor’s house; they do not desire their neighbor’s wife, male slave, or female slave; and other such things commanded in the Law. They seem to observe these things like Christians, yet they are not Christians. Often they boast, like those Pharisees, saying: “Are we also blind?” (John 9).

But they do all these things in vain, because they do not enter through the door. Instead, swollen with pride, they seek to climb in as though by themselves. Therefore the Lord set forth a likeness concerning his flock and the door through which one enters the sheepfold. For what benefit is there in the empty inflation of those who boast of living well, when their life does not reach the end of living well forever? Living well ought to benefit each person in this respect: that he may be granted to live well forever. For if someone is not granted to live well forever, what benefit is it for him to live well temporarily?

Therefore those should not even be said to live well who either do not know the end of life through blindness or disregard it through conceit. No one has true or certain hope of living forever unless he recognizes the life that is Christ and enters the sheepfold through the door.

There are some people who glory in their own conduct and seek to draw others after them, not instructing their followers from Christ’s commandments, but persuading them to live according to their own examples. Of such people Truth itself says elsewhere: “Teaching human doctrines and disregarding God’s commandments” (Mark 7).
