They seek to climb in by another way, to steal and kill, not to save and preserve like a shepherd. Of such people it is said here: “But he climbs in by another way; he is a thief and a robber.”

Such teachers are found not only among those who are without the name of Christ—for example, among many philosophers who proclaimed their wisdom with boastful mouths and promised their followers a blessed life—but also among very many who were reckoned under the Christian name and boasted that they had been enlightened by Christ. They invented for themselves various new names derived from Christ, contrary to the catholic faith, as countless heretics did, falsely supposing that they entered through the door, which is Christ.

Sabellius says: “He who is the Son is himself the Father.” But the Son is not the Father. Whoever calls the Son the Father does not enter through the door.

Arius says: “The Father is one thing, the Son another.” He would speak correctly if he said “one person, another,” not “one thing, another.” For when he says “another thing,” he contradicts the one from whom he hears: “I and the Father are one” (John 10). Therefore he too does not enter through the door. He preaches a Christ whom he invents for himself, not the Christ whom the truth possesses.

Photinus says: “Christ is merely human, not God.” Therefore he too does not enter through the door, because Christ is both human and God.

A new heresy, which arose in our own times, seems to agree with him by affirming and preaching: “Christ, like any of his own, is a titular god, and not the true God.” Why go through many examples and enumerate many empty heresies?

Hold fast to this: believe that the sheepfold of Christ is the catholic Church. Whoever wishes to enter the sheepfold should enter through the door, that is, through Christ, and should preach Christ as true God and truly the Son of God. Let him not merely preach the true Christ, but seek Christ’s glory, not his own. For many, in seeking their own glory, have scattered Christ’s sheep rather than gathered them.

Christ our Lord is a humble door. Whoever enters through this door must humble himself, so that he may enter with a sound head. These are the ones who hear the voice of the true shepherd. These are those whom the true shepherd calls by name as his own sheep. Of them it is said: “Rejoice and exult, because your names are written in heaven” (Luke 10); for this reason “he calls them by name” (John 10). And who else brings them out except the one who forgives sins, so that, freed from harsh bonds, they may be able to follow him?

And who went before them, so that they might follow him, except the one who, “rising from the dead, dies no more, and death shall no longer rule over him” (Rom. 6)? He leads these from faith to sight and goes before them, because he was the first of all to ascend into heaven. His sheep follow him, because they know the voice of his teaching. They do not follow alien teachers, but flee from them, because they do not know the voice—that is, the teaching—of strangers.

But when the Lord Jesus was speaking, those who heard did not understand. “For they had fattened hearts and heard with difficulty” (Matt. 13). [Col. 0566A] He names the door, he names the sheepfold, he names the sheep; he commends these things, but does not yet explain them. Let us therefore read on, since he is going to come to those words in which he deigns to explain certain things he has said. From his explanation he may perhaps enable us also to understand what he did not explain. For he nourishes us with what is clear and exercises us with what is obscure.

Let us listen to him explaining whom we heard proposing the parable. Jesus therefore says to them:

“Amen, amen, I say to you: I am the door of the sheep.” Behold, he has opened the very door that he had presented as closed. He himself is the door. We have recognized it; let us enter, so that we may rejoice that we have entered.

“All who came are thieves and robbers.” What does this mean, Lord: “All who came”? What then—did you not come? But understand that when he said “all who came,” he meant all except me.

Let us recall, then. Before his coming, the prophets came. Were they thieves and robbers? Certainly not. They did not come apart from him, because they came with him. He sent heralds who were to come, but he possessed the hearts of those whom he sent. Therefore they came with him, because they came with the Word of God. “I am,” he says, “the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14). If he is the truth, they came with him because they were truthful and preached the truth.

But all who came apart from him “are thieves and robbers.” They came through themselves, because they were not sent through him, as the Apostle says: “How shall they preach unless they are sent?” (Rom. 10). And because they came through themselves and were not sent by him, “they are thieves and robbers.”

Before Christ’s coming there were false prophets and false teachers among God’s people, just as after his coming there were very many false teachers under the Christian name—not teachers, but seducers; not preachers, but plunderers; practicing robbery, not adhering to sound doctrine. Of them it is said: “They are thieves and robbers,” that is, they came to steal and kill.

“But the sheep did not listen to them”—those who are truly sheep, not those who conceal a wolf’s heart beneath a sheep’s skin.

Therefore those who preached before Christ’s coming preached in the same Spirit in which the apostles and holy teachers preached who, after Christ’s coming, showed the way of truth to the world. All who at that time believed in Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Moses, or the other patriarchs and prophets who foretold Christ were sheep, and they heard Christ. They heard not a stranger’s voice, but Christ’s own voice.

For the judge cries out in the herald, while the herald announces that the judge is coming. Those whom the sheep did not hear are different: they had no voice of Christ. They wandered, spoke falsely, chattered empty things, invented vanities, and led wretched people astray, like the false prophets and the scribes and Pharisees in the Lord’s own time. These are the ones who came through themselves and were not sent by the judge.

Now that these have been driven far away with their teachings, let us see where the good shepherd calls us. For he says:

“I am the door of the sheep. If anyone enters through me, he will be saved, and he will enter and go out, and will find pasture.” This clearly shows that not only the shepherd but also the sheep enter through the door.

But what does “He will enter and go out, and will find pasture” mean? To enter Christ’s Church through the door is very good. To leave the Church, as John the evangelist himself says in his epistle, “They went out from us, but they were not of us” (1 John 2), is certainly not good. Such an exit cannot be praised by the good shepherd, so that he would say: “He will enter and go out, and will find pasture.”

There is, therefore, a good kind of entering and also a good kind of going out through the good door, which is Christ. But what is this praiseworthy and blessed going out? I can indeed say that we enter when we think something inwardly, but we go out when we act outwardly. From this it is clear, as the Apostle says, that “Christ dwells in our hearts through faith” (Eph. 3): to enter through Christ means that, according to this same faith, we should also act outwardly, that is, before human beings.

Hence it is said in the Psalm: “A person goes out to his work” (Ps. 103). The Lord himself also says: “Let your works shine before human beings” (Matt. 5).

But I am more pleased by the fact that Truth itself, as a good shepherd—and therefore in a certain sense a good teacher—admonished us how we should understand what he said, “He will enter and go out, and will find pasture,” when he immediately added:

“The thief comes only to steal, slaughter, and destroy. I came so that they may have life and have it more abundantly.” For he seems to have said that they may have life when they enter, and have it more abundantly when they go out.

No one, however, can go out through the door—that is, through Christ—to eternal life, which will exist in sight, unless through that same door, Christ, he has entered into his Church, which is his sheepfold, for temporal life, which exists in faith.

Therefore he says: “I came so that they may have life”—that is, faith working through love, through which faith they enter the sheepfold so that they may live, because “the righteous person lives by faith” (Gal. 3)—“and have it more abundantly,” because, by persevering to the end through that door, that is, through faith in Christ, they go out. For faithful people die and will have life more abundantly when they come to where that shepherd has gone before them, where afterward they will never die.

Although even here in the sheepfold there is no lack of pasture—for we can understand the saying “and he will find pasture” with reference to both entering and going out—nevertheless they will then find the true pasture, where “those who hunger and thirst for righteousness” will be satisfied (Matt. 5), the kind of pasture found by the one to whom it was said: “Today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23).

## HOMILY CIII. WEDNESDAY OF PENTECOST

(Acts 2.) “In those days: Peter, standing with the Eleven, raised his voice and spoke to them: ‘Men of Judea, and all who dwell in Jerusalem, let this be known to you, and listen carefully to my words.’” And so forth.

After the coming of the Holy Spirit upon the apostles—which we still celebrate in the present festival—the Jews heard the apostles, filled with the Holy Spirit, speaking in every kind of language, and they were greatly astonished and amazed. Others, however, mocking them, said that they were filled with new wine. Yet, although they were ignorant, they spoke the truth, because the apostles were filled with the wine of spiritual grace.

For already “new wine in new wineskins” had come (Matt. 9), when the apostles were proclaiming God’s mighty works “not in the oldness of the letter but in the newness of the Spirit” (Rom. 7).

“Then Peter, standing with the Eleven,” as you heard in the present reading, “raised his voice and said: ‘Men of Judea, and all who dwell in Jerusalem, let this be known to you, and listen carefully to my words. These men are not drunk, as you suppose, since it is the third hour of the day.’”

The Holy Spirit, about to preach the glory of the undivided Trinity to the world, fittingly descended upon the apostles at the third hour, while they were persevering in prayer. Rightly, then, they received the Holy Spirit at the hour of prayer, so that readers might understand that the grace of the Holy Spirit is not easily received unless the mind, lifted above carnal things, is continually raised to meditate upon heavenly things.

“But this is what was spoken through the prophet: ‘I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh.’” By the word “pouring out,” he shows the generosity of the gift. The Holy Spirit was not given, as formerly, only to prophets and priests; rather, the same grace was granted freely to all believers, of both sexes, conditions, and ranks.

“And I will give wonders in heaven above, and signs on earth below.” Wonders in heaven: when the Lord was born, a new star appeared; when he ascended the cross, the sun was darkened, and heaven itself was covered with darkness. Signs on earth: when the Lord gave up his spirit, the earth trembled, tombs were opened, rocks were split, and it brought forth again many bodies of saints that had been sleeping.

“Blood and fire and vapor of smoke.” He gave blood flowing from his side, from which the salvation of the whole world proceeded; the curse was destroyed, and the whole earth was sanctified. He gave fire, that is, the Holy Spirit, who burns away all vices and sins in a human being. He gave vapor, that is, the grace of compunction and tears. The fire may also be understood as the illumination of the faithful, and the vapor of smoke as the blindness of the Jews who did not believe.

[Col. 0568D] “And it shall be: everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord will be saved.” This is what Peter says elsewhere (Acts 10): “God is not a respecter of persons, but in every nation whoever fears him and practices righteousness is acceptable to him.”

Since these things are so, consider, human being, how much you are worth, and weigh what you ought to be, so that at last you may cease to be contemptible in your own eyes, and so that, through this very consideration, you may be ashamed to remain subject to vices, while you imitate your nobility from the dignity of the Creator and Restorer.

You have reasons by which you yourself may be confounded. Why should the Lord submit to the worthy one with a feigned heart, to whom eternal glory is promised? [The reading is grammatically uncertain.] As though you seemed to be honored by a twofold privilege through participation in the divine image, you are also made precious by the nobility of this exchange.

Therefore, to understand how you can be so strong [Col. 0569A] against your enemy, examine your condition: consider what free power the Lord has conferred upon you to conquer in your members the prince of this world and overcome spiritual wickedness. Thus do not think it impossible for you to be transferred to possess heavenly things if you have conquered the powers of the air.

Therefore let not a life make you degenerate and despised whom either creation or grace has shown to have been brought forth illustrious. Rather, let Christ’s faithful people confidently raise their course toward heavenly things. For those who see that they have been redeemed at a heavenly price should not hesitate to prepare themselves for heavenly things, through our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom are honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY CIV. WEDNESDAY OF PENTECOST

[Col. 0569B]

(John 6.) “At that time Jesus said to the crowds of the Jews: ‘No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him.’” And so forth.

What does “No one can come to me” mean, except “No one can believe in me unless the Father who sent me draws him”? He comes whom God’s grace has preceded, to whom we say with the Prophet: “His mercy will precede me” (Ps. 58). And again: “His mercy will follow me” (Ps. 22). It precedes the willing and follows through to completion.

The Father draws to the Son those who believe in the Son because they think that he has God as his Father. For God the Father begot a Son equal to himself. Whoever thinks, senses, and meditates in his faith that the one in whom he has believed is equal to the Father—the Father himself draws that person to the Son.

Whoever says of Christ, “He is not the true God,” is not drawn by the Father. Rather, his perverse thought draws him into refusing to agree with the truth.

The one drawn by the Father is he who says: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matt. 16). To him the Lord says: “Blessed are you, Simon son of Jonah, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven” (ibid.). That revelation is itself the drawing.

For when he said, “No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him,” he immediately added: “And I will raise him up on the last day.” He gives back what is hoped for: he will see what he has so far believed without seeing; he will eat what he has hungered for; he will be filled with what he has thirsted for. Where? In the resurrection of the dead, because he says: “I will raise him up on the last day.” [Col. 0569D]

“It is written in the prophets” (Jer. 31): “And they will all be taught by God.” Why did he say this, Jews? Has the Father not taught you, so that you are able to recognize me? All the people of that kingdom will be taught by God; they will not hear from human beings. And if they do hear from human beings, nevertheless what they understand is given within; within it flashes forth; within it is revealed.

Human beings can make the word sound outwardly, but they labor in vain unless God, teaching within, opens the senses. The person who is taught by God is the one whom God instructs inwardly in the knowledge and love of truth.

“Everyone who has heard from the Father and learned comes to me.” How does the Father draw? By teaching and delighting, not by imposing compulsion? No one has believed by compulsion, but by the will. The Son was speaking; the Father was teaching. The human being who was seen was speaking, but God was teaching inwardly in the heart of the hearer. Therefore he adds:

“Not that anyone has seen the Father, except the one who is from God; this one has seen the Father.” I am from the Father, and therefore I see the Father.

But what is being drawn by the Father except learning from the Father? What is learning from the Father except hearing the Father, hearing the word of the Father—that is, me?

Therefore, lest you say among yourselves, when I tell you, “Everyone who has heard from the Father and learned”: “We have never seen the Father; how could we have learned from the Father?”—hear from me: “Not that anyone has seen the Father, but the one who is from God; this one has seen the Father.” I know the Father; I am from him. But how am I the Word from him whose Word I am—not a word that sounds and passes away, but one that remains with the speaker and draws the hearer?

“Amen, amen, I say to you: whoever believes in me has eternal life.” The Lord wished to reveal what he was. He could have said briefly: “Whoever believes in me has me.” For Christ himself is true God and eternal life. Whoever, therefore, believes in me comes to me; and whoever comes to me has me. What does it mean to have me? To have eternal life.

Eternal life assumed death. It wished to die, but it took death from you, human being, not from itself. It received from you what would enable it to die for you. Thus life assumed death, so that life might kill death.

For he says: “Whoever believes has eternal life”—not what is apparent, but what is hidden. Eternal life is the Word who in the beginning was with God, and the Word was God, and the life was the light of human beings (John 1). He came to die, but on the third day he rose again.

“I am,” he says, “the bread of life.” And what were they proud of? “Your fathers,” he says, “ate manna in the wilderness, and they died.” Why did they eat and die? Because they believed what they saw; they did not understand what they did not see.

Therefore they are your fathers because you resemble them: murmuring fathers of murmuring children. Moses and Aaron ate, and the other holy people who were among the people ate manna, yet they did not die, because they understood the visible food spiritually, hungering spiritually.

Others ate and remained in unbelief, just as the Jews heard Christ speaking but did not understand his words spiritually. Therefore he said to them: “Your fathers ate manna in the wilderness, and they died.”

By what death, except the death of unbelief? For they died the common death, as did the holy people who were among them. Therefore the Lord signified by these words spiritual, not bodily, death.

The fathers of these people, then—that is, evil fathers of evil people, unbelieving fathers of unbelievers, murmuring fathers of murmurers—were so called because that people is said to have offended God in nothing more than by murmuring against him.

Therefore, wishing to show them to be the children of such fathers, the Lord began by saying to them: “Why are you murmuring among yourselves, murmuring children of murmuring fathers? Your fathers ate manna in the wilderness, and they died.” Not because it was evil, but because they ate it wrongly.

“This is the bread that comes down from heaven.” The manna signified this bread; the altar of God signified this bread. These are sacraments, and those were sacraments: they differ in their signs, but in the reality signified they are equal.

Hear the Apostle: “I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, that our fathers were all under the cloud, and all passed through the sea, and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea, and all ate the same spiritual food” (1 Cor. 10).

Spiritual food, certainly, not bodily food: they had manna, we have another spiritual food. But they were our fathers, not the fathers of those whom we resemble, not of those whom they resembled.

“This, then, is the bread that comes down from heaven,” [Col. 0571B] “so that if anyone eats of it, he will not die.” But this refers to the power of the sacrament, not to the visible sacrament: the one who eats inwardly, not outwardly; the one who eats in the heart, not the one who presses with the tooth.

“I am the living bread that came down from heaven.” It is living for this reason: because it came down from heaven. Manna also came down from heaven, but manna was a shadow; this is the truth.

“If anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever. And the bread that I will give is my flesh for the life of the world.”

When could flesh grasp what he called bread flesh? It is called flesh, though flesh cannot grasp it. And for this very reason flesh grasps it even less, because it is called flesh. This is what they shuddered at; this is what they said had been presented deceptively; this is what they thought could not happen.

“My flesh,” he says, “is for the life of the world.” The faithful know the body of Christ, provided that they do not neglect to be the body of Christ. Let them become the body of Christ if they wish to live from the Spirit of Christ. No one lives from the Spirit of Christ except the body of Christ.

Whoever wishes to live should believe in Christ, eat spiritually the spiritual food, be incorporated into Christ’s body, and not be a putrid member deserving to be cut off. Let him be beautiful, healthy, and suited to his head.

## HOMILY CV. THURSDAY OF PENTECOST

(Luke 9.) “At that time: Jesus summoned the twelve apostles and gave them power and authority over all things, and to cure diseases.” And so forth.

[Col. 0571D] Having first granted them the power of signs, he sent them to preach the kingdom of God, so that the greatness of their deeds might also bear witness to the greatness of the promises, and the power displayed might give credibility to their words; thus those who preached new things might perform new things.

Therefore now also, when the number of the faithful has increased within the holy Church, there are many who possess a life of virtue but do not possess signs of virtue. For it is useless to display a miracle outwardly if the work to be done inwardly is lacking. For, in the words of the teacher of the nations: “Tongues are a sign not for believers but for unbelievers” (1 Cor. 14).

“And he said to them: ‘Take nothing on the road, neither a staff, nor a bag, nor bread, nor money; and do not have two tunics.’”

It is often asked how Matthew and Luke could have recalled that the Lord told the disciples not to carry a staff, when Mark says: “And he commanded them to take nothing on the road except a staff” (Mark 6).

This is resolved by understanding that “staff” was spoken with one meaning in the passage according to Mark, where it is to be carried, and with another meaning in the passage according to Matthew and Luke, where it is not to be carried. The same distinction applies to the temptation of which it is said, “God tempts no one” (Jas. 1), and to that of which it is said, “The Lord your God is testing you, to know whether you love him” (Deut. 13). The first is temptation through seduction; the second is testing.

Both, therefore, are to be understood as having been said by the Lord to the apostles: both that they should carry no staff and that they should carry nothing except a staff.

For when, according to Matthew, he said to them (Matt. 10), “Do not possess gold or silver,” and so forth, he immediately added: “For the worker is worthy of his food.” From this he clearly showed why he did not want them to possess or carry these things—not because they are unnecessary for the support of this life, but because he was sending them in such a way as to show that these things were owed to them by those to whom they proclaimed the Gospel and who believed.

It is clear that the Lord did not command this as though evangelists ought to live from no other source than those to whom they proclaim the Gospel. Otherwise the Apostle would have acted contrary to this command when he supported himself by the labor of his own hands, so that he might not be a burden to anyone (2 Cor. 12). Rather, the Lord gave them authority, by which they would know that these things were owed to them.

When something is requested from the Lord, failure to do it is a fault of disobedience. But when authority is given, each person is permitted not to use it and, as though withdrawing from his own right, to renounce it.

Thus the Lord established what the Apostle says he established: that those who proclaim the Gospel should live from the Gospel.

He was speaking to the apostles so that, secure in this authority, they would not possess or carry the necessities of this life, neither great nor small. Therefore he mentioned “neither a staff,” showing that everything was owed by his faithful people to his ministers, provided that they demanded nothing superfluous. By adding, “For the worker is worthy of his food,” he made entirely clear and illuminated the reason for all these instructions.

For he signified this authority by the name “staff” when he said: “They should take nothing on the road except a staff,” so that it might be understood that, through the authority received from the Lord—which he signified by the name “staff”—even what is not carried will not be lacking.

The same should be understood concerning the two tunics: none of them should think that, besides the one with which he was clothed, he ought to carry another, anxious lest he should need it, since he could receive one through that authority.

But when, according to Mark, he prohibits not merely carrying or having two tunics but more expressly prohibits wearing them, saying, “and they should not put on two tunics,” what does he urge them to do except to walk not in duplicity but in simplicity?

Alternatively: by “two tunics” he seems to me to indicate a double garment—not that in places of Scythia, rigid with icy snow, a person ought to be content with one tunic, but that by the tunic we should understand clothing, so that, clothed in one garment, we should not reserve another for ourselves out of fear of the future.

[Col. 0573A] “And into whatever house you enter, remain there, and do not leave from there.” He gives a general command concerning steadfastness, so that they may observe the obligations of hospitality. For he declares it foreign to a preacher of the heavenly kingdom to hurry from house to house and violate the obligations of inviolable hospitality by changing lodgings.

Nor is it without purpose that, according to Matthew, the house into which the apostles are to enter is determined in advance, so that the opportunity to change lodgings and violate the obligations of hospitality may not prevail.

“And whoever does not receive you, when you leave that city, shake even the dust from your feet as a testimony against them.” The dust is shaken from the feet as a testimony to their labor: that they entered the city and that the apostolic preaching reached them.

Or the dust is shaken off so that they may accept nothing from those who despised the Gospel—not even what is necessary for sustenance.

Allegorically, those who humbly attend to the word, if they are obscured, as human beings, by the stains of earthly frivolity, are immediately cleansed by the traces of evangelical preaching that they receive. But communion with those who despise these things through unbelief, negligence, or even deliberate purpose is to be avoided, and their synagogue is to be shunned.

The dust of the feet must be shaken off, lest the pure mind’s footprint be polluted by empty deeds comparable to dust.

“But they went out and traveled through the villages, preaching the Gospel and healing everywhere.” What the apostles preached and how they healed, Mark explains more fully: “They preached,” he says, “that people should repent; and they cast out many demons, and anointed many sick people with oil, and they were healed” (Mark 6).

James also says: “Is anyone among you sick? Let him summon the presbyters of the Church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with holy oil in the name of the Lord; and if he is in sins, they will be forgiven him” (Jas. 5).

From this it is clear that this custom of the holy Church was handed down by the apostles themselves: that the sick person should be anointed with oil consecrated by episcopal blessing.

“They preached that people should repent,” and so forth. “He sent them,” he says, “to preach the kingdom of God,” because, following the example of John the Baptist and of the Savior himself, they preached both things: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is near” (Matt. 3).

For the kingdom of heaven’s drawing near to the doors means that each person should repent of the things by which he had departed from it.

## HOMILY CVI. FRIDAY OF PENTECOST

[Col. 0573D]

(Matthew 12.) “At that time Jesus said to the crowds: ‘If I cast out demons by the Spirit of God, by whom do your sons cast them out?’” And so forth.

Here the Trinity appears to be called a trinity because the whole is one. For although there are three, they are one, since each remains in itself, and all are in all. Therefore the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are trinity and unity: the same reality is one and the same reality is three; one in nature, three in persons. One because of the communion of majesty; three because of the distinct property of the persons.

When he says, “I cast out demons by the Spirit of God,” he shows that the Father and the Son are believed to work through the cooperation of the Holy Spirit, as the Psalmist bears witness, saying: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the breath of his mouth all their power” (Psalm 32). Because he proceeds from the Father and the Son, the Holy Spirit is therefore proclaimed God and possesses his substance. For nothing other than what the Father himself is could proceed from the Father.

He is called “Spirit” according to that which refers to something else—breathing and inspiring—and thus he is also called spirit from this. More properly, in a certain sense, he is called the Holy Spirit according to his relation to the Father and the Son, because he is their Spirit. The term “spirit,” however, is not used only according to what refers to something else, but also according to what signifies a certain nature. For every incorporeal nature is called spirit in the Holy Scriptures.

The “principal spirit” is nevertheless read in Psalm 50. Since “spirit” is repeated there three times, some understand the Trinity to be signified: in the principal spirit, the Father; in the upright spirit, the Son; in the Holy Spirit, the Holy Spirit.

“I cast out demons.” The demons are called by the Greeks δαίμονας (*daímonas*), that is, “those who are experienced and knowledgeable in matters.” They know many future things in advance, and therefore are accustomed to give certain oracles. Before their transgression they indeed bore celestial bodies; after their fall, however, they were changed into an aerial condition. They were not permitted to possess the former regions of the air, but only these dark places, which are for them like a prison until the time of judgment. Afterward they will be tormented without end in unquenchable fire. These are the transgressing angels, whose prince is the devil.

This distinction of spirits is thus shown to be plainly established in part. We must return to the consolation of believers.

[Note: [Col. 0573D] Here something is either missing or superfluous.]

“Therefore the kingdom of God has come upon you.” That is: if you believe that I cast out demons by the Spirit of God—that is, if you believe that I am equal to the Father in divinity—the kingdom of God is open to you.

The kingdom of God means that lofty throne concerning which it is sung in Holy Scripture: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is near” (Matthew 3). And again, against the reprobate: “The kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a nation producing its fruits” (Matthew 22). And elsewhere, to the disciples: “The kingdom of God is within you” (Luke 17), that is, Christ, who is the perfect portion of the kingdom of the righteous.

“Or how can anyone enter the house of a strong man and seize his goods, unless he first binds the strong man? And then he will plunder his house.”

He introduces another comparison involving a strong man, just as he had previously spoken of a kingdom and a city. The meaning is: How could I have cast out demons if I did not have their prince consenting and unbound? Or it may simply be understood that the strong man is the devil, who was bound by Christ on the cross, and whose house is the world lying in wickedness. His goods are unbelieving human beings, whom the Lord took away from him.

“Whoever is not with me is against me; and whoever does not gather with me scatters.”

It is as though he said: The works of the Savior cannot be compared with the works of Beelzebub. The one desires to hold souls captive; the other liberates them. The one preaches idols; the other the knowledge of the one God. The one draws people toward vices; the other toward virtues. The one gathers them into the knowledge of the one God; the other scatters them by persuading them of many useless things.

Or, “whoever is not with me” means the unbelieving heretic who constantly resists my faith. “Whoever does not gather with me scatters”: destroying unity, he divides it into many heresies.

Morally: “Whoever is not with me” means whoever is not obedient to my commandments and resists my will. “Whoever does not gather with me” means whoever does not collect his affections into the love of God but scatters them among the various desires of the world.

“Therefore I say to you: Every sin and blasphemy will be forgiven human beings.”

Such is the saying: “This man does not cast out demons except by the prince of demons.” “Every sin”—whatever may be said against the Son of Man—will be forgiven through repentance. But “the blasphemy of the Spirit,” by which that through which salvation is accomplished is blasphemed, “will not be forgiven.”

Whoever speaks the aforementioned sin against the Son of Man—that is, whoever is scandalized by the lowliness of my flesh, saying that I am the son of a carpenter and of Mary, and so forth—although he is not free from the guilt of error, nevertheless receives pardon, on account, namely, of the lowliness of the flesh.

“Whoever speaks against the Spirit.” This means the person who plainly understands the works of God but, unable to deny them, says through envy of the Holy Spirit that they were accomplished by Beelzebub.

“Neither in this age nor in the age to come will it be forgiven him.” He shows that there are certain sins that are forgiven in the judgment through purgatorial fire.

“Or make the tree good and its fruit good.”

He concludes them by a syllogism. If, he says, the devil cannot perform good works, and if what you see is good, you must understand that it is not the devil who performs it. For it cannot happen that good comes from evil, or evil from good.

The good tree is Christ; the bad tree is the devil. It is as though he said: “O Pharisees, good fruit will come from me when I heal the world; but evil fruit will come from you when you crucify me.”

“Brood of vipers, how can you speak good things, since you are evil? For out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks.”

It is as though he had said: The fruit of a good tree does not come forth from you, but leaves—that is, words only, and not works.

“A good person brings good things out of a good treasure, and an evil person brings evil things out of an evil treasure.”

This must be joined to what precedes. Just as a good person does not bring forth evil things, nor an evil person good things, so Christ cannot do evil, nor can the devil do good. This is to be understood of Christ and the Jews.

“But I say to you…”

It is as though he said: A word that does not edify those who hear it will not be without danger for the one who speaks it. How much more dangerous, then, is it for you, who slander the works of the Holy Spirit by saying that they are the works of Beelzebub?

“An idle word.” An idle word is one spoken without benefit to the speaker or the hearer, whether it lacks reason and piety, or whether it accomplishes neither good nor evil.

“He will give an account,” that is, of his own soul.

“For by your words you will be justified, or by your words you will be condemned.”

That is, either here or in the future. Through the speech of the mouth, therefore, the Lord indicates all that we bring forth from the heart by action, deed, or thought—things that are more naked and open to his eyes than if they were spoken to human beings.

For it is also the custom of Scripture to use words in place of realities. Hence the Psalmist says: “Say to my soul: I am your salvation” (Psalm 34). And Hezekiah says: “There was no word that I did not show them” (Isaiah 65). He plainly revealed to the Chaldeans the secrets of things, not merely of words.

Likewise the Apostle says: “No one says ‘Lord Jesus’ except in the Holy Spirit” (1 Corinthians 12), meaning: No one perceives the Lord Jesus with understanding, and no one embraces him by the will, except through the grace of the Holy Spirit.

## HOMILY 107. SATURDAY AFTER PENTECOST

(Luke 4.) “At that time: Rising from the synagogue, Jesus entered the house of Simon. Simon’s mother-in-law was held by a severe fever.” And so forth.

When Jesus had come into Peter’s house, he saw his mother-in-law lying there and suffering from fever. He touched her hand, and the fever left her. Mark and Luke relate this event before they speak of the leper. But the diversity of narration presents no difficulty when the same event is being announced, especially since Luke writes a historical account, as was said above: “Rising from the synagogue, Jesus entered the house of Simon.” Matthew, however, followed the order of the mystery.

“Synagogue,” which is said to be the place from which Jesus arose, is rendered in Latin as *congregatio*, “assembly,” a name that the people of the Jews retained as their own. Their assembly is properly called a synagogue, although it has also been called a church. The apostles, however, never called ours a synagogue, but always a church—either for the sake of distinction, or because there is some difference between a gathering, from which *synagogue* takes its name, and a calling together, from which *church* takes its name. Animals are accustomed to be gathered together, and we properly call their groups “flocks”; beings who use reason, such as human beings, are more properly called together.

“He entered the house of Simon.” Spiritually, Simon Peter’s house signifies the Church.

A mother-in-law is the mother of one’s wife; the father of one’s wife is called a father-in-law. Peter’s mother-in-law signifies the synagogue, which Jesus found lying there and feverish—that is, remaining in the letter of the law and in envy. At the end it will believe, once the Gentiles have been saved, as it is written: “When the fullness of the Gentiles has come in, then the remnant of Israel will be saved” (Romans 9).

“She was held by a severe fever, and they appealed to him on her behalf. Standing over her, he rebuked the fever, and it left her.”

If we say that the man freed from a demon—shortly above, as the Gospel text relates—morally signifies the mind cleansed from impure thought, then, correspondingly, the woman seized by fever but healed at the Lord’s command signifies the flesh restrained from the heat of its desire through the commandments of continence.

Every bitterness, anger, indignation, shouting, and blasphemy is the fury of an unclean spirit. Understand fornication, uncleanness, lust, evil desire, and greed—which is the worship of idols—as the fever of seductive flesh.

“Standing over her, he rebuked the fever, and it left her.” It is asked why Peter’s mother-in-law is healed in third place. Is it because a woman was the third person to err at the beginning of the world? Or because the synagogue arose from Noah’s third son, Shem, whose figure it bears?

But the Lord our Savior heals the sick sometimes when asked and sometimes of his own accord. He shows that, against the sufferings of sins as well, he both always inclines to the prayers of the faithful and grants those things which they themselves scarcely understand in themselves, either giving them understanding or removing them even when they do not understand them, according to the Psalmist’s petition: “Who understands his offenses? Cleanse me, Lord, from my hidden faults” (Psalm 18).

“And immediately she rose and ministered to them.”

It is natural for those suffering from fever, when health begins, to be weak and to feel the discomfort of their illness. But health that is bestowed by the Lord’s command returns all at once. It not only returns, but is accompanied by such strength that she is immediately able to minister to those who had helped her.

In accordance with the laws of tropology, the members that had served uncleanness for iniquity, as though to sacrifice to death, now serve righteousness for eternal life.

“When the sun had set, all those who had sick people suffering from various diseases brought them to Jesus. And he laid his hands on each of them and healed them.”

The setting of the sun signifies the passion and death of the one who said: “As long as I am in the world, I am the light of the world” (John 9). When the sun had set, more demoniacs than before were freed, and more sick people were healed. For the one who, while living temporarily in the flesh, taught only a few Jews, after trampling down the kingdom of death, transmitted the gifts of faith and salvation to all the nations throughout the world.

Concerning his ministers, as heralds of the way and of the light, the Psalmist sings: “Make a way for him who ascends over the setting” (Psalm 67). The Lord ascended over the setting, because from the place where he set in his passion, he manifested his greater glory by rising again.

“Demons also came out of many, crying out and saying: ‘You are the Son of God.’ And rebuking them, he did not allow them to speak, because they knew that he was the Christ.”

The demons confessed that he was the Son of God, and the evangelist bears witness: “They knew that he was the Christ.” The devil had recognized him as a human being when he was exhausted by forty days of fasting, but, unable to discover through temptation whether he was the Son of God, he now either understood—or rather suspected—through the power of his signs that he was the Son of God.

He therefore did not persuade the Jews to crucify him because he thought that he was not the Christ or the Son of God, but because he did not foresee that he himself would be condemned by his death. For the Apostle truly says of this mystery, hidden from the ages, that none of the rulers of this age knew it: “For if they had known it, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Corinthians 2).

Why does the Lord forbid the demons to speak about him? The Psalmist makes this clear when he says: “But to the sinner God says, ‘Why do you recite my statutes?’” and so forth (Psalm 49). He did this so that no one, while hearing one who preached, might follow one who was in error.

The devil is an improper teacher, who often mixes falsehoods with truths so that, under the appearance of truth, he may conceal the testimony of fraud.

Elsewhere, not only the demons, who confessed unwillingly, are ordered to keep silent about Christ, but also those who had been healed by him and wished to confess him willingly; indeed, even the apostles, who were to preach him throughout the whole world after the resurrection, are commanded to say nothing about him before his passion. This was so that, once his divine majesty had been preached, the dispensation of his passion might not be postponed, and, if the passion were delayed, the salvation of the world that was to come through it might be denied.

“When day came, he departed and went into a deserted place. The crowds searched for him, came as far as he was, and tried to keep him from leaving them.”

If the setting of the sun expresses the death of the Lord and Savior, why should his resurrection not be understood when the day returns—he who is sought in manifest light by crowds of believers and, found in the desert of the nations, is detained lest he depart—especially since this departure, search, and discovery occurred on the first day of the week, on which the resurrection was celebrated?

He said to them: “I must evangelize the kingdom of God to the other cities also, because for this I was sent.”

As Mark says (Mark 1), he went into the desert of the nations, and there he prayed in his faithful people, because by the grace of his Spirit he stirred their hearts to the virtue of prayer.

## HOMILY 108. ON THE OCTAVE OF PENTECOST

(John 3.) “At that time: There was a man from the Pharisees, named Nicodemus, a ruler of the Jews.” And so forth.

Just as the ignorance of one person can sometimes harm many, so the question of one person can benefit many. We can very easily confirm this in the text of this reading if we attend carefully to Nicodemus’s question and the Lord’s answer.

For one person is usefully ignorant when, in response to one person’s question, not one but many learn something beneficial. As the Gospel reading reported above, when the Lord was preaching in Jerusalem on a feast day, many Jews believed in his name, seeing the signs that he performed. Jesus himself, however, did not entrust himself to them, because he knew everyone and had no need for anyone to testify to him about a human being. He himself knew what was in a human being.

Among those who had believed, this Nicodemus was one. Since he had acquired some elementary knowledge of heavenly teaching and desired to be instructed more fully, he came to him at night, wishing to enjoy a more private conversation with him.

The night in which he came signifies the very ignorance by which he was oppressed. For because he did not yet believe that Jesus was the true God, but approached him as a teacher from whom he was to learn, he appropriately came not in the day but in the night.

He was not among those who deserved to hear from the Apostle: “Once you were darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Ephesians 5). Rather, he is shown to belong among those to whom it is said through the prophet: “Rise, shine, Jerusalem, for your light has come” (Isaiah 60), and through the Apostle: “Rise, sleeper, and arise from the dead” (Ephesians 5).

Or certainly, because he was a ruler of the Jews, Nicodemus came to Jesus at night because he feared that some danger threatened him, not only from the Jews but also from the Romans. For the Jews had already conspired that if anyone openly confessed him as Christ, he would be expelled from the synagogue.

He disclosed his ignorance not only by coming at night, in the literal circumstances of the time, but also in his words, when he said to him:

“Rabbi, we know that you have come from God as a teacher.”

He understood from the vision of his miracles that Jesus had been sent by God to teach heavenly doctrine, but he did not yet believe that he himself was the true God. Therefore he said: “Rabbi, we know that you have come from God as a teacher.”

“Rabbi” and “teacher” are one and the same. In Hebrew, *rabbi* is rendered in Latin as *magister*, “teacher.” If he had believed perfectly that Jesus was the true God, he would have called him Lord rather than teacher. But by calling him teacher and remaining silent about Lord, he showed that he did not yet believe perfectly.

He had not yet been filled with the one who casts out fear; rather, he belonged among those of whom it is said: “They loved the glory of human beings more than the glory of God” (John 12).

Accordingly, he appropriately represents the catechumens, that is, those who are being instructed in the faith in preparation for receiving baptism. When questioned, they confess that they believe he is God, yet they do not understand his hidden mysteries, nor do they grasp the sacrament of his body and blood.

But we who are rooted in the foundation of the faith should believe essentially concerning him what Nicodemus speaks as though foolishly. For he is the true teacher, from whom all wisdom proceeds, and with whom wisdom has always existed and exists before the ages. Without his teaching, even the one who seems wise to himself is proved foolish.

He said to his disciples: “You call me Teacher and Lord, and you speak rightly, for so I am” (John 13). And again: “Do not be called Rabbi, for one is your teacher” (Matthew 23).

Let us also believe that he came from God, according to what he himself says in the Gospel: “I have not come of myself, but my Father sent me” (John 8). And again: “He who sent me is with me” (ibid.). And elsewhere: “I am going to him who sent me” (John 16). And again: “I came forth from the Father and came into the world” (ibid.).

Paul writes concerning his coming: “When the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son,” and so forth (Galatians 4).

When Nicodemus added: “For no one can perform these signs that you perform unless God is with him,” let us believe not only that the things the Lord performed could not be done without him, but that nothing good, however small, can be done without him. He says in the Gospel: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15).

Nevertheless, through his grace many have been enabled to do what would have been entirely impossible without him, as he himself says: “Whoever believes in me will also do the works that I do, and will do greater works than these” (John 14).

From the power of the miracles, Nicodemus believed that Jesus had been sent by the Lord, or that he was some great man, such as Moses, Elijah, or one of the prophets. But he believed that Jesus could not possess this power in himself, but received it from God.

Because Nicodemus was concerned for his salvation and had come to question the teacher of truth, he heard not only about the mystery of the second birth, but also about the mystery of the passion, resurrection, and ascension into heaven. For it follows:

“Jesus answered and said to him: ‘Amen, amen, I say to you, unless someone is born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God.’”

Every human being is held bound by the chain of original sin until washed through the water of baptism and the grace of the Holy Spirit, as the Psalmist testifies: “For behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother conceived me” (Psalm 50). And as it is said through blessed Job: “No one is clean from sin, even if his life upon earth has been but one day” (Job 4; 25).

But Nicodemus, who had come to the Lord at night and did not yet understand the mystery of the second birth, said to Jesus:

“How can a person be born when he is old? Can he enter his mother’s womb a second time and be born?”

In these words he does not declare what he hears to be impossible; rather, he asks how it can happen. But what he says about a bodily birth, we must understand spiritually.

Just as a person cannot enter his mother’s womb again and be born, so one who has been baptized is not to be baptized again. Whether he has been baptized by a heretic or by any criminal, in the name of the Holy Trinity, he is not to be baptized again, lest the invocation of so great a name appear to be annulled.

Neither a wicked person can perform this sacrament worse, nor a good person better, because whatever the external minister may be, the Holy Spirit is the internal agent. Therefore, after baptism, the Church imposes penance on sinners, but does not repeat baptism.

The Lord reveals the manner in which spiritual birth is accomplished when he answered Nicodemus’s question, saying:

“Amen, amen, I say to you, unless someone is born of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God.”

In the proper order of baptism he fittingly placed both water and the Holy Spirit. Water washes the body, but the Holy Spirit renews the mind. Water would be superfluous if the Holy Spirit did not forgive sins.

Water therefore signifies outwardly what the Holy Spirit accomplishes inwardly, namely, the cleansing of sins. Thus water contributes to the washing, while the Spirit contributes the grace.

John baptized the people with water, not for the forgiveness of sins but for repentance, saying: “I baptize with water; but among you stands one whom you do not know. He is the one who baptizes with the Holy Spirit and with fire” (John 1).

After the one who, by a unique privilege, deserved to have the Holy Spirit descend upon him in the form of a dove and remain upon him had come, and after he sanctified our baptism through his own baptism, we believe that all who believe receive the forgiveness of sins.

Concerning this baptism the Lord says: “You will be baptized with the Holy Spirit not many days from now” (Acts 1). And again: “You will be baptized with my baptism.” And again: “I have a baptism with which I must be baptized” (Luke 12).

But because after sin the flaming sword and the revolving sword had been placed at the entrance of paradise (Genesis 3), it was necessary that, once sins had been forgiven through the Holy Spirit, the entrance should again be opened to believers through baptism.

Because the invisible Spirit works invisibly, he rightly adds:

“What is born of the flesh is flesh, and what is born of the Spirit is spirit.”

It is as though the Lord said: Just as flesh is born from flesh, so the human spirit is renewed through the Spirit of God.

Hence the Apostle says: “Be renewed in the spirit of your mind, and put on the new person, who according to God has been created in righteousness and the holiness of truth” (Ephesians 4).

Only the minds of the faithful understand that, when someone comes to baptism, a son of wrath descends and a son of reconciliation rises; a son of the devil descends and, through adoption, a son of God rises; a son of discord descends and a son of peace rises.

Before the eyes of the foolish and unbelieving, however, who wish to believe nothing except what they see with their eyes, everything that takes place in baptism is considered a game. Therefore, at the end, when they see the glory of the saints, they will say:

“These are the ones whom we once held in derision and as an object of reproach. We fools considered their life madness and their end without honor. How then have they been counted among the sons of God, and their lot is among the saints?” (Wisdom 5).

“Do not wonder that I said to you: You must be born again.”

Because Nicodemus could not yet fully understand what he had heard from the teacher of truth, he was greatly astonished. He knew that truth could not be mistaken, yet he did not understand how what truth had declared could happen, and therefore he wondered.

The Lord, removing his mind from astonishment, explained the mystery of the second birth more clearly, adding:

“The Spirit breathes where he wills, and you hear his voice, but you do not know where he comes from or where he goes. So is everyone who is born of the Spirit.”

The Spirit breathes where he wills because he enlightens the mind of whomever he wishes. As the Apostle says, after enumerating the gifts of the same Holy Spirit: “All these things one and the same Spirit accomplishes, distributing to each one as he wills” (1 Corinthians 12).

“And you hear his voice” when the person whom he has filled confesses God in your presence.

“But you do not know where he comes from or where he goes,” because neither his beginning nor his end can be seen.

Or certainly: “I do not know where he comes from or where he goes,” because one cannot see how he enters and leaves a human being. He has a nature that is invisible, so that even if, in your presence, the spirit of prophecy should fill someone for a time, you could not see it.

If you cannot see your own spirit with bodily eyes, although you do not doubt that you possess a spirit, how much less can you see the Spirit of God working invisibly? Yet the faithful mind does not doubt what he works invisibly.

“So is everyone who is born of the Spirit.” That is: just as the Spirit of God is invisible, so the human spirit is invisible. And just as the Spirit of God works invisibly, so the human spirit is reborn invisibly.

Whoever does not understand this invisible sacrament should inquire into it not stubbornly but humbly, just as Nicodemus continues to ask:

“How can these things happen?”

The Lord answers him: “You are a teacher in Israel, and you do not know these things?”

The Lord does not say this insultingly, as though he were mocking someone called a teacher who nevertheless remained ignorant of so great a mystery. Rather, he summons him to the way of humility, without which the door of the heavenly kingdom is not opened.

He says:

“Amen, amen, I say to you: We speak of what we know, and we testify to what we have seen, but you do not accept our testimony.”

In these words he shows the indivisible Trinity in the substance of humanity, since the one and same Son of God, speaking, says not “what I know, I speak,” but in the plural: “What we know, we speak.” For what the Son knows, the Father knows, and the Holy Spirit knows. What the Son speaks, the Father speaks, and the Holy Spirit speaks. Where there is one substance, there is no disparity of knowledge.

They did not accept his testimony because, as he himself said: “I have come in my Father’s name, and you did not receive me” (John 5).

“If I have told you earthly things and you do not believe, how will you believe if I tell you heavenly things?”

Frequently, when speaking to the disciples and the crowds, the Lord used comparisons drawn from earthly things. But if they did not believe earthly and visible things, how could they grasp heavenly things?

To give one example among many, the Lord showed him an earthly matter when he said: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2). They, however, did not understand that he was speaking about the temple of his body, and applied his words to the destruction or restoration of the material temple, saying: “This temple was built in forty-six years, and you will raise it up in three days?” (ibid.).

Whoever desires to know the heavenly mystery must gradually ascend to higher things. Therefore, after the Lord had disclosed to Nicodemus the manner of the second birth, he declared the power of his ascension, saying:

“No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven.”

Here it is asked how the Son of Man is said to have descended from heaven and, according to his own promise, to be in heaven before the ascension.

The answer is that the mediator between God and human beings, the Lord Jesus Christ, is believed to be one person from two substances, divine and human. The same person is the Son of God and the Son of Man; and the same person is the Son of Man and the Son of God.

He therefore descended from heaven through his humanity, while he was in heaven through his divinity. He ascended into heaven through his humanity, while he was always there through his divinity.

A similar statement occurs elsewhere: “I came forth from the Father and came into the world; again, I am leaving the world and going to the Father” (John 16).

Again, it is asked why he says, “No one has ascended into heaven,” and so forth, when the whole Church of the faithful believes that it will ascend to the place where it remembers that its head has gone before, according to his promise: “Father, I desire that where I am, there my servant also may be” (John 21).

The answer is that Christ is the head of all the elect, and all the elect are members of this head. The Apostle says to them: “You are the body of Christ, and individually members of it” (1 Corinthians 12).

The members, therefore, joined to their head will ascend into heaven. But because no one can ascend by his own power or merit except through the grace of the one who deigned to descend from heaven to earth, it is rightly said: “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven.”

Because the Lord Jesus Christ becomes one body with his members, whoever desires to ascend into heaven should cling to his head with all his strength.

And because the Lord’s passion had first to be completed, and only afterward his ascension declared, the Lord summons Nicodemus, a teacher of the Mosaic law, to the spiritual understanding of that same law when he adds:

“And just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up.”

Here the Lord recalls the history in the book of Numbers, where the Israelite people, afflicted by the weariness of a long journey, are said to have murmured against the Lord and Moses (Numbers 21).

For this reason the Lord sent fiery serpents among them. When many were dying from their bites, they came to Moses and said: “We are all dying; pray to the Lord for us.”

When Moses had prayed, the Lord commanded him to make a bronze serpent and place it on a pole as a sign, saying: “If anyone who has been bitten looks at it, he will live.”

A wondrous and previously unheard-of event took place. They were bitten by serpents, looked at the serpent, and were healed.

The lifting up of the bronze serpent therefore prefigured the Lord’s passion, for he was to be lifted up on the cross, as he himself deigned to explain in the present passage. Elsewhere he says concerning it: “When I am lifted up from the earth, I will draw all people to myself” (John 12).

No one should consider it unworthy that the Lord, through the humanity he assumed, is compared with a serpent. For he says of himself through the Prophet: “But I am a worm and not a human being, scorned by humanity and despised by the people” (Psalm 21).

And, as it is read in the Septuagint, the scarab cried out from the wood—that is, Christ from the cross.

Just as that serpent bore the likeness of the fiery serpents but was nevertheless free from their poison, so the Lord Jesus Christ appeared in the likeness of sinful flesh, yet drew no stain of sin from it.

The serpent was called bronze because of the infinite eternity in Christ. Bronze is a durable and highly resonant metal, and the nature of eternity had neither a beginning nor will it have an end.

Or, because bronze has a reddish color, the serpent was called bronze on account of the shedding of precious blood.

The fiery serpents, whose bites caused people to perish, signify poisonous thoughts and deadly persuasions. When these carry perverse delight as far as consent, they kill the soul as though by piercing it.

For even our first parents were deceived in paradise by the serpent’s cunning.

Thus, in a wondrous order, a serpent is set against the serpent, because by enduring passion for us, the Lord crushed the head of the ancient serpent.

Whoever wishes to be healed from the sting of original sin or from the contagion of any wound should look upon the serpent on the pole—that is, confess Christ on the cross and confess him crucified.

When, armed with such faith, he crucifies his members with their vices and desires, he will deserve not only to be freed from the danger of death but also to attain eternal life.

Hence it follows: “So that everyone who believes in him may not perish but have eternal life.”

“For everyone,” Scripture says, “who calls upon the name of the Lord will be saved” (Acts 2), just as the Savior himself says in the Gospel: “Whoever believes in me, even if he dies, will live. And everyone who lives and believes in me will never die” (John 11).

But the one truly believes who lives as Christ commands. Whoever confesses him with words but denies him by deeds does not deserve life but punishment. For, as the Apostle James says: “Faith without works is dead” (James 2). And again: “You believe that God is one? You do well. Even the demons believe—and tremble” (ibid.).

## HOMILY 109. SECOND SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST

(1 John 4.) “Beloved: God is love. In this the love of God was revealed among us, that he sent his only-begotten Son into the world, so that we might live through him.” And so forth.

As the Lord himself says: “No one has greater love than this, that someone should lay down his life for his friends” (John 15). In this the love of Christ for us was proved: that he died for us.

How was the Father’s love proved to us? Because he sent his only Son to die for us, as the Apostle Paul also says: “He who did not spare his own Son, but handed him over for us all, how will he not also give us everything with him?” (Romans 8.)

“And in this is love: not that we loved God, but that he himself first loved us.” We did not love him first; rather, he loved us first for this purpose—that we might love him. Grace, after all, precedes a human being so that he may love God, because through love he may do good works. Hence the Psalmist says: “My God, his mercy will precede me” (Psalm 58). “And he sent his Son as the propitiation for our sins.” This is also the greatest indication of God’s loving-kindness toward us: when we did not yet know how to ask him for forgiveness of our sins, he sent his Son to us, who would freely grant forgiveness to those who believe in him and call us to share in the glory of the Father.

In some manuscripts this verse is read as follows: “And he sent his Son as a *litator* [sacrificial officiant] for our sins.” A *litator* is a sacrificer. For the Son of God sacrificed himself for our sins—not an animal victim, but by offering himself. Thus Paul rightly admonishes us, saying: “Be imitators of God, as dearly beloved children, and walk in love, just as Christ loved us and handed himself over for us as an offering and sacrifice to God, for a pleasing fragrance” (1 Corinthians 4). John also brings this same teaching into harmony when he adds by way of exhortation:

[Col. 0585A]

“Beloved, if God so loved us, we also ought to love one another.” But what follows—“No one has ever seen God”—requires a more extensive discussion, since the Lord promises that those who are pure in heart will see God, and says of the saints that their angels in heaven always see the face of the Father. John himself sets forth this statement in his Gospel, where he also adds, in due sequence, how God may be seen: “The only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, he has made him known” (John 1).

[Col. 0585B]

The blessed Father Ambrose explained this as follows:

“And therefore no one has ever seen God, because no one has perceived or grasped with mind or eyes that fullness of divinity which dwells in God. ‘He saw’ must be referred to both. Finally, when it is added, ‘The only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, he has made him known,’ the vision of minds rather than of eyes is declared. For appearance is seen, whereas power is made known: the former is grasped by the eyes, the latter by the mind.”

Likewise, the blessed Augustine, discussing the same question in his book *On Seeing God*, says that, through the ineffable revelation of the Only-Begotten, who is in the bosom of the Father, the rational, pure, and holy creature is filled with the ineffable vision of God. We shall attain this vision when we have been made equal to him. For just as visible things are seen by the bodily senses, so no one has ever seen God. If he has at some time been seen in that manner, he was not seen as this nature is seen, but was seen by his will, appearing in whatever form he wished while his nature remained hidden and unchangeably within him.

[Col. 0585C]

In the manner in which he is seen as he is, he may perhaps now be seen by certain of his holy angels. By us, however, he will then be seen in this way, when we have been made equal to him. A little later, explaining the statement of Saint Ambrose, Augustine says:

“No one has ever seen God, either in this life as he is, or even in the life of the angels as visible things are seen by bodily sight, because the Only-Begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, has made him known. For what he made known was said to pertain not to the sight of bodily eyes, but to the vision of minds.”

Again, after much else:

[Col. 0585D]

“With regard to that vision by which we shall see God as he is, he urged us to cleanse our hearts. Because bodily things are called ‘visible’ in ordinary speech, God is therefore called invisible, lest he be believed to be a body. He will not deprive pure hearts of the contemplation of his substance, since this great and supreme reward is promised to those who worship and love God. The Lord himself said this when he would appear visibly to bodily eyes and promised that the invisible One would be seen by pure hearts: ‘Whoever loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and manifest myself to him’ (John 14).

“For his nature is invisible together with the Father, just as it is equally incorruptible, because the Apostle placed these qualities together when he said: ‘To the King of the ages, invisible, incorruptible’ (1 Timothy 1), commending the divine substance to human beings by whatever preaching he could. God, then, is invisible and must be sought not with the eye but with the mind. Yet just as, if we wished to see the sun, we would cleanse the eyes of the body, through which light can be seen, so, wishing to see God, let us cleanse the eye of the heart, through which God can be seen. ‘Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God’ (Matthew 5).

“But since this vision is hoped for in the future, what are we to do while we remain in the body and are pilgrims away from the Lord? What consolation are we to use, since we are not yet permitted to enjoy the divine vision?”

[Col. 0586A]

“If we love one another, God remains in us.” But no one should suppose that this love, in which God remains, is preserved by some weak and idle gentleness—or rather, not gentleness but laxity and negligence. This is not love but languor. Let love burn for correction and improvement. If there are good habits, let them expand; if there are bad ones, let them be improved and corrected. If, therefore, we love one another with sincere and disciplined love, God remains in us. The work of this love reveals him, although he does not yet appear visibly.

[Col. 0586B]

“And his love is perfected in us.” We must ask how he can say that divine love is perfected in mutual love, since the Lord declares in the Gospel that it is not a great thing if we love those who love us, unless that same love also reaches our enemies—of whom he seems here to remain completely silent. Perhaps, however, we are commanded to love our enemies as well, out of fraternal love, so that they may not remain enemies forever, but may repent of the snares of the devil and be joined to us in a brotherly covenant.

“If we love one another,” he says, “God remains in us, and his love is perfected.” Begin to love. Have you begun to love by bringing it to perfection? God has begun to dwell in you, so that, by dwelling more perfectly, he may make you perfect.

[Col. 0586C]

“By this we know that we remain in him and he in us, because he has given us of his Spirit.” How do you know that he has given you of his Spirit? Question your inmost being: if it is full of love, you have the Spirit of God, as Paul testifies when he says: “God’s love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Romans 5).

“And we have seen and testify that the Father sent his Son as the Savior of the world.” Let no one despair of salvation. Even if the diseases of sins that weigh us down are great, God almighty is the physician who saves. Let each person merely remember that the same Son of God who came in gentleness to save will come in severity to judge.

[Col. 0587A]

“Whoever confesses that Jesus is the Son of God, God remains in him, and he in God.” He speaks of a perfect confession of the heart—one that cannot be corrupted by the deception of heretics who give evil counsel, shaken by the torments of persecuting pagans, made to stumble by the example of carnal brothers, or weakened by the sluggishness of one’s own frailty.

There are indeed those who even in words deny that Jesus is the Son of God, as many are reported to have done at the very time when John was writing these things. There are also those who confess him in words but deny him by their deeds. Hence the one who now says, “Whoever confesses that Jesus is the Son of God, God remains in him, and he in God,” said a little earlier:

[Col. 0587B]

“If we love one another, God remains in us,” clearly indicating that whoever has love for the brethren bears witness that Jesus is the Son of God.

“And we have come to know and believe the love that God has for us.” We have come to know that Jesus is the Son of God and that the Father sent him as Savior of the world; and we believe in the love that God has for us. For though he had an Only-Begotten, he did not wish him to remain alone; rather, so that he might have brothers who would possess eternal life with him, he adopted them.

“God is love.” Earlier he had said this; behold, he says it again. Love could not have been commended to you more fully than by calling it God. Perhaps you were about to despise God’s gift; do you also despise God?

[Col. 0587C]

“And whoever remains in love remains in God, and God in him.” They dwell mutually in one another—the one who contains and the one who is contained. You dwell in God, but so that you may be contained; God dwells in you, but so that he may hold you up lest you fall, because, as the Apostle says of love, “love never falls” (1 Corinthians 13). How can one whom God contains fall?

“In this love is perfected with us, so that we may have confidence on the day of judgment.” Whoever has confidence on the day of judgment has love perfected in him. What is it to have confidence on the day of judgment? It is not to fear that the day of judgment will come. When someone first turns to repentance for his evil deeds, he begins to fear the day of judgment, lest, when the just Judge appears, he himself be condemned. But as he is strengthened by progress in a good way of life, he learns not to fear what he had feared, but rather to desire that the One desired by all nations may come (Haggai 2), hoping that through the merit of good action he will be crowned with the saints.

[Col. 0587D]

He explains more fully how we can have confidence on the day of judgment by adding: “Because as he is, so are we in this world.” Can a human being really be like God? We must remember what was said above: “as” does not always indicate equality, but may indicate a certain likeness. How can you say, “As I have ears, so does an image have ears”? Is it altogether so? Yet you say, “as.” If, then, we have been made in the image of God, why should we not be as God is? Not in equality, but according to our measure.

[Col. 0588A]

This, then, gives us confidence on the day of judgment: “Because as he is, so are we in this world”—namely, by imitating in this world the perfection of love whose example he provides for us daily from heaven. Concerning this the Savior says in the Gospel: “Love your enemies,” he says, “and pray for those who persecute you, so that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven, who makes his sun rise on the good and the wicked and sends rain on the just and the unjust” (Matthew 5).

“There is no fear in love”—namely, in such love as knows how, in imitation of divine goodness, to do good even to enemies and to love them—“but perfect love casts out fear.” He means the fear of which it is said: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Psalm 110). Through this fear, a person who is beginning works of righteousness fears lest the severe Judge of righteousness should come and, finding him insufficiently chastened, condemn him.

[Col. 0588B]

That love drives out fear which, on account of the merit of righteousness, has confidence on the day of judgment. Perfect love also drives from the mind fear of present adversities—the fear sought by the one who pleaded with the Lord: “Deliver my soul from fear of the enemy” (Psalm 63), and possessed by the one who said: “Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation? Or distress? Or persecution? Or famine? Or nakedness? Or danger? Or the sword?” (Romans 8), and so forth.

“Because fear has punishment.” The conscience of sins torments the heart; the thought has not yet been completed. Therefore, in the Psalm, concerning the perfection of righteousness, he says: “You have turned my mourning into joy for me; you have torn off my sackcloth and girded me with gladness, so that my glory may sing to you and I may not be pierced” (Psalm 29)—that is, so that there may be nothing to prick my conscience.

[Col. 0588C]

Fear pricks, but do not fear: love enters and heals the one whom fear wounds. “Whoever fears is not perfected in love.” Fear indeed has punishment, although, just as desired health follows the surgeon’s incision, so desired love follows fear.

Nor should it be thought contrary to these words of blessed John that the Psalmist says: “The holy fear of the Lord endures forever and ever” (Psalm 18). There are two fears. One is the fear by which people fear God lest they be sent into Gehenna. This is the fear that introduces love, but it comes in order to depart. For if you still fear God because of punishments, you do not yet love the one whom you fear in this way: you do not desire good things, but avoid evil ones.

[Col. 0588D]

Yet, because by avoiding evil you correct yourself, you also begin to desire good things. When you begin to desire good things, there will be in you holy fear—namely, fear lest you lose those very good things, lest you be sent into Gehenna, and also lest the presence of the Lord himself depart from you, since you embrace him and desire to enjoy him eternally.

“Let us therefore love God, because he first loved us.” For how could we love unless he had first loved us? Hence he himself says in the Gospel: “You did not choose me, but I chose you” (John 15). We shall therefore be perfect in love if, just as he loved us first for no reason other than our salvation, so we also love him for no reason other than love of him alone.

[Col. 0589A]

But since there are those who love God only in word, the text appropriately adds:

“If anyone says, ‘I love God,’ and hates his brother, he is a liar.” How do we prove that he is a liar? Listen: “For whoever does not love his brother whom he sees, how can he love God whom he does not see?”

What, then? Whoever loves his brother but does not love God must necessarily love God and love love itself. For God is love.
