And lest anyone dare say, “What prevents me from loving God even if I do not love my brother?” he rightly adds: “And we have this commandment from God: whoever loves God must also love his brother.”

[Col. 0589B]

How can you love the one whose commandment you hate? Who would say, “I love the emperor, but I hate his laws”? Such is not a true lover of God. Rather: “See whether I have loved your commandments, Lord,” and therefore he confidently adds, “In your mercy give me life” (Psalm 118).

# HOMILY 110. THE SECOND SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST

## (LUKE 16)

“At that time Jesus said to his disciples: ‘There was a certain rich man, and he was clothed in purple and fine linen.’” And so forth.

[Col. 0589C]

Sacred Scripture, divinely inspired, recalls not only the deeds of the good for imitation, but also narrates the torments of the reprobate, so that those whom the examples of the devout do not move to live well may at least be terrified by the punishments announced for the wicked. Both are shown in this reading, when not only Lazarus’s rest is recalled, but also the punishment of the proud rich man is brought back to memory, so that in the one the poor may have something to imitate, and in the other the rich may have something to fear.

For when the Lord had been arguing above against the vice of greed, he added an admonition, saying: “Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity, so that when it fails, they may receive you into eternal dwellings” (Luke 16). But because everyone who does not wish to be corrected of a vice becomes worse through correction, the Evangelist added, saying: “The Pharisees, who were lovers of money, heard all these things, and they mocked him.” For when the perversity of the wicked increases, preaching ought not merely to diminish, but to increase.

[Col. 0589D]

To confirm by examples what he had taught in words, the Lord added by way of a parable what we heard at the beginning of this reading, saying: “There was a certain rich man, who was clothed in purple and fine linen, and feasted splendidly every day.” He showed that the proud rich man was condemned because he had not wished to make Lazarus his friend from the mammon of iniquity.

This man is shown to have been very rich, since he is said to have been clothed in purple and fine linen. Purple is the garment of royal dignity; fine linen is a kind of exceptionally smooth and brilliantly white linen. To increase his temporal glory, he feasted splendidly every day, satisfying his belly with various arrangements of food. Feasts belong to gluttony, while costly garments belong to empty glory.

[Col. 0590A]

But the richer he was in possessions, the worse he was in torments. “The powerful,” says Scripture, “will suffer powerful torment” (Wisdom 6).

There are some who think that there is no sin in the adornment of costly clothing. If this were entirely so, the Lord would never, when mentioning the rich man clothed in purple who was tormented in hell, have prefaced it by saying: “There was a certain rich man, and he was clothed in purple and fine linen.”

And if there were no sin in the adornment of costly clothing, Peter would never have restrained women, saying: “Let there not be outward braiding of the hair, or putting on of gold, or the adornment of clothing” (1 Peter 3). The Apostle Paul likewise says in his letter to Timothy: “I want women to be adorned in proper attire, with modesty and sobriety, adorning themselves not with braided hair, or gold, or pearls, or costly clothing, but with what is fitting for women who profess devotion through good works” (1 Timothy 2).

[Col. 0590B]

And if this is to be observed by women, how much more by men? Each person’s conscience is a witness that costly clothing is sought only for empty glory. When someone is in private, where no one sees him, he does not care what sort of clothing he wears. But when he has gone out in public, he seeks costly garments—not to appear holier, but to appear more honorable than others.

Since it is a virtue to be clothed in inexpensive garments, we infer by contrast that there is sin in seeking costly clothing. If there were no virtue in plain clothing, the Evangelist would never have praised John for the roughness of his garment.

[Col. 0590C]

From these examples we can understand that we ought to seek such and such clothing as can cover nakedness and ward off the cold. The Lord showed this when, at the beginning, he clothed the first human beings not in purple but in tunics of skin. Hence Paul admonishes us, saying: “We brought nothing into this world, and neither can we take anything out of it; but having food and clothing, let us be content with these” (1 Timothy 6).

There are others who think that the precepts of the Old Testament are harsher than those of the New. But they are deceived by careless consideration, because they do not examine more subtly the precepts of both Testaments.

For in the Old Testament it is said: “You shall love your friend, and you shall hate your enemy” (Leviticus 19). But in the New the Lord says: “Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who persecute and slander you” (Matthew 5).

[Col. 0590D]

In the Old Testament, homicide is punished by death (Deuteronomy 35). In the New, the Lord says: “Whoever is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment” (Matthew 5).

In the Old it is said: “An eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth, a hand for a hand” (Deuteronomy 19). In the New it is commanded: “If someone takes what is yours, do not demand it back. And whoever wishes to contend with you in court and take your tunic, let him have your cloak as well. And whoever presses you into service for one mile, go with him two. And I say to you, do not resist evil; but if someone strikes you on the right cheek, offer him the other as well” (Matthew 5).

[Col. 0591A]

In the Old it is commanded: “You shall not commit adultery with your neighbor’s wife” (Exodus 20). In the New: “Whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matthew 5).

In the Old Testament, when another person’s property has been seized, it is restored fourfold. Here, however, the rich man is not said to have stolen what belonged to another; but because he did not give what was his, he is tormented in hell. From this we learn that the precepts of the New Testament, the more perfect they are, are also the more demanding.

“And there was a certain beggar named Lazarus.” If we examine these words of the Lord carefully, we shall find that what appears lofty among human beings is frequently low in God’s sight, and what is despised among human beings is acceptable to God.

[Col. 0591B]

Among human beings, the names of the rich are known far and wide, whereas the poor are unknown even to many of their fellow citizens and neighbors. But, on the contrary, when the Lord mentions the rich man and the poor man, he remains silent about the rich man’s name as though he were unknown, while he identifies the poor man’s name as though he were more familiar. He shows that he does not know the one whom he rejects, but knows the other whom he chooses.

For he says of the rich man: “There was a certain rich man.” But of the poor man: “There was a certain beggar named Lazarus,” as though he were saying: “I do not know the proud rich man; I know the humble poor man.” The exalted Lord, although he is not a respecter of persons, sees lofty things from afar and humble things from near, “to raise the needy from the dust and lift the poor from the dung heap” (Psalm 112).

[Col. 0591C]

The Lord therefore knows those whom he has chosen and does not know those whom he rejects. Hence at the end he will say to the reprobate: “I do not know where you are from; depart from me, workers of iniquity” (Matthew 7). But to the perfect man Moses it is said: “I know you by name” (Exodus 33). And as the Apostle says: “The Lord knows those who are his” (2 Timothy 2). From this we believe that those whose names God is said to know possess great merit.

“Who lay at his gate, full of sores, desiring to be filled with the crumbs that fell from the rich man’s table, and no one gave him anything; but even the dogs came and licked his sores.”

[Col. 0591D]

“An earthen vessel is tested by the furnace,” says Scripture, “and just men by the trial of tribulation” (Ecclesiasticus 27). We see that this happened to the poor Lazarus, who, in addition to the increase of his pain, suffered the illness of sores together with the want of food.

Poverty alone would have been enough for him, even if illness had been absent. And again, illness alone could have been enough, if need had been absent. But to increase his pain, need was added to illness, so that he might be more acceptable in God’s sight the more harshly he had been baked in the fire of tribulation.

[Col. 0592A]

Here we must consider that the almighty Lord, the most equitable judge, carried out two judgments in one and the same circumstance, so that from the same thing reward might increase for one and punishment for the other.

Perhaps this rich man would have had an excuse based on mercy if he had not seen the afflicted poor man lying before his gate. But when he saw the wretched man and refused to have compassion, he closed every avenue of excuse for himself.

The poor man, however, endured greater tribulation of mind in addition to the poverty of his body, since he saw the rich man feasting splendidly every day while he himself longed for fragments of crumbs; he saw the rich man surrounded by crowds of attendants while no one visited him.

[Col. 0592B]

That he was despised by human beings is testified by the dogs, which freely licked his sores. This happened, as we have said, by the just judgment of God, so that from the same thing testing might increase for one and condemnation for the other.

But will one of them always be in tribulation and the other always in glory? No. Hear what follows:

“Now it happened that the beggar died and was carried by the angels into Abraham’s bosom. The rich man also died and was buried in hell.”

From this passage we can gather that an angel is assigned to each of the elect for his protection, according to what the Apostle says: “Are they not ministering spirits sent out for service on behalf of those who are to inherit salvation?” (Hebrews 1). And as the Lord says of little ones: “Their angels always see the face of my Father” (Matthew 18). For it was also said concerning Peter, who was knocking at the door: “It is his angel” (Acts 12).

[Col. 0592C]

As long as the elect remain in the present life, where “the corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks of many things” (Wisdom 9), they necessarily need to be strengthened by the help of angels, according to what is written in the person of the just man: “He has commanded his angels concerning you, to guard you in all your ways. They will carry you in their hands, lest you perhaps strike your foot against a stone” (Psalm 90).

Although the eye of the divine majesty always and everywhere observes our deeds and thoughts, we nevertheless believe that worthy works and righteous almsgiving are reported by angels to God, according to what the angel of Tobit says: “When you were praying, I offered your prayers before God” (Tobit 12).

[Col. 0592D]

Hence the angel says to Daniel: “From the day when you set your heart to understand and humbled yourself before the Lord, your words were heard, and I came because of your words” (Daniel 10).

Those who assist the elect while they labor in this life receive them when they depart from the body. This is confirmed in the present example, where it is said: “Now it happened that the beggar died and was carried by the angels into Abraham’s bosom.”

Abraham’s bosom in this passage signifies the rest of the blessed, according to what he says elsewhere: “Many will come from east and west and recline with Abraham and Isaac and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 8). Just as we are confident and secure concerning something that we hold in our bosom, so the elect, gathered into the lap of the heavenly kingdom, are strengthened by eternal security.

[Col. 0593A]

But just as we should hear with joyful heart the words, “Now it happened that the beggar died and was carried by the angels into Abraham’s bosom,” so we should greatly fear what follows: “The rich man also died and was buried in hell.”

He is said to have been buried in hell, although the spirit does not need burial, in order to show the greatness of his punishments. Burial is owed to the dead; and therefore, because he was dead in body, he is said to have been buried in hell in soul, since he will be tormented without end.

For just as “the death of his saints is precious in the sight of the Lord” (Psalm 115), so, on the contrary, the death of the wicked is most evil.

Let the greedy man hear this; let the lover of money hear it. What does it profit the rich miser that he leads his days amid good things when in an instant he descends to the lower realms?

[Col. 0593B]

Here, by contrast, we can gather what punishment is prepared for plunderers, since this rich man, who is said not to have stolen what belonged to another but not to have given what was his, is narrated to have been buried in hell.

If he is tormented in hell who did not give what was his, with what punishment must he be punished who takes what belongs to another? To such people Isaiah says: “Woe to you who join house to house and connect field to field, even to the boundary of the place” (Isaiah 5).

Not only robbery, but also excessive possessiveness deserves the punishment of hell, as the Judge himself will say to those who neglected care for the poor (Matthew 25): “Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire that has been prepared for the devil and his angels. For I was hungry, and you did not give me food; I was thirsty, and you did not give me drink; I was a stranger, and you did not take me in; naked, and you did not clothe me; sick and in prison, and you did not visit me.”

[Col. 0593C]

“Then they too will answer him, saying: ‘Lord, when did we see you hungry or thirsty, or a stranger, or naked, or sick, or in prison, and did not minister to you?’ Then he will answer them, saying: ‘Amen I say to you, insofar as you did not do it for one of these least ones, neither did you do it for me.’”

“For greed,” as the Apostle says, “is the root of all evils” (1 Timothy 6). Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Woe to you who are rich, for you have received your consolation” (Luke 6). And again: “How difficult it is for those who have money to enter the kingdom of heaven” (Mark 10).

Finally, to those who customarily inquire carefully whether the soul has members like those of the body or not, the present reading gives an answer. The Lord says concerning the rich man:

[Col. 0593D]

“But lifting up his eyes while he was in torments, he saw Abraham from far away, and Lazarus in his bosom. And crying out, he said: ‘Father Abraham, have mercy on me, and send Lazarus to dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue, for I am tormented in this flame.’”

Thus the rich man had eyes and a tongue, and Lazarus a finger, because the soul, according to its subtle and spiritual nature, is believed to have members, as the body does.

This is easily proved by the fact that the members of the body can do nothing without the soul. It is also shown here that not only do the good recognize the good in glory, but the wicked recognize the wicked in punishment.

[Col. 0594A]

For the rich man recognized not only Lazarus, whom he had previously seen, but also Abraham, whom he had never seen, as he testifies when he says: “Father Abraham, have mercy on me.” And when he remembers his absent brothers, it is clearly understood that he was able to recognize those whom he saw to be wicked in the present life.

This passage also shows that not only do the good, when received into eternal rest, behold the wicked in punishment, but the wicked also behold the good in glory. This is done by God’s judgment, so that from the same thing glory may increase for the saints and punishment for the reprobate.

The reprobate are tormented in two ways when they see the saints at rest: not only because they sinned, but also because they see those whom they held in contempt being rewarded. Hence, at the end, when they see their glory, they will say:

“These are the ones whom we once held in derision and as an object of reproach. We foolishly regarded their life as madness and their end as dishonored. How then have they been counted among the sons of God, and their lot is among the saints? Therefore we have gone astray from the way of truth” (Wisdom 5).

[Col. 0594B]

The righteous, however, offer God more abundant thanks the more they consider themselves delivered from greater torments—not by their own merits but by grace. This will continue until the future judgment.

Afterward, when the wicked have been removed so that they do not see the glory of God, the saints will behold the reprobate, because those who will be joined to their Creator will see nothing in creation that they do not see.

The rich man sees Abraham from far away because he refused to become his neighbor through imitation. He earnestly asks that Lazarus be sent to cool him, so that the glory of the one whose punishment he himself had refused to relieve might become his own detriment.

In all his works the Lord is most just. His just judgment is especially made clear here when it is said: “Send Lazarus to dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue.” On the tables of the rich, crumbs appear to be superfluous, whereas even a drop of water is something small for the poor.

[Col. 0594C]

Therefore, he who had denied the smallest things cannot obtain the smallest things. Because he refused to give Lazarus crumbs of bread, while placed in the heat he could not obtain a drop of water falling from his finger.

Let the greedy hear this—those who allow the superfluities of their wealth to turn to decay rather than spend them for the needs of the poor, not fearing what the Apostle James threatens them with terrifyingly, saying:

“Come now, you rich, weep and howl over your miseries that are coming upon you. Your riches have rotted, your garments have been eaten by moths. Your gold and silver have rusted, and their rust will be a testimony against you and will consume your flesh like fire” (James 5).

Such was the rich man who said in his heart: “I will tear down my barns and build larger ones.” The Lord said to him: “Fool, this night your soul will be taken from you; and whose will these things be that you have prepared?” (Luke 12).

[Col. 0594D]

“Therefore,” as the Apostle says, “we brought nothing into this world, and neither can we take anything out of it; but having food and clothing, let us be content with these” (1 Timothy 6).

Why does he specifically ask that his tongue be cooled, when he is surrounded on every side by avenging punishments and is wholly tormented, unless it is because he judges that he burns more intensely in that member?

Here it is understood that punishment is assigned to the reprobate according to the quality and quantity of their sins. The punishment is not equal for one who has sinned little and one who has sinned much. For just as not all of us are burned equally beneath one ray of the sun, so the reprobate are not all tormented equally in the punishment of Gehenna.

The subtlety of God’s judgments has this feature: through whichever member a person sins more greatly, in that member he receives a greater punishment. Since this rich man is said above to have feasted splendidly and now is said to be tormented in his tongue, it is shown that he burned in his tongue more than in his other members.

[Col. 0595A]

At banquets, excessive and empty talk commonly abounds. When the belly has been filled with various foods and drinks, the tongue immediately gives itself over to laughter, jokes, curses, slander, and other things of this sort, as it is written: “The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play” (Exodus 32).

Because he had sinned with his tongue at banquets, he burned in his tongue in torments. “For,” as Solomon says, “by the things through which one sins, by those things one is also tormented” (Wisdom 11).

But perhaps someone will ask whether the fire of Gehenna is bodily or incorporeal. To this we must answer that it is believed to be bodily in such a way that it can torment an incorporeal soul.

[Col. 0595B]

That a bodily thing can torment an incorporeal soul is not astonishing, since, while any human being is alive, the spirit is held in the body. For who would doubt that apostate angels are incorporeal spirits? Yet they are tormented without interruption by the fire of Gehenna, as Truth will say to the reprobate: “Go, accursed ones, into the eternal fire that has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matthew 25).

There is therefore no doubt that before the judgment an incorporeal soul can be tormented by bodily fire, since this is shown to be possible in the case of unclean spirits. For it is just that those who sin in soul and body together should, before the judgment, be tormented in soul, and after the judgment, in soul and body.

“And Abraham said to him: ‘Son, remember that you received good things in your lifetime, and Lazarus likewise evil things.’” [Col. 0595C] When earlier he calls Abraham “father,” and now Abraham calls him “son,” we can understand that he belonged to that same people which derived its origin from Abraham’s stock. But this must be considered most carefully: although he calls him “son,” he does not free him from punishment, because in the rigor of God’s just judgment there will be such complete equality of justice that neither son will be able to free father, nor father son; rather, each will receive according to his deeds, according to what he has done, whether good or evil. For “the sinner shall die in his sin, and the righteous shall live in the righteousness that he has practiced.” Therefore, through the prophet Ezekiel also, when the Lord foretold that a land would perish by sword, pestilence, and famine, he added, saying: “As I live, says the Lord, even if Noah and Job and Daniel were in its midst, they would not deliver sons or daughters, but they themselves would deliver their own souls by their righteousness” (Ezek. XIV). It must also be committed to the memory without forgetfulness that the rich man is addressed in Abraham’s voice: “Son, remember that you received good things in your lifetime, and Lazarus likewise evil things.”

“Now, however, he is being comforted, but you are being tormented.” In these words we understand both that the rich man had done some good for which he received good things in this life, and that the poor man had done something blameworthy for which he was cleansed by the afflictions of the present life. For God, the supremely just judge, just as he leaves no evil unpunished, so he leaves no good without reward, because he repays either in the present or in the future. Therefore, whenever the prosperity of the present life flatters us or riches overflow, we must fear that we may receive in the present age the reward for the good we are doing, lest perhaps in the future it be said to us: “Truly I say to you, you have received your reward” (Matt. VI). Whenever, however, poverty afflicts us or scourges wear us down, we ought to rejoice and give thanks, because God’s scourges come upon us either for reward or for testing. For this reason Scripture admonishes us, saying: “My son, do not despise the discipline of the Lord your God, nor grow weary when you are corrected by him. For the Lord corrects the one whom he loves, and he scourges every son whom he receives” (Prov. III).

“And in all these things a great chasm has been fixed between us and you, so that those who wish to cross from here to you cannot, nor can they cross from there to here.” [Col. 0596B] Chaos is said to mean something compact or fixed, or a confusion of the elements. For *chaos* means a gulf or depth. But in this passage we say that hell, where the rich man was being tormented, lay far below; hence a little earlier it is said: “But lifting up his eyes, he saw Abraham from afar, while he was in torment.” Before the Lord’s coming, the souls of the saints, because they could not enter through the gate of the heavenly kingdom on account of original sin, were in hidden places without punishment; compared with them, punitive hell lay far below. Therefore the Psalmist prays: “You have delivered my soul from the lower hell” (Ps. LXXXV). Thus a great chasm has been fixed—or an impassable boundary established by the rigor of God’s just judgment—so that neither these can cross to those, nor those to these. [Col. 0596C] There is no doubt that those held in places of punishment would wish to cross over to the rest of the saints. But although the righteous, established in rest, wish through the compassion of their minds to cross over to them, nevertheless, because they cannot depart from the equity of the just Judge, they are in no way able to cross to them.

But the wretched rich man, despairing of his own salvation, turned his concern toward the liberation of his brothers whom he had left in the world, saying:

“Therefore I ask you, father, to send him to my father’s house. For I have five brothers, so that he may testify to them, lest they too come into this place of torment.” By God’s just judgment, to increase his condemnation, not only knowledge but also memory was preserved for him, so that he might be tormented not only for himself but also for his brothers, whose similar destruction he feared. For vengeance for the poor man upon the rich man would not have been complete if he had not recognized Lazarus; nor would his punishment in the torments have been complete if he had not remembered the brothers whom he had left in the world. By this example we are instructed that the souls of the saints, received into eternal blessedness, are believed to intercede for the salvation of their loved ones whom they left amid the dangers of the world. And since, according to the authority of Scripture, “the one who is wicked to himself will be good to no one” (Ecclus. XIV), the rich man, pleading for his brothers, receives this answer:

“They have Moses and the prophets; let them listen to them.” But he, constrained by grief, said: “No, father Abraham; but if someone goes to them from the dead, they will repent.” And because—as Solomon says—“there is neither work, nor reasoning, nor knowledge, nor wisdom in hell” (Eccles. IX), it is added: “If they do not listen to Moses and the prophets, neither will they believe if someone rises from the dead.” By this saying it is clearer than light that those who refused to listen to Moses and the prophets were unwilling to believe in Christ rising from the dead; or that those who despise the commandments of the Old Testament cannot at all fulfill the truth of the New Testament, which proclaims Christ’s resurrection.

But since we have spoken of these matters morally, to terrify the greed of the rich and console the poverty of the poor, let us briefly see what they signify allegorically. By the rich man and the poor man, therefore, the two peoples are signified: namely, the Jewish people and the gentiles. By the rich man the Jewish people are prefigured, who received not only carnal riches but also spiritual riches through knowledge of the Law, and used them more for ostentation than for usefulness. He was clothed in purple among the martyrs, in fine linen among virgins; or purple signifies royal dignity, and fine linen priestly glory. He feasted splendidly every day, meditating on the utterances of the Fathers.

By the poor man Lazarus, on the other hand, the gentile people are designated, who were poor when they were alienated from knowledge of the Law and knowledge of God. He lay at the rich man’s gate because he could not enter within the gate of knowledge of the Law. He was full of sores, that is, defiled by various crimes of sin. He desired to be satisfied with the crumbs falling from the rich man’s table, and no one gave him any, because that proud Jewish people did not wish to give the gentiles the words that flowed from knowledge of the Law. And while it used the precepts of the Law more for exaltation than for charity and usefulness, it swelled up, as it were, from the food it had received.

The table signifies Holy Scripture, as it is written: “You have prepared a table before me in the presence of those who trouble me” (Ps. XXII). The crumbs falling from the rich man’s table are the words that, as we have said, flowed from knowledge of the Law. This poor man, namely the gentile people, desired to receive them; among these was that Canaanite woman who, when the Lord said to her, “It is not good to take the children’s bread and throw it to the dogs,” replied: “Certainly, Lord, for even the little dogs eat from the crumbs that fall from their masters’ table” (Matt. XV).

But the one whom the rich man despises, God does not disdain. For when the exalted God became a humble human being, he deigned to send his preachers not only to the Jewish people but also to the gentiles. Hence it is rightly said: “But the dogs also came and licked his sores.”

In Scripture, dogs have various meanings. Sometimes they signify the Jewish people, as is read in the Psalm: “Many dogs have surrounded me” (Ps. XXI). Sometimes they signify false Catholics, as Solomon the wisest says: “As a dog returns to its vomit, so a fool repeats his folly” (Prov. XXVI). Sometimes they signify heretics, as the Apostle says: “Beware of dogs, beware of evil workers, beware of the mutilation” (Phil. III). Sometimes they signify bad teachers, as it is said through the prophet: “All his watchmen are blind; they are all ignorant, mute dogs unable to bark, seeing vain things and loving dreams” (Isa. LVI). And again: “Impudent dogs know no satiety” (ibid.). And John says in the Apocalypse: “Outside are dogs and sorcerers and the immoral, and everyone who loves and practices falsehood” (Apoc. XXII).

But in this passage they signify good preachers, of whom the Psalmist says: “The tongue of your dogs from the enemies, from him” (Ps. LXVII). For a dog brings the wound that it licks more quickly to healing. What, then, are wounds except sins? Just as a wound bursts forth from the inner organs onto the skin outside, so sins must be revealed through confession, so that a person may attain the soul’s healing. Therefore confession of sins is nothing other than a kind of opening of wounds. When we confess our sins, we do nothing other than open what was lying hidden, poisonous, in the mind.

Thus, because the holy preachers called the gentile people to confess their sins, they healed Lazarus’s wounds by licking them, as spiritual dogs. Hence Lazarus is rightly interpreted as “helped,” because those who taught him to confess his sins helped him toward salvation. And because the gentiles became sons of Abraham through faith, it is rightly added:

“It happened that the beggar died and was carried by angels into Abraham’s bosom.” The poor man is carried into Abraham’s bosom because through faith the gentile people are gathered into fellowship with the patriarchs, the Lord saying: “Many will come from east and west and recline with Abraham and Isaac and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. VIII).

But the Jewish people, which refused to believe, is rejected because of its faithlessness. Hence it is rightly said: “The rich man also died and was buried in hell.”

At the beginning of this reading he rightly placed the rich man first and the poor man afterward; now, however, he places the poor man first and the rich man afterward, to show that the Jewish people, which had been at the head through its pride and self-exaltation, became the tail; while the gentile people, which was last through its humility, became first, because, as Solomon the wisest says: “Disgrace follows the proud, but glory follows the humble in spirit” (Prov. XXIX). Hence the Lord also says in the Gospel: “Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled” (Luke XIV, XVIII). And again: “The first will be last, and the last first” (Matt. XIX).

He sees Abraham from afar because he refused to become close to him through imitation, as we have said. He is said to suffer more in his tongue because he despised fulfilling in his deeds the words of the Law that he held in his mouth. He is also rightly said to burn more in his tongue because the Jews sharpened their tongues like serpents when they said against the author of life: “Crucify him, crucify him. We have no king but Caesar” (John XIX).

He asks to be refreshed by the tip of Lazarus’s finger because those condemned to eternal punishment would, if it were possible, wish to share even in the smallest works of the saints. Since this cannot happen after death, the rich man is rightly addressed in Abraham’s voice:

“Remember, son, that you received good things in your lifetime, and Lazarus likewise evil things. But now he is being comforted, while you are being tormented.”

The rich man testified that he had five brothers because the Jewish people received the five books of Moses. Hence Abraham rightly says: “They have Moses and the prophets.” Or because that part of the same people which still remains in the present life consists in the five bodily senses, concerning those senses which refuse to bend themselves toward spiritual understanding the text rightly adds, in condemnation of their obstinacy: “If they do not listen to Moses and the prophets, neither will they believe if someone rises from the dead.” For they do not believe in Christ, who rose from the dead, because they do not understand spiritually the words of Moses and the prophets. Hence the Savior says in the Gospel: “If you believed Moses, you would perhaps believe me also. For he wrote about me” (John V).

## HOMILY 111. THE THIRD SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST

(I John III.) “Do not be astonished if the world hates you.” And so forth. By “the world” he means those who love the world. Nor is it surprising that those who love the world cannot love a brother separated from love of the world and intent only on heavenly desires. For religion is an abomination to the sinner, as Scripture testifies.

“We know that we have passed from death to life, because we love the brethren.” Let no one falsely exalt himself because of his virtues; let no one fear the poverty of his powers beyond measure. The clear indication is “because we love the brethren”: whoever is full of fraternal love belongs to the salvation of the elect, because he has deserved to have a share in the land of the living.

“He who does not love remains in death.” He means the death of the soul. “The soul that sins shall itself die” (Ezek. XVIII). The life of the flesh is the soul; the life of the soul is God. The death of the body is to lose the soul; the death of the soul is to lose God. Hence it is evident that, dead in soul, we are all born into this light, carrying original sin from Adam; but through Christ’s grace the faithful are regenerated so that they may be able to live in soul. Yet the mystery of baptism and faith benefits only those who sincerely love the brethren; it draws them from death to life.

Therefore it must be noted that he does not say, “He who does not love will come into death,” as though he were speaking of the perpetual punishment awaiting sinners in the future. Rather, he says, “He who does not love remains in death,” from which he could also rise in this life if he loved his brethren perfectly. Hence it is said in the Apocalypse: “Blessed and holy is the one who has a share in the first resurrection; over these the second death has no power” (Apoc. XX).

“Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer.” If someone despised fraternal hatred, would he not also despise murder in his heart? He does not move his hands to kill a person, yet he is already held by God as a murderer: the other lives, but this one is already judged a killer. “And you know that every murderer does not have abiding life in himself.” For when the time of retribution comes, anyone held by this kind of murder will also be condemned with Cain, who was of the evil one (Gen. IV), so that he is at odds and in conflict and has no peace with his brethren. It must be noted that he does not say absolutely, “A murderer does not have abiding life in himself,” but “every murderer”—that is, not only the one who attacks his brother with a sword, but also the one who pursues him with hatred.

“By this we have known the love of God, that he laid down his life for us.” We have learned from the example of the Lord’s Passion what perfect love ought to be in us. “For no one has greater love than this: that someone lay down his life for his friends” (John XV). Hence Paul also says: “God commends his love toward us, because, while we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Rom. VI).

Blessed Peter was admonished to possess this love when, after the Lord said, “Peter, do you love me? Feed my sheep,” he replied that he loved him and immediately heard: “When you grow old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will gird you and lead you where you do not wish to go.” “This he said,” the Gospel tells us, “signifying by what death he would glorify God” (John XXI). For when the Lord entrusted his sheep to the one who confessed his love, he taught him to lay down his life for those same sheep as testimony to perfect love.

“And we ought to lay down our lives for the brethren.” But someone may say: How can I possess this love? Do not quickly despair of yourself. Perhaps it has been born, but it is not yet perfect; nourish it, lest it be smothered. “And how,” he says, “do I know that love has been born in me, so that I may nourish it?” Hear what follows:

“Whoever has the substance of this world and sees his brother in need, and closes his compassion against him, how does the love of God remain in him?” This is where love begins. If you are not yet capable of dying for your brother, become capable now of giving your possessions to your brother. For if you do not sympathize with one who suffers hardship, you certainly do not suffer with him; since both of you have been regenerated, love remains in you.

“My little children, let us not love in word or with the tongue, but in deed and in truth.” In deed, that is, when a brother or sister is naked and lacks daily food, let us give them what the body requires. Likewise, when we see them lacking spiritual gifts, let us provide what we can for their need. In truth, that is, let us bestow these same benefits on them with a sincere intention—not for human praise, not for boasting, and not to the injury of others who, though endowed with greater possessions, have done nothing of the kind. For wherever the mind is stained by such blemishes, the purity of truth cannot dwell, even though it may appear to bestow works of love upon its neighbors.

“By this we know that we are from the truth,” that is, when we perform works of compassion in truth, it becomes clear that we are from the truth, which is God, since we imitate his perfection according to the measure of our ability.

## HOMILY 112. THE THIRD SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST

(Luke XIV.) “At that time Jesus told his disciples this parable: ‘A certain man made a great supper and invited many.’” And so forth.

Almighty God, at the beginning of the world’s formation, created two rational creatures—the angelic and the human—to know him and praise him perpetually. But because a great part of the angelic nature fell through pride, it envied human nature while it remained standing, drew it into the fall of sin, and deprived it of the delights of paradise. Hence it is written: “Through the devil’s envy death entered the world” (Wis. II).

The first man lost these delights when he despised the commandments of life in paradise. After being expelled from paradise, he became so distant from its delights through sinning that he could scarcely remember them even when they were mentioned, and was unable to touch spiritual delights except through likenesses and parables.

There is this difference between carnal and spiritual delights: carnal delights, when possessed, become wearisome; when not possessed, they are desired. Spiritual delights, on the contrary, are wearisome when they are not possessed; once tasted, they are enjoyed, and the more they are tasted, the more they are desired. Hence the Psalmist says: “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet” (Ps. XXXIII). First he said, “Taste,” and then, “see,” as though he were saying: You cannot perceive his sweetness if you have not tasted it. The Apostle Peter likewise says: “If indeed you have tasted that the Lord is sweet” (I Pet. II).

Because, through sinning, humanity had therefore moved far away from tasting these delights, the loving and merciful God, unwilling that human nature—which had something fragile inclined toward wrongdoing—should perish forever, prepared these delights again for the penitent. And in order to announce their flavor to human beings, he sent his servant.

For, as the evangelist related above, when the Lord said to the Pharisee by whom he had been invited (Luke XIV), “When you make a luncheon or a supper, do not invite those who may invite you in return, so that you may receive a repayment; rather, invite the poor and the weak, and you will be blessed, because they have nothing with which to repay you; for you will be repaid in the resurrection of the righteous,” some of those standing nearby said: “Blessed is the one who will eat bread in the kingdom of God.” And the Lord said to them: “A certain man made a great supper and invited many.”

Spiritually, this man is to be understood as God, of whom it is written: “He is man, and who knows him?” And again: “A man was born in her, and the Most High himself founded her” (Ps. LXXXVI). He is truly called “man” because of his humanity, since he daily displays the most kindly generosity toward the human race.

He made a great supper because he prepared unfailing satisfaction in eternal sweetness for the elect souls. He invited many: first, by preaching to the Jews through himself; afterward, by the preaching of the apostles, calling the gentile people to faith from the four quarters of the world. Concerning this calling the Psalmist says: “I announced and spoke; they were multiplied beyond number” (Ps. III). The reprobate are multiplied beyond number because they are found outside the number of the elect.

Many are called, but few come, because many enter the Church through faith, but few are saved through their works. And so that people would have no excuse based on ignorance, “he sent his servant at the supper hour to say to those who had been invited that they should come.”

This servant, who is sent to invite others, signifies the order of preachers. When they announce the divine word within the Church, they call many, as it were, to the supper. For divine mercy was not satisfied merely with preparing eternal delights for us; through servants who were sent, it also announced their sweetness to us. One of these was the man who said: “We are ambassadors for Christ, as though God were exhorting through us. We beg you, on behalf of Christ: be reconciled to God” (II Cor. V).

The supper hour is the end of the world, that is, the time of which Paul says: “We are those upon whom the ends of the ages have come” (I Cor. X), and John: “Little children, it is the last hour” (I John II).

Although among the ancients it was customary to eat only once a day, and this feast was called both luncheon and supper, nevertheless, according to the usage of our speech, supper remains after luncheon, and after supper no meal remains. Therefore, not inappropriately, this supper signifies the day of judgment or that eternal banquet. Those who deserve to reach it “will hunger no more, nor thirst anymore, nor will heat or sun strike them, because their merciful one will rule them and lead them to springs of water” (Isa. XLIX).

John speaks of this supper: “Blessed are those who are called to the marriage supper of the Lamb; over them the second death has no power” (Apoc. XIX). He knew that he had a share in this supper who said: “The Lord feeds me, and I shall lack nothing; in a place of pasture he has settled me” (Ps. XXII). And again: “I shall be satisfied when your glory is revealed” (Ps. XVI).

Therefore, we ought to hasten toward this supper all the more eagerly because we know of no other to find after it, the Lord admonishing us: “Walk while you have the light of life, lest the darkness of death overtake you” (John XII).

Then, to remove any weariness, he added: “For everything is now ready.” Everything is ready because that singular Lamb has been slain, in whose preparation all things went before. Or everything is ready because there is no example of virtue that has not been displayed for our imitation in the works of the saints. We have already heard of Abel’s innocence, Abraham’s obedience, Isaac’s constancy, Jacob’s endurance, Joseph’s chastity, Moses’ gentleness, David’s mercy, Job’s patience, and we have seen the Lord’s end.

“And they all began together to make excuses.” God offers what ought to have been requested; he is ready to give without being asked something that could scarcely have been believed he would deign to bestow even when requested. The Lord’s delights must indeed be sought, even if they had been hidden. Now, however, they are plainly prepared, and yet we are sluggish and weary when it comes to receiving them. This happens because we gape after earthly desires more than heavenly ones.

Hence it follows: “The first said to him: ‘I have bought a farm, and I must go out and see it; I ask you to hold me excused.’” What is signified by the farm except earthly substance? He went out to see the farm who, in order to acquire earthly substance, entangles himself in external affairs.

There are some who, seized by desire for temporal riches, serve earthly business through various arts and devices so that they may appear richer and more powerful than others. While they scarcely or only slowly recall eternal life, they neglect to come to God’s banquet—not in words, perhaps, but in their deeds—because, as the Apostle says: “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in worldly business” (II Tim. II). And as the Lord says in the Gospel, those who have money will enter the kingdom of heaven with difficulty (Matt. XIX).

Therefore, whoever gives his whole desire to carrying out superfluous cares and worldly concerns seems to imitate the world more than God, as the Apostle James says: “Whoever wishes to be a friend of this world is constituted an enemy of God” (James IV). And again: “Those who wish to become rich fall into temptation and the devil’s snare, and into many foolish and harmful desires” (I Tim. VI).

“Another said: ‘I have bought five yokes of oxen, and I am going to test them; I ask you to hold me excused.’” What are understood by the five yokes of oxen except the five bodily senses—sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch? They are appropriately called yokes because they are doubled in the two sexes.

We receive these senses so that we may be able to distinguish between good and evil. Yet there are some who turn the bodily senses they received for the use of nature toward the use of sin: they turn their eyes toward desire, open their ears willingly to hear detraction, their tongue toward cursing, their hands toward injuring their neighbor, and their nostrils toward illicit odors.

While forgetting themselves, they investigate the deeds of others with excessive curiosity in order to disparage them—not to correct or amend them, but to judge and despise them—and therefore do not come to God’s banquet. Hence it is rightly said of the five yokes of oxen: “I am going to test them.” For testing sometimes belongs to curiosity.

Whoever tries to remove the speck from another’s eye so that he may seem holier and more righteous than the rest, while not seeing the beam in his own eye (Matt. VII), goes out, as it were, to test the yokes of oxen and does not come to the Lord’s banquet. Curiosity is a grave vice: while judging the actions of others, a person forgets himself.

Such a person was signified by Dinah, Jacob’s daughter (Gen. XLIII), who went out to see the women of that region, namely Shechem, where she had entered with her father and brothers; she was shamefully violated by Shechem, son of Hamor, and, after her father intervened and her brothers fought, she returned to her father’s house.

When the mind scrutinizes the actions of the weak with curiosity, it leaves its father’s house like Dinah, daughter of Jacob, desiring to see the women of the region (Gen. XXXIV)—that is, it departs from itself. Thus, having lost its virginity, it returns to its father’s house, because it often happens that a person falls more deeply into the same vices in which he judged others more harshly than was fitting.

And just as Dinah, Jacob’s daughter, could not be freed except through her father’s intervention and her brothers’ fighting, so the action of curiosity cannot be escaped except through the Lord’s mercy and the intervention of the saints’ prayers.

Therefore, whoever is still in girlhood—that is, whoever is still inexperienced in his way of life—should remain in his father’s house: that is, he should place himself before himself in the secret of his heart; and, according to the Gospel’s command, he should enter his room, shut the door, and pray to his Father (Matt. VI).

But those should go out to correct the actions of others whom the gravity of their conduct, the maturity of their age, long-standing holiness, and balanced discernment render capable of doing so.

It must be noted that both the one who excuses himself on account of the farm and the one who excuses himself on account of the five yokes of oxen use the same words in their excuse when they say: “I ask you to hold me excused.” When he says, “I ask you,” humility sounds in his voice; but when he adds, “hold me excused,” pride is shown in his action.

There are some weak-minded people who fear taking up Christ’s gentle yoke, yet do not fear lying in their iniquities. Of such the Psalmist says: “There they trembled with fear where there was no fear” (Ps. XIII).

When doctors preach to them that they should abandon their wrongdoings and renounce worldly desires, they usually reply: “I ask you, pray for me, but I cannot do this.” When he says, “I ask you, pray for me,” and when he says, “I cannot do this,” what else is it but that humility sounds in his voice while pride appears in his action?

Peter signified such people while he was still in weakness, when, after seeing the miracle of the fish, he said: “Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, Lord” (Luke V). But the one who considers himself a sinner must not in any way drive God from his heart; rather, the more he understands himself to be ungodly, the more he should implore God’s mercy.

“Another said: ‘I have married a wife, and therefore I cannot come.’” What is signified by the wife except the pleasure of the flesh? Nor is this surprising. An illicit thing is often represented through something lawful. Marriage is a lawful thing, because it was granted by God, as it is written: “The two will be one flesh” (Mark X). And the Apostle says: “What God has joined, let no human being separate” (ibid.).

But while many undertake it not for the desire for children but solely to satisfy the pleasure of the flesh, they refuse to come to God’s banquet. They are compared to foolish beasts and become like them, against whom the prophet speaks in condemnation: “Lustful horses and stallions, each neighing after his neighbor’s wife” (Jer. V). And again: “Their flesh is like the flesh of donkeys, and their discharge like the discharge of horses” (Ezek. XXIII). Through the Prophet it is said to them: “Do not become like the horse and the mule, which have no understanding” (Ps. XXXI).

The Lord therefore mentioned three kinds of excuses because there are spiritually three vices in which the human race is most deeply entangled and through which it disdains to come to God’s banquet. By these also the devil tempted Jesus Christ: by greed, by curiosity—which belongs to vainglory—and by the desire of the flesh, that is, by gluttony.

The Apostle John admonishes us carefully to avoid these things when he says: “Beloved, do not love the world, nor the things that are in the world, because everything that is in the world is the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes” (I John II), “and the ambition of the age.”

The purchase of the farm belongs to the ambition of the age, that is, to greed. The testing of the five yokes of oxen belongs to the desire of the eyes, that is, to curiosity. The union with a wife belongs to the desire of the flesh, that is, to lust.

Pride inflates some; lust stains others; greed or curiosity devastates others. From their roots many branches of vices spring forth, and these call many people back from God’s banquet.

Therefore, fleeing the vices just mentioned, let us not scrutinize the wickedness of others; rather, returning to ourselves, let us consider that we have been such, or that we could become such. Let us flee desire and greed, and desire to be poor for Christ, as the Apostle says: “Having food and clothing, let us be content with these things” (I Tim. VI).

Let us not merely flee wantonness, but also abstain from the lawful use of marriage; and, according to the Apostle, “those who have wives should be as though they had none” (I Cor. VII).

“And the servant returned and reported these things to his master.” This servant, as has been said above, represents the teachers. The servant therefore reports the words of those making excuses to his master when teachers grieve over their errors and simply beseech the Lord concerning those whom they know to despise the word of God and refuse to come to the supper.

But will the place at the Lord’s banquet remain empty because the greedy, the curious, and the lustful disdain to come? No. Hear what follows:

“Then the master of the house became angry.” It is asked how this master of the house is said to become angry, when we have said that he represents God, in whom there is no anger and no change. We must answer that Scripture speaks according to our manner of speaking, so that through visible things we may understand invisible things. We could not understand otherwise.

Just as a king is said to be angry when he exercises vengeance upon sinners, so Almighty God will appear angry toward those whom he punishes for their sins. In his own nature, however, he is truly unchangeable and can never become angry, as a certain wise man testifies concerning him: “But you, Lord of hosts, judge with tranquillity.” And the Apostle says: “With whom there is no change” (James I). The Psalmist also says of him: “God is a just judge, strong and patient; does he become angry every day?” (Ps. VII).

“He said to his servant: ‘Go out quickly into the streets and lanes of the city, and compel the poor and the weak, the blind and the lame, to enter.’”

The streets are so called from their breadth; the lane takes its name from fellow diners. Therefore, when the proud disdain to come, the humble poor are gathered, because it is fitting that God should choose those whom the world despises. For, as the Apostle says: “God chose the weak things of the world to confound the strong; and God chose the low-born and despised things of the world, and things that are not, to destroy things that are” (I Cor. I).

Here we can understand that bodily infirmities express infirmities of the mind. The poor and weak are those who despise themselves in their own eyes. The blind are those whom no skill illuminates with understanding of the Scriptures. The lame are those who see the way of God through understanding, yet, because of weakness of mind, fear to run along it.

Those who are gathered are therefore also held by the bond of sin, just like those who had disdained to come. But the humble poor are gathered, while proud sinners are despised. Frequently, those whom the prosperity of the world does not bind with various occupations are more easily converted to God.

“And the servant said: ‘Lord, it has been done as you commanded, and there is still room.’” As though he were saying: Some of the Jews have already believed, but room still remains for the multitude of the gentiles to enter. Concerning these it is added further:

“Then the Lord said to the servant: ‘Go out into the roads and hedges, and compel them to enter, so that my house may be filled.’”

When above the Lord commanded that some be gathered from the streets and lanes, he wished the Jewish people to be signified, since they had taken up residence in the suburbs: for they lived in the cities as though in lanes, and were, in a certain way, cultivated through the institutions of the Law. But now, when he compels others to enter from the roads and hedges, he wishes the Gentile people to be understood—uncultivated and, in a certain sense, alienated from the worship of God.

First, therefore, he sent into the streets and lanes, because he initially sent his preachers to the Jewish people, saying: “Do not go on the road of the Gentiles, and do not enter the cities of the Samaritans, but go rather to the sheep that have perished from the house of Israel” (Matthew 10). But since for the most part they did not believe, the Gentiles are summoned when it is said: “Go out into the roads and hedges, and compel them to enter, so that my house may be filled.”

The Gentile people were in the broad and spacious road that leads to death, and were bound by various crimes and sins, with winding turns like those of hedges. Or certainly, as some wish, when above he commanded that certain rich people be gathered, he signifies the Jewish people, as has been said. By those, however, who are summoned from the streets, the people of the Gentiles are designated: through the height or length of their vices, by the preaching of the apostles, they were converted from the worship of idols to the true God.

Of them it is said: “The poor and the weak,” and so forth. The Gentile people were poor, weak, blind, and lame. They were poor because they had lost the delights of paradise; weak because they were sluggish in good works; blind because they sat in darkness and the shadow of death; lame because, limping on both feet, they ceased from the right path. Thus they were ignorant of the light of truth, unable to run along the way of God’s commandments, deprived of spiritual delights, and unable to do good.

Therefore, it is not only those who are weak in body who run to the banquet, but also those who are weak in mind. The poor person is one who, although rich, nevertheless, lacking in virtues, distributes riches as a master and does not covet them as a servant. Of such people the Lord says: “Blessed are the poor in spirit” (Matthew 5).

The blind person is one who cannot behold that light which said: “I am the light of the world” (John 8). The weak person is one who does not possess perfect faith, concerning which the Lord, commending it to his disciples, said: “If you have faith,” and so forth (Matthew 17). The lame person is one who has faith without works, or works without faith. For just as “faith without works is dead” (James 2), so works without faith are nothing.

Therefore such people are summoned to God’s banquet, because “it is not the healthy who need a physician, but those who are ill” (Matthew 9).

When he says, “Go out into the roads and hedges,” he wished those who are summoned from the roads to be understood as the Jewish people, who were called, as it were, from the roads because they possessed the Law, by which they ought to walk. By the hedges, however, the Gentile people are understood. Hedges are made from the forest. Now the nation of the Gentiles is often signified by the trees of the forest, as it is written: “Then all the trees of the forest will rejoice.”

They were summoned when they abandoned the broad, spacious, and winding road that leads to death and began to walk along the straight path. Hence, after John in the Apocalypse had said that he saw twelve thousand sealed from each of the twelve tribes, he added: “After this I saw a great multitude, which I could not number” (Revelation 7).

It should be noted that in this third invitation it does not say, “Call,” but, “Compel them to enter.” For there are many who are not easily converted to God unless they have first been constrained by illness, poverty, or some necessity. This is shown by that Gospel parable about the prodigal son, who, when he began to be in need and came to himself, said: “How many hired servants in my father’s house have bread in abundance, while I perish here from hunger! I will arise and go to my father, and I will say to him: Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you; I am no longer worthy to be called your son; make me like one of your hired servants” (Luke 15).

And concerning such people the Psalmist says: “When he slew them, then they sought him” (Psalm 77). And as he says through the prophet: “Only oppression will give understanding to the hearing” (Isaiah 28).

Some of the elect desire to run after the desires of the flesh and to live a common life with lovers of the world. But the eye of divine mercy, anticipating their ungodly actions, afflicts some with illness, weakens others through poverty, and confines others through various necessities. When they are converted to God after these scourges, they are compelled, as it were, to enter his banquet.

To such people it is said through the prophet: “You will be chastised, daughter of Zion, with rod and scourge, so that my zeal may not depart from you.”

That boy, the Amalekite, signified such people. Of him we read in the Books of Kings: when his companions were fleeing, he remained weak on the road. David, pursuing the Amalekites, found him, refreshed him with food and drink, and made him the guide of his journey; afterward he struck the Amalekites together with David, from whose company the weak man had remained behind on the road (1 Kings 30).

For “Amalekite,” which is interpreted as “the licking people,” signifies lovers of the world, who desire to grow rich from the possessions of others. There are indeed some of the elect who wish to live a common life with such people, but, through God’s mercy going before them, they are hindered by illness or some necessity and remain, as it were, weak on the road. When David—that is, the Lord Jesus Christ, the strong-handed one—finds them, he refreshes them with spiritual food and drink and kindles their minds to thirst for heavenly things.

It often happens that afterward, once converted to God, they strike lovers of the world—whom they had previously desired to accompany in worldly life—with the spiritual sword of reproof, as the prophet Hosea compassionately threatens such people, saying:

“Behold, I will hedge in your way with thorns, and I will wall it in, and you will pursue your lovers but will not overtake them; you will seek them but will not find them. And you will say: ‘I will return to my first husband, because it was better for me then than now’” (Hosea 2).

What is said at the conclusion of this parable is exceedingly terrifying:

“But I tell you that none of those men who were invited will taste my supper.”

We know that we have all been invited; but whether we shall reach the tasting of eternal blessedness, we do not yet know. God calls us in many ways: through faith, through baptism, through the examples of the fathers, through prosperity and adversity, through dreams and revelations. Since, therefore, we are without excuse concerning our calling, we must be anxious—indeed, it is necessary—to engage in good works, lest at the time of judgment we be excluded from God’s banquet and, perishing from hunger with the foolish virgins and crying, “Lord, Lord, open to us,” hear: “Amen, I say to you, I do not know you” (Matthew 25). Rather, with the prudent virgins, may we feast continually in eternal satiety upon the vision of our Creator.

## HOMILY 113. FOURTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST

(1 Peter 5.) “Beloved, humble yourselves under the mighty hand of God, so that he may exalt you at the time of visitation.” And so forth.

Just now, dearest brothers, we heard the blessed apostle Peter exhorting us to humility and saying: “Humble yourselves under the mighty hand of God.” The hand of God is understood as his power, because no joining of bodily members is found in God, who is wholly present everywhere and in all things, complete and perfect. Scripture speaks about God in human terms so that human beings may understand more clearly the majesty and power of their Creator and, understanding what God’s will is, strive to fulfill it in their deeds, thereby acquiring eternal joys for themselves.

It follows: “So that he may exalt you at the time of visitation.” For whoever in this present world submits himself to God’s will, gives his assent to his commandments, and strives to fulfill them in deeds insofar as divine grace grants him the ability—crushing the pride of the flesh—will be exalted by the Lord on the day of final recompense and will be led to the rewards of eternal blessedness.

[Col. 0609A] “Casting all your anxiety upon him, because he cares for you.” As the Psalmist admonishes us, saying: “Cast your thought upon the Lord, and he will nourish you” (Psalm 54). And elsewhere: “Those who seek the Lord shall lack no good thing” (Psalm 33). The Lord himself also says in the Gospel: “Do not be anxious, saying, ‘What shall we eat?’ or ‘What shall we drink?’ For your Father knows that you need all these things. Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you” (Matthew 6).

“Be sober and watchful.” Always live your life in sobriety and moderation, continually guarding against the devil’s cunning, and remain constantly vigilant in keeping God’s commandments and in guarding your souls.

[Col. 0609B] It follows:

“Because your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour.” The devil never sleeps and never rests from plotting against human beings; rather, day and night he continually prowls about, tempting people and laying snares, seeking how he might deceive by his suggestion any of those who are subject to God’s will, “seeking someone to devour”—not in body, but in soul—by drawing whoever he can toward harmful and useless carnal desires.

“Resist him, strong in faith.” Following the example of Christ and his saints, let us despise the sweetness of carnal desire, continually remembering what bitterness has been prepared for those who serve earthly desires and are unwilling to turn from their wickedness through repentance.

Let us therefore strive faithfully to cling to the Lord, continually meditate upon his commandments, crush the desires of our flesh, and resist with strength the devil, our most wicked enemy: in right faith, in firm hope of the mercy of almighty God, in perfect charity for his service, and in works of mercy and piety. Thus, by his gracious generosity, may we deserve both triumph over the enemy and the reward of eternal blessedness.

“The God of all grace, who has called us into his eternal glory in Christ,” through the incarnation of his only-begotten Son, whom he sent to die for the salvation of the world,

“having suffered a little”—although he remained in this world for only a short time, he endured many injuries for us and, finally, was crucified and killed for our redemption, consenting to die for us. After being held by death for a short time, he immediately rose on the third day.

“He himself will perfect” in us the good work he had begun, and will always confirm and strengthen us in his will and in divine religion, “in perseverance in good works.”

## HOMILY 114. FOURTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST

(Luke 15.) “At that time, tax collectors and sinners were drawing near to Jesus to hear him.” And so forth.

Just as the fall of one sinner often draws many into despair, because they imitate his evil example, so the recovery of one benefits many for salvation. We can readily establish this at the beginning of this reading if we carefully consider what precedes in this Gospel.

For, as the Gospel narrative reported above: “As Jesus was passing by, he saw a man named Levi sitting at the tax booth; he too was a chief tax collector, and he called him. But he, leaving everything, rose and followed him. And he made a great banquet for him in his house, and there was a great crowd of tax collectors reclining at table with him.”

Therefore, when the tax collectors and sinners saw that their chief had not only been received so kindly by God but had also been called into the order of the apostles, they finally took courage again and approached him like sick people approaching a physician, in order to hear him. They were received not only for conversation but also for eating with him.

When the scribes and Pharisees saw this—the men who applauded themselves for their false righteousness—they reproached not only the sick who were approaching the physician, but the physician himself as well, with insolent speech, saying:

“This man receives sinners and eats with them.”

From this we learn that just as true righteousness possesses compassion, so false righteousness possesses disdain. The Lord Jesus Christ, possessing true righteousness, did not disdain to receive tax collectors and sinners with compassion and mercy. The Pharisees, who falsely considered themselves righteous, not only despised sinners but reproached the physician himself for calling sinners.

Among them was one Pharisee named Simon. When he had invited the Lord to his house and had seen a sinful woman wetting his feet with her tears and wiping them with her hair, he said in his heart: “If this man were a prophet, he would surely know who and what sort of woman this is who touches him, for she is a sinner” (Luke 7).

The Lord anticipated him and said: “Simon, I have something to say to you.” He replied: “Teacher, say it.” He said to him: “Two debtors owed money to a certain moneylender: one owed five hundred denarii, and the other fifty. Since they had nothing with which to repay, he forgave both of them. Which of them, then, will love him more?” (Ibid.) Unable to deny the truth, he answered: “I suppose the one to whom he forgave more” (Ibid.).

Turning to the woman, he said to Simon: “Do you see this woman? I entered your house; you did not give me water for my feet, but she has wet my feet with her tears and wiped them with her hair. You gave me no kiss, but she has not ceased kissing my feet from the time I entered. You did not anoint my head with oil, but she has anointed my feet with ointment. Therefore I tell you, her many sins are forgiven” (Ibid.).

But when they were murmuring, the Lord employed such a comparison that he might both restrain their murmuring by reason and show that the comparison itself referred especially to the Author of all things.

“For he said this parable to them: Which of you, having a hundred sheep, if he loses one of them, does not leave the ninety-nine in the wilderness and go after the one that was lost until he finds it?”

It is as though he were saying: If you seek a lost sheep with such zeal and labor—not consulting the sheep but your own greed—how much more ought I to seek a human being made in the image of God and free him from destruction? For I came not to destroy anyone, but to save all (Luke 9).

Spiritually, this man is the one of whom the prophet says: “Behold, God and man will come from the house of David”—namely, the Lord Jesus Christ, who had a hundred sheep when he created the rational creature, angelic and human, in perfection. The number one hundred is perfect, and he had a hundred sheep when he established the nature of angels and human beings for the attainment of eternal perfection.

One sheep then perished when the first human being sinned. But he whose mercy is from eternity and unto eternity over those who fear him, unwilling that human nature should perish forever, left the ninety-nine sheep in the wilderness and went to seek the one that had perished.

Here the wilderness is understood as heaven. Since “wilderness” means “abandoned,” heaven is rightly called a wilderness in this passage, because the first human being abandoned it by sinning. Another evangelist, wishing to signify this more clearly, put “on the mountains” instead of “in the wilderness,” so that you might understand “in the heights.”

He therefore left the ninety-nine in the wilderness when, leaving those angelic spirits in heaven, he entered the earth in order to assume human nature for us and for our salvation.

It should nevertheless be noted that he did not abandon them in such a way that he was no longer with them through the power of his divinity, by which he is present everywhere and wholly present everywhere, as he abandoned us when he returned to them.

He sought the sheep that did not seek him, because human nature could not approach his divinity. Through his humanity he became near to us, as the Apostle bears witness, saying: “He emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of human beings” (Philippians 2). And again: “When the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, born of a woman, born under the Law, to redeem those who were under the Law, so that we might receive adoption as sons” (Galatians 4).

“And when he has found it, he places it upon his shoulders, rejoicing.”

By the shoulders of God the labor of his Passion is expressed. Since a human being has greater strength in the shoulders for carrying burdens than in the other limbs, the power of the Passion is rightly signified by the shoulders, as Isaiah says (chapter 9): “The principality was made upon his shoulder.”

Because we ordinarily carry burdens on our shoulders, he placed the sheep he had found upon his shoulders when, through the labor of his Passion, he recalled us to heavenly glory. Concerning this the blessed Peter says: “He himself bore our sins in his body upon the wood, so that, having died to sins, we might live for righteousness; by his bruising we have been healed. For you were like sheep going astray, but now you have returned to the shepherd and bishop of your souls” (1 Peter 2).

Or he carried it back to the flock after placing it upon his shoulders when he restored us to his likeness. Thus, to place the sheep he had found upon his shoulders means the same as, according to another parable, to place the man wounded by robbers upon a beast of burden and lead him to an inn.

“And coming home.”

The house to which the found sheep is brought back is the heavenly homeland. To it that spiritual sheep desired to be carried back upon the shoulders of the merciful shepherd when it said: “One thing I have asked of the Lord, this I will seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life, that I may see the will of the Lord and visit his temple” (Psalm 26). And again: “I have gone astray like a sheep that is lost; seek your servant, Lord” (Psalm 118).

When the sheep has been found, it returns to the Lord, because, after human nature had been liberated and after the triumph of his Passion, he returned to heaven in the glory of his Ascension.

How great a glory arose among the angels in heaven over the liberation of the human being is shown when it follows:

“He calls his friends and neighbors and says to them: Rejoice with me, because I have found my sheep that was lost.”

The friends and neighbors are the angelic spirits. They are rightly called friends because they never disagree with his truth. They are neighbors because they contemplate the vision of his glory from close at hand.

It should be noted that he does not say, “Rejoice with the sheep that has been found,” but, “with me,” showing that our salvation is his joy. Although God is most compassionate and immutable, just as he is said, in human terms, to be saddened by the destruction of human beings, so he is said to rejoice over their salvation.

That he grieves over the destruction of human beings he himself declares through the prophet, when, after enumerating Jerusalem’s sins, he adds: “In all these things you were grieving me.”

But how greatly he rejoices over its salvation the evangelist declares, saying: “In that hour Jesus rejoiced in the Spirit and said: I confess to you, Lord, Father of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones” (Matthew 11).

The Lord declares the perfection of this joy when, explaining the comparison, he adds:

“I tell you that in heaven there is such joy over one sinner who repents as over ninety-nine righteous people who have no need of repentance.”

There is therefore greater joy in heaven over converted sinners than over righteous people who remain standing, because we too recover lost earthly property with greater joy than that with which we had possessed it before its loss. That Gospel parable clearly indicates this, in which the father received his returning prodigal son with great joy, saying:

“Bring quickly the first robe and put it on him; place a ring on his hand and shoes on his feet; bring the fattened calf and kill it, and let us eat and rejoice, because this son of mine was dead and has come to life; he was lost and has been found” (Luke 15).

But perhaps someone may wonder how the angels of God, in whom supreme perfection exists, can rejoice more over the conversion of sinners than over the state of the righteous.

To this we must reply that there are some of the elect who, with God protecting them, have committed no capital crimes, yet do not exercise themselves in any of the principal virtues. Because they seem righteous to themselves by their own judgment, they live all the more securely the less they recognize themselves as sinners.

Those, however, who, after public disgraceful acts and crimes, have turned to repentance afflict themselves all the more severely the more gravely they remember having sinned. Angry with themselves, they mortify their flesh through abstinence and vigils; they deny their own wills; they devote themselves to fasting and almsgiving; they are pierced with remorse in prayers and tears; and, mortifying themselves, they “crucify their members with vices and desires” (Galatians 3).

There is therefore greater joy in heaven over the conversion of such sinners than over the state of those righteous people who, as we have said, exercise themselves less in good works because they feel themselves less bound by more serious evils. For a king also loves more in battle the soldier who, after fleeing, returns and presses the enemy vigorously than the one who never fled but nevertheless never performed any courageous deed.

Likewise, a farmer loves more the land which, after the removal of thorns and brambles, yields more abundant fruit than the land that never produced thorns but also never produced abundant fruit.

There are also other righteous people who, although they possess works of righteousness, nevertheless do not consider themselves righteous at all.
