As though conscious of great sins, they accuse themselves and afflict themselves with fasts, vigils, and prayers. Just as others lament sins of action, so these often lament sins of thought.

It must therefore be considered that if there is joy in heaven over converted sinners, there is much more and greater joy over the works of such righteous people. Nor can the angels, in whom charity is perfect, behold the salvation of human beings without joy, since they are said to grieve over their destruction.

“Or what woman, having ten drachmas, if she loses one drachma, does not light a lamp, overturn the house, and search carefully until she finds it?”

The one signified above by the shepherd is now signified by the woman: namely, the Lord Jesus Christ, the power and wisdom of God.

This woman had ten drachmas because she created the rational creature, angelic and human. There are nine orders of angels: angels, archangels, thrones, dominions, virtues, principalities, powers, cherubim, and seraphim. The tenth fell through pride. But so that the number of the elect might be completed, the human being was created as the tenth for his restoration.

For we believe that such a multitude will ascend from the souls of the faithful into heaven as the number of angels who happened to remain there, in accordance with what is written: “He established the boundaries of the peoples according to the number of the children of Israel.” And as the Lord says in the Gospel, in the resurrection they “neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like the angels in heaven” (Mark 12).

The image of the king is expressed in a drachma. Since the spirits of angels and human beings were created in the image of God, they are rightly expressed under the name of drachmas.

The woman lost one drachma when the first human being sinned. But the wisdom of God, unwilling that the human being should perish forever, lit a lamp.

He lit a lamp when he glorified through his divinity, by the power of miracles, the human nature that he assumed from us. A lamp is light in an earthen vessel: light in an earthen vessel is divinity in humanity. Just as light grows stronger in an earthen vessel, so the flesh of God passed through the fire of the Passion into immortality, as he himself says through the prophet: “My strength has dried up like a potsherd” (Psalm 21).

But after the woman lit the lamp, she overturned the house, because when the Lord appeared in humanity, he immediately turned the human heart toward repentance, as he himself said: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven will draw near” (Matthew 3).

The house is overturned when a human being, severely punishing within himself what he has wickedly done, destroys it.

“And when she has found it, she calls her friends and neighbors together, saying: Rejoice with me, because I have found the drachma that I had lost.”

The friends and neighbors are the virtues of the heavenly city—that is, the angelic spirits—who never disagree with her will and are never separated from her vision by any interval of time.

The angels will rejoice at the finding of the sheep and the drachma when they see their number, which they had observed to have been diminished through the apostate angel, completed through the recovery of the human being.

It should be noted that she does not say, “Rejoice with the drachma that has been found,” but, “with me,” showing that our liberation is the exultation of the liberator.

Great hope is held out to converted sinners, and great confidence is granted to those who repent, when it is added:

“So I tell you: there will be joy before the angels of God over one sinner who repents, more than over ninety-nine righteous people who have no need of repentance.”

Who, then, has so hard a breast and impenitent a heart that, hearing these things, will not be converted?

Since the angels are to rejoice over our conversion, it is certainly fitting that we should maintain mourning on earth, saying with the Psalmist: “Every night I will wash my bed” (Psalm 6), so that what the Lord says in the Gospel may be fulfilled in us: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matthew 5).

But we must consider what repentance ought to be, because there are many who continually call themselves sinners and yet are still pleased to sin. Some abstain from wine and meat; others give generous alms. But because they do not cease from sin, they do not produce fruits worthy of repentance.

No one can practice true repentance except one who hates sin and loves God. The person who should be called repentant is the one who so laments past sins that he does not commit again what must be lamented.

Hence repentance—*paenitentia*—is rightly named as though from *punientia*, “punishment,” because through repenting we ought to punish past evils in such a way that we do not again commit what would require repentance. Whoever laments the past and guards against the future comes to God securely.

The person who clings pleasurably and without ceasing to evil works, while abstaining from the foods that God created to be received with thanksgiving, should be called more a mocker than a penitent.

Both things are necessary for those who repent: that they have bitterness in their heart for their sins and affliction in their body, so that the flesh which, when joyful, drew us into guilt may, when afflicted, lead us back to forgiveness, following the example of the one who says: “I was turned in my affliction, while the thorn is being fixed” (Psalm 31).

Elsewhere, in the voice of the penitent, it is said: “I ate my bread like ashes, and I mixed my drink with weeping, because of the face of your anger and indignation” (Psalm 101). And again: “But while they troubled me, I clothed myself in sackcloth and humbled my soul with fasting” (Psalm 34).

Hence the practice of the Church has been accustomed to impose public penance in ashes and sackcloth, so that affliction may be felt outwardly in the roughness of the sackcloth and the remembrance of human mortality may be inwardly present in the sight of the ashes.

Hence, in the voice of blessed Job and in the person of penitents, it is said (chapter 42): “Therefore I rebuke myself and do penance in dust and ashes.”

Let no one despair because of the greatness of his sins. Even if the diseases of souls are great, the physician is almighty; he came not to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance. No wound of sin is so great that it cannot be healed through repentance, provided that the medicine of repentance is not neglected.

He does not lie who says: “On whatever day the sinner turns and groans, his sins will be consigned to oblivion.” And again: “As I live, says the Lord, I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live” (Ezekiel 18 and 33).

Therefore, calling the sinful soul to repentance, the Lord says through the prophet: “Can a mother forget her infant, so as not to have compassion on the son of her womb? And even if she should forget, I nevertheless will not forget you” (Isaiah 49).

Human nature, just as it falls easily, can also rise easily. For, as the Savior says in the present reading: “There will be joy in heaven over one sinner who repents.”

## HOMILY 115. FIFTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST

(Luke 6.) “At that time Jesus said to his disciples: Be merciful, just as your Father is merciful.” And so forth.

Among the other virtues by which the Lord Jesus Christ urged us to seek heavenly glory, he especially commended mercy. Indeed, when he was seated on the mountain teaching his disciples the eight beatitudes, he said, among other things: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matthew 5).

Therefore, whoever desires to attain this reward of blessedness should strive to possess the virtue of mercy. To show that mercy must be extended not only to the grateful but also to the ungrateful, after giving his teaching on love of enemies, he added what we heard at the beginning of this reading, saying:

“Be merciful, therefore.”

First, then, let us examine the etymology of this name, so that we may come to know its virtues more perfectly. *Misericordia*—“mercy”—is a word composed of *cor*, “heart,” and *miseria*, “misery.” This composition shows that wherever there is misery, there mercy is necessary.

We understand mercy in two ways: one is bodily and the other non-bodily; one visible and the other invisible.

Bodily mercy consists in giving food to the hungry and drink to the thirsty, clothing the naked, receiving the stranger, visiting the sick, burying the dead, forgiving from the heart those who sin against us, helping the needs of our neighbors according to our strength, and performing other works of piety similar to these.

Spiritual mercy, on the other hand, consists in teaching the ignorant, consoling the sorrowful, encouraging the one who is doing good, reproving the negligent, calling the proud to humility and satisfaction, and performing other such acts.

One is good and the other better, because spiritual mercy is better than bodily mercy to the same extent that the soul is better than the body. Through one, the body—which is destined to die—is refreshed; through the other, the soul—which will remain without end—is refreshed.

Therefore, whoever can extend both forms is perfect. But if someone is unable to extend spiritual mercy, let him at least not neglect bodily mercy, so that at the reward of the righteous he may deserve to hear: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matthew 25).

The apostle Paul wished his disciples to possess this mercy, saying to them: “Clothe yourselves, as God’s chosen ones, with compassion; be kind to one another” (Colossians 3).

The apostle Peter exhorts the faithful to possess it in his letter, saying: “Be all united in prayer, compassionate, lovers of the brotherhood, merciful, modest, humble” (1 Peter 3).

Therefore, we ought to seek this virtue with all the greater zeal the more we desire, in practicing it, to be imitators of our heavenly Father. How perfect the virtue of mercy is is clearly shown by the fact that we are urged to display it by the example of the Lord himself. Hence it follows:

“Just as your Father is merciful.”

Here it should be noted that the adverb *just as* does not always refer to equality, but sometimes to resemblance. For we cannot be in every respect as the Lord is, and yet, according to a certain likeness, as the apostle John says: “Just as he is, so are we in this world” (1 John 4). According to this manner of speaking, *just as* here too refers to resemblance. For it is fitting that, just as we glory in having the Father in heaven, so we should live justly and devoutly on earth, so that our good works themselves may show that we are children of God.

For just as in human birth we frequently recognize the likeness of a father’s face in the faces of his children, so, if we wish to be children of God, we must imitate our heavenly Father on earth. Hence the Apostle says: “If we have borne the image of the earthly, let us also bear the image of the heavenly” (1 Cor. 15). And just as the dress of kings’ sons is more costly and their dignity more exalted, so in us, who are sons of God, virtues ought to flourish in good works, so that we may appear radiant in charity, distinguished in humility, and shining in chastity, so that what the Lord says may be fulfilled: “You shall be holy, just as I am holy” (1 Pet. 1).

Be perfect, so that, just as he himself is kind and merciful—“who makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil, and sends rain upon the just and the unjust” (Matt. 5)—so we too may offer what we can not only to friends, but also to enemies and strangers, as the Lord says: “Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you” (ibid.), so that we may deserve to be counted among the children of God, and that what he himself says in the Gospel may be fulfilled in us: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called the children of God” (ibid.).

Nor should it seem superfluous if, in order to investigate more closely this imitation of our heavenly Father, we take some example from visible things. Physiologists report that it is the nature of eagles to hold their young up before the sun’s radiance; those whom they see gazing at the sun’s brightness with unblinded eyes, after the manner of their parents, they cherish and nourish with every care, but those whom they see looking toward the earth they cast down and despise as adulterous offspring.

Likewise, they say of ravens that they neglect their young until they see their own likeness in them, in the blackening of their feathers. In these likenesses we are mystically admonished that, if we desire to be children of God, we should contemplate with the eye of the mind the joys of eternal brightness and display the likeness of our heavenly Parent in good deeds, so that what he himself says in the Gospel may be fulfilled in us: “Let your light shine before men, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (ibid.).

For, as the apostle Peter testifies, whoever does someone’s works is called that person’s son. Hence Paul admonishes us, saying: “Be imitators of God, as beloved children” (Eph. 5). John says likewise: “We are children of God, but it has not yet appeared what we shall be. We know, however, that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him just as he is” (1 John 3).

“Do not judge, and you will not be judged. Do not condemn, and you will not be condemned.”

It is asked why he says, “Do not judge, and you will not be judged,” when elsewhere he is recorded as saying: “If you see your brother sinning, rebuke him” (Luke 17). And in another place: “If your brother sins against you, go and rebuke him between you and him alone. If he listens to you, you have gained your brother; but if he does not listen to you, take with you one or two others” (Matt. 18).

The answer is that in fraternal correction this rule of discernment must be observed: manifest and open evils are both to be avoided and reproved; but those things whose intention in our neighbors is unknown are not to be judged, but rather are to be kept outside the scope of reproof.

There are certain actions that can be performed with either a good or a bad intention. It is dangerous to judge such things, especially lest we ourselves be condemned. For example, if you see someone frequently not fasting, do not greatly praise him or greatly detest him, because it may be that he cannot fast on account of an infirm stomach, or that he does not wish to fast on account of an appetite for gluttony.

Such matters and others like them should not readily be judged, as the apostle Paul says: “Let the one who eats not judge the one who does not eat, and let the one who does not eat not despise the one who eats” (Rom. 14). And again: “Do not judge before the time, until the Lord comes, who will both bring to light the hidden things of darkness and disclose the purposes of hearts; and then each one will receive praise from God” (1 Cor. 4). Elsewhere, where he forbids those who ate meat to judge those who did not eat it, he says: “Let no one judge you in food or drink” (Col. 2). And again: “Who are you to judge another’s servant?” (Rom. 14). And once more: “It is better not to eat meat or drink wine” (ibid.), and so forth.

For whoever unjustly judges or condemns another will justly be judged and condemned.

There are, however, other actions that are plainly and manifestly evil in themselves, such as adulteries, thefts, murders, robberies, drunkenness, and other things of this kind. These must not only be reproved by the faithful, but also corrected by the one who holds the place of governance, and judged, especially because of what the Lord says through the prophet: “If you do not announce his iniquity to the wicked man, I will require his blood from your hand” (Ezek. 33).

Another kind of discernment must also be observed in fraternal correction: if, for example, the sin is hidden, correct and amend it secretly, because the Lord says: “If you see your brother sinning, rebuke him between you and him alone.” But if the sin is manifest and public, rebuke and amend it publicly, because the Apostle says: “Rebuke sinners in the presence of all, so that the others may have fear” (1 Tim. 5). And as it is said through Solomon: “Whoever rebukes openly makes peace.” And again: “Answer a fool according to his folly” (Prov. 26).

For this purpose divine justice established in the Church a shepherd among the people and a ruler in the world, so that one might correct sinners, while the other might punish those who remain negligent even after correction.

When your brother sins against you, forgive him with a mild reproof. Hence it is added as follows [Note: [Col. 0617D] Here something is either missing or superfluous]. But because it is not enough to turn away from evil unless each person also strives to do good, after giving the command concerning not judging one’s neighbors, he shows the pattern to which we should conform, saying:

“Forgive, and you will be forgiven.”

That is to say: forgive those who sin against you, and your sins will be forgiven you. For we must not only refrain from rashly judging others, but also forgive from the heart those who judge us unjustly.

Thus, *to forgive* pertains to pardoning sins, according to what the Lord says elsewhere (Matt. 6): “If you forgive men their sins, your heavenly Father will also forgive you your sins.” And again: “When you stand to pray, forgive whatever you have against anyone” (Mark 11).

What he adds—

“Give, and it will be given to you”—

pertains to giving alms, as the Lord says elsewhere: “Give alms, and behold, everything is clean for you” (Luke 11). We ought to forgive injuries and give alms, so that eternal life may be given to us, according to what the Lord says: “Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity, so that when you fail, they may receive you into the eternal dwellings” (Luke 16). And perhaps, if you should ask what would be given to you, he added, saying:

“A good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and overflowing.”

A good measure will be given by the rewarder of all good things, when he repays greater things for small ones, heavenly things for earthly things, and things that endure for things that pass away. It is rightly called *pressed down*, that is, full and perfect, and *shaken together*, because it will be empty and void in no part. *Overflowing* means superabundant.

This full, perfect, and superabundant measure will be given to the faithful servant when it is said: “Well done, good and faithful servant; because you have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many things. Enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matt. 25).

And because, once the glory of the blessed homeland has been received, there will be no possibility of losing any part of it, it is rightly said: “They will give into your bosom.” For just as we are certain and secure concerning something that we have in our bosom, so, after we have been gathered into the embrace of the heavenly kingdom, we shall be established in eternal security, as John says in the Apocalypse: “God will wipe away every tear from their eyes” (Rev. 21).

And because God will repay each person according to his works, it is added:

“With the same measure with which you have measured, it will be measured back to you.”

For if we willingly forgive those who sin against us, almighty God will mercifully forgive our sins. Hence every day in prayer we ask him, saying: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. 6). Whoever, therefore, does not wish to forgive one who has sinned against him asks the Lord vainly and uselessly, as he himself says: “If you do not forgive men their sins, neither will your heavenly Father forgive you your sins” (ibid.).

Hence Solomon also says: “A man keeps anger against a man” (Ecclus. 28), and so forth. And again: “Forgive your neighbor who has harmed you, and when he asks you, forgive him, and your sins will be released” (ibid.).

For whoever, for God’s sake, has taken on greater love in the present life and has given more abundant alms will receive a greater reward in eternal life, as the Apostle testifies when he says: “Whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and whoever sows in blessings will reap from blessings” (2 Cor. 9)—eternal life.

“He also told them a parable: Can the blind lead the blind? Will they not both fall into a pit?”

In this parable the Lord particularly strikes at the scribes and Pharisees, who unworthily usurp the place of teachers while abandoning the Lord, as the Lord says elsewhere: “You transgress God’s commandment because of your traditions” (Matt. 15).

Although they were blind, so that they did not know themselves to be blind, they were not ashamed to become teachers among the people. They sought not the profit of souls, but the advancement of their own ostentation and ambition—not to benefit the people, but to appear more honorable and learned among them, loving “the first couches at banquets, the first seats in the synagogues, greetings in the marketplace, and to be called Rabbi by men” (Matt. 23).

Because they saw him who said, “I am the light of the world” (John 8), yet did not recognize him, they were unquestionably blind, as the Lord says: “Leave them; they are blind, leaders of the blind” (Matt. 15). And while they taught the people what they did not know, they themselves, blind leading the blind, both fell into the pit, as the Lord reproaches them elsewhere, saying: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, lawyers, who have taken away the key of knowledge” (Luke 11). And in another place: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who shut the kingdom of heaven before men; for you yourselves do not enter, nor do you allow others to enter” (Matt. 23).

But we must take care lest the vices of the scribes and Pharisees pass over to us, so that what we condemn in them may be found in ourselves.

There are some who, before becoming disciples, desire to become teachers. Though they possess neither holiness of conduct nor maturity of age, and though learning in speech does not support them, they shamelessly seek a position of governance. Thus they become teachers of error because they refused to be disciples of truth.

When someone living perversely unworthily assumes the office of teaching, he presumes, like a blind man, to lead the blind; and therefore both fall into the pit, because one presides unworthily while the other follows a bad example, and so both fall into error. Hence James says: “Do not become many teachers” (James 3).

Everyone who desires to show others the way of truth must take the greatest care not to live differently from what he teaches, except as Christ lived and taught. Hence it is added:

“The disciple is not above the teacher; but everyone will be perfect if he is like his teacher.”

In human disciplines it commonly happens that a disciple surpasses his teacher in acuteness of mind. Here, therefore, the teacher is understood to be the one who says elsewhere: “You call me Teacher and Lord, and you speak rightly” (John 13). And again: “Do not be called teachers, for one is your teacher, who is in heaven” (Matt. 23).

This statement depends upon what was said above: “Forgive, and you will be forgiven. Give, and it will be given to you.” It is as though he were saying: If your teacher, although he could have vindicated his injuries as God, did not wish to do so, then you too can become perfect disciples if, amid persecutions, you do not repay injuries but display patience.

This does not mean that we can be perfect in the same way as he is; rather, according to the measure of our capacity, we must imitate his humility and gentleness, following the example of that true teacher who says: “Learn from me, for I am gentle and humble of heart” (Matt. 11).

There are some who appear harsher and stricter in correcting the faults of others, while they are more indulgent and lenient toward their own. Hence it is added:

“Why do you see the speck in your brother’s eye, but do not consider the beam that is in your own eye?”

As great as the difference between a speck and a beam is, so great is the difference between a lesser and a greater sin. To make this clearer, let us bring forward one example among many. Sudden anger is a speck; when it has grown old, however, it becomes a beam.

Sudden anger disturbs the eye of the mind, as it is said through the Prophet: “My eye has been troubled because of anger” (Ps. 6). Hatred, however, blinds the mind, as the apostle John testifies when he says: “Whoever hates his brother is in darkness and walks in darkness, and does not know where he is going, because the darkness has blinded his eyes” (1 John 2).

Whoever, while keeping hatred in his heart, harshly rebukes and judges a brother who has suddenly become angry is like someone trying to remove a speck from another’s eye while not seeing the beam in his own.

But because the preaching of one whose life is despised is also despised, it is rightly added:

“How can you say to your brother, ‘Brother, let me remove the speck from your eye,’ while you yourself do not see the beam in your own eye?”

Whoever wishes to correct another’s smallest sins must first correct and amend his own, lest God someday say to him: “Why do you recount my statutes and take up my covenant in your mouth? You have hated discipline and cast my words behind you” (Ps. 49).

Whoever must examine another’s life needs to have a pure eye of the mind, as the Apostle writes to Timothy: “A bishop must be blameless, as God’s steward” (1 Tim. 3). Hence the Lord, continuing his admonition, adds:

“Hypocrite, first remove the beam from your eye, and then you will see clearly to remove the speck from your brother’s eye.”

*Hypocrite* is Greek; in Latin it is called *simulator*, “one who pretends,” or *subauratus*, “gilded over.” By this name those are designated who display one thing outwardly and preserve another inwardly.

The Lord rebukes such people in the Gospel, saying: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you are like whitened tombs, which appear beautiful to men outwardly, but inwardly are full of the bones of the dead and every impurity. So you too outwardly indeed appear righteous to men, but inwardly you are full of hypocrisy and iniquity” (Matt. 23).

How grave a vice hypocrisy is, blessed Job shows when he says: “For no hypocrite shall come into the presence of the Lord” (Job 13). And again: “The assembly of hypocrites is barren” (ibid., 15). And: “The deceitful and cunning provoke God’s anger” (ibid., 36). Solomon likewise says: “The pretender deceives his friend with his mouth” (Prov. 11).

The worst kind of hypocrites are those who mortify the flesh in this world but are deprived of their reward in the future, because, as the Lord says, “They have received their reward” (Matt. 6).

There are some who, although they are servants of vices, sharply correct the sins of others so that they may appear righteous to men. Of such people Scripture says: “There is a lying correction in the mouth of the insolent” (Ecclus. 19).

To such people applies what the Lord says: “Hypocrite, first remove the beam from your eye, and then you will see clearly to remove the speck from your brother’s eye.”

By saying these things, we do not prohibit anyone from fraternal correction, especially since, as the apostle James says (James 5): “Whoever converts a sinner from the error of his way will save his soul from death and cover a multitude of sins.”

But whenever we see a brother sinning, mindful of our own weakness, we ought to correct him kindly and gently, as the apostle Paul instructs: “Brothers, if a person is overtaken in any transgression, you who are spiritual should instruct such a one in a spirit of gentleness, considering yourself, lest you also be tempted” (Gal. 6).

When, however, we see someone incorrigibly clinging to vices, we ought, kindled by zeal for righteousness, to rebuke him more harshly, following the example of the one who says: “I saw the transgressors, and I wasted away” (Ps. 118). And again: “Do I not hate those who hate you, Lord? With perfect hatred I hate them” (Ps. 138).

We seem to become angry without fault when such severity is formed not by anger but by zeal, as in the example of Moses, who went out from Pharaoh exceedingly angry because he saw that Pharaoh’s wickedness was incorrigible.

## HOMILY 116. SIXTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST

### (1 Pet. 3) “Beloved, be all of one mind in prayer.”

And the rest. The unity of brotherhood, like an impregnable city, is not exposed to the enemy’s ambushes. For, as Solomon says (Song 6), the holy Church has “an army arranged in battle formation,” which tyrants and persecutors, together with their author, the devil, cannot break through. For in Christ, who unites them, persecution does not overcome the martyrs, carnal pleasure does not overcome virgins, greed does not overcome the merciful, and ambition for temporal glory does not overcome the humble.

“Having compassion.”

For just as we ought to rejoice with those who rejoice, so also we ought to weep with those who weep, as the apostle Paul did when he said: “Who is weak, and I am not weak?” (2 Cor. 11).

“Lovers of brotherhood.”

Whoever loves human beings ought to love them either because they are righteous or so that they may become righteous, just as he ought to love himself either because he is righteous or so that he may become righteous.

Let us consider how greatly the apostle John commends brotherly love: “Whoever loves his brother,” he says, “whom he sees remains in the light, and there is no scandal in him” (1 John 2). And again: “Beloved, let us love one another, because love is from God. And everyone who loves is born of God and knows God” (ibid., 4). And the Lord says: “I give you a new commandment, that you love one another. By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you love one another” (John 13).

“Merciful.”

For it is written (Prov. 21): “To do mercy is more pleasing to God than sacrifices.” And Scripture says: “Whoever is inclined to mercy will be blessed” (Prov. 22). And the Lord says: “Be merciful, just as your Father is merciful” (Luke 6).

“Humble.”

For it is written (Ecclus. 10): “God destroys the memory of the proud and does not abandon the memory of the humble.” And the Lord says: “Learn from me, for I am gentle and humble of heart” (Matt. 11). And to whom shall I look, says the Lord (Isa. 66), except to the humble and quiet?

“Not repaying evil for good.”

For it is written: “Do not say, ‘I will repay evil for evil’; wait for God, and he will deliver you” (Prov. 20). And again: “Whoever wishes to take revenge will find vengeance from God, and he will preserve that person’s sin” (Ecclus. 28).

“Nor curse for curse.”

In this we must follow the Lord’s example, “who, when he was cursed, did not curse in return” (1 Pet. 2).

“But, on the contrary, blessing.”

As in the saying: “Bless those who curse you; bless and do not curse” (Luke 6; Rom. 12).

“For to this you were called, that you should possess a blessing as your inheritance.”

The blessing of the inheritance is the entire abundance of heavenly virtues, in which the saints become heirs indeed of God and fellow heirs of Christ, when they hear: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. 25).

“For whoever wishes to love life”—that is, eternal and blessed life, which will remain without end in the future—“and to see good days” [the printed reading *honos* is evidently uncertain, perhaps an OCR error for *bonos*], in which the saints rejoice with the saints in heaven—days that are called days not because night interrupts them, but because their light is perpetual—“let him restrain his tongue from evil,” that is, from the evil of detraction, cursing, and murmuring; or, more generally, the tongue must be restrained altogether from evil.

James says: “If anyone thinks that he is religious, not restraining his tongue but deceiving his own heart, that person’s religion is vain” (James 1). For Scripture also says: “Whoever guards his tongue guards his soul” (Prov. 25).

“And let his lips not speak deceit.”

By *deceit* is meant fraud, not sorrow: when one thing is held in the heart and another is uttered from the mouth.

“Let him turn away from evil and do good.”

That is, let him destroy vices and build virtues; let him abandon what the devil instigates, so that he may do what Christ commands.

“Let him seek peace and pursue it.”

That is, by praying diligently and asking humbly, let him seek Christ, who became our peace, and imitate him; for to follow is to imitate. Or, according to the Apostle: “Let him pursue peace and holiness, without which no one will see God” (Heb. 12).

“For the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous.”

That is, the gaze of the Divinity.

“And his ears are toward their prayers.”

That is, the divine hearing by which he deigns to hear the prayers of the righteous.

“But the face of the Lord is upon those who do evil.”

Why is “the face of the Lord upon those who do evil”? Hear what follows: “To destroy their memory from the earth” (Ps. 33)—that is, from the land of the living. And this also: “Let them be blotted out of the book of the living, and not be written with the righteous” (Ps. 68).

“And who is he who can harm you?”

The implied answer is: no one. In keeping with this statement, sufferings and persecutions do not make people miserable, but rather enable them to be blessed.

“If you are zealous for what is good.”

That is, if you are imitators of the good God, of whom it is written, “No one is good except God alone” (Matt. 19), or, more generally, if you are imitators—that is, followers—of all good virtues.

“But even if you suffer anything for righteousness, you are blessed”—the words “you will be” are understood.

Peter had heard the Lord express this sentence when he said: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5).

“Do not fear their fear”—that is, the fear of persecutors—“and do not be troubled in faith.”

The Lord also admonished this when he said: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; rather, fear him who has power to destroy both body and soul in Gehenna” (Matt. 10).

“But sanctify the Lord Christ in your hearts.”

Where ought the Lord, who sanctifies all things by creating them, to be sanctified, if not in a devout heart and a chaste body? Thus the Lord Jesus must be sanctified in our hearts, so that we are called Christians by his name and regard nothing as holier than his name.

Let us sanctify him in faith, hope, and charity, by believing, worshiping, and adoring, so that we may likewise deserve to be saved and sanctified by him.

## HOMILY 117. SIXTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST

### (Luke 5) “At that time, when the crowds pressed upon him to hear the word of God, he was standing beside the lake of Gennesaret.”

And the rest. Since we are going to speak about the fish that the apostles caught at the Lord’s command after letting down their nets, let us first examine the situation of the place.

The Gospel says: “When the crowds pressed upon Jesus to hear the word of God, he was standing beside the lake of Gennesaret. And he saw two boats standing.”

The lake of Gennesaret is the same as the Sea of Tiberias and the Sea of Galilee. The Sea of Tiberias was so called from the city of Tiberias; the Sea of Galilee from the neighboring province, which is also called Galilee.

The lake of Gennesaret was named from a Greek expression, as though meaning “producing a breeze,” because, when the winds blow and the waves ripple, it seems to generate a breeze from itself. This sea or lake is one hundred and forty stadia long and forty wide.

It is not called a sea because its waters are bitter. Rather, it is the custom of the Hebrew language to call every gathering of waters a sea, whether the waters are salt or fresh, as it is written in Genesis: “And he called the gatherings of waters seas” (Gen. 1).

Spiritually, this sea signifies the world, that is, those who love the world. For just as the sea is always in motion and cannot remain still, so the world is shaken by various disturbances and upheavals, as the Psalmist says: “You have moved the earth, Lord, and troubled it” (Ps. 59). It grows by being born and diminishes by dying; it is raised up in prosperity and cast down in adversity.

The Lord stood beside the lake when, as the Apostle says, “he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men, and being found in appearance as a man” (Phil. 2). And beautifully he is said to stand not in the lake but beside the lake, because he came into the world by nature but was alien to the world through sin, as the apostle Peter testifies: “He committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” (1 Pet. 2).

He is rightly said not to have walked or passed through, but to have stood, clearly showing himself to be the one who by the power of his divinity always remains unchanging, who is present everywhere and wholly everywhere, who neither moves nor passes from place to place. For neither do past things pass away from him nor do future things succeed them; for him being is always equal and eternal. Through the prophet he says: “I am God, and I do not change” (Mal. 3).

Or certainly, he stands beside the lake because, rising from the dead, he established the flesh that he had assumed from us upon the shore of incorruption. And thus, just as he himself is unchanging, so he establishes his elect in eternal unchangeableness.

The crowds that pressed upon him out of love for the word of God signify the multitude of believers who draw near to him by believing in and loving him. Concerning them Isaiah says: “All nations shall come to him, and many peoples shall go and say: House of Jacob, come, and let us walk in the light of the Lord” (Isa. 2). And the Psalmist says: “All the nations that you have made shall come and worship before you, Lord” (Ps. 85).

But because this crowd of believers was to come not only from the Jews but also from the Gentiles, it is rightly added: “And he saw two boats standing beside the lake.”

The two boats signify the two groups that would believe: one from the Jews and the other from the Gentiles—not that there is division within the unity of faith, but because the Church is gathered from both peoples.

Jesus is rightly said to have seen both boats, because from both peoples he foreknew those who would believe in him. For the Lord knows those who are his. To see is to choose, as the Lord says to Nathanael: “When you were under the fig tree, I saw you” (John 1).

“But the fishermen had gone down and were washing their nets.”

The fishermen are the teachers of the Church, whose first representatives were the apostles. Extending their nets of preaching into the world, they caught many from both peoples in the faith. Concerning them it is said through the prophet: “I will send my fishermen, and they will fish for them” (Jer. 16), and so forth.

The nets signify the teaching of preachers, which, strengthened by the various judgments of the Fathers, is woven together like a fabric of many threads. The nets beautifully signify the teaching of preachers because, just as nets hold the fish they catch, so the preaching of truth does not easily lose those whom it catches in the faith. Hence they are appropriately called nets, as though they were “things that retain.”

The fishermen wash their nets when holy preachers chastise their bodies and subject them to service. They do not live otherwise than as they teach others to live, taking care lest, while preaching to others, they themselves be found rejected, imitating the example of the one of whom it is written: “Jesus began both to do and to teach” (Acts 1).

Or the fishermen wash their nets when preachers carefully examine and scrutinize their teaching, lest anything heretical or perverse sound within it.

“Getting into one of the boats, which was Simon’s, he asked him to put out a little from the land. And sitting down, he taught the crowds from the boat.”

Simon’s boat is the primitive Church, gathered from the Jews. It is called Simon’s because it was specially entrusted to him, since at the beginning of his preaching many Jews believed through him. When he preached, three thousand believed in one day (Acts 2), and a great crowd of priests obeyed the faith.

To him the Lord said: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church. And whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven” (Matt. 16). Hence the apostle Paul says: “He who worked through Peter for the apostleship to the circumcision worked through me also among the Gentiles” (Gal. 2).

Or certainly Simon’s boat may be understood as the Church from the Gentiles, which was then entrusted to him by the Lord when he heard: “You are Peter,” and so forth. And again: “Simon, son of John, do you love me more than these? Feed my sheep” (John 21).

It is rightly called “one,” because the multitude of believers had one heart and one soul. None of them said that anything he possessed was his own; rather, they held everything in common (Acts 2).

He taught the crowds from the boat because holy preachers ought to commend no teaching other than that of the Church.

“When he had ceased speaking, he said to Simon: Put out into the deep.”

It should be noted that at first he commanded the boat to be moved a little from the land, but now he orders it to be taken into the deep, showing that teachers must temper their speech in preaching.

Weak hearers are not to be introduced suddenly into the depths of the mysteries. First they must be moved a little away from the land—that is, separated from earthly cares and carnal actions. The Lord indicates that their weakness must be tolerated when he orders Simon to move the boat a little from the land.

The perfect are not to be abandoned on account of such people; rather, they are to be summoned to the heights of the mysteries of God. This is what the Lord wished to signify when he said to Simon: “Put out into the deep.”

Alternatively, when he commands the boat to be moved a little from the land, he shows that the apostles’ preaching was to be extended to the neighboring nations. But when he says, “Put out into the deep,” he demonstrates that this same preaching would reach to the ends of the earth.

This was fulfilled when the apostles said to the Jews: “It was necessary that the word of God should be spoken to you first, but since you reject it and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts 13).

He rightly adds: “Let down your nets for a catch.”

A *catch* is a place suitable for catching fish, and thus the word is appropriately used. When he says, “Let down your nets for a catch,” he shows that the apostles’ preaching was to be let down where he knew there were elect who would be caught in the faith. The book of the Acts of the Apostles declares this when it says: “When the apostles wished to go into Bithynia, the Spirit of Jesus did not permit them” (Acts 16). For at that time there was no suitable place for a catch there.

When they were not planning to go into Macedonia, a Macedonian man appeared to Paul in a dream, begging him and saying: “Cross over into Macedonia and help us” (Acts 16). Understanding that the vision had been shown to him by God, he went to Macedonia, letting down his nets there for a catch.

It should be noted, however, that at one time the nets are folded and at another they are let down for a catch [the printed *plicantun* is likely an OCR error for *plicantur*, “are folded”], because not every time is suitable for teaching. At one time the nets of preaching are extended; at another the teachers attend to themselves.

“And Simon answered him: Master, we have labored throughout the whole night and caught nothing; but at your word I will let down the net.”

He rightly calls him Master, because although he had labored fruitlessly throughout the whole night in the work of fishing, as soon as he let down the nets at the Lord’s command, he caught a great multitude of fish.

In Scripture, night sometimes signifies ignorance or blindness of mind. Thus they labored throughout the whole night and caught nothing because, unless the Lord inwardly illuminates the mind of the hearer, the teacher’s speech labors outwardly in vain, as Scripture says (Ps. 126): “Unless the Lord builds the house,” and so forth. And: “Unless the Lord guards the city,” and so forth.

Whoever preaches to others ought not to trust in his own wisdom or eloquence, but in the power of God. Hence Simon rightly says: “But at your word I will let down the net.”

“And when they had done this, they enclosed a great quantity of fish.” Twice in the holy Gospel we read that, at the Lord’s command, nets cast out caught a great quantity of fish: once now, before the Passion, and a second time after the Resurrection. But there is this difference between the two catches: in this catch they are commanded to cast out the nets, but the side toward which they should be thrown is not specified; in the other, they are expressly said to have been cast on the right side. In this catch the net is torn because of the quantity of fish; in the other, many and large fish are caught, and the nets are not torn. In this catch the number of fish is not given; in the other, a definite number is stated, since one hundred and fifty-three are remembered as having been caught.

Therefore this catch signifies the Church as she is now, while the other signifies what she will be in the future. For as long as the Church remains in the present life, she contains citizens of both sides, because she receives both the good and the wicked. “For many,” as the Apostle says, “profess in words that they know God, but deny him by their deeds” (Tit. I); concerning them the Psalmist says: “I proclaimed and spoke; they were multiplied beyond number” (Ps. XXXIX). And appropriately, in that catch which took place after the Resurrection, the nets are read as having been cast on the right side of the boat, because just as the left signifies the present life, so the right signifies eternal life, as it is said through Solomon: “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand will embrace me” (Song II).

In this catch, which took place before the Resurrection, fish both good and bad are said to have been caught; in the other, only good fish, because in the present Church both good and bad are found, whereas in eternal life no wicked person is found. Nowhere are only the good found except in heaven, and nowhere are only the wicked found except in hell. This life, however, just as it lies between heaven and earth, contains within itself the citizens of both cities.

“But their net was being torn.” For those who were held in the Church by faith attempted to divide her through various heresies; such were Judas the betrayer and Simon Magus, and such were those of whom the apostle John says: “They went out from us, but they were not of us” (1 John II). But because the number of the elect was to be gathered not only from the Jews but also from the Gentiles, it is rightly added:

“And they signaled to their companions who were in the other boat to come and help them.” The other boat, as we said above, is the Church called from the Gentiles. Thus they signaled to their companions who were in the other boat to come and help them, because many were found among the Gentiles who became helpers of the apostles in preaching.

“And they came and filled both boats, so that they were almost sinking.” The filling of the boats signifies the perfection of the Church, which is filled daily through the conversion of believers and will be filled until the end of the age. The boats are endangered but do not sink, because the Church has often been shaken by the persecutions of heretics and often disturbed by the wicked conduct of false brothers, yet she could not be sunk because she had Christ as her foundation. He himself says: “Upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matt. XVI), and so forth. And as he says elsewhere: “The rivers came, the winds blew, and they struck that house, and it did not fall, because it had been founded upon solid rock” (Matt. VII).

[Col. 0628C] “When Simon Peter saw this, he fell at Jesus’ knees, saying: ‘Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, Lord.’” There are some weak people within the holy Church who, weighed down by the magnitude of their sins, fear to enter the paths of life as though they were difficult, yet do not fear to lie in their iniquities. Peter here expresses their person in himself: when he saw the miracle of the fish, he fell at Jesus’ knees, saying: “Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, Lord.” But one who regards himself as a sinner ought not, through despair, to drive God away from himself; rather, through devout groans and continual tears, he should draw near to God’s mercy, doubting nothing concerning the promise of him who says: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven will draw near” (Matt. III).

There are also others who, living according to the flesh, regard the discipline of spiritual rulers as tyranny; and while spiritual teaching seems burdensome to them, they try to cast the yoke of ecclesiastical governance from their necks. Although they live perversely, they sometimes persuade spiritual teachers—by their words, and sometimes even by the depravity of their conduct—to withdraw from them, though they are unwillingly subject to them. Peter signified their subjection by falling at Jesus’ knees; he signified the perversity of their conduct by saying: “Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, Lord.” But what spiritual teachers ought to do is shown by the example of that Shepherd of shepherds, because he did not withdraw from Simon when Simon asked him to do so, but offered him spiritual instruction. For the humble should not be abandoned because of the rejected proud; rather, the wicked should be corrected and endured together with the good, as Solomon says: “If the spirit of one who has authority rises against you, do not leave your place” (Eccli. XVIII).

“For amazement had seized him and all who were with him, at the catch of fish which they had taken; and likewise James and John, the sons of Zebedee, who were Simon’s companions.” Because these disciples were still less capable of the divine mystery, the sudden catch of fish overwhelmed them not only with amazement but also with fear. But the Lord comforts their weakness when he strengthens the frightened Simon, saying:

“Do not be afraid.” Indeed, in the frightened Simon he seems to comfort all penitents, so that they may not despair because of the greatness of their sins. Here he plainly foretells the ministry of preaching that he was about to entrust to him, when he says: “From now on you will be catching human beings.” He did not prohibit the occupation of fishing, but changed it spiritually. For after the Lord’s Resurrection we read that he went fishing. And appropriately, the one who had been a fisher of fish is foretold as destined to become a fisher of human beings, so that just as he used to draw fish from the depths of the whirlpools to the shore with a material net, so through spiritual preaching he might draw human beings from the bitter waves of the world to faith.

“And having brought the boats to land, they left everything and followed him.” It should not be thought that this was the same calling by which Matthew narrates that two disciples were called from the boats to follow Jesus. For here they are not said to have been called by him; rather, after seeing the miracle of the fish, they are remembered as having brought the boats to land, left everything, and followed him. Here it is to be understood that after these events they returned to their own affairs and took care of themselves. Later, however, when they were called by him, as Matthew and Mark relate, they left the boats and the net and followed him, so that they did not return again to their former affairs.

## HOMILY 118. THE SEVENTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST

(Matt. V.) “At that time Jesus said to his disciples: ‘Amen, I say to you, unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees.’” And so forth.

Those who think that the precepts of the Old Testament are stricter than those of the New should learn from the present reading to confess their ignorance, and should hear the Savior himself saying to his disciples: “Amen, I say to you, unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven.” The righteousness of the scribes and Pharisees was not killing a human being; but the righteousness of those who desire to enter the kingdom of heaven must be greater, so that they not only do not kill anyone, but do not even become angry or harbor hatred.

The righteousness of the scribes and Pharisees was to love a friend and hate an enemy; but the righteousness of those who are to enter the kingdom of heaven must be greater, so that they love not only a friend in God but also an enemy for God’s sake, as the Lord says: “Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who persecute and slander you, so that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. V).

The righteousness of the scribes and Pharisees was not to commit adultery with one’s neighbor’s wife; but the righteousness of those who desire to enter the kingdom of heaven must be greater, so that they not only do not commit adultery in the body, but do not even take pleasure in it in the heart, because the Lord says: “Whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (ibid.). And because of the Apostle’s statement: “God will judge fornicators and adulterers” (Heb. XIII).

The righteousness of the scribes and Pharisees was not to seize what belonged to others; but the righteousness of those who desire to enter the kingdom of heaven must be greater, so that they both give away what belongs to them and do not resist robbers, the Lord saying: “Do not resist evil” (Matt. V), and: “If someone takes what is yours, do not demand it back” (Luke VI).

These examples plainly show that the precepts of the New Testament are stricter insofar as they are spiritual. The former were given as carnal precepts to the immature and carnal, in whom perfection was not manifested but wickedness was cut away. The latter are spiritual gifts given to the spiritual, preparing not an earthly possession but a heavenly dwelling. Under the temporal righteousness of the former, a temporal reward was expected, as the Lord says: “Observe and hear the commandments of the Lord your God, so that it may go well with you, that you may live a long time, and that you may enter and possess the land flowing with milk and honey” (Deut. V, VI). The perfection of the New Testament promises eternal life, “which no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and which has not entered the human heart, what God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Cor. II). Therefore, to those who are promised a greater reward, a greater righteousness is required.

Alternatively: The righteousness of the scribes and Pharisees was thought to consist—although it was not righteousness—in disfiguring their faces so that they might appear to people to be fasting, while inwardly they were full of robbery and wickedness (Matt. VI). But the righteousness of those who desire to enter the kingdom of God must be greater, so that the holiness that appears in the body may be preserved much more in the heart.

The righteousness of the scribes and Pharisees appeared to consist in binding heavy and unbearable burdens and placing them on people’s shoulders, while they themselves were unwilling to move them with their finger (Matt. XXIII). But the righteousness of those who wish to enter the kingdom of heaven must be greater, so that they first keep God’s commandment and do not neglect what they teach or have taught others to keep.

The righteousness of the scribes and Pharisees was seen to consist in tithing mint, dill, cumin, and every garden herb, while neglecting the weightier matters of the Law (ibid.). The righteousness of those who are to enter the kingdom of God must abound more, so that they keep God’s smallest precepts in such a way that they do not neglect the greater ones.

“You have heard that it was said to the ancients: ‘You shall not kill’; and whoever kills will be liable to judgment.” It was said to the ancients—that is, to the Jewish people, to whom the Lord had commanded through Moses that they should not kill; or, if anyone killed, that he too should be killed.

“But I say to you that everyone who is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment.” That is: I, the new human being, who did not come to abolish the Law but to fulfill it, and who chose you from the world and give you a new commandment, that you love one another—I say to you: “Everyone who is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment.” Thus, in the New Testament anger is punished with as great a penalty as murder in the Old, according to what the apostle John says: “Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer” (1 John III).

In some copies it is written as follows: “Everyone who is angry with his brother without cause will be liable to judgment.” Some thought this should be understood as though anger were not a sin when we become angry because we have been harmed or provoked by others. But “without cause” must be deleted. A Christian is not permitted to become angry with his brother, either without cause or with cause; for the Lord commanded him: “Do not resist evil, but to the one who strikes your cheek, offer the other also, and pray for your persecutors” (Matt. V). “For, as the Apostle says, a servant of the Lord must not quarrel, but must be gentle toward all, even toward those who hold contrary opinions” (2 Tim. II). And as the apostle James says: “The anger of man does not accomplish the righteousness of God” (Jas. I). When charity is carefully maintained, the goad of anger is shut out, because no one can kill the person whom he truly loves.

“Whoever says to his brother, ‘Racha,’ will be liable to the council.” *Racha* is neither Greek nor Latin, but properly Hebrew. It is said to mean κενός, that is, “empty” or “vacant”; we may call such a person senseless or brainless. Some, however, have wanted to derive the etymology of this name from Greek, thinking that it means “ragged.” For in Greek a rag is called ῥάκος (*rhakos*). But, examining the force of this word more subtly, we understand *racha* to be nothing other than an inarticulate utterance signifying the agitation of an angry mind. Such are the interjections among grammarians: a grieving person says “alas,” an angry person “hei,” and one who falls “atat.” And appropriately it says: “Whoever says to his brother, ‘Racha.’” For our brother is the one who was redeemed with us at the same price and regenerated in the same baptism.

If, as the Lord says (Matt. XII), we are to give an account on the day of judgment even for an idle word, much more for an insulting one.

“Whoever says, ‘Fool,’ will be liable to the Gehenna of fire.” It should be noted in this passage that the progression rises step by step from lesser matters to greater, since he threatens punishment according to the quality of the sin. In the first place he posits only one thing, namely anger; in the second, two things, namely anger and the word expressing the agitation of anger; in the third, three things: anger, the word, and insult. Therefore, just as it is a greater sin to say “Fool” than merely to become angry or to say “Racha,” so it is more serious to be liable to the Gehenna of fire than to be liable to judgment or to the council.

In a court the case is examined, and the person thought to be guilty is sometimes found innocent. In a council, if someone has been convicted as guilty, the others deliberate what penalty should be imposed, and he may still escape. But in the Gehenna of fire there is no release. Thus the degree of punishment indicates the measure of the sin.

The name *Gehenna* is not found throughout the entire sequence of the writings of the Old Testament, but is recognized as having first been used by the Savior in the Gospel. The name *Gehenna* is compounded from *ge* and *Ennon*, for it is interpreted as “the free valley” (*vallis gratuita*). There was a valley of the sons of Ennon near Jerusalem, where, because of the crime of idolatry, many corpses of the dead lay. Therefore, wherever the name *Gehenna* is used, the punishment of hell is signified.

But lest the Savior seem to have pronounced too harsh a sentence when he said that whoever called his brother “Fool” would be liable to the Gehenna of fire, he immediately added the remedy of reconciliation, saying:

“If you offer your gift at the altar, and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar, and go first to be reconciled to your brother; then come and offer your gift.” In these words we must carefully consider how greatly he loves brotherly affection in us and how much he hates the evil of discord, since he commands us to leave our gifts unoffered before the altar and first to be reconciled to our brother. Since the Lord seeks our gifts only for our sake, we can in no way offer him the sacrifice of peace as long as we are unreconciled with our brothers.

It should not be thought that we offer gifts to him only when we carry an offering with our hands before the altar. When we devote ourselves to prayer, mortify the flesh through fasting and vigils, give alms, receive a guest, clothe the naked, and fulfill other works of piety like these, then we offer gifts to God. We must therefore be extremely careful not to retain in our heart the evil of discord against anyone, so that our gifts may not be acceptable in God’s sight; for, as has been said, we cannot offer God a pleasing sacrifice as long as we are unreconciled with our neighbors.

It should be noted that he does not say, “If you have something against your brother,” but: “If your brother has something against you.” Your brother has something against you when you have harmed him. We must therefore proceed to reconciliation; and if he wishes to ask forgiveness, what he has sinned against us must be mercifully forgiven, because the Lord says: “When you stand to pray, forgive” (Mark XI), and so forth.

If he does not wish to ask forgiveness, spiritual brothers should be sent to him more privately, to urge him to make satisfaction in humility, according to the Lord’s command: “If your brother refuses to listen to you, take with you one or two others, so that by the mouth of two or three witnesses every word may stand” (Matt. XVIII). But if he persists in being obstinate and proud, the one who has sinned against you need not be asked by you for forgiveness; nevertheless, for God’s sake forgive him from your heart, so that, approaching the altar with a clear conscience, you may say: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. VI). And so that what the Lord says may be fulfilled in us: “If you forgive people their sins, your heavenly Father will also forgive you your sins” (ibid.).

If negligence has occurred on both sides, satisfaction through forgiveness must proceed from both sides. Yet this distinction must be observed in this reconciliation: if the one who injured another caused temporal harm, he should justly restore what he unjustly took. But if he injured his neighbor only by word or insult, the mere request for forgiveness is considered sufficient satisfaction. Therefore, after reconciliation, the Lord says:

“And then, coming, you will offer your gift. Come to an agreement with your adversary while you are on the way with him.” Perhaps someone is prompted to ask who our adversary is, with whom our Lord commands us to agree. The answer is that this adversary is understood to be the word of God—not because it is rightly an adversary of our salvation, but because it contradicts our carnal will.

For example, carnal pleasure wants to drag us into adultery, but the word of God, contrary to us, cries out: “Adulterers will not possess the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. VI). And elsewhere: “God will judge fornicators and adulterers” (Heb. XIII). And again: “Whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. V). If, after hearing this voice, you avoid carnal pleasure—that is, if you restrain the heat of lust with the bridle of continence—you have agreed with your adversary for your own good.

Let us give another example. Drunkenness suggests itself to you and sends dryness into your throat until you reach intoxication, but the divine word contradicts you: “See that your hearts are not weighed down by gluttony and drunkenness” (Luke XXI). And again: “Drunkards will not possess the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. VI). Therefore, conquer the pleasure of drinking and agree with your adversary.

The same must be understood concerning the other vices, in which the flesh desires against the spirit and the spirit against the flesh; these oppose one another, so that we do not do what we wish (Gal. V). The present way is life. As long as we remain in the present life, we are, as it were, on a road and journey, and have not yet reached our homeland. We are therefore commanded to agree with our adversary on the way, because after death there will be no opportunity either to hear the word of God or to amend, as Solomon testifies: “Whatever your hand can do, do it earnestly, because there is neither work, nor reason, nor knowledge, nor wisdom in the underworld to which you are hastening” (Eccl. IX).

Thus it is said concerning those who neglect to convert until late: “They will call upon me, and I will not answer; they will rise early, and will not find me, because they hated discipline and did not listen to the fear of the Lord, nor did they accept my counsels, and they rejected all my correction” (Prov. I).

What follows is greatly to be feared: “Lest perhaps the adversary hand you over to the judge, and the judge hand you over to the officer, and you be thrown into prison.” If you refuse to listen and neglect to agree with your adversary, he will hand you over to the judge—that is, the word of God itself will be a testimony to your condemnation, the word that had prohibited your correction. And not only will the word of God be your testimony, but your very thoughts will rise against you, as the Apostle says: “Their mutually conflicting or even defending thoughts, on the day when God will judge the secrets of human beings” (Rom. II).

Even the earth on which we sin will be a testimony against us unless we have first been healed by the medicine of repentance, as blessed Job testifies: “And the earth cries out against me” (Job XIII). The officer to whom the one who refused to agree with his adversary is handed over is understood to be the devil, who will receive the ministry of just condemnation over those who voluntarily handed themselves over to wicked action. For in punishment they will have as exactors those whom they had as persuaders in guilt.

The prison is hell, “where there is the worm that will not die and the fire that will not be extinguished” (Mark IX), concerning which John says in the Apocalypse: “All blasphemers, fornicators, and adulterers will be thrown into the lake of fire and sulfur” (Rev. XXI).

As for what follows:

“Amen, I say to you, you will not come out from there until you have paid the last quadrans.” He uses the adverb *until*, which ordinarily designates a limited time, for an unlimited duration. Sacred Scripture does this not only here but in many passages, as the Lord says through the Prophet: “Until you grow old, I am.” And the Psalmist: “As the eyes of a maidservant are on the hands of her mistress, so our eyes are toward the Lord our God, until he has mercy on us” (Ps. CXXII). Surely God was not going to exist only until their old age, nor would our eyes cease to look upon him after he had had mercy on us? No; as we have said, a limited expression is used for an unlimited one.

This passage refutes the Origenists, who in a false display of piety said that the demons would be released after the judgment. For just as eternal kingdom has been prepared for the saints, so eternal punishment has been prepared for the reprobate, the Lord saying (Matt. XXV): “Go, accursed ones, into the eternal fire that has been prepared for the devil and his angels.” And again: “These will go into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life.” Hence Solomon says: “Wherever a tree falls, whether toward the south or toward the north”—that is, whether into hell or into the kingdom of God—“there it will remain” (Eccl. XI).

## HOMILY 119. THE EIGHTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST

[Col. 0634D]

(Mark VIII.) “At that time, when there was a great crowd with Jesus and they had nothing to eat, he called his disciples and said to them: ‘I have compassion on the crowd.’” And so forth.

The Lord Jesus Christ, God before the ages and made human at the end of the ages, was pleased to order his works in such a way that in one and the same miracle he might reveal himself to be true God and true human being. We quickly recognize this in the sequence of the present reading if we consider it carefully. For the statement that he was moved with compassion for the hungry crowd is an indication of human compassion; but the fact that he feeds four thousand people from seven loaves is a declaration of divine power.

It should not be thought that this is the same reading in which the other evangelists report that five thousand people were satisfied with five loaves. For there the disciples remind the Lord to dismiss the crowds so that they may buy what they need, whereas here the Lord is said to have been moved with compassion for the hungry crowd. There five loaves are mentioned, here seven; there they are said to have been barley loaves, whereas here the kind of foodstuff is not specified; there five thousand people were satisfied from five loaves, here four thousand are fed from seven loaves; there they reclined on grass, here upon the ground.

Therefore, there the crowd that was satisfied from five loaves signifies the people placed under the Law of the Old Testament, who received the five books of Moses for their instruction. Here, however, the crowd that is refreshed from seven loaves signifies the multitude of faithful people who are fed daily through the grace of the New Testament.

Isaiah had foreseen this crowd in the Spirit as one that would be fed by the Lord when he said: “All the nations will come to him, and many peoples will go and say: ‘House of Jacob, come, and let us walk in the light of the Lord’” (Isa. II). And the Psalmist says: “All the nations that you have made will come and worship before you, Lord, and they will glorify your name forever” (Ps. LXXXV).

And appropriately, in that feeding which took place from five loaves, by which we said the Jewish people were signified, the disciples are said to have reminded the Lord to dismiss the crowds so that they might buy what they needed, because before the Lord’s coming that people had their patriarchs and prophets as intercessors. Here, however, the Lord himself is moved to mercy, because the Gentile people were saved not by their own merits or through anyone’s intervention, but solely by the Lord’s gratuitous mercy, as the apostle Paul says: “You have been saved by the grace of God” (Eph. II).

And appropriately, the Lord refreshes with bodily food the crowd that he saw hungering for the word of God, so that he might fulfill in them what he promised elsewhere, saying: “Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you” (Matt. VI).

Rightly, therefore, it is said concerning this crowd: “For behold, they have already remained with me for three days, and they have nothing to eat.” The crowd remains with the Lord for three days when the faithful people persevere unceasingly in confessing the holy Trinity. A human being is said to sustain God when, even amid adversity, he does not fall away from his love, imitating the one who said: “Direct me in your truth and teach me, for you are God my Savior, and I have waited for you all day long” (Ps. XXIV).

Alternatively: The crowd sustains the Lord for three days when the elect occupy their understanding, memory, and will in good works. Or certainly, it sustains the Lord for three days when it preserves faith, hope, and charity inviolate, concerning which the Apostle says: “Let these three remain in you: faith, hope, and charity; but the greatest of these is charity” (1 Cor. XIII).

“And if I send them away fasting to their home, they will faint on the way.” The home of the elect is properly the heavenly homeland, concerning which the Lord says: “In my Father’s house there are many dwelling places” (John XIV). The one who said, “I have asked one thing from the Lord; this I shall seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life” (Ps. XXVI), longed to reach it with the most ardent love.

The present way is life. As long as we live, we are on the way and have not yet reached our homeland. The Lord therefore does not wish to send the crowd away fasting, lest they faint on the way, because the elect must be fed with the nourishment of the word of God so that they do not cease from good works in the present life. For just as the body fails without food, so the soul fails without the word of God. The one who desired to be refreshed by this food said: “The Lord feeds me, and I shall lack nothing; he has placed me in a place of pasture” (Ps. XXII).

As for what follows: “But some of them have come from far away.” If we wish to refer this to both peoples, the Jewish people came from near, because they possessed knowledge of the Law and knowledge of God; the Gentile people came from far away when, after the worship of idols, they were converted to the knowledge of God. Hence the Apostle says: “He himself is our peace, who made both one” (Eph. II).

Every day, however, in the conversion of the faithful, some come to faith from near and others from far away. Whoever follows God’s will without being defiled by any grave sins undoubtedly comes from near. The person who, having experienced lawful marriage, is converted to God also comes from nearby. But whoever is converted to God through repentance after public debauchery, adulteries, thefts, murders, drunkenness, and robberies comes from far away.

The one who dedicates himself to God’s service from infancy or childhood comes from near; the one who is converted to God in old age comes from far away. The Lord therefore promises that he will give food even to those who come from far away, because he receives and loves not only the righteous but also converted sinners, as he himself says: “I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance” (Luke V). And the Apostle says: “Coming, he proclaimed peace to those who were near and to those who were far away” (Eph. II).

He who through the prophet says, “As I live, says the Lord God, I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live,” denies neither forgiveness nor food to such people (Ezek. XVIII). And again: “On whatever day the sinner turns and laments his sin, all his sins will be handed over to oblivion” (ibid.). And again: “Can a woman forget her infant, so as not to have pity on the child of her womb? And even if she should forget, I nevertheless will not forget you” (Isa. XLIX). And in the Gospel: “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick” (Matt. IX).

“And his disciples answered him: ‘Where can anyone satisfy these people with bread here in the wilderness?’” At the other feeding, Philip is specifically reported to have said: “Two hundred denarii worth of bread would not be enough for them, so that each might receive even a little” (John VI). Now, however, all the disciples say in general: “Where can anyone satisfy these people with bread here in the wilderness?”

The more difficult the matter appeared to the disciples, the more clearly the Lord’s miracle shines forth. For the apostles, weighed down by the weakness of the flesh, did not yet perfectly understand Christ’s divinity. In the presence of him who brings bread forth from the earth and wine that gladdens the human heart, they nevertheless doubted that a multitude of people could be satisfied from a few loaves. But the Lord wished to feed the multitude from a few loaves not only to remove the disciples’ doubt, but also to refresh the crowd, exhausted by fasting.

“And he asked them: ‘How many loaves do you have?’” The Lord, who knows everything before it happens, asks the disciples not because he is ignorant, but so that through his question he may instruct their minds. They were to learn that through his presence many crowds of people could be satisfied from a few loaves—he who for forty years fed vast ranks of the people in the wilderness with manna, without the labor of the plow.

“They said: ‘Seven.’” At the other feeding, five barley loaves are reported, by which, as we said, the Scripture of the Old Testament was signified, lying hidden beneath the covering of the letter. Here, however, seven loaves are mentioned because of the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit. Enlightened by this grace, the apostles and their successors proclaimed to the world both the faith of the holy Trinity and the teaching of the four Gospels.

The number seven aptly signifies this, since it is composed of the first even number and the first odd number—that is, of three and four. Or it is because the number seven is frequently used for fullness, since through the grace of the Holy Spirit the saints have attained the perfection of righteousness.

[Col. 0637C] “And he commanded the crowd to recline upon the ground.” In the other feeding, the crowd is said to have reclined upon the grass, because the Law prohibited only carnal sins. “For all flesh is grass, and all its glory like the flower of the field” (Isa. 40). In this feeding, however, by which we have said the grace of the New Testament is signified, the crowd rightly reclines upon the ground, because the grace of the New Testament restrains not only sins of action but also sins of thought. It does not merely forbid those who seize what belongs to others, but also urges those striving toward perfection to leave their own possessions together with the earth itself, the Lord saying: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me” (Matt. 19). And as he himself says elsewhere: “Unless someone renounces all that he possesses, and does not hate father, mother, wife, children, brothers and sisters, servants and maidservants, and lands for my name’s sake, he cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14).
