In the moral sense, the crowd reclined upon the ground when the souls of the faithful, mindful of their own frailty, continually consider that they are earth and dust, saying with the Psalmist: “My soul clung to the pavement; revive me according to your word” (Ps. 118). And again: “For our soul has been humbled in the dust; our belly has clung to the earth” (Ps. 43). In this way he had reclined upon the ground who said: “I shall speak to my Lord, though I am dust and ashes” (Gen. 18).

“And taking the seven loaves, giving thanks, he broke them and gave them to his disciples to set before the people; and they set them before the crowd.” Above we have already said that the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit are signified by the seven loaves. The Lord therefore took seven loaves because, above all human beings, he possessed the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit in a special way, as the prophet says: “And the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him, the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety; and the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him” (Isa. 11).

He broke the loaves and gave them to his disciples because he distributes the gifts of that same Holy Spirit to each of the saints as he wills: to some he grants the word of wisdom, to others the word of knowledge, to others kinds of tongues, to others the interpretation of speech, and to others the discernment of spirits. Or he gave the seven loaves to his disciples to set before the crowd when, appearing to them after the resurrection, he breathed upon them and said: “Receive the Holy Spirit. Whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them; and whose you retain, they are retained” (John 20). The disciples set them before the crowd because he wished the knowledge of the sacred mystery to be made known to the world through their preaching. Beautifully, he is said to have given thanks when he was about to feed the crowd, in order to show that God must be glorified by us in all good works.

“And they had a few small fish, and he blessed these also and commanded them to be set before the people.” By the small fish, which he blessed and set before the crowd, the imitable conduct of the saints is signified. They are accustomed not only, like fish, to leap above the waters, despising the earth and loving heaven, but also to grow and advance spiritually amid the waves of various persecutions, saying with the Apostle: “Although our outward man is being corrupted, yet the inward man is being renewed” (2 Cor. 4).

With the seven loaves, therefore, he commanded a few small fish to be set before them, because preachers daily bring forward the examples of the saints, together with the preaching of the word, for our imitation. They are rightly said to have been a few small fish, because the conduct of the saints is humble and despised in their own judgment; to them the Savior says: “Do not fear, little flock, because it has pleased your Father to give you the kingdom” (Luke 12). Of these Solomon says: “The little rabbit, a feeble people, makes its dwelling in the rock” (Prov. 30).

And rightly, in that feeding which was made from five loaves, two fish are mentioned, while here an indefinite number is given: because, compared with those from the Jewish people who were going to believe, an innumerable multitude from the Gentile people came to the faith, the Lord saying: “Many shall come from the east and the west, and shall recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 8).

“And they ate and were satisfied.” They did not all eat equally, but all reached one fullness, because not all grasp the meaning of Sacred Scripture equally; nevertheless, all find spiritual nourishment in it according to their measure and condition. Hence it is rightly said of the manna: “He who had more did not have too much, and he who had less did not have too little; but all measured out a measure of a gomor” (2 Cor. 8; Exod. 16).

For Sacred Scripture is a certain river, great and small, lofty and lowly, in which the elephant swims and the lamb walks upon its feet. Spiritual and most learned men, the more fully they taste its meaning, the more they find within it that for which they hunger; while the humble and the little ones find in it what can satisfy them according to the measure of their capacity. Of these the Psalmist says: “The poor shall eat and be satisfied, and they shall praise the Lord who seek him; their hearts shall live for ever and ever” (Ps. 21).

“And they took up what remained of the fragments, seven baskets.” Here the Lord’s miracle is increased. It would indeed be a great miracle if, after four thousand people had been satisfied from seven loaves, nothing remained. But the sign grew and increased the wonder. Not only were four thousand people satisfied from the seven loaves, but seven baskets were also filled with fragments, according to the number of the loaves.

What the crowd cannot consume, the apostles carry away in baskets, because the teachers and doctors of the Church ought to store in their own hearts the more obscure meanings of Sacred Scripture, which simple people cannot grasp, so that at the time of teaching they may be able to provide each person with spiritual food. For it is shameful to be learning at the very time when one ought to be teaching. They should be among those of whom the Lord says: “The faithful and prudent servant whom the Lord has set over his household, to give them their measure of wheat at the proper time” (Luke 12).

Beautifully, in that feeding which was made from five loaves, twelve baskets of fragments remained, because the Jewish people had twelve apostles full of the Holy Spirit for their instruction. Here, however, seven baskets are carried away according to the number of the loaves, because the Church gathered from the Gentiles is celebrated, governed, and nourished through the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit. In its type, John in his Apocalypse enumerates seven churches, as well as seven golden lampstands and seven horns of the Lamb. Hence the prophet Zechariah says: “Upon one stone are seven eyes” (Zech. 9).

Rightly, the seven baskets signify the innermost hearts of the saints, who, illuminated by the grace of the Holy Spirit, preserve the unfading freshness of faith and, extinguishing the flaming darts of the wicked one with spiritual weapons, advance toward the trophy of perpetual victory. For a basket is woven from rush and palm. The rush commonly grows beside water because of its moisture, while the palm is so called as though it were *alma pacis*, “the nourishing palm of peace,” which used to adorn the victorious hand.

Holy men, therefore, become green like a rush beside water when they devote themselves to meditation upon Sacred Scripture, so that they cannot wither in faith and good works. Of them it is written: “Blessed is the man who trusts in the Lord, and the Lord will be his confidence. He shall be like a tree planted beside streams of water, sending its roots toward moisture; he shall not fear when heat comes, but his leaf shall be green, and in the year of drought he shall not be anxious, nor shall he ever cease to bear fruit” (Jer. 17).

The palm is woven together with the rush in the basket when these same holy men undertake spiritual warfare against the vices of the flesh and of thoughts, knowing that “the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh; and these are opposed to one another, so that we do not do the things we wish” (Gal. 5). Their most steadfast perseverance is revealed when it is added:

“And those who ate were about four thousand, and he dismissed them.” It is not without reason that four thousand people are fed by the Lord. For the number four is perfect and, divided into its parts, possesses perfection. It is divided into one, two, and three. One belongs to God, because there is “one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all, who is above all, and through all, and in us all” (Eph. 4). Two refers to the twofold love or to the two Testaments. Three refers to the holy and undivided Trinity, namely, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Four refers to the grace of the New Testament or to the four books of the Gospel, in which this is especially described.

Because in the four books of the Gospels we find how we are to believe in one God, how we are to possess the twofold love, and how we are to confess the holy and undivided Trinity, we rightly recognize that four thousand people were satisfied by the Lord. Or, rightly, because we have heard that four thousand people were fed by the Lord, we are mystically taught that, if we wish to be spiritually nourished, we must possess the four principal virtues: prudence, temperance, fortitude, and justice, than which nothing is more useful in human life.

Because a squared stone does not sway, but whichever way it is turned, it lies equally firm, the steadfastness of the saints is rightly signified by the number four. They are not carried about by every wind of doctrine, but, like firm stones, whether in prosperity or adversity, they persevere most steadfastly in good works and in faith, considering what the Lord says: “He who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. 24).

Or, because through the teaching of the four Gospels we learn both the faith by which we rightly believe and the steadfastness by which we live rightly, the four thousand are rightly said to have been nourished from the seven loaves. We ought not to believe or live in any other way than the four Gospels teach. Hence John testifies in the Apocalypse that he saw four living creatures before the throne of God, full of eyes before and behind, crying out: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God Sabaoth, who is, and who was, and who is to come” (Rev. 4).

## HOMILY 120. THE NINTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST

*(Matthew 7.)* “At that time, Jesus said to his disciples: ‘Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing.’” And what follows.

Foreseeing that the teaching of heretics would arise against the elect in the Church, as well as the savagery of false Catholics, the Lord first wished to reveal the character of their thoughts, so that they might be guarded against all the more easily the more clearly they were recognized. For he says: “Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly are ravenous wolves.”

This is to be understood especially of heretics, who are false prophets, since they utter many falsehoods about the substance of divinity and humanity, wishing to bend the divinely inspired Sacred Scriptures to their own meaning. So that they may deceive the hearts of simple brothers more easily, they clothe themselves, as it were, in sheep’s clothing when they insert the opinions of Catholic Fathers into their own teaching. For they know that if they always said evil things, they would be recognized and avoided more quickly. Therefore, they mix good things with evil, so that, while what is true is gladly heard, what is false may not easily be distinguished.

They imitate the practice of poisoners, who, when they wish to offer poison to someone, smear the mouth of the cup with honey, so that, while the sweet part is tasted, the drinker may reach the deadly part without hesitation. Like scorpions carrying stings in their tails, heretics display good things in their first words but teach perverse doctrines at the end, and thus they sting.

Such people are compared to ravenous wolves because, while their tongue flatters outwardly, they rage inwardly in their mind. Just as a wolf scatters, tears apart, and mangles a flock, so heretics, possessing a poisonous mind, do not cease to tear apart the minds of the simple. Those whom they cannot deceive secretly, they persecute openly. Therefore, they pretend to be good so that they may drag the minds of the simple into their heresy, or at least receive their possessions as though they were good teachers.

The apostle Paul writes of this in his Epistle, saying: “These are the ones who enter into widows’ houses and lead captive little women laden with sins” (2 Tim. 2), “and by smooth speech and blessings deceive the hearts of the innocent” (Rom. 16). The same Apostle foresaw that such wolves would come when he said: “I know that after my departure grievous wolves will enter among you, ravenous wolves who will not spare the flock. From among you men will arise speaking perverse things, and they will draw away the disciples after them” (Acts 20).

The Lord also wished the apostles to beware of these people, saying to them: “Behold, I send you as sheep into the midst of wolves. Therefore be wise as serpents and simple as doves” (Matt. 10). The Lord warns us to beware of such wolves, because just as the most learned and Catholic men ought to resist heretics, so simple people ought to avoid their company, lest, while their teaching is heard, the minds of those listening be defiled.

The apostle John gives this warning when he says: “If anyone comes to you and does not bring this doctrine, do not receive him into your house, nor say ‘Hail’ to him. For whoever says ‘Hail’ to him shares in his wicked works” (2 John 1). Hence the Apostle also writes to Titus: “Avoid a heretical person after one and a second correction, knowing that such a person is perverted” (Titus 3).

This may be compared with the words of Maro [Virgil] (*Eclogue* 3):

> You who gather flowers and strawberries growing on the ground,  
> Flee from here, boys; a cold snake lies hidden in the grass.

Alternatively, “ravenous wolves” may be understood as false Catholics, who confess that they know God but deny him by their deeds. When they assume the outward appearance of Christianity, they appear as though clothed in sheep’s skins. They are rightly compared to ravenous wolves because, while they live carnally, they sometimes draw others toward evil by their bad example and sometimes seize the possessions of others like wolves. Of such people the prophet says: “Your princes have become like evening wolves, leaving nothing for the morning” (Zeph. 3).

The Lord therefore commands us to beware of such people, because just as the company of the good greatly helps, so the society of the wicked frequently does great harm. The prophet bears witness to this when he says: “With the holy man you will be holy, and with the innocent man you will be innocent. With the chosen man you will be chosen, and with the perverse man you will become perverse” (2 Sam. 22). Solomon likewise says: “He who walks with the wise will be wise; the friend of fools will become like them” (Prov. 13).

The same Solomon warns us, saying: “Do not be a friend to an angry man, nor walk with a furious man, lest you learn his ways and take a stumbling-block for your soul” (Prov. 22). Paul writes similarly to the disciples: “If anyone is called a brother and is a fornicator, adulterer, or greedy person—which is the service of idols—with such a person do not even eat” (1 Cor. 5).

But do heretics or false Catholics always remain hidden beneath sheep’s clothing, or can they always conceal themselves? No. For the Lord revealed how they could be recognized when he added:

“You will know them by their fruits.” The word “fruit” derives its name from enjoyment; therefore works are signified by fruit. If you ask what the good fruits are by which you can recognize a person, the apostle Paul makes this clear, saying: “The fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, long-suffering, goodness, kindness, gentleness, faith, modesty, self-control, chastity” (Gal. 5).

Do not therefore seek in a heretic the beautiful leaves of words, but purity of faith. Do not look in a Christian merely for a reputation of good standing, but seek the fruit of right action. Do not look at the tongue, but at the hand. For just as a tree is not praised for the beauty of its leaves or flowers but for the abundance of its fruit, so heretics and false Catholics are not to be praised for their pretense but for the fruit of good works.

“For,” as the Lord says elsewhere (Luke 6), “there is no good tree that produces bad fruit, nor a bad tree that produces good fruit. Each tree is known by its fruit.” Hence it is also added: “Do they gather grapes from thorns, or figs from thistles?”

Thorns and thistles are trees full of prickles, so that they can scarcely be handled without injury. Opposed to them are the fig tree and the vine, which produce both the fragrance of the sweetest scent and the fruit of the sweetest taste. Therefore, by thorns and thistles vices and sins are signified, concerning which the Lord said to the first man: “Your land shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you” (Gen. 3).

By the grape and the fig, however, the sweet and pleasant fruit of charity is understood—the fruit whose taste the palate of the mind had experienced when he said: “How sweet are your words to my throat, sweeter than honey to my mouth” (Ps. 118).

Just as the thorn and thistle are difficult to handle, so heretics and false Catholics are found to be bitter and sharp toward their neighbors. Therefore the false doctrine of the former and the evil examples of the latter must be avoided, because, as Solomon says: “Whoever touches pitch will be defiled by it, and whoever breaks through a hedge will be bitten by a serpent” (Sir. 13).

Or, as some teach, by the grape and the fig the sweetness of the memory of the heavenly kingdom is understood. Thus grapes are not gathered from thorns, nor figs from thistles, because if the fruit of charity is sought in a heretic, the thorn of dissension is found; if heavenly love is sought in a false Catholic, earthly love is discovered; and if the fruit of chastity is sought, the fruit of lust is seen.

Although the thorn does not produce grapes, it nevertheless sometimes supports a vine with its cluster. For heretics and false Catholics, though evil in many respects, nevertheless sometimes teach certain good things and display certain religious practices. What, then, should be done with such people? Should the cluster be abandoned because of the thorn—that is, should good things be abandoned because of evil things? Certainly not. But, as Father Augustine says: “The cluster should be gathered in such a way that the thorn is nevertheless avoided.”

Just as the teaching of heretics must be completely avoided by simple people, so Catholics and orthodox Fathers, who know how to distinguish true doctrine from false, must reject what is evil and take up what is good within ecclesiastical authority.

The Lord showed this figuratively in the Law when, as the children of Israel were leaving Egypt (Exod. 12), he commanded them to borrow from their neighbors many vessels of gold and silver, so that they might despoil Egypt. What is understood by silver if not the splendid meaning of Sacred Scripture? “The words of the Lord are pure words, silver tested by fire” (Ps. 18). By gold, however, the brilliance of eloquence is expressed, Solomon saying: “A desirable treasure rests in the mouth of the wise” (Prov. 21).

Therefore, we borrow golden and silver vessels from our neighbors when we take from heretics and pagans, for our own benefit, necessary insights or the brilliance of eloquence. Hence elsewhere in the same Law it is figuratively commanded:

“If you go out to war against your enemies, and the Lord your God delivers them into your hands, and you lead them away captive, and among the number of the women you see a beautiful girl who pleases your eyes, and you wish to have her as a wife, you shall bring her into your house. But first you shall shave the hair of her head and cut the tips of her nails; she shall mourn her father and mother in the house for one month, and after this you shall go in to her, and she shall be your wife” (Deut. 21).

Spiritually, we go forth to war when we contend with the enemies of the Church, that is, with heretics, concerning the Christian faith and religion. When, overcome by divine authority, our Lord God has delivered them into our hands, and we find among their arguments insights necessary to strengthen our faith, we should take them to ourselves as wives, because, as Solomon says: “Wisdom is a man’s wife” (Prov. 10).

But first we must shave the hair of her head and cut the tips of her nails—that is, we must discern and reject whatever is superfluous, whatever is heretical, and whatever is corrupt and contrary to our faith. If someone from among them wishes to convert to our Catholic faith, he must not be rejected but received, provided that he first mourns his father and mother for one month—that is, that he does penance for the former way of life and heretical perversity by which he was polluted or nourished, and that he anathematizes and washes it away.

“Thus every good tree produces good fruits, but the bad tree produces bad fruits.” That trees in Scripture signify human beings the Lord makes clear when he says elsewhere: “Either make the tree good and its fruit good, or make the tree bad and its fruit bad” (Matt. 21). The blind man who had been illuminated by the Lord said: “I see people as though they were trees” (Mark 12). Daniel likewise interprets the great tree in the vision of King Nebuchadnezzar as the king himself (Dan. 4). And the Psalmist says of the righteous: “The righteous shall flourish like a palm tree, and shall multiply like a cedar of Lebanon” (Ps. 91).

What he says—“Thus every good tree produces good fruits, but the bad tree produces bad fruits”—amounts to this: Just as neither the thorn produces grapes nor the thistle figs, so bad fruit proceeds from a corrupt root, and good action arises from good intention. Hence it is also added:

“A good tree cannot produce bad fruits, nor can a bad tree produce good fruits.” Here a question troubles the mind: why does he say, “A good tree cannot produce bad fruits, nor can a bad tree produce good fruits,” when we read that the apostle Paul, surely a good tree, produced bad fruit when he persecuted the Church of God, and that Judas, a bad tree, produced good fruit when he followed the Lord with the other apostles?

The answer is that just as fruit proceeds from the root of a tree, and from the fruit itself its kind or taste is recognized, so a work is brought forth from the intention of the heart. And as the Lord says: “Whatever your intention has been, such will your work also be.” Therefore a good person cannot produce bad fruits so long as he perseveres in the root of a good intention; nor can a bad person produce good fruits so long as an evil intention endures.

According to this meaning, we also read that the apostle Peter, surely a good tree, produced bad fruit so long as he denied the Lord (Matt. 26). Jethro, however, though previously a bad tree, produced good fruit when he gave Moses useful counsel (Exod. 18). Similarly David, certainly a good tree, produced bad fruit when, through carnal desire, he committed adultery and homicide (2 Sam. 11). Nebuchadnezzar, however, though he was a bad tree, produced good fruit when he commanded the God of Daniel to be worshiped throughout the world (Dan. 6).

A bad person can nevertheless become good if he abandons evil, and one who seemed good can become bad if he turns away from goodness. But because one and the same person cannot, at one and the same time, be both good and bad, a good tree cannot produce bad fruits, nor can a bad tree produce good fruits.

What follows is extremely fearful:

“Every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire.” He does not say, “the tree that produces bad fruit,” but “the tree that does not produce good fruit.” From this, by contrast, we can gather what punishment is prepared for those who do evil, when punishment is foretold even for those who are sluggish in doing good.

If the one who did not clothe the naked is thrown into the fire, into what fire will the one be thrown who stripped the clothed? And if the one who did not give his own possessions goes to punishment, to what punishment will the one go who steals what belongs to others?

Therefore, let no one who is sluggish in good works deceive himself with false security, because every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire, in accordance with what the Lord says elsewhere: “Every branch in me that does not bear fruit must be cut off and thrown into the fire” (John 15). For it is not enough to turn away from evil unless each person also strives to do good.

Hence the Lord of the vineyard, seeking fruit on the fig tree and finding none, says to the gardener: “Behold, these three years I have come seeking fruit on this fig tree, and I find none. Cut it down, then; why should it even occupy the ground?” (Luke 13). Of this tree John the Baptist says: “Now the axe is laid at the root of the tree” (Matt. 3).

The tree is cut down when a human being dies. Once cut down, it is thrown into the fire when the wicked person, through death, encounters the burning of Gehenna, because while he lived he refused to produce the fruit of good works.

The Lord repeats the recognition of good and bad trees when he adds:

“Therefore you will know them by their fruits.” The apostle Paul shows what kind of fruits distinguish bad trees from good ones when he says: “The works of the flesh are manifest: fornications, uncleanness, licentiousness, debauchery, the service of idols, sorceries, enmities, strife, jealousies, anger, quarrels, dissensions, factions, envy, murders, drunkenness, revelries, and things like these. Those who do such things will not obtain the kingdom of God” (Gal. 5).

Of such people the prophet Jeremiah says: “Cursed is the man who trusts in man, and makes flesh his arm, and whose heart departs from the Lord. He shall be like a tamarisk in the desert, and shall not see when good comes; he shall dwell in dryness, in solitude, in a salt land and an uninhabited place” (Jer. 17).

But what fruits a good tree produces the same prophet declares, saying: “Blessed is the man who trusts in the Lord, and the Lord will be his confidence. He shall be like a tree transplanted beside streams of water, sending its roots toward moisture; he shall not fear when heat comes, his leaf shall be green, and in the year of drought he shall not be anxious, nor shall he ever cease to bear fruit” (ibid.).

Such fruits were produced by the good tree that said: “But I, like a fruitful olive tree in the house of God, have hoped in the mercy of God for ever and ever” (Ps. 51). The Lord wished his disciples, who were certainly good trees, to produce such fruits when he said to them: “I chose you from the world and appointed you to go and bear fruit, and for your fruit to remain” (John 15).

Some people, however, possess only the leaves of words in vain, refusing to produce the fruits of works. Hence it is also added: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Father who is in heaven will enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 7).

To say “Lord, Lord” seems to be the fruit of a good work, but not to do his will does not belong to a good tree. Mere confession is not enough if good action is lacking, as the Lord says elsewhere: “Why do you call me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ and do not do what I say?” (Luke 6). Hence the apostle James says: “Faith without works is dead” (James 2).

He terrified those who gloried in faith alone by the example of demons, saying: “You believe that God is one; you do well. Even the demons believe, and tremble” (ibid.). Those whom the Lord reproves through the prophet, saying, “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isa. 29), will therefore cry out at the time of judgment, without the fruit of good works, “Lord, Lord, open to us,” and will deserve to hear: “Truly I say to you, I do not know you” (Isa. 29).

Therefore, whoever wishes to enter the kingdom of heaven should desire not only to know what God wills but also to fulfill what he commands, because, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “Blessed are those who hear the word of God and keep it” (Luke 11). And again to the disciples: “You know these things; blessed are you if you do them” (John 13).

## HOMILY 121. THE TENTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST

*(Luke 16.)* “At that time, Jesus said to his disciples this parable: ‘There was a certain rich man who had a steward.’” And what follows.

It is the practice of Sacred Scripture sometimes to recount certain events according to the letter in such a way that it nevertheless requires a spiritual meaning to be sought in them, and sometimes merely to present certain matters by way of comparison, so that it may soften the mind of the listener for understanding invisible things.

This is found more frequently in the Gospel, where a comparison arises from a preceding exhortation, and from the same comparison a further exhortation follows. We recognize both in this comparison if we consider carefully what comes before and after. For when tax collectors and sinners had approached Jesus to hear him, and the scribes and Pharisees were murmuring, as the evangelist reported above, he proposed to them the comparison of the hundred sheep and the one that had been lost and found.

Then he added the comparison of the ten drachmas and said that there is joy in heaven over one sinner who repents. He also added a third comparison, concerning the prodigal son who squandered his substance with prostitutes; but after he had begun to suffer want, he was received mercifully and kindly by his father.

Having shown there that converted sinners are not merely not to be despised but are also to be received, in order to stir the minds of the disciples to mercy, he turned to them and said: “There was a certain rich man, and he had a steward.” From this comparison an exhortation arose, when, after it was finished, he said:

“And I say to you: Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity.” And what follows.

But because these things were spoken by way of comparison, I wish briefly to recall what they signify spiritually. Spiritually, this man is almighty God, concerning whom it is written: “He is a man, and who shall know him?” (Jer. 17). And, “Behold, God and man shall come from the house of David.”

He is rightly said to be rich because with him are “all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge hidden” (Col. 2). Not even the one who, after being taken up to the third heaven, said, “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments and unsearchable his ways!” (Rom. 11), was able to contemplate the greatness of his riches.

We are his stewards, whom he created in his image and likeness, to whom he also gave sense and understanding. For “steward” derives its name from *villa*, a country estate; it is one who is known to have charge of another’s estate. We may call him an *oikonomos*, or, in common speech, a dispenser.

And truly almighty God entrusted his great riches to us when, above all other creatures, he granted us rational sense and understanding, shared with the angels. We administer our Lord’s riches badly when we turn the faculty of discernment, which we received for the use of good, to the use of vices.

We are reported to the Lord as squandering his goods because he not only observes our hearts—before whose eyes everything is naked and open—to see whether anyone is understanding or seeking God, but also because angels appointed for this purpose report our deeds to him day and night, just as an angel said to the righteous man: “When you were praying, I offered your prayers before God” (Tob. 12).

Or certainly we are reported to our Lord when, by ourselves, we give a bad impression, to such an extent that we cause shame or reverence in pious minds, so that we become like those of whom the Apostle says: “The name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you” (Rom. 2).

But shall we always handle the Lord’s riches badly? No. Hear what follows.

“And he called him and said to him: ‘What is this that I hear about you? Give an account of your stewardship, for you can no longer be steward.’”

God calls us in the present to repentance and in the future to judgment. We are called to give an account of our stewardship when we are led from the present life to his judgment, where we shall give an account not only of our deeds but also of every idle word.

After this we shall no longer be able to act as stewards, because after death, as Solomon says, “there will be neither work, nor reasoning, nor wisdom, nor knowledge in the underworld” (Eccl. 9). Hence it is said to God through the Psalmist: “But in hell, who will confess to you?” (Ps. 6)—that is, no one.

Terrified by these examples, let us imitate the steward, who prudently provided for himself in the future, saying within himself:

> “What shall I do, because my master is taking the stewardship away from me? I am unable to dig; I am ashamed to beg. I know what I shall do, so that, when I have been removed from the stewardship, they may receive me into their houses.”

Digging is the work of peasants; begging is a source of shame. For by digging one brings about the appearance of the earth hidden below, so that it becomes visible above, while what appears externally is cast downward. What, then, is signified by digging except the confession of sins? Just as by digging we turn over the appearance of the earth, so, ploughing our hearts with the ploughshare of compunction, we disclose through confession the sins that lie hidden within. And by this we conceal them from the eyes of the Lord: we reveal them by confessing them through compunction of heart to the ministers of God, just as the penitent’s voice says in the Psalm: “I made my sin known to you” (Ps. XXXI). And again: “I said, ‘I will confess my injustice against myself to the Lord,’ and you forgave the wickedness of my sin” (ibid.).

Hence, in the Law it is figuratively commanded that the Israelites, when traveling, should carry pegs beside their belts, and that, having gone out to attend to the necessities of nature, they should dig in the earth and cover their excrement with soil (Deut. XXIII). Just as compunction of heart is signified by the pegs, so sins are signified by the excrement, as the prophet says: “The beasts have rotted in their dung” (Joel I). We are therefore commanded to have pegs beside our belts, so that by digging we may cover our daily sins through daily repentance and compunction.

Begging, as we have said, is a source of shame, especially that worst kind of begging in which we read that the foolish virgins begged when they said to the prudent virgins (Matt. XXV): “Give us some of your oil, because our lamps are going out.” They were told: “Perhaps there will not be enough for us and for you; go instead to those who sell, and buy some for yourselves.” Concerning this worst kind of begging Solomon also says: “Because of the cold the lazy man would not plough; therefore he will beg in summer, and nothing will be given to him” (Prov. XX).

The steward therefore says: “I am unable to dig; I am ashamed to beg.” For after death it will be possible neither to practice fruitful repentance for evils nor to exercise oneself in good works, as Wisdom’s voice says through Solomon concerning the reprobate: “They will call upon me, and I will not answer. They will rise early, and will not find me, because they hated discipline, did not accept the fear of the Lord, did not consent to my counsels, and despised all my correction” (ibid. I).

Since, therefore, on the day of judgment there can be no opportunity for repenting, correcting, or making amends, as we have said, it is necessary that while we are in this world and live, and while we have the opportunity, we should, according to the Apostle, “while we have the time, do good to all, and especially to those who belong to the household of faith” (Gal. VI). Hence the Lord admonishes us in the Gospel, saying: “Run while you have the light, lest the darkness overtake you” (John XIII). And through the Prophet: “Seek the Lord while he may be found; call upon him while he is near” (Isa. LV).

The Apostle also says: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation. Giving no one any cause for offense, so that our ministry may not be reviled. But in everything let us show ourselves as ministers of God: in great patience, in tribulations, in necessities, in distress, in blows, in prisons, in seditions, in labors, in watchings, in fastings, in chastity, in knowledge, in long-suffering, in kindness, in the Holy Spirit, in unfeigned love” (I Cor. VI). And Solomon: “Whatever your hand is able to do, do it diligently” (Eccl. IX).

Before everything and above everything, we must set the day of death before our eyes. For the person who always thinks that he will die easily despises everything. Hence the same wise man says: “On the day of evils do not forget good things” (Eccl. XI). And again: “In all your ways remember your last things” (Eccl. VII).

> “Having therefore called together each of his master’s debtors, he said to the first: ‘How much do you owe my master?’ He replied: ‘A hundred *cadi* of oil.’ He said to him: ‘Take your written agreement and sit down; quickly write fifty.’ Then he said to another: ‘And you, how much do you owe?’ He replied: ‘A hundred *cori* of wheat.’ He said to him: ‘Take your document and write eighty.’”

In this steward, whom his master was expelling from the stewardship, we must not take everything as something to imitate. We must not defraud either masters or strangers in order to give alms from the proceeds. Rather, as we said above, these things are said by way of comparison, so that we may understand that if the man who committed fraud could be praised because he prudently provided for his future, then we shall be much more praiseworthy if we give generous alms from our own possessions and, while we live in the present, provide for ourselves in the future. Likewise, from the unjust judge who was importuned by a widow, he drew a comparison with the Lord as judge, though the unjust judge is not comparable with him in any respect.

For *kados* (κἀδος) in Greek means in Latin a measure containing three urns. A *corus*, however, is filled with thirty *modii*. The fact that he ordered the debtors to write fifty instead of a hundred *cadi* of oil and eighty instead of a hundred *cori* of wheat signifies that everyone who repents of past sins ought not only mercifully to forgive those who have sinned against him, but also to distribute alms from possessions acquired justly; and he should not merely give tithes and first fruits, as was commanded in the Law, but also minister to the needy from what remains. Or certainly, he should give half of his possessions, as Zacchaeus did when he received the Lord Jesus into his house and said: “I give half of my possessions to the poor, and if I have taken anything from anyone, I will restore it fourfold” (Luke XIX).

> “And the master praised the unjust steward because he had acted prudently. For the children of this world are more prudent than the children of light in their own generation.”

The master did not praise the unjust steward because he had committed fraud, but because he had prudently provided for his future, so that by his example we may learn not to have here a lasting city, but to seek the one that is to come with all our desire (Hebr. XIII).

Those who inhabit this world in mind and desire are called children of the world. For just as those who love the inaccessible light—that is, God—with all their heart are called children of light, so those who have planted the roots of their hearts in love of this world are called children of this world, wishing to live without end in it, as the Apostle Peter testifies when he says: “Everyone is called the child of the one whose works he does.”

Therefore, “the children of this world are more prudent than the children of light in their own generation,” because while the former are crafty, cunning, ingenious, deceptive, and double-minded, the latter, by contrast, are simple, humble, pure, and kind, not knowing how to repay evil with evil. And just as the latter are simple in evil but prudent in good, so the former are wise enough to do evil but do not know how to do good. Concerning them the Lord says: “Woe to you who are wise in your own eyes and prudent in your own sight” (Isa. V).

They are rightly called prudent in their own generation, because such people are counted not in the generation of God but in their own, since the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God. Concerning this wisdom the Apostle Paul says: “The wisdom of the flesh is death” (Rom. VIII). For it is not said of them: “The generation of the upright will be blessed” (Ps. CXI), but rather they are numbered among those of whom it is written: “A wicked and adulterous generation” (Matt. XII).

But concerning the wisdom of the children of light it is said: “The wisdom that is from above is first pure, then peaceable, gentle, compliant, agreeing with what is good” (Jas. III). When the comparison had been completed, the merciful Lord turned his speech to our admonition, saying:

> “And I say to you: Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity, so that when you fail, they may receive you into eternal dwellings.”

Some have thought that this saying should be understood in such a way that stealing from others and giving the proceeds to the poor would be to make friends from the mammon of iniquity. How absurd and alien to religion this is is plainly evident. Almighty God does not command the seizure of another’s property, since he has commanded us to give what is our own; nor does he deign to receive alms from robberies, for through the prophet he cries out: “Whoever offers sacrifice from the possessions of the poor is like one who sacrifices a son before his father” (Ecclus. XXXIV).

Hence a certain wise man says: “One builds, and another destroys; one prays, and another curses: whose voice did God hear?”

*Mammon* is interpreted in Hebrew or Syriac as “riches” in Latin, because in Punic *mammon* means “profit.” Thus “mammon of iniquity” is the name given to these riches, even when they have been acquired through justice and have come by right of inheritance from parents, because they are acquired with labor, guarded with great anxiety, and can scarcely ever—or only rarely—be possessed without iniquity.

The Lord therefore commands us to make friends from the mammon of iniquity—that is, to give alms from riches acquired with labor—so that, according to the Apostle, in the present life the abundance of the rich may supply the poverty of the poor, and that in the other life the abundance of the poor may in turn be a consolation for the poverty of the rich (II Cor. VIII).

The friends whom we are commanded to make from the mammon of iniquity are the poor and needy, whom God has allowed to be in want for their purification and our testing. We make them our friends when we cover their nakedness, refresh their hunger, quench their thirst, and assist them in all their needs. They are said to receive us into eternal dwellings because the one who will receive us on their behalf is the one who says:

> “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world. For I was hungry, and you gave me food; I was thirsty, and you gave me drink; I was a stranger, and you welcomed me; naked, and you covered me; sick and in prison, and you visited me” (Matt. XXV).

And when they say:

> “Lord, when did we see you hungry and feed you, or thirsty and give you drink? When did we see you a stranger and welcome you, or naked and cover you, or sick and in prison and come to you?” (ibid.)

he replies:

> “Amen I say to you, insofar as you did it for one of the least of mine, you did it for me” (ibid.).

Because that rich man did not wish to have these friends, he was placed not in eternal dwellings but in eternal punishment, and he said: “Father Abraham, have mercy on me and send Lazarus to dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue, because I am being tormented in this flame” (Luke XVI).

The eternal dwellings are the various recompenses of merits, as the Lord declares elsewhere when he says: “In my Father’s house there are many dwellings” (John XIV).

Let the rich man hear this; let the Christian hear it; let him learn to give what is small, so that he may be able to receive what is great. For, as the Lord says, “the one who is faithful in what is least will also be faithful in what is great” (Luke XVI). Let him learn to give what is transitory, so that he may deserve to receive what is eternal. Let him receive the poor man into his house, so that he may deserve to be received by Christ into his dwellings.

In these dwellings the man wished to find a place who said (Ps. XIV): “Lord, who will dwell in your tabernacle, or who will rest on your holy mountain?” To him the divine voice immediately replies:

> “The one who enters without blemish and practices righteousness, who speaks truth in his heart, who has not acted deceitfully with his tongue, nor done evil to his neighbor, nor accepted reproach against his neighbors. The wicked person is brought to nothing in his sight, but he glorifies those who fear the Lord. The one who swears to his neighbor and does not deceive him, who has not given his money at interest and has not accepted gifts against the innocent: the one who does these things will not be shaken forever” (ibid.).

“For blessed,” says the Prophet, “is the one who understands concerning the needy and the poor; on the evil day the Lord will deliver him” (Ps. XL). For the Lord reveals how great the power of almsgiving is when he says: “Give alms, and everything is clean for you” (Luke XI). And again: “When you give a luncheon or a dinner, do not invite those who will invite you in return, but call the poor, and you will be blessed, because they have nothing with which to repay you” (Luke XIV). And elsewhere: “As water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin” (Ecclus. III).

Hence it is said in the voice of righteous men: “Almsgiving will have great confidence before the Most High God for all who practice it” (Tob. IV). And again: “My son, almsgiving delivers from death” (Tob. XII), and does not allow a person to enter into darkness. And again: “Let almsgiving sweat in your hand until you find a righteous person to whom you may hand it over.”

The poor, too, ought therefore to give alms according to their ability. Hence a good father instructing his son says: “My son, if you have much, give abundantly”; but if you have little, give even the little willingly (Tob. IV). For before the just Judge there will be no excuse concerning almsgiving, since he has promised to give a reward even for a cup of cold water (Matt. X).

Alternatively, some wish to understand this comparison as fulfilled in the Apostle Paul in the following way. This man is Almighty God, who had a steward, namely the Apostle Paul, to whom he entrusted the distribution of his riches when he instructed him in the truth of his ancestral Law at the feet of Gamaliel, a teacher of the Law.

But Paul handled his master’s riches badly when, understanding the Law carnally, he persecuted Christians, to such an extent that he received letters from the chief priests so that, wherever he found men or women of this Way, he might bring them bound to Jerusalem. He was reported to his master when it was said concerning him: “Lord, I have heard from many about this man, how much evil he has done to your saints in Jerusalem; and here he has authority from the chief priests to bind all who call upon your name.”

When the report of his persecution had risen up to the Lord, as Paul was traveling to Damascus, his master called him from heaven and said to him: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts IX). “It is hard for you to kick against the goad.” This means: “What is this that I hear about you? Give an account of your stewardship; you will no longer be able to act as steward” (Luke XVI)—that is, to practice Judaism.

It was as though he were saying: “Because until today you have been a teacher of the Law carnally, you will now begin to be a disciple of the truth spiritually.”

A steward is one who exercises care over another’s estate. Paul was exercising care over another’s estate when he taught carnally the Law given through Moses. But the stewardship was taken away from him when he was commanded to understand the carnal Law not carnally but spiritually.

> “The steward said within himself: ‘What shall I do, because my master is taking the stewardship away from me?’” (Luke XVI).

It was as though he were saying: “What shall I do, because I was a teacher in the carnal doctrine of the Law, and I am compelled to become a steward, a disciple, and a worker of the spiritual Law?”

> “I am unable to dig” (ibid.)

—that is, “I cannot scrutinize the doctrine of the Law by myself.”

> “I am ashamed to beg” (ibid.)

because he was afraid to learn the Christian faith from Ananias, whom he had held as a disciple.

> “I know what I shall do, so that when I have been removed from the stewardship, Christians may receive me into their houses” (ibid.)

—Christians whom I persecuted.

He called two debtors of his master, namely the people of the Jews and of the Gentiles, both of whom were held bound under the debt or yoke of sin, as the Apostle says (Rom. XIII): “There is no distinction between Jew and Greek. For all have sinned and lack the glory of God.”

He ordered one to write fifty instead of a hundred *cadi* of oil, and the other to write eighty instead of a hundred *cori* of wheat. The number eighty pertains to faith in the resurrection, because the Lord Jesus Christ rose from the dead on the eighth day. Fifty pertains to repentance, because the fiftieth Psalm is sung concerning repentance. The fiftieth year in the Law is also called the Jubilee, that is, the year of remission.

Therefore he made the Jewish people write eighty instead of a hundred *cori* of wheat because he taught them to believe in Christ’s resurrection. But he called the Gentile from the hundred to the fifty because he taught him to correct his former evils through repentance and to draw near to God.

> “And the master praised the unjust steward because he had acted prudently” (Luke XVI),

namely, the Apostle Paul, who had been changed from a persecutor into a preacher, [and made in doctrine: wording uncertain]. He magnified him in doctrine and preaching, saying concerning him to Ananias:

> “Go, for this man is a chosen vessel for me, to carry my name before the Gentiles and kings and the children of Israel” (Acts IX).

Thus was fulfilled the prophecy that Jacob formerly uttered when he blessed his sons, saying: “Benjamin is a ravenous wolf; in the morning he will eat the prey, and in the evening he will divide the spoils” (Gen. XLIX).

The Apostle Paul was from the tribe of Benjamin, as he himself testifies. Like a ravenous wolf, he burned with zeal in persecuting Christians. In the morning he ate the prey, because in his youth he persecuted the Church of God. In the evening he divided the spoils, because after he had been converted to faith in Christ, he sent among various nations those whom, having conquered them from the power of the devil, he had obtained for proclaiming the faith that he had previously persecuted.

# HOMILY CXXII. THE ELEVENTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST

(Luke XIX.) “At that time, as Jesus drew near to Jerusalem, seeing the city, he wept over it, saying: ‘If you too had known.’” And so forth.

In the sequence of this reading the Lord Jesus Christ commends both his natures, namely the divine and the human. It is an indication of his human nature that he has compassion, even to the point of weeping, for the city destined to perish; it is an indication of his divine nature that, as God, he foretells what was going to happen to that same city. As a human being he entered the temple, but as God he drove out from it those who were selling and buying, saying: “My house shall be called a house of prayer” (Matt. XXI).

He shows at the beginning of this reading how greatly he rejoices in human salvation and how greatly he grieves over their destruction: seeing the city that was destined to perish, he wept over it, saying: “If you too had known.” He wept not for the beauty of the houses, the height of the towers, or the buildings of the walls, but, metaphorically, for the people.

The weeping Lord is also said to say: “If you too had known,” where it must be understood: “If you had known the evils that threaten you, you would weep; but now, because you do not know that you will soon perish, you rejoice.” For, intent only upon the prosperity that was presently flowing to it, the city did not foresee at all what was going to happen. Hence the Lord also says: “And indeed, in this your day, the things that are for your peace—but now they are hidden from your eyes.”

It was as though it had peace in its own day when it was exalted in honors, gloried in riches, and rejoiced in the fruitfulness of offspring; and therefore it recognized in no way the danger that was going to come upon it. But the Lord briefly encompasses what was going to happen to it when he adds:

> “For days will come upon you, and your enemies will surround you with a rampart; they will surround you and hem you in on every side, and they will throw you and your children who are within you to the ground; and they will not leave in you stone upon stone.”

He says that days will come—days of tribulation and distress, calamity and famine, siege and death. He names the Roman commanders as its enemies: surrounding the same city with a rampart, they hemmed it in on every side, literally cast it down, and killed its children.

The historiographer Josephus, of the Hebrews, fully narrates how all these things happened to the city. But for the less educated, who perhaps do not know the history of that man, a few details from many should be recalled. After the Lord’s ascension, after the death of James who was called “the Just,” while the Jewish people persisted in wickedness, the Lord raised up against them two Roman commanders, namely Vespasian and Titus, father and son. By the just judgment of God, those who had denied the Father and the Son were killed by a father and son.

When the Roman army was ravaging the region of the Jews, as the solemnity of Passover approached, the whole people ran together into the city as one man. The just judgment of God demanded that those who had killed Christ during the solemnity of Passover should be surrounded by sieges during that same solemnity.

The city was suddenly enclosed by the enemy, so that no one could enter or leave. It remained under siege until everything they had brought with them for food appeared to have been consumed. Everything they had left outside the city had been devastated by the Roman army. Afflicted, therefore, by the long siege, they were pressed much more severely by hunger within than by the enemy without.

The same historiographer shows this when he says that the scarcity of dreadful and prolonged famine dried up even delicate entrails to such an extent that some did not refrain from eating their very shoes. Others offered scraps of old hay and the refuse of grain to be chewed by their teeth. Some stripped the coverings from the gates, so that they might at least relieve the scarcity of food with this nourishment.

If anyone wished to leave the city to gather herbs, he was seized as though he intended to flee to the Romans. No one dared set a table in the customary manner; instead, they ate their own food as though it were stolen. For everything connected with natural modesty or shame was disregarded in this necessity, since hunger had claimed all of it for itself.

Finally, women snatched food from the hands of men, children from their parents, and—what is more miserable—mothers from the mouths of their own children. No respect was shown to the elderly on account of their gray hair, and no compassion to little children on account of their innocence. Old men were beaten if they wished to conceal food. Women who attempted to hide food were dragged through the streets with their hair disheveled.

The bodies of young men lay in the streets, consumed more by hunger than by age. Neither the multitude of the dead nor the weakness of their strength allowed the bodies of the dead to be buried. Many, while wishing to bury the bodies of those dear to them, gave up their own spirits.

When an unbearable stench from the corpses of the dead began to grow in the city, they threw the bodies outside the walls. One day Titus—whom his father, having returned to Rome, had left behind in the siege of Jerusalem—was circling the city with his soldiers. Seeing the corpses of the dead almost level with the city wall, he raised his eyes to heaven with a great groan and called upon God as witness that this was not his work.

Then, turning to the soldiers, he said: “I think that if the Roman army had withdrawn even a little from this pestilence of the city, either they would have been killed by floodwaters, or burned by the fires of Sodom, or certainly swallowed up by a chasm in the earth.”

When he was about to withdraw shortly afterward, he again encouraged the soldiers against the city, strengthened the guards, and armed the army. In addition to all these evils, robbers had risen up from among the people themselves, snatching food, so to speak, from their very throats.

If they saw anyone’s doors closed, they believed it was a sign that the inhabitants were eating inside. Suddenly breaking down the doors and rushing in, they seized whatever they could find. But since it would take too long to enumerate all the evils that befell the Jews because of the shedding of the Lord’s blood, it seems appropriate to recall briefly how the city was captured.

There was a certain woman named Mary, daughter of Eleazar, noble by birth and rich in possessions. She had come with the rest of the multitude for the feast. When she had consumed everything she had brought with her during the prolonged siege, and hunger was already tormenting her delicate entrails, nature itself was turned against her.

She had a small son at her breast. Placing him before her eyes, she said: “Most wretched mother, and more wretched son, in war, famine, and the plundering of robbers, for whom shall I preserve you? For even if life could be hoped for, we are nevertheless pressed under the yoke of Roman slavery. Come, therefore, my son; become a tale among the mothers of this age and a source of fury to the robbers.”

Having said this, she slaughtered her son, roasting part of him over a fire and eating it, while reserving part for later. When the robbers, drawn by the smell of the roasted flesh, came as usual, they began to threaten her with death unless she showed them the food she had hidden.

But she, with a savage expression, more sorrowful than the robbers themselves, said: “I have reserved the best part for you.” Saying this, she uncovered the remaining limbs of the child.

When the robbers, struck with horror, dreaded such a crime, she said: “This is my offspring, my son, my food, and my crime. Eat with me. For I ate first, I who gave birth to him. Do not be more religious than a mother or more tender than a woman. But if piety overcomes you, curse my food. I who have fed on such things shall feed on them again.”

They, grieving that they had left the wretched mother nothing from all her possessions except this, reported the deed throughout the city. A great cry arose in the city of those grieving and mourning. Amid that very outcry, when the gates had been opened, Titus entered with the Roman army. He slaughtered some with the sword, burned others with fire, and sent the young into captivity.

He destroyed the city itself from its foundations so completely that, in accordance with the Lord’s word, no stone was left upon stone in it. In its destruction was fulfilled what the Lord had once figuratively foretold through the prophet Ezekiel, saying:

> “And you, son of man, take for yourself a sharp sword, a razor for shaving, and pass it over your head and beard; and you shall burn a third part with fire, and cut down a third part with the sword, and scatter the remaining third to the wind, and I will unsheathe my sword after them” (Ezek. V).

The account of this historiographer agrees with the words of the Savior, who, when he had seen the walls of the city, said: “When you see this city surrounded by an army, know that its desolation is near. Then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains. But woe to those who are pregnant and nursing in those days” (Luke XXI).

And elsewhere we read that when the disciples had shown him the buildings of the city, he said: “Do you see all these things? Amen I say to you, ‘Not one stone will be left upon another that will not be destroyed’” (Mark XIII).

The Lord reveals the cause for which the ruin of the aforesaid city occurred when he adds:

> “Because you did not recognize the time of your visitation.”

The Lord visited it through the mystery of his incarnation, when the exalted God, appearing among human beings as a humble man, displayed many signs and miracles. The man who said, “Remember us, Lord, in the favor shown to your people; visit us with your salvation” (Ps. CV), desired to see this visitation.

He had also foreseen it as near who said: “Blessed is the Lord God of Israel, because he has visited and accomplished the redemption of his people” (Luke LXVIII).

But the proud city did not recognize the time of its visitation, because it disdained to believe that the one whom it saw as a human being was God. To convict its hard-hearted unbelief, even the birds of heaven are brought forward as witnesses, when the Prophet says:

> “The kite in heaven knows its time; the turtledove, the swallow, and the stork have observed the time of their coming, but my people have not known the judgment of the Lord” (Jer. VIII).

And again:

> “The ox knows its owner, and the donkey its master’s manger; but Israel has not known me, my people has not understood me” (Isa. I).

He visited it not only through the presence of his incarnation, but also, after his ascension, displayed many signs and portents in order to soften their hearts toward repentance.

For, as the same historiographer relates, when they were celebrating a certain festival, a sudden disturbance arose among the Jewish people, and thirty thousand of them killed one another. On a certain late night the door of the Lord’s temple, which could scarcely be moved by twenty men, opened of its own accord.

On one day, when a heifer had been brought forward for sacrifice, it gave birth to a lamb. In the middle of the night such a bright light shone in the temple that some thought it was midday. Seeing this, the ignorant believed that prosperity was coming to them. But the wise were not at all unaware that the destruction of the city was being signified.

On the holy day of Pentecost, while the priests were offering sacrifices, voices were heard in the temple saying: “Let us depart from these dwellings.”

Two years before the siege, when they had gathered at Jerusalem to celebrate a certain festival, a man named Jesus, son of Ananias, filled with the Spirit, began to cry out: “A voice from the east, a voice from the west, a voice from the four winds, [‘of the age/world’: reading uncertain]. A voice against Jerusalem and the temple, a voice against bridegrooms and brides.”

When they wished to silence him with blows, he cried out more and more loudly. As he breathed out his spirit in the hands of those beating him, he said: “Woe, woe to Jerusalem.”

A star, also entirely like a sword, hung over Jerusalem for a full year, indicating the city’s destruction. A fiery chariot and fiery horses were seen being carried through the air. The merciful Lord deigned to display many other signs as well, in order to summon their hearts to repentance.

But because they were “storing up wrath for themselves on the day of wrath according to their hardness and unrepentant heart” (Rom. IV), he “sent his armies, destroyed those murderers, and burned their city” (Matt. XXII).

Their destruction was also prefigured in the Books of Kings, when, as Elisha was ascending from Gilgal, young boys mocked him, saying: “Go up, baldhead; go up, baldhead” (IV Kings II). He cursed them in the name of the Lord, and immediately two bears came out of the forest and devoured forty-two of the boys.

Elisha bore the figure of the Lord. When he was crucified at the place of Calvary, the Jews mocked him childishly, saying: “If he is the Son of God, let him come down from the cross, and we will believe him” (Matt. XXVII). And again, bending their knees, they said: “Hail, King of the Jews” (ibid.).

But because they refused to believe him, after forty-two years two bears came out of the forests of the Gentiles—namely, Vespasian and Titus—who tore that same people apart with various disasters, to such an extent that the same historiographer records that eleven hundred thousand died during the siege of the city, while one hundred thousand young men were scattered in captivity.

> “And he entered the temple and began to drive out those who were selling and buying in it.”

When the Lord foretold the city’s ruin, and “entered the temple and drove out those selling and buying in it,” he showed that the ruin of the temple came chiefly through the fault of the priests. Those who ought to have been teachers and leaders among the people, and examples of good, became examples of evil.

They sat in the temple for this purpose: to exalt those who gave gifts with empty expressions of favor, and to afflict in various ways those who refused to give. Taking thought for their avarice, they had devised an ingenious arrangement. They persuaded the children of Israel who came from distant places not to bring sacrificial victims with them, so that they could sell them at a higher price for offering in the temple of God.

For this reason, as the other Evangelists testify, sheep, oxen, and doves were sold in the Lord’s temple. They did not sacrifice the things that had been offered to the Lord according to the rite of the Law, but sold them again and again to others. And to remove every excuse from those who had nothing, they kept money-changers prepared in the temple with bronze coins; thus they made the house of prayer a den of robbers.

But the Lord entered the temple and began to drive out those who were selling and buying in it, saying: “It is written: ‘My house is a house of prayer’” (Isa. LVI). “But you have made it a den of robbers.”

After these things, “he was teaching daily in the temple.”

But what we have said pertains to the destruction of the visible city; morally, it can also be referred to the soul that is destined to perish. The Lord himself wept over the city that was destined to perish; daily, through teachers, he mourns those who fall from good works into evil.

Frequently the teachers of the Church grieve and weep over those whom they cannot correct by admonition, those “who rejoice when they have done evil and exult in the worst things” (Prov. II), just as the Apostle Paul did when he wept over the fall of his disciples, saying:

> “My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you” (Gal. IV), “I wish that I could be present with you now and change my tone, because I am perplexed about you.”

And again: “I mourn over many of those who sinned previously” (II Cor. XII).

What is said by the weeping Lord is fitting, then, for the soul that is destined to perish:

“If you had known—even you.” For if she had known the evils prepared for the condemned, if she had brought before the eyes of her mind the punishments of eternal judgment, she would not have deceived herself with false security, but rather would have lamented herself with the tears of the elect. But when she rejoices in prosperity, delights in honors, and takes pleasure in possessions, the very prosperity of this passing life hides from the eyes of her mind the evils of the punishment to come. Hence it is rightly said: “Indeed, in this your day, the things that are for your peace—but now they are hidden from your eyes.” For the unhappy soul has, as it were, its own day when it places all its hope in worldly possessions, and because of this it will suffer a stumbling-block on the day of judgment. It does not foresee the coming tribulation, because earthly love blinds the eyes of the heart. For just as dust blinds bodily eyes so that they cannot see clearly, so love of this age and present riches blind the eye of the mind, preventing it from guarding against the future judgment.

Such was that rich man who said in his heart: “I will pull down my barns and build larger ones, and I will say to my soul: Soul, you have many good things stored up for many years; feast” (Luke 12), “and rejoice.” That distinguished prophet Jeremiah regarded this day as nothing, saying: “I have not desired the day of man” (Jer. 17). The apostle Paul likewise had despised it when he said to his disciples: “But it is a very small matter to me that I should be judged by you, or by a human day” (1 Cor. 4). What evil is to come upon the sluggish soul is made clear when it continues:

“For days will come upon you, and they will surround you, and hem you in on every side, and cast you down to the ground, and your children who are within you.” The days of tribulation come upon the wretched soul when it is constricted by the pain of death—the soul that rejoiced wickedly in the present life—and then begins to quarrel with itself and say: Why did I enlarge myself in evil deeds? Why did I not repent of my past sins? Why did I not exercise myself in good works? Then, I say, it will begin to repent, when no fruit of repentance will remain, but only the severity of punishment.

Its enemies are none worse than unclean spirits. From these the Psalmist desired to be rescued when he said: “Deliver me from my enemies, my God, and rescue me from those who work iniquity” (Ps. 58). They surround it with a rampart and hem it in on every side when, as the soul departs from the body, they enumerate the evils it has committed; and it has as exactors in punishment those whom it had as persuaders in guilt. Then the unhappy soul is cast down to the ground, when, released from the flesh—which is earth and ashes—it is led away to punishment; or when it loses whatever virtue it thought it possessed.

By “children” we sometimes understand good thoughts and sometimes evil thoughts. Of the good we read: “And may you see your children’s children” (Ps. 127). Of the evil, however, it is said here:

“And they will cast you down to the ground.” But what follows is exceedingly terrifying: “And they will not leave in you a stone upon a stone.” In the destruction of a city, no stone is left upon another, because in the condemnation of a perverse soul an account will be demanded not only of evil deeds but also of perverse thoughts. Therefore, while we are in this age, living and having leisure, it is necessary not only to abstain from evil but also to strive to do good in everything.

Above all, let us place the day of death before our eyes, because one who always thinks that he will die easily despises everything. Hence Solomon exhorts us, saying: “In all your works remember your last things” (Sir. 7). And again: “In the day of evils, do not be forgetful of good things” (Sir. 11). And: “Whatever your hand can do, do it earnestly” (Eccl. 9). Therefore the merciful Lord, because he patiently awaits us here but will judge us strictly at the judgment if we have not been converted, deigned to admonish us when he said: “Run while you have the light of life, lest the darkness overtake you” (John 12). And likewise: “Be reconciled with your adversary.” The Apostle also says: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (1 Cor. 2).

Why these evils befell the unhappy soul is made clear when it is said: “Because you did not know the time of your visitation.” The time of visitation is the present life, in which almighty God deigns to visit us in various ways: sometimes gently admonishing, sometimes terrifyingly threatening, sometimes through prosperity, sometimes through adversity. But the perverse soul does not recognize the time of its visitation when it preserves neither humility in prosperity nor patience in adversity, because it neither fears committing sins nor punishes those committed with tears.

What follows—“And he entered the temple and began to drive out those who were selling and buying in it”—is seen to happen daily in the Church. Spiritually, the temple of God is the Church, which may be called a house of prayer because it does not cease daily to offer pure prayers to God, saying with the Psalmist: “Let my prayer be directed like incense in your sight” (Ps. 140).

Those who distribute the spiritual gifts they received freely either for payment or for temporal praise are sellers. Another evangelist has taken care to reveal where this commerce occurs most especially, saying that sheep, oxen, and doves were being sold in the temple.

By the ox is signified the preachers, since the Lord says to Moses: “You shall not plow with an ox and an ass together” (Deut. 22)—that is, do not join the prudent with the foolish in preaching or teaching. And again: “You shall not muzzle the ox while it is treading out the grain” (1 Cor. 9). Explaining this, the apostle Paul says: “Does God concern himself with oxen?” (ibid.) No. “But this was written for our sake.”

Therefore whoever preaches the word of God in the Church solely to receive human glory or temporal payment is, as it were, driving a saleable ox into the temple [the printed reading *minat* is uncertain]. By the sheep, that very gentle animal, innocence is signified. Whoever displays holiness before God—or before human beings in order to be praised—brings, as it were, a saleable sheep into the temple. Of such people the Lord says: “They do all their works so that they may be seen by human beings” (Matt. 23). And elsewhere: “Truly I tell you, they have received their reward” (Matt. 6).

By the dove the grace of the Holy Spirit is signified, as he himself deigned to reveal when he appeared in the form of a dove over the baptized Lord. Therefore whoever confers an ecclesiastical rank, or the laying on of hands through which we believe the Holy Spirit is given, in order to acquire temporal profit, carries, as it were, a saleable dove into the temple—that is, into the Church—not considering what the Lord says: “Freely you have received; freely give” (Deut. 16).

Of such people it is written: “Fire will consume the tents of those who gladly accept gifts” (Job 15). And again: “Do not show partiality toward the poor in judgment, because gifts blind the eyes of the wise and overthrow the words of the righteous” (Deut. 16).

The Lord drove such people from his temple, because although in the present age they may appear joined bodily to the Church, on the day of judgment they will be separated from the Church, when it will be said to them: “Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25).

The Lord drove not only the sellers from the temple but also the buyers, because not only are those guilty and alien to the Church who sell spiritual gifts, but also those who buy them so that they may sell them more dearly. Hence the great and holy synod decreed that even a layperson, if he had acted as a mediator in such transactions, should be made alien to the Church.

Such people make the house a den of thieves, because by selling spiritual gifts they produce an abominable fruit. Of them the Savior says: “Whoever does not enter the sheepfold through the door, but climbs in by another way, is a thief and a robber” (John 20).

What follows—“And he was teaching daily in the temple”—he always does spiritually in the Church, as he then did bodily in person. For he teaches in the temple when outwardly he forms teaching through preachers and inwardly illumines the heart of the hearer.

# HOMILY 123. THE TWELFTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST

*(Luke 18.)* “At that time Jesus said to certain people who trusted in themselves as though they were righteous and despised others, this parable: Two men went up to the temple.” And what follows.

In many places sacred Scripture shows how greatly the virtue of humility benefits human beings and how greatly the disease of pride harms them. Yet especially in this reading the Lord declares it under the example of two men: namely, the Pharisee, vainly exalting himself on account of his merits, and the publican, humbly confessing his sins. For he says: “Two men went up to the temple.”

[Col. 0661B] Above, the Gospel reading related how the Lord urged his disciples to perseverance in prayer and proposed the comparison of an unjust judge whom a certain widow approached daily, saying: “Vindicate me against my adversary,” while “for a long time he was unwilling” (Luke 18). Afterward he said within himself: “Although I do not fear God and have no respect for human beings, nevertheless, because this woman troubles me, I will vindicate her, lest by continually coming she wear me out” (Luke 18). Overcome by annoyance, he granted what he had been unwilling to grant as a favor.

But because everyone who approaches to worship must preserve not only humanity in the heart but also an appropriate bearing in the body, after the parable had ended he said to those who trusted in themselves as though they were righteous: “Two men went up to the temple to pray, one a Pharisee and the other a publican.”

“Pharisee” is interpreted as “divided.” By this name those among the Jewish people were designated who separated themselves from the others in order to appear more righteous, teaching certain observances and superstitions. The Lord not only exposes their vices in the Gospel but also frequently rebukes them, saying: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you are like whitened tombs, which outwardly indeed appear beautiful to human beings, but inwardly are full of the bones of the dead and every impurity. So you also outwardly appear righteous to human beings, but inwardly you are full of iniquity and hypocrisy” (Matt. 23).

And again: “The scribes and Pharisees have sat on the seat of Moses. Therefore do and observe everything they tell you, but do not act according to their works. For they say and do not do. They bind heavy and unbearable burdens and place them on people’s shoulders, but they themselves are unwilling to move them with their finger” (ibid.).

This Pharisee belonged to their number. When he had gone up into the temple to pray, he said: “God, I thank you that I am not like the rest of humanity—robbers, unjust, adulterers—or even like this publican.”

From this passage we can gather that the swelling of the arrogant is divided in four ways. First, when a person thinks he possesses what he does not possess. Second, when he thinks that what he possesses comes from his own power. Third, when he believes that he received what he possesses from God but attributes it to his own merits. Fourth, when, despising others, he thinks that he alone possesses what he possesses.
