This Pharisee suffered from that disease of boastfulness. He preferred himself not only to the publican praying humbly but also to all other people, saying: “God, I thank you that I am not like the rest of humanity.”

The Pharisee further reveals the boastfulness of his mind in words when he adds:

“I fast twice on the sabbath; I give tithes of everything I possess.” What he says—“I fast twice on the sabbath”—is to be understood as “twice in the week.” Here the lukewarmness of those who presume even to violate a fast imposed in the Church is rebuked.

Yet he gave tithes in vain from everything he possessed, because he had not placed his mind on the foundation of humility. He belonged to those of whom the Lord says: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who tithe mint and dill and cumin” (Matt. 23; Luke 11), “and every garden herb, but neglect the weightier matters of the law—that is, judgment and equity.”

Therefore careful consideration must anticipate this: whenever we do good, let us place the virtue of humility at the foundation, lest, if outwardly we seek empty glory, inwardly we be deprived of our reward.

Hence Ezekiel, when describing the bodies of the four living creatures, said: “The heads of the living creatures were full of eyes before and behind.” For the action of the saints must be watchful on every side and fortified on every side.

Behold, this Pharisee had open eyes for giving thanks to God, but closed eyes for guarding humility, when he said: “God, I thank you that I am not like the rest of humanity.” We, too, have our eyes open in what we do that is good; but if we seek empty glory from the good work, we see nothing in that respect.

What benefit is there if an entire city is fortified and surrounded everywhere by walls, but one opening is left through which it may be captured by enemies? Or what good is it if a ship placed in the midst of the sea is firmly fastened with nails and planks, but a small opening remains through which water enters and the ship sinks? None.

So it is not enough to do good unless one strives to preserve humility. For whoever gathers virtues without humility carries dust into the wind, as it were. The humble person is so called as one inclined toward the earth.

Such humility was possessed by the one who said: “I will speak to my Lord, although I am dust and ashes” (Gen. 18). The Lord also urges us to guard humility when he says: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart” (Matt. 11). And Solomon says: “The greater you are, humble yourself in all things” (Sir. 3). The apostle Peter says: “Humble yourselves under the powerful hand of God” (1 Pet. 5).

The Psalmist possessed this humility when he said: “It is good for me, Lord, that you have humbled me” (Ps. 118). And again: “I have been humbled exceedingly, Lord” (ibid.).

It commonly happens that when a bird is caught in a snare, though its whole body is sound and its wings intact, it is held by the tip of a very small claw. Thus the ancient and crafty fowler, the devil, tries to deceive those whom he cannot capture through adultery, homicide, and other obvious evils: through empty glory, so that they may take pleasure in the good they do and despise others.

But having said these few things about the swelling pride of the Pharisee, let us turn to the words of the repentant publican. For it continues:

“And the publican, standing far off, was unwilling even to lift his eyes toward heaven, but was beating his breast, saying: God, be merciful to me, a sinner.”

A publican is one who sins publicly after losing his sense of shame, or one who publicly exacts taxes and imposts. Just as the Pharisee revealed the boastfulness of his mind through words, so the publican displayed the grief of his heart in the very posture of his body.

First, by standing far off, he did not dare to approach the holy, from whose fellowship he had separated himself by sinning. Second, by refusing to lift his eyes toward heaven, he feared to look upon the one whom he remembered offending. Third, by beating his breast, which is characteristic of those who are ashamed of their sins. For in striking his breast he displayed the grief of his mind.

But because no one should despair of forgiveness on account of the magnitude of his crimes, the publican rightly says: “God, be merciful to me, a sinner.” He knew that God is the one who says through the Prophet: “As I live, says the Lord, I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live” (Ezek. 18). And again: “On whatever day the sinner turns and groans, all his sins will be given over to oblivion.”

Therefore let us also imitate this publican, we who are bound by sins. Recalling the evils we have done, let us stand far off—that is, let us judge ourselves unworthy of the fellowship of the saints. Let us look toward the earth—that is, let us continually consider ourselves earth and ashes. Let us beat our breasts, so that carnal pleasure may be turned into bitterness of mind.

As penitents, let us not despair of forgiveness, but let us humbly approach the one who grants forgiveness, praying with the Prophet and saying: “Help us, God our Savior, and for the glory of your name, Lord, deliver us and be merciful to our sins, for the sake of your name” (Ps. 78).

But because, according to Solomon’s saying, “Before destruction the heart is exalted, and before glory it is humbled” (Prov. 16), it is rightly added: “Truly I tell you, this man went down to his house justified rather than the other”—that is, rather than the Pharisee.

The one was justified by accusing himself; the other was rejected by excusing himself. Thus in these events was fulfilled what he says elsewhere: “Truly I tell you, there is joy in heaven before the angels of God over one sinner who repents, more than over ninety-nine righteous people who have no need of repentance” (Luke 5).

Allegorically, by the Pharisee and the publican we can understand the two peoples: namely, the Jews and the Gentiles. Thus by the Pharisee, who is interpreted as “divided,” the Jewish people are signified, because through circumcision and the ceremonies of the Law they were divided from the other nations.

By the publican the Gentile people are understood: alienated from knowledge of God, they were not ashamed to sin publicly without any reverence, not only in the worship of idols but also in various impurities.

But the Pharisee, trusting in his own merits, was rejected, because, as the Apostle says: “The Jewish people, seeking to establish their own righteousness, have not submitted themselves to the righteousness of God” (Rom. 10).

The publican, or Gentile, having received knowledge of God, arrived at forgiveness all the more quickly because he was all the more deeply ashamed and grieved over his sins. The Apostle bears witness to this when he says: “What Israel was seeking, it did not obtain, but the elect obtained it” (Rom. 11).

Thus one deserved to be humbled by exalting himself, and the other deserved to be exalted by humbling himself. “For pride,” says Solomon, “is followed by disgrace, and glory follows the humble in spirit” (Prov. 19). Hence it is also added:

“For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.”

But because he did not simply say, “Whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted,” but added “everyone”—“Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted”—it must be said that people are exalted and humbled in various ways, both in this age and in the age to come.

Some are exalted here and in the future, such as King David, Job, Hezekiah, Josiah, and others like them, who were glorious in this age and will be more glorious in the future.

Others are humbled here and in the future, such as proud people who are poor; or those who receive punishment for their sins in this age and pass into eternal punishment in the future, such as Herod, Antiochus, Nebuchadnezzar, and Pilate, and many others like them, concerning whom it is written: “Crush them with a double crushing, Lord” (Jer. 19).

Some are exalted here but humbled in the future, such as proud rich people who, according to the word of Scripture, spend their days in good things and in a moment descend to the underworld (Job 21).

Others are humbled here but exalted in the future, such as the poor, and especially those who, leaving all they possess for God’s sake, humble themselves voluntarily so that they may deserve to be exalted by the Lord in the future.

May he deign to lead us into their company, he who lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen.

# HOMILY 124. THE THIRTEENTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST

*(Mark 7.)* “At that time: Jesus, departing from the region of Tyre, came through Sidon to the Sea of Galilee.” And what follows.

Above, the Gospel reading related how, as the Lord approached the regions of Tyre and Sidon, he freed the daughter of the Canaanite woman from a demon. Now, intending to describe another miracle, he did not think it pointless to mention the very places through which he walked, saying: “And again, departing from the region of Tyre, Jesus came through Sidon to the Sea of Galilee, between the territories of the Decapolis.”

Tyre and Sidon were cities of the Gentiles, which had once been assigned by lot to the children of Israel but were by no means possessed by them. Situated in the heart of the sea, they were not easily captured by enemies.

In Tyre there was a very powerful king, Hiram, who greatly assisted Solomon in constructing the house of the Lord (1 Kings 5). Against Tyre the prophet Ezekiel spoke many things (Ezek. 27–28), saying that it was situated in the heart of the sea and rich in wealth, but not free from vices. He also describes Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, hastening toward its destruction.

The Decapolis, however, is a region beyond the Jordan containing ten cities, as its name itself confirms. For δέκα (*deka*) in Greek means “ten” in Latin; πόλις (*polis*) in this place means “city.” From these terms, as we have said, the name of the region, Decapolis, is composed.

Therefore, just as Tyre and Sidon, cities of the Gentiles, signify the Gentile people, so the Decapolis signifies the Jews, who had received the Decalogue of the Law for their instruction.

When he says, “He came through Sidon to the Sea of Galilee, between the territories of the Decapolis,” this does not mean that he entered the territories themselves, but that he passed alongside them. This is also not without relevance to the meaning of the mystery. For he spiritually approached the territories of the Decapolis when he assumed flesh from the Jews, as the Apostle says: “Their fathers are from them, and from them, according to the flesh, is Christ, who is blessed for ever and ever” (Rom. 9).

He did not enter those territories themselves because he was neither recognized nor received by them, as he himself reproached them, saying: “I have come in my Father’s name, and you did not receive me; if another comes in his own name, you will receive him” (John 5). Hence it is said through John: “He came to his own, and his own did not receive him” (John 1).

Or certainly he approached the territories of the Decapolis when he accepted fellowship with human nature. He did not enter them, however, because he had no participation in sin.

“And they bring him a deaf man and one who could not speak.” This deaf and mute man allegorically signifies the human race, which consists both of Jews and of Gentiles. “For there is no distinction,” as the Apostle says, “between Jew and Greek; for all have sinned and lack the glory of God” (Rom. 3).

The human race became deaf when, in the first parent, it opened its hearing to the serpent’s words. After becoming deaf, it then lost the faculty of speech when it ceased from praising God. “For praise is not beautiful,” as Scripture says, “in the mouth of a sinner” (Sir. 15).

Those who bring the deaf and mute man to the Lord to be healed signify the patriarchs and prophets, who spiritually brought the sick human race to the Lord for healing. For they not only foretold the Lord’s incarnation for its deliverance but also desired it with all their strength. Hence it follows: “And they begged him to lay his hand upon him.”

In the Scriptures, the hand of the Lord sometimes signifies the power of divinity, and sometimes the incarnation of humanity. It signifies the power of divinity, as it is written: “Into your hands, Lord, I commend my spirit” (Ps. 30; Luke 23). It signifies the humanity of the incarnation, as we read elsewhere: “Send forth your hand from on high” (Ps. 143).

Therefore, in this passage the hand of the Lord appropriately signifies the mystery of the incarnation. They beg him to lay his hand upon him because, by accepting our mortality, he freed the human race from weakness of soul.

“And taking him aside from the crowd, he put his fingers into his ears.” Why did the Lord take the deaf and mute man aside in order to heal him? Could he not heal him in the presence of the people, who created all things from nothing? Certainly he could. But first he separates him from the crowd and afterward heals him, so that the human race might understand that it cannot receive the health of the soul in any other way unless, first abandoning its former errors, it makes itself separate from the crowd of unclean spirits and the tumult of vices.

The finger of God signifies the Holy Spirit in the Scriptures, as the Lord says elsewhere: “But if I cast out demons by the finger of God” (Luke 11). Another evangelist makes this clearer, saying: “If I cast out demons by the Spirit of God” (Matt. 12).

This is the finger that the Egyptian magicians acknowledged when they said: “This is the finger of God” (Exod. 8). The tablets of the Testimony were written by this finger.

The Holy Spirit is beautifully represented by the finger of God, because just as we grasp something with our fingers in order to work, so the Father and the Son do all things through the Holy Spirit, as the Psalmist bears witness when he says: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the breath of his mouth all their host” (Ps. 32).

He had seen the marvelous operation of this finger who said: “For I shall see your heavens, the works of your fingers” (Ps. 8).

Or certainly the Holy Spirit is rightly designated by the finger of God, because just as we have no other members in which there is as much division as in the fingers, and yet there is one hand, so although the gifts of the same Holy Spirit are divided among individuals, they nevertheless remain indivisible in the same Spirit.

Hence Paul, having enumerated the gifts of the same Holy Spirit, added: “All these things one and the same Spirit accomplishes, distributing to each as he wills” (1 Cor. 12).

Therefore he puts his fingers into the ears so that he may restore hearing to the deaf man, because the ears of the heart are opened through the grace of the Holy Spirit so that they may hear the word of God and understand it spiritually.

“And spitting, he touched his tongue.” Spittle descends from the head. Therefore by the head divinity is signified, and by spittle humanity, as the Apostle says: “The head of Christ is God” (1 Cor. 2). Thus he touched the tongue with spittle so that it might recover speech, when he lowered the height of his divinity to our humanity (John 11).

He demonstrated this more clearly elsewhere when he opened the eyes of the man born blind. For he made clay from spittle and smeared it upon his eyes.

“And looking up to heaven, he groaned and said to him: Ephpheta, which means, ‘Be opened.’” When the Lord was about to heal the sick man, he looked up to heaven to show that all good and holy things are to be requested from God. From there hearing is given to the deaf, and from there speech is restored to the mute, because, as the apostle James says: “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights” (James 1).

And as it is said in the Gospel: “A person cannot do anything by himself unless it has been given to him from above” (John 9 and 19).

“He groaned.” Did he need to ask anything from the Father with a groan, when he, together with the Father, grants everything that is requested? No. But he offered us an example of groaning whenever we intercede either for our own sins or for those of others.

When he said “Ephpheta,” the evangelist explained it by adding: “which means, ‘Be opened.’” It is the custom of the evangelists sometimes to place the Hebrew words or names themselves together with their explanation. Thus in the Gospel of John we read: “Go to the pool of Siloam, which is interpreted ‘Sent’” (John 9). And in the Gospel of Mark, “Bartimaeus, son of Timaeus,” is written (Matt. 10).

Judas Zelotes is the same as Judas Chananaeus, because *Chanaan* is interpreted as “zeal.”

“Ephpheta,” therefore, which means “be opened,” properly refers to the ears. And in a most beautiful order the Lord first puts his fingers into the deaf man’s ears, then touches his tongue with spittle, and finally says, “Ephpheta,” which means “be opened,” in order to demonstrate to priests the most orderly process of baptizing.

Those who are baptized must first be illumined by the grace of the Holy Spirit, then instructed by teachers, and finally called to the confession of faith. Hence it is the custom of priests to touch with spittle the tongue and nostrils of those whom they catechize, saying the Lord’s own words: “Ephpheta,” which means “be opened.”

But because there is no distinction between the Lord’s saying and his doing—“For he spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created” (Ps. 148)—

“Immediately,” when he said “Ephpheta,” which means “be opened,” the man’s ears were opened, the bond of his tongue was released, and he spoke correctly.

It was not fitting that one who had been created by the Lord should speak in any other way than correctly. According to the higher understanding, after the Lord softened the heart of the human race to repentance through the infusion of the Holy Spirit, and after he revealed the mystery of his incarnation, the tongue that unbelief had previously bound was released by faith, and it began to praise God, saying with the Psalmist: “Lord, open my lips, and my mouth shall proclaim your praise” (Ps. 50).

And with Isaiah: “The Lord God has given me a learned tongue, that I may know how to sustain with a word the one who has fallen” (Isa. 50).

“And he ordered them not to tell anyone.” What does it mean that the one who had come into the world for this purpose—that by performing miracles he might show himself to be God—ordered the miracle he had performed to be concealed?

Clearly he offered the good an example, so that we too might avoid empty glory and boastfulness in a good work, in accordance with his command elsewhere that we enter our room, shut the door, and pray to our Father. And our Father, who sees in secret, will repay us.

Yet a distinction must be observed in this silence: one who is new in the religious life should not only refrain from the office of preaching but also conceal his good works from the sight of others, so that his left hand may not know what his right hand is doing. Otherwise, the root of the heart, which the depth of the earth has not yet firmly secured, might be torn up by the wind of elation.

But one who has been tested by a long religious life ought not only to make progress in preaching but also by example, fulfilling what the Lord says elsewhere: “Let your light shine before human beings, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 5).

The Lord showed both alternatives by his own example when he commanded one person: “Tell no one,” but said to another: “Go into the city to your own people and announce to them how much God has done for you” (Mark 1 and 5).

[Col. 0668A] “But the more he ordered them, the more abundantly they proclaimed it.” Here the sluggishness of those to whom the office of preaching has been entrusted is rebuked, though they nevertheless cease from preaching.

For it must be considered what guilt belongs to teachers when, after the Lord’s command, they place themselves in silence, since even those who were commanded not to tell anyone could not keep silent.

Let us hear, then, what they said:

“‘He has done all things well: he makes the deaf hear and the mute speak.’” He did not do well only in making the deaf hear and the mute speak; he also did well in all the things he created from the beginning, as it is written: “And God saw all that he had made, and they were very good” (Gen. I).

In the moral sense, the deaf and mute signify every sinner. Whoever turns away his ears [Col. 0668B] so as not to hear the law is deaf. Whoever speaks wickedness on high and sows discord among the brethren is also mute in the exercise of speech. Such persons are brought by the masters and teachers of the Church to the Lord, so that they may receive spiritual hearing and speech. For they bring a sick person to the Lord when, through their teaching and exhortation, they cause sinners to be converted; and on behalf of those whom they desire to convert, they pour out prayers before the Lord.

Nor does the Lord’s mercy delay in healing such people, for he came to cure the wounds of souls—provided, however, that the faith and satisfaction of penitents are not lacking. The Lord showed the proper order of making satisfaction when, intending to heal the deaf and mute man, he led him aside, away from the crowd, thereby clearly showing that if sinners wish to produce fruits worthy of repentance, they must abandon the fellowship of demons, the tumult of vices, and [Col. 0668C] the carnal communion of human beings. For just as the company of the good greatly helps, so the association of carnal people greatly harms weak minds, as the Psalmist testifies: “With the holy you will be holy, and with the innocent man you will be innocent” (Ps. XVII). “And with the chosen you will be chosen, and with the perverse you will be perverted.”

As Solomon says: “Whoever walks with the wise will become wise; the companion of fools will become like them” (Prov. XIII). Hence elsewhere he himself admonishes us, saying: “Do not be a friend to an angry man, nor walk with a furious man, lest perhaps you learn his ways and take a stumbling-block for your soul” (Prov. XXII).

The Lord, as it were, separated his faithful spiritually from the crowd of unbelievers when he said through Isaiah: “Go out from their midst, and do not touch what is unclean [Col. 0668D]” (Isa. LII). Those who are perfect, placed amid the wicked, remain apart: they neither consent in their hearts to their wicked deeds nor spare them with their mouths. What concern that man had who, placed amid royal cares, said: “Who will give me wings like a dove, and I will fly away and rest? Behold, I have gone far away in flight, and I remained in solitude” (Ps. LIV).

But because no one can perform worthy repentance unless the grace of the Holy Spirit softens his heart toward repentance, it is rightly added: “The Lord put his fingers into his ears, and, spitting, touched his tongue.” The Lord, as it were, put his fingers into the deaf man’s ears when, through the ardor of the Holy Spirit, he softens the sinner’s heart toward repentance: “For, as the Apostle says, we do not know [Col. 0669A] how to pray as we ought; but the Spirit himself pleads for us with inexpressible groanings” (Rom. VIII).

He touches the mute man’s tongue, as it were, with spittle when the sinner’s heart tastes the savor of divine wisdom. How merciful the Lord is toward converted sinners is made clear when it follows: “And immediately his ears were opened, and the bond of his tongue was loosed, and he spoke correctly.” No sin is so great that it cannot be healed by the medicine of repentance. For he does not lie who says: “As I live, says the Lord, I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live.” And: “On whatever day the sinner turns and groans, all his sins will be consigned to oblivion.”

The sinner speaks correctly after his healing when he changes the tongue [Col. 0669B] that had been twisted by insults and detraction into one that praises God and exhorts his neighbor. But because, after public repentance, no one should immediately come forth to preach, it is rightly said: “And he commanded them not to tell anyone.” He who wishes to wipe away the wounds of others must first heal himself. Hence the Apostle, speaking of those to be ordained as ministers of the Church, says: “Not one recently converted, not a novice, lest, being puffed up, he fall into the judgment of the devil” (I Tim. VIII).

But the person whom length of time and the perfection of repentance have made suitable ought also to draw others out of the pit of sin, according to what is said in the Apocalypse: “Let the one who hears say, ‘Come’” (Apoc. XXII). Hence it is rightly said: “The more he commanded them, [Col. 0669C] the more abundantly they proclaimed it, and they were all the more astonished, saying: ‘He has done all things well: he makes the deaf hear and the mute speak.’”

## HOMILY CXXV. THE FOURTEENTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST

### (Luke X)

“At that time Jesus said to his disciples: ‘Blessed are the eyes that see what you see.’” And so forth.

At the beginning of this reading it is asked why the Lord calls blessed the eyes of those who see him. Were all the eyes blessed that were able to see him bodily? Were the eyes of Pilate and Caiaphas, and of the others who saw him and crucified him, blessed? Or were the eyes of Judas blessed, who saw him and betrayed him? No. Otherwise even the eyes of beasts and birds could be blessed. Rather, he calls blessed the eyes of the apostles, to whom he deigned to reveal himself and the Father [Col. 0669D], for whom above he had glorified the Father, saying: “I confess to you, Lord, Father of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones” (Matt. XI).

The evangelist took care to make this clear when afterward he added what he had written above, saying: “And turning to them, he said: ‘Blessed are the eyes that see what you see.’” He showed that the eyes of those were blessed who, seeing a human being, believed him to be God. What they saw inwardly in that man with spiritual eyes they reveal elsewhere, when, questioned, they answer with one voice, saying: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matt. XVI). That such a vision and such a confession merit blessedness the Lord himself shows when he immediately replies, saying: “Blessed are you, Simon son of Jonah, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you [Col. 0670A], but my Father who is in heaven” (ibid.).

Nor shall we be deprived of this blessedness, although we have not seen him bodily and yet believe spiritually, as he said to one who had seen him: “Because you have seen me, you have believed; blessed are those who have not seen and have believed” (John XX).

“For I tell you that many kings and prophets desired to see what you see and did not see it, and to hear what you hear and did not hear it.”

If we understand “kings” literally, we can recognize that holy kings, such as David, Hezekiah, and Josiah, desired to see what the apostles saw but did not see it. But because “king” takes its name from ruling, spiritually we understand as kings those who, although poor in material possessions, nevertheless know how to rule and order their actions and thoughts justly [Col. 0670B]. Of them Solomon says: “The heart of the king is in the hand of the Lord” (Prov. XXI).

Hence another evangelist appropriately put “the just” in place of “kings,” saying: “Many just men and prophets desired to see what you see and did not see it” (Matt. XIII). For just as one loses royal power who, exercising tyranny, knows how to rule neither himself nor his subjects, so a poor and insignificant person is reckoned by the name of king if he knows how to rule himself well. Fortunatus briefly expressed this in a verse, saying:

> The poor man reigns in secret, possessing God.

But it is asked why the Lord says: “Many kings and prophets desired to see what you see and did not see it, and to hear what you hear and did not hear it,” when the patriarch Jacob says: “I saw the Lord face to face [Col. 0670C], and my life was preserved” (Gen. XXXII); and Isaiah: “I saw the Lord sitting upon a high and exalted throne” (Isa. VI); and he himself bears witness concerning Abraham, saying: “Abraham your father rejoiced that he might see my day; he saw it and was glad” (John VIII).

The answer is that one thing is the figure and another the reality figured; one thing the mirror and another the form reflected. Thus the holy prophets foresaw through the Holy Spirit that God would come in the flesh, but they desired to see him dwelling among them bodily, speaking with them, and eating with them, as the apostles saw him; yet they did not see him.

Therefore, concerning his bodily presence, he said: “Many kings and prophets desired to see what you see [Col. 0670D] and did not see it.” How greatly the ancient saints desired to see him in the flesh is indicated by the venerable Jacob, who, when blessing his sons as he was dying, said: “I will await your salvation, O Lord” (Gen. XLIX). Isaiah burned with this desire when he said: “Would that you would tear open the heavens and descend!” (Isa. LXIV.) David, likewise aflame with love, said: “Lord, incline your heavens and descend” (Ps. LXVI). The righteous Simeon in the Gospel (Luke II) also burned with this desire; because of the greatness of his love, he received the answer that he would not see death before he had seen the Christ of the Lord incarnate.

“And behold, a certain lawyer stood up, testing him and saying: ‘Teacher, what must I do to possess eternal life [Col. 0671A]?’”

Perhaps this lawyer, in rising to test the Lord, took his opportunity from the Lord’s words spoken above: “Rejoice because your names are written in heaven” (Luke X). For he wished to know whether he would also say that his name was written in heaven, and therefore he asks so carefully what he must do to possess eternal life.

But because it is inept to speak or to put forward something good without a proper intention, this lawyer is shown to have asked ineptly. That he questioned the Lord without a proper intention the evangelist makes clear when he says: “He stood up, testing him.” He stood up not only bodily in order to question him, but also through the elevation of his mind in order to test him. He reveals this in his very words, when he inquires of him not as the Lord but as a teacher [Col. 0671B], saying: “Teacher, what must I do to possess eternal life?”

But the Lord, whom the hidden things of the heart do not deceive and from whom no thought is concealed, so governs his answer that he responds to the scribe’s question without giving the tempter grounds for accusation. He immediately sent him back to the law, which he carried on his lips and not in his heart, saying:

“In the law, what is written? How do you read it?”

And he, who could neither deny what he had read, answered:

“You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your strength, and with all your mind, and your neighbor as yourself.”

Because the Lord recognized this answer as his own, he immediately praised it, saying:

“You have answered correctly; do this, and you will live.”

This question of the scribe [Col. 0671C] is of great benefit to us if we preserve in our deeds what he answered in words. He said: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your strength, and with all your mind, and your neighbor as yourself.”

These words show that if we wish to possess eternal life, we must love God not partially but wholly: with our whole heart, our whole soul, all our strength, and our whole mind, so that no place remains empty that is not filled with the love of God; rather, mind, hands, and tongue should resound with his love.

Here we should note that no measure is set upon the love of God when it is said: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart,” and so forth. Because God is immeasurable, he must be loved without measure [Col. 0671D], so that however greatly we love him, we confess that we love him little.

But a measure is set upon love of one’s neighbor when it is said: “And your neighbor as yourself.” Therefore we must love God more than ourselves, and our neighbor as ourselves: that is, just as we wish our own needs to be helped, so let us help our neighbor; just as we wish our own weakness to be treated with compassion, so let us have compassion on our neighbor; and just as we wish to arrive at eternal life, so let us desire that our neighbor arrive there with us. This is truly to love one’s neighbor as oneself.

We must consider in this passage that God is not truly loved without one’s neighbor, nor one’s neighbor truly loved without God. For if someone loves God in such a way that he neglects care for his neighbor, or loves his neighbor in such a way that he places the love of God second, he must be judged not to possess true love.

This is shown figuratively in the divine law when twice-dyed scarlet is commanded to be placed in the priest’s ornament [Col. 0672A] (Exod. XXV). Twice-dyed scarlet is placed in the priest’s ornament, as it were, when love is doubled in our conduct.

For just as a bird cannot raise itself to the heights without two wings, so we cannot attain perfection unless we observe the two principal commandments, namely love of God and love of neighbor. The Apostle John testifies to this when he says: “If anyone says, ‘I love God,’ and hates his brother, he is a liar” (I John IV). And again: “Whoever does not love his brother whom he sees, how can he love God whom he does not see?” (ibid.) “And we have this commandment from God: whoever loves God must love his brother also.”

“But he, wishing to justify himself, said to Jesus: ‘And who is my neighbor [Col. 0672B]?’”

For he was one of those of whom the Lord says: “They sought the glory of human beings more than the glory of God.” But the Lord so shaped his answer that he both showed himself to have become our neighbor through mercy and declared to the Pharisee whom he ought to imitate.

“Then Jesus looked up and said: ‘A certain man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and he fell among robbers.’”

Those who follow the literal sense of Scripture appropriately say that, when the Lord presented the likeness of a wounded man, he correctly mentioned that he went down from Jerusalem to Jericho. For on the road from Jerusalem to Jericho there are great rocks [Col. 0672C], hollow valleys, and places suitable for the ambushes of robbers. Josephus bears witness to this, relating that a multitude of robbers was killed by Herod in that same place.

Spiritually, however, we understand this man as Adam together with his descendants. He is rightly said to have gone down from Jerusalem to Jericho because, losing the vision of heavenly peace, he fell into the present life, which is full of miseries and troubles. Jerusalem is interpreted as “vision of peace”; Jericho, however, as “moon.” In sacred speech the moon signifies the decline of human frailty: as it waxes and wanes at monthly intervals, it expresses the mutability of our calamity, since we grow by being born and decline by dying.

The first man therefore descended from Jerusalem to Jericho when, leaving the company of the angels with whom he contemplated God [Col. 0672D], he experienced the miseries of the present life. The robbers among whom he fell are unclean spirits, who sit in ambush in hidden places in order to kill the innocent. The Prophet prayed to be freed from their snares when he said: “Keep me from the trap that they have set for me and from the stumbling-blocks of those who work iniquity” (Ps. CXL).

“They also stripped him.”

They stripped him because, after sin, they deprived him of the garment of immortality with which he had been clothed. Hence, immediately recognizing that they were naked, they sewed together fig leaves and made themselves loincloths (Gen. III).

“And after inflicting wounds on him, they went away.”

They inflicted wounds when, after disobedience, they wounded the human race, expelled from paradise, with various vices and sins. They went away [Col. 0673A] not by ceasing from temptation, but by not harming him as much as they wished. Hence it is rightly said:

“Leaving him half dead.”

For someone is half dead who is alive on one side and dead on the other. They therefore left him half dead because they stripped him of the garment of immortality, but they could not entirely remove from him the hope of returning to forgiveness.

“Now it happened that a certain priest was going down the same road, and when he saw him, he passed by.”

This priest is understood, in his order, as Aaron, to whom the honor of the legal priesthood was granted by God. He too, going down the same road, saw the wounded man and passed by, because, born from the same mortality, he understood that the human race was held under the sin of the first transgression, but he could free neither himself nor others.

“Likewise a Levite, when he was near the place and saw him, passed by [Col. 0673B].”

The Levite signifies the order of the prophets. He too saw the wounded man and passed by, because the prophets understood that the human race was bound under the chain of its first guilt, but they were able to absolve neither themselves nor others.

“But a certain Samaritan, journeying, came near him; and when he saw him, he was moved with compassion.”

The Samaritan, whose name is interpreted as “guardian,” signifies the Lord Jesus Christ, of whom the Prophet says: “Unless the Lord builds the house, those who guard it watch in vain” (Ps. CXXVI). He was the one whose guardianship was desired by the man who said: “Keep me, Lord, as the apple of your eye; protect me beneath the shadow of your wings” (Ps. XVI).

This is that guardian to whom it is said through the prophet Isaiah [Col. 0673C]: “He cries to me from Seir: ‘Guardian, what of the night?’ The guardian says: ‘Morning comes, and also night. If you seek, seek; turn back and come’” (Isa. XXI).

In the Gospel, when the Jews reproachfully said to him: “Are we not right in saying that you are a Samaritan and have a demon?” (John VIII), he denied that he had a demon, but he did not deny that he was a Samaritan.

The journey of this Samaritan was from heaven into the womb, from the womb to the cross, from the cross to the tomb, and from the tomb again into heaven. When he was making this journey, he came near the wounded man when he assumed the likeness of our flesh. Seeing his wounds, he was moved with compassion, because everything by which he freed us from everlasting death, and by which God, having become man for our redemption, humbled himself even to our human condition [Col. 0673D], was wholly mercy and not merit. The Prophet contemplated this when he said: “The mercy of the Lord is from eternity and to eternity upon those who fear him” (Ps. CII).

“And approaching, he bound up his wounds, pouring in oil and wine.”

He bound up the wounds when he prohibited sin. Or he bound up the wounds when he promised forgiveness to penitents, saying: “I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.” And again: “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick” (Matt. IX).

It is rightly said: “Pouring in oil and wine.” For these two liquids, as physicians say, are suitable for treating wounds: wine cleanses, while oil soothes. Spiritually, the Lord [Col. 0674A] poured wine into the wounds of the injured man when he imposed the severity of repentance. He poured in oil when he promised penitents the sweetness of forgiveness.

He pours in wine, as it were, when he says: “Repent.” He pours in oil, as it were, when he adds: “For the kingdom of heaven is near” (Matt. III and IV).

“And placing him on his own beast, he brought him to an inn and took care of him.”

Here the beast signifies the Lord’s undefiled body. He placed the wounded man on the beast when, through the sacred passion of his flesh, the Lord freed us from sins. Hence the beast is rightly called *jumentum*, as though it were an aid, because he helped our weakness through that which he endured for us—the passion of the flesh without sin—as it is said through Peter: “He himself bore our sins in his body [Col. 0674B] upon the tree, so that, having died to sins, we might live to righteousness; by his bruising we have been healed” (I Pet. IV).

He also wished this to be signified according to another Gospel parable, when, finding the wandering sheep, he placed it upon his shoulders and so carried it back to the flock (Luke XV; Matt. XVIII). Having placed the wounded man upon the beast, he brought him to an inn because he brought the redeemed human race to the Church. Spiritually, this is called an inn, where the holy animals are daily refreshed with the food of the divine word, and where, according to the prophecy of Isaiah, the wolf lies down with the lamb, and the ox eats straw with the lion (Isa. XI).

“And on the following day he brought out two denarii and gave them to the innkeeper.”

The following day is the time after the Lord’s resurrection [Col. 0674C]. One day, as it were, was before the passion and another after the resurrection. The two denarii are the two Testaments, the New and the Old; or the two commandments of charity, namely love of God and love of neighbor.

He gave the innkeeper two denarii when, by teaching, he entrusted the two Testaments or the two commandments of charity first to the apostles and afterward to their followers—that is, to the teachers of the Church.

How greatly the Lord cares for our salvation he makes clear when he adds: “And he said to him: ‘Take care of him.’” He entrusted care of the wounded man to the innkeeper when, speaking especially to Peter in the person of all shepherds, he said: “If you love me, feed my sheep” (John, last chapter).

To him it is rightly promised as a reward: “And whatever more you spend, I will repay you when I return.” The innkeeper spends more [Col. 0674D] when a teaching person does from devotion what he has not received by command.

The Apostle Paul did this. Although he had the right, while proclaiming the Gospel, to live from the Gospel, he did not wish to use this authority; instead, he preached by day and worked by night so that he might provide food and clothing for himself and his companions.

When the Samaritan returns, he will repay him whatever more he has spent: when he comes to judgment, he will grant a greater reward for the greater labor of preaching, saying to the faithful servant: “Well done, good and faithful servant, because you have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many; enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matt. XXV).

When the parable had ended, the Lord beautifully concluded the scribe’s question, saying:

“Which of these three seems to you to have been neighbor [Col. 0675A] to the man who fell among robbers?”

But he answered what he could not deny and what the clearest reason demonstrated:

“The one who showed mercy to him.”

The Lord confirms his answer by adding:

“Go, and you do likewise.”

As though he were saying: Just as the Samaritan, foreign by nation, became neighbor to the wounded man through charity, so you too, judging every human being to be your neighbor, should devote all the good works of which you are capable to anyone whom you can help; and in this way you will certainly have fulfilled charity, which leads to eternal life.

## HOMILY CXXVI. THE FIFTEENTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST

### (Luke XVII)

“At that time, as Jesus went to [Col. 0675B] Jerusalem, he passed through the midst of Samaria and Galilee.” And so forth.

Anyone familiar with the boundaries of the land of Judea readily understands that, as the Lord went to Jerusalem from the places where the evangelist had previously recalled him teaching, he literally passed through the midst of Samaria and Galilee. And because he became man for us and for our salvation, he not only proclaimed the kingdom of God to those who came to him, but also, journeying through various places, granted healing to many.

“And as he entered a certain town, ten leprous men met him. They stood at a distance and raised their voices, saying: ‘Jesus, Teacher, have mercy on us.’”

They did not dare to come near, for although faith encouraged their desire, lepra [Col. 0675C] prevented their approach. Those who suffered from this disease were excluded from the camps. Yet they did not doubt that they could receive healing from him by sight or speech alone, for, standing at a distance, they humbly begged his help.

Spiritually, the town that the Lord entered signifies the world. He entered the town, as it were, when, assuming flesh from the Virgin Mary, he appeared visibly to the world.

The ten leprous men who met him signify the Jewish people. They are appropriately said to have been ten because that people had received the Decalogue of the law for their instruction. They were ten, but they were leprous, because, transgressing the commandments of the Decalogue, and with the Lord appearing in the flesh, they were divided among various doctrines and polluted by different iniquities [Col. 0675D], as the Apostle testifies, saying: “There is no distinction between Jew and Greek; for all have sinned and lack the glory of God, being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus” (Rom. III). And again: “Tribulation and distress upon every soul of the human being who works evil, of the Jew first and also of the Greek” (Rom. X).

This is fitting for those from the Jews who believed in Christ: standing at a distance, the lepers cried out, saying: “Jesus, Teacher, have mercy on us.” *Jesus* in the Hebrew language is called in Latin “savior” or “salutary.” Therefore, since they hoped for salvation from him, they called him not only Savior but also asked for mercy. And because they remembered that they had offended his commandments [Col. 0676A], they called him not only Savior but also Teacher. They presumed nothing on the basis of their own merits when they so humbly begged for his mercy: “Jesus, Teacher, have mercy on us.”

Alternatively, we may not improperly understand heretics by the lepers. Just as leprosy displays various colors on the skin, so the doctrine of heretics produces various errors in speech. They are divided not only from the Catholic Church but also from one another, holding different opinions among themselves. One believes that Christ is God alone and not man; another, that he is man alone and not God; one denies that he assumed true flesh; another, conversely, asserts that he did not assume a true soul. Thus leprosy displays varied colors on the skin.

Such people must stand at a distance [Col. 0676B] and must be driven away from the Church, lest the leprosy of their uncleanness stain the simple in heart, as the Apostle says: “Avoid a heretical person after one and a second admonition, knowing that such a person is perverted” (Tit. III). Hence John also says: “If anyone comes to you and does not bring this doctrine, do not receive him into your house, nor say ‘Greetings’ to him, lest you share in his evil works” (II John I).

If they wish to return to the Church, they must not be received until they anathematize their heresy before orthodox priests. Hence it is rightly added:

“When he saw them, he said: ‘Go, show yourselves to the priests.’”

We read of no others to whom the Lord granted these bodily benefits whom he sent to the priests, except lepers [Col. 0676C]. Nor is this recorded only here. According to Matthew, when he descended from the mountain, he is said to have healed a leper, to whom he said: “Go and show yourself to the priests, and offer the gift that Moses commanded as a testimony to them” (Matt. VIII).

We believe that he did this for several reasons. First, to show honor to the priests; second, so that he would not appear to contradict the law, since the law commanded that if someone had been cleansed of leprosy, he should come to the priest and offer a sacrifice for his cleansing; third, so that when the priests saw the lepers cleansed, they might find salvation if they believed in the one who cleansed them, but if they refused to believe, they might be without excuse.

Or certainly he sent the lepers to the priests to show that the carnal priesthood prefigured the spiritual priesthood now exercised in the Church. There is an invisible leprosy in the soul [Col. 0676D] when the conscience is polluted by various sins. One commits homicide, another theft, another adultery, another robbery, another sacrilege, and others similar offenses; thus each defiles the soul with different colors of invisible leprosy.

If such people wish to receive cleansing of soul, they must stand at a distance—that is, judge themselves unworthy of the fellowship of the saints—and with loud cries appeal to Jesus, that is, with great contrition of heart implore divine clemency, saying with the Psalmist:

“Do not remember our former iniquities; may your mercies quickly come to meet us [Col. 0677A], for we have become exceedingly poor” (Ps. LXXVIII). “Help us, God our Savior, and for the glory of your name, Lord, deliver us and be favorable to our sins for the sake of your name” (ibid.).

And because they must not only confess their sins to priests but also, according to their counsel, undertake repentance and the satisfaction that obtains forgiveness, it is rightly said: “Go, show yourselves to the priests.”

Sins must be disclosed to priests in the place of God, and repentance must be undertaken according to their counsel. This was prefigured in the divine law when this command concerning lepers was given to Moses: “A man on whose skin a varied color appears shall come to the priest and show himself to him” (Lev. XIII). The priest shall shut him up in a house, separated and apart, for seven days. After seven days, having examined him, if he sees that the leprosy has grown, he shall add another seven days. After fourteen days, if he still sees the leprosy growing [Col. 0677B], he shall know that it is a persistent leprosy. Then he shall judge him to be a leper and cast him outside the camp. He shall remain with untrimmed beard, torn clothing, covered head, and uncovered mouth, judging himself unclean throughout all the days of his separation.

But if the one who suffers from this disease is healed, let him come to the priests and offer for his cleansing a sacrifice: a round loaf of bread and a sextarius of oil for preparing the lamps, and two living birds, one for sin and the other as a burnt offering.

Let us briefly see how all these things are now to be done in the Church. As we have said, leprosy signifies sin. Therefore whoever has the leprosy of sin in his soul must come to the priest and humbly confess his sins to him [Col. 0677C]. The priest, having examined him, shall shut him up for seven days in a house set apart—that is, impose upon him a period of repentance according to the nature and extent of his sin.

After seven days, having examined him, if he sees that the leprosy has grown, he shall add another seven days, because where sin is added, the punishment for sin must also increase. After fourteen days, if he sees the leprosy growing—that is, if he sees that sin has become habitual—he shall know that it is a persistent leprosy. Then he shall judge him to be a leper and cast him outside the camp—that is, repel him from the Church or judge him unworthy of the fellowship of the saints.

Let him remain with untrimmed beard, which pertains to the squalor of repentance; with torn clothing, so that through open confession he may manifest repentance or conscience; with covered head [Col. 0677D], because one who clings to sins ought to cease from preaching; and with uncovered mouth, not in defense of his sin but in accusation of himself.

“But if the one who suffers from this disease has been cleansed”—that is, if through worthy repentance he has ceased from the habit of sin—“let him offer for his cleansing a round loaf of bread,” that is, let him extend the sweetness of charity to all whom he can, not only to friends but also to enemies; “and a sextarius of oil,” that is, clothed in the inner organs of mercy, let him kindly forgive those who sin against him.

This is to be done for the preparation of lamps, so that, just as by living wickedly he destroyed many through his evil example, so by making worthy repentance he may rebuild many through his satisfaction.

“Let him also offer two living sparrows, one for sin and the other as a burnt offering [Col. 0678A]”—that is, either the two kinds of compunction, namely fear and love; or certainly body and soul, so that, just as he offered his members to serve uncleanness and iniquity for iniquity, so he may offer those same members to serve righteousness for sanctification.

Because all these things are to be done according to the judgment of the priest, it is rightly said to the lepers: “Go, show yourselves to the priests.”

This passage destroys the opinion of those who, ashamed to confess their sins to priests, have devised a kind of excuse, saying that it is enough for them to confess their sins to God alone, provided that afterward they cease from those sins. If their opinion were true, the Lord would never send to the priests the lepers whom he himself had cleansed. Nor would he send Paul (Acts IX), whom he himself had addressed on the road [Col. 0678B], to the priest Ananias.

To show that sins must be bound and loosed according to the judgment of priests, he did not permit Lazarus, whom he himself had raised from the dead after four days, to depart until he had been loosed by the disciples, as it is written in the Gospel (John XI). He rose with his hands and feet bound, he who had been dead for four days. Then he said to his disciples: “Unbind him and let him go.”

And to confirm this authority, after entrusting to the Apostle Peter the pontifical power of binding and loosing, together with the keys of the kingdom of heaven, he said: “Whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven” (Matt. XVI).

“And it happened that, as they went, they were cleansed.”

The lepers were cleansed on the way before they came to the priests not only by divine power [Col. 0678C] but also by a most merciful arrangement, so that they themselves might recognize their purifier and the priests might realize that they had contributed nothing to their cleansing.

According to the spiritual interpretation, however, the lepers are cleansed before they come to the priests because it is not priests but God who forgives sins.

“One of them, when he saw that he had been cleansed, returned, glorifying God with a loud voice. And he fell on his face at his feet, giving thanks.”

This one who returned to give thanks to his cleanser signifies the unity of the Church. Although divided across the length of the earth, because it believes one thing, understands one thing, and desires one thing, it is held together in unity. Of this it is written: “The multitude of believers was of one heart and one soul” (Acts IV). And again: “He makes those who are of one mind dwell in a house” (Ps. LXVII). And elsewhere: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together as one” (Ps. CXXXII). For the length of the earth does not separate those whom the same faith and charity unite.

[Col. 0678D]

The loud voice signifies not so much the sound of the mouth as the intention of the heart. For the great cry of the saints is a great desire, because each person cries out as much as he loves. Hence the Lord says to Moses: “Why do you cry out to me?” (Exod. XIV), although he is not recorded to have said anything at that time. The Prophet knew that he had this cry in his heart when, because of the greatness of his love, he said:

[Col. 0679A]

“I cried with my whole heart; hear me, O Lord” (Ps. CXVIII). And again: “O Lord, I cried to you; hear me; attend to my voice when I cry to you” (Ps. CXL).

And beautifully this man, who returned to give thanks to God, his cleanser, is said to have fallen on his face. For whoever falls on his face falls where he does not see. To fall on one’s face, therefore, belongs to one who worships or entreats. To fall backward belongs to one who is proud or contemptuous. Thus Abraham, after he had seen the day of Christ, fell on his face and worshiped (Gen. XVII and XVIII). But concerning the persecutors of the Lord it is written that “they went backward and fell to the ground” (John XVIII). Eli, because he did not rebuke his sons, fell backward from his seat, and, his neck broken, died (1 Kings IV). And Scripture speaks figuratively of the Antichrist: “Let his rider fall backward” (Gen. XLIX). Therefore, falling forward belongs to the elect, but falling backward to the reprobate.

“And he was a Samaritan.”

When the evangelist so carefully calls this man, who returned to give thanks to his cleanser, a Samaritan, he silently indicates that the others, who remained ungrateful, were Jews. In many places in the Gospel the faith of the Gentiles is shown to be more ready than that of the Jews, just as elsewhere the Lord praised the faith of the centurion, saying:

[Col. 0679B]

“Amen, I say to you, I have not found such great faith in Israel” (Matt. VIII).

But since Samaritan is interpreted as “guardian,” this man, through whom we have said that the unity of the Church is signified, is rightly called a Samaritan, because from that point onward he firmly guards the cleansing and virtue of his Church, since he trusts firmly not in himself but in God, saying with the Psalmist:

[Col. 0679C]

“Guard me, O Lord, as the apple of your eye; protect me under the shadow of your wings” (Ps. XVI). And again: “Unless the Lord guards the city, the one who guards it keeps watch in vain” (Ps. CXXVI).

Or, so that he might possess other virtues, he strove to retain the guardianship of humility, as did the one who said: “I have been humbled exceedingly, O Lord; revive me according to your word” (Ps. CXVIII).

“But Jesus, answering, said: Were not ten cleansed? And where are the nine?”

The Lord does not ask this because he is ignorant of anything. Before his eyes all things are naked and open, and he knows them before they come to be. Rather, he asks in order to show that he does not know them. For God’s knowing is choosing, while his not knowing is rejecting. The Lord knows those whom he has chosen, as it was said to a certain righteous man:

[Col. 0679D]

“I know you by name.” And as the Apostle says: “The Lord knows those who are his” (2 Tim. II).

Those whom he rejects, however, he does not know, as he will say at the end to the reprobate: “Depart from me, all you workers of iniquity; I do not know where you are from” (Matt. VII; Luke XIII). Therefore, he asks where those who remained ungrateful and did not return to give thanks to God are, as though they were unknown, saying: “Were not ten cleansed? And where are the nine?”

“No one was found to return and give glory to God except this foreigner.”

And fittingly those who remained ungrateful are contained in the number nine. For the number nine is imperfect and needs one in order to complete its perfection. But the number of unity is perfect and cannot be divided; it needs nothing to complete its perfection, because there is “one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all.”

[Col. 0680A]

Therefore, those contained in the number nine rightly signify those who, having received the Lord’s gifts, do not give thanks to God. But the one who gave thanks to his cleanser signifies those who, having received benefits, give thanks to him, saying with the Psalmist: “I will bless the Lord at all times” (Ps. XXXIII). For neither do the former perfectly keep the precepts of the Decalogue, nor in the future will they receive the tenfold reward promised to those who labor in the vineyard.

“And he said to him: Rise, go.”

Since he had humbly fallen before the Lord’s feet, he rightly deserved to hear: “Rise, go.” For, as he himself says in the Gospel: “Everyone who humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke XIV and XVIII). And as it is said through Solomon:

[Col. 0680B]

“Glory follows the humble in spirit” (Prov. XXIX).

A sinner is permitted to rise and go when, through worthy satisfaction, he is absolved from sins. And because “without faith it is impossible to please God” (Heb. XI), it is rightly added: “Because your faith has saved you.”

Faith is the principal virtue, because, as Scripture says: “The righteous person lives by faith.” And as the Apostle says: “Now these three remain: faith, hope, and charity” (1 Cor. XIII). True faith is that which believes with the mind what it does not see with the body, as the Apostle testifies in the Epistle to the Hebrews:

[Col. 0680C]

“Faith is the substance of things hoped for, the proof of things not seen” (Heb. XI).

# HOMILY CXXVII. SIXTEENTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST

(Matt. VI.) “At that time Jesus said to his disciples: No one can serve two masters.” And so forth.

When the Lord Jesus Christ was urging the minds of human beings to worship the one God, knowing that human nature cannot be subject simultaneously to God and the devil, he said, among other things: “No one can serve two masters.”

[Col. 0680D]

The two masters are understood to be God and the devil. For “Lord” derives its name from lordship, and this name properly belongs to him who is not only the governor but also the creator of the whole creation, who is King of kings and Lord of lords. The devil is called “lord” not properly but abusively, because he exercises the dominion of his tyranny over the minds of those who submit to him through evil works.

Therefore, one and the same person cannot serve these two masters at the same time, because what the Lord commands and what the devil suggests are greatly opposed and different. For example: the Lord commands humility, while the devil suggests pride; the Lord calls to chastity, while the devil persuades to lust; the Lord commands almsgiving and generosity, while the devil urges greed; the Lord commands peace, while the devil urges discord; the Lord commands love, while the devil urges hatred. To conclude everything briefly, the Lord calls to virtues, while the devil calls to vices.

Therefore, the human mind is not so broad and capacious that it can retain both wills and both forms of service within itself at the same time. Christ disdains to receive the service of those who submit the neck of their mind to the devil’s yoke, as the Apostle testifies when he says:

[Col. 0681A]

“What agreement is there between Christ and Belial? Or what fellowship does light have with darkness? Or what portion does a believer have with an unbeliever?” (2 Cor. VI). None.

And as another Scripture says: No one is able to do both things at once and to place his hand on both. Hence it is said through James: “A double-minded person is unstable in all his ways” (James I). And through the prophet Isaiah: Woe to the sinner who enters the land by two ways.

“Either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will endure the one and despise the other.” That is, he will hate the devil and love Christ. For whoever loves God hates evil. No one is of so savage a mind that he would admit in words that he hates God. Yet the person who does not love God is said to hate him—that is, the one who does not keep his commandments. Of such people he himself says:

[Col. 0681B]

“They saw me, and hated me without cause” (John XV).

But whoever despises God endures the devil, a harsh and destructive master. Those who serve him endure many harsh and difficult things not only in everlasting punishment but also in the present life. For just as Christ’s burden is light and his yoke gentle, so, conversely, the devil’s service is harsh and difficult.

Therefore, concerning those who follow his will, it is said through Solomon: “They do not sleep unless they have done evil; nor is sleep taken from their eyes unless they have overthrown someone” (Prov. IV). And through the prophet: “They labored to act wickedly” (Jer. IX).

But because the devil finds this servitude especially in the minds of those who burn with the fever of greed, it is rightly added: “You cannot serve God and mammon.”

[Col. 0681C]

“Mammon,” whether in Hebrew or Syriac, is interpreted in Latin as “riches.” Its usage is not far removed from that of the Punic language, since in Punic *mammon* means “profit” in Latin.

Let the greedy person hear this; let the one who is called a Christian hear it and understand that he cannot serve God and riches at the same time. For it is one thing to possess riches and another to serve riches. Whoever is master of riches distributes them as a master, fulfilling what is said through the Prophet: “He has scattered abroad; he has given to the poor; his righteousness endures forever and ever” (Ps. CXI).

But whoever is their slave is tormented by anxious servitude not only in acquiring them but also in guarding them. And therefore, while he is held entangled in the servitude of riches, he is emptied of the service of Christ. For when a river is divided into many streams, its own channel is dried up.

[Col. 0681D]

Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Riches and pleasures choke the word, so that it bears no fruit.” Thus the Apostle James says: “Whoever wishes to be a friend of this world is made an enemy of God” (James IV).

Therefore, the Lord invites those who desire to serve Christ to voluntary poverty, when he continues, saying:

“Therefore I say to you: Do not be anxious about your life, what you will eat, nor about your body, what you will wear.”

It is as though he said: Because you cannot serve God and mammon, therefore I say to you, do not be anxious about your life. For “blessed are the poor in spirit, because theirs is the kingdom of heaven.”

[Col. 0682A]

Here the simpler-minded perhaps ask whether this food pertains to the soul, since the soul is incorporeal and invisible, while food is visible. They should be answered that in this passage “soul” means the present life, whose sustenance consists of food and drink, sleep and clothing.

It is asked, however, why he said, “Do not be anxious about your life, what you will eat,” when the prophet says in praise of the holy man: “You shall eat the labors of your hands; blessed are you, and it shall be well with you” (Ps. CXXVII).

The answer is that in this passage the Lord did not prohibit labor but forbade anxiety. A person should labor for what will sustain him, not for what will make him rich, as was said to the first human being:

[Col. 0682B]

“By the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread” (Gen. III).

Hence the Apostle commanded his disciples: “Let each one labor, working with his hands at what is good, so that he may have something to give to those in need” (Eph. IV).

And lest the human mind doubt the sustenance of the present life, he added further, saying:

“Is not the soul more than food, and the body more than clothing?”

It is as though he said: The Lord who has provided greater things will not deny lesser ones; he who gave the soul will also give food, and he who bestowed the body will add clothing.

And lest the human mind make excuses on the grounds of frailty concerning the needs of the present life, the Lord offered the example of the birds of heaven, saying:

“Look at the birds of heaven, for they neither sow, nor reap, nor gather into barns, and your heavenly Father feeds them.”

[Col. 0682C]

It is as though he said: If God feeds the birds of heaven, which possess an irrational soul, without the labor of plowing and without the anxiety of reaping and gathering into barns, he will certainly not allow human beings, made in his image and likeness, to perish from hunger.

Hence it is added: “Are you not worth more than they?” This does not refer to number but to the image. It means: You are worth more than they—that is, you are rational, because you are better than they are.

Another evangelist specifically mentions ravens instead of the birds of heaven, saying: “Consider the ravens.” Naturalists report that when young ravens have been born, they are fed by their parents until, as their feathers grow black, they begin to assume their parents’ likeness. But because they are then abandoned by their parents, they are fed by God’s providence, as the Psalmist testifies:

[Col. 0682D]

“He gives their food to the cattle, and to the young ravens that call upon him” (Ps. CXL).

Hence the divine voice says to blessed Job: “Who prepares food for the raven, when its young cry out to God, plaintively crying because they have no food?” (Job XXXVIII).

If, then, God does not allow such insignificant birds, which even seem superfluous to human beings, to perish from hunger, he will in no way allow human beings, made in his image and likeness, to perish from hunger—unless perhaps, because of abundant sins, the barrenness of the earth occurs contrary to nature by God’s just judgment, as the Psalmist testifies: “I have not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his offspring seeking bread” (Ps. XXXVI). And again: “Nothing is lacking to those who fear God.”

Because the Lord had earlier forbidden anxiety, he now also prohibits excessive concern about clothing, when he adds:

[Col. 0683A]

“Which of you, by thinking, can add one cubit to his stature? And why are you anxious about clothing?”

Since it is clear to everyone that no one can add even a cubit or the smallest part of one to his stature, he who arranged all things by measure, weight, and number, just as he gave each body its measure according to his will, will also provide the necessity of clothing.

Therefore, to rebuke the excess of carnal people, he used an illustration drawn from insignificant things, saying:

“Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow; they do not labor, nor do they spin.”

[Col. 0683B]

Here he placed “the lilies of the field” for all herbs, which almighty God paints with wondrous variety without the labor of weavers: to some he gives a white color, as to lilies; to others a red color, as to roses; to others a purple color, as to violets. Yet not even Solomon in all his glory was clothed like one of these—that is, like a lily.

Although Solomon was not only exceedingly powerful but also the wisest of all kings, and although he had discoursed on all the plants of the earth, from the cedars of Lebanon to the hyssop that grows from the wall, in all his glory he could not find a kind of clothing that was white like a lily, red like a rose, and purple like a violet.

But what temporal Solomon could not find in all his glory, our spiritual Solomon—that is, our Lord Jesus Christ, who is the true peacemaker—has in his Church: a lily in virgins, a rose in martyrs, and a violet in those who practice continence.

And with a most prudent comparison the Lord rebukes human boastfulness when he adds:

[Col. 0683C]

“If, then, God so clothes the grass of the field, which is here today and tomorrow is thrown into the oven, how much more will he clothe you, O you of little faith?”

It is as though he said: If God clothes the grass of the field—that is, the herbs of the earth, which grow from an abundance of rain and dry up in the heat of the sun—with such variety and beauty, he will not allow you to perish from nakedness or cold, since he created you in his image and likeness.

But when he calls those to whom he speaks “of little faith,” he shows that faith has degrees of increase. Whoever does not believe is an unbeliever; whoever believes perfectly has right faith; but whoever believes in part and does not believe in part is of little faith. Such faith desires increase, just as the apostles said to the Lord:

[Col. 0683D]

“Lord, increase our faith” (Luke XVII).

And the centurion who had come to plead for the boy, when he heard the Lord say, “Do you believe? All things are possible to one who believes” (Mark IX), answered: “I believe, Lord; help my unbelief” (ibid.).

Having finished the comparison, he again turns his discourse to admonition, saying:

“Therefore do not be anxious, saying: What shall we eat, or what shall we drink, or with what shall we be clothed? The Gentiles seek all these things.”

By “Gentiles” he means those alien to the faith, ethnics and pagans, who do not know God and do not believe in eternal life. Therefore they are concerned only with present things: that they may have what to eat to the point of gluttony, what to drink to the point of drunkenness, and what to wear to the point of ostentation and excess.

[Col. 0684A]

For costly clothing is sought only for empty glory. Hence the Lord is rightly reported in this passage, according to another evangelist, to have said: “And do not be lifted up on high” (Luke XII).

But to us, who ought to be anxious to preserve the unity of the spirit in the bond of peace, and whose hope is in the other life, he shows where we ought to place our concern when he adds:

“For your Father knows that you need all these things.”

Our Father is the one who not only deigned to create us but also to redeem us and regenerate us through his Holy Spirit. Each day in prayer we say to him: “Our Father, who are in heaven, hallowed be your name” (Luke XI).

[Col. 0684B]

For he who created us, knowing our formation and considering our frailty, will provide food and clothing without great anxiety if he sees us being concerned for eternal life. He himself knows what we need before we ask him.

He shows, however, in what he wants us to be concerned and what we ought to ask from him when he says:

“Therefore seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you.”

He urges us to seek first—that is, chiefly—the kingdom of God and his righteousness, because before and above all things we ought to ask for, seek, love, and desire this: that we may be participants in the heavenly kingdom.

It should be noted that he did not say, “All these things will be given to you,” but “will be added,” showing that the principal good that is given is the kingdom of God and his righteousness, while all these things that will be added are necessary only in the present life—that is, food and clothing.

[Col. 0684C]

# HOMILY CXXVIII. SEVENTEENTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST

(Luke VII.) “At that time Jesus was going into a city called Nain. When he drew near the gate of the city, behold, a dead man was being carried out, the only son of his mother.” And so forth.

Jesus Christ, the mediator between God and human beings, made human for our sake, so harmonized his works in the human nature that he assumed from us that, frequently, in one and the same miracle, he might reveal himself as true God and true man.

[Col. 0684D]

This is clearly demonstrated in the sequence of the present reading, when he is first said to have been moved by compassion and then is reported to have raised the young man. For the one who is moved by compassion at the widow’s weeping is truly human; but the one who raised the young man from the dead by a mere command is without doubt truly God.

Let us see what these things signify spiritually, so that from the place where one person is raised in body, many may rise in mind.

The evangelist says: “Jesus was going into a city called Nain.” Nain is a city of Galilee, two miles distant from Mount Tabor. In our language it is interpreted as “wave” or “agitation,” and spiritually it signifies the world, which, having lost its tranquility, is in waves and agitations, as it is said through the Psalmist:

[Col. 0685A]

“You have shaken the earth, O Lord, and troubled it” (Ps. LIX).

The Lord approached as though to Nain when, having assumed our humanity, he appeared visibly to the world. Since he was about to raise the dead man, he wished not only his disciples but also a large crowd to accompany him, so that through seeing the miracle not a few but many might be called to belief in him, to faith, or to praise.

“When he drew near the gate of the city, behold, a dead man was being carried out, the only son of his mother.”

This dead man, who had been carried outside the city for burial, signifies a human being lulled into the sleep of a deadly crime. The soul dies through sin, because “the soul that sins shall itself die.”

Sin is committed in three ways: suggestion, delight, and consent. Suggestion comes through the enemy, delight through the flesh, and consent through the spirit.

[Col. 0685B]

Whoever delights in sinning in his heart lies dead, as it were, within the city. But when delight leads not only to consent but also to action, he is driven out dead, as it were, beyond the gates of the city.

For just as a human being inhabits a city, so the soul enters the body for a time, through which it can perform good or evil. We not improperly understand the gates of the city as the bodily senses: sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch. Through these gates either life or death enters our soul.

Whoever has lofty and haughty eyes, opened to desire for a woman, is driven out dead, as it were, beyond the city through the gates of his eyes. Whoever willingly opens his ears to slander, curses, and falsehoods is led out dead, as it were, through the gates of his ears.

[Col. 0685C]

Whoever, to satisfy carnal pleasure, pursues various scents through enticements is carried out dead, as it were, beyond the gates of his nostrils. Whoever speaks wickedness on high and sows discord among brothers is carried out dead, as it were, through the gates of his mouth.

Whoever has hands ready to shed blood and inflict harm upon his neighbors is dragged away dead, as it were, through the gates of his hands. To such people the Prophet says:

[Col. 0685D]

“Death has entered through your windows; it has entered your houses” (Jer. IX).

But let us despise the examples of such people and fortify the spiritual gates of our city, so that death may not enter our souls but rather life.

Let us fortify the gates of our eyes against unlawful sight, so that with the Psalmist we may be able to say: “I lifted up my eyes to the mountains” (Ps. CXX). And with blessed Job: “I made a covenant with my eyes, that I would not even think about a virgin” (Job XXXI). And with the Psalmist: “My eyes are always toward the Lord” (Ps. LXXXIV).

Let us fortify our ears, so that they may not willingly hear words of slander, cursing, falsehood, or buffoonery, so that with blessed Job we may be able to say: “With the hearing of the ear I have heard you, O Lord” (Job XLVIII). And with the Prophet: “I will hear what the Lord God speaks within me” (Ps. LXXXIV).

Let us fortify our nostrils against unlawful scents, so that, according to the Apostle, we may be “the good fragrance of Christ to God” in every place.

Let us fortify our tongue against cursing, slander, falsehood, and hateful speech, so that with the Psalmist we may be able to say:

[Col. 0686A]

“I said, I will guard my ways, that I may not sin with my tongue. I have placed a guard over my mouth” (Ps. XXXVIII).
