Let us fortify our hands against the shedding of blood and harming our neighbor, and always keep them ready to give alms and perform good works, so that with the Psalmist we may be able to say: “I will wash my hands among the innocent, and I will go around your altar, O Lord” (Ps. XXV). And with the Church: “My hands dripped with myrrh, and my fingers were full of the finest myrrh” (Song V).

Let us also guard our feet, so that they may not be swift to run into evil but rather to proclaim peace, so that what is written in Isaiah may be fulfilled in us: Blessed are the feet that carry peace. And with the Psalmist:

[Col. 0686B]

“Your word, O Lord, is a lamp to my feet” (Ps. CXVIII).

For if we guard these five senses well, we shall deserve to be raised spiritually by the Lord, and we shall be among those of whom Isaiah says: “Those who walk in their righteousness” (Isa. XXXIII), and so forth.

“And she was a widow, and a large crowd from the city was with her.”

This widow spiritually signifies the holy Church. She is called a widow because she has been deprived of the presence of her Lord and awaits his return for judgment. Of her it is written: “Blessing, I will bless her widow” (Ps. CXXXI).

This is the widow who daily appeals to the judge in the Gospel, because the Church perseveres most earnestly in prayer. Of her it is written:

[Col. 0686C]

“Do not the widow’s tears run down her cheeks, and her cry reach the one who causes them?” (Ecclus. XXXV).

The son of this widow is each believer, who dies in soul when he sins in body. The mother was weeping for her only son because the Church does not cease to mourn daily the death of her spiritual children, as the Apostle Paul did when he said: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you. I wish I could be with you now and change my voice, for I am perplexed about you” (Gal. IV). And again: “I mourn many of those who sinned previously and did not repent of the impurity they committed” (2 Cor. XII).

It often happens that many who were held in death by their own merits are raised to life through the prayers and exhortations of others. Hence it is also added:

[Col. 0686D]

“When the Lord saw her, he was moved with compassion for her and said to her: Do not weep.”

The Lord is moved to compassion by the weeping of the saints, so that he may have mercy on sinners. We learn this from the works of Moses and Elijah. One of them, interceding for the sins of the people and saying, “Either forgive them this offense, or erase me from your book which you have written,” deserved to hear: “Behold, I have been appeased; I have done according to your word” (Exod. XXXII; 2 Kings XIV). In answer to the other’s prayer, he gave rain to the earth, which he had withheld from sinners for three years.

“And he approached and touched the bier” (Luke VII).

The bier on which the dead man was being carried signifies the sinner’s conscience, made desperate by evil. A dead man is carried in a bier for burial, as it were, when a sinner, despairing because of the greatness of his crime, sins as though secure, without fear.

[Col. 0687A]

But the Lord touches the bier when, through divine grace, he softens the sinner’s hardened heart for repentance.

“Those who carried him stood still.”

Those who carried the dead man for burial signify vices and sins, such as adulteries, homicides, thefts, robberies, sacrileges, and other such things. While these succeed one another in the sinner’s actions, they carry him as though dead to burial.

But when the Lord touches the bier, those who carried it stand still, because when the sinner’s heart has been converted to repentance, the habit of sinning ceases. His actions are changed, his former iniquity is restrained, and chastity is loved in place of lust, charity in place of hatred, and sobriety in place of drunkenness.

Alternatively:

[Col. 0687B]

those who carried the dead man signify the tongues of flatterers. For flatterers throw a heap of earth over the dead, as it were, when they soothe the sinner with empty praise and flattery. But when the Lord touches the bier, those who carried it stand still, because after the sinner has been enlightened by the grace of the Holy Spirit, he begins to flee the flatteries of those who praise him, following the example of the one who says: “Let the righteous rebuke me in mercy and reprove me, but let not the oil of the sinner make my head fat” (Ps. CXL).

“And he said to him: Young man, I say to you, arise. And the dead man sat up and began to speak, and he gave him to his mother.”

The dead man rises at the divine command when the sinner comes back to life through repentance, called by the mercy of the one who says:

[Col. 0687C]

“As I live, says the Lord God, I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live” (Ezek. XVIII).

He begins to speak when he learns both to accuse his evil works and to praise God. He is returned to his mother when, through the ministry of the priest, he is reconciled to the Church, from which he had previously departed by sinning.

Frequently the abundance of divine mercy is glorified by the restoration of those whose life had previously been despaired of. Hence it is rightly added:

“Fear seized them all, and they glorified God, saying: A great prophet has arisen among us, and God has visited his people.”

The higher a person’s rank, the graver his sin. But the more he is freed by God from greater sins, the more the grace of the liberator is glorified. For the work of physicians also appears more praiseworthy the more difficult the diseases they have been able to cure.

[Col. 0687D]

We can also understand the human race allegorically through this dead man. It fell into death when it despised the commandments of life, as the Lord said: “On whatever day you eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, you shall die” (Gen. II).

The widowed mother who wept for her only son signifies the Synagogue, which in the patriarchs and prophets mourned the destruction of the human race. And because the Lord is near to all who call upon him in truth, it is rightly added:

“When the Lord saw her, he was moved with compassion for her and said to her: Do not weep.”

It is as though he said: Stop weeping for the dead man whom shortly afterward you will see rising. Do not fear death, since you have life present.

“And he approached and touched the bier.”

[Col. 0688A]

The Lord spiritually touched the bier when, having become human, he himself summoned human hearts to repentance, saying: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand” (Matt. III).

The bier is carried by four people. For before the Lord’s coming the human race was held bound in four ways: by love and fear, joy and sorrow. By love, in acquiring possessions; by fear, in guarding them; by joy, in what had been acquired; by sorrow, in what had been lost. For the one who had previously rejoiced in an abundance of possessions afterward exulted in poverty; and the one who then rejoiced in what had been acquired afterward rejoiced in what had been lost.

Those who carried the bier signify unclean spirits, which dragged the human race to the burial of death not only through the transgression of the first human being but also through many evil works. But when the Lord touches the bier, those who carried it stand still, because after human hearts have been converted to God through repentance, the power of unclean spirits ceases.

[Col. 0688B]

“And he said: Young man, I say to you, arise. And the dead man sat up and began to speak, and he gave him to his mother.”

The human race is rightly signified by the young man. For just as the body is strong and robust in youth, so in earlier times the human race flourished as though in youth: fruitful in the procreation of offspring, long-lived in the length of its life, and exceedingly abundant in possessions.

The dead man sat up when the human race returned to life. He began to speak—that is, he who had previously praised the works of his own hands began to confess God, saying with the prophet: “The Lord God has given me a learned tongue” (Isa. L). And with the Psalmist: “O Lord, open my lips” (Ps. L).

He gave him to his mother when he restored him to the Church.

[Col. 0688C]

“Fear seized them all.”

Those who were shaken by fear and astonishment signify the unclean spirits. When they saw the human race being snatched from their power through the Lord’s coming, they were so completely shaken that, speaking through a possessed man, they said: “What have we to do with you, Son of God? Have you come here before the time to torment us?” (Matt. VIII).

# HOMILY CXXIX. EIGHTEENTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST.

[Col. 0688D]

(Luke XIV) “At that time, when Jesus entered the house of a certain ruler of the Pharisees on the sabbath to eat bread.” And so forth.

Whenever we read that the Lord came to a wedding or a banquet, we must not attribute this to the allurements of gluttony, as the scribes and Pharisees did when they called him a drinker of wine and a friend of tax collectors. Rather, we must believe that he came because of a particular mystery—that is, to win souls. For just as a skilled fisherman and an experienced hunter or fowler spreads his nets in the place where he knows a multitude of fish, birds, or beasts will gather, so that some may be caught from among the many, so the Lord wished to extend the nets of his preaching in the place where more people gathered, so that some from among the many might be caught in faith. For this reason, when invited either to banquets or to weddings, he did not refuse to come.

Hence, as the present reading relates: “When Jesus entered the house of a certain ruler of the Pharisees on the sabbath to eat bread, they were watching him.” [Col. 0689A] Here it should be noted that by the word “bread” the Evangelist intended to signify everything pertaining to nourishment, because it is the usage of Scripture to signify other things by the principal element of human life, namely bread. Thus we read that it was said of Joseph’s brothers: “These men will eat bread with me today” (Genesis XLIII), although afterward they are said to have become drunk with him. Likewise, in the same Genesis we read of the Hebrew servant who was seeking a wife for his master: [Col. 0689B] “Bread was set before him” (Genesis XXIV).

When it says, “They were watching him,” this refers not to the sabbath but to the Lord himself. They were watching to see whether he would heal a man on the sabbath, perform some other deed, or utter some statement for which they could rightly rebuke him. For they were not observers of the sabbath, since they desired, if they could, to rebuke the sanctifier of the sabbath himself.

“Watching,” therefore, is used both in a good and in a bad sense. In a good sense, as when the Lord says to the Israelites: “Behold, I send my angel, who will go before you and always guard you. Therefore watch and hear his voice” (Exodus XXII). And as the Apostle says: “Watch those who walk as you have us for an example” (Philippians III)—that is, imitate those whom you see walking according to the pattern we have shown you. [Col. 0689C]

It is used in a bad sense, as the Prophet says: “The sinner watches the righteous and gnashes his teeth at him” (Psalm XXXVI), or seeks to kill him. Thus in this passage it is used not in a good but in a bad sense, when it says: “They were watching him.” They were watching him, therefore, not because they wished to imitate him, but because they wanted, if possible, to rebuke him. Watching, then, is used both in a good and in a bad sense.

“And behold, there was a certain man with dropsy before him.” Dropsy is a severe illness arising from a disorder of the bladder, with swelling from inflation and foul breath. It is characteristic of a person with dropsy that the more he drinks, the more he thirsts.

Therefore any greedy person is signified by the man with dropsy. For just as the more swollen a person with dropsy is, the more diseased he is, so the more the greedy person abounds in riches, the fuller he is of vices. [Col. 0689D] And just as the more a person with dropsy drinks, the more he thirsts, so the more the greedy person acquires the riches he desires, the more fiercely he burns to acquire them.

Someone among the wise aptly expressed this in a brief verse:

> The love of money grows as money itself grows.

And as another said:

> The miser is in need even of a penny.

For just as the entire world is a wealth of riches to the wise person, so the entire world is a field of greed to the miser: whatever he sees with his eyes, he desires in his mind and longs to possess. He counts another’s loss as his own gain, as Solomon testifies: “The greedy man will not be filled with money, nor will his soul be satisfied with good things” (Ecclesiastes IX). [Col. 0690A]

It is also not inappropriate to understand any lustful person through the man with dropsy. For just as the more a person with dropsy drinks, the more he thirsts, so the more the lustful person gives himself over to the wantonness of the flesh, the more fiercely he burns with lustful desire. Of such people the Prophet says: “Their flesh is like the flesh of asses, and their discharge like the discharge of horses” (Ezekiel XXIII). And again: “The beasts have rotted in their dung” (Joel I).

“And Jesus answered and said to the lawyers and Pharisees: Is it lawful to heal on the sabbath? But they were silent.” This response of the Lord pertains to what was said above: “They were watching him.” For he is not read to have been questioned by others here; rather, he answered their thoughts. [Col. 0690B]

With the greatest prudence the Lord hemmed in his watchers from every side, so that they could find no suitable answer. If they said, “It is lawful to heal on the sabbath,” they would be open to rebuke: why, then, were they watching to see whether he would heal a man on the sabbath? If, however, they said, “It is not lawful,” they would be challenged as to why, on the sabbath, they untied an ass or an ox from the manger and led it to drink. Thus, because they could find nothing to say, they were silent.

Nor did he hem in his critics only in this passage; he did so frequently elsewhere as well, as with the woman caught in adultery (John VIII), or concerning the payment of the denarius (Matthew XXII). He did likewise when they questioned him, saying: “Tell us, by what authority do you do these things?” (Matthew XXI). But he answered them: “You also tell me one word, and I will tell you by what authority I do these things. If you do not tell me this, neither will I tell you by what authority I do these things. Tell me: Was the baptism of John from heaven or from men?” [Col. 0690C]

They reasoned among themselves: “If we say, ‘From heaven,’ he will say to us, ‘Why then did you not accept it?’ If we say, ‘From men,’ the crowd that was baptized by John will stone us.” Therefore, having nothing to say, they fell silent.

So also here, finding no suitable answer, they were silent, and the prophecy was fulfilled which says: “The king will rejoice in God; all who swear by him will be praised, because the mouth of those who speak iniquity has been stopped” (Psalm LXII). But because the Lord frequently grants the benefit of his generosity even to the ungrateful, it is rightly added: “He took hold of him, healed him, and dismissed him.” [Col. 0690D] It was fitting that he should heal the man with dropsy in the presence of greedy men, so that while the bodily illness was healed in one person, the disease of the mind might be healed in many. The Lord rebuked their greed by a most prudent comparison when he said:

“And answering them, he said: Which of you, if his ass or ox falls into a well, will not immediately pull it out on the sabbath? And they could not answer him concerning these things.”

It was as if he said: If one of your animals falls into a well and you hasten to rescue it, not out of concern for the animal but to protect your own greed, how much more ought I to free from illness on the sabbath a human being, who is better than an animal and was made in the image of God, since it is easier to heal a human being by a word than to pull an animal from a well. [Col. 0691A]

We have already said that the greedy person is signified by the man with dropsy. The greedy person is therefore aptly compared with an animal fallen into a well, because the man with dropsy abounds in disordered fluid. When someone succumbs to the disease of greed, he falls into a well as though thirsty.

Hence the Lord also compared the woman who had been bent over for eighteen years and could not look upward (Luke XIII) to an animal being led to water. The vice of greed is therefore evil: it removes faith, destroys concord, violates charity, and generates innumerable evils. The Apostle testifies to this when he says: “The root of all evils is greed, and in pursuing it some have suffered shipwreck concerning the faith and have entangled themselves in many sorrows” (I Timothy VI). [Col. 0691B]

But a person puffed up with riches cannot enter the kingdom of heaven by the narrow and constricted way, as the Lord says: “Those who have money will enter the kingdom of heaven with difficulty. Amen, I say to you: it is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God” (Luke XVIII).

Therefore the Apostle says to Timothy: “Command the rich of this world not to be proud, nor to hope in uncertain riches, but in God, who abundantly provides all things for enjoyment.” For “those who wish to become rich fall into temptation and the snare of the devil, and into many foolish and harmful desires that plunge a person into destruction and perdition” (I Timothy VI).

The greedy person is bound by a double punishment: in this life he acquires riches unhappily and with labor, while in the future he will render an account of those same riches amid torments and sorrow. James testifies to this when he says: “Come now, rich men, weep and howl over the miseries that will come upon you. Your riches have rotted, and your garments have been eaten by moths. Your gold and silver have rusted, and their rust will be a testimony against you and will consume your flesh like fire” (James V). [Col. 0691C]

For greed lacks the inward organs of compassion; it does not know its father or acknowledge its mother; it preserves neither faith nor friendship; it does not pity a neighbor or a relative, but makes relatives as though strangers. Solomon says: “The merciful man does good to his own soul, but the greedy person even casts away his relatives” (Proverbs XI).

“He also spoke a parable to those who had been invited, observing how they chose the first places at table, saying to them: When you are invited to a wedding, do not recline in the first place.” [Col. 0691D]

As far as the literal meaning is concerned, he orders the life and conduct of a prudent and educated man, since it is an exceedingly honorable way of living at banquets, weddings, or other gatherings for the faithful to prefer one another and anticipate one another in honor, as the Apostle Peter commands when he says: “All of you clothe yourselves with humility toward one another” (I Peter V).

For just as it is an honor to be called to a higher place, so it is a disgrace when someone who has imprudently taken the first place is sent back to the last. “It is better,” Solomon says, “that it be said to you, ‘Come up higher,’ than that you be humbled before a ruler” (Proverbs XXV). And again: “Do not seek what is too high for you, and do not investigate what is too strong for you” (Ecclesiasticus III). And again: “You have sat at a great table” (Ecclesiasticus XXXI), and so forth. And again: “Disgrace follows the proud” (Proverbs XIX). [Col. 0692A]

Spiritually, however, it is most customary in Scripture for the union of Christ and the Church to be called a wedding, as in the Gospel: “The kingdom of heaven is like a king who made a wedding for his son” (Matthew XXII).

At a wedding two persons are joined: the bridegroom and the bride. The bridegroom, therefore, is Christ, of whom John says: “He who has the bride is the bridegroom” (John III). The bride is the holy Church, to whom the Prophet says: “I will espouse you to myself in righteousness and truth” (Hosea II).

The bridal chamber of this bridegroom was the womb of the Virgin, as the Psalmist says: “Like a bridegroom coming forth from his bridal chamber” (Psalm XVIII). [Col. 0692B] The apostles were the celebrants of this wedding, concerning whom it is written: “The sons of the bridegroom cannot fast as long as the bridegroom is with them” (Matthew IX).

At this wedding, therefore, the person reclines happily who, called in faith, lives humbly, piously, and justly in the Church. It is rightly said: “Do not recline in the first place.” The last place pertains to humility of mind. Spiritually, therefore, the person reclines in the last place who judges himself in his mind to be lower and less worthy than everyone else, considering that there are many not only holier but also wiser than he.

Hence it is added: “Lest perhaps someone more honorable than you has been invited by him, and he who invited you both comes and says to you: Give this man your place.” Often, through pride of mind, someone descends from a higher rank to a lower one, because when he is swollen and inflated in mind, he is allowed to fall either into the wantonness of the flesh or into some crime by which he is censured by others. [Col. 0692C]

Hence it is also added: “And then you begin with shame to take the lowest place.” This happened to Saul, to whom the Lord said when he had become proud: “Were you not little in your own eyes when I made you head over the tribes of Israel? But now, because you have exalted yourself, I have cast you down so that you may not be king” (I Samuel XV).

But after he had forbidden what should not be done, the merciful Redeemer took care to reveal what ought to be done, when he added:

“But when you are invited, go and recline in the last place, so that when he who invited you comes, he may say to you: Friend, come up higher.” [Col. 0692D]

When he finds someone humble, he blesses him with the name “friend” and calls him to ascend higher, because, as the Apostle Peter says: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (I Peter V).

He fittingly added: “Then you will have glory before those who recline with you,” so that you may not begin to seek it now in the present. For Solomon says that an inheritance “to which one hastens at the beginning will lack blessing at the end” (Proverbs XX).

Explaining what he had proposed in the comparison, the Lord added:

“Because everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.”

Here it should be noted that he did not simply say, “Whoever humbles himself will be exalted,” but added: “Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.” [Col. 0693A]

Some are exalted both in this age and in the age to come, such as David, Hezekiah, Josiah, and others like them, who were glorious in the present age and will be more glorious in the future. Others are humbled here and in the future, such as proud poor people and those who receive punishment for their sins in the present life and pass into eternal punishment in the future, such as Herod, Antiochus, and many others like them, concerning whom it is written: “Crush them, Lord, with a double crushing” (Jeremiah XVII).

Some are exalted here and humbled in the future, such as proud rich people who, in the words of Scripture, “spend their days in prosperity, and in a moment descend to the underworld” (Job XXI). Others are humbled here but exalted in the future, such as the holy poor, and especially those who abandon everything they possess for God and humble themselves through voluntary poverty, so that they may deserve to be exalted in the future. [Col. 0693B]

Let us therefore love the virtue of humility in the present life, so that we may deserve to be exalted by the Lord in the life to come, following the footsteps of him who says: “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart, and you will find rest for your souls” (Matthew XI).

He is called “humble” as though inclined toward the ground. The person is therefore truly known to be humble who continually considers himself to be earth and ashes, saying with the blessed patriarch Abraham: “I will speak to my Lord, although I am dust and ashes” (Genesis XVIII).

Humility must be preserved not only in the body but also in the mind, following the example of the one who, though established upon a royal throne, said: “I have been humbled exceedingly, Lord; give me life according to your word” (Psalm CXVIII). [Col. 0693C]

Humility is indeed the teacher of wisdom, as the Prophet testifies when he says: “It is good for me, Lord, that you have humbled me, so that I may learn your statutes” (ibid.). For the more humble each person is here for God’s sake, the more exalted he will be in the future, as the Apostle Peter testifies: “Humble yourselves under the powerful hand of God, so that he may exalt you at the time of visitation” (I Peter V).

## HOMILY CXXX. WEDNESDAY OF THE FOUR EMBER DAYS

(Mark IX) “At that time, one of the crowd answered and said to Jesus: Teacher, I brought my son to you, who has a mute spirit; and wherever it seizes him, it dashes him down.” And so forth. [Col. 0693D]

It should be noted that places always correspond to events. On the mountain the Lord prays and, transfigured, reveals to his disciples the mysteries of his majesty. Descending to the lower regions, he is met by the crowd and assailed by the weeping of the wretched. Above, he opens to his disciples the mysteries of the heavenly kingdom; below, he reproaches the crowds for the sins of unbelief. Above, he discloses the Father’s voice to those capable of receiving it; below, he drives the evil spirit from those who are tormented.

Even now, according to the quality of their merits, he does not cease either to ascend for some or to descend for others. For he strengthens, teaches, and chastises those who are still carnal and beginners, as though they were seeking the lower regions. But he glorifies the perfect, whose citizenship is in heaven, by raising them more sublimely; he instructs them more freely concerning eternal things; and he often teaches them what the crowds are not even able to hear. [Col. 0694A]

Mark records that this demoniac, whom the Lord healed as he descended from the mountain, was deaf and mute, whereas Matthew says that he was moon-struck. He signifies those of whom it is written: “Fools change like the moon” (Ecclesiasticus XXVII). They never remain in the same condition; now changed into one vice, now into another, they increase and decrease.

They are mute because they do not confess the faith; deaf because they do not hear even to some degree the word of truth. They foam when they waste away in folly. It belongs to fools, the feeble, and the dull to let saliva foam from their mouths. They gnash their teeth when they blaze with the fury of anger, and, strengthened by no discipline of virtue, live without vigor.

When it says, “I told your disciples to cast him out, and they could not,” he openly accuses the apostles, since the inability to heal sometimes relates not to the weakness of those who heal but to the faith of those who are to be healed, as the Lord says: “Let it be done for you according to your faith” (Matthew IX). [Col. 0694B]

“He answered and said to them: O unbelieving generation, how long shall I be with you? How long shall I endure you?” The gentle and meek one did not say this because he had been overcome by weariness. He did not open his mouth like a lamb before its shearer, nor did he burst into words of anger. Rather, it was as though a physician, seeing a sick person act against his prescriptions, might say: How long shall I come to your house? How long shall I waste the skill of my art, when I command one thing and you do another?

He was not angry with the man but with the vice. Through one man he rebuked the Jews for their unbelief, so that he immediately added: “Bring him to me. And they brought him. When he saw him, the spirit immediately convulsed him, and he fell to the ground and rolled about, foaming.” [Col. 0694C]

When the boy was brought to the Lord, the spirit convulsed him and dashed him down, because often, when we strive to turn toward God, we are struck by the ancient enemy with greater and new ambushes. The cunning adversary does this either to inspire hatred of virtue or to avenge the injury of his expulsion.

This is why—passing from the particular to the general—at the beginning of the holy Church he inflicted as many most grievous conflicts of persecution as he grieved that losses of souls had suddenly been brought upon his kingdom.

“And he asked his father: How long has this been happening to him? He said: From childhood. And often he has thrown him into fire and water, to destroy him.” [Col. 0694D]

Let Julian blush, since he dares to say that all human beings are born in the flesh without any contagion of sin, entirely as innocent as Adam was when he was created. What did this boy possess that he should have been tormented so severely by a demon from childhood, if he was held by no bond of original sin, when it is clear that he could not yet have committed any personal sin?

Let the Catholic confess that no one is born free from the guilt of the first transgression, and let him invoke the grace of God, by which he may be delivered from the body of death through Jesus Christ our Lord.

Let the learned scribe understand that in this demoniac healed by the Lord the salvation of all believers is signified: they come into the world bound by the guilt of original sin, to be saved by the faith and grace of the one Redeemer, Jesus Christ. [Col. 0695A]

When it is said, “He often threw him into fire and water,” this signifies the greatest crimes of human madness. The burning of fire is to be referred to the heat of anger; water, to the pleasures of the flesh, which commonly dissolve the mind through indulgence. Or certainly the demoniac is cast into the fire in which the hearts of adulterers are inflamed, and into the waters that commonly extinguish charity.

“But if you can do anything, help us and have mercy on us. Jesus said to him: If you can believe, all things are possible to the one who believes.”

The Lord gave the penitent an appropriate answer. He said, “If you can do anything, help us,” and the Lord replied, “If you can believe, I can help you in my mercy,” because unfeigned faith deserves to obtain everything it asks for beneficially. [Col. 0695B]

By contrast, the leper who faithfully cried out, “Lord, if you will, you can cleanse me,” received an answer suited to his faith: “I will; be cleansed” (Matthew VIII).

“And immediately the father of the boy cried out with tears and said: I believe, Lord; help my unbelief.”

No one suddenly becomes perfect. In a good way of life each person begins with small things, so as to reach great ones. The beginnings of virtue are one thing, progress another, and perfection another.

If faith itself were not led toward its perfection by certain stages, this man, when asked whether he believed, would not have answered: “I believe, Lord; help my unbelief.” If he believed, why did he speak of unbelief? [Col. 0695C] But if he knew that he possessed unbelief, how did he believe? Because through the hidden inspiration of grace faith grows according to the stages of one’s merits, at one and the same time the man who had not yet believed perfectly both believed and was unbelieving.

“When Jesus saw the crowd running together, he rebuked the unclean spirit, saying to it: Deaf and mute spirit, I command you: come out of him, and do not enter him again.”

The Lord’s rebuke is the divine power of command. He did not rebuke the boy who suffered the violence, but the demon who inflicted it. For one who desires to correct a sinner must indeed drive out the vice by rebuking and condemning it, but restore the person by loving him.

The Lord rightly commands the unclean spirit, which he drives from the man, not to enter him again, because the person is truly freed from demonic domination who avoids returning through evil living to the sins from which he was once cleansed by repentance. [Col. 0695D]

“And crying out and convulsing him violently, it came out of him.” As the unclean spirit was about to leave the man, it convulsed him and terrified those watching with a furious cry. For often, when the devil is expelled from the heart, he produces sharper temptations in it than he had previously aroused when he possessed it undisturbed.

“And he became like a dead man, so that many said that he was dead. But Jesus, taking him by the hand, raised him, and he arose.” The impious enemy, compelled to flee, had thrown down the one whom he had already been forced to abandon and made him appear dead; the merciful Savior raised him by the gentle touch of his right hand. [Col. 0696A]

Just as he showed himself to be truly God through the power of saving, so he also demonstrated through human touch that he truly possessed a bodily nature. For the madman Manichaeus denies that he was genuinely clothed in flesh. But when the Lord raised, cleansed, and enlightened so many sick people by his touch, he condemned that heresy even before it was born.

“When he had entered the house, his disciples asked him privately: Why could we not cast it out? And he said to them: This kind can go out by nothing except prayer and fasting.”

While teaching the apostles how the most wicked demon should be expelled, he instructed everyone for life, so that we may know that the more serious sins, or the temptations of unclean spirits, must be overcome by fasts and prayers. [Col. 0696B] The Lord’s anger also, when it has been kindled in punishment for our crimes, can be appeased by this singular remedy.

Fasting in general means abstaining not only from food but from every enticement of the flesh; indeed, it means restraining oneself from every passion of the vices. Likewise, prayer in general consists not only in the words by which we invoke divine mercy, but also in everything we do in faithful devotion for the service of our Creator, as the Apostle testifies: “Rejoice always; pray without ceasing” (I Thessalonians V).

For how can anyone invoke God with words at every hour and moment without ceasing, when he must also have time to eat or sleep? We pray without ceasing when we perform only those works that commend us to the piety of our Creator. [Col. 0696C] By this fasting and prayer, with the Lord’s help, we shall conquer and repel all the ambushes of the ancient enemy.

## HOMILY CXXXI. FRIDAY OF THE FOUR EMBER DAYS

(Luke XVIII) “At that time Jesus told his disciples this parable. And so forth.” The Apostle also says: “Rejoice always; pray without ceasing” (I Thessalonians V). [Col. 0696D]

Who can always pray without failing, or persist in prayers without interruption, so that he has no time either to eat or to sleep? Either, then, we must say that the person always prays and does not grow weary who, at the canonical hours each day, according to the rite of ecclesiastical tradition, does not cease to praise and beseech the Lord with the customary psalms and prayers. This is what the Psalmist says: “I will bless the Lord at all times; his praise shall always be in my mouth” (Psalm XXXIII).

Or certainly everything that a righteous person does according to God is to be counted as prayer. Since the righteous person acts justly without ceasing, he therefore prays without ceasing and never stops praying unless he ceases to be righteous.

“There was a certain judge in a certain city who did not fear God and did not respect human beings. There was also a certain widow in that city, and she came to him, saying: Vindicate me against my adversary. And for a long time he was unwilling. But afterward he said to himself: Although I do not fear God or respect human beings, nevertheless, because this widow is troublesome to me, I will vindicate her, lest, by coming at last, she wear me out.” [Col. 0697A]

The Lord presents parables either according to some likeness, as in the case of the man who had two sons, the elder near him in the field and the younger living dissolutely in a distant land; or he proves something from the very unlikeness, as in the saying: “If God so clothes the grass of the field, which is here today and tomorrow is thrown into the oven, how much more will he clothe you, O you of little faith?” (Matthew VI).

Thus the first kind may be joined to these words: “As this is, so is that.” The second kind may be expressed in the words: “If this, how much more that?” Or: “If this, how much less that?” Sometimes these matters are presented obscurely, sometimes openly.

Here, therefore, the unjust judge is introduced not by likeness but by unlikeness. That unjust judge in no way allegorically represents God. Nevertheless, the Lord wished it to be recognized from this that God, who is good and just, cares for those who entreat him, since not even an unjust human being can despise those who weary him with continual prayers, at least in order to avoid their trouble. For this is what he says: “Lest, by coming at last, she wear me out.” [Col. 0697B]

The widow herself may have a likeness to the Church, which appears desolate until the Lord comes, although even in secret he cares for her.

“But the Lord said: Hear what the unjust judge says. Will God not vindicate his elect, who cry to him day and night, and will he have patience concerning them? I tell you that he will quickly vindicate them.” [Col. 0697C]

If anyone is troubled by the fact that God’s elect are said to pray for vengeance—something John also says in the Apocalypse concerning the martyrs—although we are most clearly instructed to pray for our enemies and persecutors, it should be understood that the vengeance of the righteous is that all the wicked may perish.

They perish in two ways: either by conversion to righteousness or by losing through punishment the power by which they now act against the good, for as long as it is expedient for the good, they possess some temporary power. Although the righteous pray for their enemies, they are not absurdly said to desire vengeance, since they desire this end.

“Nevertheless, when the Son of Man comes, do you think he will find faith on earth?” [Col. 0697D]

Although the almighty Creator is always ready to vindicate his elect when they cry to him, nevertheless, on the day of judgment—which must be held in mind with trembling—when that same Creator appears in the form of the Son of Man, there will be such a scarcity of the elect that the ruin of the whole world will already be hastened, not so much because of the cry of the faithful unjustly condemned.

When the Lord says, as though doubtfully, “Do you think he will find faith on earth?” he is not doubting but rebuking. By the word of doubt, unbelief is reproved; divinity is not expressing an opinion.

We too sometimes use a word of doubt in rebuke concerning matters we hold as certain, although we do not doubt in our hearts. For example, if you are angry with your servant, you may say: “Do you despise me? Consider that perhaps I am your master.” And the Apostle says to certain people who despised him: “I think that I too have the Spirit of God” (I Corinthians VII). [Col. 0698A]

The one who says “I think” appears to doubt, but he was rebuking, not doubting. So also the Lord knows all things, through whom all things were made, and yet by seeming to doubt he rebukes the hearts of unbelievers.

## HOMILY CXXXII. SATURDAY OF THE FOUR EMBER DAYS

(Luke XIII) “At that time Jesus told the crowds this parable: A certain man had a fig tree planted in his vineyard.” And so forth.

This fig tree can indeed signify the nature of the human race: by the vineyard, the human race; by the fig tree, the teachers or rulers of this world. It was rightly planted—that is, it was created according to the likeness of its author. But it refused to give its master fruit for three years, because before the Law, under the Law, and under grace it disdained to obey. [Col. 0698B]

If, however, you look back to what was said above, you will recognize that by the vineyard the people of the Jews are signified, and by the fig tree the scribes and Pharisees. Although the figure applies generally to all, it bears especially the type of the Synagogue.

For after that fearful and dreadful sentence had been given—“Unless you repent, you will all likewise perish” (Luke XIII)—he immediately added the parable of the fruitless tree, clearly teaching that those to whom he spoke, like a fruitless fig tree, would be cut down if they did not repent.

“The vineyard of the Lord Sabaoth is the house of Israel,” as we are taught in Isaiah’s song (Isaiah V). The Synagogue, established within that same house, is the fig tree in the vineyard. But the one who permitted his vineyard to be plundered by passers-by also commanded that the fig tree be cut down. [Col. 0698C]

“And he came seeking fruit on it, and found none.” What he had instituted for the Synagogue to follow through Moses, the Lord revealed after being born in the flesh. Teaching frequently in the Synagogue, he sought the fruit of faith but did not find it in the minds of the Pharisees.

“And he said to the vinedresser: Behold, for three years I have come seeking fruit on this fig tree, and I find none.”

The order of the apostles and teachers is expressed by the vinedresser, through whose prayers and admonitions continual care is offered to the people of God. For the Lord frequently complained to them about the fruitless Jewish people, because during the three years of his visitation—that is, in the legal decrees, the prophetic testimonies, and the very grace of the radiant Gospel—it had remained negligent. [Col. 0698D]

“Cut it down, then; why should it also occupy the ground?”

The Jewish people were cut down not by the apostles but by the Romans, and were expelled from the promised land. “Cut it down,” he says—that is, by urging repentance, announce to it the calamity of the cutting down that is to come.

By a just judgment it lost both the land and the kingdom, for the sake of which it did not fear to persecute the citizens of heaven and to kill the King of heaven and earth himself, saying through its chief priests and Pharisees: “If we let him go on like this, everyone will believe in him, and the Romans will come and take away our place and our nation” (John XI).

The crowd of the Jewish people may also be figured by the earth occupied by the sterile fig tree. It has been pressed down by the harmful shadow of its rulers, so that it cannot receive the light of truth; and, lest it be warmed by the sun of heavenly love, it has been obstructed by the example of their perversity. Thus the Savior says to them elsewhere: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who shut the kingdom of heaven before men. For you yourselves do not enter, nor do you allow those entering to enter” (Matthew XXIII). [Col. 0699A]

“But he answered and said to him: Lord, let it alone this year also, until I dig around it.”

This is the voice of the apostles, who after the Lord’s Passion prayed most earnestly for the Jews, lest they suffer the vengeance of the Lord’s cross without repentance.

“Until I dig around it,” he says—that is, until I humble the root of the fruitless mind with the double-edged hoe of correction, inflicting the horror of present afflictions and the threat of eternal damnation. [Col. 0699B]

Every trench is at the bottom, and certainly rebuke, when it shows the mind its own condition, humbles it.

“And I will spread manure.” That is, I will bring back to the mind the abomination of the evils it has committed, so that I may raise up the grace of compunction as though from the rottenness of manure.

“And if indeed it bears fruit—but if not, in the future you shall cut it down.”

When he said, “And if indeed it bears fruit,” he added nothing, but suspended the sentence. When he added, “But if not,” he immediately attached the judgment of future condemnation, saying: “In the future you shall cut it down.” [Col. 0699C]

For the Lord saw that the Synagogue was much more inclined to deny than to confess. Hence elsewhere, acting through events according to the same figure that he expresses here in words, he condemned the fruitless fig tree to eternal sterility, showing that even if the apostles should dig around it by correcting it, and even if they should bring manure by reproaching it for its sins, it would nevertheless not be filled with the fruit of repentance, but would be removed by the strict severity of the double-edged axe.

“Now he was teaching in the synagogue of the Jews on the sabbaths. And behold, there was a woman who had a spirit of infirmity for eighteen years.” After the parable of the fig tree has been recounted, the Lord is said to have taught in the synagogue, so that it may be made clear that the parable points to nothing else but this: he sought fruit in the fig tree and did not find it; he was offering the word to the synagogue, but it was not received. Yet, lest you should think that it was to be completely uprooted because of the guilt of its barrenness, but might know that its remnants were to be saved through the election of grace, immediately thereafter, in the same place, the healing of the primitive Church follows under the figure of the bent woman. She had properly been bent over for eighteen years, a number completed by six multiplied three times, because it shows that she languished in feeble works during the witness of the Law, the prophecy of the Prophets, and the revelation of grace. For the number six, in which the creation of the world was perfected, signifies the perfection of works. There are three periods, as I have said, of the Lord’s visitation, during which Judaea, which had known how to perform earthly rather than heavenly deeds, was bent away from the uprightness of its mind, as though for eighteen years. “And she was bent over and could not look upward at all.” Since she was earthly in her understanding and sought what was below, she did not yet know how to contemplate heavenly things, hearing through the Prophet: “If you are willing and listen to me, you shall eat the good things of the earth” (Isaiah 1). In contrast, the Apostle says to the members of the Church: “Set your minds on the things that are above, not on those that are upon the earth” (Colossians 3).

“Jesus, when he saw her, called her to himself and said to her: ‘Woman, you are released from your infirmity.’ And he laid his hands upon her, and immediately she was straightened, and she glorified God.” He saw her by predestining through grace; he called her by enlightening through teaching; he laid his hands upon her by assisting with spiritual gifts; he raised her up to glorify God in good works, advancing her to firm faith. “Those whom he predestined,” he says, “he also called; and those whom he called, he also justified; and those whom he justified, he also glorified” (Romans 8).

[Col. 0700B] “But the ruler of the synagogue, indignant because Jesus had healed on the sabbath, answered and said to the crowd: ‘There are six days on which one ought to work. On those days, therefore, come and be healed, and not on the sabbath day.’” Jesus healed on the sabbath, showing that the time had already come for the day to dawn according to the prophecy of the Song of Songs and for the shadows to be removed (Song of Songs 2). But the ruler of the synagogue knew neither this nor that far more excellent mystery which the Lord indicated by healing on the sabbath: namely, that after the six ages of this world he would grant the perpetual joys of immortal life. As a figure of this, Moses commanded that on the sabbath one should abstain not from good activity but from servile—that is, harmful—action, prefiguring that time when our worldly works would cease, but not our religious works, that is, the deeds by which we praise God. The ruler of the synagogue is therefore mistaken and causes others to be mistaken, because in the sabbath the Law prohibited not healing a person but carrying burdens, that is, being weighed down by sins.

“But the Lord answered them and said: ‘Hypocrites, does not each one of you on the sabbath untie his ox or his donkey from the manger and lead it away to drink?’” He certainly reproves the unbelief of the leaders of the Synagogue and rightly marks them with the name hypocrites, that is, pretenders. Although they sought to be teachers of the people, they were ashamed to place the healing of a human being below care for livestock. But in a deeper sense, by the terms “ox” and “donkey” he signifies the Jew and the Greek, concerning whose calling it is written: “The ox knows its owner, and the donkey its master’s manger” (Isaiah 1). Both, released from the bonds of sin, laid aside their thirst and the heat of this world by drinking from the Lord’s fountain.

[Col. 0700D] “And ought not this daughter of Abraham, whom Satan has bound—behold, for eighteen years—to be released from this bond on the sabbath day?” Every faithful soul is a daughter of Abraham. The Church is a daughter of Abraham, gathered from both peoples into the unity of faith; when the time of the Law and of the Lord’s resurrection had been fulfilled, she broke free through the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit from the bond of a long captivity. Perhaps, in this way also, the mystery of the sabbath of eighteen years can appropriately be understood. Mystically, therefore, to lead an ox or a donkey, released from the manger, to drink is the same as raising Abraham’s daughter from the bond of a harmful inclination: namely, to release the Church, gathered from Jews and Gentiles, from the snares of sins through the water of baptism and to raise her up to hope for heavenly things.

It should certainly be noted that a most wicked heresy attempts, from the fact that the Lord says this to one bound by Satan, to maintain that bodily illnesses belong not to the Lord as their author but rather to the devil—as though, although the devil always has the desire to harm, he could harm anyone unless he received power from the Almighty. For what else is declared not only in the book of blessed Job—which that heresy, along with the other books of the Old Testament and with God himself who gave them, spews out like a madman as though he were a malicious ruler of the world—but also in the Gospel, where we read that the demons could not even enter the pigs unless he himself granted them permission (Matthew 8)?

# HOMILY CXXXIII. THE NINETEENTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST

## (MATTHEW 22)

“At that time: The Sadducees, who say that there is no resurrection, approached Jesus.” And so forth. While our Lord Jesus Christ was preaching, there were two principal heresies among the Jews: one of the Sadducees and the other of the Pharisees. The Sadducees were so called because they followed a certain teacher of the Law named Sadducus; they believed neither in the resurrection nor that angels or spirits existed. Accepting only the five books of Moses, they rejected the prophetic oracles. In contrast were the Pharisees, whose name is interpreted as “separated,” because they separated themselves from the others in certain observances. They believed in the resurrection of bodies, confessed that angels and spirits existed, and accepted not only the five books of Moses but also the prophetic oracles. The Sadducees, therefore, in order to be able to deny the truth of the resurrection, devised a shameful story about a woman who had had seven brothers.

“And so they questioned him, saying: ‘Teacher, Moses said’ (Deuteronomy 25): ‘If someone dies without having a son, his brother is to marry his wife, so that he may raise up offspring for his brother. Now there were seven brothers among us, and the first, having taken a wife, died; and, having no offspring, left his wife to his brother. Likewise the second and the third, up to the seventh. Last of all, the woman also died. In the resurrection, therefore, whose wife of the seven will she be? For they all had her.’”

In these words it is clear that they showed themselves incapable of understanding correctly not only in a spiritual sense but even according to the letter. It could perhaps happen through some misfortune that, among the same people who had departed from observance of the Law, seven brothers had one wife; but Moses did not command this in the Law. For although he gave a law concerning the first and the second, and remained silent about the others, he certainly did not order seven brothers to have one wife. This command, however, is to be understood spiritually rather than carnally.

For our brother is the Lord Jesus Christ, who, although by his divinity he is our Creator and Lord, deigned by his humanity to become our brother, as he himself says in the Gospel: “Whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven is my brother, sister, and mother” (Matthew 12). And through the Prophet: “I will proclaim your name to my brothers; in the midst of the Church I will praise you” (Psalm 21). His wife is the holy Church, to whom he says through the Prophet: “I will espouse you to myself in righteousness and truth” (Hosea 2). Concerning her it is said through John in the Apocalypse: “I saw the holy city, the new Jerusalem, descending from heaven, like a bride adorned for her husband” (Revelation 21).

He died without children because, before his Passion, he spiritually begot only a few Jews as children for God through his preaching and good example. He also gives the firstborn the name of the brother, because we are called Christians from Christ, so that teachers may understand that those whom they beget through preaching do not belong properly to them but to God. But because the Sadducees did not understand the Scriptures spiritually, they wished to deny the resurrection. Therefore they appropriately heard from the Lord:

“You are mistaken, knowing neither the Scriptures nor the power of God.” Since they were ignorant of the meaning of the Scriptures, they consequently had no knowledge of Christ, who is the power and wisdom of God. But what we ought to believe or think concerning the resurrection he makes clear when he says: “For in the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like the angels of God in heaven.” In these words, the propriety of the Latin language does not agree with Greek usage. Among the Latins, women are properly said *nubere*—to marry—and men are said to have wives. But here we follow the propriety of the Greek expression when we say, “They will not marry,” namely, the men, “nor will they be given in marriage,” namely, the wives. Therefore, in the resurrection men will not marry, nor will wives be given in marriage. They will indeed have true bodies, which can be given in marriage and marry, but they will be immortal and free from weakness, and therefore not only removed from pollution but also from every kind of corruption. What those who are judged worthy in this world will be like, he makes clear by saying: “But they will be like the angels of God in heaven,” that is, having become immortal:

“Concerning the resurrection of the dead, have you not read what was spoken by God, who said to you: ‘I am the God of Abraham and the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob’?” To prove the truth of the resurrection, the Lord could have brought forward many clearer testimonies from the prophetic oracles, including this one: “Wait for me, says the Lord, for the day of my resurrection in the future” (Zephaniah 3). Again, in Hosea: “He will revive us after two days, and we shall live in his sight” (Hosea 6). And in Daniel: “Many from the dust of the earth will rise, some to everlasting life and others to everlasting disgrace” (Daniel 12). And the Psalmist: “I slept and was overcome with sleep, and I arose, because the Lord received me” (Psalm 3).

But, as was said above, since the Sadducees, with whom he was discussing the resurrection, did not accept the prophetic oracles, it would have been pointless to produce testimonies from books that they did not accept. If we consider this carefully, we recognize that this testimony evidently pertains to the resurrection. For when the Lord spoke these words to Moses approximately four hundred years after Abraham’s death, he did not say, “I was the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob,” but “I am,” showing that their souls had not perished together with their bodies, as the Sadducees thought, but lived and existed. Hence it is added: “He is not the God of the dead but of the living.” He could not be their God if they did not continue to exist.

[Col. 0703A] “And when the crowds heard this, they marveled at his teaching. But the Pharisees, hearing that he had silenced the Sadducees, gathered together.” Although the wicked disagree among themselves, they often unite in the oppression of the good, as we read about Herod and Pilate: although they had been enemies of one another, they became friends in the Lord’s Passion (Luke 23). In the same way, the Sadducees and Pharisees, two Jewish heresies, although they held different opinions among themselves, came together with one mind to slander the Lord. The Pharisees were distressed that the Sadducees had been defeated by the Lord while the crowds marveled and rejoiced; if they themselves had defeated them, they would certainly have rejoiced. Thus, driven by envy, they gathered together.

“And one of them, a lawyer, questioning him in order to test him, said: ‘Teacher, which is the great commandment in the Law?’” One questioned him on behalf of all. That he questioned him in order to test him is shown by his very words, when he says, “Teacher.” For if he had truly been asking a question, he would have called him Lord rather than teacher.

From this question we understand that at that time a serious controversy had arisen among the Jews, who were disputing over the precept of the Law, some preferring one commandment and others another. Some said that circumcision was the better commandment; others thought observance of the sabbath more important; others preferred the offering of sacrifices and victims; and others wanted to place the Calends and festivals first. The Pharisee therefore asked the Lord which was the great commandment in the Law, so that, by naming one as great, he might appear to disparage the other commandments and thereby incur the hostility of those who wished to praise another commandment of the Law.

But the Lord so tempered his answer that he showed which was the great commandment while remaining beyond reproach. He said:

“You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind. For this is the greatest and first commandment.”

The love of God is therefore called the greatest and first commandment, not so much in order as in dignity. For it is the usage of Scripture to call “first” what is better, just as the Israelite people were commanded to offer the firstfruits of gold and silver—that is, what was most precious among the gold and silver. The Prophet Jeremiah also says concerning the same people: “Israel was holy to the Lord, the firstfruits of his harvest” (Jeremiah 2).

The greatest and first commandment, therefore, is love, because it holds primacy in both the New and the Old Testament, as the Apostle Paul says: “Faith, hope, and love remain, these three; but the greatest of these is love” (1 Corinthians 13). The Pharisee’s question is beneficial for us, to whom it is said: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind.”

Here we must consider that no measure is set upon the love of God, since we are commanded to love him with our whole heart, whole soul, and whole mind. Because God is immeasurable, he must be loved without measure, so that when we love him greatly, we acknowledge that we love him little; no place should remain empty within us that is not filled with the love of God, but mind, tongue, and hand should resound with his love. Yet because no one can love God perfectly unless he also loves his neighbor, he rightly adds:

“And the second is like it: You shall love your neighbor as yourself.”

We ought therefore to love God more than ourselves, and our neighbor as ourselves: that is, just as we wish our own needs to be assisted, so let us assist our neighbor; just as we wish compassion to be shown toward our weakness, so let us show compassion toward our neighbor; and just as we wish to attain eternal life, so let us desire that our neighbor attain it with us.

This is to love one’s neighbor as oneself: for God is then loved when love for him is seasoned by love of one’s neighbor. In vain does someone claim to love God if he does not love his neighbor. Hence it is read through the Apostle John: “If someone says, ‘I love God,’ and hates his brother, he is a liar” (1 John 4). And again: “Whoever does not love his brother whom he sees, how can he love God whom he does not see? And we have this commandment from God: whoever loves God must also love his brother” (ibid.).

Just as a bird cannot raise itself to the heights without two wings, so we cannot reach the perfection of true love unless we preserve the twofold love, namely, of God and of our neighbor. Hence it is commanded that scarlet wool dyed twice be placed in the priest’s vestment, so that in our good work the love of God and of our neighbor may be joined. The Lord confirms this when he adds:

“On these two commandments hang all the Law and the Prophets.”

If someone does not have time to read all the books, let him hold fast to love of God and neighbor, and he has fulfilled everything, as the Apostle testifies when he says: “Whoever loves his neighbor has fulfilled the Law. For: ‘You shall not commit adultery; you shall not steal; you shall not kill; you shall not bear false witness; you shall not covet your neighbor’s wife’; and if there is any other commandment, it is summed up in this word: ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself’” (Romans 13). And again: “Love is the fullness of the Law” (ibid.).

The commandment of love is broad and brief: broad in the performance of works, as the Psalmist says: “Your commandment is exceedingly broad” (Psalm 118); brief in the formulation of its words, as in this passage: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.” As the Prophet says: “The Lord will make a brief word upon the earth” (Isaiah 10).

There are therefore two things to be observed concerning love. First, that one harm no one; second, that one bestow the good things one is able to give. For he who said, “What you do not want done to you, do not do to another” (Tobit 4), says elsewhere: “Whatever you wish that human beings would do to you, do likewise to them” (Matthew 7).

Just as many branches of a tree emerge from one lowly root, so the other virtues are produced from love of God and neighbor. But the one who does not possess the root of love boasts in vain of having the branches of good works. The Lord shows this when he says: “To everyone who has, more will be given, and he will abound; but from the one who does not have, even what he seems to have will be taken away” (Luke 19). For the one who has love will have the other virtues added to him; but the one who does not have it boasts in vain of almsgiving, abstinence, and vigils. The Apostle testifies: “If I speak in the tongues of human beings and of angels, but do not have love, I have become like sounding brass or a clanging cymbal. And if I have prophecy” (1 Corinthians 13), and so forth.

The Lord praises this love in the Gospel, saying to his disciples: “By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (John 13). And again: “I give you a new commandment, that you love one another” (ibid.). Do you wish to know what this means? Hear the Apostle John saying: “God is love, and whoever remains in love remains in God, and God remains in him” (1 John 4).

[Col. 0705B] “When the Pharisees had gathered together, Jesus questioned them, saying: ‘What do you think concerning the Christ? Whose son is he?’” And so forth. When the Lord says elsewhere, “Do not give what is holy to dogs, and do not throw your pearls before pigs” (Matthew 7), what is the meaning of his teaching the Jews, who were tearing him apart with their questions, those things that are just and holy?

The answer is that he did not give what was holy to dogs, nor throw his pearls before pigs; rather, he disclosed his preaching to everyone because there were people in the crowd who would believe through his preaching. He did this so that those who were to believe would have something to believe, while those who refused to believe would be without excuse. But while the Pharisees were going astray through various questions, the Lord asked them what concerned faith and salvation, saying: “What do you think concerning the Christ? Whose son is he?”

But they answered “David,” because they had read this and could not deny it. For they knew that it had been said to the same David: “And it shall be, when you sleep with your fathers, I will raise up your offspring after you, which shall be from your sons, and I will establish his kingdom” (1 Chronicles 17). And again: “Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and I will raise up for David a righteous Branch, and he shall reign as king and shall act wisely” (Jeremiah 23; 33).

The Savior’s question is of great benefit to us today against those Jews who believe him to be merely a human being and not God. Taught by him, we should ask them: If Christ is merely human and not God, “How does David in the Spirit call him Lord, saying: ‘The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand, until I place your enemies as a footstool for your feet’” (Psalm 109)? If David therefore calls him Lord, how is he his son?

When they have no answer, let us confidently reply that he is both David’s Lord and David’s son: David’s Lord in his divinity and David’s son in his humanity; David’s Lord because “in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1); David’s son because “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (ibid.).

Nor is it surprising that one and the same Mediator between God and human beings, the Lord Jesus Christ, is called both David’s Lord and David’s son, since today it often happens that an ordained bishop is called his father’s father, not by the order of birth but by honor.

But it should not be passed over that the Jews, lying about many things in the Scriptures, claim that this psalm was sung in the person of Abraham by his servant Eliezer of Damascus when he was still a boy, so that the meaning would be: “The Lord said”—that is, almighty God said—“to my lord”—that is, to Abraham—“Sit at my right hand,” when he glorified him with the triumph of victory as he returned from the slaughter of the five kings, since a seat is prepared for the victor.

Let us therefore ask them how what follows in the same psalm (Psalm 109) can apply to Abraham: “From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you.” And again: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.” Let them say, then, how Abraham was begotten from God’s womb before the morning star, when we read of his origin and birth; and how he was a priest according to the order of Melchizedek, when he rather offered spoils to that same Melchizedek and asked for his blessing (Genesis 14).

When they cannot answer, let us firmly believe that this psalm was sung in the person of Christ. Its meaning is: “The Lord said”—that is, God the Father—“to my Lord”—that is, to God the Son. When it says, “The Lord said to my Lord,” the repetition of one name does not indicate a division of substance but the distinct property of each person. For the Father is what the Son is in nature, yet the person of the Father is one and the person of the Son another.

He “said” not by uttering words with his mouth, nor because the other listened attentively with his ear, but because the Son knows what the Father wills, and the Father knows what the Son wills; for with them, saying is willing.

When it says, “Sit at my right hand,” this is said to the victorious Son, because sitting is owed to the victor. After he had conquered the ancient enemy through his Passion and resurrection, he placed at the Father’s right hand the humanity he had assumed from us. The Evangelist Mark testifies to this when he says: “The Lord Jesus, after he had spoken to them, was taken up into heaven and sits at the right hand of God” (Mark 16). This does not mean that God the Father should be thought to have a right or left hand as we do; rather, he is wholly on the right, because he is wholly holy.

When it adds, “until I place your enemies as a footstool for your feet,” it uses a finite adverb for an infinite time. Scripture has the practice of using this finite adverb sometimes for a finite period and sometimes for an infinite one. For a finite period, as through the Prophet Isaiah: “My people, enter into your rooms; hide yourself for a little while, for a moment, until the indignation passes” (Isaiah 26). For an infinite period, as the Psalmist says: “Our eyes are toward the Lord our God, until he has mercy upon us” (Psalm 122). And the Prophet: “Until you grow old, I am he.” Surely God would not cease to exist after their old age, nor would our eyes cease to look toward him after he had shown us mercy? No; as we have said, a finite expression has been used for an infinite one.

Thus in this passage also, when he says, “until I place your enemies,” and so forth, this adverb, used with an infinite sense, signifies the eternity of Christ. A footstool takes its name from climbing; the feet signify his eternity of perpetual stability. The enemies who are placed beneath the footstool of his feet are not to be understood as enemies who remain enemies, but as those who were once enemies and, through conversion, have been reconciled and made friends. This is readily understood from the fact that the Son beneath whose footstool they are placed is said to sit at the right hand. Only the elect are to be placed at the right hand, as the Lord himself says: “He will set the sheep at his right hand but the goats at the left. Then he will say to those who are at his right hand: ‘Come, blessed of my Father; possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world’” (Matthew 25).

[Col. 0707B] “And no one was able to answer him a word, nor did anyone dare from that day onward to question him any further.” When the Pharisees saw that the Lord’s praise was increasing through their questions while their own disgrace was increasing, they did not dare to question him any further, because whatever they said they perceived to have been spoken against themselves. But the one whom they did not dare to question, they openly seized and handed over to Roman authority, so that we may understand that resentment and envy can be overcome, but do not know how to be quiet.

[Col. 0707C] “Then Jesus spoke to the crowds and to his disciples, saying: ‘The scribes and Pharisees have sat upon the seat of Moses. Therefore, whatever they tell you, do and observe; but do not act according to their works. For they say and do not do.’”

In this passage the Lord’s great patience is displayed, but his benevolence is shown no less clearly. The scribes and Pharisees were eager to assail him with the most serious questions, but he himself urged the crowds to submit to them and show them reverence, saying: “They have sat upon the seat of Moses,” and so forth.

A seat is a wooden chair, suited on every side to support the body, and therefore appropriate to teachers and instructors. Through the seat, sometimes good doctrine and sometimes bad doctrine is signified. Bad doctrine, as is read in the first psalm: “He did not sit in the seat of pestilence.” Good doctrine, as the Psalmist says elsewhere: “Let them exalt him in the assembly of the people, and praise him in the seat of the elders” (Psalm 106). So also in this passage it is used in a good sense when it says: “Upon the seat of Moses.”

Here the seat of Moses signifies the teaching of the Law, which is attributed to Moses because it was given by the Lord and administered to the people especially through Moses. The scribes and Pharisees therefore sat upon the seat of Moses because they rested in the teaching of the Law. For this reason the Lord urges the crowds to listen to their teaching: although they lived badly, they nevertheless spoke good things. What the common people could not understand, they had received from the Lord in a special way so that they might teach the people.

In what they taught well, they were to be heard; in what they lived badly, they were neither to be heard nor imitated. Hence it is rightly said: “Whatever they tell you, observe and do.” Since they taught not their own doctrine but the preaching of God, he invited the people to hear and observe their teaching. But after he had urged the people to observe their preaching, he now turns them away from observing their example when he adds: “But do not act according to their works.”

Anyone today in the Church who teaches well but lives badly is a scribe and Pharisee. Yet although his life is despised, it does not follow that his preaching should be rejected; good preaching must not be abandoned because of evil works. Hence the Apostle Paul says: “Whether Christ is proclaimed from pretense or from truth, in this I rejoice, and I will rejoice” (Philippians 1).

[Col. 0708B] “For they bind heavy and unbearable burdens and lay them on people’s shoulders, but they themselves do not wish to move them with their finger.” The heavy and unbearable burdens were the precepts of the Law, which were given as hard and harsh because of the stubbornness of the Israelite people, to such an extent that no one could fulfill them according to the letter, as the Apostle Peter testifies: “Why do you wish to place upon the necks of the disciples a yoke that neither we nor our fathers were able to bear? But we believe that we are saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as they are” (Acts 15).

But the scribes and Pharisees had made the heavy and unbearable burdens even heavier by adding various observances and superstitions to the Law, so that through these they might incline the simple crowd toward reverence for themselves. The Lord reproves them for this elsewhere, saying: “Hypocrites, why do you transgress God’s commandment because of your traditions? For God said: ‘Honor your father and your mother.’ But you say: ‘Whatever gift is from me will benefit you,’ and you do not honor your father; thus you have made God’s commandment void because of your traditions” (Matthew 15).

They do not wish to move these burdens with their finger because they not only failed to observe the greater commandments of the Law but were unwilling even to touch the lesser ones with the finger of action. Concerning them he says elsewhere: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who have taken away the key of knowledge” (Luke 11).

But because they did these things not from love of God but from a desire for human praise, it is rightly added:

[Col. 0708D] “But they do all their works so that they may be seen by people.” They were such as deserved to hear what the Lord says elsewhere: “You are those who justify yourselves before people, but God knows your hearts” (Luke 16). Concerning them it is said elsewhere: “Truly I say to you, they have received their reward” (Matthew 6). Hence he strongly rebukes them elsewhere, saying: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who are like whitewashed tombs” (Matthew 23), and so forth.

The Lord exposes their vices when he continues, saying: “For they enlarge their phylacteries and magnify their fringes.” When the Lord had given the Law through Moses, he added at the end: “You shall bind it upon your fingers, and it shall be immovable before your eyes, and you shall meditate upon it day and night” (Deuteronomy 6). The meaning is: “You shall bind it upon your fingers,” that is, you shall fulfill it in your works. “And it shall be immovable before your eyes,” that is, you shall meditate upon it continually.

The scribes and Pharisees, lovers of empty glory, wrote the ten words of the Law on little pieces of parchment and bound them around their foreheads, so that when they greeted and met one another they might remember the precepts of the Law. They called the little painted object itself a phylactery.

The Lord had also commanded in the Law (Numbers 15) that they place blue fringes at the four corners of their cloaks, so that the Israelite people might be distinguished. The scribes and Pharisees, therefore, followers of greed and seeking profit from poor women, made the fringes extremely long, and tied very sharp thorns to their ends, so that when they sat together at banquets or in the synagogues they might prick one another with them and thereby remember the Law, while whoever possessed such a fringe might be considered more religious.

In accordance with this comparison was the fringe of the Lord—not superfluous through Pharisaic superstition, but moderate and small according to the legal precepts—which the woman who had suffered from a flow of blood for twelve years approached and touched from behind (Luke 8). She was not pricked according to the superstition of the Pharisees but was healed by the Lord’s mercy.

The reason why he had devised these and similar superstitions is made clear when it is added:

“They love the first couches at banquets”—which pertains to gluttony; “and the first seats in the synagogues”—which pertains to empty glory; “and greetings in the marketplace, and to be called Rabbi by people”—which pertains to undeserved reverence.

After exposing their vices, the Lord restrained his own people from imitating them, saying:

“But you must not be called Rabbi. For one is your teacher.” It is as though he said: You are the elect, who have one and true teacher, namely, the one from whom all wisdom proceeds, who was always with him and exists before the ages; your confidence is in God, and he grants you earthly things so that you may be able to attain heavenly things. Do not be called Rabbi, that is, teachers, so that you may turn the honor owed to him toward your own glory.

“All of you are brothers.” In these words it is shown that not so much carnal birth as spiritual birth is to be praised, when he says: “For all of you are brothers.”

[Col. 0709D] “And do not call anyone your father on earth. For one is your Father, who is in heaven. Nor be called teachers, because one is your teacher, Christ.”

Since there is one Father, God, and one Mother, the Church, and one faith of Catholics, they ought consequently to be brothers—not according to the flesh but according to the Spirit—so that they may believe one thing, understand one thing, and desire one thing, and that what is written may be fulfilled in them: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is when brothers dwell together in unity” (Psalm 132). Such were those of whom it is said elsewhere: “The multitude of believers had one heart and one soul.
