Nor did any of them say that anything he possessed was his own, but all things were common to them” (Acts 4).

Hence the Apostle calls all believers brothers. And John says: “Beloved, we are children of God” (1 John 3).

It is asked why some dare to call those who preside over them in teaching or governance fathers or teachers, especially in monasteries, when the Lord says: “You must not be called Rabbi, and do not call anyone your father on earth,” while the Apostle Paul calls himself the teacher of the Gentiles, saying: “As long as I am the teacher of the Gentiles, I will honor my ministry” (Romans 11).

The answer is that it is one thing to be a father and teacher essentially, and another to be called one by designation. The true teacher and Father is the one who knows all things before they come to be, and whose wisdom governs and orders everything. Nevertheless, without sin we call those who preside over us teachers or fathers, because by this designation we pay reverence to their holiness, age, and wisdom; we do not, however, confess them to be the authors of our nature.

For just as “no one is good except God alone” (Matthew 10), yet many are called good from his goodness, so there is one Father who created all things and one Teacher who taught all things; nevertheless, through his teaching or imitation, many are called teachers and fathers. But he is so essentially, whereas they are so by an extended or customary designation. And because one ascends to this dignity, so as to be called teachers or fathers, not through pride but through humility, it is rightly added:

“Whoever among you is the greater shall be your servant.” In these words the pride of those who desire to ascend to a higher rank not through the merit of their life but because of temporal honor is rebuked. For this is the difference between secular power and the humility of the Church: in the former, power is chosen; in the latter, humility. And the more powerful someone is among the former, the more highly he is revered; among the latter, however, the more humble he is, the better he is. Therefore, when he says, “Whoever among you is the greater shall be your servant,” it is as though the Lord were saying: Just as the Son of Man did not come to be served but to serve, and became present among you not as one reclining at table but as one who serves, how much more ought teachers to show their disciples the way of humility? That is, the higher they are in rank, the more humble they should be in example.

The Lord wished to demonstrate this elsewhere when the disciples were disputing among themselves which of them was the greater in the kingdom of heaven. He said: “The kings of the nations lord it over them, and those who exercise authority over them are called benefactors. But it shall not be so among you. Rather, let the one who wishes to be greater be as the least of all, and the leader as one who serves” (Luke 22). And again: “Amen, I say to you, unless you turn and become like little children, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 18). He displayed this virtue when he said: “For who is greater, the one who reclines at table or the one who serves? Is it not the one who reclines? Yet I am among you as one who serves” (Luke 22). As he is also recorded as having said elsewhere: “You call me Teacher and Lord, and you speak rightly, for so I am. If then I, the Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet” (John 13). It properly belongs to those who love eternal glory more than temporal life to do this. Hence it is also added:

“Whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.” It is asked why he says, “Whoever exalts himself will be humbled,” since we see many exalted in the present world and remaining in that exaltation until the end of their lives; and again we see others in poverty and destitution, remaining in that poverty until the departure of their souls. The answer is that whoever has proudly exalted himself in the present world will be humbled in the future, while whoever has truly humbled himself in this world for the sake of the Lord Christ will be exalted in the future. Just as there are always quarrels among the proud, so among the humble unbroken peace and concord are preserved. For those who humble themselves in the present will be exalted in the future, when they will deserve to hear that desirable voice: “Well done, good and faithful servant, because you have been faithful over a little, I will set you over much; enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matthew 25).

## HOMILY 134. THE TWENTIETH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST

### (Matthew 9)

“At that time: Jesus got into a boat, crossed over, and came to his own city.” And so forth.

It often happens that one and the same thing in Scripture has a twofold or threefold meaning. Such is the case with a boat, which at one time signifies the standard of the holy cross, at another the holy Church, and at another the womb of the undefiled Virgin.

It signifies the standard of the holy cross, as we read in another passage: “When Jesus had got into a boat, his disciples followed him” (Matthew 8) [Col. 0711C]. It signifies the holy Church, as it is read in the psalm: “Those who go down to the sea in ships, doing their work upon the great waters, have seen the works of the Lord and his wonders in the deep” (Psalm 106). It signifies the womb of the undefiled Virgin, as in this passage: “Jesus got into a boat.” For the Lord spiritually ascended into a boat when he assumed flesh from the womb of the undefiled Virgin.

“He crossed over,” because, once born, he taught, performed miracles, suffered, and rose again, as it is said through the apostle Peter: “He went about doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil” (Acts 10). “He came to his own city,” that is, the holy Church—not because, when he came to it, he found it already his own, but because by coming to its aid he made it his own.

In its typological representation, his city was called Nazareth, which is interpreted as “pure” or “guarded.” It signifies the Church that he chose for himself, having neither spot nor wrinkle, since the Lord has cleansed the Church with his blood and guards it by his protection. To her he speaks in the Song of Love: “You are altogether beautiful, my beloved, and there is no blemish in you” (Song of Songs 4). And again: “You are one, my beloved, my beautiful one, my dove, my immaculate one” (Song of Songs 5–6).

It is asked, however, why Matthew says that the Lord came to his own city, when Mark reports that this miracle of healing took place not in Nazareth, which is called his city, but in Capernaum. The answer is brief and clear: Nazareth and Capernaum are situated in the region of Galilee. Just as all Galilee was called his homeland because he was conceived or brought up there, and hence he is also called a Galilean, so not only Nazareth but also Capernaum, which is situated in Galilee, can be understood as his city. Matthew and Mark do not disagree with one another: one gives the actual name, while the other simply says “his city.” Or certainly Capernaum can be called his city not because he was born or raised there, but because he glorified it by his miracles.

Again it is asked why he got into a boat. Could he not walk upon the waves of the sea, since he once enabled Peter to walk upon the waves of the sea (Matthew 14)? Or could he not dry up the sea before his own feet, since before the children of Israel leaving Egypt he dried up the Red Sea and made them cross over on dry ground (Exodus 14)? He certainly could. But he got into a boat in order that, doing everything that belongs to a human being, he might demonstrate that he had come as a true man for our salvation.

“And behold, they brought him a paralytic lying on a bed.” Paralysis is not only a very severe but also a very acute affliction. As soon as it suddenly attacks a person, it renders him useless for every task. It occurs when the natural heat of the body or of the blood is turned into cold and closes the natural passages of the veins, so that if it affects the whole person, it makes him weak; but if it seizes any particular limb, it makes it inflexible and useless.

Accordingly, the paralytic represents any sinner who, withdrawing from the warmth of divine love, is changed into the lukewarmness or coldness of iniquity, so that, even if he sometimes commits very serious crimes, he does not fear them as though they were insignificant. Of such people it is said through the prophet: “As a cistern makes its water cold, so a fool makes his wickedness cold” (Jeremiah 6).

The bed on which the paralytic was carried signifies either a human body accustomed to sins or a despairing conscience. Those who brought the paralytic to the Lord to be healed signify the teachers and masters of the Church. Ecclesiastical men bring the paralytic to the Lord for healing when they correct the sinner by their words and assist him with their prayers, so that he may repent of those sins.

According to Mark, they are rightly reported to have been four, because there are four books of the holy Gospel, in which the whole teaching of preachers is not only instructed but also strengthened. But since anyone who undertakes to govern other souls ought not to cling to earthly desires but to long for heavenly things, it is rightly said by another Evangelist that those who brought the paralytic to the Lord, finding no way to carry him in because of the crowd, went up onto the roof and lowered him with his bed through the tiles into the midst before Jesus.

Every soul that wishes to be freed from the paralysis of its iniquity must drive away the crowds of demons and the tumult of vices and seek what is lofty. He ascends to the roof who, despising earthly things, desires heavenly ones. He places the sick man before the Lord through the tiles when, mindful of human frailty, he is angry with sinners in such a way that he sympathizes with the penitent.

Or certainly those who brought the paralytic to the Lord for healing are rightly remembered as four, because there are four principal virtues, of which it is sung in praise of eternal Wisdom: sobriety and wisdom, justice and strength. Some, changing the names, call them prudence, temperance, fortitude, and justice. As Scripture says, nothing is more useful than these in human life.

Prudence is to know God and understand his will. The Lord shows how necessary and useful this virtue is when he says to his disciples: “Be prudent as serpents and simple as doves” (Matthew 10). But what sort of prudence is it if fortitude is lacking? To know what is good but not to be able to do it is more a punishment than a virtue.

Let fortitude therefore be added to prudence, so that the good known through prudence may be held indefatigably through the strength of merit, as Scripture says: “Act manfully, and let your heart be strengthened, all you who hope in the Lord” (Psalm 30).

Fortitude, moreover, will be praiseworthy if it is just, because to act courageously but not justly is not virtue but vice. Many act bravely in battles, contests, and the carrying of burdens, but because they do not act justly, such strength is attributed not to virtue but to vice.

Let justice therefore be added to fortitude, so that what is just and right may both be maintained in action and retained in memory, as Scripture admonishes: “Love justice, you who judge the earth” (Wisdom 1).

Then justice will be acceptable and pleasing to God and to human beings if it is discerning and temperate, because a good virtue practiced without temperance frequently turns into vice. Hence Scripture admonishes: “Do not be excessively just, nor be wiser than necessary, lest you become bewildered” (Ecclesiastes 7).

Let temperance, that is, discernment, therefore be added to justice. As Scripture says, it is the mother of all virtues, so that in the very good work no one may be excessive or superfluous, but discerning and temperate. For virtue practiced without watchfulness frequently turns into vice.

And because the person who wishes to offer his own soul and another’s to God must possess these four virtues, those who brought the paralytic to the Lord for healing are rightly said to have been four.

But lest anyone think it impossible for one and the same person to possess all four virtues together, I would like to bring forward one among the many who both practiced them in deed and taught them in speech: namely, the holy patriarch Abraham.

He possessed prudence, because, while others had strayed from the worship of God, he believed and recognized his Creator as God. For just as the person who says in his heart, “There is no God” (Psalm 13), is foolish, so the one who recognizes God is prudent.

He added justice to prudence when, without any delay, he obeyed the commands of the one whom he had recognized as God, departing from his land, his kindred, and his father’s house. Hence Scripture immediately adds: “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness” (Genesis 15).

But let us see how prudent, just, and strong he was. When, as an old man, he had received from his beloved wife an only son by promise, he heard from the Lord (Genesis 22): “Take your son, your beloved Isaac, and offer him to me as a burnt offering upon one of the mountains that I shall show you.” And he rose early, saddled his donkey, and so forth.

And again: “On the third day, when he lifted up his eyes and saw the place from afar, he said to his servants: ‘Wait here with the donkey; I and the boy will hasten there, and after we have worshiped, we shall return to you.’”

When he reached the place, built an altar, and placed the bound boy upon the pile of wood, he must be believed to have endured no small grief and anguish in his heart—not only because of the death of his beloved son, but also because he feared lest the boy, in the pain of death, might at least murmur against God in his heart. Yet greater fortitude conquered the great grief.

Let us see how prudent, just, strong, discerning, and temperate he was. When he was already about to sacrifice his son and held the drawn sword in his hands, he heard from the Lord: “Do not stretch out your hand against the boy, nor do anything to him.” Then, being discerning and temperate, just as he had been strong in preparing to sacrifice, so he became temperate in refraining.

Therefore he deserved to be consoled by the divine voice, when he immediately heard: “Now I know that you fear God, since you have not spared your only son for my sake. Blessing, I will bless you, and I will multiply your offspring like the stars of heaven” (Genesis 22).

I have wished to recall these things briefly concerning Abraham’s deeds so that we too may understand that we can possess these four virtues, if we are not reluctant to ask God for them.

“But when Jesus saw their faith, he said to the paralytic: ‘Take courage, son; your sins are forgiven.’”

Here we must consider how much one’s own faith helps each person, when another’s faith is shown to have helped so greatly. The Evangelist does not say, “When Jesus saw the faith of the one who was brought,” but “of those who brought him.” Since the paralytic could not come by himself, he was carried by the hands of others and healed through the faith of others.

From this we can understand that there are some in the Church who, although they are not saved by their own merits, nevertheless deserve to be saved through the intercession of others.

Here not only the Lord’s power, which must be adored, is displayed, but also his humility, which must be venerated and imitated to the best of our ability. For there is a great difference between the pride of the Jews and the Lord’s humility. The scribes and Pharisees did not consider the sick man, whose limbs were entirely paralyzed, worthy not only of touching but scarcely even of looking at; yet the Lord not only healed him of his infirmity but also called him “son,” saying: “Take courage, son.”

Faith adorned with works is also a great virtue, as the apostle James says: “Faith without works is dead” (James 2), and “without faith it is impossible to please God” (Hebrews 11). Commending this faith to his disciples, the Lord says: “If you have faith like a grain of mustard seed” (Luke 17).

And beautifully he calls him “son,” the one whom he freed from sins, so that the one who had previously been a son of malice and wickedness, and a son of the devil, after his sins had been forgiven became a son of God.

It follows: “Your sins are forgiven.” It must be noted that his sins are forgiven first, and then bodily health is bestowed. By forgiving his sins first, as we have said, and granting health afterward, the Lord shows that illnesses befall many people because of their sins.

For divine scourges touch people in the present life in five ways. Some are scourged for the sake of testing alone, as were Job and Tobias. Since their patience was known only to themselves and to God, they were scourged so that they might become more approved and their patience might serve as an example to others.

Others are scourged so that the power of the one who heals may be glorified, as happened with the blind man about whom the disciples asked the Lord (John 9): “Rabbi, who sinned, this man or his parents, that he was born blind?” They heard: “Neither this man sinned nor his parents, but so that the works of God might be manifested in him.”

Others are scourged to preserve humility, lest they become proud of the virtues they have received. This happened to the apostle Paul, who said of himself: “And lest the greatness of the revelations should exalt me, a thorn in my flesh was given to me, an angel of Satan, to buffet me. For this I asked the Lord three times that it might depart from me, and he said to me: ‘My grace is sufficient for you, for power is made perfect in weakness’” (2 Corinthians 12).

Others are scourged because of the enormity of their crimes, so that they may begin to experience in this life the punishments they will suffer in the future. Such were King Herod, Nebuchadnezzar, Antiochus, Pilate, and others like them, concerning whom it is written: “Crush them, Lord, with double destruction” (Jeremiah 17).

Others are scourged so that their past sins may be forgiven. Such was the sick man who lay beside the pool of Siloam, to whom, after his sins had been forgiven, the Lord said: “See, you have been made well; sin no more, lest something worse happen to you” (John 5). Such also was this paralytic about whom we are now speaking, whose sins were not only forgiven but whose bodily health was also restored.

“And behold, some of the scribes said within themselves: ‘This man blasphemes.’”

The scribes maintained their usual behavior. They followed the Lord not out of love but because of envy, so that they might find grounds to criticize him. Knowing that they could not deny the visible miracle that had taken place, they called it blasphemy that he invisibly forgave sins.

Accordingly, according to the Evangelist Mark, they are reported to have said indignantly: “Who can forgive sins except God alone?” (Mark 2). In these words they spoke the truth, because no one can forgive sins except God alone, who says through the prophet: “I am he who blots out your iniquities for my own sake” (Isaiah 43), and so forth.

Following him, the Psalmist said: “According to the multitude of your mercies, blot out my iniquity” (Psalm 50). And: “Wash me more and more from my iniquity” (ibid.).

But they were greatly mistaken when, seeing in his bodily presence the one who could invisibly forgive sins, they refused to believe that he was God.

Yet because it is necessary to grant a benefit even to the ungrateful, the Lord first answered the thoughts of the blasphemers and then displayed the miracle of healing. Hence it is also added:

“And when Jesus saw their thoughts, he said: ‘Why do you think evil in your hearts?’”

In this act the Lord clearly declared to his blasphemers that he must be believed to be God. For just as God alone can forgive sins, so God alone can behold the thoughts of human beings, as Scripture says: “You alone, God, know the thoughts of human beings” (2 Chronicles 6). And: “A human being looks on the face, but God looks into the heart” (1 Samuel 16).

It is as though he were saying: By the same divine power with which I behold your thoughts, I can forgive sins not only to the paralytic but also to all penitents. From your own thoughts, moreover, understand what this paralytic will receive.

“For which is easier to say: ‘Your sins are forgiven,’ or to say: ‘Rise and walk’?”

Among human beings there is a great difference between saying and doing, but with God there is none: for him, to say is to do. “He spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created” (Psalm 32).

The one who forgave them knew that his sins had been forgiven. But that he would rise and walk was known both by the one who rose and by those who saw him rise.

Yet the scribes and Pharisees were utterly blind, because they did not understand the spiritual through the bodily miracle. When they saw the paralytic cleansed, they did not believe that his sins had been forgiven.

Thus a bodily sign is performed to prove a spiritual reality, because, according to the Apostle, tongues are for a sign not to believers but to unbelievers. And so that they might not doubt that the soul’s sins had been forgiven invisibly, visible health was restored to the paralytic.

Therefore he continued and said:

“But so that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins”—then he said to the paralytic—“Rise, take up your bed.”

The Son of God and the Son of Man are one and the same; and the Son of Man who is the Son of God is one and the same person from two substances. And because the Son of Man was assumed by the Son of God, he has authority on earth to forgive sins, in accordance with what he says elsewhere: “The Father has given him authority to execute judgment, because he is the Son of Man” (John 5). And again: “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (ibid.).

Nevertheless, he preferred more frequently to call himself the Son of Man rather than the Son of God in order to make known the virtue of humility. Once the paralytic had been healed, he is rightly told: “Rise, take up your bed,” and so forth.

“And he rose and went to his own house.”

Above we said that the paralytic represents the sinful soul, and that his bed signifies flesh accustomed to sins. It is rightly said, “Rise,” because every penitent, if he wishes to obtain forgiveness, must first rise from the iniquity in which he lay, as the Apostle says: “Rise, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ will enlighten you” (Ephesians 5).

The paralytic is commanded not only to rise but also to carry his bed, because not only must the soul cease from sins, but the flesh, which was enslaved to vices, must also serve the virtues, according to the Apostle: “Just as you once presented your members as slaves to impurity and iniquity for iniquity, so now present them as slaves to righteousness for sanctification” (Romans 6).

The paralytic carries his bed when, after conversion, the sinner crucifies his flesh, putting to death his members that are upon the earth, and, according to the Apostle, “crucifies his flesh with its vices and desires” (Galatians 5).

For the one whose soul desires to see God perfectly ought also to subject his flesh to the virtues, following the example of the one who said: “My soul thirsted for you; how greatly my flesh also” (Psalm 62). And again: “My heart hoped in God, and I was helped, and my flesh flourished again” (Psalm 27). And again: “My heart and my flesh have rejoiced in the living God” (Psalm 83).

The house to which we are commanded to go after our healing is paradise. We were created for this purpose: if the first human being had not sinned, we would have remained there without any corruption. But because we departed from it by sinning, it is right that we return to it by repentance.

The one who longed to reach it with the most ardent love said: “One thing I have asked of the Lord; this I will seek” (Psalm 26). And again: “I will enter your house, Lord; I will worship toward your holy temple” (Psalm 5). And again: “I will enter the place of the wondrous tabernacle, even to the house of God” (Psalm 41).

In this house each person will find a more spacious dwelling the more justly he has lived in the present life, as the Lord himself says: “In my Father’s house there are many dwelling places” (John 14).

“When the crowds saw this, they were afraid and glorified God, who had given such authority to human beings.”

Here the difference between learned wickedness and holy simplicity is revealed. While the scribes blasphemed God, the crowds, who were less learned, saw his works and glorified God with fear and wonder.

This also happens daily in the Church in the conversion of sinners. When some criminal publicly turns to God and is healed through repentance, many people glorify God’s immense mercy in his conversion.

According to the preceding sense, the crowds who fear can be understood as unclean spirits. When they saw sinners snatched from their power through the Lord’s incarnation, they were shaken with fear and wonder. Hence, speaking through the possessed man, they said: “What have we to do with you, Son of God? Have you come here before the time to torment us?” (Matthew 8). And as the Evangelist says: “The demons begged him at length not to order them to depart into the abyss” (Luke 8).

## HOMILY 135. THE TWENTY-FIRST SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST

### (Matthew 22)

“At that time Jesus was speaking with his disciples in parables, saying: ‘The kingdom of heaven has become like a king who made a wedding feast for his son and sent his servants to call those who had been invited to the wedding, but they were unwilling to come.’” And so forth.

Since the kingdom of heaven is frequently named in the Gospel, it not inappropriately always has one and the same meaning. At times it signifies the heavenly Lord Jesus Christ, at times the teaching of the holy Gospel, at times the heavenly homeland, and at times the present Church.

It signifies the Lord Jesus Christ, as he himself says: “The kingdom of God is within you” (Luke 17). It signifies the teaching of the holy Gospel, as he said to the Jews who refused to receive it: “The kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a nation producing its fruits” (Matthew 21). It signifies the heavenly homeland, as in the saying: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 5). It signifies the holy Church, as he says elsewhere: “Whoever breaks one of these least commandments and teaches others to do so will be called least in the kingdom of heaven” (ibid.).

Therefore, in this passage the kingdom of heaven signifies the present Church, that is, the assembly of the righteous, in which the Lord not only reigns but also rests, as it is written in Solomon: “The soul of the righteous is the seat of Wisdom.”

Some think that this is the same reading that Luke described under the name of a supper, but the two passages seem to contain certain differences. There the meal is called a supper; here it is called a banquet. There no one who entered is said to have departed; here the man who had entered without a wedding garment is said to have been expelled with great disgrace.

Although it was customary among the ancients to eat only once a day, and this meal was called a banquet, a dinner, or a supper, among us it is more usual for supper to follow dinner, and after supper no meal remains. Therefore, by that supper the Church is represented as it will be in the future; by this banquet, as it is in the present.

This king spiritually is God almighty; his Son is the Lord Jesus Christ, of whom the Psalmist says: “Give the king your judgments, O God” (Psalm 71), and so forth.

He made a wedding feast for his son when, through the mystery of the Incarnation, he joined the holy Church to him, the Church having neither spot nor wrinkle, of which the Apostle says: “I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ” (2 Corinthians 11).

At a wedding two are joined: the bridegroom and the bride. The bridegroom is Christ, of whom John says: “The one who has the bride is the bridegroom” (John 3). “The friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices with joy because of the bridegroom’s voice.”

The bride is the holy Church, to whom the prophet says: “I will betroth you to myself in righteousness and truth” (Hosea 2).

John speaks of this wedding in the Apocalypse, saying: “Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb” (Revelation 19). And again: “I saw the holy city, Jerusalem, descending from heaven” (Revelation 21).

The bridal chamber of this bridegroom was the womb of his mother, from which he proceeded like a bridegroom from his chamber in order to join the Church to himself. Hence, when the Apostle was explaining the testimony spoken to the first human being, “For this reason a man will leave his father and mother and cling to his wife,” and so forth, he immediately added: “This mystery is great; but I speak with reference to Christ and the Church” (Ephesians 5; Genesis 2).

“And he sent his servants to call those who had been invited to the wedding.”

If we read “servant,” as some copies have it, we should understand Moses; if “servants” in the plural, we can understand the patriarchs and prophets.

He therefore sent servants to call those who had been invited to the wedding because he wished to announce the mystery of his Incarnation long beforehand through the patriarchs and prophets. They called many to the wedding of Christ because, foreseeing Christ’s coming through the Holy Spirit, they announced it to others.

But what follows is greatly to be lamented: “And they were unwilling to come.” It is beautifully said, “They were unwilling to come,” because many heard through the prophets that he had been announced, yet did not at all believe that he would come.

God offers what ought to have been requested. Without being asked, he is prepared to give what could scarcely be believed, so that he would grant it even when requested. But the reprobate are unwilling to come to the wedding because through many actions they oppose his commands.

There are some who not only fail to ask God for what is fitting for them, but also refuse to accept what is offered to them. Yet divine mercy does not despise those who despise it, since he sent other servants again to those who were unwilling to come.

The servants sent a second time are to be understood as the apostles, who were sent to preach the Gospel after the Lord’s Incarnation. They announced Christ’s coming with greater confidence because they had heard the divine Word more abundantly from the very mouth of Truth.

But since examples generally benefit the minds of hearers more than words do, the second invitation rightly says:

“Tell those who have been invited: ‘Behold, I have prepared my banquet; my bulls and fattened animals have been slaughtered, and everything is ready. Come to the wedding.’”

By the bulls and fattened animals we understand the holy Fathers of both Testaments, that is, of the Old and the New.

The bull is an animal with an erect neck, bearing horns on its head with which it defends itself and frightens smaller animals. Accordingly, by the bulls we not improperly understand the Fathers of the Old Testament, who, having received from the promise of the Law the command to strike down bodily the enemies of God and of themselves, bore horns, as it were, upon their heads.

But in the preparation for the wedding the bulls were slaughtered, because, while the Fathers of the Old Testament foretold Christ’s Incarnation, some of them were killed: some were cut apart, such as Isaiah; others were stoned, such as Jeremiah.

The fattened animals are so called as though they were “nourished animals,” which in ordinary speech we call hand-fed, that is, fattened. Therefore the fattened animals represent the apostles and their successors. Having learned to despise earthly riches and love the heavenly kingdom, they knew how to lift themselves upward like fattened birds on the wings of contemplation, saying with the Apostle: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Philippians 3).

Having received the nourishment of doctrine from the Lord’s own mouth, they were, as it were, fed by hand. They were fattened with spiritual richness all the more abundantly because they were filled more openly and perfectly with the gift of the same Holy Spirit, so that they could say with the Psalmist: “May my soul be filled as with marrow and fatness” (Psalm 62). And again: “You have anointed my head with oil” (Psalm 22).

But at Christ’s wedding feast the fattened animals were slaughtered along with the bulls, because the Fathers of the New Testament died bodily for the preaching of the Gospel. Some were crucified, such as Peter; others beheaded, such as Paul; others stoned, such as Stephen; others burned by fire, such as Lawrence; others were torn apart, and, according to the Apostle, “went about in sheepskins and goatskins” (Hebrews 11).

The king removes every opportunity for excuse when he says: “Everything is ready.” Everything is ready because that singular Lamb has been sacrificed, in whose figure all things came beforehand.

Or certainly everything is ready because there is no example of virtue manifested in the deeds of the saints for our imitation that has not already been set before us. We have already heard of Abel’s innocence, Abraham’s obedience, Isaac’s chastity, Jacob’s endurance, Moses’ gentleness, David’s mercy, and Job’s patience; and we have seen the Lord’s end.

But all the reprobate, while eagerly yearning to acquire earthly riches, not only disdain imitating the examples of God’s servants but also neglect to hear the words of the Lord himself as he invites them. Hence it is added:

“But they paid no attention and went away, one to his farm.”

What is signified by the farm except earthly possessions? He goes to the farm who, loving earthly and superfluous things, does not seek the heavenly homeland.

When he occupies his natural understanding not in God’s service but in earthly advantages, he goes not only to the farm but also to his business. Hence it is rightly added: “Another to his business.”

What is signified by business except cunning and skill? In business, the aim is to buy what is cheaper and sell it for more. Whoever therefore seeks unjust profit through craft or ingenuity, going, as it were, to his business, refuses to come to God’s wedding.

The Apostle undoubtedly speaks of such people: “Those who desire to become rich fall into temptation and a snare of the devil, and into many useless desires that plunge people into destruction and perdition” (1 Timothy 6).

Whoever is devoted to these things must fall not only into lies but also into perjuries. Whoever has abandoned himself to them refuses, as we have said, to come to Christ’s wedding.

Hence the Apostle says: “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in secular business, so that he may please the one to whom he has presented himself” (2 Timothy 2). And James says: “Whoever wishes to be a friend of this world makes himself an enemy of God” (James 4).

“But the rest seized his servants, treated them shamefully, and killed them.”

There is a great difference between those who neglect to hear the word of God and those who persecute its messengers. Some do not consider the word of God worthy of being heard; others hear the word of God but disdain fulfilling it in action. Still others not only despise the word of God but also persecute its preachers with hatred and swords.

Those who do not hear the word of God will certainly be condemned strictly; but those who neglect to fulfill what they have heard will be condemned still more strictly. For, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “The servant who did not know his master’s will and did not act accordingly will be beaten with few blows; but the one who knew and did not act accordingly will be beaten with many blows” (Luke 12).

Those who cannot restrain their hands from persecuting preachers will be judged more severely still. Hence it is also added:

“But when the king heard this, he was angry, and sending out his armies, he destroyed those murderers and burned their city.”

If this parable is understood specifically of the Jewish people, it is plainly evident that they treated God’s servants with contempt, when, as the book of the Acts of the Apostles says: “The disciples went away rejoicing from the presence of the council, because they had been deemed worthy to suffer dishonor for the name of Jesus” [Col. 0721B] (Acts V). They also stoned Stephen and killed James the Just by throwing him down from the pinnacle of the Temple (Acts VII). When the king heard this, while they persisted in their wickedness, he sent Vespasian and Titus—the two Roman commanders, father and son—with their armies, and destroyed those murderers. They also burned their city, that is, Jerusalem, by fire, so that, in accordance with the Lord’s word, “not one stone was left upon another in it” (Mark XXIII).

But if this parable is understood generally of all the reprobate, it is made clear that those who neglect to hear the words of God who invites them are condemned not only in their souls but also in their bodies. For the armies [Col. 0721C] of our King are angelic spirits; hence he is called “the Lord Sabaoth,” that is, “the Lord of armies.” Concerning them Daniel says: “Thousands of thousands ministered to him” (Dan. VII), and so forth. Having therefore sent out his armies, he destroyed those murderers, because he will execute all judgment upon human beings through his angels, as he himself says in the Gospel: “The Son of Man will send his angels, and they will gather out of his kingdom all stumbling-blocks, and cast them into the furnace of burning fire” (Mark XIII).

The city of the reprobate is their own bodies, because just as a human being dwells for a time in a city, so the soul inhabits the body. Therefore, not only are the murderers destroyed, but the city also is burned, because the reprobate will be condemned in their souls until the judgment, and after the judgment in their bodies as well. But since [Col. 0721D] we said above that this king bears the likeness of almighty God, it may be asked how he is said to be angry, when no anger or changeability can exist in the nature of God. The Psalmist bears witness to this when he says: “God is a just judge, strong and patient; is he angry every day?” (Ps. VII.)

To this we must reply that in many places Holy Scripture speaks in our manner, so that the hidden judgments of God may be understood through visible things. Just as an earthly king is said to be angry when he exercises vengeance upon his subjects, so almighty God appears angry with those whom, in his just judgment, he condemns and punishes on account of their sins. In his own nature, however, he always remains unchangeable and always tranquil. To him a certain wise man says: “But you, Lord Sabaoth, judge with tranquillity [Col. 0722A] and dispose us with great forbearance” (Wis. II). And through the prophet: “I am God, and I do not change” (Mal. III).

“Then he said to his servants: ‘The wedding is indeed ready, but those who were invited were not worthy. Go therefore to the outlets of the roads, and invite to the wedding whomever you find.’”

In these words the rejection of the Jews and the calling of the Gentiles are plainly signified. Formerly the Jews stood on the road, when, knowing the God of heaven, they observed the legal commandments. But when the Lord came in the flesh, those who had been invited were not worthy, because by refusing to believe in the one promised to them, they made themselves unworthy.

But will the place of God’s wedding remain empty because the Jews refuse to come? Certainly not. Immediately the servants are sent for the calling of the [Col. 0722B] Gentiles, when it is said: “Go therefore to the outlets of the roads.” The Gentile people were called from the outlets of the roads when, possessing no knowledge of God, they were brought from the worship of idols to faith in God.

But because we believe that this parable applies not only to the Jews but also to us, just as we understand the roads as actions, so we call the outlets of the roads the failure of actions. There are some who are not easily converted to God unless the prosperity of this present age first fails them, as it is written: “Only oppression will give understanding to the hearing” (Isa. XXVIII). And the Psalmist says: “When he slew them, they sought him” (Ps. LXXVII), and so forth. Frequently some who have been struck by divine scourges return to salvation; if they had remained in the prosperity of this age, they would certainly have [Col. 0722C] perished. To such people the prophet says: “You shall be chastised with rod and scourge, daughter of Zion, so that my zeal may not depart from you” (Ezek. XXIII).

That child of the Amalekites signified such people, concerning whom we read in the Books of Kings (1 Kings XXX). When the Amalekites were fleeing, he had been left behind on the road in weakness. David, pursuing them, found him, gave him food and drink, and afterward made him the guide of his journey. “Amalekite,” which is interpreted as “the licking people,” signifies lovers of the world, who desire to grow rich from other people’s wealth and to increase through the resources of strangers.

When some of the elect desire to share the common course of the present life with such people, by the most merciful goodness of God they are either crushed by scourges, weakened by poverty, or constrained by some necessity, so that even against their will they may be converted to God. [Col. 0722D] Such people are called to the Lord’s wedding not from the roads but from the outlets of the roads. To them what is said through the prophet Hosea applies: “Behold, I will hedge up your way with thorns, and I will enclose it with a wall; and you shall pursue your lovers, but you shall not overtake them; you shall seek them, but you shall not find them; and you shall say: ‘I will return to my former husband, because it was better for me then than now’” (Hos. II).

“And his servants went out onto the roads, gathered all whom they found, bad and good, and the wedding feast was filled with those reclining at table.”

These words plainly show that, as we said above, the present Church is signified by the king’s wedding. [Col. 0723A] For it is said: “His servants went out onto the roads and gathered all whom they found, bad and good.” The good alone are nowhere found except in heaven; the bad alone are nowhere found except in hell. But the present Church, which stands between heaven and hell, receives citizens from both sides, because many enter the Church through faith who cannot enter the kingdom of heaven through the merit of their life. Concerning them the prophet says: “I proclaimed and spoke; they were multiplied beyond number” (Ps. XXXIX). Nor is it surprising that the reprobate are multiplied beyond number, since grains of wheat are preserved amid a multitude of chaff, and the fragrant rose commonly grows among piercing thorns.

“But the king entered to see those reclining at table.” [Col. 0723B]

To recline at the wedding is to rest in faith within the Church, as the Lord says elsewhere: “Many will come from east and west, and will recline with Abraham and Isaac and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. VIII). Every day this king enters his wedding, because almighty God judges human actions and conduct with subtle scrutiny and weighs the intention according to which each person lives. If he sees someone adorned with good works, he rejoices to have that person sit and feast with him as a spiritual guest.

Yet it commonly happens that someone is found in the Church like the man who is mentioned next: “And he saw there a man not clothed in a wedding garment, and he said to him: ‘Friend, how did you come in here without having a wedding garment?’”

The question is what the wedding garment is [Col. 0723C], without which whoever enters the Church will not be received into the feast but will be cast out with great disgrace.

[Note: [Col. 0723D] This should be read with caution: there seems to be an error, although the archetypes agree.]

We cannot properly understand the wedding garment as faith, because without faith we cannot enter the Church. Nor do we take baptism as the wedding garment, because without baptism we do not enter the Church. Let us therefore confidently and without any contradiction understand the wedding garment as charity, without which anyone enters the Church in vain, even if he pretends to possess right faith.

We rightly understand the wedding garment as charity, because just as a garment is woven from two threads, an upper and a lower, so charity is fulfilled through two commandments: namely, love of God and love of neighbor. The lower thread therefore signifies love of neighbor; the upper thread [Col. 0723D] signifies love of God. Charity cannot exist with fewer than two persons, because we cannot truly love God without our neighbor, nor can we truly love our neighbor without God.

Hence, among the other ornaments of the priest’s garment, scarlet wool dyed twice is commanded to be placed (Exod. XXIII), so that charity may be doubled in our good work: that we may love God with all our heart, all our soul, and all our mind, and our neighbors as ourselves. As the apostle John says: “Little children, we have this commandment from God: whoever loves God must also love his brother. And whoever says, ‘I love God,’ and hates his brother, is a liar” (1 John IV).

Or, in another sense, charity is rightly [Col. 0724A] represented by the wedding garment, because just as a garment is woven from very many threads, so charity is adorned with various virtues. From it arise prudence, generosity in almsgiving, hospitality, love of one’s enemy, and other things of this kind.

If anyone wishes to know from what threads the garment of charity is woven, let him read the apostle Paul, who, after saying: “If I speak in the tongues of human beings and of angels, and if I have prophecy, and know all mysteries and all knowledge, and if I have all faith, so that I remove mountains, and if I distribute all my possessions as food for the poor, and if I hand over my body so that I may burn, but do not have charity, it profits me nothing” (1 Cor. XIII), immediately enumerated the members of that same charity, saying: “Charity is patient, is kind; it does not envy, does not [Col. 0724B] act wrongly, is not puffed up, is not ambitious, does not seek its own, is not provoked, does not think evil, does not rejoice over iniquity but rejoices with the truth; it bears all things, believes all things, endures all things; charity never fails” (ibid.).

Or again, charity is rightly the wedding garment, because just as a garment not only covers the nakedness of bodies but also gives them beauty, so charity not only generates the other virtues and covers a multitude of sins, but also adorns them. The Lord says: “To everyone who has, it will be given, and he will abound; but from the one who does not have, even what he seems to have will be taken away” (Matt. XXV). And the Apostle says: “Now these three remain: faith, hope, and charity” (1 Cor. XIII).

But it is astonishing that [Col. 0724C] he calls him “friend” whom he rejects from the feast with such great confusion. To this we must reply that, speaking figuratively through antiphrasis—that is, by mockery—he calls “friend” one who does not deserve to be loved. It is as though he said: “Friend, and not friend.” Friend through faith, but not friend through conduct. Friend, because you came to the wedding; but not friend, because you did not bring a wedding garment.

“But he was speechless.”

Rebuked by the king, the man who had entered the wedding without a wedding garment was speechless, because in that examination of strict judgment there will be no opportunity to flee, to lie, or to conceal himself from anyone. Not only will the presence of God and the multitude of angels and saints bear witness, but the sinful conscience itself will accuse itself of why it sinned. Blessed Job bears witness to this when he says: “And the earth cries out against me” (Job XXXI).

Hence, in [Col. 0724D] the person of Judas the betrayer, or of any impious person, it is said: “The heavens will reveal his iniquity, and the earth will rise up against him, and his sin will be made manifest on the day of the Lord’s wrath” (Job XX). The prophet was considering this strictness when he said: “Neither from the east, nor from the west, nor from the desert mountains”—that is, there will be no place of escape—“for God is judge” (Ps. LXXIV).

What follows after this is made clear when it is added:

“Bind his feet and hands and cast him into the outer darkness.”

If anyone wishes to know by what [Col. 0725A] cords the hands and feet of sinners are bound in punishment, Solomon makes it clear when he says: “Each person will be bound by the cords of his sins” (Prov. V). The Psalmist speaks of these cords: “The cords of sinners have entangled me” (Ps. CXVIII). A cord is made by twisting, so that it may become longer; and whoever adds sins to sins makes, as it were, a cord by which he will be bound in punishment. Isaiah cries out to such people in terror: “Woe to those who draw iniquity with cords of vanity, and sin as though with a cart rope!” (Isa. V.)

These ministers are to be understood as unclean spirits, concerning whom the Psalmist says: “He sent forth through evil angels” (Ps. LXXVII). The binding of the feet signifies vices and sins. Whoever has his hands or feet bound here, so that he cannot do good or run along the way of God’s commandments, must necessarily have his hands or feet bound there. And whoever has spread himself in every direction through evil conduct will be restrained in every direction in the retribution of vengeance.

It is fitting that the sinner’s hands and feet are bound in punishment [Col. 0725B], since here he kept them free for guilt. But since darkness is always within and never outside, why is this person said to be cast into the outer darkness?

To this we must reply that the inner darkness is blindness of mind, whereas the outer darkness is infernal punishment. It is therefore just that after death the person who, while he lived, shut himself within the inner darkness—that is, blindness of mind—should be cast into the outer darkness.

What the one cast there will suffer is made clear when it is added: “There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.” Here the quality of the torments is shown through the names of bodily members. [Col. 0725C] Eyes commonly weep when touched by acrid smoke, and teeth gnash because of excessive cold. Therefore, when he says, “There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth,” it is understood that the reprobate, condemned to eternal punishment, will endure both immeasurable cold and intolerable heat, as blessed Job bears witness: “They pass from excessive heat to waters of snow” (Job XXIV).

Here we must also consider that not only the bodies of the saints but also those of the reprobate are shown to rise at the judgment. Hence blessed Job says elsewhere: “I believe that my Redeemer lives, and on the last day I shall rise from the earth, and in my flesh I shall see God” (Job XIX). The eyes are made of flesh, and the teeth of bones. [Col. 0725D] Therefore, when he says, “There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth,” he shows that the bodies of the reprobate, which consist of flesh and bones, will truly rise, so that those who sinned in flesh and soul may likewise be punished in flesh and soul.

But what he says—

“For many are called, but few are chosen”—

is more to be feared than explained. We know that we have all been called; but whether we belong to the lot of the chosen, we do not yet know. We must therefore be all the more diligent in good works, the more clearly we know that we are without excuse concerning our calling, so that we may not hear, together with the many reprobate: “Go, accursed ones, into eternal fire” (Matt. XXV), but may deserve to hear, together with the chosen: “Come, blessed of my Father, possess the [Col. 0726A] kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (ibid.).

May he himself deign to grant this, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God, forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY CXXXVI. THE TWENTY-SECOND SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST

### (JOHN IV)

“At that time: There was a certain royal official whose son was ill at Capernaum.” And so forth.

It sometimes happens that certain people receive outward names from the quality of the mind they possess inwardly. Thus Simon was called Peter because of the firmness of his faith, since he clung to a firm rock; and the sons of Zebedee were called Boanerges, that is, “sons of thunder,” because they were going to thunder from the spiritual heaven: “In the beginning was [Col. 0726B] the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John I). Judas was also called “the Zealot,” because he burned intensely with zeal for the love of God.

So perhaps this royal official also drew his outward name from the quality of mind he possessed inwardly. “Regulus” is a diminutive name derived from “king,” as if one were called the first under a king, or a little king. And because he believed in part and did not believe in part, he deserved to be called not a king but a royal official. What we say about him in words, he himself proves by his actions. For it follows:

“When he heard that Jesus had come from Judea into Galilee, he went to him and asked him to come down and heal his son. For he was beginning to die.”

All these things are so clear according to the literal sense [Col. 0726C] that they require no explanation. Only this seems strange: why did the Lord say to the man who had come to ask on behalf of his son:

“Unless you see signs and wonders, you do not believe”—

when surely, if he had not believed, he would never have approached the Lord to ask for his son’s health?

To this we must reply that he both believed and did not believe. He believed that the Lord could restore health to his son through his bodily presence, but he did not believe that, through his divinity, he was present everywhere, since he so anxiously sought his bodily arrival, saying:

“Lord, come down before my son dies.”

Because he believed, he came to ask on behalf of his son; but because he did not believe perfectly, he deserved to hear: “Unless you see signs and wonders, you do not believe.”

Faith has growth [Col. 0726D], just as the apostles said to the Lord: “Lord, increase our faith” (Luke XVII). And that centurion who had come to ask on behalf of a boy afflicted with epilepsy, when he heard the Lord say, “Do you believe? All things are possible for one who believes,” replied: “I believe, Lord; help my unbelief” (Mark IX).

There is this difference between signs and wonders: “signs” are called unusual miracles, whereas “wonders” are those things which, although marvelous in their immediate manifestation, also foreshadow something in the future. Hence “prodigy” is so called as though from *porro digium*, “a sign pointing forward.”

But in this reading our pride is confounded if we compare it with another. For we read in the Gospel of Matthew that when Jesus entered Capernaum, a centurion approached him, asking him and saying: “Lord, my servant lies paralyzed in the house and is being severely tormented.” And Jesus said to him: “I will come and heal him” (Matt. VIII).

Who does not know that the royal official held greater [Col. 0727A] rank than the centurion? What, then, does it mean that the Lord refused to go when asked to the royal official’s son, but was ready to go, even without being asked, to the centurion’s servant?

Our pride is plainly confounded, as we have said, because in human beings we consider not the nature by which they were made in the image of God, but their power. Those whom we see as powerful we honor; those whom we fear we venerate; but the poor we despise, disdain, and neglect.

In contrast, the Son of God, who descended from heaven to earth, refused to go when asked to the royal official’s son, but was ready to go to the centurion’s servant even when he had not been asked. For, as Peter most truthfully testifies concerning him [Col. 0727B]: “God is not a respecter of persons, but in every nation whoever practices righteousness is acceptable to him” (Acts X).

Let us therefore imitate our head, and whoever we see loving God more, let us love more earnestly. In saying this, we do not forbid the honoring of the powerful, especially since the apostle Peter says: “Fear God, honor the king” (1 Pet. II). But just as we venerate their power, so we must supply the needs of the poor, so that in the Church of God the fitting honor may be shown to each person.

But because reproof often greatly benefits pious minds, after the royal official had been rebuked by the Lord, he heard: “Go, your son lives.” The man believed the word that Jesus had spoken to him, and he went. Thus faith immediately obtained its effect. [Col. 0727C]

“Now as he was going down, his servants met him and announced to him that his son was alive.”

From the fact that the royal official had earlier said to the Lord, “Come down before my son dies,” and here it is said, “Now as he was going down,” it is understood that Capernaum was situated in a valley. The name is interpreted as “fertile valley” or “most beautiful village.”

Wanting to know whether health had been restored to his son at the very hour when he had heard from the Lord, “Your son lives,” he “asked them at what hour he had improved. And they said to him: ‘Yesterday, at the seventh hour, the fever left him.’”

It is fitting that the royal official’s son is healed at the seventh hour, because there are seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, by whose grace and power not only the remission [Col. 0727D] of sins but also strength and health are granted, as the Apostle bears witness when he says: “The love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. V).

Or certainly the royal official’s son was healed at the seventh hour so that we might understand that, in the present life, which revolves through seven days, we must seek the salvation of our soul by doing good.

“Therefore the father knew that it was at that hour in which Jesus had said to him, ‘Your son lives,’ and he himself believed, and his whole household.”

In many places in the Gospel, the greater readiness of the Gentiles to believe than that of the Jews is shown, when the Lord himself says concerning the centurion: “Amen, I say to you, I have not found such great faith in Israel” (Matt. VIII).

A little earlier, [Col. 0728A] in the account of the same evangelist John, we read that when the Samaritan woman had heard from the Lord all the things she had done, she went into the city and said to them all: “Come and see a man who told me everything I have done. Is he perhaps the Christ?”

When they had come to him, the Samaritans asked him to remain there. He stayed there for two days, and many more believed because of his word. And they said to the woman: “Now we no longer believe because of your speech; for we ourselves have heard, and we know that this is truly the Savior of the world” (John IV).

There the whole city believed without the display of a miracle; here, although a great sign had been displayed, the father himself and his whole household “believed.”

## HOMILY CXXXVII. THE TWENTY-THIRD SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST

[Col. 0728B]

### (MATTHEW XVIII)

“At that time Jesus said to his disciples this parable: ‘The kingdom of heaven is like a king who wished to settle accounts with his servants.’” And so forth.

The Lord Jesus Christ, the power and wisdom of God, accommodating himself to human ignorance, has often deigned to add comparisons to his holy discourses, so that what his hearers could not grasp through the likenesses expressed in words, they might at least retain through parables and figures.

Hence, as Matthew says elsewhere: “Jesus spoke with his disciples in parables, and without parables he did not speak to them, so that what was spoken through the prophet might be fulfilled: ‘I will open my mouth in parables’ (Matt. XIII and Ps. LXXVII), ‘I will utter sayings from the beginning.’”

We recognize that he did this in the present reading if we consider more carefully what precedes in this Gospel. For when he had given the command that we should forgive our brothers who sin against us, so that this might not seem harsh and difficult, he added the comparison of a king who forgave his debtor ten thousand talents at a single supplication.

Spiritually, this man who is king is the Lord Jesus Christ, concerning whom it is written: “Behold, God and man will come from David, who is King of kings and Lord of lords” (1 Tim. VI), and whose kingdom will have no end.

The servants of this king are human beings, whom he created in his own image to serve and praise him, and to whom he also gave understanding and intelligence. To serve him is the highest freedom; to withdraw from his service is the most shameful slavery.

The Psalmist gloried in calling himself this king’s servant when he said: “I am your servant and the son of your handmaid” (Ps. CXVIII). And again: “I am your servant; give me understanding” (Ps. CXVI), O Lord.

The king settles accounts with his servants because the eye of his majesty carefully examines and distinguishes not only our deeds but also our thoughts. But when he settles accounts, it commonly happens that many are found bound not only by lesser sins but also by greater crimes. This man represents them, concerning whom it follows:

“And when he began to settle accounts, one was brought to him who owed him ten thousand talents.”

In Scripture, a talent sometimes signifies sin, or weight, or a multitude of sins, as we read in Zechariah: “I saw, and behold, a talent of lead was being carried” (Zech. V); and he cast it into the midst of the vessel and said: “This is wickedness” (ibid.). For just as a talent is weighed in various ways, so the kinds of sins are various. Whoever commits murder, adultery, sacrilege, and other things of this sort owed, as it were, ten thousand talents.

“But since he had nothing with which to repay, the master ordered him to be sold, together with his wife and children and everything he had, and payment to be made.”

The servant had nothing with which to repay the debt because, through his own merit, he cannot adequately make satisfaction to God for his sins. Or certainly the servant has nothing with which to repay the debt because, on the day of judgment, the sinner will find no excuse for his sins.

But because God is merciful and does not wish sinners to perish forever, he orders the servant to be sold when he commands the sinner to be changed through repentance. In a sale, what takes place is that one person’s property passes into another’s possession. Spiritually, therefore, the servant is sold when the sinner passes through repentance from the possession of the devil into the possession of God.

The wife and children are also sold when the flesh, which had been subjected to sins, and carnal thoughts are changed into the service of God. Let the one who served impurity and iniquity unto iniquity serve righteousness unto sanctification; let him love humility instead of pride, chastity instead of lust, and generosity instead of greed. The one who previously begot children of the devil by living wickedly—

By the wife we can understand his own flesh; by the children, vices and sins.

Or, in another sense, the servant is sold when eternal punishment is threatened to the unrepentant sinner, and he is commanded to turn away from evil and do good. The wife and children are also sold when punishment of eternal torment is proclaimed not only for souls because of their sins but also for sinful flesh.

When the servant frequently hears this after sinning, he is shaken by fear toward repentance, although he had refused to avoid sin for the love of God. Hence it also follows:

“But that servant fell down and pleaded with him, saying: ‘Have patience with me, and I will repay you everything.’”

The servant fell down before God when the sinner, recognizing his weakness, humbly asks forgiveness, saying with the prophet: “For I acknowledge my iniquity, and my sin is always before me. Against you alone I have sinned and done what is evil before you, so that you may be justified in your words and prevail when you are judged” (Ps. L).

He also asks for patience so that he may be able to offer worthy repentance, so that he may receive the days of the present life as a postponement for repenting and, according to the Apostle, may be converted to repentance through God’s patience.

How merciful God is toward converted sinners is shown when it follows:

“And the master, moved with compassion for that servant, released him and forgave him the debt.”

Behold, he not only found the patience for which he had asked, but also received release from his debt. For divine mercy is accustomed always to grant more than human weakness knows how to ask.

Therefore no one should despair because of the greatness or multitude of his sins, or lose hope in forgiveness, since the one who owed ten thousand talents and asked for patience so that he might repay everything obtained this from the Lord. God loves sinners after their conversion if they make worthy satisfaction. For, as he himself says through the prophet, he does not desire the death of a sinner, “but that he should turn and live” (Ezek. XVIII and XXXIII). And again: “On whatever day the sinner turns” (ibid.), and so forth.

And as the merciful Redeemer says in the Gospel: “I have not come to call the righteous but sinners” (Matt. IX). “There is joy in heaven over one sinner who repents more than over ninety-nine righteous persons who have no need of repentance” (Luke VII).

But one thing is supremely necessary for penitents: just as they wish their own sins to be forgiven by God, so they must mercifully forgive their brothers who sin against them. There are some who desire God to be kind toward them but are harsh, severe, and bitter toward their brothers. This man appears to represent such people, concerning whom it follows:

“And that servant went out and found one of his fellow servants who owed him a hundred denarii; and he seized him and began to choke him, saying: ‘Pay what you owe.’”

The servant goes out when he is permitted to depart free. By the choking mentioned above we can understand the tribulations and hardships that he inflicted upon him. Spiritually, each one of us, going out, finds one of his fellow servants owing him a hundred denarii when he remembers having been injured by another.

“But that servant fell down and pleaded with him, saying: ‘Have patience with me, and I will repay you everything.’”

Thus, in the same words with which he had pleaded with his master, he was entreated by his fellow servant; but he did not show his fellow servant the mercy he had received from the Lord. Hence it also follows:

“But he was unwilling; instead, he went away and had him put in prison until he should repay the debt.” The punishment of the wicked is signified by the confinement or suffocation of imprisonment. Thus, in this passage, the prison is understood as the affliction by which he was constraining him. That debt is called sin in Scripture we understand from what we ask daily in prayer, saying: “Forgive us our debts” (Matt. VI). Hence it is commanded in the Law: If your brother owes you a debt, and you take “a pledge from him, restore the pledge before sunset” (Exod. XXII). For every person is both a debtor and has a debtor. Who is there who is not a debtor to God, since no one is without sin? And who is there who does not have his brother as a debtor, except the one against whom no one has sinned? As much as ten thousand talents exceed one hundred denarii, so much greater are the things we commit against God than those by which our brothers sin against us. Therefore, we ought to forgive the lesser offenses of our brothers who sin against us with the same kindness by which we desire the greater offenses committed by us to be forgiven by God.

We recognize this more clearly if we consider the Lord’s earlier admonition, from which this parable arose. For when he had previously commanded, saying: “If your brother sins against you, go and reprove him between you and him alone” (Matt. XVIII), and the other things that follow, Peter asked him, saying: “Lord, how often will my brother sin against me, and I shall forgive him? Up to seven times?” Jesus said to him: “I do not say to you up to seven times, but up to seventy times seven” (ibid.). From this question and answer we learn that if our brother sins against us as often as human frailty does not permit a person to sin in a single day, we must always be ready to forgive.

But someone may say: “My brother sinned against me; I forgave him up to seventy times seven. Must I forgive him more than Christ commanded?” We must answer that even if he sins seventy-eight times, even a hundred times, and however many times he may sin altogether, he must always be forgiven. For just as we wish the Lord to forgive our sins not partially but completely, so we must forgive with our whole heart our brothers who sin against us, as the apostle Paul urges: “Forgive one another everything, if anyone has a complaint against another, just as he forgave us in Christ” (Col. III).

That number is established not for the quantity it denotes but for its mystery. The evangelist Luke took care to reveal the sacramental meaning of this number when, describing the order of Christ’s human generation, he counted seventy-seven generations. For while Matthew, beginning from Abraham and descending to Christ, counted forty-two generations, Luke, by contrast, describing the line upward from Christ to the first man Adam, counted seventy-seven generations, so that we may understand that “seventy times” pertains not to the quantity of the number but to sin.

From Christ therefore to Adam, seventy-seven generations are counted, because the sin which the first man committed continued through seventy-seven generations until Christ, who came without sin. Hence Luke fittingly began to count from Christ’s baptism, because all sins are absolved in baptism. Lamech showed this mystically in his own words when he said to his wives: “Sevenfold vengeance shall be taken for Cain, but for Lamech seventy times seven.” In the literal sense, sevenfold vengeance was taken for Cain, because he bore the punishment he deserved for his brother’s death throughout his own generation. But seventy-sevenfold vengeance was taken for Lamech, because seventy-seven souls came forth from his loins, all of whom perished in the Flood.

Spiritually, however, seventy-sevenfold vengeance was taken for Lamech because, as we have said, the sin which the first man committed continued through seventy-seven generations until Christ’s coming. Hence Lamech is aptly interpreted as “striking” or “struck,” because the first man sinned and struck all his offspring with the same wound. We have said this to show that “seventy times seven” pertains not to the quantity of the number but to sin.

Therefore, he commanded that we forgive everything our brothers can sin against us when he commanded us to forgive our brothers who sin against us seventy times seven. Let us therefore learn within ourselves the rule of forgiveness: just as we wish to find God merciful toward us after sin, so let us be gentle and kind toward those who sin against us, as the Savior himself admonishes: “When you stand to pray, forgive whatever you have against anyone, so that your Father who is in heaven may also forgive you your sins” (Matt. XI). For one who, forgetful of divine benevolence, wishes to avenge his own injuries will not only fail to deserve pardon for future sins, but the past sins that he believed had been forgiven him will also be recalled against him for punishment. Hence it follows:

“Therefore, when his fellow servants saw what had happened, they were very sorrowful, and they came and reported to their master everything that had taken place.” The fellow servants who, seeing these things, report them to the Lord are the angels, who are believed to announce our works to our Maker day and night, just as the angel said to Tobias: “While you were praying, I offered your prayers before God” (Tob. XII). They are called fellow servants because they minister to our lowliness, as the Apostle says: “They are ministering spirits, sent for service on behalf of those who desire to inherit salvation” (Heb. I). They are said to be sorrowful because, just as they rejoice over those who act well, so they are said to grieve over those who act badly.

Or, in another interpretation, the fellow servants who report these matters to their lord signify the teachers and masters of the Church. When they see the lesser oppressed or afflicted by the greater, they suffer with them; and while they grieve for them, they report all these things to the Lord, as it were through the affection of their hearts.

[Col. 0732C] “Then his master summoned him and said to him: ‘Wicked servant, I forgave you all that debt because you pleaded with me; should you not therefore have had mercy on your fellow servant, just as I had mercy on you?’” Behold what punishment he deserved because he wished to avenge his own injuries. For he says: “Wicked servant,” and so forth. It is as though he were saying: “Wicked servant, ungrateful servant, since I forgave you the entire debt at a single petition, why did you not consider that you too ought to have had mercy on your fellow servant, just as I had mercy on you?”

“And his master, being angry, handed him over to the torturers until he should repay the whole debt.” It is asked how the Lord is said to be angry, since no anger or changeability occurs in the nature of God, as the Psalmist bears witness, saying: “God is a just judge, strong and patient; is he angry every day?” (Ps. VII).

We must answer that in many places Holy Scripture speaks according to our manner of speaking, so that the hidden judgments of God may be understood through visible things. Just as an earthly king is said to be angry when he exercises vengeance upon his subjects, so almighty God appears to be angry with those whom, in his just judgment, he condemns and punishes on account of their sins. Yet in his own nature he remains always unchangeable and always tranquil. To him it is said by a certain wise man: “But you, Lord of hosts, judge with tranquility and dispose of us with great reverence” (Wis. XII).

The torturers to whom the ungrateful servant is handed over are unclean spirits, concerning whom it is written: “The sending of evil angels” (Ps. LXXVII). They harshly exact from us what they had persuaded us to do smoothly and gently. The sinner has as torturers in punishment the very ones whom he had as persuaders toward guilt.

When it is said, “until he should repay the whole debt,” a temporal adverb is used for an infinite time, because the reprobate, condemned to eternal punishment, will daily pay the debt of sin in punishment, yet the torments of their punishments will never come to an end. The Lord says elsewhere: “Amen I say to you, you will not come out from there until you have paid the last quadrant” (Ps. XXVI).

It must not therefore be understood that, after the universal judgment has been completed and the punishment of sinners carried out, the reprobate can obtain pardon, although the Origenists maintain this. Their opinion is not to be followed, because once they have been condemned, they will not obtain forgiveness. Explaining what he had previously set forth in the parable, the Lord added:

“So also my heavenly Father will do to you, if each of you does not forgive his brother from your hearts.” These words show that, as we said above, whoever does not wish to forgive his brothers who sin against him will have even those sins that he believed had been forgiven him recalled against him for punishment. And because God is the examiner of the heart, it is expressly said: “from your hearts.”

There are some who, when they have been injured by others, appear to forgive with their mouths but retain their injuries in their hearts. They do this either because they are compelled by others to forgive, or because they cannot defend themselves against those by whom they have been injured, or because they await an opportune time for revenge. Of such people it is said through the prophet: “With his mouth he speaks peace with his friend, but secretly he lays snares for him” (Jer. IX).

But the Psalmist declares what punishment such people will receive, saying: “Those who speak peace with their neighbor, but evil is in their hearts.” And again: “Give them according to their works, and according to the works of their hands repay them” (ibid.). Their patience will not receive the reward of virtue, because it is a covering for anger. It profits nothing, therefore, to forgive with the mouth while wishing to preserve anger in the heart.

For this reason, when the Lord had said: “So your heavenly Father will do to you, if each of you does not forgive his brother,” he added: “from your hearts.”

# HOMILY CXXXVIII. TWENTY-FOURTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST

[Col. 0733D]

(Matt. XXII.) “At that time, the Pharisees went away and took counsel together in order to entrap Jesus in his speech.” And so forth.

From the time when the monarchy of the whole world was brought under the rule of one man, in order that peace and harmony might be preserved among the peoples, it was established that each person should pay the census of his own head. The evangelist Luke bears witness to this matter, for he records that, at the time when our Lord and Savior was born, this law was introduced among the Jewish people, saying: “A decree went out from Caesar Augustus that the whole world should be registered” (Luke II).

On account of this matter Caesar Augustus appointed Herod, the son of Antipater, over the Jews, so that he might collect the taxes and obey the Roman empire. Therefore, while our Lord and Savior was preaching, a great dispute immediately arose among the Jews concerning the payment of the census. Some said that taxes ought to be paid for the sake of security and peace, because the Roman rulers fought on their behalf. The scribes and Pharisees, on the other hand, said that the people of God ought not to be subject to human laws, especially since they offered tithes, first fruits, and voluntary offerings to God.

And because, as we have often said, the scribes and Pharisees followed the Lord for the purpose of being able to accuse him either in his deeds or in his words, on this occasion they took counsel together and:

[Col. 0734A] “sent their disciples to him with the Herodians, saying: ‘Teacher, we know that you are truthful and teach the way of God in truth, and that you care for no one.
