For you do not regard the person of men. Tell us, then, what do you think? Is it lawful to pay the census to Caesar, or not?’”

They asked this so that, whatever answer he gave, he would incur the hatred either of one group or of the other. If he said, “It is lawful,” he would be reproached by those who did not wish to pay the census, or he would appear to be acting contrary to the law of God. But if he said, “It is not lawful,” he would be seized and held by the servants of Herod as one who intended to stir up rebellion against Caesar.

He calls those who publicly collected taxes the Herodians, or the servants of Herod; alternatively, he calls Herodians those whom the scribes and Pharisees, because they willingly paid tribute to Herod, mockingly called Herodians. And because, as the Lord says, the scribes and Pharisees were like whitened tombs, they prefaced their fraudulent question with flattering words, saying to him:

[Col. 0734B] “Teacher, we know that you are truthful and teach the way of God in truth, and that you care for no one. For you do not regard the person of men.”

It is characteristic of those who attempt to deceive others by fraud that they first soothe the mind of their hearer with flatteries, so that, enticed by their blandishments, he may answer not what is true but what the questioner has shown would please him.

But what they said fraudulently about the Lord, we must believe with firm and immovable faith: namely, that he is the true and unique teacher, from whom all wisdom proceeds, and who was and is eternally with the Father. He says in the Gospel: “You call me Teacher and Lord, and you speak rightly, for so I am” (John XIII). And again: “Do not be called teachers, because your one teacher is Christ” (Matt. XXIII).

He is truthful because, as Scripture says, “Every man is a liar” (Ps. CXV), while he says in the Gospel: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John XIV). He also taught “the way of God in truth” (Luke XX), because he neither deceived anyone nor could be deceived by anyone, and because he will truly give what he promised to those who keep what he commanded.

“For you do not regard the person of men” (Matt. XXII), because he neither rejects anyone on account of poverty nor chooses anyone on account of riches. Rather, whoever he sees to be more devoted in his service, he makes holier. Of him the apostle Peter says most truthfully: “In truth I have discovered that God is not a respecter of persons, but in every nation whoever works righteousness is acceptable to him” (Acts X).

By “Caesar,” however, we must understand not Augustus but Tiberius, his successor, under whom the Lord suffered. All the emperors of the Romans were called Caesars, after the first Gaius Caesar, who was given the name Caesar for two reasons: either because he came forth from his mother’s womb by incision, or because he was born with a full head of hair—that is, with hair.

[Col. 0735A] “But Jesus, knowing their wickedness, said: ‘Why do you put me to the test, hypocrites?’”

Wisdom always acts wisely. First he exposed the thoughts of those who were testing him, so that in this way at least they might be compelled to recognize his divinity. For it is proper to God to see the thoughts of human beings, as Scripture bears witness, saying: “The things that are in the heart of man, your eyes see, Lord.”

He rightly rebuked those testing him by calling them hypocrites, because they brought one thing forth with their mouths while retaining another in their hearts. The Greek term *hypocrite* means *simulator* in Latin. Those who inwardly preserve one thing and outwardly display another are rightly designated by this name. Such were these men: while they said to the Lord, “Teacher, we know that you are truthful,” they were planning to entrap him in his speech.

He further says to them:

[Col. 0735B] “Show me the coin of the census.”

A *numisma*, as Isidore says, is a solid coin of gold, silver, or bronze. It is called *numisma* because it was marked with the names and images of rulers.

“And they offered him a denarius.” The denarius was a kind of coin counted as ten *nummi*, and it bore the image of Caesar and his name inscribed above it.

“And he said to them: ‘Whose image and inscription is this?’ They said to him: ‘Caesar’s.’”

The Savior’s question did not arise from ignorance, especially since it was plainly evident whose image had been impressed upon the coin. Rather, he questioned those testing him so that, once they had answered whose image it was, he might teach reasonably and without reproach that what belongs to God must be rendered to God and what belongs to Caesar to Caesar. Hence it follows:

“And he said to them: ‘Render therefore to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s.’”

It is as though he were saying: Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s—that is, tribute, tax, and census—and to God the things that are God’s—that is, tithes, first fruits, and voluntary offerings.

We must carefully consider, therefore, that just as Caesar demanded from his subjects the census of his image, so almighty God will demand from us the likeness of his image. For the king’s image was stamped on the denarius, while human beings, according to the inner person, were made in the image and likeness of God, as the Lord himself says: “Let us make man according to our image and likeness” (Gen. I). He knew that this image had been stamped upon him when he said: “The light of your countenance, Lord, has been marked upon us” (Ps. IV).

Therefore, just as Caesar demanded from his subjects the denarius on which his image was stamped, so almighty God wishes to find his image preserved inviolate in us through pious deeds, pious conduct, and chastity.

We must also consider that, unless the first man had violated the image of God in himself by sinning, one human being would never have been subject to another. For in the beginning, when God had made man in his image and likeness, he did not say, “Let man rule over human beings,” but: “Rule over the fish of the sea, the birds of the heavens, and the beasts of the earth” (Gen. I).

But after sin began to increase among human beings, together with quarrels, conflicts, and the seed of discord, God set one human being over other human beings in order to restrain the insolence of wicked people, so that those whom the love of God did not move toward goodness might at least be restrained from evil by fear of another human being.

Now, in Christian times, divine providence has arranged that in the Church of God there should be not only a shepherd and pontiff but also a ruler in the world: the one instructs the Church of God by words, and the other defends it with arms. What the one cannot correct by words, the other may strike with the sword. Those who refuse to accept ecclesiastical discipline may be restrained from evil by royal power. Those who are not subject to the power of God may be constrained by worldly laws.

Therefore we ought to be subject and obedient to Christian rulers—unless they command us against the will of God—so that, in accordance with the Savior’s command, we may render “to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s.”

Hence the Apostle admonishes us, saying: “Be subject to the higher powers,” because “there is no power except from God. Those that exist have been ordained by God. And whoever resists the power resists the ordinance of God” (Rom. XIII). And again: “Render to all their due: tribute to whom tribute is due, tax to whom tax, honor to whom honor, fear to whom fear” (ibid.).

The Lord showed that this must be done not only by his words but also by his examples, when he rendered to God the things that are God’s by doing the will of the Father, and to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s when he ordered tribute to be paid for himself and Peter, as it is written in the Gospel (Matt. XVII):

“When those who received the didrachma came to Peter, they said to him: ‘Does your teacher not pay the didrachma?’ And he said: ‘Yes.’ And when Peter, troubled, had entered the house, Jesus anticipated him, saying: ‘What do you think, Simon? From whom do the kings of the earth receive tribute or the census: from their sons or from strangers?’ When he answered, ‘From strangers,’ he said: ‘Then the sons are free. But so that we may not scandalize them, go to the sea and cast a hook. Take the fish that first comes up, and when you have opened its mouth you will find a stater; take it and give it to them for me and for you.’”

Following this example, Peter himself admonishes his disciples in his epistle, saying: “Fear God, honor the king” (1 Peter II). And again: “Be subject for God’s sake to every human creature, whether to the king as supreme, or to governors as sent by him for the punishment of evildoers and the praise of the good” (ibid.).

# HOMILY CXXXIX. TWENTY-FIFTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST

(Matt. IX.) “At that time, while Jesus was speaking to the crowds, behold, one ruler came and worshiped him, saying: ‘Lord, my daughter.’” And so forth.

Among all the miracles that the Lord Jesus Christ displayed on earth by himself, he is recorded to have raised only three dead persons. He raised the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue, lying in the house, who is the subject of the present discussion. He also raised the son of a widow, carried outside the gate of the city for burial. Likewise, he raised Lazarus, who had been dead for four days and was already stinking in the tomb.

Since he had come to raise to life in the soul all who believe in him, it is not without reason that he is recorded to have raised only three dead persons in the body. For the threefold raising of the dead signifies the variety of sinners and of those who, after sin, rightly do penance.

The soul dies through sin, because, as Scripture says, “The soul that sins, it shall die” (Ezek. XVIII). Sin itself is committed in the mind in three ways, and in the body in three ways. In the mind it is carried out through suggestion, delight, and consent; in the body, sometimes secretly, sometimes openly, and sometimes through habit.

Whoever sins secretly lies dead, as it were, inside a house. But when divine grace kindles his heart to do penance, he is raised from the dead inside the house, as it were. Such people were signified by the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue, who was raised at a girl’s age.

Whoever sins openly is driven out, as it were, beyond the gate of the city as a dead person to be buried. But when such people, through divine grace and the correction of others, are pierced with remorse for penance, they are raised by the Lord before they reach the tomb, as it were. These were signified by the young son of the widow, whom the Lord raised outside the gate of the city (Luke VII).

There are also some who are not ashamed merely to sin publicly but turn sin itself into a longstanding habit. Such was signified by Lazarus, dead for four days, concerning whom it is rightly written: “He already stinks” (John XI). For when people are not ashamed to sin publicly through habit, they bring the stench of an evil reputation upon devout minds.

Yet even concerning such people we must not despair, because the Lord raised Lazarus, dead for four days and stinking, by his sole command. Of him it is written that Jesus wept and cried out with a loud voice: “Come out,” because such people must be instructed by teachers not only through exhortations but also through prayers, and they must be summoned with a loud voice through earnest preaching.

Often, being pierced by divine grace, they recover from their sins and afflict themselves with continual tears and prolonged fasts. They give more generous alms, and “where sin abounded, grace abounded all the more” (Rom. V). Just as they were eager to sin, so may they be even more eager to do penance.

But now let us see what the ruler and his daughter, for whom he had come to plead, signify allegorically. The evangelist says:

“While Jesus was speaking to the crowds, behold, one ruler came and worshiped him, saying: ‘My daughter has just died,’” and so forth.

Allegorically, this ruler signifies Moses. Hence, according to the evangelist Luke, he is rightly called Jairus, which is interpreted as “illuminating” or “illuminated.” For when Moses, the lawgiver, received from God the words of life that he was to minister to others, he himself was illuminated by spiritual grace, and by his teaching he illuminated others.

His daughter signifies the Synagogue, which he, as the first teacher, instructed in divine commandments and legal observances and thus, as it were, begot from a spiritual womb.

But while the Lord was speaking to the crowds, the ruler’s daughter died, because at the time when the Lord appeared in the flesh, the Synagogue had departed from the religion of its fathers and from observance of the Law.

For how did it lose its former dignity amid the confusion of affairs? Neither did priestly honor retain its proper beauty, nor were the reverence due to the temple and the offering of sacrifices observed—not only spiritually but not even historically.

Therefore the ruler pleaded for his daughter, because Moses often entreated divine mercy for the liberation of the Synagogue, as you find written in many passages of Scripture, especially where he prayed for the people of Israel so earnestly that he even wished to be blotted out of the book of life, if by this means he could avert God’s anger.

And because he understood that she could not otherwise be freed from the death of the soul except through the incarnation of the only-begotten Son of God, the voice of the same ruler rightly says: “Come, lay your hand upon her, and she will live.”

The hand of the Lord in Scripture sometimes signifies the incarnation of the Son, as it is said through the prophet: “Why do you turn your hand away, and your right hand from the midst of your bosom?” (Ps. LXXIII). And again: “Send forth your hand from on high; rescue me and deliver me from many waters” (Ps. CXLIII).

Therefore, to ask that he lay his hand upon the dead daughter was to ask that, through the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation, he visibly appear to the world. Moses asked spiritually that he lay his hand upon the dead daughter when he preached the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation to the Jews, saying: “God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers, like me; you shall hear him” (Deut. XVIII), “according to all that he will speak to you.”

And because, when the fullness of time arrived, he not only deigned to assume flesh from the Synagogue but also visibly to show himself as God among human beings, it rightly follows:

“And Jesus arose and followed him, with his disciples. And behold, a woman who had suffered from a flow of blood for twelve years came up behind him and touched the fringe of his garment.”

Just as the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue signifies the Synagogue, so “the woman who had suffered from a flow of blood for twelve years” signifies the Church from the Gentiles.

The flow of blood signifies the uncleanness of sins, as it is said through the prophet: “Theft, murder, and adultery have overflowed, and blood has touched blood” (Hos. IV). The person who wished to be freed from this flow of blood was the one who said: “Deliver me from bloodshed, O God, God of my salvation” (Ps. L).

We must not pass over the fact that this woman “suffered from a flow of blood for twelve years.” For, as the other evangelists relate, this girl, the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue, was twelve years old. Considering both accounts, therefore, we understand that when the girl was born, the woman began to fall ill: the one was twelve years old, and the other had suffered twelve years from her illness.

According to the spiritual interpretation, when the Synagogue was born, the Church from the Gentiles began to fall ill, because vices are easily recognized by comparison with virtues. Thus the Gentile people began to be regarded as more wretched from the time when the Jewish people was chosen.

If, as we have said, the girl died in the twelfth year of her life, she ended her life when the time of puberty was approaching. For, when the time of liberation or redemption was near, Judaea did not recognize its liberator and chose death rather than life.

In this sense, it is not without a mystery that the ruler of the synagogue asked the Lord to raise his daughter as the eighth miracle. When the Gospel reading is reviewed, the first miracle is found to have been performed by the Lord in Galilee: he changed water into wine. Second, descending from the mountain, he cured a leper. Third, he healed the centurion’s servant from paralysis. Fourth, he freed Peter’s mother-in-law from fever. Fifth, he calmed the troubled sea. Sixth, in the region of the Gerasenes, he healed a man from a legion of demons. Seventh, in his own city of Capernaum, he healed a paralytic. In the eighth place the ruler of the synagogue enters to plead for his daughter, unwilling to be excluded from the mystery of circumcision.

The woman healed from the flow of blood also enters. She came up behind him because the Church from the Gentiles believed not while the Lord remained in the flesh but after his ascension. Or she came up behind him because she not only recognized the mystery of his incarnation but also imitates the traces of his passion.

To come behind the Lord is to imitate his footsteps, as he says in the Gospel: “If anyone wishes to come after me,” and so forth (Matt. XVI). And again: “Whoever ministers to me, let him follow me” (John XII). Hence it is commanded in the Law: “You shall walk after the Lord your God.”

For this reason Peter admonishes the Church that has approached the Lord, saying: “Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example, so that you might follow his footsteps” (1 Peter II). And John says: “Whoever says that he abides in Christ ought himself to walk just as he walked” (1 John II).

The Church therefore approached in heart, not in body, in accordance with the prophetic saying: “Come to him and be enlightened” (Ps. XXXIII).

To touch the fringe of his garment is to recognize the mystery of his incarnation and to live spiritually according to it. Because God cannot be touched in his divinity, he presented himself as one whose garment-fringe could be touched when he showed himself visibly in his humanity.

“For she was saying within herself: ‘If I only touch his garment, I shall be saved.’”

This woman rightly spoke within herself, because the faith and activity of the whole Church are more in the heart than in the body. In order to appear more glorious in the sight of God, she frequently hides her good works from human eyes. Of her it is said through the prophet: “All her glory is within” (Ps. XLIV).

She believed that salvation lay in touching the garment because she did not doubt that the human race could be saved through the mystery of the incarnation.

[Col. 0740A] “But Jesus, turning and seeing her, said: ‘Take courage, daughter.’”

The Lord’s turning toward the woman signifies the regard of his mercy toward the Church. She saw, as it were, the Lord’s back and not his face when, running after the idols made by her own hands, she did not know her Creator as God. After she began to touch him by faith, he showed her his face when, through his grace, he illuminated the mind of the Church so that it might see him.

And because she merited to receive this through faith, it is rightly said: “Take courage, daughter; your faith has saved you. And the woman was saved from that hour.”

If someone attends only to the literal sense, he recognizes that this woman possessed no small faith. The evangelist Luke makes the perfection of her faith clearer, saying that she “had spent all her substance on physicians, and could be cured by no one” (Luke VIII).

But when she saw the Lord walking among the crowd, she believed that by touching his garment alone what many physicians had proved impossible could be accomplished. “And so she approached from behind and touched the fringe of his garment, and immediately the flow of her blood stopped” (ibid.).

To confirm the power of her faith, the Lord said: “Who touched me?” When everyone denied it, Peter and those who were with him said: “Teacher, the crowds press upon you and afflict you, and you say, ‘Who touched me?’” And he said: “Someone touched me. For I know that power has gone out from me.”

When the woman saw that she had not escaped notice, she came trembling and fell before his feet. In the presence of all the people she declared why she had touched him and how she had been healed immediately. But he said to her: “Daughter, your faith has saved you” (ibid.).

He rightly called her daughter because she possessed such perfect faith. Spiritually, as we have said, she signifies the Church, which is God’s daughter by adoption, because, as the evangelist says: “To all who received him, he gave power to become children of God” (John I).

To her it is said through the Prophet: “Hear, daughter, and see, and incline your ear” (Ps. LXVII).

She is rightly saved through faith, because, as it is written: “The righteous person lives by faith” (Gal. III), and “without faith it is impossible to please God” (Heb. XI). Hence the Lord said to the Canaanite woman: “O woman, great is your faith; let it be done for you as you wish” (Matt. XV).

It must also be noted that, while the Lord was going to raise the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue, the woman was healed on the way. For when the Lord came to teach the Synagogue, the Church from the Gentiles anticipated salvation by believing, in accordance with the prophetic saying: “Ethiopia will anticipate his hands for God” (Ps. LXXVII).

Ethiopia, which produces a black people, signifies the Church from the Gentiles, covered by the blackness of sins. Ethiopia will anticipate his hands when the Church from the Gentiles believes before the Synagogue.

We must also consider that the woman met him neither in a house nor in the city, since she was excluded far from the city, but on the road. For the Gentile people had no knowledge of God and no acquaintance with the Law, and therefore came before the Lord as naked and uncovered.

Thus, while the Lord was making his way to the girl, the woman was healed on the road, because while he was preaching to the Jewish people, he approved the faith of the Gentiles. As he says elsewhere concerning the centurion: “Amen I say to you, I have not found such great faith in Israel” (Matt. VIII).

Hence the apostles also said to the Jews: “It was necessary that the word of God should be spoken to you first, but since you reject it and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts XIII).

The woman’s greater faith is also clearly demonstrated in comparison with that of the ruler of the synagogue. The ruler asked the Lord to come to his house, and by making him labor as he went or returned, he caused him difficulty. But the woman, believing perfectly, caused him no labor at all; she merely touched the fringe of his garment.

After the Lord had healed the woman on the way, he raised the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue in the house, because near the end of the world the Synagogue will believe, in accordance with the Apostle’s saying (Rom. XI): “When the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then all Israel will be saved.”

And again: “Not first is the spiritual, but the natural; afterward the spiritual” (1 Cor. XV)—that is, the Synagogue, which was spiritual, did not believe first, but the Gentile people, which was natural; afterward the Synagogue, which was spiritual.

# HOMILY 140. THE TWENTY-SIXTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST

**(John 6.)** “At that time: When Jesus had lifted up his eyes and seen that a very great crowd was coming toward him, he said to Philip: ‘Where shall we buy bread?’” And so forth. Whenever we read that the Lord fed great crowds of people with a few loaves, this is not so much something to be wondered at as something to be revered. [Col. 0741C] For it is not surprising that he was able to do it; rather, it is worthy of reverence that he wished to do it. Since he created all things from nothing, it is not surprising that he fed great crowds from a few loaves. But we should consider that, when the Lord was about to refresh the crowds, he is first said to have lifted his eyes and looked toward heaven. For the Lord’s eyes have a twofold significance in Scripture, and so forth.

See the Sunday *Laetare* in Lent.

# HOMILY 141. ON THE DEDICATION OF A CHURCH

**(Luke 6.)** “At that time Jesus said to his disciples: ‘A good tree is not one that produces bad fruit.’” And so forth. The Lord Jesus Christ, builder and guardian of his Church, declares at the beginning of this reading what sort of trees he seeks for its construction, saying: “For a good tree is not one that produces bad fruit.” [Col. 0741D]

“Nor is a bad tree one that produces good fruit.” In Scripture, trees spiritually signify human beings, as that blind man who had been illuminated by the Lord said: “I see people like trees” (Mark 8). Daniel likewise interpreted the great tree in King Nebuchadnezzar’s vision as the king himself (Daniel 4). The fruit of a tree, moreover, signifies a person’s works, whether good or bad, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “Either make the tree good and its fruit good, or make the tree bad and its fruit bad” (Matthew 12). [Col. 0742A]

But it may be asked why the Lord himself says, “A good tree is not one that produces bad fruit, nor is a bad tree one that produces good fruit,” when we read that the apostle Peter, certainly a good tree, produced bad fruit when he denied God and his master; while, conversely, no one doubts that Judas was a bad tree, and yet he produced good fruit when he followed the Lord together with the other disciples.

The answer is that a good tree—that is, a good person—produces good fruits only as long as he perseveres in a good intention; and a bad tree produces bad fruits only as long as an evil intention endures. For just as fruit proceeds from the root of a tree, so the fruit of an action proceeds from the root of an intention. Therefore the intention must be of such a kind that it produces a corresponding fruit, as the Lord says: “As your intention has been, so also will your work be.” Moreover, one who appears to be good can produce bad fruits if he abandons a good intention; and one who is thought bad can produce good fruits if, through repentance, he corrects his past evils. [Col. 0742B]

In accordance with this meaning, we read that David, certainly a good tree, produced bad fruit when he committed both murder and adultery. Conversely, Nebuchadnezzar, although he was a bad tree, produced good fruit when he ordered the God of Daniel to be worshiped throughout his kingdom. Similarly, Jethro, although previously a bad tree, produced good fruit when he gave Moses useful advice. Paul too, although he was a good tree, produced bad fruit when he persecuted the Church of God.

And because things hidden [Col. 0742C] from human beings are pleasing to God, the Lord reveals how human beings can distinguish between good and bad trees when he adds:

“For each tree is known by its fruit.” Just as we distinguish visible trees by their fruit, determining of what kind or taste they are, so we can distinguish spiritual trees—that is, human beings—by their works, determining what sort of intention they possess.

For if the apostle Paul declares what fruits a bad tree produces, or by what they can be recognized, he says: “Now the works of the flesh are manifest: fornication, impurity, avarice, the worship of idols, sorcery, enmities, quarrels, jealousies, anger, disputes, dissensions, factions, envy, drunkenness, revelries, and things like these. I warn you, as I warned you before, that those who do such things will not obtain the kingdom of God” (Galatians 5). [Col. 0742D]

But what fruits a good tree produces, the same apostle shows when he adds: “The fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, long-suffering, gentleness, faith, modesty, self-control, chastity; against such things there is no law” (ibid.).

The Prophet rejoiced that he had produced these fruits when he said: “But I, like a fruitful olive tree in the house of God, have hoped in the mercy of God forever and ever” (Psalm 51). He also described such a tree elsewhere, saying: “Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly and has not stood in the way of sinners” (Psalm 1). He added: “And he shall be like a tree planted beside streams of water, which shall yield its fruit in its season. And its leaf shall not fall” (Psalm 1). And again: “The righteous shall flourish like the palm tree, and shall multiply like the cedar of Lebanon” (Psalm 91).

But what end a bad tree has, the Lord shows in the Gospel when he says: “Every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire” (Matthew 7). The prophet Jeremiah describes such a tree when he says: “Cursed is the man who trusts in man, makes flesh his arm, and turns his heart away from the Lord. He shall be like a tamarisk in the desert and shall not see when good comes” (Jeremiah 17). [Col. 0743A]

Of this it is further said: “For they do not gather figs from thorns, nor harvest grapes from a bramble.”

A thorn and a bramble are trees full of prickles, so that they can scarcely, or not at all, be handled without injury. [Col. 0743B] The vine and the fig tree are their opposites: they possess both the taste of sweet flavor and the fragrance of a pleasant scent. Therefore thorns and brambles signify vices and sins, of which it was said to the first man: “Your land shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you” (Genesis 3).

There are some people in whom the prickles of sins abound so greatly that their company cannot be maintained without injury. Since they live badly within themselves, they are bitter, harsh, and unpleasant toward their neighbors, either by living wickedly or by inflicting injuries. There are others, however, who, like a vine, display in their works the sweet remembrance of the heavenly homeland and give forth the fragrance of a good reputation, drawing others toward heavenly love—not only by supporting the needs of the needy with earthly possessions, but also by gently ministering the word of life through spiritual instruction. [Col. 0743C]

But because those in whom the pangs of crimes abound cannot possess such qualities, this is declared by the Lord’s voice when it says: “For they do not gather figs from thorns, nor harvest grapes from a bramble.”

By the thorn and the bramble we may also understand the wicked doctrine of heretics, which wounds and tears the souls of those who hear it. Such people must be avoided so completely that, insofar as possible, no participation or conversation should be maintained with them. For, as Scripture says, “Whoever touches pitch will be defiled by it” (Ecclesiasticus 13), and “Whoever breaks through a hedge will be bitten by a serpent” (Ecclesiastes 10). Therefore the Apostle warns us, saying: “Avoid a heretical person after one and a second correction, knowing that such a person is perverted” (Titus 3). [Col. 0743D]

Yet although a thorn does not produce a cluster of grapes, it sometimes supports a vine together with its cluster. We occasionally see in vineyards a thorny sedge (*carex*) supporting a vine with its cluster. Although the cluster proceeds from a lofty root, nevertheless a thorn often supports the vine together with its cluster.

What, then, should be done? Is the grape to be abandoned because of the thorn? No. Rather, as one of the wise men said, the cluster should be gathered in such a way that the thorn is nevertheless avoided.

Accordingly, following this comparison, because heretics teach certain good and useful things in their assertions, they must first be discerned by ecclesiastical men; afterward the good is to be gathered and the bad avoided.

This was figuratively shown in the Scriptures of the Old Testament (Exodus 11), when, as the children of Israel were leaving Egypt, he commanded them to borrow from their neighbors a great number of vessels of gold and silver and to strip Egypt.

By gold the brilliance of eloquence is signified, as Solomon says: “A desirable treasure rests in the mouth of the wise” (Proverbs 21). By silver, which both sounds and shines, the subtlety of preaching is expressed, as the Psalmist testifies: “The sayings of the Lord are pure sayings, silver tested in fire” (Psalm 11). [Col. 0744A]

We spiritually borrow vessels of gold and silver from the Egyptians when we learn from heretics or pagans useful judgments necessary for our faith. This should be done by those who are so firmly rooted in the Catholic faith that the subtlety of heretical perversity cannot harm them in any way.

Therefore elsewhere in the Law the Lord figuratively commanded, saying: “When you go out to battle against your enemies, and the Lord your God delivers them into your hands and you lead them away captive, if you see among the number of women a young woman who pleases your eyes, and you wish to have her as a wife, you shall bring her into your house. But you shall first shave the hair of her head and cut the tips of her nails; and she shall remain in your house mourning her father and mother for one month. Afterward you shall go in to her, and she shall be your wife” (Deuteronomy 21; Judges 3). [Col. 0744B]

For we spiritually go to war against our enemies when we contend with heretics concerning the Christian faith and religion. Once they have been overcome by divine authority, if we see in their discussions judgments useful and necessary to our faith, we ought to take them to ourselves as a wife, because wisdom is called a man’s wife. [Col. 0744C] Yet we must first shave the hair of her head and cut the tips of her nails—that is, we must cast away and reject whatever is heretical, distorted, and wicked in their teaching.

Moreover, if some heretics wish to convert to the Catholic faith, they should be received, but only on the condition that they anathematize their former error.

Explaining what he had said in the words, “For they do not gather figs from thorns, nor harvest grapes from a bramble,” the Lord added:

“A good person brings forth good from the good treasure of his heart, and an evil person brings forth evil from the evil.”

A treasury (*thesaurus*) is a place where gold is stored; for *thesis* (θέσις) in Greek means “placement” in Latin. Therefore, in this passage, “treasure” signifies the intention of the heart, in accordance with what he says elsewhere: “Where your treasure is, there your heart will be” (Matthew 6). [Col. 0744D]

“Thus a good person brings forth good from the good treasure of his heart” (Matthew 12), because good speech proceeds from the heart’s good desire. Likewise, “an evil person brings forth evil from the evil treasure” (ibid.), because the fruit of wicked action proceeds from an evil intention of the heart, in accordance with what the Lord says: “For from the heart come evil thoughts, adulteries, drunkenness, murders, thefts, blasphemies” (Matthew 15), and things like these.

Therefore he further adds, saying: “Out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks.”

Here someone may perhaps ask why he says, “Out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks,” since people often—and especially those who are called hypocrites— [Col. 0745A] lie by saying one thing instead of another, deceiving others and being deceived by others.

The answer is readily apparent: although these things are hidden from human beings, they are nevertheless manifest to God, who sees what is in the heart more clearly than you can see what is on the face. Scripture says: “The things that are in the human heart your eyes see, O Lord.”

Therefore “out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks” only for the one before whose eyes everything is bare and open (Hebrews 4), and who sees the intention before the tongue utters the word.

Yet hypocritical people cannot always remain hidden, because what they ardently love in their hearts they frequently bring forth in speech. Those who know God with their whole heart also reveal their desire in their words, in accordance with the saying of the wise man:

> Love presses upon the mind; ardor boils over in speech.

[Col. 0745B]

But because, as we have said, there are some who, in order to deceive human beings, do not fear God’s judgment, a fitting rebuke follows:

“Why do you call me ‘Lord, Lord,’ and do not do what I say?”

To say “Lord, Lord” appears to belong to the fruit of a good tree and to the good treasure of the heart. But not doing what he commands belongs more to disobedience than to obedience, because, as the Apostle says of false professors of the faith: “They profess to know God, but by their deeds they deny him” (Titus 1).

The Lord reproves such people through the prophet, saying: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isaiah 29). [Col. 0745C] And elsewhere in the Gospel: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 7).

Therefore, when the foolish virgins were crying at the bridegroom’s door, “Lord, Lord, open to us,” he testifies that he will say to them: “Amen I say to you, I do not know you” (Matthew 25).

He wishes his confessors to be doers of his commandments. Therefore he further adds a comparison, saying:

“Everyone who comes to me, hears my words, and does them—I will show you what he is like.”

And beautifully, after saying “and hears my words,” he added “and does them,” because, as the Apostle says: “It is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but the doers will be justified” (Romans 2).

The Savior himself, when he had said in the Gospel, “Blessed are those who hear the word of God,” added, “and keep it” (Luke 11). Therefore elsewhere the Lord blesses his disciples, saying: “Do you know these things? Blessed will you be if you do them” (John 13). [Col. 0745D]

For this reason John too, in his Apocalypse, after saying, “Blessed is the one who hears and reads the words of this book,” immediately added, “and keeps what is written [Col. 0746A] in it” (Revelation 1).

The Lord especially recognizes as his own those who join good works to right faith. Therefore the Psalmist, when praising the saints, said: “They called upon the Lord, and he heard them,” and added: “They kept his testimonies and the commandment that he gave them” (Psalm 98). And elsewhere: “Blessed are those who keep judgment and do justice at all times” (Psalm 10).

Whoever, then, is such a person rightly becomes an imitator of the Lord himself, as follows:

“He is like a man building a house, who dug deep and laid its foundations upon rock.”

In this comparison the man is the Lord Jesus Christ, because he builds a house, namely the holy Church, not from visible stones and wood, but [Col. 0746B] from the precious and incorruptible souls of the saints. Of this it is said through the Prophet: “Holiness befits your house, O Lord, for length of days” (Psalm 92).

“He dug deep,” because he completely uprooted earthly desire from the hearts of his faithful.

“And he laid the foundation upon rock,” because he established or stabilized the faith of the Church upon himself. Thus he says to Peter, whose name was given from the firmness of the rock: “Upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matthew 16). For the rock signifies Christ, as the Apostle says: “The rock was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10).

But when it adds, “When a flood came, the river struck against that house, and it could not move it,” the meaning is perfectly clear: the Church has often been shaken by persecutions, yet has not [Col. 0746C] been moved from the faith—at times by the assaults of pagans, at times by the perverse doctrines of false brothers, at times by the attacks of demons, or by its own frailty.

Against all these things the Church stands firm, because it does not trust in itself but in Christ, saying with the Prophet: “You have set me high upon a rock; you have led me, because you became my hope, a tower of strength against the enemy” (Psalm 60). And again: “He set my feet upon a rock and directed my steps” (Psalm 39). [Col. 0746D]

Therefore it is also added: “For it was founded upon rock,” that is, upon Christ. Of him the Apostle says: “No one can lay any foundation other than that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus” (1 Corinthians 3).

For just as nothing is placed before a foundation in a building, so whoever places the love of God above all things, although he may be struck, cannot fall. The things built upon it cannot totter when the things that contain them stand firmly fixed.

Therefore elsewhere it is said of the Church: “And the gates of hell shall not prevail against it” (Matthew 16).

# VARIOUS HOMILIES ON THE SAINTS

Some proper to individual saints, others common to all.

[Col. 0747]

# HOMILY 1. ON THE FESTAL DAY OF SAINT ANDREW THE APOSTLE

[Col. 0747A]

**(Matthew 4.)** “At that time: As Jesus was walking beside the Sea of Galilee, he saw two brothers, Simon who is called Peter, and Andrew his brother.” And so forth.

In all his works, which the Lord Jesus Christ graciously displayed for our imitation, he wished to make this clear: if we want to receive the virtues of the soul, we must first overcome the goads of temptations.

Accordingly, before preaching the Gospel to the world, he was first baptized by John, withdrew into the desert, and there, fasting for forty days and forty nights, overcame the devil’s triple temptation. Then, after leaving it, he walked beside the Sea of Galilee and, as the present [Col. 0747B] reading relates, chose disciples.

By this action he instructed us that, if we want to receive good, we must first turn away from evil. The proper order of living is that whoever wishes to receive virtues must first overcome vices. For after conquering the devil, the Lord wished to choose disciples, to show us that we can ascend to the summit of the virtues only when we have bravely overcome the devil’s temptations.

As the Apostle says: “Tribulation produces endurance, endurance produces testing, testing produces hope, and hope does not disappoint. Because the love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us” (Romans 5).

But since we are going to speak about the calling of the apostles, we must first recall something about the setting of the place where these things are said to have happened.

This sea, now called Galilee, is known [Col. 0747C] by various names because of the different regions lying around it. It is called the Sea of Galilee because of the neighboring province of Galilee. It is also called the Sea of Tiberias, after the city of Tiberias. It is called the Lake of Gennesaret because, when the winds blow and the waves ripple, it seems to generate a breeze from itself. It is also called the Lake of Gennesaret because of the same neighboring city. By some it is called the Asphalt Sea, because of the unsuitability of its harbor.

It extends for one hundred and forty *stadia* in length and forty in width. It is not called a sea because its waters are bitter—for they are sweet to drink and suitable for fishing—but it is an idiom of the Hebrew language to call all gatherings of waters “seas,” as it is written in Genesis (chapter 1): [Col. 0747D] “He called the gatherings of waters seas.”

But if we consider these things spiritually, it should not be thought irrelevant that the evangelist described the Lord as neither sitting nor standing, but walking beside the Sea of Galilee. The very [Col. 0748A] movement of the Lord’s body should not be considered devoid of mystery.

The sea in this passage signifies the world. And appropriately so, because just as the sea cannot be still but is always advancing and receding, so the world is shaken by various disturbances and fluctuations. Hence the Psalmist says: “You have shaken the earth, O Lord” (Psalm 59).

The sea is called *mare* from *meare* (“to move”), because it is always advancing and receding. It signifies, as we have said, the world, which grows by being born and diminishes by dying, is lifted up in prosperity and cast down in adversity.

The Lord came to this sea when, through the mystery of his incarnation, he appeared visibly to the world. As the Apostle says, he “emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of human beings, and being found in appearance as a man, he humbled himself” (Philippians 2). [Col. 0748B]

He is not said to have stood or sat, but to have walked about, because, although he was born in the world, he did not remain in the world as other mortals and other human beings do. After the teaching of the holy Gospel, after the manifestation of his miracles, and after his sacred passion, he rose from the dead and returned victoriously to heaven. As he himself says: “I came forth from the Father” (John 16), and so forth. His walking signified this.

Concerning his movement or passage, it is said through Peter: “He went about doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil.”

Nor should we pass over without consideration the fact that, when the Lord was about to choose disciples, he walked beside the sea, and is later narrated to have walked upon the waves of the sea before them.

As we have said, the sea signifies the world. While the disciples [Col. 0748C] were fishing in the sea, the Lord walked beside the sea, because although he came into the world according to nature, he was nevertheless alien to the world according to guilt. For, as Peter most truthfully testifies: “He committed no sin, and no deceit was found in his mouth” (1 Peter 2).

But perhaps someone asks why the Lord wished first to choose disciples from Galilee and not from Judea or the other regions that were considered more distinguished.

To this the curious person may answer that although the Lord’s glorious birth was first celebrated in Judea, his holy conception was first announced in Galilee by the angel to the Virgin. The evangelist Luke testifies to this, saying: “At that time the angel Gabriel was sent by God to a city of Galilee named Nazareth, to a virgin betrothed to a man whose name was Joseph” (Luke 1). [Col. 0748D]

A little later he added:

“Do not be afraid, Mary; you have found favor with the Lord. Behold, you will conceive and bear a son” (ibid.).

It was fitting that where the beginning of his birth had taken its origin, there the members of his body should receive their growth; where the sun of righteousness had first risen, there [Col. 0749A] the shining stars should appear to the world; and where the Virgin had heard, “Behold, you will conceive” (Luke 1), there the fishermen should hear, “Come after me.”

Or perhaps the Lord wished to choose disciples from Galilee for this reason: through the power of his miracles and through his manifestation, he first became known to the world in Galilee.

For we read that he performed his first miracle at Cana of Galilee, when he made wine from water, “and manifested his glory, and his disciples believed in him” (John 2). And Peter says: “You know the word that came to be throughout all Judea, after the baptism that John preached, Jesus of Nazareth, beginning from Galilee” (Acts 10).

But we say that he wished to choose his first disciples from Galilee because of the mystery of the name itself. For Galilee is interpreted as “transmigration [Col. 0749B] made” or “revelation accomplished.” When the Lord chose disciples from Galilee, he instructed us that, if we wish to cling to his discipleship, we must first migrate from riches to virtues and from love of the world to love of God, saying with the Prophet: “For we are strangers and sojourners before you, as were all our fathers” (Psalm 39).

Thus, in Galilee—that is, in eternal revelation—contemplating the face of the Lord, we may say with the Apostle: “But we, with unveiled face contemplating the glory of the Lord, are transformed from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of God” (2 Corinthians 3).

“He saw two brothers, Simon who is called Peter, and Andrew his brother, casting their nets into the sea, and he called them.”

For God to see is to choose, just as not to know [Col. 0749C] is to reject. For just as he does not know those whom he rejects—whence at the end he will say to the rejected: “I do not know where you are from” (Matthew 25)—so he is said to see those whom he has chosen for eternal presence, as it was said to someone: “When you were under the fig tree, I saw you” (John 2).

The Lord therefore saw Peter and Andrew, whom, through prevenient grace, he chose as worthy for the lot of the apostleship.

Nor should we omit the fact that in his first calling he chose brothers according to the flesh. Peter and Andrew were brothers not only in spirit but also true brothers according to the flesh. By choosing brothers according to the flesh, he showed that those who wish to cling to his discipleship must be brothers not according to the flesh but according to the spirit—not by genealogy but by love.

All of us who have been reborn in Christ have [Col. 0749D] one Father, God, to whom we say daily in prayer: “Our Father, who are in heaven” (Matthew 6). Concerning him he himself says in the Gospel: “Do not call anyone your father on earth; one is your Father, who is in heaven” (Matthew 23).

Let us glory in being his children, saying with the Apostle: “We are children of God, but it has not yet appeared what we shall be” (1 John 3).

Our mother, however, is the holy Church, which spiritually gives birth to us daily through faith and the sacrament of baptism.

Since, therefore, we have one Father, God, and one mother, the Church, it follows that we should be brothers: that is, that we should think as one, have the same mind, not disagree, and not be divided, so that we may be counted among those to whom the Savior says: “For you are all brothers” (Matthew 23). [Col. 0750A]

The Prophet admired these spiritual brothers when he said: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is when brothers dwell together as one” (Psalm 133).

It should be noted that he chose two brothers to show that he wishes his disciples to possess a twofold love: namely, love of God and love of neighbor. “Woe to the one who is alone,” says Scripture, “for when he falls, he has no one to lift him up” (Ecclesiastes 4).

For this reason the Lord chose them in pairs and later sent them in pairs to preach, to show that no one ought to undertake the office of preaching unless he bears in his heart love of God and neighbor.

Or certainly he chose them in pairs to confirm authority, so that they would become teachers of the two Testaments and what he says [Col. 0750B] elsewhere might be fulfilled in them: “Every learned scribe in the kingdom of heaven is like a householder who brings forth from his treasure new things and old” (Matthew 13).

“They were fishermen.”

The Lord chose fishermen and uneducated men so that the faith of believers, which was to be instructed through their teaching and preaching, would not be thought to arise from eloquence of words rather than from the power of God.

The teacher of humility, who came into the world saying, “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart, and you will find rest for your souls” (Matthew 11), wished to preserve an example of humility in all his works, even in the calling of the apostles.

For he did not choose a mother who was powerful, but one who was as exceedingly holy as she was exceedingly poor, so poor that she could not find a lamb to offer for her [Col. 0750C] Son. Nor was he born in cedar-paneled houses decorated with varied colors of painting; rather, he was laid in a manger, because there was no room for him in the inn.

He was not wrapped in purple garments shining with gold and pearls, but, as it is written: “She wrapped him in swaddling clothes” (Luke 2).

This humility, which he had preserved in these and similar matters, he did not abandon in the calling of the two. For he did not choose the powerful or sons of kings, nor philosophers or the wise of the world, but poor and simple men who sought their daily food by the craft of fishing.

Nevertheless, through their teaching and preaching he called the powerful and wise of the world to his faith, because, as the Apostle says: “The world did not know God through wisdom; it pleased God through the foolishness of preaching to save those who believe” (1 Corinthians 1).

And again: “Our speech and preaching were not in words of human wisdom, but in [Col. 0750D] power” (1 Corinthians 2), so that the cross of Christ might not be emptied of its power. “For not many powerful, not many noble, but what is foolish in the world God chose to confound the strong; and what is lowly and despised in the world God chose to confound the wise; and what is not, to destroy what is” (1 Corinthians 1).

But let us see what the Lord says concerning such men:

“And he said to them: ‘Come after me.’”

Peter and Andrew are rightly said first to have been seen and afterward called to follow, because all the elect are first called to follow from the inward presence of God, and it is said to [Col. 0751A] them:

“Come after me.”

What does “Come after me” mean except “Follow me; obey my commandments and not your own desires”? To go after the Lord is to imitate his footsteps, as he himself says: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself” (Matthew 16), and so forth.

And again: “Whoever does not carry his cross and come after me is not worthy of me” (Luke 14). Therefore it is commanded in the Law: “You shall walk after the Lord your God.”

But let us hear what he says in his promise. For he says: “I will make you become fishers of human beings.”

He does not say “fishers of fish,” but “fishers of human beings.” He changed the name but did not remove the [Col. 0751B] occupation. For after the resurrection we read that they went fishing.

And appropriately he wished to make fishers of human beings from fishers of fish. For just as it is the fisherman’s task to board a boat, hold nets in his hands, and draw fish from the depths of the whirlpools to the shore, so these men, received into the bosom of the Church, boarded the ship of faith and held the nets of preaching in word and deed. From the bitter and dark whirlpools of the world they drew many people toward the true light, which says: “I am the light of the world; whoever follows me does not walk in darkness” (John 8), fulfilling the prophecy that says: “The people who walk in darkness” (Isaiah 9), and so forth.

See Peter at Jerusalem holding nets in his hands and spiritually catching many fish from the depths of the whirlpools. For we read that at his preaching five thousand people believed on one day and three thousand on another.

See blessed Andrew, whose feast we celebrate today, holding nets in his hands in [Col. 0751C] Achaia and spiritually catching many fish. For we read that not only the entire city but also the entire region believed through his preaching, as he himself said: “Christ sent me to this province, where I acquired no small people.”

The Lord promised these fishermen to the Church when he said through the prophet: “I will send my fishermen, and they will fish for them; and my hunters, and they will hunt them from every mountain and from every hill” (Jeremiah 16).

It is pleasant to observe that the Lord, who chose Peter and Andrew from the craft of fishing, also called Paul, who was not lesser in grace, from the craft of tentmaking to the office of preaching.

Just as these men appropriately became fishers of human beings from fishers of fish, so Paul, who had been a builder of bodily [Col. 0751D] tents, was suitably transferred to construct spiritual tents.

He built spiritual tents when, through his preaching, he expelled the worship of demons from human minds, so that Christ might dwell in their hearts through faith. He also spiritually built tents for Christ when he filled the region from Jerusalem to Illyricum with the Gospel of Christ, so that the man who had built bodily tents for people destined to die might afterward, as we have said, begin to build spiritual tents for God in souls destined to live forever.

He built tents for God when he preached: “Repay everyone what is owed: tax to whom tax, revenue to whom revenue” (Romans 13), and so forth.

Or when he instructed how husbands should relate to wives and wives to husbands; how parents should relate to children and children to parents; how slaves should relate to masters and masters to [Col. 0752A] slaves (Ephesians 4–5).

The Prophet admired the beauty of these tents when he said: “How beautiful are your tents, Jacob, and your tabernacles, O Israel” (Numbers 24). And the Psalmist: “How beloved are your tabernacles, O Lord of hosts” (Psalm 84), and so forth.

The obedience of the apostles followed the Lord’s command. For it continues:

“Immediately they left their nets and the boat and followed him.” In their deed our pride is confounded and our hardness rebuked: we are daily worn down by scourges, frightened by threats, stirred by signs, and encouraged by promises, yet we disdain to follow the one who calls us. But they had not seen him performing miracles, nor had they been encouraged by his promises; nevertheless, at a single command they left their nets and boat and followed him.

Let us therefore follow them whom we have deserved to have as patrons in Christ, so that, stirred by their example, we may at least after many admonitions and promises willingly leave what we lose every day, so that the Lord’s promise may be fulfilled: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 5). For he sits in heaven who still admonishes us on earth concerning our conversion.

But those who wish to renounce their own wills commonly put forward poverty as an excuse, saying: “We wish to imitate those who despised the world, but we have nothing to leave.” To them we reply that Almighty God, in the renunciation of the world, weighs not one’s wealth but one’s vow; he does not consider what you have in your chest, but what sort of conscience you have. Therefore, if you have temporal possessions, sell them; but if you have none, you have been freed from a great burden. You can follow Christ all the more freely the less you are bound by the ropes of riches.

We also urge such people to consider what and how much our holy fathers left behind. Did they not leave nets and a boat? And yet afterward, when the Lord promised it, they were worthy to hear: “Everyone who has left house, fields, father and mother, wife and children, brothers and sisters for my sake will receive a hundredfold and will possess eternal life” (Matthew 13). Peter, speaking freely on behalf of them all, replied: “Lord, behold, we have left everything and followed you; what, then, will there be for us?” And he who, as we have said, weighs not wealth but one’s vow, said: “Amen, I say to you, you who have left everything and followed me: in the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty, you also will sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (ibid.).

Peter and Andrew seem to have left little in their nets and boat, yet they received great grace and reward from the Lord. Nevertheless, they had left much, since they had renounced the will to possess. For as much is left by those who follow as can be coveted by those who do not follow. The kingdom of God is worth as much as you possess. Half of his property was worth that much to Zacchaeus; a boat and nets were worth that much to Peter and Andrew. Likewise, although they had everything to leave, it profited Hermogenes and Socrates nothing, because they did not imitate Christ. A cup of cold water also has value; and if all these things are lacking, it can be acquired by good will alone. For when the Lord was born, the citizens of heaven were seen on earth, crying: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2).

After saying “having left everything,” he rightly added, “they followed him.” For he has left all his possessions in vain who does not follow Christ, that is, imitate him.

Amid all this we must consider what kind of craftsman the Holy Spirit is. Without delay, he not only changes the mind he touches but also possesses and teaches it. He touched a boy who played the lyre and made him a psalmist (1 Samuel 16). He touched a herdsman who was pruning sycamores and made him a prophet (Amos 7). He touched a young man who practiced abstinence and made him a judge of elders (Daniel 13). He touched a tax collector and made him an evangelist (Matthew 9). He touched a persecutor and appointed him teacher of the nations (Acts 9). He touched Peter and Andrew and appointed fishermen of fish as apostles.

We must therefore ask this craftsman and entreat him with the most devoted prayers to deign to touch our minds, since for him merely to touch is to teach.

“And proceeding from there, he saw two other brothers, James the son of Zebedee and John his brother, in the boat with Zebedee their father, mending their nets, and he called them. And immediately they left their nets and their father and followed him.”

The repeated calling of two pairs confirms the preceding account. For the disciples were called in pairs not only once but again, because there are two things that must be carefully observed toward our neighbors out of charity: first, that we harm no one; second, that we provide whatever good we can. For the one who said, “What you do not wish to be done to you, do not do to another” (Tobit 4), says elsewhere: “Whatever you wish people to do to you, do also to them” (Matthew 7).

“Zebedee” is interpreted as “whitening” and signifies the devil. The name “whitening” rightly suits him because, although he is dark by merit, as the Apostle says, he disguises himself as an angel of light (2 Corinthians 11). These disciples, then, who were called by the Lord, are remembered as sons of Zebedee because, as the Apostle says (Ephesians 2), we were all children of wrath before we were redeemed—not by the condition of nature, but by imitation and by the transgression of our first parent.

Zebedee’s boat signifies unbelief; the equipment of that boat is vices and sins. The Apostle Paul enumerates such things, saying: “The works of the flesh are manifest: fornications, impurities, shamelessness, greed, service of idols, magical arts, and things like these” (Galatians 5).

Just as these disciples, when called by the Lord, left their father and followed him, and are not said to have returned to their father afterward, so we, who by divine grace have been freed from the power of the devil and called to the heavenly kingdom, must not return to him either for love of our parents or under the pretext of any desire. This is because the Lord says: “No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God” (Luke 9). Rather, we must persevere tirelessly in good works to the end, because, as the Savior says: “The one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matthew 10).

Hence, when someone said, “Lord, I will follow you wherever you go, but first let me bury my father,” he replied: “Let the dead bury their own dead” (Matthew 8). But you, follow Christ.

Having said these few things about the calling of the disciples, let us consider why the Lord did not choose four disciples at his first calling without reason. The number four is perfect, and, being divided into its parts, signifies perfection. For it is divided into one, two, and three.

One, its first part, signifies perfection, because there is “one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all” (Ephesians 4). Two, another of its parts, pertains to perfection because of the two Testaments or the twofold commandment of love. Three signifies the undivided Trinity and the three periods—before the Law, under the Law, and under grace—or because the inner human being consists of three things: memory, understanding, and will.

The number four is perfect because of the four Gospels, or the four seasons of the year, or the four elements of which we consist in the outer human being—air, fire, earth, and water—which are cold, hot, dry, and moist; or because of the four rivers that flow from paradise; or certainly because of the four principal virtues: prudence, temperance, fortitude, and justice.

These virtues are signified by these disciples not only in number but also in their names. Peter, who is interpreted by some as “one who recognizes,” signifies prudence. The first part of this virtue is to know God and his will. For just as the person who says in his heart, “There is no God,” is foolish (Psalm 13), so the person who knows God is prudent. Peter possessed this virtue: seeing a human being with his heart, he recognized God and said: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matthew 16).

Andrew, whose name is interpreted as “manly,” signifies fortitude. He possessed this virtue not only in his name but also in his deeds, because he persevered manfully in the right faith even unto suffering. Indeed, when he was being led to crucifixion and saw the cross, he said joyfully:

“Hail, precious cross, which has been consecrated in the body of Christ and adorned with his limbs as with pearls. Rejoicing and exulting, I come to you, so that you may receive me from human beings and return me to my teacher, so that through you he may receive me who through you redeemed me.”

Through James, whose name is interpreted as “supplanter,” justice is signified: justice knows how to supplant iniquity and love equity. We ought to possess it in all our actions, as the prophet says: “I will show you, O human being” (Micah 6), and so forth.

John, whose name is interpreted as “grace of God,” or “in whom there is grace,” signifies temperance, which is also called discernment and is the mother of all virtues. He possessed this virtue when he said: “Are you our angel or one of our adversaries?” [The wording is uncertain in the supplied text; the source reads *Angelus noster es an adversariorum* (John 5).]

For a person to be prudent, strong, and temperate is not something he has from himself; he receives it through divine grace. When, therefore, the Lord chose his four disciples at his first calling, he made known to us through that number that, if we wish to be his disciples, we must possess these four virtues.

We must be Peter by recognizing what is good, so that we may see past, present, and future, in accordance with the Lord’s admonition: “Be prudent as serpents” (Matthew 10). Peter himself says: “Be prudent and watchful in prayers” (1 Peter 4).

We must be Andrew by holding firmly through fortitude to what we recognize as good, as the angel admonishes John in the Apocalypse, saying: “Be strong in battle and fight with the ancient serpent” (Titus 2), and so forth.

We must be James by supplanting vices through justice, so that we may maintain justice in all our actions, as the Apostle says: “Let us live justly and piously” (Titus 2). Solomon likewise says: “Love justice, you who judge the earth” (Wisdom 1).

We must be John by attaining the grace of God and possessing discernment with it, so that, distinguishing between good and evil, we may hold to the good and abandon the evil, in accordance with the Apostle’s words: “Test everything; hold fast to what is good” (1 Thessalonians 5).

When we have become such people, we will have in the chariot of the cherubim the face of a human being through prudence, of a lion through fortitude, of a calf through justice, and of an eagle through discernment.

Allegorically, these four disciples, as some say, represent two peoples. Peter, whose name is interpreted as “one who recognizes,” signifies the Jewish people, who came to know God through observing the ceremonies. James signifies the same people: by believing first, he supplant­ed his gentile brother. Andrew, whose name is interpreted as “manly,” signifies the gentile people, who, after believing in God, remained manfully in the faith. John, whose name is interpreted as “grace of God,” signifies the same people, because the gentile people deserved to be saved through the assistance of God’s grace, not through their own merits, as Paul says: “By the grace of God the nations have been saved” (Ephesians 2).

Let us therefore imitate these apostles of God, so that through his grace we may deserve to be saved, as they were. May he himself deign to grant this, who lives and reigns without end, and so forth.

## HOMILY II. ON THE NATIVITY OF SAINT JOHN THE BAPTIST

[Col. 0755D]

(Luke 1.) “At that time: The time came for Elizabeth to give birth, and she bore a son. And her neighbors and relatives heard.” And so forth.

Not only the deeds and virtues of the saints are full of wonders; sometimes the very words in which they are written for the memory of posterity are not without mysteries. The evangelist wished to show this at the beginning of this reading when, about to describe the birth of the Lord’s precursor, he said: “The time came for Elizabeth to give birth, and she bore a son.”

Sacred Scripture is accustomed to use the word “fulfillment” only in connection with the birth, activity, or death of the good. Thus, “the days of Mary were fulfilled for her to give birth to a son.” And, “the time of Elizabeth was fulfilled for her to give birth.” And Solomon “completed building the house of the Lord” (1 Kings 9). Abraham, or some other father, died old and full of days.

Fulfillment is rightly mentioned in the works of the saints because, even in a short time, they reach the summit of perfection, as it is written of one of them: “Being perfected in a short time, he fulfilled many years” (Wisdom 4), because his works were pleasing to God. Therefore, to show how great the perfection of the Lord’s precursor would be, the evangelist decided to use the word “fulfillment” in the very account of his birth.

By contrast, the days of the wicked are empty and void. Although they live happily for a long time, they never reach the summit of perfection. Of them the Psalmist says: “Men of blood and deceit will not live out half their days” (Psalm 54). And of their leader blessed Job says: “Before his days are fulfilled, he will perish; and when the sun grows hot, he will be loosened from his place” (Job 6). The Psalmist had despised their shadowy happiness, which would pass away without perfection, when he said: “I saw the wicked exalted above measure” (Psalm 36), and so forth.

“And his neighbors heard that the Lord had magnified his mercy toward her, and they rejoiced with her.”

This account of the evangelist agrees with the preceding evangelical promise. When the angel promised Zachariah that John would be born, he said among other things: “He will be your joy and exultation, and many will rejoice at his birth” (Luke 1). Now, after the child had been born, the evangelist adds: “And his neighbors and relatives heard,” and so forth.

Elizabeth’s neighbors and relatives rightly rejoiced with her, not only because she had borne a son in advanced age, but also because she had received him through a promise, in the likeness of Sarah and Hannah. Earlier the evangelist had said of Zachariah and Elizabeth that they were both righteous before God, walking blamelessly in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord. Now he demonstrates this in their actions when he says:

“And it happened on the eighth day that they came to circumcise the child, and they were calling him by the name of his father, Zachariah.”

The Law had commanded that a newborn infant be circumcised on the eighth day. This shows with what zeal they observed the other legal commandments, since they were so diligent in keeping this commandment as well.

The neighbors and relatives who had gathered were calling him by the name of his father, Zachariah, so that the dignity that seemed to have been lost in the old and speechless father might be recovered in the son. We believe that the practice of giving names to children on the day of circumcision arose from the fact that the blessed patriarch Abraham, together with the sign of circumcision, received an increase or alteration of his name (Genesis 17).

“And his mother answered and said: ‘By no means; he shall be called John.’”

She had not learned this from her husband, since he remained mute because he had not believed that a son would be born to him. Rather, he had learned it from the angel, while she had learned it from the Holy Spirit. For it was fitting that the herald of the new grace should be called by the new name assigned to him by divine election, not by carnal kinship.

“And they said to her: ‘No one in your family is called by this name.’ And they were making signs to his father, asking what he wished him to be called. And asking for a writing tablet, he wrote, saying: ‘John is his name.’”

Because the neighbors and relatives who had gathered wanted to give the son his father’s name, while the mother did not consent, they tried, by whatever signs they could, to question the mute father. But he asked for a writing tablet—that is, a writing stylus—and what he could not express in words, he expressed in writing, saying: “John is his name.”

Here we should note that he did not say, “John will be his name,” as though he were looking toward the future, but, “John is his name.” It was as if he said: “We are not giving him this name, for he already has the name we have recognized, not one we have chosen.”

This name was therefore not first given to him at that moment, but before he was born, when the angel Gabriel said to Zachariah: “Do not be afraid, Zachariah; your prayer has been heard, and Elizabeth your wife will bear you a son, and you shall call his name John” (Luke 1). There he was shown in advance as one who would become the great precursor of the Lord, when his name was foretold before his birth.

Something new is shown in advance as destined to occur in the deeds of those to whom God assigns names before they are physically born. We read this of Isaac and Ishmael, of Solomon and Josiah, of John the Baptist, and of the Lord and Savior.

This John is therefore shown to be destined for greatness because he was named before he was born. The following words spoken by the divine voice to Jeremiah can apply to him: “Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you; and before you came out of the womb, I sanctified you and appointed you a prophet to the nations” (Jeremiah 1). And also: “The Lord called me from the womb; from my mother’s belly he remembered my name, and the Lord made my mouth like a sharp sword, under the shadow of his hand” (Isaiah 49).

“And everyone was amazed,” namely, at such agreement: the mother agreeing in words and the father in writing concerning the child’s name. They were especially amazed because no one in their family was called by this name.

“Immediately his mouth and his tongue were opened, and he was speaking.”

It was fitting that the tongue bound by unbelief should be released by faith, so that what had been said to him by the angel might be fulfilled: “Because you did not believe my words, you will be mute and unable to speak until the day when these things take place.” Since the voice of one crying in the wilderness was being born, it was fitting that at his birth the tongue of his father, who had earlier become mute, should be released.

He was not speaking idle or frivolous words, but blessing God. It is the custom of the saints always to bless the Lord, but especially then to open their mouths in his blessing when they have been freed from some tribulation. The hymn of the three young men makes this entirely clear (Daniel 3). Released from the furnace of blazing fire, they walked about, blessing not only God but also urging creation to praise him.

“And fear came upon all their neighbors, and throughout all the hill country of Judea all these words were being spoken.”

Because the herald of the judge was being born, the hearts not only of the neighbors but also of others were shaken by fear. They had heard that he had been born through an angelic promise from an old father and a barren mother, and they saw that at his birth his father’s tongue had been released. Their hearts were moved not only by wonder but also by fear. Hence they said:

“What, then, will this child be?” That is: What sort of person is he? But lest you think that John obtained this grace through his own power and not through divine assistance, it is rightly added:

“For the hand of the Lord was with him.”

In Scripture, “the hand of the Lord” signifies some assistance of divine protection, as we read in the Psalms: “Into your hands, Lord, I commend my spirit” (Psalm 30).

“And Zachariah his father was filled with the Holy Spirit and prophesied.”

Since the one who was born was destined to be not only a prophet but more than a prophet—for the Savior says of him in the Gospel, “Among those born of women no one has arisen greater than John” (Matthew 11)—his father received at his birth not merely the office of speaking. Filled also with the spirit of prophecy, he proclaimed the Savior’s coming.

Because he foresaw what was soon to happen, he narrated it in prophetic fashion as though it had already taken place, saying:

“Blessed is the Lord God of Israel, because he has visited and brought about the redemption of his people.”

Here we must consider the two things he mentioned: “He has visited, and he has brought about the redemption of his people.” Visitation pertains to the sick; redemption, to captives. The Lord Jesus Christ therefore visited and brought about the redemption of his people through his coming. He freed those who believed in him from the sickness of the soul and redeemed them from diabolical captivity by his precious blood.

Hence the conclusion of this song says: “The dawn from on high has visited us, to illuminate those who sit in darkness and in the shadow of death,” and so forth.

He says “his people,” not because he found them to be his when he came, but because by visiting and redeeming them he made them his, just as he himself says through the prophet Hosea: “I will call ‘Not my people’” (Hosea 2), and so forth.

These brief remarks have been made about the birth of the Lord’s precursor according to the literal sense.

Spiritually, when John’s birth is celebrated, the sublimity of the New Testament begins. “From the days of John,” says the Savior, “the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and those who use force seize it” (Matthew 11).

Elizabeth’s neighbors and relatives rejoiced at John’s birth because joy was born in heaven among the angels over the cleansing of the righteous, as the Lord says: “There will be joy before the angels of God in heaven” (Luke 15), and so forth.

Or the neighbors and relatives rejoiced with the mother at the birth of the new child because the Church experienced spiritual joy when through baptism she gave birth to a faithful people.

The grace of the New Testament also agrees with the fact that the circumcision of this same herald is celebrated on the eighth day. The number eight pertains to faith in the resurrection, as Solomon says: “Give a portion to seven, and indeed also to eight” (Ecclesiastes 11).
