And the Lord Jesus Christ, rising from the dead on the eighth day, showed that our resurrection would take place in the eighth age of the world.

Rightly, when the New Testament begins, John is circumcised on the eighth day. It is also beautifully fitting that at the birth of the new herald the father’s tongue is released, because spiritually the dignity of the priesthood and the mystery of the Old Testament, which had been hidden and bound, were manifested and revealed after the Lord’s resurrection.

Those who wished to give the child his father’s name rather than the name John signify that part of the people who believed that a human being could be justified more by works of the Law than through faith in Christ. But the mother, speaking in the prophetic spirit, forbids this, saying: “By no means; he shall be called John.” The Church believes that the cleansing of those whom she regenerates through baptism is accomplished more through faith and grace than through works of the Law.

The name “John,” in our language, seems to signify “grace of God,” or “in whom there is grace.” For the Apostle says: “By the grace of God the nations have been saved” (Ephesians 2). And elsewhere: “Neither circumcision counts for anything, nor uncircumcision, but faith working through love” (Galatians 5).

Therefore, spiritually speaking, when they wished to impose the father’s name on the child, the apostle Peter joins Elizabeth in opposing them when he says: “Why do you wish to place a yoke upon the necks of the disciples that neither we nor our fathers were able to bear? But we believe that we are saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as they are” (Acts 15).

## HOMILY III. ON THE HOLY DAY OF THE APOSTLES PETER AND PAUL

(Matthew 16.) “At that time: Jesus came into the region of Caesarea Philippi.” And so forth.

We read of three Caesareas: two in the Promised Land and the third in Cappadocia. There is the Caesarea of the Palestinian region, on the shore of the Great Sea. It was previously called the Tower of the Station, but later Herod rebuilt it more nobly in honor of Caesar and called it Caesarea.

In it that same Herod built a magnificent house of white marble in honor of Caesar. There Herod was struck by an angel because he had not given honor to God, and, consumed by worms, expired (Acts 12). In this place also Cornelius the centurion was baptized by Simon Peter (Acts 10). There, moreover, the tombs of Philip’s four virgin daughters are shown to this day.

There is also another Caesarea in Cappadocia, which Luke the evangelist mentions in the Acts of the Apostles: “He went down to Caesarea and greeted the church” (Acts 25).

The third Caesarea is Caesarea Philippi, which the evangelist mentions in this passage. It too is in the Promised Land. Philip, the son of Herod, built it in honor of Caesar at the foot of Mount Lebanon and called it Caesarea Philippi. Two springs rise there, one called Jor and the other Dan; joined together, they form the river Jordan.

When Jesus came into this region with his disciples, he questioned them, saying: “Who do people say the Son of Man is?” Thus, where Caesar demanded a coin of tribute, the Savior would receive the coin of faith.

It should be noted that he did not say, “Who do people say that I am?” lest he seem to be asking boastfully about himself. Rather, he said: “Who do people say the Son of Man is?”

Although it might have appeared more honorable to call himself the Son of God, he wished to call himself the Son of Man, to show that humility must be preserved in all things. Or certainly he preferred to call himself the Son of Man more frequently than the Son of God so that no one would doubt the reality of the flesh he had assumed. Thus: “When the Son of Man comes, do you think he will find faith on earth?” (Luke 18); and: “The Son of Man will come in the glory of his Father with his angels” (Matthew 16); and: “Foxes have dens” (Matthew 8), and similar passages.

Wherever “Son of Man” is read in Latin, the Hebrew has “son of Adam,” as in the Psalm: “Sons of men, how long will you be heavy of heart?” (Psalm 4), where the Hebrew has “sons of Adam.”

When questioned, the disciples reported various opinions, saying:

“Some say John the Baptist, others Elijah, others Jeremiah, or one of the prophets.”

But how could people have thought that Christ was Elijah or Jeremiah, when they are said to have lived many generations earlier? This error had descended among the people from the foolishness of the pagans, who believed that some great man could, after death, give his spirit to whomever he wished.

Herod had been deceived by this error when, hearing reports about Jesus, he said: “John, whom I beheaded, has risen from the dead, and therefore many powers are at work in him” (Mark 6).

After hearing the various opinions, the Savior turned his speech specifically to the disciples and said:

“But you, who do you say that I am?”

It was as if he said: “While those people form merely human opinions about me, you, who are not of them because I chose you from the world—who do you say that I am?”

By these words he showed that they had transcended the merit of human nature in its human weakness and could in some manner be called gods in imitation of the true God, according to the Psalmist’s words: “I have said: You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High” (Psalm 81).

“But Simon Peter answered and said: ‘You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.’”

Peter not only preserves the order of his precedence by answering first when questioned; he also displays the greatness of his love. He rightly answers first because he loves him more than the others.

In many places in the Gospel we read that Peter loved the Lord more than the other disciples, as the Lord himself says: “Simon, son of John, do you love me more than these?” And he said: “You know, Lord, that I love you” (John 21), or “that I cherish you.”

When he foretold his passion to the twelve disciples, Peter, unable to bear this because of the greatness of his love, took him aside privately and said to him: “Be favorable to yourself, Lord; this shall never happen. It is not fitting for the Son of God to taste death” (Matthew 16).

When the hour of his passion was approaching, the Lord said: “You will all suffer scandal because of me on this night.” Peter replied: “Even if everyone is scandalized because of you, I will never be scandalized.” And when the Lord foretold what would happen, saying: “Amen, I say to you, before the cock crows, you will deny me three times,” Peter, presuming on himself, said: “Even if I must die with you, I will not deny you” (Matthew 26).

After the resurrection, when the Lord appeared standing on the shore while the disciples were fishing, Peter heard that it was the Lord, girded his tunic around himself, threw himself into the sea, and came to Jesus. The other disciples came by boat.

Set ablaze, therefore, by this same flame of love, Peter answered first when all the disciples had been questioned, saying: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.”

In these words he most fittingly declared the foundation of the true faith. “Christ” received his name in Greek from the anointing of chrism. By confessing him as Christ, Peter teaches belief in a true human being who was anointed not with material oil but with the gift of the Holy Spirit. Hence the Psalmist says: “God, your God, has anointed you” (Psalm 44), and so forth.

When Peter added, “the Son of the living God,” he indicated that Christ is truly God, because the Father begot what he is—that is, God begot God. He calls him the living God in contrast to the false gods whom human beings thought to be gods, although they were dead: Jupiter, Saturn, Mars, Mercury, Venus, and the other monstrosities of idols. Of these the prophet says: “May the gods who did not make heaven and earth perish” (Jeremiah 10), and so forth. The Psalmist likewise says: “All the gods of the nations are demons” (Psalm 95).

“Jesus answered and said to him: ‘Blessed are you, Simon Barjona.’”

True confession receives its reward. Because Peter confessed Christ to be the Son of the living God, he is rightly called blessed. He is surnamed “Barjona,” which in our language means “son of a dove.” The Lord himself demonstrated that the dove signifies the Holy Spirit when, after the Redeemer had been baptized, the Spirit appeared in the form of a dove.

Barjona, therefore, is said to mean “son of a dove,” that is, “son of the Holy Spirit,” because, through the revelation of the Holy Spirit, Peter confessed the Son of the living God.

Some think that Barjona should be written as *bar Joanna*, because in another Gospel passage he is called the son of Joanna, when the Lord says: “Simon, son of Joanna, do you love me?” (John 12). Joanna is interpreted as “grace of God,” or “in whom there is grace.”

It is therefore fitting that the first of the apostles is called the son of John, because he recognized the Son of God not through his own power but through the Father’s grace revealing him. Hence it is added:

“For flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven.”

“Flesh and blood” in this passage signifies the carnal teaching of the scribes and Pharisees, in accordance with the Apostle Paul’s declaration: “I did not immediately consult flesh and blood” (Galatians 1). The prince of the apostles therefore did not recognize Christ the Son of God through the teaching of the Pharisees and scribes, but through the revelation of the Father, just as the Son himself elsewhere glorifies the Father, saying: “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth” (Matthew 11).

“And I say to you that you are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church.”

It is as if he said: “Because you have confessed me to be Christ, the Son of the living God, I also say to you”—not with an empty or passing word, since for me to say is to do—“I say, then, to you that you are Peter,” and so forth.

We should not think that he first gave him the name Peter at this moment. Rather, he gave it when he came to him while Andrew was preaching the Gospel and, looking at him, said: “You are Simon, son of Joanna; you shall be called Cephas, which is interpreted as Peter” (John 1). What is called *Cephas* in Syriac is called *Peter* in Latin.

Both names derive from that rock of which the Apostle says: “The rock was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10).

When he says, “Upon this rock I will build my Church,” the meaning is as if he said: “Upon this faith—that is, upon me, whom you have confessed—I will build my Church.” For the Apostle says: “No one can lay any foundation other than the one that has been laid, which is Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians 3).

What is contained within cannot fall, because what contains it is fixed. Hence it is added:

“And the gates of hell will not prevail against it.”

By “the gates of hell” in this passage we may understand the teaching of heretics, which makes its hearers rush into hell. The gates of hell therefore do not prevail against the Church founded upon Christ, because although it has often been assailed by the persecutions of heretics, it could not be torn away from the catholic faith.

Alternatively, we can understand the gates of hell as vices and sins, such as the Apostle recalls when he says: “The works of the flesh are manifest: fornication, and things like these” (Galatians 5). They are rightly called the gates of hell because those who persevere in them are plunged into hell, as the same Apostle concludes: “Those who do such things will not obtain the kingdom of God.”

The gates of hell will not prevail against the Church, although the elect may be tempted by these vices and sins; they do not know how to persevere in them to the end. Either they conquer before they are overcome, or, after falling, they quickly rise through repentance, in accordance with what the Lord says elsewhere:

“Everyone who comes to me, hears my words, and does them—I will show you whom he resembles: he is like a man building a house, who dug down deep” (Matthew 7), and so forth.

“And to you I will give the keys of the kingdom of heaven.” The keys of the kingdom of heaven signify nothing other than the power of binding and loosing. For just as a key is placed in a door so that friends may be admitted while strangers are shut out, so the power of binding and loosing admits the righteous but excludes the unrighteous. Concerning this it continues: “And whatever you bind on earth,” and so forth.

Here we must consider that, although this man is called with such great humility, he was brought to such great glory; for because he followed Christ with the most ardent love, having left everything behind, he attained such exalted status that, in God’s place, he could forgive the sins of some and retain those of others. Yet we must not think that this power was given only to blessed Peter. Just as one spoke on behalf of all when he answered, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God,” so in one person all heard: “Whatever you bind on earth,” and the rest.

Therefore, when after the resurrection the Lord had given his disciples the Holy Spirit, he said generally to them all: “Whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them.” Nor was this power given only to the apostles, but also to bishops and priests, who now preserve their order in the Church and possess the power of binding and loosing.

Hence, in the Law, a symbolic command is given concerning lepers: if someone had been struck with leprosy, he was to show himself to the priest and, according to the priest’s judgment, either be expelled outside the camp or received back—not because the priest himself could cleanse a leper or make a cleansed person leprous, but because it belongs to the priest’s ministry to distinguish between leprosy and leprosy, that is, between a greater and a lesser sin. Seek this meaning in the Gospel at the Octave of Easter.

# HOMILY IV: ON SAINT LAWRENCE THE MARTYR

*(John 12.)* “At that time Jesus was speaking with his disciples in parables: ‘Amen, amen, I say to you, unless a grain of wheat falling into the earth dies.’” And the rest.

As the Lord was exhorting his disciples to martyrdom, he first set before them the example of his own passion, so that they would fear suffering death for his name all the less, since in this work they would prove themselves imitators of their heavenly teacher. For he says: “Amen, amen, I say to you,” and the rest.

In these words we understand that the Lord speaks of himself as being put to death and multiplied in the likeness of a grain of wheat: put to death through the unbelief of the Jews, and multiplied through the faith of all nations. We can understand this not only more easily but also more clearly if we give a little attention to the preceding passage of this Gospel.

Above, the Evangelist reported that, when the Lord was preaching in Jerusalem on the feast day, there were certain Gentiles who had come to worship in Jerusalem. They approached Philip, who was from Bethsaida of Galilee, and said to him: “Sir, we wish to see Jesus.” Philip came and told Andrew. Andrew and Philip in turn told Jesus. But Jesus answered them: “The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified.” Then he continued: “Amen, amen, I say to you,” and the rest.

When, therefore, he said to those Gentiles who desired to see him, “The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified,” and then continued, “Amen, amen, I say to you: unless a grain of wheat falling into the earth,” and so forth, he clearly indicated the order of his passion: he was first to be put to death by the Jews and afterward preached to the Gentiles. For his name grows all the more in the faith of believers the more it was extinguished through death in the unbelief of the Jews.

Nor should it seem unworthy of our Redeemer that, in the humanity he assumed, he is compared with a grain of wheat, since in that same humanity he is also likened to lowly worms, as he himself says through the prophet:

“I am a worm and not a man” (Psalm 21).

And the Lord is beautifully compared with a grain of wheat, because, just as among all crops nothing is more beautiful or more pleasing than wheat, so he surpasses all creatures, since nothing is found sweeter or more delightful than he. Or certainly he is compared with a grain of wheat because, through the food of his body and blood, he refreshes the souls of the faithful. For he himself says in the Gospel: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven” (John 6). And again: “The bread that I will give is my flesh, for the life of the world.” And elsewhere: “My flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink” (ibid.).

Having first set forth the mystery of his passion, he immediately exhorts his disciples to steadfastness in martyrdom, saying:

“He who loves his life will lose it, and he who hates his life in this world will preserve it for eternal life.”

In the Scriptures, “soul” or “life” sometimes signifies the inner person, that is, the vital spirit, and sometimes the present life. It signifies the inner person when the Lord says: “What does it profit a man if he gains the whole world but suffers the loss of his soul?” (Matthew 16). It signifies the present life when he says elsewhere: “Is not the soul more than food, and the body more than clothing?” (ibid.).

Therefore, in this passage, by “soul” he designates the present life, when it is said: “He who loves his life will lose it.” It is a remarkable thing that by loving life the soul should perish, while by hating it in this world it should be preserved for eternal life. We hate our soul rightly, and preserve it by hating it, when we resist its carnal desires, break its appetites, struggle against its passions, and regard the present life as nothing in comparison with the life to come. We carefully consider what the Lord says: “If anyone comes to me and does not hate his father and mother, wife, children, brothers, and sisters”—and even his own life—“he cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14).

Paul hated his life in this way when he said: “I am ready not only to be bound, but also to die in Jerusalem for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Acts 21). For I do not make my life more precious than myself.

And so that even the simpler may understand what we are saying, let us bring forward some examples: some who hated their lives and loved them, and others who loved their lives and hated them. For example, some were told: “Worship idols, or you will be killed.” But they, hating their lives—that is, treating their present life as nothing—fell into bodily death, yet attained the life of the soul. Others were likewise told: “Worship idols, or you will be killed.” But they, wrongly loving their lives—that is, worshiping their present life—found everlasting death.

In this way blessed Lawrence the Levite, whose feast we celebrate today, hated his life and, by hating it, preserved it for eternal life. When, for the sake of the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, he had been placed upon the gridiron after distributing the Church’s resources, he said to the most cruel tyrant: “It is roasted; turn it over and eat, for the Church’s resources that you demand have been carried by the hands of the poor into the heavenly treasuries.”

The Lord reveals whose imitators the martyrs are in their passion when he says: “If anyone serves me, let him follow me.” To follow the Lord is to imitate him, as he himself says elsewhere: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Matthew 16). And again: “Whoever does not carry his cross and come after me is not worthy of me” (Luke 14).

The faithful serve Christ in various ways. Some serve him by speaking well, like confessors; others by dying for his name, like martyrs; others by giving alms justly, like faithful laypeople. But whoever serves Christ must follow Christ. For, as the apostle John says: “Whoever says that he remains in Christ ought himself to walk as he walked” (1 John 2).

He himself declares what reward one receives for such imitation when he continues:

“And where I am, there also will my servant be.”

What more can be promised to a faithful servant than that he may deserve to be with his Lord—not only to see his humanity but also to contemplate his divinity? Hence it is also added:

“If anyone serves me, my Father who is in heaven will honor him.”

The Father will honor the Son’s servant, because for faithful service he will repay eternal life, saying: “Well done, good and faithful servant” (Matthew 25), and the rest. Then the Savior’s prayer will be fulfilled: “Father, grant that, just as you and I are one, so they also may be one in us” (John 17)—not by equality of nature, but by participation in glory.

May he deign to lead us to that glory, he who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

# HOMILY V: ON THE SOLEMNITY OF THE EVER-VIRGIN MARY

The reading from the Book of Ecclesiasticus, common to all feast days dedicated to the Blessed Virgin.

*(Ecclesiasticus 24.)* “From the beginning and before the ages I was created, and until the age to come I shall not cease.” And the rest.

This passage of the reading, which is known to have been taken from the Book of Wisdom, appears specifically to commend the praise of eternal Wisdom, through whom all things were created. But this passage has been assigned for reading by Catholic and learned Fathers on the solemnity of the ever-virgin Mary, from whom that same Wisdom of God assumed flesh.

A certain portion of it may appropriately be applied to the same Mother of God, who was created by that Wisdom of God in such a way that, through her, the Son of God might be created for the redemption of human nature without human concupiscence.

For what is absurd or contradictory if we say that the words:

“In all things I sought rest, and in the inheritance of the Lord I shall abide”

apply to the Mother of God? She indeed sought rest in all things; and, so that she might find the Father in eternal rest, she was the first of all to vow to preserve her virginity without blemish, as she replied to the angel Gabriel when he announced the Lord’s conception: “How shall this happen, since I do not know a man?” (Luke 1)—that is, “I have resolved not to know one.”

She remained in the inheritance of the Lord, for she did not depart from the Lord’s passion by sinning; rather, preserving her soul undefiled by concupiscence and her flesh from corruption, she became a portion of God’s inheritance, singing with the Prophet and saying: “Indeed, my inheritance is splendid for me” (Psalm 15).

The following also appears to apply to her person:

“Then the Creator of all things commanded and said to me, and he who created me rested in my tabernacle.”

But who is to be believed to be the Creator of all things John declares in the Gospel. After saying, “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God,” he added: “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1). And David says: “You made all things in wisdom” (Psalm 103).

This Creator of all things therefore rested in her tabernacle when the Word of God, through whom all things were made, assumed flesh within the Virgin’s womb in order to become true man.

Therefore let the presumption of the Manichaeans cease its heretical barking and growling. They dared to say that Christ did not assume true flesh from the Virgin. Let the Wisdom of God herself speak in the person of the Virgin:

“He who created me rested in my tabernacle, and he said to me, ‘Dwell in Jacob and inherit in Israel.’”

Jacob, which is interpreted as “supplanter,” signifies the actions of those who, in order to advance in the virtues of the soul, courageously trample underfoot the allurements of vices. The Wisdom of God therefore has her dwelling in those who supplant vices and possess in their deeds what Jacob signifies in his name. As he himself says: “I will dwell in them and walk among them” (2 Corinthians 6).

Israel was the name given to that same Jacob after he overcame the angel and was deemed worthy to see God. Hence it is rightly interpreted as “a man seeing God.” Therefore, after the supplanting of vices, the soul that strives toward the contemplation of God becomes the inheritance of the Wisdom of God, that is, of Christ, in accordance with the Apostle’s words: “Heirs indeed of God, and fellow heirs with Christ” (Romans 8).

She is also commanded to put down roots among the elect—that is, secretly to plant the seeds of her thoughts in the minds of those whom she knows will bring forth the fruit of good works. She therefore puts down roots not in the reprobate but in the elect, in whose hearts a good will is so firmly bound by spiritual roots that it does not wither before reaching the fruit of maturity.

But those who now go forth weeping, sowing their seed, will come with joy, carrying their sheaves (Psalm 125), and so forth, hearing from the merciful Judge: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you,” and so forth. “For I was hungry, and you gave me food” (Matthew 25), and so forth.

It continues:

“And so I was established in Zion, and likewise I rested in the sanctified city, and my power was in Jerusalem.”

Zion is situated within Jerusalem, not only more strongly fortified for defense but also more exalted for contemplation; hence it is suitably interpreted as “mirror” or “contemplation.” The interpretation of this name suits the Church, which, lest it lie exposed to the snares of invisible enemies, rises higher through spiritual desire and contemplates heavenly things through purity of mind, praying with the Prophet and saying: “Be to me, Lord, a tower of strength” (Psalm 60).

The sanctified city is the holy Church, which desires to be sanctified by him to whom it says daily in prayer: “Hallowed be your name” (Matthew 6), carefully considering the Lord’s command: “Be holy, because I am holy, your God” (Leviticus 11).

The Wisdom of God therefore rests in the sanctified city, because it rests in the minds of those who love holiness. As for what follows—“And my power was in Jerusalem”—this means that he holds power in the hearts of those who love the vision of inner peace with their whole affection.

It continues:

“And I took root among an honored people, and my inheritance is in the portions of my God.”

By an honored people he means a holy people. For, as the Apostle says: “Glory, honor, and peace for everyone who does good” (Romans 2).

He is therefore said to have taken root in such a people: people who are not carried off like ash by the blast of temptation, but who remain firmly rooted in the love of God, according to the Apostle’s admonition: “Rooted and founded in charity, so that you may be able, with all the saints, to comprehend what is the length, breadth, height, and depth” (Ephesians 3).

The inheritance of this people is in the portions of God, for they place nothing before his love and regard nothing as dear in comparison with him. Concerning them it is said in the Law: “You shall give no inheritance to the tribe of Levi, for I am his portion and inheritance” (Numbers 18). And concerning them the Psalmist says: “Blessed is the nation whose God is the Lord” (Psalm 143), and so forth. And he himself cried out to him: “Lord, you are the portion of my inheritance and my cup” (Psalm 15), and so forth.

Those who are such must therefore strive toward perseverance, and so it continues:

“And my dwelling is in the fullness of the saints.”

The fullness of the saints is the perfection of works. They possess fullness who are brought to completion in good works. May he grant us this fullness, he who is blessed forever and ever. Amen.

# HOMILY VI: ON THE HOLY DAY OF THE ASSUMPTION OF THE VIRGIN MARY, MOTHER OF GOD

*(Luke 10.)* “At that time Jesus entered a certain village, and a woman named Martha welcomed him.” And the rest.

The Lord Jesus Christ, Creator and Redeemer of human nature, not only announced the word of life to those who came to him, but also, as the Gospel reports, went through cities and villages evangelizing the heavenly kingdom to all.

As he traveled through different places according to this custom, he “entered a certain village,” as the present Gospel reading relates, “and a woman named Martha welcomed him into her house.” She welcomed him as a guest, as a stranger, as one who had nowhere to lay his head. She also welcomed him as a great man and prophet, with the same devotion with which the widow of Zarephath had once received the prophet Elijah. She welcomed him in order to be received by him, sowing her own earthly goods so that she might reap his spiritual ones.

Her sister was named Mary. Martha and Mary were sisters not only in spirit but also by birth, and their brother Lazarus had been raised by the Lord from the dead.

This Mary, sitting beside the Lord’s feet, listened attentively to the word from his mouth. For she had heard the prophet saying: “Be still and know that I am God” (Psalm 45). She had also heard what is said through Moses: “Those who draw near to his feet receive instruction from him” (Deuteronomy 33).

But because everyone who receives a guest or stranger ought, according to his ability, to provide temporal assistance, Martha was so occupied with continual service that she brought a complaint not only against her sister but also against the Lord himself, saying:

“Lord, do you not care that my sister has left me to serve alone? Tell her, then, to help me.”

But he who is not a respecter of persons, who carefully judges the merits of each and distinguishes virtues, so as to show that spiritual food is better than bodily food, praises the work of one without condemning the other:

“Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things. But one thing is necessary.”

Here Martha’s work is not criticized; rather, Mary’s is praised when it is said: “Mary has chosen the better part, which will not be taken away from her.”

When he says, “Martha, Martha,” the repetition of the name is an admonition toward devout attention. These things have been said briefly according to the literal sense.

Spiritually, however, the village that the Lord entered signifies the world. He entered, as it were, a village when he appeared visibly in the world, when “he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men, and being found in appearance as a man” (Philippians 2).

The two devout sisters who welcomed the Lord into their house signify the Church’s two ways of life: the active and the contemplative. They demonstrate the character of these ways in their actions.

When one of them was occupied with continual service, the labor of the active life is expressed. To this life belong feeding the hungry, giving drink to the thirsty, clothing the naked, receiving guests, visiting the sick, burying the dead, and also foreseeing with laborious concern what is necessary for those placed under one’s governance.

Through Mary, who sat beside the Lord’s feet and listened to his word, the sweetness of the contemplative life is signified. The more this sweetness is tasted, the more the mind is separated from visible things, from the tumult of cares, and from worldly business. Having despised every care and trampled every vice underfoot, the mind desires to be alone with God alone.

It delights to hear heavenly commands, to devote itself frequently to reading and prayer, and, insofar as mortal frailty permits, to participate in the company of angels. And because it is somewhat separated from their fellowship, it weeps most bitterly with spiritual joy.

The Lord wished to signify this immeasurable grace and incomprehensible happiness when he said: “But one thing is necessary, Mary,” and so forth. Its sweetness is so necessary that even those things which appear good here are judged superfluous in comparison with it.

There is what “no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and what has not entered the human heart, what God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Corinthians 2). That is the sweetness the one who said, “One thing I have asked of the Lord” (Psalm 26), and so forth, desired to possess.

The active life is on the way; the contemplative life is in the homeland. The active life belongs to necessity; the contemplative to love. The active belongs to labor; the contemplative to rest.

The active life begins in the present life and ends with the present life, while its reward remains. For who will feed the hungry in that homeland where no one hungers? Who will clothe the naked where clothing is immortal? Who will visit the sick where no one is sick? Who will bury the dead where eternal life is present?

The contemplative life, however, begins in the present but will be perfected in the future. Hence it is rightly said of Mary:

“Mary chose the better part, which will not be taken away from her.”

What the mind begins here to taste for a little while, it will fully receive there, where the God of gods will be seen in Zion, as the Apostle testifies when he says: “What we now see through a mirror, in an enigma, we shall then see face to face” (1 Corinthians 13). And again: “Now I know in part,” and so forth.

This, then, is the difference between the active and contemplative lives: the active is common to many, whereas contemplative vision, the higher it is, is the rarer. For rarely are those found who can truly say: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Philippians 3). And: “Whether we are beside ourselves, it is for God; or whether we are sober, it is for you” (2 Corinthians 5).

The order of these virtues requires that each person strive through active labor to reach the sweetness of contemplation. For to many, after they have labored diligently in the work of the active life, the sweetness of the contemplative life is given as a reward.

Hence it is symbolically commanded in the Law: “If you buy a Hebrew servant, he shall serve you for six years, and in the seventh he shall go out free without payment” (Exodus 21).

Hebrew is interpreted as “one who passes over.” A Hebrew servant is spiritually bought when the mind passes from earthly conduct to heavenly desire. The number six pertains to the labor of the active life, because there are six days on which work is permitted; the number seven, because of the rest of the Sabbath, expresses the sweetness of the contemplative life.

The Hebrew servant who has been bought is commanded to serve for six years and is ordered to go out free without payment in the seventh, because there are some who, after prolonged labor in the active life, pass over to the rest of contemplation. Because this happens not through their own power but by a divine gift, it is rightly said: “He shall go out free without payment.”

This properly applies to those who, after long exercises in monastic life and prolonged testing in the monastery, choose secluded places where they can fulfill the Apostle’s command: “Pray without ceasing; give thanks in all things” (1 Thessalonians 5).

He goes out free without payment because, after they have done everything, they call themselves his useless servants. Without doubt, just as the active life comes by gift, so the contemplative life also comes by grace.

Let him answer in the garment in which he entered, for it is entirely necessary that each of us persevere in what he begins and continue to the end of the work in the intention with which he began. He has passed well to the contemplative life who has not changed the garment of his intention in this life.

There are some who, burning with divine love, begin at the very outset of their conversion to fly toward the sweetness of the contemplative life, but by divine dispensation are first permitted to be set free in the active life. They reach the contemplative life all the more securely—and indeed more happily—the more perfectly they have been proved in the active life.

Such were signified by the two wives of the holy patriarch Jacob, Leah and Rachel. One of them, Leah, had weak eyes but abundant children; Rachel was beautiful in appearance but barren.

Through Leah, who had weak eyes but abundant children, the active life is signified. Although it cannot contemplate God with the clear eye of the heart, it nevertheless begets spiritual children for God through the example of good preaching. Hence Leah is rightly interpreted as “laborious,” because the active life is occupied with many labors and cares.

Through Rachel, who was beautiful in appearance but barren, the sweetness of the contemplative life is expressed. For while the mind gathers itself entirely to see God, it bears fewer children through preaching. Hence Rachel is rightly interpreted as “sheep” or “the beginning of vision,” because the mind devoted to contemplation desires to see him who says: “I am the beginning, who also speak to you” (John 8).

Jacob desired Rachel, but in the night he received Leah without knowing it. For there are some, as we have said above, who desire to attain the contemplative life but are first, by divine judgment, permitted to labor for the benefit of many in the night of the present life.

After he received Leah, he attained Rachel’s embrace, because those who have labored well in the active life will eventually, by divine gift, attain the contemplative life.

They are found steadfast and perfect in both. Such was the apostle Paul, who, while he had concern for all the churches—a concern belonging to the active life—was caught up to the third heaven, which belongs to the contemplative life.

These two lives were signified by the two devout sisters who welcomed the Lord into their house, Martha and Mary. We believe that both were holy, both good, and both righteous. But he himself deigned to declare which was better—he who needs no witness—when he said: “Mary chose the better part for herself, which will not be taken away from her,” and so forth.

# HOMILY VII: ON THE FEAST OF SAINT MICHAEL THE ARCHANGEL

*(Matthew 18.)* “At that time the disciples approached Jesus, saying: ‘Who, do you think, is greater in the kingdom of heaven?’” And the rest.

Whenever we read that the Lord’s disciples contended or asked among themselves about precedence, we must not attribute it to jealousy and envy but to human frailty and weakness. They were inexperienced and still young in the faith. For they had heard him preaching his resurrection, but had not yet been enlightened by the grace of the Holy Spirit. They had not learned to love the heavenly kingdom perfectly; as the Evangelist John says: “The Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified” (John 7).

They thought that, when he rose from the dead, he would possess a bodily kingdom and that they themselves would be exalted with honors. Hence, at the time of his passion, a dispute arose among them about which of them would be greater in the kingdom of heaven.

The mother of the sons of Zebedee had been led astray by this suspicion when she approached the Lord and said: “Lord, say that these two sons of mine may sit, one at your right hand and the other at your left, in your kingdom” (Matthew 20).

For the same reason Cleopas and another disciple, to whom the Lord appeared after the resurrection in the guise of a stranger, said: “But we had hoped that he was the one who would redeem Israel” (Luke 24). And some of the disciples, questioning him, said: “Lord, will you at this time restore the kingdom to Israel?” (Acts 1).

The occasion for asking the Lord which of them was greater in the kingdom of heaven may perhaps have arisen from what came before. For, as the Evangelist reported above, those who collected the didrachma approached Peter and said to him: “Does your teacher not pay the didrachma?” He said, “Yes.” And when he entered the house, Jesus anticipated him, saying:

“What do you think, Simon? From whom do the kings of the earth receive tribute or tax—from their own sons or from strangers?”

He said, “From strangers.” Jesus said to him: “Then the sons are free. But, so that we may not scandalize them, go to the sea and cast a hook, and take the first fish that comes up; when you open its mouth, you will find a stater. Take it and give it to them for me and for you” (Matthew 17).

Because the other disciples had seen Peter being treated as equal to the Lord in the payment of the tax, they concluded that he had been preferred above them all. At that moment they approached Jesus, saying: “Who, do you think, is greater in the kingdom of heaven?”

But the teacher of humility, who says in the Gospel, “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart, and you will find rest for your souls” (Matthew 11), wished to show that the kingdom of heaven must be sought not through pride but through humility, and that the one who humbles himself for God’s sake would be greater in it:

“Calling a little child, he set him in their midst and said: ‘Amen, I say to you, unless you turn and become like little children, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven.’”

This can be understood in two ways. We can understand the little child here as the Lord Jesus Christ. Although he is great and greatly worthy of praise, and of his greatness there is no end (Psalm 47), he was born as a little one for us and a son was given to us, in order to make us exalted.

The sense is: Unless you humble yourselves according to my example—I who did not come to be served but to serve, and who became among you as one who serves and not as one reclining—you cannot enter the kingdom of heaven, which has been prepared for the humble.

If, however, we understand simply any little child, it is clear that by this example he exhorts us not only to humility but also to preserve simplicity. It is as if he said:

Just as this child whom I have set before you as an example does not lust upon seeing a beautiful woman, does not desire another’s wealth, does not return injury when hurt, does not think one thing and say another, and, when angry, does not maintain lasting quarrels, so you too cannot enter the kingdom of heaven, which has been prepared for the humble and simple, unless you possess in your mind the innocence that this child possesses in his body.

No proud person walks on its path, and no haughty person proceeds along it, because “the way that leads to life is difficult and narrow, and few are those who find it” (Matthew 7).

When he therefore says, “Unless you turn and become like little children, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven,” he continues:

“Whoever therefore humbles himself like this little child is greater in the kingdom of heaven. And whoever receives one such little child in my name receives me. But whoever scandalizes one of these little ones,” and so forth.

It is as if he had said: If an exalted position delights you, first practice the humility of an innocent life. He did not wish the apostles to be little in body, but to possess the innocence of little children in their minds.

The Lord wished his disciples to be such little ones, to whom he said: “Let the little children come to me, for of such is the kingdom of heaven” (Mark 10). The apostle Paul also wished his disciples to possess such innocence of little children, commanding them in his Epistle: “Do not become children in understanding, but be little ones in malice and mature in understanding” (1 Corinthians 14).

The prophetic king knew himself to be such. Though exalted on a royal throne, he was humble in mind and said: “The Lord preserves the little ones; I was humbled, and he saved me” (Psalm 114). And again: “I will play, and I will become even more insignificant than I have become, and I will be humble in my own eyes” (2 Samuel 6).

A little one is someone who displeases himself in order to please God. He will be all the more beautiful before God the humbler he is in his own eyes. Hence it is also added:

“Whoever therefore humbles himself like this little child will be greater in the kingdom of heaven.”

Let us therefore possess the virtue of humility if we wish to possess a place of exaltation in the kingdom of heaven, since, as the Savior says in the Gospel: “Everyone who humbles himself will be exalted, and whoever exalts himself will be humbled” (Luke 14).

Hence Scripture also admonishes us elsewhere: “The greater you are, humble yourself in all things, and you will find grace before God” (Ecclesiasticus 3). And again: “Humble yourselves under the mighty hand of God, so that he may exalt you at the time of visitation” (1 Peter 5).

And lest you think that the one who humbles himself here for God’s sake should be despised, he added an appropriate statement, saying:

“And whoever receives one such little child in my name receives me.”

This is what the Lord announced beforehand that he would say in the future: “As long as you did it for one of the least of mine, you did it for me.” And he pointedly says: “Whoever receives one such little child in my name receives me” (Matthew 18).

Although, according to the word of Scripture, we must not choose whom we ought to benefit, nevertheless we should show special goodwill toward those who choose to be little and humble for God’s sake, because we recognize Christ in the conduct of their lives.

Thus, when a devout father instructed his son, he said: “Place your bread and your wine upon the grave of the righteous, and do not share them with sinners” (Tobit 4). And again: “Let your almsgiving sweat in your hand until you find a righteous person to whom you may give it.”

Hence the Apostle says: “While we have opportunity, let us do good to all, but especially to those who are of the household of faith” (Galatians 6).

Whoever bestows temporal goods upon those in whose life and conduct he recognizes Christ dwelling, certainly gives them to the one for whose love he bestows them. Hence it is rightly said, “in my name.”

For many give temporal goods not in Christ’s name but so that they may win human praise. Of them it is written: “They loved the glory of men more than the glory of God” (John 12). And the Lord says elsewhere: “They do all their works so that they may be seen by men” (Matthew 23). And again: “Amen, I say to you, they have received their reward” (Matthew 6).

And lest we remain sluggish in receiving guests and strangers, he promised that he himself is received in them when he said: “Whoever receives one such little child in my name receives me.”

Hence he also says elsewhere: “Whoever receives a prophet in the name of a prophet will receive a prophet’s reward, and whoever receives a righteous person in the name of a righteous person will receive a righteous person’s reward” (Matthew 10). And again: “Whoever receives you receives me, and whoever despises you despises me” (Luke 10).

Just as a reward is promised to those who receive others, so punishment is imposed on the harsh and miserly when it continues:

“Whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble, it would be better for him that a millstone be hung around his neck and that he be drowned in the depths of the sea.”

Here we must consider how grave a sin it is to cause a brother to stumble, since such vengeance is threatened even against those who cause scandal. When he says, “It would be better for him that a millstone be hung around his neck and that he be drowned in the depths of the sea,” he speaks according to the custom of the province, where among the ancient Jews capital crimes were punished by this penalty [Col. 0773D]. One must not, therefore, suppose that the scandalizing of a brother is a slight sin, since such a punishment is foretold for those who cause scandal. For, as he says elsewhere in the Gospel, “Whoever says to his brother, ‘Fool,’ will be liable to the fire of Gehenna” (Matt. VI). The Apostle shows that he took great care to avoid this when he says: “It is better for me not to eat meat or drink wine or do anything by which I might cause my brother to stumble” (Rom. XIV). He also restrains his disciples from this sin, saying: “Why do you cause your brother to stumble, or why do you despise him?” (ibid.)

Therefore, insofar as we are able, we ought, in accordance with the Apostle’s admonition, to avoid causing our brothers to stumble. If, however, scandal arises on account of [Col. 0774A] the truth, the truth must be chosen rather than avoided for the sake of preventing scandal.

Or certainly, by the millstone—which has weight but accomplishes no journey, revolving endlessly—the changeable love of the world is signified. When he therefore says, “It would be better for him that a millstone be hung around his neck and that he be drowned in the depths of the sea,” he also forbids carnal people and lovers of the world from ecclesiastical authority. For it is better that a lover of the world, living carnally in the world, should destroy only himself than that, placed in ecclesiastical authority, he should drag himself and others to destruction by living perversely. For when someone’s life is despised, it follows that his preaching is also scorned; and when weak disciples follow the example of their patron, both they perish and their destruction rebounds upon the head of the one who is the author of the crime.

Or certainly, by the millstone teachers are understood. For just as grain is broken by the millstone so that its kernel may be brought forth for the nourishment or refreshment of human nature, so teachers, opening the hidden meanings of Sacred Scripture, reveal their inner sense, whether for the life or the refreshment of holy souls [Col. 0774B].

“Woe to the world because of scandals.”

The world to which woe is pronounced is not the world that the Son of Man came to seek and save, but the world that lies in wickedness—that is, the lovers of the world. Of this world the Lord says elsewhere: “Righteous Father, the world has not known you” (John XVII). Those who dwell in the world in mind and desire are rightly called “the world”; concerning them John says: “The world will pass away, and its desire” (I John II) [Col. 0774C].

The lovers of the world, while they do not fear causing scandal to others for the sake of worldly desires, nevertheless themselves suffer scandal—sometimes in body, but always in mind. Therefore woe to them, because “they spend their days in prosperity, and in a moment they descend to the underworld” (Job XXI). James says to them: “Whoever wishes to be a friend of this world is made an enemy of God” (James IV). To them pertains what follows: “For it is necessary that scandals come; nevertheless, woe to the person through whom the scandal comes.”

When he says, “It is necessary,” it is as though he were saying: It cannot be that scandals do not come. “For there must also be heresies,” as the Apostle says, “so that those who are approved may become manifest” (I Cor. XI). Another Scripture says: “The furnace tests the potter’s vessels, and the trial of tribulation tests righteous people” (Ecclus. XXVII) [Col. 0774D].

In a time of peace it is not easy to discern who is good and who is evil. But when the wind of those who cause scandal has blown, it will cast the light and unstable away like chaff before the face of the wind, while it will gather the grain into Christ’s granaries. Woe, therefore, to the person who makes himself such that the evil that is to come is fulfilled through his ministry. Of such people the Lord says: “The Son of Man will send his angels, and they will gather from his kingdom all scandals and deliver them up to the furnace of burning fire” (Matt. XIII).

We understand this more easily if we bring forward one example, namely Judas, the betrayer of the Lord. Concerning him the Lord himself said at the time of his passion: “The Son of Man goes as it is written concerning him; but woe to that person through whom he will be betrayed” (Matt. XXVI) [Col. 0775A]. It was necessary that the Son of God suffer passion for us, but woe to Judas, who made what was our good into his own evil.

And lest anyone should think that, on the pretext of relatives or friends, he ought to withdraw from the way of God, the Teacher of truth removes every error when he adds:

“If your hand or your foot causes you to stumble, cut it off and throw it away from you. It is better for you to enter life maimed or lame than, having two hands or two feet, to be thrown into the fire of Gehenna. And if your eye causes you to stumble, tear it out and throw it away from you. It is better for you to enter life with one eye than, having two eyes, to be thrown into the fire of Gehenna.”

How abhorrent this is according to the literal sense is readily apparent. But when we are excluded from the literal meaning, the spiritual sense must be sought [Col. 0775B]. Because the hand, foot, and eye are especially necessary for our needs, the affection of relatives and dearest friends is signified here. It is as though the Lord were saying: If someone is precious to you as an eye, close to you as a foot, and necessary to you as a hand, and persuades you to withdraw from the way of God, cut off that person’s love and cast it away from you. It is better for you to enter life alone than, with a great crowd of relatives, to be cast into eternal fire.

“What does it profit a person if he gains the whole world but suffers the loss of his soul?” (Matt. XVI.) For example: A wife flatters, a father threatens, a mother persuades, a brother and sister weep; but you, stand firm in the Lord’s way. Do not, by loving them uselessly, withdraw from the love of God [Col. 0775C], but follow what he says elsewhere: “Let the dead bury their own dead; but you, follow me” (Matt. VIII).

We have not said this because we ought to be ungrateful and disobedient toward parents and friends. Rather, when they wish to remove us from the way of God, then we must cut off their love from ourselves. Otherwise, when we know that they love God, they must be honored by us for two reasons: first, because they are righteous; second, because they are our relatives. For the Lord says in the Law: “Honor your father and your mother, so that it may be well with you and you may live long” (Exod. XX). Hence the Apostle says: “If anyone does not care for his own, and especially for members of his household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever” (I Tim. V).

How great a concern and care the Lord has for those who place all their hope in him, he shows when he adds [Col. 0775D]:

“See that you do not despise one of these little ones.”

Those who are little and humble in the present life for God’s sake must in no way be despised. For, as we have said, the little ones are those who are humble and despised in their own eyes. Concerning them the Savior says in the Gospel: “Do not fear, little flock, because it has pleased your Father to give you the kingdom” (Luke XII).

Whoever, therefore, is not afraid to cause such people to stumble offends God, who dwells in them, just as he says through the prophet: “Whoever touches you is like one who touches the pupil of my eye” (Zech. II). And again: “Do not touch my anointed ones, and do not act wickedly against my prophets” (Ps. CIV). Concerning these people, it is very sweet that the following is added, explaining why they must not be despised [Col. 0776A]:

“For I say to you that their angels in heaven always see the face of my Father who is in heaven.”

Here we learn that each of the faithful has an angel assigned for his protection. That angel defends him from temptations and helps him in the virtues, just as the Apostle says in his Epistle to the Hebrews: “Angels are ministering spirits, sent into service for the sake of those who are to inherit salvation” (Heb. I). And the Psalmist says of any righteous person: “He has commanded his angels concerning you, to guard you in all your ways; they will lift you up in their hands, lest you strike your foot against a stone” (Ps. XC).

Hence, concerning Peter, we read in the Acts of the Apostles that, after he had been led out of prison by an angel and had begun to knock at the door, the faithful who had gathered there said: “It is not Peter, but his angel” (Acts XII) [Col. 0776B].

The angels of the little ones, therefore, always see the face of the Father, because, even if they go forth from him for our sake, they never depart from his vision, as the angel Raphael himself says to Tobit: “I am one of the seven spirits who stand before God” (Tob. XII). Daniel also says: “Thousands of thousands ministered to him, and ten thousand times a hundred thousand stood before him” (Dan. VII).

The angels who are guardians of our life are believed to announce our prayers and works to God, just as the angel says to Tobit: “When you prayed, I offered your prayers before God” (Tob. XII). Daniel likewise says: “From the day on which you set your heart to understand and to humble yourself before God, your words were heard [Col. 0776C], and I came because of your words” (Dan. X).

But you, O Lord, etc.

## HOMILY VIII: ON THE MARTYRS

(Luke VI.) “At that time: Jesus, coming down from the mountain, stood in a level place, with a crowd of his disciples and a great multitude of people from all Judea and Jerusalem.” And so forth.

The Lord Jesus Christ not only, through the mystery of the Incarnation, came down from heaven to earth and graciously condescended to human weakness; in his holy teaching as well, he so adapted his doctrine for instructing human ignorance that not only the perfect but also the less perfect could find the nourishment of life [Col. 0776D].

Indeed, as the evangelist reported above, when they had ascended the mountain, his disciples followed him (Matt. V). There, after giving more perfect commandments to those who were able to receive them, he did not wish to abandon the simpler crowds on their account; therefore, coming down from the mountain again, he stood in a level place. By this action he showed that, in preaching, the discourse of teachers must be adapted to the capacity of their hearers.

The mountain in this passage signifies more perfect doctrine; the level places signify a humbler and more common form of preaching. Those who are such that they can hear with the apostles, “To you it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God” (Mark IV), must be instructed in a loftier manner. But those who, because of weakness of mind, cannot ascend to the higher doctrine must be taught the smallest commandments, so that those who are altogether incapable of doing good may at least not be inclined to commit evil [Col. 0777A].

The Lord showed this elsewhere by his own example. When someone asked him, “Teacher, what must I do to possess eternal life?” (Matt. XV), as though he were dwelling in the valleys, he answered: “You know the commandments: You shall not kill; you shall not commit adultery; you shall not bear false witness; you shall not covet your neighbor’s property; honor your father and mother.”

When the man replied, “I have kept all these things from my youth,” the Lord showed him the mountain of more perfect doctrine, saying: “One thing is still lacking to you. If you wish to be perfect, go, sell everything you possess, give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; then come, follow me.”

But because those burdened with the riches of the world can scarcely climb this mountain, it is immediately added: “He went away sad, because he had many possessions” [Col. 0777B].

The Apostle Paul likewise followed this example when he had ascended the mountain with his disciples, to whom he said: “We speak wisdom among the perfect” (I Cor. II). He was, as it were, dwelling with some people in the valleys when he said: “I, brothers, could not speak to you as spiritual people but as carnal, as infants in Christ. I gave you milk to drink, not food” (I Cor. III).

Not everyone comprehends everything, nor is everyone instructed in the same manner. The proud must be admonished one way, the humble another; the chaste one way, adulterers another; the drunkard one way, the sober another; men one way, women another; the married one way, virgins another; the devout one way, the impious another; those who despise the world one way, those who love it another; the peaceful one way, the contentious another; those who give away what is their own one way, those who seize what belongs to others another. Thus the former may hear what they ought to love concerning the promise of eternal life, while the latter may hear what they ought to fear concerning eternal punishment [Col. 0777C].

Often what benefits one illness harms another. Poison, although it is a person’s death, is a serpent’s life; and a soft whistle calms horses but incites puppies. In accordance with this example, therefore, teachers ought to temper their preaching, so that the perfect may find something they can always continue learning, while the weak may hear things from which they do not recoil.

The blessed patriarch Jacob showed this to us by his own example (Gen. XXX). While he was tending the sheep of his uncle Laban and was to receive various animals as his wages, he took poplar and almond rods, peeled some portions of them, left others with their bark, and placed them in the channels when the sheep were led to water, so that, looking at them, they might conceive various offspring.

Jacob, the shepherd of sheep, signifies shepherds of souls. To these it was first said: “If you love me, feed my sheep” (John XXI). Water signifies Sacred Scripture, in accordance with Solomon’s saying: “Deep water is the word from a man’s mouth, and a flowing stream is a fountain of wisdom” (Prov. XVIII).

The various rods signify the varied meanings of the Scriptures. The sheep are led to water when the faithful gather to hear the word of God. When diverse interpretations are brought forth from the divine utterances, the rods are, as it were, placed in the channels. Some are to be peeled, while others are to be left with their bark [Col. 0777D]. For, as we have said, the more perfect are to be instructed through allegorical meaning, while the simple and less understanding are to be nourished according to the truth of the historical sense.

Thus, when the Lord taught his disciples on the mountain and wished to heal the crowds in the valleys, he showed that those who could not believe through the teaching of words should at least believe through the power of miracles.

As we have said, the Lord made this clear by his own example when, “coming down from the mountain, he stood in a level place, with a crowd of his disciples and a great multitude of people from all Judea and Jerusalem, and from the seacoast, and from Tyre and Sidon, who had come to hear him” [Col. 0778A].

[Col. 0778B]

By “the seacoast” here we must understand the regions of the Great Sea, especially since they are said to have come from Tyre and Sidon, which are situated in the heart of the sea. Here we learn that his powers had extended not only to the kingdom of the Jews but also to neighboring and foreign regions, since everyone flocked together not only to hear the word of God but also to be healed of their illnesses. Hence it is added:

“And the whole crowd was seeking to touch him, because power went out from him and healed them all.”

Many desired to touch him, from whom all power proceeds, who is the power of God and the wisdom of God, in whom the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily. Therefore, because all power went out from him, everyone wished to touch him.

For earlier he had healed a leper by touching him; and now the whole crowd sought to touch him, so that we might understand that touch brings healing. The woman who had suffered from a flow of blood for twelve years experienced this. When she touched the fringe of his garment, she was immediately healed of her infirmity [Col. 0778C].

At her touch power went out from him, to such an extent that the Lord, as though unaware, asked, “Who touched me?” His disciples said to him: “Rabbi, the crowds press around you and trouble you, and you say, ‘Who touched me?’” But he replied: “Someone touched me, for I know that power has gone out from me” (Luke VIII).

Spiritually, however, the person touches Christ who believes that he is true God and confesses him with right faith. Pagans, Jews, and heretics do not truly touch Christ, because they disdain believing him to be true God and do not wish to confess him in the right faith.

Therefore, when Mary, who did not believe that the Lord had risen but sought him dead among the dead, wished to touch him, she was told: “Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father” (John XX) [Col. 0778D]. It was as though he were saying: Because you did not wish to touch me with the hand of faith, do not touch me with the hand of the body.

The healing of demons took place not only through his presence but also through the invocation of his name in his absence. Thus the disciples, rejoicing, say to the Lord: “Lord, even the demons are subject to us in your name” (Luke X).

It follows:

“And he lifted up his eyes toward his disciples and said: Blessed are you poor, because yours is the kingdom of God.”

Although the Lord was speaking generally, he lifted his eyes particularly toward the disciples, whom he made worthy of greater grace. For the lifting of the eyes of Jesus Christ signifies the gifts of a more abundant mercy [Col. 0779A]. He raised his eyes toward the disciples, whom he enriched especially with virtues, as we read elsewhere.

When someone said to him, “Behold, your mother and your brothers are standing outside, seeking to speak with you,” he himself lifted his eyes toward his disciples and said: “Behold my mother and my brothers” (Matt. XIII).

Let us hear what he says with his eyes lifted: “Blessed are you poor, because yours is the kingdom of God.” What virtue should hold the first place among the other beatitudes if not voluntary poverty? From it the other virtues derive a certain beginning and origin.

Just as many branches and leaves grow from a single tree root, so many virtues arise from voluntary poverty. Whoever loves voluntary poverty will be merciful through generosity and not grasping through avarice [Col. 0779B]. He will consequently also be gentle, because the person who loves poverty with humility does not seek riches through boasting. He will also be peaceful, because where there is no desire to acquire, there will be no occasion for quarrelling. He will also possess purity of heart, because just as those who love riches are troubled in mind, so those who love voluntary poverty are concerned with the things of God and with how they may please God.

But we must carefully consider that the poverty deserving praise is that which either does not desire to possess or, if it happens to possess something, leaves it to be distributed for God’s sake. Therefore the evangelist Matthew, wishing to show that this poverty pertains to blessedness, added the qualification: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. V).

Some are poor in spirit and in possessions; some are poor neither in possessions nor in spirit; some are poor in possessions but not in spirit; and some are poor in spirit but not in possessions [Col. 0779C].

Poor in possessions but not in spirit are those who have nothing but desire to possess many things. Poor in spirit but not in possessions are those who, according to the Apostle, are “as having nothing and possessing everything,” such as Abraham, Jacob, and David. Although David had been raised to a royal throne, he showed himself poor in spirit, saying: “But I am a beggar and poor” (Ps. XXXIX). And again: “I am needy and in labors from my youth” (Ps. LXXXVII).

Poor neither in possessions nor in spirit are the proud rich, who, though endowed with wealth, are nonetheless puffed up in mind. Of them it is said in the Psalm: “Behold, these are sinners, and, abounding in the world, they have acquired riches” (Ps. LXXII) [Col. 0779D].

Poor in possessions and in spirit are perfect monks, who, leaving everything for God’s sake, do not even leave the power over their own bodies to their own discretion. Therefore, the poorer they are here for God’s sake, the richer they will be in future glory, in accordance with the Lord’s promise: “Everyone who has left house, fields, father and mother, brothers and sisters, wife and children for my sake will receive a hundredfold and will possess eternal life” (Matt. XIX).

“Blessed are you who hunger now, for you will be filled.”

What those who desire to attain blessedness ought to hunger and thirst for is explained more clearly by another evangelist, who says: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they will be filled” (Matt. V).

To hunger and thirst for righteousness [Col. 0780A] is to hear God’s commandments willingly and to fulfill them in action even more willingly. Such people will be filled when they are brought to behold God, whose commandments they received here with great hunger of mind. Then they will say with the Psalmist: “But I shall appear in righteousness, and I shall be satisfied when your glory is revealed” (Ps. XVI). Hence Solomon says: “Love righteousness, you who judge the earth” (Wis. I).

“Blessed are you who weep now, for you will laugh.”

Those who weep are called blessed—not those who weep because of the loss of temporal advantages or the death of loved ones, but those who weep because of the remission of sins or in expectation of the kingdom of heaven. They can truly say with the Psalmist: “O God, I have declared my life to you; you have placed my tears in your sight” (Ps. LV) [Col. 0780B]. And again: “My tears have been my bread day and night, while it is said to me every day, ‘Where is your God?’” (Ps. XLI.)

Such people will laugh when what the Lord says is fulfilled: “Now you have sorrow, but I shall see you again, and your heart will rejoice, and no one will take your joy from you” (John XVI).

We must not understand laughter here in a childish sense, but as exultation and joy of mind. Thus Sarah, rejoicing over the promised offspring, said: “God has made laughter for me” (Gen. XXI). Of this laughter blessed Job says: “The mouths of the truthful will be filled with laughter” (Job VIII). Concerning this laughter it is also said in praise of the Church: “She girded her loins with strength, and she will laugh on the last day” (Prov. XXXI).

Because the rewards of martyrdom are attained through the merit of humility, it is rightly added after the other beatitudes [Col. 0780C]:

“Blessed will you be when people hate you, and when they separate you, reproach you, and cast out your name as evil, on account of the Son of Man.”

Here it is shown that the persecution of wicked people is not to be feared but rather endured when it comes. For, as the Apostle James says: “Blessed is the person who endures temptation, because when he has been tested, he will receive the crown of life which God promised to those who love him” (James I).

But this must be examined more subtly: we must not stir up wicked people to persecute us; rather, when they have been stirred up [Col. 0780D], we should mitigate them as far as we can by justice and uprightness. If they refuse to be quiet, persecution must be endured rather than righteousness abandoned.

Another evangelist makes this clearer, saying: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. V). Murderers, adulterers, thieves, and invaders of other people’s property suffer many tribulations. Yet persecution of this kind does not lead to blessedness; only persecution endured for righteousness does.

Therefore the blessed Peter admonishes us: “Let none of you suffer as a murderer, a thief, an adulterer, or a robber. But if anyone suffers as a Christian, let him not be ashamed, but let him glorify God in this name” (I Pet. IV). “And who is there to harm you if you are zealous for what is good? But even if you suffer for righteousness, you are blessed” [Col. 0781A].

Therefore the Savior rightly concludes, saying:

“Rejoice on that day and exult, for behold, your reward is great in heaven.”

We must not grieve in persecutions but rather rejoice, so that the more harshly someone is afflicted here for righteousness, the more sweetly he may be rewarded in heaven.

Hence James admonishes us: “Consider it all joy, my brothers, when you fall into various temptations, knowing that the testing of your faith is much more precious than gold, which is tested by fire” (James I). Another Scripture says: “The furnace tests the potter’s vessels, and the trial of tribulation tests righteous people” (Ecclus. XXVII).

For this reason the Savior, when he urged his disciples to endure persecution, set forth his own example, saying: “If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you. If they kept my word, they will also keep yours” (John XV) [Col. 0781B]. And again: “If you were of the world, the world would love what was its own. But because you are not of the world, and I chose you from the world, therefore the world hates you” (ibid.).

Let us therefore strive, in accordance with the Lord’s command and example, to bear all the adversities of this world with equanimity. We know that if we have been chosen by him, we have been sent into the world not for the world’s joy but—as he himself was sent by the Father, who ordained that he become incarnate for the redemption of the human race—for sufferings.

Amid the scandals of persecutors, therefore, let there be endurance of suffering. Let us flee earthly desires that separate us from God, so that we may deserve to attain heavenly rewards. Amen.

## HOMILY IX: ON THE CONFESSORS

[Col. 0781C]

(Matt. XXV.) “At that time, Jesus said this parable to his disciples: A certain man, going abroad, called his servants and entrusted his possessions to them. To one he gave five talents, to another two, and to another one, to each according to his own ability, and he departed.” And so forth.

In the parables that the Lord has set forth to instruct our ignorance, we must carefully consider that certain things are proposed for our admonition while also pertaining particularly to the Mediator himself, God and human beings. This is demonstrated in the sequence of the present reading, where it says: “A certain man, going abroad, called his servants and entrusted his possessions to them” [Col. 0781D].

This man must be understood through the parable as the Lord Jesus Christ. Although he was God before the ages, he became human at the end of the ages. Concerning him it is written: “A man was made in her, and the Most High himself founded her” (Ps. LXXXVI).

This man went abroad when, by ascending into heaven, he raised his flesh, which he had assumed from human beings. From the time when it was first said to the first human being, “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Gen. III), the proper place of flesh is earth. But this man went abroad because the flesh he assumed did not see corruption; rather, after the resurrection, it ascended into heaven.

The servants of this man are human beings, whom he created as rational creatures to serve him and praise him [Col. 0782A]. To serve this man is the highest freedom; to withdraw from his service is the most shameful slavery.

Paul gloried in being his servant when he said: “Paul, a servant of Christ Jesus” (Rom. I). And again: “I give thanks to my God, whom I serve from my forefathers.” The Psalmist likewise says: “I am your servant and the son of your handmaid” (Ps. CXV). And again: “I am your servant” (Ps. CXVIII).

The possessions of this man are spiritual gifts, that is, virtues of the soul, which arose from his goodness and were bestowed upon us by his generosity: love, peace, patience, humility, chastity, sobriety, and things of this kind.

Therefore, as he was about to depart abroad, he called his servants and entrusted his possessions to them, because he granted spiritual gifts to spiritual people. And because not everyone receives the same gifts equally, but, according to the distribution of the giver, one makes greater progress and another less, it is rightly said:

“To one he gave five talents, to another two, and to another one, to each according to his own ability, and he departed immediately.”

Just as a talent was weighed in different ways among the ancients, so the gifts of the Holy Spirit are diverse according to the merits of those who receive them—not in themselves, but in the recipients. For diverse gifts are given by one Lord to his servants, in accordance with what the Apostle says:

“To one is given through the Spirit a word of wisdom; to another, a word of knowledge according to the same Spirit; to another, faith in the same Spirit; to another, gifts of healing in the one Spirit; to another, the working of miracles; to another, prophecy; to another, discernment of spirits; to another, kinds of tongues; to another, interpretation of speeches. But one and the same Spirit works all these things, distributing to each one as he wills” (I Cor. XII).

By the five talents, therefore, the five bodily senses are signified, through which the outer person is governed: sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch. By the two, understanding and action are signified. By the name of one talent, understanding alone is expressed.

Thus the person who receives two talents receives more than the person to whom five talents are entrusted, because there are some who perform whatever works they can through the external senses and yet make little progress in spiritual understanding. There are also some who accomplish great things outwardly and understand still greater things inwardly.

There are likewise some who receive only one talent, because they understand good things but take no trouble to put them into practice. Concerning them it is written: “They are wise in doing evil but have not known how to do good” (Jer. IV).

That we must diligently persist in multiplying good works is made clear when it follows:

“He who had received five talents went away, worked with them, and gained another five. Likewise, he who had received two gained another two.”

We have already said above that the five talents signify the five bodily senses, and the two signify understanding and action. To double the five talents, therefore, is to serve God most devoutly through the external senses: giving food to the hungry, drink to the thirsty, clothing to the naked, visiting the one in prison, visiting the sick, burying the dead, and fulfilling other works of compassion [Col. 0783A].

The talents are doubled, as it were, through multiplication when some who are slower in understanding make progress in spiritual understanding through the practice of good works.

Those who double the two talents are people who, by living well and teaching well, do not neglect to increase the Church of God. They heed what is written to Timothy: “Entrust to faithful people the teaching that you have received from me, people who are able to teach others also” (II Tim. II).

The Apostle urged spiritual servants to double the talents they had received in this manner when he said: “Having gifts that differ according to the grace given to us: whether prophecy, according to the proportion of faith; or ministry, in ministering; or the one who teaches, in teaching; or the one who exhorts, in exhortation; the one who gives, in simplicity; the one who presides, with diligence; the one who shows mercy, with cheerfulness” (Rom. XII) [Col. 0783B].

“But he who had received one, went away, dug in the ground, and hid his master’s money.”
