He buries one talent in the ground, as it were, who occupies the ability he received from God in earthly pursuits and binds himself entirely to the love of the world.

But the time will come when spiritual people rejoice over the profit they have acquired, while lovers of the world are ashamed of their desires. Hence it follows:

“After a long time the master of those servants came and settled accounts with them.”

The Lord is said to return after a long time because a long interval lies between the Lord’s Ascension and his second coming [Col. 0783C]. Accounts will then be settled with the servants when he strictly demands from us the gifts that he mercifully bestowed upon us, when we stand before the tribunal of Christ to render an account, as the Apostle says, for what we have done (II Cor. V).

Blessed is the person who at that hour of examination is found to be such as this servant is said to have been. Of him it follows:

“He who had received five talents came forward and offered another five talents, saying: Lord, you entrusted five talents to me; behold, I have gained another five.”

He gains another five talents from the five talents who performs whatever good he can through the five bodily senses mentioned above. There are some people in the Church who, although they appear slower in intellect, nevertheless, when they faithfully serve through external ministry, are brought by his gift to spiritual understanding, to such an extent that they are sometimes even chosen for ecclesiastical teaching [Col. 0783D].

What reward he will receive is made clear when it follows:

“His master said to him: Well done, good and faithful servant; because you were faithful over a little, I will set you over much. Enter into the joy of your master.”

Everything in the present life is little in comparison with future goods, however great it may seem. Therefore, the person who was faithful over a little is set over much, because the one who has administered earthly substance well will receive an everlasting reward in place of transient things, hearing from the judge himself:

“Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. XXV).

“Then the one who had received two talents also came forward and said: ‘Lord, you entrusted me with two talents; behold, I have gained two more.’” Likewise, he gains another two talents who had received two from his lord, when one who possesses both understanding and practical ability calls many to the love of God not only by living well but also by teaching well.

It should be noted that the one who returned ten from five talents and the one who returned four from two are praised in equal words, since the lord says to both: “Well done, good and faithful servant,” that is, “Rejoice well.” How the servant rejoices with his lord is explained when it follows: “Because you were faithful over a little, I will set you over much.” [Col. 0784B] To him it is rightly said: “Enter into the joy of your lord,” because he will receive a reward corresponding to, and as great as, the number of those whom he has gained by living well and teaching well.

From these words we understand that those will receive a greater reward from the Lord in eternal life who, by living well—as we have said—and teaching well, devote themselves spiritually to the instruction and teaching of others. The Lord makes this clearer elsewhere, when the apostles asked, “Lord, are you telling this parable to us, or to everyone?” He replied: “Who, then, do you think is the faithful and prudent servant whom his lord appointed over his household, to give them their food at the proper time? Blessed is that servant whom his lord, when he comes, finds doing so. Truly I tell you, he will set him over all his possessions (Luke XII).” For whoever is set over all his possessions will receive a double reward: not only the one who lived holily, but also the one who taught worthily.

Accordingly, when Daniel was speaking of the resurrection of the dead, to show that spiritual teachers would be set over all things, he said: “Those who are learned will shine like the splendor of the firmament, and those who instruct many in righteousness like the stars for everlasting eternities (Dan. XXI).”

Desiring to hear this desirable saying and ineffable joy, our most blessed father, whose feast we celebrate today, took pains to expend the talent entrusted to him by teaching well and living well, so that he might return it doubled to the Lord—not only by admonishing the devout but also by restraining the reprobate. And because, according to the saying of Scripture, “a wise son is his father’s joy,” the merits of this man’s joys increase in proportion to the growth of his spiritual children.

Therefore, dearest brothers, it is necessary that each one of us, following the footsteps of this most blessed father, not bury in the earth the talent we have received from God, but strive with great eagerness to expend it, so that we may return it doubled to the Lord. Since one has received the talent of reading, another of singing, another of preaching, another of painting, and another of making things pertaining to the adornment of the church, each should strive to expend what he has learned.

Nor are such talents found only in ecclesiastical ministries. There are also people in this assembly who possess various crafts by which they earn their livelihood: some are masons, some carpenters, some smiths, and some cutters. Each person’s craft, by which he is fed, will be reckoned as the commendation of his talent; and if he instructs others in what he knows, he will receive a reward in the future.

The Lord shows how such a person ought to expend the talent he has received when he says: “You received without payment; give without payment (Matt. X).” Therefore, beloved brothers, each one of us must consider with the utmost diligence and vigilance how he may present to the Lord the talent he has received doubled.

But if he does not wish his talent to benefit others, let him fear the rebuke heard by the one who hid his single talent in the earth from the Lord: “Wicked and lazy servant, why did you not give my money to the money-changers, so that when I came I might at least have received what was mine with interest?” [Col. 0785B] And what follows will be fulfilled:

“Take the talent from him and give it to the one who has ten talents.” For whatever he has done without love is not good in God’s sight, even though it may appear good before human beings. The more generously each person expends the talent he has received for the Lord’s love, the greater the glory he will possess with the Lord. May he deign to grant this, who lives with the Father and the Holy Spirit, and so forth.

## HOMILY X. ALSO ON CONFESSORS

**(Luke XII.)** “At that time Jesus said to his disciples: ‘Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning in your hands.’” And so forth.

Among the other virtues that our Lord Jesus Christ taught his disciples, and through his disciples taught us, he presented chastity as the greatest and foremost. For after he had urged us above to love voluntary poverty, saying, “Make for yourselves purses that do not grow old, an unfailing treasure in heaven, where no thief approaches and no moth destroys (Luke XII),” he immediately added concerning the preservation of chastity: “Let your loins be girded.”

That lust resides in the loins of men and in the navel of women, the Lord testifies when, speaking of the devil to blessed Job, he says: “His strength is in his loins, and his power in the navel of his belly (Job XL).” Here the word “loins” signifies lust, when it is said: “Let your loins be girded.” We gird our loins when we restrain the heat of desire through love of chastity.

John the Baptist had his loins girded in this way. It is written of him that he was clothed in camel’s hair, with a leather belt around his loins (Mark I). He was not among the unclean, who because of the discharge of semen were expelled outside the camp; rather, he displayed in the clothing of his body the chastity he possessed in his mind. Elijah likewise wore a belt around his loins.

Those who are joined not for love of children but to satisfy lust do not have girded loins. Rather, they belong among those who, because of their uncleanness, are expelled outside the camp, being compared to senseless beasts. Whoever, taking the members of Christ, makes them members of a prostitute, certainly does not have girded loins, since, as the apostle Paul truly says: “Without peace and chastity no one will see God (Heb. XII).”

How pleasing the incorruption of the flesh is to God, he himself testifies through the prophet, saying: “Thus says the Lord to the eunuchs who keep my Sabbaths, choose what I desire, and hold fast to my covenant: ‘I will give them in my house and within my walls a place and a name better than sons and daughters, an everlasting name that shall not perish (Isa. VI).’” And in the Apocalypse it is said of such people: “These are they who have not been defiled with women, for they are virgins (Apoc. XIV).”

Although this must generally be observed by all the faithful, [Col. 0786B] it is nevertheless specially enjoined upon ministers of the ecclesiastical order. Thus, under the old law, they were not permitted to eat the flesh of the lamb—sacrificed as a figure of the Lord’s body and blood—before they had their loins girded, the Lord saying: “Thus you shall eat it: you shall gird your loins and have sandals on your feet (Exod. XII).”

Again: “The Lord said to Moses: ‘Speak to Aaron and to his sons: No man of your offspring who has a blemish shall approach the altar. If he is hunchbacked, or weak-eyed, or has a white spot in his eye, or a skin disease on his body, or a continual scab; if he is blind or lame, if he has a broken foot or a twisted nose, if he is swollen or has a hernia (Lev. XXI).’”

Those who must handle the sacred mysteries with their hands and minister them to others [Col. 0786C] ought to be free from every unclean pollution, so that they may be chaste in mind and modest in body. We learn this from the deed of David. When he came to the priest Ahimelech, he did not wish to receive the consecrated loaves before he had testified that he and his men were clean from women—not merely from other women or concubines, but even from their own wives. For he said: “Indeed, if the matter concerns women, we have abstained from them since yesterday and the day before, when we set out, and the vessels of the young men were clean (1 Kings XXI).”

Therefore, let each person examine his conscience; and if he feels himself incontinent in body, let him abstain from holy communion, lest he receive for judgment what was given to the faithful for healing. Let him fear what the Apostle proclaims so terribly, saying: “Whoever eats the bread or drinks the cup of the Lord unworthily will be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord. Let a person examine himself, and so let him eat of the bread and drink of the cup. For whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself, not discerning the Lord’s body (1 Cor. XI).”

Or, alternatively, we gird our loins when we set aside all the impediments of the world, so that we may firmly plant the step of our mind on the way of God’s commandments. One who is ungirded is hindered by his own garments from walking freely; but one who is girded can move freely in every direction. A soldier girds himself for battle and carries a sword around his loins with which to strike his adversary.

And so you, who desire to be a soldier of God, gird your loins—that is, set aside all that is fleeting and all the impediments of the world—so that you may fight “not against flesh and blood, but against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in the heavenly places,” so that what the same Apostle adds may be fulfilled in you: “Stand therefore, having your loins girded with truth, and having put on the breastplate of righteousness, and having shod your feet in the preparation of the gospel of peace (Eph. VI).”

In this way the soldier of the camp had girded his loins when he heard: “Gird your loins like a man (Job XXXVIII).” Hence also it is said in praise of the Church: “He girded his loins with strength and strengthened his arm (Job XL).”

Whoever is such must be set before others as an example for imitation, because, as the Lord says: “No one lights a lamp and puts it under a bushel, but on a lampstand, so that it may shine for all who are in the house (Luke XI).”

Therefore, after saying, “Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning,” what is signified by the lamps if not good works? To have burning lamps is to display good works to others for imitation, according to what the Lord says elsewhere: “Let your light shine before human beings, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven (Matt. V).”

It should be considered that two things are commanded: to gird the loins and to have burning lamps. For chastity is of no benefit without good works, nor is good work of any value without chastity. First we are commanded to restrain our loins, and afterward to hold the lamps, because the one to be advanced as an example to others is the person in whose breast salutary desires are alive and whose mind is not occupied by carnal pleasure.

This was prefigured in the law when Moses commanded that the Levites should minister until their fiftieth year, but after the fiftieth year should become guardians of the vessels, observing the prescribed age whether for governance or for undertaking the office of preaching (Num. VIII).

But one may ask why he commands them to hold lamps when elsewhere he says: “But when you pray, go into your room and, after shutting the door, pray to your Father (Matt. VI).” The answer is that those are commanded to display good works for the example of others who are so perfect that they are not lifted up when praised by human beings. But to those who are imperfect, or whom human favor exalts, it is commanded: “But when you pray, go into your room. And when you give alms, do not let your left hand know what your right hand is doing (ibid.).”

And because, according to John’s saying, “If our heart does not condemn us, we have confidence on the day of judgment (1 John III),” all who have their loins girded and their lamps burning ought not so much to fear the Lord’s coming as to love it. Hence it follows:

“And you must be like people waiting for their lord when he returns from the wedding, so that when he comes and knocks, they may immediately open to him.”

Our Lord went to the wedding when, ascending into heaven, he joined to himself the multitude of angels as the new man. He will then return to his servants when he begins to be revealed through judgment.

Or, alternatively: certainly the Lord comes to us every day when, through his grace, he visits our consciences and inflames our heart with his love. He knocks when, through the distress of illness, he announces approaching death. The person who gladly departs from the body immediately opens to him, desiring to see the appearance of the one whom he has always longed for.

The person who knows that he has scarcely obeyed the Lord’s commands is afraid to open to the Judge who knocks; as he departs from the body, he trembles at seeing the one whom he remembers having despised. He fears seeing as judge the one whose commands he does not know himself to have obeyed.

Just as the righteous love the arrival of a judge in his city, while thieves and robbers fear it, so those who know that they have scarcely obeyed the Lord’s commands fear his coming. Only those love it who remember that they have lived rightly. This is the conduct of those who, insofar as human frailty permits, preserve their life blameless and place their heart, withdrawing it from earthly love, in the joy of the heavenly homeland.

Such was the apostle Paul, who, secure concerning his good deeds, said: “I am already being poured out, and the time of my departure is at hand. I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith. Henceforth the crown of righteousness is laid up for me (2 Tim. IV).” And again: “I desire to depart and to be with Christ, for that is far better (Phil. I).” And once more: “I live, yet it is no longer I, but Christ lives in me (Gal. II).”

Blessed Martin was prepared to open in this way to the Judge who knocked. When he was afflicted by illness and moved by the tears of his disciples, he said: “The struggle of labor through which I have fought until now is grievous, Lord; but if I am still necessary to your people, I do not refuse the labor on their account. Let your will be done.”

What reward is prepared for such people the Lord reveals when he adds:

“Blessed are those servants whom the lord, when he comes, will find watching.”

To watch is for each person to be diligent in good work. The person watches well who believes rightly and lives rightly. The person watches who keeps the eyes of his mind open to the sight of the true light. Or certainly, the person watches who shakes off torpor and negligence from himself and clings to the divine commandments with ardent spirit.

The apostle Paul urged people to watch in this way when he said: “Awake, righteous ones, and do not sin (1 Cor. XV).” And again: “It is already the hour for us to rise from sleep (Rom. XIII).” And once more: “Watch and pray, and stand firm in the faith (1 Cor. XVI).”

The nature of the reward itself is also indicated when it follows: “Truly I tell you, he will gird himself and have them recline, and he will pass by and minister to them.”

God’s being girded means that he prepares himself for repayment. Our reclining means resting in eternal blessedness, according to what he himself says elsewhere: “Many will come from east and west and recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven (Matt. VIII).”

He is said to pass by when, after the judgment, he hastens to the kingdom. Or certainly, the Lord will pass by and minister to us when he leads us from the form of his humanity to the contemplation of the love of his divinity.

For he will appear to all at the judgment in the form of his humanity, to the righteous and the unrighteous alike, as it is written: “And all flesh shall see the salvation of our God (Isa. XL).” But after the reprobate have been condemned by a just judgment, according to what is written, “Let the ungodly be taken away, lest he see the glory of God (Isa. XXVI),” he will pass by only to the elect, whom he will raise from the vision of his humanity to the contemplation of the love of his divinity, so that those who now see only a human being may then be worthy to see God face to face, and perceive how the Father remains in the Son and the Son in the Father.

But since the end of the present life is uncertain for everyone, it rightly follows:

“And if he comes in the second watch, and if in the third watch he comes and finds them so, blessed are those servants.”

The ancients divided the night into four watches, so that each watch contained three hours. The variations of the hours signify the diversity of human calling.

The first watch is the earliest period of our age, that is, childhood. The second watch is adolescence or youth, which are nearly the same, as Solomon says: “Rejoice, young man, in your adolescence (Eccl. XI).” The third watch is old age.

When the Lord calls some who are doing good in childhood from this life, he comes, as it were, to servants watching in the first watch. When he leads others from this life in adolescence or youth, he comes, as it were, in the second watch.

Therefore, if someone does not wish to watch in the first watch, let him at least watch here in the second—that is, if someone was sluggish in childhood concerning good work, let him at least shake off the sleep of torpor in adolescence or youth and, while the strength of his body is vigorous, exercise himself in good work.

But if someone is found so negligent and idle that he has watched neither in the first nor in the second watch, let him at least come to his senses in the third, that is, in old age, and then not fear watching when he will have little time left for it.

For divine mercy does not despise those who convert late. Through the prophet it says (Ezek. XVIII): “As I live, says the Lord, I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live.” And again: “On whatever day the sinner turns and repents, he will be saved.”

But because the ancient enemy often deceives lukewarm Christians in this regard—persuading them toward sin while promising them a long life—the Lord further adds, by way of warning, a likeness concerning the uncertainty of the end, saying:

“But know this: if the master of the house had known at what hour the thief would come, he would certainly have watched and would not have allowed his house to be broken into.”

According to the literal sense, this is so: if a master of a house who had a hidden treasure stored in his house knew of the thief’s arrival, he would set watches, establish guards, reinforce the weaker places, and carefully take precautions so that his house could not be broken into by any deceit. Spiritually, however, this master of the house is our mind. It sleeps in wrongful security when, forgetting the day of death, it grows sluggish in good work and promises itself the very brief time of the present life as though it were long.

The thief’s arrival is death. It comes suddenly and unexpectedly, when it is not anticipated, and carries the treasure of our soul away to punishments. Therefore, to be able to guard against the arrival of this thief, we must always keep the day of death before our eyes.

It greatly helps us against sin if the end of life does not depart from our memory, as Scripture warns: “In all your works remember your last things, and you will never sin (Eccl. VII).” Hence the Lord adds by way of admonition:

“You also must be ready, because the Son of Man will come at an hour you do not expect.”

If we knew the end of our life, we would assign another time for repentance. But since the hour of death is uncertain to everyone, the conscience must not be secure apart from good work. For the almighty Lord, who does not wish anyone to perish but everyone to come to knowledge of the truth, wanted the final day to remain hidden from us so that, while one day is unknown, we might observe them all.

When he says, “because the Son of Man will come at an hour you do not expect,” if we refer this to the day of judgment, it is clear that the day is uncertain and unknown to everyone, as he himself says in the Gospel: “Concerning that day and hour no one knows, neither the angels in heaven nor the Son of Man, but the Father alone (Mark XIII).” And again: “As it was in the days of Noah, so will be the coming of the Son of Man (Matt. XXIV).” And once more: “As lightning comes out from the east and reaches to the west, so will be the coming of the Son of Man (ibid.).”

After his resurrection, when the disciples asked him, he said: “It is not for you to know the times or seasons that the Father has established by his own authority (Acts I).” Hence the apostle Peter says: “The day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night (2 Peter III).”

But what will then happen universally to all in the resurrection of souls and bodies happens daily to individuals in their souls. The Son of Man comes when we do not expect him, when, overtaken by sudden death, we have the same limit for sinning as for living. And while we do not abandon evil, but are abandoned by evil, we undertake repentance too late, failing to heed what is written: “Do not delay turning to God, nor postpone it from day to day, lest his anger suddenly come and destroy you in the time of vengeance (Eccl. V).”

## HOMILY XI. ON VIRGINS

[Col. 0790D]

**(Matt. XIII.)** “At that time Jesus said to his disciples this parable: ‘The kingdom of heaven is like a treasure hidden in a field, which a man found and hid.’” And so forth.

The Lord Jesus Christ, the power and wisdom of God, not only deigned to humble himself out of compassion for human beings by assuming human nature, but also, accommodating himself to human ignorance, frequently employed likenesses drawn from temporal things in his holy sayings, so that by comparing visible things he might stir the minds of his hearers toward love of invisible things.

Therefore, when he teaches that heavenly glory must be loved earnestly, he employs the likeness of things that human beings usually love greatly, saying: “The kingdom of heaven is like a treasure hidden in a field, which a man found and hid.”

By the name “treasure” we must spiritually understand the love of the heavenly homeland, where there are riches that do not fail and a treasure that never withers—where the Lord urges us to store up treasure, according to what he says elsewhere: “Store up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither rust nor moth destroys, and where thieves do not break in or steal”; and, “Where your treasure is, there your heart will be also (Matt. VI).”

This treasure is certainly accumulated all the more as earthly treasure and resources are spent more earnestly for God. Hence it is said of the one who found the treasure: “And for joy over it he goes and sells all that he has and buys that field.”

The field in which the hidden treasure is found is ourselves, provided that heavenly desire remains within us. The person who buys it by selling everything is the one who disciplines his body for the sake of the heavenly homeland through fasting, vigils, and prayers.

The person who, having given everything, buys the field together with the treasure he has found is also the one who crucifies his members with their vices and desires, follows Christ, and in a certain sense exchanges himself through a spiritual sale, turning away from evil and doing good.

The Lord persuaded a certain person to buy this hidden treasure in the field when he said: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me (Matt. XIX).”

It should be noted that the treasure, once found, is kept hidden so that it may be preserved. From this we are to understand how carefully we must avoid empty glory in good work.

The present life is like a road, while the robbers beside the road are unclean spirits. They especially envy those whom they see journeying toward the heavenly homeland with a spiritual treasure, as the Prophet says concerning their leader: “He sits in ambush with the rich in secret places, to kill the innocent (Ps. X).”

These robbers seize the riches of those who expose their good works before human beings through empty boasting. Therefore, when we perform a good work outwardly, we must always keep our intention of pleasing God hidden, according to his admonition: “When you give alms, do not let your left hand know what your right hand is doing (Matt. VI).” And again: “But when you pray, go into your room, and after shutting the door, pray to your Father; and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you (ibid.).”

To kindle the mind in love of heavenly desire, another likeness is given when it follows:

“Again, the kingdom of heaven is like a merchant seeking fine pearls; and when he found one precious pearl, he went and sold all that he had and bought it.”

By the name “precious pearl” we understand the sweetness or brightness of the eternal homeland, which is more precious than every precious thing [Col. 0792A] and sweeter than every delight.

Spiritually, we are merchants who are commanded to earn heavenly glory from earthly resources. It should be noted that he says, “He sold all that he had and bought it,” because the person who buys the one precious pearl—that is, the heavenly homeland—by giving everything is the one who renounces not only earthly resources but also his own capacities.

The person who gives his possessions to the poor but still serves his own desires has not yet bought the precious pearl, because he has retained what he could have offered to God at greater cost. For God seeks not our possessions but us; he commanded us to give earthly substance only for the gain of souls.

Since, therefore, we have been compared with the merchant seeking fine pearls and with fine pearls themselves, we must preserve in our work what we have received in the name.

Just as earthly merchants are not prevented from practicing their trade by the dangers of the sea, frightened by the ambushes of robbers, deterred by the hardships of the journey, held back by winter’s cold or summer’s heat, provided only that they can acquire earthly profit, so we, who are spiritual merchants, must not be held back from love of the heavenly homeland by any worldly allurements. No adversity of the world should frighten us, nor any tribulation prevent us, so that, loving the precious pearl, we may be able to say with the Apostle:

“Who, then, will separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or danger, or the sword? But I am certain that neither death nor life, nor angels nor principalities, nor powers, nor things present nor things to come, nor strength, nor height nor depth, nor any other creature will be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord (Rom. VIII).”

Let us imitate another practice of merchants. Those who devote themselves to commerce have this characteristic: if they suffer losses in one transaction, they apply themselves more diligently to trade until they recover in another what they lost in one matter.

So too, if we suffer harm to the soul through some circumstance, let us devote ourselves more diligently to the good work we have begun, so that what we lost through negligence we may recover through good work. In this way we may attain the profit of the precious pearl and be worthy to hear the Lord’s voice saying: “Well done, good and faithful servant, because you were faithful over a little, I will set you over much; enter into the joy of your lord (Rom. VIII).”

This pearl is so dear that it cannot be compared with any earthly riches, and yet so inexpensive that it can be acquired by good will alone.

Zacchaeus sought to purchase this precious pearl with many possessions. When he had received the giver of this pearl into his house, he said out of excessive joy: “Lord, half of my goods I give to the poor, and if I have defrauded anyone of anything, I restore it fourfold (Luke XIX).”

The widow also bought this pearl with two small copper coins cast into the treasury. The Lord himself, the witness of her conscience, praised its price, saying: “Truly I tell you, this poor widow has put in more than all those who have put into the treasury. For they all gave out of their abundance, but she, out of her poverty, put in all that she had, her entire livelihood (Mark XII).”

Blessed N., whose feast we celebrate today, acquired the beauty of this pearl by giving many possessions, when, for its love, she abandoned the power of a kingdom and rejected the marriage bed of a royal union, embracing voluntary poverty.

Therefore, undoubtedly, because she despised marriage to an earthly king, she became the bride of the heavenly King. She who did not wish to reign with an earthly king in the world now reigns with Christ in heaven. And because she avoided the salutations and services of royal ministers, she now ministers with Christ, joined to the companies of angels.

Therefore it is fitting that, while we venerate an earthly queen with due honor, we should beseech this queen, acceptable to God, with devout prayers, so that, because she gathered us together in Christ’s name through her example, she may make us joyful in the present life through her merits and prayers and make us acceptable in the future.

“Again, the kingdom of heaven is like a net cast into the sea and gathering fish of every kind.”

The Church is beautifully likened to a net, because it has been entrusted to a fisherman and daily catches human beings within the net of faith. Just as it belongs to fishermen to draw fish from the depths of the whirlpools to the shore with a net, so the Church daily strives, through the teaching of preachers, to draw human minds from the turbulent and bitter whirlpools of the world to the true light.

And because, so long as it remains in the present life, the Church gathers both the good and the wicked, it rightly follows concerning the same net:

“When it was full, they drew it ashore, sat down, and collected the good into containers, but threw the bad away.”

When the good and the wicked are named, the Church of the present age is signified. The good are nowhere found alone except in heaven, and the wicked nowhere alone except in hell. This Church, which stands between the two, receives citizens of both homelands, as the Psalmist says: “I proclaimed and spoke; they were multiplied beyond number (Ps. XXXIX).”

Here it should be considered that many reprobates may now enter the Church beyond the number of the elect, but they cannot enter the kingdom of heaven. Hence it is rightly said: “They collected the good into their containers, but threw the bad away.”

These words clearly show that the separation of the elect and the reprobate will occur at the end of the age. Just as the sea signifies the world, so the shore of the sea signifies the end of the age. Sitting on the shore, they “collected the good into their containers, but threw the bad away,” because at the end of the age the elect will be taken up to glory and the reprobate separated for punishment, according to what the Lord says elsewhere in the Gospel: “On that night there will be two in one bed: one will be taken and the other left (Luke XVII).”

Therefore, in explaining the likeness, the Lord adds:

“So it will be at the consummation of the age. The angels will go out and separate the wicked from among the righteous, and they will throw them into the furnace of fire; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.”

This is what the Lord says elsewhere in the Gospel: “The Son of Man will send his angels, and they will gather out of his kingdom all causes of stumbling (Matt. XIII).” Again, when asked about the weeds that the enemy had sown over the wheat, he said: “Let both grow until the harvest, and at harvest time I will say to the reapers: ‘First gather the weeds and bind them in bundles to burn them, but gather the wheat into my barn (ibid.).’”

The same thing is said elsewhere by the Lord: “When the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty, all nations will be gathered before him, and he will separate them from one another as a shepherd separates the sheep from the goats (Matt. XXV),” and so forth.

In the words that follow—“There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth”—the nature of the punishments is plainly described. Eyes commonly shed tears because of excessive smoke, while teeth gnash because of intense cold. When he says, “There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth,” he shows that the reprobate in Gehenna will endure both intolerable cold and immeasurable heat, according to what is said through blessed Job (chap. XXIV): “They pass from waters of snow to excessive heat; down to the underworld is his sin. May mercy forget him; his sweetness is a worm.”

When the likeness had ended, the Savior asked the disciples about its meaning, showing pious teachers that, if they are to instruct others, they must sometimes ask questions. For he said:

“Have you understood all these things?”

And when they said to him, “Yes,” he rejoiced over their progress, saying:

[Col. 0794C] “Therefore every scribe instructed in the kingdom of heaven is like a householder who brings forth from his treasure new things and old.” That this pertains especially to the apostles is made clear by the fact that they are compared to a householder “who brings forth from his treasure new things and old.” For if by “new and old” we understand the Old and New Testaments, we recognize that Abraham, Moses, and the other Fathers who lived before the Lord’s coming did not bring forth new things together with the old. Although they proclaimed new things, they did not see the Lord’s new incarnation with bodily eyes, just as he himself said to his disciples: “Many kings and prophets desired to see what you see, and did not see it; and to hear what you hear, and did not hear it” (Luke X). The apostles, however, understood the new and the old spiritually, and saw the new with bodily eyes. To them he himself said: “I give you a new commandment, that you love one another” (John XIII).

Or otherwise: the old pertains to punishment, the new to glory. For it was old for human beings, after sin, to go to punishment; something new occurred through the coming of the Redeemer, when glory was promised to those who do good. When, therefore, the Lord commends his disciples, saying, “Every scribe instructed in the kingdom of heaven is like a householder who brings forth from his treasure new things and old,” he shows that teachers must observe this order in preaching: they should bring forth the old concerning the terror of punishment, and the new concerning the promise of reward. The Lord also demonstrates this by his own example in the course of this reading [Col. 0795A]: in the preceding parables he urged people toward reward, and in those that follow he threatens punishment. Thus, as has been said, he shows teachers that they must promise glory to those who do good, yet must not cease to threaten punishment to sinners.

He also presented this figuratively in the Law, when through Moses he gave the following command: “You shall not take the upper or the lower millstone as a pledge, for he has handed over his life to you” (Deut. XXIV). The upper and lower millstones are understood as hope and fear. We take a pledge from debtors, as it were, when we receive a sinner’s confession. If we do not promise the penitent hope, we deny forgiveness and take away the upper millstone. If, however, we give the sinner security, we remove the lower one. Both must therefore be observed: we must promise forgiveness to the penitent in such a way that we threaten punishment to those who persist in sin, so that those whom promised rewards do not move to do good may at least be frightened by announced punishments. But you, Lord, have mercy on us.

# HOMILY XII. SERMON ON JESUS’ CONFESSION TO THE FATHER, AND ON THE SWEETNESS OF HIS YOKE AND THE LIGHTNESS OF HIS BURDEN

## (Matthew XI)

“At that time Jesus answered and said: I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent.” And the rest.

At the beginning of this Gospel reading a question arises, since neither above nor below is it described that anyone had asked him anything. For elsewhere we read that he was questioned by his disciples and answered; the scribes and Pharisees questioned him, and he answered. Here it is understood that nothing of this sort is found, but that it simply says, “Jesus answered.”

The agreement with the evangelist Luke must be established, for he explains this more suitably when he says (Luke X): “The Lord appointed also another seventy-two and sent them two by two before his face into every city and place where he himself was about to come,” and “gave them” power to tread upon serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy, “and nothing shall harm you,” and to heal the sick and perform other miracles. Luke himself bears witness to this in what follows, saying that they went and did as Jesus had appointed them, performing many miracles and, among other things, casting out demons. When they returned from there with joy to the Lord, they said: “Lord, even the demons are subject to us in your name.” And Jesus said to them: “I was watching Satan fall like lightning from heaven. Nevertheless, do not rejoice in this, that the spirits are subject to you; but rejoice that your names are written in heaven” (ibid.).

Then he adds and says: “In that same hour Jesus rejoiced in the Holy Spirit and said” (ibid.): “I confess to you, Lord.” This is what Jesus says. For it must be understood that in one human being there are two human beings, the inner and the outer. The inner commonly answers the outer, and the outer the inner, as we read concerning Nebuchadnezzar, who, while he was walking about in the hall of his royal palace in Babylon, swollen with pride, answered: “Is this not that Babylon which I built by the strength and power of my might?” (Dan. IV.)

But the Lord did not answer in the manner of Nebuchadnezzar. Rather, humanity answered Divinity—or rather, the Son answered the Father. For he saw the images of demons being destroyed, the prince of this world being cast out, and the number of his own people increasing; therefore he rejoiced and said: “I confess.”

Confession is spoken of in three ways. There is confession in faith, confession of sins, and confession in praise. There is confession in faith, as the universal Church confesses when it says: “I believe in God.” There is confession of sins, concerning which the apostle says: “Confess your sins to one another” (James V). There is also confession in praise, concerning which the Prophet says: “Confess to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy endures forever” (Ps. CV).

The Lord, however, is said to confess neither in faith nor in sins, but only in praise. Or certainly he is said to confess because he causes the saints to do this. “I confess to you, Lord.”

At this the heretics rose up and said that the Lord Jesus Christ was not truly the Son of God by the propriety of his nature. They argued that if he had been the true Son of God, he would never have called him “Lord,” failing to consider that in his humanity he is less than the Father, as he himself says: “The Father is greater than I” (John XIV), while in his divinity he is equal to the Father, as he himself says: “I and the Father are one” (John X). It is according to his humanity that he calls him Lord. Hence the Father says to him through the Prophet: “Do not fear, my servant.” Blessed Mary also calls herself his handmaid and says: “Behold the handmaid of the Lord” (Luke I).

“Father of heaven and earth.” He rightly calls him Father, because, having ascended into heaven, he said: “I am ascending to my Father” (John XX).

Some wish to understand this by hyperbaton—that is, by a transposition of the words—saying: “I confess to you, Father,” and then adding: “Lord of heaven and earth,” so that the sense is that he is the Father of the Son and the Lord of heaven and earth. Although it can be understood in this way, it should nevertheless be taken according to the sense stated above, because he is equal to the Father according to his divinity.

He is the Father of heaven—that is, of the angels—and of earth—that is, of human beings. Alternatively, he is the Father of heaven, that is, of holy souls. Hence it is written: “The heavens declare the glory of God, and the works of his hands” (Ps. XVIII), and so forth; and of earth, that is, of human beings who are still entangled in earthly things, who cannot yet contemplate heavenly things with the eye of the mind, nor are able to say with the Apostle: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. III).

He is rightly called the Father of heaven and earth because he created all things, visible and invisible, from nothing, as it is written: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth” (Gen. I). And elsewhere: “He who remains forever created all things together” (Ecclus. XVIII). Hence we also say daily in prayer: “Our Father” (Luke XI). And elsewhere he himself says: “You have one Father” (Matt. XXIII).

“He who has hidden these things from the wise and prudent.” Here we must inquire what the Lord hid from the wise and prudent. Was humanity hidden from the scribes and Pharisees, when Simeon says: “My eyes have seen your salvation” (Luke II)? And elsewhere it is written: “Every eye will see him.” It was not humanity that he hid from them, but divinity, because the scribes and Pharisees did not recognize the divinity concealed in humanity. For “if they had known it, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (I Cor. II).

The wise and prudent were the holy apostles, concerning whom the Lord says to the Jews: “Behold, I send to you prophets and wise men and scribes” (Matt. XXIII). And again he says to the apostles: “Therefore be prudent as serpents” (ibid. X). The apostle Peter also says: “Be prudent and watchful in prayers” (I Peter LV).

But was divinity hidden from these people? No. It was hidden from those concerning whom the Lord says through the Prophet: “Woe to you who are wise in your own eyes and prudent in your own sight” (Isa. V). And again: “They are wise to do evil” (Jer. IV). The Apostle says: “Because the world could not believe God through wisdom, God was pleased through foolishness to save believers. For God chose the foolish things of the world to confound the strong” (I Cor. I), and so forth.

“And you have revealed them to infants.” Who are these infants? Clearly, the holy apostles. For you have in the Gospel that Jesus summoned an infant, set him in the midst, and said: “Unless you turn and become like infants” (Matt. XVIII), and so forth. And again: “Let the infants come to me” (ibid. XIX).

He calls them infants not because of bodily smallness or ignorance, but because of innocence. Hence the Apostle says to his disciples: “Do not become children in your understanding” (I Cor. XIV).

The Lord revealed his Son to the holy apostles, as to Thomas, who said: “My Lord and my God” (John XX), and as he said to Peter: “Flesh and blood has not revealed this to you” (Matt. XVI). For the blessed eyes of the righteous, to whom the Lord has deigned to reveal himself and the Father, will possess the kingdom of God.

“Indeed, Father, for this was pleasing before you.” For it was pleasing to God the Father to send his only-begotten Son for the salvation of the human race. Or also, it was pleasing to him to hide his Son from the wise and prudent of this world and reveal him to infants. Or certainly, in the presence of God the Father, before all ages, it was determined whom he would choose from the world, sending his Son into the world. For, as the Apostle says: “Those whom he foreknew, he also predestined; and those whom he predestined, he also called; and those whom he called, he also justified” (Rom. VIII).

“All things have been handed over to me by my Father.” In Christ we must always understand two natures and two operations, namely, the divine and the human. According to the divine nature he is equal to the Father, and possesses all things with the Father, as he himself says to the Father: “Father, all that is mine is yours” (John XVI). According to the human nature, by which he is less than the Father, all things have been subjected to him by the Father. Hence the Father says to him: “Ask of me, and I will give you” (Mark VI). And in this passage: “All things have been handed over to me by my Father.” And in the Psalm: “You have subjected all things beneath his feet” (Ps. VIII).

Therefore, after his resurrection, the Lord himself joyfully said to his disciples: “All power has been given to me” (Matt. XXVIII), and so forth.

The Father possesses what the Son does not possess; the Son possesses what the Father does not possess; the Holy Spirit possesses what the Father and Son possess. The Father has eternity without birth. The Son has eternity with birth. The Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son. Therefore, the Father is unbegotten, the Son begotten, and the Holy Spirit—take care not to be deceived—is neither begotten nor unbegotten, but proceeds from the Father and the Son.

[Col. 0798B] “And no one knows the Son except the Father; nor does anyone know the Father except the Son and the one to whom the Son wishes to reveal him.” We must inquire very carefully why he says, “No one knows the Son,” and so forth, when the Apostle says: “But when it pleased him who set me apart” (Gal. I), and so forth. John also bears witness that he saw him clothed in a robe reaching to his feet, up to his breast (Rev. I).

And not only in the New Testament, but also in the Old, saints are found who testify that they saw God, such as Abraham, who saw three and worshiped one; and Jacob, who said: “We have seen face to face” (Gen. XXXII). Moses also spoke with him face to face (Exod. XXXIII). Isaiah likewise says: “I saw the Lord seated upon a lofty throne” (chap. VI); and the apostle John says: “What we have seen, what we have heard” (John III).

Yet here he says: “No one has seen the Son except the Father” (Matt. XI). If no one knows the Son except the Father, then the saints believe in vain that they will ascend to where Christ is. But this question is easily resolved if we consider what we said above: that there are two natures in Christ, divine and human.

For it must be understood that, since he is coeternal and coequal with the Father, no one knows him, nor can know him, as John says: “No one has ever seen God” (John I). For how can anyone know—or be able to know—God, light from light, almighty from almighty, as the Prophet says: “Who will recount his generation?” (Isa. LIII.) This is what the Apostle considered when he said: “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God!” (Rom. XI), and so forth.

For the Lord says to Moses: “A human being shall not see me and live” (Exod. XXXIII). Or, again, no one knows how he was in the womb of the blessed Virgin Mary. For the angel said to blessed Mary: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you” (Luke I). Hence John says: “After me comes a man” (John I), and the Prophet: “To whom shall I reveal the arm of the Lord?” (Isa. LIII.)

Therefore, the Father knows the Son whom he begot coeternal and consubstantial with himself. “And to whom the Son wishes to reveal him.” For although the saints do not now see him bodily, the time remains when they will see him. Hence John says: “Beloved, now we are children of God” (I John III). To whomever he wishes, and as much as he wishes, he reveals himself and the Father.

“Come to me, all of you.” In sacred Scripture we find four callings: two in the Old Testament and two in the New.

The first in the Old Testament is: “Come, children, hear me” (Ps. XII). The second is: “Come, let us worship” (Ps. XCIV). The first in the New Testament is the one recited at present: “Come to me, all of you” (Matt. XI). The second is: “Come, blessed of my Father” (Matt. XXV), and the rest.

Just as the synagogue admonished its children to come and learn the fear of God, saying, “Come, children, hear me,” and so forth, and afterward urged them to worship, saying, “Come, let us worship,” so the holy Church exhorts us when it says: “Come to me, all of you.” What the synagogue said—“Come, children, hear me”—the Church says: “Come to me, all of you.” And what it said—“Come, let us worship”—Christ likewise was to say to the saints: “Come, blessed of my Father.”

Three callings have already been fulfilled and are fulfilled daily. The fourth remains, which will be fulfilled on the day of judgment. Those who are worthy to hear it will rejoice without end.

“You who labor and are burdened.” The people of the Gentiles labored in the worship of demons and in the shrines of idols, and also in the desires of the flesh, concerning which it is written: “They have woven spiders’ webs” (Isa. LIX). The Apostle says: “You know that when you were Gentiles, [you were] to mute idols” (I Cor. XII), and so forth.

“And I will refresh you.” What did he promise? Refreshment, not only in bodily food but in spiritual food. Concerning this refreshment it is written in the Apocalypse: “Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb” (chap. XIX). Receiving it, the saints will say: “How great is the abundance of your sweetness, Lord!” (Ps. XXX), and so forth.

Concerning this refreshment the Lord said to the Samaritan woman: “Whoever drinks the water that I shall give will become in him a fountain of water springing up into eternal life” (John IV).

“Take my yoke upon you.” A human being can never be without a yoke, either Christ’s or the devil’s. Formerly the Jewish people bore the yoke of the Law, concerning which the apostle Peter says: “Why do you wish to place a yoke upon us?” (Acts XV), and so forth. For the Lord afterward says: “They impose heavy and unbearable burdens on people’s shoulders” (Matt. XXIII).

The people of the Gentiles bore the devil’s yoke, namely, the burden of sins upon their backs. Concerning this it was said above: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened” (Matt. XI).

It should be noted that he did not call the devil’s burden his yoke. We can understand Christ’s yoke as his teaching, which all the saints who wished to follow him will bear, as he himself says: “Whoever wishes to come after me” (Matt. XVI), and so forth.

It should also be noted that people who cause others to come to them and desire to instruct them say to them, “Learn from us.” Likewise, the Lord wishes to instruct us in his teaching when he says: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart.”

He did not say: Learn to perform miracles, heal the sick, raise the dead, and other such things. For above he had already given them power to do these things. Here nothing of the sort is found; he said only: “Learn from me.” What, if not humility?

It should also be noted that he said he was gentle. For he had already promised the earth to the gentle, saying: “Blessed are the gentle, for they shall possess the earth.” And lest what the Lord commanded should seem burdensome, he had already shown it by examples. It is rightly said that he is “humble of heart,” because he humbled himself, as the Apostle says: “Although he was in the form of God, he did not consider equality with God something to be seized, but emptied himself” (Phil. II), and so forth.

Many appear humble outwardly but are inwardly swollen with pride. A good conscience bears such fruit and always preserves humility within.

“And you will find rest for your souls.” Elsewhere he says: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matt. X). The saints will receive rest after tribulation.

“For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.” His yoke is easy. Why is it easy? Or why is it light? Because he first fulfilled what he taught, as Luke says in Acts I: “Jesus began to do and to teach.” He commanded us to be humble, and he first displayed humility in himself. He commanded nothing that he did not himself demonstrate.

Some teachers also commonly impose “heavy and unbearable” things upon their disciples which they themselves are unable to do. They speak with their mouths but destroy by their deeds; therefore such things seem burdensome to their disciples. But the Lord did not act in this way.

“His yoke is light.” Whatever the saints suffer in this world, they bear lightly—the yoke which the faithless Jews refused to carry, saying: “Let us break their bonds” (Ps. II). Therefore they refused to bear the knowledge of the Father, the Son, or the Holy Spirit, saying: “We do not wish to know your ways” (Job XXI).

# HOMILY XIII. SERMON ON THE LORD’S PRAYER

## (Luke XI)

“At that time one of Jesus’ disciples said to him: Lord, teach us to pray, just as John taught his disciples.” And the rest.

The evangelist Luke relates that when the Lord had risen from prayer, one of his disciples approached him, saying: “Lord, teach us to pray, just as John also taught his disciples.” After he had said to them, “When you pray, do not speak at length, as the Gentiles do, who think that they will be heard because of their many words” (Matt. V), he taught them a prayer brief in words but full of mystery, saying:

“Therefore pray in this way, saying: Our Father, who are in heaven,” and so forth.

In this prayer seven petitions are especially commended. The first three pertain to the future life, while the remaining four appear to pertain to the present life, though they are understood with a view to receiving the future life. For what he says—“Hallowed be your name; your will be done, as in heaven and on earth”—pertains to the blessedness of the future life. But what follows—

“Give us today our daily bread”—appears, even to the end, to pertain to the necessities of the present life. Let us examine everything in order.

[Col. 0801A] He says: “Our Father, who are in heaven.” Here we must consider that, although he taught each person to say this prayer, we do not say “my Father” in the singular, but “our Father” in the plural, so that we may understand that this fatherhood pertains not to nature but to grace.

The emperor says this, and the soldier also; the lord, and the servant; the rich, and the poor. All say equally, “Our Father,” because “God is not a respecter of persons, but in every nation whoever works righteousness is acceptable to him” (Acts X).

Here a great act of condescension is truly granted to human beings: they dare to call their Lord and Creator Father. Or certainly, by teaching us to invoke him commonly as Father, he indicates that we ought to be spiritual brothers, according to what he says elsewhere: “For you are all brothers” (Matt. XXIII).

Those who invoke one Father ought to have a united brotherhood, according to what is said through the Psalmist: “Behold, how good and pleasant it is when brothers dwell together in unity” (Ps. CXXXII).

Although God is wholly everywhere and present everywhere, he is said particularly to be in heaven, where he appears near the hosts of angels and is praised more sublimely. By this he suggests to us that those who glory in having the Father in heaven must live rightly on earth, so that one day, stripped of earthly dust, we may deserve to ascend into heaven, where we invoke the Father daily.

“May your name be hallowed.” Since God’s name is always holy in itself, we ask that it be hallowed in us—that is, that we, in whom his name has been invoked, may live holily and justly. Therefore we must take the greatest care lest that terrible sentence be directed against us: “You have profaned my holy name” (Ezek. XXXVI). Rather, let us be such that what he says elsewhere may pertain to us and be fulfilled in us: “Be holy, because I, the Lord your God, am holy” (Lev. XI).

“May your kingdom come.” Here he specially recalls that kingdom of God which will come through the universal judgment, where the saints will reign with the Lord in glory—those who do not now allow sins to reign in their mortal body.

Such were the apostles, to whom the Lord said: “You are those who have remained with me in my temptations, and I appoint for you a kingdom, as my Father appointed one for me, so that you may sit upon twelve thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Luke XXII).

This kingdom will come whether we wish it or not. Nevertheless, if we are confident that we belong to it, we ought with all our strength to desire that it come.

When we add, “Your will be done,” we recognize that we must not obey our own pleasures, but must seek the will of God in all things. Thus, according to the Apostle’s exhortation, testing what the good, pleasing, and perfect will of God is, we must carry out in deed what has been shown to be pleasing to his will.

When we say, “As in heaven and on earth,” we may understand “heaven” as the angelic creation and “earth” as the human creation, to which it was said: “You are earth, and to earth you shall return” (Gen. III). We ask that, just as his angels do his will in heaven, so we may do it on earth.

Or alternatively, by “heaven” we understand the righteous, concerning whom it is written: “The heavens declare the glory of God” (Ps. XVIII); by “earth,” sinners. When we say, “Your will be done as in heaven and on earth,” we ask that, just as the righteous do his will, sinners also may be converted to follow his will.

Or certainly, by “heaven” we may understand the Church, and by “earth” unbelievers and pagans. When we say, “Your will be done,” and so forth, we ask that unbelievers and pagans also may be converted to the faith.

“Give us today our daily bread.” Daily bread pertains to food and clothing, with which, according to the Apostle, we ought to be content. In these words voluntary poverty is requested. For as the Lord says: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. V). Whoever asks for daily bread does not seek an excess of riches.

When “today” is said, it signifies the whole time of the present life. Those who say, “Give us today our daily bread,” are therefore commanded not to think about tomorrow. Or certainly, since according to the Lord’s words, “Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God” (Luke IV), when we say “our bread,” we pray that he grant the soul spiritual food, namely, the word of God.

And just as he daily gives food to the flesh that is destined to die, so may he grant the soul, which will live without end, a hunger for the word of God. For, as the Lord says: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied” (Matt. V).

Or alternatively, when we say, “Give us today our daily bread,” we may understand this as referring to the reception of the Eucharist, to receiving the body and blood of the Lord. We pray that, because we cannot be without sin, he may grant us to pass through the present life without serious offense, so that we may not be separated from receiving the Eucharist.

“And forgive us our debts.” That debt pertains to sin is indicated by the Gospel parable in which a servant who owed ten thousand talents obtained release through a single petition. Therefore, when we say, “Forgive us our debts,” we ask him to forgive our sins. Without doubt he will not refuse this if we do what follows: “As we also forgive our debtors.”

We have within ourselves the rule for the forgiveness of our sins: just as we wish God to forgive our sins, so we must forgive whatever our neighbors have sinned against us. And just as we wish to find God merciful after sin, so we must be compassionate and kind toward those who have sinned against us, because the Lord says: “When you stand to pray, forgive whatever you have against anyone, so that your Father who is in heaven may also forgive you your sins” (Mark XI).

Here discernment is also necessary, so that we may distinguish between the sins which our brothers commit against us and those which they commit against God. When they sin against us, we should forgive readily; when they sin against God, however, we should not do so without correction or reproof, or, if necessity requires, without applying stricter discipline.

A person walks on a perverse path if he displays vengeance toward those who sin against him, but patience toward those who sin against God.

It should be noted that forgiveness of sins is granted in the Church not only through baptism but also after baptism in other ways. Forgiveness of sins is believed to be given in seven ways.

First, through baptism, as the Lord says: “Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved” (Mark XVI).

Second, through repentance, concerning which the Lord says elsewhere: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is near” (Matt. IV), and so forth.

Third, through almsgiving, according to what the Lord says elsewhere: “Give alms, and behold, everything is clean for you” (Luke XI).

Fourth, through the forgiveness of one’s neighbors, concerning which the Lord says: “If you forgive people their sins, your heavenly Father will also forgive you” (Mark XI), and so forth.

Fifth, through correction arising from true charity, concerning which it is said through the apostle James: “Whoever turns a sinner back from the error of his way will save his soul from death” (James V), and so forth.

Sixth, through receiving the body and blood of the Lord. Thus, when the Lord handed the same sacrament to his disciples, he said: “This cup is the New Testament in my blood, which will be poured out for you and for many for the forgiveness of sins. Do this whenever you do it, into my …” (Luke XXII), and so forth.

Seventh, through the shedding of blood in martyrdom, as it is said by the voice of the angels in the Apocalypse: “These are those who came out of the great tribulation and washed their robes in the blood of the Lamb” (Rev. XXII).

In what follows—“And do not lead us into temptation”—we ask that he not permit us to fall into temptation. God is said to lead us into temptation, as it were, when he does not free us from temptation. Thus it was said concerning Pharaoh: “I will harden Pharaoh’s heart” (Exod. IV), although for God to harden means nothing other than not to free from hardness.

Therefore, considering our weakness, let us entreat him with heartfelt cries not to lead us into temptation, but, according to the Apostle’s sentence, to provide along with the temptation a way of escape, so that we may be able to endure it (I Cor. X).

What we add—“But deliver us from evil”—may be understood generally as our request to be delivered from everything that is evil, or specifically from the devil, who is the inventor of all evils. Concerning him the Lord says elsewhere: “Everyone who hears the word of the kingdom and does not understand it—the evil one comes and snatches away” (Matt. XIII).

From his malice, therefore, we can in no way be delivered except through the help of him who says: “No one is good except God alone” (Mark X), who is blessed forever and ever. Amen.

# HOMILIES ON VARIOUS EPISTLES OF PAUL

[Col. 0803]

# HOMILY I. THE NINETEENTH SUNDAY AFTER TRINITY

[Col. 0803C]

## (Ephesians IV)

“Brothers: Be renewed in the spirit of your mind, and put on the new man, who was created according to God in righteousness and the holiness of truth.”

These words of the Apostle depend upon what precedes. For he speaks thus to the Ephesians:

“Put off, according to your former manner of life, the old man, who is corrupted according to the desires of error.” Then he adds: “But be renewed in the spirit of your mind.”

The former manner of life is for a sinner to remain in sins; the old man is the former manner of life of the human being Adam. Whoever remains in sin has the manner of life of the old man. That man—that is, that manner of life—is corrupted and depraved according to the desires of errors and vices.

“Be renewed,” he says, “in the spirit of your mind.” We ought to understand “spirit” and “mind” in a good sense, according to blessed Augustine—that is, as the rationality of the mind.

There are two renewals. One is sudden and instantaneous, which takes place in baptism, in which we are renewed from all original and actual sins. The other takes place over a period of time, through constant reading and through the practice of good works; it is this renewal of which he speaks here.

For when the mind daily understands through devoted reading things about God that it previously did not know, and when it advances daily from virtue to virtue, it is renewed daily. It is therefore as though he were saying: You were renewed in baptism; be renewed daily through devoted reading, understanding about God what was previously hidden from us, and growing from virtue to virtue.

“And put on,” he says, “the new man”—that is, the manner of life of the new man, or the Lord Jesus himself.

Let us see how he himself is the new man and how he was created according to God. He was conceived in the Virgin’s womb through the work of the Holy Spirit, from the seed of a woman without the seed of a man; this was new. He performed miracles which no one else performed. He lived in this world without sin, true God and true man. He rose from the dead. All these things were and are new.

“He was created according to God in righteousness,” because he is righteous; “in holiness and truth,” because he is holy and true. And not only holy, righteous, and true, but also righteousness itself, holiness itself, and truth itself.

Therefore, when he says, “Put on the new man,” it is as though he were saying: Put on the Lord Jesus Christ—that is, the manner of life of the new man—and all the virtues which you understand to exist in Christ. For whoever assumes righteousness, holiness, truth, wisdom, love, and all the virtues which he recognizes as existing in Christ truly puts on Christ.

“Therefore, putting away falsehood, speak the truth, each one with his neighbor.” Since all falsehood is from the devil, who is a liar and the father of falsehood (John VIII), all who are children of truth must put away and cast off falsehood, deceit, and duplicity, and speak the truth from a pure heart with every person—not only with a Christian, but also with a heretic and a pagan, because all are our neighbors (Eph. V).

And why must we speak the truth with our neighbor? “Because we are members of one another.”

Christ is the head; his chosen ones are his members. Just as the members of our body are mutually necessary to one another and provide one another with what is necessary—for example (I Cor. XII; Rom. XII), the eye is necessary to the hand and foot, and the hand and foot to the eye, and therefore the eye supplies the hand and foot with light, while the hand wipes and washes it from impurities—so in the holy Church every preacher who is an eye ought to supply the light of knowledge and preaching to those who are hands and feet, that is, to those who give alms, who run to bury the dead, and who are devoted to the active life.

Conversely, they ought to sustain the preaching eye from their resources, providing him with food and drink and supplying whatever else he needs. By doing these things, they will be members of one another.

It follows:

“Be angry, and do not sin” (Psalm 4). We may understand this in two ways. Whenever you sin and, persuaded by the devil, depart from the path of uprightness, be angry with yourselves and be indignant, so that you may not do such things again, disciplining your body with vigils and fasts. Alternatively: “If,” he says, “you become angry, do not carry your anger through to completion.” The Apostle permits anger, which is human, but forbids seeking vengeance, which is no longer human, because “the anger of man does not accomplish the righteousness of God.”

“Do not let the sun go down upon your anger.” This too may be understood in two ways. Let us explain it simply: “Do not let the sun go down upon your anger”—that is, if you have been stirred up against your neighbor for a time, be reconciled before sunset, and let anger depart from you. Alternatively, “sun” is called Christ in the sacred Scriptures, as in: “For you who fear my name, the sun of righteousness shall rise” (Malachi 4; Luke 1). This sun often sets for you because of anger that seeks vengeance, and because of discord—that is, it withdraws from you—just as it set for the sons of the prophets, of whom it is said: “Their sun went down while it was still midday” (Jeremiah 15). “Do not let the sun go down upon your anger”: beware lest, because of your anger and your sin, Christ, the sun of righteousness, withdraw from you.

“Do not give place to the devil”—that is, do not seek vengeance, and do not become angry beyond measure, lest Christ, the sun, withdraw from you and the devil, the prince of darkness, come. Whenever we sin, we give the devil a place in us.

[Col. 0806A] “Let the one who was stealing” the goods of others “steal no longer.” Or, let the one who was stealing the words and teaching of the Gospel through heretical perversity—as did the sons of the prophets, of whom it is said: “They see vanity and divine lies, saying, ‘Thus says the Lord God,’ when the Lord has not sent them” (Ezekiel 13; Jeremiah 3)—steal no longer, but let him depart from his error. “Rather, let him labor, working with his own hands at what is good, so that he may have something to give to the one suffering need.” The one who formerly stole must not merely cease from theft; he must work with his own hands so that he may have something with which to support others who suffer want.

## HOMILY II. THE TWENTIETH SUNDAY AFTER TRINITY

[Col. 0806B] (Ephesians 5.) “Brothers, see carefully how you walk, not as fools but as wise.” The Apostle speaks to the Ephesians, and in them he exhorts all people to live cautiously and thoughtfully, like the wise and not like fools. He calls them “brothers” in faith and in the fellowship of love, because we all have one Father, God almighty—not by nature, but by adoption (Matthew 23).

“See, brothers”—that is, consider—“how carefully” and orderly “you walk”: how you live and conduct yourselves amid a corrupt and perverse nation; and “not as fools”—that is, unbelievers who do not possess true wisdom, namely Christ dwelling within them—“but as wise”: that is, as believers who possess substantial wisdom within yourselves. For as great as the difference is [Col. 0806C] between darkness and light, between believer and unbeliever, so great is the difference between fool and wise person, because light and wisdom cannot be in one who does not possess faith in almighty God.

“Redeeming the time, because the days are evil.” How is time evil, when, according to God’s ordering, it continually revolves, with months, days, and nights, hours and moments passing by? Just as a house is called evil because it has evil inhabitants, so days are called evil on which evil things are done by evil people. What does he mean by “redeeming the time”? That is: make it your own. For example, others sell it by doing evil to their own harm; you redeem it by doing such works as will bring you a reward. Whoever does what is useful to him redeems and acquires time for himself, because he makes it his own and occupies it for his salvation.

“Therefore”—understand: because the days are evil—“do not become imprudent, but understand what the will of God is.” A prudent person is so called as one who looks ahead, because he considers from afar what end his works will have, and knows what he ought to seek and what to avoid; he also considers what pleases or displeases God. Conversely, the one who does everything thoughtlessly and without foresight, who does not consider toward what end his works lead or what pleases the will of God, is called imprudent and foolish. Hence the Apostle says: “Therefore,” he says, because the days are evil, in which many evil things are done, “do not become imprudent [Col. 0807A] or thoughtless,” but “be understanding of what the will of God is”—that is, what pleases God and in which works God’s will is fulfilled.

“And do not become drunk with wine, in which there is debauchery.” By debauchery we should understand all the vices that ordinarily arise through drunkenness, because, as a certain teacher says, drunkenness excuses no vice. Here, however, we should note that just as those who are filled with wine are filled with shamelessness, impatience, debauchery, immodesty, pride, and other vices, so those who are filled with the Holy Spirit are filled with chastity, humility, gentleness, and other virtues.

“Speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs.” We speak to one another when we sing psalms antiphonally. Psalms are so called from *psallere*, because they are found in the psaltery. *Hymnos* in Greek, in Latin speech, means “the praise of God.” A hymn is a hymn when it is composed and sung in praise of God. Among the Latins, especially Ambrose and Hilary, men of great renown, composed hymns. Why, then, after saying “songs,” did he add “spiritual”? Because there are songs that are not spiritual and are not sung in praise of God, such as the songs of worldly people. Spiritual songs are those composed by prophets inspired and filled with the Holy Spirit, such as the songs of Moses, the song of Hannah, the song of Deborah, the song of Isaiah, the song of Hezekiah, and those of the other prophets.

The distinction between a song and a psalm is this: a song is not merely spoken but sung, whereas a psalm is accompanied by an instrument of musical art, namely the psaltery. “Singing and making melody in your hearts to the Lord.” He said “singing in your hearts” because there are many who sing only with their mouths, whose minds do not agree with their voices, and who attend more to the pleasantness of their voices, so as to please their listeners, than to considering in their minds what they are saying. Those sing in the heart whose minds agree with their voices, according to the saying of blessed Benedict: “Let us stand for psalmody in such a way that our mind may accord with our voice.”

“Giving thanks always for all things in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ to God the Father.” For all the benefits freely given to us by God, and for all prosperous and adverse circumstances, we must always give thanks to God the Father—that is, to God almighty the Father, who is the Father of all creatures, meaning their creator and maker. And how? In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, saying to him: “We give you thanks, holy Father, who through your Son made and redeemed us and opened for us the way to the heavenly homeland.” Therefore we must give thanks to God the Father in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, because through him, who is our mediator, we offer and send our prayers and sacrifices to God the Father, saying: “Receive, O Lord, the prayers of your people, through our Lord Jesus Christ your Son, who with you, and so forth.”

“Submitting to one another in the fear of Christ.” Just as hearers and subjects are subordinate to their superiors through obedience and reverence, so superiors also ought to humble themselves toward their subjects insofar as they see them equal to themselves in virtues and the merits of their lives. But insofar as they see them rising up in pride against them and pursuing vices, they ought to display the authority of their office and leadership, and rebuke and reprimand them firmly.

This can be demonstrated from the deeds of the apostle Peter. When he saw the centurion Cornelius humbly wishing to adore him with his entire household, Peter, conversely, humbled himself before him, saying: “Rise, for I too am a man” (Acts 5). But when he saw Ananias and Sapphira departing from the way of truth and subject to vices, he displayed the power of his office and leadership by killing them with a single word (Acts 5). Yet all these things must be done in the fear of Christ—that is, through love of God, not for the sake of flattery or favoritism, as some do in order to win the favor of a superior and more freely perform what pleases them.

## HOMILY III. THE TWENTY-FIRST SUNDAY AFTER TRINITY

(Ephesians 6.) “Brothers, be strengthened in the Lord and in the power of his might. Put on the armor of God.” And so forth. After the spiritual commands by which the Apostle admonished men and women, fathers and children, masters and servants, he added these general instructions—not only for the Ephesians to whom he was sending this letter, but for every sex and every condition—and said:

“Finally”—that is, from now on, and apart from what we have said above—“my brothers” in faith and love, who have one God, the almighty Father [Col. 0808C] (Matthew 25), “be strengthened in the Lord and in the power of his might.” Do not trust in your own strength, in your merits, or in the power of the rulers of this age, but be strengthened in the Lord and in the power of his might. “Put on the armor of God.”
