“So that you may be able to stand against the snares of the devil.” The word “armor” includes all weapons of war: breastplate, helmet, shield, lance, missiles, and the other instruments of warfare. More particularly, however, we should understand the armor of God as the Lord Jesus Christ, by whose protection all the elect are defended, and whom they put on, according to what the same Apostle says elsewhere: “All who have been baptized into Christ have put on Christ” (Romans 6; Galatians 3).

The elect put on Christ when, with his help, they assume the virtues that are in Christ. Thus what he says—“Put on the armor of God”—is as though he said: “Put on the Lord Jesus Christ”; that is, assume into yourselves all the virtues that you know to be in him. For example, he is just, truthful, patient, chaste, and gentle. He is called a lamb, a lion, and a calf. Put on justice, truth, patience, charity, chastity, and gentleness. Be a lamb—that is, gentle; a lion—strong in faith and in good works against the devil; and also a calf, mortifying yourselves with your vices and desires, so that you may be able to stand against the snares of the devil.

For the devil lies in wait for us in many ways. Finally, he lies in wait through evil suggestions. He lies in wait through the vices of our flesh and the incitements of evil pleasures. He lies in wait through his servants, such as heretics, false brothers, and pagans. Against all these we must fight manfully, so that we may overcome them.

Someone might say: “O Paul, why do you command us to put on the whole armor of God?” To this he adds:

“Because our struggle,” he says, “is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers,” and so forth. In this passage the Apostle calls “flesh and blood” all human beings, who consist of flesh and blood and by whom we are often attacked at the devil’s prompting. He says that our struggle—that is, our battle—is not only against them, [Col. 0809B] but against demons who rule wicked people and, exercising power over them, direct them toward evil rather than good.

These are called “spiritual forces”—understand, demons—of wickedness, that is, of malice, which dwell in this air (Luke 12). In the sacred Scriptures, the air is called heaven; hence birds are called “the birds of heaven.” As the philosophers have said, and our teachers believe, the air is as full of demons and evil spirits as a sunbeam is full of the smallest atoms.

We must therefore fight against them as much as against human beings consisting of flesh and blood, because whatever evil people devise against us is suggested by those spirits. If we overcome those who are the princes of wickedness, at whose instigation the vices of our flesh rage against us, then we shall easily be able to overcome all their servants—just as, when the commander has been defeated, the army is easily put to flight.

This can be demonstrated from the Book of Judith, where we learn that, after Holofernes, the commander of the army, had been killed, the multitude of his forces was thrown into flight and was very easily defeated by the Jews (Judith 13).

But it may be asked how we can fight against demons, who are spirits. It is clear to everyone that a spirit cannot be fought with material weapons (2 Corinthians 10). Therefore, since they are spirits and invisible, it is necessary to take up spiritual weapons—namely, the virtues mentioned above. We should engage them in the manner in which we read that Jacob wrestled with the angel: by praying, fasting, keeping vigil, and persevering in other good works, so that just as Jacob deserved to be blessed by the holy angel with whom he wrestled through prayer (Genesis 32), so we too may deserve to be blessed by the Lord after overcoming the devil.

It may also be asked where the Apostle obtained the practice of calling demons and evil spirits “principalities,” “powers,” and “rulers of this darkness”—that is, of unbelieving, God-ignorant, sinful people—over whose service those people had once been, to whom he said: “You were once darkness” (Ephesians 5), meaning unbelievers ignorant of God and sinners.

The answer is that he took this from the Book of Daniel, where we read: “The prince of the Greeks and the prince of the Persians” (Daniel 10). He also took it from the Book of Ezekiel, where it is said to the prince of Tyre: “You were the seal of likeness in the paradise of God” (Ezekiel 28), along with the other things said there about him and about the princes of other peoples—the Egyptians, Assyrians, and Idumeans. By those princes, the demons appointed over those nations are understood.

For just as each of the faithful has a good angel assigned to guard him, so pagans have evil angels who rule them by God’s permission. And just as Michael is appointed over the Jewish people—of whom it is said, “I have no helper except Michael, our prince” (Daniel 10)—so the nations remaining in unbelief also have evil princes.

Let us speak more profoundly. The Apostle, filled with God’s grace, understood through the Holy Spirit that just as the good kings of the Israelites signified the Lord Jesus Christ, and the princes who are in the Church—for example, David, whose name is interpreted as “strong-handed” or “desirable,” and many others—and just as the people of Israel signified the people of believers, who are the true Israelites, so the evil kings and princes with their nations, who fought against God’s people, and who were kings of the Ishmaelites, Idumeans, and Philistines, signified the demons who rule pagans and heretics, who continually attack the Church of God.

“Therefore”—understand: because our struggle is against principalities and powers—“take up the armor of God,” about which we spoke above, that is, all the virtues, “so that you may be able to resist on the evil day and stand perfect in all things”—that is, persevere firmly in faith and good works amid all prosperity and adversity. He calls the present time “the evil day,” not because it is evil in itself, but because many evil things are done in it. Or he calls the day of judgment “the evil day,” on which all the wicked will be condemned.

“Stand, therefore, with your loins girded in truth.” We gird our loins when we restrain debauchery. “Stand,” he says, in faith—that is, in good works—restraining your loins from the debauchery in which it is especially strong; and do this in truth, not in falsehood or hypocrisy, nor in order to obtain human praise. Or by “in truth” he means for love of the name of Christ, who is the truth (John 14).

“Put on the breastplate of righteousness.” Righteousness is rightly compared with a breastplate, because just as a breastplate is woven from many rings, so righteousness consists of many virtues. Alternatively, righteousness can well be compared with a breastplate because, just as a breastplate guards the chest, constricts the belly, and protects the thighs, so righteousness repels excessive thoughts that ordinarily move in the chest, restrains the belly’s gluttony, and also suppresses lust.

“And let your feet be shod”—understand, let them be for you—“in the preparation of the gospel of peace.” The meaning is this: just as one whose feet are shod despises serpents and regards thorns and every roughness of the road as nothing, so you too should despise the devil, the ancient serpent, as well as thorns—that is, the sufferings of stinging wounds—and every harshness of this life, and go freely to preach the Gospel.

Alternatively, by footwear, which is made from dead animals, we should understand [Col. 0811A] the sayings and examples of the fathers who preceded us. Thus we have shod feet when, strengthened by the sayings and examples of earlier fathers, we go confidently to preach the Gospel of peace.

It is called the Gospel of peace because it contains the peace that Christ commended to the apostles (John 14), and through the apostles to all believers; or also because, through observance of the Gospel, we deserve to be reconciled to God.

“In all” battles and contests “take up the shield of faith, with which you may extinguish all the flaming darts of the wicked one.” Anything that is hurled and thrown can be called a missile; properly, however, the word refers to something extended lengthwise, such as a lance. For the Greeks call a long object *telon*; hence *mustela* means “a long mouse.” Just as a shield protects the one who holds it and repels missiles, [Col. 0811B] so faith fortifies a person and defends him from the devil’s arrows and assaults—provided that faith is adorned with good works.

He calls the devil’s missiles “flaming” because they are evil suggestions by which he inflames us to perform evil works. They are extinguished—that is, overcome—through the power of faith.

“And take the helmet of salvation.” The helmet is placed on the head and fortifies—that is, protects—all the bodily senses: sight in the eyes, hearing in the ears, taste in the mouth, smell in the nostrils, and touch throughout the head. What, then, should we understand by the helmet which, as we have said, protects all the bodily senses? Our Lord Jesus Christ and his protection.

By the head, however, we should understand the mind, because just as the limbs are governed by the head, so thoughts are ordered by the mind. [Col. 0811C] Let us therefore place Christ’s protection upon the head—that is, in the mind—and remember him in the secret of our mind, having confidence in him and not in ourselves. Then he will guard all our senses, so that they cannot be wounded by the devil, the ancient enemy.

“And the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God”—understand, take it up. The word of God is understood as the sword of the Holy Spirit, as the Apostle says (Hebrews 4): namely, the teaching and knowledge of the divine Scriptures, which are bestowed upon us through the Spirit. It is called a sword because just as enemies are put to flight by a sword, so through reflection on the divine Scriptures, which are given to us through the Holy Spirit, we can drive away all the devil’s snares and schemes by pursuing what sacred Scripture teaches and avoiding what it forbids.

And we can overcome through its knowledge and help not only demons, but also convict heretics by its authority and destroy their error.

“Grace”—that is, faith and the forgiveness of sins—“be with all who love the Lord Jesus Christ in incorruption”—that is, in the integrity of faith. Or alternatively: May grace—that is, faith, forgiveness of sins, and eternal fellowship—be with all the saints in incorruption, that is, in the general resurrection, where all the elect will receive incorruption and immortality in the body and unchangeability in the soul (1 Corinthians 15), shining like the sun in the kingdom of their Father (Matthew 13), and with him remaining happily forever and ever.

## HOMILY IV. THE TWENTY-SECOND SUNDAY AFTER TRINITY

[Col. 0812A]

(Philippians 1.) “Brothers, we are confident in the Lord Jesus that he who began a good work in us will bring it to completion until the day of Jesus Christ.” Christ, who gave us the beginning of faith and good conduct, will also give us perseverance until the day of our death, or successively until the day of judgment.

“As it is right for me to feel this about all of you”—that is, it is right for me to understand this about you: that you will remain in the faith of Christ, and therefore I ought to rejoice. “Because I have you in my heart and in my bonds”—that is, I remember you—“and in the defense and confirmation of the Gospel, sharers [Col. 0812B] in my joy,” that is, in the promise of eternal life.

He defended and confirmed the Gospel in many ways: by rightly healing, by living justly, and by teaching well. He also defended and confirmed that the teaching of the Gospel is holy when they said to him: “Deny Christ and cast aside this teaching, and you will flourish in great honor in my palace”; yet he preferred to be scourged and bound by that ruler rather than agree with him. In this way he defended the Gospel. Seeing this, others said: “Truly, unless this teaching were true, and unless Christ were truly the Son of God, Paul would never endure such things for his name.”

“I wish all of you”—understand, I desire you to be—as you are partners in the labor of preaching, so also partners in the reward. Someone might say: “Paul truly travels throughout the world, is talkative, and does not love us.” Therefore he says in response: “God is my witness, how I long for all of you in the bowels of Christ Jesus.”

“Bowels” are called sons, and *viscus* means “flesh,” although it is situated between the flesh; therefore the expression may be understood in two ways. “I desire,” he says, “that you all be sons of God,” or, “I desire that he himself be your temple, and that you, sharing in his body and blood, remain in him.”

“And this I pray: that your charity may abound more and more.” Just as faith has a beginning, an increase, and perfection, so does charity. “I pray,” he says, “that your charity may extend not only toward God and your neighbor, but also toward your enemies.” “In knowledge”—understand, of the law—“and in all perception,” that is, in the teaching of the Gospel.

[Col. 0812D] “So that you may discern what is better”—that is, understand greater things about God—“so that you may be sincere,” that is, perfect in faith and in every goodness. Pure material is whole, solid, and firm, not stained by variation in anything; so faith too ought to be solid “and without offense on the day of Christ”—that is, without stumbling on the day of your death or on the day of judgment.

“Filled with the fruit of righteousness”—that is, may you be filled with all the virtues of which the Apostle says: “The fruit of the Spirit is joy, peace” (Galatians 5)—“through Jesus Christ, to the glory and praise of God,” that is, so that God may be glorified in us and the Lord Jesus, through whom we have all good things, may be praised.

## HOMILY V. FOR THE DAY OF THE DEDICATION OF A CHURCH

[Col. 0813A]

(Revelation 21.) “I saw the holy city, the new Jerusalem, coming down from heaven from God, prepared like a bride adorned for her husband.” This holy city is the Church. It is called a city because it is inhabited by many and extends into the four parts of the world, having the Lord as its inhabitant. Hence Paul says: “The holy temple of God is what you are” (1 Corinthians 3, 6).

It is called holy because it is sanctified daily through baptism. It is also called Jerusalem, which is interpreted as “vision of peace,” because it labors for this purpose: to behold God in the heavenly places. It is called new because it is stripped of the oldness of sin; the committing of sin belongs to the old Adam. Therefore, when the Church is cleansed from original sin and from the oldness of sin, it comes to newness. Hence the Apostle says: “Strip off the old man and put on the new, who is renewed in the knowledge of God” (Colossians 3; Ephesians 4).

This city is said to descend from God because, from its beginning, it has already descended with its head. Hence the same Lord says: “No one has ascended into heaven” (John 3), and so forth. Alternatively, it is said to descend from heaven because the grace by which the Lord made it a Church is heavenly. According to the saying: “I am the Lord who makes you” (Isaiah 43). Whatever it possesses in faith, hope, charity, the other virtues, and baptism has been given to it from above. Hence James says: “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, descending from the Father of lights” (James 1).

“Prepared”—that is, adorned with faith and the other virtues. Hence it deserves to be called a bride. “Like a bride adorned for her husband.” He says two things: “bride” and “husband,” in which “wife” is implied, because it is customary for sacred Scripture to call bridegrooms “husbands” and brides “wives.” Hence Joel says: “Let the bridegroom go forth from his chamber and the bride from her bridal room” (Joel 2). And Zipporah says to Moses: “You are a bridegroom of blood to me” (Exodus 4). In the Gospel the angel says: “Joseph, her husband” (Matthew 2). And in the Law: “If a man finds a betrothed girl in the field and sleeps with her, he shall die, because he has humbled his neighbor’s wife” (Deuteronomy 22).

The holy Church is therefore now a bride through faith, hope, and charity; but then she will be a wife when she reaches the embraces of her husband—that is, the contemplation of God almighty. This occurs throughout the whole day in individual elect persons, but will be completed universally at the end. Then all together will hear: “Come, blessed of my Father” (Matthew 25), and so forth.

“Adorned,” he says—that is, composed in all virtues. According to the Psalmist: “The queen stood at your right hand” (Psalm 44), and so forth.

“And I heard a loud voice from the throne.” The throne here is understood as holy human beings and angels in whom God dwells; therefore this loud voice is understood as the voice of almighty God. It is called loud because God speaks of great things.

“Behold, the tabernacle of God is with human beings.” Great indeed is God’s grace: that human beings should become the tabernacle of him whose greatness the world cannot contain. “The tabernacle of God is with human beings”—that is, human beings themselves are God’s tabernacle.

John here represents the holy Church, which hears the voice saying, “Behold, the tabernacle of God is with human beings,” when, through inward inspiration, she recognizes herself as God’s tabernacle.

“And he will dwell with them”—that is, with those who have deserved to be God’s tabernacle. Hence the Lord himself says: “Behold, I am with you all the days” (Matthew 28).

“And they will be his people.” According to the saying: “Israel is my inheritance” (Isaiah 19).

“And he himself, their God, will be with them.” He dwells in their faith and love, as he himself says: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word. And my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him” (John 14). Hence the same John says in his Epistle: “Whoever remains in love remains in God, and God in him” (1 John 4).

And almighty God is the God of those with whom he deigns to dwell. Hence the Psalmist says: “The Lord is the portion of my inheritance” (Psalm 15). And he himself speaks in the Law, saying: “You shall not give an inheritance to the sons of Levi, for I am their inheritance” (Deuteronomy 18).

When a person departs from God by sinning, he is not God’s people and does not possess God. But when, through repentance, he returns to God, he is God’s people, because he possesses God and is possessed by God.

“And God will wipe away every tear from their eyes.” These words do not refer to the present life, which is full of mourning and tears, [Col. 0814C] but to the future, when all mourning will be taken away from the faithful and everlasting joy will be possessed. According to the saying: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matthew 5).

We must consider why he says that every tear will be taken from the eyes of the saints, when it would have been sufficient to say: “He will wipe away the tear from their eyes.” We should know that there are different kinds of tears by which the elect are afflicted in this life.

Sometimes they weep because of fear of punishment, lest on account of the demerits of their iniquity they be handed over to avenging penalties. Sometimes they weep because of love and fellowship with the citizens above. For after they obtain forgiveness of sins, they begin to weep again—not because they fear condemnation, but because they are delayed from the kingdom. Sometimes also they lament the sins of others, as Samuel wept for Saul because the Lord regretted that he had made him king over Israel (1 Samuel 15), and as Paul mourned for the Corinthians, who had not repented of fornication and idolatry (2 Corinthians 12).

The Lord will therefore wipe away every tear from the eyes of the elect, because they will neither be oppressed by fear of punishments nor be delayed from the kingdom, which they will possess immediately; nor will they lament the sins of others, because once the reprobate have been condemned by God’s just judgment, no one thereafter will be able to sin.

“And death shall be no more.” After we have all risen from the dead, death will no longer exist among the elect—neither the death of the body nor that of the soul. For the first human being was created in paradise under this condition: that, if he did not sin, he would remain immortal. When the number of the elect had been completed, he would have passed from that earthly paradise to the heavenly homeland without the intervention of death. Yet he was created in such a way that, if he sinned, he could die.

Because he incurred this death through sin, it was destroyed through the Lord’s death. Therefore death will have no place among the elect. After we have all risen to life, having been transformed so that thereafter we can neither die nor sin, “neither will there be mourning” in that Church, which, as was said above, occurs in many ways in the present.

“Neither will there be crying nor pain anymore.” Crying here means the complaint of an evil suggestion. Before the human being sinned, he was in great tranquility, and all his members were subject to him, possessing no form of opposition. But after he sinned, he immediately felt the cry of an evil suggestion rising up against him; seeing the woman, he desired her. By God’s judgment it came to pass that the one who had refused to be subject to God could not have his own members subject to him.

We continue to endure this cry, by which Paul too showed himself wearied, saying: “O wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from the body of this death? For I see another law in my members” (Romans 7), and so forth. This cry is always present, because the flesh always resists the spirit. But when this corruptible body has put on incorruption, and this mortal body has put on immortality, the cry that did not allow the elect to rest in this life will cease to rage against them.

There every evil suggestion will cease, because there will be no pleasure of the flesh. Nor will pain exist thereafter, because the flesh of the elect will no longer produce thorns and stings of sin for which they ought to grieve.

“These things, which were first, have passed away,” because in the present age they endure all these things. But when heaven and earth have been renewed, the elect too will be renewed, [Col. 0816B] and they will no longer suffer their former afflictions.

“And he who sat upon the throne said”—that is, almighty God, who presides over his Church—“Behold, I make all things new,” namely, the things mentioned above, including the renewal of heaven and earth.

# THE THIRD PART OF THE WORKS OF HAYMO, BISHOP OF HALBERSTADT—MISCELLANEOUS

## ON THE BODY AND BLOOD OF THE LORD

[Note: [Col. 0815D] The treatise of Aimo or Haymo, bishop of Halberstadt, *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*, was appended to his sermons in a manuscript codex of Saint-Germain in Paris, where Aimo’s name was inscribed. Therefore there is no reasonable doubt that it should be attributed to him, since the title asserts this.]

In Acherius’s *Spicilegium*. (G)*
[Col. 0815C] But since the occasion afforded by this Letter permits something more extensive to be said about so great a sacrament, let what the grace of him who willed to leave this sacrament of his body and blood on earth for the salvation of the souls of the faithful has bestowed be brought into the open, so that the integrity of faith may be strengthened more earnestly and the merits of believers may be increased more abundantly.

Therefore, to doubt that the substance of the bread and wine placed upon the altar becomes the body and blood of Christ through the mystery of the priest and thanksgiving, God effecting this by divine grace and secret power, is the most unspeakable madness in the minds of the faithful. Thus we believe, faithfully confess, and hold that that substance—namely, of bread and wine—is, through the operation of divine power, as has already been said, that is, the nature of bread and wine, substantially changed into another substance, namely, into [Col. 0816C] flesh and blood. For it is not impossible for the power of divine reason to change established natures into whatever it wills, since it was not impossible for it, when it willed, to establish those same natures out of nothing, when they did not exist. For if it can make something from nothing, then making something from something is not impossible.

The invisible priest therefore changes his visible creatures into the substance of his flesh and blood by secret power. In this body and blood of Christ, however, because of the horror of those who receive it, the taste and appearance of bread and wine remain, while the nature of the substances has been wholly changed into the body and blood of Christ. But the senses of the flesh report one thing, and the faith of the mind reports another. The senses of the flesh can report nothing other than what they perceive; but the understanding of the mind and faith report and confess the true flesh and blood of Christ, [Col. 0817A] so that the more completely it believes what is entirely removed from the senses of the flesh, the more greatly it may receive the crown of its faith and its reward.

It must also be noted that that consecrated bread and the chalice are called signs. This, however, is not to be understood with respect to the flesh and blood of Christ, although certain people, wholly devoted to the senses of the flesh and blinded in mind, foolishly think so. For the body and blood of Christ would then no longer be present. Nothing is a sign of itself, nor is any thing called the sign of itself, but of something else. Absolutely every sign, insofar as it is recognized to be a sign, is different from what it signifies.

The body and blood of Christ are therefore called a sacrament, that is, a sacred sign—not a sign of themselves, as was stated and proved above—but they are truly called signs in the likeness of those who receive them. For just as the bread that is consecrated and becomes the body of Christ is made from many grains into one bread, and that drink which is sanctified and becomes the blood of Christ is made from many grapes into one drink, so all who worthily receive this sacrament are made from many into one body in Christ.

The body and blood of Christ may also be called signs in another way, because what we eat and transfer into our body appears in a certain manner to be incorporated and united with us. This bodily and temporal eating and incorporation of Christ’s flesh and blood signifies that spiritual and everlasting vision of eternal fellowship and refreshment by which, in the future, we shall be incorporated and united with him, remaining with him without end. We should confidently hope that we can be led to this by whole-hearted faith, joyful hope, and burning charity. [Col. 0817C]

This also must be firmly held by the faith of those who receive this sacrament: however little one may seem to receive of the sacrament, one receives the body of Christ not divided and separated into parts, but wholly and entire. For a grain of wheat, cast into the earth and having died, then rising again into the multiplication of its fruit, must necessarily be wholly present in each of the individual grains produced from it. Unless we hold this by reason, how could such a great and extensive diminution of parts occur that individual grains would be formed from each individual part of that grain?

But if we were to judge ourselves—that is, examine and test our life, whether or not we were worthy—and if we corrected ourselves and our errors, we would certainly not be judged; that is, we would not be condemned by Christ, either in this age or in the age to come. When, however, we are judged in a few matters—namely, in those who are weak and feverish in the present time, and also in those who die—we are chastised by the Lord and scourged in the body through them, so that we ourselves, terrified by fear, may not be eternally condemned with this world (I Cor. XI, 31), that is, with unbelievers and lovers of the world.

For there is no difference between such a person and an unbeliever: whoever, irreverently and stained with all criminal sins, presumes to approach the Lord’s table is worse than an unbeliever and worthy of a greater punishment, because it is better not to know the way of truth than, after knowing it, to turn back (II Petr. II, 21).

Therefore, my brothers, when you assemble in the church to eat the body and blood of Christ, wait for one another, so that the offering of many may be celebrated together, and all may communicate together from one bread, because that offering is one bread and ought to be common to all. If anyone is hungry, let him eat at home—that is, let the one who is impatient and unwilling to fast with the others eat earthly bread at home—so that you may not assemble for judgment; that is, so that you may not receive the body of Christ reprehensibly, to your condemnation. “The other matters”—that is, whatever remains disordered—“I will arrange when I come” (I Cor. XI, 33).

[Col. 0817]

# Haymo, Bishop of Halberstadt: Epitome of Sacred History, or Ten Books on the Memory of Christian Affairs

[Col. 0817] (From the edition published at Cologne in the year 1600 by Antonius Hierat.) (G)*

## Haymo’s Preface

[Col. 0817D] It has been our experience to learn how much learning and how much knowledge of divine and human affairs ecclesiastical history imparts to devout readers, since by reading it often and diligently we have made this evident to you yourselves. To recommend it briefly: it teaches the truth of events accomplished from the beginning; recounts the pious deeds of the primitive Church; describes the exploits of brave men; records the struggles of martyrs; exalts the merits of confessors; and recalls the sayings and writings of teachers, who are also called Fathers.

But since, on account of the multiplicity and immense size of the volume, it tires the understanding, burdens the attention, and entangles the memory, we have decided, if the Lord wills, to reduce that immense book to a little volume. We therefore wish this to become a handbook, with this usefulness in mind: when you have read Eusebius—eloquent indeed in expression and fertile in learning, but, because of the abundance of the Greek language from which he was translated, varied and lengthy in style, and therefore easily slipping from the memory—you may wish to look at this work and consult our excerpt from it in order to restore your memory to completeness.

[Col. 0820A] Forgive me, blessed Eusebius, forgive me: I am not undertaking this as an attack upon you. Spare me, I ask, and pay attention: I am repeating that discourse, my friend, not doing you an injury, just as ecclesiastical men before us have done. By gathering little flowers from the books of learned men, they have clarified obscure matters and shortened lengthy ones.

Therefore I do not set my work alongside your divine work; rather, I reproduce you, looking upon you and reverencing you, whom I follow almost completely in your footsteps, but by a shorter road. Let your book, then, be the model, and this one the copy. Let that be the more fully expressed form, and this its representation and image. Let that be knowledge of events, and this memory; for what the former leads to knowledge, the latter brings back to memory.

# Book One

[Col. 0819]

## Chapter One. On the time of Christ’s birth according to the flesh

(Eusebius, book I, chapter 2, *Ecclesiastical History*; Nicephorus, book I, chapter 9, *Ecclesiastical History*)

Jesus Christ, our Lord and Savior, was born in the sixth age of the world at Bethlehem, a town of Judea, while Caesar Augustus was ruling among the Romans and Herod, a foreigner and a man of alien stock, was reigning among the Jews. This Herod, under whom the Lord was born, is understood to have been Herod the Great, in contrast with the younger Herod under whom he suffered. According to Josephus, he was an Idumean on his father’s side; according to Africanus, he was the son of a certain Antipater, once captured by Idumean bandits and brought up in the life and customs of those bandits. This Herod, born from such a man, obtained the kingdom of the Jews in the following manner.

## Chapter Two. How he came to the kingdom

(The same author, in the *Chronicle*)

When Pompey attacked Jerusalem, captured it, and sent Aristobulus, king and high priest of the Jews, bound to Rome with his children, he appointed Aristobulus’s brother Hyrcanus as high priest—through whom the final Jewish priesthood descended. Soon afterward, when Hyrcanus was captured by the Parthians, the aforementioned Herod obtained the kingdom of Judea by decree of the Senate, while Augustus was emperor, perhaps with certain Jews supporting him. For this Herod’s father had been very close to the aforementioned high priest Hyrcanus.

## Chapter Three. On Herod’s criminal deeds

Having obtained the kingdom, Herod wished to destroy the nobility of the Jews. He rejected the noble and legitimate succession of the lineage, promised priesthoods to any lowborn persons, and threw the whole order into confusion. To crown his wickedness, he concealed under seal the sacred vestment worn by the high priest and never permitted the high priests during his lifetime to use it. His son Archelaus did the same. After them, the Romans likewise maintained this custom of violating the high-priesthood.

## Chapter Four. On Herod’s cruelty toward infants

After Christ had been born [Note: [Col. 0819D] “After Christ had been born.” In the thirty-third year of Herod’s reign, as we said above, and according to Epiphanius against the Alogi.], and when, according to the testimony of the evangelist Matthew (Matt. II), three Magi came to him [Note: [Col. 0819D] “When the Magi came.” In the same year, the thirty-fifth.], guided by a star [Note: [Col. 0819D] “Guided by a star.” Concerning this star, see also the Platonist Chalcidius. This star appeared two years before Christ was born. Nicephorus and other ecclesiastical historians.], Herod was disturbed, incredibly fearing for the security of his position and kingdom. After investigating from the Magi [Note: [Col. 0819D] “The Magi.” Concerning them David the Psalmist had spoken so many centuries before their conversion (Ps. LXXII).] and learning from the prophecies of Micah the place of Christ’s birth, he ordered all boys from two years old and younger to be killed [Note: [Col. 0820D] “He ordered all boys from two years old and younger to be killed.” Josephus seems to remember the slaughter of these infants. Book XVII, chapter 3, *Jewish Antiquities*.], according to the time he had ascertained from the Magi, so that he might destroy the Lord along with them. But Joseph, warned by an angel [Note: [Col. 0820D] “Joseph takes the child to Egypt.” He remained there for three years, or two, according to Epiphanius; after Herod’s death he returned to his homeland, when Jesus Christ was approximately six years old. Nicephorus.], transferred the child to Egypt.

## Chapter Five. How he destroyed the genealogy of the Jews

(Nicephorus, in the same place)

At that time, while Herod held supreme power, since he was lowborn and jealous of the nobility of the Jews, he ordered their genealogical books, which were kept in the more secret archives of the temple, to be burned, together with certain genealogies of foreigners, such as Achior among the Ammonites and Ruth among the Moabites. Certain diligent men, recovering these by divine favor—partly because they already had copies at home, and partly because they retained the order of their ancestry in memory—preserved them down to us. Among them were certain members of the royal household, or apostles of the Lord, [Col. 0821A] because of their kinship with Christ’s lineage; they too taught his genealogy, according to what the truth of the Gospels contains.

## Chapter Six. On God’s vengeance against him

(Eusebius, book I, chapter 8, *Ecclesiastical History*; Nicephorus, book I, chapter 11)

Thus, on account of the sacrilege he had committed against the Savior and his contemporaries, divine vengeance soon tormented Herod (Josephus, book XVIII of the *Antiquities*). He began to be tortured by a wondrous and pitiable pain; inwardly and outwardly he was burned by a fire; he was swollen by excessive gluttony and greed for food; and, swollen down to the pubic region, he teemed with worms around his genitals (the same author, book II). The physicians decided that he should be fomented with hot oil. When he had been placed in that treatment, all his limbs became so relaxed that even his eyes were loosened from their sockets.

## Chapter Seven. On the notorious wickedness he committed at his death

(Josephus, book XVII, chapter 3)

From this point, it is said, he became desperate enough for an accursed deed. He summoned the nobles from all Judea, shut them up in the place called the Hippodrome, and ordered them to be killed at the hour of his death, having prepared soldiers for this purpose and hired them at a price, so that he might at least have a mournful funeral. For he knew that the Jews would rejoice at his death.

## Chapter Eight. That he killed three of his sons

(Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, book II, chapter 4)

Shortly before he died, after already killing two sons, he ordered his third son to be butchered. This impious parricide, when he sensed that the end of his life was already near, upon receiving the evil news, asked for a knife. He was accustomed to eat an apple that had been peeled and cut up by himself in this way. Then, looking around to see whether anyone was present who might stop him, he raised his right hand and struck at himself. This was the end of Herod.

## Chapter Nine. On Archelaus

(Eusebius, chapter 10 of the same book)

After him Archelaus reigned, with his father Herod and Caesar Augustus assigning the kingdom to him. After ten years, because of his arrogance, he was deposed, and the kingdom was divided into tetrarchies, [Col. 0822A] for his younger brother Herod, together with Philip and Lysanias.

## Chapter Ten. On Herod, the son of Herod

(The same author, chapter 13 of the same book) [Note: [Col. 0821D] This younger Herod punished John the Baptist by beheading him. This younger Herod was called Herod Antipas, son of Herod the Ascalonite, born of his wife Malthace. For there were many other Herods, concerning whom see Josephus, book V of the *History of the Jews*.]

This younger Herod, after a short interval, punished John the Baptist by beheading him, a very good man [Note: [Col. 0821D] “John the Baptist, a good man.” Josephus the Hebrew also gives him such a testimony; he too mentions this wicked slaughter and the Baptism. He further adds that, for this very reason, many grave misfortunes befell Herod, especially these two: first, that his forces were routed and defeated by Aretas, king of Arabia Petraea; and second, that he was condemned to exile, book XIX, chapter 7. He is said to have lived in exile at Vienna in Gaul. Nicephorus.], who instructed the Jews to practice virtue, to maintain justice among themselves, to preserve piety toward God, and to come together through baptism both for the washing away of sins and for the preservation of bodily and spiritual purity.

## Chapter Eleven. Why he punished John

This man, I say, he punished by beheading because John rebuked him [Col. 0822B] concerning Herodias, whom he had taken from his brother Philip after dismissing his own legitimate wife; and because he feared that, on account of John’s teaching, very many people would depart from his kingdom. Thus, solely because of Herod’s suspicion and John’s rebuke, John was bound and taken away to the fortress of Machaerus, where he was beheaded (Matt. XIV; Luke III; Mark VI).

## Chapter Twelve. On the Lord Jesus our Savior

At this time the Lord Jesus spread the preaching of the Gospel widely, and from among all people he chose twelve, whom, setting them above his followers, he specially called apostles. After these he chose seventy-two disciples.

[Note: [Col. 0821D] He completed the entire period of his preaching within four years. This reckoning of four years is also found in Eusebius, book I, chapter 1, and in Nicephorus, book I, chapter 19. They cite Josephus, book XVIII, chapter 7, as the authority for this period. But in this matter credence must be given to the evangelist Luke, from whom we understand that the period of Jesus Christ’s preaching was three years. Nicephorus also asserts this in book I, chapter 10, and book II, chapter 4. The words of Josephus that they cite must plainly be understood of another period.]

He completed the entire period of his preaching [Col. 0822C] within the span of four years, under the high priests Annas and Caiaphas, beginning his preaching during the high priesthood of Annas and extending it until the beginning of Caiaphas’s term (Josephus). For from Annas to Caiaphas there were four high priests in succession: after Annas came Ishmael; after Ishmael, Eleazar; after Eleazar, Simon; after Simon, Joseph, who was also called Caiaphas.

A Hebrew writer bears witness concerning who the Lord Jesus Christ was, and wrote of him in these words:

## Chapter Thirteen. Testimony of Josephus concerning Christ

[Note: [Col. 0822D] “Josephus’s testimony concerning Jesus Christ.” Book XVIII, chapter 6, *Jewish Antiquities*, specifically in the Greek and Latin text. For it is not found in the Hebrew, owing to the impious wickedness of the Hebrews. It is not believable that Josephus, a thoroughly good man, would have remained silent in Hebrew about what he had said at length in Greek.]

(Josephus, book XVIII, chapter 6, *Antiquities*)

At that time there was Jesus, a wise man—if indeed it is proper to call him a man. For he was a doer of marvelous works and a teacher of those who gladly receive what is true; and he also drew many Gentiles to himself. He was the Christ. When Pilate, at the accusation of the leading men of our nation, had condemned him to the cross, those who had loved him from the beginning did not abandon him. For he appeared alive on the third day, in accordance with what the divinely inspired prophets had foretold, whether this or other miracles concerning him. And to this day the name and race of Christians has not ceased.

## Chapter Fourteen. On the disciples

(Eusebius, book I, chapter 13, *Ecclesiastical History*; Epiphanius, book I, tome I, chapter 20, *Against Heresies*)

The names of the apostles are clear from the Gospels. We do not find the seventy written down anywhere, but it is said that one of them was Barnabas. Clement, in the fourth book of the *Dispositions*, mentions Cephas, concerning whom Paul says: “When Cephas came to Antioch, I opposed him to his face” (Gal. II, 11). He says that this man was one of the seventy and was surnamed Peter the apostle. He also says that Matthias was one of them, as was the one appointed with him by lot; he says that Thaddeus was also among them. But you will find that there were many other disciples if you observe what Paul indicates when he says that after the resurrection the Lord appeared to Cephas, then to the other eleven, and after them to more than five hundred brothers at once (I Cor. XV, 5–6).

(Haymo.) The Lord therefore lived with these men throughout the whole period of his assumed mortality, formed them in faith, and instructed them in knowledge, until, having completed the duty of the dispensation he had undertaken, he suffered, rose again, and ascended into heaven, according to the faith of the Gospels.

# Book Two

[Col. 0823]

## Chapter One. On the election of Matthias the apostle and the appointment of the seven deacons

(Eusebius, tome II, chapter 1, *Ecclesiastical History*)

It remains for us to speak of what immediately followed the Lord’s ascension. The apostles cast lots and chose Matthias in place of Judas the traitor (Acts I). They also appointed seven deacons for the ministry of the widows. One of them was stoned immediately after his appointment; for this reason he was crowned by the Lord in his own name, for **Στέφανος** (*Stephanos*) means “crown.”

## Chapter Two. On James, the first bishop of Jerusalem

(The same work; Nicephorus, book II, chapter 3, *Ecclesiastical History*)

Then James, the brother of the Lord, first assumed the seat of the Church of Jerusalem, distinguished by the merit of his virtues and the privilege of his life.

(Clement, in the sixth and seventh books of the *Dispositions*)

For although Peter, James, and John were honored above all after the Lord’s ascension, they did not claim the glory for themselves; rather, they appointed James, who was called the Just, as bishop. For to this James, Peter, and John the Lord gave all knowledge after the resurrection; and they gave it to the other apostles, who in turn gave it to the seventy-two.

It is established that there were two Jameses: one the brother of John, the other this James the Just, the brother of the Lord, [Note: [Col. 0823D] He is called the brother of the Lord because he was the son of Joseph, who was regarded as Christ’s quasi-father. James, the son of Joseph, was born from another wife. Since he was raised together with Jesus Christ, by this association in upbringing he was regarded as the Lord’s brother—not, certainly, by nature. Epiphanius explains the whole matter in book III of *Against Heresies*, as do we above.] who was called the brother of the Lord because he was the son of Joseph, who was regarded as Christ’s quasi-father.

## Chapter Three. Haymo on the same subject, according to what he found in the sayings of the Fathers

Those who have carefully investigated the matter also know that he was called the brother of the Lord because he was regarded as a kinsman. For it is the custom of the Hebrews to call or name kinsmen and relatives “brothers.” He was therefore called the brother of the Lord because he was born of Mary, the sister of the Lord’s mother, and of Alphaeus, and hence James is called “the son of Alphaeus.”

But since the occasion has now presented itself, let us resolve the entire question concerning the two Jameses and trace the origin of their families from a higher point. Mary, the mother of the Lord; Mary, the mother of James, the Lord’s brother; and Mary, the mother of James, the brother of John the evangelist, were sisters, born of different fathers but of the same mother, namely Anna.

Anna first married Joachim, and by him bore Mary, the mother of the Lord. After Joachim’s death, she married Cleophas, and by him had another Mary, who is called in the Gospels Mary of Cleophas. [Col. 0824C] Cleophas, moreover, had a brother Joseph, to whom he betrothed his stepdaughter, the blessed Mary, while he gave his own daughter to Alphaeus. From the latter was born James the younger, who is also called the Just, the brother of the Lord, and another Joseph.

After Cleophas died, Anna married a third husband, namely Salome, and had by him a third Mary. Betrothed to Zebedee, this Mary bore James the elder and John the evangelist. But let us now return to the order of the historical narrative.

## Chapter Four. On Thaddeus, sent to Edessa

At this time, then, Thaddeus was sent by the Lord to Abgar, king of the Edessenes. He cured him of his illness and freed the city from error.

[Col. 0824D] (Haymo.) I found a more extensive account of this matter in a certain written work (Eusebius, book I, chapter 15), but I do not know whether it is apocryphal; God knows. Since it proceeds from the piety of faith, I considered it necessary to insert it into this work.

It is said that, while our Savior was still dwelling in the flesh and the happy report of his miracles was being spoken of everywhere, Abgar, king of the Edessenes, sent him a letter in which he earnestly begged him to come to him and cure him of leprosy. He also said that he had long desired to see him, and therefore urged him to come to him, escape the hatred of the Jews, and live with him, since he possessed a city that could be sufficient for them both.

The Lord, however, wrote back to him with his own hand. In the letter he first declares him blessed because he believes in one whom he does not see. Second, he says that he cannot come in person, because he must fulfill the Father’s command and obedience in the land of Jerusalem. Third, he promises him healing in these words: “When I have been taken up, I will send you one of my disciples, [Col. 0825B] who will cure you of your illness.”

## Chapter Five. On the Lord’s face impressed upon a linen cloth

It is said that, in order to fulfill the desire of the aforementioned king, the Lord in some manner impressed his face upon a linen cloth and sent it to him, so that he who could not be seen in his own form might at least be seen through the image impressed upon the cloth. Thus Thaddeus, the disciple who was sent to Edessa, was worthy to carry there the aforementioned image of the Lord. It remained there for a long time, until it was carried to Constantinople with the other relics.

## Chapter Six. The dispersion of the Lord’s disciples follows

(Eusebius, book II, chapter 1, *Ecclesiastical History*)

After Stephen, the protomartyr, had been stoned, all the disciples except the twelve were scattered throughout Judea and Samaria; some of them even reached Phoenicia, Cyprus, and Antioch. There they preached to a few Jews, not daring to entrust themselves either to Jews or to Gentiles, while Saul was at that time laying waste to the Church (Acts VIII, 9).

## Chapter Seven. The deeds of Philip the deacon

(Eusebius, in the same place; Nicephorus, book II, chapter 6, *Ecclesiastical History*)

Philip, one of the seven deacons, went down to Samaria and was granted the favor of preaching, so that by his preaching he confounded Simon Magus, who was so famous among the Samaritans. Simon also received baptism from him, but deceitfully. Philip likewise converted and baptized an official of a certain Candace, queen of Ethiopia.

## Chapter Eight. The calling of Paul the apostle

(Eusebius, in the same place)

At this time Paul was called to the apostleship, a heavenly voice being conveyed to him (Acts VIII).

## Chapter Nine. Pilate’s report to Tiberius

(The same author, chapter 2)

Meanwhile, when reports about the Lord Jesus Christ were spreading everywhere, Pilate informed the emperor Tiberius about his miracles and resurrection, and about the belief of many that he was blessed. For it was the custom among the Romans that, if anything new occurred in the provinces, it should be reported to the emperor or the Senate.

## Chapter Ten. How Tiberius, informed about Christ, was pleased

Tiberius, therefore, having been informed by Pilate, reported to the Senate what he had learned.

(Tertullian, in the *Apology against the Gentiles*)

For a decree had been issued that no one was to be consecrated as a god by the emperor unless he had been approved by the Senate. But the Senate is said to have rejected him because the matter had not first been referred to it, although the opinion of the populace had anticipated its authority. Tiberius nevertheless maintained his decision and threatened danger to the accusers of the Christians.

By divine providence, he thus acted mercifully toward our people. Soon, within a short time, preaching spread throughout the whole earth; innumerable multitudes were converted and, through the teaching of Christ and miracles of virtue, gathered into the churches.

(Eusebius, chapter 3 of the same book)

Cornelius was the first in Caesarea to be converted while Peter was ministering. In Antioch very many Gentiles believed, and there a flourishing Church was gathered through the disciples who had been scattered during the first persecution under Stephen. Among them were men of the prophetic order, including Paul and Barnabas.

## Chapter Eleven. How the Christian name was first established at Antioch by being assigned

(The same author, in the same place; Nicephorus, book II, chapter 6, *Ecclesiastical History*)

There the disciples were first called Christians, the name having been assigned at the baptismal font. There also Agabus, one of the prophets among those who were present, prophesied about a future famine under Claudius. Tiberius reigned for twenty-two years.

## Chapter Twelve. How many evils befell the Jews

(Josephus, book XVIII, chapter 15, *On the Jewish War*)

Meanwhile Tiberius died after twenty-two years of rule. Gaius succeeded to the empire, granting Agrippa the kingdom of the Jews, and giving Philip, Lysanias, and Herod their tetrarchies, while imposing upon the aforementioned Herod the perpetual punishment of exile.

(Haymo.)

About this time many evils befell the Jews because of the crime they had committed against the Savior, while Gaius was persecuting them. Philo, then the most distinguished writer [Col. 0826D] among the Hebrews, undertook an embassy on behalf of his fellow Jews (Philo, book V, *On the Embassy to Gaius*).

When a sedition arose at Alexandria between the Greeks and the Jews, Philo himself, in *Against Apion*, most forcefully cleared the Jews of the accusations brought against them; Apion belonged to the Greek side. But Gaius despised him, because Gaius hated the Jews on the grounds that they made neither altars nor temples nor images for him. For he was so insane and presumptuous that he wished to be called a god.

He even filled the temple of the holy city with images and statues—a temple that alone had remained untouched by the contamination of profane religion—and dared to transform it into a temple bearing his own name, so that, shameful to say, the Lord’s temple, that most noble building, might be called the temple of Jupiter and of the new god Gaius. Philo describes all these matters more fully in his books (book II, *On Virtues*), and says that countless other disasters, beyond all tragic lamentations, were inflicted upon the Jews at Alexandria.

## Chapter Thirteen. What happened in the time of Tiberius

But Josephus (book II, *Jewish War*) enumerates the evils that befell them at Jerusalem and explains how Pilate brought images of Caesar into Jerusalem.

## Chapter Fourteen. That Pilate condemned himself to death

(Eusebius, book II, chapter 7, *Ecclesiastical History*; Nicephorus, book II, chapter 10, *Ecclesiastical History*)

At this time, while divine vengeance was thus tormenting the Jews, it did not permit Pilate either—who had acted as an unjust judge in Christ’s death—to remain unpunished. Thus, after being afflicted by Gaius with many disastrous sufferings, he finally pierced himself with his own hand and condemned himself to death.

## Chapter Fifteen. From the histories of the Greeks concerning the dire famine that was prophesied

(Eusebius, chapter 8 of the same book; Nicephorus, chapter 11 of the same book)

Meanwhile Gaius ended his life after less than four complete years. Claudius succeeded him, under whom a terrible famine occurred, as Agabus had prophesied. Then the brothers at Antioch sent, according to their means, what was necessary to the holy inhabitants of Jerusalem through Paul and Barnabas, who had been appointed to minister to the saints.

## Chapter Sixteen. On the younger Herod, who was the son of Aristobulus, the son of Herod the Great

At this time Agrippa, surnamed Herod, obtained the kingdom of all Judea. Luke calls him Herod in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts XII), while Josephus calls him Agrippa (Josephus, book XVIII, chapter 12, *Jewish Antiquities*). This man, retaining much of the cruelty of his uncle, persecuted the apostles, imprisoned Peter, and killed James, the brother of John, with the sword.

## Chapter Seventeen. On the death of James, the brother of John

(Clement of Alexandria, book VII of the *Dispositions*)

To recount something about his passion: it is said that when one of the attendants had brought him to Herod for martyrdom, the very man who had brought him, moved by repentance, was himself stirred and confessed that he was a Christian. Both were then led together to punishment. As they were being led away, the man asked James on the road to grant him forgiveness. James, after pausing to deliberate, said, “Peace be with you,” and kissed him. Thus both were beheaded. But God’s avenging right hand immediately came upon the aforementioned Herod.

## Chapter Eighteen. On God’s vengeance against Herod

(Josephus, book XIII of the *Jewish Antiquities*)

When he later held spectacles at Caesarea in honor of Caesar, dressed with extraordinary arrogance in a garment wondrously woven with gold and silver, the astonished crowds suddenly called him a god because of the radiance of the shining metal, and begged him to be favorable to them.

But because he did not restrain either the title or his pride, he was immediately struck by an angel and seized by an incredible pain and swelling of the belly. Looking toward his friends, he said: “Behold, I am your god; behold, I am suddenly struck and dragged away from life.”

## Chapter Nineteen. Luke in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts XII)

Then, swarming with worms, he breathed his last, in the seventh year of his reign: four years under Caligula and the remaining three under Claudius.

## Chapter Twenty. On Simon Magus

(Augustine, letter 86; Epiphanius, book I, tome I, *Against Simon*)

At this time a certain Samaritan named Simon, the head of all wickedness and the beginning of every heresy, was elevated under Caesar Claudius by magic arts and the assistance of demons. In the city of Rome he was declared a god and received the honor of a statue, which was placed between the two bridges of the Tiber, bearing an inscription in Latin words: “To Simon, the holy god.” But this did not last long, for the deception was exposed by divine power.

## Chapter Twenty-One. The arrival of Peter in the city of Rome

[Note: [Col. 0827D] “The arrival of Peter in the City.” This has been transmitted in the writings of all authors, and has been expressed not only in Greek but also in Hebrew, Syriac, Arabic, and almost the language of every nation. It has also been declared by the expression of the very favorable will of all rulers toward the Roman See, as we have shown elsewhere in a volume against the history of heretics. They dare to deny this because they are utterly shameless in speech, although it is widely known in the writings and language of every nation.]

(Eusebius, book I, chapter 14)

For immediately, during the very time of Claudius, through divine providence the apostle Peter, after first founding the Church at Antioch, was escorted with honor to the city of Rome. He brought with him from the regions of the East, like a heavenly merchant, the merchandise of divine light, if anyone was ready to purchase it.

Through his magnificent authority, the bright light of God immediately arose for the City, and Simon’s deception was extinguished together with its author.

(Haymo.) He possessed such grace for preaching that, illuminating the minds of all with peaceful speech, he drew them to himself and quickly made the name of Christ renowned in the capital of kingdoms. This was beautifully accomplished by divine providence, so that the title of the Savior might be raised there with greater glory precisely where, at the beginning of the faith, the Savior himself had been rejected by the Romans with greater contempt.

## Chapter Twenty-Two. Philo’s commendation and conversion

(Eusebius, chapter 17 of the same book; Nicephorus, book II, chapter 11)

At that time Philo, the Hebrew writer whom we mentioned above—most subtle, profound in thought, and exceedingly rich in eloquence, discovering matters abundantly and expressing them even more abundantly—attached himself to the apostle Peter as he preached. He finally left us, in many books, monuments of his intellect.

## Chapter Twenty-Three. On the Gospel according to Mark
(Eusebius, chapter 15 of the same book.) At that time Mark wrote the Gospel on the following occasion. Since merely hearing Peter was not sufficient for them, those who listened to him begged Mark, his disciple, with great eagerness and earnest entreaties, to commit his preaching to writing as a memorial. Clement, in the sixth book of the *Outlines*: “When Peter learned that he had been deprived by this pious theft, he was pleased, confirmed the deed, and handed it over to the churches to be read in perpetuity.” Afterwards Mark, sent by Peter to Egypt, preached this same Gospel there and was the first to be appointed bishop at Alexandria, where he won many peoples, an example of great sobriety and self-control. Meanwhile, while the apostle Paul was preaching from Jerusalem round about and as far as Illyricum, the emperor Claudius expelled the Jews who were causing disturbances from the city. Then Aquila and Priscilla, together with the other exiles, came to Asia, and there they joined the Apostle as he was laying the foundations of the churches.

## CHAPTER XXIV. The Evils That Befell the Jews

(Josephus, book XX of the *Jewish Antiquities*.) At that time, while Agrippa was reigning at Jerusalem, Felix was procurator of the province, and Claudius still remained in power, such great evils befell the Jews that, when a sedition arose on the very day of Passover, thirty thousand were counted among those who died in the crowding at the entrances of the Temple alone; Jonathan the high priest was also killed there. At that time a certain Egyptian magician, pretending by magical art to be a prophet, gathered Jews from every quarter and promised them their ancient liberty and the liberation of their city. Relying on their assistance, he came through the desert as far as the Mount of Olives. But Felix forestalled his attempt; when battle was joined with weapons, he put the Egyptian to flight and either killed or captured the others, as many as thirty-eight thousand men.

## CHAPTER XXV. The Death of the Emperor Claudius

Meanwhile, after Claudius had completed thirteen years and eight months in power, Nero assumed the principate. He sent Festus to Judea to succeed Felix, before whom Paul, after his case had been heard, was sent to Rome in chains, accompanied by Aristarchus, and remained there for two years in unrestricted custody. After this he was released for preaching, while Nero had not yet erupted into the extent of crimes that histories recount about him, but was still acting more mercifully by divine providence. Thus Paul’s preaching might meanwhile be completed and his Epistles written, whether to individuals, to the heads of provinces, for the strengthening of the faith, for the adornment of the Gospel, or, finally, for the benefit of the whole Church.

## CHAPTER XXVI. The Martyrdom of James, the Brother of the Lord

(Eusebius, book II, chapter 13, *Ecclesiastical History*.) Therefore, after Paul had been sent to Rome, when the Jews saw that the plots they had devised against him had failed, they turned against James, the brother of the Lord and bishop of Jerusalem, in order to take vengeance. They then demanded that he deny Christ; but he confessed in a free voice before all the people that Christ was the Son of God. Then he was thrown down from the pinnacle of the Temple by the wicked Jews. Kneeling, he prayed even for those who were stoning him; finally, struck with a fuller’s club, he died in the thirtieth year of his episcopate. (Clement.) He had been holy from his mother’s womb: he drank neither wine nor strong drink, ate no animal flesh, no razor came upon his head, he was not anointed with oil, did not use the bath, and wore no woolen garment, but only linen. He alone was permitted to enter the Holy of Holies, where, bending his knees, he prayed without ceasing, so that his knees became calloused like those of a camel. Because of his extraordinary self-control and supreme justice he was called Oblias, that is, “the bulwark of the people” and “justice.” Not long afterwards Vespasian’s attack followed, so that even the prudent among the Jews believed that the immediate assault upon Jerusalem had occurred because they had laid their criminal hands upon James, the most just and, by universal confession, most devout man, who was the brother of the Lord who is called Christ.

(Haymo.) I, however, think that this happened to them rather because they committed an offense against the Lord Jesus, so that, since they had cried, “His blood be upon us and upon our children,” they might be punished, both in themselves and in their successors, by an almost continuous shedding of blood. Meanwhile Festus died in Judea; Albinus succeeded him by the appointment of Caesar, and Florus succeeded Albinus. Unable to endure his avarice, luxury, and other crimes—for he had flogged even men of rank and had hanged some on the gallows in the holy city—the Jews rebelled against the Romans. On this account Vespasian was sent as military commander to wage war against the Jews.

## CHAPTER XXVII. Nero’s Cruelty

Nero, the most cruel emperor, progressed so far in wickedness that he became a parricide toward his mother, brothers, wives, and all his near blood-relatives, and committed incest. Above all, he persecuted the Christians.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. Peter and Paul Are Crowned Together

(Eusebius, chapter 25 of the same book.) In Rome itself he condemned both Peter and Paul, the leaders and standard-bearers of the apostles and of Judea’s people: one to the sword, the other to the cross. Peter was crucified head downward because he asked not to appear equal to the Lord.

Dionysius, bishop of the Corinthians, says that they were not teaching separately or at different times, as some maintain, but that both were crowned with martyrdom together, at one and the same time, in the aforementioned city. With their most glorious end, let us also bring this second volume to an end.

# BOOK THREE

## CHAPTER I. The Division of the Apostles among the Provinces

(Eusebius, book III, chapter 1, *Ecclesiastical History*; Nicephorus, book III, chapter 1.) This third book begins with the division of the apostles. Since the Jews were being pressed by punishments they had deserved, the apostles of the Lord, together with the other disciples, were sent through the provinces to preach.

## CHAPTER II. In What Places the Apostles Were Scattered after the Division

Origen, in his explanation of Genesis (book III): “Thomas received Parthia by lot; Matthew, Ethiopia; Bartholomew, Hither India; John, Asia; Andrew, Scythia; Peter, Pontus, Galatia, Bithynia, and Cappadocia; Paul filled the whole region from Jerusalem as far as Illyricum with the Gospel of Christ. The others were sent either through these regions or through other places, according to the will of the Holy Spirit, as their own acts record.”

Perhaps Origen remained silent about them for this reason: their lives and deeds are less authentic, or were written by heretics and impostors. Peter therefore left memorials of his preaching and wrote two Epistles; likewise James, the brother of the Lord, wrote one; John, three; Jude, who is also Thaddeus, one. Paul wrote fourteen.

[Note: The Epistle to the Hebrews was at times doubted among the Latins. The reason for the doubt was, in fact, very slight. As for the fact that it was entirely Paul’s, there are many and very weighty arguments advanced by those who have undertaken this line of inquiry. Since the matter is already evident and requires no debate, I do not wish to cast into doubt something certain and already established, which defends itself by its own truth. For what is true has no need to be brought to external supports of proof.]

Nevertheless, the Epistle to the Hebrews was at times doubted among the Latins.

## CHAPTER III. Paul’s Epistle to the Hebrews

(Clement of Alexandria, in the book *Reform*.) Although Paul the apostle’s writings are manifest, some nevertheless doubt the Epistle to the Hebrews. But it should be understood that it was written by Paul in the Hebrew language, as being addressed to Hebrews, and translated into Greek by Luke, his disciple. Hence its style seems more similar to that little book which Luke himself wrote concerning the Acts of the Apostles. The reason why it does not bear the customary subscription is that the Hebrews had been instructed not to accept statements made under Paul’s name; therefore he prudently omitted his name, lest the reading should immediately be rejected at the outset upon seeing Paul’s name.

## CHAPTER IV. Saint Luke

(Eusebius, chapter 3 of the same book.) Luke, a disciple of that same Paul, an Antiochene by birth and a physician by profession, wrote two books for us: the Acts of the Apostles, which he himself saw with his own eyes, and the Gospel, which, as is said, he transcribed from Paul’s own mouth. Paul also calls it his own when he says, “According to my Gospel” (2 Timothy 2). But let us now return to the order of the history.

## CHAPTER V. Nero’s Death

Thus, after thirteen years of his reign, Nero died. Galba and Otho seized power. When they had died after one year and three months, Vespasian, then serving in the army in Judea, was recalled and given the empire, while responsibility for the war and the assault on Jerusalem was entrusted to Titus, his son. Under him the aforementioned city was captured and overthrown.

## CHAPTER VI. Josephus

[Note: The overthrow of Jerusalem. Nicephorus in his *Chronology* and book III, chapter 3; Josephus and Hegesippus, and almost innumerable others.]

The overthrow of Jerusalem by Titus Vespasian.

(Eusebius, book III, chapter 5.) The church of the faithful that had assembled there, having received a divine response, forestalled the destruction and emigrated across the Jordan to a town called Pella. (Nicephorus, book III, chapter 3.) Then an unbelievable slaughter of the Jews took place. First, as a punishment for the dreadful and unheard-of calamity of famine, an intolerable scourge was sent by God, to such an extent that wars and killings broke out between parents and children, while they struggled to snatch food from one another not only from their hands but from their very mouths. (Josephus, book IV, chapter 9, *The Jewish War*.) In the end they spared neither leather straps, belts, nor even their own shoes. Tearing away the coverings of the gates, they put them into their mouths to be consumed by their teeth; some even ate pieces of old hay. Moreover, an abominable crime was committed there, such as had not yet been heard of either among the Greeks or among the barbarians. (Hegesippus, book IV, chapter 6.)

## CHAPTER VII. The Woman Who Ate Her Son

(Josephus, book VII, chapter 8, *The Jewish War*.) A certain woman named Mary, noble by birth and wealth, who had come with the others from the region beyond the Jordan for the festival, when the danger of famine grew more severe and the enemy’s plundering left her utterly exhausted by hunger, followed the advice of the worst counselors: she slaughtered her little son, who was still at her breast, placed him over a fire and roasted him. She ate half and kept half. When the plunderers soon entered, having detected the smell of the meat, she offered them the portion, saying: “This is my child. Do not prove either more scrupulous than a mother or more tender than a woman. Eat, for I have already eaten first.” Immediately the entire region was filled with the report of so monstrous a crime.

Not long afterwards the magnificent and most famous city of Jerusalem was captured. (Nicephorus, book III, chapter 7; Eusebius, book III, chapter 6; Josephus, book VII, chapter 26.) Its devastation and the slaughter by various kinds of death can scarcely be comprehended in writing. There, eleven hundred thousand people killed by hunger and the sword were counted, apart from the chosen young men who, because of the beauty and height of their bodies, were reserved for the triumph, and the others who were assigned to labor in Egypt, to cut marble, or to extract metals, or who were sold into slavery in chains throughout the provinces. Their number reached ninety thousand. (Josephus, book VII, chapter 27.) But so that no one may doubt the multitude of those captured or killed, let him know that at that time, for the feast of Passover, thirteen hundred thousand Jews had gathered at Jerusalem, at the just retribution of God, who had chosen this time for vengeance. Thus those who during the days of Passover had condemned the Lord and Savior to the most shameful death were themselves condemned during those same days to the most shameful deaths and unheard-of calamities.

(Haymo.) Those who had celebrated solemn feast days in connection with his condemnation now made those same days mournful through their own condemnations. They rightly perished from hunger, too, so that those who had given the Lord, when he was hungry, gall for food might be deprived of every pleasant kind of nourishment.

## CHAPTER VIII. The Time of the Destruction of Jerusalem

This destruction of Jerusalem occurred forty years after the Lord’s Passion, the vengeance having been delayed until the second year of Vespasian’s reign. Meanwhile, if they had wished, the Jews could have found a place for repentance, since the apostles had often warned them that the city’s overthrow was at hand. While James, the brother of the Lord, was still alive, they were also instructed through signs and wonders shown from heaven before the time of the catastrophe. (Josephus, book VII, chapter 12, *The Jewish War*.) For a brilliant star, entirely like a sword, was seen hanging over the city from above, and, in addition, a comet burned throughout the year with destructive flames.

## CHAPTER IX. A New Portent

A heifer, too, brought to the priests for sacrifice on the feast of Unleavened Bread, gave birth to a lamb in the hands of the attendants. The gate in the inner court of the Temple, being of such great weight that it could scarcely be closed by twenty men and secured with bars and bolts, opened of its own accord during the night. Chariots and companies of armed men were also seen carried through the air, along with many other things that do not contribute to the concise scope of this work, especially since we must pursue the history of the Christians.

## CHAPTER X. Hegesippus on Simon, Bishop of Jerusalem after James

(Nicephorus, in his *Chronology*.) Thus, after the destruction of Jerusalem and not long after James’s martyrdom, when the apostles and the Lord’s relatives according to the flesh had assembled together, Simon, the son of Joseph, was appointed bishop by common agreement.

## CHAPTER XI. Titus Succeeds His Father Vespasian

Meanwhile Vespasian died. His son Titus succeeded him in the empire: a military commander, pious, wise, and warlike. He was so eloquent that he pleaded cases in Latin and composed poems and tragedies in Greek.

(Bede.) He was so warlike that, in the conquest of Jerusalem, he ranked among the finest fighters. Yet he was so good and merciful in the exercise of power that he punished no one at all, and even released all who conspired against him and retained them in the same intimacy they had previously enjoyed. For he used to say that it was unbecoming for anyone to depart from the emperor’s presence in sadness. Among all his sayings, this one became famous: he had lost a day whenever he had done nothing good. Thus he was remarkable in every kind of virtue, so much so that he was called the love and delight of the human race. He did not harm the Christians.

At this same time Linus, the Roman pontiff, died after completing twelve years in the priesthood; Cletus succeeded him.

## CHAPTER XII. Domitian

Titus died after two years and two months of his reign. Domitian, his younger brother, was appointed to the empire. In the fourth year of Domitian’s reign, Ammanus died at Alexandria after twenty-three years as bishop. Abilius succeeded him. Cletus, the Roman pontiff, also held office for twelve years, and at his death left the papacy to Clement.

Those who have investigated the succession of the Roman Church say that:

[Note: Linus and Cletus did not sit as pontiffs. While Peter was still alive, they did not do so; but after his death, first one and then the other sat at the helm of the Roman see. Thus Linus is counted second and Cletus third among the Roman pontiffs. I do not wish to say anything about Clement, for many count him second, while others write that he was fourth; the latter opinion seems more probable to most.]

Linus and Cletus did not sit as pontiffs, but as assistants to the supreme pontiff. Blessed Peter entrusted them with the administration of ecclesiastical affairs, while he himself devoted his time only to prayer and preaching. Therefore, having been endowed with such authority, they deserved to be placed in the catalogue of pontiffs.

## CHAPTER XIII. Domitian’s Persecution

(Nicephorus, book III, chapter 10, *Ecclesiastical History*; Eutropius, book IX, at the end.) Meanwhile Domitian, a portion of Nero and the successor to his impiety, fiercely persecuted the Christians. He slaughtered some, punished others by confiscating their property, and sent others into exile. Among them he ordered Flavia Domitilla, an outstanding virgin of Christ whose deeds are recorded, to be deported to the island of Pontia. He also banished the blessed John the Evangelist into exile; there he wrote the Apocalypse, having first been sent into a cauldron of boiling oil, yet remaining unharmed.

He ordered the family of David and the blood-relatives of Christ to be sought out so that he might kill them, lest any Jew of royal descent remain. When they were brought before him and answered that Christ’s kingdom was not of this world, he ordered them to depart free, but held them in contempt.

## CHAPTER XIV. Domitian Reigns for Fifteen Years

Thus Domitian held the empire for fifteen years. Afterwards, by decree of the Senate, all who had been exiled at his command were recalled; the blessed John returned with them.

## CHAPTER XV. Nerva Reigns Scarcely a Year

(Eusebius, book III, chapters 21–23, *Ecclesiastical History*.) When Nerva had died after approximately one year, Trajan obtained the empire. In the first year of his reign Abilius of Alexandria died after thirteen years as bishop, and Cerdon succeeded him in the priesthood as the third bishop. At that time Clement still held the pontificate at Rome after Peter; but at Antioch Evodius had been Peter’s successor, and Ignatius was second after him. At Jerusalem, after James, the brother of the Lord, Simeon, the Lord’s cousin, still presided.

(Irenaeus, book II, *Against Heresies*.) Meanwhile the blessed John the Evangelist, still alive, presided over the churches of Asia, residing at Ephesus, and continued living until the time of Trajan. There he built up the churches that Paul had first founded. He had Papias and Polycarp as hearers and fellow disciples. He also instructed and educated very many by composing books and Epistles. Near the end of his life he wrote the Gospel, compelled by the bishops of Asia because heretics had invaded the churches during his exile with various and perverse doctrines.

For this reason he wrote about Christ’s birth, saying little about his temporal deeds and pursuing only what the other evangelists had omitted.
