The other three, in fact, follow the Lord’s deeds beginning with the imprisonment of John the Baptist, whereas this one especially recounts what the Lord did at the beginning of his preaching, before John’s imprisonment. He also profoundly sets forth much concerning the mystery of the Trinity and unity, as we have said, against the heretics whose errors were then flourishing.

## CHAPTER XVI. Menander the Magician and Heretic

(Epiphanius, book IV, volume II, chapter 22; Eusebius, book III, chapter 26; Nicephorus, book III, chapter 12, *Ecclesiastical History*.) At the same time a certain Menander, a disciple of Simon the Samaritan magician, himself also a Samaritan and magician, polluted Antioch with blasphemous error. He mocked the immortality of the soul and the resurrection of the dead, asserting that he himself was the savior of humanity. He claimed that no one could overcome the angels of this age except by first receiving instruction in magical art from him, and that through the baptism he administered each person became immortal and, having been made eternal, became everlasting in this life.

## CHAPTER XVII. The Heretical Ebionites

(Eusebius, chapter 27 of the same book.) His disciples, the Ebionites, although belonging to another sect, also deceived many. They said that Christ was a mere human being, begotten by ordinary birth from a man and a woman, while still observing the ceremonies of the Law. “Ebionites” is interpreted as “poor,” and in understanding they truly were poor.

## CHAPTER XVIII. The Cerinthian Heretics

(The same, chapter 28.) The heretic Cerinthus also introduced new doctrines: namely, that Christ’s kingdom would be earthly in Jerusalem, that in the meantime human beings would be subjected to vices and desires, and that wedding festivities would take place—ideas intended easily to deceive those devoted to lust.

## CHAPTER XIX. The Heresy of the Nicolaitans

(The same, chapter 29 of the same book.) Another heresy also arose, called that of the Nicolaitans, which boasted that it derived from Nicolaus, one of the seven deacons ordained together with Stephen.

## CHAPTER XX. The Heretical Nicolaitans and Nicolaus

(Clement of Alexandria, book II, *Stromata*.) This Nicolaus had a beautiful wife. After the Lord’s Ascension, when the apostles reproached him for jealousy, he brought her forward publicly, insulted by the accusation, and freely permitted anyone who wished to have her. From this incident they concluded that, according to this deed or saying of Nicolaus, each person ought to abuse his own flesh in whatever way he took pleasure.

Hence even now those who adopt a sect according to their own lust, under his name, seek promiscuous and illicit intercourse.

## CHAPTER XXI. More about Nicolaus; Clement’s Defense of Nicolaus

I have learned that Nicolaus knew no woman at all except the one joined to him in marriage. His daughters, certainly, remained chaste until extreme old age; his son himself preserved the holiness of an undefiled body. It is therefore clear that he brought out his wife and allowed her to depart freely out of contempt for lust and vice, rather than exposing her for anyone else to abuse.

But, to return to what we began, it should be understood that the heresies mentioned above were quickly quieted, especially through the writings and preaching of the blessed John. After long periods of great self-control and sobriety, after his distinguished preaching of the Gospel and his incredible working of signs, he finally ordered that a grave be dug for him. He, both martyr and teacher, now sleeps at Ephesus, having completed a good and venerable old age of ninety-eight years. With his praiseworthy end, let us also bring the third volume to a close.

# BOOK FOUR

## CHAPTER I

After the death of the blessed John and the departure of the apostles, or of that choir which had received living instruction from the Lord’s own voice, immediately, as into an empty house, pestilential heretics thrust themselves into the Church.

## CHAPTER II. The Persecution of the Emperor Trajan

(Eusebius, book III, chapter 32, *Ecclesiastical History*; Epiphanius, *On the Sects*; Nicephorus, book III, chapter 16, *Ecclesiastical History*; Tertullian, in the *Apology*.) The emperor Trajan also launched a very great persecution against the Christians. Under him Simeon, bishop of Jerusalem, was afflicted for several days with tortures after being accused by heretics, and at last was crucified. The judge himself marveled that a man of one hundred and twenty years had endured the punishment of the cross.

Then the Church was pressed beneath the weight of persecutions; then many thousands of martyrs were slaughtered. Moved by this, Pliny the Younger, the governor, wrote to the emperor and pleaded on behalf of our people, asserting that there was no crime in them except that they sang hymns before dawn to a certain Christ as God.

## CHAPTER III. Hegesippus on the Martyrdom of Simeon, Bishop of Jerusalem

(The same.) Thus, after Simeon had been released through martyrdom, a certain Justus took over his episcopate. At that time Clement, pontiff of the city of Rome, after serving nine years in the priesthood, left the ministry of the papacy to Evaristus.

## CHAPTER IV. Ignatius, the Strong Athlete

(Eusebius, chapter 36 of the same book; Nicephorus, chapter 19 of the same book.) At that time Ignatius, bishop of Antioch, second in succession after Peter, was sent from Syria to the city of Rome and condemned to the beasts for his confession of Christ. This strongest athlete of Christ, in one of his letters written to the Romans, also begged them not to deprive him of the hope of martyrdom. In it he uses these very words, as one truly Christian and immovable in faith:

“O saving beasts, which are prepared for me! When will they come? When will they be sent out? When will it be permitted them to enjoy my flesh? I pray that they be prepared more fiercely, and I will invite them to devour me. I will beg them not to fear touching my body, as they have feared with some others; indeed, if they hesitate, I myself will use force, I myself will thrust myself upon them. Grant me pardon, I beg you, for I know what is expedient for me.”

(Nicephorus, book III, chapter 19, *Ecclesiastical History*.) “Now I am beginning to be Christ’s disciple. Let fires, crosses, beasts, scattering of bones, tearing apart of limbs, punishments of the entire body, and every torture devised against me by the devil’s art be inflicted upon me, provided only that I may deserve to attain Jesus Christ.”

He also wrote many other Epistles. Sailing from Syria to Rome, exhorting every church he entered and strengthening them in the Lord, he finally, as he himself also writes, happily departed to the Lord, bound and chained to ten leopards—that is, soldiers assigned to guard him.

## CHAPTER V

(Haymo.) He is rightly placed in the canon of the Mass after the commemoration of the holy apostles, together with the distinguished martyrs. For the one who greatly pleased God and his Christ by his renowned confession of faith and his illustrious writings and deeds can greatly intercede for us, being truly most worthy and the heir of the apostle Peter, both in succession of character and in succession to his see.

## CHAPTER VI. Ignatius’s Successor

(Eusebius, book III, chapter 37, *Ecclesiastical History*.) After Ignatius, Heros succeeded to the episcopate. At that time there flourished an equally distinguished man, Quadratus, renowned for prophetic grace, whose little works are also extant.

## CHAPTER VII. Distinguished Preachers and Leaders of the Church

It would be lengthy to enumerate each of the leaders who were in the churches after the apostles. We shall therefore commemorate those whose faith and preaching have reached us, whose examples instructed and strengthened the Church, who consecrated themselves to the word of God through a more ardent philosophy, and who, first distributing their possessions to those in need in obedience to the saving command, became ready to preach and fulfilled the office of evangelists.

At the beginning of the faith, the grace of the Holy Spirit accompanied them just as it had accompanied the apostles, and the mighty effect of miracles followed them. Among their number was Cerdon, bishop of Alexandria, mentioned above, who died in the twelfth year of Trajan’s reign. (The same, chapter 21 of the same book.) A certain man named Primus succeeded him, fourth after the apostles.

## CHAPTER VIII

[Note: Evaristus. Born of a Jewish father, yet Roman pontiff, as was Theodore. Likewise, not everyone agrees about the years of his pontificate.]

Evaristus, the Roman pontiff, also died after eight years as bishop, and Alexander, a venerable and apostolic man, succeeded him.

## CHAPTER IX

(Dionysius, Orosius, Eusebius, book IV, chapter 1.) Meanwhile, as the Church grew, the Jews, fomenting sedition in Alexandria, throughout Egypt, and in various lands, were struck down under Trajan in a slaughter both deserved and beyond counting.

## CHAPTER X. Trajan Reigns for Twenty Years Less Six Months

(The same, chapter 3 of the same book.) After completing a reign of twenty years less six months, Trajan was succeeded on the throne by Hadrian.

## CHAPTER XI. Hadrian’s Reign

(The same.) Then Quadratus, a disciple of the apostles, whom we mentioned above, and the Athenian bishops wrote books on the Christian religion to Hadrian. These works are considered distinguished as evidence of apostolic teaching and of great intellects.

## CHAPTER XII. Pope Alexander Held Office for Ten Years

Then Pope Alexander was crowned with martyrdom in the third year of Hadrian, and was buried at the seventh milestone from the city, where he had been beheaded, as his deeds recount. (Eusebius, book IV, chapter 4.)

## CHAPTER XIII

(Haymo.) We find in the revision of Eusebius’s *Chronicles*, which Bede prudently arranged and abridged, that the aforementioned pontiff did not suffer under Hadrian but under Trajan. This can easily be demonstrated from the fact that Hadrian, instructed by Quadratus’s books composed concerning our religion, ordered by letter that Christians should not be punished without charges of crimes.

## CHAPTER XIV. The Final Destruction of the Jews

(Bede.) Finally, this Hadrian subdued the Jews, who had rebelled for the second time, in a final slaughter. He also took away their permission to enter Jerusalem, which he himself had begun to rebuild with excellent walls, and ordered it to be called Aelia after his own name.

He established annual games in honor of Antinous, his beloved, began to call them the Antinoia, founded a city named Antinoopolis, dedicated a temple to him, and appointed priests and prophets. Meanwhile, after Alexander had ended his life through martyrdom, Xystus was appointed at Rome; at Alexandria, after Primus had died, Justus was chosen bishop.

## CHAPTER XV. Bishops of Jerusalem from among the Jews

(The same, chapter 5 of the same book.) At Jerusalem, however, Mark, the first bishop from the Gentiles, was appointed, after those who had been Jews ceased to serve. They numbered fifteen: James, the brother of the Lord; Simon; Justus; Zacchaeus; Tobias; Benjamin; John; Matthias; Philip; another Justus; Levi; Effren; Joseph; and Judas.

## CHAPTER XVI. Basilides and Saturninus, Heresiarchs

At that time the ancient enemy of the human race hissed as though with a forked tongue through Basilides, a heresiarch who arose at Alexandria, and Saturninus, born at Antioch, disturbing the churches.

(The same, chapter 6 of the same book.) Basilides gathered disciples for himself and made them remain silent for five years, after the Pythagorean custom. He taught them to taste things sacrificed without regard for conscience and, during persecutions, to deny the faith without scruple and indifferently.

## CHAPTER XVII. The Blasphemy of Saturninus and Carpocrates

Saturninus devised the same things as the aforementioned Menander. A certain Carpocrates, however, a disciple of Simon Magus, brought forth his tricks not secretly like him, but openly and publicly. Through these men accusations were directed against Christians of shameful acts, incest, and promiscuous intercourse among brothers, sisters, and mothers. But by the Lord’s grace, the credible way of life and learning found among our people at that time easily refuted and overcame them.

Hegesippus in particular, a contemporary of the apostles of Christ and their disciple, whose distinguished books are extant, refuted them in discussions and writings. Thus, when the fictions of the aforementioned heretics quickly vanished, the reputation of Christians flourished, so that every kind of person, abandoning ancestral laws and superstitions, hastened from the gods to the Lord Jesus and hurried to learn from him who is gentle and humble of heart.

## CHAPTER XVIII. Hadrian Reigns for Twenty-One Years. Telesphorus Holds Office for Eleven Years. Hyginus Holds Office for Four Years. Pius Holds Office for Twelve Years

(The same, chapter 10 of the same book.) Meanwhile Hadrian died, and Antoninus, surnamed Pius, became emperor. Telesphorus died, released through martyrdom. Hyginus succeeded to the apostolic office. Under him Valentinus, Cerdon, and a certain Marcion taught heretical fictions as doctrines.

When Hyginus died, Pius of Rome assumed the priesthood. Mark was appointed at Alexandria after Eumenes died. But when Mark also died after ten years, Celadion governed the church. In Rome, after completing his priesthood, Pius left the see to Anicetus. Under Anicetus, Hegesippus came to Rome and remained there until the episcopate of Eleutherius, who followed Anicetus.

At that time Justin the philosopher, defender of Christ and of our faith against Marcion both by living speech and by his writings, wrote a book on the Christian religion to Antoninus and obtained favor for our people.

## CHAPTER XIX. Polycarp, the Distinguished Martyr

At that time Polycarp, ordained and instructed by the apostles, bishop of the Smyrnaeans and venerable for his long and blameless life, went to Rome and rebuked Valentinianus and Cerdon, corrupted by heretical pollution.

(Nicephorus, book III, chapter 14, *Ecclesiastical History*.) It is reported that he elegantly related the following about the apostle John: when John had entered a bathhouse at Ephesus in order to bathe and saw Cerinthus there, he immediately went out without bathing, saying, “Let us flee from here, lest the bath itself collapse in which Cerinthus, the enemy of the truth, is bathing.”

Some distinguished little works of his are extant, as is his powerful Epistle to the Philippians, containing exhortations concerning faith and salvation. After Antoninus Pius, under the reign of Marcus Aurelius Verus, his son Antoninus, and Lucius, his brother, he ended his life in martyrdom.

## CHAPTER XX. Antoninus Pius Held Office for Twelve Years
(HAYMO.) This man is worthy to be granted perpetual remembrance by the Church, having been released through a most celebrated passion. Because of his distinguished merit and the support of his intercession, we have taken care to record him in this brief work, although in abridged language. Three days, then, before he was arrested, he saw in a nocturnal vision the headrest of his bed consumed by fire; and when he awoke, he interpreted the vision to the brethren in this way: that he would burn for Christ. Not long afterward his arresters rushed upon him. Advancing toward them with a calm countenance, he ordered a table to be set before his enemies as though they were guests, and abundant food to be served, having obtained an hour’s time for prayer. Then, seated on a donkey, he was led to the tribunal. When he had entered, he heard a voice from heaven: “Be strong, Polycarp.”

The proconsul accordingly admonished him at length to respect his age, to swear by the fortune of Caesar, and to utter insults against Christ. In an elegant voice, truly worthy of John’s disciple, he replied: “For eighty-six years,” he said, “I have served him, and he has never wronged me. How can I curse and blaspheme my king, who has given me salvation? I will not do it.” When the judge threatened to release wild beasts against him, he said steadfastly: “Let them be brought.” When he likewise threatened fire, he said: “Bring it confidently.”

Then, when the peoples of the city of Smyrna, both Jews and Gentiles, shouted, “Let him be burned alive,” he was condemned to the fire. When it had been prepared, he laid aside his older garments and loosened his belt; he also tried to remove his shoes from his feet, although he had never been accustomed to remove them except with the help of the religious men who had always preceded him in doing so [Note: It seems that the words “who had always preceded him” should be deleted.]—for thus he was revered by everyone. Thereafter, with his hands bound behind his back, he was handed over to the fire. But when, by a miracle wrought by God, the fire could not consume him, he was finally pierced through by the executioners’ sword. He was offered to God as both sacrifice and burnt offering, for a pleasing fragrance.

## CHAPTER XXI. On Justin, teacher and martyr

(Eusebius, Book III, chapters 3, 12, and 16; Book IV of the Ecclesiastical History.) At that time the aforementioned philosopher Justin presented to the judges a second book composed in defense of our religion. He received the reward of a faithful and learned tongue, the gift of martyrdom, after a certain philosopher named Crescens, a treacherous informer, accused him and laid snares for him, especially because the aforementioned Justin had often publicly confounded him in debates.

Before he entered his own contest, Justin also described the struggles of those who had become martyrs before him. Other distinguished works of his also survive, showing great learning; it would take too long to enumerate them.

## CHAPTER XXII. Pope Anicetus of Rome held office for eleven years

(Eusebius, Book IV, chapter 19, of the Ecclesiastical History.) Meanwhile, when Anicetus died, Soter succeeded him, and Celadion succeeded him in Alexandria. Agrippinus, the bishop mentioned above, Dionysius, bishop of the Corinthians, and Irenaeus were then regarded as distinguished men (the same author, chapters 21, 23, and 24 of the same book). They wrote books and letters, instructed the Church, and strengthened it. Monuments of their learning still survive.

There survives a particularly lucid letter of the aforementioned Dionysius to the Athenians, inviting them to martyrdom and reproving those who had fallen away. In it he also explains how Dionysius the Areopagite, instructed by Paul, was ordained the first bishop of Athens (Nicephorus, Book IV, chapters 8, 9, and 10, of the Ecclesiastical History).

Theophilus also, whom we mentioned above, wrote commentaries at Antioch and refuted with brilliant arguments the heretics who had arisen at that time, especially Marcion, against whom Irenaeus and Modestus also labored magnificently. Melito, bishop of Sardica, and Apollinaris of Hierapolis were likewise held in the highest esteem, and they wrote books on behalf of our appeal to the Roman emperor Antoninus.

Many distinguished works of Melito survive. In them he depicts the rule of the Church’s faith with remarkable skill. In a little book that he wrote on the explanation of the Scriptures, he lists, as though in a preface, the books of the Old Testament and which of them ought to be observed in the canon.

## CHAPTER XXIII. Irenaeus on the heresy of the Encratites

(Eusebius, Book IV, chapters 28 and 29; Irenaeus, Book I, chapter 30, of the Ecclesiastical History; Epiphanius, Book III, Treatise I, “On the Encratites.”) At that time the heresy of the Encratites arose, descending from Saturninus and Marcion. They condemned the foods of animals, which God established to be received for human use with thanksgiving; and they judged marriage, fornication, and corruption by the same law.

They are said to have had as their founder a certain Tatian, who was initially a hearer of Justin and displayed nothing of this kind during Justin’s lifetime. But after Justin had been released through martyrdom, Tatian separated himself from the Churches, puffed up with the arrogance of a teacher; and, in order to be esteemed greater than the others, he established his own method of teaching.

(Nicephorus, Book IV, chapter 11, of the Ecclesiastical History.) This Tatian, however, making a certain compilation of the Gospels, somehow composed one Gospel from the four, which they call the *Diatessaron*; for it is still possessed by many. One of his many treatises survives, written against the nations. It is judged the foremost and most useful of all his writings.

At the same time innumerable heresies sprang up, especially in Mesopotamia. A certain Bardesanes, powerful in speech and doctrine and an energetic dialectician, vigorously opposed them with his most eloquent arguments. He wrote books especially against Marcion; his disciples translated these works, composed in his own language—that is, Syriac—into Greek.

Soter held office for seven years. During this period Soter, bishop of the Roman Church, a pious and gentle man toward the brethren and a holy man who generously supplied the needy with whatever bodily use required, also brought his life to an end. Let us here bring the end of the fourth book.

# BOOK FIVE

[Col. 0843]

## CHAPTER I

(Eusebius, Book V, at the beginning.) Accordingly, Eleutherius succeeded Soter, the twelfth bishop after the apostles, in the twenty-second year of the reign of Marcus Antoninus Verus. At that time, throughout many provinces of the Roman world, the populace’s shouting and rebellion against our people stirred up extremely severe persecutions, so that many thousands of martyrs were made in each place.

## CHAPTER II. On the Letter of the Church of Lyons

(The same author, chapter 3 of the same book; Nicephorus, Book I, chapters 16, 17, and 18, of the Ecclesiastical History.) At that time the servants of Christ living in Lyons and Vienne, the most distinguished cities of Gaul, were afflicted by the gravest tribulations. To summarize briefly and rapidly all the kinds of persecution, the enemy attacked them with all his strength.

First, they were forbidden to live in their houses; then they were forbidden the use of baths; afterward, access to public places; and finally, both public and private places. Thus, after being subjected to insults, they were confined, beaten, stoned, and tortured, to such an extent that no one could describe each individual kind of torment.

But the saints endured these things with composure, like steadfast pillars of Christ. They not only bore the assaults already brought against them, but even sought them voluntarily. Some weaker persons, unable to undergo what was required of them—perhaps because their sins demanded it—fell away, nearly ten in number. By their fall they left the Church in profound mourning, for the Church is more saddened by the fall of our people than by their torments.

Then, at the devil’s instigation, the unbelieving populace invented new and deadly lies against our people. Having seized some pagan slaves of Christians, they extorted from them, through fear of torture, the claim that Christians ate their own children and abused their mothers and sisters.

For this reason Christians were held in execration by everyone, especially by those who had previously treated them with greater clemency. Among them were a certain holy deacon named Viennensis; Blandina, a noblewoman; and Photinus, the venerable bishop of Lyons. Although he was already ninety years old and, because of weakness and old age, was carried to the tribunals rather than led there, he was released through martyrdom, as their acts relate.

A certain Attalus also suffered with them. During his torments, while his flesh was being roasted and the smell of burnt flesh was perceived, he uttered that famous statement: “This is what you are doing—eating human beings. We do not eat human beings, nor do we do anything else evil.”

When he was asked what name God has, he replied elegantly: “Those who are many are distinguished by names; the one who is one has no need of one.”

## CHAPTER III. Again, from the Letter of Lyons

The humanity and humility of the blessed martyrs were so great that, although they had frequently become martyrs after wild beasts, fires, and metal plates, they absolutely refused to be called martyrs, whether in speech or in the letters of the brethren. If anyone did this, they rebuked him more severely, saying that this title was owed to Christ alone, or certainly to those who, after a good confession, had deserved to depart from this life and go to God.

“We, however,” they said, “are humble and needy, and we desire that at least the confession itself may remain secure in us.”

Their humility was therefore so great that, although they were martyrs in reality, they nevertheless shunned the boastfulness of the name: humble among the brethren, exalted among their persecutors. They accused no one, released everyone, quarreled with no one, and prayed for their persecutors, using the words of the holy martyr Stephen: “Lord, do not hold this sin against them.”

Because of the excessive love that they had in Christ Jesus, they clung with every compassion to those who had fallen away, pouring out rivers of tears for them before almighty God. They did not say that the journey to the Lord would be pleasing to them if part of their members were torn from the Churches and snatched away by the devil.

These words, therefore, which derive from the authority of such great men, have been stated for the sake of and against those who are carried away, proud and arrogant, against their brethren; and against those who, if they happen to have stumbled, think that the mercies of Christ must be entirely excluded from them.

## CHAPTER IV. On Irenaeus, an illustrious man

(Eusebius, Book V, chapter 20.) Accordingly, when Photinus, bishop of Lyons, had been crowned with the other martyrs, Irenaeus—who in his youth had been a hearer of Polycarp—succeeded him in the priesthood. He wrote many books and left behind distinguished monuments of his talent. Among his many and countless works, he relates an elegant and wondrous account concerning the seventy translators.

## CHAPTER V. On the seventy translators

(The same author, chapter 8 of the same book.) “Ptolemy,” he says, “the son of Lagos, wishing to obtain greater glory for his library, which he was constructing at Alexandria from the volumes of all the Greeks, also requested from Jerusalem that he be given their Hebrew Scriptures translated into the Greek language.

“But since they were subject to the Macedonians, they sent to Ptolemy seventy elders, chosen men highly skilled in the sacred Scriptures in both languages. Yet in this the will and plan of God were at work.

“Ptolemy wished to receive the testimony of each one individually, and feared that they might conceal the truth inserted in the divine books through their translation. Therefore he separated them from one another and ordered each of them, placed apart, to translate independently, requiring them to observe the same order of translation in each book.

“Then he ordered them to be brought together before him in a single group and to compare with one another what each had translated. And now God was truly glorified, and the sacred Scripture was recognized as truly divine. For all of them translated the same things in the same words and with the same names, from beginning to end, so that even the Gentiles who were present recognized that the Scriptures had then been translated by God’s command.

“Nor is this surprising, since God inspired the priest Ezra to restore the Hebrew books that had been corrupted during the captivity under King Nebuchadnezzar.”

## CHAPTER VI

[Note: This is Irenaeus’s testimony. There are many histories and testimonies concerning the seventy translators, some of which agree with Irenaeus and some of which do not entirely agree. Justin plainly agrees with him and relates that their chambers were separated, claiming that he himself saw them with his own eyes. But Aristaeus, who was sent by Ptolemy to Eleazar, the Hebrew high priest, under that name and who embraced the whole history, mentions nothing of the kind; nor do Josephus or Philo, whose authority Justin uses. The matter of their chambers is therefore disputed, including among the Latins, by Jerome and Augustine. Epiphanius, however, correctly explains the whole of this account in the little book that he wrote on measures.]

(HAYMO.) We have included this testimony of Irenaeus out of reverence for the divine Scriptures, although certain ecclesiastical writers consider it apocryphal, chiefly because Josephus, the Hebrew historian, affirms nothing of the kind but writes that they compared their work together in one and the same basilica. Blessed Jerome also testifies to this in the preface to the Pentateuch. But let us now return to the order of the narrative.

## CHAPTER VII. On the miracle performed by Christians in the army of Christians

(Nicephorus, Book IV, chapter 12; Eutropius; Orosius, Book VII, chapter 15; Julius Capitolinus, in *Macrophil*.) Accordingly, during the times of Antoninus, when so many evils are reported to have been inflicted, Marcus Aurelius, his brother, waged war against the Sarmatians and Germans. When his army was endangered by thirst, certain Christian soldiers who were present prayed. In answer to their prayers, abundant rain poured down from heaven and refreshed the army, while frequent flashes of lightning drove the enemies away into the distance.

Pagan histories also relate this event, but they conceal and disguise the fact that it was obtained through our people.

## CHAPTER VIII. Antoninus reigned nineteen years

(Eusebius, Book V, chapter 10.) Meanwhile Antoninus died, and Commodus succeeded to the empire. At that time Julian assumed the priesthood at Alexandria.

At that time Pantaenus the Stoic, head of the ecclesiastical school there, was held in the highest esteem for his eloquence in disputing our doctrine. Inflamed by the heat of faith, he preached the word of God as far as Nearer India. In the school of his divine learning Clement of Alexandria especially blossomed.

At that time Narcissus, presiding over the Church of Jerusalem, was celebrated for his outstanding faith and his works of signs. Among all his miracles, it is related that by a wondrous and unheard-of exercise of power he changed water into oil when, on a solemn day of the Paschal vigils, oil had happened to run out for the lamps.

(The same author, chapter 16 of the same book.) At that time the enemy of the human race, never having any rest, raised up various and diverse heresies in every place. Among them he produced in Asia and Phrygia a great serpent of his own kind, Montanus, who called himself the Paraclete. He also falsely presented certain women, namely Maximilla and Priscilla, as prophetesses inspired by him.

He impiously taught that marriages should be dissolved, and he was the first to impose laws of fasting. He called Pepuza and Tymion, towns of Phrygia, “Jerusalem,” and decreed that everyone should assemble in them. He appointed collectors of money and, under the name of offerings, skillfully received gifts. He provided salaries for those preaching his word, so that, bound by this arrangement, they might devote themselves more zealously to his doctrine.

It is reported, however, that in the end he and his women ended their lives by hanging at different times, the demon by whom they had been inspired having brought this about, after the example of Judas the traitor.

At this time also, in the city of Rome, the rule of ecclesiastical tradition was disturbed by the schismatics Blastus and Florinus. But by the grace of God there were then men of faith and virtue who destroyed both the aforementioned heresies and the schismatics, writing books or letters against them, such as Irenaeus, Melitides, Serapion, Apollonius, Apollinaris, and many others.

## CHAPTER IX

[Note: A question arose concerning the time of Easter. It was later explained and defined by a synod of the Roman Church, namely the synod held at Rome by Pope Victor, whose judgment the remnants of the synod followed. For, while Commodus was emperor, a synod was held at Jerusalem by Narcissus, at Caesarea in Palestine by Theophilus, in Gaul at Lyons by Irenaeus, at Corinth by Bacchylides, in Asia by Palmas, and likewise at Edessa by eighteen bishops; in Mesopotamia it was held by others. This was held against the synod of Polycrates, which he convened at Ephesus. Finally, at Nicaea, with the frequent agreement of the Fathers, a canon was issued. Epiphanius nevertheless mentions Theodoret, although Socrates denies this, while Ambrose and Gregory of Cappadocia remember him.]

A question arose concerning the time of Easter.

Meanwhile, under the emperor Commodus, while distinguished priests presided over the Churches—Victor at Rome, Demetrius at Alexandria, Serapion at Antioch, Theophilus at Caesarea in Palestine, Narcissus at Jerusalem, and Polycrates at Ephesus—a considerable dispute arose in the provinces of Asia. It arose from their ancient observance: they thought that Easter ought always to be observed on the fourteenth day of the moon, namely when the Jews are commanded to sacrifice the lamb. They affirmed as necessary that the fast should be ended on whatever day of the week the fourteenth day of the moon occurred.

Such a custom had never been observed in the other provinces or Churches. For this reason assemblies of bishops and councils were convened both at Caesarea in Palestine and at Rome. Victor, the Roman pontiff, and the other western bishops disputed against the Asians, saying that it was not permissible to celebrate the mystery of the Lord’s Pasch except on Sunday, the day on which the Lord rose, and that the fast ought to be ended only on that day.

## CHAPTER X. Polycrates’ argument for observing Easter on the fourteenth day of the moon

The Asians, and especially Polycrates, bishop of Ephesus, who seemed to hold primacy among them, argued in opposition that nothing could be added to or subtracted from that undefiled day of Easter on which, according to the Gospel, the Lord himself celebrated his Pasch, so that it might be celebrated after or before the fourteenth day.

They also appealed to ancient custom and the tradition of their ancestors. They said that Philip the evangelist, who sleeps in Asia with his daughters; John the Apostle, who reclined upon the Lord’s breast at the supper; and Polycarp, his disciple, had observed it.

At length, when very many bishops of sounder faith and knowledge had been brought together in agreement through divine inspiration, Victor, the Roman pontiff, issued a solemn decree concerning agreement over Easter [Note: The word “and” appears to be subject to deletion.] With the venerable bishops Narcissus of Jerusalem, Theophilus of Caesarea, and Irenaeus of Lyons subscribing, together with the other bishops of Gaul, they confirmed that the mystery of Easter ought in every way to be celebrated on the Sunday of Christ’s resurrection.

## CHAPTER XI

(HAYMO.) It seems to me that the Roman Church chose this course rather through prudent counsel and a sounder judgment, so that we might not appear to Judaize or still observe the Mosaic and figurative Pasch if we celebrated the solemnity of Easter on the fourteenth day of the moon.

Since Christ, therefore, after the old and typological observance had ended, instituted the new Pasch and, in place of the eating of the typological lamb, handed over the mystery of his immaculate body and blood, it is right that, just as we do not take the typological lamb, so we should now disregard the figure, since we possess the reality.

Accordingly, we do not observe that observance of the fourteenth day with the Jews; instead, on the day of the Lord’s resurrection, we celebrate our new Pasch. Since “Pasch” is interpreted as “passage,” and signifies our passage either from vices to virtue or from death to life, rightly and truly our passage—which begins with the Lord’s passion—is completed when the Lord rises. Therefore we celebrate Easter at that time.

For Christ’s death would have profited us nothing if his resurrection had not also profited us. There are perhaps other explanations of the Fathers, which a diligent and studious reader may find elsewhere. But now, returning to the order of the narrative, let us pause here briefly, so that afterward, refreshed, we may complete the sixth book.

# BOOK SIX

[Col. 0847]

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 0847C]

(Eusebius, Book V, chapters 27 and 28, of the Ecclesiastical History.) Accordingly, after Commodus had ruled for thirteen years, and Aelius Pertinax had ruled after him for only six months, Severus assumed the principate. Likewise, after Pope Victor had completed ten years in the episcopate, Zephyrinus assumed the priesthood.

Many ecclesiastical men flourished at that time, distinguished in style [Note: The conjunction “and” appears to be subject to deletion]: Heraclitus, who wrote a commentary on the Apostle; Maximus, who discussed the most famous of all questions concerning heretics; Candidus, who wrote on the Hexaemeron; the same man also wrote on the beginning of Genesis; and Appius as well.

Together with certain others, these men refuted the heresies that arose in their time, especially the heresy of Paul of Samosata, which derived authority from a certain Artemon, who said that the Savior was a mere man and without God, and falsely claimed that this had been handed down from ancient times by the apostles.

Meanwhile, while Severus also raged against the Church, many became martyrs, especially at Alexandria, where athletes were brought from all Egypt and the Thebaid as though into a kind of arena of piety. Among them Leonides, the father of Origen, was beheaded for the faith of Christ, leaving behind the aforementioned boy, who was still of tender age.

## CHAPTER II

(HAYMO.) If anyone wishes to know more fully the life, deeds, and doctrines of this Origen, let him read Eusebius (Book VI, chapter 13). From him we have transferred these matters; he writes so much and so extensively about Origen that it is not fitting to insert all of it into this brief work, especially since we know that the aforementioned Eusebius was somewhat censured by certain ecclesiastical men for having been excessive in praising Origen.

We shall briefly relate about him, however, what even orthodox and religious men cannot deny.

## CHAPTER III. On Origen

(Eusebius, Book VI, chapters 23, 4, 5, and 6, of the Ecclesiastical History; Nicephorus, Book V, chapters 2–8, 11–19, 29, 32, and 33, of the Ecclesiastical History.) Origen, son of the martyr Leonides, was himself, almost from childhood, a martyr by intention and perhaps in deed, had not his mother, secretly taking away his clothing at night, prevented him by a pious deception. He received from God a great and manifest grace of knowledge. He was powerful in *grammateia* and in the other ordinary literary studies, thoroughly trained in every philosophical discipline, and especially powerful and famous among the investigators of that age in the reading and teaching of the divine books.

Because of his great and extraordinary excellence in knowledge, Demetrius, bishop of that place, appointed him a teacher of the Church at Alexandria. He occupied the teacher’s chair as the third after Pantaenus and Clement; he himself had been a hearer of Clement.

There, while openly teaching the word of God to both men and women, and wishing to remove from unbelievers every opportunity for shameful slander, he undertook an act in his own body that reflected an imperfect understanding but proceeded from fervent faith and extraordinary chastity.

For, although previously he observed and commanded the observance of all the evangelical precepts and sayings of the Savior, he paid attention to the Gospel saying, “These are eunuchs who have made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of God,” and immediately undertook to fulfill the Lord’s word in himself, both in reality and in deed.

From that time, therefore, he devoted himself most intensely to teaching and preaching, when no suspicion of slander remained for his adversaries. Then, as the Apostle says, he preached the word of God “in season and out of season” (2 Timothy 4), by day and by night, publicly and privately, with very great abstinence, unceasing fasts, and almost continual vigils. If natural necessity ever demanded a little sleep, he was found sleeping not on a bed—for he used none at all—but on the bare ground.

It is reported that many from his school, both men and women, became martyrs. Many books of his learning survive, among them extremely learned commentaries on the sacred Scriptures. He also wrote thirty books commenting on a certain portion of the prophet Isaiah, twenty-five books on Ezekiel, and the same number on the Song of Songs.

He also wrote a book on martyrs to Ambrose, with such great and disciplined spiritual power that by his arguments, like very strong walls, he strengthened many for martyrdom. There are also almost innumerable other works, which there is no need to enumerate in this brief account.

The following remarkable fact is reported about him: he never permitted what he discussed in the Churches to be taken down by notaries, except when, having reached the age of sixty, he had acquired through long practice and labor great confidence in the word of God—when, that is, gravity of life, maturity of age, and the authority of extensive experience had come to him.

Among his studies of learning, Origen also did not neglect to investigate and learn the force of the Hebrew language, so that he might know what the readings used by the Jews were like and how great was the diversity of learning among the other translators who had translated apart from the Seventy.

In addition to the versions that are in use—those of Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion—he even discovered other translations hidden away in secret places, in which he found that the names of certain translators were not written. He says that he found one on the Actian coast near Nicopolis, another at Jericho, and still others in other places.

He also labored to refute heretics through eloquent disputations, both orally and in books. By debate he refuted Beryllus, bishop of Bostra, a city of Arabia, who said that our Savior had neither existed before his birth in the flesh nor possessed a distinct existence of divinity, but only that the inner deity dwelt in him. He also refuted a certain Epicurean philosopher named Celsus, who had written books opposing the faith.

(HAYMO.) I cannot sufficiently express my amazement that a man so illustrious, who so openly rebelled against and opposed heretics, should have fallen into a very notorious heresy and error: namely, that in Isaiah he interpreted the Seraphim as the Holy Spirit; that elsewhere he wrote about the repentance of the devil and the release of the reprobate after a thousand years; and that he advanced many other things opposed to orthodox faith.

This is especially astonishing since he is reported to have lived a most abstinent and chaste life and to have possessed such distinguished learning and such pure and lucid speech.

(HAYMO.) In good faith and without violating the judgment of the Fathers, I would say of him either that he did not write these things at all, but that heretics maliciously invented and composed them in order to obscure his illustrious name and placed them under his name; or, if he did write them, that he did not establish them as his settled opinion but discussed them as a matter of inquiry.

For, as he himself says, he had learned the doctrines of philosophers and heretics so that he would not be less prepared to refute them if he were ignorant of what they held. Perhaps, when he touched upon their errors in writing in certain places, he was falsely accused of having said these things on his own authority.

But even if, as some think, he wrote the aforementioned heresies as his settled opinion, great compassion is due to so learned a man, who supplied us with such an abundance of learning. If there are faults in his writings, the luminous and heavenly splendor of what he wrote faithfully may surpass them.

The Fathers also said of him: “Where he wrote well, no one wrote better.”

As for what Origen got wrong and what he wrote against orthodox faith, I think this happened because he embraced philosophers with excessive devotion to reading. For he had touched and entirely mastered the secrets of Plato, Pythagoras, Zeno the Stoic, Cerinthus, and the books of the other philosophers.

Perhaps because he lingered too long among them and drank too deeply from the gilded cup of Babylon, he was somehow compelled to pour some of its dregs into sacred Scripture.

From this ecclesiastical men must take great and vigilant care not to devote themselves excessively to philosophical teachings. Otherwise, when they have been intoxicated by empty cups and puffed up by inflated assertions, they may be recalled to the humility of Christ with greater difficulty and submit more slowly to our faith, since they have been instructed in contrary doctrines.

In saying this we do not condemn either the readers of the liberal arts or the arts themselves. They are not read without usefulness for untying difficult questions and working through arguments; indeed, sacred Scripture itself is mistress of the arts, while the others serve her as attendants.

We severely criticize certain scholars, however, who cling so familiarly to the books of the pagans and immerse themselves wholly in them that they spend almost the entire course of their lives and learning in them. How much more honorable and how much more correct and easier it would have been to devote themselves to ecclesiastical discipline!

If they applied themselves to learning the books of sacred Scripture, they would certainly transfer the whole library into themselves in fewer spans of time than they spend on all those frivolous and almost useless little branches of knowledge with which they occupy themselves.

But behold: while we are devoting too much attention to Origen and using him as an occasion for this digression, contrary to the law of a brief work, we have almost forgotten the others who lived at the same time and helped the Church by word and example. Let us now return to the order of the narrative.

## CHAPTER IV. Severus reigned eighteen years

(Eusebius, Book VI, chapter 7, of the Ecclesiastical History.) Accordingly, after the emperor Severus had ruled for eighteen years, and his son had then been handed over to him, Alexander—the man mentioned earlier, sufficiently distinguished by the title of confessor—was appointed bishop of the Church of Jerusalem.

He had happened to come to Jerusalem from Cappadocia, where he was bishop of a distinguished city, in order to pray. By a divine oracle this was made known to everyone through a heavenly voice: “Receive the bishop who has been appointed for you by God.”

After he had been taken, he was not permitted to return to his own bishopric but was compelled to remain there, although Narcissus, the aforementioned bishop of that place, was still alive; he was worn out by old age and unable to fulfill the episcopal ministry.

Meanwhile Serapion, bishop of Antioch, a man of great learning, whose many works are known, also died. Asclepiades succeeded him, himself one of the distinguished number of confessors.

## CHAPTER V. Antoninus reigned seven years and six months

The emperor Antoninus also died, and Macrinus succeeded him. After Macrinus had been brought to an end after a short time—that is, after one year—the emperor Antoninus succeeded him.

In the first year of his reign Zephyrinus, the Roman pontiff, died, and Callistus succeeded him. Pope Zephyrinus had held office for eight years. When he too had reached the end of his term, Urban presided; he also left the see after eight years to Pontianus (Eusebius, Book VI, chapter 16, of the Ecclesiastical History).

After Antoninus had ruled for four years, Alexander succeeded him.

## CHAPTER VI

(HAYMO.) At that time very eloquent men flourished in the Church. Alexander, the venerable bishop of Jerusalem, carefully caused the letters that they sent to one another—both eloquent and fruitful—to be placed in the library of Jerusalem, which he himself had built with much labor and expense for the benefit of those who would come after.

We give thanks for the great diligence of the Fathers, whose fervent devotion and unceasing care concerning the sacred Scriptures were so great that they not only wrote books or explained them, but also, through much labor and great expense, gathered into the work of their scribes the divinely inspired writings of every distinguished man, for the advancement of the universal Church.

Such, then, were precious investments; such was a living treasure: to acquire for oneself the writings of one’s predecessors, to establish a library, and to gather books in the archives of the temples, rather than coins in a money box.

Let the ecclesiastical persons of the present age hear this and blush with shame. They have so shamelessly and foolishly departed from the footsteps of the Fathers that they have become slaves of maidservants—slaves of ambition and money. Although they might perhaps have investigated the sublime Scriptures more easily than our predecessors, since through their diligence they possess a greater abundance of copies, shamefully they now turn to the lowest and most contemptible matters, to civil lawsuits and moneyboxes.

But enough of this.

In those days Hippolytus, a bishop and author of many works, among his other writings produced a treatise on Easter. In it he also beautifully set forth, by a well-ordered method, a calendar of the times and a certain description of them.

(Bede.) Having discovered the nineteen-year cycle of Easter, he was the first to provide Eusebius with the occasion to compose a treatise on that same nineteen-year cycle.

## CHAPTER VII. Alexander reigned nineteen years

Meanwhile, when the emperor Alexander had died, Maximinus Caesar succeeded him. He was the first to become emperor from the military ranks without a decree of the Senate.

(The same author, in the same place.) Because of his hatred for the household of his predecessor Alexander, for Alexander’s mother Mamaea—especially because she was a Christian—and for the presbyter Origen, whom Mamaea had summoned to Rome, treated honorably, and heard, a man then famous not only at Alexandria but throughout the whole world, Maximinus began a persecution throughout the Churches, especially against the teachers of the Churches.

## CHAPTER VIII. Maximinus reigned three years

But by God’s providence he was brought to an end shortly afterward, and thus he ended both his life and the persecution.

## CHAPTER IX

After him Gordian becomes emperor.

When Pontian, the Roman pontiff, was bringing his life to an end, Antherus succeeded him. After he had served for no more than one month, he relinquished the priesthood to Fabian.

## CHAPTER X

(Bede.) At this time he was ordained bishop, with the testimony of the Holy Spirit descending in the form of a dove upon his head; others report that this happened to him, while others say it happened to Bishop Zephyrinus (Eusebius, Book VI, chapter 21; Nicephorus, Book V, chapter 26, *Ecclesiastical History*).

At the same time Africanus was regarded as distinguished among ecclesiastical writers. He wrote many books and letters, among them a work in which he most clearly demonstrates the agreement of Matthew and Luke in their genealogies of Christ; he also composed a *Chronicle*.

## CHAPTER XI

Gordian rules for six years.

Meanwhile, when the emperor Gordian was coming to his end, Philip succeeded him together with his son Philip. He was the first of all the emperors to be a Christian (Eusebius, chapter 25 of the same book). When he wished to take part in the vigils of Easter and to share in the mysteries, Pope Fabian resisted him and did not permit it until he had confessed his sins and stood among the penitents.

After the third year of his reign, when the thousandth year from the founding of Rome had been completed, he celebrated the birthday of the City with magnificent games.

## CHAPTER XII

Philip rules for seven years.

(The same author, chapter 29.) After him Decius succeeded. After he had killed Philip, the father, and his son, and was hostile to Christians because of his hatred for them, he launched a persecution against the churches. In it Fabian was crowned with martyrdom in the city of Rome; Cornelius succeeded him and was himself also released through martyrdom.

At Jerusalem as well, Alexander, a most learned man and illustrious bishop, one of the confessors, after the venerable grayness of a long life, after many tortures and imprisonments, collapsed amid tortures that followed one another in turn.

(Bede.) At that time the holy monk Antony is said to have arisen in Egypt. Meanwhile, under Decius, the persecution inflicted upon Christians blazed up with great force, and innumerable holy men and women endured their contests, especially at Alexandria, so that one might have thought that the early periods of the persecutions had been renewed. Dionysius, bishop of Alexandria, reports these events most fully in his letters to Bishop Fabian; Dionysius himself was later condemned to death by beheading.

But because there was also chaff with the wheat on the Lord’s threshing floor, some at that time denied Christ at the first appearance of the judge and rushed to the altars, fearing the loss of temporal goods more than they loved the highest good. The Lord had foretold concerning them: “Those who love money do not fall with difficulty.”

At this time Novatus, a presbyter of Bishop Cyprian, arose.

(Cornelius, in his letter to Fabian, bishop of Antioch.) From his youth he had been afflicted by an unclean spirit. After spending time among exorcists, he contracted a serious illness and despaired of recovery. Consequently, while lying in bed, he was poured over with water out of necessity; the other rites that those who are baptized ordinarily receive were not solemnly completed in him. For this reason he was never able to obtain the Holy Spirit.

When he came to Rome, swollen with arrogance, he attempted by a new doctrine to deprive the lapsed entirely of the hope of salvation, even if they had repented worthily. From this he became the leader of the heretics known as the Novatians. Separated from the Church, they called themselves by a new name, *Cathari*, that is, “the pure.” For this reason a very famous council of priests was assembled in the city of Rome, whose proceedings the following little book will explain.

# BOOK SEVEN

## CHAPTER ONE

(Eusebius, Book VI, chapter 33, *Ecclesiastical History*.) While Cornelius was sitting as pontiff with sixty bishops, an equal number of presbyters, and very many deacons, a vigilant discussion was held against the heresy of the Novatians. With the testimony of both parts of Scripture supporting the decision, it was determined that those who had fallen should be treated and healed with the remedies of repentance, and that Novatus, who possessed no brotherly charity, should be separated from the Church together with his remaining followers.

There survives a letter from Cornelius to Fabian, bishop of Antioch, and also a magnificent work published by Cyprian, in which he both consoles the lapsed and anathematizes those who oppose them.

## CHAPTER II

Decius rules for two years and three months.

(The same author, Book VII, chapters 1–3.) Meanwhile Decius, after ruling for less than two complete years, was killed together with his sons. At that time Origen also is said to have died, when he was full of days and almost seventy years old.

Then Gallus obtained the empire with his son Volusianus. Although his reign flourished at the beginning and everything went according to his wishes, following the example of Decius he persecuted the holy men who, on behalf of his realm, were praying to God; together with them he drove away both his prosperity and his peace.

At the same time a question arose in the regions of Africa concerning whether heretics should be rebaptized or not. Cornelius and the other western bishops, however, maintained this position: after rejection of the heretical doctrine, such persons should be cleansed by the laying on of hands alone.

## CHAPTER III

Cornelius occupied the see for approximately three years.

Accordingly, when Cornelius had completed his course through martyrdom, Lucius succeeded him. After Lucius had held the apostolic office for only eight months, Stephen was raised to the episcopate. He maintained the same opinion as Cornelius concerning the non-rebaptism of heretics.

## CHAPTER IV

Concerning Dionysius, bishop of Alexandria.

At that time Dionysius, bishop of Alexandria, was held in renown. Writing many and varied works, he left us an abundant store of instruction and teaching.

There survives a letter of his to Pope Stephen, discussing many ecclesiastical matters. There also survive his letters directed against the Sabellian heresy, which had arisen in his time. This heresy was full of blasphemies against God the Father and denied that our Lord Jesus Christ was the true Son or the firstborn of all creation; at the same time it removed any proper understanding of the Holy Spirit.

## CHAPTER V

Emperor Gallus rules for two years, not quite complete.

(The same author, chapter 9 of the same book.) Meanwhile Emperor Gallus died, and Valerian succeeded him together with his son Gallienus. Stephen died.

## CHAPTER VI

Xystus is chosen bishop.

Valerian persecuted Christians with particular severity, although at first he had been kind and humane. Later he was led astray by a certain master of magical arts, the chief of the Egyptian magicians.

Dionysius writes about this persecution in various works of his, especially in his letter to Hermammon. In them he recounts the glorious deeds of the martyrs, mentions his own persecution, and recalls a certain Asterius, a man of great renown among the holy martyrs and a senator of the city of Rome.

It happened that Asterius was once present at Caesarea Philippi at a spectacle famous in that place. On a fixed and solemn day, a victim was sacrificed there at the foot of the mountain. By a certain demonic art, although the demon appeared nowhere, the gentiles believed that the victim was being lifted into heaven.

Then Asterius, pitying human error and earnestly praying to God on their account, the victim was suddenly restored to the sight of everyone. After that, this error no longer existed in those places.

(Eusebius, Book VII, chapters 13–14, *Ecclesiastical History*.) They say that the woman whom our Savior healed from an issue of blood was a citizen of this city, and her house is still shown there. In front of the house, on a raised site, a kind of base is displayed, on which a bronze image appears to have been fashioned of the woman falling, as it were, upon her knees before the Savior and extending her hands supplicatingly.

Another bronze statue stands beside it, likewise cast in metal, in the form of a man wearing a cloak wrapped around his head and extending his right hand toward the woman. At the foot of this statue and its base a plant of unusual appearance grows. Once it has emerged, it regularly grows as high as the fringe of that bronze garment. When the plant, growing upward from its very top, has touched the fringe, it acquires the power to drive away every weakness and disease, so that whatever the bodily illness may be, it is removed by drinking a small amount of liquid in which the grass has been moistened. But the plant has no power at all if it is plucked before it has touched the top of the fringe.

They reported that this statue had been fashioned in the likeness of the face of Jesus. It remained until our own times, and we saw it with our own eyes.

(Bede.) Divine vengeance immediately overtook this Valerian. For he was captured by Sapor, king of the Persians, and there, deprived of his sight, he grew old in miserable age.

His son Gallienus, after gaining sole control of the empire, was terrified by this evident judgment of God. Acting more moderately, he brought the persecution against our people to an end.

Nevertheless, on account of either his father’s guilt or his struggle against God, he suffered innumerable losses to his kingdom when the barbarians rose against it.

At that time Cyprian, bishop of Carthage, whose most learned works remain in existence, was crowned with martyrdom. Stephen and Xystus, bishops of Rome, also died as martyrs.

## CHAPTER VII

Concerning Paul of Samosata, the heretic.

(The same author, chapters 24–25 of the same book.) After Xystus, Dionysius was appointed Roman pontiff. Paul of Samosata assumed the priesthood, but fell into heresy, saying that Christ was merely a human being of common nature.

A council was then celebrated, and Dionysius was invited to attend. Because of his old age he was prevented from coming, but he was present by letter.

Paul was placed in the midst of the assembly and refuted through frequent discussion and debate, while venerable bishops sat in judgment and publicly exposed his blasphemy: Firmilian of Caesarea in Cappadocia, Helenus of Sardis, Nicoma [or Nichomachus] of Iconium, Hymenaeus, the chief priest of Jerusalem, Theotecnus of nearby Caesarea, and Athenodorus and Gregory, priests of the province of Pontus.

This Gregory was renowned in the speech of everyone and powerful in the working of signs. On one occasion, two brothers possessed a fishpond and often quarreled over the fish they caught, even to the shedding of human blood. Gregory intervened between them and, after praying, put an end to their bloody contention. He ordered the waters to depart, and they receded; the place became productive soil for crops, though previously it had borne boats.

Again, when in a certain place a rock obstructed the construction of a church, he spent the night in prayer and moved the rock.

On another occasion, as he was crossing the Alps, he was compelled by the snow to turn aside to a shrine of Apollo, where he spent the night. When he departed in the morning, the demon also departed. When the people asked it to give responses as before, it became silent. The priest consulted it, and it gave as the reason for its departure the arrival of Gregory.

The priest immediately took to the road and, reaching Gregory, explained his complaint about the deity’s expulsion and lamented the loss of his income. Gregory then wrote a letter in these words:

> Gregory to Apollo: I permit you to return to your place and perform what you were accustomed to perform.

The priest carried this letter to the shrine and placed it beside the image. The demon returned and again gave responses.

Then, turning inward upon himself, the priest said: “How much better is Gregory than this Apollo, who obeys his commands!” He went down at that very hour to Gregory, returned the letter, and explained the whole matter in order. He asked Gregory to present him to God.

Then, abandoning paganism, he became Gregory’s catechumen. After devoting himself to a most chaste and exceedingly temperate life, he also received baptism. He advanced so far in faith and virtue that he became the blessed Gregory’s successor in the episcopate.

From this Gregory also left us great monuments of his intellect in a small compass.

## CHAPTER VIII

Note on the paraphrase of Gregory, martyr and bishop of Neocaesarea.

[Note: This Gregory is the subject of a book by Gregory of Nyssa.]

Concerning Ecclesiastes he wrote a most magnificent paraphrase, containing briefly the following exposition of the catholic faith:

“One God, the Father of the living Word, of subsisting Wisdom, and of his own Power and Image; the perfect begetter of the Perfect One, Father of the only-begotten Son; one God, alone from the alone God; the figure and image of deity; the Word penetrating all things; Wisdom comprehending all things; and the Power through which the whole creation was able to come into being.

“The true Son of the true One; invisible from the Invisible; incorruptible from the Incorruptible; immortal from the Immortal; everlasting from the Everlasting.

“One Holy Spirit, possessing his substance from God, who appeared through the Son: the perfect image of the perfect Son; the cause of holiness to living beings and the giver of sanctification. Through him God, who is above all and in all, is known, and through the Son all things are.”

(Eusebius, Book VII, chapter 25.) This perfect Trinity is not divided or separated in majesty, eternity, or kingdom. Therefore there is nothing made or servile in the Trinity, nor anything introduced into it as though previously it had not subsisted and later had entered into being.

Nor was the Son ever lacking to the Father, nor the Holy Spirit to the Son. Rather, the same Trinity is always unchangeable and immutable.

Thus far concerning Gregory.

## CHAPTER IX

Emperor Gallienus rules for fifteen years.

Meanwhile Dionysius died at Alexandria in ecclesiastical peace, after serving in the priesthood for eighteen years. Maximus succeeded him.

## CHAPTER X

Claudius rules for two years.

(Nicephorus, Book VI, chapters 28–29.) When Gallienus died, Claudius succeeded him. He soon died, and Aurelian succeeded him.

During Aurelian’s reign, a council was assembled at Antioch, and Paul of Samosata was condemned to the ultimate penalty. He was debated by a certain Malchion, a man of perfect learning, while notaries recorded the proceedings.

Malchion conducted the debate so magnificently and precisely that it remains a source of wonder even now to those who read it. Thus Paul, already for the second time, was openly refuted as a heretic. Letters were sent to Dionysius, the Roman pontiff, and Maximus of Alexandria (Eusebius, Book VII, chapter 30).

His heresy and condemnation, as well as his character, became known: how he denied that the Son of God had descended from heaven, but asserted that he had begun from Mary and had his origin from the earth; how he had also caused the psalms that were sung concerning our Lord Jesus Christ to cease, as though they were recent and newly invented; and how he had women whom he himself—horrible to hear—had trained sing compositions made by him personally in the midst of the Church on the days of Easter.

It also became known how, when walking through the street, he indulged in such ambition that he publicly reread letters and dictated them in the hearing and sight of everyone, while notaries stood beside him in the street. He had even arrogantly placed a tribunal for himself in the church much higher than it had previously been. When speaking, he would throw back his right hand excessively and strike his thigh with his palm; he would also leap with his foot and beat the footstool, and, in theatrical fashion, demand loud acclamations and applause from his listeners.

He had also, with the utmost shamelessness, permitted women to live with him and had granted similar license to the presbyters and deacons who imitated his conduct.

## CHAPTER XI

(Eusebius, Book VII, chapter 26, *Ecclesiastical History*; Nicephorus, Book VI, chapter 19.) After Paul had been condemned and expelled from the Church, but refused to leave, Domnus by name succeeded him as bishop of the Church of Antioch by public authority, at the command of the emperor Aurelian.

Meanwhile Aurelian was corrupted by evil counsels and began to devise a persecution against our people. He went so far that, when he was about to sign written orders, the hand of God intervened and prevented his signature. Lightning also fell before him, to the great terror of those standing around.

Not long afterward he was condemned by a sudden death.

## CHAPTER XII

Aurelian rules for six years.

Probus succeeded him. After Probus had likewise completed six years, Carus succeeded him with his sons Numerian and Carinus. When they had soon completed their lives, Diocletian became emperor. Shortly before his reign, however, Dionysius, the Roman pontiff, died.

## CHAPTER XIII

Pope Dionysius occupied the see for nine years. Carus rules with his sons for two years, not quite complete.

Blessed also is he who at that time deserved to be snatched from the world, so that he would not see the evils that this Diocletian soon inflicted upon the churches beyond anything that can be believed.

Felix then succeeded to the apostolic office. At that time a certain magician named Manes, acting madly in accordance with his name, a Persian by birth, from whom the heresy of the Manichaeans derives its name, formed a new sect. He put forward doctrines borrowed from various heretics; now he pretended to be Christ, now he called himself the Paraclete, and he chose twelve disciples in imitation of Christ.

## CHAPTER XIV

Pope Felix occupied the see for six years.

Accordingly, when Pope Felix had completed his course, Eutychianus succeeded him. After Eutychianus soon completed his life, Gaius was chosen bishop.

By the time of Eusebius, Gaius had already served fifteen years in the priesthood. He left Marcellus as his successor, and Marcellus was soon overtaken by the time of persecution.

# BOOK EIGHT

## CHAPTER ONE

Eutychianus occupied the see for five years.

Meanwhile it was the nineteenth year of Diocletian’s reign, and an exceedingly great persecution of Christians began under him. It was justly imposed by the judgment of God and necessary for correction, since the conduct of our people had already been corrupted by excessive freedom and indulgence, and the discipline of the churches had been ruined (Eusebius, Book VIII, chapters 1–4 and following).

Our faith was being divided by various doctrines and was for that reason becoming despised. The prelates, rulers, and leaders of the people, having forgotten Christian humility and sincerity, were inflamed against one another by hatred and disputes.

Then the emperor’s impious edicts were published: all the churches were to be destroyed to their foundations, and the sacred Scriptures burned in fire. If any of our people held an office of honor, he was to be stripped of it and left disgraced.

Finally, those in authority were ordered to sacrifice to idols; otherwise they were to be thrown into prison and tortured.

At Nicomedia, in the Thebaid, Phoenicia, Alexandria, throughout Egypt, Phrygia, Syria, Cappadocia, and all the other regions everywhere, the storm of persecution was so immense and intolerable that its very excess and brutality makes the accounts of the martyrs seem almost unbelievable.

(Nicephorus, Book VII, chapter 17, *Ecclesiastical History*.) Some were torn apart by whips; others were gouged with claws; others were burned with blazing flames; others were beheaded with the sword; others were fastened to crosses; others were hurled into the sea; others were hung with their hands bound behind their backs and stretched on pulleys until their limbs were torn apart.

Some were lacerated with fragments of earthen vessels until all their skin had been scraped away. Others were given to wild beasts—lions, bears, leopards, bulls, boars, and every kind of animal.

The priests of the churches were stripped shamelessly and dragged here and there by the impious. What a crime! The instruments that had been made for murderers, adulterers, poisoners, and violators of graves now bound the necks of bishops, presbyters, deacons, and other religious persons, so that criminals had neither chains left for them nor room in the prisons.

The satellites of the wicked ruler were so eager to torture that they had leisure to devise new torments. They drove sharp reeds under the fingernails of some. For others they poured molten lead down the back, as far as the private parts where natural bodily excretion is produced. In the case of women, masses of glowing iron and burning lead were thrust through their private parts into their entrails, without any regard for human decency.

If the torturers found two neighboring trees in some place, they bent the branches toward one another and tied one foot of a martyr to each branch. When the branches returned to their natural position with their force, they tore apart the entrails and dragged away the limbs attached to them.

At Antioch, among the other contests, a remarkable deed occurred that I must not leave unmentioned. Two young men were arrested and forced to sacrifice. They said: “Lead us to the altars.”

When they had been taken there, they placed their hands beneath the fire and said: “If we withdraw them, consider that we have sacrificed.” They remained motionless until all their flesh had fallen away into the fire.

When the emperor had been somewhat sated with cruelty and began to recover his senses, he issued an edict that Christians were no longer to be put to death, but were to remain alive after having the right eyes dug out with iron and the thumb of the left hand wounded.

But the eternal and ever-watchful Eye did not fail to see the state of the Church being devastated by cruel punishment. After chastising his own household in a few matters, the avenging right hand of God immediately came upon the emperors Diocletian and Maximinus, one of whom had devastated the Church in the West and the other in the East.

By divine command they were suddenly transformed: having laid aside the purple and the other imperial ornaments, they became commoners and private citizens after their reign.

Then, after the Roman Empire had been divided by force and contention into two administrations, Maximinus ruled in the regions of the East, forcibly seizing the title of Augustus, while Constantius ruled in the West. Constantius acted mercifully toward our people.

Maxentius, son of Maximian Herculius, Diocletian’s colleague, seized power in the city of Rome and exercised tyranny. Following magical practices, he filled the whole of Rome with criminal outrages and the filth of impurity; he obscured the glory of the noble, proscribed senators, and abused noble matrons.

## CHAPTER III

The reign of Constantius and Maximinus.

In the regions of the East and Egypt, Maximinus was like him in every respect. Stripped of the character of a ruler, he put on that of a raging tyrant. He worshiped idols, pursued auguries, was an impure banqueter and drunkard, and fluctuated in every kind of debauchery. He was especially hostile to Christians and their persecutor, inflicting upon them fire, metal plates, crosses, and particular tortures upon each limb.

When ten years of this persecution had passed, divine providence again came to the aid of our people and led those whom it had tested by fire into refreshment.

For the same Maximinus, struck by divine vengeance, suddenly became swollen and was distended in his innards. Later, when his wounds had putrefied, he vomited forth worms and breathed out an intolerable stench.

## CHAPTER II

(Haymo.) We now have, in a certain sense, a resurrected Herod, suffering from a similar disease. Because he persecuted Christ, that Herod became swollen as far as his private parts and swarmed with worms. This man likewise suffered the same shameful end because he persecuted Christians.

It was accomplished through the beautiful design of divine providence so that the connection between the head and the members might be understood, as well as how great and indivisible Christ’s love is, and how great his zeal for the Church is, since he inflicts upon the persecutors of his people the same vengeance that he inflicted upon the persecutor of himself.

(Eusebius, Book IX, chapter 9, *Ecclesiastical History*.) When all hope of recovery had been abandoned, Maximian, led by belated repentance, wrote a law ordering that the persecution of Christians should cease and that the churches should be rebuilt.

Then, as though the sun had been restored to the earth, all the imprisoned were released. Those condemned to the mines were brought back; the churches were restored and the priesthoods renewed. The pagan crowds were astonished at so great and so sudden a change of affairs.

But after six months Severus Maximinus, the colleague of the aforementioned Maximinus, exercising tyranny in the regions of the East and Egypt, immediately disturbed the peace that had been restored to our people.

Persecution against our people was renewed, and the priests of the idols were stirred up to hatred and slaughter against Christians. To make the persecution appear to be carried out with some justification, certain documents were fabricated as though they had been composed before Pilate concerning our Savior. In them every blasphemy against Christ was written down.

(The same author, chapters 6–8 of the same book.) Then many martyrs endured their contests again at Tyre and in Phoenicia, as well as in many other places.

The aforementioned Severus Maximinus added this to his impiety: he had our laws written on bronze tablets, as though they were to last forever. In them he impiously and arrogantly declared that, as a result of the persecution of Christians, the climate had become milder and the fertility of the earth more abundant.

(Nicephorus, Book VII, chapters 21–23 and following.) God immediately contradicted these proud laws, and events turned in the opposite direction. On account of the persecution of our people, the sky soon withheld its rains and an intolerable drought arose; a dreadful famine raged there.

The climate also changed into such corruption that human bodies became swollen with the worst ulcers, which are called “sacred fire.” Thus two powerful plagues and pestilences devastated the people. Yet, wonderfully, neither famine nor pestilence held sway over our people.

Consequently, the Christian religion was later proclaimed by everyone to be true and perfect, and our people were asked to provide assistance with food and prayer.

God also added this just retribution to Maximinus’s disgrace: the Armenians, previously friends of the Romans, rebelled because of his impious edicts. In the war, Maximinus himself was disgracefully put to flight, and his army perished by the sword.

(The same author, chapters 31 and 39 of the same book.) He then ordered the priests of his gods, and the diviners whose responses had led him to wage war, to be killed as deceivers.

Finally, after being seized by a severe illness and pains in his internal organs, and after losing his sight to the disease—so that he could then see more clearly what he had committed against Christ—he brought his life to an end, having first issued a law for the liberation of Christians.

## CHAPTER IV

Concerning the emperor Constantine.

At that time Constantine, a most religious emperor, arose. He was the son and heir of Constantius, that most moderate ruler whom we mentioned shortly before, and he obtained the Roman Empire.

In the observance of religion he surpassed all the emperors who had preceded him.

Near the end of the persecutions, when God wished to be reconciled to his saints and to establish his Church in the stable tranquility of peace, Constantine became a Christian.
