He granted Christians permission to assemble councils freely and to build churches. He himself founded very many churches and bestowed very many gifts, having been prompted by the divine Spirit and by the following heavenly miracle.

When he was about to fight against Maxentius, the tyrant of the city of Rome, and was praying for divine assistance, he saw during sleep, at night, a fiery sign in the sky and an angel standing beside it, saying:

> Constantine, by this sign you will conquer.

Accordingly, he proceeded to war after transforming this sign into military standards. He himself carried in his right hand the same sign, fashioned from gold, and prayed to God that, if possible, he would not allow that right hand to be stained with Roman blood.

God granted him this: he drowned the tyrant Maxentius, who was preparing for battle, together with all the ships with which he had covered the river, plunging them into the depths.

Then the Roman Senate and people, freed from the tyrannical plague, welcomed Constantine as the restorer of their liberty and had an image of him made in honor of his triumph.

Constantine ordered the sign of the cross to be painted on the right hand of this image, with the words written beneath it that the City had been restored to liberty by its power.

He then issued a law, with Licinius—his sister Constantia’s husband and his colleague in the empire—also agreeing with him, that the God of the Christians, who had given him victory and liberty to the City, should be worshiped by everyone. He sent this law as far as the eastern regions, where the persecution was still raging.

Then, through the more open indulgence of the legitimate ruler, the condition of the churches plainly began to be restored. The word and teaching of Christ spread freely; festivals were celebrated; bishops assembled; churches were dedicated.

The persecutors through whom Maximian had kindled the fires of impiety were tortured by the ruler’s command. The sculpted or painted images of the tyrant himself were ordered to be thrown down, blackened with dark pigment, or obliterated with colors.

While the Church was thus advancing before God and humanity, and was regarded on earth as a kind of image of heavenly things, the aforementioned Licinius, jealous of Constantine because his great devotion caused him to be honored by everyone, especially by Christians, devised secret plots against him.

When these proved ineffective, he soon declared open war. He in turn persecuted Christians and, with a new and unheard-of cruelty, sent them to prison and denied them food and drink.

Those who refused to sacrifice he tortured with new and monstrous punishments and handed over to butchers, so that they might be hung up like pigs, laid across blocks, chopped to pieces, and thrown into the sea as food for fish.

Those whom he sent into exile he deprived of their lawful wives and joined the women to his own attendants.

[Note: Understand “them,” that is, the wives.]

He also overturned the churches of the faithful that he had previously ordered to be built.

Finally, moved by such tyranny, Constantine prepared to go out against him. Victory was not difficult where the cause was more just and the valor more eminent.

After the tyrant Licinius had been overthrown, Constantine alone held the stability of the Roman Empire together with his sons, restoring the condition of the churches with incredible diligence. Thereafter they undertook to enlarge and exalt them through expenditures, privileges, and honors.

Thus far Eusebius of Caesarea. Rufinus continues the remainder.

# BOOK NINE

## CHAPTER ONE

At these times, when a convenient peace and tranquility had been restored to the churches, another storm of persecution arose.

For a certain Arius, a presbyter of Alexandria, taught wicked doctrines and attempted to sever the Son from the eternal and ineffable substance or nature of God the Father, saying:

> God the Father did not always exist; the Word of God did not always exist. There was a time when God the Father did not exist, and the Word of God was made from things that did not exist.

(Socrates, Book I, chapter 14, *Tripartite History*.) For the Existing One made the Existing One from what did not exist; therefore there was a time when he did not exist.

The Son is merely a creature and something made. He is not like the Father according to substance. He is not true, nor is he the Father’s true Wisdom, nor is he naturally his true Word. Rather, he is one among creatures and things made. He is called “Word” and “Wisdom” improperly, himself also having been made in the Word of God and in the Wisdom of God, in which God made all things, including him.

Therefore he is changeable and mutable by nature, just as all rational beings are. The Word is foreign, alien, and removed from the Father’s substance, and the Father is invisible to the Son.

For the Son does not know the Father perfectly and completely; indeed, he cannot see him perfectly. For the Son does not even know his own substance as it is.

He was made for our sake, so that God might create us through him as through a mystery. He would never have existed had God not wished to make us.

Therefore he is not naturally the Son of God, nor does he possess any special relationship with God. When he exists as a mutable nature, God loves him on account of his moderation and chooses in him a virtue that has not changed for the worse. Even if Paul and Peter had reached this same state, they could differ in nothing from the Son’s filial status.

This blasphemous error of Arius therefore disturbed the Church, and the question became widely known. Alexander, bishop of Alexandria, opposed him and brought Arius to prominence through his zeal for the faith.

The matter reached the emperor Constantine. He then, following the decision of the priests, summoned an episcopal council at the city of Nicaea. There, with 318 bishops in session, together with other honorable persons, philosophers, dialecticians, and every kind of highly reputed scholar, he ordered Arius to be present and commanded that judgment be rendered concerning his propositions and questions.

## CHAPTER II

The account has been rearranged from both histories.

A subtle discussion of the faith was then held there, and Arius’s error was condemned by the clear words of Scripture: the Son is naturally the only-begotten Son of God, the Word, Power, and Wisdom of the Father alone, and the true God, as John says; he is the radiance of glory and the image of the Father’s substance.

After a long and extensive discussion, everyone approved the writing of the term ὁμοούσιον (*homoousion*), that is, the confession that the Son is of the same substance as the Father.

The decision of the priestly council was presented to Constantine. He revered it as having been pronounced by God and threatened exile to those who contradicted it.

The text of the decision, or of the Nicene faith, is as follows:

## CHAPTER III
(Rufinus, Book X, chapter 6, *Ecclesiastical History*; Socrates, Book II, chapter 9, *Tripartite History*.) We believe in one God, the Father [Col. 0864B] almighty, of all things visible and invisible; and in one Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, born from the Father, only-begotten—that is, from the substance of the Father—God from God, light from light, true God from true God, begotten, not made, *ὁμοούσιον* (*homoousion*), that is, of the same substance as the Father; through whom all things were made, both those in heaven and those on earth; who for us human beings and for our salvation came down from heaven and was incarnate—that is, was made human. He suffered, rose again on the third day, and ascended into heaven; from there he will come to judge the living and the dead.

But those who say, “There was a time when he was not,” “He did not exist before he was born,” or “He did not exist before he was made,” or, “Because he was made from things that did not exist,” or “from another substance” [Col. 0864C] or subsistence; and those who say that the Son of God is changeable or mutable—the catholic and apostolic Church anathematizes them. (Theodoret, Book II, chapter 1; Book V, chapter 45, *Tripartite History*.)

Three hundred and eighteen bishops embraced this venerable faith. Among them there was an even greater number of confessors of Christ and martyrs. For James, a certain man of Antioch in Mygdonia, who raised the dead, healed the living, and performed many other miracles, was present; as was Paul of Neocaesarea, a fortress situated beside the Euphrates, who had both hands bound and burned with red-hot iron in the fury of Licinius; and Paphnutius the Egyptian, one of those whom Maximian had condemned to the mines after gouging out their right eyes and cutting off their left thumbs.

Spiridion too, a Cypriot bishop, is said to have been among them: a man from the order of the prophets, who remained a shepherd of sheep even after becoming a bishop. The following deed of his is reported, remarkable and worthy of wonder in every age. He had a daughter who, after having administered his affairs well, died a virgin. After her death, a certain man came saying that he had entrusted a deposit to her. Her father knew nothing of the matter. The whole house was searched for what was being requested, but it was found nowhere. The man who had entrusted it persisted and pressed his claim with weeping and tears, even threatening to kill himself unless he recovered the deposit. The old man, moved by his tears, hurried to his daughter’s tomb and called to her by name. Then she answered from the tomb: “What do you want, father?” He replied: “Where did you put the deposit entrusted to you by that man?” She, indicating the place, said: “There you will find it buried.” He returned to his house, found the deposit where his daughter had answered from the tomb, and handed it over to the claimant. Many other deeds of his are also related.

These and other most reverend men sat at Nicaea. (Haymo.) Hence we believe without hesitation that the aforesaid synod was assembled there by the Holy Spirit through a certain divine providence, so that it might be understood by us who came later, and by those of subsequent and modern times, that whatever was promulgated there concerning the mystery of faith is firm and catholic.

Indeed, such divine and spiritual men spoke these things—men unlike us, unworthy and sinful, who because of our injustice can both deceive and be deceived in the Holy Scriptures. For the Holy Spirit could not have spoken falsehood through men by whom he performed such great and extraordinary miracles. Therefore, with the Lord cooperating and confirming their speech by the signs that followed, certain bishops, both at the synod itself and around the time of the synod, performed various acts of power and signs. (Rufinus, Book X, chapter 3, *Ecclesiastical History*.)

For when a certain philosopher, distinguished in the art of dialectic, opposed our faith by raising objections and could not be refuted by anyone, one of the confessors—a man of exceedingly simple nature, who knew nothing except Jesus Christ, and him crucified—confronted the philosopher who was mocking him with only a few words. Having set forth a certain simple account of the faith, he immediately transformed him through ineffable piety and made him a Christian. Then it was shown to the philosopher that the kingdom of God consists not in speech but in power.

## CHAPTER IV. From the *Tripartite History*: What occurred at Constantinople.

(Sozomen, Book I, chapter 4, *Tripartite History*.) Alexander of Constantinople too, a man of admirable conduct, performed a miracle in the name of Christ. Certain philosophers were bringing accusations against the emperor because he was introducing a new form of worship into the state, and they wished to oppose Alexander concerning doctrine. By such great power of the Spirit he commanded their chief philosopher not to speak, so that, together with his speech, his mouth was completely stopped.

But let us now return to the history. When the Nicene faith had been dictated and communicated both by the emperor himself and by the bishops, Eusebius, bishop of Nicomedia, together with four other bishops who were more favorably disposed toward Arius, refused to subscribe to the word “consubstantial.” They criticized it, saying that “consubstantial” means something that comes from another thing, whether by division, separation, or planting: by planting, as a shoot comes from a root; by separation, as a son comes from a father; and by division, as two or three golden rings come from a mass of gold. “But,” they said, “the Son of God is not consubstantial with the Father in any of these ways. Therefore one must not assent to the consubstantial faith.”

The universal synod, therefore, together with the emperor, condemned them and sent them into exile with Arius and his followers. (Rufinus, chapters 7 and 8 of the same book.)

At the same time, the cross of the Lord was discovered by Helena, the mother of Constantine, a religious woman, in the place where the ancient persecutors had once set up an image of Venus at the site of the tomb, so that if anyone wished to worship Christ there, he would instead appear to be worshiping Venus. The inscription written by Pilate was also found, together with the other two crosses.

When the three crosses had thus been found, Macarius, bishop of that place, knelt with his knees fixed to the ground and earnestly entreated God with the queen, asking that it be revealed which of the crosses was destined for the Lord’s glory. Two of them were then brought to the body of a certain half-dead matron, but nothing happened. He brought the third, and immediately the woman rose and glorified God.

Having received this evident sign, the queen built a magnificent church on the spot where she had found the cross. She also carried to her son the nails with which the Lord’s body had been fastened. From them he fashioned bridles and a helmet for use in war, fulfilling the prophecy of Zechariah: “And that which is on the bridle shall be holy to the Lord Almighty.” Of the saving wood, she conveyed one part to her son and kept another part for herself.

## CHAPTER V.

[Col. 0866C] (Sozomen, Book II, chapter 18, *Tripartite History*.) Concerning this wood, the Sibyl said among the pagans: “O thrice-blessed wood, upon which God was fastened!”

Moreover, the mother of the aforesaid emperor died in the eightieth year of her life, leaving her son many instructions concerning piety. He soon set these aside, however, having been led astray by his sister Constantia and repeatedly entreated by her. He ordered Arius to be recalled from exile and sent to the bishops who happened at that time to have gathered at Jerusalem for the dedication of the church, so that his faith might be examined.

Arius then wrote out a statement of faith which appeared to contain our understanding, our words, and our profession.

## CHAPTER VI.

(Socrates, Book III, chapter 10, *Tripartite History*.) The emperor, still wishing to test Arius, summoned him to the palace. When questioned about the Nicene faith, he subscribed deceitfully and gave an oath, in a certain way mocking the oath by trickery. It is said that he had written his own doctrine on a sheet of paper which he carried beneath his arm. Thus he believed that he had truly sworn, saying that he held the same view as he had written.

The emperor, therefore, believing him, ordered that he be received into communion by Alexander, bishop of Constantinople. Since Alexander still refused, avoiding him because of his infamy and the suspicion of heresy, the emperor ordered a synod to be convened at Constantinople.

Before the day appointed for the council, Alexander prostrated himself beneath the altar and cried out to the Lord throughout the night, saying: “Judge, Lord, between the threats of Eusebius and the oath of Arius.” While he was earnestly entreating God, divine vengeance soon pursued Arius’s presumption and lying oath.

For when Arius was hurrying to the church the following morning for the customary service, surrounded by a crowd of bishops and people, he turned aside to a private place because of a bodily necessity. As he sat there, his intestines and all his entrails poured out into the holes of the privy. Thus Eusebius of Nicomedia, together with the other Arians, was put to shame. Yet the Arian doctrine was not thereby put to shame permanently; it was only concealed for a time.

## CHAPTER VII.

[Note: [Col. 0867D] In the meantime, the emperor Constantine. Eusebius, Socrates, and Sozomen, who are suspected of heresy, recalled certain matters concerning Constantine’s baptism in order to undermine the authority of the most holy Nicene council—matters that certainly expose their heresy. For the man who was baptized by an Arian in the Jordan River at the end of his life was Constantine the son, not Constantine the father. The writings of Damasus, Hadrian, Gelasius, and other ancient Roman pontiffs declare that the father was baptized at Rome by Sylvester; and the writings of all Greek authors who hold the correct view plainly testify to the same, while the monuments left in memory of that event clearly indicate it. Although this matter is evident, we shall nevertheless take care elsewhere to demonstrate it in due order, so that those who are obstinate in mind may be clearly recognized as mistaken, even if they refuse to yield to the truth.]

In the meantime, while the emperor Constantine was residing at Nicomedia, weighed down by illness, he was baptized at the point of death. For he had postponed it until that time, wishing to obtain this blessing in the Jordan. After drawing up his will and appointing his three sons as heirs—Constantine first, in the West; Constantius second, in the East; and Constans, the younger, appointed Caesar—he died in the western regions after the fifty-fifth year of his life. Beforehand, he had recalled the great Athanasius to Alexandria, where he had been in exile because of the persecution of the Arians.

Thus, when the most Christian emperor had died, the Arian doctrine sprouted again. The emperor Constantius, led astray by heretics, fell back into the same error and condemned the great Athanasius, who taught the truth. Later, when the heretics conspired grievously against him during his persecution and brought forward many accusations, the whole world joined together against him: the rulers of the earth, the peoples, kingdoms, and armies gathered against him.

When bishops were assembled at Milan and compelled to subscribe to his condemnation, Hilary of Poitiers alone refused to consent, although some of the others had been deceived. For this reason he was sent into exile with certain other bishops.

The heretics then assembled a synod at Rimini. There they removed *ὁμοούσιον* (*homoousion*), as though it were an unfamiliar expression and alien to the Scriptures, from the exposition of the faith. They established their wicked formula and said that one ought to believe Christ alone and not affirm *ὁμοούσιον*.

## CHAPTER VIII.

(Rufinus, Book X, chapter 22, *Ecclesiastical History*.) In the meantime Pope Liberius was sent into exile, and Felix, his deacon, was installed in his place by the heretics. At Jerusalem, Cyril succeeded Maximus in the episcopate, at times wavering in faith and at times in communion.

(Socrates, Book VI, chapters 1–2, *Tripartite History*.) At the same time the emperor Constantine died, and Julian succeeded to the kingdom, beginning well but ending badly. For at first he was a cleric and distinguished philosopher, but afterward he turned to idols.

At first peaceful, he released the bishops from exile and acted kindly toward our people; afterward he persecuted them and inflicted punishments. Out of hatred for Christ, he permitted the Jews to rebuild the temple at Jerusalem. Gathered from every province, they laid new foundations for the temple, but these suddenly collapsed in a divinely caused earthquake, with enormous stones scattered far and wide.

And so that this might not be thought to have happened by chance, on the following night the sign of the cross appeared on everyone’s garments. Astonished by the miracle, very many believed in Christ.

This same Julian, to crown his supreme wickedness against God, rather shamelessly removed an image of Christ which a woman whom he had freed from a flow of blood had set up at Caesarea. In its place he installed an image of himself. Later, when fire fell from heaven, it was struck by lightning: its head and neck were cast down together onto the ground, while the remaining part has been preserved until the judgment of the lightning. The pagans then smashed the image of Christ, but Christians later gathered up its pieces and placed them in a church.

## CHAPTER IX. From the council held at Alexandria.

(Sozomen, chapter 19; Socrates, chapter 20, *Tripartite History*.) In the meantime, a small number of confessors gathered at Alexandria—though they were many in merit of faith—and deliberated on calming the storms raised by the heretics.

Some, adhering to the rigor of the Church, said that those who had in any way stained themselves with the contagion of heresy ought not to be received into the priesthood. Others, moved by compassion, declared that access should not be denied to those who returned after renouncing the error of their faithlessness.

A fuller discussion of the Holy Spirit was also added to the decree of that council, so that he might be believed to possess the same substance and divinity as the Father and the Son, and so that nothing at all in the Trinity might be said to be created, inferior, or subsequent.

The Scriptures prompted them to discuss the difference between substances and subsistences, which the Greeks call *οὐσίαι* (*ousiai*) and *ὑποστάσεις* (*hypostaseis*). Some said that substance and subsistence appeared to be the same, because we do not speak of three substances in God and therefore ought not to speak of three subsistences either. Others, however, for whom substance plainly seemed quite different from subsistence, said that substance designates the nature and rational constitution by which a thing exists, whereas subsistence indicates, in each person, that very thing which exists and subsists.

## CHAPTER X. The heresy of Sabellius briefly noted.

Therefore, because of the heresy of Sabellius, who confused the persons and said that the same God is the Father when he wishes, the Son when he wishes, and the Holy Spirit when he wishes, it was necessary to confess three subsistences, since this appeared to signify three subsisting persons. Otherwise we might seem to give grounds for suspicion that we were followers of that faith which confesses the Trinity only in names and not in realities and subsistences.

Concerning the Lord’s incarnation, it was understood that the body which the Lord had assumed was not assumed without sensation or without a soul. When these matters had been carefully and moderately settled, the council was dissolved.

Eusebius, an illustrious man, powerful in the teaching of the word, then traveled through the East and Italy. Carrying its decrees with him, he recalled each Church to the soundness of the orthodox faith. The bishop Hilary of Poitiers, a man naturally learned and exceptionally suited to persuasion, was laboring toward the same end. Many short works of his survive, as well as books nobly published concerning the faith against the tricks of the heretics.

Meanwhile, the emperor Julian, preparing to fight against the Persians, offered sacrifice to Apollo and sought an oracle, but received no answer. When the demons were questioned about the reason for their silence, they said that the nearby tomb of the martyr Babylas was obstructing them.

Julian then ordered the “Galileans”—for he was accustomed to call our people by this name—to come and remove the martyr’s tomb. Our people gathered, singing with rejoicing in the ears of the impious ruler the Psalmist’s words: “Let all who worship graven images be confounded, and those who trust in their idols.”

Provoked to anger by this, Julian imprisoned the Christians and inflicted martyrdoms upon them, threatening them with still greater torments after his victory in the war. While he was planning this, however, events turned out contrary to his expectation. He did set out, but there was no return: there he was pierced by a dart whose source—whether one of his own men or an enemy—is uncertain.

It is said that when he had been wounded, he immediately filled his hand with his own blood and threw it into the air, saying: “Galilean, you have conquered!” Thus, even while blaspheming, he confessed the victory.

# BOOK TEN

[Col. 0869]

## CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0869B]

(Theodoret, Book I, chapters 1 and 3, *Tripartite History*.) After Julian, Jovian was drawn from the army to assume the insignia of imperial power. He excused himself, saying that he could not rule over sacrilegious men because he was a Christian, and he did not consent until the army acclaimed: “We too are Christians.”

He persecuted the heretics and honored the Church. He sought Athanasius and received from him the form of the faith and the manner of organizing the Churches. But death, arriving prematurely, soon cut short these very happy beginnings.

After him, Valentinian assumed the empire together with his brother Valens. Julian had once expelled him from military service because of our faith. Valentinian chose the western regions for himself, while he left the eastern regions to his brother.

Valentinian therefore administered the Roman state in faith and religion. Valens, however, by favoring the heretics, followed the path of his fathers. He persecuted all orthodox Christians, tortured them, and condemned them to exile—but this occurred after the death of Athanasius, for while Athanasius was alive, Valens was prevented from doing so as if by a certain divine power.

## CHAPTER II. Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, dies in the forty-sixth year of his priesthood.

(Rufinus, Book X, chapter 3, *Ecclesiastical History*.) Thus, after Athanasius had died in peace following many struggles, and Peter had been appointed in his place—Peter whom Athanasius himself had chosen after asking him about his successor—the Arians, stirred up by the favor of the emperor against our people, rose against them with greater violence.

Then Lucius, a bishop of the Arian pestilence, drove out Peter and ravaged the Church, already suffering the persecutions of the pagans; he ravaged the desert as well and declared war upon those who were living in quiet.

He therefore undertook to attack with armed force more than three thousand men dispersed throughout the entire desert in solitary dwellings. He sent into exile the fathers of the Egyptian monks—Macarius, Isidore, another Macarius, Heraclides, and Paul, the disciples of Antony—men regarded as distinguished for the merit of their lives and admirable for their virtues.

Omitting the rest for the sake of brevity, I shall relate one notable miracle of Macarius. A certain blind man came to Macarius’s cell. When he did not find him at home, he was at first sorrowful, but soon grew fervent with the ardor of faith. “Bring me,” he said, “to that part of the wall where the old man usually sleeps.” When he had been brought there, he placed his palm upon a little of the dry mud with which the wall had been plastered. He dissolved it with water from the well from which Macarius himself drank, anointed his eyes, and immediately regained his sight. (Rufinus, Book X, chapter 4, *Ecclesiastical History*.)

The same Macarius also freed from blindness the blind cubs of a lioness which their mother had brought to him, as though the beast were pleading on their behalf. In return, the animal gave him many torn skins as a gift, killing them with her own mouth and laying them down before his cell.

Yet Lucius the Arian did not yield to these great and wondrous miracles. Instead, he ordered that the aforementioned fathers be secretly seized and transported to a fiery island of Egypt, where they performed many miracles and converted unbelievers. Lucius, terrified by this and fearing the people, who were rioting on behalf of the just men, recalled them and sent them back to the desert.

While Lucius was doing this in Egypt, the emperor Valens, an Arian, raged no less violently against our people in other regions, especially at Edessa, a city of Mesopotamia adorned with the relics of the Apostle Thomas. There, having expelled the Catholics from the church, he did not even permit them to hold an assembly in the open country.

Then, like gold tested in a furnace, the Church shone amid persecution. Thus the faith was approved not only in words, but also in prisons, exiles, and chains.

In the meantime, when a certain obscure teacher named Lucius was darkening the people at Alexandria, like a lamp of divine light, the Lord kindled Didymus. (The same author, chapter 1 of the same book.) Although deprived of his eyesight from childhood, he devoted himself no less to letters and, wondrously enough, by a divine miracle attained such learning in the Scriptures that he became the greatest teacher of the ecclesiastical school of his time.

When the blessed Antony had come down from the Thebaid to bear witness to the faith of Athanasius against the Arians, he consoled Didymus with magnificent words: “Let nothing offend you, Didymus, because you appear to be deprived of bodily eyes. You lack the eyes that mice, flies, and lizards possess; but rejoice, because you have the eyes that angels possess, by which God is seen, and through which the great light of knowledge is kindled for you.”

## CHAPTER III. Concerning the illustrious men Basil and Gregory.

(The same author, chapter 7 of the same book.) At that time Basil and Gregory, of Cappadocia, shone like two luminaries of heaven. Both were noble, and both had been most thoroughly educated at Athens. Finally, setting aside the books of the secular Greeks, they sought a monastery, devoting themselves solely to Holy Scripture.

Basil clung to monastic contemplation and became humbler through contempt for the world; Gregory devoted himself to ecclesiastical activity and was freer in preaching.

Basil therefore became bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia. When Valens was forcing him into exile and he was standing before the tribunal, he is said to have replied elegantly to the threatening prefect: “Would that I had some worthy gift to offer the man who would sooner release Basil from the knot of this bag!” When time was granted him for deliberation, he said: “Tomorrow I shall be what I am today; may you not change!”

That very night, when the emperor’s wife was being tormented by severe distress and her only son was suddenly struck down by divine vengeance, Basil was summoned and detained at her intercession—the man who a little earlier had been driven out to punishment.

Thus, after Valens had expelled all the Catholics, Basil alone remained in the Church, preserving the sacrament of communion undefiled until the end of his life.

## CHAPTER IV. Gregory of Nazianzus was transferred to Constantinople.

Gregory was appointed in place of his father as bishop in the town of Nazianzus. He was most renowned for his learning and a most formidable opponent of the heretics. For this reason he was transferred to Constantinople to teach the Church.

(Rufinus, Book XI, chapter 10, *Ecclesiastical History*; the same author, chapter 11 of the same book.) At the same time, when Liberius, the Roman pontiff, had died, Damasus succeeded him in the apostolate. Against him the schismatic Ursinus presumed to occupy the apostolic see. Each side defended itself and raised armed conflict, to such an extent that the places of prayer were filled with human blood.

But God, the defender of innocence, stood by Damasus, a prudent and innocent man.

At Milan, when Auxentius, the bishop of the heretics, had died, Ambrose, a man who had first been a consular official, was suddenly elected bishop amid the shouting of the people. He was still a catechumen, but he was baptized shortly before his ordination.

## CHAPTER V. Valentinian reigns for ten years.

(The same author, chapter 12.) In the meantime, the emperor Valentinian died, leaving the empire to his sons Gratian and Valentinian. His brother too, when the Goths rose up, fled from battle and was burned by flames.

## CHAPTER VI. Concerning the illustrious emperor Gratian.

Gratian therefore assumed the empire together with his very young brother, after Valens had also died in the East. He was pious and religious, brave in arms, swift in body, good in understanding, and more modest than was advantageous for the state.

For this reason he summoned Theodosius to undertake the care and administration of affairs, a useful man and seasoned in war, entrusting him with the government of the East.

After Gratian had accomplished many things piously and bravely, and had been killed by Maximus, the tyrant of Britain, he left Valentinian behind in the western regions. Meanwhile his mother Justina, an Arian, persecuted the Church, threatening the priests with exile unless they accepted the Arian decrees.

She also harassed Ambrose, a most powerful tower against the heretics, with many attacks. Having persuaded her son, she prepared to condemn him to exile, but was prevented by the people, who loved Ambrose beyond belief.

Ambrose did not defend himself against the queen with weapons or physical force, but persisted without ceasing in fasts and prayers, until, with God acting as avenger and the tyrant Maximus pressing forward, Justina was put to flight and shared exile with her son.

## CHAPTER VII. Concerning the pious and religious emperor Theodosius.

In the meantime, Theodosius, mindful of Gratian’s benefits, rose with all the strength of the East to avenge him, avenged the innocent blood, recovered the kingdom, and restored the catholic faith which Justina had violated.

Returning from there to the East, he continued from the beginning of his reign to overthrow the idols completely, drive out the heretics, gather the Catholics, and persevere in faith, religion, and generosity.

He established a pious law that the sentences issued by rulers concerning punishment should be delayed by the executioners until the thirtieth day, so that an opportunity for mercy—or, if circumstances required it, for repentance—might not be lost.

## CHAPTER VIII. A notable history of various matters.

At that same time, at Laodicea, the bishop Apollinaris, a man otherwise well instructed, gave birth to a heresy. In a dispute he asserted that the Lord had assumed only a body in the economy of salvation, not a soul as well; and he maintained that, in place of that rational part, the Word of God himself had been present.

From this arose the heretics called Apollinarians, who had their own sects and doctrines.

A council was then gathered at Rome by Damasus and Peter of Alexandria, and the Apollinarians were condemned. This decretal judgment was issued: if anyone said that the Son of God possessed anything less, whether in humanity or in divinity, he was to be separated from the Church.

A synod was also held at Constantinople under three hundred and fifty Fathers, at which all the heretics were condemned.

At that time Martin, bishop of Tours, a city of Gaul, shone forth through many signs of miracles.

At that time the presbyter Jerome was held in renown at Bethlehem—indeed, throughout the whole world. Concerning him I cannot, without great astonishment, understand why Rufinus omitted to mark him out in this historical narrative, especially since he honored in eloquence other illustrious men, including his contemporaries, who were either inferior to him in knowledge or, if his equals or superiors, certainly less useful to the Churches in every respect.

Perhaps Rufinus did this deliberately, lest he appear to do an injury to that little book which the blessed Jerome himself wrote concerning illustrious men, where he also mentions himself at the end.

It is also said that they once had disagreements with one another and—if it is permissible to say this of such holy and prudent men—looked upon each other with sidelong glances and reproached one another in their words. Perhaps for this reason the blessed Jerome turned aside from this historical account.

Whether he omitted him for this reason or for that, I do not know; God knows. I know only this: he ought not to have been omitted. Therefore I have now considered it appropriate to supply Rufinus’s omission and to insert this one man into the narrative, so that the history, mutilated as though in one of its golden horns, might be restored by this insertion.

Accordingly, I intend briefly to gather into one place the things I have found written about him in scattered form, with his merits lending support. But let us now return to the history.

Meanwhile, the pious emperor Theodosius, making himself accessible to the priests of God, governed the Churches in great peace and quiet, after the heretics had been destroyed.

(The same author, chapters 33 and 34 of the same book.) At that time the idols were completely destroyed and the temples of the pagans overthrown.

At Alexandria the enormous temple of Serapis was demolished. In it stood such a vast image of Serapis that its right hand touched one wall and its left hand another. This monstrous figure was said to have been composed of every kind of metal and material.

They said that this idol was greeted by the sun on appointed days, because it had been constructed so that a direct ray of sunlight, passing through a small window, illuminated its mouth and lips while the people looked on.

In the same temple there was also an image of the sun made of very fine iron. A magnetic stone fastened above in the ceiling drew it upward, and it moved downward while being pulled, then rose higher as though to greet Serapis.

When our people rose up to overthrow this image, they were delayed for a little while by fear. The pagans confidently asserted that if a human hand touched it, the earth would immediately gape open and dissolve into chaos, and heaven would collapse headlong.

Then, behold, one of the soldiers, kindled by faith, seized a double-headed axe and struck the old fraud in the jaw. Yet heaven did not fall, nor did the earth split apart. With others helping to cut it down, the ancient idol was torn apart and burned in the sight of the clergy of Alexandria.

This was the end of Serapis. Some think that he was Jupiter; others, the power of the Nile River; others, Apis, the king of Egypt; and others assert that the image was fashioned in honor of our Joseph, because of the distribution of grain by which he aided Egypt.

When the image was also cast down in the temple of Saturn, the fraud of the tyrant who was the priest of that shrine was discovered. He would declare, as though from an oracle of the deity, that women pleasing to his lust were worthy of the god Saturn and of his summons. He would make them spend the night in the temple with the doors closed and the keys handed over. Then, when he appeared to leave, he would enter from behind through underground passages into the image, which had been hollowed out and carefully joined to the wall, and he would summon the woman as though with Saturn’s voice while she was praying and concentrating on her devotions.

Many other frauds of the pagans were also exposed at that time.

Thus, after the very head of idolatry at Alexandria had been cast down, the remaining idols were trampled underfoot, and churches of the true God were built.

Meanwhile, Valentinian ended his life in the western regions by hanging, through the treachery, as is said, of his commander Arbogast. After him, the tyrant Eugenius seized Italy.

Theodosius was inflamed to seek vengeance. After consulting John the Anchorite, a monk endowed with a prophetic spirit, he defeated the tyrant Eugenius, trusting as much in arms as in fasts and prayers.

He then returned east from his enemies. There he created his son Arcadius Augustus and also appointed Honorius emperor over the western regions. He himself, after subduing his enemies, eliminating the idols, and restoring peace to the Church, departed to the Lord after seventeen years of Roman rule, destined to receive the rewards of his merits together with the most pious rulers.

Here Rufinus brings his ecclesiastical history to an end. We too, now that the persecutions have ended, the heresies have been quieted, and the Church has been founded and built up, shall end with him the compendium of the work we undertook. After the enumeration of so many martyrs, confessors, teachers, and Fathers, nothing more worthy or illustrious remains.

[Col. 0875]

# THREE BOOKS OF HAYMO, BISHOP OF HALBERSTADT, ON THE VARIETY OF BOOKS, OR ON THE LOVE OF THE HEAVENLY HOMELAND

Now brought back to the press for the first time from the Cologne edition of the year 1531. (C, G)*

[Col. 0875]

# HAYMO’S PROLOGUE

[Col. 0875A] Since you are the unique and most holy example of true humility and compunction, crucified to this world, and with the world crucified to you, you have often asked, my most reverend lord Father William, that I should pass through the meadows of the sacred Scriptures with all speed and gather from them for you eternal flowers beneficial to the salvation of your soul: both concerning the love of the heavenly homeland and the steps of good works by which it may be reached, and also concerning the fear and nature of punishment.

You desired this so that, by the generosity of the giver of all good things, stirred and admonished by divine sayings, you might continually possess the mortification of carnal desires, fountains of tears, and constant compunction.

For all of us who know that your crucified life is not hidden know that, after you were released from worldly and courtly bonds, abandoned earthly and perishable things, and happily hastened toward poverty, your whole life has been mortified to this world, cleansed outwardly and inwardly from every vice, and thoroughly purified by divine fire from all secular cares and carnal desires. We know that, without any interruption, with continual sighs and tears, you hurry with the greatest speed toward your everlasting homeland.

Therefore, most blessed saint, I did not dare to be disobedient to your command. Nor did I wish—or ought—I to refuse, although I am without eloquence and entirely unlearned both in life and speech. Instead, I did not delay to obey your most radiant Holiness, insofar as the author and source of light has deigned to grant me. I have divided into three books certain passages excerpted from the little works of the holy Fathers.

The first little book concerns the nature of the heavenly homeland; the second, by what holy works this blessed life may be acquired; the third, the nature of punishment and everlasting penalties.

# BOOK ONE

[Col. 0875]

## CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0875B] Concerning the nature of the future and everlasting life.

Concerning the future life, more must be believed than can be written. For it is impossible to express in words as much as the mind can comprehend. (Prosper.) Indeed, even the mind’s deepest capacity of understanding grasps less than the magnitude of the reality itself. Therefore the future life is believed to be blessed eternally and eternally blessed: there is certain security, secure tranquility, tranquil joy, happy eternity, eternal happiness. There is perfect love, no fear, an eternal day, lively movement, and one spirit shared by all, secure in the contemplation of their God and in abiding with him.

There is the city itself, the blessed assembly of angels, saints, and human beings, shining with radiant merits. Eternal salvation abounds there, and truth reigns. No one deceives, and no one is deceived; hence no blessed person is expelled, because no wretched person is admitted. Those who reach it through the completion of good works will be like the blessed angels and will reign without end together with their God.

What they believed here, they will see there. Contemplating the substance of their Creator with pure hearts, they will rejoice in eternal exultation. Possessed by divine love and mutual delight, they will cleave forever to their God and happily to one another. In that eternal life all the saints will see God, and there they will rejoice without end.

There they will rejoice where they will receive their reward; there they will receive their reward where they will triumph not only over conquered enemies but also over enemies brought to an end; there they will triumph where they will fear no adversary any longer. There the cleansing of human sins will be so great and so perfect that they will have reason to give thanks to their cleansing God, not reason to blush at having been stained by any sins that could offend him.

(Gregory.) For there will be neither sins nor sinners, and those who are there will no longer be able to sin. There they rejoice, and there they will rejoice without end. There are the choirs of angels singing hymns; there is the company of the citizens above; there is the sweet solemnity of those returning from the sad labor of this pilgrimage. There are the discerning choirs of the prophets; there is the judicial company of the apostles; there is the victorious army of innumerable martyrs, all the happier there because they were afflicted more harshly here. There is the steadfastness of the confessors, consoled by receiving their reward. There are faithful men whom worldly pleasure could not soften away from the strength of their youthful vigor. There are holy women who conquered both the world and their sex.

(Prosper.) There are children who here surpassed their years in character. There are old men whom age here made weak and whom the strength for good works did not abandon. All who will be there, although they were separated from one another by differing merits, will nevertheless be blessed in a single perfection. For each will have rewards sufficient for him, and those already perfected will no longer be able to contain greater rewards than their own. In that great realm of blessedness, no one will claim greater merits for himself, because there will be no arrogance there; nor will an inferior envy a superior, because envy cannot exist there. And therefore, even if there are different dwellings there, there will be in them all the supreme equality of a single perfection, and they will possess one happiness of the heavenly kingdom.

That one denarius is equal for all of them which the householder commands to be given to everyone who worked in the vineyard, without distinguishing on that account between those who labored less and those who labored more (Matthew XX). (Augustine.) By that denarius, certainly, eternal life is signified, in which no one lives more than another, since no difference in living is to remain in eternity. The many dwellings, however, signify different dignities of merit within eternal unity. “The glory of the sun is one, the glory of the moon another, and the glory of the stars another; for star differs from star in glory. So also is the resurrection of the dead” (1 Corinthians XV).

Like stars, the saints receive different dwellings of different brightness in the kingdom, as though allotted in heaven; yet, because of the one denarius, no one is separated from the kingdom. Thus God will be all in all. Since God is love, through love he makes what each person possesses common to all. For each person also possesses what he himself does not have when he loves it in another. There will therefore be no envy of unequal brightness when the unity of love reigns in all.

(Gregory.) Although in that perpetual recompense the same dignity will not belong to everyone, there will nevertheless be one blessed life for all. Hence the Lord himself says: “In my Father’s house are many dwellings” (John XIV). Yet those who were brought into it, although they came at different hours, nevertheless received one denarius. How, then, do many dwellings accord with one denarius? Surely because the dignities of the blessed citizens will indeed be different, but the repose of the eternal recompense will be one.

Even if the merit of each person is unequal, there will be no difference in their joys. For although one is exalted less and another more, the sight of their Creator delights all with one joy. Once they have become participants in that blessed life, they gaze upon the author of their blessedness with inexhaustible delight. Made eternally happy by the stability of their condition, they are secure in their continuance; they receive their highest and solid joy, which they enjoy without exhaustion, from the contemplation of God, and they serve their God tirelessly and lovingly.

They will be perfectly blessed, so that they neither desire nor are able to become more blessed. In that blessed homeland they will have understanding without fear, memory without forgetfulness, thought without wandering, love without pretense, perception without offense, health without weakness, salvation without pain, life without death, ease without impediment, fullness without weariness, and complete soundness without disease.

There can be no weeping or groaning there. All the saints will have perfect love, no fear, and everlasting joy. There the will will be rightly ordered and desire will be absent. For, enjoying the heavenly goods to which they longed to attain, they will lack nothing further to desire. Perfectly blessed in that perpetual realm of security and peace, they will suffer neither the goads of fear nor pain.

There will be the complete salvation of all faithful Catholics, no corruption, and blessed immortality. There will be the true perfection of prudence and wisdom, and complete knowledge of all things. Whoever is saved there will no longer be able to perish; rather, the soul subject to God will reign in everlasting peace together with the flesh subject to it.

What tongue or understanding is sufficient to describe or comprehend the joys of that heavenly city: to take part in the choirs of angels, (Gregory.) to stand with the blessed spirits before the glory of their Creator, to behold the face of God present, to see the unbounded light, to be touched by no fear of death, and to rejoice in the gift of perpetual incorruption? No mortal can say or imagine how great are the joys of the righteous in that perpetual realm, as Scripture says: “Eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the human heart what God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Corinthians II).

Let us therefore love God, dearest brothers, by keeping his commandments.

For to love God is to keep his commandments. He himself says: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my words” (John XIV). And John says in his Epistle: “Whoever says, ‘I love God,’ and does not keep his commandments, is a liar” (1 John II).

Let us take care to keep all God’s commandments, insofar as he grants us to keep them: by giving alms, devoting ourselves to prayers, tears, vigils, and fasts; doing good works wherever we can; avoiding what is evil; and, with his help, doing with all our strength what is holy and pleasing to God. Thus may we deserve to reach the holy fellowship of the angelic citizens, the eternal Jerusalem, in which there is the holy company of all the elect, certain solemnity, secure rest, true peace, and perpetual life.

May we deserve to ascend to it, aided by the merits and prayers of all who are there, through the gift of him who lives through infinite ages. Amen.

## CHAPTER II. The Greatness of the Glory of the Elect: Seeing God

(Bede.) No speech can explain, and no understanding can comprehend, how great are the joys of the righteous when they come to Mount Zion and the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to the assembly of many thousands of angels, and when they behold God himself, the craftsman and founder of that city—not through a mirror and in a riddle, as now, but face to face.

The blessed Peter speaks of this vision when he says to the faithful concerning the Lord: “Though you do not now see him, you believe in him; and when you see him, you will rejoice with inexpressible and glorified joy” (1 Peter I).

(John Chrysostom.) The greatness of that joy cannot be explained: the soul, having returned to its own nobility, will then begin confidently to see its God, before whom the holy assembly of angels and archangels, thrones and dominions, principalities and powers will stand. No voice is sufficient to tell what glory it is to see the eternal King reconciled; no thought can comprehend it. That beauty, that loveliness, that power, that glory, that magnificence, that majesty escapes every word and exceeds every capacity of the human mind.

O how unspeakably happy and supremely blessed is the one who deserves to see God in that perpetual realm, where he will rejoice happily with the angels and archangels without end.

## CHAPTER III. That Before the Saints Reach Future Blessedness They Cannot See God Perfectly

(Prosper.) In that blessed life which is to come, the saints will see God perfectly as he is, and there they themselves will be perfected in the attainment of eternal life and the heavenly kingdom.

But if human frailty could have contemplated God’s substance perfectly here, the holy Evangelist would never have said: “No one has ever seen God” (John VI). He did not say, “No one will see him.” Finally, to show clearly that the vision of God was not denied to holy people but postponed—what he denied in the present, he promised in the future—he said: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God” (Matthew V). Here too he did not say, “For they see God.”

Therefore God, who in this life could not and cannot be seen without the reception of some means of nourishment, is to be seen in the future life. There the perfection of divine contemplation is to be hoped for, where there will be the fullness of all good things. For this reason the contemplative life, in which the intellectual creature, purified from every sin and healed in every respect, will see its Creator, receives its name from contemplating, that is, from seeing.

If this is the nature of that life in which God can be seen, then that life must be believed to be contemplative. In the present life, however, which is full of miseries and errors, it is beyond doubt that God cannot be seen as he is.

Nor should it disturb us that we read that God was seen here by certain righteous people of ancient times. He was not seen in this condition of our humiliation as he will be seen in that glory. For when he appeared in the visible form of a creature, in accordance with the dispensation of the times, wherever and to whomever he willed, he could not and cannot be seen as he is. But he will be able to be seen when our pilgrimage reaches the heavenly homeland, when our mortal nature has been clothed with blessed immortality, and when faith itself, which here believed in what was to come, has brought all the truly faithful to divine contemplation and to the reception of heavenly rewards.

## CHAPTER IV. That God Can Be Seen Here through Faith, but in the Future through Direct Vision

(Prosper.) The holy Apostle says: “We walk by faith, not by sight” (2 Corinthians V). Faith, therefore, is that by which one walks, and sight is that which is seen. In this life, where by living well through faith we advance, we walk, so to speak, with the steps of good works. In the future, however, when we reach direct vision, there will no longer be anywhere for us to walk as though advancing farther; rather, we will have reached the very vision toward which we walk through spiritual faith, and we will behold it with insatiable delight.

Insofar as the human mind is capable—for its Creator made it in his own image—let it strive even here to see God intelligibly through faith, so that it may see him more fully when, by the gift of its Creator, it reaches direct vision.

## CHAPTER V. With What Great Brightness God Will Be Seen by His Elect in His Kingdom

(Bede.) He will be seen by all the saints in his kingdom after judgment, in the same brightness in which the disciples saw the Lord shining on the mountain (Matthew XVII). What the mortal and still corruptible eyes of the disciples could not then endure, the entire Church of the saints, made incorruptible through the resurrection, will then be able powerfully to behold. Of this Church it is written: “Their eyes will see the King in his beauty” (Isaiah XXXIII).

No human voice could or can say what that beauty, glory, loveliness, magnificence, power, brightness, and majesty are in every respect.

(John Chrysostom.) Let us turn our eyes toward the mountain on which Christ was transfigured and behold his splendor, the splendor with which he then shone in his transformation. Even so, we will not find the whole brightness of that glory and of the future age revealed to us. For that transformation took place not according to the full reality of future goods, but only to the extent that the eyes were able to endure the sight.

Thus the Gospel says that he “shone like the sun” (Matthew XVII). The glory of incorruptible bodies, however, does not emit merely as much brightness as proceeds from this corruptible light, nor such a light as mortal eyes can now receive. Rather, the splendor of the future light will be so great that bodily sight could not endure it—although it endured the one who shone in the transformation on the mountain.

This shows that as much was revealed as mortal eyes were able to bear. Yet they did not bear even that completely; instead, it says, “they fell on their faces upon the ground.”

## CHAPTER VI. Concerning the Resurrection and Life of the Saints

The bodies of the saints will therefore rise without any defect, without any deformity, just as they will be without any corruption, burden, or difficulty. In them there will be as much ease as blessedness. Having received bodies with incorruption and immortality, they will receive citizenship in the heavenly homeland; made its citizens forever, they will receive the promised rewards.

There such great joy and such abundant grace of heavenly delights will overflow for them that they will give thanks to their rewarder for such gifts and will suffer no weariness from the very abundance of the goods they receive. No secret will remain hidden from the perfectly blessed there, since, what is far more excellent, they will see God himself with pure hearts.

For the human creature will then be so perfected that it can no longer be changed for the better or the worse. Whatever the bites of beasts may have taken from human bodies, whatever unforeseen accident may have removed, whatever varieties of illness may have torn away, whatever human cruelty may have amputated, whatever fire or any other thing may have inflicted as weakness, and whatever old age itself, burdensome even to the healthy, may have denied—all such bodily losses and those like them one resurrection will restore there, and incorruptible health will possess bodies restored in all their members.

Let us also consider the condition of that holy resurrection and perpetual life, insofar as it is possible for us to consider it. No speech will suffice to comprehend it as it truly is, but let us take from what we read and receive through riddles some faint conception of it, as far as we can.

It is said of it in one passage that “pain, sadness, and groaning will flee from there.” What life could be more blessed than one in which there is no fear of poverty and no injury from the affliction of illness?

(Augustine.) No one is angry, no one envies, no desire burns, no longing exists there, and no ambition for honor beats through the exercise of power. Every stain of vice is put to sleep and utterly extinguished; peace contains all things, and joy fills them.

Everything is tranquil and quiet; there is perpetual brightness and light—not the light that exists now, but light so much more splendid and clear as the sun is more splendid than a lamp. There is no night, no darkness, no gathering of clouds, no harshness of cold or heat. There is no old age, nor the misery of old age; everything that belongs to corruption is banished, and the glory of incorruption surrounds all things.

Hence Paul says: “The creation itself will be liberated from the slavery of corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God” (Romans VIII).

(Gregory.) For now the elect are weighed down by the punishment of corruption, but then the glory of incorruption will exalt them. As far as the burdens of present necessity are concerned, freedom shows nothing of itself in the children of God now; but as far as the glory of the freedom that follows is concerned, then no trace of slavery will appear in God’s servants.

Creation, therefore, stripped of the slavery of corruption and having received the dignity of freedom, is transformed into the glory of the children of God. United to God through the Spirit, it thereby declares that it has, as it were, passed beyond and subdued the very condition of being a creature.

## CHAPTER VII. That the Loss Caused by the Fall of the Angels Is Repaired from among Holy Human Beings

(Augustine.) Through the redemption of human beings, the loss caused by that angelic fall is repaired. The holy angels, instructed by God, whose eternal truth they contemplate in blessedness, certainly know how many human beings are needed to complete the integrity of that city.

For this reason the Apostle says: “To restore all things in Christ, those in heaven and those on earth” (Ephesians I). The things in heaven are restored in him when what fell among the angels is restored from among human beings. The things on earth are restored when the human beings predestined to eternal life are renewed from the oldness of corruption.

That heavenly city consists of angels and human beings. We therefore believe that the human race will ascend to it in such a number as corresponds to the number of elect angels who remained there, as it is written: “He established the boundaries of the nations according to the number of the angels of God.”

## CHAPTER VIII. That the Elect in the Eternal Homeland Recognize All the Good

(Gregory.) In the eternal homeland the elect recognize not only the good whom they knew in this world; they also recognize as though seen and known the good whom they never saw. For when they see the ancient fathers in that eternal inheritance, those whom they have always known through their works will not be unknown to them through vision.

Since all there behold God in a common brightness, what could they not know there, where they know the one who knows all things?

A certain religious man among us, whose life was highly praiseworthy, died three years ago. As other religious men who were present testified, at the hour of his departure he began to look upon the prophet Jonah, as well as Ezekiel and Daniel. Saying that they had come to him, he lowered his eyes and offered them the service of reverence; then he was led out of the flesh.

This makes it plainly understood what knowledge there will be in that incorruptible life, if this man, while still placed in corruptible flesh, recognized the holy prophets whom he had certainly never seen.

## CHAPTER IX. That the Souls of the Blessed Go Immediately to Christ as Soon as They Leave the Body

(Gregory.) Whether the souls of the righteous can now, before the restoration of their bodies, be received into heaven, we can neither affirm of all the righteous nor deny of all. There are souls of certain righteous people that are delayed in certain dwellings in the heavenly kingdom. What does the loss involved in this delay suggest except that they possessed somewhat less than perfect righteousness?

Nevertheless, it is as clear as daylight that the souls of the perfected righteous are received into heavenly dwellings as soon as they leave the confinement of this flesh. Truth itself bears witness to this: “Wherever the body is, there the eagles will be gathered” (Matthew XXIV). For wherever our Redeemer is bodily, there, without doubt, the souls of the righteous are gathered.

Paul desires “to be dissolved and to be with Christ” (Philippians I). Whoever does not doubt that Christ is in heaven cannot deny that Paul’s soul is in heaven. He also speaks of the dissolution of his body and of dwelling in the heavenly homeland: “We know that the earthly house of this dwelling will be dissolved, and that we have a building from God, a house not made by hands, eternal in the heavens” (2 Corinthians V).

## CHAPTER X. That Now the Elect Enjoy the Blessedness of Souls Alone, but after the Resurrection of Souls and Bodies Together

(Gregory.) The elect now enjoy the blessedness of souls alone, but afterward they will enjoy also the blessedness of their bodies, so that they may rejoice in the very flesh in which they endured pains and sufferings for the Lord. Concerning this doubled glory it is written: “In your land they will possess double” (Isaiah LXI).

For this reason, even before the day of the resurrection, it is written concerning the souls of the saints: “White robes were given to each of them, and they were told to rest for a little while” (Revelation VI), until the number of their fellow servants and brothers should be completed.

Those who have now received single robes will therefore have two robes at the judgment. For now they rejoice in the glory of souls alone, but then, in the glory of both souls and bodies, they will rejoice in two white robes.

## CHAPTER XI. That the Perpetuity of Our Future Rest Is Mystically Shown through the Number Fifty

(Bede.) It was not without a great mystery that the number fifty was observed in the giving either of grace or of the law. For on the fiftieth day after Passover, the law was given to the people on the mountain, and the grace of the Spirit was sent to the disciples in the upper room.

This number certainly signifies the perpetuity of the future rest. In it, fittingly, either the Decalogue of the law is given or the grace of the Holy Spirit is bestowed upon human beings, so that it may be clearly shown that all who, with the help of the Spirit’s grace, fulfill the commands of the divine law are surely advancing toward true rest.

The number fifty is therefore suited to signify inner rest because it is completed from seven weeks and one additional day. The people were commanded in the law to work for six days and rest on the seventh; to plow and reap for six years and cease in the seventh, because the Lord also completed the adornment of the world in six days and ceased from his work on the seventh.

Through all these things we are mystically admonished that those who in this world—which consists of six ages—devote themselves to good works for the Lord are enclosed in the future Sabbath, that is, in eternal rest from the Lord.

The fact that seven days are mentioned signifies the abundant multiplicity of that same rest. In it the sublime reward is given to the elect, of which the Apostle says: “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart, God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Corinthians II).

Moreover, the fiftieth day itself, which follows the seven weeks and was venerable with a greater solemnity than the others, indicates the time of the future resurrection. Then the rest now enjoyed by the souls of the elect will be crowned by the glory of their bodies also, once received.

For in the law the fiftieth year was commanded to be called the Jubilee, that is, “releasing” or “changed” (Leviticus XXV). In it the people were to rest from every labor, all debts were to be released, slaves were to return free, and the year itself was to surpass the others in greater solemnities and more exalted divine praises.

Rightly, therefore, this number indicates that tranquility of supreme peace, when, as the Apostle says, at the sound of the last trumpet the dead will rise and we will be changed in glory. Then, when the labors and troubles of this world have ceased and the debts of all faults have been released, the entire people of the elect will rejoice forever in the sole contemplation of the divine vision, when that desirable command of our Lord and Savior has been fulfilled: “Be still and know that I am God.”

## CHAPTER XII. That the Present Life Is Shown by Good Friday, the Rest of Souls by the Sabbath, and the Glory of the Resurrection by the Lord’s Day

The whole of time unfolds through seven days. The eternal day that follows when the succession of seven days has been completed is the eighth; this is why the Lord wished to rise from the dead after the Sabbath.

The Lord’s Day, which is the third day after the Lord’s death, is counted as the eighth day from the creation of the days, because it follows the Sabbath. Hence the passion of our Redeemer and his true resurrection also prefigured something concerning his body during the days of his passion.

He suffered on Good Friday, rested in the tomb on the Sabbath, and rose from the dead on the Lord’s Day. The present life is still our Good Friday, because it is spent in pain and tormented by distress. But on the Sabbath, as though in the tomb, we rest, because after the body we find rest for the soul.

On the Lord’s Day—namely, the third day from the passion and, as we have said, the eighth from the creation of the days—we will rise from death in the body and rejoice in the glory of the soul together with the flesh.

What our Savior wonderfully accomplished in himself, he truly signified in us, so that pain may receive us on the sixth day, rest on the seventh, and glory on the eighth.

## CHAPTER XIII. What and How Great Is the Difference between the Two Lives of the Holy Church of God

(Augustine.) The Church knows and commends two lives divinely proclaimed to it: one is in faith, the other in direct vision. One is in the time of pilgrimage, the other in the eternity of dwelling; one in labor, the other in rest; one on the way, the other in the homeland; one in the work of action, the other in the reward of contemplation.

One turns away from evil and does good; the other has no evil from which to turn and possesses a great good in which to rejoice. One fights with an enemy; the other reigns without an enemy. One is strong in adversity; the other experiences nothing adverse. One restrains carnal desires; the other is free for spiritual delights.

One is anxiously concerned with the struggle for victory; the other is secure in the peace of victory. One is helped amid temptations; the other rejoices in the very helper without any temptation. One assists the needy; the other is where it finds no needy person.

One forgives the sins of others so that its own may be forgiven; the other neither suffers anything requiring forgiveness nor does anything for which it would ask forgiveness. One is scourged by evils lest it be lifted up by good things; the other, in such fullness of grace, is free from every evil, so that without any temptation to pride it shines with the supreme good.

One distinguishes good and evil; the other sees only what is good. Thus one is good but still wretched; the other is better and blessed.

## CHAPTER XIV. That the Present Life Is Shown by the Affliction of Lent and Eternal Joy by the Fifty Days

(Bede.) The holy Church of God still labors on earth in some of its members for eternal rest, while in others, every labor having ended, it already reigns with Christ in heaven.

In remembrance of both lives, our fathers established these two fitting religious solemnities: the forty days of affliction and fasting, as the time of the Lord’s resurrection approached, and the Paschal joys. Through the former they wished to recall to us more frequently that through labors and abstinence, through vigils and prayers, and through the other weapons of righteousness mentioned by the Apostle (Romans VI), we must attain the rewards of immortal life.

They wished the fifty days beginning with the very day of the Lord’s resurrection to be celebrated with joys and divine praises rather than fasts, so that through its annual festivals we might be more sweetly admonished to direct and fix our desire upon obtaining the feasts that are not annual but perpetual, not earthly but heavenly.

For true happiness is not to be sought in the time of this mortality but in the eternity of the incorruption to come; true solemnity is to be found there, where, once all anguish has ceased, life is spent entirely in the vision and praise of God.

In accordance with this, the Prophet, rejoicing in God both in heart and flesh, said: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house; forever and ever they will praise you” (Psalm LXXXIII).

## CHAPTER XV. No One Can Be Perfectly Blessed before Reaching Future Blessedness

(Prosper.) In the present life, no matter how greatly someone may stand out in holiness or how highly someone may excel in perfection, he can indeed be perfect according to the measure of this life. Yet he is not so secure in his perfection that he need not be anxious about falling.

Where there is anxiety, there is not complete blessedness. Blessedness cannot be believed perfect unless it is secure, and it will not be secure unless eternal security has consumed every anxiety.

Therefore those who are called blessed in this life are blessed in hope of future blessedness. In reality, however, they are not blessed here but will be blessed in that life, because the blessedness of all the blessed will be perfect there. Human nature, perfectly blessed, will see the glory of its Creator and its own glory, and will cling to him without any defect in its blessedness.

## CHAPTER XVI. Then the Heart and Soul of All the Elect Will Be Perfectly One, When God Is All in All

(Bede.) Just as at the beginning of the Church’s birth in Jerusalem the multitude of believers had one heart and one soul, and all things were common to them (Acts IV), so in that vision of supreme peace God will be one heart and one soul to the multitude of believers, as they love and praise him by whose grace they will see themselves saved.

There, truly, all things will be common to all, because, as the Apostle says, “God will be all in all” (1 Corinthians XV).

(Prosper.) All who will be there will be one body, and each will rejoice in his own happiness and in the happiness of every other. This is the true and blessed unanimity of the holy angels and blessed human beings in that perpetual realm: their one will is to proclaim the glory of God’s kingdom and to speak of the power of his might.

## CHAPTER XVII. That Holy Jerusalem Is Eternal in Part and Captive in Part

(Augustine.) Holy heavenly Jerusalem is eternal in part and captive in part: eternal in the angels, captive in human beings. Not all the citizens of that city are captives; only those who are on pilgrimage away from it are captives.

The human being, whose home is Jerusalem, has, sold under sin, become a pilgrim. Just as that people was led from the land of Jerusalem into captivity in Babylonia and returned to its city after seventy years, and as the seventy years signify the whole period that unfolds through seven days, so, when all time has passed, we too will return to our homeland, eternal Jerusalem, where our fellow citizens, the angels, are.

We are on pilgrimage from them on earth. In pilgrimage we sigh; in the city we will rejoice.

## CHAPTER XVIII. How Ardently Pilgrims Should Desire the Region of Their Heavenly Homeland

(Augustine.) That pilgrim ardently desired to return to the heavenly homeland who, grieving and groaning, said: “Woe is me, for my sojourn has been prolonged” (Psalm CXIX).

It is as though he were saying: “Lord, I have withdrawn far from you; my pilgrimage has become long. I have not yet come to that homeland where I will live with no evil. I have not yet come to that fellowship of angels where I will fear no scandal. Why am I not there yet? Because my sojourn has become long.”

A sojourn is a pilgrimage. An inhabitant is one who lives in a foreign land, not in his own city. “My sojourn has become long.” And where has it become long?

Sometimes, my brothers, when a person is on pilgrimage among better people and lives among them, he might perhaps live in his homeland; but it is not so when we are pilgrims from that heavenly Jerusalem. A person changes his homeland, and sometimes he is well off in pilgrimage. While on pilgrimage, he may find faithful friends whom he could not find in his homeland; he may have had enemies who drove him from his homeland into pilgrimage, and in pilgrimage he may find what he did not have in his homeland.

It is not so with that homeland, Jerusalem, where all are good. Whoever is a pilgrim from it is among the wicked. He cannot withdraw from the wicked except when he returns to the company of the angels—to the place from which he is on pilgrimage—where all the righteous and holy enjoy the Word of God without reading and without letters.

What is written for us on pages, they see through the face of God. What a homeland! A great homeland—and wretched are those who are pilgrims from that homeland.

But what does this man say? “My pilgrimage has become long.” Now, wishing to return, he recognizes the misery of his pilgrimage because he has come to know that homeland. He returns and longs to ascend to the blessed homeland.

## CHAPTER XIX. How Captives Should Lament Their Eternal Homeland, Jerusalem
(Aug.) Let us all groan, let each of us groan, in this captivity, in this mortality; let us sigh for and desire our homeland, the heavenly Jerusalem. Let us strive toward our Creator, the builder of that same city; let us ask him for the sustenance of good works, so that we may deserve to reach him and dwell in his house all the days of our life—that is, in everlasting [Col. 0888A] life. That eternal house, which we have from God in heaven, was loved by the one who said: “Lord, I have loved the beauty of your house and the place where your glory dwells” (Ps. LXXXIII). And again: “How lovely are your tabernacles, Lord of hosts! My soul longs and languishes for the courts of the Lord, because one day in your courts is better than thousands” (ibid.). He himself also ardently desired to reach the Lord when he said: “My soul thirsted for God, the living fountain. When shall I come and appear before the face of the Lord?” (Ps. XLI). In this pilgrimage, therefore, let us, who have been placed here, weep before the Lord who made us, because he himself is the Lord our God.

(Aug.) Held fast in this sorrowful mortality, let us desire with complete contrition of heart and body to return to that heavenly Jerusalem, [Col. 0888B] which is the mother of us all. From it we are exiles in this wretched life; let us sigh for our return to it. We remain wretched and laboring until we return there, where we shall be able to see the God of gods on the holy mountain of Zion.

## CHAPTER XX. No mortal can say how great the joys of the righteous are in heaven

(Aug.) Human speech can neither explain nor imagine what and how great the joys in heaven are, as the Apostle Paul testifies: “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart—what God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Cor.
