II). Let us therefore love God with our whole heart and with all our strength, desiring the blessedness that he promised to his elect. Let all earthly [Col. 0888C] and transitory things become worthless to us in comparison with love of our heavenly homeland; with all the powers of our soul let us strive there, and with the inward affections of our hearts let us sigh for it. Let us all ask God with tears, let each of us ask, that we may dwell in his house all the days of our life and deserve to see his good things in the land of the living. Let these few excerpts concerning the nature of future blessedness, drawn from the divine books of the holy Fathers, suffice. Now, therefore, with the Lord’s help, let us show by gathering flowers from the pronouncements of the Catholic Fathers by what steps of good works we must hasten toward it.

# BOOK TWO

[Col. 0887]

## CHAPTER I. On the praise of charity, and that it is the mother of all virtues

[Col. 0887D]

(Aug.) Charity is the mother, fountain, and origin of all holy virtues, and the end of every commandment. Concerning it the Apostle says: “The end of the commandment is charity from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith” (1 Tim. I). Every commandment is referred to charity. Hence the Lord says: “This is my commandment, that you love one another” (John XIII).

(Greg.) Every commandment concerns love alone, and all are one commandment, because whatever is commanded is made firm in charity alone. Just as many branches of a tree grow from one root, so many virtues are generated from one charity. A branch of good works has no verdure if it does not remain in the root of charity. The Lord’s commandments, therefore, are both many and one.

(Aug.) Many in the diversity of their works, but one in the root of love. For charity concerns God and one’s neighbor. Certainly, upon these two commandments hang the whole Law and the Prophets. Add the Gospel; add the Apostles. The saying is not excessive: “The end of the commandment is charity” (1 Tim. I). And: “God is charity, and whoever remains in charity” (as the Apostle John says) “remains in God, and God in him” (1 John IV).

(Prosp.) Charity is a right will, wholly turned away from all earthly and present things, joined inseparably to God, and kindled with a certain fire of the Holy Spirit, from whom it comes and to whom it is directed. A stranger to every defilement, incapable of corruption, subject to no fault of changeability, exalted above all things loved carnally, most powerful over every affection, eager for divine contemplation, always unconquered in all things, the summit of good actions, the salvation of morals, the end of heavenly commandments, the death of crimes, the life of virtues, the strength of those who fight, the palm of the just, the soul of holy minds, the cause of good merits, and the reward of the perfect.

It raises the dead in their sins, heals the sick, restores the lost, and inspires hope in the despairing. It dwells in peaceful minds; it is fruitful in penitents, joyful in those making progress, glorious in those who persevere, victorious in martyrs, and active in absolutely all the faithful. Faith conceives it; hope hastens toward it; the progress of all serves it. From it every good work lives; under it obedience grows; through it patience conquers; because of it religious devotion despises carnal allurements; without it no one has pleased God, and with it no one could sin, nor will anyone be able to sin.

This is true, genuine, perfect charity, which the holy Apostle calls “a still more excellent way” (1 Cor. XII). Truly, it is the way that leads those who walk in it to their homeland. For just as no one reaches the destination toward which he is traveling without a way, so without charity—which has been called the way—people cannot walk but only wander.

## CHAPTER II. That charity extends in many ways to countless good things

The fullness of the Law, as the Apostle Paul says, is love (Rom. XIII). Again he says of it: “Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ” (Gal. VI). What can the law of Christ more fittingly be understood to mean than charity? We truly fulfill it when, out of love, we bear our brothers’ burdens. Hence it is also said through blessed Job that his law is manifold (Job XI). What should the law of God mean in this passage except charity, through which the commandments of life are always read in the mind, so that they may be observed in action?

This same law is called manifold because, through vigilant devotion, charity diligently expands into every work of virtue. It begins, indeed, with two commandments but extends to countless things. The beginning of this law is love of God and love of one’s neighbor. Love of God, however, is divided into three parts, because the Creator commands that he be loved with the whole heart, the whole soul, and all one’s strength (Exod. XX). Here it must be noted that when divine speech commands that God be loved, it not only says from what part he is to be loved but also teaches to what extent, when it adds “with the whole”: namely, that whoever desires to please God perfectly should leave nothing of himself for himself.

Love of one’s neighbor is derived into two commandments. A certain righteous man says: “What you hate to have done to you by another, see that you do not do to another.” Truth itself says: “Whatever you wish people to do to you, do likewise to them” (Matt. VII). By these two commandments of the two Testaments, evil is restrained by one and kindness is offered by the other: each person ceases from doing harm by not doing the evil he does not wish to suffer; and, by providing the good he desires to have done to himself, he exercises himself in kindness for his neighbor’s benefit.

When these two things are considered with attentive intention, the heart is directed toward countless ministries of virtue, so that the restless mind may neither burn with desires to inflict what it ought not to inflict nor grow slack through idleness in providing what it ought to provide. For when one takes care not to do to another what one absolutely does not wish to endure from another, one looks around oneself attentively: lest pride elevate one; lest, lowering the mind to the point of despising one’s neighbor, it exalt itself; lest ambition tear the mind apart when it expands it toward desiring what belongs to another, and then constrict it; lest lust defile the heart and corrupt it by subjecting it to unlawful desires; lest anger embitter it and inflame it even to the utterance of insult; lest envy bite it and, rivaling the happiness of others with a sweetness that is really destructive, draw it on even to the wantonness of slander; lest hatred arouse malice and provoke it even to the dart of cursing.

Again, when one considers doing to another what one expects another to do to oneself, one carefully weighs how to answer evil with good and good with better: so that toward the insolent one may show the long-suffering of gentleness; toward those weakened by the plague of malice one may offer the grace of kindness; that the divided may come to peace; that those at peace may be girded for the desire of true peace; that one may provide necessities to the needy; show the way of uprightness to those who err; soothe the afflicted by word and compassion; restrain by reproach those inflamed by the desires of this world; mitigate the threats of the powerful by reason; lighten the distresses of the oppressed with whatever help one can; oppose patience to those who resist outwardly; and inwardly show discipline with patience to those who are proud.

Toward the errors of subordinates, gentleness should temper zeal so that it does not weaken the pursuit of justice. Let zeal against flatteries burn, but let it not, by burning, cross the boundary of compassion. Let it provoke the ungrateful to love by benefits, and preserve them in love even through freely given services. When one cannot correct the wrongs of neighbors, let one be silent; but when they can be corrected by speaking, let one fear that silence may be taken for consent. Let one tolerate what one keeps silent about in such a way that one does not conceal the poison of grief in the soul. Let one show less kindness to the malicious, but not, under the guise of grace, depart from the law of uprightness. Let one give one’s neighbors everything one is able to give, but not become swollen with pride in giving it. In the good one displays, let one fear the precipice of pride, but not grow sluggish in the practice of goodness.

Let one give away what one possesses in such a way as to consider the greatness of the rewarder’s generosity, lest, when giving earthly things, one darken the light of joy in the offering by grieving over one’s own poverty more than is necessary. Well, therefore, in the words of blessed Job, the law of God is called manifold (Job XI), because although charity is one and the same, when it fully possesses the mind it kindles it in many different ways toward countless works.

## CHAPTER III. What and how great good works charity has produced in the holy Fathers

(Orig.) Charity, through Abel, both offered gifts chosen for God and endured his brother’s sword without resistance. Charity taught Enoch to live spiritually among human beings and even withdrew his body from among them to a sublime life. Charity taught Noah, disregarding everything else, to show that only God was worthy of pleasing: it engaged him in the construction of the ark through the devotion of long labor, and by his pious work he survived the world.

Through Shem and Japheth, charity was humbly ashamed of their father’s shame and, having thrown a cloak over their backs, concealed what they had not seen. Charity made Abraham, whose right hand he obediently raised to kill his son, the father of innumerable nations. Charity expanded Isaac’s mind—which he had always kept pure—so that, although his eyes were dim with age, he could see things destined to come long afterward.

Charity compelled Jacob both to mourn from the depths of his being for the loss of his good son and to endure with equanimity the presence of his wicked sons. Charity taught Joseph, sold by his brothers, to endure servitude without a broken spirit and afterward to rule over those same brothers without an exalted mind.

Charity cast Moses prostrate in prayer when the people sinned, even to the point of asking for death; and, through the zeal of his devotion, raised him even to the slaughter of the people, so that he might both offer himself to death for the perishing people [Col. 0891C] and immediately rage against the sinning people in the place of the angry Lord.

Charity raised Phinehas’ arm in vengeance against sinners, so that he seized a sword and pierced the couple who were joining together, and, becoming angry, appeased the Lord’s anger. Charity taught Joshua the scout, so that he first defended the truth in words against lying fellow citizens and afterward bound it by the sword against enemies.

Charity made Samuel humble in his rule and kept him upright in his humiliation. Although he loved the people who persecuted him, he himself bore witness that he did not love the position from which he had been cast down. Charity moved David, before an unjust king, both to flee in humility and to be filled with humility for forgiveness: he fled from his persecutor in fear as from the Lord, yet, when he found an opportunity to strike him, he did not regard him as an enemy.

Charity raised Nathan against the sinful king to the authority of free reproach, yet, when the king’s guilt was absent, laid him humbly prostrate in supplication. Through Isaiah, charity was not ashamed to expose the nakedness of the flesh in preaching, and, withdrawing the carnal veil, penetrated heavenly mysteries.

Charity taught Elijah to live spiritually through the zeal of his fervor and also withdrew him bodily into life. Charity taught Elisha to love his master sincerely and filled him twice over with his master’s spirit. Through charity Jeremiah resisted the people’s descent into Egypt; yet, because he loved the disobedient whom he forbade to descend, he himself descended.

Charity caused Ezekiel, because he had first lifted himself away from earthly desires, afterward to be suspended in the air by the lock of his head. [Col. 0892A] Charity, in Daniel, who restrained his appetite from the king’s food, also closed the mouths of hungry lions for him.

Charity, in the three young men, because it subdued the fires of vices while they were at peace, also tempered the flames of the furnace in the time of tribulation. Charity, in Peter, bravely resisted the threats of terrifying rulers and humbly listened to the words of a lesser man concerning the abolition of circumcision. Charity, in Paul, humbly endured the hands of persecutors and yet, in the matter of circumcision, boldly and discerningly reproved those far his superiors and predecessors.

## CHAPTER IV. The ways in which charity consists

(Pelag.) Charity consists in four ways: first, in love of God; second, in loving ourselves according to God; third, in loving our neighbors; and fourth, also in loving our enemies. We must therefore love God more than ourselves, our neighbor as ourselves, and our enemy as our neighbor.

## CHAPTER V. That no good things are beneficial without charity

(Prosp.) The Apostle Paul says: “If I speak in the tongues of human beings and of angels, but do not have charity, I have become like sounding bronze or a clanging cymbal” (1 Cor. XIII). By the tongues of human beings or angels we should understand the empty eloquence of certain people who undertake the office of teaching more out of the vanity of pleasing than out of charity for giving help. They desire their words to be praised rather than put into practice, and are concerned not with the holiness of their work but with the beauty of carefully polished speech.

Such people are rightly compared with sounding bronze or a clanging cymbal: like ringing bronze or a cymbal, they prefer to make splendid things sound rather than to do them. The Apostle continues: “If I have prophecy and know all mysteries and all knowledge, and if I have all faith, so as to move mountains, but do not have charity, I am nothing” (ibid.). He does not say this as though anyone could possess some good things without charity, but because those things benefit their possessors nothing if they fall away from charity.

“And if I distribute all my possessions to feed the poor, and if I hand over my body so that I may burn, but do not have charity, it profits me nothing” (ibid.). Charity itself, therefore, must be possessed and pursued; without it neither almsgiving, nor the killing of the body, nor any of the things mentioned above, nor any other good things, bring anyone to salvation. For no good action or suffering can benefit us unless it arises from faith working through love. Therefore nothing of damnable sin can remain in those who have it, and nothing good will be lacking to those who possess charity, the cleansing of every defilement and the mother of all good things.

## CHAPTER VI. How the words of blessed Paul the Apostle concerning charity are to be understood

(Greg.) “Charity is patient; it is kind; it does not envy; it is not inflated; it does not act improperly; it is not ambitious; it does not seek its own; it is not provoked; it does not think evil; it does not rejoice over iniquity but rejoices with the truth” (1 Cor. XIII).

Charity is patient because it tolerates inflicted evils with equanimity. It is kind because, in return for evils, it generously supplies good things. It does not envy because, desiring nothing in the present world, it does not know how to envy earthly success. It is not inflated because, while it anxiously desires the reward of inward recompense, it does not exalt itself over external goods. It does not act improperly because, as it expands itself solely in love of God and neighbor, it ignores whatever departs from uprightness.

As for what it means to act improperly, Saint Basil defines it among other things as follows: “Whatever is done not for necessary uses but either for adornment or for some kind of elegance is acting improperly.”

(Greg.) Charity is not ambitious, because, the more ardently it strives inwardly for what belongs to it, the less it covets what belongs to others outwardly. It does not seek its own, because it neglects as foreign everything transitory that it possesses here, recognizing that nothing is its own except what remains with it. It is not provoked, because even when challenged by injuries it does not stir itself to any movement of vengeance, while it awaits greater rewards after great labors.

It does not think evil because, grounding the mind in love of purity and uprooting all hatred from its foundations, it does not know how to turn over in the mind what defiles. It does not rejoice over iniquity because, desiring all people through love alone, it does not exult in the destruction of those who oppose it. It rejoices with the truth because, loving others, it rejoices in what it sees to be upright in them as though it were an increase in its own progress.

(Prosp.) It bears all things because, with the tranquility of a steadfast mind, it bears all restless people and disturbances. It believes all things because, after this life, it believes in the punishments threatened by God without fear. It hopes all things because it hopes joyfully for the promised rewards. It endures all things because it firmly endures while desiring the revelation of the children of God.

(Pelag.) “Charity never fails”: by “does not fail,” he means that it has not slipped away or passed away. It alone remains into the future; or, rightly, because it is true, it will not change.

## CHAPTER VII. How charity is to be shown toward God and how toward one’s neighbor

Therefore, if we show charity toward God and our neighbor from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith, we easily resist sin, abound in every good thing, despise the allurements of the world, and accomplish with love everything that is difficult or even harsh for human frailty—provided that we love God with the charity we have received from him, with our whole heart, our whole soul, and all our strength.

A person sins from that part of himself by which he loves God less. If we love him with our whole heart, there will be nothing in us by which we serve the desires of sin. And what is it to love God except to occupy the mind with him, to conceive hatred of sin for the sake of attaining the enjoyment of his vision, to despise the world, and also to love the neighbor whom he has judged should be loved in himself?

Those who love God wholly and more than themselves are the ones who, for his love, do not spare their own temporal safety, but hand themselves over to tribulation and dangers. They are prepared to be stripped of their possessions, made exiles from their homeland, and to renounce parents, wives, and children. In short, they not only do not flee bodily death itself but even welcome it gladly, desiring to depart from the life of their body rather than from God, the life of their life.

We must love our neighbors as ourselves. We should not regard only those joined to us by degrees of blood relationship as our neighbors; all human beings who share our nature must be regarded as our neighbors. We love all our neighbors as ourselves when we care for their salvation as we do for our own, directing them toward good conduct and the attainment of eternal life; when we think of ourselves in their sins and dangers; and when, just as we would wish to be helped, we help them according to our ability—or, if we lack the means, retain the will to help them.

Therefore the whole love of one’s neighbor consists in this: that you should wish the good to be conferred on your neighbor that you wish to be conferred on yourself. Indeed, you should regard your neighbor’s progress as your own and mourn mercifully over the sins of others as though they were your own.

(Basil.) This is the charity that we ought to have for one another, as the Lord showed and taught when he said: “Love one another as I have loved you. No one has greater love than this: that someone should lay down his life for his friends” (John XIII). If one ought even to lay down one’s life, how much more must the intention and devotion in other matters be understood—not according to human desires, but according to that vision in which the common purpose of all is to please the Lord.

## CHAPTER VIII. How charity is of such great power that we can fulfill the whole Law and all God’s commandments through it

The Apostle demonstrates the great power of charity in what follows when he says (Rom. XIII): “Whoever loves his neighbor has fulfilled the Law. For: ‘You shall not commit adultery, you shall not kill, you shall not steal, you shall not bear false witness, you shall not covet,’ and if there is any other commandment, it is summed up in this saying: ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’” Finally, briefly gathering the reason for this great good, he says: “Love of one’s neighbor does no evil; love is the fullness of the Law” (ibid.).

Above he had said that whoever loves his neighbor has fulfilled the Law. Since it seemed difficult to understand how anyone could fulfill the whole Law in one saying, he gives the fullest explanation: “Love of one’s neighbor does no evil.” Therefore love is the fullness of the Law. Apply love to each individual commandment of the Law and see how easily all are fulfilled.

Can one who loves his neighbor kill him? Certainly no one kills someone whom he loves. Love, therefore, is what fulfills the commandment that says, “You shall not kill.” Similarly, one who loves his neighbor does not commit adultery with his wife. One who loves his neighbor does not steal what belongs to him. One who loves his neighbor does not bear false witness against him. Likewise, if love exists toward one’s neighbor, the other commandments of the Law are observed without difficulty.

It can also be understood that our neighbor is Christ, according to the Gospel’s teaching: he came, found us lying wounded by robbers and stripped by demons, placed us upon the beast of his body, carried us to the inn of the Church, and so forth. If, then, we love this neighbor, we fulfill the whole Law and all the commandments in love of him.

## CHAPTER IX. How, through charity, a friend is loved in God and an enemy is loved for God’s sake

(Greg.) If someone loves another person but does not love him for God’s sake, he does not have charity, although he thinks he does. True charity exists when a friend is loved in God and an enemy is loved for God’s sake. The person who loves those whom he loves for God’s sake also knows how to love those by whom he is not loved.

Charity is usually proved by the adversity of hatred alone. Hence the Lord himself says: “Love your enemies; do good to those who hate you” (Matt. V). Therefore the person loves securely who loves even the one whom he understands not to love him, for it is difficult to express the whole power of charity, since charity alone possesses all God’s commandments. Blessed Augustine says:

“Charity securely possesses the whole breadth and height of the divine words, by which we love God and our neighbor. It tolerates adversities, exercises moderation in prosperity, is strong in harsh sufferings, joyful in good works, most secure in temptation, most generous in hospitality, broadest among true brothers, and most patient among false ones.”

Let what has been written about charity suffice. We must now proceed to the other virtues, insofar as the Author of light will grant us ability.

## CHAPTER X. On hope

(Cassiod.) Hope is the expectation of future good things, expressing a humble disposition and the service of diligent obedience. It is called hope because it is like a foot for advancing—*pes*, a foot. Conversely, despair is so called because it has no ability to advance. For whoever loves sin does not hope for future glory. The person awaits confidently who faithfully keeps God’s commandments.

## CHAPTER XI. That hope benefits only those who cease from evil action

(Isid.) Those who do not cease from doing evil seek forgiveness from God’s mercy in vain, although they would seek it rightly if they ceased from evil action. We must be very careful neither to sin persistently because of the hope of pardon that God promises nor to despair of forgiveness because he justly punishes sins. Let us avoid both dangers: let us turn away from evil and hope for forgiveness from God’s mercy. Every righteous person shines through hope and fear: now hope raises him toward joy, now the terror of Gehenna subjects him to fear.

## CHAPTER XII. That hope must not be placed in a human being

(Aug.) “By hope,” as the Apostle says, “we have been saved” (Rom. VIII). Hope must not be placed in a human being, because, as the divine utterances testify, “Cursed is everyone who places his hope in man” (Jer. XVII). Consequently, anyone who places hope in himself is also bound by the chain of this curse. Therefore we must ask from the Lord God alone whatever we hope either to do well or to obtain for good works.

Let us therefore place our hope in the Lord, as David instructs when he says: “But for me it is good to cling to God, to place my hope in the Lord God” (Ps. LXXII). And again: “My hope is in God” (Ps. LXI).

## CHAPTER XIII. How hope grows amid adversity

(Greg.) Hope in God rises all the more firmly the more serious the things one has endured for its sake. For the joy of recompense from eternity is never gathered unless it is first sown here through devout tribulation. Hence the Psalmist says: “Going they went and wept, casting their seeds. But coming they shall come with rejoicing, carrying their sheaves” (Ps. CXXXV).

## CHAPTER XIV. On faith

(Prosp.) Faith is the foundation of righteousness, preceded by no good works and from which all good things proceed. It cleanses us from every sin, enlightens our minds, reconciles us to God, joins us to all who share our nature, inspires in us hope of future reward, increases holy virtues in us, and confirms us in possession of them.

## CHAPTER XV. That no one can come to rest except through faith working through love

[Col. 0896D] No one can attain true blessedness except through faith. Without faith, as Scripture says, it is impossible to please God (Heb. XI)—that is, the faith that works through love, because, as the Apostle James says: “Faith without works is dead” (James II). And again: “What good is it, my brothers, if someone says he has faith but does not have works? Can faith save him?” (ibid.). Faith without works is idle.

Blessed is the person who both lives well by believing rightly and preserves right faith by living well. The one who is not adorned with good works flatters himself in vain concerning faith alone. Many are Christians in faith only, but in their works they disagree with Christian teaching. Faith is a splendid virtue, through which the holy Fathers were united to God. Read the Epistle of the Apostle Paul to the Hebrews (Heb. II), and you will find this.

## CHAPTER XVI. What difference there is between faith and hope

(Aug.) Faith concerns both good and evil things, since both good and evil things are believed—and this is good faith, not evil faith. Faith also concerns past, present, and future things. We believe that Christ died, which is past; we believe that he sits at the right hand of the Father, which is present; and we believe that he will come to judge, which is future.

Faith also concerns one’s own things and the things of others. Each person believes that he himself began at some time and was certainly not eternal. We also believe many things about others and about other matters—not only about other human beings, many things pertaining to religion, but also about angels.

Hope, however, concerns only good things, only future things, and things pertaining to the person who is said to possess hope of them. Since this is so, for these reasons faith must be distinguished from hope both in name and by rational distinction.

As far as not seeing is concerned, however, what is believed and what is hoped for have this in common in faith and hope. In the Epistle to the Hebrews (Heb. II), which the distinguished defenders of the Catholic rule used as their authority, faith is said to be knowledge of things that are not seen.

Nevertheless, sometimes someone says that he has believed—not because of words, witnesses, or any arguments, but because of the evidence of present things; that is, he has given his faith to them. It does not seem so absurd that he should rightly be corrected in his wording and told, “Did you see it? Then you did not believe it.” From this it may be thought that it does not follow that a thing believed cannot be seen. But we more properly call faith what the divine utterances have taught: faith concerning things that are not seen.

The Apostle also says concerning hope: “Hope that is seen is not hope. For who hopes for what he sees? But if we hope for what we do not see, we await it with patience” (Rom. VIII). Therefore, when we believe that good things are to be in the future, we do nothing other than hope for them.

What shall I say about love, without which faith profits nothing? Hope cannot exist without love. Finally, as the Apostle James says: “The demons believe and tremble” (James II); yet they neither hope nor love. Rather, by believing, they fear that what we hope for and love will come. For this reason the Apostle Paul approves and commends the faith that works through love (Gal. V), and that faith certainly cannot exist without hope. Accordingly, love does not exist without hope, hope without love, or either without faith.

## CHAPTER XVII. That hope, faith, and charity differ from one another

“Now,” says the Apostle Paul, “there remain hope, faith, and charity; but the greatest of these is charity” (1 Cor. XIII). Faith advances into hope, and hope into charity. In the present there are these three; in the future there will be only the charity of the saints, the angels, and God (Prosp.).

Whatever faith and hope promised, charity will bring to completion. That which will always exist is therefore greater than that which will at some point cease. Moreover, prophecy and knowledge or understanding of all mysteries, as well as faith itself and other such things—which are shown to be necessary not for the perfection of the faithful but because of their weakness—will not be necessary in that perfection of the righteous to which those rooted in charity strive to attain. There only perfect charity will remain, when it has joined the perfected to God, from whom it was given.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On prayer

(Cypr.) Our Lord Jesus Christ taught us to pray not only in words but also by deeds. He himself frequently prayed and entreated, and by the testimony of his example showed what we ought to do, as it is written: “But he withdrew into the wilderness and prayed.” And again: “He went out to the mountain to pray, and he spent the night in the prayer of God” (Matt. XIV; Luke VI).

If he prayed who was without sin, how much more ought sinners to pray. And if he prayed throughout the whole night, keeping continual watch and offering uninterrupted prayers, how much more ought we to keep watch at night in frequent prayer.

On this subject blessed Ambrose, bishop, also says: “That the Lord Jesus spent the night in the prayer of God sets before you a pattern that you ought to imitate.”

(Ambr.) What ought you to do for your salvation, when Christ spends the night in prayer for you? What is fitting for you to do when you wish to undertake some work of piety, since Christ, when he was about to send the Apostles, first took care to pray?

## CHAPTER XIX. On the praise and usefulness of prayer

(Joan.) How praiseworthy, useful, and altogether necessary prayer is, Saint John, bishop of Constantinople, says among other things:

“Ecclesiastical prayer loosed Peter’s chains. Paul’s prayer enlarged the boldness of preaching. Prayer extinguished the furnace of fire. Prayer closed the mouths of lions. Prayer restrained rebellion. Prayer opened paradise. Prayer unlocked the hinges of heaven. Prayer made the barren fruitful. Cornelius’s prayer penetrated the heavens.”

(Isid.) “Prayer justified the tax collector. Frequent prayer drives away the devil’s darts. Frequent and continuous prayer overcomes the devil’s weapons. Frequent prayer extinguishes the flames of vices. Prayer is a great fortification of the soul.”

(Basil.) Through the purest prayers, the Lord grants us everything useful, [Col. 0898D] and without doubt all harmful things are driven far away.

## CHAPTER XX. On reverence and devotion in prayer
(Cyprian.) When we stand at prayer, as the most holy martyr Cyprian says, we must watch and devote ourselves to prayer with our whole heart. Let every carnal and worldly thought depart, and at that moment let the mind think of nothing except what it is praying for. For this reason, before prayer the priest, having prefaced it with an exhortation, prepares the minds of the brethren by saying, “Lift up your hearts,” so that when the people respond, “We have them lifted up to the Lord,” we may be reminded that we ought to think of nothing other than the Lord. Let the breast be closed against the adversary and open to God alone; let it not permit the enemy of God to approach it during prayer [Col. 0899A]. For he frequently creeps in and penetrates within, and, subtly deceiving us, diverts our prayers from God, so that we have one thing in our heart and another in our mind, whereas, with sincere intention, it ought not to be the sound of the voice but the mind and understanding that pray to God. What negligence it is to be distracted and captured by foolish and profane thoughts when you are beseeching the Lord—as though there were something else you ought to think about more than speaking with God!

(Benedict.) The most blessed and holy Father Benedict also demonstrates with what devotion and reverence one ought to pray, saying: “If we wish to make some request of powerful men, we presume to do so only with humility and reverence; how much more, then, must we beseech the Lord God of all things with complete humility and devout purity. And let us know that we are heard not through much speaking, but through purity of heart and tears of compunction” [Col. 0899B].

## CHAPTER XXI. That the prayer acceptable to God is the prayer poured forth without hatred of one’s brother

(Gregory.) “When you stand at prayer,” says the Lord, “forgive, if you have anything against another” (Mark XI). Again he says: “Unless you forgive people their sins, neither will your Father who is in heaven forgive you your sins” (Matthew VI). Again he says: “Give, and it will be given to you; forgive, and you will be forgiven” (Luke VI). Again, in establishing the condition of the petition, he set forth the requirement of mercy, saying: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matthew VI). A person rightly asks forgiveness for his own offense when he first releases what has been committed against him [Col. 0899C]. Let us forgive what is owed to us, so that what is owed by us may be forgiven. “Release your neighbor,” says Solomon, “who has injured you, and then your sins will be forgiven when you pray” (Ecclesiasticus XXVIII). For the apostle Paul says: “Therefore I wish men to pray in every place, lifting holy hands without anger or dispute” (I Timothy II).

(Ambrose.) The mind ought to be peaceful in prayer, so that the prayer may attain its effect. For hands are holy when the heart is clean.

## CHAPTER XXII. How we can pray always, without any interruption

(Bede.) For the Lord says: “We ought always to pray and not grow weary” (Luke XVIII). And the apostle Paul says: “Rejoice always and pray without interruption” (II Thessalonians II) [Col. 0899D]. But who can pray always in this way and persist in prayer without weariness or interruption, so that he has no time even to take nourishment or sleep?

It must therefore either be said that the one prays always and does not grow weary who does not cease daily, at the canonical hours, according to the rite of ecclesiastical tradition, to praise and entreat God with psalmody and customary prayers; and that this is what the Psalmist meant when he said: “I will bless the Lord at all times; his praise shall always be in my mouth” (Psalm XXXIII).

Or certainly everything that a righteous person does and says according to God must be regarded as worship. For because the righteous person continually does what is just, the righteous person will therefore pray without interruption and will never cease from prayer—unless he ceases to be righteous. Whether the righteous person eats and drinks, sleeps, works, speaks, or does anything else, if he does it for the glory and praise of God and according to his will, it is prayer [Col. 0900A].

## CHAPTER XXIII. That everything must be done with prayer

(Ambrose.) The servant of God ought to be constant in prayer and, as the apostle Paul says, pray without interruption (I Thessalonians II). For persistent prayers move the mind of the judge to grant mercy. The same Apostle also admonishes us, saying: “Devote yourselves to prayer, keeping watch in it” (Colossians IV).

(Cyprian.) He teaches and shows, of course, that those who ask can obtain from God what they request if God sees them keeping watch in prayer.

(Augustine.) Do not be without prayer by day or by night; rather, when sleep has fallen from your eyes, let your understanding keep watch in prayer [Col. 0900B].

(Jerome.) Just as it is not fitting for a soldier to go out to war without weapons, so it is not beneficial for a Christian to go anywhere without prayer. As we leave our lodging, let prayer arm us; as we return from the street, let prayer meet us. Whatever a Christian begins, let him first direct a prayer to God. Whatever he completes, let him complete that also with prayer. Let him always pray to almighty God in understanding, mind, voice, and deed, asking that God grant him to think, desire, say, and likewise do what is right and pleasing to him, and to reach happily the perseverance of good work and everlasting life.

For he should frequently devote himself to prayer and confess his past sins to God daily in prayer, with tears or groaning [Col. 0900C]. Let him beware lest he fall again into what he recognizes that he lamented with tears. For he must remember what is said: “Do not repeat a word in your prayer” (Ecclesiasticus VII). By this saying the wise man certainly does not forbid us often to ask forgiveness, but forbids us to repeat our sins. It is as though he were plainly saying: “When you have mourned your evil deeds, do not again do what you would then have to lament once more in your prayers.”

## CHAPTER XXIV. That prayer becomes more precious when joined with almsgiving

(Cyprian.) Those who pray must not come to God with fruitless and raw prayers. A petition is ineffective when one asks God with a barren prayer. For since every tree that does not produce good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire, a word that bears no fruit cannot please God when it is made fruitful by no action [Col. 0900D]. Therefore divine Scripture instructs us, saying: “Prayer is good with fasting and almsgiving” (Tobit XII).

Since he will render a reward for works and almsgiving on the day of judgment, he is also today a gracious hearer of the one who comes to prayer with good works. Thus, finally, the centurion Cornelius deserved to be heard when he prayed: “He was making many alms among the people and always praying to God.” At about the ninth hour an angel stood beside him, bearing witness to his works and saying: “Cornelius, your prayers and your almsgiving have ascended as a memorial before God” (Acts X) [Col. 0901A].

(Gregory.) Prayers ascend quickly to God when they bear to him the merits of our works. Hence it is said through the prophet Jeremiah: “Let us lift up our hearts with our hands to God” (Jeremiah III). To lift up one’s heart with one’s hands to God is to join the devotion of our prayer to the merit of good works. Saint Leo, pope, also speaks of this.

(Leo.) Through prayer the mercy of God is sought; through fasting the desire of the flesh is extinguished; through almsgiving sins are redeemed. In prayers faith remains upright, in fasts an innocent life, and in almsgiving a benevolent mind.

## CHAPTER XXV. On the fasting of the outer and inner person

(Augustine.) We say that fasting is the chastisement of the whole body. One must not fast only from the desire for food, but from every delight in temporal pleasures. Therefore the person who devoutly imposes fasts upon his body must renounce vices above all. He must restrain the fuel of desires, break the impulses of the mind, conquer lusts, extinguish the torches of burning avarice, extend the power of love more broadly through his deeds, and generously distribute the expenses of his elaborate preparations as food for the poor [Col. 0901B]. Thus all the shameful sins of the body must be trampled down by the strength of the soul, so that the soul may also be assisted by the holiness of the body.

(Isidore.) This is the perfect and reasonable fast: when our outer person fasts and the inner person prays. Through fasting, prayer more easily penetrates heaven. Fasts are strong weapons against the temptations of demons, for through abstinence they are quickly overcome. Fasts accompanied by good works are pleasing to God [Col. 0901C]. Those who abstain from food but act wickedly imitate the demons, who have no food but always have wickedness. A person abstains well from food when he also fasts from deeds of evil and from the ambitions of the world.

(Cassian.) Hence Cassian, defining the matter among other things, says: “Let us not believe that this fast from visible foods can by itself suffice for perfection of heart and purity of body, unless the fast of the soul also has been joined to it. For the soul too has its harmful foods, by which, even without an abundance of nourishment, it is attacked and brought down into the precipices of luxury. Detraction is its food, and indeed a very sweet one. Anger also is its food, although by no means gentle; yet for a time it feeds it with an unhappy consumption and at once lays it low with a deadly flavor. Envy is food for the mind, and vainglory is its food. Every desire and unstable wandering of the heart is a kind of nourishment for the soul, feeding it with harmful foods [Col. 0901D]. For if, while fasting bodily, we become entangled in the most destructive vices of the soul, our bodily affliction will profit us nothing, since the more precious part has been polluted. Therefore, while the outer person fasts, the inner person must likewise abstain from harmful foods.”

## CHAPTER XXVI. That the perfect fast is commended together with prayer and mercy

(Augustine.) Fasts are necessary for our soul, like medicine for wounds. They bring healing for eternal life, provided, however, that they are commended by the testimony of two things: prayer and mercy [Col. 0902A].

That fasting alone cannot be beneficial, the eloquent teacher Cassian demonstrates in his twenty-first Conference through prophetic testimonies. “The Lord,” he says, “detests the fast of certain people. Speaking in their person, he had first objected to himself, saying: ‘Why have we fasted, and you have not looked upon us? We have humbled our souls, and you have not known it?’ Immediately afterward he revealed the reasons why they did not deserve to be heard: ‘Behold, on the days of your fasting your own will is found, and you exact all your debts. Behold, you fast for lawsuits and quarrels, and you strike with the fist wickedly. Do not fast as you have done until this day, so that your cry may be heard on high. Is this the fast that I have chosen, for a person to afflict his soul for a day? Is it to twist his head like a circle and spread sackcloth and ashes? Will you call this a fast and a day acceptable to the Lord?’” (Isaiah LVIII) [Col. 0902B].

Then he continues, explaining how the restraint of the one who fasts becomes acceptable, and clearly declaring that fasting by itself cannot be beneficial unless it has the following accompanying conditions: “‘Is this not the fast that I have chosen?’ he says. ‘Loose the bonds of wickedness; undo the bundles that oppress; set free those who are broken, and break every burden. Break your bread for the hungry, and bring the poor and homeless into your house. When you see the naked, cover him, and do not despise your own flesh. Then your light will break forth like the morning, and your healing will arise quickly; your righteousness will go before you, and the glory of the Lord will gather you [Col. 0902C]. Then you will call, and the Lord will hear you; you will cry out, and he will say: “Here I am”’” (ibid.).

You see, therefore, that fasting is by no means judged by the Lord to be the principal good, since it becomes good and pleasing to God not through itself but through other works. Again, because of the conditions that accompany it, it is judged not only vain but even hateful, as the Lord says: “When they fast, I will not hear their prayers” (Jeremiah XIV).

(Gregory.) God therefore approves that fast which raises the hands of almsgiving to his eyes; which is performed with love of one’s neighbor; which is prepared from compassion. Therefore give to another what you take away from yourself, so that what afflicts your own flesh may restore the flesh of your needy neighbor.

For this reason the Lord says through the prophet: “When you fasted and mourned, did you fast for me? And when you eat and drink, do you not eat for yourselves and drink for yourselves?” (Zechariah VII) [Col. 0902D]. For the person who receives the nourishment of the body—goods that are common gifts of the Creator—without sharing with the needy eats and drinks for himself. And each person fasts for himself if he does not give to the poor what he temporarily takes away, but keeps it to offer afterward to his belly.

Hence it is said through the prophet Joel: “Sanctify a fast” (Joel I). To sanctify a fast is, by adding other good works, to demonstrate a bodily abstinence worthy of God.

## CHAPTER XXVII. On almsgiving

(Augustine.) Whoever wishes to give alms properly ought to begin [Col. 0903A] with himself and first give them to himself. For almsgiving is a work of mercy, and it has been said most truly: “Have mercy on your own soul, pleasing God.” We are reborn for this purpose: that we may please God, whereas what we contracted by birth rightly displeases him. This is the first almsgiving that we owe ourselves.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. That the virtue of almsgiving is manifold

(Augustine.) “Give alms,” says the Lord, “and behold, everything is clean for you” (Luke XI). Therefore not only does the person give alms who gives food to the hungry, drink to the thirsty, clothing to the naked, shelter to the traveler, a hiding place to the fugitive, visitation to the sick or imprisoned, redemption to the captive, support to the weak, guidance to the blind, consolation to the sorrowful, treatment to the unhealthy, a way to the lost, counsel to one deliberating, and whatever is necessary to anyone in need [Col. 0903B]. The person who gives forgiveness to one who sins also gives alms.

And the person who corrects with a blow one over whom authority has been given, or restrains him with some discipline, yet forgives from the heart the sin of the one by whom he has been harmed or offended, or prays that it may be forgiven him, gives alms—not only in forgiving and praying, but also in rebuking and correcting him through some more appropriate punishment—for he shows mercy.

(Cyprian.) The angel Raphael also urges that almsgiving be performed willingly and generously, saying: “Prayer is good with fasting and almsgiving” (Tobit XII). “For almsgiving delivers from death, and it itself purifies sins.” He shows that our prayers and fasts can accomplish little unless they are assisted by almsgiving, and that mere petitions have little power to obtain anything unless they are joined to the addition of deeds and works [Col. 0903C]. The angel reveals, declares, and confirms that through almsgiving our petitions become more effective, through almsgiving life is rescued from dangers, and through almsgiving souls are delivered from death.

(Isidore.) There are two kinds of almsgiving: one bodily, to give the needy whatever you are able; the other spiritual, to forgive the person by whom you have been injured.

## CHAPTER XXIX. On the praise and usefulness of almsgiving

“Sell,” says the Lord, “what you possess and give alms” (Luke XI). And again: “Give alms, and behold, everything is clean for you” (Luke XII). Solomon says: “A man’s wealth is the ransom of his soul. But whoever has mercy on the poor will be blessed” (Proverbs XIII) [Col. 0903D]. Again Scripture says: “Enclose almsgiving in the bosom of the poor, and it will plead for you against every evil” (Ecclesiasticus XXIX). As water extinguishes a burning fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin.

Again: “Whoever closes his ears so as not to hear the poor will himself call upon the Lord, and there will be no one to hear him” (Proverbs XXI).

(Cyprian.) For the one who has not been merciful cannot obtain the mercy of God, nor will the person who has not been humane toward the poor person’s plea obtain anything from divine compassion through his own prayers. The Holy Spirit declares and confirms this again in the Psalms, saying: “Blessed is the one who understands concerning the needy and the poor; on the evil day the Lord will deliver him” (Psalm XL).

Daniel, moreover, is read to have given King Nebuchadnezzar this counsel [Col. 0904A]: “Therefore, O king, let my counsel please you: redeem your sins with almsgiving and your iniquities with compassion for the poor, and God will be merciful to your sins” (Daniel IV). If he had wished to redeem his sins, he could indeed have escaped the evils he suffered.

For God lends at interest on alms given to the poor, and when it is given to the least, it is given to Christ. For in his judgment he himself will say: “I was hungry and you gave me food; I was thirsty and you gave me drink; I was naked and you clothed me; I was a stranger and you welcomed me; I was sick and in prison and you visited me,” and so forth. And: “What you did for one of the least of mine, you did for me.” Then they will hear that blessed voice: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matthew XXV).

## CHAPTER XXX. That through almsgiving the forgiveness of all sins is granted [Col. 0904B]

The blessed Tobias, admonishing his son to give alms, says among other things: “From your substance, my son, give alms, and do not turn your face away from any poor person; for then it will happen that the face of the Lord will not be turned away from you. Be merciful as you are able. If you have much, give abundantly; if you have little, willingly strive to share even a little. For you are storing up a good reward for yourself on the day of necessity, because almsgiving delivers from every sin and from death and will not allow the soul to go into darkness” (Tobit IV).

## CHAPTER XXXI. How divinely, piously, and beneficially Scripture instructs us to pursue almsgiving [Col. 0904C]

“Almsgiving will have great confidence before the Most High God for all who practice it” (Tobit IV). Hence also a certain wise man says: “My son, do not defraud the poor of almsgiving, and do not turn your eyes away from the poor. Do not despise the hungry soul, and do not embitter the poor in his poverty. Do not afflict the heart of the needy, and do not delay giving to one in distress” (Ecclesiasticus X).

Therefore whoever wishes to learn more about the virtue of almsgiving should read the book that the most holy martyr Cyprian wrote on Almsgiving, and the book that the blessed Maximinus, bishop of Turin, likewise wrote on Almsgiving; there he will find sufficient instruction.

## CHAPTER XXXII. On humility [Col. 0904D]

(Basil.) Humility is this: to consider all people superior to ourselves and ourselves inferior and more insignificant than everyone—not merely to declare this in humble speech, but also to believe it with the innermost feeling of our heart.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. On the praise of humility

Our Lord and Redeemer, to summon us to humility, showed us through his Gospel the pattern of humility, saying: “Learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls” (Matthew XI). For he himself says through the prophet [Col. 0905A]: “And upon whom shall I look, except upon the humble and quiet person who trembles at my words?” (Isaiah LXVI).

Hence the blessed apostle Peter says: “All of you, practice humility toward one another. For God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble” (I Peter V). Be grounded in humility; be the last of all. Humble yourself so that you may be exalted. Make yourself least of all; put yourself before no one and consider yourself superior to no one. Consider everyone superior to you, even if you are the highest. Hold fast to humility, because if you hold fast to humility, you will be glorious. For the more humble you are, the more exalted a glory follows you. Descend so that you may ascend; humble yourself so that you may be exalted, lest, once exalted, you be humbled.

Humility does not know a fall; humility does not experience a collapse. The person who is insignificant in his own eyes is great before God. And the person who displeases himself pleases God [Col. 0905B]. Therefore be little in your own eyes, so that you may be great in the eyes of God. You will be all the more precious before God the more despised you are in your own eyes.

Always bear shame upon your face in remembrance of sin. You are dust; sit in dust. You are ashes; live in ashes. In the highest honor let the highest humility be yours; let honor not lift you up. Show yourself with the greater humility the more distinguished you are in rank.

(Gregory.) The occasion of our destruction was therefore the devil’s pride, while the instrument of our redemption was found in God’s humility. Our enemy, created among all things, wished to be exalted above all things; but our Redeemer, remaining great above all things, deigned to become little among all things [Col. 0905C]. Thus let it be said to the humble: “While they abase themselves, they ascend to the likeness of God.” Let it be said to the exalted: “While they raise themselves up, they fall in imitation of the apostate angel.”

## CHAPTER XXXIV. How holy men, by the authority of humility, strike at the faults of sinners

Holy men, through the authority of humility, spare no powers that act against the truth. Those whom they see being lifted up through pride, they press down by the authority of the Spirit.

Hence Moses, coming from the desert, approached the king of Egypt with authority, saying: “Thus says the Lord God of the Hebrews: How long will you refuse to submit to me? Let my people go, so that they may sacrifice to me.” When Pharaoh, oppressed by plagues, said to him, “Go, sacrifice to your God in the land,” Moses immediately replied with greater authority: “It cannot be done so, for we will sacrifice to the Lord our God the abominations of the Egyptians” (Exodus V).

Hence Nathan approached the sinful King David. First presenting to him a likeness of the transgression he had committed and holding him guilty by the voice of his own judgment, he immediately added: “You are that man who has done this thing” (II Kings XII).

Hence the man of God sent to destroy idolatry in Samaria, when King Jeroboam was burning incense upon the altar, neither fearing the king nor constrained by fear of death, fearlessly exercised the authority of free speech against the altar, saying: “Altar, altar, thus says the Lord: Behold, a son shall be born to the house of David, Josiah by name, and he shall sacrifice upon you the priests of the high places” (III Kings XIII).

Hence proud Ahab, enslaved to the service of idols, presumed to rebuke Elijah, saying: “Are you the one who troubles Israel?” Elijah immediately struck down the foolishness of the proud king with a rebuke spoken in free authority, saying: “It is not I who have troubled Israel, but you and your father’s house, because you have abandoned the commandments of the Lord and followed the Baals” (III Kings XVIII).

Hence Elisha, following the true greatness of his teacher, convicted that same Ahab, who came to him with King Jehoshaphat, of the guilt of his faithlessness, saying: “What have you to do with me? Go to the prophets of your father and your mother.” And: “As the Lord of hosts lives, before whom I stand, if I did not respect the face of Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, I would neither pay attention to you nor look upon you” (IV Kings III).

Hence the same man stopped Naaman at his door when he came to him with horses and chariots. Though accompanied by an abundance of talents and garments, Elisha did not go out to meet him or open the door of the house, but sent word that he was to wash seven times in the Jordan. Therefore Naaman departed in anger, saying: “I thought that he would come out to me” (IV Kings V).

Hence, when the priests and rulers prohibited Peter from speaking in the name of Jesus, even savagely beating him, he immediately replied with great authority: “Whether it is right in the sight of God to listen to you rather than to God, judge for yourselves. For we cannot fail to speak of what we have seen and heard” (Acts IV).

Hence, when Paul saw the high priest resisting the truth, and when the high priest’s attendant struck him on the mouth, Paul did not respond in confusion with a curse; rather, filled with the Spirit, he prophesied in a free voice, saying: “God will strike you, whitewashed wall! Do you sit judging me according to the law, while contrary to the law you order me to be struck?” (Acts XXIII).

Hence Stephen, even as he was about to die, did not fear to exercise the authority of speech against the violence of his persecutors, saying: “You stiff-necked people, uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit, just as your fathers did” (Acts VII) [Col. 0906D].

But because holy men rise to words of such height through zeal for truth, not through the vice of pride, they themselves plainly demonstrate this: by their other deeds and words they show both how much humility they possess and how greatly they burn with love toward those whom they rebuke.

Pride generates hatred; humility, love. Therefore the words that love makes severe certainly flow from the fountain of humility. How could Stephen have uttered rebuke through pride, when he prayed on bent knees for those whom he had rebuked, as they grew worse and stoned him, saying: “Lord, do not hold this sin against them” (Acts VII)?

How could Paul, in proud harshness, have spoken against the priest and ruler of his own people, when in humility he subjected himself even to the service of his disciples, saying: “For we do not preach ourselves, but Jesus Christ our Lord; and ourselves as your servants through Christ” (I Corinthians I)?

How could Peter have resisted the rulers through pride, when, having compassion on their error, he excused their offense as though it were guilt arising from ignorance, saying: “I know that you acted through ignorance, as did your rulers. But God fulfilled what he had foretold through the mouth of all the prophets, that his Christ would suffer” (Acts III) [Col. 0907A]. He drew them toward life through mercy, saying: “Therefore repent and be converted, so that your sins may be blotted out” (ibid.).

How could Elisha have refused to see Naaman through pride, when he permitted himself not only to be seen but also to be touched by a woman? It is written of her: “When she had come to the man of God on the mountain, she seized his feet. And Gehazi approached to remove her. But the man of God said: ‘Leave her, for her soul is in bitterness’” (IV Kings IV).

How could Elijah have spoken words of rebuke to the proud king because of his arrogance, when he humbly ran before his chariot, as it is written: “And, with his loins girded, he ran before Ahab” (III Kings XIII)?

How could he have despised Jeroboam’s presence through pride, when in compassion he immediately restored his withered right hand to its former health, as it is written: “When the king heard the word of the man of God, which he had cried out against the altar at Bethel, he stretched out his hand from the altar, saying: ‘Seize him!’ And his hand withered” (ibid.)? And shortly afterward: “The man of God prayed before the face of the Lord, and his hand returned to him and became as it had been before” (ibid.) [Col. 0907B].

Since pride does not know how to produce virtues, the voice of rebuke is shown to have come from humility by the signs that accompany it.

How could Nathan have raged against King David through words of rebuke, when, as he rebuked the king’s guilt, he prostrated himself upon the ground before him, as it is written: “They announced to the king, saying: ‘Nathan the prophet is here.’ And when he had entered before the king, he worshiped him, prostrate on the ground”?

How could Moses, freely resisting the king of Egypt, have despised him, when, conversing familiarly with God, he humbly worshiped Jethro, his kinsman who followed him? He also showed such obedience to Jethro’s counsel that, after his secret conversations with God, he considered it a great gain to hear outside from the mouth of a human being.

From the other deeds of the saints, then, we learn what we ought to consider about others. Holy men are neither outspoken through pride nor submissive through fear. When uprightness raises them to freedom of speech, consideration of their own weakness keeps them in humility [Col. 0907D]. Although they strike the faults of sinners from a height when they rebuke them, they nevertheless judge themselves more subtly within and, as it were, place themselves among the lowly. In whatever way they pursue what is wrong in others, they make themselves more severe in restraining it within themselves.

Again, precisely because they do not spare themselves when they are doing better things, they rebuke the faults of others all the more vigilantly. What could those who despise themselves even when they inwardly grasp the stronghold of exaltation marvel at in human power? They therefore rightly judge outwardly the height of earthly eminence, because inwardly the weight of pride does not burden their eye.

## CHAPTER XXXV. On patience

(Cyprian.) True patience is to endure the evils of others with equanimity and not to be gnawed by pain even against the person who inflicts those evils. For whoever bears the evils of his neighbor while nevertheless suffering inwardly in silence and awaiting the time of a fitting repayment does not display patience but merely pretends to do so. For it is written: “Charity is patient, charity is kind” (I Corinthians XIII). It is patient in order to tolerate the evils of others; it is kind in order to love even those whom it bears.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. On the praise of patience

(Cyprian.) Patience, dearly beloved brothers, not only guards what is good but also repels adversity. Cherishing the Holy Spirit and clinging to heavenly and divine things, it resists deeds of the flesh and body—by which the soul is attacked and captured—with the bulwark of its virtues [Col. 0908B].

The virtue of patience extends widely. Its abundance and generosity proceed from the source of a single name, but through its overflowing channels they spread along many paths of glory. Nothing in our actions can advance toward perfect glory unless it receives from patience the firmness of completion.

Patience is what both commends us to the Lord and preserves us. It moderates anger, restrains the tongue, governs the mind, guards peace, directs discipline, breaks the impulse of lust, suppresses violent pride, and extinguishes the fire of hostility. It restrains the power of the rich and revives the poverty of the poor. It protects blessed integrity in virgins, laborious chastity in widows, and undivided chastity in married men and women. It makes people humble in prosperity, courageous in adversity, and gentle in the face of injuries and insults [Col. 0908C].

It teaches sinners to forgive quickly and, if one has sinned oneself, to ask forgiveness for a long time and earnestly. It conquers temptations, endures persecutions, and brings sufferings and martyrdoms to completion. It is the virtue that firmly fortifies the foundations of our faith. It is the virtue that grants growth to hope through sublimity. It directs us so that we may be able to hold to the way of Christ, as we enter it through its endurance. It makes us persevere as children of God, as we imitate the patience of the Father.

For this is the highest expression of Christianity: to return love to those who love us and patience to those who injure us. Therefore whoever is more patient under injury will be established more powerfully in the kingdom.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. Examples of the holy Fathers concerning patience [Col. 0908D]

(Cyprian.) Peter, upon whom the Lord’s Church was founded by his gracious will, sets forth and says in his Epistle: “Christ suffered for you, leaving you an example so that you might follow in his footsteps. He committed no sin, and no deceit was found in his mouth. When he was reviled, he did not revile in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten. But he handed himself over to the one who judged unjustly” (I Peter II).

Finally, we find that the patriarchs, the prophets, and all the righteous, who bore the figure of Christ with the image preceding them, guarded nothing more carefully among the praises of their virtues than the fact that they maintained patience with strong and steadfast equanimity.

Thus Abel, beginning and dedicating the origin of martyrdom and the suffering of the righteous man, does not resist or struggle against his fratricidal brother, but is humbly and gently killed with patience [Col. 0909A].

(Bernard.) Noah endured long labors for a hundred years in building the ark, but bore them patiently and without murmuring.

(Cyprian.) Thus Abraham, believing God and first establishing the root and foundation of faith, when tested in his son neither doubts nor hesitates, but obeys God’s commands with the complete patience of devotion. Isaac, prefigured in the likeness of the Lord’s sacrifice, is likewise found patient when he is offered by his father to be sacrificed.

Jacob, driven from his home by his brother, departs patiently; afterward, with even greater patience, he recalls that same impious persecutor, still as a suppliant, to reconciliation through peaceful gifts.

Joseph, sold and banished by his brothers, not only forgives patiently but also generously and mercifully distributes grain without payment to those who come [Col. 0909B].

(Gregory.) Moses is frequently despised by an ungrateful and treacherous people and is almost stoned, yet, gentle and patient, he prays to the Lord on behalf of those same people. Samuel, moreover, is expelled from his leadership by a wicked people, yet with tearful prayers he patiently entreats the Lord for those same people.

(Cyprian.) In David, from whom Christ’s birth according to the flesh arose, what great, wondrous, and Christian patience appeared! He often had Saul, the king who was persecuting him and desired to kill him, in his power; he could have killed him, yet preferred to preserve him when he was subject to him and delivered into his hands. He did not repay his enemy in kind, but even avenged him after he had been killed.

[Col. 0909C]

(John Chrysostom.) The prophet Isaiah is reported to have endured patiently being sawn apart by the treacherous. The prophet Jeremiah, bound with a cord, is nevertheless said to have endured everything patiently for the Lord. Ezekiel, placed in captivity, is known to have been patient in all things. Daniel was thrown into the lions’ den and was found to have been patient in all his tribulations for the love of God. The three young men, cast into the furnace of fire for the love of God, endured patiently; hence they earned a celebrated name in the holy Church.

Job, struck by the loss of his children, deprived of immeasurable possessions, afflicted with the most grievous torments of his body, harassed by his wife with many reproaches, and mocked by his friends, never uttered an unworthy word from his mouth, but endured everything patiently. Tobias, struck with blindness and reproached by his wife, never let a word of complaint escape from his mouth, but is always recognized as having been patient in all things.

The Maccabean martyrs patiently endured countless tortures for the law of their God. John the Baptist was thrust into prison by the most impious king Herod, and there was patiently put to death for asserting the truth. Peter, the chief of the apostles—as is read in the Acts of the Apostles—was often scourged, together with his fellow apostles, for the worship of the Divinity, and is always found to have been patient and joyful. Therefore Scripture says: “The apostles went away rejoicing from the presence of the council, because they had been deemed worthy to suffer dishonor for the name of Jesus” (Acts IV).

The apostle Paul suffered many things for the love of Christ, which it is difficult even to enumerate:

[Col. 0910A]

prisons, chains, blows, scourges, punishments. He was stoned by the Jews, beaten with rods, thrown down, encountered robbers, and endured ambushes from false brothers; within there was fear, outside there was conflict. He suffered hunger, nakedness, slanders, ambushes, and tribulations. He endured wild beasts—and why say more? He dies daily, yet in all these things he rejoices and glories, and, patient and exultant, says: “I rejoice in my sufferings” (Col. I). And again: “But not only that, we also glory in tribulations” (Rom. V).

If, then, such a man rejoiced and gloried while suffering so much, what forgiveness or excuse will there be for those who are impatient over small injuries and blows, or over whatever tribulations—which are certainly lesser than those—may befall them?

The apostle and evangelist John, thrown into a boiling vat and banished into exile on the island of Patmos, patiently endured, for the love of Christ, every adversity inflicted upon him. Stephen, ordained a deacon by the apostles, with a peaceful heart prays for his very enemies amid the hands of those stoning him, kneeling with his knees fixed on the ground.

Behold, instructed by divine Scripture, we recognize that our holy fathers who preceded us earned heavenly crowns through the virtue of patience.

(Gregory.) Therefore, brothers, preserve patience in your minds and exercise it in action whenever circumstances demand it. Let no losses of your possessions disturb you. If you fear losses that will remain fixed in your mind, you do not regard the losses of passing things as grievous. If you behold the glory of eternal recompense, you do not grieve over a temporary injury. Therefore, endure your adversaries,

[Col. 0910C]

but love as brothers those whom you endure.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. Testimonies of the Sacred Scriptures concerning patience

Our Lord and Redeemer, whom the prophet calls the Prince of Peace (Isa. IX), at whose birth according to the flesh the angelic host sang, “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke II), said before ascending in the flesh to the heavenly realms: “By your patience you will possess your souls” (Luke XXI).

Thus also the apostle Paul says: “You have need of patience, so that, by doing the will of God, you may receive the promise” (Hebr. X). Again: “Pursue peace with all and holiness, without which no one will see God” (Hebr. XIII).

Hence James says: “Let patience have its perfect work, so that you may be perfect and complete, lacking in nothing. Blessed is the man who endures temptation, for when he has been tested he will receive the crown of life which God promised to those who love him” (James I).

Hence Solomon says: “The patient man is better than the strong, and he who rules his spirit is better than he who captures cities” (Prov. XVI).

Therefore, beloved, let us have peace, because God has commanded the peaceful and harmonious to dwell in his house, so that we who have begun to be sons of God may remain in God’s peace, and that those who have one Spirit may also have one mind and one understanding (Cyprian).

For the most blessed martyr Cyprian wrote an exceptionally elegant book On the Good of Patience. Whoever wishes to read it will be able to find in it fully what a good patience is.

[Col. 0911A]

## CHAPTER XXXIX. On forbearance

(Gregory.) If we are sons of the elect, it necessarily remains for us to walk by their examples. For he was not good who refused to tolerate the wicked. Hence blessed Job asserts this concerning himself, saying: “I was a brother to dragons and a companion to ostriches” (Job XXX).

Hence, through Solomon, the holy Church is addressed in the voice of the Bridegroom: “As a lily among thorns, so is my beloved among the daughters” (Song II).

Hence the Lord says to Ezekiel: “Son of man, do not fear them, nor dread their words, because they are unbelievers and subversives with you, and you dwell among scorpions” (Ezek. II).

Hence Peter glorifies the life of blessed Lot, saying: “He rescued righteous Lot, oppressed by the injury and wanton conduct of the wicked. For by sight and hearing he was righteous while living among them, who from day to day tormented his righteous soul with unlawful deeds” (II Pet. II).

Hence Paul both praises and strengthens the life of the disciples, saying: “In the midst of a crooked and perverse nation, among whom you shine like lights in the world, holding fast the word of life” (Phil. II).

Hence John bears witness to the Church at Pergamum, saying: “I know where you dwell, where Satan’s throne is; yet you hold fast my name and have not denied my faith” (Rev. II).

Behold, dearest brothers, as we review almost everything, we recognize that no one was good whom the wickedness of the evil did not test. For, so to speak, the iron of our soul is never brought to the sharpness of an edge unless the file of another’s wickedness has rubbed it.

[Col. 0911C]

Therefore, let us tolerate our adversaries, but without ceasing let us love those whom we tolerate, and let us freely give them whatever good we can. For God accepts only that sacrifice which the flame of charity kindles before his eyes on the altar of good works.

Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Love your enemies; bless those who hate you, and pray for those who persecute and slander you, so that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. V).

## CHAPTER XL. What the forbearance of God’s servants ought to be in time of tribulation

[Col. 0911D]

You ought, O Christian, to move always with an even—or rather a more joyful—heart amid hatred in people’s hearts, insults of their tongues, and the very hands of persecutors.

And if your possessions have been taken from you, say: “Naked I came from my mother’s womb, and naked I shall depart from here” (Job I). Add also that apostolic saying: “We brought nothing into this world, and neither can we take anything away” (I Tim. VI).

If you hear yourself cursed, slandered among people, and burdened with insults, remember and place before your eyes the word of the Lord, who says: “Woe to you when all people speak well of you” (Luke VI). And again: “Rejoice and exult when they cast out your name as evil, for the sake of the Son of Man” (ibid.).

You have been driven from your homeland and your house: remember that “we have no enduring city here, but we seek the one that is to come.” Why, then, do you think you have lost your homeland, when you are a stranger throughout the whole earth?

But if you have also fallen into a very serious illness, use that apostolic saying in which he says: “Even if our outward man is corrupted, yet the inward man is renewed day by day” (II Cor. IV).

You have been shut in prison, and a cruel death threatens and is being prepared for you: bring before your eyes John, struck on the neck in prison, and yet the prophet’s head was given to a dancing girl as the reward of lust.

[Col. 0912A]

Thus, whenever each of these injuries is inflicted, in view of the glory that is repaid for them, the person who suffers this is not only absolved from sins but also acquires righteousness—provided only that faith and steadfastness do not abandon him.

## CHAPTER XLI. On forgiveness

The Lord says: “If you forgive people their sins, your heavenly Father will also forgive you your sins. But if you do not forgive people their sins, neither will your Father forgive you your sins” (Matt. VI).

Hence Peter says: “Not returning evil for evil, nor curse for curse, but on the contrary blessing, because you were called to this, so that you may possess the inheritance of blessing” (I Pet. III).

Hence Paul says: “Supporting one another with patience” (Eph. IV), and forgiving one another. “If anyone has a grievance against another, just as God forgave you in Christ, so also do you; returning evil to no one for evil.”

Hence divine Scripture says: “Do not seek revenge, nor remember the injury done by your fellow citizens” (Lev. XIX).

Hence Solomon says: “Do not say, ‘I will repay evil for evil’; wait for the Lord, and he will deliver you” (Prov. XX).

Forgive your neighbor who harms you, and then your sins will be released when you pray. Therefore, whoever wishes to receive forgiveness of his sins must forgive all who sin against him, because each person will receive from the Lord such forgiveness as he himself has granted to his neighbor.

## CHAPTER XLII. On mercy

Mercy received its name from compassion for another’s misery. All sins are cleansed by the resources of mercy, but let the person who grants mercy beware of sinning. Otherwise there is no forgiveness of an offense when mercy comes first in such a way that sins follow it.

No one can be merciful toward another who, by living wickedly, is not merciful toward himself. For if he is wicked toward himself, toward whom is he good? No crimes can be redeemed by acts of mercy if a person remains in sins. Forgiveness then obtains the fruit of mercy when one ceases from the work of crimes.

Therefore, let us be merciful toward all, so that we too may obtain mercy from the Lord, who says: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matt. V). And again: “Be merciful, therefore, just as your Father is merciful” (Luke VI).

[Col. 0913A]

Hence Paul says: “Be kind and merciful to one another; clothe yourselves, as God’s elect, with compassion” (Eph. IV).

Hence Solomon says: “To practice mercy and judgment is more pleasing to the Lord than sacrifices” (Prov. XXI).

Hence it is said through a certain wise man: “Whoever practices mercy offers a sacrifice” (Ecclus. XXXV).

## CHAPTER XLIII. On compassion
