Through his Gospel the Lord admonishes us, saying: “Whatever you wish people to do to you, do likewise to them; for this is the law and the prophets” (Matt. VII).

What you do not wish to happen to you, do not desire to happen to your neighbor. Grieve over the calamities of others; be filled with tears. In another’s labors and in another’s tribulation, you too should be sad.

Be toward others as you wish others to be toward you. What you do not wish to suffer, do not do, nor inflict evils upon another, lest you suffer similar things. Be as merciful toward another’s offenses as toward your own, so that you do not judge yourself one way and others another. Judge others as you wish to be judged.

Do not cease to assist those placed in tribulation; do not fail to console the grieving.

## CHAPTER XLIV. On chastity

Chastity is a sweet fruit; the chastity of the saints is inviolate beauty, security of mind, and health of body. For unless each person perseveres in chastity, he will not be able to reach everlasting rest or see God, as the apostle Paul testifies: “Pursue peace with all and holiness, without which no one will see God” (Hebr. XII).

Here too he clearly declared that without holiness—which he ordinarily calls integrity of mind or purity of body—God cannot be seen at all.

(Cassiodorus.) Hence it is said through the same apostle: “This is the will of God, your sanctification: that you abstain from fornication, that each of you know how to possess his own vessel in honor and sanctification, not in the passion of desire, like the nations that do not know God” (I Thess. IV).

Therefore, let us love chastity, because God dwells in chaste minds and chaste bodies, but condemns the lustful and unclean. For however many good things a person may have done—however much he may pray, spend nights in prayers and vigils, give all his possessions to the poor, wear down his body through hunger and prolonged fasts, and fulfill the other divine commandments—if he has not had chastity, none of it will benefit him.

[Col. 0913D]

Hence the Lord also commanded in the Gospel, saying: “Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning in your hands” (Luke XII).

Two things are commanded: to gird the loins and to hold lamps, so that there may be both the purity of chastity in the body and the light of truth in action. Our Redeemer cannot possibly be pleased with one without the other: if someone who does good has not yet abandoned the stains of lust, or if someone who excels in chastity has not yet exercised himself in good works.

Therefore chastity is not great without good works, nor is good work anything without chastity.

## CHAPTER XLV. [Col. 0914A] On obedience

Obedience is the holy way that leads its followers to the heavenly homeland. Along this way our Lord Jesus Christ deigned to walk for us and for our salvation. Of him the apostle Paul says: “Christ became obedient unto death, even death on a cross” (Phil. II).

Along this way the patriarch Abraham ran when, at the Lord’s command, he led his beloved son to be sacrificed. Along this way the holy apostles Peter and Andrew followed the Lord’s call, leaving their nets. Along this way Matthew followed the Lord, abandoning the profits of the tax office. Along this holy way all the patriarchs, prophets, apostles, martyrs, and other elect deserved to reach God.

Although it is a narrow and confined way, it nevertheless led its travelers to everlasting life, as the Lord says: “Narrow and confined is the way that leads to life” (Mark VII).

Let it not seem hard or harsh to you when you hear that obedience is a narrow and confined way; rather, rejoice because of what follows: “which leads to life.”

For if people, because of a king’s command or that of some powerful man, travel to foreign regions—even overseas and alien, wholly unknown, and extremely dangerous places—for some temporary profit, which can be taken from them as soon as they possess it, and are so obedient that they willingly and eagerly cross countless regions and homelands, endure the difficulties of lands, rough and hard roads, dangerous shipwrecks on rivers,

[Col. 0914C]

terrible waves and sea billows, hostile swords, the ambushes of robbers, and attacks by enemies; if they willingly endure all this, abandoning their own country, parents—father, mother, brothers, sisters, relatives—wives, children, homes, slaves, and all their possessions, while friends mourn, parents grieve, children weep, and slaves are saddened, not knowing whether they will ever see them again—and yet none of these things can draw them back from the command of the one who ordered it, but with complete devotion they obey a powerful man who exists today and perhaps will not exist tomorrow—if, as we have already said, they endure all these things in order to receive some earthly profit in return, what will we wretched people say on the day of judgment in our defense before our God, since we are disobedient to his holy and saving commands and do not obey the salutary admonitions of our fathers?

What worldly people do for a perishing thing, let Christ’s soldiers do for glory that will remain without end. What they do in obedience for empty exaltation, let Christ’s servants do in obedience for unfailing excellence. What they do in obedience for the perishing glory of a perishing man, let Christ’s servants do in obedience for the perpetual glory of the perpetual Redeemer.

Therefore, let no sluggishness, insolence, delay, or laziness hold us back from the good work of obedience, because even if the way by which we travel is harsh, the homeland to which we arrive is blessed.

Let us therefore obey our fathers and elders insofar as they issue commands according to God. But if what they command is against God, let us say to them humbly and reverently: “We must obey God rather than men” (Acts V).

## CHAPTER XLVI. How subjects ought to obey their superiors

Therefore, dearest brothers, let us obey our superiors and fathers with a joyful spirit and a most willing mind, because the divine voice commands us through the apostle Paul, saying: “Obey your superiors in the Lord and submit to them” (Hebr. XIII).

For the more humble and obedient we are, the more lightly and sweetly we shall feel the Lord’s yoke upon us. The more obedient we are to our superiors and fathers, the more God will obey our prayers. The prayer of one obedient person is heard more quickly than ten thousand prayers of a contemptuous person.

Therefore, with holy intent and complete speed, let us obey the commands of our elders. As soon as something has been ordered to us by a superior, let us not tolerate delay in doing it, as though it had been commanded by God himself, because the obedience shown to superiors is shown to God.

For he himself said: “Whoever hears you hears me” (Luke X). For the love of God, let us submit ourselves in all obedience to our superiors, so that we may be able to imitate our Lord, of whom the apostle says: “Christ became obedient unto death” (Phil. II).

## CHAPTER XLVII. How we ought to obey one another

We ought to obey one another as servants of the Lord, according to what the Lord commanded: “Whoever wishes to be great among you, let him become the least of all and the servant of all” (Matt. XX).

He added this also, to incline us more toward humility: “Just as the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve” (ibid.).

And there is also what the apostle said: “Through charity of spirit, serve one another” (Gal. V).

## CHAPTER XLVIII. Those who truly love God desire to obey beyond their strength

Whoever faithfully and purely loves God, and is certain of the Lord’s recompense, does not consider what has been enjoined upon him sufficient. Rather, he always seeks an increase in his work and desires and longs for greater things to be enjoined, even if what he does appears to be beyond his strength.

He is never secure as though his work were complete; on the contrary, he is anxious and troubled, as one who has done nothing worthy of the Gospel commandments, remembering that saying of the Lord: “When you have done all that I have commanded you, then say: ‘We are unworthy servants; we have done what we ought to have done’” (Luke XVII).

## CHAPTER XLIX. On the praise and character of obedience

Obedience alone is the virtue that implants the other virtues in the mind and preserves them once implanted. Hence the first man received a command to keep; if he had willingly submitted himself to it in obedience, he would have reached eternal blessedness without labor.

Hence Samuel says: “Obedience is better than sacrifices, and to listen than to offer the fat of rams” (I Sam. XV).

Obedience is rightly placed before sacrifices, because through sacrifices another’s flesh is slaughtered, but through obedience one’s own will is put to death. Therefore each person pleases God more quickly when, with the pride of his own will suppressed before God’s eyes, he sacrifices himself with the sword of the commandment.

But because we are sometimes commanded the prosperous things of this world and sometimes its adversities, we must understand with the greatest care that obedience is sometimes nothing if it has something of its own, while at other times it is very little if it has nothing of its own.

When success in this world is commanded and a position of superiority is imposed, the person who obeys in order to obtain these things empties obedience of its virtue if he also yearns for them from his own desire. For he does not direct himself under obedience who, in seeking the prosperity of this life, serves the lust of his own ambition.

Again, when contempt of the world is commanded, when reproaches and insults are ordered, unless the mind itself desires these things, it diminishes the merit of obedience, because it descends unwillingly and reluctantly to what is despised in this life.

[Col. 0916B]

Obedience is brought to its detriment when the mind is accompanied by none of its own wishes in receiving the reproaches of this age. Therefore obedience ought to possess something of its own in adversities, while in prosperity it ought in every way to possess nothing of its own, so that in adversities it may be more glorious insofar as it is joined even by desire to the divine order, and in prosperity it may be more genuine insofar as the present glory it receives from God is completely separated from the mind.

We can show the weight of this virtue more clearly if we recall two heroes of the heavenly homeland.

When Moses was tending sheep in the desert, he was called by the Lord through an angel speaking in fire to preside over the entire multitude of Israelites, who were to be rescued. But because he was humble in his mind, he immediately feared the glory of such great leadership when it was offered to him, and at once took refuge in a defense based on his weakness, saying: “I beg you, Lord, I am not eloquent; for yesterday and the day before, and from the time when you began to speak to your servant, I have become slow and impeded in speech” (Exod. IV).

And, setting himself aside, he asks for another, saying: “Send whom you will send” (ibid.). Behold, he speaks with the authority of his tongue, yet, so as not to receive the power of such great leadership, he claims to be speechless.

Paul, too, had been divinely instructed when he ought to go up to Jerusalem, as he himself says to the Galatians: “Then after fourteen years I went up again to Jerusalem, taking Barnabas and Titus with me. I went up according to a revelation” (Gal. II).

On the journey, when he encountered the prophet Agabus, he heard how much adversity awaited him in Jerusalem. For it is written: “The Jews will bind in Jerusalem the man whose belt this is” (Acts XXI).

[Col. 0917A]

Paul immediately responds: “I am ready not only to be bound but also to die in Jerusalem for the name of Jesus” (ibid.); “for I do not consider my life more precious.”

Thus, going to Jerusalem after receiving the revelation, he recognizes the adversities and then willingly embraces them. He hears what he should fear, but he burns more ardently to meet it.

Moses, therefore, has nothing of his own with respect to prosperity, because he asks to be excused so that he will not be placed over the Israelite people. Paul, on the other hand, is led toward adversity even by his own desire, because he learns of the evils threatening him, yet through the devotion of his spirit he grows fervent even for harsher things.

The former, at God’s command, wished to avoid the glory of present leadership. The latter, with God promising harsh and difficult things, strove to prepare himself for still greater hardships.

Therefore, following the unbroken virtue of both leaders, let us establish that if we truly strive to grasp the palm of obedience, we should serve in the prosperity of this age solely because of a command, but in adversities also out of devotion.

It must be understood, however, that evil is never to be done through obedience, though sometimes the good being done ought to be interrupted through obedience. For the tree in paradise was not evil, the tree which God forbade man to touch. But so that the well-formed human being might grow through the better merit of obedience, it was fitting that God should also prohibit him from something good, so that the virtue of his action might be more genuine insofar as, abstaining from a good thing, he showed himself more humbly subject to his Creator.

## CHAPTER L. On manual labor

A soldier of Christ ought to work with his hands, devoting his diligence to various crafts and labors of every kind, following the apostle who says: “We did not eat bread freely, but laboring in work and toil night and day” (I Thess. III).

And again: “If anyone does not wish to work, neither should he eat” (ibid.).

Through idleness, lusts and the nourishment of harmful thoughts grow dense; through the exercise of labor, vices likewise melt away.

The patriarchs tended flocks, and the pagan philosophers were shoemakers and tailors. Joseph the righteous, to whom the Virgin Mary was betrothed, was a blacksmith. Peter, the chief of the apostles, also practiced the occupation of a fisherman, and all the apostles performed bodily work by which they supported their physical lives.

If men of such great authority devoted themselves to labors and even rustic occupations, how much more should we, who ought not only to provide the necessities of our own life with our hands but also to refresh the needs of others through our labors, according to the apostle’s saying: “Let the one who stole steal no longer, but rather let him labor, working with his hands at what is good, so that he may have something to give to those suffering need” (Eph. IV).

The blessed apostle Paul also worked with his hands for this reason: to offer us an example of working. For among other things he says: “Not as though we had no authority, but so that we might give ourselves as a model for you to imitate” (II Thess. III).

He explains why he imposed so much labor upon himself: “For this reason,” he says, “so that we might give you a model to imitate.”

The Acts of the Apostles records that when Paul came to Corinth he did not permit himself to stay anywhere except with Aquila and Priscilla, because they practiced the same craft that he himself had been accustomed to practice. For it says:

“After this Paul departed from Athens and came to Corinth. Finding a certain Jew named Aquila, a native of Pontus, and his wife Priscilla, he approached them because they were of the same craft, and he stayed with them and worked; for they were tentmakers” (Acts XVIII).

He worked not only enough for himself, but also enough to support those who were with him. For it is written in the Acts of the Apostles that, setting out from Miletus and sending to Ephesus, he summoned the presbyters of the Church of Ephesus and gave them instructions about how they ought to govern the Church of God in his absence. He said:

“I coveted no one’s silver or gold, as you yourselves know, because these hands ministered to the things that were necessary for me and for those who are with me. I showed you everything, because by laboring in this way we ought to support the weak” (Acts XX).

Manual work also cuts away many vices. For it is written: “Every idle person is in desires.” And again: “Idleness is the enemy of the soul.” The incentive to Sodomitical vice is known to have grown from idleness, as the prophet says: “This was the iniquity of Sodom: they ate their bread in fullness and idleness” (Ezek. XVI).

Therefore, let us fear the evil of idleness; let us devote ourselves to the good resources of our hands, fulfilling the Psalmist’s saying: “You shall eat the labors of your hands; blessed are you, and it shall be well with you” (Ps. CXXVII).

For just as it is hardly fitting for any time of idleness to be allowed among God’s servants, so a limit should be placed on spiritual meditation. It is necessary to exercise the virtues of body and soul together: the bodily sustenance of the outer person and the spiritual nourishment of the inner person.

On this subject the blessed Augustine, that eminent teacher, says among other things: “Those who work with their hands can easily sing divine songs and console the labor itself as though by a divine summons. Do we not know that all craftsmen, while their hands do not cease from work, give their hearts and tongues to idle tales, and often even to shameful things? What, then, prevents a servant of God who works with his hands from meditating on the law of the Lord and singing psalms to the name of the Most High?”

## CHAPTER LI. That it benefits nothing those who cast away their possessions if they do not abandon their own wills

It benefits nothing those who cast away their possessions if they do not abandon their own wills, since it is far more excellent to renounce one’s own will than one’s possessions.

Even the philosophers of this world were able to abandon their possessions, and now any heretics can do so. But neither did those philosophers, when they became lovers of their own will, live according to the will of God; and these heretics, through their devotion to their own will, contradict the Lord’s will.

Therefore, it is not that which even God’s enemies do that commends us to God, but that by which only true Christians—and through this, lovers of God—make progress.

These are the people who, casting aside their own wills and possessions, subject themselves wholeheartedly to their Creator, suspend their own desire upon his will, and therefore, whatever the senses of the flesh suggest that they should pursue or do, they reject, captured by the delight of righteousness.

## CHAPTER LII. How those who desire to imitate Christ ought to live

Therefore, if we wish to be in him what we ought to be, let us walk spiritually as the apostle John says: “As he walked, so let us walk” (I John II).

What is it to walk as he walked, except to despise all the prosperity that he despised; not to fear the adversities that he endured; willingly to do what he caused to be done and commanded to be taught; hope for what he promised; follow where he went before us; grant benefits even to the ungrateful; not repay the malicious according to their deserts; pray for enemies; love the good; show mercy to the perverse; invite adversaries; receive in charity those who have been converted; and endure the deceitful and proud with equanimity?

To this also belongs what the apostle Paul says: “If you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God” (Col. III).

Those rise with Christ who die to sin as he did, with this distinction preserved: he died to sin not his own but ours. Each one of us, however, dies not to everyone’s sin but to his own.

What is it to die to sin except not to live at all for works deserving condemnation? It means to desire nothing carnally, to pursue no ambition, so that, dead in the flesh, one no longer detracts from anyone, turns away from or despises anyone, corrupts no one’s chastity through crafty deception, acts violently toward no one, slanders or oppresses no one; envies no good person and insults no afflicted person.

He does not serve the lust of the flesh; he is not devoted to drunkenness, so that by drinking he increasingly kindles in himself a thirst for drinking; he does not burn with bundles of hatred; he does not pursue unjust profits; he does not flatter the powerful and rich; he is not carried away by restless curiosity; he is not distracted by the cares of domestic concern; he does not delight in the dutiful greetings of those who come to him, nor is he wearied by the injuries of the proud.

Pride does not inflate him; boastful ambition does not hurl him down; empty glory does not disgracefully vaunt him; the desire for a glorious reputation does not inflame him; distinction based on another’s conduct does not ensnare him; love does not invite him into association with shamefulness; savage rage does not agitate him; devotion to costly pleasures does not destroy him; the heat of spirited contention does not exhaust him.

Audacity does not make him shameless; injustice does not make him unjust; mercilessness does not make him savage; inconstancy does not make him changeable; obstinacy does not make him stubborn; madness does not make him insane; gluttony does not make him pleasure-loving; disobedience does not make him rebellious; boastfulness does not make him vain; treachery does not make him faithless; prosperity does not make him gentle; cruelty does not make him savage; gluttony does not make him a shameful eater; volatility does not make him impatient; instability does not make him fickle; spiritual weakness does not make him wandering; spiritedness does not make him angry; perversity does not make him suspicious; vanity does not make him talkative; malice does not make him a mocker.

He is removed entirely from worldly enticements, removed from hostilities, removed from the ambushes of others, removed from robberies whether hidden or open, removed from malice and perjury, and finally removed from every kind of disgraceful act or crime by which those who live carnally offend God. Dead to sin, they do not serve it.

As I have said, just as one dead in the flesh can neither do nor suffer the things I have mentioned, so those who live for God do not live at all for these and similar vices; they crucify their flesh with its vices and desires.

## CHAPTER LIII. On the active life
The active life is for the devoted servant of Christ to persist in righteous labors: first, to keep himself unstained by this world; to restrain his mind, tongue, hand, and the other members of his body from every defilement of tempting sin; and continually to subject himself to divine service. Then also, according to his strength, to come to the aid of the needs of his neighbor: food to the hungry, drink to the thirsty, clothing to the cold. By ministering to the needy, receiving wanderers into his home, visiting the sick, burying the dead, and rescuing the poor from the hand of one stronger than he; by delivering the needy and the poor from those who rob them, showing the way of truth to one who has gone astray, and devoting himself to the other services of brotherly love; and, moreover, by contending for justice even unto death.

## CHAPTER LIV. On the Contemplative Life

The contemplative life is to retain love of God and of one’s neighbor with the whole mind, yet to rest from outward action and cleave solely to the desire for the Creator, so that one no longer wishes to do anything else, but, with every care trampled underfoot, the soul burns to behold the face of its Creator. Thus one already knows how sorrowfully to bear the burden of corruptible flesh, while longing with all one’s desires to take part in those hymn-singing choirs of angels, to be mingled with the citizens of heaven, and to rejoice in the incorruption that is eternal in the sight of God.

## CHAPTER LV. What and how great is the perfection of the contemplative life in this flesh, and how those who despise the world should cleave to it in order to enjoy it

Therefore, the follower of the contemplative life should approach his Creator with a heart that must be enlightened; he should serve Him watchfully by contemplating Him and enjoying Him without satiety. Let him continually desire Him, and for love of Him flee everything by which he could be turned away from Him. Let him suspend all his thoughts and his entire hope upon delight in Him. Let him devote himself to the sacred meditations of the divine Scriptures and, divinely enlightened, take delight in them. There let him contemplate himself entirely, as though in a shining mirror: let him correct whatever he finds to be perverse in himself; retain what is upright; set in order what is deformed; preserve what is beautiful; cultivate what is healthy; and strengthen what is weak through continual reading.

Let him read the commands of his Lord without weariness, love them without satiety, fulfill them effectively, and, sufficiently instructed by them, recognize what he must avoid and what he must pursue. Let him apply himself to searching out the mysteries of those same divine Scriptures. Let him read Christ promised there and see Him represented; let him understand the destruction foretold for the obstinate people, grieve that it is fulfilled, and rejoice in the salvation of the nations. Let him hold fast to what has been foretold and fulfilled in the past, and believe the promises concerning the future.

Far removed from the tumult of worldly affairs, let him ardently consider those things by which he may inflame his soul with desire for the reward to come. Let him keep watch over spiritual pursuits by which he may become better and better each day. Let him love holy leisure, in which he may carry on the business of his soul; let him reckon the world dead to him, and present himself crucified to the allurements of the flattering world. Let him place the contemplation of his Creator incomparably above the enjoyment of present spectacles, and raise his continual progress to the summit of divine contemplation.

Let him never turn away, even for a moment, from considering the promises of the future in order to look back upon earthly things. Let him direct the gaze of his mind without ceasing toward the place he desires to reach. Let him set the blessedness of the life to come before the eyes of his soul and love it. Let him neither fear nor desire anything temporal, lest either fear of losing a temporal possession or desire to acquire one weaken the concentration of his mind. Let flattering things not corrupt him, nor adverse things shake him; let favorable opinion not inflate him, nor unfavorable opinion cast him down; let false blame or praise neither increase nor diminish his joys. Let him neither rejoice in temporal things at all nor grieve over them. Amid joy and sorrow alike, let him preserve one expression of soul with invincible constancy. Let nothing that the world promises or threatens shake the stable firmness of his heart. Rather, always the same and remaining like himself, let him feel neither the losses nor the gains of this world.

And when, moved by desire for the contemplative life, he has fulfilled these and similar duties, let him believe firmly that he is not yet perfect here in every respect, but is still to be perfected in that blessed life which is to come. Let him stretch himself toward that place where he may see the substance of God with unveiled face.

## CHAPTER LVI. How the active and contemplative lives differ from each other

The active life, however, comes to an end with the body. For who would offer bread to the hungry in the eternal homeland, where no one hungers? Who would give drink to the thirsty, where no one thirsts? Who would bury the dead, where no one dies? Therefore, when the present life is taken away, the active life is taken away; but the contemplative life begins here in order to be perfected in the heavenly homeland. For the fire of love, which begins to burn here, burns more intensely when it sees the one whom it loves.

The contemplative life, therefore, is not taken away, because, when the light of the present age has been removed, it is perfected. The active life labors sweatily in the contest, whereas the contemplative life, once the disturbances of the vices have been calmed, enjoys the desired repose in Christ. It belongs to the active life to advance amid human affairs and to restrain the rebellious movements of the body under the command of reason. It belongs to the contemplative life to rise above human desire toward perfection and to devote oneself continually to the increase of the virtues.

The active life possesses perfection; the contemplative possesses the summit. The former makes a person holy, the latter perfect. It belongs to this life to inflict injury upon no one at all; to that one, to endure injuries inflicted upon it with equanimity. Or, to put it more precisely: the practitioner of the active life strives to dismiss from himself the one who sins against him, whereas the follower of the contemplative life, when assailed by offenses, is not even shaken, being more ready to disregard them than to forgive them.

The former restrains anger by the power of patience and places the bridle of moderation upon immoderate desires. He is touched by carnal desires but does not consent; he is assailed by curiosity about this world but is not carried away; he is shaken by demonic attack but is not overcome. Subject to his God with devoted mind, he is not crushed by various temptations but tested by them.

The latter overcomes with holy virtues all the afflictions by which mortal life is varied. Free from every desire and disturbance, he enjoys blessed repose; having become superior to allurements and pleasures with a mind set free, he is made capable of the ineffable joy of divine contemplation.

The active person, by receiving the stranger, clothing the naked, governing the subordinate, redeeming the captive, and protecting the one violently oppressed, continually cleanses himself from all his iniquities and enriches his life with the fruits of good works. The contemplative person, distributing his possessions for the use of the poor, strips himself of the world once for all and draws himself toward heaven with all his strength. He casts the things of the world back upon the world and restores himself to Christ with devoted mind. From Him he asks, as a poor man, to be given immortal riches; as a weak man, he daily requests protection; as a naked man, he desires to be clothed with immortality; as one oppressed by the frailty of the flesh, he begs to be defended from the assault of invisible enemies; and as a pilgrim, he longs for a heavenly homeland to be granted him.

The active life has an anxious course; the contemplative, everlasting joy. In the former, discipline is acquired; in the latter, it is received. The former makes one knock at the door of good works as though with hands; the latter calls the perfected into the homeland. In the former, the world is despised; in the latter, God will be seen.

And, to pass over many things that I cannot recount: in this life, those who have become stronger than unclean spirits are, in that contemplative life which is blessed in the highest degree, made equal to the holy angels by the Lord’s rewarding hand, and will reign happily with them forever in that heavenly city.

## CHAPTER LVII. On Compunction of Heart

Compunction of heart is humility of mind arising with tears from the remembrance of sin and the fear of judgment. For those who have been converted, that affection of compunction is more perfect which drives away from itself the affections of desire and fixes its purpose with the whole devotion of the mind upon the contemplation of God.

For this is true compunction of heart in a baptized person: to do great things and speak humbly, to act justly, and to fear and tremble on account of sinners. For just as fire burns up and removes every defect of the soul, so compunction of heart, whatever evils it finds, frightens away all of them and utterly destroys them. If it finds the flames of desire, it extinguishes and kills them like a cleansing river. If it sees multitudes of cares and disturbances, it drives them out and scatters them as with a whip, commanding them to remain far from the dwelling places of the soul. And just as dust cannot stand before the face of the wind, so no evil thought can remain in the soul where compunction of heart is present.

## CHAPTER LVIII. That there are two kinds of compunction

There are two kinds of compunction by which the faithful sacrifice themselves upon the altar of the heart. For the soul thirsting for the Lord is first pierced by fear, and afterward by love. At first it afflicts itself with tears, because, when it recalls its evils, it fears to suffer eternal punishments for them. But when the dread has been consumed by a long anguish of sorrow, a certain security concerning the presumption of pardon already arises, and the soul is inflamed with love for heavenly joys.

The one who first wept lest he be led to punishment afterward begins to weep most bitterly because he is delayed from the kingdom. For the mind contemplates what the choirs of angels are, what the fellowship of blessed spirits is, what the majesty of the eternal vision of God is; and it grieves more because it is absent from everlasting blessings than it grieved before when it feared everlasting evils.

Christ has graciously deigned to accept both sacrifices of our compunction: for those who mourn and are afflicted over sin He mercifully forgives their transgressions, and those who burn with the whole intention of their mind for entrance into heavenly life He refreshes with the eternal light of His vision.

## CHAPTER LIX. That compunction of heart and pleasures are opposed to each other, and that David possessed great compunction

Just as it is impossible for fire to be kindled in water, so it is impossible for compunction of heart to flourish amid pleasures. These things are opposed to and destructive of one another. The former is the mother of weeping; the latter, the mother of laughter. The former constricts; the latter relaxes. The former fastens wings to the soul and makes it fly to heaven; the latter lays upon it the weight of lead and plunges it into hell.

The prophet David, pierced in heart, continually weaving within himself the memory of the future judgment and always keeping that day before his eyes, was never free from anguish of spirit and compunction of heart. What we scarcely ever, and only very rarely, recall to mind, his mind and thought always possessed within itself; and with his whole mind he trembled before the judgments of God.

For that blessed David was also a king, yet, when everything that seemed to surround and constrain him had been broken away, he was placed in such a position of submission as though he himself were subject to all. In purple he lay as though in sackcloth, sprinkled with ashes and pierced in heart. The royal palace was for him like the vastest solitude of the wilderness. Compunction of heart accomplished all these things in him.

Would you know how great his fear of divine judgment was? Hear what he says: “If you observe iniquities, Lord, who will endure?” (Psalm 50). For he knew—and knew very well—that we are liable before God for many crimes. And because even small sins, including those of which we do not even suspect ourselves, are brought to judgment, his compunction of heart was therefore great.

There are four qualities of affection by which the mind of the righteous is pierced with a salutary weariness: the memory of past crimes; the recollection of future punishments; consideration of one’s pilgrimage throughout the length of this life; and desire for the heavenly homeland, so that one may be able to reach it as quickly as possible.

## CHAPTER LX. On the Remembrance of Sin

It is good for a person always to place his own offenses before his eyes, according to the saying of the Psalm: “My sin is always against me.” For just as one ought not to retain affection for sin, so it is always necessary to remember one’s own sin in mourning it. The servant of God ought to have such remembrance of sin that he always confesses with tears the things he has done.

Hence the Psalmist also says: “I was turned in my anguish when the thorn was fixed in me. I made my sin known to you, and I said: I will declare my injustices against myself to the Lord; and you forgave the iniquity of my sin” (Psalm 31).

## CHAPTER LXI. On the Confession of Sin

Solomon says: “He who hides his crimes will not be set right; but he who has confessed and abandoned them will obtain mercy” (Proverbs 28). Hence blessed Job says: “Therefore I will not spare my mouth” (Job 7). For he spares his mouth who is ashamed to confess the evil he has done. To put the mouth to labor is to employ it in confessing the iniquity committed.

But the righteous person does not spare his mouth, because, strictly anticipating the anger of the judge, he rages against himself with words of his own confession. Hence the Psalmist says: “Let us anticipate his face in confession” (Psalm 94). Hence it is written: “Declare your iniquities, that you may be justified” (Ecclesiasticus 43). Each righteous person begins to be righteous from the moment he becomes his own accuser.

For confession displays repentance; repentance manifests satisfaction; and satisfaction wins pardon for itself through divine goodness. Nor can indulgence be granted unless confession is able to appease the anger of God.

O venerable goodness of God! We sin, and He spares us; we transgress, and He forgives; we offend, and He nevertheless remains reconciled. Thus He shows what He is toward the righteous by displaying Himself in this way toward sinners. Nor can the sinner now be excused if he has not hastened to embrace confession, through which pardon arises. He may be held guilty of a double crime: first, because he despised the law in order to transgress; and then because he refused to embrace the means of confession and so perished.

Seize the remedies, whoever you are, who by sinning have despised the divine commandments. Let confession bring salvation to the one for whom contempt had brought death. Let each person confess his offense, I beg you, brothers, while the one who sins is still in this world, while his confession can still be admitted, while satisfaction and remission made through priests are pleasing to the Lord.

Let us turn to the Lord with our whole mind, expressing repentance for our crime with true sorrow, and let us implore the mercy of God. Let the soul prostrate itself before Him; let the whole mind make satisfaction to Him; let all hope rest upon Him.

He Himself tells us how we ought to pray: “Return to me with all your heart, with fasting, weeping, and mourning. And tear your hearts and not your garments” (Joel 2). Let us return to the Lord with our whole heart and, as He Himself admonishes, appease His anger and offense with fasting and tears.

## CHAPTER LXII. On Repentance

Blessed John, the forerunner of our Lord, than whom no one greater has arisen among those born of women (Matthew 11), of whom the prophet had said, “Behold, I send my angel before your face” (Malachi 3), uttered this first proclamation, saying: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is near” (Matthew 3).

From this we understand that Christ spoke through him. Therefore, beloved, all of you, together with us, receive in your hearts the mercy of our Lord, who says: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is near.” O sweetness—that there is nothing intermediate between repentance and the kingdom of heaven!

Let us therefore repent of our crimes, and in an instant the kingdom of heaven will be opened to us. Thus says the blessed prophet: “Cease from your evils; learn to do good, for your sins separate you from God” (Isaiah 59). Therefore, if sins separate God and man, let sins be removed from the midst through repentance, and man is joined to God, as the Apostle instructs and teaches: “He who clings to God is one spirit” (1 Corinthians 6).

But someone may say: “How can I remove sins from the midst?” Hear the forerunner of the Lord crying out and teaching: “Bear fruits worthy of repentance; for now the axe is laid at the root of the trees. Every tree that does not bear good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire” (Matthew 3).

And what are the fruits worthy of repentance except that you do what is contrary to sin? You served idolatry or demons; now, having been converted, serve God through faith. You were an adulterer and fornicator; now, on the contrary, be chaste. You were devoted to drunkenness; now occupy the place of sobriety. You were fraudulent and predatory; now be faithful and generous. You were puffed up and proud; now be gentle and meek. You were greedy and deceitful; now be devout and truthful.

Behold what the fruits worthy of repentance are: that you who formerly acted contrary to God should now act contrary to the devil, according to the Lord’s saying: “Neither will I condemn you. Go, and now sin no more” (John 8). And again: “Her many sins are forgiven, because she loved much” (Luke 7).

The Lord also exhorts us to repentance through the apostle John, saying: “Remember from where you have fallen, and repent, and do the first works. But if you do not repent, I will come and remove your lampstand from its place” (Revelation 2). This is said to one who is known to have fallen and whom He urges to rise again through good works.

Elsewhere, time is granted for repentance, and the Lord threatens the one who does not repent. “I have a few things against you,” He says, “because you allow the woman Jezebel, who calls herself a prophetess, to teach and seduce my servants to fornicate and to eat food sacrificed to idols. And I gave her time to repent, but she does not wish to repent of her fornication. Behold, I cast her onto a bed, and those who fornicated with her will be in the greatest tribulation unless they repent of their works.”

He would certainly not exhort her to repentance unless He promised pardon to those who repent. And in the Gospel He says: “I tell you, there will be such joy in heaven over one sinner who repents as over ninety-nine righteous persons who have no need of repentance” (Luke 15).

For since it is written, “The Lord did not make death, nor does He rejoice in the destruction of the living” (Wisdom 1), He who wishes no one to perish certainly desires sinners to repent and through repentance return again to life.

The devil has cast us down and shattered us through sin; it is necessary, therefore, to rise again through repentance and once more stand against him. Blessed David fell into the most serious sin of adultery, and he added murder to adultery. What happened after this—did he remain lying there? Did he not rise and stand again against the enemy, and so subdue him that even after his death his merits benefited his descendants?

O repentance, salvation of the soul, restoration of virtues, destruction of vices, conqueror of demons, closing of hell, gate of heaven, way of the righteous, refreshment of the blessed! Blessed is the one who loves you; happy is the one who holds fast to you; exceedingly blessed and happy is the one who keeps you until the last day of his life!

You raise up those dead in sins; you call the despairing back from the precipice of death and restore them to hope. You encourage your followers and workers toward hope, summon them to faith, and urge them to love of God and neighbor. You make them humble in prosperity and strong in adversity. You make them gentle in the face of insults and mockers. You endure persecutions and injuries; you patiently bear sufferings and scourges. You restrain anger, soften the tongue, preserve peace, and govern the mind.

In virgins and those consecrated to God you preserve blessed integrity; in widows, laborious chastity; in married people, undivided chastity. O repentance, most chaste mother, teach your children to hold and love chastity, to flee luxury, impurity, and every lustful stimulation of the body. For you bring no one to everlasting glory unless he is chaste, humble, patient, and benevolent.

O repentance, most devout mother, bring forth and produce from your holy womb continual groans, abundant sighs, and unceasing sobs. Shake profuse tears from your eyes. Do not cease; do not grow sluggish, until with swiftest course you reach the final day.

## CHAPTER LXIII. What the Measure of Repentance Should Be

To repent is to mourn the evils committed and not commit the evils that ought to be mourned. For one who laments some things while nevertheless committing others either does not know how to repent or pretends not to.

What does it profit someone to mourn the sins of lust while still panting with the fires of greed? Or what does it profit someone to grieve the faults of anger while still wasting away in the flames of envy?

But what I have said is still far too little: the one who laments sins must not commit what ought to be lamented, and the one who mourns a vice must fear to commit vices. One must think with the greatest care that whoever remembers having committed illicit acts should strive to abstain even from certain licit ones, so that by this he may make satisfaction to his Creator. Whoever has committed what was forbidden should cut himself off even from what is permitted, and should reproach himself in small matters who remembers that he has sinned in great ones.

A great part of justice is to know oneself—to know that one is small—so that one may be humbly subjected to divine power from the moment one recognizes one’s weakness. A person judges himself well in this life so that he may not be judged by God with everlasting condemnation. Each person passes judgment upon himself when, through worthy repentance, he condemns his evil deeds.

The bitterness of repentance makes the mind examine both its deeds more subtly and the gifts of God that it despised, recalling them with tears. Nothing is worse than to recognize guilt without mourning it. Every sinner ought to have a twofold weeping in repentance: either because through negligence he did not do good, or because through presumption he committed evil. He failed to do what he ought to have done, and he did what he ought not to have done.

That person repents worthily who mourns his guilt with legitimate satisfaction, condemning and lamenting what he has done. The deeper one must be in mourning, the more inclined one has been to sin. However sinful and impious a person may be, if he turns to repentance, he is believed able to obtain pardon.

And however much the appeasement of sins is achieved through repentance, a person must nevertheless not be without fear, because the satisfaction of repentance is weighed only by divine judgment, not by human judgment. Therefore, since God’s mercy is hidden, it is necessary to weep without interruption. A penitent ought never to have security concerning his sins.

Let us therefore at last look for our Lord Jesus Christ, like good and useful servants, and let us not despair while we live in this light that we cannot obtain pardon through repentance. After death, the remedies of repentance will be of no benefit; but while we are placed in this light, even if you undertake true repentance at the end of life, believe me, you will be healed.

For this reason the devil moves and does everything in order to instill despair in us. He knows that even if a person practices repentance for a short time, although it may be brief, his conversion will nevertheless not be fruitless. Just as the one who offers a cup of cold water by no means loses the reward due to him, so the one who repents of past evil deeds, even if his repentance may seem less worthy in proportion to the weight of his sins, will nevertheless not be deprived of the reward of good things, however small that gesture of repentance or moment of conversion may be.

For no good work, however small, will be despised before God the just judge. Even if a person has not been able to complete the whole order of making satisfaction, He will not reject repentance carried out to whatever extent and for however brief a time; He will receive it and will not allow the reward of even the slightest conversion to perish.

Isaiah appears to teach this when he says concerning the people of the Jews: “Because of sin I afflicted him for a little while and struck him, and I turned my face away from him; he was grieved and walked in sorrow, and I healed him and comforted him.”

The impious king Ahab will also give even clearer testimony. Through his wife’s wickedness he sought the prey of his desire; but, troubled by the enormity of that crime, he repented, mourned his deed in sackcloth, and so moved God’s mercy toward himself that God absolved him from all evils. For it is written: “And the Lord said to Elijah: Have you seen how Ahab has been pierced before me, and because he wept in my sight I will not bring evils in his days” (1 Kings 21).

After him came Manasseh, who surpassed all tyrants in the enormity of his crimes and had overthrown the worship of divine religion and the observance of the law, leaving all things bereft of heavenly worship [the Latin construction is uncertain]. Yet because he repented, although he surpassed every memory of impiety in the enormity of his crimes, he was afterward counted among the friends of God.

The prodigal son also, who consumed his substance with prostitutes, through repentance recovered the status of his former glory. You see, therefore, how great is the usefulness of repentance and how great the hope of conversion is. There is no sin, no iniquity, that cannot be healed by the remedy of repentance, if the conversion is pure and sincere.

As long as we are in this life, whatever sins may befall us, it is possible for all of them to be washed away through repentance; after death, however, repentance will be of no use. Let no sinner despair of God’s mercy, but while he still lives, let him repent of his sins, and the Lord will be merciful toward his offenses and crimes.

## CHAPTER LXIV. On the Praise and Usefulness of Repentance

With prudent mind and profound reflection, two distinct matters must be understood: namely, how far good differs from evil. This knowledge, which must be traced back to the beginning, arises from the fact that evil is one thing when sin is committed, while good is another thing, namely the repentance we perform for what has been committed.

This is the distinction between the two matters: the serpent in paradise persuaded Eve to sin, while repentance opened the way; and from this came the origin of good and evil.

Who was more worthy before God than David? Yet he sinned, and he would have fallen from the summit if he had not been pierced with compunction. Who was more criminal than Manasseh? Yet repentance recalled him. God repented that He had chosen Saul as king. Why? Because Saul himself did not know repentance. Who was wiser than Solomon? Yet, because he did not know repentance, he lost grace.

O repentance, which, through God’s mercy, forgives sins and unlocks paradise; which heals the contrite, gladdens every sorrowful person, recalls life from destruction, restores one’s condition, renews honor, reforms confidence, and pours back more abundant grace!

O repentance, what new thing shall I say about you? You loosen everything bound; you open everything unfastened; you soothe every adversity; you heal everything broken; you enlighten everything confused; you enliven everything in despair.

O repentance, more radiant than gold, more splendid than the sun, whom sin does not overcome, grief does not defeat, and despair does not destroy! Repentance rejects greed, shudders at lust, flees rage, strengthens love, tramples pride, restrains the tongue, composes conduct, hates malice, and excludes envy.

Perfect repentance compels the sinner willingly to endure everything. If a violent person seeks what he possesses, it does not forbid him; if someone removes his garment, he does not resist. He offers the other cheek to the one who strikes him; when pressed into service, he adds himself willingly; when chastised, he gives thanks; when provoked, he is silent; when exasperated, he responds gently. He is suppliant toward his superior and submits to his inferior.

In his heart there is contrition, in his mouth confession, and in his conduct complete humility. This is perfect and fruitful repentance.

Through repentance, God becomes a nourisher to the hungry and a giver of drink to the thirsty. What is considered foolish tastes wise to the repentant; what is sad pleases him; what is soft displeases him; what is fleeting he dreads.

O repentance, mother of mercy and teacher of virtues! Great are your breasts, by which you release the guilty and restore those who have transgressed, raise up the fallen, and revive the despairing.

Through you David, after his crime, was blessed and received the Holy Spirit again. Through you Manasseh, after bloody crimes, was deemed worthy to be received. Through you the apostle Peter, after denying three times, was granted the hand of pardon. Through you the prodigal son, returning to his father, deserved to obtain not only a paternal embrace and kiss but also the distinction of the banquet of the fattened calf.

Through you the sinful woman shed copious tears and immediately washed the font of her own baptism—the feet of Christ—and wiped them with her hair. Through you the great city of Nineveh and the whole people of the barbarians suddenly came to know God, experienced your power, received your fragrance, grasped your savor, tasted your sweetness, put on your sackcloth, poured out your tears, and perceived your groaning and sighing. It displayed the fruits of your abundance in profusion, and thus not only escaped the danger of the death that had been decreed but also received the crown of a life previously unknown.

Therefore, while we are in this life, let us repent with tears and prayers, fasts, almsgiving, and other good works for our sins and crimes, lest we be tortured without end in everlasting punishments, where there is no repentance and no pardon, but only anger and torments without cessation.

## CHAPTER LXV. On the Praise and Usefulness of the Tears of Repentance

For almighty God seeks contrition; He is moved by tears; He makes those who mourn joyful; He is present to those who repent. Great is the progress brought by tears. By weeping, a servant appeases his master; by tears, a son softens his father; and a little child, by crying, soothes an austere mother.

Thus also the sinner, reformed in Him, removes God’s anger through abundant tears. Peter washed away his threefold denial with tears. For it is written: “And Peter remembered, and so forth, and he wept bitterly” (Mark 26).

David says: “Come, let us adore and weep before the Lord who made us” (Psalm 94). And again: “My tears have been my bread day and night, and I mingled my drink with weeping; every night I will water my bed with tears” (Psalm 101). And again: “God, I have declared my life to you; you have placed my tears in your sight” (Psalm 55).

Therefore we ought to mourn our salvation, which has been lost, and lament our dead soul, so that, when we have been taken away from this world, we may deserve to attain everlasting life.

## CHAPTER LXVI. What the Fruits Worthy of Repentance Are, and How the Kingdom of Heaven Can Suffer Violence

*(Greg.)* Blessed John the Baptist, the forerunner of our Lord Jesus, speaks to the crowds, saying: “Therefore, bear fruits worthy of repentance” (Matthew 3).

From these words it is clear that the friend of the Bridegroom admonishes them to produce not merely fruits of repentance but fruits worthy of repentance. For it is one thing to produce fruit and another to produce fruit worthy of repentance.

To speak, then, of fruits worthy of repentance: it must be understood that whoever has committed no illicit act is rightly permitted to make use of licit things. Thus he should perform works of mercy, yet, if he does not wish to, he need not abandon the things of the world. But if someone has fallen into the guilt of fornication, or perhaps—what is more serious—into adultery, he ought to cut off from himself licit things in proportion as he remembers having committed illicit ones.

For the fruit of good work ought not to be equal for one who has sinned little and one who has sinned greatly, nor for one who has fallen into no crimes and one who has fallen into certain crimes. Therefore, by the words, “Bear fruits worthy of repentance,” each person’s conscience is confronted, so that through repentance he may seek gains in good works proportionate to the greater losses he has inflicted upon himself through guilt.

Because John urges us to great works by saying, “Bear fruits worthy of repentance” (Matthew 3), and again, “Let the one who has two tunics give to the one who has none; and let the one who has food do likewise” (Luke 3), it is now plainly understood what the Truth means when He says: “From the days of John the Baptist until now, the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it” (Matthew 11).

These words of the heavenly pronouncement must be examined with the greatest care. For it must be asked how the kingdom of heaven can suffer violence. Who inflicts violence upon heaven? And again, if the kingdom of heaven can suffer violence, it must be asked why it endured this same violence from the days of John the Baptist and not before.

But when the law says, “If anyone does this or that, let him die,” it is clear to all who read that it struck sinners with the punishment of its severity, but did not lead them to life through repentance.

But when John the Baptist, preceding the grace of the Redeemer, preaches repentance so that the sinner who is dead through guilt may live through conversion, then certainly from the days of John the Baptist the kingdom of heaven suffers violence. For what is the kingdom of heaven except the place of the righteous? The rewards of the heavenly homeland are owed only to the righteous, so that the humble, chaste, meek, and merciful may attain eternal joys [Col. 0931A]. But when someone who was swollen with pride, stained by the crime of the flesh, inflamed with anger, or impious through cruelty returns to repentance after his sins and receives eternal life, he enters, as a sinner, into something like another’s domain. Therefore, from the days of John the Baptist the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it, because the one who imposed repentance upon sinners taught nothing other than how violence might be done to the kingdom of heaven.

Let us therefore recall, dearest brothers, the evils we have committed, and let us wear ourselves down with continual lamentation; let us seize through repentance the inheritance of the righteous, which we did not possess through our life. Almighty God wishes to endure such violence from us. For he wishes the kingdom of heaven to be seized by our tears, although it is not owed to our merits [Col. 0931B]. Therefore, let no quality or quantity of our evils break us in the certainty of hope. That venerable thief provides great confidence in pardon—venerable not for the reason that he was a thief: a thief because of his cruelty, venerable because of his confession. Consider, therefore—consider what incomprehensible depths of mercy the almighty God possesses. This thief was dragged away from the throat of the road with bloodstained hands; he was hung upon the gallows of the cross; there he confessed, there he was healed, and there he deserved to hear: “Today you will be with me in paradise.” What is this? Who is sufficient to speak of or to estimate such great goodness of God? From the very punishment for his crime he reached the rewards of virtue.

For this reason almighty God permitted his elect to fall into certain lapses: so that, when others are lying in guilt, if they rise to him with their whole heart, he might restore to them hope of pardon and open to them, through the lamentation of repentance, the way of mercy [Col. 0931C]. Let us therefore exercise ourselves in lamentation; let us extinguish our guilt with tears and worthy fruits of repentance. Let us not allow the time granted to us to perish, because when we see many already healed of their impieties, what else do we possess but a pledge of heavenly mercy? We ought to contemplate the immense mercy of our Creator, who has placed before us, as a sign and example of repentance, those whom he caused to live through repentance after their fall.

For I weigh Peter, I consider the thief, I look upon Zacchaeus, I contemplate Mary, and I see in them nothing other than examples of hope and repentance placed before our eyes. Perhaps someone has fallen in faith: let him look upon Peter, who wept bitterly over what he had denied through fear. Another has burned against his neighbor with the malice of cruelty [Col. 0931D]: let him look upon the thief, who even at the very moment of death reached the beginnings of life through repentance. Another [Col. 0932A], panting in the heat of avarice, has seized what belongs to others: let him look upon Zacchaeus, who, if he had taken anything from anyone, restored it fourfold. Another, inflamed by the fire of lust, has lost the purity of the flesh: let him look upon Mary, who burned out the love of the flesh within herself by the fire of divine love.

Behold: the Almighty everywhere places before our eyes what we ought to imitate; everywhere he sets before us examples of his mercy. Let the evils we have experienced therefore now displease us. Almighty God readily forgets that we were guilty; he is prepared to count our repentance as innocence for us. Though defiled after the waters of salvation, let us be reborn from tears. Thus, in accordance with the voice of the first shepherd: “Desire the milk as newborn infants” (1 Peter II). Return, little children, to the lap of your eternal mother, Wisdom. Suck the abundant breasts of God’s mercy. Mourn what has passed [Col. 0932B]; avoid what threatens. Our Redeemer will console your momentary tears with eternal joy.

## CHAPTER LXVII. On Perseverance in Good Works

The virtue of a good work is perseverance, and the voice of Truth says: “But whoever perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matthew X). For good is done in vain if it is abandoned before the end of life. By the command of the Law (Leviticus III), the tail of the sacrificial victim is ordered to be offered. For the end of the body is in the tail. And the one who carries the sacrifice of a good work through to the end of the required action makes a good offering.

For this reason Joseph is described as having had a long tunic among his other brothers (Genesis XXXVII). A tunic reaching to the ankle signifies a good work carried through to completion [Col. 0932C]. Our conduct is pleasing to God when we complete with a persevering conclusion the good that we begin. Therefore, virtue consists not in having begun something good, but in having completed it. The reward is not promised to those who begin, but given to those who persevere.

The end of every person’s life must always be considered, because God does not regard what we were before, but what we will be near the end of life. God judges each person according to his end, not according to his past life. Let us therefore persist, dearest ones, with complete devotion in divine supplications, so that he may cause us, with his blessing, to begin what pleases him and bring it through to the perseverance of good completion—he who is α and ω, the beginning and the end, Jesus Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns as God with the Father, [Col. 0932D] in the unity of the Holy Spirit, forever and ever. Amen.

# BOOK THREE

[Col. 0931]

## PREFACE

[Col. 0931D]

This third little book begins on purgatorial fire, on Christ’s coming to judgment, and also on eternal punishment; by the Lord’s generosity, it is made up of excerpts from the brief works of the holy Fathers. I earnestly beseech your most excellent [Col. 0932D] Paternity humbly and unceasingly to implore the divine majesty of the eternal Judge, so that together with you I may deserve to be snatched away from such great evils and reach everlasting life. Amen.

## CHAPTER I. That a purgatorial fire before the judgment is to be believed to exist for certain lesser sins

[Col. 0933A]

A purgatorial fire before the judgment is to be believed to exist for certain lesser sins, because Truth says: “Whoever speaks blasphemy against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, either in this age or in the age to come” (Matthew XII). In this statement it is made understood that certain sins can be forgiven in this age and certain others in the age to come. For when forgiveness is denied in one case, the consequent meaning is clear: it is granted in certain others.

Nevertheless, since he said this beforehand concerning small and very minor sins, it must be believed that it can happen in such cases. Such sins include continual and idle talk, immoderate laughter, or the sin involved in concern for household affairs—things that are scarcely carried out without some fault even by those who know how they ought to avoid fault—or an error of ignorance in matters that are not serious. All these things continue to burden a person even after death if they have not been forgiven while he is still in this life [Col. 0933B].

For when Paul says that Christ is the foundation and adds: “If anyone builds upon this foundation gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, straw, the work of each person will become evident; the Day will disclose it, because it will be revealed in fire, and the fire will test the quality of each person’s work. If anyone’s work that he has built upon it remains, he will receive a reward. If anyone’s work is burned, he will suffer loss, but he himself will be saved, yet as through fire” (1 Corinthians III)—although this may be understood as referring to the fire of tribulation applied to us in this life, nevertheless, if anyone fittingly understands this as referring to a future purification, it must be carefully considered.

For he said that the person can be saved through fire—not one who builds iron, bronze, or lead upon this foundation, that is, greater sins, which are therefore harder and by then already insoluble, but wood, hay, and straw, that is, minor and very light sins, which are easily consumed by fire [Col. 0933C]. Yet this must be understood: even there, no one will obtain purification from the smallest sins unless, while still in this life, he earns it through good works, so that he may obtain it there.

## CHAPTER II. On those who are saved through fire—that is, those who build gold, silver, and precious stones upon the foundation that is Christ, and also those who build wood, hay, and straw

[Col. 0933D]

Concerning those who build upon the foundation that is Christ not gold, silver, and precious stones, but wood, hay, and straw—for it is said of them that they will be saved through fire, since they will not perish because of the merit of the foundation—this must be understood in such a way that these statements, once made clear, do not appear contradictory.

Wood, hay, and straw can reasonably be understood as worldly possessions, even when they have been lawfully permitted. Such desires cannot be lost without pain of spirit. But when this pain burns, if Christ has a place in the heart as its foundation—that is, if nothing is preferred to him—and if a person who is burned by such pain would rather be deprived of the possessions he loves in this way than of Christ, he is saved through fire.

But if, at the time of temptation, he prefers to retain such temporal and worldly possessions rather than Christ, he did not have Christ as his foundation, because he placed those possessions first, whereas nothing should be placed before the foundation in a building [Col. 0934A].

The fire of which the Apostle spoke must be understood as one through which both pass: those who build gold, silver, and precious stones upon this foundation, and those who build wood, hay, and straw. After saying this, he added: “The work of each person will become evident; the fire will test it. If anyone’s work that he has built upon it remains, he will receive a reward. But if anyone’s work is burned up, he will suffer loss, yet he himself will be saved, as through fire” (1 Corinthians III). Therefore, the fire will test the work not of one of them but of both.

There is indeed a fire of the trial of tribulation, concerning which it is plainly written elsewhere: “The furnace tests the potter’s vessels, and the trial of tribulation tests righteous people” (Ecclesiasticus XXVII). In the meantime, this fire in the present life does what the Apostle says. Suppose it comes upon two faithful people: one thinking about the things of God and how to please God, that is, building gold, silver, and precious stones upon Christ the foundation; the other thinking about the things of the world and how to please his wife, that is, building wood, hay, and straw upon the foundation.

The work of the first is not burned, because he has not loved those things whose loss would torment him. The work of the second is burned, because things possessed with love do not perish without pain. But because, when the alternative is presented, he would rather be deprived of those things than of Christ, and because he does not abandon Christ through fear of losing them, he is saved, as through fire. He suffers when he loses the things he had loved, but this pain does not overturn or consume the stability of the foundation, which is protected by incorruption.

It is not incredible that something of this kind also occurs after this life. Whether this is so may be asked; and it may either be discovered or remain hidden whether some of the faithful are saved through a certain purgatorial fire. “The more or less they loved perishable goods, the more slowly or quickly they will be saved.” Yet these are not those of whom it was said that they will not possess the kingdom of God, unless the same crimes are remitted to them after suitable repentance. I have said “suitable” so that they may not be barren in almsgiving.

## CHAPTER III. That one fire is purgatorial, while the other is everlasting, in which sinners are tortured without end

[Col. 0934D]

There is another fire that is to come, concerning which, when the Lord judges, it will be said to the impious: “Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire.” There is another fire, properly called purgatorial, because of those who are saved through it. No one will be saved through the fire that is to come for the impious, because, according to what is written, “These will go into eternal fire.”

But salvation is clearly promised through this fire, which both tests and purifies; concerning it, it is said: “The Day will disclose it, because it will be revealed in fire, and the fire will test the quality of each person’s work” (1 Corinthians III). Into that eternal fire only those on the left will be sent for final and everlasting condemnation [Col. 0935A].

This purgatorial fire tests those on the right, but it tests some of them in such a way that it does not burn up or consume the building it finds constructed by them upon Christ’s foundation. It tests others in such a way that what they have built upon the foundation burns, and they suffer loss because of it. Those are saved who have held Christ, firmly established as their foundation, with surpassing love.

No one will be saved from that everlasting fire, because all who go there will go into eternal punishment, where “their worm will not die and their fire will not be extinguished.”

## CHAPTER IV. That those who are saved through purgatorial fire will not all endure the torment of the spirit for the same length of time

[Col. 0935B]

Just as not all the reprobate who will be plunged into the eternal fire are to be condemned with one and the same measure of punishment, so all those who are believed to be saved through purgatorial punishments will not endure the torment of the spirit for one and the same length of time. Thus, what is accomplished among the reprobate through distinctions of punishment will be accomplished among those who are to be saved through fire.

Their purgatorial punishment will extend for a shorter or longer time according as, in this life, they loved transitory goods less or more.

## CHAPTER V. That some suffer purgatorial punishments in this life and others after death

[Col. 0935C]

We confess that there are certain purgatorial punishments in this mortal life, but they are temporal punishments. Some suffer them only in this life, others after death, and others both now and then. Nevertheless, those who suffer temporal punishments undergo them before that most true and final Judgment; not all of them enter the everlasting punishments that will come after that judgment.

For certain people, what is not forgiven in this age is forgiven in the age to come, so that they may not be punished with eternal suffering. Let no one suppose that there will be purgatorial punishments except those that precede that final and terrifying Judgment and that fire into which all the impious will be plunged when Christ judges.

## CHAPTER VI. Against those who believe that people are saved through purgatorial fire by faith alone, without good works

Some people believe that those who do not abandon the name of Christ [Col. 0935D], who are baptized in his washing within the Church, and who are not cut off from it by any schism or heresy, will be saved through the future fire, no matter how great their crimes, even if they neither wash them away through repentance nor redeem them through almsgiving, but persist in them stubbornly until the final day of this life—even though, because of the magnitude of their crimes and their long-continued wickedness, they deserve to be punished with eternal fire.

But those who believe this, although they may be Catholics, nevertheless seem to me to be deceived by a kind of human benevolence. For the faith that can save is the faith of which the Apostle Paul says: “In Christ Jesus neither circumcision nor uncircumcision has any power, but faith working through love” (Galatians V). But if faith works evil, then, unquestionably, according to the Apostle James, it is dead in itself. He says again: “If someone says that he has faith but does not have works, can faith save him?” (James II).

Moreover, if a wicked person is saved through fire on account of faith alone, and if this is how we must understand what the blessed Apostle Paul says—“He himself will be saved, yet as through fire” (1 Corinthians III)—then, if faith can save without works, what the Apostle James, Paul’s fellow apostle, said will be false; and this statement of Paul himself will also be false: “Do not be deceived: neither fornicators, nor those who serve idols, nor adulterers, nor the effeminate, nor men who have intercourse with males, nor thieves, nor the greedy, nor drunkards, nor slanderers, nor robbers will possess the kingdom of God” (1 Corinthians VI).

For if those who persist in these crimes will nevertheless be saved because of faith in Christ, how will they not be in the kingdom of God? [Col. 0936B]

## CHAPTER VII. That those assigned to purgatorial punishments are purified from them when the Church prays for them in this life

Those spirits who depart from here without such perfect holiness that they can immediately go to paradise upon the dissolution of their bodies, yet do not live so criminally and damnably that they persist in their crimes to the point of deserving condemnation with the devil and his angels, are purified from medicinal punishments when the Church effectively intercedes for them here. They will receive their bodies together with blessed immortality, and, made participants in the heavenly kingdom, they will remain in it without any diminution of their blessedness.

## CHAPTER VIII. That some righteous people are received immediately into blessed rest when they leave the body, while others are received by the flames of purgatory

[Col. 0936C]

There are many righteous people in the Church who, after the dissolution of the flesh, are immediately received into the blessed rest of paradise. They await, in great joy and among great choirs of those rejoicing with them, the time when, having received their bodies, they will come and appear before the face of God.

But some, although preordained through good works to the lot of the elect, are received after death into the flames of purgatorial fire to be severely chastised because of certain evils with which they depart from the body. Either they are cleansed from the stain of their vices through this lengthy examination until the day of judgment, or, having first been freed from their punishments through the prayers, almsgiving, fasts, tears, and offerings of the saving sacrifice made by faithful friends, they too reach the rest of the blessed [Col. 0936D].

## CHAPTER IX. That the souls of faithful departed people, if their sins are not insoluble, are aided by the devotion of their living relatives when a sacrifice and other good works are offered for them

The period between a person’s death and the final resurrection is the time in which souls are held in hidden receptacles, each according to what it deserves, whether rest or distress, in accordance with what it received in the flesh while it lived.

Nor should it be denied that the souls of the departed are relieved by the devotion of their living relatives when the sacrifice of the Mediator is offered for them or almsgiving is performed. But these things benefit them if, while they were alive, they earned for themselves the benefit of these acts afterward [Col. 0937A].

For there is one manner of life that is not so good that it does not require these things after death. There is another that is so good that it does not require them. And again, there is one so evil that, once a person has passed from this life, these things cannot help him. Therefore, every merit by which someone may be relieved or burdened after this life is acquired here. But let no one prepare himself to deserve the Lord after death if he neglected him here.

Therefore, the things that the Church regularly performs for the commendation of the dead are not opposed to that apostolic statement which says: “For we will all stand before the tribunal of Christ, so that each one may receive according to what he did through the body, whether good or evil” (Romans XIII). For each person acquired this merit for himself while he lived in the body, so that these things might be of benefit to him. They are not beneficial to everyone.

And why are they not beneficial to everyone? Is it not because of the difference in the life each person lived in the body? Thus, when sacrifices—whether of the altar or of any kind of almsgiving—are offered for all baptized departed people, for the very good they are thanksgivings; for those who are not very bad, they are propitiations; for the very bad, even if there is no assistance for the dead, they are nevertheless some kind of consolation for the living [Col. 0937B].
