The same teacher says elsewhere, among other things: “There are four things that help people after death: the offerings of priests, the prayers of the righteous, the almsgiving of loved ones, and the fasts of friends. Yet these things do not help after death those who did not earn this in the present life” (Gregory).

For the blessed Pope Gregory says concerning this: “If sins are not insoluble after death, the sacred offering of the saving sacrifice often helps souls even after death, so that sometimes the souls of the departed themselves seem to seek it.”

In the fourth book of the Dialogues of the same blessed Gregory it is read that a certain spirit assigned to the heat because of his sins, who appeared like a man, said to a certain priest offering him bread: “For my sins, Father, offer this bread to almighty God, and then know that you have been heard when you come here and do not find me.” With these words he disappeared. The same priest afflicted himself with tears for him for an entire week, offered the saving sacrifice daily, and when he returned there afterward, he no longer found him [Col. 0937D].

From this it is shown how much the sacrifice of the sacred offering benefits souls, since the spirits of the dead themselves ask the living for it and give signs by which they appear to be released through it.

For a certain monk named Justus, instructed in the art of medicine—as the blessed Pope Gregory relates in the aforementioned book—was led to the punishment of fire because, contrary to the authority of the regular life, he had illicitly kept three gold pieces hidden among his medicines. Thirty days after his death, it pleased the aforementioned venerable father Gregory, who at that time was living as a monk in the same monastery under the discipline of the regular life, that throughout those thirty days no day should pass on which the saving sacrifice was not offered for his release. This was done [Col. 0938A].

The same brother who had died appeared one night in a vision to his own brother, whose name was Copiosus, and indicated that on the thirtieth day, when the sacred sacrifice had been offered for his release, he had received communion and had already been freed from his punishments. Then the matter became plainly clear: the brother who had died had escaped punishment through the saving sacrifice.

For in the aforementioned book it is read that one day, when the blessed Germanus, bishop of Capua, was bathing at the Angulares Baths for the medical needs of his body, he saw Paschasius, a deacon of the holy Roman See, standing in the heat, and asked him what he was doing there. Paschasius explained why he had been assigned after death to that place of punishment and afterward said: “I beg you, pray to the Lord for me [Col. 0938B], and know that you have been heard if, when you return here, you do not find me.”

For this reason the man of God, Germanus, applied himself earnestly to prayer; and when he returned after a few days, he no longer found the aforementioned Paschasius in that place. Since he had sinned not through malice but through an error of ignorance, he was able to be purified from his sin after death. Nevertheless, this must be believed: through the generosity of his almsgiving he obtained the possibility of deserving pardon at a time when he could no longer perform any work. (Gregory.)

If sins are not insoluble, as was said above, the victim of the sacred offering can be of the greatest benefit for release, even to the dead—those who obtained this while living. Yet it must be understood that the sacred victim benefits the dead so that the good works performed here on their behalf by others may aid them even after death [Col. 0938C].

Among these matters, it must be considered that the safer course is for each person to perform personally, while alive, the good work that he hopes others will perform for him after his death. For it is more blessed to depart free than to seek freedom after imprisonment.

## CHAPTER X. That sometimes fear alone purifies the souls of the righteous from their sins as they depart

Very often, fear alone, as the souls of the righteous depart, purifies them from minor sins. Thus it is related of a certain holy man who, as he approached death, was greatly afraid, but after death appeared to his disciples in a white robe and indicated that he had been received most gloriously.

For we read that the same blessed Father Gregory [Col. 0938D] gave the following advice to the superior of that monastery for the purification of a dying brother who had illicitly retained three gold pieces in secret, as was mentioned above: “Go,” he said (Gregory, Book IV of the Dialogues), “and let none of the brothers approach him as he is dying, nor let him receive words of consolation from the mouth of any of them. But when, at the point of death, he asks for the brothers, let his own blood brother tell him that, because of the coins he secretly possessed, he is hated by all the brothers, so that at least at death the bitterness of this may pierce his mind because of his guilt and purify him from the sin he committed.”

When this monk reached the point of death and anxiously sought to be commended to the brothers, and none of the brothers deigned to approach or speak with him, his blood brother, who was present, told him why he was hated by everyone. Immediately he groaned bitterly over his guilt and departed from the body in that very sorrow [Col. 0939A].

The blessed Gregory would never have ordered this to be done unless he had recognized that it was beneficial for the purification of the dying man. Up to this point we have treated of purgatorial fire; from here onward we must address the final judgment.

## CHAPTER XI. On the exceedingly fearful coming of Christ to judgment

Let us hear how Christ’s coming is proclaimed by the prophets, insofar as it was permitted that it be announced to human beings. One of them says: “God will come manifestly, our God, and he will not be silent. [Col. 0939B] Fire will burn before him, and a mighty tempest will surround him. He has summoned heaven above and the earth to distinguish his people” (Psalm XLIX).

Another, Isaiah, who also shows us the forms of punishment, says—listen to how he speaks: “Behold, the day of the Lord will come, incurable, a day of fury and anger, to make the whole earth desolate and destroy sinners from it” (Isaiah XIII). “The stars of heaven and Orion, and all the adornment of heaven, will not give their light; the sun will be darkened at its rising, and the moon will not give its light. I will command evils against the whole world and their sins against the impious; I will destroy the insolence of the wicked and humble the arrogance of the proud. Those who are left will be more precious than gold refined by fire, and a human being will be more precious than a sapphire stone. For heaven will be shaken and the earth will be moved from its foundations [Col. 0939C], because of the fury of the anger of the Lord of hosts, on the day when his fury comes upon it” (Isaiah XIII).

Malachi the prophet also speaks in agreement with these words, saying: “Behold, the almighty Lord is coming, and who will endure the day of his coming? Or who will withstand his appearance? For he himself enters the refining fire and will sit, “melting like the chaff of winnowers” [text as printed, uncertain], and purifying like gold and silver” (Malachi IV).

And again he says: “Behold, the day of the Lord will come, burning like a furnace, and it will consume them; and all foreigners and all who commit iniquity will be like straw. That day, which is coming, says the almighty Lord, will burn them, and neither root nor branch will be left” (Malachi III).

But the man of desires speaks in this way: “And behold, I saw, and thrones were set in place, and the Ancient of Days sat; his clothing was white as snow, and the hair of his head like pure wool. His throne was a burning fire. A river of fire flowed before him. He held judgment, and the books were opened” (Daniel VII) [Col. 0939D].

And shortly afterward: “I saw,” he says, “in a vision of the night, and behold, one like a Son of Man was coming in the clouds of heaven; he came even to the Ancient of Days, and was brought before him, and dominion, honor, and a kingdom were given to him. All peoples, tribes, and languages will serve him. His dominion is an eternal dominion that will not pass away, and his kingdom will not be destroyed. My spirit shuddered. I, Daniel, was terrified by these things, and the visions of my head disturbed me” (ibid.).

When these things begin to happen, the gates of heaven will undoubtedly be opened—or rather, heaven itself will be removed from the midst, as though the coverings of someone’s tents were being gathered up, so that it may be restored and transformed for the better. Then everything will be filled with fear, and dread and trembling will fill the universe. Then fear will shake the angels themselves, and not only the angels but perhaps also the archangels, thrones, dominions, principalities, and powers. For this is indicated by the statement: “The powers of heaven will be shaken.”

They are fellow servants of those who are to be judged and who will have to render an account of this life. If, when a single city is to be judged by earthly judges, the other cities are afraid and tremble even when they fear no danger, how much more will this happen when the entire world comes to judgment and is to be judged by a judge who needs no witness [Col. 0940A], who seeks no arguments, and who requires no advocate for the case.

But with all such things set far aside, he himself will lay bare their deeds, words, and thoughts, set them in the midst, and display to their eyes, as if portrayed in certain images, all that they committed, both they and all who appear to be standing there. How then will the whole creation be shaken and be in fear? [lacuna]

## CHAPTER XII. That the second coming of the Savior is to be shown not in humility as before, but in glory

“For just as lightning comes out from the east,” the Lord says in the Gospel, “and appears as far as the west, so will be the coming of the Son of Man” (Matthew XXIV).

This too must be understood: the second coming of the Savior is to be manifested not in humility as before, but in glory [Col. 0940C]. And shortly afterward the Lord adds and says: “The sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light; the stars will fall from heaven, and the powers of heaven will be shaken” (ibid.).

This does not mean a diminution of light—for elsewhere we read that the sun will have seven times its present light—but by comparison with the true light everything will be seen to be darkness. If, therefore, this sun, which now shines throughout the whole world, and the moon, which is the second luminary, and the stars, which have been kindled for the consolation of the night, and all the powers, by which we understand the multitudes of angels, will be reckoned as darkness at Christ’s coming, let the arrogance of those who consider themselves holy and do not fear the presence of the Judge be struck down.

“And then,” says the Lord, “the sign of the Son of Man will appear in heaven.” Here let us understand the sign of the cross, so that the Jews may see, according to Zechariah and John, the one whom they pierced [Col. 0940D]. Or let us understand the banner of the triumphing victory, because then all the tribes of the earth will mourn. Those will mourn who do not possess citizenship in heaven but are written on earth.

## CHAPTER XIII. How it is to be understood that Christ, coming from heaven, will judge the living and the dead

We confess that Christ is to come from heaven and to judge the living and the dead. This does not pertain to the life we live here, since it is neither among the things he has done nor among those being done now, but among the things to be done at the end of the age.

To this belongs what the Apostle adds afterward: “When Christ appears, your life, [Col. 0941A] then you also will appear with him in glory” (Colossians III).

The statement that he will judge the living and the dead can be understood in two ways. Either we understand by “the living” those whom his coming will find not yet dead here, but still living in this flesh, and by “the dead” those who have departed from the body before he comes or who will depart before then.

Or we understand the living as the righteous and the dead as the unrighteous, since the righteous will be judged. Sometimes God’s judgment is spoken of in an evil sense, as in the statement: “Those who have done evil will rise to the resurrection of judgment” (John V). But sometimes it is spoken of in a good sense, according to what is said: “Save me, O God, by your name, and judge me by your strength” (Psalm LIII).

For through God’s judgment the distinction between the good and the wicked is made, so that the good may be separated to the right, to be delivered from evil and not destroyed with the wicked. For this reason he cries out: “Judge me, O God”; and, as though explaining what he has said, he adds: “And distinguish my cause from an unholy people” (Psalm XLII).

## CHAPTER XIV. That we will not be able to offer any excuses for good works on the day of judgment

[Col. 0941B]

Come now: we have reached the final judgment, where we are to be judged by the Judge who can neither be deceived by the concealment of crimes nor corrupted into granting impunity by the offering of any gift, when everyone’s secrets begin to be revealed, and not only acts and words but even thoughts themselves are displayed.

What will we do beneath the majesty of such a Judge? What excuse will we be able to offer? By what skill of defense will we clear ourselves? [Col. 0941C] What repentance, which we despised in this flesh, will come to our aid? What good works, which we did not perform in this life, will defend us? To which apostles, or to which other saints, will we flee for refuge, whose examples and words alike we disregarded?

Or perhaps the weakness of the body will excuse something there? But against such an excuse all the examples of the saints will protest. While living in the flesh, they taught that what they did could indeed be done despite the weakness of the flesh, especially since they themselves resisted sin not by their own strength but through the help of the merciful Lord. He revealed himself even to those who were not seeking him, so that he might be sought and believed in; and he defended those who believed in him with unconquerable protection, so that they would not be overcome by sin.

What, then, will they answer if the Lord says to them: “If you were able, why did you not [Col. 0941D] resist the desires of sins? If you were not able, why did you not seek my help against sins? Or, when you were wounded, why did you not apply the remedy of repentance to your wound?”

Will we be silent in response to these things? What excuse will remain? To those who have nothing, he says: “Bind them hand and foot and cast them into the outer darkness; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth. There their worm will not die, and their fire will not be extinguished.”

## CHAPTER XV. That even the smallest sins are brought to the future judgment unless they have been erased in this life through repentance
Small sins, even those of which we have no suspicion, are brought to judgment unless in this life they have been cleansed through repentance and the other good works. For the Lord also says concerning idle words, about which we take the least care: “For every idle word that people have spoken, they will give an account of it on the day of judgment” (Matthew XII). What shall we wretched people do on that day, since we are entangled in every evil? Let us not despair, but let us do penance, so that our sins may be blotted out.

## CHAPTER XVI. On the twofold divine judgment; and that at the final judgment Christ will appear gentle to the elect and terrifying to the reprobate.

Divine judgment is twofold. One kind is that people are judged both here and in the future. The other is that they are judged here precisely so that they may not be judged there; and therefore temporal punishment benefits some for purification. For others, condemnation begins here, and there their complete destruction is expected.

At the judgment the reprobate will see Christ’s humanity, in which he will judge, so that they may grieve; but they will not see his divinity, lest they rejoice. For when divinity is shown to anyone, it is certainly displayed for joy. According to the diversity of consciences, Christ will also appear gentle in judgment to the elect and terrifying to the reprobate. For each person will have such a judge as the conscience he has brought with him, so that, while Christ remains in his own tranquility, he appears terrifying only to those whom conscience accuses of evil.

## CHAPTER XVII. That at the future judgment there will be two orders of the elect and two of the reprobate.

There are two orders of the elect at the future judgment. One consists of those who judge with the Lord, who left everything and followed him. Of them it is said: “You who have left everything and followed me, at the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty, you also will sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matthew XIX).

The other order consists of those who will be judged by the Lord. They did not likewise leave all their possessions, but from what they had they took care to give daily alms to the poor on behalf of Christ. Therefore they will hear at the judgment: “Come, blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world. For I was hungry and you gave me food; I was thirsty and you gave me drink; I was naked and you clothed me,” and so forth (Matthew XXV).

We likewise learn from the Lord’s account that there will be two orders of the reprobate at the judgment. One consists of those who, having been initiated into the mysteries of the Christian faith, nevertheless disdain to practice the works of faith. To them, as the testimony declares, it will be said at the judgment: “Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire which has been prepared for the devil and his angels. For I was hungry and you did not give me food,” and so forth (ibid.).

The other consists of those who either never received the mysteries of the Christian faith or rejected them after receiving them through apostasy. Of them he says: “But whoever does not believe has already been judged” (John III), because he does not believe in the name of the only-begotten Son of God. Since they were unwilling even to honor Christ in word, they do not deserve even to hear his words by which they might be convicted at the judgment. Nevertheless, they will come to judgment so that, together with the sinners who are judged, they may be sent into eternal damnation.

## CHAPTER XVIII. How the two orders of the elect and the two of the reprobate differ among themselves at the judgment, and what is set against each order.

There are two distinctions, or orders, of people at the judgment, namely, of the elect and of the reprobate; yet these are divided into four. There is one order of the perfect: those who judge with God; and another, those who are judged. Nevertheless, both will reign with Christ.

Similarly, the order of the reprobate is divided into two: those who are evil within the Church will be judged and condemned; but those who are found outside the Church will not be judged, but only condemned.

The first order, that of those who are judged and perish, is opposed to the order of the good, consisting of those who are judged and reign. The second order, that of those who are not judged and perish, is opposed to the order of the perfect, consisting of those who are not judged and reign. The third order, that of those who are judged and reign, is opposed to the order consisting of those who are judged and perish. The fourth order, that of those who are not judged and reign, is opposed, conversely, to the order consisting of those who are not judged and perish.

## CHAPTER XIX. On sin which is either expiated here or reserved for future judgment.

For it is not without reason that the day on which the judge of the living and the dead will come is properly called the day of judgment. Conversely, certain things are judged here, and yet, if they are forgiven, they will certainly do no harm in the world to come. Therefore, concerning certain temporal punishments inflicted in this life upon sinners and not reserved for the end, the Apostle says: “If we judged ourselves, we would not be judged by the Lord. But when we are judged, we are chastised by the Lord, so that we may not be condemned with the world” (1 Corinthians XI).

## CHAPTER XX. That each person appears at the judgment as he departs this life, except that purgatorial fire is believed to precede the judgment for lighter faults.

**(Gregory.)** In the Gospel the Lord says: “Walk while you have the light” (John XII). Through the prophet he also says: “At an acceptable time I have heard you, and on the day of salvation I have helped you” (Isaiah XLIX). The Apostle Paul, explaining this, says: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (2 Corinthians VI). Solomon also says: “Whatever your hand is able to do, perform diligently. For there is neither work, nor reason, nor wisdom, nor knowledge in the underworld, where you are hastening” (Ecclesiastes IX). David likewise says: “For his mercy endures forever” (Psalm CXXXV).

From these statements it is plainly established that each person departs this life in the condition in which he will appear at the judgment. Nevertheless, it must be believed that for certain lighter faults there is a purgatorial fire before the judgment, as has already been written above. Therefore, while anyone lives in this present life, let no one neglect to do the good he is able to do, because after this life, if he wishes, he will no longer be able to do so **(Cassiodorus).** Since we do not know the time of the coming death and cannot work after death, it remains for us to seize the time granted before death. Death itself is conquered when, before it comes, it is always feared.

## CHAPTER XXI. How strictly the eternal Judge will come on the day of judgment, and that that day is exceedingly dreadful.

**(Gregory.)** Considering the severity of the coming Judge, Paul says: “It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God” (Hebrews X). Hence the Psalmist declares: “God will come manifestly, our God, and he will not be silent. Before him fire will burn, and around him a mighty storm” (Psalm XLIV). A storm and fire accompany the strictness of such great justice, because the storm tests those whom the fire will consume.

Therefore, dearest brothers, place that day before your eyes, and let whatever now seems grievous be light in comparison with it. Concerning that day the prophet says: “The great day of the Lord is near; it is near and exceedingly swift. The voice of the day of the Lord is bitter; there the mighty man will be troubled. That day is a day of wrath, a day of tribulation and distress, a day of calamity and misery, a day of darkness and gloom, a day of cloud and whirlwind, a day of trumpet and blast” (Zephaniah I).

Again, concerning this day the Lord says through the prophet: “Yet once more, and I will shake not only the earth but also heaven” (Haggai II). Therefore contemplate that day with complete attention, correct your life, change your conduct, overcome the evils that assail you by resisting them, and punish the evils you have committed with tears. For you will one day see the coming of the eternal Judge with greater security in proportion as you now anticipate it by fearing his strictness.

## CHAPTER XXII. That no one should neglect God’s longsuffering and patience, because he will judge strictly at the judgment.

**(Gregory.)** Let no one neglect God’s longsuffering. For he will exercise that much stricter justice at the judgment in proportion to the longer patience he has shown before the judgment. Hence Paul says: “Do you not know that the kindness of God leads you to repentance? But according to your hardness and unrepentant heart, you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and of the revelation of God’s righteous judgment” (Romans II).

Hence the Psalmist says: “God is a just judge, strong and patient” (Psalm VII). By saying “patient” before “just,” he indicates that the one whom you see patiently enduring the sins of sinners for a long time will at some point judge strictly. Hence it is said through a certain wise man: “The Most High is a patient requiter.” He is called a patient requiter because he bears human sins and repays them. **(Augustine.)** For those whom he patiently tolerates for a long time so that they may convert, if they do not convert he condemns more harshly. Therefore whoever wishes to escape eternal punishment without end must obey God’s command without interruption.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On the difference in perpetuity between the good and the evil.

After the resurrection has taken place and the whole judgment has been completed, the two cities will attain their final states: one, that of Christ; the other, that of the devil; one of the good, the other of the evil. Each, however, will contain both angels and human beings. The good will have no will to sin, while the evil will have no ability to do so; neither will there be any condition of dying.

**(Prosper.)** While the former live truly and happily in eternal life, the latter endure unhappily in eternal death, without the power to die. Both will remain without end: the former in blessedness, the latter in misery. Thus neither will those who have been rewarded bring their reward to an end, nor will those who have been condemned bring their punishment to an end.

For this reason incorruption and immortality will also be given to the bodies of the wretched, so that they neither end their eternal punishment nor are themselves consumed by immortal punishment, but are punished by it. Therefore the bodies of the righteous will be endowed with blessed incorruption and immortality, so that they themselves may remain in glory and glory may remain in them forever.

## CHAPTER XXIV. **[Col. 0945B]** On hell, which is believed to be beneath the earth.

Some have thought that hell exists in a certain part of the earth, while others believe that it is beneath the earth. This consideration nevertheless presses upon the mind: we call it “hell” (*infernus*) because it lies below; and what the earth is in relation to heaven, that which is below ought to be in relation to the earth. Hence perhaps the Psalmist says: “You have delivered my soul from the lower hell” (Psalm LXXXV).

The upper hell seems to be upon the earth, while the lower hell seems to be beneath the earth. John’s statement also agrees with this understanding. When he said that he had seen a book sealed with seven seals, and that no one was found worthy to open the book and loose its seals, neither in heaven, nor on earth, nor beneath the earth, he added: “And I wept greatly” (Revelation V).

Later, however, he says that this book was opened by the Lion from the tribe of Judah. In this book, what else is signified but Sacred Scripture, which our Redeemer alone opened? By becoming human, dying, rising again, and ascending, he disclosed all the mysteries that had been closed within it.

No one was found in heaven, because no angel was able; no one on earth, because no human being living in the body was able; and no one beneath the earth, because no souls separated from their bodies were able to open for us the secrets of sacred discourse apart from the Lord. Since, then, no one beneath the earth is said to have been found worthy to open the book, I do not see what prevents us from believing that hell is beneath the earth.

## CHAPTER XXV. **[Col. 0945D]** On Gehenna.

**(Bede.)** The name Gehenna is not found in the ancient books, but it is first used by the Savior. Let us therefore ask what occasion gave rise to this expression.

We read that the idol Baal stood near Jerusalem, at the foot of Mount Moriah, where the waters of Siloam flow. This valley and plain of small fields was watered and wooded, full of delights, and contained a grove consecrated to the idol. The people of Israel had fallen into such madness that, abandoning the vicinity of the Temple, they sacrificed victims there; pleasures overcame the strictness of religion, and they burned or initiated their children for the demon. The grove itself was called Gehenon, that is, “the valley of the sons of Hinnom.”

The Book of Kings, Chronicles, and Jeremiah describe this most fully. God threatens that he will fill that very place with the corpses of the dead, so that it will no longer be called Topheth or Baal, but Polyandron, that is, “a burial place of the dead.” Thus the future punishments and everlasting penalties with which sinners will be tormented are designated by the name of this place. In Job we read at great length that Gehenna has a twofold character, of excessive fire and cold.

## CHAPTER XXVI. That the punishment of the condemned in Gehenna is twofold, namely, of mind and body alike.

The punishment of the condemned in Gehenna is twofold: grief burns their mind, while flame burns their body in turn, so that those who conceived in the mind what they carried out in the body may be punished in both mind and body.

The fire of Gehenna possesses light for one purpose, namely, for condemnation, so that the wicked may see the source of their grief; and it lacks light for another purpose, namely, for consolation, so that they may not see anything from which they could rejoice.

## CHAPTER XXVII. That the one fire of Gehenna does not torment all sinners equally.

There is indeed one fire of Gehenna, but it does not torment all sinners in the same way. Each person will feel there as much punishment as his guilt requires. For just as many people stand beneath one sun and yet do not feel the heat of that same sun equally, since one burns more and another less, so there, in one fire, the degree of burning will not be the same for all.

What diversity of bodies accomplishes here, the diversity of sins accomplishes there: they will have a fire that is not different in kind, yet it will burn each of them differently.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On the difference among punishments.

The mildest punishment of all will certainly be that of those who, apart from the original sin they carried with them, added no further sin. Each person will have a more tolerable condemnation there in proportion to the lesser iniquity he had here.

When the reprobate angels and human beings remain in eternal punishment, the saints will then know more fully what good grace has bestowed upon them. Then it will become more evident in reality what is written in the Psalm: “I will sing mercy and judgment to you, O Lord” (Psalm C). For no one will be liberated except through undeserved mercy, and no one will be condemned except through deserved judgment.

## CHAPTER XXIX. Why it is called unquenchable fire.

**(Chrysostom.)** The fire that exists in the present life consumes everything it receives. That perpetual fire always torments those whom it takes in and preserves them forever intact for their punishment. Therefore it is called unquenchable not only because it itself is not extinguished, but also because it neither extinguishes nor destroys those whom it receives.

Scripture teaches that sinners too will put on incorruption—not for the honor of life, but for the enduring of punishment. No voice can express the force of this punishment or the power of that fire; no speech can explain it. Nothing among corruptible things, whether good or evil, is like it. Nevertheless, in order to gain some image of that fire from the punishment of this one, we have compared them.

## CHAPTER XXX. That the torments of the wicked are without end.

Just as there is no end to the joy of the good, so there is no end to the torments of the wicked. For when the Truth says: “These will go into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life” (Matthew XXV), since what he promised is true, what God threatened will undoubtedly not be false.

## CHAPTER XXXI. Against those who say that God threatened sinners with eternal punishment in order to restrain them from committing sins.

**(Gregory.)** If what he threatened is false, so that he might correct people from injustice, then what he promised is also false, so that he might call them to justice. But who would dare say this unless insane? And if he threatened what he was not going to fulfill, then, while we wish to assert that he is merciful, we are compelled to proclaim him deceitful—which it is impious to say.

**(Augustine.)** Blessed Augustine says among other things concerning this: Some, indeed many, in a human spirit of pity, unnecessarily commiserate the eternal punishment of the condemned and their everlasting torments without interruption, and do not believe that this will be their future state. They do not oppose the divine Scriptures as such, but, following their own inclination, soften whatever seems harsh and bend toward a milder interpretation what is thought to have been stated in them more terribly than truthfully.

“Will God,” they say, “forget to show mercy? Or will he restrain his mercies in his anger?” This is indeed read in a holy psalm. But without any hesitation it is understood of those who are called vessels of mercy, because they too are liberated from misery not by their merits but by God’s mercy.

Or, if they think that this applies to everyone, it is not therefore necessary for them to suppose that the condemnation of those of whom it was said, “These will go into eternal punishment,” can come to an end—unless in the same way they also suppose that blessedness will at some point end, since it is added: “But the righteous into eternal life” (Matthew XV).

## CHAPTER XXXII. That it is just for a fault committed within time to be punished without end.

**(Gregory.)** This would rightly be said if the strict Judge weighed not human hearts but deeds. The wicked sinned within time because they lived within time. For, if they could, they would certainly have wished to live without end so that they could sin without end. They show that they desire always to live in sin because, while they live, they never cease sinning.

It therefore belongs to the great justice of the Judge that those should never be without punishment who in this life never wished to be without sin.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. That in eternal condemnation there is death without death, and the desire to die without the ability to die.

**(Gregory.)** Eternal punishments both torment their victims in various ways beyond their strength and preserve them by extinguishing the support of life, so that the end of life punishes them while the end continually prolongs their torment through sufferings, and the torment endures by defining itself without end.

Thus for the wretched there is death without death, an end without end, decay without decay, because death lives, the end always begins, and decay does not know how to decay.

**(Augustine.)** The renowned teacher Augustine says among other things concerning this: “There is nothing worse in death than to be in death without death, and to wish to die without being able to die.”

## CHAPTER XXXIV. How the soul is immortal, although it is established that it dies in perpetual fire.

**(Gregory.)** Just as life is spoken of in two ways, so the soul must also be understood in two ways. One thing is that by which we live in God; another is that by which we have also been formed or created in this condition. That is, one thing is to live blessedly, another to live essentially.

The soul is therefore understood to be both mortal and immortal. It is mortal because it abandons blessed life; but it is immortal because it never ceases to live essentially and cannot lose the life of its nature, not even when it has been condemned to perpetual death.

Placed there, it will lose blessedness but not existence. Consequently, it is always compelled to suffer both death without death and decay without decay, an end without end, so that for it death is immortal, decay unceasing, and the end infinite.

## CHAPTER XXXV. That the souls of the wicked descend into hell as soon as they leave the body.

If we believe, on the testimony of sacred discourse, that the souls of the saints are in heaven, we must also believe in every respect that the souls of the wicked are in hell. For from the retribution of eternal justice by which the righteous already rejoice, it necessarily follows that the unrighteous are tormented in every respect.

Just as blessedness gladdens the elect, so we must believe that fire consumes the reprobate from the day of their departure.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. That whichever receives the soul leaving the body—whether holy angels or demons—retains it forever without any change.

Scripture says: “In whatever direction a tree falls, whether toward the south or toward the north, there it will remain” (Ecclesiastes XI). This means that when, at the time of death, a holy or evil spirit receives a human soul departing from the prison of the flesh, it will retain that soul with it forever without any change, so that, once raised up, it will not fall into punishment, nor, once submerged in eternal punishments, rise again to the remedy of deliverance.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. That the reprobate whose guilt is shared in their conduct are also led after death to places they share in common.

If the reprobate, whose guilt is shared in their conduct, were not also led after death to places shared in common, the coming Judge would certainly not declare to the reapers: “Gather the weeds and bind them into bundles to burn” (Matthew XIII).

The reapers, who are angels, bind the weeds into bundles for burning when they join those who are alike to those who are alike in similar torments, so that the proud burn with the proud, the lustful with the lustful, the greedy with the greedy, the deceitful with the deceitful, the envious with the envious, and the faithless with the faithless. When those who are alike in guilt are brought to similar torments, the angels who assign them to places of punishment bind them, as it were, into bundles of weeds for burning.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. That just as the good recognize the good in rest, so the wicked recognize the wicked in torments.

Just as the good recognize the good in rest, so the wicked recognize the wicked in torments. For if Abraham had not recognized Lazarus at all, he would certainly not have spoken to the rich man placed in torments about his past distress, saying that he had received evil things during his life (Luke XVI).

And if the wicked did not recognize the wicked, the rich man placed in torments would certainly not have remembered his brothers, who were already absent. For how could he fail to recognize those present who, even in their absence, took care to plead on behalf of their memory?

This also demonstrates that the good recognize the wicked and the wicked recognize the good. The rich man is recognized by Abraham, himself a rich man, to whom it is said: “You received good things during your life” (ibid.). The elect Lazarus is also recognized by the reprobate rich man, who asks that he be sent by name: “Send Lazarus, so that he may dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue” (ibid.).

In this recognition of both parties the fullness of retribution increases: the good rejoice more because they see those whom they loved rejoicing with them; and the wicked are tormented with those whom, while despising God, they loved in this world. They are consumed not only by their own punishment but also by the punishment of those others.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. Whether the souls of the saints pray for their enemies who are tormented in eternal fire.

**(Gregory.)** The souls of the elect pray for their enemies at the time when they can turn their hearts to fruitful repentance and save them through that conversion. For what else should be prayed for on behalf of enemies than what the Apostle says: “That God may grant them repentance for knowledge of the truth, and that they may recover from the snares of the devil, by whom they are held captive for his will” (2 Timothy II)?

But how will prayer then be offered for those who can no longer be changed from iniquity to works of justice in any way? The reason why prayer is not then offered for people condemned to eternal fire is therefore the same as the reason why prayer is not now offered for the devil and his angels, who have been assigned to eternal punishment.

This is also now the reason why holy people do not pray for deceased unbelievers and ungodly people: they know that these have already been assigned to eternal punishment, and they refuse to have the merit of their prayer canceled before the presence of the just Judge.

If even now the living righteous do not greatly pity the dead and condemned unrighteous, although they themselves still know that they are suffering something subject to judgment concerning their own case, how much more strictly will they then regard the torments of the wicked, when, stripped of every fault of corruption, they themselves will cling more closely and firmly to justice?

For their minds will be so absorbed by the power of destruction because they cling to the most just Judge that they will have no inclination at all toward anything that differs from the exactness of that eternal rule.

## CHAPTER XL. On the unregenerate and their torment.

Whoever is not liberated from that mass of perdition which came through the first human being by the one mediator between God and humanity will indeed rise, each with his own flesh, but in order to be punished with the devil and his angels.

Whether they will rise with the defects and deformities of their bodies—those who bore defective and deformed limbs—is it necessary to labor over this question by investigation? The uncertain condition or beauty of those whose condemnation will be certain and everlasting ought not to weary us.

Nor should it trouble us how they will have an incorruptible body if they can suffer pain. For there is no true life except where life is lived happily, nor true incorruption except where health is not corrupted by any pain. But where the unhappy are not permitted to die, and, so to speak, death itself does not die, and where perpetual pain does not destroy but afflicts, corruption itself does not end.

In the Holy Scriptures this is called the second death. Yet neither the first death, which compels the soul to leave its body, nor the second, by which the soul is not permitted to leave its punitive body, would have happened to human beings if no one had sinned.

## CHAPTER XLI. That the demons, who were made from angels and cast from heaven because of pride, were struck by irrevocable punishment.

The demons who now exist were once created without sin and appointed to serve their God in happiness. Corrupted by their own will, they were unwilling to remain what they had been made. When, in the form of pride of place, they had raised themselves in hostility against their Creator, they were cast from the heavenly region. Divine judgment condemned them under this sentence: because they were unwilling to persevere when they could have done so, they would neither wish nor be able to be restored.

They were struck by the punishment of their transgression, which was an irrevocable judgment; and it certainly belonged to the most just condemnation that they entirely lost both the will and the ability to return. Conversely, it was through the will of the holy angels that, when the evil angels fell voluntarily, they themselves remained in their dignity.

## CHAPTER XLII. That Gehenna was made not for human beings but for the devil.

Almighty God did not make us for the purpose of handing us over to Gehenna and perpetual fire. The kingdom of heaven was made for us; Gehenna was made for the devil. I will show from the Gospels that this is so.

The Lord himself says to those who are on his right: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom that was prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matthew XXV). But to those who are on his left he says: “Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire which was prepared”—he did not say “for you,” but “for the devil and his angels” (ibid.).

Thus, from the foundation of the world, the fire of Gehenna was prepared for the devil and the kingdom of heaven for humanity. The only concern is that, by stubbornly persisting in evil, we do not exclude ourselves from entering into good things.

## CHAPTER XLIII. What it means for the hands and feet of the reprobate to be bound; what the outer darkness means; what the weeping and gnashing of teeth mean; and other matters.

**[Col. 0951B] (Prosper.)** In the future the king will say to his ministers concerning the reprobate: “Bind them hand and foot and cast them into the outer darkness; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth, where their worm will not die and their fire will not be extinguished” (Matthew XXII; Mark IX).

What does it mean to bind them hand and foot, leaving them speechless, except that they are deprived forever of action by which they might confess God? To be cast into the outer darkness will mean nothing other than to be expelled by the Lord, who is the light of minds.

The weeping and gnashing of teeth show their most bitter pains. Assigned to the punishment of everlasting death, they will not possess the sensation of living, but of suffering. Their continual groaning, eternal torment, and supreme pain torture their souls without destroying them; they punish their condemned bodies without bringing them to an end.

Therefore unquenchable fire, to which they have been assigned, will not extinguish them, so that, while the life of sensation remains, punishment may remain also. It will keep their eternal bodies shackled for suffering rather than for living, while immortality, in the flames of the second death, kills them.

“Now their worm will not die, and the fire will not be extinguished”: these words refer to the whole punishment of the condemned person. The fire of ineffective repentance burns him, and the immortality of the worm that consumes his conscience gnaws him.

## CHAPTER XLIV. That repentance is of no benefit after death.

As long as we are in this life, brothers, whatever sins may befall us, it is possible for everything to be washed away through repentance. But when we have been taken from this world, even if there is great repentance there—and there will be great repentance—it will be of no benefit.

Even if there is gnashing of teeth, even if there are howling and weeping, even if we pour out prayers and countless entreaties, and even if we cry aloud, no one will hear and no one will help. No one will dip even the tip of a finger in water for our tongue lying in the flames. Instead, we will hear what the rich man heard from Abraham: “A great chasm has been fixed between us and you, and neither can anyone cross from here to there nor from there to here” (Luke XVI).

While we live in this light, let us know that we can obtain forgiveness through repentance; but in hell, as we have said, the remedies of repentance will be of no benefit.

## CHAPTER XLV. **[Col. 0952A]** What and how great are the evils suffered by those who are said to be killed in Gehenna.

**(Prosper.)** All who are said to be killed in Gehenna are not treated in such a way that, consumed by the greatest pains, they eventually perish; rather, they are made to live in punishment.

We ought willingly to hear or read these things and things like them, constantly bring them before the eyes of the mind, believe them to be future, and fear them without disturbance.

Consider what an evil it is to be excluded from the joy of divine contemplation, deprived of the most blessed company of all the saints, made an exile from the heavenly homeland, to die to blessed life, to live for death everlasting, and to be cast into eternal fire with the devil and his angels.

There the second death is exile for the condemned and life is punishment: they do not experience in that fire what gives light, but experience what torments. They suffer the terrifying crackling of the raging blaze; their eyes are blinded by the bitter darkness of the smoking abyss; they are plunged into the depths of surging Gehenna; they are torn forever by the most ravenous worms—and they are not brought to an end.

## CHAPTER XLVI. That the torments in hell are so great that no voice can express them and no speech can explain them.

(Greg.) For blessed Pope Gregory, in the ninth book of the *Moralia*, where he appears to be expounding the words of Saint Job, says the following concerning the eternal punishments, when he writes: “Before I go—and do not return—to the land that is dark and covered with the gloom of death” (Job 10):

“What else is signified by the name ‘dark land’ than the dreadful prisons of Tartarus, which the darkness of eternal death covers, which forever separates the condemned from the light of life? Nor is it without reason that hell is called ‘land,’ because whoever is seized by it is held there securely. For it is written: ‘One generation passes away and another generation comes, but the earth stands forever’ (Ecclesiastes 1). Thus the dark prisons of hell are rightly called ‘land,’ because those whom they receive for punishment they do not torment with a transitory penalty or a merely imagined fantasy, but preserve through solid retribution in everlasting damnation.

“Sometimes, however, they are also designated by the name ‘pit,’ as the prophet bears witness when he says: ‘They bore their shame with those who go down into the pit’ (Ezekiel 31). Hell, therefore, is called both ‘land,’ because it holds those whom it has received securely, and ‘pit,’ because those whom it has once seized it always swallows, tossing and trembling amid the punishments that surge around them.

“But the holy man, whether speaking in his own voice or in that of the human race, asks to be released before he goes—not because the one who laments his guilt is going to the dark land, but because without doubt the one who neglects to lament is going there. Just as a creditor says to his debtor, ‘Pay the debt before you are bound by the debt’; yet he is not bound if he does not delay in paying what he owes.

“Here it is rightly added: ‘I shall not return.’ For the mercy of the One who spares will in no way thereafter free those whom the justice of the Judge has once condemned in places of punishment.

“These places are described still more precisely when it is said: ‘a land of misery and darkness.’ Misery pertains to suffering, darkness to blindness. Thus that which holds those expelled from the sight of the strict Judge is called a land of misery and darkness, because outwardly pain torments those whom inward blindness obscures, separated from the true light.

“Yet ‘land of misery and darkness’ may also be understood in another way. For this earth on which we are born is indeed a land of misery, but it is also a land of darkness, because here we suffer many evils arising from our corruption; nevertheless, through the grace of conversion, we return to the light within it, as the Truth urges when he says: ‘Walk while you have the light, lest the darkness overtake you’ (John 12). But that other land is simultaneously a land of misery and darkness, because whoever descends there to endure its evils never returns thereafter to the light.

“In its further description it is added: ‘Where there is the shadow of death and no order’ (Job 10). Just as outward death separates flesh from soul, so inward death separates the soul from God. The shadow of death, therefore, is the darkness of separation, because every condemned person, while being kindled by eternal fire, is darkened by eternal light.

“Fire by its nature both gives light from itself and burns; but that avenging flame of past sins has burning without light. Hence the Truth says to the reprobate: ‘Depart from me, you accursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels’ (Matthew 25). Again, signifying the whole of them in the person of one man, he says: ‘Bind his hands and feet, and cast him into the outer darkness’ (Matthew 22). If, therefore, the fire that torments the reprobate could possess light, the one who is rejected would not be said to be cast into darkness.

“Hence the Psalmist says of them: ‘Fire fell upon them, and they did not see the sun’ (Psalm 57). Fire falls upon the impious, but the sun cannot be seen by the fire that burns brightly, because the flame of Gehenna devours those whom it blinds to the vision of the true light, so that outwardly the pain of burning torments them, while inwardly the punishment of blindness darkens them.

“Thus, in body and heart alike, they are punished according to the manner in which they sinned against their Creator in body and heart. They feel punishment in both respects, since while they lived here they served their depraved pleasures through both. Hence the prophet rightly says: ‘They descended into hell with their weapons’ (Ezekiel 32). The weapons of sinners are the members of the body, by which they carry out the perverse desires they covet. Therefore Paul rightly says: ‘Do not present your members as weapons of iniquity to sin’ (Romans 6).

“To descend into hell with one’s weapons, then, is to endure the torments of eternal judgment with those very members by which one fulfilled the desires of pleasure: so that pain may then absorb from every side those who now, subjected on every side to their pleasures, fight against the justice of the just Judge.

“It is indeed very remarkable that it says, ‘where there is no order.’ For almighty God, who orders evil well, does not in any way permit either the punishments themselves or their infliction to be without order. Those penalties, too, which proceed from the balance of justice, cannot possibly be inflicted without order. For how could there be no order in punishments, when retribution follows each condemned person according to the measure of his crime?

“Thus it is written: ‘The powerful will suffer powerful torments, and a harsher punishment awaits the stronger’ (Wisdom 6). Likewise, in the condemnation of Babylon it is said: ‘As much as she glorified herself and lived in luxury, so much give her torment and mourning.’ If punishment is distinguished according to the measure of guilt, it is plainly evident that order is maintained in punishments.

“And unless the totality of torments separated them according to the deeds of their merits, the coming Judge would not be said to tell the reapers: ‘Gather the weeds and bind them into bundles to burn’ (Matthew 13). For if no order is maintained in punishments, why are the weeds to be burned bound into bundles? To bind bundles for burning plainly means to associate those who are to be handed over to eternal fire with their equals, so that those whom a similar guilt stains may be restrained by an equal punishment; and those who are not polluted by unequal wickedness may not be tormented by unequal punishment. Thus the same condemnation crushes those whom the same arrogance exalted; the same affliction constricts those whom ambition similarly inflated; and an equal flame of punishment torments those whom an equal flame of sin kindled in the fire of lust.

“For just as there are many mansions in the Father’s house according to the diversity of virtue, so the disparity of crimes subjects the condemned to different punishments in the fires of Gehenna. Although Gehenna is one for all, it does not burn all with one and the same intensity. For just as we are all touched by the same sun, yet we do not all grow hot beneath it in the same way—for the weight of the heat is felt according to the quality of the body—so for the condemned there is one Gehenna that afflicts, but it does not burn all with the same intensity. What the differing bodies effect here, the differing causes of merit effect there.

“How, then, is it said that there is no order in punishment, when each person is certainly tormented according to the measure of his guilt? . . .

“But after the holy man has introduced the shadow of death, he adds how great is the confusion in the minds of the condemned. For the punishments themselves, which come in an ordered manner through justice, are certainly not ordered within the hearts of those who die. As we said a little earlier, every condemned person is burned outwardly by flame and inwardly devoured by the fire of blindness; placed in pain, he is confused both outwardly and inwardly, so that he is tormented still more severely by his own confusion.

“Thus there will be no order in the punishment of the rejected, because at their death the confusion of mind itself rages more cruelly within them. What wondrous power of the judging One: his equity orders punishment in such a way that the punishment confuses the soul as though it were disordered.

“Or certainly punishment is said to lack order because the individual character of those crying out in punishment is not preserved. Hence what follows immediately is: ‘and everlasting horror dwelling there.’ In the torments of this life, fear does not possess pain, and pain does not possess fear, because fear does not torment the mind once it has begun to suffer what it feared.

“But hell is obscured by the shadow of death, and everlasting horror dwells there, because those delivered over to its fires both feel pain amid their punishments and, struck by the anguish of pain, are continually assailed by terror. Thus they suffer what they fear, and again they continually fear what they suffer.

“Of these it is written: ‘Their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be extinguished’ (Mark 9). Here the flame that kindles also gives light; there, as we have shown above from the words of the Psalmist, the fire that torments also darkens. Here fear is lost once what was feared has begun to be endured; there pain tears apart and terror constricts. In a dreadful manner, therefore, the reprobate will then have pain with fear, punishments with darkness.

“Thus the weight of supreme equity ought to be felt by the condemned, so that those who, while living, did not fear to depart from the will of the Creator may eventually find, in their destruction, even their torments at variance with their own qualities. Thus the torments that assail them may increase, and because they arise in various forms, may be felt in manifold ways.

“Yet these punishments torment those who are diverse in themselves beyond their strength, and preserve them by extinguishing the support of life, so that the end of life punishes them in such a way that the end of torment is always extended through their sufferings, and their failing endures without end. Thus for the wretched there is death without death, an end without end, failure without failure: death lives, the end is always beginning, and failure does not know how to fail.

“Therefore, although death destroys, it does not extinguish; pain torments, but in no way drives away terror; flame burns, but does not disperse the darkness. As far as can be gathered from our knowledge of the present life, punishments have no order because they do not retain their own character in every respect.

“Nevertheless, although the fire there does not shine for consolation, it does shine in some fashion in order to torment more severely. For the reprobate will also see their companions in torment, illumined by the flame with them—those for whose love they sinned. Thus those who loved their lives in a carnal manner, against the commandments of the Creator, will be afflicted by the destruction of those same companions, to the increase of their own damnation.

“We have gathered this, as the Gospel bears witness, from the account in which the Truth tells us that the rich man who descended to the torments of the eternal fire remembered his five brothers and asked Abraham to send Lazarus to instruct them, lest they should one day come there and be tormented by the punishment (Luke 16). Since he remembered absent relatives for the increase of his own pain, it is undoubtedly established that he could also later see them present, to increase his punishment.

“What wonder, then, if he sees the reprobate burning with him for the increase of his pain, when he saw Lazarus, whom he had despised, in Abraham’s bosom? If the chosen man appeared so that the punishment might increase, why should we not believe that he can also see in his punishment those whom he had loved against the Lord?

“Therefore it is inferred that those whom the reprobate now love in a disordered manner they will then see with themselves amid torments, by a wondrous ordering of judgment, so that their own punishment may be intensified: the carnal relationship placed before its Creator will be condemned before their eyes by an equal retribution. The fire, therefore, which torments in darkness is to be believed to retain light for the sake of torment.

“If we cannot establish this by testimonies that explicitly express it, it remains for us to demonstrate it from the opposite direction. Three boys of the Hebrew people were thrown, with their hands and feet bound, into a furnace whose fires had been kindled at the command of the Chaldean king. Yet when that same king inspected them amid the furnace’s blaze, he saw them walking about unharmed and with their garments intact.

“Here it is plainly inferred that, through the wondrous dispensation of the Creator, the nature of the fire was tempered with different powers: it did not touch the garments, but burned the bonds. For the holy men the flame was cool for the infliction of torment, yet it burned for the mystery of release.

“Just as fire knows how to burn for the consolation of the elect, yet does not know how to burn for their punishment, so conversely the flame of Gehenna neither shines for the reprobate as a gracious consolation, nor does it fail to shine for their punishment. Thus, in the eyes of the condemned, the fire of punishment will glow without any brightness, yet it will show them how those they loved are being tormented, to increase their pain.

“What wonder if we believe that the fire of Gehenna possesses punishment together with both darkness and light, when experience teaches us that even the flame of torches shines while remaining dark? Then the devouring flame will burn those whom carnal pleasure now defiles. Then the bottomless abyss of hell will swallow those whom empty exaltation now exalts. Those who here fulfilled the will of the cunning persuader through whatever vice will then arrive at torments under their leader.

“And although the nature of angels and human beings is very different, one punishment nevertheless entangles those whom guilt binds in one crime. The prophet aptly and briefly indicates this when he says: ‘There is Asshur and all his multitude, and around him are his graves’ (Ezekiel 32).

“For whom is Asshur expressed under the name of the proud king, if not that ancient enemy who fell through arrogance? Because he drags many into guilt, he descends with his entire multitude into the prisons of hell.

“Graves cover the dead; and who suffered death more grievously than the one who, despising his Creator, abandoned life? When human hearts receive this dead one, they undoubtedly become his graves. But his graves are around him, because those in whose minds he now buries himself through desires he later joins to himself through torments. And because the reprobate now illicitly receive malignant spirits by perpetrating evil within themselves, then the graves will burn together with the dead.

“Up to this point in this chapter the words of Saint Pope Gregory concerning eternal punishments have been set down. Now the sayings of John Chrysostom must be presented. He says, among other things:

“No one among you, and no speech, will be able to set forth the force of this punishment or explain the power of the eternal fire. For nothing among corruptible things, whether good or evil, resembles it. Nevertheless, to form some image of that fire and punishment, remember when someone is consumed by the excessive heat of fever: what anguish and what torments of body and soul reside there. From this temporal punishment measure how great are those punishments kindled by the eternal fire, which the fiery river flowing before that dreadful tribunal will inflict through its punitive waves.

“What shall we do there? What shall we answer? Nothing but the gnashing of teeth, nothing but wailing and weeping, while help ceases on every side and punishments grow stronger everywhere—and not even any consolation anywhere. For no one will meet our eyes except the ministers of punishment alone, and everywhere the dreadful faces of the torturers; and, worst of all, there will be no relief even from the air itself or from light.

“For the places of punishment, the outer darkness, will surround us. But that fire, just as it does not possess the nature of consuming, so neither does it possess the nature of illuminating; it is a dark fire and a shadowy flame. Once placed amid these things, what trembling—indeed, what dissolution of the entrails and tearing apart of the limbs—and what or how great the savage punishments inflicted upon all the senses will be, no speech can now explain.

“For the forms of punishment are diverse and varied, and according to the measure of the sins, punishments are multiplied for each individual. But if you ask how the body will suffice for punishment amid so many evils, when it knows no end of time, consider what sometimes happens in this life, and infer great things from these small ones. How often do we see some people worn down by the longest illness, yet no end of life is thereby granted them? Or, if the body is eventually dissolved by death, the soul is not consumed.

“Thus it is clear that when the body too has received immortality, neither punishment will thereafter destroy the soul nor will it destroy the body. In the present life it cannot happen that bodily punishment is both severe and perpetual; one yields to the other, because the fragility of the body cannot endure both. But when both have been freed from corruption, punishment will rage with the power it has received, while incorruption, once attained, will admit no end.

“Let us not suppose, therefore, that the excess of punishments itself will bring an end to the pains. Rather, as we have said, sins kindle punishments, while the incorruption of soul and body will grant no termination to the punishments.

“Tell me, then, how many periods of luxury, what spans of pleasure, do you wish to set against such punishments? Suppose we grant a hundred years to pleasures; add another hundred if you wish, and add ten times a hundred. What compensation will these provide in comparison with eternity? Does not the whole time of this life, during which we seem to enjoy pleasures and indulge lust, appear like the dream of a single night when compared with eternity?

“The pleasures of this life pass like a shadow and flee swiftly, but the punishments remain forever. Now bring your thought back to that dreadful tribunal of divine judgment, which a burning river surrounds with streams of flame: where there are weeping and gnashing of teeth, where there is outer darkness, where there is that worm of conscience which never dies, and the fire which is never extinguished.

“Recall the parable of Lazarus and that rich man, who was clothed in purple and fine linen and could not find even a single drop of water when he was placed in the necessity of burning heat (Luke 16). Tell me, I beg you, what more does this life possess than a dream?

“For just as those condemned to the mines, or placed under any other punishment, when after great labor they have been granted a brief easing of life and have fallen asleep, see themselves seated amid abundant banquets and enjoying rich feasts, yet when they rise understand that none of the pleasure of the dream has remained with them, so that rich man possessed the riches of this life as though in a dream. When he departed, nothing remained with him except regret for the past and punishment in the present.

“Remember this now, friend, and set that fire of Gehenna against the flames of lust and desire that now torment you. For this is a remarkable kind of medicine: that fire may be extinguished by fire. If these fires that now torment you are not extinguished, they will make those eternal fires sharper and inextinguishable for you.

“That fire always torments those whom it receives, and always preserves them intact for its punishment. It is called inextinguishable not only because it is not itself extinguished, but because it neither extinguishes nor destroys those whom it receives.

“Therefore, lest we too come into these torments of the soul, let us at last awaken while there is time. Behold, now is the acceptable time; now is the day of salvation; now there is opportunity for repentance, and a time in which the penitent also receives its fruit.

“For we must remember the multitude of our sins; we must also remember the stains of conscience. Let us ask the Lord to enable us to mourn for ourselves and to dissolve the burden of our sins through a multitude of tears. Yet after this we must not always be weeping and doing nothing. Let us therefore embrace a life pleasing to God and leading to heaven, lest perhaps we descend with our evils into hell, where no one can confess to him, and there suffer what the impious suffer, when no one will any longer exist to intercede for us.

“While we are in this life, let us do all the good we can. But once we have gone there, neither friend, brother, nor father will be able to rescue the one assigned to punishments. For how can one who is in the light approach one who is held in darkness? There, when no refreshment from the consolation of the saints is available to us, we shall nevertheless undergo eternal punishments, whose effects cannot be escaped, amid immortal flames.”

We have learned what punishment awaits the condemned; and since sacred teaching instructs us, we have no doubt whatever how great is the fire in damnation, how great the darkness in the fire, and how great the terror in the darkness. [Col. 0958D] But this knowledge is useful if, through our tears, prayers, fasts, almsgiving, and other good works, we redeem our sins, so that, freed from everlasting punishments, we may deserve to attain everlasting life: through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns throughout infinite ages. Amen.

## In the Year of Our Lord 865. Saint Anscharius, Bishop of Hamburg.

[Col. 0959]

# Life of Saint Anscharius, by Saint Rembert, His Disciple and Successor

*(In Mabillon, Benedictine Annals, volume VI.)*

## Preface. To the Monks of Old Corbie

[Col. 0959A] 1. To the most holy lords, fathers, and brothers serving God in the most sacred monastery of Corbie, to be remembered and loved with especial veneration in the love of Christ: the sons and disciples of the most reverend Father Anscharius pray, in the Lord who rules, for your perpetual peace and salvation in eternal blessedness.

[Note: [Col. 0959C] The author’s dedication of this Life to the monks of Old or French Corbie is made clear by the text itself, so that it is surprising that Adam should be mistaken on this point, followed as he is by most more recent writers. Henschenius corrected this error, and after him Peter Lambecius. This is especially clear from section 3, where Rembert, addressing the monks of this monastery, says: “Tonsured among you and placed among the monastic disciplines, among you he was offered to God and promised obedience; together with your other brothers he was sent to these regions of Saxony, where a monastery had begun to be built and had taken its name from the place of your habitation, so that it might be called New Corbie.” Nothing clearer than these words can be adduced. The author continues to address the same monks throughout the entire course of the little book.]

Long delighted, through the Lord’s grace, by the office of a good shepherd, instructed by his preaching and example, and supported by his merits and intercession, now at last bereft of his presence, we weigh carefully what we ought to mourn on our own behalf and what we ought to rejoice over on his account. For, being a true worshiper of God, abstaining from every evil deed and remaining in the moderation of simplicity, he gave us firm confidence concerning himself that, once taken from here, he would without delay have reached God, whom he had always loved with complete devotion and toward whom he had always directed his mind.

Therefore we believe that we should truly rejoice over the reward of his recompense, but that we must necessarily pray because of our own desolation, so that although humanly deprived of so great a shepherd, we may deserve to be fortified from heaven by divine assistance. For placed amid various pressures and anxieties, we now truly feel what we have lost and understand well what we ought to mourn on our own behalf.

While he was alive, we believed that nothing was lacking to us. Kings honored his holiness, the shepherds of the churches venerated him, the clergy imitated him, and the whole people admired him. While everyone proclaimed him holy and just, we too, as the body of its head, seemed venerable and praiseworthy on account of his goodness.

But now, deprived of so great a gift, we do not rely upon our own merits; rather, with fearful hearts we tremble lest, because our sins deserve it, we begin to lie exposed to the bites of wolves. For the world, which lies in wickedness, seeks more to overturn what is just and holy than to raise up what is religious; and the devil, the enemy of the human race, the more holy and religious a person he sees leading his life, the more vigorously sets every adversity against him, so that he may destroy what is holy and, through cunning persuasion and wicked intentions, prevent others from imitating it.

Thus, sighing amid fearful dangers, although we temporally fear many evils, we nevertheless believe that divine assistance will not be absent from us, unworthy though we are. Therefore, with humble hearts we ask and beseech your most devoted holiness to deign to remember us and intercede for us with the Lord, so that his mercy may not now abandon us, but that our most kindly helper may drive every harmful thing away from us. May he be our refuge in tribulation, who does not abandon those who hope in him.

Relying, then, upon his presence, placing our hope in his mercy, and leaving to his judgment what will happen to us and how we ought to endure in the future, we praise and thank his goodness with the whole affection of our hearts and minds, because he granted us the use of so great a patron, even for a time.

We also offer immense thanks to your most holy fatherhood, because by your favor and permission we deserved to have such a Father, whose example, if anyone should wish to imitate it, would in a certain sense give him a heavenly way of life on earth. If anyone remembers his teaching, he will be able to walk without error along the way of God’s commandments. If anyone heeds his exhortations, he will strive to avoid the snares of the enemy.

We have therefore resolved to inscribe the memory of this most holy Father with the pen and to make known in writing to your reverence how he lived among us and what we came to know about him, so that your devotion may join ours in praising divine mercy in the blessed man, and so that his most holy devotion may become an example of salvation for those who wish to imitate him.

# The Life Begins

[Col. 0961]

## Anscharius Is Recalled from Empty Childhood Amusements by Heaven

2. The holiness of the religion of the most blessed Father Anscharius [in the Corbie manuscript: “the holiness of whose religion”], by the gracious gift of divine grace, began to grow from the beginning of his life, and at every moment of his age multiplied its increase in virtues.

[Note: [Col. 0961D] The author is silent about Anscharius’s homeland, as is also the poet Gualdo. The French Corbie monks maintain the opinion that he was born there as well. Anthony de Caulincourt (who has sometimes seemed to me to be Jacobus Baro), in a manuscript Chronicle of Corbie, says that he was born in the town of Corbie; and in the suburb of Foliot, down to the present time, there was a village called Saint Anscharius, perhaps because his paternal house once stood there. Certainly, while still a boy, he was entrusted to the monks of Old Corbie some years before the death of Charlemagne, as is clear from what follows, and therefore before his tenth year. For he was born in 811 and died in the year of Christ 865, having reached the age of sixty-four. Those who assert that he was born in Frisia and became a monk at New Corbie are mistaken, since he was already a monk more than twelve years before the foundation of New Corbie.]

For from childhood he was inspired by heavenly spiritual revelations and was often admonished by a heavenly visitation through the Lord’s grace, so that, separating his mind from earthly things, he might yearn with all his heart for heavenly things. He had made these revelations known to certain of us who clung to him more closely, but under the condition that they should reveal them to no one during his lifetime.

After his death, we chose to insert them into this work for the praise of the Lord, so that all who read might recognize with how great a grace the Lord deigned to correct his servant from his earliest age and thereafter glorify him through the successive merits of good works.

For he related that, when he was about five years old, his mother, a woman exceedingly religious in the fear of God, died. Not long afterward, his father sent him to school to learn letters. Once there, he began, as is customary at that age, to behave childishly with his companions and to devote himself more to aimless running about and games than to applying himself to the discipline he was meant to learn.

While he was thus devoted to childish pursuits, it seemed to him one night that he was in a very muddy and slippery place, so that he could escape from it only with great difficulty. Beside that place was a most pleasant road, on which he saw approaching what appeared to be a woman distinguished by every adornment and propriety. There were also several other women clothed in white, among whom was his mother.

When he recognized her, he began to wish to run toward her; but he could not easily escape from that muddy and exceedingly slippery place. When that chorus of women had drawn near him, it seemed to him that the one who appeared to be the leader of the others—the one whom he unquestionably believed to be Saint Mary—said to him: “Son, do you wish to come to your mother?”

When he answered that he eagerly wished to do so, she continued: “If you wish to share in our way of life, you must flee every kind of vanity, abandon childish games, and preserve yourself in the gravity of life.
