For we detest exceedingly everything that is vain and idle, and whoever delights in such things cannot be in our company.”

After this vision he immediately began to conduct himself more seriously and to avoid childish companionship. He occupied himself more closely with reading, meditation, and other useful pursuits, so that his companions greatly wondered that he had so suddenly been transformed into a different way of life.

## Having Heard of Charles’s Death, He Becomes More Fervent

3. After this, when he had been tonsured among you and placed in the monastic disciplines, and had become somewhat older, human frailty began to make him grow somewhat cold toward the rigor of his former resolve.

Meanwhile it happened that he heard of the death of the most excellent lord, the Emperor Charles, whom he had previously seen glorious in great power and had heard to have governed the scepter of the kingdom commendably and with great prudence.

Struck, therefore, by excessive terror and dread at the death of so great an emperor, he began once more to return to himself and to recall to mind the words of the holy Mother of God’s admonition. Abandoning every kind of levity, he began to languish with love of divine compunction, and turning his whole self toward God’s service, he devoted himself to prayer, vigils, and abstinence.

## In Ecstasy, Saints Lead Him to Purgatory

[Col. 0962D] 4. While the true athlete of God persisted in these exercises of virtue, and while the world became dead to him and he to the world as he persevered in this seriousness, the holy day of Pentecost arrived. The grace of the Holy Spirit, which was poured out upon the apostles on that feast, also—so we believe—illuminating and gladdening his mind, it seemed to him that on that same night he was about to die through a sudden accident.

At the very moment of death, he called upon the holy Apostle Peter and blessed John the Baptist for assistance. When, as it seemed to him, his soul was departing from the body and immediately appeared in another, exceedingly beautiful form of body, free from every mortality and anxiety, the men mentioned above appeared at that same moment of death and wonder.

One of them was an elder, with gray hair, smooth and thick hair, a flushed face, a somewhat sorrowful expression, a white and colored garment, and short stature. Without anyone telling him, he immediately recognized this man as Saint Peter. The other was a young man, taller in stature, beginning to grow a beard, with darkish and slightly curly hair, a lean face, a cheerful expression, and a silk garment. He firmly believed this one to be Saint John.

They stood around him on either side. His soul, having departed, immediately seemed to be in an immense radiance that filled the whole world. Through that radiance, in which he experienced no distress whatever, the saints mentioned above led him in a wondrous and ineffable manner. When they reached a certain place which, without anyone telling him, he knew with complete certainty to be purgatorial fire, they left him there.

There he seemed to endure many things, but above all the densest darkness, monstrous pressures, and suffocations. With every other memory taken away, he could scarcely think of anything except how such a monstrous punishment could exist. When he had been tormented there for three days, as he supposed—a period that seemed longer to him than a thousand years because of the immense punishment—the men mentioned above returned.

They again stood around him on either side, rejoicing with far greater liveliness than before and proceeding with much greater sweetness in every respect. Walking without bodily pathways, with an immovable step, through an even greater radiance, if such a thing can be said, they led him onward.

## Then into Paradise.

5. And, to use his own words: “I saw,” he said, “at a distance, various orders of saints, some nearer and some farther away, standing in the east but looking toward the east and praising him who appeared in the east. Some worshiped with bowed heads, others with faces turned upward and hands outstretched. When we had reached the place of the east, behold, the twenty-four elders, as it is written in the Apocalypse, appeared seated on thrones, with a very spacious entrance preserved. They too, looking reverently toward the east, uttered the Lord’s praises, beyond all words. The praises sung by them together provided me with the sweetest refreshment; but after returning to the body I could in no way retain them.

“In that very place of the east there was a marvelous splendor, an inaccessible light of excessive and immeasurable brightness, in which every most precious color and every delight were present. All the orders of saints who stood rejoicing all around drew their joy from it. That splendor was of such magnitude that I could contemplate neither its beginning nor its end. Although I could look all around, far and near, within that immensity of light I could not contemplate what was inside it, but saw only its surface. Yet I believed that he was present there of whom Peter says: ‘Into whom the angels desire to look’ (1 Peter 1:12). From him proceeded an immense radiance, by which every length and breadth of the saints was illumined. He himself was also, in a certain manner, in all things, and all things in him. He surrounded them all externally; inwardly, by satisfying them, he governed them all. Above, he protected them; below, he sustained them.

“The sun and moon did not shine there, nor were heaven and earth seen there. Nor was the brightness itself of such a kind as to obstruct the eyes of those contemplating it; rather, it most delightfully satisfied their eyes. And when I said that the elders were seated, they were, in a certain manner, seated in him; for nothing corporeal was there, but all things were incorporeal, although they possessed the appearance of bodies, and for that reason were beyond description. Around those who were seated, a splendor proceeding from him was held like a rainbow among the clouds.”

**He understands that he is to become a martyr: how this occurs**

6. “When, therefore, I had been presented by the aforesaid men before this immensity of light, where the majesty of almighty God seemed to me to be, although no one pointed it out, a voice of the sweetest kind, clearer than every sound—for it seemed to me to have filled the whole world—proceeded from that same majesty and addressed me, saying: ‘Go, and return to me crowned with martyrdom.’ At this voice the entire assembly of saints, who were praising God on every side, fell silent and worshiped with bowed faces. In fact, I did not see at all the form from which this voice had been produced.

“After that voice I became sad, because I was being compelled to return to the world, but secure in the promise of returning, I went back from there with the aforementioned guides. Both as they went and as they returned with me, they said nothing, but looked upon me with such loving affection as a mother gazes upon her only son. Thus I returned to the body. In going and returning there was neither labor nor delay, because wherever we were headed, we were immediately present.

“And although I seem to have related something of so great a sweetness of sweets, I nevertheless confess that no writing could express how much the soul felt. Yet the soul itself does not feel it as it truly was, because it seemed to me to be that which ‘eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man.’”

From this vision, which we have related in his own words just as he dictated it, the aforementioned servant of God, both terrified and consoled, began to exercise himself more diligently in the fear of God, to cling more ardently from day to day to good works, and to place his hope in God’s mercy, trusting that God would provide some occasion by which he might attain the palm of martyrdom. Since this did not occur bodily, with a sword threatening him, we shall explain more fully, when we begin to relate his death, how it was completed, by God’s mercy, in the mortification of the cross which he continually bore in his body for the honor of Christ’s name.

**A schoolmaster is admonished by Christ concerning the confession of sins**

[Col. 0965A]

7. After this, when he had been schoolmaster at Saint Peter’s [Note: [Col. 0965D] That is, in the monastery of Corbie, whose principal basilica is consecrated in honor of Saints Peter and Paul and Saint Stephen. Nearby was an oratory of Saint John the Baptist, now occupied by Benedictine nuns; but the church of Saint John the Evangelist was closer to the cloister, and this may perhaps be what is meant here.], he had made it his custom, when going to or returning from the cloister, to spend time more privately in the oratory of blessed John the Baptist. Thus, two years after the preceding vision, one night it seemed to him that he had turned aside to the same oratory for the sake of prayer. When he had risen from prayer, behold, a man was coming through the door, tall in stature, dressed in the Jewish manner, handsome in appearance; from his eyes a radiance of divinity shone like a flame of fire. When he looked at him, he immediately believed him to be Christ the Lord, and rushing forward he fell at his feet.

When he was lying prostrate on his face, the other commanded him to rise. As he rose and stood reverently before him, unable, because of the excessive brightness flashing from his eyes, to look into his face, he addressed him in a gentle voice, saying: “Tell your iniquities, so that you may be justified.”

The servant of God replied: “Lord, why is it necessary for me to tell you? You know everything, and nothing is hidden from you.”

But the other continued: “I indeed know everything, but for this reason I want people to confess their sins to me, so that they may receive forgiveness.”

When he had disclosed to him everything he had done from childhood, and afterward the other had stood upright while he himself lay prostrate in prayer, he said: “Do not be afraid, for I am the one who erases your iniquities.”

After these words, the one who had appeared withdrew. The man of God awoke from sleep, strengthened by confidence in the forgiveness of his sins, and rejoiced with immense joy. [Col. 0965C]

**He sees Fulbert’s soul carried away into heaven**

8. At that same time it happened—as is well known to Your Reverence—that a certain little boy in the school, named Fulbertus [Note: [Col. 0966D] Gualdo calls him Filbertus in the metrical Life, if the manuscript reading is sound.], was struck with a tablet by one of his companions and brought to the point of death. The aforementioned servant of God became exceedingly sad on account of this, because such negligence toward those under his care had allowed so serious an event to occur.

As the hour of the boy’s death approached, the man of God happened to be lying on his bed, overcome by sleep. Behold, in a dream he saw the boy’s soul taken from the body and carried to heaven by angelic ministry; by a marvelous and ineffable dispensation of God, he himself accompanied it as well.

When they had penetrated the secrets of heaven, he saw the soul of the aforementioned boy brought into a certain purple dwelling and placed among the ranks of martyrs. There he was allowed to understand that, because the boy had borne with sufficient patience the wound inflicted upon him and, loving his brother even unto death, had earnestly interceded for his assailant, he had been numbered among the choirs of the martyrs, divine mercy rewarding his patience and kindness.

This was shown to him so promptly, at the very hour of the boy’s death, that while the boy was still dying, the venerable Father Witmarus—who at that time governed the boys’ school together with him and is present as a witness of this event—awoke him and announced the death of the pupil, and he replied that he had already known this as well. Certainly the grace of the Lord permitted him to see this for his consolation, so that, since he was excessively saddened by the matter, the boy’s salvation might relieve the grief of his heart.

**He moves from Old Corbie to New Corbie, where he becomes master and teacher**

9. Inspired from heaven by these and many other revelations and visions, how greatly the grace of holiness and goodness afterward grew among you will be better established by the testimony of those of your number who were then present. But since we wish to relate what took place among us, it seems necessary first to investigate, for those who perhaps know less about this matter, on what occasion he withdrew here from the place of his stability; and, since he had been offered to God among you and had promised obedience there, by what prompting he emigrated to these regions and was raised among us to the office of bishop.

We have thought it necessary to write this so that no one might perhaps attribute to frivolity what the man of God undertook, prompted by divine compunction and love of pilgrimage, for the salvation of souls.

Long ago, therefore, a monastery began to be built in these regions, namely in Saxony. It was founded, in the first place, through the authority and direction of Your Holiness, and in succeeding time, by God’s gift, was happily completed. It took its name from the place of your dwelling, so that it was called New Corbie.

To this place, then, the servant of God was first sent together with other brothers of yours, so that he might carry out there the office of teaching. In this he was found to be so worthy and acceptable in every respect that, by the choice of all, he also publicly preached the word of God to the people in the church. Thus it came about that he became the first schoolmaster of that place and teacher of its people.

**On what occasion he was sent to Denmark with King Heriold, at the request of Louis the Pious**

10. After this it happened that a certain king named Heriold, who held part of the kingdom of the Danes, was attacked with hatred and hostility by the other kings of that province and expelled from his kingdom. He approached the most serene emperor Louis, asking to be deemed worthy of his assistance so that he might regain his kingdom.

The emperor kept him with him and, both personally and through others, encouraged him to accept Christianity, so that greater intimacy might exist between them and the Christian people might come more readily to his and his people’s aid if both worshiped one God. At last, by divine grace, he converted him to the faith, and, after he had been washed in sacred baptism, the emperor himself received him from the sacred font [Note: [Col. 0967D] Namely, at Mainz, in the monastery of Saint Alban, and indeed in the year 826, as is established by Einhard and by the book On the Life of Louis the Pious. There it is reported that Heriold, with his wife and a considerable number of Danes, was baptized with all his people at Saint Alban in Mainz and received many gifts from the emperor, together with a certain district in Frisia called Rhiustri. Thegan adds that his wife, the queen, was lifted from the sacred font by the empress Judith. Adam incorrectly adds Heriold’s brother.] and adopted him as his son.

When he wished to lead him back again to his own people and, strengthened by his assistance, have him reclaim the borders of his kingdom, he began to seek more diligently whether he could find a man of holy devotion who could go with him, remain constantly at his side, and become for him and his people a teacher of sound doctrine, to strengthen them and bring them to accept the faith of the Lord.

Accordingly, the aforementioned Augustus began to discuss the matter publicly in an assembly of his nobles, with his priests and other faithful, and earnestly to ask them all to find someone both willing and worthy for such a task.

**They disapprove of this pilgrimage, although Wala, his brother, consents**

11. When all declined, saying that they knew no man of such devotion who would be willing to undertake so dangerous a pilgrimage for Christ’s name, there was at that time the venerable Wala, abbot of your monastery. He told the aforesaid emperor that he knew one monk in his monastery [Note: [Col. 0967D] That is, in Old Corbie, to which Anscharius had by then returned. He had previously been sent to New Corbie for the purpose of teaching, but perhaps Wala recalled him from there after Abbot Adalhard’s death.], who burned with great zeal for divine religion and desired to suffer much for God’s name. He praised both his training and his character and declared him sufficiently suitable for this task, while nevertheless testifying that he did not know whether the man would willingly endure this pilgrimage.

What more need be said? At the king’s command, Anscharius was summoned to the palace. The abbot told him everything that had taken place and explained why he was being summoned. He replied that he was prepared for God’s service in everything that might be imposed upon him in the cause of obedience.

He was then led into the presence of the Augustus. When the emperor asked him whether he wished to become Heriold’s companion for the sake of God’s name, to preach the Gospel among the Danish peoples, he firmly replied that he most certainly did.

When the abbot added that he was in no way imposing so great a burden upon him by command, but that it would please him and he would grant him permission as a matter of his authority if Anscharius himself chose this of his own accord, Anscharius nevertheless replied that he both chose it and wished to carry it out in every way.

When they publicly declared these things, and all who lived in the abbot’s household learned of them, many began to marvel at such a great transformation in him: namely, that, abandoning his homeland and his relatives, as well as the brothers with whom he had been raised and to whom he was most affectionately attached, he wished to seek foreign nations and associate with unknown and barbarous peoples.

Many also began to condemn him for this and assail him with reproaches; some tried to recall him from his purpose. But the man of God remained immovable in the intention he had begun.

Finally, while the abbot went to the palace each day, Anscharius remained at home, avoided everyone’s company, chose for himself a secluded place in a vineyard [Note: [Col. 0968D] I understand this to mean a vineyard situated near the palace, not the vineyards of Old Corbie, concerning which a certain anonymous writer says in On the Destructions of the Church of Corbie, in Chesne’s second volume: “Attached to Corbie were vineyards around the monastery, containing twelve bunaria of land and more; there ninety modii of wine and more could be gathered.” The entire field surrounding the monastery has now been turned over to the cultivation of grain.] nearby, and devoted himself to prayer and reading.

**Autbertus is joined to him**

12. At that time there was also with the lord abbot a certain brother of your monastery named Autbertus. When he saw Anscharius excessively anxious and sad, withdrawing into solitude each day and having no company or conversation with anyone, he began to sympathize with him.

One day he went to the place where Anscharius was sitting alone in the aforementioned vineyard and began to ask whether he truly wished to undertake that pilgrimage. Anscharius, suspecting that he was asking this not out of compassion but rather through cunning [Col. 0968B], replied: “Why do you care about this? Do not disturb my mind with such questioning.”

Autbertus, however, declared that he was not at all trying to deceive him in this matter, but sincerely wished to know whether Anscharius intended to persevere in the purpose he had undertaken.

Then, rejoicing in his goodwill, Anscharius replied: “I was asked whether I wished, for God’s name, to go to foreign peoples to preach the Gospel of Christ. I did not dare resist that proposal in any way; rather, I desire with all my strength that I be granted the opportunity to go for this purpose. No one will be able to change my mind from this intention.”

The aforementioned brother then replied: “I shall never allow you to go alone, but I desire to set out with you for the love of God—provided only that you obtain for me the lord abbot’s permission.”

When this pious contest between them had been firmly established, Anscharius met the returning abbot and told him that he had found a companion who willingly wished to accompany him on this journey. When the abbot asked who the man was and Anscharius named Brother Autbertus, he was struck with great amazement, never imagining that someone who was of noble birth in the world, who was then close to the abbot and was regarded as the steward of his household after him, would wish to undertake such a thing.

Nevertheless, he summoned Autbertus and questioned him about it. Autbertus replied that he could in no way bear to let Anscharius go alone, but that, for Christ’s name, he wished to become his comfort and assistance, if he had the permission of the abbot and the brothers.

The lord abbot replied that he would grant permission if Autbertus freely chose this journey, but that he would assign them no companion from his household for the service of their needs—unless perhaps they themselves could persuade someone to go with them willingly. The venerable abbot did not do this out of lack of affection, but because it seemed abominable and unjust to compel anyone unwillingly to live among pagans.

**Both set out for Denmark with Heriold. They are well received at Cologne. They reach the Danish frontier**

13. After this both were brought to the king. Delighted by their willingness and desire, he himself gave them ecclesiastical equipment [Note: [Col. 0969D] That is, ecclesiastical furnishings—a chalice, ornaments, and other things for the use of the altar—which they call a capella by a single term.] He gave them chests, tents, and other provisions that seemed necessary for so long a journey. He ordered them to go with the aforementioned Heriold, warning them to devote the greatest care to his faith and continually to labor, through pious exhortation, to prevent him and his people, who had been baptized together with him, from being led back into their former errors at the devil’s instigation. At the same time, they were to urge others vigorously by the word of preaching to accept Christianity.

After they had been dismissed by the emperor, they had no companion to provide them with any service, since no one from the abbot’s household wished to go with them voluntarily, and the abbot did not wish to compel anyone unwilling.

Heriold, to whom they had been entrusted, was still inexperienced and a neophyte, and did not know how the servants of God ought to be treated. His own people, who had only recently been converted and had been brought up in a very different manner, also paid them little attention.

Undertaking this pilgrimage with great difficulty, they reached Cologne. There the venerable bishop Hadelbod, moved by their need, gave them an excellent ship in which to store their belongings and which contained two quite well-prepared cabins. When the aforementioned Heriold saw it, he chose to remain with them on the same ship, so that he might occupy one cabin and they the other. Thus familiarity and goodwill began to grow between them, and his people also thereafter provided them with more diligent service.

From there they entered by way of Dorestad [Note: [Col. 0969D] A town of the Batavians on the Rhine, from which Anscharius and his companions traveled downstream into the Ocean and then by sea to Denmark in the year 827.], crossed the neighboring territory of the Frisians, and reached the borders of the Danes.

Because King Heriold was sometimes unable to remain peacefully in his kingdom, the aforementioned Augustus granted him an estate beyond the Elbe, so that, whenever necessary, he might stay there.

**They instruct pagans and open schools for boys. Autbertus dies at Corbie**

14. The aforementioned servants of God, sometimes situated with him among Christians and sometimes among pagans, began to devote themselves to the word of God and to admonish as many as they could to follow the way of truth. Many were converted to the faith by their example and teaching, and each day the number of those being saved in the Lord increased.

Inspired by divine love to spread the religion of their devotion, they also began carefully to seek out boys whom they could purchase and educate for God’s service. The aforementioned Heriold likewise placed some of his own people under their care for instruction. Thus it came about that within a short time they established there a school of twelve boys or more.

They also took other people here and there into their service as assistants and helpers, and their reputation and religious work began to grow more fruitfully in God’s name.

When they had remained in this holy undertaking for two years or somewhat longer, the aforementioned Brother Autbertus happened to be afflicted by the burden of illness. For this reason he was taken from there to New Corbie. As his prolonged illness grew worse, he ended his life there in a blessed passage—as we believe—at Eastertide, just as the Lord had previously revealed to them.

**When the Swedes ask for preachers, Anscharius is sent to them by Louis; he is strengthened by a heavenly vision in his desire to suffer**

[Col. 0970B]

15. Meanwhile it happened that envoys of the Swedes came to the aforementioned Louis [Note: [Col. 0969D] Namely, in the year 829, since Anscharius had already spent two years among the Danes, according to section 14, although the writers of his age make no mention of this embassy. It must certainly have occurred before the year 830, when Abbot Wala, with whom the emperor discussed the matter, was ordered by him to return to his monastery and observe the rule there, as the author who wrote the Life of Louis puts it.], who reported among the other matters entrusted to their embassy to the most merciful Caesar that there were many among their people who desired to accept the practice of the Christian religion. Their king’s disposition was also sufficiently favorable to permit God’s priests to be present there, provided only that the emperor’s munificence deemed them worthy enough to send suitable preachers.

When the most religious emperor heard this, he was greatly delighted and began again to seek whom he might send to those regions, to test whether that people was ready to believe, as the envoys had reported, and to begin introducing the practice of the Christian religion to them.

Thus it happened that the most serene emperor again began to discuss the matter with your aforementioned abbot, asking whether he might find among his monks someone willing to go to those regions for Christ’s name—or whether, at least, Anscharius, the servant of God who was staying with Heriold, might undertake that embassy.

For this reason Anscharius was summoned to the palace by royal command. He was instructed not to shave himself [Note: [Col. 0970D] Was it then customary for monks going to visit the king to renew their tonsure so that they might appear more well-groomed?] before coming into the emperor’s presence.

The man of God, knowing in advance why he was being summoned, began to burn with the whole fervor of his heart in the love of God and to regard it as the greatest joy if he were permitted to devote himself to winning souls. If any difficulty or adversity could befall him on such a journey, he resolved in his mind to endure it patiently for Christ. He held no doubt in his heart concerning such a work, because he was comforted by the gift of the divine vision he had previously received.

Indeed, at the time mentioned above, while he was living among you and had already been inspired from heaven by two visions, it seemed to him one night that he had come into a certain house where several men of the order of Preachers stood prepared for the office of preaching. Before them, he was suddenly carried away in an ecstasy of mind and saw the radiance of an immense light, above a ray of the sun sent forth from heaven, shine around him.

As he wondered what this might be, a voice almost like the one he had reported hearing in the first vision addressed him, saying: “Your sin has been forgiven.”

He, inspired—as we believe—by the Holy Spirit, replied: “Lord, what do you wish me to do?”

Again the voice sounded, saying: “Go and announce the word of God to the nations.”

Reflecting upon this vision in his mind, the servant of God rejoiced happily in the Lord, seeing that what had been commanded him was already partly fulfilled; and, wishing to announce the word of God also to the Swedes, he desired to add to the total of his labor. [Col. 0971B]

**He obtains Witmarus as his companion, with Gislemarus substituted in Denmark. He is robbed by pirates**

16. When he had been brought into the Caesar’s presence and asked by him whether he wished to undertake this embassy, he replied openly that he was prepared for everything that the emperor, by his authority, might decree and impose upon him for Christ’s name.

Then, through God’s providence, the venerable abbot found for him from your brotherhood a certain nonnus [Note: [Col. 0971D] Saint Benedict prescribes that the abbot be called *domnus* and the priors *nonnus*, meaning a form of paternal respect, in chapter 63 of the Rule.], Witmarus, sufficiently worthy and willing for so great a task.

For his stay with Heriold, he appointed the most devoted Father Gislemarus, proven in faith and good works and most fervent in zeal for God.

He therefore undertook the embassy entrusted to him by the Caesar, to go to the regions of the Swedes and test whether that people was ready to believe, as the aforementioned envoys had reported. How many and how serious were the hardships he endured on this embassy can better be related by the aforementioned Father Witmarus, who was present himself [Note: [Col. 0971D] Thus Witmarus was still alive at that time and had apparently already returned to Old Corbie.].

For us, it is enough to relate that, when they were nearly halfway through the journey, they encountered pirates. The merchants who were traveling with them defended themselves bravely and at first indeed won a victory; but in the second encounter they were defeated and overcome by those same pirates, who took their ships and everything they possessed, while the travelers themselves barely escaped by fleeing on foot to the shore.

There they lost both the royal gifts they were supposed to carry there and everything else they had, except for a few things which they may perhaps have been able to seize and carry away when they leapt from the ship.

Among these losses were nearly forty books, which they had gathered for the service of God; the pirates plundered them and they lost them.

After this, when some of the company intended to return and others to continue onward, the servant of God could not be turned from the journey he had begun. Rather, placing in God’s hands whatever might happen to him, he resolved not to return until he learned by God’s will whether permission to preach could be granted in those regions.

**He is kindly received by the king of Sweden and successfully undertakes the conversion of the people**

17. After this, traveling on foot with great difficulty for a very long distance and crossing the intervening seas by ship wherever appropriate, they finally reached the port of their kingdom called Birca. There they were kindly received by their king, who was called Bern [Note: [Col. 0971D] Adam calls him Biorn in Book I, chapter 16, of his History. In chapter 50 the same author describes the location of the town of Birca in these words: [Col. 0972D] “Birca is a town of the Goths situated in the middle of Sweden, not far from the temple which the Swedes hold in the highest renown in the worship of the gods, called Uppsala. At this place a certain inlet of the strait called the Baltic or Barbarian Sea, turning northward, makes a harbor desirable to the barbarian peoples who inhabit the shores of this sea. Thus far the island has retained the name Biorko.”], after his envoys had reported the reason for their arrival.

When their embassy had become known, and the king had discussed the matter with his faithful advisers, with the unanimous vote and consent of all he granted them permission to remain there and preach the Gospel of Christ, allowing anyone who wished to seek out their teaching.

Thus the servants of God, with joyful hearts, seeing that what they had desired had prospered, began to announce the word of salvation to the people settled there. Many also supported their embassy. Many Christians were held captive among them, and they rejoiced that at last they could participate in the mysteries.

It was proven that everything was exactly as the king’s envoys had truthfully reported to the most serene Caesar, and several people earnestly sought the grace of baptism.

Among them, the prefect of the town itself and an adviser of the king, a man especially dear to him named Herigarius, received the gift of holy baptism and remained most steadfast in the Catholic faith. He built a church on his own estate and devoted himself with great religious zeal to the service of God.

Various distinctions of this man are recorded, and many indications of his unconquered faith are attested; we shall explain these more clearly in what follows.

**Anscharius reports the matter to the emperor**

18. After the aforementioned servants of God had completed another half-year among them, they returned to the most serene Augustus with a reliable account of the success of their embassy and with letters written in their customary manner by the king’s own hand. He received them honorably and with the greatest benevolent piety. They related how greatly the Lord had acted with them and that, in those regions, a door of faith had been opened for the calling of the nations.

When the most devout emperor heard this, he rejoiced with immense joy. Recalling at the same time what had long ago been conceived concerning the worship of God among the Danes, and offering praises and thanks to almighty God, he began, inflamed by the zeal of faith, to seek how he might establish an episcopal see in the northern regions, at the very edge of his empire. From there it would be appropriate for a bishop residing there to visit those regions more frequently for the sake of preaching, and from there all those barbarian nations could more easily and abundantly receive the sacraments of the divine mystery.

While he was pursuing this concern with vigilant care, some of his faithful reported to him that, when his father of glorious memory, Charles Augustus, had subdued all Saxony by the sword and subjected it to the yoke of Christ, he had divided it among bishoprics but entrusted no bishop with the last part of that province, which lay in the north beyond the Elbe. Instead, he had resolved to reserve it so that he might establish an archiepiscopal see there, from which, by the grace of the Lord, the succession of the faith might also advance among foreign nations.

For this reason he had first caused a church to be consecrated there by a certain bishop of Gaul named Amalarius [Note: [Col. 0973D] I believe he was the bishop of Trier, a different man from Amalarius the writer of books on the divine offices, who traveled to Rome in the year 831, according to Book 1, chapter 58, of On the Order of the Antiphonary. At that time Amalarius’s successor Hetti had presided over the church of Trier since the tenth year of his episcopate. In an imperial privilege cited later, Louis Augustus says that a certain bishop from the distant regions of Gaul, named Amalarius, consecrated the church at Hamburg, without mentioning his see.].

Afterward he entrusted that parish for special governance to a priest named Heridach, and did not wish the neighboring bishops to have any authority at all over that place. He had also decided to consecrate this priest as bishop, but Heridach’s earlier departure from this life prevented it.

**He obtains the see at Hamburg, designated by Charles and established by Louis; he is consecrated archbishop**

19. After the death of the Augustus of such illustrious memory, when his son—the aforementioned emperor Louis—had been placed upon the throne of his kingdom, certain advisers persuaded him to divide that part of the province which lay beyond the Elbe into two and, for the time being, to entrust it to two neighboring bishops [Note: [Col. 0973D] Namely, the bishops of Bremen and Verden, Willericus and Heligaudus, concerning whom more will be said below.]. For he did not pay sufficient attention to his father’s arrangement concerning this matter, or else was entirely unaware of it.

When an opportunity thus arose, and the faith of Christ had already begun, by God’s grace, to bear fruit in the regions of the Danes and Swedes, he learned of his father’s intention. So that none of his father’s work might remain unfinished, and with the agreement of the bishops and the participation of a large synodal assembly, he established an archiepiscopal see in the aforementioned farthest region of Saxony beyond the Elbe, in the city of Hamburg.

The entire Church of the Nordalbingians was to be subject to it, and authority over all the northern regions was to belong to it, so that bishops or priests might be appointed there and sent to those regions for Christ’s name.

Accordingly, the aforementioned emperor solemnly had our lord and father Anscharius consecrated archbishop of this see [Note: [Col. 0973D] This occurred in the year 832, though Adam gives the year 833 incorrectly. Since the same author testifies that Anscharius died in the year 865, this was the twenty-fourth year of his episcopate.], through the hands of Drogo, bishop of Metz and then archchaplain, holding the highest and sacred dignity of the palace. The archbishops Ebbo of Rheims, Hetti of Trier, and Otgar of Mainz were present, together with many other bishops assembled at the imperial council.

The bishops Heligaudus and Willericus also assisted, consented, and jointly consecrated him; the portions of that parish mentioned above had begun to be entrusted to them.

Because that diocese had been established in dangerous places, lest it perish in any way on account of the barbarians’ impending savagery, and because it was very small in every respect, he granted to that same see, for its perpetual support, a certain cell in Gaul called Turholt [Note: [Col. 0973D] The cell of Turholt, now the town that is the capital of the county of Thurolt, adjoining Flanders, was granted to Anscharius in the year 833, as Adam testifies in Book I, chapter 17. This cell is mentioned in the Life of Saint Bavo, second century.], to serve that see and its mission permanently.

**Confirmed by Gregory IV, he is appointed legate of the northern peoples**
20. And so that all these things might retain forever the full force of their stability, he honorably sent him to the apostolic see and, through his envoys, the venerable bishops Bernold and Ratold, together with the most illustrious count Gerold,

[Note: [Col. 0974D] It is uncertain to which place he belonged. There does exist a formal letter from Wolfeo, bishop of Constance, to Bernalt, bishop of Strasbourg, in Sirmond’s third volume of the Councils of Gaul; this Bernalt is omitted by Guillimann. But since that letter was issued in 817, and Utho—clearly Bernalt’s successor—is said to have subscribed to the Council of Aachen in 819, another Bernold must be understood here. Count Gerold was prefect of the Pannonian frontier, according to Einhard under the year 826.]

he caused this entire arrangement to be reported to the most holy Pope Gregory for confirmation. The pope himself strengthened it both by the authority of his decree and by the bestowal of the pallium, according to the custom of his predecessors. He appointed him, who was then present, legate among all the surrounding peoples of the Swedes or Danes, as well as of the Slavs and the other peoples settled in the northern regions,

[Col. 0974C]

together with Archbishop Ebo of Rheims, who had previously undertaken that legation. Before the body and shrine of the holy Apostle Peter he granted him public authority to preach the Gospel, and, so that none of these arrangements might in future be rendered void, he struck with the sword of anathema anyone who resisted or contradicted them, or in any way plotted against these holy endeavors of the most devout emperor, and condemned him as guilty to everlasting punishment in the lot of the devil.

Moreover, as we have already stated, this same legation had previously been entrusted by the authority of Pope Paschal to Archbishop Ebo of Rheims.

[Note: [Col. 0974D] Philip Caesar reports letters of Paschal concerning this legation, and Henschenius follows him; in them the pontiff grants Ebo authority to spread the Gospel in the northern regions together with Halitgar as his assistant. Baronius assigns this to the year 823.]

For he himself—as we believe, inspired by the Holy Spirit—burned with the most ardent desire for the calling of the nations, especially the Danes, whom he had often seen at the palace and whom he grieved to see deceived by diabolical error.

[Col. 0975A]

He desired to devote himself and all that he possessed to the salvation of the nations for the sake of Christ’s name. The lord emperor had also given him a place beyond the Elbe called Welanao,

[Note: [Col. 0975D] Commonly Wehl or Wedel, below Hammaburg.]

so that whenever he went into those regions he would have a place there in which to stay. He therefore came to that place many times, distributed much in the northern regions for the winning of souls, brought many people into the Christian religion, and strengthened them in the Catholic faith.

He Receives Bishop Gauzbert as an Assistant, and Others from Old Corbie.

21. But after the ordination of our lord and father Anscharius described above, when they were conferring among themselves about the same legation, it seemed necessary to them that an assistant should be ordained for him, who would exercise the episcopal ministry among the Swedes. For in a region situated so far away the bishop ought to be present, and he alone was not sufficient for both places.

Therefore, with the consent and approval of the aforesaid emperor, the venerable Ebo sent to the land of the Swedes a certain relative of his named Gauzbert [also Gautbert], chosen for this work and invested with episcopal honor. He abundantly supplied him with ecclesiastical furnishings and the necessary expenses, both from his own resources and from royal gifts. He appointed him as legate among the Swedish peoples, almost as his representative,

[Note: [Col. 0975D] Yet Ebo did not remain continuously in those regions from 823 until that time. Certainly he was present in his own diocese of Rheims in 827, when Louis Augustus sent him to the monastery of Dervent, then occupied by secular clerics, to examine carefully whether the place was suitable for the observance of the monastic order, as is clear from Louis’s own charter.]

since Ebo had earlier undertaken there the office of preaching by apostolic authority.

[Col. 0975C]

Later, at the suggestion of that same venerable bishop Ebo, the most clement Augustus gave him the cell that Ebo himself had built at the aforementioned place of Welanao, as a place of refreshment, so that it might serve the ministry of his office in perpetuity and with lasting stability.

The aforesaid Gauzbert, whom the men who consecrated him called Simon in honor of the apostolic name,

[Note: [Col. 0975D] This shows that it was at times customary then for the name of a bishop to be changed at his consecration. Thus Saint Willibrord was called Clement by the pope.]

came to the land of the Swedes and was honorably received by both king and people. He began, with the goodwill and unanimous support of all, to build a church there and to preach publicly the Gospel of the faith. Joy over salvation arose among the Christians living there, and the number of believers increased day by day.

Meanwhile, our lord and pastor vigorously fulfilled his office in the diocese entrusted to him and in the regions of the Danes, and by the example of his good conduct he drew many toward the grace of faith. He also began to purchase some boys from the Danish and Slavic peoples, and to ransom others from captivity, so that he might raise them for the service

[Col. 0976A]

of God. He placed some of them in the aforementioned cell of Turholt to be educated. With him there were some of your community, our holy fathers and teachers, whose doctrine and instruction happily caused the esteem of divine religion to grow among us.

Hammaburg Is Ravaged by Pirates, and Anscharius Patiently Endures the Loss of Everything.

22. But while these things were being commendably and worthily accomplished before God in both regions, it happened unexpectedly that pirates arrived and surrounded the city of Hammaburg by ship. Since this occurred suddenly and without warning, there was no time to gather the country people; especially since the count who at that time held the prefecture of that place, the illustrious Bernarius, was absent.

The lord bishop, who was stationed there, together with those who were present in the city itself or living in its suburb, at first, upon hearing of their arrival, wished to hold the place until greater assistance should come. But when the pagans pressed forward and the city was already blockaded, he saw that they could not be resisted and prepared to carry away the relics of the saints.

[Note: [Col. 0976D] Namely, those of the holy confessors and pontiffs Xystus and Siricius of Rheims, according to Adam in Book I, chapter 23. Later, in their honor, he established a monastery on the estate of Ramsola, which the noblewoman Ikia had given him, not far from Hammaburg. Anscharius had received these relics from Ebo, together with the body of Saint Martinianus, which he placed at Helingastad, and the treasures of blessed Remigius, which he preserved with great honor at Bremen.]

Thus, while the clergy had fled in various directions, he himself barely escaped, even without his cloak. The people also left the place and wandered here and there; many fled, some were captured, and most were killed.

Finally, after plundering the city and stripping everything that was in it or in the neighboring settlement, the enemy—who had arrived there in the evening—remained there through that night, the following day, and the following night.

[Col. 0976C]

Then, after setting everything on fire and carrying off the spoils, they departed. The church, constructed with remarkable workmanship under the direction of the lord bishop, together with the monastery buildings magnificently arranged, was burned there. The library, which the aforementioned serene emperor had given to our father and which had been excellently written out, perished in the flames together with many other books.

Thus everything he had there, whether in ecclesiastical furnishings or in other treasures and possessions, was seized by hostile violence, either through plunder or through fire, so that they left him as though completely stripped. For scarcely anything had previously been carried away from the place, nor was anything rescued then, except what some fugitive perhaps happened to seize and carry off with him.

For all these losses, the most holy lord and father was not at all troubled in heart, nor did he sin with his lips. Rather, although he had lost in what seemed a single moment almost everything that, from the beginning of his episcopate, he had been able to accumulate or devote to the construction of buildings, he repeatedly recited in the words of blessed Job:

“The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away; as it pleased the Lord, so it has happened; blessed be the name of the Lord” (Job 1:21).

Gauzbert Is Harassed by the Swedes, and Nithard Is Killed.

23. After these things had taken place, while the lord bishop and his people were suffering many hardships and calamities, and the brothers of his community, together with the most holy relics, wandered here and there through various places without settling anywhere in peace, the wicked plot prevailed. By diabolical instigation it happened that the people of the Swedes, inflamed by the heat of zeal, began treacherously to persecute the aforesaid Bishop Gauzbert.

A group of the people then burst into the house in which he was staying, unanimously agreeing to plunder it. They killed his nephew, named Nithard, with the sword, and, struck down by hatred of the Christian name, made him—as we believe—a martyr of God.

They bound Gauzbert himself together with the other companions who were present with him. After plundering everything they could find among them, they expelled them from their territory amid insult and abuse. This, however, was not done by royal command, but was carried out solely through a popular conspiracy.

The mercy of the divine majesty did not permit this to go unpunished. Almost all who had taken part were punished within a short time, each in a different manner. Much could be said about them, but, so as not to weary the readers, we have chosen to mention only one, so that from his destruction it may become clear by what punishment the others were avenged.

The Swedes Are Punished.

24. There was in that land a certain powerful man whose son had taken part in the same conspiracy with the others and had brought home to his father’s house the goods that had fallen to him from the spoils taken there. After this, the man’s property began to diminish, and his livestock and household to perish. His son also died, struck down by divine vengeance. His wife, together with their son and daughter, died soon afterward.

When he saw himself deprived of all his possessions except his little son, the wretched man began to fear the anger of the gods and considered in his mind that he was suffering all these things because he had offended some god.

[Col. 0977D]

Accordingly, as was customary there, he went to a diviner and asked him to tell him which god he had offended and how he ought to appease him. The diviner performed the rites that he was accustomed to observe in matters of this kind and declared that all their gods were favorably disposed toward him, but that the God of the Christians was altogether hostile to him.

“Christ,” he said, “holds you as one destroyed. Because something belonging to him, something consecrated to him, remains stored in your house, all these evils that you have suffered have come upon you. You will not be able to escape them so long as it remains in your house.”

When he heard this and anxiously considered what the object might be, he remembered that his son had brought home from the aforementioned spoils a certain book. He was struck with tremendous horror, and, since there was then no priest present, he was completely uncertain what to do with the book. He did not dare to keep it with him any longer.

At last, having scarcely found a solution, he brought it before the people who lived in the same village and told them what he had suffered. When they all declared that they did not know what should be done about it and were afraid to receive or keep such a thing in their houses, he himself, astonished and unwilling to retain it any longer, fastened it neatly to a certain hedge. He announced that whoever wished might take it from there, and he vowed to offer the Lord Jesus Christ voluntary satisfaction for the offense he had committed.

A Christian took the book from there and brought it into his own house. From his account we also learned these things. He later became a man of great faith and devotion, so that he afterward learned the psalms among us by heart, without books.

Thus the others too were punished, some by death, some by disease, and some by the loss of their possessions. It became clear to everyone that those who had dared to treat the holy bishop of God and his companions dishonorably and to despoil them had experienced the gravest vengeance of our Lord Jesus Christ.

After Seven Years Anscharius Sends Ardgarius to Them.

25. After these events, that place remained without a priestly presence for nearly seven years. Our lord and pastor Anscharius, therefore, deeply distressed by this absence and unwilling to allow the faith of the Christian religion that had begun there to perish—and especially grieving for the son whom we mentioned above—sent into those regions a certain anchorite named Ardgarius and ordered him to remain especially close to Herigarius.

When he arrived, Herigarius received him with due honor, as did the Christians who were there, and they showed great joy at his presence. They began, as they had done at first, to seek devotedly the things of God and to observe the Christian rite with willing hearts.

No unbeliever dared to resist his preaching, because they remembered with fearful minds the punishment inflicted on those who had expelled the servants of God from that place. At the urging of the aforementioned Herigarius, and by the command and permission of the king who was then ruling, he began publicly to celebrate the mysteries of God.

That most faithful man Herigarius, during the time when no priestly presence was available there,

[Col. 0978D]

suffered many insults from unbelievers. But by divine grace, through signs from heaven obtained at his request, the praises of the true faith were made manifest. Of these, as we promised, we have decided to insert some here, so that the invincible strength of his faith may be made clear.

Herigarius, Who Himself Suffered Much, Performs Miracles.

26. On one occasion he was sitting at a certain public assembly, with a platform prepared in the open field for the discussion. During the conversation, the people praised their gods, whose favor brought them many successes, and reproached him for wandering alone from the company of all others in an empty faith.

Since he was fervent in spirit, he is said to have replied:

“If there is such doubt concerning the divine majesty—although there ought to be no doubt at all—let us prove by miracles which possesses greater power: your many gods, as you call them, or my one almighty Lord Jesus Christ.

“Look, the time for rain has come”—for rain was indeed threatening at that moment. “Invoke the names of your gods, so that the rain may not descend upon you, while I shall invoke my Lord Jesus Christ, so that not a single drop of rain may touch me. If anyone in this matter hears those who invoke him, let that one be God.”

After they had made this agreement among themselves, they all sat on one side while he sat on the other with a single boy. Each of them began to invoke his own god, and Herigarius also invoked the Lord Jesus Christ.

An immense rain then descended from heaven and drenched all the others with water, so that they appeared to have been thrown into a river with their clothing on. Even the leaves of the branches falling upon them from the shelter erected there showed that they were overwhelmed by the divine power.

But upon Herigarius and the boy who was with him not a single drop of rain fell.

When this had happened and the others were confused and amazed, he said:

“Behold, you see who is God. Do not attempt, wretched men, to turn me away from his worship. Rather, be confounded by your errors and learn the way of truth.”

Other Miracles of the Same Man.

27. At another time it happened that he suffered such severe pain in his shin that he could not move from the place where he was unless he was carried. When he had endured this affliction for some time, many people began to come to visit him.

Some urged him to sacrifice to the gods for his health; others attacked him with insults, saying that he was without a god and therefore lacked health. When this occurred repeatedly and he steadfastly resisted their evil suggestions, at last, unable to endure their abuse, he replied that he had no intention of seeking help from empty images, but from his Lord Jesus Christ, who, if he wished, could heal him of his infirmity in an instant.

He immediately called his servants and ordered them to carry him to his church. There, placed before all who were present, he poured out humble prayers to the Lord, saying:

“My Lord Jesus Christ, so that these wretched men may know that you alone are God and that there is no other besides you, grant to me, your servant, at this hour the former health of my body. Let your enemies, when they see your mighty works, be confounded by their errors and be converted to the knowledge of your name.

“Do, I beg you, what I ask for the sake of your holy name, which is blessed forever. Let there be no shame for those who trust in you, O Lord.”

After these words, divine grace healed him, and he was immediately restored to perfect health. He left the church by himself and gave thanks to God for his recovery. Growing stronger in the faith of Christ, he increasingly confounded the unbelievers.

King Avoundus Attacks Birca with the Danes.

28. At approximately the same time it happened that a certain Swedish king named Avoundus,

[Note: [Col. 0979D] So the manuscript codices read, as does the poet Gualdo. Bollandus has Anaundus, or Anoundus.]

having been expelled from his kingdom, was an exile among the Danes. Wishing to recover the borders of his former kingdom, he began to seek their help, promising that, if they followed him, many gifts would come to them.

He proposed to them the settlement called Birca, saying that many wealthy merchants were there, together with an abundance of every good thing and great quantities of treasure-money. He promised to lead them to that settlement, where they could enjoy abundant advantage for their needs without risking the loss of their army.

Delighted by the promised gifts and eager to acquire the treasures, they filled twenty-one ships with men equipped for battle and sent them with him. He himself had eleven ships of his own.

Departing from Denmark, they unexpectedly came to the settlement mentioned above. As it happened, their king was then far away, and the leaders and the multitude of the people could not assemble. Only the aforementioned Herigarius, prefect of the place, was present with the merchants and people who lived there.

Placed in great distress, they fled to the nearby city. They also began to promise and offer vows and sacrifices to their gods—or rather, to demons—that they might be saved from such danger by their help.

But because the city itself was not very strongly fortified and they had few men to resist, they sent envoys to the Danes, requesting a pledge of peace and an agreement. The aforesaid king ordered them to pay one hundred pounds of silver as the price of ransoming the settlement, and then they would have peace.

They immediately sent what he demanded,

[Col. 0980C]

and it was accepted by the aforesaid king.

Herigarius Urges the People of Birca to Invoke Christ.

29. The Danes, however, were deeply displeased with this agreement, because matters had not turned out as they had planned. They began to wish to attack them suddenly and completely plunder and burn the place, saying that any one merchant there possessed more than had been offered to them and that they could in no way endure so great an insult.

While they were discussing these things among themselves and preparing to plunder the city into which the inhabitants had fled, this plan also became known to the people inside. They therefore gathered together again. Since they had no strength to resist and no hope of refuge, they encouraged one another to offer greater vows and sacrifices to their gods.

But the faithful servant of the Lord Herigarius, angered against them, said:

“May your vows and sacrifices, together with your idols, be cursed by our God. How long will you serve demons and reduce yourselves to ruin through empty vows and poverty? Look: you have offered much, made even greater vows, and moreover given one hundred pounds of silver. What benefit has this brought you?

“Behold, they are coming to plunder everything you possess. They will lead your wives and children away as captives, burn your city and settlement with fire, and you will perish by the sword. What benefit, then, do your images bring you?”

At these words they were all terrified and did not know what to do. With one accord they replied:

“Let our safety and counsel depend upon your decision. Whatever you advise us, we shall certainly do.”

He said to them:

“If you wish to make vows, make them and fulfill them to the almighty God who reigns in heaven, whom I serve with a pure conscience and upright faith. He is Lord of all; everything rests in his will, and no one can resist his dominion.

“If you therefore seek his help with all your heart, you will find that his omnipotence will not fail you.”

Having accepted his counsel, they then went out unanimously and willingly into the open field, as was customary there, and vowed to the Lord Christ a fast and almsgiving for their deliverance.

They Are Freed from the Enemy’s Attack.

[Col. 0981B]

30. Meanwhile, the aforesaid king began to deal with the Danes, asking them to determine by lot whether it was the will of the gods that the place should be destroyed by them.

“There are many powerful gods there,” he said. “A church was once built there, and Christ is worshiped by many Christians there. He is the most powerful of the gods and is able to help those who hope in him, in whatever way he wishes. It is therefore necessary to inquire whether you are being moved to this action by the divine will.”

Since this was their custom, they could not refuse. They therefore consulted the lots, and it was discovered that they could not accomplish this undertaking with success and that the place had not been granted by God for their plunder.

They inquired again in what direction they should go, where they might acquire money, so that they would not return home empty-handed after being frustrated in their vain hope. The lot fell that they should go to a certain city situated farther away, in the territory of the Slavs.

Believing, therefore, that this had been divinely commanded them, the Danes withdrew from the place mentioned above. They hurried by a direct route to that city, attacked its peaceful and secure inhabitants, and unexpectedly captured the city by force of arms. After taking much plunder and many treasures there, they returned home.

The king, who had come with them to plunder the place, made peace with them, returned the silver he had received from them, and remained among them for some time, wishing to be reconciled with his own people.

Thus, by the grace of the Lord and because of the faith of his servant Herigarius, the people of that place were freed from the attack of the enemy and restored to their possessions.

Herigarius Urges the Inhabitants to Believe in Christ and Then Dies Devoutly.

[Col. 0981D]

31. After this, he himself brought the matter before a public assembly and urged them to consider more attentively which god truly existed, saying:

“Alas, wretched people, understand at last that it is vain to seek help from demons, who cannot assist you in tribulation. Accept the faith of my Lord Jesus Christ, whom you have proved to be the true God, who, when you had no refuge, granted you help through his mercy.

“Do not continue to seek superstitious worship or to appease idols with empty sacrifices. Worship the true God, who rules over all that is in heaven and on earth, and submit yourselves to him. Adore his omnipotence.”

After this, he became all the more joyful as he grew stronger in the faith through the Lord’s repeated benefits. Wherever he was present, he publicly announced to everyone, partly with exultation, the power of the Lord and the grace of faith.

Thus he carried the good fight through to the end of his life. When he had completed the course of good works and his illness grew worse, he was commended to divine mercy in the presence of the aforementioned priest Ardgarius. Having received holy communion, he happily died in Christ.

Much more could still be said about the steadfastness of his faith, but because we have aimed at brevity, what has been said here may suffice.

Frideburg Remains Steadfast in the Faith and Arranges for Wine to Be Kept as Viaticum.

[Col. 0982B]

32. In those same times there was among them a certain matron of great piety whom no perversity of wicked people could ever turn from the uprightness of her faith.

Whenever she was placed in any difficulty, people repeatedly urged her to sacrifice to idols according to their custom. But she remained firm and did not abandon the duties of her faith. She said that it was useless to seek help from mute and deaf images and that it seemed abominable to her to turn again toward those things to which she had renounced allegiance at baptism and thus break the promise she had made to Christ.

“For if it is wrong,” she said, “to lie to human beings, how much more wrong is it to lie to God? And if it is good among human beings to remain faithful, how much more must one who accepts the faith of the Lord never depart from it?

“My Lord Jesus Christ is almighty. If I persevere in his faith, he will be able to grant me both health and everything I may need.”

This devout woman, named Frideburg, praiseworthy for the goodness of her life and the steadfastness of her faith, lived out her days into old age.

When the day of her death was approaching, and after the departure of the lord Simon no priest was then present there, she—out of love for the sacrifice that she had heard was the viaticum

[Note: [Col. 0981D] I cited this passage in the preface to the third century as evidence for viaticum under both kinds. In the eleventh century certain Frisians had fallen far from this matron’s devotion; Baldericus calls them Aquatici in Book III, chapter 22 of his Chronicle of Cambrai.]

of Christians—had a little wine set aside in a certain small vessel. Commending it to her daughter’s faith, she ordered that, if her final hour should ever approach, some of that wine should be dripped into her mouth, since she had no sacrifice, so that in this way she might commend her departure to the grace of the Lord.

That wine was preserved with her for nearly three years. Then it happened that the aforementioned priest Ardgarius arrived there. Once he had settled there, she exercised the devotion of her religion for as long as she had strength, diligently seeking from him the solemn celebrations of the Mass and salutary instruction.

Meanwhile, when illness overtook her, she began to grow weak. Concerned about her death, she had the aforementioned presbyter summoned to her. Having received from his hand the desired viaticum, she happily departed to the Lord.

She Orders Her Possessions Distributed to the Poor; While Her Daughter Carries This Out, the Money Does Not Diminish.

[Col. 0983A]

33. Since she had always been devoted to almsgiving and was wealthy in worldly possessions, she had instructed her aforementioned daughter, named Cathla, that after her departure from this life she should distribute everything that belonged to her among the poor.

“And because there are few poor people here,” she said, “after my death, as soon as the opportunity arises, sell everything that has not been distributed here, take the money with you, and go to Dorestad. There are many churches and priests and clerics there, and a multitude of those in need.

“When you arrive there, seek out people who can teach you, as faithful Christians, how to distribute these things, and distribute everything for the remedy of my soul.”

After her mother’s death, the daughter diligently fulfilled what her mother had commanded. She set out on her journey and arrived at Dorestad, where she sought devout women who would go with her around the holy places and instruct her what she ought to distribute to each person.

One day, as they were going around the holy places for the purpose of distributing the money, and half had already been given away, she said to her companions:

“Now we are tired. It would be better to buy some wine so that we may refresh ourselves, and then complete what we have begun.”

They therefore spent four denarii for this purpose. After recovering their strength, they completed what they had begun.

When this was finished, she returned to her lodging and placed the sack in which the money had been kept, now empty, in a certain place. But when she went again to that place through the gift of heaven, she found it full as it had been before.

Overwhelmed by so great a miracle, she summoned the women who had previously gone with her and showed them what had happened. Counting the money in their presence, she found as much as she had brought there, except for the four denarii.

Following their advice, she went to the priests who appeared most reputable there and made the miracle known to them. They praised God’s grace for such goodness and declared that the Lord had repaid her labor and good intention.

“Because,” they said, “you obeyed your mother, preserved your faith toward her unblemished, and diligently fulfilled her almsgiving, the Lord, the rewarder of all good things, has granted you this as support in your need. He is sufficient for all and needs nothing from anyone. Everything distributed in his name he will repay in the heavenly kingdom.

“So that you would not doubt that this is true, and so that you would not regret the distribution of the money given to you, God has deigned to assure you by this miracle.

“Believe firmly from this sign that your mother is safe with the Lord. Having been admonished by this miracle, do not be afraid to give your own possessions for Christ.”

Ardgarius Returns from Sweden to His Solitude.

34. After the death of the aforementioned man Herigarius, the already-mentioned priest of God Ardgarius, out of love for the solitary life that he had previously led, left those regions and returned to his own place. Thus the Christians settled there were once again deprived of a priestly presence.

It therefore became clear by evident indication that the anchorite Ardgarius had been sent to those regions both to strengthen the faith of the aforementioned man Herigarius and of the matron mentioned above, and likewise to commend their departure to divine mercy, so that they might receive, as their final viaticum, the mystery of holy communion that they had faithfully desired.

After the Death of Louis the Pious, Anscharius Is Deprived of Necessary Resources and Abandoned by His Companions.

35. In the midst of the events described above, it happened by the judgment of God that the most serene emperor Louis, of blessed memory, departed from this present life.

[Col. 0984B]

After his death, when great confusion arose concerning the division of the kingdom, our pastor’s legation also began at times to falter. Since the aforementioned cell of Turholt had fallen to the share of the venerable King Charles, he removed it from the service that his father had assigned to it and, as you know well, gave it to Reginarius.

Although he was repeatedly admonished about this by his most glorious brothers, the kings, and by many others, he refused in any way to yield to their requests. Our father therefore began to be worn down by needs and want.

As a result, your brothers who were then present here with him returned to your community, and many others also abandoned him because of his poverty. He alone, with the few who remained with him, managed as best he could. Although he lived in poverty, he did not wish in any way to abandon the office entrusted to him.

While Louis, King of Germany, Was Ruling, Anscharius Receives the Bishopric of Bremen with the Approval of the Council.

36. The Lord also, seeing his humility and steadfastness in patience—for the heart of a king is in the hand of the Lord—inspired the mind of our most clement lord and senior, King Louis, who had assumed the governance of this kingdom after his father, to begin seeking a means by which he could provide Anscharius with support for his subsistence, so that he might complete the charge of his legation.

Since he had no cell in this province suitable for that legation, and since the church of the bishopric of Bremen was then without a pastor, he resolved to give it to him.

[Note: [Col. 0983D] This occurred in the year 849, as the Saxon Chronicle indicates in these words: “In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 849, Leuderic, the third bishop of the church of Bremen, died; Anscharius the monk, the first archbishop of Hammaburg, succeeded him. Under him the union of the dioceses of Bremen and Hammaburg was made.”

[Col. 0984D] The book of donations cited by Adam agrees, in Book I, chapter 24, where this union is said to have taken place “in the ninth year of Louis II,” when “Ansgarius was led into the bishopric by Aldric the cleric and Count Reginbald, the emperor’s envoys.”]

He therefore began to discuss the matter with the other bishops and his remaining faithful men in a public assembly, asking whether he could lawfully do this according to canonical authority.

Our lord and pastor, fearing in some way that this would be dangerous for him and prudently taking care lest he be accused by anyone of the stain of greed, did not readily consent to this arrangement. At the king’s command, the matter was therefore examined in a council of bishops.

They proved by many preceding examples that it could rightly be done: because the diocese to which Anscharius had been ordained was very small—for it had only four baptismal churches—and because these too had often been devastated by barbarian incursions, this additional charge could be joined to it as a means of support.

The Portion of the Diocese Is Restored to the Bishop of Verden, While Anscharius Retains the See of Hammaburg.

### 37. The Diocese of Bremen and the Diocese of Verden Restored

But lest the bishop of Verden should have any scruple that he himself was retaining both the portion of his episcopate taken from beyond the Elbe and the whole diocese of Bremen, they decreed that, just as they had been in the time of Lord Louis I, the two bishoprics—Bremen and Verden—should be restored, and that he should retain Bremen, from which the greater part of his diocese had been taken, and which at that time was likewise bereft of the presence of its pastor. After the bishops had established this by decree, he, at the king’s command, undertook the governance of the diocese of Bremen. Meanwhile Waldgar, then bishop of Verden, received the portion of the diocese beyond the Elbe that ought to belong to him.

When matters had remained thus for some time, the same question was examined more carefully at another council of bishops. They judged that it was not right for the see to which he had been ordained to be held by another bishop—for at that time Hammaburg had fallen to Waldgar—although they said that the king certainly had the power to enlarge a small and greatly diminished diocese; nevertheless, a place established by apostolic authority for episcopal dignity must not be altered in any way. Therefore, by unanimous agreement and with the consent of the most devout king mentioned above, Louis, the bishops assembled there decreed that our Father Anscharius should recover the see to which he had been consecrated; and, if he retained anything beyond the Elbe from the diocese of Verden, he should restore to the bishop of that see a portion from the parish of the church of Bremen. This was accordingly carried out by royal command, by synodal decree of the bishops, and also with the will and consent of the aforementioned Waldgar, bishop of Verden.

### The Bishop of Cologne Initially Opposes This Union

### 38.

While these things were being done, the city of Cologne, to which the parish of Bremen was suffragan, was at that time without episcopal blessing; and because this situation had lasted a long time, it was necessary to decide this matter even without the presence of the prelate of that place. [Col. 0985D] **Note:** For nearly ten years. Gunthar first raised a dispute over this union in the year 857, as Henschen correctly proves from the Annals of Fulda, where Louis is said to have held a conference with his nephew Lothar at the castle of Confluentia in February, and, during Lent, to have held a public assembly at the city of the Vangiones, which is Worms. More will be said below about this assembly or conference. Nevertheless, the matter was confirmed by Pope Nicholas I in the following year, in which these words occur in the Saxon Chronicle manuscript: “In that same year the union of the parishes of Bremen and Hammaburg was made, at the end of the life of Saint Ansgarius, by the authority of Pope Nicholas, who appointed both him and his successors as legates and vicars among all the peoples of the Swedes, Danes, and Slavs, just as Pope Gregory had previously granted.” This union was again opposed during the pontificate of Pope Formosus, whose letters on the matter are preserved in favor of Hermann, archbishop of Cologne.

Afterward, however, when the venerable bishop Gunthar had been consecrated to that place, our Lord and Father endeavored to persuade him that this arrangement should also be confirmed by his authority. Gunthar, however, was strongly opposed to it. For this reason, when the two kings—Louis and Lothar—were later staying in the city of Worms, in the presence of a large assembly of bishops from both kingdoms and of our venerable Father, this same matter was brought forward. When everyone approved the arrangement as properly ordered, so that the aforementioned bishop Gunthar should also confirm it by his authority, they all entreated him to do so. At first he began stoutly to resist them, demonstrating in many ways that it was unjust for a suffragan see to be transformed into an archiepiscopal see, and that he ought not in any way to diminish the honor of his own see. Finally, however, when both kings and all the bishops assembled there urged him to do this and declared that necessity made it entirely permissible, he replied that, if it were confirmed by apostolic authority, he too would regard it as valid.

### Legates Sent to Rome: Nicholas I Confirms the Union. The Legation of the Northern Regions Is Granted to Anscharius

### 39.

After this response had been received, and after all his suffragans had likewise agreed to the same proposal, the most devout king Louis mentioned above, wishing both to increase in every respect the almsgiving of his father and to have what he himself had arranged confirmed in every detail, sent the most reverend Solomon, bishop of the city of Constance, to the apostolic see for this purpose. With him our Lord and Father Anscharius, since he could not go in person, sent his son and our brother Nordfrid, a presbyter. The holy Pope Nicholas received them with the greatest courtesy, and they reported to him fully and clearly the commission of their embassy. Carefully and prudently considering what they said, and, by God’s inspiration, judging this arrangement just for the winning of the souls of the gentiles, he confirmed the will of our king by his authority.
