Finally, so that we may set forth more clearly the matter after his careful examination of it, we have decided to insert his own words. After he had briefly and fully recapitulated the purpose of the embassy and the other matters related above, he added:

“Of this delegation, authority, and reception of the pallium, a document has been sent to us by Louis, our son, through the most holy bishop Solomon, sealed according to the custom of the holy Roman Church. From the contents of this document we have learned that these matters are as the piety of the aforementioned king has communicated to us through his faithful servant, namely Bishop Solomon. Therefore, following the footsteps of so great a pontiff and our predecessor Gregory, and recognizing there the whole arrangement established in a manner worthy of God, we have determined, by this apostolic precept of authority and also by the granting of the pallium, according to the custom of our predecessors, to strengthen the desire of the great princes: namely, of Louis Augustus, of blessed memory, and of his most excellent son, the king of the same name. Thus, founded upon so great an authority, the aforementioned Anscharius, first archbishop of the Northalbingians, and after him his successors, devoted to winning the peoples, may be stronger against the assaults of the devil.

“We also grant to our aforementioned son Anscharius public authority to preach the Gospel among all the neighboring peoples of the Swedes, Danes, and Slavs, and among any others in those regions wherever divine mercy may open a door. We decree that the see of the Northalbingians, called Hammaburg, consecrated in honor of the holy Savior and of his holy and undefiled mother Mary, shall henceforth be an archiepiscopal see. Moreover, under the testimony of divine judgment, we establish that after the death of the oft-mentioned Archbishop Anscharius, a person suitable for this great office shall always be chosen to succeed him as a vigorous preacher and bishop.

“But because King Charles, brother of the oft-mentioned King Louis, after the death of his father, the emperor Louis of pious memory, took away from the aforementioned place called Hammaburg the monastery called Turholt—which, after the partition among his brothers, seemed to lie within his own kingdom, in West Francia—although his father had given it to provide sustenance and maintenance for the bishop and his clergy, all the ministers of the altar, as is reported, began to withdraw. For, when the necessary revenues failed, they departed from those peoples, and by this action the same mission to those nations declined; the metropolis of Hammaburg itself also became almost deserted.

“While these things were taking place, the bishop of the diocese of Bremen died; this diocese is said to be adjacent to it. When the aforementioned king saw both this diocese vacant and that new institution failing, and, moreover, saw both churches of God greatly weakened by the ferocity of the barbarians, by a hidden judgment permitted by God, he began to seek how the aforementioned church of Bremen might be united to and placed under the aforementioned new archiepiscopal see, with our decree strengthening this desire. Therefore, through the venerable envoy repeatedly mentioned—namely Solomon, bishop of the city of Constance—this matter was reported to us for confirmation, and our authority was requested to strengthen it.

“Accordingly, having weighed the matter with careful examination, we perceived that, because of the pressing necessity and the gains of souls made evident among the gentiles, it would be useful. For we do not doubt that everything which is proved beneficial to the Church and does not conflict with divine commands is lawful and ought to be done, especially in the planting of so new a Christianity, in which various events commonly occur.

“Therefore, by the authority of almighty God and of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, and by this our decree, in accordance with the desire of the most reverend King Louis, we decree that the aforesaid dioceses—namely Hammaburg and Bremen—shall henceforth not be two but one, and shall be so called; and that they shall be subject to the see which, by the decree of our predecessor, has been elevated to the rank of an archiepiscopal see. Only the portion taken from the possessions of the church of Bremen shall be restored to the bishopric of Verden.

“Moreover, let no archbishop of Cologne henceforth claim any authority for himself in that same diocese. Indeed, we urge both him and all worshipers of the true religion to give aid and support to those carrying out this holy mission, so that they may deserve to receive the full reward of this benefit from him who said: ‘Go, teach all nations’ (Matthew 28:19), and, ‘Whoever receives you receives me’ (Matthew 10:40).

“Accordingly, everything assigned by our beloved son, King Louis, to this office worthy of God, together with his pious desires, we also confirm by our authority. And because the events of the past make us cautious for the future, we strike with the sword of anathema anyone who opposes or contradicts this, or in any way lays snares for these pious endeavors of ours; and we condemn such a person, by the lot of the devil, as guilty of eternal vengeance. Thus, by zealously defending the apostolic dignity and the cause of God according to the devotion of our predecessors, we may be more securely protected from adversaries on every side.” [Col. 0987D] **Note:** The complete letter of Nicholas is reproduced by Philip Caesar, Bollandus, and in the history of the bishops of Hammaburg.

### 40.

By these decrees and institutions of the most holy Pope Nicholas, the church of Bremen, joined and united to the see of Hammaburg—which had previously been established as a metropolis—was made an archiepiscopal see. [Col. 0987D] **Note:** By this union, Hammaburg and Bremen became not two churches but one, and likewise one archiepiscopal see, although the bishops appear to have preferred Bremen.

### Anscharius, a Friend of Horic, King of the Danes, Builds a Church with His Consent and Is Granted Freedom for the Christian Religion

### 41.

Since we have anticipated the account by speaking of the organization of that diocese as though it had already been firmly established—for it had been nearly ten years [Col. 0988D] **Note:** Nearly ten years, according to what was noted above at section 38—since he had undertaken the governance of that see before it was confirmed by apostolic authority, let us return to the events that occurred earlier.

After receiving the parish of Bremen, he again began to burn inwardly with spiritual zeal, because he now had something to give if he could accomplish anything for the name of Christ in the regions of the Danes. Accordingly, he began to visit Horic more frequently. [Col. 0988D] **Note:** Others call him Horuc or Ericus. He was the son of King Godfrey, who was killed in 810; Henschenius proves that he was wrongly confused with Roruc or Rorich, the brother of King Heriold.

Horic at that time alone held the monarchy of the Danish kingdom. Anscharius endeavored to win him over through gifts and every service he could provide, so that by his permission he might exercise the ministry of preaching in his kingdom. Several times he was even sent to him on royal embassies, and he energetically and faithfully carried out matters concerning peace treaties and the welfare of both kingdoms.

When the aforementioned King Horic learned of the holy man’s faith and goodness, he began to honor him with great affection, willingly to use his counsel, and to keep him as his closest confidant in every matter. Thus, when he discussed affairs of the kingdom with his counselors, Anscharius was permitted to be present even during his private deliberations. He also refused to have the agreements that were to be established between the people of this land, namely the Saxons, and his own kingdom confirmed in any other way than on Anscharius’s word, declaring that he considered wholly trustworthy whatever Anscharius had approved and promised to him.

Having gained such intimacy, Anscharius also began to persuade him to become a Christian. Horic listened graciously to everything he explained to him from divine Scripture, praised it as altogether good and truly salutary, and said that he took great pleasure in it and gladly wished to merit Christ’s grace.

After such expressions of willingness, the most holy Father patiently began to suggest that he should show this goodwill to the Lord Christ by permitting a church to be built in his kingdom, where a priest might always be present and distribute the seeds of the divine word and the grace of baptism to all who wished to receive them.

Horic granted this with the greatest kindness. In a harbor of his kingdom, most suitable for this purpose and close to that region, called Scleaswich, [Col. 0989D] **Note:** This trading center has been discussed above. Sleaswich, or Sleswicum, formerly the dwelling-place of the Angles and now the name of the duchy of Schleswig; concerning Sleswich—there—where merchants gathered from every direction, he permitted Anscharius to build a church, granting him a place where the presbyter could live. He likewise granted permission for anyone in his kingdom who wished to become a Christian to do so.

### Why Baptism Was Delayed by Some and Received by Others with Bodily Healing

### 42. [Col. 0989C]

After our lord bishop had received this permission, he immediately accomplished what he had long desired. Once a presbyter had been appointed there, the grace of God began to increase more fruitfully in that place.

Many Christians had already been there, having been baptized either at Dorestad or at Hammaburg. Some of them were regarded as leading men of the settlement, and they rejoiced that the opportunity had been granted them to observe their Christianity. Following their example, many other men and women, abandoning the superstitious worship of idols, were converted to faith in the Lord and baptized.

Great joy arose in that place, so that even the people of that nation, without any fear and—something that had not previously been permitted—merchants both from there and from Dorestad, freely visited the settlement, and through this opportunity an abundance of every good thing flourished there.

Although many who had been baptized there lived on, an innumerable multitude of the newly robed thereafter ascended to the kingdoms of heaven. For they willingly received the sign of the cross, so that they might become catechumens, [Col. 0989D] **Note:** For the rite by which catechumens were made in the ninth century, see the letter of Jesse, bishop of Amiens, where he explains more fully the same matters that Augustine touches upon in these words: “I had already been marked with the sign of the cross and seasoned with his salt from the womb of my mother,” in Book I, chapter 11 of the *Confessions*—so that they might be permitted to enter the church and attend the sacred offices. Yet they postponed receiving baptism, judging this to be beneficial for themselves: they would be baptized at the end of their lives, so that, purified by the saving bath, they might enter the gates of eternal life pure and undefiled, without any delay.

Many among them who were afflicted by illnesses, when they saw that they had sacrificed to idols in vain for their health and were given up for dead by their relatives, took refuge in the Lord’s mercy and vowed to become Christians. When they had summoned a priest and received the grace of baptism, they immediately became well by divine generosity. Thus God’s mercy increased in that place, and a multitude was converted to faith in the Lord.

### Anscharius, Having Requested Permission from Horic, Undertakes the Mission to the Swedes Again, Although Gauzbert Refuses

### 43.

Meanwhile, our lord and Father Anscharius, deeply grieving for the Swedish people because they were then deprived of the presence of a priest, began to ask the aforementioned King Horic, who was entirely devoted to him, that he might seek the borders of that kingdom with his assistance. Horic received this request with the greatest goodwill and promised that he would fulfill it in every respect.

For this reason our lord bishop began to discuss the matter with the aforementioned Bishop Gauzbert, saying that it was necessary to make another attempt, in case that people, warned by divine providence, might allow priests to remain among them, lest the faith of Christ that had begun in those regions should at some time perish through their negligence.

Bishop Gauzbert, also called Simon, replied that, having been expelled from that place, he did not dare to seek it again. Nor, he said, could this be very profitable; indeed, it might be more dangerous if, remembering what had happened before, they should again stir up some disturbance against him. It seemed more appropriate to him that Anscharius should go, since he had undertaken this mission at the beginning and had been received there most kindly. He himself would send his nephew with him, so that, if an opportunity for preaching were found there, the nephew might remain and perform the priestly ministry among them.

Having established this agreement between them, they came into the presence of the most clement King Louis, reported the matter to him, and begged that it might be permitted to take place with his authorization. When he asked whether the two of them were united in this intention, he received the following answer from the venerable Bishop Gauzbert:

“In the service of God,” he said, “we have always been and remain in agreement, and by unanimous consent we wish this to be done.”

Accordingly, the most serene king, ever willing to advance God’s cause, assigned this mission, as they had agreed, to our most religious pastor in the name of Christ, entrusting him with messages from his own side to the king of the Swedes, just as his father had done.

### He Is Strengthened by a Heavenly Vision

### 44.

Our most devoted Father therefore began to prepare himself for this journey, and, in order to complete it as quickly as possible, he was impelled by an increasingly fervent spirit. He believed that this journey had also been imposed upon him from heaven, because he had previously been granted a certain vision.

He seemed to himself to be greatly anxious about the journey and to arrive at a certain place where there was a large complex of buildings and various dwellings. There a man met him and said:

“Do not be excessively distressed about the journey that troubles you and about the things that are in your heart, for here is a prophet who will make you certain about all these matters. And, so that no doubt about this may remain in your mind, I shall tell you who this prophet is. A certain most renowned abbot, Adalhard, is now a prophet sent by the Lord to you; he will announce to you the things that are going to happen.”

When he heard this, Anscharius was gladdened in spirit and seemed to answer him:

“Lord, where shall I find him?”

The other replied:

“You will find him with difficulty, and you are not permitted to reveal this to anyone.”

Then he seemed to go around the dwelling, searching for him, and to reason within himself:

“If he announces to me, without my asking him, what is in my mind, I shall then prove him to be a true prophet.”

When he reached a certain most beautiful dwelling, he saw Adalhard sitting there on his throne and immediately recognized him. Adalhard at once began to speak, addressing him intently:

“Listen, islands, and attend, peoples from afar. The Lord called you from the womb; from your mother’s belly he remembered your name. He made your mouth like a sharp sword; in the shadow of his hand he protected you and made you like a chosen arrow. He hid you in his quiver and said to you: ‘You are my servant, because in you I shall glory.’”

After saying this, he extended his arm and began to raise his right hand toward him. Anscharius, seeing this, approached his knees, hoping that he intended to bless him. But Adalhard continued:

“‘I have given you as a light to the nations, so that you may be their salvation to the ends of the earth. Kings shall see, and princes shall arise, and they shall worship your God and the Holy One of Israel, because he has glorified you.’”

The servant of God had seen this vision long before that departure. He therefore firmly believed that he was being impelled to those regions by God’s command, especially because of the words spoken to him: “Listen, islands,” since almost the whole of that country consists of islands. He also understood the words that followed—“You shall be their salvation to the ends of the earth”—because the end of the world lies in the northern regions, among the territories of the Swedes.

Finally, the words that had been altered at the end of the passage from the prophet Jeremiah—namely, “because he will glorify you”—nourished the ardor of his desire exceedingly, because he believed that they signified the crown of martyrdom that had once been promised to him.

### Recommended to the King of the Swedes by Horic, Anscharius Arrives in Sweden, Which Has Been Thrown into Confusion by the Instigation of Demons

### 45.

As he was about to undertake this journey, he carried with him both an envoy and a token from the aforementioned King Horic. Horic ordered that the following message from his side be delivered to the king of the Swedes, named Olef. [Col. 0991D] **Note:** Gualdo likewise has this form. More recent authors call him Olaum. The servant of God who had been sent on behalf of King Louis and was traveling to the borders of the Swedish kingdom was known to Horic in every respect; he had never seen so good a man in all his life, nor had he ever found such faith in any mortal. Therefore, having recognized Anscharius’s most holy goodness, Horic had granted him permission to arrange whatever he wished in his kingdom for the sake of the Christian religion. He asked Olef likewise to permit Anscharius to establish the Christian faith in his own kingdom, as Anscharius desired, since he wished to accomplish nothing except what was good and right.

Proceeding on his journey, Anscharius spent nearly twenty days traveling by ship and arrived at Byrca. There he found the king and a multitude of people confused by great error.

For, at the instigation of the devil, who fully foreknew the arrival of the blessed man, it happened at that very time that someone arrived there claiming that he had been present at an assembly of the gods, who were believed to possess that land, and that he had been sent by them to announce the following to the king and the people:

“‘For a long time you have had us favorable toward you, and by our help you have held the land of your settlement in peace and prosperity, with great abundance. You have also paid us the sacrifices and vows that were owed, and your services were pleasing to us.

“‘But now you withdraw your customary sacrifices and offer your voluntary vows less diligently; and, what displeases us most, you are introducing a foreign god over yourselves. Therefore, if you wish to keep us favorable toward you, increase the sacrifices that you have neglected and pay greater vows. Do not receive among you the worship of another god, which is taught in opposition to us, and do not devote yourselves to his service.

“‘Moreover, if you desire to have more gods, and we are not enough for you, we have unanimously enrolled your former king Eric in our company, so that he may be one of the number of the gods.’”

[Col. 0991D] **Note:** Hence Adamus, when discussing the superstitions of the ancient Swedes in chapter 233, says: “They also worship gods made from men, whom they grant immortality because of their great deeds, just as we read in the *Life of Saint Anscharius* that King Hericus did. To all the gods, naturally, they assign priests to offer the sacrifices of the people.” If Adamus has correctly expressed the meaning of this passage, it should be understood that King Hericus enrolled his like-named predecessor among the gods and dedicated sacrifices and priests to him.

This diabolical message, publicly proclaimed, disturbed everyone’s minds upon the arrival of our lord bishop, and great error and confusion overwhelmed all their hearts. They even built a temple in honor of the aforementioned king, who had long since died, and began to offer vows and sacrifices to him as though he were a god.

### Although His Friends Discourage Him, He Invites the King to a Feast, and the King Approves the Mission, Subject to the Casting of Lots

### 46. [Col. 0992D]

When our lord bishop arrived there, he began to ask his friends, whom he had once known in that place, how he should approach the king about this matter. They all resisted with all their might, declaring that his mission could accomplish absolutely nothing on that occasion; but if he had anything of value, he ought to give it in order to escape alive.

He replied:

“I shall give nothing here for the redemption of my life. For if my Lord has so ordained, I am prepared to undergo torments here and to suffer death for his name.”

While he was thus placed in the greatest anxiety over this matter, he finally took counsel and invited the king to his lodging. He offered him a banquet, presented whatever gifts he could, and reported the commission of his embassy. The king had already been informed of the reason for Anscharius’s arrival both by Horic’s envoy and by the faithful men of our lord bishop who remained there.

Delighted both by Anscharius’s graciousness and by the presentation of gifts, the king replied that he was indeed glad to accept what Anscharius had proposed. But he added:

“Previously there were clerics here who were expelled from this place by a popular uprising, not by royal command. Therefore I can neither confirm nor dare to approve your mission until I have consulted our gods by casting lots and also asked the people’s will about it. Let your envoy attend the next public assembly with me, and I shall speak to the people on your behalf. If, with the gods favorable, they agree to your wish, what you seek will prosper; but if not, I shall also make that known to you. For among us it is customary that every public matter depends more upon the unanimous will of the people than upon royal authority.”

### Anscharius Is Strengthened by Divine Inspiration. The Lots Favor His Undertaking

### 47.

After our most devoted pastor had received this reply from the king, he turned entirely to the Lord as his refuge, devoting himself to fasting and prayer and humbling himself before God in contrition and affliction of heart.

While he was placed amid these distresses, and the day of the public assembly was approaching, heavenly inspiration was infused into him one day during the celebration of the Mass, while the priest stood at the altar blessing the sacred mysteries and Anscharius lay prostrate on the ground. Strengthened inwardly by the gift of the Holy Spirit and fortified in his soul with the greatest confidence, he understood that everything would turn out as he wished.

After the Mass he announced to the priest, who was entirely familiar with him, that he ought to have no fear, because God’s grace would accompany him. When the priest asked how he knew this, Anscharius replied that it had been divinely inspired in him. [Col. 0993D] The brother recognized this illumination of his mind very clearly, since he had previously established through many signs that Anscharius was divinely consoled in this way.

The outcome immediately confirmed this confidence of his spirit. For the king first gathered his leaders and began to discuss our Father’s mission with them. They decided that the will of the gods concerning the matter should be sought by casting lots. [Col. 0993D] **Note:** This was a custom familiar among the Germans, according to Tacitus in his *Germania*. Julius Caesar also reports that among the Germans it was customary “that their matrons, by lots and divinations, declared [Col. 0994D] whether or not it was advantageous to join battle,” in Book I of *The Gallic War*. See the Acts of Saints Wulfram and Willibrord. They went out into the field according to their custom and cast the lots, and the lot fell in such a way that, by God’s will, the Christian religion should be established there.

One of the leading men, a friend of our lord bishop, immediately informed him of what had happened and urged him to take comfort, saying:

“Take courage and act manfully, because God does not reject your desire and your mission.”

Thus, taking confidence and gladdened by the inner spirit, Anscharius rejoiced and exulted in the Lord.

### The Assembly Also Gives Its Consent

### 48.

When the day of the public assembly arrived—it was held in the aforementioned settlement of Byrca—the king, according to their custom, had the nature of the mission announced to the people by the voice of a herald. When they heard it, they, who had previously been confused by error, began to hold different opinions and to raise a tumult.

While they were making this uproar, an elderly man arose and spoke in the midst of the people:

“Listen to me, king and people. Many among us already know well what this God’s worship can accomplish for those who hope in him: it can provide them with great help. For many of us have repeatedly proved this, both in dangers at sea and in various necessities. Why, then, do we reject what we know to be necessary and useful to us?

“Once, some of us who went to Dorestad, recognizing that the observance of this religion would benefit them, accepted it of their own free will. Now many dangers intervene, and because of the attacks of pirates that journey has become extremely dangerous for us. Why, then, do we not accept what we previously sought so far away and what is now offered to us here? And since we have proved in many matters that this God’s grace is useful to us, why should we not willingly agree that his servants remain among us?

“Consider our counsel, people, and do not reject your own advantage. When we cannot have our own gods favorable to us, it is good for us to have the grace of this God, who always can and wishes to help those who call upon him in every circumstance.”

After he had concluded in this manner, the whole multitude of the people became unanimous and chose that priests should remain with them and that whatever pertained to the mysteries of Christ should be carried out without any opposition.

The king then rose from the assembly and immediately sent his messenger with the envoy of our lord bishop, ordering him to report that the unanimity of the people had turned toward his desire and that this pleased him in every respect. Nevertheless, he said that he could not yet grant Anscharius full permission until another assembly, which was to be held in another part of his kingdom, where he would announce the same matter to the peoples living there.

Then our Father, of good memory, again sought his customary supports and prayed more earnestly for divine mercy. And behold, the time of the assembly arrived. The king had the mission of our lord bishop announced by the voice of a herald, together with everything that had been said and done at the earlier assembly.

By divine providence, the hearts of all were so united that everyone praised the decision of the earlier assembly and openly declared that they too wished to agree to it in every respect.

### He Receives Permission to Build Churches

### 49. [Col. 0995A]

After this had been done, the king summoned our lord bishop and reported what had taken place. Then, by the unanimous will and consent of all, he decreed that churches should be built among them, that priests should be present, and that anyone among the people who wished to become a Christian should do so without opposition.

Our lord and pastor commended to the king’s protection the aforementioned nephew of the venerable Bishop Gauzbert, named Erimbert, so that, strengthened by the king’s assistance and defense, he might perform the divine mysteries there. The king also gave him a courtyard in the aforementioned settlement for the construction of an oratory.

Our lord bishop bought another place, together with a house, for a presbyter to live in. The king likewise showed our lord bishop the most gracious affection and promised that he would prove entirely faithful in every respect in his support of the practice of the Christian religion.

Thus, by the grace of the Lord, when everything had been properly completed, our lord bishop returned to his own people.

### Through Reflection on the Passion He Learns to Endure Adversity

### 50.

Our most holy Father had already foreseen, by the Lord’s revelation, the great anguish of mind that he would suffer during that journey while it was being prepared. One night he seemed to see the time of the Lord’s Passion. The Lord Jesus Christ was present as he was led by Pilate to Herod and again from Herod to Pilate. Finally, as he suffered spitting and insults from the Jews and soldiers and, as it seemed to Anscharius, was scourged over all his limbs, Anscharius could not endure seeing him punished in this way. He ran forward and placed himself behind Christ, between him and those who were striking him, receiving in his own body all the blows inflicted upon Christ. Yet Christ’s stature appeared taller, with his head rising above Anscharius’s, and for that reason Anscharius could not protect it.

The invincible soldier of Christ did not at first understand what this vision signified. Only after he had returned from the journey did he reflect upon how many insults and mockeries he had endured there, how great his distress had been, and how many blasphemies against God he had borne.

Insofar as it concerned his own spirit, Christ had undoubtedly suffered there in Anscharius’s person; and there Christ again endured in his servant the insults that had previously been inflicted upon him. As for Anscharius’s inability to defend Christ’s head, he thought that this signified that God is the head of Christ, and that the sufferings which the saints endure for Christ in this world partly extend even to the majesty of God himself. God, in a certain manner, receives them by sharing in their suffering; for a time he tolerates them, but eventually he judges them with strictness.

### The Swedes, Victorious over the Danes, Attack the Curonians
### 51. Nor should it be passed over how the power of the Lord was revealed to the Sueons mentioned above after this expedition.

For a certain people living far away from them, called the Chori [Note: Adam of Bremen writes about Courland: “This people, as he himself says, exceedingly savage, is enclosed by the Baltic Sea and the Gulf of Livonia; it borders Livonia, Samogitia, and Lithuania. From the whole world answers are sought there,” says Adam in Book III, chapter 75, “especially by Spaniards and Greeks”; he also adds that the inhabitants are dressed in monastic clothing.], had once been subject to the authority of the Sueons; but by that time they had long refused, through rebellion, to submit to them.

Finally, when the Danes learned at the time mentioned above that the lord bishop had already arrived in the territory of the Sueons, they assembled a large number of ships and proceeded to that same country, wishing both to plunder their goods and to bring them under their own rule. The kingdom itself had five cities.

The people living there, learning of their arrival, gathered together and began to resist courageously and defend their possessions. Victory was granted to them: half of the Danish force was struck down in the slaughter, and they also seized half of their ships, taking gold, silver, and many spoils from them.

When the aforesaid King Olef and the Sueon people heard this, they wished to acquire the reputation of doing what the Danes had not done. Since these people had also formerly been subject to them, they assembled an innumerable army and marched into that region.

First, advancing unexpectedly against a certain city of their kingdom called Selburg [Note: Seburg, or Selburg, is still a fortress of the Duke of Courland on the right bank of the River Dvina, as Henschenius noted.], in which there were seven thousand warriors, they utterly devastated and plundered it and set it on fire.

Then, encouraged in spirit, they left their ships and, undertaking a journey of five days, hastened with savage determination toward another of their cities, called Apulia [Note: Gualdo has “Appulia.” Henschenius suspects that this was the city of Pila, on the borders of Courland and Samogitia.]. There were fifteen thousand warriors in that city.

When they had arrived there, the inhabitants were shut inside the city. Those outside began to attack the city, while those within courageously resisted: the latter defended it from within, the former attacked it from without. Thus eight days passed, as they fought from morning until evening each day and many fell on both sides, yet neither party obtained victory.

### With their gods invoked in vain, they turn to Christ.

### 52.

Then, on the ninth day, the Sueon people, wearied by the prolonged slaughter, began to be distressed. Frightened in their hearts, they could think only of how they might escape from there.

“Here,” they said, “we are making no progress, and our ships are far away.” For, as we have said, it was a five-day journey to the harbor where their ships lay.

Since, exceedingly troubled, they did not know at all what they ought to do, they decided to consult the lots to determine whether their gods wished to help them, so that they might either gain victory or escape alive.

Accordingly, after the lots had been cast, they could find none of their gods who wished to come to their aid. When this was announced among the people, immense wailing and lamentation arose in the camp, and all courage departed from them.

“What shall we wretched men do?” they said. “The gods have abandoned us, and none of them is our helper! Where shall we flee? Look, our ships are far away, and if we flee, these men will pursue us and destroy us to the last man. What, then, will become of us?”

While they were placed in such great distress, some merchants, remembering the teaching and instruction of the lord bishop, began to advise them.

“The God of the Christians,” they said, “often helps those who cry out to him, and he is most powerful in giving aid. Let us inquire whether he is willing to be with us, and let us freely promise him vows pleasing to him.”

At the supplication of them all, therefore, a lot was cast, and it was found that Christ wished to help them. When this had been publicly announced and became known to everyone, the hearts of all were suddenly so strengthened that they immediately wished to approach the city fearlessly and attack it.

“What should we now fear, or what should we dread?” they said. “Christ is with us. Let us fight and act courageously; nothing will be able to stand in our way. Certain victory will not be lacking, because we have the most powerful of the gods as our helper.”

Thus they all gathered with joyful and courageous hearts and set out to attack the city.

### They obtain victory by making a treaty; they vow fasts; they devote themselves to almsgiving.

### 53.

When they were standing around the city and wished to begin the battle, those inside requested that they be granted an opportunity to speak. When the king of the Sueons had agreed, they continued:

“Peace now pleases us more than battle, and we wish to make a treaty with you. First, whatever gold and weapons we acquired from the Danish spoils in the previous year, we give you as a gift for the treaty. Next, for every person established in this city, we offer you half a pound of silver. In addition, we shall pay the tribute which we formerly used to give you. After giving hostages, we wish from now on to remain subject and obedient to your rule, as we were before.”

Although these offers had been made, the young men’s spirits still could not be calmed. Rather, becoming more eager and fearless, desiring only to fight, they said that they would destroy the city and everything it contained with weapons, and lead the inhabitants away as captives.

But the king and the leading men, accepting their right hands with wiser counsel, made the treaty. After receiving innumerable treasures and thirty hostages, they returned joyfully to their own territory.

Finally, when peace had been established between them, the Sueons immediately began to praise the omnipotence of Christ our Lord and to proclaim with all their strength his magnificence, declaring that he was truly greater than all the gods. They carefully began to inquire what vows they ought to make to him through whom they had obtained so great a victory.

Accordingly, instructed by the Christian merchants who were present with them, they vowed a fast pleasing to Christ the Lord: when they had returned home and had spent seven days there, they would all together abstain from meat for another seven days; and after a further forty days had passed, they would likewise, by unanimous agreement, abstain from meat for the following forty days.

This was also done, and all who had been present there willingly fulfilled what had been established. Many of them afterward, out of reverence and love for Christ, began to observe the fasts practiced by Christians and to help any poor people with alms—for they had learned that this was pleasing to Christ.

Thus, with everyone favoring him, the priest Erimbertus was freely able to carry out the things of God among them. While all were praising Christ’s power, devotion to the divine religion in those regions began from that time to increase through him, without anyone’s opposition.

### With the younger Horicus succeeding his father, access to the church is closed, then granted at the king’s wish; permission is given to build another church.

### 54.

Meanwhile, by divine judgment, it happened that King Horicus, already mentioned, was killed in battle during an attack by pirates, when certain relatives were attempting to invade his kingdom [Note: In the year 854, according to the Annals of Fulda, Bertin, and Metz, and the book On the Deeds of the Northmen. Their leader Gudurm, born of the brother of King Horicus, returned to his homeland after carrying out pirate attacks in the regions of Gaul, attacked his uncle Horicus, and caused such slaughter over three days that no one remained from the royal line of Godefrid except one boy.]. Along with him, all the leading men of that land, who had formerly been regarded as familiar and friendly to the lord bishop, perished by the sword.

After the younger Horicus had been established in his kingdom, some of those whom he then had as princes, and who had previously been less known to the lord bishop, began to persuade him that the church established among them should be destroyed and the Christian religion begun there should be abolished. They said that their gods were angry with them, and that so many evils had therefore befallen them because they had accepted among themselves the worship of another and unknown God.

For this reason the count of the aforesaid settlement, namely Scleswich, named Hovi [Col. 0998C], who especially resisted this religion and incited the king to destroy the Christian faith, ordered the church established there to be closed and prohibited the practice of the Christian religion there. Consequently, the priest who was present there, compelled by the severity of the persecution, withdrew.

Because of this, the lord bishop became exceedingly anxious and sorrowful. At that time he had none of the friends of the younger Horicus whom he had previously made familiar to himself through very generous gifts, and through whom he might reconcile the king to the Lord’s will.

Since he had been deprived of human assistance, therefore, he resorted, as usual, to divine help. Nor did his hope deceive him. The Lord consoled him with spiritual consolation in his heart, and he became entirely certain that the religion begun there would in no way perish, as the enemies of Christ were plotting. With the Lord’s consent, this happened not long afterward.

For when he was preparing to go to the aforementioned king for this very reason, the grace of the Lord went before him. The same king, having first expelled the aforesaid count from the settlement—so that afterward he could never regain the king’s favor—sent a messenger willingly to his lord bishop, instructing him to send his priest back to his own church. He declared that he wished to earn Christ’s favor no less than the elder Horicus had and to obtain the friendship of the lord bishop.

After this, our most reverend Father himself came into the presence of that king with the assistance of the illustrious Count Burchard, who had previously also been the elder Horicus’s helper in everything and had influence with both kings, since he was their relative. The younger Horicus received him with such favor that he immediately granted him everything which his predecessor had allowed to be done in his kingdom for the sake of Christianity.

Moreover, he consented to something that previously seemed impious to the pagans: that a bell should be kept in the church.

In another settlement of his kingdom, called Ripa, he likewise granted a place where a church could be built, and he gave permission under his authority for a priest to be present there.

### Various ministers are sent to the Sueons.

### 55.

While these things were taking place, the aforesaid venerable Bishop Gauzbertus sent to the Sueon people a certain priest named Anfrid, who was of Danish origin and had been raised for the service of the Lord by the lord Ebo.

When he arrived there, the priest Erimbert, already mentioned, returned from that place. Anfrid remained there, greatly desired by everyone, for three years or more.

Afterward, when he heard of the death of the lord Gauzbertus, he too returned from there and, after spending some time among us, died as his illness grew worse.

After this, the lord bishop, unwilling to allow the Christian faith begun there to perish, sent there his priest named Raginbert. Although he was quite suitable for this task and very willing to undertake so long an expedition, as he was traveling toward the aforementioned harbor of Sleaswich, he was surrounded on the road by an ambush of Danish robbers and stripped of what he possessed. On the day of the Assumption of Saint Mary, he too happily completed the course of his good intention.

When this had afflicted the lord bishop’s heart with immeasurable sorrow, he nevertheless could not be drawn away from the intention he had begun. Instead, the bishop appointed another priest for this work, born of Danish stock and named Rimbertus [Note: This priest Rimbertus is different from Rimbert the deacon, disciple, successor, and herald of Anscharius. To these two must be added another, the priest Raginbert, mentioned above.].

When he sent him to those regions in the name of Christ, he was kindly received there by the king and the people, and, with the Lord granting it, he has freely celebrated the divine mysteries among them until now.

Finally, just as he had done with the others whom he had previously appointed among the pagans, he also instructed the priests that they should desire or request nothing belonging to anyone, but that, following the example of the blessed Apostle Paul, they should themselves work with their hands and be content with food and clothing. He piously exhorted them to this.

Nevertheless, for them and their followers he abundantly supplied from his own resources whatever they needed, as well as anything that had to be given in order to win friends.

### Anscharius is repeatedly strengthened by Ebo. He bears adversity with equanimity.

### 56.

Amid these many and varied pressures of distress, by which, as we have related, he was continually strengthened by inspiration concerning the same mission, so that he would not abandon the work he had begun, he was also greatly consoled in this matter by the devotion of spirit and fervor of heart of the aforementioned lord Ebo, archbishop of Rheims, who had first undertaken this mission.

For Ebo himself, burning inwardly with zeal for the calling of the nations, continually urged him to proclaim the grace of the faith in these regions and earnestly reminded him not to abandon what he had begun.

Provoked by Ebo’s words of exhortation and by the immense ardor of mind with which he burned for this work, this blessed man unquestionably took care of the duty entrusted to him. No adversity or hardship could ever turn him away from the work he had begun.

Although the aforesaid bishop gave innumerable exhorting admonitions, by which our Father was inwardly comforted with great joy, he nevertheless always remembered the speech they had exchanged at the time of their final conversation concerning this mission.

When our lord bishop, after recounting the many distresses that had befallen him, asked Ebo what he thought about the same mission and earnestly requested what consolation he wished to give him concerning it, Ebo, as though inspired by a prophetic spirit, replied:

“I am certain,” he said, “that what we have begun to undertake in the name of Christ will bear fruit in the Lord. For this is my faith, and this is what I firmly believe—indeed, what I truly know: because—” [The text is corrupt or incomplete here.]

He had indeed encountered and entirely mastered the secrets of Plato and the books of Pythagoras, Zeno the Stoic, and Cerinthus, and of the other philosophers; and perhaps because he had lingered too long and drunk too deeply from Babylon’s gilded cup, he was somehow compelled to pour some of its dregs into Sacred Scripture.

From this ecclesiastics must be very carefully and vigilantly on guard, so that from the one from whom they will undoubtedly receive the reward of their labor—[the sentence is incomplete in the supplied text].

The intention of this devotion never departed from the heart of our Lord and Father, and he never ceased to pray for the salvation of the nations. Rather, while his diocese was being devastated all around by the almost continual attacks of pirates coming from the peoples already mentioned, and his household was being plundered, he nevertheless continually prayed for those who opposed and ambushed him. He unceasingly entreated God’s mercy for the conversion of those who harmed him, asking that what they did should not be counted against them as sin, since, ignorant of God’s justice and deceived by diabolical error, they were hostile to the possessions of Christians.

His concern burned so intensely that even when he was lying in his final illness, he never ceased to consider and arrange the affairs of the mission mentioned above, until he breathed out his final breath of life.

Having been received from this world in such fervor of religion, we believe that, accompanied by the greatest multitude of the faithful whom he had won for the Lord from the Danish and Sueon peoples, he entered gloriously and happily into the kingdoms of the blessed on the day of the resurrection of all, through the rewarding mercy of God.

### Anscharius was an exemplary monk and an imitator of the saints as bishop. He constantly wears a hair shirt. He loves solitude.

### 57.

Since we have already said much about the purpose of his mission and the care with which he wished to save others, it is now time to explain what sort of man he was in himself, for the salvation of his own soul, and how he afflicted his body.

What he was among you in the monastery, in all the zeal of his devotion, is perfectly known to you. Nevertheless, as we have heard, even as a young man and adolescent he seemed admirable and worthy of imitation to the elders and the very old.

After he had assumed the episcopate among us, he strove in every way to increase what he had begun in the monastery and to imitate the life of all the saints, especially that of the blessed Martin.

He wore a hair shirt next to his flesh not only by day but also by night, and he earnestly sought to benefit the people by preaching the word of the Lord.

Sometimes, however, in order to exercise himself in divine philosophy, he remained in solitude. For this purpose he had a suitable cell built for himself, which he called a quiet place and a friend to sorrow.

Whenever he could be free from preaching and ecclesiastical duties and from the disturbance of the pagans, he lived there with a few companions. Yet he never placed his own comfort or his love of solitude above the welfare of the flock entrusted to him.

### Sparing in food and therefore tempted by vainglory, he is divinely freed from that fault. In old age he compensates for diminished austerity by almsgiving.

### 58.

As long as he possessed some of the strength of youth, he very often took bread by weight and water by measure, especially for as long as he was permitted to use solitude.

At that time, as he himself stated, he was seriously tempted by the spirit of vainglory. The enemy of the human race was attempting to infect his soul with that already-mentioned pestilence, and he seemed great in his own eyes because he abstained in such a manner.

Becoming troubled over this, he turned in prayer to the Lord’s mercy and asked that the Lord’s grace free him from this most destructive impiety. This was indeed done.

While he was more earnestly devoted to prayer for this reason, one night, having fallen asleep, he saw himself as though carried up to heaven, while the whole world had been gathered together as if into a most dreadful valley. From it, however, the souls of the blessed, although rarely, were carried away by angelic ministry and led into heaven.

In this dark valley there was also shown to him what seemed like a certain seed-bed from which the human race derives its origin.

As he gazed upon all these things in wonder and horror, he was ordered to observe from what beginning he entered this life. And it was said:

“From what source,” he said, “could any boastfulness belong to a human being who was begotten from so vile an origin in the valley of tears, and who received whatever good he possessed not from himself but from him from whom every good gift and every perfect gift comes?

“If, therefore,” he said, “you are ever again tempted by the plague of vainglory, bring this to mind and remember from whom you were begotten; and you will be freed by God’s grace.”

This was indeed done.

After he grew old, however, he could no longer abstain from food to the same degree. Water was nevertheless always his drink, except that, in order to avoid vainglory rather than to obtain any pleasure, he would mix a little [wine] into the water he was going to drink [the supplied text reads “de potu,” with “de vino” supplied editorially].

Since in his old age he could no longer practice his customary austerity, he strove to compensate for it through almsgiving, prayers, and many other good works.

For this reason he redeemed many captives and gave them their freedom. Some of them, however, he ordered to be educated for the service of God and instructed in the divine writings.

### Anscharius writes books out of devotion. He is devoted to tears and uses passages of Scripture for this purpose.

### 59.

How diligently he sought to sharpen his devotion in the love of God is shown by the large books preserved among us, which he wrote with his own hand in shorthand [Note: Such shorthand as Cicero’s freedman invented, so that the hand of the writer might keep up with the speed of the tongue.]. They are known to contain only material concerning the praise of almighty God, the rebuke of sinners, the praise of blessed and eternal life, and the terror of Gehenna, as well as everything pertaining to contrition and lamentation.

The brothers among us [Note: That is, in the church of Bremen, where monks established according to Anscharius’s instruction were therefore settled.] and those living in New Corbie are also witnesses. He frequently requested them for this work, and they sent him some writings of this kind.

Yet it could never be enough for him; he wished to spend his entire life in mourning and tears. Although contrition of heart stirred tears in him, they never seemed sufficient to him, except that in the final year of his life, through the Lord’s generosity, he obtained the grace he had long sought: whenever he wished, he could weep.

Finally, from the very passages of Scripture conducive to contrition, he composed a little prayer for each of the psalms [Note: In ancient books of the Psalms, individual prayers occur after each psalm, as in the book which Saint Rotbert, abbot of Molesme, brought to Cîteaux. This was sometimes observed by the monks of the East: instead of the verse “Glory to the Father,” which Westerners sang after each psalm, a prayer was said, as Cassian testifies in Book II, chapter 9, of the Institutions. Such compositions are attributed to Bede, under the title Scintilla; similar ones are also attributed to Alcuin.]. He used to call these prayers “compounds” or “confections” (*pigmenta*), so that the psalms would become sweet to him for this reason.

In these *pigmenta* he did not concern himself with the arrangement of words, but sought only contrition of heart. In them he sometimes praised the omnipotence and judgment of God; sometimes he reproached himself; sometimes he pronounced blessed the saints who obey God; sometimes he mourned the wretched and sinners, among whom he always declared himself the worst.

When others sang with him, after the psalm had ended he alone would silently meditate on these prayers. He did not wish to reveal them to anyone.

One of our number, however, who was especially close to him, scarcely obtained, through great force of entreaty, that he dictate these very *pigmenta* to him as he himself used to sing them.

Although this man wrote them down while Anscharius was still alive, he made them known to no one. After Anscharius’s death, however, he displayed them to anyone who wished to read them.

### He recited various psalms according to place and time.

### 60.

While singing the psalms [Note: Thus the Egyptian monks practiced manual labor and the recitation of the psalms at the same time, according to Cassian, in chapters 13 and 14 of the same book. Thus Saint Adalhard, in Book II, chapter 4, of the Statutes, orders those who work in the kitchen service to sing psalms without interruption—that is, to recite them. This word is used here in the same sense.], he also frequently used to work with his hands, for in those days he worked at a net.

Regarding the psalms themselves, he had arranged which ones he would sing by day, which by night, which while preparing himself for Mass, and which when he wished to go barefoot to bed.

In the morning, whenever he put on his shoes and washed his hands, he always sang litanies. Then, having gone to the church, he had three or four Masses celebrated, standing by and performing the office himself.

At the appointed regular time during the day, unless some illness or inconvenience afflicted him, he himself sang the public Mass [Note: Therefore Anscharius did not perform sacred work every day, but only on the more solemn days.].

### Generous toward the poor, he endows a hospice for them. He cares for everyone. He carries a purse at his belt. During Lent he feeds four poor people and serves them.

### 61.

Who could describe how extraordinarily generous he was in giving alms, since he wished to supply everything he possessed, according to the Lord’s will, to those suffering need?

Wherever he knew anyone to be in need, he worked to help him as much as he could. He provided the assistance of his support not only in his own diocese but also in distant regions.

In particular, he maintained a hospice for the poor established at Bremen [Note: A college of twelve canons was later established in that place, together with a church dedicated to Saint Anscharius, which still exists, as Philip Caesar testifies. When he was still *ἀκαθολικός*—“not yet Catholic”—he served there as canon and pastor; afterward he was converted, as he himself believed, chiefly through the prayers and merits of this saint, whose Life he had diligently and carefully sought out.], and he assigned tithes from certain villages to it, so that the sick might be refreshed there through the daily reception of the poor.

Throughout his entire episcopate he distributed to the poor the tithes of animals and of all revenues [Note: Adalhard, abbot of Corbie, had arranged the same thing, as is clear from his Statutes.], as well as the tithes of the tithes belonging to him. Whatever silver or any other revenue came to him, he tithed for the use of the needy.

Moreover, every fifth year he made a second complete tithe of all the animals, even though they had already been tithed, for distribution in alms. From the silver that came to the churches in the monasteries, he also assigned a fourth part for this same purpose.

He always showed the greatest care for orphans and widows. Wherever he knew that anchorites—whether men or women—were living, he strengthened them in God’s service through frequent visits and gifts and strove to assist them with whatever support they needed.

He also always kept a purse with coins at his own belt, so that if a needy person came and the dispenser of his alms was absent, he himself would have something to give without delay.

He strove in every respect to fulfill the saying of blessed Job, so that he would not even make a widow’s eyes wait. Thus he endeavored to be the eye of the blind, the foot of the lame, and altogether the father of the poor.

During Lent he ordered four poor people to be received daily at Bremen for food: two men and two women. He himself and the brothers washed the men’s feet; the women were served in the aforesaid hospice for the poor by a woman consecrated to God, whom he regarded as tested in God’s will and in love of religion.

Finally, when he traveled through the parishes according to episcopal custom, he ordered the poor to be brought in before he himself went to the meal. He also offered them water with which to wash their hands [Col. 1004B] and, after giving the *eulogiae*, served them drink [Note: That is, he provided a drink. The verb *miscere* is frequently used in this sense by authors of the Middle Ages. See the Glossary of the distinguished scholar Charles Fresne.]. After a table had been set before them, he then went to his own meal with his guests.

[Note: From this point until number 68 below, the poet Gualdo changes from prose into verse.]

To confirm by examples the compassion and piety of his heart, we once saw that, among many others, he had redeemed and brought back to his own country the son of a certain widow who had been carried away captive to a distant region, namely to the land of the Sueons.

When his mother joyfully saw him returned and, as is the custom of women, stood weeping for joy in his presence, the bishop himself, moved to contrition, also began to weep no less. Immediately he restored the widow’s son to his mother as a free man and allowed them to return home rejoicing.

### He foreknows the future and consults God about what must be done. He learns from heaven that he will be pastor of the church of Bremen.

### 62.

Because, according to the blessed Apostle Paul (Philippians 3:20), his manner of life was always in heaven, he was sometimes illumined on earth by heavenly revelations—as we have already said, although we have omitted much—so that almost everything that was going to happen to him became known to him beforehand, either through a dream, through an inward revelation in his mind, or through an ecstatic experience.

What we have said occurred in his mind we think was of the following kind, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles: “The Spirit said to Philip” (Acts 8:29).

For whenever he had to decide something especially important, he wished to have time for reflection. He arranged nothing rashly before, illumined by God’s grace, he sensed in his mind what was better. Thus, assured in his mind by a heavenly visitation, he arranged without hesitation what had to be done.

The things he saw in dreams, as many examples have already been included above, were so true that we do not remember any of them ever being proved false.

To offer, as proof of this, an example that we have omitted [Note: Something had been added here concerning the designation of Rembert as his successor, as is clear from chapter 6 of the Life of Saint Rembert. Rembert himself seems to have deleted it out of modesty.], before he was invited to the church of Bremen, one night he seemed to himself to have come to a most beautiful region, where he found the blessed Apostle Peter.

As he gazed at him in wonder, certain men came asking that the blessed Peter himself send them a pastor and teacher.

When Peter replied to them, “This is the one whom you ought to have as your pastor,” presenting the lord bishop as standing before him, it seemed to Anscharius that a great earthquake occurred, that he fell to the ground, and that a voice came over him, accompanied by great sweetness in his mind—an anointing, namely, of the Holy Spirit—so that he felt himself renewed, as it were, in the grace of Christ.

The voice that came poured a blessing over him.

After this, as it seemed to him, the men mentioned above again urged the apostle to send them some teacher—for they appeared to be contradicting what he had previously proposed to them. Peter replied to them as if in anger:

“Did I not tell you that this man, who now stands here, ought to be the one? Why did you doubt? Did you not hear the voice of the Holy Spirit descend upon him for the purpose of consecrating him as your pastor?”

After saying this, he awoke from sleep. Since he had seen the vision three years before he was invited to govern the church of Bremen, he became entirely certain that he ought to go somewhere in the name of the Lord; but he did not know where.

After he came to the church of Bremen by royal command, learned that it had been consecrated in honor of Saint Peter, and found that some people had not received him willingly, he remembered his vision. For this reason he consented to assume the governance of that diocese.

He used to affirm that he had never otherwise wished to do this.

### He raises Northmen boys at Turholt. He foresees Reginarius’s punishment for taking them away.

### 63.

At the time when he possessed the aforesaid cell of Turholt, since all his concern was directed toward the calling of the nations, so that he might benefit them in his mission, he had placed there certain boys bought from the Northmen or Slavs, to be raised in that same cell for sacred service and educated in learning.

Some of these the aforementioned Reginarius took away when the cell itself was given to him and sent them into his own service.

Because the lord bishop was exceedingly distressed over this, it shortly afterward seemed to him that he had come to a certain house and had found there both the venerable King Charles and Reginarius himself.

As it appeared to him, he rebuked them concerning the boys, asserting that he had intended to raise them for the service of almighty God, not so that they would serve Reginarius.

After he had said this, it seemed to him that Reginarius raised his foot and kicked the lord bishop in the mouth.

Then, immediately after this had happened, it seemed to him that Jesus Christ stood near him and said to the aforesaid king and to Reginarius alike:

“Whose man is this whom you are dishonoring so shamefully? Know that he has the Lord, and you will not go unpunished in this matter.”

After these words they became terrified and disturbed, while the lord bishop awoke.

How true this vision was is attested by the divine vengeance that came upon Reginarius himself. Not long afterward he incurred the king’s anger, lost the cell together with everything he held from the king, and could never again recover his former favor.

### How concerned he was for the flock; gentle and severe in preaching.

### 64. How great and excellent he was in pastoral grace; gentle and severe in preaching

But lest we seem to have passed over what and how great his pastoral grace was, in him [Col. 1006B] we certainly proved how true is what blessed Gregory said, in his exposition of the shepherds who were keeping watch over their flock at the Nativity of the Lord, concerning the shepherds of the Church:

“What,” he says, “is meant by the fact that, while the shepherds were keeping watch, an angel appeared to them and the glory of God shone around them? Is it not that those who know how to preside diligently over faithful flocks deserve, more than others, to see sublime things? And while they themselves piously keep watch over the flock, divine grace shines more abundantly upon them.”

For we proved through many experiences that the grace of God accompanied him in all his actions. That he was solicitous in guarding his flock, that he was granted the privilege of seeing many sublime things, and that his mind was frequently inspired by heavenly visitation, we have already shown above in many instances. Finally, since the grace of God shone more abundantly in him outwardly [Col. 1006C], his preaching too was suffused with great sweetness, yet was partly terrifying, so that it might be clearly established by sound judgment that his words were governed by spiritual infusion. In this way, mingling gentleness with terrors, he displayed the force of divine judgment—the judgment in which the Lord will come appearing terrible to sinners and gentle to the righteous.

By this grace he was admirable in both speech and countenance, so that the powerful and the rich, but especially the insolent and arrogant, regarded him as terrifying; people of moderate means embraced him as though he were a brother; and the poor venerated him with the deepest affection, as though he were a father.

### 65. He forbids labor on a feast day. God punishes transgressors

Although he cautiously avoided signs of miraculous power, as though they were instruments of vainglory [Col. 1006D], nevertheless, without his seeking them, such signs were not lacking. This was established by clear evidence: the command of the Lord, uttered through his mouth, did not remain without effect.

For once, when he was preaching to the people in Frisia, in the district called Ostergao [al., Ostargao], on the Lord’s Day, and among other things forbade anyone to perform servile labor on a feast day, some of them—as obstinate and foolish people are—returned home and, since the weather was fair, went into the meadow and made haystacks. When this had been done and evening was approaching, all the stacks that had been made that same [Col. 1007A] day were consumed by divine fire, while those that had been prepared in the middle of the field on earlier days remained unharmed.

When this occurred, the people living in the surrounding area saw the smoke from afar and, thinking that enemies were present, were greatly afraid. But, on investigating the truth of the matter more carefully, they determined that the obstinacy of certain people had been punished.

### He secures the liberation of captives

### 66.

Nor do we think this should be passed over in silence: once, when the people of Nordalbingia had committed a very serious offense, their offense was of this kind. Certain wretched Christian captives, who were being oppressed among the pagans, escaped from them and came to the Christians, to the aforementioned Nordalbingians, who are known to be neighbors of the pagans. The Nordalbingians seized these people and placed them in chains [Col. 1007B]. Some they sold again to the pagans; others they made their slaves, or sold to other Christians.

When this became known to the lord bishop, he was deeply distressed that such a great crime had occurred in his diocese. Yet he could not adequately determine how it might be corrected, because many people were entangled in this most heinous offense, including men who were considered powerful and noble among them.

Finally, when he was exceedingly anxious about this matter, divine consolation appeared to him one night. It seemed to him that the Lord Jesus was present in this world, just as he once had been, when he preached the teaching and examples of his presence to the peoples. He seemed to be with a multitude of believers, and the lord bishop himself appeared to be traveling with him on the same road, joyful and glad. As it seemed to him, divine terror had been brought upon all the obstinate, the oppressed were being rescued, and there was great peace everywhere, so that no opposition appeared to exist anywhere along that road.

Strengthened, therefore, after this vision, he prepared to set out for the people mentioned above, with the intention of freeing by whatever means he could the wretched people who had been irrationally enslaved and sold, and of preventing, with the grace of the Lord, anyone from daring to commit such an offense in the future.

On this journey the Lord granted him such great grace and struck such terror into the obstinate through his authority that, although they were noble and powerful in wrongdoing [Col. 1007D], none of them dared oppose his command. The wretched were sought out wherever they had been sold, and, having been granted freedom, were released to go wherever they wished.

Moreover, so that no fraud might be alleged in the future concerning this matter, they made the following agreement: none of those who had been stained by the aforesaid act of robbery would defend himself by oath or witnesses, but would commit himself to the judgment of almighty God—either the person accused of such a crime, or the captive whom another accused.

By this action, on that very journey the Lord truly demonstrated what he promised to the faithful, saying: “Behold, I am with you all the days [Col. 1008A] until the consummation of the age” (Matthew 28:20). He completed that journey with such prosperity and joy that some of those traveling with him said that never in their lives had they undertaken so good and pleasant a journey.

### He heals the sick with oil. He flees vainglory

### 67.

How many were healed through his prayer and the anointing of oil, we cannot enumerate. For, as we learned through the testimony of many, sick people used to come eagerly to him not only from his own diocese but also from distant places, seeking from him the medicine of salvation.

He, however, always preferred that such things be concealed rather than publicized. Indeed, when a discussion of signs of this kind once took place in his presence, he said to one of his close companions: “If I were worthy before my God, I would ask him to grant me one sign—namely, that by his grace he would make me a good man.”

### A martyr throughout his life. Afflicted with dysentery. Grieved that martyrdom had been taken from him

### 68.

Furthermore, although his life was such, he was nevertheless almost constantly afflicted by illness of his own body. Indeed, nearly his entire life was a martyrdom: through the very many hardships he endured within his diocese because of the incursions and plundering of the barbarians, as well as the opposition of the wicked; and, in addition, through the personal torment that, for love of Christ, he never ceased to inflict upon his own body.

But what are we to do, when after so many sweet and beneficial matters we are compelled to relate something that we cannot explain [Col. 1008C] without grief? In the sixty-fourth year of his life, and the thirty-fourth of his episcopate, he began to suffer from a serious bodily illness—continuous dysentery. As he struggled fiercely with it for many days, indeed for four months and more, and felt himself being driven toward death, he always gave thanks to God and said that this suffering was less than his wickedness deserved, often repeating the words of blessed Job: “If we have received good things from the hand of God, why should we not receive evil things?” (Job III, 10.)

Nevertheless, because of the visions mentioned above, he believed that he ought to be brought to completion by martyrdom rather than by such an illness. He became extremely sad and began to reckon it against himself and his sins that, as though by a most certain hope, he had been deprived through his own fault, often repeating the Psalmist’s words: “You are righteous, O Lord, and your judgment is right” (Psalm 118:137).

When his most faithful disciple, Rombert—this Life’s author, as Adam explains in Book I, chapter 31 [Note: [Col. 1007] Rombert, namely, the author of this Life, as Adam explains in Book I, chapter 31.]—learned of this sorrow by questioning him and earnestly tried to console him, saying that it had not been promised him that he would be slain by the sword, burned by fire, or drowned in water, but that he was to come to the Lord with the crown of martyrdom, he was nevertheless unable to accept consolation.

Finally, when his disciple, who was privy to nearly everything concerning him, often discussed the same matter with him and wished with all his strength to console him, he tried to recall to the bishop’s mind how much he had endured in God’s service, how much bodily suffering he had borne [Col. 1009A], and that this final illness itself, so exceedingly severe and prolonged, could quite sufficiently have been reckoned to him as martyrdom. Yet he accepted consolation in no way and remained in the sorrow mentioned above.

### He is strengthened by God. He has the privileges granted to him written down and entrusts their execution to the king

### 69.

For this reason it came about that the Lord deigned to console his servant—not now as before through a dream, but more openly—in order to provide a remedy from his grace for so great a sorrow.

One day, while he was standing in the oratory at Mass and was extremely troubled about this very matter, he was suddenly carried away in an ecstasy of mind. Then, as though awake, he heard a voice sharply rebuking him because he ought in no way to have doubted God’s promise, as though any iniquity could overcome God’s mercy [Col. 1009B].

“Believe most firmly,” it said, “and do not doubt in any way, because by his grace God will do both things for you: he will forgive the sins about which you are now anxious, and he will fulfill everything that he has promised.”

After receiving this consolation, he also consoled himself. From then on he began to arrange more diligently whatever required attention in his diocese. Moreover, he ordered the apostolic privileges that had been issued concerning his legation to be copied in many booklets and sent to almost all the bishops of the lord King Louis [Note: [Col. 1009D] This appears to refer to the letter of Ansgar reported at the end of this Life, in which he commended these privileges to the German bishops.].

He also sent the same document to King Louis himself and to his son of the same name, adding letters bearing his own name, in which he asked them to keep these matters in remembrance and, as circumstances required, to provide assistance, so that the legation itself, with the grace of God helping and with their support, might bear fruit and grow among the peoples [Col. 1009C].

### He wishes to die on the feast of the Purification of blessed Mary; on its vigil he orders three candles to be lit. On the feast day, after Masses have been celebrated for him, he awaits the public Mass while fasting

### 70.

After he had suffered from the aforesaid illness for three continuous months and the Epiphany of the Lord had passed, he began to desire that he might pass to the grace of the Lord on the Purification of holy Mary.

As that feast approached, therefore, he ordered a banquet to be prepared for the clergy and the poor, so that they might dine on that most holy day. He also ordered three large candles to be made from his own special wax. When they had been made, on the vigil of the aforesaid feast he had them carried before him and ordered one to be lit before the altar of holy Mary, another before the altar of Saint Peter, and the third before the altar of Saint John the Baptist. He wished these saints, who had once been his guides in the vision mentioned above, to receive him as he departed from the body.

Meanwhile, he had been so exhausted and wasted by the illness that scarcely anything remained in his body except bones bound together by sinews and covered with skin. Nevertheless, he always devoted himself to the praise of the Lord [Col. 1010A].

When the day of the said feast dawned, all the priests who were present celebrated Masses for him, as they had been accustomed to do every day. He began to arrange how an address to the people should be delivered, declaring that he would taste nothing that day until the public Mass had ended.

When it was finished, and he had eaten and drunk a little, he devoted the whole day with particular diligence to admonishing his people and kindling them for the service of the Lord—sometimes collectively, sometimes individually, encouraging each one to divine service as he was able. His chief care and concern, however, was for his legation to the peoples. He spent the following night continuously in such admonitions.

### After the litanies have been recited, he receives the viaticum after the Masses. He repeats prayers for himself and for others. He dies

### 71.

The brothers who were present were reciting the litany and, according to custom, singing psalms for his departure. He instructed them also to sing the hymn composed in praise of God, namely *Te Deum laudamus*, and the Catholic faith composed by blessed Athanasius.

When morning came, while all who were present were celebrating the solemn Masses for him, he received communion of the Lord’s body and blood. Then, raising his hands, he prayed that divine mercy might forgive anyone who had sinned against him in any way.

Afterward he began to repeat these verses frequently:

“According to your mercy, remember me, for the sake of your goodness, O Lord”; and, “God, be merciful to me, a sinner”; and, “Into your hands, O Lord, I commend my spirit.”

When he had repeated these words many times and, because of his frequent gasping, could no longer keep repeating them, he ordered one of the brothers to sing the same words repeatedly in his place.

And so, with his eyes fixed upon heaven, he breathed out his spirit, commended to the grace of the Lord [Note: [Col. 1009D] “He died in the year of the Lord 865, in the thirteenth indiction, which is the twenty-sixth year of Louis II, and was buried in the basilica of Saint Peter before the altar of holy Mary, Mother of God [Col. 1010D],” says Adam in Book I, chapter 31. Albert of Stade and the Saxon Chronicle indicate the same year: “He sat [as bishop] for thirty-four years; his deposition is celebrated with the greatest veneration on the third day before the Nones of February,” according to Adam.].

### All mourn. Epilogue of his encomium

### 72.
