When his body had been prepared according to custom and placed upon the bier, and was being carried to the church, the mourning of everyone seemed to be renewed, and there was one voice among the mourners—especially among the clergy, orphans, widows, children without parents, and the needy.

Although there can be no doubt about his salvation, what religious or faithful person could restrain himself from weeping when he has left us desolate—he in whom alone, almost, the examples of all the saints of old flourished [Col. 1010D]?

For, to begin with the very head of all the elect, he followed Christ in poverty, himself poor; with the apostles he abandoned everything; and with Saint John the Baptist, leading his earliest years apart from the crowds, he sought the solitude of a monastery.

Then, as time passed, he grew through daily progress and went from virtue to virtue. He was appointed, with the blessed apostle Paul, as a chosen vessel to bear the name of Christ before the nations [Col. 1011A]; afterward, with Peter, prince of the apostles, he assumed responsibility for feeding Christ’s sheep.

What he was and how great he showed himself in that office seems especially clear from this: standing midway between heaven and earth, a mediator between God and his neighbor, he was at one time occupied with divine vision and heavenly revelations, and at another arranging the conduct and life of those entrusted to him.

He was therefore sufficient for these two wings, the active and the contemplative, because, according to the faith of the Gospels, only the pure in heart are believed to see the Lord. He, chosen by the Lord as a virgin, remained a virgin forever in mind and body, together with the holy apostle and evangelist John. Moreover, he was bound to everyone by such great charity that, together with blessed Stephen, the first martyr [Col. 1011B], he even prayed for his persecutors.

O truly blessed man, worthy of every proclamation of praise! Who has had the good fortune to imitate such a man, so great, or to possess alone so many virtues all at once? Holy in mind and chaste in body, he will follow the Lamb with the virgins wherever he goes. Always persevering in confession of Christ, he will hold a most glorious place among the confessors. He will sit with the apostles upon that sublime judgment-seat in the regeneration, and will judge the world that he had despised; and with the martyrs he will receive the crown of righteousness and the palm of martyrdom.

### How he was a martyr

### 73.

It is agreed that there are two kinds of martyrdom: one hidden, in the peace of the Church; the other manifest, arising when persecution breaks out. He possessed both in intention; he attained one of them in effect.

Because every day he continually sacrificed to God upon the altar of his heart tears, vigils, fasts, mortification of the flesh, and the putting to death of carnal desires, he certainly attained by his resolve the martyrdom that he could not attain during a time of peace.

Because a persecutor’s hostile intent was not lacking against him for an open bodily martyrdom, he attained by his will what he could not fully attain in deed. Nor can we altogether deny that he possessed this martyrdom in deed as well, if we consider, according to the Apostle, his many labors for the Lord: often in journeys, dangers from rivers, dangers from robbers, dangers from his own people, dangers from the nations, dangers in the city [Col. 1011D], dangers in the wilderness, dangers at sea, dangers among false brothers; in labor and hardship, in many vigils, in hunger and thirst, in many fasts, in cold [Col. 1012A] and nakedness; besides those things that come from outside, his daily burden and concern for all the churches.

Who was weak, and he was not weak? Who was scandalized, and he did not burn?

Therefore, since he was tempered in so many and such great bodily adversities and trials of spirit for the Lord, how can he rightly be denied the status of martyr?

For if only a life ended through suffering were counted as martyrdom, the Lord would never have testified that the holy evangelist John would drink his cup, although we know that he did not end his life by martyrdom.

Accordingly, if we do not doubt that John must be enrolled among the number of martyrs according to the Lord’s judgment, we must not doubt at all concerning the holy and most blessed man whom we have just mentioned.

For he was a martyr because, according to the Apostle, the world was crucified to him and he to the world. He was a martyr because, amid the devil’s temptations, the allurements of the flesh, persecuting pagans, and opposing Christians, he remained to the end of his life fearless, steadfast, and unconquered in confessing Christ.

He was a martyr because *μάρτυρ* (*martyr*) means “witness”: he was always a witness to the divine word and to the name that bears Christ.

In this matter no one should be surprised that he did not attain the martyrdom he himself desired with the greatest longing and believed had been promised to him, because he is shown, according to the interpretation of this name, not to have been promised even that.

Indeed, in the martyrdom of the body that he received, some elation might perhaps have crept into his mind. To guard against this, divine wisdom both promised and granted the following: that nothing should be diminished from his merits, and that provision should be made for humility, the guardian of all virtues [Col. 1012C].

### 74.

Therefore, since from what we have recalled above it is clear how great this man’s holiness was and how great his merit before God, it remains for us to strive to be his imitators, just as he was an imitator of Christ in all things.

In this way it can come about that he may continue to live with us on earth until the consummation of the age, and that we may deserve to live with him in heaven after the course of this present life has ended.

For he will live with us on earth if the holiness of his life and the memory of his teaching represent him to us; and we shall live with him in heaven if, following his examples, we strive toward him always with the whole of our desire and strength—toward Jesus Christ our Lord, to whom he went before us [Col. 1012D], who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God forever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 1013]

# LIFE OF SAINT WILLEHAD, FIRST BISHOP OF BREMEN, by Saint Ansgar

*(Mabillon, Benedictine Annals, volume IV.)*

[Col. 1013]

## [ON THE LIFE OF SAINT WILLEHAD]

## AUTHOR’S PROLOGUE

[Note: [Col. 1013C] Philippus Caesar counts this as the first chapter and continues the same sequence of chapters through the end of the book on the Miracles.]

[Col. 1013A]

When the devout affection of the faithful proclaims the praises and deeds of the saints, it strives truly to preach Christ in them and to glorify Christ. For they became victorious through the power of the one whose grace had proved them faithful in good conduct. According to the Apostle, the saints are what they are by the grace of God. And because his grace is always good, through it human beings also become people of good will.

It is likewise by God’s grace that the good will which has already begun to exist is increased in goodness, and so, growing, is multiplied, enabling every righteous person to fulfill God’s commands—to fulfill fully and perfectly whatever he wills.

The saints, therefore, are to be praised for their good merits; indeed, Christ is to be praised in them even more, since by his grace they received the ability to become good and holy. Although such proclamations of praise are rightly bestowed through the devotion of the faithful upon many who live piously and religiously in this life, they are more properly and reasonably offered to holy people after they have lived through and happily completed the most perilous life of this world.

For it is then most fitting to extol and proclaim the holiness of each person, when neither can the one being praised be tempted by elation nor the one praising be accused of flattery. Hence the most just custom of the holy Church has arisen: that after their departure, the conduct and religious devotion of the saints who were distinguished and praiseworthy in this life for miracles, devotion to the faith, and perfection in good works should be described.

Thus later generations may have examples of virtue to imitate, and may also have the means to contemplate the grace of divine mercy. They should not despair of being able to accomplish things that perhaps seemed impossible, when they see fulfilled in these saints what they themselves, surrounded here by fragile flesh and aided by the wonderful and extraordinary grace of God, accomplished.

Since all the faithful rightly owe these things to the saints, the most blessed citizens of that heavenly homeland, each person should nevertheless show them more diligently to those whose protection he firmly and faithfully believes will especially guard and assist him [Col. 1014A].

Therefore we have judged it worthy to write the religious and entirely God-devoted life of our blessed father Willehad, the first bishop of the Church of Bremen, so that, while recounting his triumph of virtue, we may proclaim the divine glory in him and propose the example of his holiness for others to imitate.

## CHAPTER I. His homeland and what he did there

There was, then, a venerable man from the people of the Angles, from Northumbria, named Willehad. From childhood he was educated in sacred letters and instructed in spiritual disciplines. He began to live diligently in the worship of God and, devoted to the service of almighty God, applied himself day and night to fasts, vigils, and prayers [Col. 1014B]. His deeds were therefore, for all who lived there, not only honorable and good but also lovable and praiseworthy.

As he grew older, through the favor of all and by the grace of election, he was promoted there to priestly honor. He strove continually to adorn and increase that honor more and more by the merit of his holiness and by outstanding exercises of good works.

After receiving priestly ordination, he heard that the Frisians and Saxons—peoples who until then had been unbelieving and pagan—had abandoned the worship of idols and had begun in some fashion to seek the ministries of the Catholic faith, desiring to be cleansed from the stains of their former condition through the sacrament of baptism.

When the man of God heard this, he was filled with great joy. Kindled by an inward love [Col. 1014C], he began eagerly to seek how he might travel to those regions for the love of God. And because, inspired by the Holy Spirit, the servant of God burned with this zeal more intensely from day to day, the lamp that had been lit could not remain hidden under a bushel in darkness. It was placed upon a lampstand, so that it might shine openly for all who were then or would later be in the house of the Lord.

He therefore approached the king who at that time ruled among the English, named Alachrat [Note: [Col. 1014C] More correctly Alachart than in John of Leiden, and corruptly Alachintum in Surius. Turgot, in Book II, chapter 4, *On the Church of Durham*, and Simeon of Durham, *On the Kings of the English*, record that he was Alchred, who succeeded Moloni to the kingdom of Northumbria in the year 865; in the ninth year of his reign, however, he exchanged the kingdom for exile through the treachery of his leading men. Hence the time when Willehad crossed into Frisia must be considered.], and tearfully explained to him how greatly he was inflamed with zeal for the service of the Lord. He asked that, with the king’s permission and authorization, he might be allowed to go to the regions already mentioned to preach the word of the Lord.

When the king learned of his most holy purpose, he summoned a considerable gathering of bishops and other servants of God. In the presence of all, he made known Willehad’s most fervent devotion and, with the unanimous consent of everyone—for the credible holiness of the blessed man had long been recognized by all—sent him to the regions mentioned above to preach the word of the Lord, commending him to the grace of heaven.

## CHAPTER II. How he came to Frisia and how matters began to proceed for him there

He undertook this pilgrimage with the greatest willingness [Col. 1015B], crossed the neighboring sea as quickly as possible, and came to Frisia, to a place called Docyncyrea [Note: [Col. 1015D] Concerning the town of Docken on the river Burdine, mentioned in the *Life of Saint Boniface* under the year 754. A little beyond the Burdine one sees the river Lavica, which is discussed below. Adam begins the account of Saint Willehad’s preaching in Frisia from the year of Saint Boniface’s martyrdom, that is, from the year 754; for he says that Willehad held this office in Frisia and Saxony for thirty-five years. But Willehad went to Germany later, as is clear from the beginning of Alchred’s rule, with whose consent he left his homeland.], in the district of Hostracha, where the lord Bishop Boniface had long before been crowned with martyrdom.

Since many there had previously been instructed in the faith through the preaching of the aforesaid martyr, Willehad was received by them with great honor. He lived there for a long time, teaching the things of God. Many noblemen also entrusted their children to him for education. By the word of teaching and the example of a devout life, he continually stirred them to the love of God, and he recalled many who had formerly strayed from the faith to true and Catholic knowledge. In that place he displayed himself as a great light of heavenly radiance, and there he baptized a very large crowd of pagans instructed by the word of holy preaching [Col. 1015C].

## CHAPTER III. How he was about to be killed and was divinely freed by lot

Proceeding from there, he crossed the river Loveke [Note: [Col. 1015D] Surius published *fluvium Lavinca*, “the river Lavinca.” Bishop Liudger is said to have been appointed by Charlemagne as teacher among the Frisians on the eastern side of the river Labeki, over five districts whose names are Hugmerchi, and so forth; this district seems to be none other than the Humarcha mentioned here. The river Lavica or Laubacum is now called Lawers in the vernacular. John of Leiden also mentions it in Book IV, chapter 7 of his *Belgian Chronicle*, where he writes about Saint Willehad; he also interprets Humarcha as Hucmerk.], and came to a place called Humarcha. There he began to preach the name of the Lord to the barbarians and to persuade them that, abandoning the superstition of idols, they should receive knowledge of the one true God, so that through the washing of holy baptism they might merit forgiveness for their sins.

He said that it was madness and vanity to seek help from stones and to hope for assistance from mute and deaf images [Col. 1016A].

When the fierce people, excessively devoted to idolatry, heard this, they were all aroused together in great anger. They gnashed their teeth at him and said that the profane man ought not to live any longer; indeed, that he deserved death, since he had dared to utter such sacrilegious words against their invincible gods.

Some among them, however, advised the others with sounder judgment, saying that this rule of religion was unknown to them and that it was uncertain whether it had been proposed by divine will. The man himself was entirely free of any crime, and therefore ought not to perish by so doubtful a death. Rather, they should cast lots [Note: [Col. 1016D] Tacitus, in *Germania*, teaches that the use of lots was especially familiar to the Germans; Adam applies this chiefly to the Saxons. Read the *Acts of Saints Willibrord and Wilfram*, bishops.], so that heaven might reveal whether he deserved death; otherwise, they should release him free, and they themselves would be shown to be in no way guilty.

What they had proposed was therefore done, and, according to the custom of the pagans, a lot was cast concerning him, whether he should live or die. But, with divine Providence directing the outcome, the lot of death could not fall upon him. For this reason they did not dare harm him in any way. Instead, after taking counsel, they allowed him to depart from them unharmed.

## CHAPTER IV. How, beaten with blows and a sword, he was miraculously preserved

From there he crossed over and came to Thrianta [Note: [Col. 1016D] John of Leiden: “After this he came to Trentonia, that is, Drenterlant”; according to Philippus Caesar, this place is still called Drente today.]. While he was preaching the word of the Lord there, a very large crowd of pagans believed and received the sacrament of baptism.

He remained in that place for a considerable time, instructing those who did not believe and diligently strengthening those who believed in the way of truth by both words and examples. Many began to love the good life of their teacher [supplement: “to love”] and to hate the errors of the pagans, and to venerate with devoted purpose the Christian religion that they professed.

It therefore happened that some of his disciples, pierced by divine zeal, began to destroy the pagan shrines erected throughout the surrounding area and to reduce them to nothing as far as they could.

When this had been done, the barbarians who still happened to remain unbelieving, inflamed with immense fury, suddenly rushed upon them with force, wishing to destroy them utterly. There they beat God’s servant with clubs and inflicted very many blows upon him.

One of them, drawing his sword, also rushed upon the servant of God and attempted to cut off his head. But at that moment the blessed man was wearing around his neck a reliquary containing holy relics [Note: [Col. 1016D] The ancients call this a *phylacterium*, a reliquary suspended from the neck. Yet *capsa* and *chrismarium* are also found in the same sense in the *Life of Saint Wilfrid*, bishop, under the year 709.] [Col. 1017A].

When the attacker’s blow fell upon his neck, it cut through the strap of the reliquary but could not wound the man himself in any way. Terrified by this miracle, the pagans allowed him and his companions to depart unharmed and did not thereafter dare trouble them in any way.

## CHAPTER V. How he was sent to Saxony by Emperor Charles
After this, the most glorious king of the Franks, Charles, who had already labored many times among the Saxon people so that they might be converted to the faith of the Christian religion—but they, always hostile in heart, repeatedly abandoning the faith they had accepted, became ever more entangled in their former errors—heard the fame of the man of God and ordered that he be summoned to him. Receiving him honorably and reverently when he came, he willingly gave his attention to his conversation and teaching. Having found him approved by holy conduct and by the steadfastness of an unfeigned faith, he sent him into the regions of Saxony, to the district called Wigmodia [Note: [Col. 1017D] Philip thinks this was the tract beyond the Weser in Saxony, which now contains the bishoprics of Verden and Bremen. Compare the diploma of Charlemagne above. (See volume XCVII of the Patrologia.)], so that there, by royal authority, he might establish churches, offer the peoples the teaching of holy preaching, and freely proclaim the way of eternal salvation to all who lived there. He devoutly accepted this ministry and carried it out with the greatest diligence. Passing through the whole surrounding diocese, he converted many to the faith of Christ by evangelizing, so that in the second year both the Saxons and the Frisians living in the surrounding area all together promised that they would become Christians [Col. 1017C].

This took place in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 780 [Note: [Col. 1017D] Eginhard assigns this to the year 780. He says that all the Saxons of the eastern regions came to meet Charlemagne at the river Ocker [Col. 1018D], where a very great multitude of them is said to have been baptized at a place called Horheim, according to their customary pretense—not that all of them, but that many of them, falsely received baptism. A letter of Pope Hadrian to Charlemagne on this subject is extant as number 80 in the Carolingian Codex (see the same work).], and in the fourteenth year of the reign of the aforementioned prince Charles, who had not yet been raised to the imperial dignity. Later, in the thirty-fourth year of his reign, the Catholic Church throughout Europe, venerating and rejoicing together, received him as emperor after he had been consecrated at Rome by the hands of the most reverend apostolic Leo. For the imperial power, which after Constantine, the most devout Augustus, had until then ruled among the Greeks from the seat at Constantinople, was administered in those days more by feminine governance, since men of royal lineage were by then failing there. In his time, through the election of the Roman people, at a great council of bishops and other servants of God, dominion was transferred to the Franks [Col. 1017D], because he himself appeared to hold that city, which had been the head of the empire, as well as many other provinces throughout the world; for this reason he was also worthy, by right, of the title Caesar.

At the aforementioned time of his reign, therefore, the servant of God Willehad began to build churches throughout Wigmodia and to ordain priests over them, who could freely confer upon the peoples the grace of salvation and baptism.

## CHAPTER VI. [Col. 1018A] How He Fled Widukind’s Persecution, and What His Companions Suffered

But in the following year, at the instigation of the devil, who envies every good thing, there arose a man of more perverse counsel, Widukind, who appeared to rebel against King Charles and gathered a great multitude of Saxons around him. They unanimously began to persecute and punish those who appeared steadfast in the faith of Christ; they also began to scatter the servants of God, wandering from place to place, and to drive them from their territories.

Moved by this persecution, it happened that the servant of God, in accordance with the Lord’s command: “If they persecute you in one city, flee to another” (Matthew 10:15), crossed from Wigmodia into Utriustri [Corb., Utristi]. There, having boarded a ship [Col. 1018B], he crossed the sea toward Frisia, and thus, with the help of Christ’s grace, escaped their persecution.

The Saxons, however, exercised more fiercely upon his disciples, in the heat of their raging anger, the cruelty which they had been unable to exercise against their master. For they killed Folcard the priest together with Count Emming in the district called Leri; Benjamin in Cibhriustri; Atreban the cleric in Thiatmaresgau; and Gerwal, together with his companions, in Bremen—slaying them with the sword out of hatred for the Christian name. After these men had thus been happily summoned to the heavenly kingdom by the shedding of their own blood, the storm of persecution continued for a long time afterward to rage against the rebellious Saxons.

## CHAPTER VII. [Col. 1018C] How, During the Persecution, He Went to Rome and Returned to Frisia

After this, the man of God, recognizing that at that time he had no opportunity to preach, set out and visited Pippin, king of the Lombards; then, proceeding on a prosperous journey, he reached Rome. There he remained and, with many tears and prayers, diligently and devoutly commended himself and the entire company of the faithful to the divine mercy at the most sacred shrine of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles. He especially commended those for whom he was most deeply concerned, lest perhaps the Christianity accepted in the regions of Saxony should then be utterly destroyed by diabolical plotting.

Departing from there, the servant of God, strengthened not a little by the consolation of the venerable Pope Hadrian [Col. 1018D], returned joyfully toward Francia. On this journey it happened that divine power was also manifested through him. For the servant of the man of God, named Aldo, who provided his master’s food, had a wooden dish, commonly called a *scutella*, which he regularly kept clean and shining and placed before him at table. One day this servant found it broken by accident.

At mealtime, when the man of God asked for it, the servant did not wish to conceal from him the negligence that had occurred, but told him that it had been broken. The holy man ordered that it be brought to him just as it was. But when the servant returned to the place where it lay, he found it whole, as though it had never suffered any damage. He brought it and placed it before him, happy and cheerful, whereas previously he had trembled and feared the anger of a just reprimand.

It is certain that this happened from heaven through the grace of the holy man, although he himself, fleeing self-exaltation, preferred that it be done secretly rather than publicly.

Having thus returned from the journey he had undertaken, he went to a place called Asternacha [Note: [Col. 1019C] That is, the monastery of Asternacum, called Epternacum by later writers. Adam says: “Willehad himself came to Rome with Liudger, where, relieved by the consolation of the most holy Pope Hadrian, Liudger withdrew to Monte Cassino [Col. 1019D] for the confession of Saint Benedict, while Willehad returned to Gaul, to the tomb of Saint Willibrord. Thus, each remaining in seclusion for two years, they devoted themselves to the contemplative life.” Read the Acts of Saint Willibrord and Saint Liudger.]. There his disciples, who had been scattered in various places because of fear of the persecution, were reunited with him.

He refreshed them with kindly consolation and earnestly admonished them to conduct themselves steadfastly in all things for the faith of Christ. Having remained in that same place for nearly two years, he chose to lead a solitary and enclosed life. While living there in no ordinary way, he devoted himself to reading and prayer, and was also at times especially occupied with writing. For there he wrote the Epistles of blessed Paul in a single volume, along with many other works, which his successors preserved as a memorial of his holy remembrance and which remain intact to this day. Many people in that same place were corrected and brought to a better life by his example and admonitions, and were vigorously inspired to the service of the Lord.

## CHAPTER VIII. The Ordination of Saint Willehad as Bishop

After this, the venerable priest of the Lord again visited King Charles, who at that time happened to be staying in the Saxon fortress of Eresburg [Note: [Col. 1019D] Eresburg, a town of Saxony on the river Weser, frequently visited by Charlemagne.]. He explained his most devoted desire to prepare the Gospel of peace and sought from the king an entirely favorable command in this matter.

To console him for his labor and to provide for what would follow, the king granted him as a benefice a certain estate in Francia called Justina, and ordered him to return once more to the parish he had begun for the name of Christ. He gratefully and religiously accepted this [Col. 1020A], returned again to Wigmodia, and publicly and energetically preached the Lord’s faith to the peoples. He also restored the churches that had been destroyed and appointed approved men to preside in each place, so that they might give the peoples admonitions concerning salvation.

Thus, in that same year, by divine providence, the Saxon people again received the Christian faith that it had lost. In that same year Widukind, the author and instigator of every evil and of treachery, submitted himself to King Charles [Note: [Col. 1019D] That is, in the year 785, as Eginhard testifies, reporting that Witikind was baptized at Attigny, a royal estate in the region of Reims. Adam correctly records the eighteenth year of Charles’s reign. On this subject, read the letter of Pope Hadrian to Charlemagne in volume III of the *History of the Franks*, where it is number 91 among the papal letters.], received the grace of baptism, and thus for a time the evils brought about by his destructive influence were calmed.

Afterward, when everything seemed peaceful, and when the ferocity of the Saxons, although compelled, was already softening its neck beneath Christ’s gentle yoke, the aforementioned most excellent prince, while staying in the city of Worms, had the servant of God Willehad [Col. 1020B] consecrated bishop on the third day before the Ides of July [Note: [Col. 1019D] Charlemagne assigns the same day in the diploma cited above. It is necessary to place the year in 787, both because, according to the author’s account below, Willehad was ordained bishop seven years after Charles sent him into Saxony—he was sent at the beginning of the year 780, as stated above in chapter 5—and because, after completing two years of episcopal office, he died in 789. Certainly the Chronicle of Moissac places this ordination in the year 787, in these words: “Blessed Wlradus [Col. 1020D] (to be read Wilhadus) was ordained bishop on the Ides of July over Wimoda, Kiusleri, Asterga, Cara or Sordedi, and Wangia; and there he first taught the word of God and baptized them.”]. He appointed him pastor and ruler over Wigmodia, Laras, and Ruistri [Note: [Col. 1020D] The people of Rustri in eastern Frisia, or the county of Emden, are divided into two parts by the middle of the gulf called the Jade. Those on this side of the Jade are called Rustri and Rustringi; those beyond the Jade are called Buljadae, that is, Transjadani, Stadlandi, or Stedingii. Asterga, included within the county of Emden, is commonly called Ostringa. Read Ubbo Emmius, Book II of the *History of Frisia*.], as well as Nordendi and Wanga, so that there he might preside over the peoples with episcopal authority and, as he had begun, diligently labor to benefit them as a watchman from above through salutary teaching and outstanding works.

Thus he himself first obtained the episcopal see in that diocese. This had nevertheless been delayed for so long because the people, resisting divine belief, scarcely allowed priests to remain among them even when compelled to do so, and would not tolerate being governed by episcopal authority. For this reason he had been shown among them as a priest for seven years previously, although he was called bishop [Note: [Col. 1020D] Here Willehad is called bishop before his episcopal consecration, evidently because he exercised episcopal functions—namely, preaching, conferring baptism, establishing priests in various places, and other activities of that kind. Hence one may infer why many saints, especially in Belgium, are called bishops although they were nowhere consecrated bishops.], and arranged everything as far as he could with the full authority of one presiding [Col. 1020C].

After receiving episcopal consecration, he began to conduct himself with devotion in every respect, and, multiplying and increasing the practices of virtue that he had previously undertaken, he amassed them in still greater measure.

## CHAPTER IX

His Continence and Other Pious Works

From his earliest years this great man was exceedingly continent, and from the beginning of his life he devotedly served the almighty Lord. He did not drink wine, strong drink, or anything by which one might become intoxicated. His food [Col. 1021A] was bread and honey, vegetables and fruit. He abstained from eating meat, and from milk and fish, except that the aforementioned apostolic Adrian, near the end of his life, ordered him to eat fish because of the frequent illnesses he suffered in his body. Obeying that authority, he began to be somewhat more indulgent in this respect.

Moreover, scarcely a day passed on which he did not celebrate the sacred solemnity of Mass with abundant weeping and contrition of heart. He was continually intent upon reading and meditating on sacred doctrine, and was also most diligently devoted to psalmody, so that almost every day he chanted the Psalter, and sometimes even two or three times.

Supported by these and other exercises of good works, the man of God displayed to the peoples, in the manifestation of his own life, the great grace of the Lord [Col. 1021B]. Thus his teaching shone forth with a twofold testimony: what he preached with his mouth he confirmed by his example.

This blessed man passed throughout his diocese, strengthening the Christian people who had formerly been baptized and piercing, by the word of his preaching, the hearts of many who had wandered from the way of salvation. He also built a house of God of marvelous beauty at a place called Bremen, where he established the episcopal see, and dedicated it on the Kalends of November, a Sunday [Note: [Col. 1021D] Therefore in the year 789, which had the Sunday letter D.], in honor of our Lord Jesus Christ, under the invocation of the apostle Saint Peter.

## CHAPTER X. How He Fell Ill at Plexem [Note: [Col. 1021D] In the text, Plecateshem. Adam calls it the estate of Pleccazzem, situated in Rustris. Surius printed Bleckensee; today the name Plexem remains attached to the place. It lies on the Weser below Bremen and the new port of Fegesack, and is a safe anchorage for ships, says Philip Caesar.] and Died, and Was Buried at Bremen [Col. 1021C]

After this, as he diligently visited the entire surrounding parish with pious purpose and strengthened many in the faith by teaching the things of God, he came to a place called Pleccateshem. While staying there, he began to suffer from a severe bodily fever, and from day to day his illness grew extremely serious, so that the disciples who were with him began to despair of his continued life.

One of them, named Egisriki [Philip, Egisrik], who happened to speak with the blessed man more familiarly, approached him and tearfully and plaintively made known to him their fear that he might die. He also pointed out the extremely dangerous abandonment of the people entrusted to him, who under the pastor’s governance now seemed at last to be obedient to divine worship.

“Do not,” he said, “venerable priest, abandon so quickly those whom you have recently acquired for the Lord. Do not leave so soon the people and clergy gathered through your efforts, lest the flock, still tender in faith, be exposed to the bites of wolves and devoured [Col. 1022A]. Do not deprive us, your humble dependents, of the presence of your holiness, lest we seem to wander about like sheep without a shepherd.”

The blessed man, moved by these words, replied:

“Do not, my son, keep me away any longer from the sight of my Lord. Do not use plaintive words to tell me of the troubles of temporal life. I neither desire to live longer here nor fear to die. I wish only to pray to my God, whom I have always loved with my whole heart and served with complete devotion, that in his mercy and favor he may grant me, according to his good pleasure, the reward of a good recompense for my labors.

“As for the sheep he entrusted to me, I commit them to him to guard; for if I have been able to do anything good, I accomplished it by his power rather than my own. His mercy will not fail, for the whole earth is filled with his mercy” [Col. 1022B].

Thus, with pious devotion, the man of the Lord always directing his thoughts toward heaven and continually sending the vows of his prayer to God, on the sixth day before the Ides of November, a Sunday [Note: [Col. 1021D] In the same year, 789, eight days after he had dedicated the church at Bremen, as stated above in chapter 9. Compare chapter 1 of the book of *Miracles*. Nevertheless, in the Saxon manuscript chronicle his death is placed in the year 790.], after sunrise, the precious confessor of the Lord rested in the name of Christ.

The devoted people came running from every direction to his funeral and carried the most blessed father and teacher with praises and hymns to the seat at Bremen. There they committed him to a fitting burial, with honor and reverence, in the new basilica [Note: [Col. 1021D] Adam says: “His body was carried to Bremen [Col. 1022D] and buried in the basilica of Saint Peter, which he himself built.” In the Saxon Chronicle it is recorded that he dedicated that church on the sixth day before the Ides of November, a Sunday.] that he himself had built.

## CHAPTER XI. Miracles Concerning Him After His Death, Both in His Own Basilica and in the Other Basilica to Which He Was Transferred

In that place it was repeatedly demonstrated by many evident signs that the same blessed man was truly an elect soldier of the Lord. Yet, through carelessness and negligence, these things were not recorded anywhere, although not a few people acknowledged that they knew the divine power had often appeared in that place.

Later, after he himself had been transferred to another basilica [Note: [Col. 1022D] The following words of Adam, from Book I, chapter 19, refer to this: “Willeric built three churches at Bremen. The first, namely the church of Saint Peter, he made of stone instead of wood, and, after the body of Saint Willehad had been transferred from there, he placed it in the eastern oratory that he built. Later generations say that this was done out of fear of pirates, who, because of the power of the miracles of our confessor, preferred to carry away his body.” Archbishop Unwan is said to have repaired the chapel of Saint Willehad after it had burned down.], in the time of his successor, Bishop Willeric of blessed memory, although he is said to have performed many things there also through divine power, no one committed these events to memory, even though the testimony of many proves that they were accomplished by true miracles.

Yet what God has divinely revealed for the glory of the blessed man must not be concealed in silence. It has remained preserved to this day in the church at Bremen. For the staff of the holy man, which [Col. 1022D] he himself was accustomed to carry in episcopal fashion, had after his death been placed through the devotion of the faithful in a certain chest.

It happened that the house in which this chest stood suddenly caught fire. The house, together with the chest and everything stored inside it, was completely consumed [Col. 1023A]. But the fire was utterly unable to touch the staff itself. Rather, it was found unharmed in the midst of the fire, with not even the slightest sign of burning visible upon it.

Therefore almighty God is truly to be praised in his saints, for even in the smallest things he reveals their merit to his faithful.

Another event also occurred, which likewise demonstrates that the blessed man possessed great merit before the Lord. His chalice, with which he was accustomed to offer sacrifice to the Lord every day [al., continually], was kept in a certain place by the most faithful devotion of his disciples. When fire entered there and consumed everything, and anything that happened to have been fashioned from metal melted and ran down through the heat [Col. 1024A], the chalice, although made of silver, was found completely intact.

Truly, the Lord’s power appeared wondrously in it: the earthly fire could not prevail over the relics after death of one who, while alive, had been kindled by the true fire of divine love. For creation, subject to the Creator’s command, loses even the force of nature when it attends to the order of its ruler. It cannot bring about any harm, even when nature dictates it, since the power of each nature depends upon the all-powerful will of the Creator.

Blessed Willehad, the Lord’s chosen pontiff, remained in the episcopate for two years, three months, and twenty-six days [Note: [Col. 1023B] Adam gives the same calculation, adding: “He preached to both the Frisians and the Saxons for thirty-five years after the martyrdom of Saint Boniface [Col. 1024B]. He died old and full of days in Frisia, in the estate of Plecazze, which lies in Rustris.”]. Having completed the course of his good combat, he happily departed to the Lord, to whom are honor, glory, power, and dominion throughout infinite ages of ages. Amen.

# HERE BEGIN THE MIRACLES OF THE SAME SAINT

## PREFACE OF SAINT ANSGAR

By the gift of almighty God, who by the gratuitous preordination of his goodness appoints pastors and teachers in the holy Church, Ansgar, bishop of the church at Bremen, prays eternal peace and blessedness in Christ for the entire fellowship of the faithful dwelling throughout the world in harmonious brotherhood [Col. 1023C].

We have often learned, from the examples of the Fathers, that the praises of God attested by the wondrous deeds of his saints ought not to be passed over in silence. They diligently committed to writing many of the things that the Lord’s goodness accomplished through his servants in this world—not only things that displayed the religious holiness of the living, but also things that displayed the immortal glory of those who reign with Christ in eternal life.

Indeed, those who have been transferred from this life, yet are still seen to be present among the peoples here through miracles and the assistance of various powers, show us the great dignity of their glorification and make clear to the hearts of the faithful, more brightly than light [Col. 1023D], how great is their merit before God.

A great indication of Catholic faith is also revealed in this: although the divine majesty accomplishes its work invisibly, Christian belief does not doubt that what it sees as though with its own eyes has been accomplished from heaven. It attributes to the merits of the saints the deeds that take place in those places where their most sacred relics have been buried, remain, and are venerated.

For although the God of Israel alone is almighty, and he gives strength and power to his people, he is nevertheless proclaimed and worshiped as wondrous in his saints. Through their prayers and merits the divine majesty performs prodigies and signs.

Nor are the saints seen to benefit only where they appear to be temporally present in their ashes and relics. Rather, wherever they are faithfully invoked, they are believed to assist the faithful in every place under God’s dominion, through the power and majesty of the Creator, who is present everywhere and rewards their merit [Col. 1024B].

This has often been made evident by many clear healings [Col. 1024C], since many people, whether caught in storms or placed in other dangers, have suddenly felt themselves divinely aided at the invocation of some saint.

Therefore, if the Lord deigns to perform anything wondrous through his saints, such deeds are rightly brought to the knowledge of many [supplied: *deducuntur*], so that posterity may retain in memory the hope that earlier generations received through the grace of faith.

For this reason our humility has decided to investigate in writing those things that in our own days have shone forth, revealed through the power of divine action to display the merits of the blessed bishop and confessor Willehad. Thus the miracles that we rightly proclaimed in former times as belonging to the ancient saints, now renewed in our own time by him who was the first bishop of our church at Bremen [Col. 1024D], may be received and praised together with the joyful effort of our whole heart.

For God has not, even now, forgotten or abandoned the people he redeemed. Rather, amid the countless dangers posed by hostile pagans, when they were almost deprived of every consolation, he wished to bestow this grace of heavenly visitation, so that those who had come to know that such a great and acceptable patron to God was with them in spirit as though also in body might rely with much greater certainty upon divine mercy. They would not fear inhabiting again their devastated homeland, since they did not doubt that the merits of the most holy Father were present with them.

Indeed, they would joyfully return to their deserted dwellings. Although hostile invasion had made them exiles, divine goodness would once again reconcile them, overflowing with blessings. Nor would they despair of receiving in every respect the protection of the saint whose manifold power they had felt burning through the healing of bodies afflicted in various ways [Col. 1025A].

## CHAPTER I. The Time of the Miracles of Saint Willehad

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 860, in the twenty-eighth year of the reign of our most serene lord, Prince Louis, and in the eighth indiction, miracles began to be performed divinely in the church at Bremen. From day to day they increased more abundantly, so that throughout distant regions and among many peoples the report grew ever stronger that divine glory had truly appeared in that place and that the merits of blessed Willehad, resting in that basilica, were flourishing with the honorable bloom of miracles.

When these things were repeated by many mouths, and when many people obtained public benefits of healing there, both in our presence [Col. 1025B] and while we were absent, we resolved to commit them to writing and hand them down to the memory of posterity, so that every nation of the faithful might rejoice with us and praise the God who works in his saints.

Just as those who are present proclaim with rejoicing, in the praises of the Lord, each of the wondrous events that then occurred, so may the religious community of the future also marvel, rejoicing together, at the heavenly power manifested in the blessed man.

Beginning, therefore, to recount the deeds of the miracles, we first indicate the very time at which these things began to occur: namely, after Pentecost, in the aforementioned year of the Lord’s Nativity, about seventy years after the blessed man’s departure. Yet he had previously shown himself worthy of God in many ways [Col. 1025C], although, because of neglect, these things had not been widely disseminated by celebrated report.

Next, we have woven into the account the names of those who were healed, together with the illnesses from which they suffered, and also the places where they had been born or lived, insofar as the circumstances allowed. In this way the truth of the miracles may be confirmed more abundantly, and each person may more devoutly acknowledge, through relatives or neighbors healed by his assistance, how great a grace they experienced from the blessed man.

## CHAPTER II. Four Other Miracles Performed After His Death

A certain woman from Osteveshusun, named Dida, had been blind for seven years. One Saturday, when she asked her mistress that they might go forward to the church, her mistress replied that it was not possible for them to go then, but that they would go together the next morning, on Sunday.

Dida rose immediately at first light and hurried to precede her mistress. An old woman led her, and she hastened toward the church with rapid steps. When she arrived there and, devoted to prayer, lay prostrate upon the ground, she suddenly received back the light she had lost through the gift of divine grace.

When her mistress later arrived and entered the inner part of the basilica, recognizing from her voice that Dida was present, she suddenly ran to her joyfully and said: “My most beloved mistress, I give thanks and praise to almighty God, because through the merits of blessed Willehad I have been deemed worthy to see you with my eyes” [Col. 1026A].

The mistress marveled at what had happened, immediately related it to all who stood nearby, and made it clear, with the testimony of many confirming it, that the woman had truly been given sight. Thus this miracle was publicly manifested among the people for the glorification of God.

Again, from the district of Emisga, a certain woman named Wimod had suffered blindness for nine years. One evening she came to the aforementioned church, and after praying there following Vespers, returned to the lodging where she was to stay. During the following night it was revealed to her in a vision that she would receive there a remedy for the health she had lost through the loss of her sight.

Trusting this revelation, though in whatever measure her faith allowed, she immediately hastened to the church. There, invoking the saint’s merits with her whole heart and aided by divine grace, she recovered the use of the light she had lost [Col. 1026B]. This too was immediately made known and clearly confirmed by the testimony of many, to the glory of God.

After this, on the feast of the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist, seven sick people were freed from various illnesses in the midst of a very great gathering of the people. Since we did not consider it necessary to recount each case individually, we have nevertheless briefly described two of the miracles that occurred, so that the others too may be understood from them.

One of these was a woman named Simod, from a village nearby called Luidwinenshusun. After being deprived of the light of her eyes for three months or more, she received there, by God’s will, the grace of her former sight.

Another was a woman from that same place, namely Bremen, who had been contracted by an illness [Col. 1026C]. When she was an infant, her foot had been burned by an accidental fire. Since no medicine provided relief, the joints, turned upward, had almost completely twisted and deformed her foot. After suffering this affliction for many years, on the aforementioned day, in the presence of everyone, the extension of her foot and joints obtained healing.

Furthermore, from Laras, from a village called Sluttra, there was a woman who had been bent over for many years. She could walk in no other way than by crawling on her hands, and she could not look upward at all. Finally, as the disease pressed upon her more severely, she had become so weak that she could not go anywhere unless she was carried.

She also had a daughter whom blindness, present from infancy, had deprived of her natural sight. When the woman heard of the power of the miracles, relatives or neighbors carried her together with her daughter to the door of the church at Bremen [Col. 1026D].

When she had been placed there and arrived supported by the faith of others, through divine compassion she was deemed worthy both to rejoice at her daughter’s illumination and to carry herself upright. Straightening herself, she returned on her own feet to her familiar dwelling.

## CHAPTER III. Five Other Miracles of Saint Willehad

Likewise, from Laras, from a village called Falathorp, two women—one crippled and the other blind—were brought to the same place. Through the generosity of the divine gift, they returned home unharmed.

From the district mentioned above, from the village of Bokkenhusun, a certain young man who had long been paralyzed was brought to the same place [Col. 1027A]. By divine will he was restored to his former health and returned home sound.

Again, from the district of Ostarburge, from a village called Baldrikeswich, there was a woman named Adsuit who had been severely and for a long time afflicted by paralysis. One Sunday she was brought there. On that same day many people—seven or eight, namely—were healed of various illnesses. After the celebration of Mass, this was announced to the people, and both clergy and people sang the praises due to God in measured voices for the miracles that had been displayed.

Suddenly Adsuit rose from the midst of the crowd and began to run toward the steps of the altar, where the other sick people who had been healed were lying. Those standing nearby tried to restrain her lest she leap into the choir of the singing clerics. But she eagerly declared that she had been instructed to place herself with the others before the altar [Col. 1027B].

For it had appeared to her that the priest who had announced the healing of the others to the people had also beckoned to her with his hand to rise and proceed with the rest to the altar. When her illness and healing had been examined and made known, everyone, moved to tears and with tears of joy springing forth, once again resounded with greater eagerness in praise of the majesty of almighty God and in exalting the merits of the most blessed man, because the repeated miracle was all the more desirable.

Finally, from Waldsatis, from a village called Willianstedi, there was a woman named Ikkia who had suffered blindness for seven years. When reports of the miracles from the aforementioned place were already spreading everywhere, one of her neighbors encouraged her and said:

“Why do you not also try to seek the saint of God, so that the light of your eyes may likewise be revealed and shine for you?”

She replied that she very much wished to do so, but that one thing opposed her desire: she had no guide. The other answered:

“Look, if you have no one else, I will lead you there however I can.”

Since she knew of no other refuge, Ikkia accepted the promise most gratefully. Both women were very poor. They therefore set out, the two of them alone, with the grace of the Lord accompanying them, and eventually reached the aforementioned shrine.

When they were devoutly engaged in prayer there, the woman who had been blind was suddenly given sight. Turning to her companion, she said with a smile and congratulations:

“Oh, how well—how very well—it has turned out that I listened to your advice and sought the saint of God! Look: together with you I see the light of heaven.”

This event was immediately proclaimed publicly and gave the people great hope in divine mercy. For, according to the Psalmist’s saying, “The poor man is left to him” [Col. 1027D]. Therefore he himself is the refuge of the poor in tribulation; he will also be a ready helper of the fatherless and orphan (Psalm 9:34).

Having recovered the sight of light, she now returned to her own hut, no longer led by her companion but accompanying her equally, while continually singing the praises of the Lord and constantly exalting her companion’s salutary advice with thanks.

From the same district there had also been a woman named Ikkia. For many years she had been so contracted by paralysis from the waist [Col. 1028A] downward that she felt nothing at all in those limbs and could go nowhere unless she dragged herself along with a stool. When she reached the holy place, the Lord in his mercy restored her strength, and she carried herself wherever she wished on her own feet.

## CHAPTER IV. Six Other Miracles of Saint Willehad
A certain native man, going about seeking alms because of his poverty, had once come to the basilica of Saint Alexander. He had with him a blind stepdaughter who traveled about with him; and he himself too had long endured the twofold affliction of blindness. While they were staying there, it happened through the merits of the saint that the aforesaid stepdaughter received sight in one eye. Elated by this gift, they proceeded farther and reached the oratory at Bremen; where, while they were engaged in prayer, through the intercession of blessed Willehad they were enriched with manifold increase. For he himself also received sight in both eyes, and his stepdaughter likewise rejoiced in the illumination of her other eye. When this was reported on the testimony of the faithful who had been present, the whole people gave praise to God with rejoicing.

Moreover, a certain man from the district of Nordwidu had formerly passed over to the threshold of the aforesaid martyr Alexander. Mute and deaf alike, he had suffered a miserable affliction from infancy through prolonged suffering; through the merits of the aforesaid Martyr he received hearing. Proceeding farther, however, and reaching the basilica of the Bremen Church, through the clemency of divine generosity he deserved, while blessed Willehad interceded for him, to speak as well as to hear.

Likewise, from Laris, from the village of Otishusun, the daughter of a certain Fridebern had long been contracted in all her limbs by illness. She was brought to the aforesaid basilica and for seven days endured the gravest distress in her body, so that, because of the magnitude of the pain, she was almost believed to have expired. But at length, with divine clemency consenting, she began to fare better; and, restored to her former function, she received health through the merits of the saint. Returning to her father’s house, sound in all her limbs, she plainly displayed festive joy to her parents and neighbors.

From Steornigis also, from the village of Grandikehard [al., Gandrikesard], a certain woman named Herimod had been deaf for two years. Coming to the aforesaid place, through the saint’s intercession she deserved to have her hearing restored.

Likewise, from Laris, from the village of Falathorpe, two women came there: one bent over, named Hataburg, and the other blind, named Macswid. Begging divine protection there, both returned joyfully to their own homes, rejoicing in restored health.

Furthermore, from the public village of Wege, a certain girl had long been ill in all her limbs and retained no strength at all in her body. Brought, therefore, to the saint’s confession, through the munificence of divine generosity she recovered both the capacity for strength and the health of her entire body.

## CHAPTER V. Seven Other Miracles of Willehad.

Moreover, from Sturmi, from the village of Ekina, a certain woman named Gerswid, who had suffered blindness for a long time, was placed in the same spot and was granted the gift of light.

Similarly, from the district of Stenthorpe [pagi; read: pago], a certain woman who had long been blind, while she lay in prayer, was cured of her blindness through the help of the blessed man.

Finally, from Frisia, from the village of Vestanko, a certain blind man named Meinrad came there and, enlightened by heavenly grace, recovered the use of sight.

From Laris, from the village of Hahthoreimund, a woman who had been blind for nine years deserved there, through the prayers of the most holy man, to receive the long-desired grace of sight.

From Wigmodis, from the village of Midlistanfadarwrd, a certain man whose hand had been severely contracted for many years returned from there unharmed, the Lord granting it.

Likewise, from Wigmodis, from the village of Westristanbeverigisaeti, a woman named Thiadgardis, long blind, was there given sight.

From Sturmi, however, from the village of Ekgnon [al., Ekynon], a certain man named Akko had already been wounded in one arm. Since no medicine helped him, he had kept the arm useless for all work for many years. Coming there, lamenting the idle waste of his days and asking for the help of the blessed man, he was long tormented by pain in the arm; at last, healed by heavenly grace, he extended his outstretched right hand. When everyone had given thanks to God for his recovery, he returned home, reminded by the confidence of his restored health and placing the firmest trust in God’s mercy. He himself then brought his wife, who had already remained blind for a long time, with him back to the same church.

There, while the man, strengthened in faith for the remedy he had received, eagerly asked that the Lord be present to the woman with his beneficence, and the woman likewise, admonished by the teachings of her husband, begged the Lord to be favorably disposed toward her, suddenly, with light inspired from heaven, the woman began clearly to see everything. This was immediately proclaimed among the people and furnished great encouragement to faith, confirming the minds of all in belief in the divine power. When clergy and people resounded with prayers for their health, they returned home rejoicing, and began to devote themselves to work with all the greater eagerness and diligence, the more they remembered that they had previously lost many days in idle inactivity.

## CHAPTER VI. Five Other Miracles of Saint Willehad.

From Laris also, divine miracles, once begun, continued to increase. For a certain Rhoudwig, from the village of Stenbike, had been mute for three years. When he was placed there and silently implored the help of the blessed man, by the mercy of divine grace he suddenly began, with opened mouth, to proclaim the mighty works of the Lord.

Likewise, from the village of Restereflet [al., Rehrereflet], a certain woman had been so contracted by illness for many years that she could not, without assistance, turn herself to the other side even in bed, nor enjoy the proper use of any limb at all. When friends, roused by faith, carried her to the saint’s confession and laid her there in the middle on a pallet, as though she were almost dead and lying in a coffin, she suddenly sprang healthy from the bed and, bursting into the midst, sang praises to the Lord. No longer caring for the support of the pallet, she was dismissed in peace and fearlessly walked on her own feet along the road by which she had been carried there.

Furthermore, from the village of Bouchem in the district of Lohingaho, a woman named Hiberin [al., Siberin], whose illness had rendered all her limbs weak, so that there was no strength at all in her body, obtained complete health there through the merits of the blessed man.

Again, from Laris, from the village of Eggrikeshusun, a certain woman had been crippled from infancy, so that one of her hands had never been fit for any use. When she was placed in the holy place and asked with the inmost devotion of her heart for the help of divine mercy, she suddenly became sound, clapped with both hands, and gave God a joyful cry of jubilation.

There was also from Liastmona a certain female servant of the venerable Count Hirimann, whom he had ordered to be in his house at Hethas with other female servants for the work of weaving. While she was there engaged in the Lord’s service, by the hidden but just judgment of God, though otherwise healthy she was afflicted only with loss of speech. When she was oppressed by this trouble for a long time and could make no sound at all by speaking, the aforesaid count, moved by the Lord’s mercy, granted her freedom as a remedy for his soul; thus he allowed her, once dismissed from there, to return freely to her own people.

Led, therefore, by companions, she reached Bremen and immediately took care to enter the church with devout intention, as is believed. For the effect of the event made clear what she had contemplated with faithful mind. Hastening to the church doors, she immediately felt the Lord’s mercy meet her. At the very entrance of the basilica, as she entered through the doors of the atrium, the impediment of her tongue was suddenly loosened, and she began to cry out loudly and sing praises to God. When those who were present asked her the cause, she recounted plainly and clearly what had happened. Thus this power, also made known among the people through the testimony of others, greatly increased the distinguished merits of the blessed man. Returning from there to her father’s house, she went happily and joyfully, endowed at once with health and freedom, and by her arrival and good fortune made her parents and relatives rejoice as well.

## CHAPTER VII. Seven Other Miracles of Saint Willehad.

Likewise, from Bremen, a certain girl named Wige, long mute and also contracted in all her limbs, so that she could not move from one place to another except when carried by others, received in that same place, through the merits of the blessed man, both the use of speech and the proper function of all her limbs.

After this, also from Upriustri, a certain woman named Tethileis, crippled on the right side from the time of her birth, was healed there with the Lord’s help.

From Wigmodis, moreover, from the village of Medemahem, a certain woman named Ida, who had suffered blindness for nine years, was there granted by the Lord’s grace the shining brightness of her eyes.

Again, from Riustri, from the village of Smalonflet, a certain woman named Dissith had been blind in one eye for eleven months. Coming there, she rejoiced, through the merits of the blessed man, to have received sight in both eyes.

A certain woman from the village of Thadingen, named Egilmate, had long been afflicted by paralytic illness in a horrible manner. At last, coming by divine mercy to the holy place and earnestly beseeching God there, she was freed from paralysis, gave thanks to God with her strength restored, and returned home with joy.  
[Note: [Col. 1031C] The printed editions vary in the wording.]

Similarly, from a place called Citirothe, a certain woman who had long been deprived of the use of sight came to the same place. There, devoted to prayer, she lay prostrate on the ground, and suddenly, by the gift of divine favor, received back the light she had lost.

Again, from Liastmona, a certain lame woman named Rotgardis, when she earnestly implored the help of the blessed man there, was healed by the mercy of divine grace and fearlessly walked on her own feet with the greatest joy of heart.  
[Note: [Col. 1032C] Here the Corbie manuscript ends.]

## CHAPTER VIII. Conclusion of the Miracles of Saint Willehad.

There were also many others hastening to the same place to recover their health who were healed on the way through the merits of the most blessed bishop. Their health became known through the reports of others, because they did not continue, as they had begun, to seek the holy place; rather, having been granted health, they returned home quickly and joyfully from the road, proclaiming the Lord and blessed Willehad with magnificent praises.

But, lest a longer narrative become burdensome to readers, we have omitted these and many other accounts, which nevertheless are publicly known among the people through the mouths of many. The body of the saint himself, which had already at that time been transferred from the place of his rest to another basilica, we lifted from there with a very great crowd of the faithful and an innumerable assembly of the clergy, placed it on a bier, and, amid the voices of the people resounding in praise of God and the blessed man, deposited it on the day of his deposition in the new basilica that we then dedicated. There, honorably arranged, it later shone forth magnificently through innumerable signs of virtues, and from day to day the signs of manifold miracles increase there through the merits of the blessed man.

His day of deposition and at the same time of the translation of his body is observed on the sixth day before the Ides of November, to the praise and glory of the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, who, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, lives and reigns as one true God through immortal ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 1031]

# Letter of Ansgar

[Col. 1031]

[Col. 1031C] In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Ansgar, archbishop by the grace of God, to all the prelates of the holy Church of God residing in the kingdom of King Louis.

I wish you to know that this little book contains an account of how Ebo, archbishop of Rheims, inspired by the Holy Spirit, in the time of Lord Emperor Louis, with his consent and that of a synod assembled from nearly his whole kingdom, went to Rome and there received from the venerable Pope Paschal public permission to evangelize in the northern regions; and how afterward Emperor Louis elevated this work and showed himself generous and kindly in every respect; and the other events that befell this mission.

Therefore I humbly beseech you to intercede with God so that this mission may deserve to grow and bear fruit in the Lord. For already, by Christ’s favor, the Church of Christ has been founded both among the Danes and among the Swedes, and priests perform their office without prohibition. I also ask that you have these letters placed in your library for perpetual remembrance and, as occasion dictates, that both you and your successors, whenever you discern its usefulness, make this known to everyone. May almighty God make you all participants in the pious goodwill of this work and coheirs with Christ in heavenly glory.

# APPENDIX

[Col. 1033]

## Decree of Louis the Pious concerning the mission of Saint Ansgar and his ordination

[Col. 1033A] In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the favorable clemency of God, Emperor Augustus.

If imperial authority shows that we must assist when the particular needs of each of our faithful have been recognized, how much more does it belong to the proper general care, as something equitable and worthy, that we should show pious and attentive concern in all things for the Catholic and apostolic Church, which Christ redeemed with his precious blood and entrusted to us to protect and govern; and that we should apply appropriate diligence to its advancement and exaltation, providing new decrees—indeed, necessary and useful ones—concerning matters newly arising for its need, usefulness, and dignity.

Therefore we wish it to be certain to the sons of the holy Church of God, both present and future, how, by the ordering of divine grace in our days, in the northern regions, namely among the people of the Danes or Swedes, the grace of heavenly preaching or acquisition has opened a great door, so that a multitude on every side, converted to the faith of Christ, eagerly sought the heavenly mysteries and ecclesiastical assistance. Hence, rendering immense praises to our Lord God, we exalt him who in our times and through our efforts allows his holy Church, his bride, to spread and advance in unknown places.

Accordingly, together with the priests and the other faithful of our empire, seeing this cause worthy of God, exceedingly necessary, and beneficial to the dignity of the future Church, we judged it right to choose more clearly a suitable place within our borders where, by this decree of our authority, we might establish an episcopal see. From there all those barbarian nations might more easily and abundantly receive the nourishment of eternal life, and might continually have the grace of salvation before their hands and eyes; moreover, the sacred zeal of our great forebears for winning people might never fail in our days.

For our father, Charles, of glorious memory, subjected all Saxony to ecclesiastical religion and taught the yoke of Christ, subduing fierce hearts with the sword, as far as the borders of the Danes and Slavs. Observing there the last part of Saxony, situated between these two peoples—namely the Danes or Vandals—and lying amid diverse temporal and spiritual dangers, he decreed that an episcopal see should be established there beyond the Elbe.

Afterward, when he had ordered the land of the Nordalbingians, freed from the captivity that they had endured for seven years because of the great treachery committed at the very beginnings of Christianity, to be restored to Count Ecbert lest that place be invaded by barbarians, he no longer wished to entrust it to neighboring bishops. But, lest any of them should thereafter claim that parish for himself, he sent from the distant regions of Gaul a certain bishop named Amalarius, who was to consecrate the primitive church there. He also took care, in pious generosity, to send specially to that church sacred relics and numerous ecclesiastical gifts.

Later, when the captives streamed from every side to their desired homeland, he entrusted the same parish specially to a certain priest named Heridac. He had arranged for him to be consecrated bishop of the entire Church of the Nordalbingians, lest they relapse into the rite of the pagans, and also because that place appeared most suitable for winning still more peoples. In this way, by that occasion and supreme authority, the holy Church might be diligently multiplied among those peoples in their very borderlands, since even the considerable concern required by the extent of the territory did not suffice for the neighboring bishops to range everywhere.

He also assigned to the same priest a certain cell called Hrodnace, so that it might serve as a supplement to that place, surrounded on every side by dangers. But because the swift departure from this life of my pious father prevented the consecration of the aforesaid man from taking place during his lifetime, I, whom divine clemency had called to his royal throne, while occupied with arranging many affairs of the kingdom, failed to attend carefully enough to this work of my aforesaid father carried out at the kingdom’s borders. Persuaded by certain persons, I gave the aforesaid cell to the monastery of Inda and meanwhile entrusted the neighboring parish to neighboring bishops.

Now, both because of the ecclesiastical gains among the peoples described above and because of the vow of our pious father, lest any of his work remain unfinished, we have determined, with ecclesiastical consent, to establish the aforesaid farthest region of Saxony beyond the Elbe, in the place called Hamburg, together with the entire province of the Nordalbingians, as a see possessing its own authority.

We appointed Ansgar archbishop to preside over it first and to be solemnly consecrated by the hands of Drogo, bishop of Metz and prelate of the supreme holy palatine dignity. The archbishops Ebo of Rheims, Hetti of Trier, and Otgar of Mainz were present, together with many other prelates of our whole empire gathered in a general assembly. Also specially assisting, consenting, and consecrating were the bishops Helingand and Willeric, from whom we received the portions of the aforesaid parish formerly entrusted to them by us.

To him, namely Ansgar, because in the aforesaid peoples the most worthy gains had been displayed in our days through the summoning of the nations and the redemption of captives, we entrusted this God-worthy mission among the peoples by the authority both of ours and of the see of the holy Roman Church, and decreed that it should be endowed with the dignity of its own authority.

And so that this new foundation, begun in dangerous places, might be able to endure and not perish through the prevailing savagery of the barbarians, we offered to the divine Majesty, for our perpetual reward and that of our offspring, a certain cell called Turholt, which would serve perpetually both this new foundation and his mission, and that of his successors, among the peoples.

We also absolved from every expedition, military service, occupation, or other obligation the men who appear to possess the benefits of that cell, so that the same venerable bishop might suffer no impediment in carrying out at the appointed times this mission worthy of God. The gifts which they were accustomed to render from that cell to our fisc we likewise wish to be rendered to us and to our successors.

With these exceptions, whatever may be greater or lesser, whether for summoning pagans, redeeming captives, supplying the same see surrounded by manifold dangers, or supporting those who serve God there, we permanently assign it for the love of God and of his confessor, blessed Sixtus.

We wish the property of the aforesaid see and of the aforementioned monastery to remain and be protected under the fullest defense and safeguard of immunity. Thus no public judge, nor any other person invested with public authority, may presume to take from their property fines, tributes, lodging dues, provisions, tolls, or sureties; nor may such a person distrain their men, whether dependents or free, residing on their land; nor demand or exact any public services, payments, or unlawful exactions.

Rather, let the aforesaid venerable bishop and his successors, and all the clergy placed under their rule, be permitted to live peacefully in the service of God and to implore divine mercy for us and our offspring and for the condition of our entire empire. And, so that this authority may retain the lasting firmness of its force, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it sealed with the impression of our ring.

Given on the Ides of May, in the twenty-first year, with Christ favorable, of the empire of Lord Louis, most pious Augustus, in the twelfth indiction. Done at the royal palace of Aachen, prosperously, in the name of God. Amen.

[Col. 1035]

## Copy of the Decree of Gregory IV, Pope of Venerable Memory, on the Same Matter

[Col. 1035]

[Col. 1035B] Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God.

We wish it to be certain to the understanding of all the faithful how the most excellent King Charles, of blessed memory, in the time of our predecessors, inspired by the Holy Spirit, subjected the Saxon people to sacred worship and taught the yoke of Christ, which is gentle and light, as far as the borders of the Danes or Slavs, subduing their fierce hearts with the sword. He had also determined to subject by proper episcopal authority the last part of that kingdom, situated beyond the Elbe amid the deadly dangers of the pagans, lest it relapse into the rite of the gentiles, and also because it appeared especially suitable for winning still more peoples.

But because death prevented this from being carried into effect, his most excellent son, Louis, Emperor Augustus, succeeding him, effectively fulfilled the pious undertaking of his holy father. This matter was reported to us for confirmation by the venerable bishops Ratold and Bernod, as well as by Count Gerold or a venerable envoy.

We, therefore, recognizing the entire God-worthy provision established there, and instructed also by the presence of our brother and son Ansgar, first bishop of the Nordalbingians, consecrated by the hands of Drogo, bishop of Metz, have determined to strengthen the holy undertaking of the great emperors both by this present authority and by the bestowal of the pallium, according to the custom of our predecessors, so that our aforesaid son, founded upon such authority, and his successors, devoting themselves to winning peoples, may stand stronger against the temptations of the devil.

We establish this same son of ours, Ansgar, as legate in all the surrounding peoples of the Swedes and Danes, as well as of the Slavs, and wherever divine mercy may open a door to them in those regions. Together with Ebo, archbishop of Rheims, before the body and Confession of Saint Peter, we grant him public authority to preach the Gospel. We decree that the same see of the Nordalbingians, called Hamburg, consecrated in honor of the Savior and of his holy and undefiled mother, the ever-virgin Mary, shall henceforth be archiepiscopal.

We meanwhile entrust the consecration of succeeding priests to the sacred palatine authority, until the number of consecrators increases among the peoples. Let a succession always be chosen of vigorous preachers suited to so great an office.

Whatever the venerable prince has assigned to this God-worthy office, together with his father’s pious vows, we confirm by our authority. We strike with the sword of anathema anyone who resists or contradicts, and condemn him as guilty to perpetual vengeance according to the lot of the devil, so that, zealously guarding the apostolic dignity and the cause of God with pious affection according to the custom of our predecessors, we may protect it more securely from opposing forces on every side.

And because divine clemency has appointed you, dearest son Ausgari, to be the first archbishop in the new see, we too grant you the pallium for celebrating the solemn rites of the Mass. We grant you its use during your lifetime, while the privileges of your church remain perpetually established. Therefore the honor of this garment must be preserved by you through the vigor of your conduct.

If shepherds of sheep keep watch with ever-vigilant eyes, in sun and frost, for the protection of their flock, lest any of them perish by wandering or be carried off to be torn apart by the bites of wild beasts, let us consider with what labor and care we must remain watchful, who are called shepherds of souls. We admonish you not to entangle the office you have undertaken in earthly affairs to any extent.

Let your life, therefore, be a road for your sons: if they possess any strength, let them direct it in that way; let them look upon what they should imitate in it; let them advance by continually examining themselves in it, so that after God the good life they lead may appear to be your work.

Let neither prosperous things, which flatter temporarily, lift up your heart, nor adversities cast it down. Let the wicked recognize you as strict, and let the kindly experience you as merciful. Let another’s malice not make the innocent culpable before you; let favor not excuse the guilty. Let your defense assist widows and orphans unjustly oppressed.

Behold, dearest brother, among many other things, these are the duties of the priesthood; these are the duties of the pallium. If you diligently preserve them, what you have shown that you received outwardly, you will possess inwardly.

May the Holy Trinity deign to preserve your fraternity unharmed for a long time and, after the bitterness of this age, lead you to everlasting blessedness.
